stem: You are a general practitioner in a regional South Australian practice. Your next patient is Mia Delacruz, a 25-year-old woman, who has presented complaining of excessive nausea and vomiting. Her last menstrual period was 8 weeks ago and she has had a positive home pregnancy test. Antenatal screening bloods have been performed and are normal. She has not had any ultrasound scan.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Perform a physical examination by asking the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient

dx: **Hyperemesis gravidarum at 8 weeks** — but this is a **differential diagnosis station wearing a hyperemesis costume**. Everyone knows the diagnosis at the door; the marks are in what you ruled out.

Defined as severe nausea and vomiting of pregnancy causing **dehydration, ketonuria, electrolyte disturbance and weight loss over 5% of pre-pregnancy weight**. VERIFY. **Morning sickness is not hyperemesis** — it is severity plus consequence plus exclusion.
Mechanism is a reaction to **beta-hCG**. Anything that raises beta-hCG raises the risk — **a twin pregnancy, and above all a molar pregnancy**. That is why the ultrasound is not optional.
CORRECTION — the source teaching says "postural hypertension". The finding is **postural (orthostatic) hypotension: a fall of ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing**.

Red flags, each of which takes you **out** of the diagnosis: **bilious (green) vomit · abdominal pain, guarding, fever · sudden onset after 10 weeks or first onset in the second trimester · headache, visual change, photophobia, rash, neck stiffness · haematemesis · vaginal bleeding · haemodynamic instability · confusion, ataxia or abnormal eye movements (Wernicke)**.

The four referral triggers: **positive ketones with clinical dehydration · unable to tolerate any oral intake · persistent vomiting despite adequate oral antiemetics · haemodynamic instability**. Plus bilious vomiting, haematemesis, peritonism, meningism or neurological signs at any time.

Drug ladder, stepwise and never skipped: **1. pyridoxine (vitamin B6) with doxylamine · 2. metoclopramide or ondansetron wafers, which dissolve under the tongue · 3. intravenous fluids with intravenous ondansetron in hospital**. Corticosteroids are a specialist option in refractory disease. VERIFY all doses.
**Thiamine** before or with any glucose-containing intravenous fluid, and in any woman with protracted vomiting — **Wernicke encephalopathy**. VERIFY dose and route. Saying the word marks you out.

Counselling on the two step-2 drugs: ondansetron carries a **small absolute increase in orofacial clefting** reported in the first trimester; metoclopramide carries **extrapyramidal effects**. VERIFY.

Diet — say all six: **small frequent meals · small sips rather than glasses · cool drinks and ice chips · a dry cracker before getting up · avoid spicy, fatty and strong-smelling food · ginger is safe in pregnancy**. SA: the scan means travel, so **PATS**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unstable; molar pregnancy to the **Women's and Children's Hospital** with serial beta-hCG; **TIS National 131 450**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222** after hours.
plan: WIPE. To the examiner before you sit: **'May I have the blood pressure, and whether there is a postural drop, the pulse rate and the temperature?'** Asking is scored, and **postural drop by name is scored again**.

Confirm name and date of birth. **'How can I help you today?'** One acknowledgement of how exhausting it is, then signpost: questions, examination, then what I think. **Empathy once** — there are two task blocks after the history.

Characterise the vomit: **when did it start · is it getting worse · what colour is it · any blood in it · does it have a bad smell · how many times a day · anything make it better or worse**. Then the two severity questions: **are you feeling dizzy, particularly standing up** and **are you able to keep anything down at all**. Add **have you lost weight**.

Bucket 1, obstetric, signposted aloud: **when was your last period · any other pregnancy symptoms · any vaginal bleeding · have you had your pregnancy bloods and a scan · is this your first pregnancy · any twins in the family · was this IVF or assisted**. The last three are multiple-pregnancy risk questions.

Bucket 2, acute abdomen, never skipped: **do you have any abdominal pain at all · any diarrhoea or constipation · any bloating, and are you passing wind · any yellowing of the skin or eyes · any heartburn · do you take anti-inflammatories**. Something is coming out of the top — ask what is coming out of the bottom.

Bucket 3, infection: **any fever or chills · pain or burning passing urine, or going more often · any headache · vision problems or dislike of bright light · any rash or neck stiffness · any recent travel or contact with anyone unwell**.

Buckets 4 and 5 if time: **hot or cold weather preference · family history of thyroid problems · palpitations, tremor or sweating · are you passing more urine than usual · any weakness or numbness**. Breadth across five beats depth in one.

Examination from the examiner — **two systems properly, not six in outline**. General and dehydration, weight against booking, the postural drop. Abdomen: inspection, palpation with **mass** and organomegaly, bowel sounds.

**'I would like to perform a pelvic examination, with the patient's consent and in the presence of a chaperone'** — one phrase, every time. Inspection, then **speculum: is the os open or closed**, then bimanual: **cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, tenderness and border, adnexae**.

Office tests: **'a urine dipstick — and first, the ketones'**, then nitrites, leucocytes, protein and blood, and a **blood glucose**. Ketones 3+ with a normal glucose is the finding that sends her to hospital.

Diagnosis in lay language, then the differentials **as groups, named before the examples** — the pregnancy itself, the tummy, infections, hormone and sugar problems, the head. Answer **'is my baby alright?'** when it comes.

Management: the ketones explained, **emergency department for intravenous fluids and intravenous antiemetics**, bloods there, and **'I'm arranging an ultrasound regardless'**. Then diet, the stepwise ladder, and safety-netting **including green vomit**.
Address the hidden concern if it has not surfaced — **a friend told her vomiting this badly means something is wrong with the baby**. Summarise in one sentence and close.
pefe: Ask for the **vital signs before you sit down**, and ask for the **postural drop by name** — it is the objective sign of volume depletion. If you forget, you can still recover it during the examination block.

You have about three minutes. **Two systems done properly — abdomen and pelvis — plus the office tests** beats six systems in outline. Say out loud what you are deliberately omitting rather than silently skipping it.
General: **alert or drowsy, degree of clinical dehydration, weight against booking weight**.
Abdomen: inspection for **distension and symmetrical movement**; palpation for **tenderness, guarding, mass and organomegaly**; **bowel sounds**.

**Why you ask about a mass at 8 weeks**: the uterus is not normally palpable abdominally until about **12 weeks**. A suprapubic mass at eight means the uterus is larger than dates — **twin or molar pregnancy** — and makes the scan urgent. In the first trimester the uterus is assessed **bimanually, not by fundal height**.

Pelvic, as one package: **consent and a chaperone**; inspection for bleeding or discharge; **speculum for the cervical os, open or closed**, and any bleeding, discharge or products; bimanual for **cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, tenderness and border, and the adnexae**. A sterile speculum is not routinely required.

Office tests — the mark you must not lose: **urine dipstick, ketones first**, then nitrites, leucocytes, protein and blood; and a **blood glucose**. **Ketones with a glucose of 20 is diabetic ketoacidosis before it is hyperemesis.** A urine pregnancy test adds nothing once pregnancy is established.

Investigations in priority order, numbered and justified — never a flat shopping list. **1. Ultrasound, preferably transvaginal** — multiple pregnancy, molar pregnancy (**snowstorm or cluster-of-grapes, no fetal parts**), and **fetal cardiac activity, expected from about 6–7 weeks**. The stem told you it has not been done.

**2. Urea, electrolytes and creatinine** — hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypochloraemic alkalosis, renal impairment. **3. TSH and free T4** — thyrotoxicosis, noting beta-hCG itself causes transient biochemical hyperthyroidism. **4. Urine MCS, FBE, LFTs, blood glucose, lipase**.
If investigations are **not** a listed task they belong **inside your management** — say 'I would arrange an ultrasound' out loud, or you lose the mark.

stem: Lily Fraser, 30, is 36 weeks pregnant and has come for a routine antenatal visit. The pregnancy has been uneventful and all antenatal screening is complete and normal.

Last week she developed swelling of both legs. The baby is kicking well. Today: blood pressure raised on two readings, urine protein 3+. Fundal height 36 cm, fetal heart rate 140, longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your investigations and your management

dx: **Pre-eclampsia with severe features at 36 weeks** — severe **on the clonus, not on the number**. The stem hands you the diagnosis; what is marked is whether you can tell stable disease from disease about to become eclampsia.

Definition: **new hypertension after 20 weeks together with maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction**. CORRECTION — **proteinuria is no longer required** for the diagnosis under current SOMANZ and ISSHP criteria; it is the commonest manifestation, not a mandatory one. VERIFY

The four numbers every answer is built from: **140/90** is hypertension in pregnancy, on two readings · **160/110 or above** is severe · **under 135/85** is the target · **37 weeks** is when you plan birth in stable disease.
CORRECTION — **do not aim for a normal blood pressure**. Placental perfusion is pressure-dependent and aggressive lowering causes fetal compromise. The target is **under 135/85, not 120/80**.

Oral control: **labetalol first line**, with **methyldopa (slow onset) or modified-release nifedipine** as alternatives and oral hydralazine a further option. **Avoid ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and diuretics in pregnancy.** VERIFY doses.

Severe (**160/110 or above**) is an emergency department presentation: **IV labetalol, IV hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine** in a monitored setting. **Do not attempt intravenous therapy in a general practice** — no monitoring, no CTG, no obstetric or anaesthetic support.

**Magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour**, continued **24 hours after birth or the last seizure**. Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output — **loss of reflexes is the earliest sign of toxicity**. CORRECTION — name which of its three indications you mean: **treating eclampsia · seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia · fetal neuroprotection in very preterm birth**. VERIFY
**Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart**, if birth is anticipated before about **34–35 weeks**. At 36 weeks she is past the usual threshold. VERIFY

CORRECTION — **HELLP is a diagnosis made on blood tests, not on symptoms**: haemolysis, elevated transaminases, low platelets. Right upper quadrant pain with pre-eclampsia is hepatic involvement. Do not name HELLP before you have the **film, LDH, liver function tests and platelet count**.

Prevention and aftercare: **aspirin 100–150 mg nightly from 12 weeks (before 16) until about 36 weeks** in high-risk women — one high factor or two moderate factors is enough. VERIFY. **6–12 week postnatal blood pressure review**; pressure can worsen for days after birth. SA: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, transfer **in utero** wherever safe, give the first antihypertensive dose and load magnesium before transfer; **PATS** for the partner's travel, Country Health Connect, the Aboriginal Family Birthing Program, **TIS National 131 450** — never a family member.
plan: To the examiner before you begin: **'could I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and oxygen saturations?'**

**'Hello Lily, I'm Dr ___. I understand you've come for your antenatal check and there's been some swelling in your legs. Tell me about it.'** Acknowledge the worry in one sentence, signpost, proceed. Do **not** congratulate her on the pregnancy at 36 weeks, and do **not** open with 'try not to worry'.

Explore the swelling: **when did it start · is it getting worse · how far up does it go · both legs or one**. Then the key question — **'is the swelling there when you first wake up in the morning?'** Physiological oedema is worse by evening and settles overnight; oedema present on waking and climbing above the ankles is the pathological kind. Name it as a red flag out loud.

Neurological group first, because the seizure is what you are preventing: **any headaches · any change in your vision, blurring, flashing lights, spots or floaters · any dizziness · any confusion**. Do not visibly react and do not stop screening — four organ groups remain.
Hepatic: **any pain in your tummy, particularly up under the ribs on the right · any nausea or vomiting · any yellowing of your skin or eyes**.

Cardiorespiratory, haematological, renal: **any chest pain or shortness of breath, particularly lying flat · any rashes, or bruising more easily than usual · have you noticed you're passing less urine than usual**.

Obstetric complications — the block most often forgotten: **any bleeding from down below · any discharge or leaking of fluid · is the baby moving as much as usual**. Pre-eclampsia raises the risk of abruption, preterm birth and growth restriction.

Background: **have you ever had high blood pressure or kidney problems, before this pregnancy or in a previous one · anyone in the family with high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia**. Then confirm quickly, not at length: booking bloods, dating scan, screening, the 18–20 week scan, the glucose test, the 36-week swab, previous pregnancies, medications and allergies.

**'Examiner, findings rather than technique please.'** General appearance and repeated vitals; neurological — **fundoscopy, deep tendon reflexes, and specifically is there ankle clonus**; cardiovascular; respiratory — **particularly bibasal crackles**; abdomen — **tenderness over the liver and over the uterus**, then fundal height and fetal heart rate; lower limbs — oedema, pitting or non-pitting, to what level; and a **urine dipstick**.

Say it out loud the moment you are told clonus is present: **'sustained clonus indicates central nervous system irritability and marks impending eclampsia — that makes this severe pre-eclampsia regardless of the blood pressure number.'**

**Name pre-eclampsia in the first sentence**, then explain it, then give the four reasons: the blood pressure on two readings, the 3+ protein, the headaches and flashes, and the clonus. Say what you are trying to prevent — **eclampsia, a fit**.

Differentials as **other hypertensive and multisystem disorders**, with the reason for and against each. When she becomes tearful about her sister: **'your sister's pregnancy isn't a script for yours'** — she is 36 weeks, not 33.

Investigations, **CTG first**, then ultrasound for growth, liquor and cord Dopplers, then FBC, LFTs with LDH, UEC and eGFR, coagulation profile, **urine protein-creatinine ratio**, and a midstream urine to exclude infection.

Management split at **160/110** in the first sentence. Non-severe by number but **severe by features because of the clonus**: admission under the obstetric team today, oral labetalol to **under 135/85**, magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, **birth is the only cure** — at 36 weeks, days rather than weeks.

Safety-net in her words: **worsening headache · any change in vision · pain under the ribs · vomiting · breathlessness · swelling that suddenly worsens · any bleeding · reduced fetal movements** — emergency department, not an appointment. **Ask her to say them back.** Summarise and close.
pefe: Ask for **findings, not technique**, and ask in this order — **neurological first, because the seizure is the thing you are trying to prevent**.
General appearance: **alert or drowsy** (a drowsy pre-eclamptic is an emergency), **rash, bruising, jaundice** — these point toward HELLP. Then repeat the vital signs.

Neurological: **fundoscopy** for papilloedema, **deep tendon reflexes**, and **specifically ankle clonus**. **Do not stop at hyperreflexia** — it is common and non-specific in pregnancy. Clonus is the finding that carries weight. It is tested at the ankle by briskly dorsiflexing the foot and holding.
Cardiovascular and respiratory: heart sounds, murmurs, added sounds; **equal air entry and added sounds, particularly bibasal crackles** — pulmonary oedema is an emergency.

Abdomen: **tenderness over the liver** (hepatic involvement) **and over the uterus** (abruption risk), then Leopold's for **fundal height and fetal heart rate**. If challenged on why you want Leopold's when the stem gave you the lie: **'because I want the fundal height and the fetal heart rate — the lie and presentation don't change my management today.'**
Lower limbs: **oedema, pitting or non-pitting, and to what level**. Then a **urine dipstick**.

**The three findings that change everything**: sustained ankle clonus (severe disease regardless of pressure) · bibasal crackles (pulmonary oedema, an emergency) · liver tenderness with a tender uterus (hepatic involvement plus abruption risk).

Investigations, in the order to say them. **1. CTG — first, because it is the one candidates leave out.** Name four things on the trace: **baseline 110–160 bpm, variability 5–25, accelerations present, decelerations absent**, then comment on the tocograph. A reassuring trace does not mean mild disease — it means the baby is currently coping.

**2. Ultrasound** for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Dopplers. **3. Bloods: FBC for platelets, LFTs with LDH, UEC with eGFR, coagulation profile.** **4. Urine protein-creatinine ratio** to quantify the protein.
**Midstream urine** — a urinary tract infection is a common cause of a false-positive protein and must be excluded before you commit.

stem: Jenny Mahoney, 28, G1 P0. At 30 weeks everything was normal and her symphysis–fundal height was 29 cm. Today, at 34 weeks, it is 30 cm.
tasks: Take a history
Tell the examiner the investigations you would request
Results are then handed to you. Explain the results
Explain the diagnosis
Tell her the outcome for the baby

dx: **Fetal growth restriction in a small-for-gestational-age pregnancy, most likely placental insufficiency** — and the reason said aloud: **estimated fetal weight and abdominal circumference both below the 10th centile** at 34 weeks.

The distinction that separates a strong candidate: **SGA is a statistical label** — estimated fetal weight or abdominal circumference **below the 10th centile**. **Growth restriction is a pathological one** — a fetus failing to reach **its own** growth potential. Not all SGA babies are restricted, and a restricted baby may never be SGA.

On the chart, growth restriction is confirmed by **weight or abdominal circumference below the 3rd centile alone, or both below the 10th**. The **most sensitive single measure is the abdominal circumference**, used with estimated fetal weight.

**Symphysis–fundal height = gestation in weeks ±3 cm** VERIFY (some Australian services use ±2). A discrepancy of **3 cm or more mandates a scan**. **Oligohydramnios = AFI under 5 cm or deepest vertical pocket under 2 cm**; normal AFI 5–24 cm. VERIFY

**Asymmetrical** restriction — abdomen falls away, head spared by blood redistribution — is a **late, placental** insult and is the pattern here. **Symmetrical** — head and abdomen equally small, roughly 20–30% of cases — is an **early** insult: chromosomal, congenital infection, teratogen. Asymmetry points at Doppler; symmetry points at microarray and serology.

CORRECTION — say the right test timings: **OGTT 75 g at 24–28 weeks** (not 26–28), **GBS swab 35–37 weeks** (not 'about 36'), combined first-trimester screening **11+0 to 13+6**, NIPT from **10 weeks**, morphology scan **18–20 weeks**, amniocentesis from **15 weeks** reported by **chromosomal microarray, not karyotype alone**.

CORRECTION — three things not to say. **Not hyperglycaemia** — the newborn risk is **hypoglycaemia** (small liver, poor glycogen stores, little fat). **Not 'stop exercising'** — moderate exercise is recommended in pregnancy and that advice is marked wrong. **Not uric acid** as a key investigation — it is not diagnostic in pre-eclampsia and does not change management.

CORRECTION — **dogs are not a toxoplasmosis risk**. The exposures are **cat faeces and litter trays, undercooked meat, soil and gardening, and unwashed produce**. Antiphospholipid antibodies done properly are **lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin IgG and IgM, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I** — the third is usually forgotten — needing a clinical criterion **plus persistent positivity at least 12 weeks apart**.

Management: **obstetric referral the same day** — growth restriction at 34 weeks is not a general practice problem. Surveillance with **umbilical artery Doppler, CTG, liquor volume, and serial growth every 2–3 weeks** (more often and measurement error swamps real change) VERIFY. **Corticosteroids if birth before about 34–35 weeks** is anticipated; **magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection if birth before 30 weeks** VERIFY. **Do not name a delivery week** — say the obstetric team decides, guided by the Doppler and the CTG.

SA: a growth scan, CTG and Doppler are not in every country town — arrange them where they are, with **PATS** for travel and accommodation and **Country Health Connect** for follow-up. **In-utero transfer** to the WCH, FMC or Lyell McEwin beats retrieving a sick newborn — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, RFDS for remote fixed-wing. **Quitline 13 7848** offered as treatment, not a lecture; Aboriginal Family Birthing Program, ACCHS, Closing the Gap PBS; **TIS National 131 450**, never the partner and never a child.
plan: WIPE, sit at eye level. **'You're Jenny? What's been happening?'** She opens with the worry. **Acknowledge it before the first question** — 'I understand why that's worrying, and I'm glad you came in' — then signpost. **Do not congratulate her at 34 weeks.**

**'Was this a planned pregnancy?'** and **'how has the pregnancy been going so far?'** (Version C only: **'can I ask what made it hard to get to your appointments?'** — one kind sentence, no judgement. The approach-to-patient marks are sitting there.)

The obstetric spine, all six at 34 weeks, one at a time: **routine bloods at the start · a dating scan · the Down syndrome screening · the 18–20 week scan, and was it normal · the sweet drink test at 24–28 weeks · the swab at 35–37 weeks**. Use her answers later — 'I had a dating scan' is how you close wrong dates out loud.

**'Is the baby kicking as usual?'** She says less than usual. Respond immediately: **'thank you for telling me — that's important, and it's one of the reasons I want to check on him today rather than wait.'** Then **any headaches, blurred vision, swelling in your legs, passing less urine** and **previous pregnancies — was that baby a small one?**

M D I S C, group named before the questions. **Maternal: any high blood pressure · kidney disease · high blood sugars or diabetes · clots in your legs or lungs · joint pain or rashes · lupus or arthritis in the family.** Diabetes belongs here — long-standing diabetes with vascular disease damages the placental bed and restricts growth.

**Dates: when was your last period · are you sure of that date · were your cycles regular · did you have a dating scan.** **Infections: any fever or rash in the pregnancy · contact with anyone unwell, especially with a rash · do you have a cat or empty a litter tray · any undercooked or raw meat.**

**Growth: has anyone been checking your weight, and were there concerns?** **Substances: do you smoke · any alcohol · any other drugs · any medicines, including anything you buy yourself.** **Constitutional: do small babies run in your family — how big were you and your partner at birth?**

The two added questions the mnemonic omits: **'have you had any leaking of fluid from below?'** and **'any bleeding, or any pain in your tummy?'** Then close: **'any allergies? That's everything I need to ask.'**

**STOP, whatever is unasked.** To the examiner: **an ultrasound growth scan** — liquor volume, estimated fetal weight, abdominal and head circumference, femur length, and a look for malformation. **A CTG** for fetal heart rate and wellbeing. **An umbilical artery Doppler** for placental function. For the mother: **blood pressure and dipstick with a protein-creatinine ratio if positive, UEC, antiphospholipid antibodies, toxoplasma and CMV serology.**

**Prompt bell. Charts handed over.** Read them out loud, never silently: **'the estimated fetal weight plots below the 10th centile. The abdominal circumference is also below the 10th centile. Head circumference and femur length are less useful here. Both measurements that matter are low, which confirms growth restriction.'**

Diagnosis in four sentences, **umbrella term first**: small for gestational age → most likely intrauterine (fetal) growth restriction → in plain terms, not growing and gaining weight as expected → **and the reason I'm saying that is the scan**. Never lead with 'restriction'.

Causes, **each with its reason**: maternal disease (she has none) · wrong dates (**dating scan, set aside**) · infection (serology will tell us) · **the placenta not working as well as it should — most likely here** · smoking, alcohol and drugs (none) · and **constitutionally small, but only once we've ruled the others out**. If she asks 'is it something I did?' — **'no. Nothing you've told me points to anything you've done.'**

The outcome answer, **six plain words in order**: **breathing · help at birth · temperature · blood sugar · feeding · jaundice** — all things the nursery watches for, which is why she should give birth somewhere with a special care nursery. Then the plan, **in-utero transfer**, and the safety-net: **movements slow or stop · bleeding · leaking fluid · regular tightenings · bad headache or sudden swelling**.
pefe: **Ultrasound and CTG named together, out loud, with the reason for each, BEFORE the five-minute prompt.** The published critical error is failing to request at least an ultrasound and at least a CTG. Almost everyone asks for the scan; **the CTG is the one that is forgotten, and it fails the station on its own**. Said after the bell, it does not count.

**1. Ultrasound growth scan** — say what you want from it: **estimated fetal weight, abdominal circumference, head circumference, femur length, the amount of amniotic fluid, and a look for malformations**.
**2. CTG** — fetal heart rate and wellbeing. With reduced movements it needs doing **today**.

**3. Umbilical artery Doppler** — the lecture omits it entirely and it is the surveillance test with the best evidence for reducing perinatal death in high-risk pregnancy. Name it third and you stand out. **Absent or reversed end-diastolic flow means urgent tertiary referral and probable delivery.**
**4. Blood pressure and urine dipstick**, with a **protein-creatinine ratio** if positive. Growth restriction is itself a feature of pre-eclampsia, so screen every time.

Maternal work-up: **urea, electrolytes and creatinine; full blood count; antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I); toxoplasma and CMV serology**; confirm the booking rubella and syphilis results.
**Amniocentesis with chromosomal microarray only if** the ultrasound shows a structural abnormality or early symmetrical restriction — not first line.
Reading the chart: **find two lines and ignore the rest**. Estimated fetal weight, then abdominal circumference. Say the centiles aloud — **the interpretation is what is marked, not the conclusion**.

Version C, the mannequin: **'I'm finding the top of the symphysis pubis, palpating for the fundus, and measuring with the tape blinded. I make it thirty centimetres, at 34 weeks.'** If you measure 15 cm at 34 weeks you have found the wrong landmark — **re-measure once, out loud, then report**.

Causes of oligohydramnios if asked: **placental insufficiency, ruptured membranes, fetal renal abnormality or obstruction, post-dates, and drugs such as ACE inhibitors and NSAIDs**. The fetus makes the liquor — no kidneys, no fluid.

stem: Chloe Bennett, 28, G2 P1, who believes she is about 20 weeks pregnant. The pregnancy was unplanned. She has been travelling with her partner, has had no antenatal screening or check-ups, and has a history of irregular periods. On examination the symphysis–fundal height is well above the gestation.
tasks: Take a focused history
Explain the diagnosis with your reasons
Give your differential diagnoses
(Older versions) Tell the examiner your investigations

dx: **Large for gestational age — a FINDING, not a diagnosis.** There is nothing to diagnose here. The station is a **differential-generation exercise dressed up as a consultation**, and the emptiness of Version A (no scans, no bloods, no antenatal care) is deliberate: the only thing left to score is **the breadth and reasoning of your causes**.

Definition: **SFH more than 3 cm above the gestation in weeks**, or on ultrasound an **estimated fetal weight above the 90th centile**. VERIFY — some Australian services use **±2 cm**; if challenged, say **'a discrepancy of about 3 cm, and any discrepancy that concerns me, prompts an ultrasound.'**

The four mechanisms every differential belongs to: **the fetus · the fluid · the uterus itself · the dates**. Or six buckets said in order — **maternal endocrine (diabetes) · maternal other (obesity, fibroids) · fetal (macrosomia, multiple, malformation) · infection · placental and fluid · artefact** — which is a complete answer in under forty seconds.

The numbers: **macrosomia = birthweight over 4000 g**, high-risk over **4500 g** VERIFY · **polyhydramnios = AFI over 24 cm or deepest pocket 8 cm or more**; normal AFI **5–24 cm**, pocket **2–8 cm** · **EFW error roughly 10–15% near term**, so never make a delivery decision on one number · **about half of polyhydramnios is idiopathic**.

CORRECTION — say the right timings: **OGTT 75 g at 24–28 weeks** (not 26–28), earlier at booking or 12–16 weeks if she has risk factors and repeated at 24–28 if the early one is normal · **GBS swab 35–37 weeks** · combined first-trimester screening **11+0 to 13+6**, NIPT from **10 weeks** · morphology scan **18–20 weeks**. Diagnostic OGTT: **fasting 5.1, 1 h 10.0, 2 h 8.5 mmol/L**. VERIFY

CORRECTION — **TORCH does not cut both ways.** **Toxoplasma and CMV characteristically cause growth RESTRICTION**, not uterine enlargement. The infections that enlarge a uterus do it through **fetal anaemia, hydrops and placentomegaly** — chiefly **parvovirus B19 and syphilis**. Screen for the congenital infections, but **add parvovirus serology and check the syphilis result**, and say the mechanism differs if challenged.

CORRECTION — **do not interpret raw weight figures.** '56 kg to 76 kg' means nothing on its own; gain is judged against **booking BMI**. Ask instead: **'has the gain felt rapid or unusual to you?'** And **SFH is unreliable above a BMI of about 30** — saying so is a mark for insight.

CORRECTION — **no bed rest** (not evidence-based, raises thromboembolic risk) · **no reflexive steroids** (antenatal corticosteroids are for anticipated preterm birth, usually under 34–35 weeks, not for polyhydramnios itself) VERIFY · **no pelvic examination** — past the first trimester the uterus is an abdominal organ, and a bimanual adds nothing to the size assessment. Be able to say that in one sentence.

**Do not commit to polyhydramnios without an amniotic fluid index.** 'Probably' is the honest word, and the AFI is the confirming measurement. **The AFI is the sum of the deepest vertical pocket in each of four quadrants.**

Investigations, named with what you want from each: **ultrasound — amniotic fluid index, fetal biometry with an estimated weight, the NUMBER of fetuses, a look for fibroids, and a structural survey** · **75 g OGTT** · **catch-up booking bloods** — FBE, group and antibody screen, rubella, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, HIV · **CTG** in the third trimester or with reduced movements. SA: obstetric ultrasound means travel — **PATS**; fetal medicine at the **WCH or FMC**, Lyell McEwin for the north; **in-utero transfer** rather than retrieving a sick baby — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, RFDS for remote; **TIS National 131 450**, never the partner and never a child; **Quitline 13 7848**.
plan: WIPE, sit at eye level. **'You're Chloe? What's brought you in today?'** She hands you the agenda — her friend said her tummy looks too big. **Acknowledge before any question**: **'that's a very reasonable thing to be worried about, and I'm glad you came in.'** Then signpost. **Approach to the patient is a scored domain and it is won or lost in the first fifteen seconds.**

The two opening obstetric questions, asked **separately**: **'was this a planned pregnancy?'** then **'how has the pregnancy been going so far?'** Congratulate only if it was planned, she sounds pleased, and it is early — **at 34 weeks it lands badly**.

The non-judgemental line, asked **once**: **'you mentioned you haven't had your check-ups — was there a reason, or was it just the travelling? I'm only asking so we can make it easier from here.'** The answer barely matters; **the asking is what is marked**, and it is where the approach-to-patient marks sit in Version A.

The obstetric spine, **one question at a time, stopping at her gestation**: **routine bloods at the start · a dating scan · the Down syndrome screening · the scan at 18 to 20 weeks — AND DID THEY SAY ONE BABY OR MORE THAN ONE · the sweet drink test at 24 to 28 weeks · the swab at 35 to 37 weeks.** Every 'no' is a differential you have just opened, and you must say so later.

The three that close every second- and third-trimester history: **'are you feeling the baby move?'** · **'any headaches, blurred vision, or swelling in your legs?'** (ask even at 20 weeks — eight seconds, and it is a scored habit) · **'have you been pregnant before, any problems in the pregnancy or the birth — and was the baby large?'**

**I M D D, infections — signpost the group first**: **'can I ask a few questions about infections in pregnancy?'** Then **any fever or rash since you fell pregnant · contact with anyone unwell, especially with a rash · any pets or a cat litter tray · any undercooked or raw meat.** **Never say 'TORCH' to the patient** — name them in plain words.

**Macrosomia: do big babies run in your family · have you noticed any rapid or unusual weight gain.** She says her sister had a huge baby — **write it down, because that sentence is the reason you attach to macrosomia later**. Hearing it and never using it is a named failing.

**Multiple: were you unusually sick early on · any twins in the family · was this an IVF or assisted pregnancy.** **Masses: have you ever been told you have fibroids · were your periods heavy before the pregnancy.** **Malformations has no question of its own — the morphology scan IS the question.**

**Dates — the answer the stem is steering you toward: when was your last period · are you sure about that date · were your cycles regular or irregular.** **Diabetes: are you passing more urine than usual · are you thirstier than usual · any diabetes in the family.** Do not drop diabetes because the OGTT was never done — **symptoms and family history are still yours to ask for**.
Close the history: **do you smoke · any alcohol · any other drugs · any medicines, including anything you buy yourself · any allergies.** Then stop, whatever is unasked.

Examination, asking for **what you are looking for, not the region**: **blood pressure · urine dipstick for protein and glucose · fundal height in centimetres · uterine contour, regular or irregular · tenderness, then tone · Leopold's for lie and presentation, then the fetal heart rate · capillary blood glucose.** **No pelvic examination**, and say why in one sentence if asked.

The frame, three sentences: **the finding** — 'your womb is measuring larger than we'd expect at this stage; we call that large for gestational age' · **the reason** — the measurement itself, expected within about three centimetres of the weeks · **the honesty line** — **'that's a measurement, not a diagnosis.'**

**The causes, each with its reason attached.** Wrong dates (irregular periods, no dating scan — **most likely and least worrying**) · a big baby (**her sister**) · extra fluid, polyhydramnios · **more than one baby — 'you haven't had the 20-week scan, so I can't rule twins out'** · gestational diabetes (no sugar test) · a fibroid · less commonly, **certain infections, or a problem with the way the baby's food pipe or stomach has formed** that stops the baby swallowing the fluid. **Six causes with reasons beats nine recited.**

When she pushes **'so what is it, doctor?'** — **'I can't tell you which one yet, and I don't want to guess. That's exactly what the scan is for. But I can tell you everything it could be.'** Then name the five things the ultrasound answers, the OGTT and the catch-up bloods, and safety-net: **bleeding · leaking fluid · regular tightenings · reduced movements once established · bad headaches or swelling.** Offer a catch-up antenatal schedule.
pefe: **No pelvic examination.** Past the first trimester the uterus is an abdominal organ; there is no routine indication for a speculum or bimanual here, and asking for one wastes the clock and reads as reflex.

Ask in this order, naming what you are looking for: **general — consciousness, pallor, oedema · vitals, blood pressure above all · symphysis–fundal height in centimetres · uterine CONTOUR, regular or irregular · tenderness, then TONE · Leopold's for lie and presentation, then the FETAL HEART RATE explicitly · office tests — urine dipstick for protein and glucose, and a capillary blood glucose**.

**Tense but not tender with no bleeding = over-distension, so probably polyhydramnios. Tense AND tender with bleeding = abruption**, and the station stops being this station. **An irregular contour suggests a fibroid.**
**Say the pre-eclampsia exclusion out loud** — normal blood pressure, no proteinuria. The examiner cannot mark what you do not verbalise.

**Ultrasound, and name the five things you want from it**: **amniotic fluid index · fetal biometry with an estimated weight · the number of fetuses · a look for fibroids · a structural survey** (she has never had a morphology scan). Ordering 'an ultrasound' and stopping is the named fail — the five things **are** the differential list restated as a test.

**75 g OGTT**, brought forward if necessary. **Catch-up booking bloods**: FBE, blood group and antibody screen, and serology — **rubella, syphilis, hepatitis B and C, HIV**. Add **parvovirus B19, toxoplasma and CMV** if polyhydramnios is confirmed.
**CTG** if she is in the third trimester or reports reduced movements. Reduced movements are assessed **today**, not at the next appointment.

If the scan confirms **polyhydramnios**: find the cause — **OGTT, detailed anomaly scan, fetal echocardiography, antibody screen, parvovirus and syphilis serology, and middle cerebral artery Doppler if anaemia is suspected**. Then obstetric-led care, **serial growth and liquor**, birth in a unit with neonatal support, and a **controlled rupture of membranes with an obstetrician present**. **Amnioreduction is reserved for maternal respiratory compromise.** VERIFY — indomethacin is now rarely used, because of fetal ductal constriction.

If the scan confirms **macrosomia**: OGTT if not done, **serial growth scans**, shoulder dystocia discussed honestly and without alarm, and **'the obstetric team will discuss timing and mode of birth with you'** rather than quoting a week or a weight threshold. Induction is commonly considered around **39 weeks**. VERIFY

Complications of polyhydramnios to have ready: **preterm labour · prelabour rupture of membranes · malpresentation · cord prolapse when the membranes go · abruption on sudden decompression · postpartum haemorrhage from an over-distended uterus · maternal respiratory discomfort**.

stem: Lily Chen, 30, is 36 weeks pregnant and has presented with a headache.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you would like
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Eclampsia at 36 weeks** — but run it as a **HEADACHE station with pre-eclampsia at the top of the list**. The stem effectively hands you pre-eclampsia the moment the examiner reads out 150/90, so **the diagnosis is worth very little on the mark sheet**. What scores is holding **two differential columns** — pregnancy-specific and not-to-miss general — and screening both under time pressure.

**Pre-eclampsia: new hypertension after 20 weeks with maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction. Eclampsia: a generalised seizure in a woman with pre-eclampsia, not attributable to another cause.** The prefix is the whole point — **pre-eclampsia is the stage before eclampsia, and everything you do is aimed at keeping her there**.

**The name change: no fit → pre-eclampsia. Fit → eclampsia.** Nothing else about the explanation changes — same multisystem disease, same high blood pressure, same leaking kidneys, one more feature. Only **the name and the urgency**. A candidate who has just watched a seizure and says 'you have pre-eclampsia' has told the examiner they were reciting a recall.

**The four priorities, in order, said as headings**: **1. Resuscitate** — DRS ABC, protect from injury, **LEFT LATERAL**, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, move to resuscitation. **2. Stop the fit** — **magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour**; benzodiazepine (midazolam or diazepam) only if it continues. **3. Stop the pressure** — if above **160/110**, IV labetalol or hydralazine, down promptly but **not to normal**. **4. Stop the pregnancy** — delivery is definitive; at 36 weeks, as soon as she is stable.

**Why left lateral**: the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when supine, reducing venous return and cardiac output — **and it protects the airway from aspiration**. It is the step candidates most often leave out.

**Magnesium continues for 24 hours after birth or the last seizure, whichever is later.** CORRECTION — **toxicity is detected by LOSS OF REFLEXES FIRST**, before respiratory depression. That is why you check them **hourly**. Order: **reflexes → respiratory rate → urine output**. **Antidote calcium gluconate.** Magnesium is renally cleared, so check renal function — impaired excretion is the usual reason for toxicity.

CORRECTION — **severe hypertension is 160/110, not 160/100**. The pair that matters is **140/90 and 160/110**, target **under 135/85**. VERIFY. CORRECTION — **eclampsia can occur without preceding hypertension or proteinuria, and it can occur POSTPARTUM** — most within the first 48 hours, described up to four weeks after birth. **Do not exclude eclampsia because she has delivered.**
**Strict fluid balance** — these women are at risk of **pulmonary oedema**, so avoid over-filling. Catheterise and measure **hourly urine output**. **'I'd run a litre of saline' is a named fail.**

**Imaging is not routine** for a typical eclamptic seizure. Image for **focal signs, failure to regain consciousness, recurrent seizures despite magnesium, or an atypical presentation** — **MRI in preference to CT** in pregnancy.

CORRECTION — **dengue and Ross River virus are mosquito-borne, not tick-borne** (relevant in the fever variant). Investigations if asked: **CTG first — the one most often omitted** · ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler · FBE · LFTs with LDH and a film for HELLP · UEC, eGFR, urate, urine protein-creatinine ratio · coagulation, group and hold · **magnesium level only if toxicity is suspected or she has renal impairment**. SA: an eclamptic seizure at an MM5 site is a **MedSTAR retrieval — call 1300 13 12 33 at the same time as you start magnesium, not afterwards**, because the aircraft takes time. Load magnesium and give the first antihypertensive **before** transfer. Receiving units WCH, Lyell McEwin or FMC; **PATS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: Before you sit: **'Examiner, could I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturations AND TEMPERATURE?'** The temperature is not a formality here — **meningitis is on your list, and examiners notice when it is requested by name.**
**'I understand you've come in with a headache. Tell me what's been happening.'** Acknowledge the worry in one sentence, then signpost: assess the headache, examine, find the cause, make a plan.

SICORA: **where is the headache, one side or both · out of ten how bad · is it throbbing, a pressure or tightening, or a dull ache · when did it start, is it constant or intermittent, is it getting worse · does it spread · does anything make it better or worse**. **Offer the options for character** — 'describe the quality' produces silence; 'throbbing, pressure or dull ache?' produces an answer.

**The four discriminators, and they are the marks**: **'did it come on suddenly, over seconds?' · 'is this the worst headache of your life?' · 'is it worse when you cough, sneeze or strain?' · 'does it wake you at night?'** She says no to all four — **you are being marked for asking, not for the answers**.

The pre-eclampsia set: **any change in your vision, blurring, flashing lights, spots · any dizziness · any tummy pain, particularly up under the ribs on the right · any nausea or vomiting · any yellowing of your skin · any swelling in your legs, hands or face · any chest pain or shortness of breath · passing less urine than usual**. She volunteers blurring and puffy ankles **only if asked**.

The obstetric block, **faster than in a pure pre-eclampsia station** — the dating scan can go, the fetal movement question cannot: **were the routine bloods normal · Down syndrome screening, the 18–20 week scan and the sweet drink test · is the baby kicking as usual · any bleeding, discharge or leaking of fluid · any high blood pressure in a previous pregnancy · any kidney problems ever**.
**Signal the second column out loud**: **'I'm now going to ask about some other causes of headache that I need to rule out.'** The examiner is marking whether you know you are screening two columns.

**Meningitis: any fever or chills · any rash · any stiffness in your neck · do bright lights hurt your eyes.** **Space-occupying lesion: any weakness or numbness anywhere in your body** (the cough and night-waking questions are already done). **Brain tumour questions are awkward in pregnancy — early-morning vomiting and weight loss are both unusable at 36 weeks; use raised-pressure features instead.**

**'Examiner, findings rather than technique please.'** General appearance, **blood pressure and temperature in particular**, then — **'because this is a headache case'** — **fundoscopy, deep tendon reflexes and specifically ankle clonus, a FULL CRANIAL NERVE examination, upper and lower limb tone, power, reflexes and sensation, and neck stiffness**. **Say the word back**: **'Thank you — so there is papilloedema, hyperreflexia and clonus. That tells me this is severe disease with central nervous system irritability, and it changes my plan from monitoring to admission and treatment.'**

**The examiner interrupts: 'your patient is now having a fit.'** **Turn to the examiner, not the patient.** Say the four headings out loud, with the left lateral reason attached, and keep going until you are told to stop.

Told she is stable and alert, go back to the task. **Orient her first**: **'you've just had a seizure, and I know that will have been frightening. You're safe, we're treating it, and I'm going to tell you exactly what's happening.'**

**'The condition you have is called eclampsia'** — a condition that only happens in pregnancy, involving several organs at once. Then the reasons **all together**: the headache and blurred vision, **150/90**, a large amount of protein in the urine, **papilloedema**, exaggerated reflexes and clonus, **and the seizure itself**. Answer **'is the baby all right?'** with the continuous CTG, and **'will it happen again?'** with the magnesium and the reflex checks.

**The differentials, still headache differentials**: infection in the brain — meningitis or encephalitis; bleeding in the brain — subarachnoid haemorrhage; a growth in the brain; **a clot in one of the veins draining the brain, which pregnancy makes more likely**; then migraine, tension headache, sinus or dental infection, or a problem with her glasses. Close with **delivery as the definitive treatment** and ask who to call.

**Imaging only** for focal signs, failure to regain consciousness, recurrent seizures despite magnesium, or an atypical presentation — **MRI in preference to CT** in pregnancy.

stem: You are the medical officer in a country emergency department. Jess Tuiono, 26, has come in with vaginal bleeding that started yesterday and is getting worse, together with lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was six weeks ago.
A urine pregnancy test has already been done in triage. You will be told the result only if you ask.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain the most likely diagnosis to the patient

dx: **Ectopic pregnancy at 6 weeks with a NEGATIVE urine test** — empty uterus of normal size, **CMT positive**, right adnexal tenderness, constant pain that **preceded** the bleeding. Everything else here is a standard early-pregnancy-bleeding assessment; the negative test is handed to you to see whether you fold.

The sentence that passes the station: **'That does not change my diagnosis. A negative urine pregnancy test does not exclude an ectopic at this gestation, because βhCG rises slowly in an ectopic and may sit below the urine threshold of about 20 to 25 IU/L. I would send a quantitative serum βhCG and arrange an urgent transvaginal ultrasound. My working diagnosis remains an ectopic pregnancy.'** Then continue as though nothing happened.

Why it can be negative: in an ectopic the **trophoblast is poorly implanted**, so βhCG **rises slowly and plateaus far below** what the same gestation would produce in the uterus. **Urine assays detect from about 20–25 IU/L; serum detects from around 5.** Dilute urine lowers it further.

The mirror-image trap: a **βhCG below the discriminatory zone does not exclude an ectopic either**, and a level **above** it with an empty uterus is **suspicious rather than diagnostic**. **Transvaginal zone roughly 1500–2000 IU/L, transabdominal about 6000.** The zone guides **when to image**; it never makes the diagnosis. VERIFY locally.

CORRECTION — **do not refuse the bimanual.** The diagnosis is reached through it: cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and the adnexal findings all come from it. What you avoid is **vigorous or repeated** examination in a suspected **rupture**; an unstable woman is resuscitated and taken to theatre, not examined.

The risk-factor sweep the examiner is waiting for, and she volunteers none of it: **previous ectopic · tubal or uterine surgery · an intrauterine device or progestogen-only pill · IVF or assisted conception · chlamydia or PID · smoking**. She has **chlamydia at 20, a hit-and-miss mini-pill, and ten cigarettes a day** — only if asked.

Reading the card: **os closed** = not incomplete or inevitable · **no tissue passed** = not complete · **uterus empty and normal size** = not a miscarriage at all (a miscarriage leaves the uterus either equal to dates or small and contracted, with a history of tissue) · **CMT positive** = pelvic peritoneal irritation · **right adnexal tenderness** = the site.

Management, and **this is not a general practice problem**: **IV access · FBE, quantitative serum βhCG, group and antibody screen, cross-match if any instability · urgent transvaginal ultrasound · urgent gynaecology · nil by mouth · anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours**. **If she becomes unstable she goes to theatre, not to the scanner.**

Definitive treatment is the gynaecologist's call — **do not offer methotrexate yourself or quote thresholds you cannot defend**. The safe, complete answer: **'the options are methotrexate or surgery, and the gynaecologist will decide which is appropriate'** — methotrexate for a **stable, small, unruptured ectopic with a low βhCG and no fetal cardiac activity**; otherwise **laparoscopic salpingectomy or salpingostomy**.

SA: there is **no transvaginal ultrasound at 2 a.m.** in a Yorke and Northern hospital, and a suspected ectopic does not wait for the morning list. Ring the on-call gynaecologist early and discuss **retrieval rather than self-transport** — a woman who ruptures on the Copper Coast Highway has no options. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** or RFDS. Know your **SA Pathology** βhCG turnaround before you rely on it. **PATS covers planned travel, not this.** Chlamydia retesting and contraception through **SHINE SA**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: Before you sit: **'Examiner, could I have her blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature, and is there a postural drop?'**

WIPE, confirm identity, one open question. She is hunched and guarding her right side. **'Which came first — the pain or the bleeding?'** The pain, two days ago. Pain preceding the bleeding points **away** from miscarriage.

The bleeding: **is it getting worse or settling · have you passed any tissue, anything solid · any clots · how many pads**. Worsening but **light and dark** fits an ectopic better than a miscarriage, and **the blood loss does not explain how unwell she is** — a warning sign.
The pain: **where exactly · out of ten · is it there all the time, or does it come and go in waves**. **Constant and worse on movement = ectopic. Waves = a contracting uterus.**

The two questions that change the urgency: **'any pain at the tip of your shoulder?'** — yes, on the right, lying down — and **'have you felt faint or dizzy?'** — light-headed this morning. **Pre-syncope with minimal external bleeding means concealed loss.** Volunteer both in your presentation.
**P1 — when was your last period, are your cycles regular.** **P2 — any pregnancy symptoms, sickness, sore breasts?** Symptoms are often **mild** in an ectopic.

**P3, the risk-factor sweep, one at a time — this is the block the examiner is waiting for: is this your first pregnancy · any previous ectopic pregnancy · any miscarriage or termination · any surgery on the tubes or the womb · are you using contraception, or do you have a coil · was this conceived with help such as IVF.**

**'Have you ever been told you had a sexually transmitted infection, or pelvic inflammatory disease?'** — chlamydia at 20, and **she will not volunteer it**. Then **'do you smoke?'** — a genuine independent risk factor — and **'do you know your blood group?'**

Examination in order: **general inspection → abdomen, where is she tender, guarding or rebound → 'a pelvic examination with her consent and a chaperone' → is the os open or closed → tissue or active bleeding at the os, any lesion → bimanual: cervical motion tenderness → uterine size, and is the uterus empty or full → adnexal mass or tenderness**.
**'And may I have the result of the urine pregnancy test?'** The examiner hands you **NEGATIVE** and watches. **Everything before this moment is preparation for the next thirty seconds.**
Say the sentence to the examiner, then do not soften it, do not re-open the differential, and do not offer to repeat the urine test.

To her: **'I'm concerned that this pregnancy may have settled outside the womb, most likely in the tube on your right side.'** Then the reasons — **empty uterus of normal size, right-sided tenderness, pain before the bleeding**.

**Deal with the negative test before she raises it** — she will push back with 'I'm not even pregnant' and hold that position. **'The hormone level rises slowly in this kind of pregnancy and can be too low for a urine test to pick up. It doesn't reassure me.'**

Why it matters, without terrifying her: **'a pregnancy can't grow safely in a tube. If it keeps growing the tube can rupture and bleed, and that is an emergency — which is why I want this sorted out today rather than next week.'**

The plan out loud: **drip, bloods including the hormone level and blood group, internal scan now, ringing gynaecology, nil by mouth, anti-D because she is B negative.** Fertility question answered honestly: **most women go on to have normal pregnancies, no promises today.** Escalation: **severe pain, shoulder pain, feeling faint, heavy bleeding — tell the nurse immediately.**
pefe: **Observations before you sit**, including the postural drop. She is stable now; that can change in minutes.

Order: **general inspection → abdomen (site of tenderness, guarding, rebound, uterus palpable) → consent and chaperone → speculum: the os first, then tissue or bleeding at the os, then lesions → bimanual: CMT, then uterine size and whether the uterus is empty or full, then adnexal mass or tenderness → and finally the urine pregnancy test result**.
**Ask for the urine test result deliberately, and last.** The examiner gives it at that point specifically to see what you do with it. **Silence scores as not knowing.**
**No palpable adnexal mass is expected.** A palpable ectopic is the exception, not the rule — its absence is not reassuring.
Investigations: **IV access · FBE · quantitative serum βhCG · group and antibody screen · cross-match if any instability · URGENT transvaginal ultrasound**. Nil by mouth.
**A sac seen inside the uterus is the only thing that excludes an ectopic.** Nothing else does — not a negative urine test, not a low βhCG, not the absence of a mass.

If the βhCG comes back **below** the discriminatory zone (~1500–2000 transvaginal): an empty uterus at that level is **uninformative**. **Repeat at 48 hours and rescan**, with the same safety advice meanwhile. βhCG should rise by **at least about two thirds in 48 hours** in a normal intrauterine pregnancy; it rises slowly in an ectopic.
**Do not observe her overnight without a scan and a βhCG.** The diagnosis is unresolved and tubal rupture can be catastrophic within minutes — observation alone is not a plan.
**If she becomes unstable she goes to theatre, not to the scanner.**
**Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours** — she is B negative and **ectopic pregnancy is a first-trimester indication**. VERIFY.

**Reasonable as a differential, wrong as a conclusion — rank it second.** Ultrasound of the adnexa. Urgent

Ultrasound with Doppler; **surgical emergency if suspected**

**CMT positive**, bilateral adnexal tenderness

**Against here — she has passed no tissue and the pain preceded the bleeding.** Prompt

**Os open, tissue at the os**, uterus smaller than dates
**Excluded** — os closed, no tissue. Urgent if present
**Heterotopic pregnancy**
**Assisted reproduction**; an intrauterine sac **plus** adnexal findings
Both a sac **and** an adnexal mass
Careful adnexal imaging. **After IVF this is a real differential, not a curiosity.** Immediate
Pregnancy of unknown location
No sac, no adnexal mass, βhCG below the zone
Empty uterus, nothing else to find
**Treat as an ectopic until proven otherwise.** Serial βhCG at 48 h, rescan in 7–10 days, written red flags

stem: You are a general practitioner in a rural South Australian practice. Mary Whitfield, 27, has come in this morning with vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was eight weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive three weeks ago.
tasks: Take a focused history (approximately six minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain the diagnosis and your management to the patient

dx: **Threatened miscarriage with a subchorionic haematoma at 8 weeks** — a viable intrauterine pregnancy, os closed, and the whole station is the **order in which you say it**.

CORRECTION — the card says **"retroplacental clot"**. At 8 weeks there is no mature placenta, so the accurate term is a **subchorionic haematoma** (some reports say retrochorionic). **Retroplacental clot and abruption are second- and third-trimester diagnoses.** Management is identical; saying this gains marks rather than losing them.

Reassurance first, label second, always: **'the pregnancy is in the right place, the right size, and I can see the heartbeat. The neck of the womb is closed. You are not having a miscarriage.'** Then attach the name and stress the word **threatened**.

The clot in words she will keep: **'a bruise, essentially, where the pregnancy has attached to the wall of the womb. That is where today's bleeding came from.'** Do **not** say haematoma to her, do **not** say abruption at all, and do **not** promise it will resolve — **'most settle, which is why I want to scan you again.'**

CORRECTION — **bed rest is not treatment.** No evidence it changes the outcome, and prolonged immobility carries a **thrombosis risk** in pregnancy. **'Carry on as normally as you feel able.'** Answer the self-blame before she asks it: **'there is nothing you did that caused this.'**

**Progesterone** — vaginal micronised progesterone has a role only in a woman with bleeding **and at least one previous miscarriage**, once an **intrauterine pregnancy is confirmed on ultrasound**. This is her first pregnancy, so it is not indicated. None at all in a pregnancy of unknown location.

**Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours** if Rh D negative — for ectopic, molar, termination, and miscarriage managed medically or surgically. **NOT for a threatened miscarriage before 12 weeks.** She is **O positive**, so it does not arise. VERIFY
**No serial βhCG once cardiac activity has been seen** — the ultrasound is the better test. Serial levels belong to a pregnancy of unknown location.

Milestones to have exact: **sac from about 5 weeks · yolk sac 5½ · fetal pole and cardiac activity 6 weeks**. Non-viability is **MSD ≥ 25 mm with no embryo, or CRL ≥ 7 mm with no heartbeat**. Once a heartbeat is seen at 8 weeks the great majority continue — give that reassurance **without quoting false precision**. VERIFY

Plan: **repeat scan in 1–2 weeks**, written red flags, a follow-up appointment and a phone number. Red flags: **heavier bleeding · a pad soaked within an hour · any tissue passed · severe pain · feeling faint · fever or offensive discharge**. SA: scan not on site in a Yorke and Northern town — ring the unit first, **PATS** for planned travel, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unstable; EPAS at TQEH, RAH, FMC and the WCH; **TIS National 131 450**.

CORRECTION — do not congratulate, but **do ask**: **'before we go on, was this a planned pregnancy?'** Four seconds, and it stops you assuming grief where there may be relief, or the reverse.

The bleeding, timing then CCVO: **when exactly did it start · is it getting worse or settling · have you passed any tissue, anything solid apart from blood · any clots · how many pads, and were they fully soaked · bright red or darker**.

Pain, always linked to the bleeding: **are you having any tummy pain · where exactly · out of ten how bad · is it there all the time or does it come and go in waves**. Waves = a uterus contracting to expel. Constant = ectopic. Do not run a full pain assessment.

The early pregnancy 5 Ps. **P1 Periods — when was your last period · are your cycles regular · any heavy or irregular bleeding before this.** **P2 Pregnancy symptoms — are you tired · any morning sickness**, and if she vomits, **how many times a day** (ten a day plus large for dates is molar).

**P3, the ectopic risk sweep — is this your first pregnancy · was it conceived with help such as IVF · any previous miscarriage · any terminations · any caesarean or surgery on the womb.** One at a time. This also decides whether progesterone is even a discussion.

**P4 Partner — are you in a stable relationship · is he supportive · ever been told you had a sexually transmitted infection.** **P5 Pap — are you up to date with cervical screening, and was it normal?** P5 is the cervical-source sweep; do not drop it for time.

One screening question, not a full social history: **'do you smoke, drink alcohol, or use any other drugs?'** Smoking is a genuine ectopic risk factor. Then **medications, allergies, and do you know your blood group** — the blood group is the anti-D decision.

Examination, **the os before anything else**: general inspection → abdomen → **'a pelvic examination with her consent and a chaperone'** → **is the os open or closed** → tissue or active bleeding at the os → lesion on cervix or vaginal walls → bimanual for **cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, adnexae** → **'has she had an ultrasound, and what does it show?'**

Plan: **no tablet, no bed rest, and say why honestly** · normal activity as tolerated · **repeat scan in 1–2 weeks** · **O positive, so no anti-D**. Then the written red flags and a phone number.

What you avoid is **vigorous or repeated** examination in a woman you suspect has a **ruptured** ectopic — and an unstable woman is resuscitated, not examined.

**Uterine size against dates is the cheapest discriminator in the block** and the examiner hands it to you if you ask. Eight weeks in size with a closed os and a sac seen inside the uterus is what makes this threatened rather than anything else.

stem: You are a hospital medical officer in the early pregnancy assessment clinic. Sarah Nguyen, 25, was referred yesterday with light vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was eight weeks ago. She has had an ultrasound this morning and has come back for the result. She is on her own.

Information you have been given: observations BP 112/70, HR 76, T 36.6, she is well. Speculum yesterday: os closed, scant old blood, cervix healthy. Bimanual yesterday: uterus consistent with dates, non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, adnexae normal. Transvaginal ultrasound today: single intrauterine gestational sac, crown–rump length consistent with 8 weeks, no fetal cardiac activity, no adnexal mass, no free fluid. Blood group A negative. Her own words at reception: 'Is everything all right? Nobody would tell me anything.'
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings to the patient
Counsel her about further management
Answer any questions she has

dx: **Missed miscarriage at 8 weeks** — sac of 8 weeks' size with **no fetal cardiac activity**. Also called early fetal demise or silent miscarriage, but **never say those words to her**.

**Non-viability is a measurement, not an impression**: **mean sac diameter ≥ 25 mm with no embryo**, or **crown–rump length ≥ 7 mm with no heartbeat**. At 8 weeks the CRL is well past 7 mm, so the diagnosis is **secure on a single scan**. VERIFY

If the numbers were borderline — a small sac, or a pole **under 7 mm** — the correct action is a **repeat scan in 7 to 10 days** and you do **not** use the word miscarriage today. Saying this shows you know the thresholds rather than the label.

The sequence, and it fails in two opposite directions: **warning shot → one plain sentence → ten seconds of silence → and still reach the three options**. Some candidates break the news beautifully and run out of time with no management; others rush to the options and never let her react. You must do both.

The sentence itself, no hedging: **'The scan shows that the pregnancy has stopped growing. I'm very sorry — you have had a miscarriage.'** Then stop. No 'unfortunately the sonographic appearances are consistent with'.

Volunteer the blame answer before she asks it: **'there is nothing you did that caused this. It isn't the gym, it isn't your work, it isn't coffee, and it isn't anything you ate.'** Most early miscarriages happen because the pregnancy did not develop as it should from the very beginning. She still feels pregnant **because the hormones take a while to fall**.

The three options, **none more correct than the others**: **expectant** (no drugs, no surgery, at home — but no one can say when) · **medical** (**mifepristone, then misoprostol a day or two later**) · **surgical** (day-case **suction curettage** under anaesthetic — planned, least bleeding, tissue to the laboratory). If she asks which you would choose, **decline**, then help her weigh it: **'what matters more to you — knowing when, or avoiding an anaesthetic?'**

CORRECTION — medical management does **not** fail 5% of the time. Roughly **15–25% go on to need surgical evacuation**. Quote a range, and tell her that needing the operation afterwards is **common, not a complication**. CORRECTION — curettage does **not** meaningfully cause later ectopic pregnancy or placenta praevia; the real risks are **uterine perforation, cervical injury, infection, retained tissue and rarely intrauterine adhesions**.

CORRECTION — the **nine-week / 63-day limit is the MS-2 Step registration limit for medical TERMINATION**, not a ceiling for managing a miscarriage. Gestation affects how much bleeding and pain to warn her about, not her eligibility.

**Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours** — she is **A NEGATIVE**, so it is needed **if managed medically or surgically**. VERIFY. Then: **histology on any tissue obtained** (which also excludes a molar pregnancy) · red flags · **no medical need to wait beyond one normal period** before trying again, and that is only to make dating easier · **about one in five pregnancies ends this way**, and after one miscarriage the next is essentially the same as anyone else's · continue folic acid. SA: **PATS** for travel to EPAS at TQEH, RAH, FMC or the WCH; **Sands**, **Red Nose Grief and Loss**, **Miscarriage Australia**; Country Health Connect; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: There is **no history to take** — do not spend the station taking one. Set up instead: **'Sarah, come and sit down. We won't be interrupted.'** Then **'before we start, is there anyone you'd like me to call to be with you?'**
Find out what she already knows: **'can you tell me what you understand so far about why you came in?'** She says the closed os was called a good sign.

**Give the normal findings first** — **'that's right, the neck of the womb was closed, and the pregnancy is in exactly the right place, inside the womb.'** It is true, and it makes the next sentence land as information rather than ambush.
**Warning shot: 'I'm afraid I don't have good news for you today.'** Then pause. Let her brace — two seconds is enough.
**One plain sentence: 'The scan shows that the pregnancy has stopped growing. I'm very sorry — you have had a miscarriage.'** Then stop talking.
**Ten seconds of silence.** Offer tissues if she is crying. **Do not fill the gap.** If she puts a hand up, wait longer.
**'I'm so sorry, Sarah. Take whatever time you need.'** Then volunteer the blame answer **without being asked** — the gym, work, coffee, food — and explain why she still feels pregnant.
Ask permission before pivoting: **'when you're ready, I'll explain what happens from here. Would that be all right?'**
Frame the choice: **'there are three ways this can be managed, and none of them is more correct than the others. It is your choice, and you don't have to decide today.'**
**Expectant** — wait and let your body pass the pregnancy; no drugs, no surgery, at home; **the difficulty is we can't tell you when**, and there will be bleeding and cramping.

**Medical** — **one tablet, then a second medicine a day or two later** which brings the bleeding on; avoids an anaesthetic, can be at home; causes **cramping, heavy bleeding and often nausea**, and **a proportion still need a small operation afterwards**.

**Surgical** — a **small operation under anaesthetic as a day case**; planned and predictable, least bleeding, **tissue goes to the laboratory**; downsides are the anaesthetic, and small risks of **infection, injury to the womb and rarely scarring inside it**.
If she asks which you would choose: **decline honestly**, then **'what matters more to you — knowing when, or avoiding an anaesthetic?'** Reflect her answer back without deciding for her.

**Anti-D: 'your blood group is A negative, so if we manage this with tablets or with an operation you'll need an anti-D injection within 72 hours — I'll organise that.'** Then **histology** on any tissue obtained.
Red flags: **soaking a pad within an hour · severe pain · fever · offensive discharge** — come straight back.

Answer the two questions she will ask: **can we try again** — no medical need to wait beyond one normal period, and that is only for dating; wait until you both feel ready. **Will it happen again** — about one in five, and after one the next is the same as anyone's. **Keep taking the folic acid.**
**'I'll write all of this down, and I'd like to see you again next week — not because anything is wrong, but because this is a great deal to take in on your own.'** Offer **Sands** and **Red Nose**.
pefe: **No examination task and no history task** — everything is handed to you on the door. The work is entirely in interpreting the scan and counselling.

The scan, read properly: **single intrauterine gestational sac · CRL consistent with 8 weeks · NO fetal cardiac activity · no adnexal mass · no free fluid**. The intrauterine sac is what excludes an ectopic; the absent cardiac activity at this CRL is what makes it a miscarriage.
**Non-viability thresholds: MSD ≥ 25 mm with no embryo, or CRL ≥ 7 mm with no heartbeat.** Below those, the answer is a **repeat scan in 7–10 days**, not a diagnosis. VERIFY

Yesterday's examination, already given: **os closed, scant old blood, cervix healthy; uterus consistent with dates, non-tender, no cervical motion tenderness, adnexae normal**. A closed os with a uterus at dates and no tissue is what makes this **missed** rather than incomplete or complete.

**Blood group and antibody screen** is the anti-D decision and it is already done — **A negative**. **Anti-D 250 IU within 72 hours if managed medically or surgically**; not required for expectant management of a **threatened** miscarriage before 12 weeks, but this is a confirmed miscarriage. VERIFY with the receiving unit.
**Histopathology on any tissue obtained** — it also excludes a molar pregnancy. Say it as part of the plan for the medical and surgical options.
**No serial βhCG** — this is a confirmed intrauterine miscarriage, not a pregnancy of unknown location. Serial levels would add nothing.
If challenged on a **5 mm CRL**: **'then I could not call it a miscarriage. Below 7 mm with no heartbeat the correct action is a repeat scan in 7 to 10 days, and I would not use the word today.'**

If she chooses expectant management and goes home to think — **that is entirely acceptable**. There is no urgency in a woman who is well and not bleeding heavily. Written information, red flags, and a review appointment.
