stem: Jenny Hollis, 58, presents to your general practice with palpitations.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 150 · BP 124/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% · alert and comfortable.
The ECG you will be handed: rate 150 · regular R-R intervals · no visible P waves · PR not measurable · narrow QRS · ST segments normal.
tasks: Take a focused history (about 6 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient

dx: **Supraventricular tachycardia** — a **fast, regular, narrow-complex rhythm arising above the ventricles**, in a patient with a heavy stimulant load.

Strictly SVT is an umbrella term covering atrial fibrillation, flutter, AVNRT and AVRT. **For this strip the answer they want is 'supraventricular tachycardia'; AVNRT is also acceptable.** **'PSVT' simply means paroxysmal — do not get drawn into the distinction.**

To the patient in three parts: **name it → 'your heart is beating faster than usual, but still regularly' → 'because of abnormal electrical signalling: your heart has its own wiring that sets the pace, and here an extra circuit takes over and drives it much faster than it should.'**

Then the contributing factor you found: **eight cups of coffee a day is very likely provoking it.** And **the planted hidden finding — a blood pressure she was told was raised once and never followed up** — which needs **its own line in the plan**, not a dismissal because 'it's just an SVT'.

**Address the stated fear before she asks again**: **'this is not a heart attack. There's nothing on your tracing to suggest one, and you don't have the symptoms that go with it — no chest pain, no sweating, no nausea. It's a rhythm problem, and it's very treatable.'**

**Unstable** = hypotension, altered conscious state, ischaemic chest pain or ECG change, breathlessness at rest or pulmonary oedema, syncope, a rate that will not settle, **a broad-complex tachycardia**, or known structural or ischaemic disease → **senior help and synchronised DC cardioversion**, not a leisurely history.

Stable: **continuous monitoring, IV access, 12-lead ECG → vagal manoeuvres first.** The **modified Valsalva** — blow against resistance, then lie flat with the legs raised — is **more effective than the standard technique**. **Carotid sinus massage only with care, and never with a bruit or a previous stroke.**

**Adenosine if vagal manoeuvres fail: rapid intravenous push through a large proximal vein with an immediate saline flush, 6 mg then 12 mg.** Warn her it causes **brief, very unpleasant flushing and chest tightness that passes within seconds**. **Avoid in severe asthma.** VERIFY against local protocol, with senior involvement.

Long term: **reduce or stop the stimulants · teach her to perform the vagal manoeuvres herself · refer for electrophysiology assessment, since catheter ablation is curative for recurrent SVT.** And **recheck the blood pressure, arrange follow-up, and assess absolute cardiovascular risk**.

SA — **adenosine only where resuscitation facilities and monitoring are available**; discuss early with the receiving cardiology service; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if she is unstable or needs repeated cardioversion. **Electrophysiology and ablation are metropolitan** — referral means a trip to Adelaide, so raise travel, **PATS** and support when counselling a country patient.
plan: To the examiner: **'before I begin, may I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, and the rhythm if it's available, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** If told you don't have the rhythm yet, **accept it without fluster** — the mark is for asking, and the ECG is coming.
WIPE, open question, acknowledge: **'I understand how concerning this must be. Let me ask you some questions and look at your heart tracing, and we'll find the cause together. Is that all right?'**

**Box 1 — describe it**: **can you describe what you mean by palpitations — is your heart beating fast, does it feel irregular, or does it feel like it's missing or skipping a beat? · could you tap out on the desk what the rhythm feels like?** **Expect the refusal. Ask once, accept it, move on** — role-players have declined to tap since 2019.

**Box 2 — timing and course**: **when did it start · is it there all the time or does it come and go · how long does an episode last, and how does it stop · is this the first time, or have you had episodes before · is it getting worse or more frequent?**

**Box 3 — triggers**: **is there anything that makes it better or worse · do you notice it more when you stand up, bend forward or lie down · is it worse on exertion, and do you get it at rest as well · is there a particular place or situation that brings it on?** The positional trigger is classic for SVT; **exertion-only points to ischaemia and changes the case.**

**Group 1 — the full cardiovascular block, five sub-blocks, not one**: **any chest pain with the palpitations, any breathlessness, nausea or sweating · do you feel dizzy, have you ever fainted or blacked out · any swelling in your legs, any breathlessness lying flat, how many pillows · ever been told you have a murmur or valve problem, or had a heart attack · any family history of heart attack or stroke, any high blood pressure, high blood sugar or cholesterol, do you smoke, how much alcohol · any fever or recent flu-like illness?**

Groups 2 to 4: **any cough, noisy breathing or wheeze · any swelling or pain in your calves, recent long travel, previous clots in you or the family · any weather preference, do you find hot weather hard to tolerate, any weight loss, diarrhoea or tremor · how much coffee, tea or energy drink in a day · any recreational drugs · any asthma puffers or nasal decongestant sprays · any Chinese takeaway or very salty food before it started?**

Groups 5 to 8, compressed to one question each if the clock is tight — **but never at the expense of the cardiovascular block or the stimulant count**: **any stress at home or work · how has your mood been · during an episode did you ever feel you were going to die · unusually tired, or more breathless on exertion · any headaches, sweating episodes or tremor · did you miss any meals before it started, any diabetes treatment · when was your last period, and any hot flushes?**

**Name it, define it, explain it** in plain words — then **address the heart-attack fear with your reasons, before she raises it again**.

Plan and close: **monitoring and IV access · vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine · bloods including thyroid function · cut the coffee down substantially · recheck and follow up the blood pressure · electrophysiology referral given recurrent episodes.** Safety net: **chest pain, feeling faint, blacking out, or breathlessness with it → come back straight away.**

**12-lead ECG read in seven steps: rate → regular? → P waves? → PR interval → QRS duration → ST segments → impression.**

**The rule at step 3: a P wave and a T wave must both be present and separate.** If there is only one deflection between QRS complexes at 150, **it is the T wave** and there is no P — the commonest error on this strip.

stem: Raymond Doyle, 68, attends your general practice with three days of palpitations and increasing breathlessness on exertion. He describes his heart 'racing steadily, not jumping about'. He has hypertension on perindopril, BMI 33, and drinks around 30 standard drinks a week. An ECG has been performed and is available.
Observations: BP 128/76 · PR 148 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 96% RA · Temp 36.5 °C · no chest pain, alert and well perfused.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to the examiner
Give your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Outline your management

dx: **Typical atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular block**, ventricular rate 150, in a stable 68-year-old. **A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at or near 150 is flutter with 2:1 block until proven otherwise** — say that sentence and you have already separated yourself from the field.

The read: **atrial rate about 300 · a continuous sawtooth baseline with no isoelectric segment · negative in II, III and aVF, positive in V1 · two flutter waves per QRS · narrow QRS.** **2:1 gives 150 · 3:1 gives 100 · 4:1 gives 75.** At 2:1 **one flutter wave hides in the QRS and the other in the T wave**, which is why it looks like sinus.

Why not sinus: **sinus tachycardia is a response and requires a driver** — pain, fever, hypovolaemia, sepsis, anaemia, PE, thyrotoxicosis, drugs — and he is afebrile, comfortable and well perfused at rest. **Sinus rates also vary with respiration; this is metronomically regular.**
**Adenosine unmasks flutter; it does not terminate it.** It terminates AVNRT and AVRT. Say this unprompted — it is the discriminator an examiner listens for.

Keep **two separate lists**. Differentials **of the rhythm**: sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT, atrial tachycardia, and AF with a very rapid response that can look deceptively regular. Causes **of the flutter**: by system. Candidates who blur them sound muddled.

Rate control: **a beta-blocker first line, or verapamil or diltiazem where a beta-blocker is unsuitable — never both together**, because of profound bradycardia and heart block. **Expect it to work less well than in AF**; a rate stuck near 150 is the nature of flutter, not your failure, and it is the argument for a rhythm strategy sooner.

Stroke prevention is **identical to AF**. **CHA₂DS₂-VA: he scores for hypertension and age 65–74 — that is 2, so anticoagulate**, with a **DOAC preferred** over warfarin (warfarin for mechanical valves and moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis). **Aspirin is not stroke prevention in flutter or AF**, and saying so unprompted is worth a mark. VERIFY which score is current.

**Three days is outside the 48-hour window.** Either **three weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation beforehand, or a transoesophageal echo to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus** — then cardiovert, then **at least four weeks afterwards**, because the atrium remains mechanically stunned even once the rhythm looks normal. **Instability overrides the rule.**

**Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is curative in typical flutter** — high success, low complication rate, considerably better than AF ablation — so **raise it early, not as a last resort**. But **a substantial proportion go on to develop AF**, so anticoagulation follows **the stroke score, not the rhythm on the day**. And **never flecainide without an AV nodal blocker on board** — a slower atrial rate can conduct **1:1 at over 200**.

The drivers are sitting in the stem, and naming them turns a rhythm diagnosis into a management plan: **hypertension · 30 standard drinks a week against the NHMRC limit of 10 a week and 4 in a day · BMI 33 with likely undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea** — plus **thyroid function in every tachyarrhythmia**. SA: sleep study and cardiology via **Country Health Connect** and **PATS**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if he destabilises.
plan: To the examiner, before touching the tracing: **'I would confirm his haemodynamic stability — blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, saturations and temperature — and ask specifically about chest pain, syncope and breathlessness at rest.'** Then **say it**: **'he is stable, which means I can work through this properly rather than proceeding to immediate cardioversion.'**

The ECG in seven steps: **rate ~150 · regular · no discrete P waves, a continuous sawtooth baseline negative in II, III and aVF and positive in V1 · atrial rate ~300 · two flutter waves per QRS, so 2:1 block · narrow QRS · no acute ischaemic change.** Impression: **typical atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction.**

Defend the call when challenged: **sinus needs a driver and he has none; sinus varies with respiration and this does not; and if I were uncertain I would increase AV block with vagal manoeuvres or adenosine under continuous ECG recording — in flutter that is diagnostic, not therapeutic.**
Diagnosis, then **the two lists kept apart**: the rhythm differentials, then the causes by system — **cardiovascular, respiratory, endocrine, drugs and lifestyle**.

To the patient — **loop and filter, never the bare number**: **'the electrical signal gets caught in a loop, going round and round the top chamber about 300 times a minute. Your heart has a natural filter that only lets some of those through, which is why your pulse is 150 and not 300.'** If he says that sounds like he should be dead: **'that is the top chamber — the filter is doing its job, which is why you walked in here talking to me.'**

The two things that matter, in his words: **a heart running at 150 for three days gets tired, which is why you are breathless**; and **when the top chamber flutters rather than squeezing, blood can sit still and form a clot — if that travels to the brain it causes a stroke.** So **a blood thinner is a major part of the treatment.**

His three questions. **'Am I going to have a stroke?'** — higher than it should be, which is exactly why the tablet starts today. **'Can you shock it back today?'** — the highest-value thirty seconds in the station: **explain that a clot may already have formed, and cardioverting now could push it out and cause the very stroke we are preventing.** **'Is this from the drinking?'** — **be honest with a number: thirty a week against a recommended ten.**

Management, five headings out loud: **rate · rhythm · anticoagulation · ablation · the drivers.** Rate first with a beta-blocker and the warning not to combine agents; anticoagulate on the named score; defer cardioversion with the reason; raise CTI ablation early; then blood pressure, alcohol, weight and sleep apnoea.

Investigations: **FBC, electrolytes including magnesium, renal and thyroid function, glucose and lipids · chest X-ray · transthoracic echocardiogram** — and **a repeat ECG once the rate is controlled**, because the sawtooth is far clearer at a slower rate.

dx: **Pulmonary embolism arising from a left leg deep vein thrombosis**, provoked by **immobility on a long road journey and oestrogen exposure**. **Name the source in the leg**, not just the lung.

The chain: **clot forms in the leg → embolises to the pulmonary arteries → pulmonary vascular resistance rises sharply → right ventricular strain → pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia, and sometimes infarction of the lung.**

To the patient, plain and short: **'most likely you have a pulmonary embolism — a clot in the blood vessels of your lungs. The clot most likely formed in your leg during that long drive, when you were sitting still for a long time, and then a piece of it travelled up to your lung.'**

**Wells** awards points for: **clinical signs of DVT · PE as likely as or more likely than an alternative · heart rate over 100 · immobilisation or surgery within 4 weeks · previous VTE · haemoptysis · malignancy.** **Two-level: above 4 means PE likely → image.** She scores on leg signs, tachycardia and immobility, so **straight to CTPA**. **PERC applies only where suspicion is already low, and all eight must be negative**: **age under 50 · HR under 100 · SpO2 at least 95% · no haemoptysis · no oestrogen · no previous VTE · no unilateral leg swelling · no surgery or trauma needing hospitalisation in 4 weeks.** **She fails several.** **D-dimer is a rule-out test only** — it rises in pregnancy, infection, malignancy, surgery and older age.

Treatment: **apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily**, or **rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days, then 20 mg daily**. **Start anticoagulation before imaging if clinical suspicion is high and there is no bleeding contraindication.** Duration **at least 3 months for a provoked event**, longer or indefinite if unprovoked or recurrent. VERIFY

Fold the breathlessness in, **three questions only**: **what do you mean by shortness of breath — difficulty getting air in, not getting enough, or tightness · anything that makes it better or worse · any cough, any noisy breathing or wheeze?** Then **have you coughed up any blood, and have you felt dizzy or faint?**

Respiratory group — **where the case turns**: **any injury or trauma to your chest · have you had any long travel or long periods sitting still recently · any swelling, pain or redness in your legs, especially the calf · any fevers, chills or coughing up phlegm · any weight loss, loss of appetite, or lumps and bumps?** **Ask the open version of the travel question** — it is the immobility, not the aircraft.

**Interpret the findings out loud, do not recite them**: the tachycardia, tachypnoea and hypoxia fit an acute pulmonary problem; **the loud P2 and the parasternal murmur mean raised pulmonary pressures with tricuspid regurgitation from right ventricular strain**; **the basal dullness is infarction with a small effusion, not consolidation**; **and the swollen tender calf gives you the source.**

stem: You are the doctor in the emergency department. James Okafor, 22, has presented with sudden onset chest pain that started while he was exercising today. He is already on oxygen when you enter the cubicle.
Information available: HR 98 · BP 122/74 · RR 22 · SpO2 94% · T 36.8 °C · alert and orientated.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
Version A: at about five minutes a chest X-ray is provided — explain the X-ray to the patient. Version B: ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you require
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Primary spontaneous pneumothorax** in a tall, thin 22-year-old who vapes — **rupture of a subpleural bleb**, air in the pleural space with no underlying lung disease.

**Say the conclusion out loud — this is a marked moment**: **'that's a sharp, well-localised pain that came on suddenly and is worse when you breathe in. We call that pleuritic, and it points me towards your lungs and the lining around them rather than your heart. I still need to check both properly.'**

**The conclusion does not change the structure.** You have narrowed your suspicion; **you have not earned the right to skip the cardiac block.** Run CVS first, in full, **exactly as you would for a 60-year-old with central crushing pain** — that is what would have caught pericarditis, myocarditis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy if the case had been one of those.

**The new question in a young person with exertional chest pain: family history of sudden cardiac death** — **anyone who died suddenly and young, or unexpectedly during sport or in their sleep.** Ask it **inside the cardiac block, not at the end with family history**, because the end of the station is where you run out of time.

**The X-ray script, six steps**: **'this is the X-ray of your chest' → three colours, white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air → landmarks: heart, spine, and the windpipe, and say you are checking it sits centrally → the normal side, markings running to the edge and a sharp angle at the base → the abnormal side, lung edge visible with no markings beyond it → name it.** **Comment on the trachea even when it is normal** — that is how you demonstrate you were looking for tension.

**No radiology language to the patient.** 'A lucency with absent peripheral vascular markings and a visible visceral pleural line' is a correct description and **a failed communication task**. If the film is genuinely poor: **say what you can see, lean on the history, and ask to review the digital image** — that is what a safe doctor does, not a weakness.

**Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis: hypotension, trachea deviated away, distended neck veins, hypoxia not correcting on oxygen.** **Immediate needle decompression with a large-bore cannula — 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line, with the 2nd space midclavicular line as the traditional alternative — then an intercostal catheter straight away, because decompression is only temporising. Do not wait for an X-ray.** VERIFY against local protocol.

**Intervention rule: symptomatic or unstable → pleural intervention** — aspiration, or a **small-bore 8–14 French catheter by Seldinger technique in the safe triangle, 5th intercostal space anterior to the mid-axillary line**. Minimally symptomatic and stable → **conservative or ambulatory care with review**. **Led by symptoms and stability rather than size alone — but still measure it and factor it into the conversation.**

**The counselling is where a 22-year-old's life is actually affected**: **stopping the vaping is the single most effective way to prevent recurrence · recurrence is about 30%, mostly in the first one to two years · no flying until fully resolved on imaging and typically a week beyond · and no scuba diving ever, without definitive surgery.** **Surgical referral** after a second ipsilateral event, a first contralateral event, bilateral disease, a persistent air leak, or a high-risk occupation. **High-flow oxygen speeds reabsorption** in conservative management.

**The clock is the second discriminator.** **Diagnosis in 30–40 seconds, three differentials with one reason each, then the rest as a rapid list.** **A beautiful forty-second explanation of pleural physiology eats the time the list needed — and the examiner cannot award marks for differentials you did not say.** Safety net: **more breathless, worse pain, feeling faint or a racing heart, or blue lips or fingers → come back or call an ambulance.**
plan: Face-to-face: **'may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature?'** Online, a closed statement instead: **'I'll take you through to the treatment area and put you on the monitor to check you're stable while we talk.'** **A gate you walk through, not a place to spend thirty seconds.**

WIPE, confirm identity, open question — then **empathy once, properly**: **'I understand, and I can see this is worrying you. Let me ask you some questions and get you examined; we'll find the cause, and you're in safe hands. I'll come back to your concerns as soon as I know more.'** **Once, then work** — and again only if he becomes newly distressed, which role-players do when the X-ray appears.

SOCRATES in full: **where exactly — is it an area, or can you point to one spot · when did it start and what were you doing, sudden or gradual · sharp, dull, heavy, tight or burning · does it go anywhere · out of ten · constant or in waves, and getting worse?**

**The three named modifiers — patients rarely volunteer them, and the open question alone gets 'not that I've noticed'**: **does taking a deep breath make it worse · does it change with rest or activity · does leaning forward help at all?**
**Say 'pleuritic' out loud**, and say what it points you towards and away from.

**The cardiovascular block, in full, despite his age**: **any breathlessness, sweating or nausea with it · blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, smoking, family history of heart disease · any recreational drugs, particularly cocaine or amphetamines · any fever or flu-like illness in the last week or two, and is it better sitting forward · breathless walking or lying flat, waking at night, ankle swelling, any condition you were born with · ever fainted or felt faint, especially during exercise · and any family history of sudden cardiac death?**

Respiratory: **any calf swelling or pain, long flights or car trips, recent surgery or immobility, clotting problems in the family, coughing up blood · what exercise were you actually doing, and did you take any knock or tackle to the chest · ever had a collapsed lung, or anyone in your family · do you smoke, vape or use cannabis · any fever, cough or coloured phlegm · and though it's unlikely at your age, any weight loss, lumps or bumps, night sweats?**

The rest of the sweep, briskly: **any tummy pain, vomiting, heartburn or sour fluid coming up, related to food · any rash on the chest, worse on pressing or twisting · any stress at home or uni, and how's your mood** — then **SADMA, past history, allergies**, and **'is there anything you were particularly worried this might be?'**

The bell. **Version A — the six-step X-ray script, 60–75 seconds, trachea named.** **Version B — the ten-step examination request**, opening with your reasoning: **'given the pleuritic character I'll go into more detail on the respiratory examination, with a relevant cardiovascular examination alongside it'**, then **expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation and vocal resonance by name**.

**Diagnosis in 30–40 seconds, no more**: **'a pneumothorax — air collected in your chest cavity, outside the lung, usually because small bubbles on the surface of the lung burst and let air leak out.'** Then **three reasons**: sharp not heavy · worse on deep breathing, which is pleuritic · and the X-ray shows air around the lung with the lung edge visible.

**Differentials — three with reasons, then the rest as a list.** Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but no family history of sudden death · a clot on the lung, but no travel, immobility or calf symptoms · a chest infection, but no fever or cough. Then name **valve narrowing, heart failure, heart attack, pericarditis, a tear in the main artery, a growth in the lung, shingles, costochondritis, reflux or ulcer, and panic attack** in one sweep.

Plan and counselling: **oxygen, analgesia, monitoring · drainage by needle or a small tube between the ribs under local anaesthetic · admission and a repeat film.** Then the three that matter to him: **stop the vaping · no flying until cleared · no diving, ever, without an operation.** Safety net, summarise, check understanding.

**Ask for the trachea by name, in inspection and palpation.** 'Is the trachea midline or deviated?' If you ask only for 'a respiratory examination' you will not be told.

**If you get one positive, complete the system.** 'Air entry reduced on the left' is a **prompt, not an answer** — expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation and vocal resonance are **four separate marks**.

**Interpret the card aloud**: reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance on the left with a midline trachea = **a left pneumothorax without tension physiology**. **Hyper-resonance rather than dullness rules out effusion or consolidation.**

**Erect chest X-ray** — and **trace the whole periphery of both lungs, apices included**. Two things that fool you: **a skin fold has lung markings crossing it**, and **bullous emphysema has an edge concave towards the chest wall**, which is dangerous to drain.
**ECG and troponin if there is any doubt about the cardiac differentials** — and ask for the ECG even when told it is pending.
**Lower limbs for oedema and calf asymmetry** — pulmonary embolism stays on the list of every pleuritic chest pain.

**In the traumatic variant**: large-bore IV access, **group and hold with crossmatch**, FBE and coagulation, erect CXR and consider **CT chest**, a **larger-bore drain rather than a small-bore catheter**, and surgical involvement early.

stem: Your next patient is a 25-year-old man brought to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset chest tightness and shortness of breath that began while watching a movie at home. He has had similar episodes before and was told nothing was wrong. His parents are separated, he lives alone, works as an accountant, and has been under stress.
Vitals: T 36.7 · HR 96 · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 99% RA · alert, anxious.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis to the patient
Explain your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain the pathophysiology of the condition

dx: **Panic attack occurring within a panic disorder**, with **early agoraphobic avoidance**, in a 25-year-old under psychosocial stress.

**The trap the whole station is built on: the psychosocial detail in the stem is bait.** Candidates who recognise the recall walk in and take a full psychiatric history — mood, sleep, appetite, psychosis screen — **and fail**. **This is a chest pain and shortness of breath presentation. You approach a case from the complaint, not from the diagnosis you remember**, and **psychogenic causes sit at the END of the chest pain list**, which is where you reach them legitimately.

**Panic attack: an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort peaking within minutes — typically under ten — with four or more of thirteen physical symptoms, characteristically including a fear of dying or of losing control.** Name the cluster and the fear of dying; **you are not expected to recite thirteen items**.

**Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks PLUS, for at least one month, persistent worry about further attacks OR a maladaptive change in behaviour to avoid them.** **Agoraphobia: fear or avoidance of two or more of — public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, queues or crowds, being outside the home alone — typically six months or more.**

**The three key questions, word for word**: **'During the attack, did you feel that you were going to die — were you afraid of dying?' · 'Since then, have you been worried about having another attack?' · 'Have you changed any of your routines or your behaviour because of that worry?'** **Question 1 names the attack; questions 2 and 3 convert it into the disorder.** Without them you cannot justify the diagnosis you are about to give.

**Do not convert to GAD on 'I'm generally an anxious person.'** **GAD requires excessive, hard-to-control worry about multiple everyday matters for at least six months, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension or sleep disturbance — and prominent discrete physical attacks are NOT a core feature.** The two can coexist; **the attacks define this presentation**.

**When asked for differentials, give the differentials of the COMPLAINT** — cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal — **not a list of anxiety disorders**. Listing GAD, OCD, PTSD and adjustment disorder is the wrong answer; one or two psychiatric alternatives at the end are fine.

**The pathophysiology task is the one nobody rehearses.** Patient version: **your body has an alarm system — fight or flight. When it fires you release adrenaline: heart pounding, breathing faster, muscles tense, sweating. In a panic attack the alarm goes off when there is no danger. Then, because you feel you can't breathe, you over-breathe, which blows off carbon dioxide and causes the tingling in your fingers and around your mouth, the dizziness and the unreal feeling. And those sensations feel so much like a heart attack that your brain reads them as proof something terrible is happening — which fires the alarm again. That's the vicious cycle.** **It is real, not imagined — and it is not dangerous.**

Examiner version if asked technically: **a perceived threat activates the amygdala and sympathetic nervous system, producing a catecholamine surge with tachycardia, raised cardiac output, sweating and tremor. Hyperventilation causes hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis; cerebral vasoconstriction produces light-headedness and derealisation, and the fall in ionised calcium produces perioral and peripheral paraesthesiae and, if severe, carpopedal spasm. Catastrophic misinterpretation amplifies fear in a positive feedback loop, and repeated attacks produce conditioned anticipatory anxiety and avoidance.**

Management: **validate and explain — that is itself therapeutic → CBT is first line, with breathing retraining, cognitive work on the catastrophic interpretation, and graded exposure to avoided situations → a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan for subsidised sessions → an SSRI if needed, started low and increased slowly, warning that anxiety can briefly worsen in the first week or two and benefit takes several weeks → AVOID benzodiazepines beyond very short-term use, because of dependence and because they become a safety behaviour that reinforces avoidance → cut caffeine, energy drinks, alcohol and stimulants → GP follow-up and safety-net.** **NEVER say 'there's nothing wrong with you', 'it's all in your head', 'it's just stress, try to relax', or 'your tests are normal so you can go home'** — each is a marked communication failure. SA: **telehealth CBT and online programs matter more where psychology access is limited**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer or a local Aboriginal health service; **Closing the Gap PBS** if an SSRI is started. VERIFY
plan: To the examiner: **'may I have his vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Then **say he is stable with a mild tachycardia**.

Open question, then **acknowledge the frustration explicitly — it buys the rapport you need for the diagnosis later**: **'I can hear how worrying this is, especially as it's happened before and you were told nothing was wrong. That's a frustrating place to be. Let's go through it properly and find the cause.'** Then signpost: **chest tightness first, then the breathing, then questions to rule out the important causes.**

Full pain analysis — **and do not skip the trajectory question**: **where exactly · when did it start and how quickly did it come on · HOW LONG DID IT TAKE TO REACH ITS WORST · tight, sharp, heavy or burning · does it go anywhere · out of ten · anything that makes it better or worse, breathing, moving, position, pressing · how long did it last and how did it settle?**

Breathlessness folded in, **three questions only — do not re-time it**: **what do you mean by shortness of breath — difficulty getting air in, not getting enough, or tightness · anything that made it better or worse · any cough or noisy breathing?**

Cardiovascular and respiratory sweep: **any sweating, nausea, racing heart or dizziness with it · smoking, blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol, family heart disease · any fever or recent flu-like illness, and is it better sitting up and leaning forward · breathless lying flat, how many pillows, leg swelling, ever fainted especially on exertion · any long travel or sitting still, calf swelling or pain, coughing up blood · any injury to your chest · any fevers, chills, phlegm, weight loss or lumps?** **Note the perioral and finger tingling — it is the fingerprint of hyperventilation, and you will use it in the mechanism.**

GI, musculoskeletal, drugs and endocrine — **the rows candidates drop because 'it's obviously anxiety'**: **any abdominal pain or vomiting, acid or bitter taste, heartburn, relation to eating · worse on moving or pressing, any rash · how much coffee or energy drink in a day, any recreational drugs, how much alcohol, have you recently stopped anything · any weight loss, feeling hot all the time, tremor or loose bowels?**

**Announce the negative organic screen out loud — this is the transition that earns the diagnosis honestly**: **'I've asked about your heart, your lungs, your stomach and your chest wall, and I haven't found anything pointing that way, which is reassuring. Now I'd like to ask about the episodes themselves.'** Then: **how many, over what period · out of the blue or always a trigger · what was happening in the film · any trembling, choking, or a sense things aren't real?**
**The three key questions, verbatim and in sequence.** Ask all three. **Question 1 names the attack; 2 and 3 name the disorder.**

**The agoraphobia screen** — places you now avoid, public transport, crowds, queues, being far from home alone, **and whether the avoidance is because you fear an attack there**. Then **the GAD criteria asked properly rather than assumed**, the stressors in one or two questions, mood, and **a brief, calm risk question** — fifteen seconds, matter-of-factly, with a response if positive.

Diagnosis, at **both levels**: **'what you've had is a panic attack'** — then the worry and avoidance — **'when that whole pattern is present, we call it panic disorder.'** Then **validate**: **'your symptoms are real. The tests being normal doesn't mean nothing happened.'** If he asks **'is it all in my head?'** — **'no, it's in your body.'**

**Differentials of the complaint, with why each is less likely**: heart attack or angina — 25, no risk factors, not exertional, no radiation, but we'll still do a tracing · clot on the lung — no travel, no leg symptoms, normal oxygen · collapsed lung — no injury · pericarditis — no viral illness, no positional change · **a rhythm disturbance, which is another reason for the tracing** · reflux or ulcer — no heartburn, no meal relation · chest wall — pressing doesn't reproduce it · and **two to check on bloods: thyrotoxicosis, and the caffeine.**

**The pathophysiology, in the patient version** — alarm, adrenaline, over-breathing, the tingling and unreality, then the catastrophic misinterpretation that fires the alarm again. **Check understanding once in the middle, not only at the end**, and draw it if you can.

Management and close: **CBT first line with a mental health plan · an SSRI if needed, low and slow · avoid sedatives · cut the coffee right down · ECG and bloods today, and say why you will stop there.** Safety net: **come back if the pattern changes, or you get pain with exercise, faint, or cough up blood.**
pefe: **Vital signs first** — and note that normal saturations and observations are part of your evidence, not just a formality.
**ECG in every chest pain presentation** — it is also a genuine differential test here, because **an arrhythmia such as SVT mimics panic closely and is easy to miss**.
**Bloods: FBC, electrolytes and renal function, thyroid function, glucose.** **Thyrotoxicosis is the classic organic mimic of anxiety** and must be excluded before you settle.
**Troponin only if the story or the ECG warrants it.**
**Urine drug screen where stimulant use is suspected** — asked non-judgementally, and disclosure handled without moralising.
**Chest X-ray only if a respiratory cause is genuinely in play.**

**Then stop — and say why out loud.** **'I don't want to keep repeating tests, because that tends to feed the worry rather than settle it.'** Ordering a CT, echocardiogram and Holter 'to be safe' is a listed fail.

dx: **Ischaemic heart disease presenting as stable exertional angina** — a narrowed, unruptured plaque, so demand outstrips supply on exertion and settles within minutes of rest. **Say both terms.**

**The discriminating issue is diagnostic overshadowing, not the angina.** People with severe mental illness die **15 to 20 years earlier**, mostly of cardiovascular disease. Treat his chest pain exactly as you would anyone's.
The stem names schizophrenia for two reasons: **antipsychotic cardiometabolic risk explaining coronary disease at 40**, and the **three-question psychiatric screen** the examiner is waiting for.

Three reasons to give him, in plain words: **the character of the pain — central, heavy, to the neck, worse on exertion, better with rest · his risk factors — father's MI at 50, a pack a day, weight, diet, no exercise · the medication that keeps him well raises his heart risk.**

**Because it is new within 48 hours, do not discharge without excluding ACS.** Classically, new-onset angina within two months sits in the unstable category whatever the pattern — say so and you satisfy either examiner.

The test that makes the diagnosis is **functional: exercise stress ECG (Bruce protocol, steps every 3 minutes) or stress echo**. **ST depression of 1 mm or more, horizontal or downsloping, is positive.** Add that **CTCA is increasingly first-line**.

Secondary prevention: **aspirin 100 mg daily** (300 mg stat if ACS suspected), **atorvastatin 40–80 mg nocte**, **GTN spray 400 microg SL, repeat every 5 minutes up to 3 doses**, **metoprolol 25–50 mg BD**.

**The medication review is the mark most candidates miss.** Risperidone carries a real cardiometabolic burden — **switch via his psychiatrist, to something like aripiprazole; never stop it yourself**, abrupt cessation risks relapse. Metabolic monitoring: **baseline, 3 months, then at least annually**.

Hold a delusion without colluding or arguing: **'that sounds frightening, and I don't see it the same way you do — but I have no doubt the pain is real and I'm taking it seriously.'** Then add a mental health review to the plan.

Safety-net verbatim: **'if the pain comes on while you're resting, or lasts more than ten minutes, or comes with sweating, vomiting or breathlessness — call an ambulance on triple zero. Don't drive yourself.'** **Quitline 13 7848.**
plan: **'Before I start, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?'** Then WIPE and the psych habit: **'everything we discuss stays between you and me, unless there's a risk of harm to you or someone else.'** Four seconds, and it unlocks the risk question later.

**'Jack, tell me more about this pain'** — then stay quiet. Follow with the empathy line: **'I'm sorry to hear that, and I understand your concern. I'll do my best to find the cause today.'** Both are separately scored.

SOCRATES as one fluent run: **where exactly, can you point · what does it feel like, sharp, burning or a heaviness · out of ten · does it travel · constant or coming and going · what brings it on · what makes it better?**

**The question that decides the station, said out loud and unmistakably: 'do you ever get this pain when you are resting — sitting still, or lying in bed at night? And what's the longest one has lasted?'** No rest pain → stable angina. Rest pain, over 20 minutes, or crescendo → ACS.

Signpost, then the four questions for any known condition: **'I noticed you have schizophrenia — can I ask a few quick questions, because it may be relevant to your chest pain?'** → **when were you diagnosed · what treatment, and can you take it regularly · any side effects — weight gain, dizziness on standing, shakiness, dry mouth · do you see your GP and psychiatrist regularly?**

**Three questions, not thirty.** **'I ask everyone this — have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming anyone else?'** → **'do you ever hear, see or feel things that other people don't?'** → **'do you ever feel anyone is trying to harm you, or that someone is controlling you?'** Then get out.

Cardiovascular risk factors in one continuous run — **this case was built around them**: **family history of heart attack or stroke · ever told you have high blood pressure, cholesterol or diabetes · smoking, how much and how long · alcohol · recreational drugs · what do you usually eat in a day · any regular exercise?**

The system sweep, rapid fire: **sweating, breathlessness, nausea, palpitations · fever or recent flu-like illness, worse lying flat or better sitting forward · breathless at night, ankle swelling · long travel, calf pain or swelling, haemoptysis · chest injury, cough, phlegm · weight loss, appetite, lumps · tummy pain, vomiting, acid taste, related to meals · any rash, worse on pressing or moving?** Then **SADMA**.

Diagnosis in plain words — **a blood tube supplying the heart has narrowed, not blocked** — then **the three reasons**, then the five-second insurance line: **'I did also think about inflammation around the heart, a clot on the lung and reflux, but they don't fit.'**

Management under **three headings**: tests to confirm it (**ECG now, troponin to exclude a heart attack, then the exercise stress test**) · treatment to protect the heart (**aspirin, statin, spray under the tongue, quitting smoking, alcohol, diet, 30 minutes walking most days**) · **the antipsychotic — don't stop it, I'll speak to your psychiatrist about switching**.

Safety-net with **triple zero**, summarise, invite questions. If concerns were never elicited he volunteers it here: **'are you actually going to look into this, or is this going to get put down to my head again?'**
pefe: **Vitals before you greet the patient** — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations. This man could be infarcting in front of you.
**12-lead ECG**, and repeat vitals, **BMI and waist**, and **BP in both arms**. A normal resting trace does not exclude stable angina; look for old infarct, LVH and **QTc**.

**Serial high-sensitivity troponin at 0 and 2 hours** — because he is in the ED with symptoms new within 48 hours. In primary care troponin has little role in assessing stable angina; say which setting you are in.

**The test that makes the diagnosis: exercise stress ECG or stress echo.** Positive is **ST depression of 1 mm or more, horizontal or downsloping**. **CT coronary angiography is increasingly first-line** in low-to-intermediate risk new chest pain.

**Do not exercise-stress a patient you have not first cleared of ACS**, and do not discharge on a single negative troponin.
If he were on **clozapine with a fever**: consider **clozapine-induced myocarditis** — troponin, CRP, ECG, echo, and urgent discussion with his psychiatrist and cardiology.

Explain the situation to the patient

Ramipril, spironolactone, metformin, atorvastatin. He calls them 'a blood pressure one and a fluid one'. ASK BY NAME: he admits IBUPROFEN for his knee only if asked, and never volunteers it. Also ask trimethoprim and salt substitutes

must: FAIL — Not asking for an ECG and cardiac monitoring. A fail on its own, whatever else you score.
FAIL — Saying calcium lowers the potassium. It protects; it does not lower.
FAIL — Treating acutely and leaving him on ramipril and spironolactone.
FAIL — Being reassured by a normal ECG, or treating a haemolysed sample before repeating it.
ASK — Was the sample haemolysed? In your first sentence, before you read the panel.
ASK — Anti-inflammatories, trimethoprim, salt substitutes — by name, or he won't tell you.

dx: **Severe hyperkalaemia, K 7.2, WITH ECG changes** — acute-on-chronic kidney injury in stage 4 CKD. **The number is not the emergency; the ECG is.**
**Severity: mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe 6.5 or more · ANY level with ECG change is severe.** That last row overrides every row above it.
ECG progression: **tall peaked T waves → flat P and long PR → wide QRS → P waves lost → sine wave → VF or asystole**. A normal ECG at 7.2 is **not reassurance**.

**Four mechanisms at once, and saying all four is what separates a good answer from a list**: **stage 4 CKD sets the baseline · gastroenteritis and poor intake have caused an AKI on top · ramipril and spironolactone together are additive · the acidosis (HCO3 16) shifts potassium out of cells.**
**Three jobs, and know which drug does which. PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE.** The follow-up question is asked almost every time.

**PROTECT: calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV over 2–3 minutes** on the monitor, **repeat at 5 minutes if the ECG has not improved**. **It does not lower the potassium** — it stabilises the myocardium for **30 to 60 minutes**.

**SHIFT: 10 units of short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% glucose IV over 15–30 minutes** — onset 15–30 min, lasts 4–6 h. **Hourly BGL for at least 6 hours, said unprompted** — delayed hypoglycaemia is the commonest complication. Plus **salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised**, additive. **Bicarbonate only if acidotic**, and the evidence is weak.

**REMOVE: haemodialysis is definitive here** — oliguric, eGFR 16. **Involve renal and retrieval NOW, not after two failed rounds** — transfer time is the rate-limiting step. Loop diuretic only if passing urine and not volume deplete. **Modern binders, not resonium, and never as the acute answer.**

**Withhold ramipril and spironolactone**, and sweep the class list: **ACEi/ARB · potassium-sparing diuretics · NSAIDs · trimethoprim · heparin · beta-blockers · ciclosporin and tacrolimus · digoxin in toxicity · supplements and salt substitutes.** **Recheck K at 1–2 hours** on continuous monitoring.

To the patient, **explain the effect, never the number**: **'a salt called potassium is much higher than it should be · when it gets too high it upsets the electrical rhythm of your heart · the calcium does not lower it, it protects your heart while the rest works · two of your tablets hold potassium in, I am stopping both today, please do not restart them until you are reviewed.'**
plan: **The single highest-scoring sentence in the station, before you read the rest of the panel: 'Examiner, before I go through these results in full — the potassium is 7.2, which is in the severe range. I would attach cardiac monitoring and obtain a 12-lead ECG immediately, and I would check whether the sample was reported as haemolysed.'**

Read the ECG **in order — rate · P · PR · QRS · T — then conclude**. A short ordered read-out beats a list of adjectives. If challenged on ischaemia: **hyperacute T waves are broad-based and asymmetrical; it is the company they keep — flat P, long PR, wide QRS — that makes the diagnosis.**

The biochemistry: **severe hyperkalaemia · creatinine 312 and eGFR 16 = advanced renal impairment · urea 24 with that creatinine suggests a prerenal component, so AKI on CKD · bicarbonate 16 is a metabolic acidosis, which itself shifts potassium out of cells · mild hyponatraemia fits volume depletion.**

**The causes — all four, not one.** Then add the three questions you must ask by name: **over-the-counter anti-inflammatories · recent trimethoprim · potassium-based salt substitutes.** He is taking ibuprofen for his knee and will not mention it unless asked.
Management as **three jobs, naming which drug does which**. Protect, then shift, then remove — and say **'this does not lower the potassium'** as you say calcium, before the examiner can ask.

Say unprompted: **hourly BGL for 6 hours · recheck K at 1–2 hours · continuous monitoring · withhold ramipril and spironolactone · cautious volume replacement · renal referral and retrieval now.** Rurally, a **point-of-care blood gas** gives a potassium in minutes — treat on the ECG while awaiting the formal result. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
Explain to the patient in plain words. **Never quote 7.2** — he will look blank and say 'is that bad?'. Effect, then what you are doing, then the two tablets you are stopping.

His three questions, in order. **'Am I going to have a heart attack?'** → not in the usual sense, this affects the rhythm rather than blocking an artery, **but do not understate it**. **'Is it something I did?'** → **'you have not done anything wrong.'** **'Do I have to go to Adelaide?'** → possibly, and **'I am arranging that conversation now rather than waiting. Is there someone you would like me to call?'**
pefe: **ECG and cardiac monitoring in your first sentence** — before you finish reading the panel. Not asking for an ECG is a fail on its own regardless of the total.

**Ask whether the sample was haemolysed**, whether processing was delayed, and what the platelet and white cell counts were — **but only as an exclusion after the ECG, never as an opening assumption**.

Three questions to ask every time: **was it haemolysed · is the patient passing urine** (anuria removes your safest route and moves dialysis up) **· is anything still making it worse** — rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, or a drug still in the system.
**Point-of-care blood gas** for a potassium in minutes where you are. **Recheck the potassium at 1–2 hours.** **Hourly BGL for at least 6 hours** after insulin.

Causes of a **falsely high** result: **haemolysis** (red cells hold potassium at about 25 times plasma) **· tight tourniquet or fist clenching · delayed processing or a cold sample · marked thrombocytosis or leucocytosis — a plasma rather than serum sample resolves it · contamination from a drip upstream**.

**Version B: ECG first, repeat the sample second, conclude third.** Repeat with a **wider-bore needle, no prolonged tourniquet, no fist clenching, straight to the laboratory**. Do not treat and do not cancel her procedure until a clean result is back.
ddx: **Spurious — pseudohyperkalaemia**
**Always consider it first.** A well patient, an implausible result, a lab haemolysis comment
Difficult venepuncture, tight tourniquet, fist clenching, delayed or cold sample, high platelets or white cells, drip-arm contamination
**ECG first, then repeat the sample properly.** Exclusion is a conclusion, not an opening assumption
**Reduced excretion — CKD and AKI**
**Creatinine 312, eGFR 16, urea 24** with a prerenal pattern; gastroenteritis and poor intake
Urine output, volume state, recent illness, nephrotoxins
**Volume replacement, stop contributors, dialysis if refractory or anuric**
**Drugs — the additive combination**
**Ramipril AND spironolactone together** in advanced CKD — classic and avoidable
**ACEi/ARB · potassium-sparing diuretics · NSAIDs · trimethoprim · heparin · beta-blockers · ciclosporin, tacrolimus · digoxin**
**Withhold every contributor.** Ask about NSAIDs, trimethoprim and salt substitutes **by name**
**Shift out of cells — metabolic acidosis**
**Bicarbonate 16**
Acidosis, DKA or insulin deficiency, hyperosmolality
Treat the acidosis; **bicarbonate only where the acidosis is significant**
Rhabdomyolysis
Crush or prolonged immobility, dark urine, very high CK
Muscle pain, the circumstances of the injury
**Aggressive fluids — and expect it to rise again as muscle keeps breaking down**
Tumour lysis syndrome
24–48 hours after chemotherapy; high phosphate and urate, low calcium
Recent chemotherapy, bulky disease
**Hydration, rasburicase, involve renal early**
Addison disease and hypoaldosteronism
**Low sodium with high potassium**, weight loss, pigmentation, postural dizziness, low glucose
Postural BP, pigmentation, fatigue
**Hydrocortisone and fluids** — the hyperkalaemia is the clue, not the diagnosis. Also type 4 RTA
Digoxin toxicity
Nausea, yellow-green visual disturbance, on digoxin
Digoxin level, renal function, recent dose change
**Digoxin-specific antibody fragments are definitive.** Discuss calcium with toxicology rather than improvising
Increased intake
**Rarely sufficient alone** — only in someone who already cannot excrete
Salt substitutes, supplements, large transfusions of stored blood
Stop the source; treat the excretion problem underneath it
**Hyperkalaemia mimicking VT**
**Broad complex regular tachycardia in a dialysis patient**
Missed dialysis sessions, known renal failure
**Calcium first, and get him dialysed.** Treating it as VT alone misses the cause

versions.doorStem: A results-interpretation station: a potassium result is handed to you. Tasks are the same in both versions — interpret the results and any further investigation to the examiner → state the likely causes → outline immediate management → explain the situation to the patient. The two versions land on DIFFERENT answers.
rows: A · the sick one

68-year-old man, CKD stage 4, rural ED, two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness after gastroenteritis last week, drinking little. On ramipril, spironolactone, metformin, atorvastatin. BP 104/62, PR 52. K⁺ 7.2, urea 24.1, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, bicarbonate 16. ECG: bradycardic, flat P, long PR, broad QRS, peaked T.

SEVERE HYPERKALAEMIA with ECG changes — MULTIFACTORIAL: CKD sets the floor, acute illness and dehydration precipitate, ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone are additive, acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells. Treat now.
B · the well one

44-year-old woman, entirely well, routine bloods before a minor procedure. Lab phones K⁺ 6.1. No symptoms, no relevant medications, normal renal function, lab comments 'specimen haemolysed'. ECG normal.
PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA — repeat the sample properly. But get the ECG FIRST and confirm it is normal before concluding the result is spurious, not after.
versions.note: The trap in version B splits candidates two ways and both fail: treating a haemolysed sample with insulin–dextrose in a well patient, or dismissing it as artefact with no ECG and no repeat. ECG first, repeat second, treat only if confirmed. Severity: mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · ANY level with ECG change = severe, and that row overrides the rest. A normal ECG at 7.2 is not reassurance. Practice cards in the source (crush injury/rhabdomyolysis, Addison, trimethoprim interaction, tumour lysis, dialysis patient with broad-complex tachycardia) are partner drills, not recalls.

stem: A 52-year-old man has presented complaining of chest pain and shortness of breath that started one hour ago. The pain began while he was chopping wood.
Vital signs: BP 135/85 · pulse 78 regular · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on room air · T 36.8°C. He has no history of bleeding disorders.
The ECG is handed to you with the stem.
tasks: Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your management plan to the patient

dx: **Acute anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction, proximal LAD territory.** **The declared predominant assessment area is management — task 1 will not fail you, task 2 will.** Most candidates finish early; **that is a warning sign, not a comfort**.
**Six numbers, and only six: 300 · 600 · 400 micrograms · 2.5–5 · 4–8 · 92%.** Say **drug, dose, route and when you would repeat it**, every time. The examiner is holding a checklist of numbers.
**Notify the cardiac team first — before any drug**, and say so out loud. **'The first thing I've already done is let the cardiac team know, so they're getting ready for you.'**

**Aspirin 300 mg chewed** rather than swallowed — faster buccal and gastric absorption — dissolved in water if he cannot chew. **Clopidogrel 600 mg as a single load before PCI**; **ticagrelor 180 mg is the more commonly preferred agent in Australian practice**, and is **never given with fibrinolysis**. VERIFY

**GTN spray 400 MICROGRAMS sublingual, repeatable every 5 minutes up to three doses** — micrograms, not milligrams; **one wrong unit undoes an otherwise specific answer**. Withhold for **right ventricular infarction, hypotension, bradycardia or extreme tachycardia, severe aortic stenosis, HOCM, or a PDE-5 inhibitor within 24–48 hours**. CORRECTION — the danger is profound **hypotension**, not hypertension, because the right ventricle is preload dependent.

**IV access ×2 · troponin plus FBE, UEC, glucose, lipids and coagulation · morphine 2.5–5 mg IV for pain · ondansetron 4–8 mg IV for nausea.** And the sentence that matters: **'we are not waiting for the blood test — the tracing is enough to act on, and waiting would cost you heart muscle.'**

**Oxygen only if SpO2 falls below 92% — say the threshold instead of giving it.** Routine oxygen in a normoxic patient **causes coronary vasoconstriction** and offered no benefit in randomised trials. Some Australian guidance uses 93%; quote 92% and say 'per Therapeutic Guidelines'. VERIFY

**The reperfusion decision must be spoken, not assumed. PCI if achievable within 120 minutes of first medical contact, with a target first-medical-contact-to-device time of 90 minutes or less.** In lay words: **a very fine tube passed from the wrist, sometimes the groin, dye injected to see which tube is blocked, then opened with a balloon — 'ballooning' — or a stent, 'a tiny metal scaffold that props the tube open'.** **Awake but comfortable**, and cardiology takes consent.

**'Am I going to die?' is answered with action, never with 'no': 'I'm not going to pretend this isn't serious — it is. But you got here fast, we've caught it early, and the treatment works well. I'm going to stay with you.'** Then **support, family — 'is there anyone you'd like me to call?' — concerns, and a one-line summary.**

Long term, **SAVA**: **Statin high-intensity and lifelong — atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg** (CORRECTION — simvastatin is not a high-intensity option) · **ACE inhibitor lifelong unless contraindicated** · **beta blocker once euvolaemic and haemodynamically stable** · **dual antiplatelets for 12 months, then aspirin 100 mg lifelong**, adding **pantoprazole or rabeprazole** if a PPI is needed, because **omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and reduce clopidogrel activation**. **Cardiac rehabilitation for everyone.** **No private driving for about 2 weeks after an ACS.** VERIFY
plan: **Park the patient in one sentence, then turn away**: **'Hello James, I'm one of the doctors looking after you. I can see you're in pain and I'm going to treat that very shortly. I've been asked to look at your heart tracing with my examiner first — give me one minute and I'll come straight back with the plan.'** **No full WIPE and no stability ritual — every vital sign is printed in the stem.**

The ECG to the examiner, **one minute, fixed order**: **patient details, date and calibration · rate · rhythm · axis · PR · QRS · ST segments naming every lead · reciprocal change · Q waves · territory.** End on **acute anterolateral STEMI, most likely proximal LAD, time-critical.** **Three minutes here cannot pass you — it only steals the time management needs.**

Turn back and **give the diagnosis before the plan, in the words 'heart attack'**: **'one of the blood tubes supplying the muscle of your heart has become blocked by a clot, so part of that muscle isn't getting the blood and oxygen it needs — and that's what's causing this pain. It is serious. It is also very treatable, and we're starting right now.'** Then: **the cardiac team already knows.**

**'There are six things I'm going to do in the next few minutes. Let me take them one at a time.'** Steps 1 and 2: **aspirin 300 mg chewed, and clopidogrel 600 mg as a single dose — 'between them, these stop the clot from getting any bigger while we work on opening it.'**

Step 3, **the nitrate with the question attached so they are one action, not two**: **'a spray under your tongue called glyceryl trinitrate, 400 micrograms — it widens the blood tubes and should take the edge off the pain, and I can repeat it every five minutes up to three doses. Before I give it, one quick question I have to ask everybody: have you taken Viagra, Cialis or anything similar in the last 24 hours?'** If yes — **withhold it, say why, and use morphine instead.**

Steps 4 and 5: **a small drip in the arm · bloods through it, the important one a troponin, 'a chemical released when heart muscle is injured' · morphine 2.5 to 5 mg as a starting dose · ondansetron 4 to 8 mg for the nausea.** When he asks how long the blood test takes: **'an hour or so — but we are not waiting for it.'**

Step 6, **oxygen as a threshold, not a reflex**: **'it's 97 per cent at the moment, which is good, so you don't need oxygen — but if it falls below 92 per cent I will start it.'** Plus **repeat tracings every hour or two.**

**Reperfusion — the sentence the station is built around, then translated.** **'Because we're in a hospital with a catheter laboratory, the right treatment is to physically reopen the artery, and we aim to do that within 90 minutes.'** Then the lay explanation, and answer **'is that surgery, are you cutting my chest open?'** with **'no cut to the chest at all — a small needle puncture at the wrist, and most people go home within a couple of days.'**

**Support, family, concerns — do not leave these out.** **'I'm going to stay with you, and you are in the safest place you could be right now. Is there anyone you'd like me to call?'** Then **'do you have any questions or concerns about anything I've said?'**

**A one-line summary**: tracing shows a heart attack · aspirin and clopidogrel to stop the clot growing · spray and morphine for pain · cardiac team preparing to reopen the artery within the hour. **If time remains, move to the long-term plan — SAVA and cardiac rehabilitation — and never to history taking.**
pefe: **No history and no physical examination in this station** — the stem gives you the vital signs precisely so you skip them. **Two or three targeted questions only, each tied to a contraindication.**
**ECG within 10 minutes of arrival**, read in fixed order to a **named territory**, then **serial ECGs every 1–2 hours and after reperfusion**.
**Troponin, repeated — but never a reason to delay reperfusion.** **FBE, UEC, glucose, lipids and coagulation** as a baseline.
**Right-sided leads, particularly V4R, if the changes are inferior** — ST elevation in V1 alone does not exclude right ventricular infarction.
**Posterior extension: tall R with ST depression in V1–V3 → do V7 to V9.**
**Blood pressure in both arms before you give antiplatelets** — aortic dissection is an absolute contraindication to lysis and antiplatelets are harmful in it.
**Chest X-ray** for mediastinal width and pulmonary oedema — **must not delay reperfusion**. **Bedside echocardiogram** for wall motion and mechanical complications.
**Compare with an old ECG if one exists** — the question is always whether the change is new. And say the other half aloud: **a normal ECG does not exclude coronary ischaemia**.
ddx: **STEMI**
Crushing central pain radiating to arm, neck, jaw or back; sweating, nausea, breathlessness; exertional trigger; risk factors
**ST elevation in contiguous leads with reciprocal depression**
**It is the diagnosis here. Reperfuse — do not wait for troponin** — immediate
NSTEMI · unstable angina
The same pain, **no ST elevation**
ST depression, T inversion, or a normal ECG
Serial ECG and high-sensitivity troponin; risk-stratify; **no lysis** — immediate
**Aortic dissection**
**Tearing pain to the back, maximal at onset**, BP asymmetry between arms, pulse deficit, new aortic regurgitation
**BP in both arms**; widened mediastinum on CXR
**CT aortogram. An absolute contraindication to lysis — and antiplatelets are harmful** — immediate
Pericarditis
Sharp, pleuritic, worse lying flat and better sitting forward; rub; recent viral illness
**Widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and NO reciprocal change**
Echocardiogram; NSAID plus colchicine. **Reciprocal change is the discriminator** — urgent
**Pulmonary embolism**
Pleuritic pain, sudden breathlessness, tachycardia, hypoxia, calf swelling, immobility or travel
Sinus tachycardia, right heart strain, S1Q3T3
Wells score, D-dimer or CTPA — immediate
Pneumothorax
Sudden pleuritic pain and breathlessness; tall thin young man, or trauma
Reduced expansion, hyper-resonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal shift
**Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — decompress before imaging** — immediate
Myocarditis · Takotsubo
Recent viral illness; or an intense emotional trigger, often an older woman
Troponin out of keeping with the ECG; apical ballooning on echo
Echocardiogram, cardiology — and angiography still excludes occlusion
Oesophageal spasm · GORD · peptic ulcer · biliary colic
Burning, related to meals or lying flat, waterbrash, responds to antacid
Normal ECG and troponin
**A diagnosis of exclusion only. Never label chest pain as reflux with an abnormal ECG**
Musculoskeletal · herpes zoster
Reproduced by palpation or movement; dermatomal burning preceding a rash
Local tenderness; unilateral vesicles in a dermatome
Clinical. **Both are common decoys in this cluster**

rows: A · metropolitan

52-year-old man, HMO in a metropolitan ED, pain began while chopping wood. BP 135/85, pulse 78, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% room air. 'No history of bleeding disorders.' Tasks: interpret the ECG → explain your management plan to the patient.

Anterolateral STEMI → PRIMARY PCI. Say the number: first-medical-contact to device ≤90 min. Clopidogrel 600 mg (ticagrelor 180 mg commoner in Australian practice). Activate the cardiac team before you take bloods.

55-year-old man brought by ambulance, HMO in a rural hospital, nearest tertiary centre 400 km. Known hypertension. BP 160/95, pulse 88, RR 20, SpO₂ 93% on oxygen. Tasks: interpret the ECG (to examiner or medical student) → explain your diagnosis → explain your management.

Anterolateral STEMI with NO PCI ACCESS → FIBRINOLYSIS within 30 min. Screen the four bleeding questions out loud first. Lytic PLUS an anticoagulant and dual antiplatelets; clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg, no load, if over 75) — never ticagrelor or prasugrel with lysis. stem: A 55-year-old man has been brought in by ambulance complaining of chest pain that started suddenly one hour ago while he was working. He is a known hypertensive.

dx: **Acute anterolateral STEMI with no PCI access → FIBRINOLYSIS within 30 minutes.** **The initial six steps are identical to version A. Everything that separates the two is one sentence about time and distance.**

**The trap built into this version:** the case became so well known that the AMC began **writing 'you do not have access to PCI' explicitly into the stem**. **If you talk about arranging a catheter laboratory, you have failed to read the case that was written to test whether you can read it.**

**Say the decision out loud with the numbers**: **'the nearest hospital that can reopen the artery mechanically is 400 kilometres away — about four hours. The cut-off is two hours, and we cannot meet it. So the right treatment here is a clot-dissolving medicine, and I want to give it within the next 30 minutes.'**

**The four bleeding questions before you name the drug** — ten seconds, and all the examiner needs to see. **Absolute contraindications**: any previous intracranial haemorrhage · ischaemic stroke within 6 months · cerebral vascular malformation or intracranial tumour · **suspected aortic dissection** · active bleeding or bleeding diathesis · significant closed head or facial trauma within 3 months · recent major, intracranial or spinal surgery.

**The lytic, plus what goes with it — never instead of it.** **Tenecteplase**, a single weight-based IV bolus, is the agent used in most Australian rural STEMI pathways because it is far easier and safer to give in a small hospital. **Alteplase** is the accelerated alternative: **15 mg IV bolus, then 0.75 mg/kg over 30 minutes, then 0.5 mg/kg over 60 minutes.** Either is given **with enoxaparin (or unfractionated heparin) and with dual antiplatelets**. VERIFY weight bands and age adjustments over 75.

**CORRECTION — clopidogrel is not one dose for both versions. With fibrinolysis: 300 mg load if 75 or younger, and 75 mg with NO load if over 75**, because the loading dose increases intracranial bleeding in the elderly. **Ticagrelor and prasugrel are not given with fibrinolysis.** VERIFY

The rest is unchanged from version A: **aspirin 300 mg chewed · GTN 400 micrograms sublingual, repeatable every 5 minutes up to three doses, after the sildenafil question · IV access ×2 · troponin and baseline bloods · morphine 2.5–5 mg IV with ondansetron 4–8 mg IV · oxygen only if SpO2 below 92%**, and **the cardiac team notified first, before any drug**.

**Say all four of these out loud after the lytic**: **continuous cardiac monitoring · serial ECG and troponin · liaison with the nearest cardiac unit · a plan for transfer for angiography at 3–24 hours, or immediately if the pain and ST elevation do not settle, which means reperfusion has failed.** **PCI usually settles the situation; fibrinolysis is where the complications begin.**

**In lay words**: **'a clot-dissolving medicine given through the drip that breaks the clot down and reopens the tube. It works well — but because it thins the blood very powerfully it carries a risk of bleeding, so I need to ask you four quick questions first.'** If he asks **'can't you fly me?'** — **'retrieval is being arranged, but the medicine can be given now, and now is what matters.'**

SA — **from Wallaroo the nearest catheter laboratory is about 160 km and two hours by road, which sits right on the 120-minute boundary — exactly why the decision must be made explicitly and early rather than assumed.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** and **RFDS** for fixed-wing transfer; **PATS** afterwards; **Country Health Connect** for follow-up; **TIS National 131 450**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer early, with **Closing the Gap PBS** for ongoing cardiac medicines.

rows: A · metropolitan

52-year-old man, HMO in a metropolitan ED, pain began while chopping wood. BP 135/85, pulse 78, RR 18, SpO₂ 97% room air. 'No history of bleeding disorders.' Tasks: interpret the ECG → explain your management plan to the patient.

Anterolateral STEMI → PRIMARY PCI. Say the number: first-medical-contact to device ≤90 min. Clopidogrel 600 mg (ticagrelor 180 mg commoner in Australian practice). Activate the cardiac team before you take bloods.
B · rural, 400 km out

55-year-old man brought by ambulance, HMO in a rural hospital, nearest tertiary centre 400 km. Known hypertension. BP 160/95, pulse 88, RR 20, SpO₂ 93% on oxygen. Tasks: interpret the ECG (to examiner or medical student) → explain your diagnosis → explain your management.

Anterolateral STEMI with NO PCI ACCESS → FIBRINOLYSIS within 30 min. Screen the four bleeding questions out loud first. Lytic PLUS an anticoagulant and dual antiplatelets; clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg, no load, if over 75) — never ticagrelor or prasugrel with lysis. Monitor, serial ECG/troponin, transfer for angiography at 3–24 h, or immediately if lysis fails.
versions.note: The trap built into version B: this case became so well known that the AMC began writing 'you do not have access to PCI' explicitly into the stem. Talking about arranging a catheter laboratory means you failed to read the case written to test whether you can read it. Starred fails common to both: no doses, not screening lysis contraindications, giving a nitrate without asking about sildenafil, waiting for the troponin. Practice scenarios in the source (the nitrate/sildenafil trap, the inferior/RV version, the recent bleeding ulcer who cannot be lysed, the silent MI in a diabetic woman) are partner drills, not recalls.
