stem: Robert Hale, 60, a farmer in rural Queensland, presents with shortness of breath. He had a myocardial infarction one year ago treated with thrombolysis, and has had no GP follow-up since.
Vitals: BP 140/90 · PR 96 · RR 14 · T 36.5 °C · SpO2 99% room air.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient
findings: Vital signs
BP 140/90 · PR 96 · RR 14 · T 36.5 · SpO2 99% on room air. A NORMAL SATURATION DOES NOT EXCLUDE HEART FAILURE
General appearance
No respiratory distress, not cyanosed, alert
CVS — inspection
JVP RAISED, MORE THAN 3 cm above the sternal angle. Say you are starting with the cardiovascular examination, and why
CVS — palpation
APEX BEAT DISPLACED. PARASTERNAL HEAVE PRESENT
CVS — auscultation
First and second heart sounds normal, NO MURMUR. GALLOP RHYTHM WITH AN AUDIBLE THIRD HEART SOUND. Ask for the gallop and the S3 by name
Respiratory
Chest movements symmetrical. Percussion NORMAL. BIBASAL CREPITATIONS. Vocal resonance NORMAL
Abdomen
HEPATOMEGALY with a POSITIVE HEPATOJUGULAR REFLUX
Lower limbs
BILATERAL PITTING OEDEMA TO MID-SHIN. Ask whether it PITS and whether it is BILATERAL — a size difference is a DVT question, not this one
Office tests — ECG
Sinus rhythm around 75. PATHOLOGICAL Q WAVES IN V1 AND V2 with POOR R WAVE PROGRESSION — a previous septal infarct. Also look for LVH, LBBB, AF and ischaemic ST or T change
If the findings arrive on a printed card
READ IT SILENTLY. Do not read it aloud and do not narrate it back. Absorb it and move on
findingsLabel: Examiner stage — vitals and the examination findings · open when you would ask
must: FAIL — A thin differential list. History and differentials are scored separately.
FAIL — Not opening the stem's clue: when, treated how, on what now, compliant, followed up.
FAIL — Never asking about haemoptysis, weight loss or the farm exposures.
FAIL — Asking whether it is tightness or difficulty getting the air in, and skipping it.
ASK — Are you managing to take them every day? The key question of this case.
ASK — Are you short of breath when you're resting as well? The severity question.

dx: **Congestive heart failure from ischaemic cardiomyopathy after a thrombolysed MI**, in a man on no secondary prevention who has had no follow-up for a year.

**A patient one year post-MI who takes nothing and sees nobody has TWO complications waiting: heart failure, and RECURRENT ISCHAEMIC HEART DISEASE.** Ask about both — the second is the one candidates forget.

**The discriminating issue is the differential list you give after you already know the answer.** You can score six of seven on history, score one on differentials, and fail. **Name eight to ten, one reason each.**
**The question that splits heart from lung, asked first: 'is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?'** In a man with known IHD, tightness reopens another coronary event.
The stock AMC line is **six months, worse on walking, better with rest, walking less far** — **do not stop there. 'Are you short of breath when you're resting as well?'**

Heart failure signs: **raised JVP over 3 cm · displaced apex · S3 gallop · bibasal creps · hepatomegaly with positive hepatojugular reflux · bilateral pitting oedema.** **Definitive test: echocardiogram.**

**Four pillars of HFrEF: ACE inhibitor (or ARB or sacubitril–valsartan) · a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure — bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol CR, nebivolol · a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · an SGLT2 inhibitor.** Start low, titrate slowly, monitor potassium and renal function. **Frusemide relieves congestion but does not change prognosis.**

Self-management: **daily weights with an action plan for a gain over 2 kg in 2 days · fluid restriction around 1.5 L daily if congested · salt reduction · cardiac rehabilitation · influenza, pneumococcal and COVID vaccination.** Plus the **secondary prevention he has been missing — aspirin, a high-intensity statin, blood pressure control.**

The rural exposures the stem plants: **wheat, hay and birds → hypersensitivity pneumonitis · cattle, sheep and goats → Q fever, and the vaccine needs PRE-VACCINATION SKIN TESTING AND SEROLOGY because vaccinating someone already exposed can cause a severe reaction · old sheds → asbestos and mesothelioma.**

**Reframe the name when he reacts to it**: it does not mean the heart is about to stop, it means it is not pumping as strongly as it should, and treatment makes people feel better and live longer. **Ask what he drives** — Austroads: symptoms at rest or on minimal exertion means not fit for an unconditional licence. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **'Before I start, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, temperature and oxygen saturation?'** Then introduce, open question, and your own fixed acknowledgement line: **'thank you for coming in to get this assessed today. Let me ask some questions and examine you, and we'll find the cause together.'**

**Character first: 'is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?'** Then **how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · what makes it worse and better · how far could you walk six months ago and how far now · AND ARE YOU SHORT OF BREATH AT REST AS WELL?**
**Cough and noisy breathing** — cough, wheeze, phlegm and colour. Cheap, and it closes off asthma and COPD before you open the clue.

**The stem's clue — the heart of this station.** **When did you have your heart attack · what treatment did you have at the time · what medications are you on for it NOW · ARE YOU MANAGING TO TAKE THEM EVERY DAY · have you had regular follow-up with a GP?** → ran out at three or four months, never got a new script, three-hour round trip. **Thank him and normalise it; do not judge.**

**Both post-MI complications.** Recurrent IHD: **any chest pain with the breathlessness, especially on exertion · racing of the heart · dizziness or blackouts?** Heart failure: **worse lying down · HOW MANY PILLOWS · waking at night gasping · swelling in the legs or ankles?**
**The cancer block, done anyway**: **weight loss without trying · appetite · lumps or bumps · night sweats · HAVE YOU COUGHED UP ANY BLOOD · any previous cancer?**

**Occupation and exposures**: **what's your occupation · do you work with hay, grain or birds · ever exposed to ASBESTOS · contact with cattle, sheep or goats — and HAVE YOU HAD THE Q FEVER VACCINATION?**

The remaining sweep: **childhood chest infections or repeated pneumonias · fevers or chills · recent cold or flu · travel or TB contact · joint pains or rashes · bruising, tiredness, bowel change or black stools.** Then **SADMA with pack-years and quit date, past history, family history.**

**'Given the history, I'd like to start with the cardiovascular examination'** — say why. Then **JVP · apex and parasternal heave · heart sounds, murmurs, GALLOP OR THIRD HEART SOUND** → respiratory → **hepatomegaly and hepatojugular reflux** → **oedema, and is it pitting** → **ECG and spirometry.**

**Diagnosis with THREE reasons**: the pattern of the breathlessness and the three pillows · the swelling in both legs · the examination findings named one by one. Then reframe the term if he reacts to it.

**'I was also thinking about…' — said once per differential.** Recurrent IHD, arrhythmia, valve disease; then lung cancer, COPD, asthma, hypersensitivity pneumonitis from the grain, ILD, bronchiectasis, pneumonia and Q fever, TB, and anaemia. **If you realise you forgot to ask something, name it as a differential anyway — do not go back and re-take history.**
pefe: **Vitals before you sit down**, then **cardiovascular FIRST and say why** — changing the order signals you are adapting to the case rather than reciting a template.

The order: **general appearance — distress, cyanosis, drowsiness · JVP · apex beat and parasternal heave · heart sounds, murmurs, GALLOP AND THIRD HEART SOUND · respiratory — symmetrical movement, percussion, breath sounds and added sounds, vocal resonance · abdomen — hepatomegaly and HEPATOJUGULAR REFLUX · lower limbs — oedema, AND IS IT PITTING · office tests — ECG and spirometry.**

**ECG always, even when heart failure is obvious** — prior infarction, LVH, atrial fibrillation, bundle branch block. **A pathological Q wave is at least 40 ms wide or deeper than 25% of the following R wave, in two or more contiguous leads**, and is permanent. **Small narrow septal Q waves under 40 ms in I, aVL, V5 and V6 are normal — do not call those an old infarct.**
**Echocardiogram is the definitive test** — ejection fraction, regional wall motion abnormality, valves, chamber sizes.

**Chest X-ray**, read as **A B C D E — Alveolar oedema (bat-wing) · Kerley B lines · Cardiomegaly · Dilated upper lobe vessels · Effusions.** **The cardiothoracic ratio over 0.5 is only valid on a PA film at full inspiration** — on an AP or portable film say the ratio cannot be assessed reliably. **And screen the lungs while you are there.**

**Spirometry** for obstructive versus restrictive. Bloods: **FBE for anaemia, UEC and eGFR, LFT, fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, TSH, iron studies.** **24-hour ambulatory BP** where hypertension is part of the picture.

**A natriuretic peptide 'if available to me'** — BNP and NT-proBNP are guideline tests to rule out heart failure but community access in Australia is limited and they are not universally MBS-rebated. **Echocardiography is definitive regardless.**
**Avoid the shotgun list.** Relevance scores, not length — and do not stop at 'chest X-ray' as an entire investigation answer.

tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials to the patient, and your investigations to the examiner
findings: Pulse
TACHYCARDIC
JVP
NOT RAISED
Apex beat and heaves
Not displaced, no parasternal heave
Auscultation
A MURMUR is present. NO GALLOP, NO THIRD HEART SOUND
Respiratory
NO CREPITATIONS. Percussion and vocal resonance normal
Abdomen
NO HEPATOMEGALY, no hepatojugular reflux
Lower limbs
BILATERAL LOWER-LIMB OEDEMA
What the absences mean

The sparse findings are DELIBERATE. With no raised JVP, no gallop, no crepitations and no hepatomegaly, 'heart failure' is OVER-CALLING IT. Oedema alone could be a calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine
The answer to give
CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE — and then say what it could be within that: narrowing of the arteries, heart failure, a problem with the muscle itself, or a rhythm disturbance. 'I'd rather test than guess'
findingsLabel: Examiner stage — the sparse findings, and what the absences mean
must: FAIL — Over-calling it. Do not say 'heart failure' on oedema, tachycardia and a murmur.
FAIL — Skipping the respiratory differentials because the picture looks cardiac.
FAIL — Never asking about haemoptysis, weight loss or previous cancer.
FAIL — An investigation answer that stops at 'chest X-ray', or a shotgun list with no reasons.
ASK — Are you short of breath when you're resting as well? And how many pillows?
ASK — What medications are you on — and are you managing to take them every day?

dx: **Cardiovascular disease — and that is the answer.** Months of exertional breathlessness, chest heaviness, ankle swelling and long-standing hypertension, in a man in his seventies with **no previous MI**.
**The vagueness is the design.** The sparse findings exist so that the investigation task has something to do. **Refusing to over-call it is what is being marked.**

Say it as a range within cardiovascular disease: **narrowing of the heart's arteries · heart failure · a problem with the heart muscle itself · a rhythm disturbance — the heart is running fast today. 'I don't yet have enough to tell you which, and I'd rather test than guess.'**

**Bilateral oedema alone is not heart failure.** With **no raised JVP, no gallop, no crepitations and no hepatomegaly**, the commonest innocent explanation is a **calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine** — so take the medication list seriously.

**Long-standing hypertension is the thread**: it drives ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease with diastolic dysfunction, and atrial fibrillation. **24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring earns its place here.**
A murmur with tachycardia keeps **valvular disease — especially aortic stenosis in this age group — and arrhythmia** live. **Echocardiogram answers both.**
**The lung list still has to be said**: **lung cancer at the top, then COPD, asthma, bronchiectasis and interstitial lung disease.** History and differentials are separately scored.

Investigations, with a reason attached to each: **ECG because this could still be ischaemic heart disease · echocardiogram for heart failure and the murmur · 24-hour ambulatory BP given the hypertension · chest X-ray, which may show cardiomegaly or an effusion and screens the lungs · spirometry · FBE for anaemia.**
**Avoid the shotgun list** — 'FBE, ESR, CRP, LFT, TFT, renal function and an echo'. **Relevance is what scores, not length.**

If the tests confirm HFrEF, the **four pillars** follow: **ACE inhibitor or ARNI · a beta-blocker licensed for heart failure · a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · an SGLT2 inhibitor**, with **frusemide for congestion only**. Until then, **investigate rather than commit**.
plan: Vitals from the examiner, introduce, open question, and the acknowledgement line.

**Character first: 'is it more a tightness in your chest, or difficulty getting the air in?'** Then **how long · constant or intermittent · getting worse · aggravating and relieving · how far could you walk before and now · AND AT REST?**

The **chest heaviness** — treat it as angina until proven otherwise: **on exertion, relieved by rest, how long does an episode last, any radiation, sweating or nausea, any racing heart, dizziness or blackouts?**
Heart failure questions: **worse lying down · HOW MANY PILLOWS · waking at night gasping · swelling in the legs, and is it both sides?**

**The hypertension thread**: **how long have you had it · what are you taking for it · ARE YOU TAKING IT EVERY DAY · when was it last checked · any kidney trouble, diabetes or high cholesterol?** And go through **the whole medication list by name** — the oedema may be in it.
**The cancer block, done anyway**: **weight loss without trying · appetite · lumps or bumps · night sweats · HAVE YOU COUGHED UP ANY BLOOD · any previous cancer?**

**The oestrogen is the risk.** Combined pills, patches and rings count; **progestogen-only pills, implants and hormonal IUDs do not.** And **it is the immobility, not the aeroplane** — a long bus or car trip, bed rest or a leg cast all count.

**Stable, non-pregnant adult: rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily, or apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily.** Alternative **enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg daily or 1 mg/kg twice daily** bridging to warfarin, **target INR 2–3**. **In pregnancy LMWH only — DOACs and warfarin are contraindicated.** **At least 3 months when provoked.**

stem: A 68-year-old man with tachypnoea. History of hypercholesterolaemia, hypertension and previous myocardial infarction.

SpO2 89% RA · BP 132/84 · HR 112 · RR 28 · T 36.8 °C. Distended neck veins; apex not displaced; systolic murmur at the apex; S1 and S2 muffled with an S3 gallop; bibasal dullness and crepitations; pitting oedema to the knees.
tasks: Explain your diagnosis to the medical student
Explain your immediate management plan
findings: Observations
SpO2 89% ON ROOM AIR · BP 132/84 · HR 112 · RR 28 · T 36.8. Tachypnoeic, tachycardic and hypoxic — and NORMOTENSIVE, which is the finding that settles the tamponade question
Neck veins
DISTENDED — the systemic venous side of the same raised pressure
Apex beat
NOT DISPLACED
Heart sounds
FIRST AND SECOND HEART SOUNDS MUFFLED, with a THIRD HEART SOUND PRESENT — GALLOP RHYTHM. The S3 is rapid filling into a stiff, dilated ventricle
Murmur
SYSTOLIC MURMUR AT THE APEX — expect radiation to the axilla. FUNCTIONAL (SECONDARY) MITRAL REGURGITATION from a dilated ischaemic ventricle, NOT mitral valve prolapse
Chest
DULLNESS TO PERCUSSION AT BOTH BASES with BIBASAL CREPITATIONS. Fine, bibasal and SYMMETRICAL — the dullness is transudative pleural effusion
Legs
PITTING OEDEMA TO THE KNEES
Test Beck's triad out loud
HYPOTENSION · RAISED JVP · MUFFLED HEART SOUNDS. He has TWO OF THREE — but at 132/84 he is NORMOTENSIVE, so THIS IS NOT TAMPONADE. Order the echocardiogram anyway to answer the pericardium
VERSION — cardiogenic shock

BP 78/50, cool peripheries, lactate 4.2, oliguric. NO NITRATE — it will drop him further. Oxygen and non-invasive ventilation, cautious or withheld diuretic until perfusion improves, INOTROPE OR VASOPRESSOR, urgent bedside echo, cardiology and intensive care now. SAY THE WORDS CARDIOGENIC SHOCK
VERSION — the flash one

Two hours of severe breathlessness, BP 210/120, lungs clear yesterday, NEW LOUD PANSYSTOLIC MURMUR three days after an inferior infarct → PAPILLARY MUSCLE RUPTURE with acute severe mitral regurgitation. Urgent echo and cardiothoracic surgery
findingsLabel: Findings given in the stem · open before you teach
must: FAIL — Half a diagnosis. 'Heart failure' alone, or 'pulmonary oedema' alone.
FAIL — Calling tamponade in a normotensive man. Beck's triad is HYPOTENSION.
FAIL — Leaving him flat, or a management list that opens with oxygen or frusemide.
FAIL — No ECG and no troponin after a previous infarct; or starting a beta-blocker today.
ASK — the student first: what did you make of him? Then teach, don't recite.
ASK — at the end: does that hang together? Anything you want me to go back over?

dx: **Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, secondary to decompensated heart failure.** **Say the whole phrase** — 'heart failure' alone misses the emergency, 'pulmonary oedema' alone misses the cause.

**The chain, six links, not a list**: hypertension, cholesterol and a previous infarct are the substrate → **the left ventricle cannot eject enough** → pressure backs into the left atrium and the pulmonary veins → **pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure exceeds the oncotic pressure holding fluid in the vessel** → fluid crosses into the interstitium and then the alveoli → **gas exchange fails**.

**Hang every sign on a link.** Raised JVP and pitting oedema = the systemic venous side of the same pressure. **S3 = rapid filling into a stiff dilated ventricle.** Crepitations = alveoli opening against fluid. Basal dullness = **transudative effusion**.
**Crackles are not pneumonia when they are fine, bibasal and symmetrical and sit beside a raised JVP, an S3 and oedema.** Consolidation is focal, with bronchial breathing and a fever.

**CORRECTION — the murmur is functional mitral regurgitation, not mitral valve prolapse**: annular dilatation and papillary muscle displacement in a dilated ischaemic ventricle. **Prolapse gives a mid-systolic click with a late systolic murmur, usually in a younger patient.**

**CORRECTION — Beck's triad is HYPOTENSION, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds** (plus **pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg** and electrical alternans). **Reversing it to hypertension is a hard fail.** Muffled sounds are far more often obesity, hyperinflation or crackles drowning them.

**Seven ordered steps, numbered aloud: 1 sit him upright with legs dependent · 2 oxygen to 92–96% (88–92% if CO2 retention is a risk) · 3 IV access, cardiac monitoring, 12-lead ECG · 4 GTN 300–600 microg sublingual or 400 microg spray, repeated while systolic stays above 100 · 5 IV frusemide 20–40 mg or the usual daily oral dose, with a catheter to chart output · 6 STOP ANY IV FLUIDS · 7 CPAP 5–10 cmH2O if still hypoxic, and call cardiology.**

**Nitrate before diuretic when the pressure allows** — much of the acute picture is **redistribution rather than total body overload**, and nitrates drop preload and afterload within minutes while the diuretic only addresses volume.

**Deliberately not doing: no IV fluids · no NSAIDs · no beta-blocker today.** **CORRECTION — morphine is no longer routine**; observational data associate it with worse outcomes, more ventilation and longer stay. Reserve it for severe distress or ischaemic pain.

**Four pillars of HFrEF once euvolaemic: ACE inhibitor or ARNI · a beta-blocker with heart failure evidence — bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol CR, nebivolol, started low and slow · a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist · an SGLT2 inhibitor.** A loop diuretic sits alongside for congestion, **not as disease-modifying therapy**. **Action plan: 2 kg in 2 days. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**

Film — three colours
White is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air. Say it to the patient in those words, not in jargon
Film — landmarks and THE TRACHEA
Heart, spine, and THE TRACHEA RUNNING DOWN THE CENTRE — CENTRAL. This is the discriminating item of the whole station and it is step 2, not an afterthought
Film — the normal side first
On the left the lung goes right out to the chest wall, sitting against the inside of the ribs the way it should
Film — the abnormal side
On the RIGHT, a BLACK SHADOW between lung and chest wall. PLEURAL LINE with ABSENT LUNG MARKINGS BEYOND IT — uniform blackness. NAME IT: PNEUMOTHORAX
How to find it on a poor film

Do NOT hunt for the pleural line. Pick a side, find the fine peripheral lung markings, FOLLOW THEM OUTWARDS — on a normal side they reach the inner rib margin. WHERE THEY STOP SHORT is the pleural line; beyond it, blackness. Then compare sides

TRACHEA CENTRAL → simple pneumothorax → management by SYMPTOMS AND STABILITY. TRACHEA PUSHED AWAY from the black side → TENSION → IMMEDIATE NEEDLE DECOMPRESSION, before imaging, before anything else

The patient's left is on the RIGHT of the image. Describe it in THEIR sides. Adapt the script to whichever side you actually see

**The trachea is the discriminating issue.** **Central → simple → treat by symptoms and stability. Deviated AWAY from the affected side, with hypotension, distended neck veins and distress → TENSION → needle decompression within seconds, before any imaging.**

**CORRECTION — guidance has changed. **Stable and asymptomatic → observe 4 hours → discharge with a follow-up film, an appointment and red-flag advice. Unstable, or still symptomatic after analgesia → pleural intervention regardless of size.** **Oxygen if hypoxic, and analgesia — pneumothorax hurts, and pain drives the respiratory rate.**

**Needle decompression: 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line, entering JUST ABOVE THE THIRD RIB to avoid the neurovascular bundle — or the 5th space in the anterior axillary line, which many now prefer in adults because the anterior chest wall is often too thick.** Leave the cannula, withdraw the needle, then a **definitive intercostal catheter in the SAFE TRIANGLE — pectoralis major laterally, latissimus dorsi anteriorly, the 5th intercostal space below.**

**The rest question, which is the severity marker and is POSITIVE here: 'does rest make it better — and are you breathless at rest, just sitting here now?'** Then **any cough · any noisy breathing or wheeze?**

stem: Jane Marsh, a 47-year-old woman, presents with cough.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **ACE inhibitor–induced cough — but never only that.** Three findings are planted in this version: **lisinopril, post-nasal drip, and a viral illness two weeks ago.**

**The discriminating issue: this station scores how many differentials you EXCLUDED, not which diagnosis you reached.** Candidates who memorised 'cough equals ACE inhibitor' name the right drug **and still fail**. **Multiple findings are a sign you are passing** — rehearse that reframe before the exam, because the instinct when the second and third appear is panic.
**Chronic cough is more than 8 weeks** — subacute 3–8, acute under 3. **Every recalled version of this station has been chronic.** **A chest X-ray is indicated for any cough beyond 3 weeks.**

**ACE inhibitor cough: around 1 in 10, a class effect, commoner in women. Onset anywhere from days to months after starting — so a year on the drug does NOT exclude it. Settles 1–4 weeks after switching, occasionally longer.** **The '-prils': perindopril, ramipril, lisinopril, enalapril, captopril.** VERIFY — reported incidence ranges from about 5% to 20%, so say 'around one in ten'.
**Never tell her to simply stop the tablet.** It must be **substituted with an ARB**, not ceased — do not leave hypertension untreated.

**The four boxes: timing · triggers · character · SOUND.** Character runs **C·C·C·V·O — Colour, Consistency, Content, Volume, Odour** — and **Content is haemoptysis**, buried there deliberately because it is the most forgotten question. **Box 4 is the one everyone drops**: you ask about cough sound reflexively in paediatrics and abandon it in adults.

**Cough sounds: honking = psychogenic or habitual · an inspiratory whoop = pertussis · harsh and barking = croup or laryngeal · bovine and weak = recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy**, which in a chronic cough raises lung cancer.

**The scoring rule nobody tells you: examiners are instructed NOT to reward grouping.** Six differentials that are all infections score roughly one to two marks, not six. **Aim for at least five differentials from at least four different systems.**

**The sentence that reads as real understanding**: in a non-smoker with a normal chest X-ray who is not on an ACE inhibitor, **the overwhelming majority of chronic cough is upper airway cough syndrome (post-nasal drip), asthma or cough-variant asthma, and gastro-oesophageal reflux** — and that maps exactly onto the findings AMC plants.

**The delivery: one most likely with a reason → 'you also have features of…' for each remaining finding → then the exclusion list with the reassuring negatives**, which simultaneously answers her stated fear about her lungs. **The exclusion list IS the differential task.** Plan: **chest X-ray and spirometry · substitute the ACE inhibitor · intranasal corticosteroid for the drip · review in four weeks to confirm resolution.**
plan: **'Examiner, before I begin, may I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature?'** Then WIPE, open question — and **acknowledge the stated fear before interrogating**: **'I'm sorry to hear that, and I'm glad you've come in to have it looked at.'** Then **signpost the breadth**: **'some of my questions will seem unrelated to a cough — there are a lot of possible causes and I'd like to go through them properly.'** That buys permission to fire rapid questions.

**Box 1 — timing**: **how long have you been coughing · is it on and off or there constantly, are there weeks when you're fine · is it getting worse · and do you cough at night, or does it wake you from sleep?** **Anything that wakes a patient from sleep is significant** — and it is an asthma discriminator in the same sentence.

**Box 2 — triggers, open THEN specific**: **has anything made it better or worse?** … then, whether or not she answers, **is there a particular place or situation that sets it off — at work, outdoors, in certain seasons, when you exercise, or when you lie down?** The specific follow-up is what produces the wheat farm, the springtime park and the positional reflux clue.

**Box 3 — character**: **is the cough dry, or chesty — do you bring anything up?** Use **'dry or chesty', never 'productive' or 'wet'**. If chesty, **C·C·C·V·O**: **what colour · thin and watery or thick and sticky · HAVE YOU EVER NOTICED ANY BLOOD IN IT · a teaspoonful or more like an eggcupful · any bad smell?**

**Box 4 — the sound, and then the brothers**: **'a slightly unusual question — what does the cough sound like? Is it a loud, honking cough, one single explosive bark? Do you make a whooping sound at the end of a bout? Is it harsh and barking?'** Then **any shortness of breath, any noisy breathing or wheeze?** Cough and breathlessness are brothers — asking here costs ten seconds and buys a whole symptom axis.

**Red flag 1 — the lung cancer block, asked EARLY, not last**: **have you lost any weight or appetite · noticed any lumps or bumps · been unusually tired · have you ever coughed up blood · have you ever had cancer anywhere · what's your occupation now, AND what did you do before that · have you ever been exposed to asbestos?** **Asking only the current occupation misses decades of latency.**

**Red flag 2 — heart failure, because the cough that isn't in the lungs still counts**: **any chest pain · shortness of breath on exertion · breathless lying flat, how many pillows · any swelling in your legs or ankles?**

Infections: **any fevers, chills or night sweats · any sore throat or runny nose — NOW, OR RECENTLY · any body aches · do you ever vomit after a coughing bout · any travel overseas, or contact with anyone unwell or with tuberculosis?** **The past-tense follow-up is what uncovers the post-viral cough.**

Airways: **is the cough worse at night or on exercise · any family history of asthma, eczema or hay fever · do you smoke NOW OR HAVE YOU EVER, and does anyone smoke at home or at work · did you have recurrent chest infections as a child?** **A non-smoker can still develop COPD.**

**THE OTHERS — protect this block, it is where the planted findings live**: **are you on any medications at all · do you get heartburn, an acid or bitter taste, a sudden rush of saliva · do you feel secretions dripping down the back of your throat, any facial pain or blocked nose · any rashes or joint pains · do you keep birds at home, or work around hay, grain or mouldy dust · and how is this affecting your life, any stress, how's your mood?**

**Self-check at four minutes**: have I asked **haemoptysis · weight loss · occupation BEFORE · medications · heartburn · secretions behind the throat?** If any is missing, ask it now and let something else go.

SADMA and background **only if time remains** — and **if she reports social drinking, note it and move on**. Offering a separate consultation to counsel her about alcohol in a six-minute cough history answers a question nobody asked and costs you the differentials block.

**Task 2, in three moves**: **the most likely, with a reason drawn from the duration and daily dry pattern → the other findings named as contributors, because a cough often has more than one cause → and the exclusion list**, led by lung cancer with the reassuring negatives, then heart failure, infections, airways, reflux, bird and dust exposure and sarcoidosis. Close with **chest X-ray, spirometry, and switching the tablet** — and check understanding.
pefe: **No examination and no management have ever been asked in this station.** Do not volunteer either — and do not let them eat the history.
**Ask the examiner for vital signs anyway**, because the stem does not state whether the cough is acute.

**Chest X-ray for any cough persisting beyond 3 weeks**, and **mandatory with haemoptysis, weight loss or a significant smoking history**. **Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility** alongside it.
**Post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 defines COPD.**

Targeted tests when the history points there: **FBC and CRP · sputum MCS and AFB if TB is suspected · pertussis PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab if under 3 weeks, serology later · serum ACE if sarcoidosis · ECG and BNP if cardiac · HRCT for bronchiectasis or interstitial lung disease**.
If PEFE were ever asked: **clubbing, cervical and supraclavicular nodes, cachexia, and whether she can complete a sentence in one breath** — then the respiratory examination in full.
**Include the ENT examination — nasal mucosa, post-nasal secretions, sinus tenderness.** Two of your top three differentials sit above the clavicles.

Management when asked: **cease the ACE inhibitor and substitute an ARB** · **PPI trial and lifestyle measures for reflux** · **intranasal corticosteroid for post-nasal drip** · **inhaled corticosteroid trial for asthma** · **remove the exposure** where relevant. Safety-net for **haemoptysis, weight loss, fever, worsening breathlessness or chest pain**.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with a cough of ten weeks. She has smoked for 25 years. She has coughed up blood twice, has lost 6 kg without trying, and her voice has become hoarse.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Lung cancer until proven otherwise.** Four red flags together — **haemoptysis twice, 6 kg of unintentional weight loss, a hoarse voice, and 25 years of smoking, in a 62-year-old with a ten-week cough.**

**The differing delivery — be honest, and do not soften it**: **'the combination of coughing up blood, losing weight without trying, the change in your voice and your smoking history means I'm concerned about a serious cause in the lung, including the possibility of a cancer. I'm not able to tell you that today — but I'm not going to wait either.'**

**Then the concrete next step, and the human one**: **'I'd like a chest X-ray today and I'll arrange an urgent CT scan of your chest and a specialist review. Is there someone who can come with you?'**

**The trap: delivering the reassurance script from the standard version.** The stem is the same four words in every variant — **read the findings, not the recall.** The exclusion list with reassuring negatives belongs to a patient who has no red flags; this patient has four.

**The hoarseness is not incidental.** A **bovine cough — weak and non-explosive — with a hoarse voice suggests recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy**, and in a chronic cough that points directly at a lung lesion involving the mediastinum.
**Urgent chest X-ray criteria, worth saying out loud**: **haemoptysis · weight loss · cough beyond 3 weeks in a smoker over 40 · hoarseness · clubbing.** This patient meets four of them.

**Still run the whole structure.** The red flags do not excuse you from the rest of the cancer block — **lumps, fatigue, previous cancer, occupation now AND before, asbestos** — nor from heart failure, infections, airways and the others. **The station still scores breadth**, and TB and pneumonia can also present exactly this way.

**The other serious causes of haemoptysis with weight loss** to name: **tuberculosis** — ask travel, sick contacts, night sweats and country of birth; **bronchiectasis** with large-volume purulent sputum; **pulmonary metastases** from a previous cancer; and **mesothelioma or asbestosis** if there is any asbestos history.

**Do not offer reassurance you have not earned, and do not promise a benign outcome.** Equally, do not deliver a diagnosis you cannot yet make — **'I'm concerned about' and 'I'm not able to tell you that today' are the safe forms of words.**

SA: **urgent CT and respiratory or cancer-service review usually mean transfer from a regional centre — PATS for travel, Country Health Connect for follow-up. Cancer Council SA 13 11 20** for support; **TIS National 131 450**; **Quitline 13 7848**, which still matters at this point and should be offered without lecturing. **Aboriginal Liaison Officer** and **Closing the Gap PBS** where relevant.
plan: Vitals from the examiner, WIPE, open question — and **acknowledge the concern without promising anything**. She has come in with symptoms that frighten her; do not say 'I'm sure it's nothing'.
**Box 1 — timing**: ten weeks, constant or intermittent, getting worse, nocturnal, **and whether it wakes her**.
**Box 2 — triggers, open then specific.**

**Box 3 — character, and quantify the blood properly**: **dry or chesty · colour · thin or thick · HOW MUCH BLOOD, HOW MANY TIMES, FRESH OR OLD, MIXED WITH PHLEGM, IS IT STILL HAPPENING · volume, a teaspoon or an eggcupful · any smell?**

**Box 4 — the sound**, which matters more here than in any other version: **honking, whooping, barking — or weak and bovine, which with the hoarse voice points at the recurrent laryngeal nerve.** Then **shortness of breath and noisy breathing**.

**The rest of the cancer block, in full despite what the stem gave you**: **lumps or bumps · unusually tired · ever had cancer anywhere · occupation now, AND what did you do before · ever exposed to asbestos?** And **quantify the smoking in pack-years.**
Heart failure: **chest pain · exertional breathlessness · flat-lying breathlessness and how many pillows · ankle swelling.**

Infections, which matter more with this symptom set: **fevers, chills, NIGHT SWEATS · sore throat or runny nose now or recently · vomiting after coughing · travel overseas, contact with anyone unwell or with tuberculosis · country of birth.**

Airways: **worse at night or on exercise · family atopy · smoking now and before, passive and occupational · recurrent chest infections as a child**, which raises bronchiectasis with the large-volume sputum question.

**The others**: **medications including any '-pril' · the reflux triad · secretions behind the throat · rashes and joint pains · birds, hay, grain or mouldy dust · and impact, stress and mood** — asked last and framed as impact of illness.
SADMA briefly if time remains — **and ask what she understands and what she is most worried about**, because you are about to confirm it.

**Task 2 — the honest delivery.** Name the concern, give the four reasons, say plainly that you cannot tell her today and that you will not wait. **Chest X-ray today, urgent CT chest, specialist review.** Then **'is there someone who can come with you?'**

**Still give the differential list** — tuberculosis, pneumonia, bronchiectasis, pulmonary metastases, mesothelioma if asbestos, heart failure, COPD — **because the station still scores breadth**, and because naming them is what makes the cancer concern a reasoned conclusion rather than a guess.
pefe: **No examination or management task** — but ask the examiner for vital signs as in every version.
**Chest X-ray TODAY.** A CXR is mandatory with **haemoptysis, weight loss or a significant smoking history**, and this patient has all three.
**Urgent CT chest and specialist referral** — do not wait for the plain film to be abnormal before arranging review when the clinical picture is this strong.
**Spirometry with reversibility** still belongs in the workup, but it does not delay the imaging.
**FBC and CRP · sputum MCS and AFB if TB is on your list · pertussis PCR only if the story fits**.

If PEFE were asked: **clubbing · cervical and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy · cachexia · hoarse voice · can she complete a sentence in one breath** — then chest expansion, trachea, percussion, auscultation and vocal resonance.
**Look specifically for signs of local invasion and metastasis**: supraclavicular nodes, hoarseness, facial or arm swelling, bony tenderness, hepatomegaly.
Safety-net regardless of the pathway: **return immediately for worsening haemoptysis, breathlessness, chest pain or collapse.**

stem: A 25-year-old man, an accountant, presents with a cough that has been present for five years. He denies any stress.

dx: **Habitual cough — a diagnosis of exclusion, reached only after a complete organic workup.** The 2019 one-off version: **a 25-year-old accountant, cough for five years, entire history normal.**

**The differing delivery, and it must be framed as a habit rather than a psychiatric problem**: **'having gone through everything, I can't find any features pointing to a problem in your lungs, your heart, an infection, reflux or a medication. When a cough goes on this long with nothing else to find, one recognised explanation is a habitual cough. That means there is no physical problem in your lungs — after a chest infection people sometimes get into the habit of clearing their throat, and the cough simply stays.'**

**The trap: attributing it to stress when the patient has explicitly denied stress.** He is an accountant who says work is fine. **Telling him it is stress contradicts what he told you and reads as disbelieving him** — which is both clinically wrong and a communication failure.

**Still arrange the tests, and say why**: **'I'd still like a chest X-ray and breathing tests to be certain, because this is a diagnosis we only make once everything else is excluded.'** That sentence is what makes the diagnosis defensible rather than dismissive.

**The sound box is where this version pays.** **A honking cough — a single, loud, explosive bark — is classically psychogenic or habitual, and is characteristically absent during sleep.** Candidates who drop box 4 in adults have no positive feature to build on here.

**Psychogenic cough comes LAST for a reason.** Raising it before you have worked through the organic list is both clinically wrong and reads badly. **Ask the stress and mood questions at the end, framed as impact of illness rather than as a psychiatric probe.**

**The organic list must still be complete, and five years does not excuse shortening it.** **Lung cancer block — including occupation now and before, and asbestos — heart failure, infections, airways, and the others.** The station still scores **breadth, not the diagnosis**.
**The scoring rule still applies: examiners do not reward grouping.** Five infections score one to two marks. **Aim for at least five differentials from at least four different systems.**

**What must be actively excluded before you land here**: **no ACE inhibitor** — he is on no medications at all; **no reflux triad**; **no post-nasal drip**; **no nocturnal or exertional wheeze and no family atopy**, which would suggest cough-variant asthma; **never smoked**; **no bird or dust exposure**; and **a normal chest X-ray and spirometry**.

Management: **reassure with the reasoning rather than with a platitude · explain the habit mechanism · speech pathology or cough-suppression techniques and behavioural therapy are the treatments that help · review after the investigations return.** **Do not prescribe on the assumption of reflux or asthma without evidence**, and do not leave him feeling disbelieved. SA: **telehealth speech pathology where local access is limited**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**. VERIFY current management options before quoting them.
plan: Vitals from the examiner, WIPE, open question, acknowledge the frustration of five years without an answer — **and signpost the breadth**, which matters especially here because he has probably been asked some of this before.

**Box 1 — timing**: **five years · constant or on and off, are there weeks when you're fine · getting worse · do you cough at night, or does it wake you?** **The night question is the discriminator in this version** — a habitual cough is characteristically absent during sleep.

**Box 2 — triggers, open then specific**: **anything that makes it better or worse · any particular place or situation — at work, outdoors, in certain seasons, when you exercise, or when you lie down?**
**Box 3 — character and C·C·C·V·O**: **dry or chesty · colour · thin or thick · any blood, ever · how much · any smell?**

**Box 4 — the sound, and this is the version where it pays**: **'is it a loud, honking cough — one single explosive bark? Do you make a whooping sound at the end of a bout? Is it harsh and barking?'** Then **shortness of breath and noisy breathing.**

**The lung cancer block — asked in full despite his age**: **weight or appetite loss · lumps or bumps · unusually tired · ever coughed up blood · ever had cancer · occupation now, AND before · asbestos exposure.** Skipping it because he is 25 and well is still the automatic fail.
Heart failure: **chest pain · exertional breathlessness · flat-lying breathlessness and pillows · ankle swelling.**

Infections: **fevers, chills, night sweats · sore throat or runny nose now or recently · vomiting after coughing · travel or contact with anyone unwell or with TB.** **A remote post-infective trigger is worth hunting** — the habit often starts after an illness years ago.

Airways: **worse at night or on exercise · family history of asthma, eczema or hay fever · smoke now or ever, passive and occupational · recurrent chest infections as a child.** **Cough-variant asthma is the main organic competitor and must be excluded properly.**

**THE OTHERS, and protect this block**: **any medications at all — and in this version the answer is none, which removes the ACE inhibitor · heartburn, acid taste, sudden rush of saliva · secretions dripping down the back of your throat, facial pain or blocked nose · rashes or joint pains · birds at home, hay, grain or mouldy dust.**

**Impact, stress and mood — last, and framed as impact of illness**: **'how is all this affecting your life? Is there much stress at home or at work, and how has your mood been?'** He will deny stress. **Accept that answer and do not argue with it.**
SADMA briefly if time remains — alcohol, drugs, allergies, other conditions, family history.

**Task 2**: **name what you could not find, before you name what you think.** Then the habitual cough explained as a habit, **with the chest X-ray and spirometry still arranged and the reason for them said out loud**. Then the exclusion list — cancer, heart failure, infections, airways, drugs, reflux, post-nasal drip, dust and birds — **spanning systems, not grouped** — and check understanding.
pefe: **No examination or management task** — but ask the examiner for vital signs, as in every version.
**Chest X-ray** — indicated for any cough beyond 3 weeks, and non-negotiable before a diagnosis of exclusion. **Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility.**
**Post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC below 0.7 defines COPD**; reversibility supports asthma.
**Cough-variant asthma is the organic diagnosis most easily missed here** — consider a trial of inhaled corticosteroid if spirometry is equivocal and the story allows.

Targeted only if the history points there: **FBC and CRP · sputum MCS and AFB · pertussis PCR · serum ACE · HRCT for bronchiectasis or interstitial disease**. **Do not over-investigate a well 25-year-old.**
If PEFE were ever asked: **general appearance, clubbing, lymphadenopathy · respiratory examination in full · ENT for nasal mucosa, post-nasal secretions and sinus tenderness.**
**The positive feature to look for is behavioural, not physical**: **a honking quality, and absence of the cough during sleep.**
Management: **explain the mechanism · speech pathology and cough-suppression techniques · behavioural therapy · review once imaging and spirometry return.** VERIFY current options.

stem: Peter Callaghan, a 62-year-old man, has had three months of increasing breathlessness and a cough. He has lost about 6 kg without trying. He has smoked around 20 cigarettes a day for forty years and worked as a boilermaker in his twenties. You have already taken a history and examined him. His chest X-ray is on the screen in front of you.
tasks: Interpret the chest X-ray
Explain the chest X-ray to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Outline your management plan
findings: Examination findings you were given

No distress at rest, no cyanosis. REDUCED CHEST EXPANSION AT THE LEFT BASE. TRACHEA CENTRAL. DULLNESS TO PERCUSSION at the left base. ABSENT BREATH SOUNDS there. REDUCED VOCAL RESONANCE. Cardiovascular normal, no leg oedema — the four signs of an effusion. TIE THE FILM BACK TO THEM
Film — details and RIPE quality

PA ERECT chest radiograph. Confirm name and date, compare with old films. NOT ROTATED — sternal ends of the clavicles equidistant from the spinous processes. ADEQUATE INSPIRATION — six anterior ribs (5–6 anterior or 8–10 posterior). ADEQUATELY EXPOSED — hemidiaphragm just visible through the cardiac shadow. QUALITY BEFORE FINDINGS, so you have somewhere to retreat to
Film — soft tissue, bones, AIRWAY

Bones and soft tissues unremarkable, no rib fracture, no surgical emphysema. TRACHEA CENTRAL, mediastinum not widened, no hilar mass or lymphadenopathy. THE TRACHEA IS THE MOST COMMONLY OMITTED COMMENT IN THIS TASK, IN BOTH REGISTERS
Film — the NORMAL side first
RIGHT LUNG FIELD CLEAR — dark all the way down, costophrenic angle sharp and pointed. Naming the normal side first costs five seconds and buys the comparison mark
Film — the abnormal side
HOMOGENEOUS OPACIFICATION OF THE LEFT LOWER ZONE with a BLUNTED COSTOPHRENIC ANGLE and a RISING LATERAL MENISCUS, and NO AIR BRONCHOGRAM
Why it is fluid and not consolidation

THE MENISCUS AND THE ABSENCE OF AN AIR BRONCHOGRAM. Consolidation is confined by fissures and CONTAINS air bronchograms — air-filled bronchi standing out against fluid-filled alveoli, an AIR-SPACE process. Say BOTH
Film — circulation and diaphragm

LEFT HEART BORDER OBSCURED, so CARDIAC SIZE CANNOT BE RELIABLY ASSESSED — say that rather than guessing. Right hemidiaphragm normally sits HIGHER than the left, by up to about one interspace, because of the liver. No lines, drains or devices
Conclusion
A LEFT-SIDED PLEURAL EFFUSION. In a 62-year-old smoker with 6 kg of weight loss, the principal concern is a MALIGNANT effusion
VERSION — a mass instead
A ROUND WHITE SHADOW, golf-ball sized, in the upper zone → LUNG MASS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. WARN, PAUSE, NAME, PAUSE — never narrate your way into a cancer diagnosis by accident
VERSION — the normal film

Reported NORMAL. A NORMAL FILM IS A FINDING, NOT AN ENDING: 'it's reassuring, but a chest X-ray can miss small cancers, early scarring and clots, so given your symptoms I still want a CT.' 'Your x-ray is clear, so there's nothing to worry about' is the single most dangerous sentence in this station
findingsLabel: The examination findings and the film, read in order
must: FAIL — Naming a cancer with no warning shot and no pause, or hiding from it entirely.
FAIL — Never mentioning the trachea, or pouncing on the abnormality without the normal side.
FAIL — Describing without diagnosing, or false reassurance on a normal film.
FAIL — Four minutes on the film, so the diagnosis-and-management task goes unfinished.

dx: **A left-sided pleural effusion — and the diagnosis you must say out loud is 'a pleural effusion, AND I am concerned about what is causing it'.** Naming the effusion and stopping answers half the question.
**Three densities: WHITE is bone · GREY is soft tissue · BLACK is air.** Every finding is one of those appearing where it should not, or missing where it should be.

**Two registers, two scripts — decide which before you open your mouth. For the PATIENT, seven moves: orientate → three colours → landmarks → THE AIRWAY IS MIDLINE → the NORMAL side → the abnormal side → a name → a next step.** **For the EXAMINER or a student: Details · RIPE · Soft tissue and bones · Airway · Breathing · Circulation · Diaphragm · Extras · impression.** **Never deliver RIPE to a patient.**
**Keep the film to 60–90 SECONDS.** It is a sub-task inside a bigger station and **the marks are in the plan.**

**Words to swap out: opacity → white area · consolidation → infection filling the air spaces · effusion → fluid around the lung · costophrenic angle → the angle where the lung meets the chest wall · hyperinflation → the lungs are over-blown and can't empty · cardiomegaly → the heart is bigger than it should be · pneumothorax → air has leaked out into the space around the lung · hilar lymphadenopathy → swollen glands at the centre of the lungs.**

**The warning shot: 'before I go on — is there anyone you'd like to have with you?' → 'the fluid isn't the whole problem; the question is why it's there' → PAUSE → 'putting together the fluid, the weight you've lost and your smoking history, the possibility I'm most concerned about is a cancer in the lung. I'm sorry to have to say that, and we do not know it yet.' → PAUSE, AND DO NOT FILL THE SILENCE.**

**The differentials given to HIM, not just the examiner: a heart problem with fluid backing up · an infection including tuberculosis · MESOTHELIOMA, linked to the asbestos he met as a boilermaker · liver or kidney problems making the body hold fluid.**

**To 'how long have I got?': 'I'm not going to give you a number I can't stand behind. What matters is the type and whether it has spread, and that's exactly what the scan and the sample will tell us. I won't keep anything from you.'**

**Plan: ULTRASOUND-GUIDED DIAGNOSTIC PLEURAL ASPIRATION — protein, LDH, cytology, Gram stain and culture, applying LIGHT'S CRITERIA · CT CHEST AND UPPER ABDOMEN · bloods · respiratory referral and the LUNG CANCER MDT — all this week.** **Safety-net: worse breathing, haemoptysis, chest pain or fever → emergency department, not the appointment.**

**Offer Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 — he can ring without giving his name.** Hand the disclosure question back with support attached, offer his wife at the next appointment, and offer **smoking cessation — Quitline, nicotine replacement, varenicline.** **PATS for travel · TIS 131 450 — never explain a film through a family member.**
plan: **Ask permission before showing him: 'your x-ray is back and I've had a good look at it. I'd like to show it to you, because it's easier to follow when you can see it. Is that all right?'**

**Orientate BEFORE naming anything abnormal — twelve seconds that buys you the rest: 'this is a picture of your chest. There are really only three colours. WHITE IS BONE — ribs, collarbone, spine. GREY IS SOFT TISSUE, like your heart here in the middle. And BLACK IS AIR, which is what healthy lung looks like.'** **Point as you speak, even online.**
**The airway — the sentence nobody says: 'this dark line running down the centre is your main airway, your windpipe, and IT IS SITTING STRAIGHT DOWN THE MIDDLE, WHICH IS WHAT WE WANT.'**

**The NORMAL side first: 'let me show you this side first — your right. The lung is dark all the way down, and this sharp little angle right at the bottom, where the lung meets the chest wall, is nice and pointed. THAT SIDE LOOKS NORMAL TO ME.'**

**The abnormal side, named plainly: 'on your left, that same angle isn't sharp any more. It's filled in, it's white, and the white curves up like this. THAT WHITE IS FLUID, sitting around the outside of the lung and pressing on it — and that is why you've been so short of breath. The name for it is a PLEURAL EFFUSION.'** Then **tie it back to the examination: that side was dull when I tapped it, and I couldn't hear the breath sounds.**
**The warning shot, the pause, the word cancer, and the second pause.** Then **'what's going through your mind?'** and **wait.** If he asks how long, **do not invent a number.**
**The differentials, given to him in plain words** — heart, infection including TB, mesothelioma from the asbestos, liver and kidney. **'The tests are designed to tell those apart.'**
**The plan with a timeframe: ultrasound-guided sample of the fluid · CT chest and upper abdomen · bloods · respiratory referral this week.** **'This is not something we wait on.'**

**Safety-net: worse breathing, coughing up blood, chest pain or fever → straight to the emergency department, don't wait for the appointment.** Then **'should I tell my wife?'** handed back with support attached, and **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20.**
**Smoking cessation offered concretely**, then **summarise and offer to see him with his wife once the results are back.** **Do not go back and take more history.**
pefe: **Quality before findings.** Commenting on rotation, inspiration and exposure first gives you permission to say **'this heart looks large but the film is AP'** or **'there is apparent basal shadowing but this is a poor inspiration'**. Candidates who pounce have nowhere to retreat.

**RIPE: Rotation — clavicle sternal ends equidistant from the spinous process · Inspiration — 5–6 anterior or 8–10 posterior ribs · Picture — PA or AP, erect or supine · Exposure — hemidiaphragm just visible through the heart.** **CTR over 0.5 is cardiomegaly on an ERECT PA FILM ONLY.**

**Effusion workup: ULTRASOUND-GUIDED TAP with protein, LDH, cytology, Gram stain and culture, applying LIGHT'S CRITERIA · CT CHEST AND UPPER ABDOMEN.** **A few hundred millilitres are needed to blunt the costophrenic angle on a PA film; far less shows on a lateral or on ultrasound.**

**Two signs worth naming: the AIR BRONCHOGRAM — branching black airways against white alveolar filling, so the process is in the AIR SPACES, pointing to consolidation and AWAY from an effusion or mass. The SILHOUETTE SIGN — lost right heart border = right middle lobe; lost left heart border = lingula; lost hemidiaphragm = lower lobe.**

**Trachea PUSHED AWAY: tension pneumothorax, massive effusion. PULLED TOWARDS: lobar collapse, fibrosis, pneumonectomy. Central with a big white hemithorax → think consolidation rather than collapse.**

**Tension pneumothorax is a CLINICAL diagnosis — decompress before imaging.** Saying that out loud is worth a mark on its own. **Free gas under the diaphragm on an erect film is a perforated viscus — make the diaphragm and what lies beneath it a fixed step.**

**Do not miss: a small APICAL pneumothorax above the clavicles · a mass hidden BEHIND THE HEART or the diaphragm · a rib lesion or pathological fracture · a Pancoast tumour at the apex · an incidental breast lesion.** **A repeat film at 6 weeks after pneumonia in a smoker over 50.**

30 mmol/L (normal 22–26), base excess +4. THE KIDNEYS HAVE BEEN COMPENSATING, and that only happens slowly — so this is LONG-STANDING, not new. This is the reassuring sentence to pair with the word acidosis
Blood gas — PaO2
62 mmHg. LOW oxygen WITH high CO2 = TYPE 2 RESPIRATORY FAILURE. Partially compensated CHRONIC respiratory acidosis
Do NOT offer home oxygen

PaO2 62 does NOT meet the threshold. Long-term oxygen needs PaO2 55 mmHg OR LESS (or 59 or less with cor pulmonale or polycythaemia), stable, non-smoking, 15 hours a day or more, and it is arranged by RESPIRATORY SERVICES. Saying so confidently is a mark
The two numbers NOT in the stem — ask for them

mMRC BREATHLESSNESS GRADE (grade 2 = walks slower than people the same age; he stops on the stairs, so at least 2) and EXACERBATIONS IN THE PAST 12 MONTHS. They drive the inhaler choice. Asking out loud shows you know what decides treatment

dx: **COPD, confirmed on POST-bronchodilator spirometry, with a partially compensated CHRONIC respiratory acidosis — type 2 respiratory failure.** **Persistent respiratory symptoms with airflow limitation that is not fully reversible.** Emphysema and chronic bronchitis both sit under COPD and **are managed identically.**

**The single biggest error is reading the result silently and announcing 'you have COPD'. This is a COUNSELLING station: the marks are in the reasoning you SPEAK and the plan you BUILD**, not in a diagnosis most candidates already have from the stem.

**The discriminator: convert the results into a complete, specific, FIVE-PART plan the patient could act on tonight, WITH a written action plan, a rescue pack and a call-000 threshold.** Candidates fail by spending five of eight minutes on the spirometry and then offering 'a preventer and a specialist referral'.

**COPD-X: C confirm the diagnosis · O optimise function · P prevent deterioration · D develop support and self-management · X manage eXacerbations.** Recite the five letters and the examiner can see the structure.

**Four steps on every gas: 1 pH — acidaemic, alkalaemic or normal · 2 PaCO2 — does it explain the pH? if yes, respiratory · 3 bicarbonate and base excess — compensating, or a second problem? · 4 PaO2 — type 1 (low O2 alone) or type 2 (low O2 with high CO2).**

**Inhalers: keep salbutamol as the RELIEVER, THROUGH A SPACER. Add a long-acting bronchodilator — salmeterol 50 microg BD or tiotropium 18 microg daily. EITHER is acceptable first; say which you chose and why.** **CHECK TECHNIQUE IN THE ROOM.**

**Do NOT start an inhaled corticosteroid first line** — it raises pneumonia risk. **Add only for 2 or more moderate exacerbations, or 1 or more hospitalisations, in 12 months, or blood eosinophils 0.3 x10^9/L or above.** VERIFY.

**Prevent: continued abstinence (Quitline 13 7848) plus THREE vaccines, named with intervals — INFLUENZA annually, funded · PNEUMOCOCCAL, one conjugate dose then 23vPPV at 2–12 months, then a second 23vPPV at least 5 years after the first · COVID-19, 65–74 recommended 12-monthly and eligible 6-monthly; 75 and over 6-monthly.** VERIFY against the Handbook.

**Pulmonary rehabilitation: about EIGHT WEEKS, TWO TO THREE SESSIONS A WEEK** — supervised exercise, inhaler technique, flare-up education, breathing and coughing techniques, dietitian and exercise physiologist, outcome assessment. **Better evidence for breathlessness and quality of life than any third inhaler — say that sentence.**

**CORRECTION — the 'hypoxic drive' explanation is out of date.** CO2 retention on high-flow oxygen is driven mainly by **worsening ventilation–perfusion matching and the Haldane effect.** Say: **target saturations 88–92% in someone at risk of hypercapnia, and titrate.**
plan: WIPE, **confirm name and date of birth**, consent, and check he is comfortable enough to talk for ten minutes. Then **the agenda question: 'before I start — what have you already been told, and what were you hoping to get out of today?'**

**Signpost, and it buys you the whole eight minutes: 'I'll do this in two parts. First the two tests and what they show. Then we'll spend MOST of our time on the plan — what I'm going to start, what you can do yourself, and what to do on a bad day. Stop me any time.'**

**Spirometry, three sentences. THE RATIO: 'we measure the total amount of air you can blow out and the amount in the first second, then divide one by the other. Your ratio is 67, and for a man of your age and size we'd expect about 76. It is REDUCED — and a reduced ratio means an OBSTRUCTIVE pattern, which is my way of saying the airways are narrowed.'**

**THE REVERSIBILITY: 'then I look at what happened after the puffer. If the airways open up a lot, that points to asthma — we look for at least 200 MILLILITRES AND 12 PER CENT. Yours improved by 120 millilitres, about 3 per cent, so it is NOT significantly reversible. Put those together and the diagnosis is COPD.'**

**The gas, four sentences: 'a sample from an artery that measures the gases in your blood. CARBON DIOXIDE is the waste gas your body makes after it uses oxygen, and your lungs are meant to blow it off. Because your airways are narrowed, some is staying in. It dissolves to make an acid, so your blood is slightly acidic — pH 7.33 where we'd want 7.35 to 7.45. We call that RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS.'** **Then immediately the reassuring half: 'your BICARBONATE is up at 30 — your kidneys have been quietly correcting this for a long time, which tells me this is long-standing rather than something that has happened this week.'**

**Name it, then STOP AND CHECK: 'you have COPD — long-term narrowing of the airways, in your case from years of smoking. What does that word mean to you, and what questions has that raised?'** He will ask about cancer or about oxygen. **Answer honestly and briefly, then move.**

**THE PIVOT, whether or not you have finished: 'I don't want to spend the whole appointment on tests, because the plan matters more. There are FIVE parts. The puffers. Getting you fitter and lighter. Stopping it getting worse. Support and education. And what you do on a bad day — the one I most want you to remember.'**

**One, INHALERS: the blue one is a RELIEVER, for the moment, THROUGH A SPACER because far more reaches the lungs. Adding SALMETEROL twice a day, morning and night, whether or not he feels breathless — THAT is the one that changes how far he walks. Tiotropium if that is not enough. 'Before you go, show me how you use them.'**

**Two, OPTIMISE: PULMONARY REHABILITATION — eight weeks, two to three sessions a week, supervised exercise from where he is now, inhaler classes, flare-up education, physiotherapist for breathing and coughing. Plus an EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST, because 150 minutes a week is useless advice to a man breathless after five. Plus a DIETITIAN for the BMI of 32 — 'losing some weight will do more for your walking than another inhaler.'** Answer the rural access question: **Country Health Connect, telehealth-supported, PATS for travel.**

**Three, PREVENT: congratulate the abstinence and confirm no slips (Quitline 13 7848), then NAME ALL THREE VACCINES WITH INTERVALS — flu yearly and free; pneumococcal one now, another in a few months, a third at least five years on; COVID booster yearly at his age, eligible six-monthly.** **Reciting 'vaccinations' as one word loses the specificity mark.**

**Four, SUPPORT: Lung Foundation Australia 1800 654 301, printed COPD fact sheets, Lungs in Action.** **Five, the WRITTEN ACTION PLAN — 'I'm writing this down, because nobody remembers it in the moment.'** **Step one: reliever 4–8 puffs every 3–4 hours. Step two: prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days. Step three: ONLY if the phlegm has BOTH increased AND changed colour, amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days.** Both boxes handed over today.

**Call 000 for sudden severe breathlessness, chest pain, confusion or drowsiness, or the reliever no longer lasting three hours — don't drive.** Then **TEACH-BACK: 'can you tell me back what you'd do if your phlegm turned green tomorrow?'** Then **GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement, review in 4–6 weeks.**
pefe: **Confirm on the POST-bronchodilator ratio, not the pre.** If challenged: **'a pre-bronchodilator reduction can be reversible and would then be asthma.'**

**Do now: chest X-ray if not already done, CT if anything focal · FBC for anaemia and polycythaemia, blood EOSINOPHILS · resting oximetry.** **Formal oxygen assessment only if persistently below 92%.** **Alpha-1 antitrypsin level once, especially with a family history.**
**Ask for the two numbers that choose the inhaler: mMRC grade and exacerbations in the last 12 months.** Neither is in the stem.

**Screen the comorbidities: osteoporosis (smoking, steroids, inactivity) · anxiety and depression, common and under-treated · cardiovascular risk · obstructive sleep apnoea — he snores and has a BMI of 32, so Epworth and a sleep study.**

**Cor pulmonale — ankle oedema and a raised JVP — and undiagnosed heart failure coexisting with COPD are the two things not to miss.** **Lung cancer shares the risk factor and the symptoms: a normal film does not exclude it.**
**Softened claims: MUCOLYTICS are not part of routine care here and are not PBS-listed for COPD. LABA versus LAMA first is a choice, not a rule — say which you chose and why.** VERIFY.
**Avoid: antibiotics for stable disease · prescribing without checking technique · home oxygen without formal assessment · promising lung function will return to normal.**

stem: You are a general practitioner. Your next patient is Ken Ballard, a 60-year-old man, with fever, cough and shortness of breath for three days, coughing up yellow phlegm, more than usual. He has known COPD and uses puffers. Investigations are available.
T 37.8 °C · SpO2 93% RA · RR 22 · HR 92 · BP 130/80 · WCC 14.5 · CRP raised · COVID-19 PCR negative · CXR: hyperinflated, no consolidation.
tasks: Interpret the investigations to the patient
Explain the reasons for his condition
Explain your further management
findings: Temperature
37.8 — LOW-GRADE FEVER, consistent with a flare-up
Oxygen saturation

93% ON ROOM AIR. ACCEPTABLE IN COPD — not a reason to panic and not a reason to give oxygen. ASK WHAT HIS USUAL READING IS (he says 93 or 94). If oxygen is ever needed, TARGET 88–92% — but NEVER WITHHOLD IT FROM A GENUINELY HYPOXIC PATIENT
Respiratory rate and pulse
RR 22 and HR 92 — both MILDLY RAISED. BP 130/80 normal
White cell count and CRP
WCC 14.5 and CRP RAISED. NON-SPECIFIC — the cells that fight infection, so the body is responding to something. IT DOES NOT ON ITS OWN TELL YOU HOW SICK HE IS
COVID-19 PCR
NEGATIVE. SAY IT OUT LOUD — he will want it
Chest X-ray — finding 1
HYPERINFLATED — bigger and blacker than usual, FLATTENED DIAPHRAGMS. This is CHRONIC. It tells you he has COPD; IT PROVES NOTHING ABOUT TODAY. Describing it and stopping is the trap
Chest X-ray — THE PIVOT OF THE WHOLE STATION

NO CONSOLIDATION. Say the words out loud even if nobody asks: 'THERE IS NO WHITE PATCH ANYWHERE ON THIS FILM — NO CONSOLIDATION, WHICH IS WHAT WE'D SEE IF YOU HAD PNEUMONIA. SO YOU DO NOT HAVE PNEUMONIA.' MANAGING THIS AS A PNEUMONIA FAILS THE STATION
The three cardinal symptoms — ANTHONISEN

INCREASED BREATHLESSNESS · INCREASED SPUTUM VOLUME · INCREASED SPUTUM PURULENCE. TWO OF THREE, PROVIDED ONE IS PURULENCE, is the usual threshold for antibiotics. KEN HAS ALL THREE. Naming the framework lifts the answer above 'yellow sputum so amoxicillin'
What he hides unless you ask

HE IS FRIGHTENED THIS IS PNEUMONIA — HIS FATHER DIED OF IT. Given only if you ask what he was worried about. And the BROWN PREVENTER: 'most mornings' → only if you ask HOW MANY MORNINGS A WEEK does he admit HALF THE TIME, and HE HAS NEVER USED A SPACER
VERSION — the deteriorating one

DROWSY, CONFUSED SINCE LUNCHTIME, SpO2 88% → POSSIBLE TYPE 2 RESPIRATORY FAILURE. Controlled oxygen to 88–92%, ARTERIAL BLOOD GAS, and ADMIT. NIV if pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 from a country site
findingsLabel: The results handed to you at the door
must: FAIL — Treating it as a pneumonia. Say 'no consolidation' before you go near management.
FAIL — A good verbal plan with nothing handed over, or no red flags and no 000 trigger.
FAIL — Panicking at 93%, or promising high-flow oxygen.
FAIL — Ignoring confusion or drowsiness, or missing pneumothorax, PE, heart failure or cancer.
ASK — What were you most worried it might be? Before you touch the results.

dx: **An acute exacerbation of COPD, most likely triggered by a chest infection.** To the examiner: **'infective exacerbation of COPD, WITHOUT RADIOGRAPHIC CONSOLIDATION'.** Both halves matter — a flare-up of a condition he already has, with an identifiable trigger.

**An exacerbation is defined CLINICALLY, not radiologically. The three ANTHONISEN cardinal symptoms: increased breathlessness · increased sputum VOLUME · increased sputum PURULENCE. Two of three, provided one is purulence, is the antibiotic threshold.**

**Three things must physically happen: 1 you SAY 'no consolidation — this is not a pneumonia' · 2 you WATCH him use his inhaler and correct it · 3 you WRITE AND HAND OVER a three-zone plan with doses and a 000 trigger.** Everything else is recoverable; these three are not.

**The three medicines, with numbers: SALBUTAMOL 4–8 PUFFS THROUGH A SPACER every 3–4 hours while unwell, then as needed — a pMDI with a spacer is as effective as a nebuliser and is preferred · PREDNISOLONE 30–50 mg each morning for 5 DAYS, NO TAPER needed for a course of 14 days or less · AMOXICILLIN 500 mg three times daily for 5 days, or DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg twice daily (200 mg on day 1) for 5 days if penicillin-allergic.** VERIFY.

**The written THREE-ZONE plan, said aloud as you write it: GREEN when well — usual breathlessness, usual phlegm, sleeping through; keep the daily preventer, reliever as needed, off the cigarettes, vaccinations current. AMBER, a flare-up starting — more breathless, more phlegm, colour change; reliever 4–8 puffs every 3–4 hours, start the prednisolone, start the amoxicillin, and ring us for review in 48–72 hours. RED, an emergency — breathless at rest or when talking, reliever not helping or needed sooner than every three hours, chest pain, drowsy, confused, or blue lips: RING 000.**

**Admission criteria — give the list and say which he does not meet: marked increase in symptoms or breathlessness at rest · severe underlying COPD or frequent prior exacerbations · new cyanosis, new peripheral oedema, confusion or drowsiness · failure to respond to initial treatment · significant comorbidity · INSUFFICIENT SUPPORT AT HOME, the criterion that decides most rural cases · diagnostic uncertainty.**
**Blood gas if saturation is below 92%, if he is drowsy, or before considering NIV. NIV is for a RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS — pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 mmHg — NOT for hypoxia alone.**

**Causes of an exacerbation: INFECTIVE, about 70% — viral (rhinovirus commonest, influenza, RSV, coronaviruses) and bacterial (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis; Pseudomonas in severe or bronchiectatic disease). NON-INFECTIVE — smoking and smoke exposure, pollution, cold air, NOT TAKING THE MAINTENANCE INHALER or poor technique, sedatives and opioids, decompensating comorbidity.** **Up to a third have no identifiable trigger.**

**If the film HAD shown consolidation it becomes a different station**: community-acquired pneumonia, **CURB-65 or SMART-COP, amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days** with atypical cover where indicated, and **a much lower threshold for admission**. Different antibiotic, different dose, different disposition.

**Do NOT change maintenance therapy or start rehabilitation during the flare** — that is a review-appointment job. **At the 48–72 hour review and then at 4–6 weeks: smoking cessation with Quitline 13 7848 and PBS nicotine replacement, vaccination, maintenance reassessment, pulmonary rehabilitation.** **healthdirect 1800 022 222 after hours.**
plan: **Introduce, confirm identity, consent — then SET THE AGENDA covering all three tasks: 'I'd like to go through the results, explain what I think has caused this, then agree a plan including SOMETHING WRITTEN DOWN to take home.'** Then **'before I start — WHAT WERE YOU MOST WORRIED IT MIGHT BE?'** → pneumonia, his father died of it. **Answering it explicitly is scored.**

**Results one at a time, chunk and check. Temperature 37.8, slightly up, fits an infection. Oxygen 93 per cent — for someone with your lungs that's a reasonable number — CAN I ASK WHAT IT USUALLY SITS AT WHEN YOU'RE WELL?** Then **white cells 14.5, the cells that fight infection, so your body is responding to something — IT DOESN'T ON ITS OWN TELL ME HOW SICK YOU ARE.** Then **the COVID swab is negative.**

**The X-ray, two things. First: 'your lungs look bigger and blacker than usual and your diaphragms are flattened — that means your lungs are holding on to air they can't push out. THAT IS YOUR COPD, AND IT HAS BEEN THERE A LONG TIME; IT ISN'T NEW TODAY.'**

**Second, and the sentence the station is built around: 'this is what I was looking hardest for. THERE IS NO WHITE PATCH ANYWHERE ON THIS FILM — no consolidation, which is what we'd see if you had pneumonia. SO YOU DO NOT HAVE PNEUMONIA.'** Then **'anything you want me to go back over?'**

**Task 2 — what a flare-up IS: 'your airways are permanently narrowed and inflamed, mostly from years of smoking. Day to day you have a level you live at. A flare-up is when something irritates or infects those airways, so they swell, make more phlegm and narrow further. NOTHING ABOUT YOUR UNDERLYING LUNGS HAS SUDDENLY CHANGED — but they are temporarily much worse than your normal.'**

**Name HIS trigger and the three changes: 'three things have changed together — you're MORE SHORT OF BREATH, you're bringing up MORE PHLEGM, and that phlegm HAS TURNED YELLOW. Those three together are what tell me this is an infective flare-up, and they are the reason I'm giving you an antibiotic as well.'**

**'Why do I keep getting these?' — smoking first, then whether the daily preventer is actually being taken AND getting into his lungs, then vaccination, then pulmonary rehabilitation. 'I'd like to sort those out at your review, not today while you're unwell.'**
**Admission criteria named, and which he does not meet** — then **'I'm happy to treat you at home, provided you have the written plan and someone with you tonight.'**

**The three medicines WITH NUMBERS: reliever 4–8 puffs through a spacer every 3–4 hours, then back to as needed — the spacer gets far more in · prednisolone 50 mg each morning for 5 days, then STOP, no weaning, and name the side effects: sleep, appetite, mood, blood sugar · amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for 5 days, because the phlegm has changed colour.**

**'Before you go — CAN YOU SHOW ME HOW YOU TAKE YOUR PUFFER? I ask everyone; it's the commonest reason treatment doesn't work.'** Then correct what you see: **shake, upright, seal the lips, SLOW AND DEEP for a pMDI (fast and forceful for a dry powder device), hold ten seconds, wait before the second puff, always a spacer, rinse after any inhaled steroid.**

**The written plan, handed over, chunked with a check after each zone: 'I'm writing this down for you, because at two in the morning nobody remembers what the doctor said. Three boxes — GREEN when you're well, AMBER when a flare-up starts, RED when it's an emergency.'** **Read the red zone slowly, and name 000.**

**Follow-up in 48 to 72 hours, booked now, sooner if worse. healthdirect 1800 022 222 after hours.** Then **smoking without a lecture — ask permission, assess readiness, offer Quitline 13 7848 and PBS nicotine replacement, book a dedicated appointment** — plus vaccination and rehabilitation at review. **Summarise and check: 'what have I not covered?'**
pefe: **There is no examination task and no examiner presentation — everything is said to the patient.** If asked to present instead, **switch register**: infective exacerbation of COPD without radiographic consolidation, all three Anthonisen cardinal symptoms, meeting no admission criteria.
**Read the film before you open your mouth. Hyperinflation is chronic. The absence of consolidation is the examinable finding.**
**Get an arterial blood gas if SpO2 is below 92%, if he is drowsy, or before considering NIV.** **NIV for pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 — not for hypoxia alone.**
**Oxygen: 93% needs none. If required, target 88–92% delivered in a controlled way — and DO NOT WITHHOLD OXYGEN FROM A HYPOXIC PATIENT for fear of CO2 retention.**

**Say the alternatives as excluded, with the reason: PNEUMONIA — no consolidation on the film · PNEUMOTHORAX — sudden onset, unilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds in a bullous lung · PULMONARY EMBOLISM — hypoxia out of proportion, pleuritic pain, unilateral calf swelling, commonly missed in COPD · HEART FAILURE — orthopnoea, raised JVP, oedema · LUNG CANCER in a smoker over 50 · TYPE 2 RESPIRATORY FAILURE — drowsy, confused, flapping tremor.**

**Avoid: uncontrolled high-flow oxygen · sedatives, benzodiazepines and opioids, which suppress respiratory drive · prescribing without watching him use the inhaler · antibiotics with no purulence and only one cardinal symptom · sending him home with a verbal plan and nothing written.**

**Language rules: never say consolidation, hyperinflation, exacerbation or purulent without translating on the spot.** Say **flare-up · a patch of infection · your lungs are holding more air than they should · the phlegm has changed colour.**

Bronchiectasis

High-resolution CT, sputum culture
