stem: You are a general practitioner. Your next patient is Jenny, a 57-year-old woman, who has booked an urgent consultation after she coughed up blood. It happened while she was eating dinner.
Observations from the examiner on request.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
findings: Vital signs, requested first
RR 16 · SpO2 97% ON ROOM AIR · BP 128/78 · PULSE 84 · T 37.1. Ask for RESPIRATORY RATE AND SATURATION FIRST, then BP, pulse and temperature — 'because she is bleeding and infection is on my list'
General appearance
Comfortable, NOT DISTRESSED, NOT PALE. NO CLUBBING. NO CERVICAL OR SUPRACLAVICULAR LYMPHADENOPATHY. No cachexia
ENT — the system you ADD in this case

NOSE on speculum examination: NO SOURCE OF BLEEDING. THROAT: no source of bleeding, no visible posterior bleed. NO SINUS TENDERNESS. Say you are adding ENT and say WHY — a posterior nosebleed or a bleeding throat lesion presents exactly like this. Omitting it is a named, scored miss
Respiratory
Chest movements SYMMETRICAL, trachea CENTRAL, percussion RESONANT, breath sounds NORMAL with NO added sounds, vocal resonance NORMAL
Cardiovascular and abdomen
JVP NOT raised, apex UNDISPLACED, heart sounds dual, NO murmur. Abdomen soft, NO HEPATOMEGALY
Lower limbs and bedside tests
CALVES EQUAL, no oedema. ECG SINUS RHYTHM. Spirometry UNAVAILABLE
THE EXAMINATION IS DESIGNED TO BE NORMAL

Say it out loud BEFORE you interpret: 'A COMPLETELY NORMAL EXAMINATION DOESN'T REASSURE ME HERE — EARLY TUBERCULOSIS AND A CENTRAL LUNG CANCER CAN BOTH EXAMINE NORMALLY. My diagnosis rests on the history and on imaging.' A NORMAL CHEST X-RAY DOES NOT EXCLUDE LUNG CANCER EITHER
What she gives only if you ask the right way

'How much blood?' → 'I don't know, some.' GIVE HER THE ANCHOR — 'a few drops, or a large amount?' → 'ABOUT TWO TEASPOONS.' 'Lost weight?' → 'about five kilos' → ASK OVER WHAT PERIOD → 'THE LAST MONTH OR TWO.' 'Any travel?' → 'MISSIONARY WORK IN CAMBODIA' AND SHE STOPS THERE
The follow-up that wins the station
'CAN I ASK WHAT THAT WORK INVOLVED?' → 'I WAS THERE TO HELP SICK PEOPLE.' She will NEVER say she nursed people with tuberculosis. You have to do the joining up yourself
Her hidden agenda
HER LATE HUSBAND DIED OF LUNG CANCER and she is convinced this is the same thing. Given only at the end, and only if you ask whether she has any worries or questions

FAIL — Never asking travel and sick contacts, then what the work actually involved.
FAIL — 'I'm sure it's nothing serious.' Reassure about your care, never about the diagnosis.
FAIL — Continuing a history through a massive bleed, or a plan with no chest X-ray.
ASK — Did you cough it up, or did you vomit it? And was there any choking beforehand?
ASK — How much weight, and over what period? Never accept a number without a denominator.

dx: **Pulmonary tuberculosis** — and **lung cancer named aloud beside it.** **Two diagnoses have to leave your mouth in this station.**
**The four reasons, said as four: she has been in DIRECT CONTACT WITH SICK PEOPLE IN A HIGH-PREVALENCE COUNTRY · she has LOST 5 KG · she has NIGHT SWEATS · she has COUGHED UP BLOOD.**
**Haemoptysis is the coughing up of blood or blood-stained sputum arising from BELOW THE LARYNX. It is always abnormal and always requires an explanation.**

**Settle the source BEFORE building a differential list. HAEMOPTYSIS: coughed not vomited, bright red, often frothy, mixed with sputum, alkaline, preceded by a tickle. HAEMATEMESIS: vomited, dark or coffee-ground, mixed with FOOD, acidic, may be followed by melaena, with retching and epigastric pain. NASOPHARYNGEAL: spat or trickled, blood-streaked only, worse on waking, nosebleeds and sinusitis.**
**'It happened while she was eating dinner' is NOT decoration** — it is there to make you ask whether she vomited it rather than coughed it, and whether she choked.

**A 57-year-old with haemoptysis and 5 kg of unintentional weight loss has a cancer question attached to her until imaging says otherwise.** **Never-smokers get lung cancer — smoking changes the probability, not the differential.** **Weight-loss red flag: more than 5% of body weight in 6–12 months.**

**CORRECTION — Horner's syndrome is PTOSIS, MIOSIS and ANHIDROSIS, not facial droop.** Facial droop is a facial nerve palsy and points somewhere else entirely. **Pancoast invades the lower trunk of the brachial plexus at C8 and T1 and the sympathetic chain.**

**TB workup: CHEST X-RAY in every case · SPUTUM x3 for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture and NUCLEIC ACID AMPLIFICATION (Xpert MTB/RIF also reports rifampicin resistance) · AIRBORNE ISOLATION, negative-pressure room where available, N95 for staff · HIV serology with consent · NOTIFIABLE.** **IGRA and Mantoux support exposure only — they neither diagnose nor exclude active disease.**

**TB treatment: SIX MONTHS — two months of RIFAMPICIN, ISONIAZID, PYRAZINAMIDE and ETHAMBUTOL, then four months of RIFAMPICIN and ISONIAZID, plus PYRIDOXINE to prevent isoniazid neuropathy.** Counsel: **curable if taken in full · non-infectious within weeks of effective treatment · never stop early, that is how resistance develops · rifampicin turns urine, tears and sweat ORANGE and interacts with the pill · ethambutol can affect vision and colour vision · report jaundice, nausea or dark urine · contacts will be screened.** **In SA, TB treatment is FREE, including for people without Medicare — say so, it is often her first fear.**

**Massive haemoptysis: more than about 100 mL/hour or 200–600 mL in 24 hours — or ANY volume causing respiratory or haemodynamic compromise.** **ABC, high-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, cross-match, reverse anticoagulation, LIE THE PATIENT WITH THE BLEEDING SIDE DOWN to protect the good lung, urgent bronchoscopy or bronchial artery embolisation.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · TIS 131 450.**
plan: **To the examiner: 'before I start, could I have her vital signs — RESPIRATORY RATE AND OXYGEN SATURATION FIRST, and also blood pressure, pulse and temperature, because she is bleeding and infection is on my list.'** Then **open question.**

**The concern statement, and use all of it: 'I can see how stressful and frightening this must be. I'm going to ask you a few questions and examine you, and I'd like to reassure you that YOU ARE IN SAFE HANDS — we will work out what is causing this.'** To 'please tell me it's not something awful': **'I can't answer that until I've asked you some questions and examined you — but I promise I'll tell you exactly what I think before you leave.'**

**Explore the bleed: when exactly · is this the FIRST time · what colour, bright red or darker · HOW MUCH — A FEW DROPS, OR A LARGE AMOUNT · was it mixed with phlegm · how many times, and is it getting worse?**

**Explore the EVENT, and the four questions that eliminate the mimics in twenty seconds: WHAT WERE YOU DOING EXACTLY WHEN IT HAPPENED · WAS THERE ANY CHOKING BEFOREHAND · DID YOU NOTICE ANY BLEEDING FROM YOUR NOSE · DID YOU VOMIT ANY BLOOD, OR WAS IT DEFINITELY COUGHED UP?**

**The lung cancer block, which must not be skipped: have you lost any weight — HOW MUCH, AND OVER WHAT PERIOD · appetite · lumps or bumps · unusually tired · WHAT IS YOUR OCCUPATION NOW, AND WHAT DID YOU DO BEFORE · ever exposed to ASBESTOS · cough, breathlessness, noisy breathing · ever had cancer anywhere · AND TWO UNUSUAL ONES — any numbness or weakness in your hands, and have you noticed a DROOPING EYELID or a difference in pupil size?**

**The infection block, where the diagnosis lives: any fever or chills · ANY NIGHT SWEATS, waking up drenched · sore throat or runny nose · facial pain or secretions down the back of the throat · HAVE YOU TRAVELLED ANYWHERE RECENTLY · AND HAVE YOU HAD ANY CONTACT WITH PEOPLE WHO HAVE BEEN UNWELL, OR WITH ANIMALS?**

**The follow-up that is worth more than any other sentence in the station: 'CAN I ASK WHAT THAT WORK INVOLVED?'** Then **join it up OUT LOUD: 'so you've been directly caring for unwell people in a country where tuberculosis is common, you've lost five kilograms, you're having night sweats, and now you've coughed up blood.'**

**The remaining systems, fast, as rapid pairs — 'a few quick ones to make sure I'm not missing anything': ever smoked, now or before · repeated chest infections as a child, and daily phlegm volume · leg swelling or pain, long travel, family clots, pleuritic chest pain · chest pain, exertional breathlessness, breathless lying flat, HOW MANY PILLOWS, ankle swelling · blood thinners, family bleeding disorders, easy bruising, frequent nosebleeds · rashes, joint pains, BLOOD IN YOUR URINE · any injury to your chest.** Then **SADMA gaps only.**

**Request the examination in the standard sequence WITH ENT ADDED, and say why you are adding it:** general appearance including **pallor, clubbing, cachexia and cervical or supraclavicular nodes** · **ENT — nose on speculum, throat, sinus tenderness** · respiratory in full · cardiovascular aimed at heart failure · abdomen for **hepatomegaly** · lower limbs for calf asymmetry · **ECG and spirometry if available.**

**Say the normal-examination sentence BEFORE you interpret**, then **the diagnosis with the four reasons**, then **'I'm also concerned about the possibility of lung cancer, mainly because of the weight loss, so I'll check for that too — less likely than the infection, but I'm not going to leave it unchecked.'**

**The differentials, each with a one-line lay explanation AND the reason it is less likely**: bronchiectasis — no childhood infections · COPD — never smoked · heart failure — no orthopnoea, no ankle swelling · clot in the lung — no leg swelling or recent travel · bleeding from nose or throat — nothing found · lupus and the vasculitides — no rashes or joint pains.

**The plan and the infection-control sentence nobody says: chest X-ray, bloods, THREE SPUTUM SAMPLES, and a CT chest.** **'Because tuberculosis can spread through the air, I'm going to ask you to wear a mask while you're here, and if it is confirmed the public health team will contact the people close to you and offer them testing — that's routine, and it's for their protection, not because you've done anything wrong.'** Then **safety-net for a large bleed or breathlessness, and ASK WHETHER SHE HAS ANY WORRIES OR QUESTIONS.**
pefe: **Run the same sequence every time and ADD the relevant extra system.** The three you add only when relevant are **neurological, thyroid and ENT** — and **haemoptysis is the case where ENT earns its place.**

**Do now: full observations · MASK HER AND MOVE HER OUT OF THE SHARED WAITING ROOM if TB is on your list, before anything else · CHEST X-RAY, mandatory in every case of haemoptysis · FBE, CRP, U&E, LFT, coagulation profile and INR, group and hold if bleeding is significant · URINALYSIS, which is cheap and screens the pulmonary–renal syndromes.**

**For TB: sputum x3 for AFB smear, culture and nucleic acid amplification · airborne isolation and N95 · IGRA or Mantoux support exposure only · HIV serology with consent · NOTIFY — the Communicable Disease Control Branch coordinates contact tracing.**

**For lung cancer: CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST REGARDLESS — do not be reassured by a normal chest X-ray, a meaningful minority are missed on plain film.** Then **bronchoscopy or biopsy, and the lung cancer MDT.**
**For the rest: CTPA if embolism is suspected · echocardiogram for heart failure · high-resolution CT for bronchiectasis · ANCA, ANA and anti-GBM if vasculitis is on the list.**
**If Pancoast is suspected, add: Horner's syndrome — ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis — and an upper limb neurological examination testing the C8 and T1 dermatomes and the small muscles of the hand.**

**She is NOT a candidate for the National Lung Cancer Screening Program — not because of her age, but BECAUSE SHE IS SYMPTOMATIC. Symptomatic patients are investigated, not screened.** (NLCSP: 50–70, 30 or more pack-years, quit within 10 years, asymptomatic.) VERIFY.

stem: Your next patient is a 20-year-old woman with cough and shortness of breath. She developed flu-like symptoms three days ago and is now short of breath and feels feverish.
Her oxygen saturation is 92% on room air.
tasks: Take a focused history
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Request the investigations you would order
You are handed a chest X-ray — explain it to the patient
Explain the diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **Community-acquired pneumonia — with a severity attached, every time.** Not simply 'pneumonia': **the qualifier tells the examiner you considered where it was acquired, and it leaves the organism open** when you cannot yet say bacterial, atypical or viral. **A diagnosis without a severity is incomplete here, because severity chooses the drug, the route and the ward.**

**The station is not failed on the diagnosis. It is failed on the investigation list and on a differential that dies at three.** Documented pattern: **5 for history, 5 for examination, 5 for differentials, 1 for investigations — and a fail.**

**The nine-item list, four headings, one breath**: **Bedside — full observations including respiratory rate, continuous oximetry, bedside glucose, a 12-lead ECG, and an arterial blood gas. Imaging — chest X-ray, PA and lateral. Microbiology — sputum for Gram stain, culture and sensitivities; two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics; a nasopharyngeal swab for respiratory viral PCR including influenza and COVID-19; urinary antigens for pneumococcus and Legionella. Bloods — FBE; UEC, and I want the urea specifically because it is a CURB-65 item; LFTs including albumin, which is a SMART-COP item; CRP as a baseline; and a lactate if I am concerned about sepsis.**

**Saying WHY you want the urea and the albumin is worth more than the tests themselves.** And **the opposite error is penalised too** — a published examiner prompt instructs markers to mark down candidates who recite every test they can name. **Nine relevant items with reasons beats twenty without.**

**'Thank you — before I read this, may I finish my investigations?'** **The film arriving does not close the list**, and treating it as the end of the task is one of the two behaviours that produce the 1.

**Vocal resonance is the finding that separates consolidation from effusion over a dull zone.** **Increased, with bronchial breathing = consolidation. Decreased, with absent breath sounds = effusion** — and that answer is a chest ultrasound and a diagnostic tap.

**CRB-65 / CURB-65: confusion · urea >7 mmol/L · RR ≥30 · systolic BP <90 or diastolic ≤60 · age ≥65.** **SMART-COP ≥3 = high risk of needing intensive respiratory or vasopressor support; S, O and P score 2 each; albumin <35 g/L; pH <7.35; HR ≥125; multilobar shadowing.** **Her CRB-65 is 0 — but her saturation is 92% and the film is multilobar, so score SMART-COP formally with a gas and albumin before deciding disposition**, rather than sending her home on CRB-65 alone. VERIFY

**Say 'multilobar' if you see it.** It is a scored SMART-COP item and an admission argument on its own. **Candidates describe the obvious patch and never mention the second one — look at both bases and both apices before you speak.**

**The PE screen is mandatory in a hypoxic 20-year-old woman**: **pleuritic chest pain, calf pain or swelling, the combined oral contraceptive pill, long-haul travel, immobility, previous or family history of clots.** Then **say out loud why PE is less likely once you have focal consolidation** — **complete the screen, then reason; do not abandon pneumonia, and do not skip the screen.**

Antibiotics by severity: **low — amoxicillin 1 g oral 8-hourly for 5 days, plus doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly for atypical cover · moderate — benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV 6-hourly plus doxycycline · severe — ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily for 7 days · severe allergy — moxifloxacin 400 mg IV daily.** **Oxygen to 92–96%, or 88–92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure. Antibiotics within 1 hour in septic shock. Review at 48 hours. Repeat film at 6 weeks in a smoker over 50 — radiographic clearance lags clinical recovery by 4–6 weeks.** **Notifiable in SA: legionellosis, tuberculosis, Q fever, pertussis, invasive pneumococcal disease.** VERIFY
plan: **The stability statement before any question — the 92% is in the stem precisely so you say something about it**: **'before anything else I want to make sure you're safe. I'd like to move you to the resuscitation cubicle, put some oxygen on, and get a full set of observations. Then I'll ask some questions, look at your tests, and tell you what I think.'** Then to the examiner: **'could I have the blood pressure, pulse rate and temperature? I have the saturation from the stem.'**

Open question, then **one empathy line** — and **when she asks 'is it serious?', do not promise she will be fine**: **'that's exactly what I'm going to find out, and I'll tell you straight once I know.'**

The four complaints together: **when did the cough and breathlessness start · constant or coming and going · getting worse · difficulty getting air IN or tightness · at rest or only on moving · can you speak in full sentences · CAN YOU LIE FLAT.** **Do not spend a question on which came first — it changes nothing. Spend it on orthopnoea or exercise tolerance.**

**The sputum in full — C·C·C·V·O**: **dry or bringing something up · what colour · watery or thick and sticky · ANY BLOOD OR CLOTS · roughly how much · any bad smell?** Then the fever: **have you actually measured it · have you taken anything · DID IT BRING THE TEMPERATURE DOWN · any rigors or drenching night sweats · any whoop at the end of the cough · any vomiting after a coughing fit?** **A fever that settles then climbs is ordinary; a fever that will not come down at all in a hypoxic patient raises sepsis — say that reasoning aloud.**

**Box 1, upper airway**: **sore throat · runny or blocked nose · facial pressure · ear pain or discharge · lumps in the neck?** **Box 2, lower airway and the PE screen**: **any noisy or wheezy breathing · coughed up blood · ANY SHARP PAIN WHEN YOU BREATHE IN · any pain, swelling or tenderness in your calves · ever had asthma?**

**Box 3, atypical**: **diarrhoea, nausea or vomiting · bad headache or confusion · aching all over · recent travel, hotels or spas · anyone around you unwell · contact with birds, farm animals, or potting mix or compost?** **Box 4, risk**: **do you smoke — OR VAPE · alcohol · any long-term conditions · any medications including steroids or immune drugs · ARE YOU ON THE PILL · are your flu and COVID vaccinations up to date?**

**Close the PE loop out loud**: **'I asked about the pill and your calves because a clot on the lung can look like this.'** And **the vaping**: accepting 'I don't smoke' and moving on is the trap — ask it explicitly, then note it irritates the airway.

**Examination from the examiner — closed questions only, every one answerable with yes, no or a number.** General appearance → vitals → **ENT** → chest: expansion, trachea, percussion, breath sounds vesicular or bronchial, added sounds, **and vocal resonance increased, normal or decreased** → cardiovascular → abdomen. Then **name it**: **'dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance over one zone is consolidation.'**
**The full nine-item investigation list, grouped, with the two reasons attached.** If the film arrives mid-list: **'thank you — before I read this, may I finish my investigations?'**

**The film in plain English, forty-five seconds**: **bone white, soft tissue grey, air black · heart, spine, main airway · the left side, normal black lung with a sharp angle at the bottom · the right side, grey instead of black, where air has been pushed out and replaced by infection · AND a smaller patch at the left base.** **No opacity, consolidation, air bronchogram or silhouette sign to the patient — say which register you are in.**

Her two questions: **'isn't pneumonia only something old people get?'** — **'it's commoner in older people, but healthy young adults get it too, which is exactly why we treat it properly.'** And **'am I going to have to stay in?'** — **do not guess**: **'your oxygen is low and more than one part of the lung is involved, so I'll answer that once the gas and bloods are back and I've scored the severity.'**

**The diagnosis with its severity**, then **the differential in named groups** — above the voice box, in the lungs, in the circulation, and overall sepsis — **at least eight items, and name PE explicitly with why it is less likely.**

**Plan and safety net**: oxygen, the listed tests, antibiotics once cultures are taken, severity scored before disposition. **Come straight back if your breathing worsens, if you become confused or drowsy, if you can't keep fluids down, or if the fever won't settle.** Then **'is there anything you're worried about that I haven't covered?'** — **that is the only way the exams come out.**
pefe: **Ask the examiner for the vital signs in the first ten seconds** — you have the saturation from the stem.
**Closed questions only.** 'I'd like to examine the respiratory system' gets you nothing; every request must be answerable with yes, no or a number.

**The four-sentence sequence, fifteen seconds**: is expansion symmetrical, where is the trachea → is there dullness, and in which zone → are breath sounds vesicular or bronchial, any added sounds → **is vocal resonance increased, normal or decreased?**
**Do not skip ENT** — throat, nose, ears, neck nodes. The answer will be no; **the mark is for asking.** Then cardiovascular and abdomen in fifteen seconds each.

**Investigations, four headings**: **bedside** — observations, oximetry, glucose, ECG, **arterial blood gas** (pH and PaO2 are two of the three double-weighted SMART-COP items); **imaging** — CXR PA and lateral; **microbiology** — sputum, two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, viral PCR swab, urinary antigens; **bloods** — FBE, UEC with the urea, LFTs with albumin, CRP, lactate.

**The Legionella urinary antigen detects only serogroup 1 of L. pneumophila — it does NOT detect L. longbeachae**, which in Australia is at least as common and is the one associated with potting mix and compost. **If the history smells of Legionella, ask for lower respiratory PCR and culture on selective media as well.**
**Blood cultures ×2 before antibiotics — but do not delay antibiotics to obtain them.**

**Decline spirometry and say why.** **Avoid** the undifferentiated panel — naming ten irrelevant tests is explicitly penalised — routine CT chest at first presentation, and waiting for microbiology before treating.

Sudden onset, pleuritic pain, **hypoxia out of proportion to the film**, low-grade fever, tachycardia; oestrogen-containing pill, travel, immobility, malignancy
Calf swelling or tenderness; **a clear chest with a low saturation**

**Sepsis / septic shock**

Lactate, urine output, capillary refill, conscious state
**Lactate and cultures; antibiotics within one hour; fluids; senior review** — immediate

Rapid onset, rigors, **purulent or rusty sputum**, focal signs, lobar shadowing
**Dullness, bronchial breathing, increased vocal resonance**
**This is the diagnosis** — confirm with the film and cultures — same day

**Diarrhoea, nausea, headache, myalgia, fatigue**; travel, air-conditioning, spas, **potting mix**, farm animals, birds

Preceding coryza, sick contact with influenza

**Tuberculosis**

Upper-lobe or cavitating shadowing
**Three sputum specimens for AFB and PCR; respiratory isolation; notify** — urgent

Wheeze, atopy, previous attacks — or sudden pleuritic pain in a tall thin young person with hyper-resonance

Bronchodilator response and peak flow; erect film. **If tension is suspected, decompress before imaging** — immediate

**A whoop at the end of the cough; vomiting after a coughing fit**
Ask both — uncommon in adults, but adults transmit it to unvaccinated infants
**Pertussis PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab. Notifiable**
**Malignancy with post-obstructive pneumonia**
Smoker over 50, weight loss, haemoptysis, **a pneumonia that will not clear**
Persisting shadowing in the same lobe; clubbing; nodes
**Repeat film at six weeks; CT chest; respiratory referral** — urgent
Named upper airway infection
Sore throat, blocked nose, facial pressure, ear pain, **no hypoxia**
Pharynx, tonsils, sinuses, drums, nodes
**Say pharyngitis, tonsillitis or rhinosinusitis — never just 'URTI'**
Heart failure / pulmonary oedema
Orthopnoea, PND, **frothy pink sputum**, ankle swelling
Raised JVP, third heart sound, bibasal fine crackles
ECG, NT-proBNP, echocardiogram

stem: A 70-year-old man has been diagnosed with a high-severity community-acquired pneumonia. He is confused and disoriented. eGFR 50. Documented allergy to amoxicillin and penicillin.
His daughter is with him. An antibiotic table is displayed on the screen.
tasks: Take a three-minute history (from the daughter)
Explain the condition and why it is high severity to the daughter
Explain your antibiotic choice

dx: **High-severity community-acquired pneumonia in a 70-year-old with a documented penicillin allergy.** **This is a management case wearing an unfamiliar costume — three minutes of history is not enough for anything else.** Spend it on **the two questions that choose the antibiotic**, then on severity risk factors and comorbidity.

**The two allergy questions, and they must both be asked**: **'what actually happened — a rash, an upset tummy, or swelling of the lips or face, wheezing, collapse?'** and **'how soon after the dose — within an hour or two, or days later?'**

**CORRECTION — cross-reactivity is about the SIDE CHAIN, not the beta-lactam ring.** The old teaching of a blanket 10% penicillin–cephalosporin cross-reactivity is wrong. **Ceftriaxone and cefotaxime share no R1 side chain with amoxicillin, so they are acceptable in non-severe amoxicillin allergy. Cefalexin and cefaclor DO share it — those are the ones to avoid.**

**The answer for a delayed rash**: **'that was a rash, three days later — a non-severe delayed reaction. That means I can safely use ceftriaxone: it shares no side chain with amoxicillin. I'd give ceftriaxone 1 g intravenously daily plus azithromycin 500 mg intravenously daily, for seven days, switching to tablets once he's stable.'** VERIFY

**The answer for anaphylaxis**: **'if instead he'd had swelling and collapse within twenty minutes, I would avoid all penicillin-type drugs and use moxifloxacin 400 mg intravenously daily.'** **Avoid all beta-lactams only in a severe immediate reaction such as anaphylaxis, or a severe delayed reaction such as SJS, TEN or DRESS.** VERIFY
**If challenged**: **'Therapeutic Guidelines permits cephalosporins with a dissimilar side chain in non-severe penicillin hypersensitivity. Ceftriaxone qualifies.'**

**Name the severity tools while speaking to the daughter — this is the warfarin-counselling manoeuvre.** She does not care that it is called CURB-65, but **the examiner needs to hear it**: **'we use a tool called CURB-65 — whether the person is confused, whether a kidney blood test called urea is high, whether they are breathing fast, whether the blood pressure is low, and whether they are over 65. This one is not.** **The two stems differ by one line, and the one line is the station.** One recent stem states explicitly: **do not explain palliative care.**

**Read the directive out loud, early**: **'before I go through the plan — I have read your father's advance care directive, and I can see he has asked for all treatment that may help him. We will be following that.'** Then confirm standing: **'can I check — are you his substitute decision-maker, and do you have his consent for me to discuss his condition with you?'**
**Candidates who reach for palliative care are told flatly by the role-player that the family does not want it, and the station never recovers.** Say the acknowledgement, then move on to management.

**Short-term**: **ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily for seven days, switching to tablets once he is stable.** **If he deteriorates, intensive care; if his breathing becomes too laboured to sustain, intubation and mechanical ventilation — and that is within what he has asked for.** VERIFY doses against Therapeutic Guidelines.

dx: **Post-operative atelectasis on day 1.** Splinting from wound pain → shallow tidal volumes → alveolar collapse, basal or mid-zone, with fever, tachypnoea and desaturation. **Loss of lung volume from collapse of alveoli that are no longer being inflated — not an infection, though it predisposes to one.**

**Nobody is marked on knowing the answer.** You are marked on **a differential list generated by the post-operative TIMELINE**, on including **the two things that kill — myocardial infarction and venous thromboembolism** — and on **asking for the one finding that separates collapse from consolidation**.

**Say the list in this shape: in the first few hours — the inflammatory response itself, drug or transfusion reaction, malignant hyperthermia, or an infection he brought in with him. In the first three days — atelectasis and pneumonia, myocardial infarction, UTI, early wound infection, VTE. After day three — wound infection, a surgery-specific complication such as a collection or bile leak, thrombophlebitis, hospital-acquired infection, drug fever. He is on day one, so my list narrows to the middle group.**
**Vocal resonance is the discriminator. NORMAL OR REDUCED = atelectasis. INCREASED = consolidation.** Air entry, crepitations and a dull percussion note are **identical in both**.

**Pain is a respiratory question.** A painful abdominal wound means no deep breath, and shallow breathing without periodic sighs collapses dependent alveoli within hours — **which is why analgesia is the first line of treatment, not physiotherapy.**

Management, in this order: **1 optimised multimodal analgesia — paracetamol 1 g every 6 h, max 4 g in 24 h, an NSAID if renal function and the surgical team allow, an opioid or PCA for breakthrough · 2 paracetamol also treats the fever · 3 continuous saturation, oxygen to 92–96% · 4 chest physiotherapy TODAY — deep breathing and effective cough with wound support · 5 sit up and mobilise, which is also VTE prophylaxis · 6 smoking cessation now, Quitline 13 7848 · 7 review in a few hours.**
**ANTIBIOTICS ARE NOT INDICATED FOR ATELECTASIS.** Say it deliberately — prescribing them is the reasoning error the examiner is watching for.

**CORRECTION — it is malignant HYPERthermia**, a pharmacogenetic hypermetabolic crisis triggered by volatile agents and suxamethonium, treated with **dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV**. **CORRECTION — ask for FBE and CRP, not ESR**: ESR rises non-specifically after any surgery and lags by days, and CRP is raised by the operation itself on day 1, so use the trend.

**The Five Ws are second-best**: Wind d1–2 · Water d3–5 · Walking d4–6 · Wound d5–7 · Wonder drugs d7+. **They omit myocardial infarction and anastomotic or bile leak entirely** — the two things that will actually fail you. Use the timeline, keep the Ws as a cross-check.

**Escalate tonight for: systolic under 90 · heart rate over 130 · respiratory rate over 25 despite oxygen · new confusion · lactate 2 or more · bilious drain output · generalised abdominal tenderness.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS 131 450.**
plan: **To the examiner first: 'before I begin I'd like this patient on continuous observations, and I'd move him to a monitored bed if he deteriorates. I have the chart, so I'll proceed.'** Six seconds, and it is a scored line. Then gel, introduce, open question.

**The concern statement — do not skip it**: **'I completely understand why a temperature after an operation is worrying. Let me ask you some questions and examine you, then we'll work out the cause together and I'll tell you exactly what we're going to do.'**

**Box 1, the fever itself: do you feel feverish? any shivering or shaking chills? when did it start? DID YOU HAVE ANY FEVER BEFORE THE OPERATION? is it getting worse?** Rigors point to bacteraemia rather than collapse; fever before the list means the infection came in with him.

**Box 2, the post-operative review — the block everyone skips: any nausea or vomiting? have your bowels worked, have you passed wind? any tummy pain apart from the wound? any dizziness? have you started eating and drinking? HAVE YOU BEEN OUT OF BED? ARE YOU IN PAIN RIGHT NOW — AND ARE THE PAINKILLERS HELPING?** When he says it hurts to breathe in, **react to it in the room**: 'that's really important — I think the pain is part of what's causing this.'
**Box 3, chest: any cough — dry or bringing anything up, what colour? any shortness of breath? any noisy breathing? ever had a lung condition? do you smoke, or have you ever?**

**Box 4, heart — the box that decides Version B and the single most dangerous omission: ANY CHEST PAIN OR TIGHTNESS, EVEN BRIEFLY? have you noticed your heart racing or thumping? any previous heart trouble, heart attack or angina?** If he has known ischaemic disease, **which cardiac medicines were withheld for surgery** — abrupt beta-blocker cessation causes rebound ischaemia.
**Box 5, urine: any burning or pain passing urine? going more often? cloudy or offensive? any back or loin pain? HAVE YOU HAD A CATHETER?**

**Box 6, the wound: any discharge or weeping? any redness or swelling? is it more painful than yesterday?** Discharge is the discriminating symptom — some redness after a fresh incision is normal, **escalating pain is not**.
**Box 7, legs: any swelling or pain in the calves? any sharp chest pain on breathing in, or coughed up blood? have you had the blood-thinning injection each day?**

**Box 8, travel — and say why: 'did you travel anywhere in the weeks before the operation? I ask because an infection picked up before surgery can present like this'** — not because you are chasing a clot.

**Box 9, lines, drugs and blood: any redness or pain around the drip site — AND WHEN WAS IT PUT IN? have you ever had a fever after an operation before, after a blood transfusion, or after starting a new medicine?** That last sentence ticks off drug fever, transfusion reaction and a family history of malignant hyperthermia at once.
**Closure: any other medical conditions, regular medicines, allergies, anything in the family? And is there anything you were hoping I'd ask that I haven't?**

**The examination request, specific not generic**: general appearance · 'I have the vital signs, so I'll move on' — **say it, don't silently skip it** · **respiratory in full ending with VOCAL RESONANCE** · cardiovascular · **abdomen with the four asks — wound, suprapubic, renal angle, masses, plus distension and drain** · **cannula site, I'm looking for thrombophlebitis** · **lower limbs for oedema, calf size difference and tenderness** · **urine dipstick**.

**Say 'I've grouped my differentials by how long it is since the operation'**, deliver the timeline list, **then** name atelectasis in plain English — **'because of the pain you haven't been breathing deeply, and a small part of your lung has collapsed down'** — and **name the differentials to the patient** so he could repeat them back.

**Management with ANALGESIA FIRST**, then paracetamol for the fever, chest X-ray and bloods, urine to the lab, monitoring and oxygen, **physiotherapy today**, sitting up and out of bed, no smoking, **'antibiotics don't treat a collapsed lung'**, review this afternoon, and the safety-net: **breathing worse, chest pain, racing heart, wound leaking or much more painful, feeling faint — tell the nurses immediately.**
pefe: Request it in this order: **general appearance — respiratory distress, cyanosis, IS HE IN PAIN · vital signs (say you have them) · respiratory — symmetrical movements, tracheal position, percussion note, breath sounds and added sounds, AND VOCAL RESONANCE · cardiovascular — S1, S2, murmurs, gallop · abdomen — the surgical site, SUPRAPUBIC tenderness, RENAL ANGLE tenderness, masses, distension and what is in the drain · cannula site for erythema, tenderness or discharge · lower limbs for oedema, calf size difference and calf tenderness · and a urine dipstick.**

**Do now, before you leave the room: full observations with a repeat temperature · urine dipstick · 12-lead ECG if any chest pain, palpitations, tachycardia or hypertension · inspect the wound, cannula and drain yourself · oxygen to 92–96% · and FIX THE ANALGESIA NOW rather than deferring it to the plan.**

**Do next: CHEST X-RAY — the single most useful test, separating collapse from consolidation · FBE and CRP · urine MCS, because a UTI can be present with a negative dipstick · two sets of blood cultures if septic or rigoring · serial troponin if the ECG or history raises cardiac concern · U&E, LFT and lipase with abdominal signs, and CT abdomen with contrast if a collection or bile leak is suspected · venous lactate if any sepsis features.**
**Do not order more than this** — a scattergun panel reads as absent reasoning, and you still have to talk about management.
**D-dimer is unreliable post-operatively** — go to compression ultrasound or CTPA. **Dipstick alone misses infection and is unreliable with a catheter.**

**Cannulae are reviewed daily and generally resited by 72 hours** unless clinically indicated sooner. VERIFY against local SA Health policy — some sites work to 72–96 hours or replace on clinical indication only.
**Avoid: diagnosing atelectasis without a chest X-ray · antibiotics 'just in case' · treating the fever and ignoring the pain · 'the physio will sort it out' as your whole plan.**

stem: James Whitmore, 45, is two to three days post-cholecystectomy and has developed a fever. The nurse asks you to review him.
Observations: temperature 38.4°C · pulse 112 · BP 168/96 · respiratory rate 16 · SpO2 97% on room air.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
Outline your management plan
findings: Observations
T 38.4 · PULSE 112 · BP 168/96 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% ON ROOM AIR. THE RESPIRATORY RATE AND SATURATION ARE NORMAL — that is the entire point of this version
Chest examination
ENTIRELY NORMAL. Air entry equal, NO crepitations, percussion normal, vocal resonance normal. THERE ARE NO CHEST SIGNS
Abdomen and limbs
Abdomen soft, wound clean and dry. Calves soft and equal
The history that flips the station

CHEST TIGHTNESS FOR ABOUT TWENTY MINUTES OVERNIGHT — 'I thought it was indigestion' · HEART THUMPING · FATHER HAD A HEART ATTACK AT 50 · HIS BLOOD PRESSURE TABLETS WERE WITHHELD FOR SURGERY. None of it is volunteered unless you ask Box 4
What you do before anything else
12-LEAD ECG NOW and SERIAL TROPONIN, on cardiac monitoring, and involve the medical team. Post-operative MI is frequently SILENT OR ATYPICAL
The honest caveat if pressed

This pilot case was never definitively resolved. Do not invent an answer: 'with normal respiratory observations and no chest signs I cannot call this atelectasis. My working diagnosis is a cardiac event until the ECG and troponin say otherwise, and I would also want to exclude an intra-abdominal complication given the abdominal surgery.' That answer scores whatever the truth was
VERSION — day 4, the bile leak

Pain spread across the WHOLE abdomen, no flatus since yesterday, vomiting, DRAIN BAG HAS GONE GREEN, mild jaundice → BILE LEAK or subhepatic collection. Blood cultures and lactate, FBE, CRP, U&E, LFT, lipase, CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast, fasted with IV fluids, SURGICAL REGISTRAR NOW. Not physiotherapy and reassurance
VERSION — the septic turn mid-station

The nurse reports BP 85/50 and heart rate 132. STOP THE HISTORY. High-flow oxygen, two large-bore cannulae, blood cultures, venous lactate, fluid bolus, empirical IV antibiotics within the hour, catheterise for urine output, escalate to the surgical registrar and intensive care, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 EARLY
findingsLabel: Observations and what the absences mean
must: FAIL — Diagnosing atelectasis with a normal respiratory rate, normal saturation and no chest signs.
FAIL — A differential list with no cardiac entry. That is why this version exists.
FAIL — Continuing the history through a deteriorating patient instead of naming the pathway.
FAIL — Inventing a definitive diagnosis when the honest answer scores better.
ASK — Any chest pain or tightness, even briefly? Have you noticed your heart racing?
ASK — Which of your usual cardiac and blood pressure tablets were withheld for surgery?

dx: **A cardiac event until proven otherwise — post-operative myocardial infarction.** Fever, tachycardia and hypertension **with a normal respiratory rate, normal saturation and no chest findings is not atelectasis.**

**This version was piloted once and almost nobody diagnosed it**, because candidate differential lists for post-operative fever traditionally contain **no cardiac entry at all**. **Keep MI on the list in every post-operative fever station you ever sit.**

**Surgery is a major physiological stressor, and post-operative MI is frequently silent or atypical.** In a 45-year-old with cardiovascular risk it is **the single most dangerous omission in this station**.
**ECG and serial troponin before anything else**, cardiac monitoring, and involve the medical team. **Do not wait to be asked.**
**Ask which cardiac and antihypertensive medicines were withheld peri-operatively** — **abrupt beta-blocker cessation causes rebound ischaemia**.

**The same observations also fit a surgery-specific complication** — **bile leak or subhepatic collection** — and that must be voiced in an abdominal case, alongside **pulmonary embolism**, which fever does not exclude.

**The honest caveat scores**: 'with normal respiratory observations and no chest signs I cannot call this atelectasis. My working diagnosis is a cardiac event until the ECG and troponin say otherwise, and I would also want to exclude an intra-abdominal complication.' **Do not invent a final diagnosis.**

**Say it to the patient without frightening him**: **'I'm concerned the operation may have put strain on your heart. I want to rule out a heart attack first, because that's the one that can't wait — so I'm doing a heart tracing and a blood test right now, and asking the medical team to see you.'**

**Escalation triggers: systolic under 90 · heart rate over 130 · respiratory rate over 25 · new confusion · lactate 2 or more · bilious drain output · generalised abdominal tenderness.** **Never keep taking a history through a deteriorating patient** — name the change, name the pathway, name who you are calling.

**The timeline still drives the list: day 2–3 is the EARLY group** — atelectasis and pneumonia, **myocardial infarction**, UTI, early wound infection, VTE. **The Five Ws omit MI and anastomotic leak entirely.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **Stability statement to the examiner**, then gel, introduce, open question, **and the concern statement.** Note the observations aloud: **fever with tachycardia and hypertension, but a NORMAL respiratory rate and saturation.**
**Box 1, the fever: feverish yourself? shivering or shaking chills? when did it start? any fever before the operation? getting worse?**

**Box 2, the post-operative review — the block everyone skips: any nausea or vomiting? have your bowels worked, have you passed wind? any tummy pain apart from the wound? any dizziness? have you started eating and drinking? HAVE YOU BEEN OUT OF BED? ARE YOU IN PAIN RIGHT NOW — AND ARE THE PAINKILLERS HELPING?** When he says it hurts to breathe in, **react to it in the room**: 'that's really important — I think the pain is part of what's causing this.'
**Box 3, chest: any cough — dry or bringing anything up, what colour? any shortness of breath? any noisy breathing? ever had a lung condition? do you smoke, or have you ever?**

**Box 4, heart — the box that decides Version B and the single most dangerous omission: ANY CHEST PAIN OR TIGHTNESS, EVEN BRIEFLY? have you noticed your heart racing or thumping? any previous heart trouble, heart attack or angina?** If he has known ischaemic disease, **which cardiac medicines were withheld for surgery** — abrupt beta-blocker cessation causes rebound ischaemia.
**Box 5, urine: any burning or pain passing urine? going more often? cloudy or offensive? any back or loin pain? HAVE YOU HAD A CATHETER?**

**Box 6, the wound: any discharge or weeping? any redness or swelling? is it more painful than yesterday?** Discharge is the discriminating symptom — some redness after a fresh incision is normal, **escalating pain is not**.
**Box 7, legs: any swelling or pain in the calves? any sharp chest pain on breathing in, or coughed up blood? have you had the blood-thinning injection each day?**

**Box 8, travel — and say why: 'did you travel anywhere in the weeks before the operation? I ask because an infection picked up before surgery can present like this'** — not because you are chasing a clot.

**Box 9, lines, drugs and blood: any redness or pain around the drip site — AND WHEN WAS IT PUT IN? have you ever had a fever after an operation before, after a blood transfusion, or after starting a new medicine?** That last sentence ticks off drug fever, transfusion reaction and a family history of malignant hyperthermia at once.
Closure and the concerns question.

**The examination request, specific not generic** — general appearance · respiratory in full **including vocal resonance**, which will be normal · **cardiovascular in detail here, not briefly** · abdomen with the four asks and the drain · cannula site · lower limbs · urine dipstick.

**Name what the findings do NOT support**: with a normal respiratory rate, normal saturations and no chest signs, **this is not atelectasis.** Then **'my working diagnosis is a cardiac event until proven otherwise.'**

**To the patient, plainly**: strain on the heart, ruling out a heart attack first because it is the one that cannot wait, a heart tracing and a blood test **right now**, medical team to see him. Then the others still on the list — a chest problem, a urine infection, a clot, a problem at the operation site.

**The plan: 12-lead ECG and serial troponin, cardiac monitoring, medical review, and ask which cardiac medicines were withheld.** In parallel keep **PE and an intra-abdominal complication** live. Safety-net and review.
pefe: **ECG and serial troponin first**, then everything else. **Cardiac monitoring.** Ask **which cardiac and antihypertensive medicines were withheld peri-operatively.**
Request the examination in the same nine-part order as Version A, but **cardiovascular is central here, not brief** — S1 and S2, murmurs, added sounds, gallop rhythm.
**Ask for vocal resonance anyway** — it will be normal, and saying so is what lets you exclude the chest confidently rather than by assumption.

**Still ask the four abdominal items — wound, suprapubic, renal angle, masses — plus distension and drain output**, because the same observations fit a bile leak or subhepatic collection after cholecystectomy.

Bloods: **FBE and CRP** (not ESR — it rises non-specifically after surgery and lags by days) **· U&E, LFT, lipase if abdominal signs · venous lactate if any sepsis features · two sets of blood cultures if rigoring or septic.** **CT abdomen with contrast** if a collection or leak is suspected.
**D-dimer is unreliable post-operatively** — go to compression ultrasound or CTPA if VTE is suspected.
**Escalate rather than review in the morning** for MI, PE, anastomotic or bile leak, necrotising surgical site infection, or sepsis of any source.

stem: A 40-year-old woman has been brought to the clinic feeling unwell. Her relative is with her and will speak to you.
Vital signs: BP 85/55 · pulse 122 · respiratory rate 18 · SpO2 93% on room air · temperature 36.8°C.
tasks: Take a history from the relative
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials
findings: Vital signs in the stem

BP 85/55 — SHOCK · PULSE 122 · RR 18, DECEPTIVELY NORMAL · SpO2 93% on room air · T 36.8, which ARGUES AGAINST SEPSIS. React to them: 'with those observations I'd take her to the treatment room now, LIE HER FLAT, continuous monitoring, and a colleague with her'
General appearance
PALE AND DISTRESSED, no cyanosis, MILD FLUSHING OVER THE CHEST, alert
AIRWAY — asked FIRST, before the routine systems

NO LIP OR TONGUE SWELLING. NO STRIDOR. Stridor belongs to no single system examination, so ask for it DELIBERATELY or you will lose it. If you start at the top of the respiratory examination you run out of time before the tongue — and THE TONGUE IS THE ONE THAT KILLS
The sting

AN INSECT BITE ON THE NECK; NO RETAINED STING. Ask the whole sentence: 'DO I SEE A STING? IF SO, MAY I REMOVE IT?' — a honeybee leaves a barbed sting whose venom sac keeps pumping; flick or scrape it out, DO NOT hunt for tweezers
Respiratory

AIR ENTRY EQUAL with WIDESPREAD EXPIRATORY WHEEZE. WHEEZE is expiratory, polyphonic, LOWER airway. STRIDOR is inspiratory, monophonic, harsh, loudest over the neck, UPPER airway — and far more ominous
Cardiovascular
Heart sounds dual, no murmur. CAPILLARY REFILL 3 SECONDS, PERIPHERIES WARM — WARM, VASODILATED shock, which argues AGAINST a cardiac cause
Abdomen and neurological
Abdomen SOFT, non-tender, NO MASSES and NO EXPANSILE PULSATILE MASS, no flank or periumbilical bruising. Neurological examination NORMAL
Bedside tests
BLOOD GLUCOSE 6.2 · urine dipstick NEGATIVE · ECG SINUS TACHYCARDIA. CORRECTION — the glucose is to exclude HYPOglycaemia, not hyperglycaemia
What the relative gives only if you ask

THE STING comes only when you ask 'WHAT WAS SHE DOING JUST BEFORE THIS STARTED?' — otherwise she holds it until five minutes. Blotchy chest that BLANCHES on pressure. Throat 'felt funny' but voice unchanged. Nearly collapsed on standing. Hay fever and mild childhood asthma. No known allergies, no EpiPen, no medications
Read the findings back before you interpret
'So: an insect bite, wheeze, warm shocked peripheries, no airway swelling and a normal glucose.' Saying it aloud shows you heard it and buys three seconds to think
findingsLabel: Examiner stage — airway and the sting first, then the systems
must: FAIL — A perfect history, the word anaphylaxis at 7:45, and adrenaline never named.
FAIL — Wrong dose, route or site; or letting her stand or walk while hypotensive.
FAIL — Explaining the diagnosis to the relative without the consent gate.
FAIL — Antihistamine or steroid first, or missing meningococcaemia by not asking if the rash blanches.
ASK — Has she agreed to my discussing her condition with you?
ASK — What was she doing just before this started?

dx: **Anaphylaxis to an insect sting** — a severe, rapid-onset, generalised IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reaction with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise. **It is a CLINICAL diagnosis: treat, do not test.**
**The one sentence to memorise: nobody dies from a dose of intramuscular adrenaline; people die from the dose that was not given. If you are in any doubt at all, give it.**

**ASCIA — two routes. ROUTE 1: acute onset with typical SKIN features PLUS respiratory OR cardiovascular OR persistent severe gastrointestinal involvement. ROUTE 2: acute HYPOTENSION or BRONCHOSPASM or UPPER AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION after a likely trigger, EVEN WITH NO SKIN SIGNS.** **This case runs on Route 2.**

**The ten-second line, said the moment the sting emerges: 'that changes things. While we talk — I want her LYING FLAT and not standing up, I'm giving her an injection of ADRENALINE INTO HER THIGH now, and I'm CALLING AN AMBULANCE. I'll keep asking questions while that happens.'** That sentence is the difference between a candidate who recognised anaphylaxis and one who described it.

**ADRENALINE: 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 (1 mg in 1 mL — the SHORT ampoule), INTRAMUSCULAR into the OUTER MID-THIGH, MAXIMUM 0.5 mg. A 100 kg adult still gets 0.5 mg, not 1 mg. REPEAT EVERY 5 MINUTES. Never IV bolus outside a monitored setting.** **Autoinjectors: 150 microg for 7.5–20 kg · 300 microg for over 20 kg, the ADULT dose · 500 microg Anapen over 50 kg where supplied.** VERIFY.

**POSITION KILLS PEOPLE. LIE FLAT. Do not stand, do not walk — standing empties an already-empty heart and sudden death has occurred on standing.** Sit with legs outstretched ONLY if breathing is too difficult supine; **left lateral in pregnancy; recovery position if unconscious.**

**ANTIHISTAMINES AND STEROIDS ARE NOT TREATMENT.** Neither reverses airway obstruction or hypotension, and reaching for them DELAYS ADRENALINE. **Promethazine and other sedating antihistamines can worsen hypotension.** **Corticosteroids are no longer recommended routinely to prevent biphasic reactions.** VERIFY.

**The consent gate is a scored LEGAL step: taking a history from a relative is receiving information; EXPLAINING the diagnosis is a DISCLOSURE and needs the patient's consent unless she lacks capacity.** Being a husband, sister or cousin confers nothing. **If she is too unwell: 'she isn't well enough to consent right now, so I'll share what I need to in her best interests and to get her treated.'**

**Then: 000 and say the word anaphylaxis · high-flow oxygen and airway support · IV access with NORMAL SALINE 20 mL/kg rapidly for persistent hypotension · continuous monitoring.** **Poor response means REPEAT IM ADRENALINE — most failures are under-dosing or a delayed first dose, not resistance.** **Nebulised adrenaline for persistent upper airway obstruction; salbutamol for wheeze AFTER adrenaline, never instead; glucagon if she takes a beta-blocker.**

**After-care: OBSERVE AT LEAST 4 HOURS after the last adrenaline dose, longer if severe, repeated doses, asthma, or remote from help · TWO autoinjectors with hands-on training · a completed ASCIA Action Plan · a medical alert bracelet · avoidance advice · referral for VENOM IMMUNOTHERAPY, which is highly effective for bee, wasp and jack jumper ant.** **Tryptase 15 min–3 h with a later baseline supports it retrospectively but must NEVER delay treatment.** **000 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **To the examiner FIRST: 'given these observations I'd move her to the treatment room now, LIE HER FLAT, put her on continuous monitoring and have a colleague stay with her. I'll take the history while that happens.'** Then introduce and open: **'I can see you're both worried. Can you tell me what has happened?'**
**Concern statement, then THE CONSENT GATE — six seconds, and the item most candidates omit: 'before we go further — HAS SHE AGREED TO MY DISCUSSING HER CONDITION WITH YOU?'**

**Unpack 'unwell' by GIVING EXAMPLES — a lay person cannot answer it cold: 'does she seem CONFUSED or SLEEPY? Is she WEAK or exhausted? Does she feel HOT or FEVERISH? Is she STRUGGLING TO BREATHE?'** Then **when did this start · is it getting worse · has anything like this happened before?**

**The highest-value question in the station, asked open: 'WHAT WAS SHE DOING JUST BEFORE THIS STARTED?'** If it does not come: **'has she eaten anything unusual, taken any new medicine, or been stung or bitten?'**
**Say the ten-second treatment line the moment the sting emerges** — flat, adrenaline, ambulance — **then carry on with the history, because the answers still matter.**

**The four systems. SKIN: any rash, hives or welts · itchy · swelling of face, lips or eyes? RESPIRATORY: any noisy breathing and what does it sound like · short of breath · cough — AND IS HER TONGUE SWOLLEN · DOES SHE SAY HER THROAT FEELS TIGHT · HAS HER VOICE CHANGED?**

**CARDIOVASCULAR: has she felt dizzy or faint · did she lose consciousness or collapse? GASTROINTESTINAL: any nausea or vomiting · any tummy pain?** **After a sting, persistent vomiting or abdominal pain ARE anaphylaxis, not a mild reaction.**

**The mimics, signposted: 'I'm confident this is an allergic reaction, but I want to be sure I'm not missing an infection, a cardiac problem or a bleed.' INFECTION: any fever or chills · DOES THE RASH FADE WHEN YOU PRESS ON IT · any headache, neck stiffness or dislike of bright light · any flu-like illness recently?**

**CARDIAC: any chest pain · has she said her heart was racing or thumping? NEUROLOGICAL: any numbness or weakness in her arms or legs · slurred speech · trouble with balance · any sudden severe headache?**

**THE ABDOMINAL CATASTROPHE: any tummy or back pain · vomiting or diarrhoea · black or bloody bowel motions · and, flagging the awkwardness, DO YOU KNOW WHEN HER LAST PERIOD WAS?** Ruptured AAA and ruptured ectopic are both famous AMC stems.

**Background: any medical conditions, IN PARTICULAR ASTHMA — the strongest predictor of a fatal reaction · any known allergies, any previous reaction like this · does she carry an EpiPen · what medicines, anything for DIABETES or BLOOD PRESSURE · alcohol or drugs?**

**The examination request — AIRWAY AND THE STING FIRST, then the systems: general appearance · IS THERE SWELLING OF THE LIPS OR TONGUE · IS THERE STRIDOR · DO I SEE A STING, AND MAY I REMOVE IT · respiratory · cardiovascular including CAPILLARY REFILL AND PERIPHERAL TEMPERATURE · abdomen including AN EXPANSILE PULSATILE MASS and flank bruising · neurological · and bedside BLOOD GLUCOSE, urine dipstick and a 12-lead ECG.**

**Read the findings back, then the diagnosis with THREE REASONS in plain English** — it started within minutes of the sting; her blood pressure is low and her heart is racing, which is what a severe reaction does to the circulation; and she is wheezing because the small airways have tightened. **Then the treatment, given, and the four hours in hospital.**

**The differentials in lay language, six buckets each with a reason** — a serious infection in the blood, a heart problem, a stroke, a bleed inside the tummy, a low blood sugar, a reaction to a medicine. **'Nothing points to those, but I've specifically checked each one.'** Then **after-care and 'is there anything you'd like me to go over?'**
pefe: **Order matters more than completeness. Ask the anaphylaxis-specific items FIRST — lips, tongue, stridor, the sting — and only then run your standard structure.**

**Say the whole sting sentence: 'do I see a sting? If yes, I'd like to remove it now — I'll flick or scrape it out rather than looking for tweezers, because speed matters more than technique.'** Eight seconds, and it shows recognition, treatment and reasoning at once.

**Four abdominal questions sweep the whole catastrophe group in fifteen seconds: swelling or redness · tenderness · masses, IN PARTICULAR AN EXPANSILE PULSATILE MASS · flank or periumbilical bruising.** Say what you are looking for, not just where.

**Bedside blood glucose is the cheapest, fastest test in the station — and it is to exclude HYPOglycaemia.** Diabetes medication raises that risk; **beta-blockers blunt the response to adrenaline and may require glucagon.**
**Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis — treat, do not test. Serum tryptase (15 min to 3 hours plus a later baseline) offers retrospective support only and must not delay adrenaline.**

**Do not miss: delaying adrenaline for an antihistamine or steroid · letting her stand or walk · IV bolus adrenaline in an unmonitored clinic · discharging without observation · disclosing to a relative without consent · promethazine.**
**Premature closure works both ways** — the subtler trap is seeing a sting and stopping. **Ask the mimic questions even when you are certain, and say why you are asking.**
ddx: **Anaphylaxis** — the answer
**Onset within minutes of a sting**, hypotension with tachycardia, wheeze, urticaria, vomiting after a sting

**E — endocrine: do you have a weather preference, are you intolerant of cold or of heat? are you passing more urine than usual? any increase in thirst?** Positive → weight, bowels, hair and skin, voice, neck swelling, periods; or blurred vision, thrush, numb feet.

**M — malignancy: have you lost any weight without trying? how is your appetite? any lumps or bumps anywhere? any night sweats? any cancer in you or the family?** Positive → quantify the loss in kilograms and months, then a site-specific screen.

**I — infection: any fevers or chills? any flu-like illness or sore throat recently? HAVE YOU EVER BEEN SEXUALLY ACTIVE — and do you use condoms? have you travelled anywhere recently?** Never 'are you' sexually active. Travel → where, when, how long, rural or urban, bites, prophylaxis, fresh-water swimming.

**A — anaemia and autoimmune: any racing of the heart or shortness of breath on exertion? ANY RECENT BLOOD LOSS — heavy periods, blood in the stool, recent surgery or delivery? any shoulder or hip stiffness, or new headaches? any joint pains or rashes?**

**D — drugs and depression: do you use any drugs? are you on any medicines, including over the counter? HOW HAS YOUR MOOD BEEN? are you still enjoying the things you used to enjoy? any stress at home or at work?** A positive mood screen OBLIGES a risk assessment — self-harm, suicidal thoughts, plans, protective factors.
**C — coeliac and cardiopulmonary: any greasy stools? any blood in your bowel motions? any chest pain or swelling in the legs? any cough — have you ever coughed up blood? do you smoke?**
**O — OSA and occupation: has anyone told you that you snore or gasp during sleep? WHAT IS YOUR JOB — do you work night shifts?** The occupation question is how you find the truck driver.
**P — pregnancy and perimenopause: WHEN WAS YOUR LAST MENSTRUAL PERIOD? have you had any hot flushes or night sweats?** Ask it INSIDE the differential block, never inside SADMA at 7:30.
**Probe the one positive.** The LMP comes back at about eight weeks — then **any morning nausea? any breast tenderness? any chance you could be pregnant? what contraception are you using?**
**Closure in one breath if the clock allows** — smoking, alcohol, allergies, other conditions, family history.

**Name it, explain it, give the three reasons**, then **two or three differentials excluded by one finding each**, then **'I don't have long, so let me list the rest I've been checking through'** and keep going until the bell.

**Never omit: LMP in any woman of reproductive age · a risk assessment after a positive mood screen · driving advice in a sleepy commercial driver.**

stem: Jane Sotiris, a 35-year-old woman, presents to your general practice complaining of tiredness. Nothing else is given in the stem.
Version A (online): history 6 minutes, then examination findings appear on screen. Version B (face to face): history 4 minutes, then physical examination from the examiner.
tasks: Take a focused history from the patient
You will then be given the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
findings: General appearance and vitals
Sitting comfortably. NO pallor, NO jaundice, NO cachexia, NO rash or bruising, no scratch marks. Temperature NORMAL, pulse and BP normal
Thyroid
NORMAL
Lymph nodes — request EVERY chain by name

OCCIPITAL · PRE- AND POST-AURICULAR · SUBMENTAL · SUBMANDIBULAR · ANTERIOR AND POSTERIOR CERVICAL · SUPRACLAVICULAR · AXILLARY · EPITROCHLEAR · INGUINAL · POPLITEAL. Eight seconds, and it is a marked item
What you are given
TWO ENLARGED LYMPH NODES IN THE LEFT AXILLA. No other group enlarged. THEN THE EXAMINER WAITS to see whether you characterise them
THE FOUR CHARACTERISING WORDS

SIZE — about 2 cm · CONSISTENCY — STONY HARD, not rubbery · MOBILITY — FIXED · TENDERNESS — NON-TENDER. That is the MALIGNANT end of the spectrum, and it is the reason the word cancer has to be said out loud. ACCEPTING 'TWO ENLARGED NODES' AND MOVING ON IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL
The breast examination — NOT optional

BOTH BREASTS AND THE AXILLARY TAIL, and INSPECT THE SKIN OF THAT ARM. NORMAL here. An AXILLARY node in a 35-year-old woman is a BREAST question until proved otherwise — a hard fixed node can be the presenting sign of breast cancer with an IMPALPABLE primary
Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdomen
Heart sounds normal, no murmur. Air entry equal, no added sounds. NO HEPATOMEGALY, NO SPLENOMEGALY
Bone tenderness
Ask for it over the STERNUM AND SPINE — NONE here. Sternal tenderness would push you towards leukaemia
Office tests
Blood sugar NORMAL · urine dipstick NORMAL · URINE PREGNANCY TEST NEGATIVE
What she gives only on probing

Weight loss: 'about five kilos over a few months, and I haven't been trying.' Lumps: TWO IN THE LEFT ARMPIT, two months, SLIGHTLY BIGGER, PAINLESS. Night sweats: 'I have to change my nightie' — DRENCHING. NO fevers, no itching, no alcohol-induced pain, no breast lumps, NO FAMILY HISTORY OF CANCER. Her hidden fear: 'my friend had lumps and it turned out to be cancer'
findingsLabel: Examiner stage — the nodes, and the four words you must ask for
must: FAIL — Never saying the word cancer. 'Swollen glands, we'll do some tests' is avoidance.
FAIL — Never characterising the nodes. Four words: size, consistency, mobility, tenderness.
FAIL — No malignancy screen, or offering fine-needle aspiration as the diagnostic test.
FAIL — Giving a prognosis or cure rate, or false reassurance on a negative family history.
ASK — Have you lost weight recently? How much, and over what period?
ASK — Any night sweats — do you have to change the sheets or your nightclothes?

dx: **Lymphoma — Hodgkin or non-Hodgkin — with LEUKAEMIA alongside it.** Malignant clonal proliferation of lymphocytes, usually presenting as **painless lymphadenopathy with or without systemic B symptoms**.
**The triad you are handed: WEIGHT LOSS + PAINLESS HARD FIXED NODES + DRENCHING NIGHT SWEATS.**

**The sentence that passes: 'Jane, tiredness can have many different causes. In your case, I am concerned about the possibility of LYMPHOMA, WHICH IS A TYPE OF CANCER OF THE LYMPH GLANDS. I am not certain yet — a biopsy is what confirms it — but I would not be honest with you if I said anything less.'** Then **ONE feelings check**, then **the reasons**, then **move on to the differentials.**

**B symptoms have a definition. 'Night sweats' alone is not one. The three are: unexplained fever above 38°C · DRENCHING night sweats · unintentional weight loss of MORE THAN 10% of body weight over SIX MONTHS.** Say 'she has weight loss and drenching sweats, which are B symptoms' and you sound like a clinician rather than a list.

**FINDINGS OUTRANK A REASSURING HISTORY.** No family history, no fever, no exposures — none of that touches the diagnosis, because you can feel two hard fixed nodes. **A history that fails to support a finding does not cancel the finding.** **And most lymphoma is SPORADIC — a negative family history reassures you about nothing.**

**An axillary node in a 35-year-old woman is a breast question until proved otherwise.** Asking about breast lumps in the history is not enough — **REQUEST A BREAST EXAMINATION**. If challenged: 'I keep lymphoma at the top of my list, but the site of the node obliges me to examine both breasts and the skin of that arm before I settle on it.'

**EXCISION BIOPSY OF A WHOLE NODE is the diagnostic test — NEVER fine-needle aspiration, which cannot show nodal architecture and delays the diagnosis.** **A node over 1 cm persisting beyond 4 weeks without an explanation warrants biopsy.** VERIFY local criteria.

**Do not miss: a LEFT SUPRACLAVICULAR NODE (Virchow) — name it every time · CYTOPENIAS or blasts on the film · SUPERIOR VENA CAVA OBSTRUCTION, which is facial swelling, distended neck veins and breathlessness lying flat, and is a same-day emergency · STERNAL TENDERNESS · an impalpable breast primary.**

**Do NOT run a full SPIKES sequence.** There are two minutes left and a differentials task still to complete, and **the role-player is briefed not to give a strong emotional reaction — if you wait for one, you lose the time to silence.** **Do not give a prognosis or cure rate: you have no histology, no subtype and no stage.**

**Plan: FBE and blood film — the single most useful test · LDH, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFT, calcium, urate · HIV, EBV and CMV serology, plus hepatitis B and C before any chemotherapy · chest radiograph then CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis · URGENT referral for excision biopsy, phoned through, not a routine letter.** **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20 · PATS · RAH or TQEH haematology · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **'Good morning, I'm Dr [name], one of the doctors here. What has brought you in today?'** She volunteers the worry in her first sentence — **acknowledge it back or you lose a communication mark in the opening ten seconds.** Then the contract: **'some questions will sound unrelated — I ask everyone. Is that all right?'**

**Explore in five questions, not a conversation: IS IT A LACK OF ENERGY, FEELING SLEEPY, OR FEELING FEVERISH · how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · anything better or worse · how is it affecting your life?** **Energy rather than sleepiness moves anaemia, thyroid, malignancy and mood UP and sleep apnoea DOWN.**

**H — liver and iron: any tanning of the skin · yellowing of the eyes · dark urine or pale stools? E — endocrine: passing more urine · more thirsty · do you prefer hot or cold weather?** **Ten seconds each when the answer is no. Do not slow down on negatives.**
**M — AND THIS IS WHERE THE STATION IS WON. 'HAVE YOU LOST WEIGHT RECENTLY — HOW MUCH, AND OVER WHAT PERIOD?'** → five kilos. **Now STOP AND PROBE, do not move to the next letter.**

**The probe, eleven questions: appetite · ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS ANYWHERE · how long, getting bigger, painful · ANY NIGHT SWEATS, DO YOU HAVE TO CHANGE THE SHEETS OR YOUR NIGHTCLOTHES · any fevers that come and go · any ITCHING ALL OVER WITHOUT A RASH · do the lumps ACHE AFTER ALCOHOL · ANY BREAST LUMPS, SKIN DIMPLING OR NIPPLE DISCHARGE · any cancer in you or your family · when did you last have a cervical screening test?**

**I — the second-place group, so do it properly: any fevers or chills · sore throat or flu-like illness recently · ARE YOU SEXUALLY ACTIVE, DO YOU USE CONDOMS · any travel · any pets, ANY CAT SCRATCHES OR BITES ON THAT ARM · anyone around you with tuberculosis?** **Do not skip the sexual history — HIV can present exactly like this.**

**A — breathless or heart racing on exertion · shoulder or hip stiffness · headaches, joint pains, rashes. D — any medicines · how has your mood been, still enjoying things, any stress. C — greasy stools · blood in the stool · chest pain · how many pillows · ankle swelling · cough, do you smoke.**

**O — has anyone said you snore or gasp · what is your occupation. P — WHEN WAS YOUR LAST PERIOD, are they regular, are they heavy, ANY CHANCE YOU COULD BE PREGNANT?** Then **'was there anything you were worried this might be?'** → her friend's lumps.

**Request the examination, naming every chain**: general appearance including **bruising, petechiae and scratch marks** · vitals, particularly temperature · thyroid · **the full node examination by chain.**

**The examiner gives you two axillary nodes and WAITS. Immediately, without pausing: 'HOW LARGE ARE THEY? ARE THEY STONY HARD OR RUBBERY? ARE THEY FIXED OR MOBILE? ARE THEY TENDER?'** Then **both breasts and the axillary tail, the skin of that arm, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly, BONE TENDERNESS over sternum and spine, and office tests including a URINE PREGNANCY TEST.**

**Name it. ONE feelings check — 'how are you feeling about what I have just said?' — then CONTINUE.** Then **the reasons from her own findings: five kilos without trying · two lumps that are hard and not moving · drenching night sweats. Those three together point that way.**

**The differentials, top three REASONED against her findings, the rest rapid-fire: breast cancer — examination normal today but imaging anyway · infections, EBV, HIV, toxoplasmosis, TB, cat-scratch — no fever, no travel, safe sex, but INCLUDE AN HIV TEST · pregnancy — excluded today.** Then thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, hepatitis, haemochromatosis, coeliac, autoimmune, medications, depression, sleep apnoea, heart failure.

**The plan: bloods today, chest X-ray, URGENT referral for a small operation to remove one gland WHOLE — 'a needle sample is not enough' — phoned through today.** **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20** for information and travel. **Safety-net: fever, facial or neck swelling, breathless lying flat, bruising or bleeding → straight back or to hospital.** **'Is there someone who can come with you?'**
pefe: **Name every node chain out loud** — occipital, pre- and post-auricular, submental, submandibular, anterior and posterior cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal, popliteal. **'Are there any lymph nodes?' is not a request.**

**Characterise what you are given, in four words: size, consistency, mobility, tenderness.** **Stony hard, fixed and non-tender is the malignant end; rubbery and mobile is more typical of lymphoma than of metastatic spread — but it does not change what you do.**
**Request BOTH BREASTS and the axillary tail, and inspect the skin of the arm.** A hard fixed axillary node in a woman of this age can be breast cancer with an impalpable primary.
**Do now: full node examination, breast examination, abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly, bone tenderness over sternum and spine, temperature, urine pregnancy test.**

**Do next: FBE AND BLOOD FILM — the single most useful test, because cytopenias or blasts change everything today · LDH, ESR or CRP, U&E, LFT, calcium, urate · HIV, EBV, CMV serology and hepatitis B and C · chest radiograph then CT neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis · EXCISION BIOPSY OF A WHOLE NODE.**
**Avoid: fine-needle aspiration as the diagnostic test · a 'trial of antibiotics' in a hard fixed node · telling her it is 'probably just glands' · promising a timeframe you cannot control.**
**If a chest film appears, read it systematically before interpreting. Bulky mediastinal nodes also raise SVC obstruction, which is an emergency.**

**Painless hard or rubbery nodes, weight loss, drenching sweats**, fever, pruritus, alcohol-induced nodal pain
**Every node chain, spleen and liver, B symptoms**
**EXCISION BIOPSY OF A WHOLE NODE. FBE and film, LDH, ESR, CT neck/chest/abdomen/pelvis** — urgent
**Leukaemia**
**Bruising, bleeding, infections, pallor, sternal or bone tenderness**
Bruising, petechiae, gum bleeding, sternal tenderness
**FBE with film — blasts; urgent haematology referral** — emergency if cytopenic

**Breast examination, skin of the arm**, thyroid, chest
**Mammography and breast ultrasound; core biopsy; CT for a primary** — urgent

Flu-like illness, cat exposure, undercooked meat
Monospot or EBV serology, CMV and Toxoplasma serology — same week
**HIV**
**Generalised lymphadenopathy, weight loss, sweats, thrush — can be clinically identical**
**Sexual history and injecting drug use, asked of EVERYONE**
**Offer an HIV antigen/antibody test explicitly** — same week
Tuberculosis · cat-scratch disease · local sepsis
**Matted or fluctuant nodes**, sinus, country of birth, contacts; **a scratch or bite on that arm**
Country of birth, TB contacts, pets, breaks in the skin
Chest radiograph, IGRA, node aspirate for culture; Bartonella serology — same week
Hypothyroidism · diabetes
Cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, weight gain; or polyuria and thirst
Weather preference, bowels, thirst
**TSH; fasting glucose or HbA1c** — on every tiredness screen
Anaemia · coeliac · haemochromatosis · hepatitis
Pallor, heavy periods, greasy stools, **tanning**, jaundice
Menstrual loss, diet, bowel habit, skin colour
FBE and ferritin, coeliac serology, iron studies, LFT and hepatitis serology
Pregnancy · autoimmune disease · depression
Missed or late period; joint pain and rash; low mood and anhedonia
Last menstrual period, joints, rash, mood screen
**Urine pregnancy test**; ANA and dsDNA if indicated; PHQ-2
Drugs — phenytoin, carbamazepine, allopurinol
Drug-induced pseudolymphoma or hypersensitivity
**Full medication list including recent starts**
Cease the suspect agent — **but still biopsy if the node persists**
