stem: You are the HMO. Blood results have returned on Mr Arthur Nolan, 78, a resident of a nearby aged-care facility, currently an inpatient. Sodium 118 mmol/L (135–145), chloride low, serum osmolality low. Nothing else is given.
tasks: Report and explain the investigation results to the nurse
Take a history from the nurse
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the nurse
findings: Conscious state — ASKED BEFORE THE RESULTS
ALERT AND ORIENTED TO HIS USUAL LEVEL. NO FITTING. A sodium of 118 can seize — discussing the number before you know he is awake fails the safety domain however good the rest is
Observations
BP 128/76 · PULSE 78 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% on air · T 36.6. Stable
Orientation from the nurse
Admitted THREE DAYS AGO after a FALL at his aged-care facility, no fracture. History: HYPERTENSION, osteoarthritis, mild memory impairment. NO recent surgery. CT head on admission CLEAR
The medication chart — read in full

HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE · paracetamol · atorvastatin. Nothing changed since admission. SHE NEVER VOLUNTEERS THE THIAZIDE AS A CAUSE — and if you ask only about NEW medications she says 'nothing new since admission' and lets you miss it
Symptoms
NO change from his baseline confusion. No drowsiness, headache, dizziness, nausea or vomiting. Unsteady — but that is what brought him in. NO seizure
Pseudohyponatraemia screen
GLUCOSE 5.4 · TRIGLYCERIDES NORMAL · TOTAL PROTEIN NORMAL. Say the conclusion out loud: 'then this is a TRUE HYPOTONIC hyponatraemia, not an artefact and not glucose-driven'
Hypovolaemic block
NO vomiting or diarrhoea. Eating and drinking normally. No burns or large wounds
Hypervolaemic block
NO breathlessness, ONE pillow, no ankle swelling. No jaundice, dark urine or pale stools. Urine output normal — FLUID CHART ROUGHLY BALANCED, about 1400 in and 1300 out
VOLUME STATUS — the question that decides the station

'CAN I ASK YOU TO LOOK AT HIM FOR ME?' → MOUTH MOIST, NO POSTURAL DROP, NO OEDEMA, CHEST CLEAR, WEIGHT STABLE = EUVOLAEMIC. SHE WILL NOT OFFER THIS. Volume status is an EXAMINATION finding, and on the telephone the only way to get it is to ask her to examine him
SIADH cause groups — four questions

INFECTION: no fever, chills, cough, breathlessness, headache or neck stiffness. MALIGNANCY: no weight loss, lumps, night sweats or cancer history. INTRACRANIAL: did not hit his head, CT clear. POLYDIPSIA: drinking normal for him
findingsLabel: What the nurse gives — and the one thing she withholds
must: FAIL — Discussing a sodium of 118 before asking whether he is alert or has fitted.
FAIL — Never asking the nurse to assess his fluid state. Volume status is examined, not asked.
FAIL — Asking only about NEW medications, so the long-standing thiazide is missed.
FAIL — Saying 'SIADH' and stopping, or changing the drug by telephone instead of escalating.
ASK — Is he alert and oriented, or drowsy? Has he had any fitting?
ASK — Can you check his glucose, triglycerides and total protein?

dx: **Euvolaemic hypotonic hyponatraemia due to SIADH, most likely drug-induced — the hydrochlorothiazide.** **Almost every AMC hyponatraemia recall lands on SIADH caused by a medication: thiazide, SSRI or carbamazepine.**

**Pseudo → volume → group.** Rule out pseudohyponatraemia, establish volume status, then run the three volume groups as three labelled blocks. **Volume status is an examination finding, not a history answer** — on the telephone you must ask the nurse for it; in clinic you must say out loud that you would look for it.

**Explain in THREE LAYERS, not one word. LAYER 1: SIADH, and the drug that triggered it. LAYER 2: the other causes of SIADH — malignancy (lung cancer, lymphoma) · infection (pneumonia, TB, meningitis) · intracranial pathology (bleed, head injury). LAYER 3: the other causes of hyponatraemia — hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency, the hypovolaemic group, the hypervolaemic group.** **Saying 'it's SIADH' and stopping is the commonest reason this station scores poorly.**

**SIADH diagnostic criteria: hyponatraemia with SERUM osmolality under 275 mOsm/kg · URINE osmolality over 100 mOsm/kg · urine sodium over 30–40 mmol/L · clinical euvolaemia · normal thyroid, adrenal and renal function · no diuretic on board.** **Serum low, urine high** is the memory hook.

**CORRECTION — hyperglycaemia is NOT pseudohyponatraemia.** **High triglycerides and high protein cause a laboratory artefact with a NORMAL serum osmolality. Hyperglycaemia causes a real dilutional hyponatraemia with a HIGH serum osmolality**, because glucose pulls water out of cells. Same screen, different boxes on the algorithm.

**Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia has a urine sodium UNDER 20** — the kidney is holding on to sodium. **In SIADH the urine sodium is HIGH because the patient is volume replete and there is no stimulus to conserve it.** That contrast separates the two.

**Register: you are talking to a senior colleague. Use ISBAR and clinical language — hyponatraemia, serum osmolality, euvolaemic, SIADH.** **Translating 'sodium' into 'a salt in your blood' for a registered nurse costs communication marks.**

**Drugs to name first: THIAZIDES · SSRIs · CARBAMAZEPINE.** Then **ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, chemotherapy, MDMA, desmopressin.** **Review the chart with the pharmacist; discuss substitution with the prescriber rather than stopping unilaterally.**

**Correction: no faster than about 8 mmol/L in 24 hours**, and less in the malnourished, alcohol-dependent, hypokalaemic or those with liver disease. **Faster risks OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME — dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis or a locked-in state, appearing days later and usually irreversible.** VERIFY.

**Management is NOT a task here — one sentence if asked, then return to the diagnosis.** **Never give normal saline in SIADH: the kidney concentrates the urine above the tonicity of the saline, so salt is excreted and water retained and the sodium falls further.** **Severe and symptomatic: 3% sodium chloride in small boluses to lift by 4–6 mmol/L, then stop.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **Pick up the phone: 'Hello, this is Dr [name], the HMO covering the ward this evening. WHO AM I SPEAKING WITH, and WHICH WARD are you calling from?'**

**Before the numbers — the scored safety behaviour: 'IS HE ALERT AND ORIENTED, OR IS HE DROWSY OR MORE CONFUSED THAN USUAL? HAS HE HAD ANY FITTING? And can you give me his latest observations — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, saturations and temperature?'** Fifteen seconds, and it banks the domain.

**Report the results in colleague register**: sodium 118 against 135–145, a significant hyponatraemia · chloride low, which tends to track the sodium · **and the serum osmolality is low, which tells me this is a TRUE HYPOTONIC hyponatraemia rather than a laboratory artefact.** Then ask permission to work through the causes.

**Orient: can you tell me more about him · WHAT IS HE ADMITTED WITH · what does his past medical history include · CAN YOU READ ME HIS MEDICATION CHART, EVERYTHING ON IT INCLUDING ANYTHING STARTED OR CHANGED IN THE LAST FEW WEEKS · and has he had any recent surgery?** Note the thiazide and **deliberately keep going**.
**Symptoms: is he confused or more confused than his baseline · any drowsiness · any headache, dizziness, nausea or vomiting · any unsteadiness or falls since admission · HAS HE HAD ANY SEIZURE?**

**The pseudohyponatraemia screen: can you check whether there are recent results for his BLOOD GLUCOSE, his TRIGLYCERIDES and his TOTAL PROTEIN?** Then **say the conclusion aloud** — it converts a silent thought into scored reasoning.
**Block one, losing fluid — announce it: any vomiting or diarrhoea · is he eating and drinking as usual · any burns or large wounds · is he on a fluid tablet?**

**Block two, retaining it: any chest pain or breathlessness, worse lying flat, HOW MANY PILLOWS · any swelling in the legs · any yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or pale stools · has he been passing less urine · DOES HE HAVE A FLUID BALANCE CHART, what are the intake and output?**
**Block three, euvolaemic: any weather preference, is he intolerant of the cold · any constipation or weight gain?**

stem: Mr John Whitfield, 60, known end-stage kidney disease on maintenance haemodialysis, attends for his scheduled session. He has had several days of palpitations and diarrhoea. ECG provided: tall, narrow-based, symmetrical peaked T waves, most marked in the mid-precordial leads; QRS normal; P waves preserved.
tasks: Take a further focused history (3 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant investigations
Explain the condition to the patient
findings: The ECG, handed to you OUTSIDE the room

TALL, NARROW-BASED, SYMMETRICAL PEAKED T WAVES, most marked in the mid-precordial leads. QRS DURATION NORMAL. P WAVES PRESERVED. You do NOT have to request it — you are expected to have interpreted it BEFORE you sit down, and to say so in your first sentence
Vital signs — ask for them by name
BP 132/78 · PULSE 88 REGULAR · RR 16 · SpO2 97% RA · T 36.7. HE IS HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE — SAY SO OUT LOUD. Candidates who never ask are marked down even when the patient is well
Investigation 1 — UEC
POTASSIUM 5.9. Ask for it by ANALYTE: 'urea, electrolytes and creatinine — SPECIFICALLY THE POTASSIUM, along with sodium and bicarbonate.' 'Renal function tests' scores NOTHING
Investigation 2 — eGFR against baseline
eGFR 10–12, consistent with his known end-stage disease
Investigation 3 — blood gas

ESSENTIALLY NORMAL. Ask for arterial or venous, 'for the pH, bicarbonate and a RAPID potassium'. If challenged: 'ACIDOSIS DRIVES POTASSIUM OUT OF THE CELLS, so it changes both my interpretation and my management'
Reading the numbers back

'The potassium is 5.9 — MILDLY ELEVATED BY THE NUMBER, BUT HE HAS ECG CHANGES, WHICH MAKES THIS SIGNIFICANT REGARDLESS OF THE LEVEL. The gas shows no significant acidosis, so this is REDUCED CLEARANCE AND INCREASED RETENTION rather than a shift out of the cells.' Saying '5.9 is only mildly high' without the ECG sentence reads as false reassurance
The medication list, handed to you on paper
PERINDOPRIL · HYDROCHLOROTHIAZIDE · ERYTHROPOIETIN. READ IT ALOUD — if you glance at it silently the examiner cannot mark that you registered the ACE inhibitor
THE TWO FACTS HE WITHHOLDS

1 HE MISSED MONDAY'S DIALYSIS — given only if you ask about MISSED OR SKIPPED SESSIONS. 2 HIS GP INCREASED THE DOSE OF ONE TABLET LAST WEEK — given ONLY if you ask about A CHANGE to existing medication. ASK ONLY ABOUT 'NEW' MEDICATIONS AND THE BRIEFED ANSWER IS A FLAT 'NO'. Asked which tablet, he does not know
The third precipitant
FOUR DAYS OF WATERY DIARRHOEA six or seven times a day, HARDLY DRINKING ANYTHING, LIGHT-HEADED ON STANDING — volume depletion causing AKI on CKD. No vomiting, no falls, no muscle pain, no dark urine
His hidden fear

HE THINKS HE IS HAVING A HEART ATTACK — his brother died that way at 58. He interrupts at about one minute: 'MY HEART'S BEEN GOING LIKE A DRUM — SHOULD I BE WORRIED?' Name it, park it with a promise, and come back to it

dx: **Acute kidney injury on end-stage kidney disease, with hyperkalaemia — MULTIFACTORIAL.** Precipitated by **(1) an INCREASED DOSE OF HIS ACE INHIBITOR, perindopril · (2) a MISSED DIALYSIS SESSION · (3) VOLUME DEPLETION from days of diarrhoea and poor intake.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: hyperkalaemia is a STATE, not a diagnosis.** Everyone finds the high potassium — it is handed to you on the ECG before you enter. **The mark is for naming a DIAGNOSIS and attaching a CAUSE.** **Fails: 'you have a condition called hyperkalaemia.' Passes: 'you have an ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY ON TOP OF YOUR LONG-STANDING KIDNEY DISEASE, and it has pushed your potassium up.' Distinguishes: the same sentence PLUS 'and the main reason is the increase in your blood pressure tablet.'**

**A three-minute history is NOT a shortened long history — it is a DIFFERENT TASK.** Pathway one, analysing the diarrhoea and palpitations in full, **uses the entire three minutes and reaches no cause.** Pathway two, accepting the presenting complaints as given and spending the time on **WHY THE POTASSIUM ROSE**, passes.

**THE FOUR PRECIPITANT QUESTIONS: 1 any big change in your DIET · 2 have you MISSED ANY DIALYSIS SESSIONS · 3 any new medications OR ANY CHANGE to the ones you already take, including anything from the chemist or herbal · 4 with the diarrhoea, can you KEEP FLUIDS DOWN, any vomiting, DIZZY ON STANDING?** **The words 'or any change' are worth more than any other five words in this station.**

**THE THIAZIDE TRAP.** Candidates routinely blame the thiazide. **Thiazides are potassium-DEPLETING** — they are combined with ACE inhibitors precisely because the two effects OPPOSE each other, which is also why **spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor is the dangerous combination.** **Erythropoietin does not cause hyperkalaemia.** By mechanism and by elimination, **it is the perindopril.**

**CORRECTION — diarrhoea causes potassium LOSS, so it does not raise potassium directly.** It contributes by **causing volume depletion and an AKI, and by losing bicarbonate and worsening acidosis.** **Do not tell the patient the high potassium is causing his diarrhoea — the diarrhoea came first and helped cause the hyperkalaemia.**

**Thresholds: MILD 5.5–5.9 · MODERATE 6.0–6.4 · SEVERE 6.5 or above — BUT ANY LEVEL WITH ECG CHANGE IS TREATED AS SEVERE.** **ECG order of progression: PEAKED T → FLAT P → LONG PR → WIDE QRS → SINE WAVE → VF or asystole.**

**Management: continuous cardiac monitoring and IV access · CALCIUM GLUCONATE 10%, 10 mL IV over 2–5 MINUTES if there are ECG changes, repeated if they persist — it STABILISES THE MEMBRANE and DOES NOT LOWER THE POTASSIUM · INSULIN–DEXTROSE, 10 units short-acting in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 15–30 min, onset about 15 min, lasts 4–6 h, with HOURLY BSL FOR 6 HOURS because LATE HYPOGLYCAEMIA is the commonest complication · SALBUTAMOL 10–20 mg nebulised as an ADJUNCT, which may worsen his palpitations so warn him · HAEMODIALYSIS is DEFINITIVE, and he already has access.** VERIFY.

**STOP THE PERINDOPRIL and document why, so it is not restarted by default. Bring dialysis forward to TODAY. Recheck potassium at 1–2 HOURS because shifting agents wear off and it rebounds. Repeat the ECG after treatment, before you reassure him.** **Recheck U&E 1–2 weeks after any ACE inhibitor dose change.**

**The blame moment: 'I can understand why it feels that way. That medicine was increased FOR A GOOD REASON — to protect your heart and your blood pressure — and in most people it is entirely safe. In someone whose kidneys are as far along as yours, it needs A BLOOD TEST A WEEK OR TWO AFTERWARDS, and that's the part we need to tighten up. I'll write to your GP today. PLEASE DON'T STOP ANY OF YOUR OTHER TABLETS ON YOUR OWN.'** **Never say 'your GP made a mistake.'**
plan: **Outside the room, read the ECG: peaked, narrow-based T waves, QRS narrow, P waves present.** Then **to the examiner: 'before I begin, could I have his blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation? And I NOTE THE ECG PROVIDED SHOWS PEAKED T WAVES WITH A NORMAL QRS, so I will be treating this as hyperkalaemia from the outset.'**

**Greet, confirm identity, and WARN ABOUT THE PACE: 'I've only got a few minutes, so I'm going to ask some quick, direct questions — is that all right?'** That gives you permission to be brisk without appearing rude. **Do not open with 'tell me all about it' — in a three-minute history that single question can eat fifty seconds.**

**Block 1, the kidney background: HOW LONG have you had the kidney problem · WHAT TREATMENT, how often is dialysis and WHICH DAYS · WHAT MEDICATIONS are you on · are you seeing your GP and your kidney specialist regularly?** **READ THE MEDICATION LIST ALOUD.**

**Block 2, symptoms of hyperkalaemia — a rapid string, 25 seconds, no analysis: apart from the racing heart, any unusual TIREDNESS OR WEAKNESS · any NUMBNESS OR TINGLING, or weakness in your arms or legs · any CHEST PAIN or shortness of breath · have you felt SICK or been vomiting · have you FAINTED or come close?**
**Block 3, the four precipitants — THE MARKS LIVE HERE. 1 HAS THERE BEEN ANY BIG CHANGE IN YOUR DIET RECENTLY?**

**2 HAVE YOU MISSED ANY DIALYSIS SESSIONS?** → Monday. **Acknowledge without lecturing: 'that's important — it means a whole session's worth of potassium hasn't been removed.'** **And if it is a rural case, ASK WHY — the barrier is usually logistic, not wilful.**

**3 ANY NEW MEDICATIONS — OR ANY CHANGE TO THE ONES YOU ALREADY TAKE? Including anything from the chemist, or herbal.** → the GP put the dose up on one. Ask which; he does not know; **reason it out aloud to the examiner: 'of the three, the one that raises potassium is the perindopril. I'll confirm from his dispensing record.'**
**4 WITH THE DIARRHOEA — have you been able to KEEP FLUIDS DOWN · any vomiting · DO YOU FEEL DIZZY WHEN YOU STAND?**
**Block 4, tissue breakdown — ten seconds, and do NOT open a falls assessment: any FALLS, INJURIES or a LONG LIE recently · any SEVERE MUSCLE PAIN or DARK URINE?**

**Three named investigations: UEC, SPECIFICALLY THE POTASSIUM with sodium and bicarbonate · eGFR COMPARED WITH BASELINE · ARTERIAL OR VENOUS BLOOD GAS for pH, bicarbonate and a rapid potassium.** Then, flagged as secondary: **FBC, calcium, phosphate and magnesium, BSL, CK if any fall, stool MCS if the diarrhoea persists.**
**Read the numbers back with the ECG sentence attached.**
**Name the DIAGNOSIS, not the number: 'your kidneys have taken a further, sudden knock on top of the long-standing damage — an ACUTE INJURY ON TOP OF CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE.'**

**Say 'THREE REASONS' and then give three: the PERINDOPRIL dose went up and it makes the body hold on to potassium, a mineral in the blood · you MISSED A DIALYSIS SESSION, so a whole session's worth wasn't taken off · the DIARRHOEA HAS DRIED YOU OUT.**

**Link it to HIS symptom: 'the potassium is now high, and THAT is what's causing the racing of your heart — potassium controls the heart's electrical rhythm, which is why we take it seriously. But we can bring it down today, and you're in exactly the right place.'** Then **handle the blame moment if it comes.**

**The plan: heart monitor · DIALYSIS BROUGHT FORWARD TO TODAY · HOLD THE PERINDOPRIL · a letter to the GP · 'don't stop any of your other tablets on your own.'** Then **SAFETY-NET: racing heart again, chest pain, feeling faint, or weak limbs → tell a nurse straight away.**

**TEACH-BACK: 'would you mind telling me in your own words what you'll say to your wife?'** Then **'is there anything you're still worried about?'** — and if the cardiac fear has not surfaced, this is where it does.

**Name the ANALYTE, not the category. The three: UEC with potassium, sodium and bicarbonate · eGFR against baseline · blood gas for pH, bicarbonate and a rapid potassium.**

dx: **Mild THIAZIDE-INDUCED HYPOKALAEMIA in an otherwise well man due for elective surgery.** Thiazides block Na/Cl reabsorption in the distal tubule, **more sodium reaches the collecting duct, and aldosterone-driven Na–K exchange wastes potassium** — producing a **hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: the diagnosis is written into the stem, so NO MARKS LIVE THERE.** Candidates read it, feel clever, say 'it's your fluid tablet' and stop — **and fail.** **Every remaining mark sits in (1) a STRUCTURED DIFFERENTIAL SPOKEN ALOUD in plain English and (2) the patient's real agenda — his operation.**

**THE FOUR BUCKETS, NUMBERED, IN PATIENT LANGUAGE: ONE — not taking enough in, if the diet is very restricted. TWO — losing it through the bowel: vomiting, diarrhoea or laxatives. THREE — losing extra through the kidneys, either from a tablet like yours or from a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone that dumps potassium. FOUR — potassium moving out of the blood into the cells, which some puffers, insulin and a rare adrenaline-producing tumour can do.** Then: **'nothing you've told me points to those — but they're the reasons I asked.'**

**Severity: MILD 3.0–3.4 · MODERATE 2.5–2.9 · SEVERE below 2.5, or symptomatic or ECG change AT ANY LEVEL.** **Normal range is laboratory-dependent — commonly 3.5–5.2; use the range printed on the report, not a memorised figure.**

**Management: repeat the sample · ECG · MAGNESIUM · oral potassium — slow-release KCl 600 mg = 8 mmol, or effervescent = 14 mmol per tablet.** VERIFY doses. **Replace magnesium CONCURRENTLY if low, or potassium will not rise.**

**FIX THE CAUSE, and in a hypertensive man this is elegant: reduce the thiazide or SWITCH CLASS — an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or add a POTASSIUM-SPARING agent (amiloride, or spironolactone if aldosteronism is suspected) — which treats the blood pressure AND raises potassium at once.** **Never tell him to stop the tablet himself.**

**Surgical timing: discuss with the anaesthetist. Hypokalaemia RAISES ARRHYTHMIA RISK, POTENTIATES NON-DEPOLARISING NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKERS and CAN CAUSE ILEUS.** **Mild, corrected, asymptomatic hypokalaemia usually PROCEEDS; moderate to severe or symptomatic is a reason to DEFER an elective list.**

**VERSION B, scripted: 'that combination — a low potassium with a blood pressure that's hard to control — makes me think about a specific, TREATABLE condition: a small gland above the kidney making too much of a hormone called ALDOSTERONE, which pushes blood pressure UP and potassium DOWN. It's commoner than people used to think, and the treatment is different — a particular tablet, or sometimes surgery.'** **Correct K and magnesium first, adjust interfering antihypertensives, then the ALDOSTERONE–RENIN RATIO.** VERIFY washout periods.
**CORRECTION — primary aldosteronism causes RENAL POTASSIUM WASTING, not a shift into cells.** **Only the beta-2 adrenergic causes, including phaeochromocytoma, work by shift.**

**CORRECTION — 'potassium down, aldosterone up' is a mnemonic, not physiology.** **Potassium is itself a STIMULUS for aldosterone release, so hypokalaemia SUPPRESSES aldosterone.** **The true rule is ONE-WAY: excess aldosterone lowers potassium. Do not offer the reverse to an examiner.**
plan: **WIPE, confirm identity, and straight to the task: 'I can see you're booked for your hernia repair in about ten days and we did some blood tests to get you ready — I have those results here and I'd like to go through them with you.'**

**Explain the results in NINETY SECONDS AND NO MORE. Good news first — THE KIDNEYS ARE NORMAL. Sodium 135, normal at the low end. POTASSIUM 3.1, a little below normal. 'Potassium is the salt that helps your MUSCLES AND YOUR HEART work properly, so it's worth sorting out — particularly before an anaesthetic. IT'S NOT AN EMERGENCY.'** Then **permission to ask questions.** **Do NOT teach renal physiology — the explanation mark is already in the bag.**

**Signpost and ask the agenda: 'was there anything in particular you were hoping to sort out today?'** This is where **'will my op be cancelled?'** comes out. **If it comes early, acknowledge and PARK it explicitly — 'that's exactly what I want to sort out, and I'll answer it properly once I've asked you a few things' — then COME BACK TO IT.**

**Block 1, surgical context, 30 seconds: when was the hernia diagnosed · is it painful · HAS IT EVER BECOME STUCK OR GONE HARD AND TENDER · ANY CHANGE IN YOUR BOWEL MOTIONS?** The bowel question **doubles as your first GI-loss screen** and excludes obstruction before an elective list.

**Block 2, the hypertension — highest yield: when diagnosed · WHAT TABLET AND WHAT DOSE · HAS THE DOSE BEEN CHANGED RECENTLY, OR ANYTHING ADDED · do you take it every day · who follows it up · HAVE THE READINGS BEEN UNDER CONTROL?** Then **complications: chest pain · breathlessness or waking at night breathless · blurring of vision · weakness or numbness down one side.**
**Block 3, reduced intake: any recent changes to your diet · TALK ME THROUGH A TYPICAL DAY · any fruit and vegetables · have you lost weight without trying · how much alcohol?**

**Block 4, GI loss: any VOMITING and for how long · any DIARRHOEA or looser motions · DO YOU USE ANY LAXATIVES — TABLETS, POWDERS OR TEAS · any stoma, tube feeds or bowel surgery?** **Name laxatives explicitly — patients do not count senna, Coloxyl or 'regularity tea' as medication.**

**Block 5, renal loss and mineralocorticoid excess: any MUSCLE CRAMPS · any WEAKNESS, trouble with stairs or lifting at work · ARE YOU PASSING MORE URINE, OR GETTING UP AT NIGHT · any excessive thirst or pins and needles · any weight gain around the middle, easy bruising, purple stretch marks · DO YOU EAT LIQUORICE REGULARLY?**

**Block 6, phaeochromocytoma: 'do you get episodes of HEADACHE, HEAVY SWEATING and YOUR HEART RACING — ALL TOGETHER, coming on suddenly and settling? Do you go PALE or feel anxious during them?'** **The triad is headache, sweating and palpitations — NOT flushing. Phaeochromocytoma patients typically go PALE; flushing points to carcinoid or menopause.**

**Block 7, the rest of the drug history BY CATEGORY: any other prescription medicines · ANY PUFFERS, how many times a day · ANY STEROID tablets, creams or injections · INSULIN or diabetes tablets · any over-the-counter, HERBAL, vitamin or protein products · HAVE YOU EVER TAKEN ANYONE ELSE'S FLUID TABLETS · any recent antibiotics or antifungals?**

**Name it plainly and give the mechanism in one sentence, ANCHORING THE TIMING: 'the dose was doubled four weeks ago, which fits the timing exactly.'**

**THE FOUR BUCKETS, NUMBERED, OUT LOUD — the pass point.** Numbered so the examiner can tick four things, in patient language, **and explicitly saying why you asked the questions**, which converts your history into visible reasoning.

**The plan: REPEAT the blood test · a HEART TRACING TODAY · check MAGNESIUM · start a potassium supplement · REVIEW THE BLOOD PRESSURE TABLET.** Then **answer the operation question with a concrete plan and commit to contacting the surgeon and anaesthetic team.**

**Safety-net: marked muscle weakness, palpitations, fainting, or vomiting or diarrhoea that will not settle → come back immediately.** Then **recheck in 3–7 days and again before theatre**, summarise, and invite questions.
pefe: **No physical examination in this station — the examiner gives findings only if asked.**

**Do now: REPEAT U&E on a fresh, promptly processed sample — confirm before treating · ECG · SERUM MAGNESIUM · bicarbonate or venous gas, glucose, calcium, phosphate · CHECK THE LIST FOR DIGOXIN and other QT-prolonging drugs.**

**Do next: SPOT URINE POTASSIUM:CREATININE RATIO or 24 h urinary K, which separates RENAL loss from GI loss or poor intake · ALDOSTERONE–RENIN RATIO if hypertensive with renal wasting · TFTs if thyrotoxic features · METANEPHRINES if the episodic triad is present · repeat potassium before the operation, copied to the pre-admission clinic.**
**Before any of that, exclude a SPURIOUS result — a delayed or haemolysed sample, a very high white cell count, or blood taken shortly after insulin.**

**Escalate to IV replacement with cardiac monitoring if K is below 2.5, or at ANY level with weakness, palpitations, arrhythmia or ECG change, or if he is on DIGOXIN. Peripheral concentration and rate are capped; higher rates need central access and a monitored bed.** VERIFY local protocol.

**Do not miss: HYPOMAGNESAEMIA · primary aldosteronism in hypertension with spontaneous hypokalaemia · ECG changes and arrhythmia risk under GA · DIGOXIN co-prescription, where hypokalaemia precipitates toxicity · thiazide-induced hyponatraemia alongside the low potassium.**

**Avoid: rapid or concentrated IV potassium peripherally · oral potassium alone when magnesium is low · anchoring on the thiazide without voicing a differential · blanket reassurance about the surgery before the recheck.**

stem: James Whitfield, 45, warehouse supervisor, married with two children, not seen here for two years, no recorded chronic disease: 'I've been feeling very thirsty and I'm drinking far more water than usual.' Nurse observations: BP 128/78, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.8, weight 84 kg, BMI 27; blood glucose not yet done.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
Explain the most likely cause and the other conditions you considered
Answer his questions and outline the plan
findings: NO EXAMINATION AND NO RESULTS in this station
Nurse observations only: BP 128/78 · HR 76 regular · RR 14 · SpO2 98% · T 36.8 · WEIGHT 84 kg, BMI 27 · BLOOD GLUCOSE NOT YET DONE. The examiner may ask what you would order
The complaint, QUANTIFIED

TEN DAYS of thirst, CONSTANT and WORSENING. FOUR TO FIVE LITRES A DAY, UP FROM TWO. Nothing makes it better or worse. Up once or twice at night TO DRINK, NOT TO PASS WATER. 'Are you drinking more?' with no number is not enough — THE FIGURE IS WHAT MAKES THIS TRUE POLYDIPSIA rather than a dry mouth, and very few candidates ask for it
THE SUGAR BLOCK — all negative
NO polyuria, NO nocturia to pass water, NO polyphagia, NO weight loss, NO blurred vision, NO recurrent boils, thrush or urinary infections. FATHER HAS TYPE 2 DIABETES — which is what set him worrying
The sentence that earns the mark

'THIRST WITHOUT PASSING MORE URINE MAKES DIABETES A GOOD DEAL LESS LIKELY, and I'll check your sugar with a finger-prick before you leave either way. Can I move on to the next group?' SAY OUT LOUD WHY YOU ARE MOVING ON — do not spend three of six minutes here because the family history looked like a lead
Marrow, brain and thyroid — four questions each, all negative

MARROW: no bone or back pain, energy normal, no weight loss, night sweats, infections or bruising. BRAIN: no morning headache, no vomiting, no visual blurring or field loss. THYROID: no heat intolerance, bowels normal, no palpitations or tremor
THE QUESTION THE STATION TURNS ON

'Any medications?' → 'NO, NOTHING FROM THE DOCTOR.' AND HE STOPS. Only 'ANYTHING YOU BUY YOURSELF — PAINKILLERS, HERBAL THINGS, ANY VITAMINS OR SUPPLEMENTS?' gets 'just vitamin D — THAT'S NOT REALLY A MEDICINE, IS IT?' IF YOU NEVER ASK, THE STATION IS UNPASSABLE
Then quantify it — do not react with alarm

'WHAT DOES THE BOTTLE SAY, HOW MANY UNITS PER CAPSULE?' → 1000. 'HOW MANY A DAY?' → FOUR EVERY MORNING. 'FOR HOW LONG?' → SIX WEEKS. 'ANYTHING WITH CALCIUM IN IT?' → no. Repeat it back: 'so that's FOUR THOUSAND UNITS A DAY for about six weeks'
THE HIDDEN AGENDA — ask why he started

'WHAT MADE YOU START TAKING IT?' → HIS MOTHER HAS OSTEOPOROSIS AND HAS BROKEN TWO BONES THIS YEAR. He is frightened of ending up like her. The counselling marks sit here. If you never ask about his worries, he pushes in at about five minutes: 'is this going to happen to my bones like my mum?'
The hypercalcaemia sweep — STONES, BONES, GROANS, MOANS

Loin pain or kidney stones · aching bones · nausea or vomiting · tummy pain or indigestion · CONSTIPATION · mood, memory and concentration · muscle weakness or daytime drowsiness. HERE: all negative EXCEPT BOWELS 'A BIT SLUGGISH THIS LAST WEEK'. A negative sweep means MILD and outpatient; vomiting, constipation, confusion or drowsiness means SYMPTOMATIC and a SAME-DAY pathway
VERSIONS B and C

B — TRUE TOXICITY: bought 50 000 IU capsules online, label said weekly, HE TAKES ONE DAILY for three months, plus calcium carbonate and a multivitamin. Nausea, constipation, aching legs. SAME-DAY bloods, low threshold for ED. C — RED FLAG: 68-year-old, thirst, tiredness, MID-BACK PAIN WORSE AT NIGHT, 5 kg weight loss, NO supplements. MYELOMA until proven otherwise
findingsLabel: What he withholds — and the question that makes or breaks the station
must: FAIL — Never asking about vitamins or supplements. The station is then unpassable.
FAIL — Never asking whether he is passing more urine.
FAIL — No bone pain, weight loss or infection screen in a man over forty.
FAIL — Declaring vitamin D toxicity as established fact with no blood test offered.
ASK — Anything you buy yourself — any vitamins or supplements?
ASK — What does the bottle say, how many units per capsule, and how many a day?

dx: **Polydipsia caused by mild HYPERCALCAEMIA from excess vitamin D intake.** **The mechanism in one line: vitamin D drives gut calcium absorption → serum calcium rises → calcium BLOCKS THE RENAL RESPONSE TO ANTIDIURETIC HORMONE → a NEPHROGENIC DIABETES INSIPIDUS picture → water loss → thirst.**

**THE STATION TURNS ON ONE QUESTION: 'any medications?' IS NOT THE SAME QUESTION as 'do you take any vitamins or supplements?' — and only the second one passes.** Ask the three-part question every time: **prescribed · bought over the counter · vitamins or supplements.**

**Explain in an UNBROKEN FOUR-LINK CHAIN, never skipping a link: VITAMIN D helps your body absorb CALCIUM from your food → too much pushes the calcium in your blood UP → high calcium makes your KIDNEYS PASS OUT MORE WATER, which dries you out → and what your body feels when it's drying out is THIRST.** Then translate: **'hypercalcaemia just means more calcium in the blood than there should be.'**

**HONEST UNCERTAINTY: 'I can't be certain until I CHECK A CALCIUM LEVEL.'** **CORRECTED CALCIUM IS THE BRANCH POINT — do not diagnose without it.** **High calcium with SUPPRESSED PTH → vitamin D excess, malignancy, granulomatous disease. High calcium with NORMAL OR HIGH PTH → primary hyperparathyroidism, which vitamin D may simply have unmasked. NORMAL calcium → vitamin D is not the answer, and you go back to glucose, TSH and paired osmolalities.**

**HONEST DIVERGENCE FROM THE TEACHING CASE: 4000 IU/day is NOT established toxicity.** It sits inside the range prescribed for deficiency and rarely causes hypercalcaemia with normal kidneys; **documented toxicity usually needs sustained intake of the order of 10 000–50 000 IU/day, or 25(OH)D above 250 nmol/L.** If challenged: **'I'd call this EXCESSIVE SUPPLEMENTATION rather than established toxicity until I have a calcium and a 25(OH)D. If the calcium is high on only 4000 IU, I'd look for a SECOND reason — hyperparathyroidism or granulomatous disease UNMASKED by the supplement.'**

**Numbers: corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 x (40 − albumin g/L). NORMAL 2.10–2.60 · MILD below 3.00 · MODERATE 3.00–3.40 · SEVERE above 3.40 or symptomatic → ED.** **25(OH)D: SUFFICIENT 50 or above · insufficient 30–49 · moderate deficiency 12.5–29 · severe below 12.5. HALF-LIFE 2–3 WEEKS, so levels fall SLOWLY — which is why you recheck rather than reassure.** VERIFY.

**Adequate intake with minimal sun: roughly 200 IU/day at 19–50, 400 IU at 51–70, 600 IU over 70. Deficiency treatment: 1000–2000 IU/day mild; 3000–5000 IU/day for 6–12 weeks moderate to severe, then maintenance.** VERIFY against Therapeutic Guidelines.

**By severity: NORMAL calcium — stop the supplement, reassure, recheck in 4–8 weeks. MILD — stop all vitamin D and calcium, oral fluids 2–3 L/day, AVOID THIAZIDES, repeat in 1–2 weeks. MODERATE or symptomatic — same-day bloods, discuss with the physician, usually IV saline. SEVERE — ED: IV 0.9% sodium chloride, ECG monitoring (SHORT QT), IV bisphosphonate ONCE REHYDRATED, and CORTICOSTEROIDS, which are SPECIFICALLY useful in vitamin D-mediated and granulomatous hypercalcaemia because they reduce 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and gut absorption. LOOP DIURETICS ONLY for fluid overload, not routinely.**

**SEPARATE HIM FROM HIS MOTHER, out loud: 'your mum's dose was worked out FOR HER BONES AND HER BLOOD TEST. Yours hasn't been. That's not your fault — it's a very common thing to do.'** And **'PLEASE DON'T CHANGE YOUR MUM'S TREATMENT — that's a conversation for her own GP.'** **Do not make him feel foolish.**

**PREMATURE CLOSURE IS THE COMMONEST WAY THIS FAILS — hearing 'vitamin D' and stopping.** You still owe the examiner **the myeloma screen, the thyroid block and the brain block**, and you still owe the patient **'a blood test will confirm it.'** **Primary polydipsia is a DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION and goes LAST, if at all — never label it psychogenic.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS.**
plan: **WIPE, open question, ACKNOWLEDGE, then SIGNPOST THE GROUPS: 'I'd like to ask you a set of questions in groups — about your waterworks, your general health, anything you take — and then I'll tell you what I think.'**

**ASK HIS WORRY EARLY, NOT LATE: 'before I start — was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'** → diabetes, because his father has it. **Asked at the start it is a communication mark AND it tells you to test his glucose early; asked at the end there is no time to address it.**

**Explore in 45 seconds: how long · constant or coming and going, getting worse · HOW MUCH ARE YOU ACTUALLY DRINKING, CAN YOU PUT A NUMBER ON IT · anything better or worse · ARE YOU GETTING UP AT NIGHT TO DRINK, OR TO PASS WATER · how is it affecting your day and your work?**

**BLOCK 1, SUGAR — cap it at five questions: ARE YOU PASSING MORE URINE · getting up at night to go · hungrier or eating more · lost weight without trying · blurred vision · recurrent infections, boils, thrush, water infections · family history of diabetes?**
**Say out loud that diabetes is now less likely, promise the finger-prick, and announce the next block.**

**BLOCK 2, MARROW — non-negotiable in a man over 40, four questions, twenty seconds: any pain in your BONES OR YOUR BACK, WORSE AT NIGHT OR AT REST · unusually tired · WEIGHT LOSS, NIGHT SWEATS, or infections you've struggled to shake · any easy bruising or bleeding?**
**BLOCK 3, BRAIN: any headaches, PARTICULARLY FIRST THING IN THE MORNING · any vomiting with them · any blurring or loss of vision, or bumping into things at the side · any fits or blackouts?**
**BLOCK 4, THYROID: do you prefer hot or cold weather, feeling the heat more · any looser bowels · any racing or pounding heart · any shakiness in the hands · eating well but losing weight?**

**BLOCK 5, DRUGS AND SUPPLEMENTS — THE DIAGNOSIS LIVES HERE, in this order: any regular medicines from a doctor · ANYTHING YOU BUY YOURSELF, painkillers, herbal things · DO YOU TAKE ANY VITAMIN D, OR A MULTIVITAMIN?**

**Then, WITHOUT CHANGING YOUR TONE: what does the bottle say, HOW MANY UNITS PER CAPSULE · HOW MANY DO YOU TAKE A DAY · FOR HOW LONG · anything with calcium in it · any fluid tablets, LITHIUM, or steroids · AND WHAT MADE YOU START?**

**BLOCK 6, LIFESTYLE — must be asked before you can dismiss it: how much coffee or energy drinks · alcohol, how much and how often · do you add a lot of salt or eat a lot of takeaway · how much exercise, and are you working somewhere hot?**

**THE HYPERCALCAEMIA SWEEP, 40 seconds: loin or side pain, EVER PASSED A KIDNEY STONE · aching in the bones · NAUSEA OR VOMITING · tummy pain or indigestion · HOW ARE YOUR BOWELS, ANY CONSTIPATION · mood, memory and concentration · MUSCLE WEAKNESS or feeling DROWSY in the day?** **The answers set the SEVERITY.**
**Finish the spine: SADMA · past history — kidney stones, SARCOIDOSIS, TB, cancer, kidney disease · family history · impact and ICE if still outstanding.** Then **a one-line summary back to him.**

**Summarise and check permission, then THE FOUR-LINK CHAIN, then HONEST UNCERTAINTY, then the differentials IN PLAIN ENGLISH with a reason each — diabetes, thyroid, brain, marrow, and the everyday causes.**

**Separate him from his mother.** Then **the plan: STOP THE CAPSULES TODAY and bring the bottle in · FINGER-PRICK SUGAR NOW · bloods for CORRECTED CALCIUM, kidney function, 25(OH)D, glucose and thyroid · drink to thirst, 2–3 litres · review with the results, and a phone call sooner if anything needs acting on.**

**SAFETY-NET, said unprompted and by NAMED symptom: 'come back straight away, or go to the emergency department, if you start VOMITING, get bad TUMMY PAIN or become badly CONSTIPATED, feel WEAK, or if you or your wife notice you're CONFUSED OR UNUSUALLY SLEEPY.'** Then **'is there anything I haven't covered?'**

stem: Ms Janine Whitfield, 45, teacher's aide, attends to discuss blood tests taken at a routine check-up two weeks ago. Hypothyroidism for eight years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medicines on file; non-smoker; she has no complaint and feels perfectly well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 14 (10–20), albumin 31 g/L (low, 35–50), total calcium 2.56 (normal, 2.10–2.60), corrected calcium 2.78 — HIGH.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Explain the blood results you already have, in plain language
Tell the examiner the further investigations you would request, in order of priority
The examiner will give you those results. Explain your diagnosis and your reasoning to the patient, including the differentials you considered
findings: The results already in front of you
TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0) NORMAL · FREE T4 14 (10–20) NORMAL · ALBUMIN 31 g/L — LOW (35–50) · TOTAL CALCIUM 2.56 — LOOKS NORMAL (2.10–2.60) · CORRECTED CALCIUM 2.78 — HIGH
READ THE ALBUMIN, NOT JUST THE CALCIUM

CORRECTED Ca = total + 0.02 x (40 − albumin in g/L) = 2.56 + 0.02 x 9 = 2.78. ACT ON THE CORRECTED VALUE ONLY. Saying 'your calcium is actually normal, so there's nothing to worry about' is a STATION-ENDING false reassurance. A LOW ALBUMIN IS ITSELF WORTH A SENTENCE — it can point to malignancy, liver disease or nephrotic syndrome
The severity band
MILD, below 3.00 — usually asymptomatic, outpatient work-up. MODERATE 3.00–3.50 — symptoms likely, look hard for malignancy. SEVERE above 3.50 — confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia, ADMIT
THE HOOK — the question that turns a number into a story

'HAS ANYONE EVER TOLD YOU BEFORE THAT YOUR CALCIUM WAS HIGH?' → 'Yes — last year. My GP told me to stop my supplements and cut back on dairy, and I did. AND HERE I AM, IT'S STILL HIGH.' CHRONICITY makes hyperparathyroidism far more likely than an acute malignancy — but it does NOT exclude it
What the history returns — Version A

ALL NEGATIVE except a little more thirst ('I keep a bottle on my desk') — give it only if asked. No nausea, vomiting, constipation, bone or back pain, stones, mood change. No weight loss, lumps, night sweats, breast change, cough, haemoptysis, haematuria. Mammogram clear last year. Never smoked. NO supplements now, Gaviscon once a month. No thiazide, no lithium. No TB contact, no rash, no joint pain, no phaeo episodes
Her hidden agenda — and when she releases it

HER MOTHER HAD BREAST CANCER AT 60. If you ask ICE at any point she gives it quietly. IF YOU NEVER ASK, SHE VOLUNTEERS IT AT ABOUT MINUTE SEVEN, just as you are summarising, so you must handle it under time pressure. She also challenges mid-station after the breast question: 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ALL THIS?'
What the examiner hands back — Version A
PTH ELEVATED · VITAMIN D NORMAL · PHOSPHATE LOW-NORMAL · eGFR 88 · FULL EXAMINATION NORMAL. PTH high or INAPPROPRIATELY NORMAL confirms primary hyperparathyroidism
VERSION B — the flip

Same stem, but on direct questioning she takes a HIGH-DOSE VITAMIN D from a health-food shop and chews CALCIUM ANTACIDS daily. Corrected Ca 2.88. The examiner returns: PTH SUPPRESSED below 1.0 · 25-OH VITAMIN D 310 nmol/L · eGFR 74. DIAGNOSIS FLIPS TO VITAMIN D TOXICITY, with milk-alkali. A SUPPRESSED PTH IS THE MALIGNANCY ARM — finish the work-up anyway
The ECG, if asked
HYPERCALCAEMIA SHORTENS THE QT — the ST segment is almost abolished so the T wave appears to arise straight off the QRS. Severe cases also show OSBORN (J) WAVES and bradyarrhythmia
The levothyroxine red herring

It is in the stem ONLY TO TEMPT YOU. A NORMAL TSH MEANS THE DOSE IS CORRECT. Levothyroxine raises calcium only if it causes frank thyrotoxicosis — and then the TSH would be SUPPRESSED. Two questions on the thyroid — how long, taking it as prescribed — then MOVE ON
findingsLabel: The results, the hook, and what the examiner hands back
must: FAIL — Never saying PTH, or burying it at position nine in an unranked list.
FAIL — No malignancy screen: no weight, no lumps, no night sweats.
FAIL — Acting on the total calcium and reassuring her that it is normal.
FAIL — Blaming the levothyroxine and reducing the dose on a normal TSH.
ASK — Has anyone ever told you before that your calcium was high?
ASK — Was there anything in particular worrying you about these results?

dx: **Primary hyperparathyroidism** — a single parathyroid adenoma in about 85%, four-gland hyperplasia in most of the rest. **The commonest cause of hypercalcaemia in the community, and the answer here.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: this is a REASONING-OUT-LOUD station, not a history station.** Everything hinges on one thirty-second turn — **when the examiner asks what you would request, do you deliver a RANKED list with PTH at the top and a REASON attached to each item, or an unranked recitation?**

**THE SCORING REALITY: divide 100 marks across the list. PTH, vitamin D with phosphate, and renal function take about NINETY; everything else shares the last ten. A candidate who lists twenty tests and never says PTH does not pass.** **The word that buys the mark is BECAUSE.**

**'My first priority is SERUM PARATHYROID HORMONE, because primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause in the community and PTH IS THE SINGLE TEST THAT DIVIDES THE DIFFERENTIAL IN TWO. Second, 25-HYDROXY VITAMIN D with SERUM PHOSPHATE — calcium, phosphate and vitamin D are read as a set, and a low phosphate would support hyperparathyroidism. Third, UEC AND eGFR, for renal function and any hypercalcaemic nephropathy.'**
**PTH HIGH OR INAPPROPRIATELY NORMAL → PTH-dependent → the GLAND. PTH SUPPRESSED → PTH-independent → hunt CANCER, VITAMIN D and GRANULOMA.**

**Explain the glands in plain English: 'you already know about your thyroid gland, here in the front of your neck. SITTING BEHIND IT ARE FOUR TINY GLANDS called the PARATHYROID glands — DIFFERENT GLANDS, DIFFERENT JOB. Their only job is to keep the calcium in your blood at the right level. One of them appears to be OVERWORKING, and that pulls extra calcium OUT OF YOUR BONES into your blood.'** Then: **'it is NOT a cancer, and it is NOT caused by your thyroid tablets or by what you eat.'**

**'Calcium isn't really controlled by what you eat — your body controls it with a HORMONE.'** **Do NOT endorse a low-calcium diet: dietary calcium is not the driver, and severe restriction can WORSEN bone loss. Adequate hydration matters more.**

**Surgery indications in asymptomatic primary disease — ANY ONE of: AGE UNDER 50 · corrected calcium MORE THAN 0.25 mmol/L above the upper limit · eGFR BELOW 60 · 24-hour urine calcium ABOVE 10 mmol/day · stones or nephrocalcinosis · T-SCORE MINUS 2.5 OR LOWER, or a vertebral fracture.** **She is 45, so AGE ALONE already makes her a surgical candidate — a strong point to make.** VERIFY.

**CORRECTION — localisation imaging does NOT make the diagnosis.** It is a **TECHNETIUM-99m SESTAMIBI scan and neck ultrasound, with 4D-CT if they disagree — ordered BY THE SURGEON to plan the operation.** If challenged: **'the diagnosis is BIOCHEMICAL; imaging is for surgical planning.'**

**CORRECTION — thiazides cause HYPOnatraemia and HYPOkalaemia, together with HYPERcalcaemia, hyperuricaemia and hyperglycaemia.** Some notes have this the wrong way round. **And EXCLUDE FAMILIAL HYPOCALCIURIC HYPERCALCAEMIA with a urine Ca:Cr clearance ratio below 0.01 BEFORE anyone is referred for surgery — those patients are HARMED by it.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS.**
plan: **WIPE, confirm identity, and ASK AN OPEN QUESTION FIRST — never lead with the abnormal number.** Then **name it early and size it honestly: 'I can see one of the numbers, your calcium, is a little higher than we'd like. IT ISN'T AN EMERGENCY, but it does need explaining. Would it be alright if I asked you some questions first, so I can work out why?'** That converts a no-complaint stem into a consultation and **buys you four minutes of history.**

**The two questions that open the story: 'WHAT MADE YOU HAVE THE BLOOD TEST IN THE FIRST PLACE?' and 'HAS ANYONE EVER TOLD YOU BEFORE THAT YOUR CALCIUM WAS HIGH?'** Then **'did anyone do further tests, or start any treatment for it?'**

**BLOCK 1, symptoms of hypercalcaemia — STONES, BONES, GROANS, MOANS, THRONES, at least five: nausea or vomiting · tummy pain or CONSTIPATION · BONE OR BACK PAIN · muscle WEAKNESS or unusual tiredness · MORE THIRSTY or PASSING MORE URINE, especially at night · kidney stones or loin pain · change in MOOD, MEMORY OR CONCENTRATION?** **This block is also your ENTIRE history for hyperparathyroidism — say so when you present.**

**BLOCK 2, THE MALIGNANCY SCREEN — 60 seconds, never skip. Signpost it: 'I'm going to ask some questions I ask everybody with this result, just to be thorough.' Weight loss without meaning to · change in appetite · LUMPS in neck, armpits or groin · NIGHT SWEATS that soak the sheets · fevers.**

**Organ-directed: any LUMP OR CHANGE IN EITHER BREAST or nipple discharge, are MAMMOGRAMS up to date · a COUGH THAT WON'T GO or HAEMOPTYSIS, do you smoke or have you ever · BLOOD IN YOUR URINE · BACK PAIN ESPECIALLY AT NIGHT · any cancer in you or your family?** **Myeloma needs back pain, fatigue and infections; RENAL CELL CARCINOMA secretes PTHrP, so ask haematuria and loin pain.**

**If she challenges — 'why are you asking all this?' — STOP, TURN TOWARDS HER, and answer honestly: 'a high calcium has several possible causes. Most are not serious, and the commonest by far is a small gland problem. But a few cancers can also raise calcium, so I check for them IN EVERYBODY — not because I suspect it in you.'**

**BLOCK 3, SUPPLEMENTS — question three, not question nine, because it is the only immediately reversible cause and in Version B it is the answer: any VITAMIN D, multivitamins or CALCIUM TABLETS, what dose and how long · anything for INDIGESTION OR HEARTBURN, antacid tablets or liquid, how often · anything else you buy yourself, herbal or health-food-shop?**

**BLOCK 4, prescription drugs — name them BY THEIR USE, not their class: 'apart from the thyroid tablet, any other regular medicine — ANYTHING FOR BLOOD PRESSURE OR FLUID, or ANY TABLET FOR YOUR MOOD?'** That is **thiazide and lithium.**

**BLOCK 5, lung, TB and SARCOID: any cough, breathlessness or chest pain · fevers or night sweats · contact with TUBERCULOSIS or living where it is common · ANY JOINT PAINS, OR ANY RASH, PARTICULARLY TENDER RED LUMPS ON YOUR SHINS?** **Erythema nodosum plus hilar lymphadenopathy plus hypercalcaemia is SARCOIDOSIS.**

**BLOCK 6, phaeo and MEN, 15 seconds: episodes of HEADACHE WITH SWEATING, FLUSHING OR YOUR HEART RACING · FAMILY HISTORY OF THYROID OR PARATHYROID PROBLEMS, or tumours of the adrenal gland?** **The family-history question is the one that scores — MEN links hyperparathyroidism to phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid cancer.**

**BLOCK 7, thyroid in TWO questions then close: how long, taking it as prescribed · any tremor, heat intolerance or palpitations?** Then **SADMA and, crucially, ICE: 'is there anything you were hoping we'd cover today, or anything worrying you?'** **ICE BEFORE you explain, not after.**

**Explain the results: the thyroid is normal so the dose is right. Then the calcium: 'some floats free, some is carried by a protein called ALBUMIN. Your albumin is a bit low, so the RAW number looks normal — but once we adjust for that protein, the true level is 2.78, and we'd expect it under 2.60.'** Then **check understanding.**

**Turn to the examiner and deliver THE RANKED LIST, with a reason on each — PTH first.** Then the lower-priority items: **chest X-ray · FBC, ESR, protein electrophoresis and free light chains · 24-hour urine calcium · and a full examination including breasts and lymph nodes.**
**Take the results, turn back, and give the diagnosis in lay terms — four glands, one overworking, and IT IS NOT A CANCER.** Then **check understanding before moving on.**

**Name the differentials you excluded and WHY — cancer, vitamin D and antacids, fluid tablets and lithium, overactive thyroid excluded on the normal TSH, sarcoidosis and TB.** Then **the plan: specialist referral, generous oral fluids, and at 45 the age-based surgical indication.**

**SAFETY-NET by named symptom: 'if you become very thirsty and are passing a lot of urine, if you start VOMITING, become DROWSY OR CONFUSED, or develop severe tummy, back or loin pain, I want you seen THE SAME DAY.'** Then **summarise and offer to write it down.**
pefe: **Do now: CONFIRM IT IS REAL — repeat corrected calcium with albumin on a fresh, properly taken sample · then SERUM PTH (intact), said FIRST every time · 25-OH VITAMIN D and PHOSPHATE · UEC and eGFR · review every medicine and supplement · FULL EXAMINATION INCLUDING BREASTS AND LYMPH NODES.**

**Do next: CHEST X-RAY for lung cancer, TB, sarcoidosis and lymphoma · FBC, ESR, LFT, LDH · SERUM PROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS and FREE LIGHT CHAINS for myeloma · 24-HOUR URINE CALCIUM or Ca:Cr clearance ratio to exclude FHH · ECG for a short QT. Once diagnosed: DEXA and renal tract ultrasound.**

**In THIS station you do nothing intravenous — 2.78 is mild and asymptomatic. Stop any contributor, repeat the calcium, request PTH, encourage generous oral fluids, arrange bloods and review, and refer once PTH confirms it.**

**If severe: SALINE 0.9%, commonly 4–6 L over 24 hours titrated to cardiac and renal reserve — this alone brings most of the fall · stop the contributors · ZOLEDRONIC ACID 4 mg IV over at least 15 minutes AFTER rehydration, onset 2–4 days so NOT the first move · calcitonin 4 units/kg 12-hourly when a fast fall is needed · PREDNISOLONE 20–40 mg daily for VITAMIN D-MEDIATED and granulomatous causes · dialysis if refractory.**

**Do not miss: MALIGNANCY, especially myeloma in anyone with anaemia, renal impairment or back pain · corrected calcium above 3.5, or confusion, vomiting or dehydration at any level · FHH before referring for surgery · LITHIUM as the cause · a LOW ALBUMIN as a clue in its own right.**

**Avoid: acting on the total calcium · a long undifferentiated list instead of a priority order · advising a low-calcium diet as treatment · ROUTINE FRUSEMIDE, which is only for fluid overload during rehydration · a bisphosphonate BEFORE rehydration · localisation imaging to make the diagnosis.**
**Never stop lithium unilaterally — it needs PTH measurement and psychiatric liaison.**

**Middle-aged woman; calcium ALSO HIGH PREVIOUSLY; asymptomatic or vague tiredness and constipation; PHOSPHATE LOW**
Stones, bones, groans, moans, thrones. **No cancer symptoms**
**PTH HIGH OR INAPPROPRIATELY NORMAL confirms it.** Add phosphate, 25-OH vitamin D, eGFR, urine calcium

**PTH SUPPRESSED. FBC, ESR, LDH, chest X-ray, PROTEIN ELECTROPHORESIS and FREE LIGHT CHAINS, imaging** — must not miss
**Vitamin D excess · calcium antacids (milk-alkali)**
**High-dose supplement or health-food product; heavy antacid use — VERSION B**
**Exact preparation, dose, duration.** Alkalosis and renal impairment suggest milk-alkali

Treat the renal disease; **calcimimetic (cinacalcet) or surgery under specialist care**
**Spurious result**
**Prolonged tourniquet, dehydration, raised serum proteins**
How was the sample taken? Was she fasting or unwell?

stem: Marianne Kovac, 50, presents with two days of nausea and vomiting on a week of feeling weak, tired and lethargic. She is holding a vomit bag. Known hypertension and chronic kidney disease. Current medications: perindopril 5 mg daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings and investigations you want
Explain the most likely diagnosis and outline your immediate management
findings: Vital signs — ask for the BLOOD SUGAR in the same breath

BP 142/86 · PULSE 72 regular · RR 16 · SpO2 98% RA · T 36.6 · BSL 5.4. She is AFEBRILE AND HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE — say so. The normal sugar is a cheap move that QUIETLY CLOSES OFF DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS without spending a history question on it
The visual cue in the room

SHE IS HOLDING A VOMIT BAG. Acknowledge it — 'I'm sorry, that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first?' costs three seconds and is MARKED. But DO NOT let it push you into a purely gastrointestinal frame
Fluid status — ask for it FIRST
DRY MUCOUS MEMBRANES · POSTURAL DROP OF 20 SYSTOLIC · JVP NOT VISIBLE. It is the finding that EXPLAINS THE MECHANISM and the one candidates forget to request
The rest of the examination
Abdomen SOFT AND NON-TENDER, no palpable bladder. Heart sounds dual, chest clear. NO pallor, NO pigmentation, NO oedema, NO ASTERIXIS
The bloods

eGFR 22, DOWN FROM A BASELINE OF 45 · CREATININE ROUGHLY DOUBLED · POTASSIUM 6.3 · BICARBONATE 18 · TROPONIN NOT RAISED. A doubled creatinine meets criteria for a STAGE 2 ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY — saying the stage aloud is a cheap mark
The ECG — done in the clinic, before she leaves
PEAKED T WAVES WITH A NARROW QRS. Request it for BOTH hyperkalaemia AND ischaemia. K 6.3 is MODERATE BY NUMBER, but WITH ECG CHANGES IT IS TREATED AS SEVERE
THE DRUG SHE DOES NOT CALL A MEDICATION

'What medications are you on?' → 'PERINDOPRIL AND A FLUID TABLET.' AND SHE STOPS. Only 'ANY PAINKILLERS?' or 'ANYTHING FROM THE CHEMIST, or not on prescription?' gets IBUPROFEN 400 mg THREE TIMES A DAY FOR THREE WEEKS for her knee — bought herself at first, then a LOCUM wrote a script because her own GP was away
The follow-up questions that complete it
'WHO STARTED IT, AND WHEN?' → the locum, about a fortnight ago. 'DID WHOEVER PRESCRIBED IT KNOW ABOUT YOUR KIDNEYS?' → 'I don't think it came up. IT'S ONLY IBUPROFEN'
What she gives only on direct questioning

MUCH LESS URINE than usual — the single most useful volume question, and candidates skip it constantly. DIZZY ON STANDING. EVERYTHING TASTES OF METAL — a free uraemia mark. Vomit is FOOD AND FLUID ONLY, no blood, nothing green. She FELT CLAMMY YESTERDAY and blamed the vomiting
Her hidden fear

HER MOTHER DIED ON DIALYSIS. She volunteers it only in the last two minutes, or when you ask what worries her. She also pushes back once on the transfer: 'DO I REALLY HAVE TO GO TODAY? Can't I just stop the tablets and come back Friday?'
findingsLabel: Examiner stage — and the painkiller she does not call a medication
must: FAIL — Never screening for ACS. Four minutes of renal questions and no cardiac question.
FAIL — Missing the NSAID by asking only 'what medications are you on?'
FAIL — Sending her home with K 6.3 and ECG changes to 'come back Friday'.
FAIL — Saying hyperaldosteronism causes hyperkalaemia. It causes HYPOkalaemia.

dx: **Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease, with HYPERKALAEMIA and URAEMIA — caused by the TRIPLE WHAMMY: an ACE inhibitor, a diuretic and an NSAID taken together.**

**The mechanism, in one sentence: the NSAID CONSTRICTS THE AFFERENT arteriole by blocking prostaglandins · the ACE inhibitor DILATES THE EFFERENT arteriole by blocking angiotensin II · the diuretic DROPS THE CIRCULATING VOLUME. Perfusion pressure across the glomerulus collapses.** **Each drug alone is reasonable; together they remove every compensatory mechanism the glomerulus has.**
**SPOTTING THREE DRUGS IS NOT THE MARK. EXPLAINING WHY THOSE THREE TOGETHER BREAK A KIDNEY IS THE MARK.**

**THE TRAP THIS STATION WAS BUILT AROUND: the medication list is DELIBERATELY OBVIOUS.** Candidates who spot it in the first ten seconds **spend the remaining four minutes confirming what they already believe and never ask a single question about her heart.** **Work out the diagnosis early, then say NOTHING about it until you have spent sixty seconds actively trying to DISPROVE it — the examiner is marking the disproving.**

**THING TWO: nausea, vomiting and lethargy WITHOUT chest pain is a recognised presentation of MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION in women and in people with kidney disease.** Say it out loud: **'although the drug combination makes acute kidney injury far the most likely explanation, I have screened for it and I WOULD NOT DISCHARGE HER WITHOUT AN ECG AND A TROPONIN.'** **That demonstrates you can hold a likely diagnosis and a dangerous one at the same time — which is the whole assessment.**

**To the patient, in plain English: 'the painkiller NARROWS THE VESSEL BRINGING BLOOD IN, the perindopril WIDENS THE VESSEL TAKING BLOOD OUT, and the fluid tablet LOWERS THE AMOUNT OF FLUID IN YOUR CIRCULATION. Each is sensible on its own. Together, with kidneys like yours, they're too much. In Australia we have a name for it: the TRIPLE WHAMMY.'**
**To 'it's only ibuprofen, you can buy it anywhere': 'you can — and THAT'S EXACTLY WHY IT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT. Being sold without a prescription doesn't make it harmless for your kidneys.'**

**STOP THE IBUPROFEN PERMANENTLY. WITHHOLD the perindopril and hydrochlorothiazide — a temporary SICK-DAY HOLD, framed as temporary, NOT a permanent stop, because the ACE inhibitor has long-term renal and cardiac benefit.** **With K 6.3 and ECG changes this is an EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT TRANSFER TODAY, not a clinic recheck. Arrange transport; DO NOT LET HER DRIVE.**

**CORRECTION — the aldosterone rule runs in ONE DIRECTION ONLY. Aldosterone makes the kidney EXCRETE potassium. So HYPOaldosteronism → HYPERkalaemia; HYPERaldosteronism → HYPOkalaemia.** **Primary aldosteronism classically presents with hypertension and a LOW potassium with metabolic alkalosis. If a source lists hyperaldosteronism as a cause of hyperkalaemia, that is an error — do not repeat it to an examiner.**

**The blame moment: 'he was treating your knee, and ibuprofen is a perfectly ordinary choice for most people. The problem is THE COMBINATION with the two medicines you were already on, and that is exactly the kind of thing that gets missed WHEN A DOCTOR DOESN'T HAVE YOUR FULL RECORD. What matters now is that we've found it. I'll write to your usual GP today and put a note on your file.'** **Never say the other doctor was negligent.**
plan: **To the examiner: 'before I begin, could I have her blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature AND BLOOD SUGAR?'** Then **say what it means: 'stable, afebrile, and a normal sugar, which makes a diabetic emergency unlikely from the outset.'**

**Greet, ask how she would like to be addressed, and ACKNOWLEDGE the bag: 'I'm sorry you've been feeling so unwell — that sounds miserable. Would you like some water first? Let me ask you some questions and I'll work out what's causing it.'**

**BLOCK 1, the symptom package in ONE block — do not run SOCRATES four times: when did all of this start · is it getting worse · anything better or worse · WHEN YOU SAY TIRED, DO YOU MEAN LOW IN ENERGY, SLEEPY, OR BREATHLESS ON EXERTION?**

**Then the vomiting: how many times · WHAT DOES THE VOMIT LOOK LIKE, ANY BLOOD OR IS IT GREEN · have you been able to keep anything down · DID PAIN COME BEFORE THE VOMITING OR AFTER?** **Content of the vomitus is the highest-yield vomiting question — blood or coffee-grounds points to an upper GI bleed in someone on an NSAID; bilious or faeculent points to obstruction. Pain first suggests a surgical cause.**

**BLOCK 2, background: when were you diagnosed with the kidney problem and the high blood pressure · what treatment, and are you taking it regularly · are you up to date with your GP and kidney specialist reviews?**

**THE KEY QUESTION: 'WHEN DID YOU START THE PAINKILLER — AND WHO STARTED IT FOR YOU? What was it for, and how much are you taking? ANYTHING ELSE AT ALL — ANYTHING FROM THE CHEMIST, OR ANYTHING HERBAL?'** Then, neutrally: **'did whoever prescribed it know about your kidneys?'**

**BLOCK 3, RULE OUT THE HEART — ten seconds, and SAY WHY YOU ARE DOING IT: 'a few quick questions to make sure I'm not missing something serious. Any discomfort or TIGHTNESS IN THE CHEST, ARM, JAW OR BACK · any BREATHLESSNESS, especially on exertion or lying flat · any COLD SWEATS · palpitations · blackouts?'**

**BLOCK 4, rule out the abdomen in four questions: any tummy pain and WHERE · any change in your bowels, any diarrhoea, HAVE YOU STOPPED PASSING WIND · ANY BLACK OR TARRY MOTIONS · any fevers or chills · any yellowing of the eyes or skin?**

**BLOCK 5, metabolic and fluid status: any excessive thirst or passing more urine · HOW MUCH URINE HAVE YOU PASSED IN THE LAST DAY, MORE, LESS OR THE SAME · any DIZZINESS ON STANDING · any ankle swelling · any CONFUSION, HICCUPS, ITCH OR A METALLIC TASTE?** The last line **screens for uraemia.**

**BLOCK 6, close: any past medical problems I haven't covered · any allergies · AND IS THERE ANYTHING YOU'RE PARTICULARLY WORRIED ABOUT?** **The final question is scored — if time runs out, carry it into the explanation.**

**Examination request, FLUID STATUS FIRST: postural blood pressure, mucous membranes, JVP, capillary refill · abdomen for tenderness, guarding, organomegaly and a palpable bladder · cardiorespiratory · and a look for PALLOR, PIGMENTATION, OEDEMA AND ASTERIXIS.**

**Investigations, NAMED: an ECG HERE IN THE CLINIC NOW, for both hyperkalaemia and ischaemia · UEC with eGFR, SPECIFICALLY THE POTASSIUM, SODIUM AND BICARBONATE, AGAINST HER BASELINE · a venous or arterial blood gas · a TROPONIN · then FBC, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, LFTs, lipase, BSL · urinalysis and bladder scan if oliguric.**

**Read the numbers back and NAME THE STAGE: 'her eGFR has halved from 45 to 22 with a roughly doubled creatinine, which meets criteria for a STAGE 2 acute kidney injury. The potassium of 6.3 is moderate by number BUT SHE HAS ECG CHANGES, so I treat it as severe. The bicarbonate of 18 indicates a metabolic acidosis, which itself drives potassium out of the cells.'**

**Name the diagnosis and answer the dialysis fear HONESTLY rather than deflecting: 'not today, and in most cases like yours this is REVERSIBLE once we take the pressure off — that's exactly why we're acting now.'** Then **the mechanism in plain English, and handle the blame moment.**

**THREE THINGS: the IBUPROFEN STOPS TODAY and never again without checking · we HOLD the perindopril and the fluid tablet while you're unwell, TEMPORARILY, and don't stop anything else on your own · your potassium is high enough to affect the heart's rhythm and you can't keep fluids down, so YOU'RE GOING TO THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT TODAY. I'll ring ahead and send the results with you.**

**SAFETY-NET: don't drive, is there someone who can take you · on the way, CHEST PAIN, PALPITATIONS, FEELING FAINT, OR MUSCLE WEAKNESS means call an ambulance rather than waiting.** Then **the follow-up: repeat renal bloods in 2–3 days, a WRITTEN SICK-DAY PLAN, and a safer plan for the knee — PARACETAMOL first line and physiotherapy.** Then **TEACH-BACK: 'could you tell me back what you'll say when you get to the hospital?'**
pefe: **Ask for FLUID STATUS FIRST — it is the finding that explains the mechanism.**
**'Renal function tests' scores nothing. Name the analyte, and name the baseline you are comparing against.**

**If challenged on the troponin in a patient with no chest pain: 'because nausea and lethargy WITHOUT chest pain is a recognised presentation of infarction in women and in patients with chronic kidney disease.'**

**In the emergency department: CALCIUM GLUCONATE 10%, 10 mL IV over 2–5 minutes if ECG changes are present — MYOCARDIAL PROTECTION ONLY, it does not lower potassium, repeat if changes persist · INSULIN–DEXTROSE, 10 units short-acting in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 15–30 min, onset about 15 min, lasts 4–6 h, HOURLY SUGARS FOR 6 HOURS · SALBUTAMOL 10–20 mg nebulised as an adjunct · sodium bicarbonate only for significant acidosis · isotonic fluid titrated to fluid status · dialysis if refractory, anuric or severely acidotic.** VERIFY.
**Repeat the potassium at 1–2 HOURS after any shifting agent — it rebounds. Recheck renal function 48–72 HOURS after stopping the drugs, and 1–2 WEEKS after restarting an ACE inhibitor.**

**Avoid: ANY NSAID, including topical, over-the-counter and COX-2 selective agents — the renal risk is a CLASS EFFECT from prostaglandin inhibition, not COX-1 selectivity · resins as the acute answer, since binders are for ongoing control · stopping the perindopril PERMANENTLY by default.**

**The analgesia alternative, ready to offer: PARACETAMOL first line · physiotherapy, weight management, a walking aid, specialist referral for intra-articular options · topical NSAIDs still best avoided in significant CKD · OPIOIDS are a poor answer for chronic osteoarthritis and ACCUMULATE in renal impairment.**

stem: Mr Colin Whitfield, 58, semi-retired farm contractor, returns for the results of blood tests taken a fortnight ago when he attended feeling tired. Hypothyroidism for six years on levothyroxine 100 µg daily; no other regular medication recorded. BP 138/82, HR 76 regular, RR 14, SpO2 98%, T 36.7; he looks well. Results: TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0), free T4 15 (10–20), total calcium 2.58 (2.15–2.60), albumin 28 (low), corrected calcium 2.82 (HIGH), phosphate 0.68 (low, 0.75–1.50), creatinine 88/eGFR >60, FBE and LFT normal, PTH sent — result not yet available.
tasks: Explain these blood results in language he can understand
Take a focused, relevant history
Give your most likely diagnosis and your differentials
Explain what happens next
findings: The results card handed to you

TSH 2.1 (0.4–4.0) · FREE T4 15 (10–20) — thyroid NORMAL, dose is right · TOTAL CALCIUM 2.58 (2.15–2.60) — LOOKS NORMAL · ALBUMIN 28 g/L, LOW (35–50) · CORRECTED CALCIUM 2.82, HIGH · PHOSPHATE 0.68, LOW (0.75–1.50) · creatinine 88, eGFR above 60 · FBE and LFT normal · PTH SAMPLE SENT, RESULT NOT YET AVAILABLE
The arithmetic, done out loud

CORRECTED Ca = total + 0.02 x (40 − albumin) = 2.58 + 0.02 x 12 = 2.82. ABOUT HALF of circulating calcium is bound to albumin, so a LOW albumin lowers the TOTAL without lowering the physiologically active IONISED fraction. READ EVERY LINE OF THE CARD IN THE TWO MINUTES OUTSIDE THE DOOR — saying 'all your bloods are fine' ends the station
THE PHOSPHATE IS A FREE CLUE

PTH DRIVES PHOSPHATE OUT IN THE URINE, so primary hyperparathyroidism AND PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia both give a LOW phosphate. A HIGH or high-normal phosphate with a high calcium points instead to BONE METASTASES, MYELOMA, VITAMIN D EXCESS or GRANULOMATOUS DISEASE. Saying this marks you as someone who reads the whole panel
Observations
BP 138/82 · HR 76 regular · RR 14 · SpO2 98% · T 36.7 · BMI 27. HE LOOKS WELL — so this is an OUTPATIENT problem
What he gives ONLY on the right question

STONES: 'a stone about three years ago — WORST PAIN OF MY LIFE', and UP TWICE A NIGHT, thirsty. BONES: hips ache, 'but I've been on tractors forty years'. GROANS: CONSTIPATED, NEW THIS YEAR. MOANS: 'I've been FLAT. Denise has mentioned it.' He does NOT hand over the stone unless you ask about stones or urine, or the constipation unless you ask about bowels
The cancer block — clean negatives

WEIGHT STEADY · NO night sweats, fevers or lumps · NO cough or haemoptysis · NEVER SMOKED A DAY. A CLEAN SET OF NEGATIVES HERE IS WHAT MAKES PRIMARY HYPERPARATHYROIDISM THE LIKELY ANSWER RATHER THAN A GUESS
Drugs and family

'JUST THE THYROXINE. I DON'T HOLD WITH VITAMINS.' No fluid tablets, no lithium, no calcium or vitamin D, no antacids. No family history of high calcium, stones, neck surgery, or pituitary or pancreatic tumours. Four or five beers Friday, more at harvest — which explains the LOW ALBUMIN
THE HIDDEN AGENDA

HIS BROTHER WAYNE DIED LAST YEAR AT 55 OF BOWEL CANCER. He does not raise it in the first six minutes. IF YOU ASK what he was worried about, he tells you and his voice drops. IF YOU NEVER ASK, HE RAISES IT IN THE LAST THIRTY SECONDS — 'it's not cancer, is it?' — when there is no time to deal with it properly
VERSION B — the dangerous one

CORRECTED Ca 3.35 · ALP 260 · Hb 96 · ESR 88 · 6 kg WEIGHT LOSS · 40 PACK-YEARS · THORACIC BACK PAIN · DROWSY. PTH SUPPRESSED. MALIGNANCY — PTHrP, bone metastases or myeloma. SAME-DAY IV FLUIDS AND ADMISSION, not a follow-up appointment
VERSION C — the drug one

CORRECTED Ca 2.74 · phosphate 1.0 · eGFR 55. On INDAPAMIDE, LITHIUM for bipolar, and CALCIUM 600 mg WITH VITAMIN D. PTH mid-normal to mildly raised. THE DRUG LIST IS THE DIAGNOSIS. Change the diuretic, stop the supplement — BUT NEVER STOP THE LITHIUM YOURSELF
