stem: Jane Whitmore, 30, has come in feeling unwell. She reports there has been an incident at work. No further detail is given. T 38.1, HR 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
tasks: Take a focused history (6 minutes)
You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: Vitals in the stem — your first check
T 38.1 · HR 92 · BP 118/72 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% RA. SHE IS NOT SEPTIC AND NOT DEHYDRATED — but CHECK THE VITALS AGAINST A SEPSIS PATHWAY before settling on a benign diagnosis
THE INCIDENT — open it, or fail the approach domain

'You mentioned an incident at work. CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT IT?' → 'My job is COLLECTING SAMPLES FROM THE SEWER. I was climbing in, I SLIPPED, AND I FELL INTO THE SEWAGE.' SAY IT ALOUD: 'so you were EXPOSED TO URINE AND FAECES.' That sentence is the pivot of the case
THE FOUR EXPOSURE QUESTIONS

1 WERE YOU WEARING PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT? 2 DID ANY FLUID GET INTO YOUR EYES OR YOUR MOUTH? 3 DID YOU FILE AN INCIDENT REPORT? 4 DID YOU HIT YOUR HEAD, or injure yourself anywhere else? PPE DOES NOT PROTECT THE MOUTH RELIABLY, and the whole faecal-oral route runs through the mouth — the eyes-and-mouth question is what JUSTIFIES YOUR DIFFERENTIAL LIST
What she says about PPE — and why it changes nothing

'I WAS WEARING PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT' and 'I took all the measures I had to.' DO NOT REFRAME THE DIFFERENTIAL. Ask the eyes-and-mouth question anyway — SHE CANNOT REMEMBER. And CONFIRM AND REINFORCE the incident report: IT IS WHAT OPENS HER ReturnToWorkSA CLAIM
VERSION A CARD — the recalled version

TENDER HEPATOMEGALY · BILIRUBIN POSITIVE ON URINE DIPSTICK · NO VISIBLE JAUNDICE. History: fever, NIGHT SWEATS, RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT PAIN. BILIRUBIN APPEARS IN THE URINE BEFORE THE SKIN TURNS YELLOW — so no jaundice does NOT exclude hepatitis
VERSION B CARD — written to catch the recall

NO JAUNDICE · NO HEPATOMEGALY · NORMAL URINE DIPSTICK. History: fever, chills, night sweats, LOWER ABDOMINAL PAIN, NON-BLOODY DIARRHOEA, nausea without vomiting. THE EXAMINERS WROTE THIS VERSION BECAUSE EVERYONE KNOWS THIS AS 'THE SEWER HEPATITIS CASE' — AND STILL HEAR CANDIDATES ANNOUNCE HEPATITIS
The hepatitis group — ask it in full
ANY YELLOWING OF SKIN OR EYES · ANY TUMMY PAIN, WHERE · NAUSEA OR VOMITING · HAS YOUR URINE GONE DARK, OR YOUR STOOLS GONE PALE?
The gastroenteritis group — TWO stool questions only

ANY DIARRHOEA · IS IT LOOSE OR COMPLETELY WATERY · ANY BLOOD IN IT · ANY MUCUS · ANY FEVER OR CHILLS? CONSISTENCY GRADES SEVERITY and BLOOD SEPARATES INVASIVE BACTERIAL COLITIS from viral and toxin-mediated illness. SKIP VOLUME AND ODOUR — they add nothing you will act on and cost you a question you cannot afford
The water-contact group — the sewer-specific organism

ANY RASH · ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS in neck, armpits or groin · ANY SEVERE MUSCLE ACHES, ESPECIALLY IN YOUR CALVES · ANY RED OR SORE EYES? LEPTOSPIROSIS comes from RODENT URINE — the classic sewer vector. CALF MYALGIA plus CONJUNCTIVAL SUFFUSION, and in WEIL DISEASE jaundice with acute kidney injury
THE PSYCHOLOGICAL SCREEN — a scored omission if skipped

'FALLING INTO A SEWER WOULD SHAKE ANYONE. HOW HAVE YOU BEEN COPING SINCE?' Then MOOD · SLEEP, ANY NIGHTMARES OR FLASHBACKS · HAVE YOU AVOIDED GOING BACK TO WORK · any other stress. THE NIGHTMARE AND AVOIDANCE QUESTIONS are what tell the examiner you are screening for PTSD rather than depression
findingsLabel: The incident, the four exposure questions, and the card that overrules the recall
must: FAIL — Never asking about the incident. Straight from 'unwell' into jaundice questions.
FAIL — Diagnosing hepatitis in Version B when the card says no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, normal dipstick.
FAIL — Missing the head injury question after a fall into a confined space.
FAIL — Omitting the psychological screen in a frankly traumatic incident.
ASK — Did any of the fluid get into your eyes or your mouth?
ASK — Did you hit your head, or injure yourself anywhere else?

dx: **VERSION A — ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS, most probably HEPATITIS A, with HEPATITIS E named alongside it.** Both are **faecal-orally transmitted and there is NO WAY TO SEPARATE THEM on history and examination alone. Say 'hepatitis A or E' and move on.** **VERSION B — INFECTIVE GASTROENTERITIS, viral, bacterial or protozoal, acquired from the sewage. NOT hepatitis.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: whether you let the EXAMINATION CARD OVERRULE THE RECALL.** Almost every candidate knows this as 'the sewer hepatitis case' — **the examiners know that too, which is why Version B exists. READING THE CARD AND CHANGING YOUR ANSWER IS THE SINGLE BEHAVIOUR BEING TESTED.**

**ITS TWIN: whether you OPENED THE INCIDENT AT ALL. A candidate who diagnoses hepatitis correctly WITHOUT ASKING ONE QUESTION ABOUT THE SEWER has failed the approach and differential domains even with the right diagnosis.**

**Do NOT hedge with 'it's probably EARLY hepatitis' in Version B. It reads as an UNWILLINGNESS TO ABANDON THE RECALL and costs you the diagnosis domain.** If challenged 'why not hepatitis?': **'no jaundice, no hepatomegaly and NO BILIRUBIN IN THE URINE. In acute hepatitis I would expect at least BILIRUBINURIA, since conjugated bilirubin appears in urine BEFORE the skin discolours.'**

**If asked 'could it be both?': 'it could — A SINGLE SEWAGE EXPOSURE CAN TRANSMIT MORE THAN ONE ORGANISM. I would still call gastroenteritis the leading diagnosis and check liver function and hepatitis serology to be sure.'**

**NAME THE ORGANISMS — a bare 'gastroenteritis' scores far less than a specific list. VIRAL: rotavirus, norovirus, adenovirus. BACTERIAL: Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli, Campylobacter. PROTOZOAL: Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba.** One or two from each subgroup, every time.

**Hepatitis A incubation 15–50 days, average about 28. Hepatitis E 15–60 days. BOTH faecal-oral, and NEITHER becomes chronic in an immunocompetent adult.** **Jaundice becomes visible at a bilirubin of roughly 40–50 micromol/L — BILIRUBINURIA COMES FIRST.** VERIFY.

**PTSD REQUIRES SYMPTOMS PERSISTING BEYOND ONE MONTH — before that it is an ACUTE STRESS REACTION.** Screen in the room, review at four weeks, and offer **a mental health treatment plan** if symptoms persist.

**Hepatitis A or E management: SUPPORTIVE — rest, oral fluids, AVOID ALCOHOL AND HEPATOTOXIC DRUGS, small frequent meals. NOTIFY. EXCLUDE FROM WORK while infectious, and she is a sewage worker. VACCINATE CLOSE CONTACTS and offer immunoglobulin where indicated. REVIEW IN 48–72 HOURS with repeat LFT and INR.** **Gastroenteritis: oral rehydration, hygiene advice, WORK EXCLUSION UNTIL 48 HOURS AFTER SYMPTOMS SETTLE, faecal testing given the occupational source, antibiotics only if a specific treatable organism is identified.** VERIFY.

**Explain it in plain words: 'PICKED UP BY SWALLOWING SOMETHING CONTAMINATED WITH SEWAGE' — not 'faecal-oral transmission of hepatotropic viruses'.** **NOTIFIABLE in SA: hepatitis A and E, leptospirosis, salmonellosis, shigellosis, campylobacteriosis, Shiga-toxin E. coli.** **The incident report opens a ReturnToWorkSA claim; SafeWork SA has jurisdiction over the confined-space entry. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **WIPE — and in the online format SAY IT: 'I would normally wash my hands here.' Introduce, confirm the name, and frame it: 'I understand you've been feeling unwell and that SOMETHING HAPPENED AT WORK. I'd like to ask you some questions, then examine you, and we'll talk about what I think it is.'**
**AGENDA — eight seconds, and a marked item: 'before I start — is there anything in particular you're worried this might be?'**

**BLOCK 1, explore 'unwell' in FOUR questions, 45 seconds: can you describe what you mean by feeling unwell — tiredness, feverish, pain, or something else · how long, constant or coming and going, getting worse · anything better or worse · how is it affecting your day-to-day life?**
**BLOCK 2, THE INCIDENT — open question FIRST: 'you mentioned an incident at work. CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT IT?'** Then **SAY THE EXPOSURE BACK: 'so you were exposed to urine and faeces.'**

**THE FOUR EXPOSURE QUESTIONS, signposted: 'I want to ask a few specific questions about that, because it changes what I need to test for.' PPE · FLUID IN EYES OR MOUTH · INCIDENT REPORT · OTHER INJURIES AND HEAD STRIKE.**
**Confirm and reinforce the report: 'that's important — it's what opens your compensation claim. Keep a copy yourself.'**

**BLOCK 3, signpost the symptom groups: 'I'm going to run through some symptoms quickly — mostly yes or no.' HEPATITIS GROUP: yellowing of skin or eyes · tummy pain, WHERE · nausea or vomiting · DARK URINE OR PALE STOOLS?**
**GASTROENTERITIS GROUP: any diarrhoea · LOOSE OR COMPLETELY WATERY · ANY BLOOD · any mucus · any fever or chills?**

**WATER-CONTACT AND RARER GROUP: any rash · LUMPS OR BUMPS in neck, armpits or groin · SEVERE MUSCLE ACHES, ESPECIALLY IN THE CALVES · RED OR SORE EYES?** That is **leptospirosis, CMV and toxoplasmosis in one block.**

**BLOCK 4, THE PSYCHOLOGICAL SCREEN — 45 seconds, five questions. Open it without implying she is imagining her symptoms: 'FALLING INTO A SEWER WOULD SHAKE ANYONE. HOW HAVE YOU BEEN COPING SINCE?'** Then **mood · sleep, NIGHTMARES OR FLASHBACKS · AVOIDING GOING BACK TO WORK · other stress.**
**MALIGNANCY, then TRAVEL AND SEXUAL HISTORY: weight loss, night sweats, lumps, bruising · recent travel · sexual history if the picture fits.**
**The rest of the unwellness list as far as time allows, then past history, medications, allergies, alcohol and smoking.** **At five minutes: 'a last few quick questions, then I'll examine you.'**
**Take the card and READ IT BEFORE YOU COMMIT.** **Let the findings decide which version you are in.**

**VERSION A: 'you have a fever, pain over your liver, your liver is ENLARGED AND TENDER when I press, and there is BILE PIGMENT IN YOUR URINE. The most likely diagnosis is ACUTE HEPATITIS — inflammation of the liver, most probably HEPATITIS A, or a closely related one called HEPATITIS E. Both are picked up by swallowing something contaminated with sewage, which fits exactly with what happened to you.'**

**VERSION B: 'I want to be careful here, because THE EXAMINATION CHANGES WHAT I THINK. You are not yellow, your liver is not enlarged or tender, and your urine test is normal — SO THIS IS NOT HEPATITIS. What you have is GASTROENTERITIS: an infection of the bowel, most likely from a bug you swallowed when you fell into the sewage.'**

**The differentials IN ORDER OF THE EXPOSURE, with organisms named: LEPTOSPIROSIS · liver abscess · gastroenteritis with named viral, bacterial and protozoal organisms · other infections including EBV, CMV, HIV and syphilis · PTSD, screened for and relevant here · malignancy · and the general causes of feeling unwell.**
**SAFETY-NET: return immediately for CONFUSION OR DROWSINESS · vomiting that prevents fluids · BLEEDING OR BRUISING · worsening jaundice · REDUCED URINE OUTPUT · blood in the stool.**
pefe: **Do now: VITAL SIGNS and HYDRATION, with a POSTURAL blood pressure if she has been vomiting or has diarrhoea · URINE DIPSTICK for BILIRUBIN, blood and protein · a NEUROLOGICAL SCREEN if she struck her head.**

**Bloods: FBE, UEC, LFT, INR, CRP, LIPASE, blood glucose.** **Serology: ANTI-HAV IgM, HEPATITIS E IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and core IgM, hepatitis C antibody.** **FAECAL PCR or MCS in Version B, and in either version if there is diarrhoea.** **LEPTOSPIRA SEROLOGY AND PCR — because of the sewer.**

**What the results change: ALT and AST in the HUNDREDS OR THOUSANDS with a modest ALP means HEPATOCELLULAR injury · a RISING INR OR FALLING ALBUMIN means FAILING SYNTHETIC FUNCTION, and THAT is the finding that turns an outpatient into an inpatient · anti-HAV IgM positive confirms acute hepatitis A · bloody stool with acute kidney injury and anaemia means HAEMOLYTIC URAEMIC SYNDROME · an ULTRASOUND collection means LIVER ABSCESS, not hepatitis.**

**Do not miss: FULMINANT HEPATIC FAILURE — confusion, drowsiness, ASTERIXIS, rising INR, HYPOGLYCAEMIA · LEPTOSPIROSIS, the sewer-specific and TREATABLE diagnosis · HEAD INJURY from the fall · SEPSIS · PTSD, which unscreened is a scored omission.**

**Avoid: ANTIBIOTICS for undifferentiated diarrhoea, and specifically IF SHIGA-TOXIN E. COLI IS POSSIBLE · ANTIMOTILITY AGENTS such as loperamide in BLOODY OR FEBRILE diarrhoea · paracetamol above the reduced ceiling in acute hepatitis, and ALCOHOL ENTIRELY · naming a hepatitis subtype you cannot prove on history · reassuring her the sewage was harmless.** VERIFY the paracetamol ceiling in liver impairment.
**Treat leptospirosis EMPIRICALLY with DOXYCYCLINE or BENZYLPENICILLIN if suspected — do not wait for serology.**
**If she struck her head: STOP the infection history and assess — loss of consciousness, amnesia, vomiting, headache — with CT brain if any Canadian CT head rule criterion is met.**

stem: Ben, 27, hospitality, attends alone: feeling unwell for eight days; for the last two days he has noticed a rash. BP 110/71, HR 88, RR 12, SpO2 98%, T 38.5.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
Physical examination findings will be provided
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: ASK FOR STABILITY AT THE DOOR

'Examiner, before I begin — IS MY PATIENT HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE?' BP 110/71 · HR 88 · RR 12 · SpO2 98% · T 38.5. You do NOT open every tiredness case this way — you open THIS one this way BECAUSE MENINGOCOCCAEMIA IS ON THE LIST FROM THE DOOR. Say that reason out loud and a tick becomes a mark
If the numbers are abnormal, STOP

Systolic under 90, HR over 130, RR over 24 or altered conscious state: 'THIS PATIENT IS NOT STABLE — I would start resuscitation, take BLOOD CULTURES and give CEFTRIAXONE IMMEDIATELY for presumed meningococcal sepsis BEFORE completing my history.' The teaching that you will 'never' get an unstable patient describes PAST PAPERS, NOT A CLINICAL RULE
The findings card

FEBRILE · GENERALISED LYMPHADENOPATHY · ALL OTHER SYSTEMS NORMAL. DO NOT READ IT SILENTLY — say the two findings out loud, then ask THREE TARGETED EXTRAS: IS THERE RASH ON THE PALMS AND SOLES · IS THE SPLEEN ENLARGED · IS THERE ANY ORAL ULCERATION?
What the extra question buys you
'THERE ARE LESIONS ON THE PALMS.' No splenomegaly, mouth clear. ASKING FOR THE PALMS IS WHAT TURNS 'probably HIV' INTO 'HIV AND SYPHILIS, AND HERE IS WHY'
The rash, characterised BEFORE you theorise

REDNESS, not blisters or bruising · started on the CHEST, spread to BACK AND ARMS · NOT ITCHY AND NOT PAINFUL · IT BLANCHES. Ask 'IS IT REDNESS, BLISTERS, OR BRUISING?' before anything else about the rash — that one question decides which four differentials you spend the station on
Two precisions that earn marks

The third timing question for a rash is 'IS IT SPREADING?' — NOT 'is it getting worse'. A rash does not get worse, and the role-player is briefed to answer 'I DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU MEAN'. And ADD 'DOES IT FADE WHEN YOU PRESS ON IT?' — the GLASS TEST asked as a question, and the difference between an outpatient and an ambulance
THE PIVOT OF THE STATION
'DO YOU USE CONDOMS?' → a pause, then 'NO. NOT REALLY.' STOP THE GENERAL SWEEP. Everything for the next NINETY SECONDS is sexual health
THE HIDDEN DETAIL he will not volunteer

'There was a LITTLE PAINLESS SORE down there A COUPLE OF MONTHS BACK. It went away by itself so I forgot about it.' Offered ONLY if you ask SPECIFICALLY about SORES OR ULCERS ON THE GENITALS. Asked 'any other symptoms?' he does not mention it. THAT IS THE PRIMARY CHANCRE — miss it and you name HIV alone
THE HIDDEN AGENDA

HE IS FRIGHTENED IT IS HIV AND HAS NOT SAID SO. HIS UNCLE DIED OF AIDS IN THE 1990s. If you ask what he is worried about, he tells you. IF YOU NEVER ASK, he waits until you name the diagnosis and says quietly: 'MY UNCLE DIED OF THAT'
VERSION B — two ways it gets harder

THE RASH IS NON-BLANCHING with HEADACHE AND NECK STIFFNESS — this is MENINGOCOCCAEMIA, not an STI station. OR he says 'I'M NOT SEXUALLY ACTIVE' and only a DIFFERENTLY WORDED SECOND QUESTION — 'HAVE YOU EVER BEEN?' — opens the history. OR amoxicillin five days ago, or overseas travel
findingsLabel: Stability at the door, the card, the pivot, and the sore he forgot
must: FAIL — No sexual history: two closed questions asked, then on to past medical history.
FAIL — Partner gender never asked, and a female partner assumed.
FAIL — Meningococcaemia never excluded: no headache, neck, photophobia or blanching question.
FAIL — HIV test taken without naming it. Naming the test IS the consent.
ASK — Are your partners male, female, or both?
ASK — Any sores or ulcers on your genitals, now or in the past few months?

dx: **ACUTE HIV SEROCONVERSION, SECONDARY SYPHILIS, OR BOTH.** A febrile illness with a GENERALISED RASH and GENERALISED LYMPHADENOPATHY in a man who has condomless sex with men **is that combination until proven otherwise.**

**NAMING BOTH SCORES BETTER THAN NAMING ONE, and it is NOT hedging — it is the clinically correct answer. The presentations OVERLAP COMPLETELY, they share the same route, and CO-INFECTION IS COMMON ENOUGH THAT THE STANDARD OF CARE IS TO TEST FOR BOTH.** Say so: **'I can't tell which of these it is by looking at you — they look IDENTICAL at this stage, which is exactly why we test for both.'**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: whether the SEXUAL HISTORY IS TAKEN IN FULL, AT THE MOMENT THE CASE TURNS, and whether BOTH diagnoses are then named with reasons drawn from that history.** **Everything else is recoverable. Candidates who ask two sexual-health questions and diagnose 'a viral illness' FAIL. Candidates who ask nine and name two diagnoses PASS, even if the infection sweep was patchy.**

**HIV SEROCONVERSION ILLNESS: the acute symptomatic phase 2–4 WEEKS after infection — fever, sore throat, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, headache, sometimes diarrhoea and mouth ulcers. IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE INFLUENZA, WHICH IS WHY IT IS MISSED.**

**SECONDARY SYPHILIS: the disseminated stage weeks to months after an OFTEN-UNNOTICED PRIMARY CHANCRE — SYMMETRICAL COPPERY PAPULOSQUAMOUS rash INCLUDING PALMS AND SOLES, NON-ITCHY, fever, lymphadenopathy, mucous patches.**

**GIVE THE REASONS FROM YOUR OWN HISTORY: from the history — sex with men, no condoms, several casual partners. From the symptoms — eight days unwell, fever, body aches, headaches, a rash that started on the chest and spread. From the examination — fever, GENERALISED GLANDS, and RASH ON THE PALMS.** Plus **the painless sore two months ago.**

**THEN HOLD THE SILENCE. When he goes quiet after you say HIV, DO NOT FILL IT with reassurance — rushing in reads as discomfort and is scored as poor communication.** Wait two seconds, then: **'that's a lot to hear. WHAT'S GOING THROUGH YOUR MIND?'**

**Two honest things to say. 'HIV TODAY IS NOT THE ILLNESS IT WAS IN THE NINETIES — with treatment people live A NORMAL LIFE SPAN and CANNOT PASS IT ON. And syphilis is CURED WITH AN INJECTION.' But DO NOT PROMISE A RESULT YOU DON'T HAVE.**

**CONTACT TRACING, said supportively: 'if it's positive we do need to let your recent partners know so they can be tested — but THE CLINIC CAN DO THAT ANONYMOUSLY ON YOUR BEHALF. YOUR NAME DOES NOT HAVE TO GO ANYWHERE, and you won't have to make those calls yourself.'**

**Treatment. SECONDARY SYPHILIS: BENZATHINE BENZYLPENICILLIN 1.8 g (2.4 million units) IM AS A SINGLE DOSE; penicillin allergy DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg twice daily for 14 DAYS. WARN ABOUT THE JARISCH-HERXHEIMER REACTION — fever, chills and myalgia WITHIN HOURS of treatment, self-limiting.** **MENINGOCOCCAEMIA: CEFTRIAXONE 2 g IV, or IM if no access, IMMEDIATELY, BEFORE TRANSFER.** **HIV: SAME-DAY referral; antiretroviral therapy AS SOON AS POSSIBLE regardless of CD4.** VERIFY.
plan: **STABILITY FIRST — ask the examiner for BP, pulse, respiratory rate, saturations and temperature. Online, say it to the patient as a statement instead.** Then **introduce, confirm how he likes to be addressed.**

**Acknowledge both things: 'I'm sorry you've been feeling like this for over a week, and I can see THE RASH IS WORRYING YOU. Let me ask you some questions, then I'll examine you, and I'll explain what I think and what we do next.'**

**DEFINE THE VAGUE WORD: 'when you say unwell — do you mean LOW IN ENERGY, do you mean SLEEPY, or do you mean FEVERISH?' Then how long · constant or intermittent · getting worse · better or worse with anything · how is it affecting your day-to-day life?**

**CHARACTERISE THE RASH BEFORE YOU THEORISE: IS IT REDNESS, BLISTERS, OR BRUISING · when did it start · WHERE did it start · HAS IT SPREAD · is it ITCHY, PAINFUL, OR NEITHER · AND DOES IT FADE WHEN YOU PRESS ON IT?**
**FEVER: have you actually MEASURED your temperature · any CHILLS OR SHAKES · have you taken anything for it, and did it help?**

**TRAVEL — one question, one whole group: 'have you travelled anywhere at all in the last few months, overseas or interstate?' THEN SAY THE NEGATIVE OUT LOUD: 'good — that makes dengue, malaria and the other travel infections much less likely, though we do have ROSS RIVER VIRUS and Q FEVER here in Australia.'** **A negative you ANNOUNCE is a mark; a negative you note silently is nothing.**
**THE PIVOT: are you sexually active · DO YOU USE CONDOMS?** When the answer comes, **STOP THE SWEEP.**

**HEADS-UP, THEN ASK WITHOUT APOLOGISING: 'I'm going to ask a few questions about your sex life. They're ROUTINE for anyone who's unwell with a rash, and what you tell me STAYS BETWEEN US. Is that okay?'** **Confidentiality is worth ONE CLAUSE, not a paragraph — you do not have the time. And 'sorry, I have to ask this' signals discomfort and DRIES THE HISTORY UP.**
**PARTNERS: are you sexually active · do you have a STABLE PARTNER · have you ever had MULTIPLE partners · ARE YOUR PARTNERS MALE, FEMALE, OR BOTH?**

**METHODS AND RISK: do you use condoms — EVERY TIME · WHAT KIND OF SEX DO YOU HAVE — oral, vaginal, anal? I ASK BECAUSE IT TELLS ME WHICH SITES I NEED TO SWAB · have you EVER BEEN DIAGNOSED with an STI before · has any of this happened when you'd been DRINKING OR USING DRUGS?**

**THE STI COMPLICATION SCREEN: ANY SORES, ULCERS OR RASH ON YOUR GENITALS · any LUMPS IN YOUR GROIN · any YELLOWING of skin or eyes, tummy pain, nausea or vomiting · any DISCHARGE from the penis or BURNING passing urine · any SWELLING OR PAIN IN THE SCROTUM?**
**MENINGOCOCCAEMIA — four questions, fifteen seconds: any DIZZINESS · any HEADACHE · any PAIN OR STIFFNESS IN YOUR NECK · are your EYES SENSITIVE TO LIGHT?**
**VIRAL EXANTHEMS: did you have ALL YOUR CHILDHOOD IMMUNISATIONS · any sore throat, runny nose or cough · HAVE YOU TAKEN ANY ANTIBIOTICS RECENTLY · any diarrhoea or tummy pain?**
**THE RARE, NAMED: any INSECT OR TICK BITES, or bushwalking · any contact with ANIMALS OR FARMS · any CHEST PAIN OR RACING OF THE HEART, any RECENT DENTAL WORK · HAVE YOU INJECTED ANY DRUGS?**

**MALIGNANCY AND DRUGS: any WEIGHT LOSS you weren't trying for · appetite · ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS anywhere · NIGHT SWEATS · family history of cancer · any medications INCLUDING FROM THE CHEMIST, and HAVE YOU STARTED ANYTHING NEW · joint pains · medical conditions, allergies, smoking, alcohol.**
**HARD STOP ON HISTORY AT SIX MINUTES, even mid-sentence. The differential list is worth more than the last question.**
**Take the findings, SAY THEM ALOUD, and ask the three targeted extras.** Then **NAME BOTH DIAGNOSES with reasons from history, symptoms and examination.** Then **PAUSE.**

**THE GROUPED DIFFERENTIAL LIST out loud — meningococcaemia and why excluded · other STIs · viral exanthems · travel and vector-borne · endocarditis · haematological malignancy · drug reaction.** Then **the plan, NAMING THE HIV TEST FOR CONSENT, three swab sites, sexual health referral, and SPECIFIC SAFETY-NETTING.**
pefe: **Do now: vital signs and A LOOK AT THE WHOLE SKIN including PALMS, SOLES, MOUTH AND GENITALS · PRESS THE RASH — blanching or not · PALPATE ALL NODE GROUPS AND THE SPLEEN.**

**CONSENT, THEN BLOOD: HIV Ag/Ab (4th-generation) · SYPHILIS SEROLOGY, treponemal EIA PLUS RPR · hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B and C serology · FBE with FILM · LFT, EUC, CRP.** **NAMING THE HIV TEST IS THE CONSENT — 'one of these tests is for HIV. Is that all right with you?'**
**NAAT SWABS FROM EVERY EXPOSED SITE — THROAT, ANORECTAL, AND FIRST-PASS URINE. Three sites, every time.**
**REPEAT HIV TESTING AT SIX WEEKS if the first test is early and negative; HIV RNA if within the window period.**

**If the sexual screen is clean: EBV, CMV and toxoplasma serology. If endocarditis is possible: THREE SETS OF BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, and echocardiogram. If unimmunised with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis: MEASLES PCR and IgM, AIRBORNE ISOLATION and SAME-DAY notification. If pustular or anogenital: LESION SWAB FOR MPOX PCR.**

**Do not miss: a NON-BLANCHING rash means CEFTRIAXONE NOW and 000, do not wait · CONSENT before the HIV test · CONTACT TRACING for HIV and syphilis, with SA Health partner-notification support · BOTH HIV AND SYPHILIS ARE NOTIFIABLE in South Australia · TEST FOR ALL OF THEM, because CO-INFECTION IS THE RULE, NOT THE EXCEPTION.**

**Avoid: 'it's probably just a virus' and send him away · AMOXICILLIN empirically for the sore throat · promising a negative or a positive result · ASKING WHY HE DOESN'T USE CONDOMS, or commenting on the number of partners · deferring the sexual history to 'the sexual health clinic'.** **Risk-reduction advice belongs in MANAGEMENT, offered once, without judgement.**

stem: Gary, 26, attends alone feeling unwell. He has recently returned from an overseas trip in South-East Asia, and used heroin while he was away.
tasks: Take a relevant history (6 minutes)
You will be given a physical examination card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: THE STEM GIVES YOU THREE LEADS — every one carries marks

FEELING UNWELL · RECENTLY RETURNED FROM SOUTH-EAST ASIA · USED HEROIN WHILE AWAY. SIGNPOST THEM OUT LOUD: 'there are three things I want to cover — what the unwellness actually feels like, your trip, and the heroin. I'll take them in that order.' Twelve seconds, and it tells the examiner your whole plan before you execute it
VERSION 1 CARD — acute hepatitis
TENDER HEPATOMEGALY with RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT PAIN · JAUNDICE · URINE DIPSTICK BILIRUBIN POSITIVE. History: abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, needle sharing, and REPEATED EXPRESSIONS OF GUILT
VERSION 2 CARD — HIV seroconversion

MORBILLIFORM RASH · GENERALISED LYMPHADENOPATHY · INFLAMED TONSILS WITH EXUDATE. History: NO abdominal pain, NO jaundice; rash, sore throat, night sweats, needle sharing. AND HE HAD A HEPATITIS VACCINE BEFORE TRAVELLING. SECOND DIFFERENTIAL IS EBV — which is what most candidates say INSTEAD
VERSION 3 CARD — the confusion built deliberately

MURMUR, PLUS RAISED JVP, BIBASAL CREPITATIONS AND ANKLE OEDEMA. History: chest pain and palpitations with fever, needle sharing. IT IS INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS COMPLICATED BY HEART FAILURE — NOT A DIAGNOSIS OF HEART FAILURE
THE VACCINATION TRAP

'I saw my GP before I went and GOT A HEPATITIS SHOT.' A SCRIPTED FINDING placed to test whether you know what it covers. HEPATITIS A AND B ARE VACCINE-PREVENTABLE. THERE IS NO HEPATITIS C VACCINE. A hepatitis shot before the trip DOES NOT TAKE ACUTE HEPATITIS OFF YOUR LIST — say so
THE DESIGNED TRAP — 'I'M NOT SEXUALLY ACTIVE'

'NO SEX OVERSEAS' IS WRITTEN INTO THE ROLE-PLAYER BRIEF PRECISELY SO CANDIDATES TICK THE BOX AND MOVE ON. The virus was not contracted overseas by sex — it was contracted BY A NEEDLE. But the man in front of you CAN NOW TRANSMIT IT, and to whom is a question you must ask
THE PSYCHOLOGICAL CUE, repeated

'I FEEL SO GUILTY ABOUT IT' — said FOUR TIMES and never picked up by most candidates. Ask: HOW ARE YOU COPING · HOW HAS YOUR MOOD BEEN · ARE YOU STILL ENJOYING THE THINGS YOU USED TO · HAVE YOU HAD ANY THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF?
'I just went for a holiday, nothing special'
DO NOT ACCEPT THE VAGUE ANSWER. RUN A B C D E F G S ANYWAY — the findings are IN THE SPECIFICS, NOT THE SUMMARY. Nobody passes this station on two travel questions
EXPOSE THE ARMS
The examination card may say INJECTION SITES and expect you to have asked. LOOK AT BOTH ANTECUBITAL FOSSAE, BOTH FOREARMS AND THE GROINS for TRACKS, CELLULITIS, ABSCESS and THROMBOPHLEBITIS
Peripheral stigmata in Version 3

SPLINTER HAEMORRHAGES, JANEWAY LESIONS and OSLER NODES — individually non-specific, but MINOR CRITERIA when there is fever and a murmur. OSLER EQUALS OUCH — PAINFUL, ON THE PULPS. JANEWAY LESIONS ARE PAINLESS, ON THE PALMS AND SOLES
findingsLabel: Three leads, three cards, and the two answers you must not accept
must: FAIL — Two travel questions. A B C D E F G S is the biggest block of marks in the station.
FAIL — Sexual history never revisited after 'no sex overseas'.
FAIL — Diagnosing heart failure in Version 3 instead of endocarditis.
FAIL — Antibiotics before blood cultures, or an HIV test without named consent.
ASK — Tell me more about the heroin. How did you use it? Did you share needles?
ASK — Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?

dx: **EVERY VERSION IS A CONSEQUENCE OF SHARED NEEDLES: ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS · ACUTE HIV SEROCONVERSION · INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS. BUILD ONE STRUCTURE AND LET THE ANSWERS TELL YOU WHICH — do not chase whichever recall you memorised.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: whether you GO BACK FOR THE SEXUAL HISTORY after he says he did not have sex overseas — and, in Version 3, whether you NAME ENDOCARDITIS RATHER THAN HEART FAILURE.** Both are the same skill: **refusing to let a single answer, or a single set of signs, CLOSE A LINE OF REASONING PREMATURELY. Candidates fail not because they miss hepatitis or HIV, but because THEY STOP ASKING.**

**THE HEROIN HISTORY, IN THREE STEPS AND IN THIS ORDER: 'TELL ME MORE ABOUT THAT' → 'HOW DID YOU USE IT, HOW DID IT GO IN?' → 'DID YOU SHARE NEEDLES WITH ANYONE?'** **Leading with 'did you share needles?' ANNOUNCES THAT YOU HAVE MEMORISED THE RECALL — and it is poor practice: an OPEN question first gets you the guilt, the frequency, whether it was a one-off, and whether there is ongoing use.**

**SHARED NEEDLES OPENS ONE BOX, WHICH CONTAINS THREE — ASK ALL THREE IN EVERY VERSION. BOX 1 HEPATITIS: jaundice, RUQ pain, nausea, DARK URINE OR PALE STOOLS, appetite, itch. BOX 2 HIV: sore throat, RASH, fever, NIGHT SWEATS, weight loss, LUMPS in neck, armpits or groin, diarrhoea. BOX 3 INJECTION-RELATED: redness or swelling AT THE INJECTION SITE, CHEST PAIN, PALPITATIONS, breathlessness, MARKS OR SPOTS ON THE HANDS, FINGERS OR PALMS.**

**THE RETURN TO THE SEXUAL HISTORY, WITH THE REASON GIVEN: 'I asked earlier whether you had sex while you were away and you said no. I NEED TO COME BACK TO IT, because THE SAME INFECTIONS WE'RE TALKING ABOUT ARE ALSO PASSED ON SEXUALLY, and IF YOU HAVE PICKED ONE UP I NEED TO KNOW WHO ELSE MIGHT NEED TESTING. HAVE YOU EVER BEEN SEXUALLY ACTIVE?'** Then **condoms · multiple partners · PARTNER GENDER.**

**VERSION 1 CORRECTION — the teaching says the TYPE does not matter. FOR THE PATIENT that is true; FOR YOUR MANAGEMENT IT IS NOT. Given the needle sharing the likely types are HEPATITIS B OR C, and that matters because IT CHANGES WHO WE VACCINATE, WHO WE TEST, AND WHETHER WE CAN CURE IT.** **HEPATITIS C IS NOW CURABLE — direct-acting antivirals, typically 8–12 WEEKS, PBS-listed.** VERIFY.

**VERSION 2 — HIV SEROCONVERSION ILLNESS is the acute phase 2–4 WEEKS after infection: fever, sore throat, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, headache, sometimes diarrhoea and weight loss. IT IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM INFLUENZA OR GLANDULAR FEVER, which is why EBV is the strong second differential — TEST FOR BOTH.**

**VERSION 3, SAID PLAINLY: 'those HEART-FAILURE SIGNS ARE A COMPLICATION OF THE INFECTION, NOT A SEPARATE ILLNESS.'** If challenged: **'the heart failure is explained by ACUTE VALVULAR REGURGITATION from the infection. Heart failure is one of the TWO CLASSICAL COMPLICATIONS of endocarditis, the other being SYSTEMIC EMBOLISM. Diagnosing heart failure alone in a febrile injecting drug user with a new murmur would MISS THE TREATABLE CAUSE and delay blood cultures and antibiotics.'**

**In injecting drug use the TRICUSPID VALVE is classically involved and STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS is the commonest organism.** **THREE SETS OF BLOOD CULTURES FROM SEPARATE SITES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS; TTE then TOE; MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA.** **Empirical therapy must cover S. AUREUS INCLUDING MRSA — typically vancomycin-based.** VERIFY.

**FALCIPARUM MALARIA — South-East Asian travel with undifferentiated fever. IT KILLS IN DAYS. THICK AND THIN FILMS, THREE SETS, plus a rapid antigen test, in EVERY febrile returned traveller.** **In DENGUE, AVOID NSAIDs AND ASPIRIN.** **PEP window is 72 HOURS. Hepatitis A, B, C, HIV and malaria are ALL NOTIFIABLE in SA.** **ADIS 1300 13 1340 · Clinic 275 · SHINE SA · Lifeline 13 11 14 · take-home naloxone free without prescription.**
plan: **Introduce, confirm the name, and acknowledge the fear: 'a week of feeling that unwell, to the point you can't get out of bed, is frightening, and I understand why you're worried something serious is going on.'**
**SIGNPOST THE THREE LEADS OUT LOUD, in the order the stem gives them.**

**BLOCK 1 — DEFINE THE UNWELLNESS: 'when you say you feel unwell — do you mean LOW IN ENERGY, do you mean SLEEPY, or do you mean FEVERISH?'** **'Low in energy' puts you in the tiredness cluster; 'sleepy' in sleep disorders; 'FEVERISH' puts you in INFECTION — and with travel and needles, that is where you want to be.** Then **how long · constant or intermittent · getting worse · better or worse with anything · effect on life.**

**BLOCK 2 — THE TRAVEL HISTORY IN FULL, A B C D E F G S. ACTIVITIES: what did you do, any swimming in fresh water, caves, farms? BITES: any mosquito, tick or insect bites, any animal bites or scratches?**
**CONTACT: anyone around you unwell, any contact with animals? DRUGS: what did you take — and any prophylaxis, DID YOU TAKE MALARIA TABLETS, and did you finish them?**

**EXPOSURE TO BLOOD: any MEDICAL OR DENTAL WORK, SURGERY, TATTOOS, PIERCINGS or A BLOOD TRANSFUSION while you were there?** **It sounds odd in an Australian consultation — it is not. HEALTH TOURISM IS COMMON, and screening standards differ.**

**FOOD AND WATER: street food, unbottled water, ice, shellfish, unpasteurised dairy? GP BEFORE TRAVEL: did you see your GP for VACCINATIONS — and which ones? SEX: did you have sex while you were away?**

**BLOCK 3 — THE HEROIN, IN THREE STEPS: 'the referral mentions you used heroin while you were away. CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THAT?'** Let him talk. Then **'can you tell me HOW YOU USED IT — how it went in?'** Then **'and DID YOU SHARE NEEDLES with anyone?'** Then **'has there been ANY USE SINCE YOU GOT BACK?'**

**BOX 1, HEPATITIS: any YELLOWING of skin or the whites of your eyes · any pain in your tummy, PARTICULARLY ON THE RIGHT SIDE UNDER THE RIBS · nausea or vomiting · HAS YOUR URINE GONE DARK, OR YOUR STOOLS PALE · how's your appetite · any itch?**
**BOX 2, HIV: any SORE THROAT · ANY RASH anywhere · fever or chills · NIGHT SWEATS · weight loss without trying · appetite · ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS in your neck, armpits or groin · any diarrhoea?**

**BOX 3, INJECTION-RELATED: any REDNESS, SWELLING OR PAIN AT THE INJECTION SITE · any CHEST PAIN · any RACING OR POUNDING of your heart · any breathlessness · HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY MARKS OR SPOTS ON YOUR HANDS, FINGERS OR PALMS?**
**GO BACK FOR THE SEXUAL HISTORY, with the reframe and the reason.**
**THE PSYCHOLOGICAL CUE — pick up the guilt: coping · mood · ANHEDONIA · AND THE SELF-HARM QUESTION.**
**Close out: family history of cancer · regular medications · allergies · alcohol and smoking · medical conditions · 'is there anything you were PARTICULARLY WORRIED this might be?'**
**If time remains, sweep the tiredness mnemonic for what you have not covered — but DO NOT SACRIFICE THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST TO REACH IT. HARD STOP AT SIX MINUTES.**
**Take the card, SAY THE FINDINGS ALOUD, and name the diagnosis WITH REASONS FROM BOTH HISTORY AND EXAMINATION — and in Version 3, name the heart failure AS THE COMPLICATION.**

**THE GROUPED DIFFERENTIAL LIST, then the plan: consented testing with the HIV test NAMED, the full BBV and STI screen, MALARIA FILMS, contact tracing, mood and safety assessment, and HARM REDUCTION — needle and syringe program, take-home naloxone, opioid treatment referral.**

stem: Jack Mullins, 30, has come in feeling unwell and feverish. He is a known case of HIV and stopped his antiretroviral medication six months ago.
tasks: Take a history from the patient (about 6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings, or read them from the card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: ASK FOR OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU START

FEVER PLUS IMMUNOSUPPRESSION EQUALS A HIGH RISK OF SEPSIS, so asking first is defensible and is the same judgement you would show on a real ward. T 38.0 · HR 104 · BP 118/74 · RR 24 · SpO2 92% ON ROOM AIR. ASK FOR ALL FIVE — SATURATION IS THE FINDING THE CASE IS BUILT AROUND, and it is the one candidates leave out
RESPIRATORY EXAMINATION ENTIRELY NORMAL
Symmetrical expansion · RESONANT percussion · NO added sounds · NORMAL vocal resonance. A NORMAL EXAMINATION IN SOMEONE WITHOUT AN IMMUNE SYSTEM IS NOT REASSURANCE — IT IS THE EXPECTED FINDING
THE SENTENCE THAT SAVES THE STATION

'Although his chest examination is normal, HE IS HYPOXIC AND TACHYPNOEIC WITH A FEVER. A patient with advanced HIV CANNOT MOUNT THE INFLAMMATORY RESPONSE THAT PRODUCES CONSOLIDATION, CRACKLES OR AN EFFUSION, so a normal examination does not exclude pneumonia here. This is the same principle as FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA in a child on chemotherapy'
WHITE PATCH IN THE MOUTH — three possible answers
DO NOT SAY 'THRUSH' AND STOP. Describe it, then ask: IS IT PAINFUL WHEN TOUCHED WITH A TONGUE DEPRESSOR · CAN IT BE SCRAPED OFF · WHAT COLOUR IS IT, AND WHERE IS IT?
CORRECTION — colour settles it faster than scraping

CANDIDIASIS: white, creamy, SCRAPES OFF. KAPOSI SARCOMA: VIOLACEOUS, raised, does NOT scrape, HARD PALATE. ORAL HAIRY LEUKOPLAKIA: white, CORRUGATED, LATERAL TONGUE, does NOT scrape. The lecture frames it as candidiasis versus Kaposi — but a GENUINELY WHITE patch is far more likely candidiasis or hairy leukoplakia, and HAIRY LEUKOPLAKIA BELONGS ON THE LIST
The rest of the card
ALERT · no rash, no jaundice, MILDLY DEHYDRATED · NO significant lymphadenopathy · thyroid normal · heart sounds dual, no murmur · abdomen soft, NO organomegaly · DIPSTICK NORMAL
What he gives on the HIV history
Diagnosed ABOUT FIVE YEARS AGO. Stopped because 'I COULDN'T COPE WITH THE SIDE EFFECTS' or 'I MOVED AND LOST TRACK' or 'I FELT FINE SO I STOPPED'. NO SPECIALIST FOLLOW-UP FOR ABOUT A YEAR
HE COUGHS HARSHLY THROUGHOUT — acting as data
NOTICE IT AND USE IT: 'I can hear that cough. Tell me about it — IS IT DRY OR CHESTY? ANY BLOOD? ANY SHORTNESS OF BREATH?'
Everything else on the screen is NEGATIVE

Fever with chills a few days, PARACETAMOL UNHELPFUL, cough, shortness of breath. NO haemoptysis, NO weight loss, NO night sweats, NO diarrhoea, NO urinary symptoms, NO headache or neck stiffness, NO genital symptoms, NO travel, NO injecting drug use, NO animal contact
VERSION B — the sister case

Same stem, but UNWELL AND FEVERISH WITH DIARRHOEA. The differential becomes INFECTIVE DIARRHOEA — CRYPTOSPORIDIUM, ISOSPORA, MICROSPORIDIA, CMV COLITIS, MAC. THE CONCEPT IS IDENTICAL: two headings, a wide infection list and a malignancy list. ONLY THE ORGAN CHANGES
findingsLabel: The normal chest that is the finding, and the white patch with three answers
must: FAIL — Abandoning the diagnosis because the chest is clear.
FAIL — Never mentioning malignancy. That is half the question the case was built to ask.
FAIL — Premature closure on the white patch: 'that'll be thrush' and moving on.
FAIL — Naming Pneumocystis as the diagnosis with no CD4 count, viral load or film.
ASK — Can you tell me what led to stopping the tablets? Are you still seeing anyone?
ASK — Any ulcers or patches in your mouth? Any new purple or red marks on your skin?

dx: **PNEUMONIA — or equivalently a LOWER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION. You then ADD that because his immune system is affected you are CONCERNED ABOUT OPPORTUNISTIC INFECTION, without claiming to have diagnosed one.**

**WHY NOT SIMPLY 'PNEUMOCYSTIS PNEUMONIA': because you have NO CD4 COUNT, NO VIRAL LOAD, NO WHITE CELL COUNT AND NO CHEST RADIOGRAPH. Naming a specific opportunistic organism in front of the patient on this evidence is PREMATURE CLOSURE. Naming pneumonia and LISTING the possibilities is both safer and better scoring.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE, IN ONE LINE: COMMITTING TO PNEUMONIA DESPITE A NORMAL CHEST EXAMINATION, AND THEN OPENING THE MALIGNANCY HEADING.** **BOTH HALVES ARE REQUIRED. A candidate who backs away from the diagnosis because the chest is clear has MISUNDERSTOOD IMMUNOSUPPRESSION. A candidate who lists twelve infections and no cancers HAS ANSWERED HALF THE QUESTION.**

**TWO HEADINGS, AND SAY THEM OUT LOUD WHEN YOU DELIVER THE DIFFERENTIALS — it is what makes the list sound DERIVED rather than RECITED. The examiner is not testing whether you can diagnose pneumonia. They are testing whether the LOSS OF IMMUNITY changes two parts of your thinking: A WIDER AND STRANGER LIST OF INFECTIONS, and A SECOND HEADING FOR MALIGNANCY THAT MOST CANDIDATES NEVER OPEN.**

**THE MALIGNANCY HALF, said plainly: 'HIV RAISES THE RISK OF CERTAIN CANCERS. Because you have a cough I'm thinking about LUNG CANCER. And because of the WHITE PATCH IN YOUR MOUTH I want to exclude a particular cancer that occurs in HIV called KAPOSI SARCOMA. I'm also thinking about LYMPHOMA, which is more common in people with HIV.'** **SAY THE WORD CANCER BEFORE THE BELL.**

**NEVER SAY A CATEGORY NAME TO A PATIENT. 'ENT infections' and 'GI infections' ARE NOT DIAGNOSES AND THEY SCORE NOTHING. Say TONSILLITIS, PHARYNGITIS, SINUSITIS. Say GASTROENTERITIS. SPECIFICITY IS THE WHOLE MARK.**

**CD4 LANDMARKS: BELOW 200 → PNEUMOCYSTIS and TOXOPLASMOSIS. BELOW 50 → MYCOBACTERIUM AVIUM COMPLEX and CMV RETINITIS. KAPOSI SARCOMA OCCURS AT ANY COUNT.** **You are NOT given a CD4 count in this station, and SAYING SO IS PART OF THE ANSWER — it is precisely why you name pneumonia and list opportunistic infection as a concern.**

**DO NOT LECTURE HIM about stopping treatment, whatever the reason. Note it, stay warm, and come back to it in the plan: 'one of the most important things we do is GET YOU BACK ON TREATMENT, and we can look at WHAT MADE IT DIFFICULT LAST TIME.'** **Asking WHY is a communication mark; the reason does not change your management here.**

**If he asks 'am I dying?': 'I CAN'T TELL YOU THAT TODAY, AND I'M NOT GOING TO GUESS. What I CAN tell you is that THIS LOOKS TREATABLE, and that getting you back on your HIV treatment CHANGES YOUR OUTLOOK CONSIDERABLY.'**

**The two films you must be able to name: in PNEUMOCYSTIS the radiograph is often FAR MORE ABNORMAL THAN THE EXAMINATION — BILATERAL PERIHILAR INTERSTITIAL SHADOWING with normal auscultation is the classic MISMATCH. In TUBERCULOSIS look at the UPPER ZONES and for CAVITATION.** **Neither film is given — being able to say what you EXPECT turns a differential list into a plan.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Clinic 275 · SA TB Services · PATS.**
plan: **ASK THE EXAMINER FOR ALL FIVE OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU START.** Then **introduce, acknowledge, and open: 'I understand you've been feeling unwell. I'm sorry to hear that — tell me what's been happening.'**

**THE SIGNPOST THAT BUYS BREADTH: 'Jack, I'm going to run through the WHOLE BODY fairly quickly, asking about each area in turn. MOST OF THESE WILL BE A SIMPLE NO, AND THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT I'M HOPING FOR.'** **That one sentence gives you licence to fire twenty screening questions without appearing to interrogate him.**

**BLOCK 1 — UNWELL, THEN FEVER: what do you mean by unwell — SLEEPY, LOW IN ENERGY, OR FEVERISH · how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · anything better or worse.** Then **HAVE YOU MEASURED YOUR TEMPERATURE · any chills · have you taken anything, DID IT HELP?**

**BLOCK 2 — THE HIV HISTORY, four questions: WHEN WERE YOU DIAGNOSED · CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT LED TO STOPPING THE MEDICATION · ARE YOU STILL HAVING REGULAR FOLLOW-UP with your GP or infectious diseases specialist · HAVE YOU HAD ANY COMPLICATIONS from it before?**

**BLOCK 3 — THE INFECTION SCREEN, ONE QUESTION PER SYSTEM. ENT: sore throat · runny nose · facial pain · ear pain. LOWER RESPIRATORY: any cough, DRY OR CHESTY · shortness of breath · noisy breathing.**
**GASTROINTESTINAL: nausea or vomiting · tummy pain · diarrhoea. URINARY: burning passing urine · passing urine more often. CNS: HEADACHE · STIFF NECK · SENSITIVE TO LIGHT?**

**SEXUAL HEALTH: sexually active now or in the last three months · condoms · discharge from the penis · rash or ulcers on the penis · swelling or pain in the scrotum. LIVER: yellowing of skin or eyes · dark urine · pale stools.**

**SKIN: any rash anywhere · any red, hot, painful areas. ENDOCARDITIS: any recreational drugs, HAVE YOU EVER INJECTED · any chest pain or racing of the heart. EXPOSURE: any travel here or overseas · ANY CONTACT WITH ANIMALS, INCLUDING PETS?**
**BLOCK 4 — THE MALIGNANCY SCREEN, the heading most candidates never open. GENERAL: WEIGHT LOSS WITHOUT TRYING · loss of appetite · ANY LUMPS OR BUMPS anywhere · NIGHT SWEATS?**

**KAPOSI: any ULCERS OR PATCHES IN YOUR MOUTH · ANY NEW PURPLE OR RED MARKS ON YOUR SKIN? LUNG CANCER: HAVE YOU EVER COUGHED UP BLOOD · do you smoke · what work have you done, ANY ASBESTOS? SKIN: any new or changing moles or lesions?**
**If time remains: mood and adjustment, anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac disease, sleep apnoea. Do not sacrifice the differential list to reach them.**
**EXAMINATION, ASKED BY REGION AND TARGET: general appearance — alert or drowsy, rash, jaundice, dehydration · THE FIVE VITAL SIGNS · throat and mouth — any swelling, redness, LESIONS.**
**THE WHITE PATCH — three questions before you name it: IS IT PAINFUL WHEN TOUCHED · CAN IT BE SCRAPED OFF · WHAT COLOUR, AND WHERE?**

**FULL LYMPH NODE examination, every chain · THYROID · RESPIRATORY IN FULL — expansion, percussion both sides, added sounds, VOCAL RESONANCE · cardiovascular, heart sounds and murmurs · abdomen for tenderness and HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY · URINE DIPSTICK.** If time: **neck stiffness, and FUNDOSCOPY FOR CMV RETINITIS.**
**SAY THE SENTENCE about the normal chest OUT LOUD before the examiner asks.**

**NAME PNEUMONIA with the reasons IN HIS WORDS — fever, cough, feeling unwell, paracetamol not helping, LOW OXYGEN, breathing faster than normal.** Then **the opportunistic concern: Pneumocystis and tuberculosis, WITHOUT claiming to have diagnosed either — and the typical causes, COVID, influenza, pneumococcus, Legionella, Mycoplasma.**
**OPEN THE MALIGNANCY HEADING — lung cancer, Kaposi sarcoma because of the mouth, lymphoma.** Then **the other infection sources BY NAME, not by category.**

**If asked about management: ADMIT · oxygen, IV access, fluids · BLOOD CULTURES AND LACTATE BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS · empirical community-acquired pneumonia treatment while the workup runs · RESPIRATORY ISOLATION UNTIL TUBERCULOSIS IS EXCLUDED.**
pefe: **Do now: ADMIT — fever, hypoxia and tachypnoea in advanced HIV is NOT an outpatient problem · oxygen to target, IV access, fluids · BLOOD CULTURES AND LACTATE BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS · empirical CAP treatment while the workup runs · RESPIRATORY ISOLATION UNTIL TB IS EXCLUDED.**
**Investigations: CHEST RADIOGRAPH, and CT CHEST IF IT IS NORMAL BUT HE IS HYPOXIC · CD4 COUNT AND VIRAL LOAD · FBE, UEC, LFT, LDH, CRP, arterial or venous BLOOD GAS.**

**SPUTUM: Gram stain and culture · ACID-FAST BACILLI TIMES THREE plus XPERT MTB/RIF · PCR FOR P. JIROVECII on induced sputum or lavage.** **Plus URINARY LEGIONELLA AND PNEUMOCOCCAL ANTIGEN, respiratory viral PCR, SERUM CRYPTOCOCCAL ANTIGEN, TOXOPLASMA SEROLOGY, a FULL STI SCREEN INCLUDING SYPHILIS, and BIOPSY OF ANY SUSPICIOUS MUCOSAL LESION.**

**Treatment principles: if Pneumocystis is confirmed or strongly suspected, HIGH-DOSE TRIMETHOPRIM-SULFAMETHOXAZOLE with ADJUNCTIVE CORTICOSTEROID if there is significant hypoxia. If TB is confirmed, STANDARD QUADRUPLE THERAPY under specialist supervision, NOTIFY and arrange CONTACT TRACING.** VERIFY doses and the hypoxia threshold.

**RESTART ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY IN CONSULTATION WITH INFECTIOUS DISEASES — TIMING MATTERS BECAUSE OF IMMUNE RECONSTITUTION INFLAMMATORY SYNDROME.** **Reinstate prophylaxis where the CD4 count indicates it.** VERIFY thresholds.
**Red flags: systolic below 90 · SATURATION BELOW 92% · respiratory rate above 30 · CONFUSION · haemoptysis · severe headache with neck stiffness or photophobia · NEW FOCAL NEUROLOGY · VISUAL LOSS.**

**CONFIDENTIALITY IS A LIVE ISSUE IN A SMALL TOWN — say so, and OFFER HIM THE CHOICE OF WHERE FOLLOW-UP HAPPENS.** **From Kadina he needs a hospital that can do BRONCHOSCOPY with infectious diseases input — the RAH or Lyell McEwin.**

stem: Jane Whitmore, 40, has come in feeling unwell — tired and nauseated, no fever. She has recently returned from a trip to the Philippines. No sexual activity overseas, no mosquito bites, no needle exposures. Appendicectomy ten years ago.
tasks: Begin with a physical examination, asking the examiner for the findings — there is no history taking
At four minutes you are given the investigation results; explain them to the patient
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: THE FORMAT IS THE DIFFICULTY

NO HISTORY-TAKING TASK. A long stem holds ALL the history you will get, you go straight to examination, a card arrives AT FOUR MINUTES, and you explain. Two things go wrong: candidates WALK PAST THE PATIENT to talk to the examiner, losing the relationship they need for the second half — and they EXAMINE FOR THE DIAGNOSIS THEY ALREADY KNOW rather than ACROSS THE DIFFERENTIALS, which is what the examination task is scoring
READ THE NEGATIVES AS DELIBERATELY AS THE POSITIVES

A long stem is doing the work a history task would otherwise do. NO FEVER pushes cholangitis down · NO SEXUAL AND NO NEEDLE EXPOSURE pushes hepatitis B and C down · NO MOSQUITO BITES softens but does NOT exclude dengue and malaria · TRAVEL TO THE PHILIPPINES puts FAECAL-ORAL INFECTION AT THE TOP
General and vitals
ALERT · JAUNDICED · no rash, no pallor, MILDLY DEHYDRATED · BP 120/80 · HR 88 · RR 12 · T 36.9 — AFEBRILE
The abdomen — and what to ask NEXT

HEPATOMEGALY, THREE CENTIMETRES below the costal margin. DO NOT ACCEPT 'HEPATOMEGALY' AND MOVE ON: WHAT IS THE SPAN · IS IT TENDER · IS THE BORDER REGULAR OR IRREGULAR? Answer: NON-TENDER, BORDER SMOOTH AND REGULAR. No splenomegaly, NO SHIFTING DULLNESS, no scratch marks, no bruises, bowel sounds normal
Why each NORMAL finding was worth asking for

NO FEVER argues against ASCENDING CHOLANGITIS · NO LYMPHADENOPATHY argues against EBV, CMV, LYMPHOMA and HIV · NO SPLENOMEGALY the same · REGULAR BORDER argues against CIRRHOSIS and METASTATIC disease · NO ASCITES, SCRATCH MARKS OR BRUISING means no chronic liver disease and no synthetic failure
CORRECTION — the non-tender liver

The lecture describes a NON-TENDER liver as pointing towards CANCER. Worth saying out loud, BUT acute viral hepatitis FREQUENTLY produces a MILDLY TENDER liver, and absence of tenderness ALONE neither confirms nor excludes malignancy. USE IT AS ONE FEATURE AMONG SEVERAL, NOT AS A RULE
TWO OFFICE TESTS — the second is the one forgotten

URINE DIPSTICK: BILIRUBIN POSITIVE, UROBILINOGEN RAISED, no leucocytes or nitrites, no glucose or ketones. AND A URINE PREGNANCY TEST: NEGATIVE. Six words — 'and a urine pregnancy test' — in a 40-year-old woman with nausea
THE CARD AT FOUR MINUTES

WCC 13.2 (RAISED) · Hb and platelets normal · BILIRUBIN 68 · ALT 780 · AST 640 · ALP 130 mildly raised · GGT 110 · ALBUMIN 38 NORMAL · INR 1.1 NORMAL · HEPATITIS B SURFACE ANTIGEN NEGATIVE · HEPATITIS C ANTIBODY NEGATIVE. THE PATTERN IS HEPATOCELLULAR
ADDED — ask for INR and albumin
They are NOT in the original recall. ASK FOR THEM AND SAY WHY: they are THE TESTS OF SYNTHETIC FUNCTION, and A RISING INR IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT MARKER OF PROGRESSION TO ACUTE LIVER FAILURE
CORRECTION — the raised white cell count

The lecture reads it as confirming 'there is an infection'. IN ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS THE WHITE CELL COUNT IS MORE OFTEN NORMAL OR LOW, WITH A RELATIVE LYMPHOCYTOSIS. A frankly raised NEUTROPHIL count should make you think again about a BACTERIAL cause — ASCENDING CHOLANGITIS — or LEPTOSPIROSIS. It does not change the answer here, but be able to say it if challenged
findingsLabel: Examination first — the card, the two office tests, and two source corrections
must: FAIL — Never greeting the patient before turning to the examiner.
FAIL — Reciting a generic tiredness list first. The stem made travel the loudest thing in the case.
FAIL — Missing acute liver failure: no mention of INR, glucose or encephalopathy anywhere.
FAIL — Omitting consent and a chaperone before the pelvic examination.
ASK — Is the liver tender, and is the border regular or irregular?
ASK — And a urine pregnancy test.

dx: **ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS, MOST LIKELY HEPATITIS A — faecal-orally transmitted, self-limiting, acquired from contaminated food or water overseas.** **HEPATITIS E SITS ALONGSIDE IT AND IS WORTH NAMING, particularly after travel to South and South-East Asia.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: GREETING THE PATIENT BEFORE YOU TURN TO THE EXAMINER, and then NAMING TRAVEL-RELATED INFECTION AS YOUR FIRST DIFFERENTIAL GROUP rather than reciting a generic tiredness list.**

**ORDER IS THE MARK. Every candidate knows the same differentials for a tired patient — WHAT SEPARATES THEM IS WHETHER THE ORDER IS DERIVED FROM THIS PATIENT. If your first sentence is 'I was thinking about anaemia, thyroid disease and depression', YOU HAVE TOLD THE EXAMINER YOU MEMORISED A LIST AND DID NOT READ THE CASE.**

**FIFTEEN SECONDS AT THE START PROTECTS THE LAST FOUR MINUTES: 'Hello Jane, I'm Dr [name]. I'll be looking after you today. I'm just going to SPEAK TO MY COLLEAGUE for a few minutes and go through an examination, and then I'LL COME STRAIGHT BACK TO YOU and explain everything. Is that all right?'** **Otherwise you turn, four minutes later, to a role player you have never acknowledged and try to break significant news.**
**SAY 'THIS IS A HEPATOCELLULAR PATTERN' BEFORE YOU NAME A DIAGNOSIS — it is worth a mark on its own. GGT rises with EITHER pattern and DOES NOT DECIDE between them.**

**EXPLAIN THE RESULTS IN THREE SENTENCES, UNDER A MINUTE. 'The part I'm interested in is the WHITE BLOOD CELLS — the cells of your immune system — and they're higher than normal, which tells me your body is FIGHTING AN INFECTION OR INFLAMMATION.' 'Your LIVER ENZYMES are raised, and that tells me there's INFLAMMATION IN YOUR LIVER.' 'We tested for two viruses that commonly cause this — HEPATITIS B AND HEPATITIS C — and BOTH CAME BACK NEGATIVE.'**
**DO NOT explain what AST, ALT and GGT each are. DO NOT walk her through the three cell lines. 'KEEP IT SIMPLE' IS THE INSTRUCTION AND IT IS ALSO THE MARK.**

**THE DIAGNOSIS WITH REASONS, all six: your LIVER IS ENLARGED · you have YELLOWING of skin and eyes · BILIRUBIN IN YOUR URINE, which tells me THE PROBLEM IS IN THE LIVER · RAISED LIVER ENZYMES · the two other common causes, HEPATITIS B AND C, ARE NEGATIVE · and YOU HAVE RECENTLY TRAVELLED, with nausea and feeling unwell. HEPATITIS A SPREADS THROUGH CONTAMINATED FOOD AND WATER, WHICH FITS.**

**REASSURANCE WITH A REASON, not without one: 'HEPATITIS A DOES NOT BECOME CHRONIC AND GIVES LIFELONG IMMUNITY. In most people this settles by itself over a few weeks. There's no specific treatment and no lasting damage in the great majority — but I do want to keep an eye on you while it settles.'** **If she travels again, THE VACCINE IS THE ANSWER.**

**Spread and prevention, in her words: 'it spreads through contaminated food and water, and PERSON TO PERSON BY UNWASHED HANDS AFTER USING THE TOILET. So while you're unwell: WASH YOUR HANDS THOROUGHLY, DO NOT PREPARE FOOD FOR OTHER PEOPLE, and DO NOT SHARE TOWELS. This is a condition we're REQUIRED TO NOTIFY, which is routine — it means YOUR HOUSEHOLD CAN BE OFFERED A VACCINE.'** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · PATS · healthdirect 1800 022 222.**
plan: **ANSWER THE EXAMINER'S 'any questions?' WITH 'no questions, thank you' — THEN TURN TO THE PATIENT FIRST.** Greet, name your role, say what will happen and that you will come back. **Then** turn to the examiner: **'thank you — I'd like to start with general appearance.'**

**NEVER NAME A REGION WITHOUT NAMING THE FINDING, or you get 'what are you looking for?' after every request. GENERAL APPEARANCE: is she ALERT OR DROWSY · any JAUNDICE · any rash · any PALLOR · any DEHYDRATION? Then the FOUR VITAL SIGNS.**

**ENT: on throat examination any swelling, redness or exudate · on ear examination a red bulging tympanic membrane? NECK: is the THYROID normal · and a FULL LYMPH NODE EXAMINATION, any lymphadenopathy in any chain?**

**RESPIRATORY: is air entry equal, any added sounds? CARDIOVASCULAR: first and second heart sounds normal, any murmurs?** **Your examination is scored on COVERING THE DIFFERENTIALS — nodes, thyroid, chest, heart, pelvis — not on finding the liver.**
**ABDOMEN, INSPECTION: any distension · any redness or bruising on the abdominal wall? PALPATION: any tenderness · any HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY?**
**CHARACTERISE THE LIVER — three questions: WHAT IS THE SPAN · IS IT TENDER · IS THE BORDER REGULAR OR IRREGULAR?**
**SIGNS OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE: is there SHIFTING DULLNESS · any SCRATCH MARKS · any BRUISING? Then AUSCULTATION: are bowel sounds normal?**

**'And I'd like to perform a DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION.'** **Defensible here because you have four minutes — in a two-minute examination request it is the first thing to drop. The judgement is about TIME, not about correctness.**

**PELVIC — SAY THE WHOLE PHRASE: 'WITH THE PATIENT'S CONSENT AND IN THE PRESENCE OF A CHAPERONE.' On inspection, any discharge or rash · on speculum, any discharge from the cervix · on bimanual, CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS, uterine size, uterine tenderness, and are the adnexae normal?** **Make the consent-and-chaperone phrase automatic before every pelvic, breast or scrotal examination.**
**OFFICE TEST 1: a URINE DIPSTICK — 'given the picture I'm looking for BILIRUBIN, and also leucocytes, nitrites, glucose and ketones.' OFFICE TEST 2: A URINE PREGNANCY TEST.**
**Take the card. ASK FOR INR AND ALBUMIN if they are not on it, and SAY WHY.** Then **NAME THE PATTERN: 'this is a hepatocellular pattern.'**
**EXPLAIN THE RESULTS IN THREE SENTENCES — white cells, liver enzymes, the two negative viruses. UNDER A MINUTE, THEN MOVE.**
**NAME THE DIAGNOSIS with all six reasons in plain English.**

**DIFFERENTIALS, TRAVEL FIRST: 'because you've been overseas, the first group I thought about was TRAVEL-RELATED INFECTIONS — MALARIA, DENGUE, TYPHOID, LEPTOSPIROSIS, and also HEPATITIS E, which spreads the same way. I also considered GLANDULAR FEVER, HIV and TUBERCULOSIS.'**

**THEN LIVER AND ABDOMEN: hepatitis B and C, negative today · AUTOIMMUNE HEPATITIS · MEDICATION-RELATED LIVER INJURY including antibiotics · gallstones and CHOLANGITIS · and CANCER of the liver or pancreas, PARTICULARLY BECAUSE YOUR LIVER WAS NOT TENDER.**

**THEN PREGNANCY — 'which is why we did the urine test, and that was negative' — AND ONLY THEN the general tiredness list: anaemia, thyroid, diabetes, coeliac, haemochromatosis, lymphoma and leukaemia, autoimmune disease, depression, heart failure, sleep apnoea.**

**Close with the plan and the public health piece: confirmatory serology, ultrasound, supportive care with ALCOHOL AVOIDED COMPLETELY, NOTIFICATION, CONTACT VACCINATION, WORK EXCLUSION if relevant, and the ESCALATION TRIGGERS — CONFUSION, BRUISING, A RISING INR.**
pefe: **Do now: ANTI-HEPATITIS A IgM — the confirmatory test · HEPATITIS E IgM · INR AND ALBUMIN for synthetic function and severity · BLOOD GLUCOSE, because HYPOGLYCAEMIA IS A FEATURE OF LIVER FAILURE · MALARIA FILMS if there is any doubt about the itinerary.**
**Do next: UPPER ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND to exclude biliary obstruction and a mass · EBV and CMV serology · HIV and syphilis serology · autoantibodies if the picture does not resolve.**

**Treatment: NO SPECIFIC ANTIVIRAL. Rest, oral fluids, small frequent meals. AVOID ALCOHOL COMPLETELY until liver function normalises. REVIEW EVERY MEDICATION FOR HEPATOTOXICITY — paracetamol is not absolutely contraindicated but the dose should be REDUCED AND DISCUSSED.** VERIFY the current maximum in acute hepatitis.
**Repeat liver function and INR to confirm recovery. MOST PEOPLE RECOVER FULLY IN TWO TO EIGHT WEEKS; a relapsing or prolonged cholestatic course occurs in a minority.** VERIFY.

**Do not miss ACUTE LIVER FAILURE: CONFUSION, DROWSINESS OR ALTERED BEHAVIOUR · A RISING INR · HYPOGLYCAEMIA. Admit and discuss with a liver unit.** Other red flags: **easy bruising, FEVER WITH RIGORS, PAINLESS JAUNDICE WITH WEIGHT LOSS, ASCITES.**
**NOTIFIABLE in South Australia.** **CONTACTS: household and close contacts offered HEPATITIS A VACCINE, or normal human immunoglobulin where indicated, IDEALLY WITHIN 14 DAYS of exposure.** VERIFY.

**OCCUPATION: FOOD HANDLERS, CHILDCARE AND HEALTHCARE WORKERS ARE EXCLUDED FROM WORK — conventionally UNTIL SEVEN DAYS AFTER THE ONSET OF JAUNDICE.** VERIFY current SA Health exclusion period. **If she cannot work, discuss income support and, if occupational, ReturnToWorkSA.**

stem: Ben Alderton, 25, has come in feeling unwell. He attends a sauna regularly with friends, and his friends have similar symptoms. He is currently taking PrEP. T 38.4, HR 96, BP 122/76, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
tasks: Take a focused history (5 minutes)
You will be given the examination findings on screen or card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses
findings: TWO LEAD POINTS IN ONE STEM — open BOTH
THE SAUNA and THE PrEP. Opening only one of them is THE COMMONEST WAY TO FAIL AN OTHERWISE EASY STATION. T 38.4 · HR 96 · BP 122/76 · RR 16 · SpO2 98% RA
The published card

JAUNDICE · ENLARGED TENDER LIVER with a SPAN OVER 12–13 cm · BILIRUBIN ON URINE DIPSTICK. NO cough, NO breathlessness, NO diarrhoea, NO rash, NO genital ulcer or discharge, NO scrotal symptoms, NO travel, NO weight loss, NO lymphadenopathy
What he says about the sauna
'A FEW TIMES A WEEK, same group of us. I DON'T REALLY KNOW WHAT THEY'VE GOT.' A dead end — and THE MARK IS FOR ASKING. Then run the three water infections
'I HAVE SEX IN THE SAUNA'
NOW THE SAUNA IS BOTH A WATER EXPOSURE AND A SEXUAL EXPOSURE. Say so out loud, and take the FULL sexual history — not a two-question screen
The PrEP answers — three separate marks

'MOST DAYS, I MISS THE ODD ONE.' · 'LAST REVIEW WAS TWO MONTHS AGO.' · 'I'VE NEVER ACTUALLY BEEN CHECKED FOR STIs.' · 'I'M NOT SURE ABOUT THE VACCINES.' PrEP SCRIPTS RUN THREE-MONTHLY WITH A FULL STI SCREEN EACH TIME — he is due, and never being screened is UNUSUAL ON PrEP. Say it kindly and correct it
THE SENTENCE HE PUSHES BACK WITH

'BUT I'M ON PrEP, SO I CAN'T GET HIV.' Answer: 'PrEP is VERY EFFECTIVE, and taking it was a good decision. But IT'S NOT ABSOLUTE, and HOW WELL IT WORKS DEPENDS ON TAKING IT CONSISTENTLY — you've told me you miss doses. Testing costs you ONE BLOOD TEST, and IF IT'S NEGATIVE WE BOTH STOP WONDERING'
He does not use condoms — DO NOT REACT
Continue NEUTRALLY into practices and previous infections. COUNSELLING COMES LATER, NOT MID-HISTORY. Launching into condom advice the moment he says it is a scored fail
VERSION — the HIV card

PHARYNGITIS · MACULOPAPULAR TRUNK RASH · GENERALISED LYMPHADENOPATHY · NO HEPATOMEGALY · DIPSTICK NORMAL. History: sore throat, widespread NON-ITCHY rash, MOUTH ULCERS, aching all over, STOPPED PrEP TWO MONTHS AGO. SAME STEM, DIFFERENT DIAGNOSIS
VERSION — the Legionella card

CRACKLES AT THE LEFT BASE · SpO2 91% · SODIUM 126. History: dry cough, breathlessness, high fever, WATERY DIARRHOEA, MUDDLED THINKING, and TWO FRIENDS ALSO COUGHING. PNEUMONIA WITH DIARRHOEA IS THE CLASSIC PAIRING — add CONFUSION and HYPONATRAEMIA and the picture is complete
VERSION — the confidentiality opener

He opens with 'BEFORE WE START — MY BROTHER WORKS ON RECEPTION HERE.' Handle it honestly WITHOUT OVERPROMISING, and still take the full history. CONFIDENTIALITY MATTERS MORE, NOT LESS, IN A SMALL TOWN
findingsLabel: Two lead points, the PrEP block, and the sentence that fails the station
must: FAIL — A two-question sexual screen instead of a full history.
FAIL — Never opening the sauna: straight from 'unwell' to hepatitis questions.
FAIL — Excluding HIV because he is on PrEP. The most dangerous sentence available here.
FAIL — Testing urine only in a man who has oral and anal sex.
ASK — Are you taking your PrEP every day, without missing doses?
ASK — Tell me more about the sauna and your friends. What symptoms do they have?

dx: **ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS. DO NOT TRY TO NAME THE SUBTYPE. It could be HEPATITIS A from the faecal-oral route OR from sexual contact between men, or HEPATITIS B OR C from unprotected sex. YOU CANNOT SEPARATE THEM ON HISTORY AND EXAMINATION, and naming a subtype you cannot prove GAINS NOTHING. Say 'acute viral hepatitis' and LET SEROLOGY DECIDE.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: whether you OPEN BOTH BOXES — the RECREATIONAL WATER and the SEXUAL HISTORY — rather than pattern-matching straight to hepatitis.** **This station is EASY TO DIAGNOSE AND EASY TO FAIL: candidates recognise the recall, ask the hepatitis questions, name hepatitis, and are marked down because they NEVER ASKED ABOUT THE FRIENDS' SYMPTOMS, never mentioned Legionella or Pseudomonas, and took a two-question screen.**

**ITS TWIN: WHETHER HIV STAYS ON YOUR LIST. 'You're on PrEP so HIV is unlikely' AND MOVING ON IS THE SINGLE MOST DANGEROUS SENTENCE AVAILABLE IN THIS STATION.** **PrEP is ADHERENCE DEPENDENT, he misses doses, he does not use condoms, and in some versions HAS NEVER BEEN SCREENED.**

**WHY PrEP IS IN THE STEM AT ALL: it tells you TWO THINGS AT ONCE — this man HAS IDENTIFIED HIV RISK, and he IS IN REGULAR THREE-MONTHLY CARE. BOTH ARE HISTORY YOU MUST TAKE.** **Treating PrEP as a medication to be listed rather than A HISTORY BLOCK TO BE OPENED loses three separate marks: ADHERENCE, SCREENING INTERVAL, VACCINATION.**

**PrEP PROTECTS AGAINST HIV ONLY — NOT syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, hepatitis or mpox.** **Review is THREE-MONTHLY, not monthly: script, full STI screen and RENAL FUNCTION each time. The monitored adverse effect is RENAL IMPAIRMENT.** VERIFY.

**NORMALISE ONCE, EARLY, THEN ASK WITHOUT FLINCHING: 'I'm going to ask some personal and quite detailed questions about your sex life. I ASK EVERYONE THESE QUESTIONS, they're relevant to working out what's making you unwell, and everything you tell me is confidential.'** **HESITATING BEFORE EVERY QUESTION IS MORE UNCOMFORTABLE FOR THE PATIENT THAN ASKING DIRECTLY.**

**NAME ALL THREE WATER INFECTIONS OUT LOUD, INCLUDING THE ONES HE DOES NOT HAVE AND WHY: LEGIONELLA — less likely, no cough or breathlessness · PSEUDOMONAS FOLLICULITIS, itchy pustules where swimwear sits — no rash · CRYPTOSPORIDIUM, which SURVIVES CHLORINE — no diarrhoea.**

**THREE SITES, ALWAYS: THROAT, ANORECTAL AND FIRST-PASS URINE. If challenged on why: 'because PHARYNGEAL AND ANORECTAL GONORRHOEA AND CHLAMYDIA ARE COMMONLY ASYMPTOMATIC and are MISSED ENTIRELY by a urine test alone.'** **The practices question is NOT PRURIENCE — IT DECIDES WHICH SITES YOU SWAB.**

**CONFIDENTIALITY, HONESTLY AND WITHOUT OVERPROMISING: 'what you tell me stays between us. SOME INFECTIONS I'M REQUIRED TO REPORT TO PUBLIC HEALTH, but that's reported AS A CASE, NOT AS A NAME IN THE COMMUNITY. If anything comes back positive, your partners do need to know they may have been exposed — and THERE ARE SERVICES THAT CAN CONTACT THEM ANONYMOUSLY ON YOUR BEHALF. What I CANNOT do is tell them your results without your permission. THAT IS YOURS.'**

**If HIV is reactive: URGENT sexual health or infectious diseases referral, and STOP PrEP — PrEP ALONE IN ESTABLISHED HIV RISKS RESISTANCE.** **Notifiable in SA: HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, hepatitis A, B and C, and LEGIONELLOSIS — which triggers A PUBLIC HEALTH INVESTIGATION OF THE WATER SOURCE, and that matters here because OTHERS USE THE SAME SAUNA.** **Clinic 275 · SHINE SA · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
plan: **Introduce, then ADDRESS THE CONCERN BEFORE THE HISTORY — five seconds and a scored item: 'I can hear that you're worried, and I want to get to the bottom of it. Let me ask you some questions, then I'll examine you, and we'll make a plan together.'**

**BLOCK 1 — EXPLORE 'UNWELL', four questions: can you describe what you mean · how long, constant or coming and going · is it getting worse · what makes it better or worse, and how is it affecting your life?**
**BLOCK 2 — THE SAUNA, open then narrow: 'TELL ME MORE ABOUT THE SAUNA AND YOUR FRIENDS. HOW OFTEN DO YOU GO? DO YOU KNOW WHAT SYMPTOMS YOUR FRIENDS ARE HAVING?'**
**BLOCK 3 — THE THREE WATER INFECTIONS. LEGIONELLA: any cough · any shortness of breath · fever or chills · ANY DIARRHOEA · HAVE YOU FELT CONFUSED OR MUDDLED?**

**HEPATITIS A: any tummy pain · nausea or vomiting · ANY YELLOWING of your skin or eyes · HAS YOUR URINE GONE DARK, OR YOUR STOOLS PALE? PSEUDOMONAS: any rash anywhere — PARTICULARLY ITCHY SPOTS WHERE YOUR SWIMWEAR SITS?**

**BLOCK 4 — THE PrEP BLOCK, three questions: ARE YOU TAKING IT EVERY DAY WITHOUT MISSING DOSES · ARE YOU HAVING YOUR THREE-MONTHLY SEXUAL HEALTH SCREENING, and seeing your GP or specialist regularly · HAVE YOU HAD YOUR HEPATITIS A AND B VACCINATIONS?**
**NORMALISE, ONCE — then BLOCK 5, THE FULL SEXUAL HISTORY. WHO: are you sexually active · stable partner · ever had MULTIPLE partners · ARE YOUR PARTNERS MALE, FEMALE OR BOTH?**

**HOW: do you use condoms — ALWAYS · WHAT KIND OF SEX DO YOU HAVE — oral, vaginal or anal? RISK: have you EVER BEEN DIAGNOSED with a sexually transmitted infection · have you ever had sex UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF ALCOHOL OR DRUGS?**

**BLOCK 6 — THE STI SYMPTOM PACKAGE: any SORE THROAT · any RASH on your body · any LUMPS OR BUMPS in neck, armpits or groin · NIGHT SWEATS · any rash, sore or ULCER ON YOUR PRIVATE PARTS · any DISCHARGE from the penis · any PAIN OR SWELLING IN THE SCROTUM · ANY PAIN OR DISCHARGE FROM THE BACK PASSAGE?**
**BLOCK 7 — THE REST, FAST. Malignancy first: weight loss, appetite, lumps, night sweats. Then travel, mood, past history, medications, allergies, alcohol, smoking and recreational drug use.**
**Take the card. Name the LIVER SPAN, the tenderness and the bilirubinuria out loud.**
**NAME ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS with the reasons — enlarged tender liver, yellowing, BILE PIGMENT IN THE URINE — and SAY EXPLICITLY THAT YOU ARE NOT GOING TO GUESS THE SUBTYPE, and why.**
**THE WATER BOX, all three named WITH the reason each is less likely.**

**THE SEXUAL BOX, WITH HIV AT THE TOP: 'HIV is HIGH ON MY LIST — you're on PrEP, which is very effective, but IT DEPENDS ON TAKING IT EVERY DAY, and you've told me you miss doses and don't use condoms.' Then SYPHILIS, HERPES, GONORRHOEA AND CHLAMYDIA — which can affect THE THROAT AND THE BACK PASSAGE as well as the urine.**
**Then further down: glandular fever and CMV, travel-related infections, LYMPHOMA AND LEUKAEMIA, depression, and the general causes — thyroid, diabetes, anaemia, coeliac.**

**Handle the PrEP pushback and the confidentiality question with the scripted answers.** Then **SAFETY-NET: return immediately for CONFUSION OR DROWSINESS, BRUISING OR BLEEDING, worsening jaundice, BREATHLESSNESS, or inability to keep fluids down.**
pefe: **Do now: vital signs and hydration, ASSESS FOR SEPSIS · URINE DIPSTICK for BILIRUBIN · FBE, UEC, LFT, INR, CRP, blood glucose.**

**Serology: ANTI-HAV IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and CORE IgM, hepatitis C ANTIBODY AND RNA · FOURTH-GENERATION HIV ANTIGEN/ANTIBODY TEST, and HIV RNA IF SEROCONVERSION IS SUSPECTED · SYPHILIS SEROLOGY.**
**THREE-SITE NUCLEIC ACID TESTING for gonorrhoea and chlamydia: THROAT, ANORECTAL, FIRST-PASS URINE.** **If there is ANY cough or breathlessness: CHEST RADIOGRAPH and URINARY LEGIONELLA ANTIGEN.**
**The fourth-generation test detects the p24 ANTIGEN and turns positive EARLIER. RETEST AT 6 WEEKS AND 3 MONTHS — ONE EARLY NEGATIVE TEST DOES NOT CLOSE THE QUESTION.** VERIFY.

**What the results change: HEPATOCELLULAR pattern with BILIRUBINURIA → acute hepatitis, NOTIFY and manage supportively · RISING INR OR FALLING ALBUMIN → failing synthetic function, ADMIT · REACTIVE HIV → urgent referral and STOP PrEP · positive gonorrhoea or chlamydia → treat, PARTNER NOTIFICATION, retest · NON-IMMUNE to hepatitis A or B → VACCINATE.**

**Do not miss: ACUTE HIV INFECTION — being on PrEP does not exclude it and neither does one early negative test · FULMINANT HEPATITIS — confusion, drowsiness, bruising, RISING INR · SEVERE LEGIONELLA · TESTICULAR TORSION MASQUERADING AS EPIDIDYMO-ORCHITIS · PARTNER NOTIFICATION, an omitted public health responsibility.**

**Avoid: naming a subtype you cannot prove · testing urine only · reassuring him PrEP makes HIV impossible · CONTINUING PrEP ALONE IF HIV IS CONFIRMED · MORALISING about the sauna, the number of partners, or condom use · TELLING HIS PARTNERS YOURSELF WITHOUT CONSENT — use anonymous partner notification services.**

stem: Mary Ellis, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has come in because she has been feeling unwell for the past few days. First pregnancy; antenatal care so far uncomplicated.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings (2 minutes)
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient
findings: FOUR TASKS IN EIGHT MINUTES — the clock is the station

History 4 min → examination 2 min → diagnosis and differentials 1 min → MANAGEMENT 1 min. A candidate scoring 7, 7, 7 WHO NEVER REACHES MANAGEMENT FAILS. A candidate scoring 4, 4, 4, 4 PASSES. The moment you read FOUR TASKS on the door, decide to move faster than usual and PROTECT THE LAST TWO MINUTES
ASK FOR OBSERVATIONS AT THE DOOR

Normally you would NOT open an unwell case with a stability check. You do it here BECAUSE THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST IS GENUINELY DANGEROUS AND SHE IS PREGNANT. Eight seconds, and it reads as clinical judgement. Online there is no examiner — say it to the patient: 'I'm going to take you through to the treatment room first so we can check your observations'
The findings

T 38.7 · HR 108 · BP 110/70 MAINTAINED · RR 18 · SpO2 98% · FLUSHED, MILDLY DEHYDRATED, alert, no jaundice, no rash. Throat normal · chest clear · heart sounds dual. Abdomen: MILD SUPRAPUBIC TENDERNESS · RIGHT RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS POSITIVE · no RUQ tenderness · no organomegaly
THE UTERUS — three questions, ten seconds

FUNDAL HEIGHT 20 cm, CONSISTENT WITH DATES · UTERUS NON-TENDER · FETAL HEART RATE 145. These are the difference between a candidate who examined A WOMAN and one who examined A PREGNANT WOMAN. Fundal height larger or smaller than dates matters; A TENDER UTERUS RAISES CHORIOAMNIONITIS OR ABRUPTION; NORMAL FETAL HEART RATE IS 110–160
The dipstick — ask for it BY NAME
'I'd like a URINE DIPSTICK. I'M LOOKING FOR LEUCOCYTES AND NITRITES.' Result: LEUCOCYTES +++ · NITRITES POSITIVE · BLOOD ++ · protein trace · glucose negative
VERSION A versus VERSION B

THE RULE THAT DECIDES VERSION B
RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS ON EXAMINATION OVERRIDES THE SITE OF PAIN THE PATIENT DESCRIBED. Hearing suprapubic pain, deciding it is cystitis, and stopping asking is the trap

Feverish with CHILLS for a few days, GETTING WORSE · PARACETAMOL UNHELPFUL · VOMITED THREE OR FOUR TIMES · BURNING AND FREQUENCY. NO discharge, NO rash, NO sore throat, NO cough, NO headache, NO travel · NO visual symptoms, NO swelling · NO jaundice, NO itch · BABY MOVING NORMALLY
She has almost certainly NOT measured her temperature
