stem: Gary, 52, has presented after two episodes of falls. He is concerned about the reason for these falls.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Examination findings will be provided on screen or on a card
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: THE EXAMINATION CARD — read every line

BLOOD PRESSURE NORMAL · PULSE 42 PER MINUTE, REGULAR · TEMPERATURE 36.5 · CARDIOVASCULAR NORMAL, NO MURMURS · NEUROLOGICAL NORMAL · BLOOD SUGAR NORMAL. ONE NUMBER CARRIES THE ENTIRE STATION, and IT IS EASY TO SKIM PAST BECAUSE EVERYTHING ELSE IS REASSURINGLY NORMAL
HIS OPENING SENTENCE CONTAINS THE CONCERN

'I've fallen twice, doctor. I'M REALLY WORRIED, BECAUSE LAST TIME MY DAUGHTER WAS THERE TO HELP ME. WHAT IF IT HAPPENS WHEN THERE'S NO ONE AROUND?' NAME IT BACK AND ANSWER IT — and CLOSE THE LOOP AT THE END. It is a SCORED COMMUNICATION ITEM
THE QUESTION THAT UNLOCKS THE STATION

'GARY, CAN YOU PLEASE DESCRIBE EACH OF THE PREVIOUS EPISODES FOR ME?' ROLE-PLAYERS ARE BRIEFED WITH A FULL PARAGRAPH PER EPISODE and will volunteer it in detail ONCE INVITED. Candidates who ask a generic 'what happened?' GET A GENERIC ANSWER AND NEVER REACH THE THUMP
EPISODE 1 — his account

'The first time, I WAS GETTING OUT OF BED, and I fell. MY DAUGHTER SAW IT — she said I WAS LOOKING VERY PALE.' Could be orthostatic — BUT THE PALLOR AND COMPLETE LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS FIT A LOW-OUTPUT EVENT EQUALLY WELL
EPISODE 2 — THE DIAGNOSTIC SENTENCE

'I WAS SITTING ON THE COUCH. I FELT A THUMP IN MY CHEST — A BIG HEAVY BEAT — and then I had the fall.' HE WAS SEATED, SO GRAVITY IS NOT THE EXPLANATION, AND IT WAS PRECEDED BY A PALPITATION. SYNCOPE WHILE SEATED, PRECEDED BY AN ABNORMAL BEAT, IS A CONDUCTION PROBLEM UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE
THE FOLLOW-UP THE CASE IS BUILT AROUND

When he says YES to racing of the heart, A 'YES' RECORDED AND MOVED PAST SCORES NOTHING. Ask: 'WAS YOUR HEART BEATING FAST, OR BEATING IRREGULARLY? COULD YOU TAP THE RHYTHM OUT ON THE DESK?' HE WILL SAY HE DOESN'T KNOW AND DECLINE TO TAP. THAT IS THE SCRIPTED ANSWER AND IT DOES NOT MATTER — THE MARK IS FOR ASKING
'NO WARNING AT ALL'

MOST SYNCOPE ANNOUNCES ITSELF — a few seconds of dizziness, sweating, nausea or greying vision. CARDIAC SYNCOPE CHARACTERISTICALLY DOES NOT. Combined with a rate of 42, THE ABSENT PRODROME IS NOT A SMALL NEGATIVE; IT IS THE FINDING THAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS. AND BECAUSE NOTHING IS VOLUNTEERED, YOU ONLY GET IT IF YOU ASK
THE FOUR FEATURES THAT MAKE IT CARDIAC

1 NO WARNING SYMPTOMS WHATSOEVER before either episode · 2 PALPITATIONS IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THE SECOND · 3 ONE EPISODE WHILE SITTING ON THE COUCH — not standing, not in heat, no trigger · 4 RESTING PULSE OF 42. ANY ONE IS A RED FLAG. ALL FOUR MAKE THIS A MONITORED BED, NOT A REASSURANCE
Everything else negative

COMPLETE LOC, unaware of everything · witnessed BY HIS DAUGHTER BOTH TIMES · A MINUTE OR TWO each · NO jerking, tongue bite or incontinence · NOT CONFUSED AND NOT TIRED afterwards · NO injuries · no chest pain, breathlessness, cough or leg swelling · NO medications and NONE RECENTLY STOPPED · no family history of sudden death
SAME STRUCTURE, DIFFERENT ENDING

This is the FOURTH RECALL BUILT ON ONE STRUCTURE. The previous case ended in AORTIC STENOSIS; this one ends in a BRADYARRHYTHMIA. THE CANDIDATE WHO MEMORISES RECALLS FAILS THE VERSION THEY HAVE NOT SEEN; THE CANDIDATE WHO RUNS THE STRUCTURE PASSES ALL OF THEM
findingsLabel: One abnormal number on the card, and the episode description that unlocks it
must: FAIL — Naming a rhythm you cannot see: 'you have complete heart block', from a pulse rate.
FAIL — Discharging him. 'Everything else is normal, see your GP for a tracing next week.'
FAIL — Not asking him to describe each episode, so the thump is never elicited.
FAIL — Recording 'racing heart: yes' and moving on without the fast-or-irregular follow-up.
ASK — Did you have any warning at all — did you know you were about to go down?
ASK — Do you take any medications regularly, or have you recently stopped any?

dx: **CARDIAC SYNCOPE SECONDARY TO A BRADYARRHYTHMIA. BRADYCARDIA IS A RESTING RATE BELOW 60. Syncope occurs because THE RATE IS TOO SLOW TO MAINTAIN CEREBRAL PERFUSION, or because of A PAUSE BETWEEN BEATS.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: NAME THE SYNDROME, NOT A RHYTHM YOU CANNOT SEE. Faced with syncope and a pulse of 42, the recall-memoriser reaches for a specific label. BUT YOU HAVE A PULSE RATE, NOT A RHYTHM STRIP.**

**A REGULAR RATE OF 42 IS COMPATIBLE WITH SINUS BRADYCARDIA, SECOND- OR THIRD-DEGREE AV BLOCK, SINUS NODE DISEASE, OR AN ISCHAEMIC CONDUCTION PROBLEM. EVERY ONE CAN CAUSE SYNCOPE. NOTHING IN THE HISTORY OR THE CARD LETS YOU CHOOSE — and he could not even tell you whether his palpitations were fast or irregular.**

**WHY THE SYNDROME ANSWER IS STRONGER: IT IS DEFENSIBLE FROM THE FINDINGS YOU ACTUALLY HAVE · IT STILL DEMONSTRATES YOU KNOW THE INDIVIDUAL RHYTHMS, BECAUSE YOU LIST THEM · IT NATURALLY JUSTIFIES YOUR INVESTIGATION PLAN · AND IT CANNOT BE WRONG. NAMING COMPLETE HEART BLOCK ON A PULSE RATE CAN.**

**If the examiner pushes for one answer: 'GIVEN THE PALPITATIONS PRECEDING SYNCOPE TOGETHER WITH A RESTING RATE OF 42, I'D FAVOUR SINUS NODE DYSFUNCTION WITH A TACHY-BRADY PATTERN — BUT I'D WANT THE TELEMETRY BEFORE COMMITTING.'**

**To the patient: 'you have a condition called BRADYCARDIA, which simply means YOUR HEART IS BEATING MORE SLOWLY THAN IT SHOULD. Your pulse here is 42, where a normal resting rate is 60 TO 100. When the heart beats too slowly, IT CAN'T PUSH ENOUGH BLOOD UP TO THE BRAIN — and that's why you blacked out, WITH NO WARNING, BOTH TIMES.'**

**Then the causes in plain words: 'there are several reasons a heart can beat too slowly, and WE NEED A TRACING OF YOUR HEART OVER TIME to tell which one. It could be THE HEART'S OWN NATURAL PACEMAKER RUNNING SLOW, or A BLOCK IN THE ELECTRICAL WIRING BETWEEN THE TOP AND BOTTOM OF THE HEART, or A PROBLEM WITH THE BLOOD SUPPLY TO THE HEART.'**

**CORRECTION — LONG QT IS NOT A CAUSE OF BRADYCARDIA. The source lists it beside sinus bradycardia and heart block. LONG QT CAUSES SYNCOPE THROUGH TORSADES DE POINTES, A POLYMORPHIC VENTRICULAR TACHYCARDIA — THE RATE IS FAST, NOT SLOW.** **The genuine link runs THE OTHER WAY: BRADYCARDIA AND LONG PAUSES ARE TRIGGERS FOR PAUSE-DEPENDENT TORSADES, and some congenital forms are associated with a slow resting rate.**

**Safe wording: 'the slow regular pulse points to a BRADYARRHYTHMIA — sinus node disease or AV block. I'D ALSO MEASURE THE QT INTERVAL, because the palpitations he describes RAISE THE POSSIBILITY OF AN INTERMITTENT TACHYARRHYTHMIA, and BRADYCARDIA ITSELF CAN PRECIPITATE PAUSE-DEPENDENT TORSADES IN A PROLONGED QT.'**

**VOICE THE NEGATIVES — THEY ARE THE REASONING. Almost everything here is normal, AND THAT IS THE POINT. 'No jerking, tongue bite or postictal confusion' EXCLUDES SEIZURE. 'No prodrome' EXCLUDES REFLEX SYNCOPE AND MAKES IT CARDIAC. 'No medications taken or ceased' EXCLUDES THE COMMONEST REVERSIBLE CAUSE OF BRADYCARDIA.**
plan: **To the examiner: blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature.** Then **WIPE and the open question: 'I can see you've been having some falls — can you tell me more about them?'**

**DO NOT TALK OVER HIS ANSWER. When he raises the fear of being alone: 'I completely understand how frightening that must be, and it's a very reasonable thing to worry about. I'LL DO MY BEST TO FIND THE CAUSE TODAY SO THAT WE CAN PREVENT THIS HAPPENING AGAIN.'**
**RECONFIRM, even though the stem says it: 'can you just confirm for me — DID YOU LOSE CONSCIOUSNESS, or were you AWARE of your surroundings?' Then DID ANYONE WITNESS IT?**
**THE SEIZURE SCREEN: any JERKY MOVEMENTS of your arms or legs · did you BITE YOUR TONGUE · did you WET OR SOIL YOURSELF?** Then **HOW LONG WERE YOU UNCONSCIOUS · IS THIS THE FIRST TIME?**
**THE UNLOCKING QUESTION — ask him to describe EACH episode separately, and let him talk.**

**Still complete the ENVIRONMENT sweep, because orthostatic and reflex causes remain live and YOU ARE SCORED ON IT: hot or humid · after a CHANGE OF POSITION · after STRONG EMOTION OR FEAR · PROLONGED STANDING?**

**BEFORE — FOUR QUESTIONS: DID YOU HAVE ANY WARNING AT ALL, did you know you were about to go down · did you MISS ANY MEALS, were you drinking normally · any HEAD INJURY before it happened · any FEVER OR RASH?**

**AFTER — THREE QUESTIONS: when you came round, were you CONFUSED OR JUST TIRED · did you INJURE your head or any other part of you · DID ANYONE SAY YOU LOOKED PALE?** **Record the pallor and MOVE ON — it is common to many causes and does not overturn the cardiac picture.**
**SIGNPOST: 'for the next questions, tell me if you had it BEFORE this happened, AFTER it, or NOT AT ALL — I won't ask twice.' CNS: headache · blurred vision · slurred speech · weakness · numbness.**
**CVS AND RESPIRATORY: chest pain · RACING OF THE HEART · shortness of breath · leg swelling · cough.**

**THE PALPITATION FOLLOW-UP — the whole reason the case exists: 'CAN YOU DESCRIBE IT — WAS YOUR HEART BEATING FAST, OR BEATING IRREGULARLY? COULD YOU TAP THE RHYTHM OUT ON THE DESK FOR ME?'** **The honest conclusion — that you CANNOT CHARACTERISE THE RHYTHM FROM THE HISTORY — is precisely WHY YOUR DIAGNOSIS MUST STAY AT THE LEVEL OF 'BRADYARRHYTHMIA'.**

**GI: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain. SUBSTANCES: alcohol, how much · recreational drugs · DO YOU TAKE ANY MEDICATIONS REGULARLY, OR HAVE YOU RECENTLY STOPPED ANY?** **Drugs are THE COMMONEST REVERSIBLE CAUSE OF BRADYCARDIA — ask even when the answer is no, or you cannot say they are excluded.**

**THE ADDED THREE — in a six-minute history you should reach these: LONG TRAVEL · WEATHER PREFERENCE · YELLOWING OF THE SKIN.** Then **PSYCHOGENIC LAST: breathing fast before · any stressful news beforehand.**
**PAST AND FAMILY HISTORY: any past medical history I should know about · family history of similar episodes · FAMILY HISTORY OF SUDDEN DEATH?**
**READ THE CARD PROPERLY, LINE BY LINE. The one abnormal value IS the station.**

**NAME BRADYCARDIA to the patient in plain words, with the reason it caused a blackout — then GIVE THE POSSIBLE RHYTHMS AS CAUSES rather than picking one.** Then **the differentials across systems, with the negatives voiced.**

**ANSWER THE CONCERN HE RAISED AT THE START: 'you asked what happens if you're on your own — THAT'S EXACTLY WHY I WANT YOU ON A HEART MONITOR HERE RATHER THAN AT HOME.'** Then **DRIVING ADVICE, no heights, no machinery, no swimming alone, no ladders.**
pefe: **Do now: 12-LEAD ECG — rate, rhythm, PR INTERVAL, DEGREE OF AV BLOCK, ESCAPE RHYTHM, QTc, ischaemic changes · CONTINUOUS CARDIAC MONITORING FROM THE MOMENT HE ARRIVES · IV access · bedside glucose · ASSESS PERFUSION — IS HE COMPROMISED AT 42, OR TOLERATING IT?**

**Bloods: EUC INCLUDING POTASSIUM, CALCIUM AND MAGNESIUM · TSH · FBC · TROPONIN · LFT. Plus ECHOCARDIOGRAM for structural disease and ventricular function, and a FULL MEDICATION REVIEW INCLUDING RECENT CESSATIONS.** **If the ECG is non-diagnostic: HOLTER, and an IMPLANTABLE LOOP RECORDER for infrequent events.**

**REVERSIBLE CAUSES TO EXCLUDE. DRUGS: BETA BLOCKERS, VERAPAMIL AND DILTIAZEM, DIGOXIN, AMIODARONE, CLONIDINE, SOME EYE DROPS. METABOLIC: HYPERKALAEMIA, HYPOTHERMIA, HYPOTHYROIDISM — hence the weather-preference question — HYPOXIA. CARDIAC AND NEUROLOGICAL: INFERIOR MI, myocarditis, RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE, obstructive sleep apnoea, infiltrative disease.**
**PHYSIOLOGICAL bradycardia — athletic conditioning and sleep — DOES NOT CAUSE SYNCOPE, so it does not apply here.**

**If HAEMODYNAMICALLY COMPROMISED — hypotensive, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure or reduced consciousness: ATROPINE 600 MICROGRAM IV, REPEATED TO A MAXIMUM OF 3 mg; then TRANSCUTANEOUS PACING or an ISOPRENALINE OR ADRENALINE INFUSION as a bridge to transvenous pacing, with urgent cardiology.** VERIFY.
**PERMANENT PACING IS THE DEFINITIVE TREATMENT for symptomatic bradycardia from sinus node disease or high-grade AV block.**

**Avoid: reassuring and discharging because the examination is otherwise normal · ATTRIBUTING EPISODE 1 TO A POSTURAL DROP AND STOPPING THERE — EPISODE 2 HAPPENED SITTING DOWN · treating physiological bradycardia in a well person, BUT HE IS NOT WELL, HE IS SYNCOPAL.** **ADMIT TO A MONITORED BED. In MM5, telemetry, echo and pacing require transfer — PATS for stable transfers, MedSTAR if unstable.**

stem: Lily, 15, brought in by ambulance after fainting at school. Her mother is on the way. She has had two previous similar episodes, and an ECG has already been done.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Interpret the ECG to your examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differentials
findings: READ THE STEM LIKE A CLUE SHEET

'AN ECG HAS ALREADY BEEN DONE' — STEMS DO NOT MENTION INVESTIGATIONS FOR DECORATION. If the AMC tells you an ECG exists AND ASKS YOU TO INTERPRET IT, THE ABNORMALITY IS ON THAT ECG AND THE HISTORY WILL NOT GIVE YOU THE DIAGNOSIS. Only FIVE minutes of history for a case with almost no positives — BECAUSE THE MARKS ARE DOWNSTREAM
Vitals on request
BP NORMAL · PULSE 50 · RESPIRATORY RATE AND TEMPERATURE NORMAL. NOTE THE BRADYCARDIA
THE ONLY TWO POSITIVES IN THE WHOLE HISTORY

1 NO WARNING SYMPTOMS BEFORE ANY OF THE THREE EPISODES — and one occurred WHILE SHE WAS SITTING QUIETLY IN CLASS. 2 FAMILY HISTORY: 'MY MUM USED TO FAINT WHEN SHE WAS YOUNGER.' EVERYTHING ELSE IS NEGATIVE. THAT IS THE CASE, NOT A FAILURE OF YOUR HISTORY
THE SEVEN-STEP ECG READ

1 RATE — six large squares, about 50, A BRADYCARDIA · 2 RHYTHM regular · 3 P WAVES present and normal before every QRS, SO SINUS BRADYCARDIA · 4 PR INTERVAL normal · 5 QRS normal duration · 6 ST SEGMENTS no elevation or depression · 7 T WAVES AND QT
THE ONE SENTENCE TO LEARN VERBATIM

'EXAMINER, I'D NOW LIKE TO CHECK THE T WAVES AND CALCULATE THE CORRECTED QT INTERVAL. COULD YOU TELL ME WHAT THE QTc IS?' → 'THE CORRECTED QT IS 0.54.' THE EXAMINER IS HOLDING THE NUMBER AND WILL HAND IT TO YOU. THAT IS THE ENTIRE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN PASSING AND FAILING
THE EYEBALL CHECK — and why you still ask

At normal rates THE QT SHOULD BE LESS THAN HALF THE RR INTERVAL. The classic bedside trick is TO FOLD THE TRACING IN HALF — BUT EXAM ECGs ARE LAMINATED AND YOU CANNOT FOLD THEM, and AT A RATE OF 50 THE HALFWAY RULE IS UNRELIABLE ANYWAY. USE THE EYEBALL CHECK TO RAISE SUSPICION; ASK THE EXAMINER FOR THE NUMBER
FIVE EXTRA QUESTIONS, HIGHLY SPECIFIC HERE

HAS IT EVER HAPPENED WHILE EXERCISING, OR SWIMMING? · HAS IT EVER BEEN SET OFF BY A SUDDEN LOUD NOISE — AN ALARM CLOCK, THE PHONE? · ANY MEDICATIONS AT ALL, INCLUDING FOR ACNE, ALLERGIES, NAUSEA OR MOOD? · HAS ANYONE DIED SUDDENLY, DROWNED, OR HAD AN UNEXPLAINED CAR ACCIDENT, ANY COT DEATHS? · IS ANYONE IN YOUR FAMILY DEAF FROM BIRTH?
The rest of the history

COMPLETE LOC · NO jerky movements, tongue bite or incontinence · THIRD EPISODE — first in class, second at home, third today in class · JUST SITTING, LISTENING TO THE TEACHER · not hot, not stressed, no prolonged standing, no change of position · NO warning · no missed meals, head injury, fever or rash · NOT confused or tired after, not pale, not injured · neuro, CVS, GI, drugs, psychogenic ALL NEGATIVE
THE MOTHER IS NOT JUST A RELATIVE
She is on her way, SHE USED TO FAINT HERSELF, AND SHE HAS NEVER BEEN INVESTIGATED. She is A COLLATERAL HISTORY AND A SCREENING TARGET. Welcome her, CHECK WITH LILY FIRST, then bring her in
A RARE RECALL, BUT A CHEAP ONE TO PREPARE

A fixture before the 2020 pause, NOTORIOUS FOR FAILING ALMOST EVERYONE WHO SAT IT. The syncope structure is already built and THE ONLY NEW CONTENT IS THE QT INTERVAL AND ONE SENTENCE. THE CASES WITH THE WORST HISTORICAL PASS RATES ARE THE ONES WHERE PREPARATION BUYS THE MOST
findingsLabel: A near-empty history, seven ECG steps, and the one sentence that decides it
must: FAIL — Not asking for the QTc: silent staring, an attempt to fold laminated paper, then a guess.
FAIL — Answering 'sick sinus syndrome' on seeing a bradycardia of 50.
FAIL — Blurting 'this is long QT' with no interpretation. The seven steps are scored.
FAIL — Wrong primary diagnosis with long QT third in the differential list. That does not rescue it.
ASK — Examiner, could you tell me what the corrected QT interval is?
ASK — Has anyone in the family died suddenly, drowned, or had an unexplained accident?

dx: **LONG QT SYNDROME — DELAYED VENTRICULAR REPOLARISATION, seen on the ECG as a prolonged QT interval.** **THE DANGER IS NOT THE LONG QT ITSELF BUT WHAT IT PREDISPOSES TO: TORSADES DE POINTES, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. TORSADES CAUSES SYNCOPE WHEN IT SELF-TERMINATES, AND SUDDEN CARDIAC DEATH WHEN IT DOES NOT.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: THINK OUT LOUD, AND ASK. This station has been failed, repeatedly, BY CANDIDATES WHO KNEW THE ANSWER.** **The QTc CANNOT BE MEASURED BY EYE on a laminated ECG under exam pressure, so the candidate who tries to calculate it privately RUNS DOWN THE CLOCK, PANICS, AND DEFAULTS TO SINUS BRADYCARDIA OR SICK SINUS SYNDROME. BOTH ARE REASONABLE-LOOKING ANSWERS. BOTH ARE WRONG.**

**WHY THINKING OUT LOUD IS A GENERAL RULE, NOT A TRICK: THE EXAMINER CANNOT SEE YOUR REASONING. If you work silently you are scored on your FINAL ANSWER ALONE, and every intermediate step you performed correctly EARNS NOTHING. IN AN OSCE, UNSPOKEN REASONING IS UNSCORED REASONING — and if you need a number you cannot obtain, ASKING FOR IT IS NOT A WEAKNESS. IT IS THE CORRECT CLINICAL BEHAVIOUR, AND IT IS WHAT THE STATION IS TESTING.**

**DIAGNOSIS, THEN THREE REASONS: 'ONE, on your heart tracing a measurement called THE QT INTERVAL IS LONGER THAN IT SHOULD BE. TWO, you told me YOUR MUM USED TO FAINT when she was younger, and there is a version of this that RUNS IN FAMILIES. THREE, YOU FAINT WITHOUT ANY WARNING, AND THAT USUALLY MEANS THE CAUSE IS IN THE HEART.'** **NEVER GIVE A DIAGNOSIS WITHOUT ITS REASONS.**

**A BETTER LAYPERSON EXPLANATION THAN 'YOUR HEART BEATS SLOWER THAN USUAL' — the slow rate is AN ASSOCIATION, NOT THE MECHANISM: 'your heart has an ELECTRICAL SYSTEM that makes it beat. In this condition, after each beat, THE ELECTRICAL SYSTEM TAKES LONGER THAN NORMAL TO RESET. Most of the time that causes no problem — but sometimes it CAN TIP THE HEART INTO A VERY FAST, DISORGANISED RHYTHM, and while that's happening THE HEART CAN'T PUMP PROPERLY, SO YOU BLACK OUT.'**

**WHERE THE QT IS MEASURED: from the START OF THE QRS COMPLEX to the END OF THE T WAVE — the time the ventricles take to depolarise AND THEN FULLY RECOVER. IT VARIES WITH HEART RATE: SLOWER RATES GIVE LONGER QTs. Since long QT syndrome typically comes WITH A BRADYCARDIA, THE RAW QT IS MISLEADING AND MUST BE RATE-CORRECTED.**

**CORRECTION — BAZETT'S FORMULA IS QTc = QT DIVIDED BY THE SQUARE ROOT OF THE RR INTERVAL IN SECONDS, NOT BY RR ITSELF. Dividing by RR alone gives a SUBSTANTIALLY DIFFERENT NUMBER, so if you quote the formula, QUOTE IT CORRECTLY.**

**THRESHOLDS: QTc is generally prolonged ABOVE ABOUT 450 ms IN MEN AND BOYS and 460–470 ms IN WOMEN AND GIRLS; ABOVE 500 ms IS MARKEDLY PROLONGED AND HIGH RISK.** **The source's 'less than 0.40 or 0.44' is A CONSERVATIVE NORMAL RANGE and will not mislead you — AT 0.54 SHE IS UNAMBIGUOUSLY ABNORMAL ON ANY THRESHOLD.**

**CONGENITAL SUBTYPES BEHAVE DIFFERENTLY: one is typically triggered by EXERCISE, ESPECIALLY SWIMMING; another by EMOTION OR SUDDEN LOUD NOISE; a third by REST OR SLEEP, and is THE SUBTYPE MOST ASSOCIATED WITH BRADYCARDIA.** **She fainted three times SITTING QUIETLY with a resting rate of 50 — A REST-TRIGGERED PATTERN.** A rarer inherited form **combines long QT with CONGENITAL DEAFNESS, which is why you ask about hearing.**

**ACQUIRED CAUSES — EXCLUDE IN EVERYONE. ELECTROLYTES: LOW POTASSIUM, LOW MAGNESIUM, LOW CALCIUM, check all three. DRUGS, many of them ordinary prescriptions: ANTIPSYCHOTICS, CITALOPRAM AND TRICYCLICS, ONDANSETRON AND DOMPERIDONE, MACROLIDES, FLUOROQUINOLONES, antifungals, SOTALOL AND AMIODARONE, METHADONE. OTHER: HYPOTHYROIDISM, ANOREXIA NERVOSA, hypothermia, raised intracranial pressure, significant bradycardia or heart block.**
plan: **To the examiner: blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate and temperature.** Then **WIPE, PITCHED FOR A 15-YEAR-OLD: 'I hear you're waiting for your mum — she's on her way. How can I help you today?'**

**Empathy, then permission: 'I'm so sorry you fainted again today — that must have been really frightening, ESPECIALLY IN FRONT OF EVERYONE. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions so we can find the reason for these faints?'**
**Confirm and exclude: did you lose consciousness COMPLETELY, or were you AWARE of your surroundings · any JERKY MOVEMENTS · did you BITE YOUR TONGUE · did you WET OR SOIL YOURSELF?**
**IS THIS THE FIRST TIME · CAN YOU DESCRIBE EACH EPISODE · WHAT WERE YOU DOING?** Then **the environment sweep: hot day · stressed · standing a long time · change of position?**
**BEFORE: DID YOU GET ANY WARNING BEFORE YOU FAINTED · missed meals and fluids · head injury · fever or rash? AFTER: confused or tired · pale · injured?**

**Signpost, then the system buckets, asked once: CNS · CVS · RESPIRATORY · GI · DRUGS AND ALCOHOL · PSYCHOGENIC LAST.** **EXPECT NEGATIVES AND DO NOT LET THEM RATTLE YOU — repeating questions and losing structure means arriving at the ECG FLUSTERED AND SHORT OF TIME.**

**THE FIVE SPECIFIC QUESTIONS: exertional or SWIMMING-triggered episodes · STARTLE triggers, an alarm clock or the phone · ANY MEDICATIONS INCLUDING ACNE, ALLERGY, NAUSEA OR MOOD TREATMENTS · sudden deaths, DROWNINGS, unexplained car accidents, COT DEATHS in the family · ANYONE DEAF FROM BIRTH?**
**THE FAMILY HISTORY QUESTION THAT CLOSES EVERY SYNCOPE HISTORY: 'any family history of similar episodes, or of sudden death?'** Then **FOLLOW IT UP — half the diagnostic evidence is here.**
**Past medical history, then close the history. Five minutes is the allocation and THE MARKS ARE DOWNSTREAM.**
**Take the ECG and DELIVER ALL SEVEN STEPS OUT LOUD, even if you recognise it instantly. THE INTERPRETATION IS SCORED, NOT JUST THE ANSWER.**
**STEP SEVEN — ASK FOR THE QTc, VERBATIM.**
**The impression: 'SINUS BRADYCARDIA AT 50 WITH A MARKEDLY PROLONGED QTc OF 540 MILLISECONDS. My impression is LONG QT SYNDROME.'**
**SPEAK TO LILY, NOT OVER HER. Name the diagnosis and GIVE THE THREE REASONS.** Then **the plain-language mechanism if there is time.**
**The differentials by bucket, WITH THE NEGATIVES VOICED — here the negatives ARE the reasoning, and unvoiced they make the presentation sound thin.**

**The plan: MONITORED BED · potassium, magnesium and calcium corrected and KEPT HIGH-NORMAL · medication review · echocardiogram · URGENT PAEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY for BETA BLOCKADE and genetic assessment.**

**THE FAMILY: 'your mum needs an ECG today too' — first-degree relatives get screened, STARTING WITH THE MOTHER.** Then **a WRITTEN LIST OF QT-PROLONGING DRUGS TO AVOID FOR LIFE, and 000 for any further blackout, chest pain or palpitations.**
pefe: **Do now: 12-LEAD ECG WITH QTc and CONTINUOUS CARDIAC MONITORING FROM ARRIVAL · POTASSIUM, MAGNESIUM AND CALCIUM — correct aggressively and KEEP POTASSIUM IN THE HIGH-NORMAL RANGE · bedside glucose · TSH · FBC · REVIEW EVERY MEDICATION, INCLUDING OVER-THE-COUNTER AND ACNE TREATMENTS.**

**Do next: PAEDIATRIC CARDIOLOGY REFERRAL — in Australia to an INHERITED HEART DISEASE SERVICE · ECHOCARDIOGRAM to exclude structural disease · serial ECGs, Holter or exercise testing as directed · SCREEN FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVES WITH AN ECG, STARTING WITH THE MOTHER · GENETIC TESTING AND COUNSELLING for the family.**
**BETA BLOCKERS ARE FIRST-LINE — PROPRANOLOL OR NADOLOL — and reduce arrhythmic events. SPECIALIST-INITIATED.** **An ICD if she has had A CARDIAC ARREST, or SYNCOPE DESPITE BETA BLOCKADE.** VERIFY.

**IF SHE DETERIORATES INTO TORSADES DE POINTES: PULSELESS → DEFIBRILLATE and follow the arrest algorithm. WITH A PULSE → INTRAVENOUS MAGNESIUM SULFATE IS THE TREATMENT OF CHOICE EVEN WHEN MAGNESIUM IS NORMAL; correct potassium; STOP EVERY QT-PROLONGING DRUG; and INCREASE THE HEART RATE WITH OVERDRIVE PACING OR ISOPRENALINE TO SHORTEN THE QT, since torsades here is PAUSE-DEPENDENT.** **This is why she is on a monitored bed and not in the waiting room.**

**Avoid: PRESCRIBING QT-PROLONGING DRUGS — check before any new medication, INCLUDING ANTIBIOTICS AND ANTIEMETICS · LETTING ELECTROLYTES RUN LOW · DISCHARGING RECURRENT UNHERALDED SYNCOPE IN A TEENAGER · CLEARING HER FOR COMPETITIVE SPORT OR UNSUPERVISED SWIMMING before specialist assessment.**

**If asked how you would measure the QT yourself: 'from the START OF THE QRS to the END OF THE T WAVE, in the lead where the T wave ends most clearly — CONVENTIONALLY LEAD II OR V5 — then rate-corrected using BAZETT'S FORMULA, QT DIVIDED BY THE SQUARE ROOT OF THE RR INTERVAL IN SECONDS.'** **Rate from large squares: 300 DIVIDED BY THE NUMBER OF LARGE SQUARES — six squares equals 50.**

**SA: admit to a MONITORED PAEDIATRIC BED. In MM5, paediatric cardiology means transfer — PATS for stable transfers, MEDSTAR, WHICH INCLUDES A PAEDIATRIC AND NEONATAL RETRIEVAL SERVICE, if unstable.** **Driving: she is 15 and close to a learner's permit. LONG QT IS NOTIFIABLE UNDER AUSTROADS and she will need CARDIOLOGY CLEARANCE — FLAG IT FOR THE FUTURE rather than dwelling on it now.**

**Recurrent syncope AT REST, NO PRODROME, FAMILY HISTORY, bradycardia, QTc 540 ms**
**Exertional or swimming triggers, STARTLE triggers, family deafness, sudden deaths and drownings**
**ECG WITH QTc; electrolytes; cardiology and GENETIC assessment** — ADMIT
**Sick sinus syndrome or heart block — THE CLASSIC WRONG ANSWER HERE**
**A bradycardia of 50 tempts you to stop reading**
**RHYTHM IS REGULAR SINUS WITH NORMAL P WAVES, PR AND QRS — you have not finished reading the ECG**

stem: Gary, 40, brought in by his tennis partners after he collapsed on court this morning. BP 110/70, PR 84 regular, RR 12, T 36.5, SpO2 98% RA, GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you want — given only if requested specifically
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: FINDINGS ARE GIVEN ONLY IF YOU ASK FOR THEM SPECIFICALLY
BP 110/70 · PR 84 REGULAR · RR 12 · T 36.5 · SpO2 98% RA · GCS 15, alert and orientated. Ask for vitals AND 'IS HE HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE?' before you sit down
THE TRAP THAT HAS FAILED REAL CANDIDATES

A candidate asked 'ARE S1 AND S2 NORMAL?' — 'yes' — and 'ARE THERE ANY ADDED SOUNDS?' — 'no' — AND WAS NEVER TOLD ABOUT THE MURMUR, because THE EXAMINER IS INSTRUCTED TO ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. ASK FOR 'MURMURS' BY NAME, then SITE, TIMING, RADIATION
THE PUBLISHED CRITICAL ERROR
FAILING TO REQUEST EXAMINATION FOR BOTH CAROTID AND CARDIAC BRUITS
The murmur, once you ask properly

EJECTION SYSTOLIC MURMUR, LOUDEST AT THE RIGHT SECOND INTERCOSTAL SPACE, RADIATING TO THE CAROTIDS. Severity signs to ask for: LATE PEAK · SOFT OR ABSENT A2 · SLOW-RISING LOW-VOLUME PULSE · NARROW PULSE PRESSURE · A THRILL
The rest of the examination

Alert, NO pallor, NO dehydration, NO rash, NO injury · NO POSTURAL DROP · pulse 84 regular · neurological examination NORMAL · JVP not raised · PROMINENT BUT UNDISPLACED APEX BEAT, forceful — CONCENTRIC HYPERTROPHY, NOT DILATATION · chest clear · abdomen and limbs normal · ECG NORMAL · BSL NORMAL
A NORMAL ECG DOES NOT EXCLUDE SEVERE AORTIC STENOSIS
THE ECHOCARDIOGRAM DOES THE WORK
WHAT HE WILL NOT VOLUNTEER

THE ROLE-PLAYER IS BRIEFED NOT TO VOLUNTEER THE CHEST TIGHTNESS OR THE BREATHLESSNESS. IF YOU DO NOT ASK, IT DOES NOT EXIST. On asking: HEAVY CENTRAL CHEST PAIN RADIATING TO THE LEFT ARM AND NECK DURING PLAY, plus EXERTIONAL BREATHLESSNESS
What he does say

'I BLACKED OUT — I GOT NO WARNING AT ALL' · it happened WHILE PLAYING TENNIS · OUT FOR A FEW MINUTES · FIRST EPISODE · 'MY MATES WERE RIGHT THERE' — use them: jerking, duration, pallor · cholesterol 'HIGH-NORMAL' 3–4 years ago, A RISK FACTOR NOT A DIAGNOSIS
VERSION B — the hypertensive variant

IDENTICAL STEM, but BP 158/94 and SIX MONTHS OF BREATHLESSNESS CLIMBING STAIRS. SAME MURMUR. STILL AORTIC STENOSIS — add BP control and cardiovascular risk to the plan, but DO NOT LET THE RAISED BP DRAG YOU INTO A HYPERTENSION STATION
VERSION C — the family history twist

dx: **SEVERE SYMPTOMATIC AORTIC STENOSIS — obstruction to LEFT VENTRICULAR OUTFLOW at the aortic valve. IN A 40-YEAR-OLD THE USUAL CAUSE IS A BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE; calcific degenerative disease dominates OVER 65; RHEUMATIC DISEASE IS A THIRD CAUSE AND MATTERS IN ABORIGINAL AND TORRES STRAIT ISLANDER PATIENTS.**
**WHY IT FAINTS: FIXED OUTFLOW OBSTRUCTION PLUS EXERCISE-INDUCED PERIPHERAL VASODILATATION → CARDIAC OUTPUT CANNOT RISE → CEREBRAL HYPOPERFUSION. Sudden, no prodrome, rapid full recovery.**

**THE TRIAD: EXERTIONAL ANGINA · EXERTIONAL DYSPNOEA · EXERTIONAL SYNCOPE. He has ALL THREE.** **SYMPTOM ONSET IS THE INFLECTION POINT: untreated, mean survival is roughly 5 YEARS WITH ANGINA, 3 YEARS WITH SYNCOPE, 2 YEARS WITH HEART FAILURE.** **SEVERE = valve area BELOW 1.0 cm², mean gradient 40 mmHg OR MORE, peak jet velocity 4.0 m/s OR MORE.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS NOT NAMING AORTIC STENOSIS. IT IS TIME DISCIPLINE IN THE LAST TWO MINUTES: candidates who diagnose correctly THEN SPEND 90 SECONDS TEACHING CARDIAC ANATOMY RUN OUT OF TIME AND NEVER DELIVER THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST — WHICH IS AN EXPLICITLY MARKED TASK.**

**THE STATION GIVES YOU THREE CHANCES TO LOSE IT: 1 ACCEPTING 'CHEST PAIN' WITHOUT EXPLORING IT · 2 ASKING FOR 'ADDED SOUNDS' INSTEAD OF NAMING MURMURS, AND FAILING TO ASK SITE, TIMING, RADIATION AND BOTH CAROTID AND CARDIAC BRUITS · 3 OVER-EXPLAINING THE VALVE.**

**THE 15-SECOND EXPLANATION, VERBATIM: 'most likely you have a condition called AORTIC STENOSIS. The aortic valve is THE GATEWAY BETWEEN YOUR HEART AND THE MAIN BLOOD TUBE that carries blood and oxygen out to your organs — and in your case THAT GATEWAY HAS BECOME NARROWED.'**

**THEN JUSTIFY IT IN 15 SECONDS — NEVER ASSERT WITHOUT REASONS: 'FIRST, you have THE WELL-KNOWN TRIO OF SYMPTOMS that goes with it — CHEST PAIN, SHORTNESS OF BREATH, AND BLACKING OUT WITH EXERCISE. SECOND, when I listened to your heart I HEARD AN ABNORMAL SOUND THAT FITS WITH THAT NARROWING.'**

**MARKS ARE SPREAD THIN ACROSS SIX ASSESSED THINGS — DEPTH IN ONE AREA CANNOT RESCUE AN UNTOUCHED AREA. BETTER TO TOUCH EVERY SYSTEM BRIEFLY THAN TO COMPLETE ONE SYSTEM PERFECTLY. BREADTH SCORES HERE.** Questions you may drop if the clock beats you: **weather preference, long-haul travel, jaundice, detailed occupational history.**

**ENDOCARDITIS PROPHYLAXIS — an examiner probe. Under current Australian Therapeutic Guidelines, ISOLATED AORTIC STENOSIS ALONE IS NOT AN INDICATION FOR ROUTINE ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS before dental procedures. Prophylaxis is reserved for DEFINED HIGH-RISK CONDITIONS — a PROSTHETIC VALVE, PREVIOUS ENDOCARDITIS, specified congenital lesions, and RHEUMATIC HEART DISEASE IN ABORIGINAL AND TORRES STRAIT ISLANDER PATIENTS.** Say: **'I'd check current Therapeutic Guidelines for this patient's specific risk category.'**

**SA DRIVING: cardiac syncope AND symptomatic severe aortic stenosis make a person NOT FIT TO HOLD AN UNCONDITIONAL LICENCE until the cause is treated and A SPECIALIST CLEARS THEM; commercial standards stricter again. IN SA AND THE NT THE DRIVER MUST NOTIFY AND THE DOCTOR HAS A STATUTORY DUTY TO REPORT to the Registrar of Motor Vehicles — unlike most other states, where reporting is DISCRETIONARY.** VERIFY.
plan: **To the examiner before you sit: blood pressure, pulse rate, respiratory rate, saturation, temperature — AND IS HE HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE?**

**WIPE and acknowledge: 'I know how stressful and concerning this must be. Let's go through a few things together — I'll ask you some questions, then I'll examine you, and WE'LL TRY TO FIND THE CAUSE TOGETHER.'**
**CONFIRM IT REALLY IS SYNCOPE: did you lose consciousness COMPLETELY, or were you AWARE of what was going on · HOW LONG were you unconscious · HAS THIS EVER HAPPENED BEFORE?**

**EXCLUDE SEIZURE — three questions, all must be asked: did your friends say you had any JERKY MOVEMENTS · did you BITE YOUR TONGUE · did you WET OR SOIL YOURSELF?** **The fourth pillar, POST-EVENT CONFUSION, comes in the after block.**

**THE MONEY QUESTION: 'DID YOU GET ANY WARNING SIGNS AT ALL BEFORE YOU FELL — DIZZINESS, LIGHT-HEADEDNESS, SWEATING, NAUSEA, RINGING IN YOUR EARS, OR YOUR VISION GOING DARK?'** Then **SAY THE DEDUCTION OUT LOUD: 'no warning signs — that makes me think about a cardiac cause.'**

**'WHAT EXACTLY WERE YOU DOING AT THE MOMENT IT HAPPENED — WERE YOU MID-PLAY, OR HAD YOU JUST STOPPED?'** **DURING exertion means obstruction or arrhythmia; AFTER STOPPING is more often reflex.** Then **hot or humid day · standing a long time · missed meals and fluids · anything frightening or emotional · head injury before · fever or rash.**

**DURING AND AFTER: when you came round, were you CONFUSED OR DROWSY, or back to normal straight away · did anyone say you LOOKED PALE OR YOUR LIPS WENT BLUE · DID YOU INJURE YOURSELF — head, face, shoulder, wrist?**
**Signpost the review: 'for each one, tell me if you had it BEFORE OR AFTER the collapse.' CNS: headache · blurred or double vision · slurred speech · weakness or numbness anywhere?**

**CVS — AND EXPLORE THE CHEST PAIN, DO NOT ACCEPT IT: 'ANY CHEST PAIN?' → 'WHERE EXACTLY? DOES IT TRAVEL ANYWHERE? WHAT DOES IT FEEL LIKE?' Then SHORTNESS OF BREATH · RACING OR POUNDING OF THE HEART · ANKLE SWELLING · BREATHLESSNESS LYING FLAT OR WAKING YOU AT NIGHT.**

**RESPIRATORY: cough · haemoptysis · pain worse on breathing in · CALF PAIN OR SWELLING · RECENT LONG FLIGHTS, SURGERY OR IMMOBILITY. GI: nausea or vomiting · tummy pain · BLACK OR BLOODY MOTIONS. ENDOCRINE: ever been told you have diabetes?**
**PSYCH, briefly: breathing very fast before · tingling in hands or around the mouth · anything stressful going on?**

**SADMA AND HISTORY, WITH TWO COMBINED QUESTIONS THAT SAVE THIRTY SECONDS: smoking, alcohol per week, recreational drugs · regular medications AND ANYTHING STARTED OR STOPPED RECENTLY, allergies · 'HAVE YOU EVER BEEN TOLD YOU HAVE HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE, HIGH BLOOD SUGAR, OR HIGH FATS IN YOUR BLOOD?' · 'HAVE YOU EVER BEEN TOLD YOU HAVE A HEART MURMUR, OR HAD RHEUMATIC FEVER AS A CHILD?'**
**FAMILY: any heart attacks or strokes · HAS ANYONE DIED SUDDENLY AT A YOUNG AGE, or had episodes like this?** **Sudden cardiac death under 50 raises HOCM, LONG QT, BRUGADA, ARVC.**

**EXAMINATION REQUESTS, NAMED: general appearance · POSTURAL DROP · PULSE CHARACTER, IS IT SLOW-RISING, IS THE PULSE PRESSURE NARROW · neurological · JVP, APEX BEAT DISPLACED OR HEAVING, THRILL IN THE AORTIC AREA, PARASTERNAL HEAVE.**
**THEN THE MURMUR, BY NAME, WITH THE THREE FOLLOW-UPS — AND BOTH CAROTID AND CARDIAC BRUITS.** Then **respiratory, abdomen, limbs, and the OFFICE TESTS: ECG, blood sugar, urine dipstick.**
**THE 15-SECOND EXPLANATION, THEN THE TWO REASONS. THEN STOP — DO NOT TEACH ANATOMY.**

**SPRAY THE DIFFERENTIALS ACROSS SYSTEMS: HOCM, arrhythmia, ACS, pulmonary embolism, aortic dissection, seizure, intracranial pathology, hypoglycaemia, vasovagal and heat, drugs.** Then **SAFETY-NET: STOP TENNIS AND HEAVY EXERTION · NO DRIVING · TRY NOT TO BE ALONE · come straight back for another blackout, chest pain, breathlessness at rest or a racing heart.**
pefe: **Do now: ABC and CONTINUOUS CARDIAC MONITORING · IV access · 12-LEAD ECG looking for LVH WITH STRAIN, LBBB, conduction block, prolonged QT, ischaemic change · BEDSIDE GLUCOSE · SERIAL TROPONIN with repeat ECG to exclude ACS · FBE, UEC WITH CALCIUM AND MAGNESIUM, CRP · ERECT AND SUPINE BP · ASSESS FOR INJURIES SUSTAINED IN THE FALL.**

**Do next: TRANSTHORACIC ECHOCARDIOGRAM — THE SPECIFIC TEST AND THE ONE THAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS: valve area, mean gradient, peak velocity, LVH and ejection fraction, BICUSPID MORPHOLOGY, aortic root · chest X-ray · HOLTER OR INPATIENT TELEMETRY if ECG and echo are unrevealing · CORONARY ANGIOGRAPHY BEFORE VALVE SURGERY · CTPA only if PE is genuinely suspected · brain imaging ONLY for head injury or focal neurology.**
**AVOID A SHOTGUN PANEL. The published marking notes treat AN UNDIFFERENTIATED BATTERY OF TESTS AS EVIDENCE THAT THE CANDIDATE DOES NOT UNDERSTAND THE CONDITION. Name specific tests and say why.**

**DO NOT PERFORM AN EXERCISE STRESS TEST — CONTRAINDICATED in symptomatic severe aortic stenosis.** **BE VERY CAUTIOUS WITH GTN, OTHER NITRATES AND VASODILATORS — A PRELOAD-DEPENDENT, FIXED-OUTPUT VENTRICLE CAN DROP ITS BLOOD PRESSURE PRECIPITOUSLY. Avoid aggressive diuresis.**

**Definitive management: ADMIT for monitoring and EXPEDITED ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY. URGENT CARDIOLOGY — SYMPTOMATIC SEVERE AORTIC STENOSIS IS A CLASS I INDICATION FOR AORTIC VALVE REPLACEMENT. SURGICAL REPLACEMENT IS STANDARD FOR A FIT 40-YEAR-OLD — MECHANICAL VALVE MEANS LIFELONG WARFARIN with an INR target set by valve type and position; BIOPROSTHETIC MEANS LATER RE-OPERATION. TAVI IS RESERVED FOR OLDER OR HIGHER-RISK PATIENTS.** VERIFY.

**Do not miss: ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME · VENTRICULAR ARRHYTHMIA OR COMPLETE HEART BLOCK · PULMONARY EMBOLISM · AORTIC DISSECTION · HYPOGLYCAEMIA · INTRACRANIAL HAEMORRHAGE · INJURY FROM THE FALL, including HEAD, CERVICAL SPINE AND WRIST.**

**Avoid: DISCHARGING BEFORE THE ECHOCARDIOGRAM · premature closure on ACS, because EXERTIONAL SYNCOPE PLUS A MURMUR REFRAMES THE CASE — KEEP BOTH · anchoring on the recall, since SEVERAL RECALLS SHARE THIS STEM AND DIVERGE ON THE FINDINGS · FALSE REASSURANCE. Say instead: 'IT'S SERIOUS BUT VERY TREATABLE, AND WE CAN FIX IT.'** **Advise against competitive and strenuous exertion, INCLUDING TENNIS, until the valve has been assessed.**

findings: THE HISTORY IS BAIT AND THE EXAMINER BUILT IT DELIBERATELY

INSULIN · SKIPPED BREAKFAST, 'JUST AN APPLE' · HOURS OF WALKING. EVERYTHING IN THE FIRST FIVE MINUTES POINTS TO A HYPO. THE PASS IS RESERVED FOR THE CANDIDATE WHO READS THE ECG AS THOUGH THE HISTORY HAD NEVER HAPPENED
ASK FOR A CAPILLARY GLUCOSE ANYWAY

The stem says vitals are stable, so you need not open with haemodynamic stability. But say once: 'COULD I PLEASE HAVE A BEDSIDE BLOOD GLUCOSE WHILE WE TALK?' VERSION B — the 2019 recall, the one that is out now

ST ELEVATION IN II, III AND aVF WITH RECIPROCAL ST DEPRESSION IN aVL → ACUTE INFERIOR STEMI. Candidates fail because THEY HAVE ALREADY DECIDED IT IS A HYPO, GLANCE AT THE ECG, AND MISS AN EVOLVING STEMI IN FRONT OF THEM

The history, IDENTICAL IN BOTH VERSIONS

PRESYNCOPE LASTING A FEW SECONDS, NO LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS · FIRST EPISODE · took her usual insulin, NO DOSE CHANGE, no new medicines · NO WARNING SIGNS BEFORE THE EPISODE · no jerking, no incontinence, no post-event confusion, no injury · NO CHEST PAIN, no breathlessness, no palpitations, no ankle swelling
'NO CHEST PAIN. NONE AT ALL.'

IN DIABETES, PAINLESS ISCHAEMIA IS COMMON. ABSENCE OF CHEST PAIN DOES NOT REMOVE ACS — SAY THIS TO THE EXAMINER. Roughly A QUARTER TO A THIRD OF INFARCTS ARE CLINICALLY UNRECOGNISED at the time. 'NO CHEST PAIN' LOWERS THE PROBABILITY; IT NEVER REMOVES IT
'I had no warning at all'
FLAG IT INTERNALLY: ABSENT PRODROME ARGUES AGAINST VASOVAGAL AND RAISES CARDIAC CAUSES. ASK FOR THE ECG WITH REAL INTENT
'WE WALKED FOR HOURS TODAY' — two readings at once
UNACCUSTOMED EXERTION RAISES HYPOGLYCAEMIA RISK AND IS AN ISCHAEMIC TRIGGER. MENTION BOTH

dx: **ACUTE INFERIOR ST-ELEVATION MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION PRESENTING AS PRESYNCOPE WITHOUT CHEST PAIN — a 'SILENT' MI. DIABETES CAUSES BOTH THE ACCELERATED CORONARY DISEASE AND THE LOSS OF THE WARNING PAIN.**

**PRESYNCOPE IS THE PRODROME OF SYNCOPE WITHOUT ACTUAL LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS. ITS CAUSES, ITS RISK AND ITS ASSESSMENT ARE THE SAME AS FOR SYNCOPE — IT IS NOT A BENIGN VERSION.** **'I was about to faint but I didn't' DOES NOT SEND YOU DOWN A FALLS PATHWAY.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: YOU MUST LET THE ECG OVERRULE YOUR HISTORY.** The pass goes to the candidate who **READS THE ECG SYSTEMATICALLY, NAMES AN INFERIOR STEMI WITH ITS RECIPROCAL CHANGE, EXPLAINS WHY THERE IS NO CHEST PAIN, AND THEN ACTS — ASPIRIN, AMBULANCE, NO PARTY.**
**THE MOMENT YOU SAY STEMI, THE NEXT SENTENCE IS ASPIRIN AND 000.** Naming the infarct correctly and then **continuing to counsel is a fail in its own right.**

**THE TWO-PART EXPLANATION: 'DIABETES, OVER TIME, DAMAGES THE SMALL BLOOD VESSELS THAT SUPPLY THE HEART. When one suddenly blocks, part of the heart muscle stops getting blood — that's a heart attack. Now you'll ask why you have NO CHEST PAIN, and that's the second part: DIABETES ALSO DAMAGES THE NERVES, INCLUDING THE NERVES THAT CARRY PAIN FROM THE HEART. So instead of pain, the only thing you felt was BEING UNWELL AND ABOUT TO FALL.'**

**SAY EXPLICITLY THAT BOTH CAN BE TRUE: 'a low blood sugar is very possible given you'd skipped breakfast and walked for hours — AND THAT MAY STILL BE PART OF IT. The tracing is what moves the heart attack to the top of that list.'** **Dropping hypoglycaemia entirely once you see ST elevation is a fail.**

**THE ECG DRILL, SAID IN THIS ORDER EVERY TIME: rate · rhythm and P waves · PR INTERVAL, AND IMPORTANTLY WHETHER THERE IS HEART BLOCK · QRS width · axis · ST SEGMENTS · T waves · Q waves.** Then: **'I would also look for ST DEPRESSION IN V1–V3 that might indicate POSTERIOR EXTENSION, and I would immediately do RIGHT-SIDED LEADS, PARTICULARLY V4R, to look for RIGHT VENTRICULAR INVOLVEMENT.'**

**TERRITORIES: INFERIOR II, III, aVF with reciprocal change in I and aVL — RIGHT CORONARY IN ABOUT 80%, circumflex in the rest, and WATCH FOR BRADYCARDIA, AV BLOCK, RV INFARCT AND HYPOTENSION. RIGHT VENTRICULAR — V4R, PROXIMAL RCA, PRELOAD-DEPENDENT SO NITRATES CAN CAUSE PROFOUND HYPOTENSION. POSTERIOR — V7–V9, with TALL R AND ST DEPRESSION IN V1–V3, EASILY MISSED BECAUSE IT LOOKS LIKE ANTERIOR ISCHAEMIA.**

**STEMI VOLTAGE CRITERIA: new ST elevation at the J point in TWO CONTIGUOUS LEADS — 1 mm OR MORE in all leads other than V2–V3; in V2–V3, 2.5 mm in men UNDER 40, 2 mm in men 40 AND OVER, and 1.5 mm in women.** **RECIPROCAL DEPRESSION STRONGLY SUPPORTS TRUE INFARCTION rather than pericarditis or early repolarisation.** VERIFY.

**WHY YOU ASK CARDIAC RISK FACTORS: because EVERY LOSS-OF-CONSCIOUSNESS HISTORY INCLUDES A CARDIOVASCULAR SCREEN, NOT BECAUSE YOU KNOW HOW THE RECALL ENDS. IF YOU ONLY START ASKING ABOUT SMOKING, CHOLESTEROL AND FAMILY HISTORY AFTER THE ECG APPEARS, THE EXAMINER CAN SEE YOU WERE RECITING AN ANSWER.**
plan: **WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, check comfort, and SIGNPOST THE WHOLE STATION: 'I'd like to ask about what happened this morning, look at your heart tracing, and then we'll work out the cause together.'**
**Acknowledge: 'thank you for coming in to get checked — YOUR FRIENDS GAVE YOU VERY GOOD ADVICE.'** Then **ASK FOR THE BEDSIDE GLUCOSE.**

**BLOCK 1, THE EPISODE: did you lose consciousness COMPLETELY, or were you AWARE of your surroundings · any JERKING of the arms or legs, ANY TWITCHING ON ONE SIDE · did you WET OR SOIL YOURSELF · HOW LONG did it last · IS THIS THE FIRST TIME?** **FOCAL SEIZURES CAN OCCUR WITH PRESERVED AWARENESS, so the seizure screen is still worth ten seconds.**

**BLOCK 2, CONTEXT AND BEFORE: what were you doing just before · was it HOT, had you been STANDING a long time, did it come on when you CHANGED POSITION · any stressful news · DID YOU GET ANY WARNING — light-headed, sweaty, SHAKY, HUNGRY, palpitations, vision greying, ringing in the ears · HAVE YOU MISSED ANY MEALS TODAY, were you drinking enough · any knock to the head · any fever or rash?**
**BLOCK 3, AFTER: were you CONFUSED OR DROWSY, how long before you felt normal · did you INJURE yourself · did anyone say you looked PALE, GREY OR SWEATY?**

**BLOCK 4, THE DIABETES BLOCK: when were you diagnosed · ARE YOU TAKING YOUR INSULIN EXACTLY AS PRESCRIBED, AND DID YOU TAKE IT TODAY · HAS THE DOSE BEEN CHANGED RECENTLY, BY YOU OR YOUR DOCTOR · ANY NEW MEDICINES, OVER-THE-COUNTER PRODUCTS, SUPPLEMENTS OR HERBAL REMEDIES?**

**Then: TALK ME THROUGH WHAT YOU EAT IN A DAY — DO YOU TAKE YOUR MID-MORNING AND MID-AFTERNOON SNACKS · do you test your sugars at home, what are they usually running · DO YOU GET WARNING SYMPTOMS WHEN YOU GO LOW · do you see your GP regularly and have your HbA1c done?**

**COMPLICATIONS — not box-ticking: any NUMBNESS, TINGLING OR BURNING IN YOUR FEET, any ULCERS · any CHANGE OR BLURRING OF VISION, when was your last eye check · any kidney problems on your blood tests · DO YOU GET DIZZY ON STANDING, FEEL FULL VERY QUICKLY AFTER MEALS, OR HAVE BLADDER TROUBLE?**

**Established microvascular disease tells you TWO THINGS AT ONCE: AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHY CAN CAUSE ORTHOSTATIC PRESYNCOPE AND CAN ABOLISH THE PAIN OF MYOCARDIAL ISCHAEMIA. A patient with retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy IS EXACTLY THE PATIENT WHO HAS A PAINLESS INFARCT — SAY THIS WHEN YOU PRESENT.**

**BLOCK 5, SYSTEM SCREEN, QUICK AND COMPLETE. CNS: headache, weakness, numbness, slurred speech, double vision, unsteadiness. CVS: ANY CHEST PAIN, TIGHTNESS OR HEAVINESS — EVEN A LITTLE · breathlessness on exertion or lying flat · RACING OR THUMPING of the heart · ankle swelling.**

**GI: nausea, vomiting, tummy pain, diarrhoea, BLACK OR BLOODY STOOLS. SADMA: smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs, other medications, allergies. PSYCHOGENIC: breathing very fast, stress or panic episodes. EXERTION: MORE PHYSICAL ACTIVITY THAN USUAL TODAY?**

**RISK AND BACKGROUND, IN THEIR PROPER PLACE: blood pressure, cholesterol, weight · ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH HEART DISEASE OR A HEART ATTACK AT A YOUNG AGE?** Then **IMPACT: do you drive · who is at home with you?**
**THE ECG DRILL, OUT LOUD, IN FIXED ORDER — AS IF THE HISTORY HAD NEVER HAPPENED.**

**WARNING SHOT, THEN PLAIN WORDS: 'I need to tell you something important, and I want you to hear the whole of it. YOUR HEART TRACING SHOWS THAT YOU ARE HAVING A HEART ATTACK RIGHT NOW.'** Then **THE TWO-PART DIABETES EXPLANATION.**

**WHAT HAPPENS NOW: 'I give you an aspirin to chew, WE CALL AN AMBULANCE, and you go straight to hospital where they can OPEN THAT BLOCKED VESSEL — THE SOONER THAT HAPPENS, THE MORE HEART MUSCLE WE SAVE.'** Then **'tonight's party isn't possible, AND YOU MUST NOT DRIVE. IS THERE SOMEONE I CAN CALL FOR YOU?'**

**THE DIFFERENTIAL SHE MUST STILL HEAR, briefly: a low blood sugar WHICH MAY STILL BE PART OF IT · a high sugar or diabetic emergency · an abnormal rhythm or valve problem · a clot on the lung · a stroke or mini-stroke · a seizure · a salt disturbance · dehydration · anaemia or bleeding · medications or alcohol.**
pefe: **Do now: BEDSIDE GLUCOSE · 12-LEAD ECG WITHIN 10 MINUTES OF PRESENTATION, repeated if it evolves · ASPIRIN 300 mg CHEWED unless true allergy · CALL 000 FOR AN AMBULANCE TO A PCI-CAPABLE CENTRE — do not let her drive or take a taxi · IV access, CONTINUOUS MONITORING, DEFIBRILLATOR TO HAND · OXYGEN ONLY IF SpO2 BELOW 93% · repeat blood pressure AND DO V4R.**

**Do next: NOTIFY THE RECEIVING TEAM DIRECTLY AND TRANSMIT THE ECG · antiplatelet loading — TICAGRELOR 180 mg or CLOPIDOGREL 300–600 mg — and anticoagulation as directed by the receiving centre · troponin, FBE, UEC, CMP, lipids, HbA1c, coagulation, BUT NEVER DELAY REPERFUSION FOR A TROPONIN · analgesia if she has pain — GTN 300–600 microg SL, morphine 2.5–5 mg IV titrated · contact her family.** VERIFY.

**REPERFUSION NUMBERS: PRIMARY PCI PREFERRED, target FIRST MEDICAL CONTACT TO DEVICE 90 MINUTES OR LESS, up to 120 minutes if transfer is required. If that cannot be met, FIBRINOLYSIS WITHIN 30 MINUTES of first medical contact, then TRANSFER FOR ANGIOGRAPHY AT 3–24 HOURS, or immediately if reperfusion fails. findings: THE STATION IS A DESIGNED TRAP

THE HISTORY IS DELIBERATELY CLEAN OF RESPIRATORY SYMPTOMS. THE EXAMINER IS MARKING WHETHER YOU NAME PULMONARY EMBOLISM AND CTPA ANYWAY. A TOTAL KNEE REPLACEMENT WAS CHOSEN OVER, SAY, A HERNIA REPAIR PRECISELY BECAUSE THAT PATIENT CANNOT WALK

'THEY GAVE ME A NEEDLE IN THE TUMMY EACH NIGHT'

dx: **PULMONARY EMBOLISM CAUSING SYNCOPE, PROVOKED BY POST-OPERATIVE IMMOBILITY after total knee replacement.** **SYNCOPE OCCURS IN ROUGHLY ONE IN SEVEN PE PRESENTATIONS AND SIGNALS A LARGER, MORE CENTRAL CLOT WITH RIGHT-VENTRICULAR STRAIN — A SYNCOPAL PE IS A SICKER PE, NOT A MILDER ONE.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: NAMING PULMONARY EMBOLISM FIRST AND CTPA EXPLICITLY, WHEN EVERY SYMPTOM YOU ASKED ABOUT WAS NEGATIVE.** **THE NEGATIVE RESPIRATORY REVIEW IS THE TRAP, NOT THE ANSWER.** **Candidates have failed WITH A FLAWLESS STRUCTURE because PE was absent from their differential list and CTPA was absent from their investigations.** **'There was no cough and no shortness of breath' IS NOT ACCEPTED AS A DEFENCE.**

**THE SENTENCE TO REHEARSE: 'EVEN WITH A NORMAL RESPIRATORY HISTORY, THE CONTEXT OF MAJOR JOINT SURGERY AND IMMOBILITY MAKES PULMONARY EMBOLISM MY LEADING CONCERN, SO I WOULD PROCEED TO CT PULMONARY ANGIOGRAPHY.'**

**VERSION A SCRIPT: 'everything you've told me is reassuring, and that is GENUINELY GOOD NEWS. But I have to be guided by YOUR SITUATION AS WELL AS YOUR SYMPTOMS. You had major knee surgery yesterday and have barely been able to move since — THAT IS ONE OF THE STRONGEST RISK FACTORS THERE IS FOR A BLOOD CLOT, and a clot in the lung CAN CAUSE EXACTLY THIS KIND OF BLACKOUT WITH NO WARNING AT ALL. So even though your breathing is fine, I AM NOT WILLING TO LEAVE THAT POSSIBILITY UNTESTED.'**

**VERSION B SCRIPT, WHICH VALIDATES WITHOUT CONCEDING: 'what you describe — straining, feeling hot and light-headed — DOES SOUND LIKE A SIMPLE FAINT, AND THAT MAY WELL BE EXACTLY WHAT IT WAS. I still want to be careful, because after this operation A CLOT IN THE LUNG CAN LOOK IDENTICAL, and it is THE ONE CAUSE I CANNOT AFFORD TO BE WRONG ABOUT. So I'll TREAT THE SIMPLE FAINT AS LIKELY AND RULE OUT THE DANGEROUS ONE AT THE SAME TIME.'**
**SAY IT IN PLAIN WORDS: 'A CLOT IN THE BLOOD TUBES OF YOUR LUNGS' — not 'thromboembolic occlusion of the pulmonary vasculature'.**

**D-DIMER HAS NO ROLE HERE, AND SAYING SO CONVERTS A WEAK ANSWER INTO A STRONG ONE. IT IS RAISED IN ESSENTIALLY EVERY PATIENT 24 HOURS AFTER MAJOR SURGERY, SO A POSITIVE RESULT IS UNINFORMATIVE AND A NEGATIVE ONE WILL NOT BE BELIEVED. GO STRAIGHT TO CTPA.**

**ECG IN PE: SINUS TACHYCARDIA IS THE COMMONEST FINDING. LOOK FOR RV STRAIN — T-WAVE INVERSION V1–V4, NEW RIGHT BUNDLE BRANCH BLOCK, RIGHT-AXIS SHIFT. S1Q3T3 IS UNCOMMON AND ITS ABSENCE EXCLUDES NOTHING.**

**PERI-OPERATIVE MI PEAKS DAYS 0–3 AND IS OFTEN SILENT AND OFTEN TYPE 2 — age 60, first exertion, anaemia and tachycardia. ECG PLUS TROPONIN IN EVERY POST-OPERATIVE COLLAPSE OVER 50.** **FAT EMBOLISM SYNDROME sits 12–72 HOURS after long-bone or joint surgery: HYPOXIA PLUS CONFUSION PLUS PETECHIAE IN THE AXILLAE OR CONJUNCTIVAE.**
**ATTACH EACH TEST TO THE DIFFERENTIAL IT ANSWERS, OUT LOUD. Reciting a generic screen — FBE, ESR, CRP, LFT, blood cultures — WITH NO STATED LINK IS READ BY THE EXAMINER AS AN ABSENT DIAGNOSIS.**
plan: **STABILITY FIRST: 'could I have the patient's BLOOD PRESSURE LYING AND STANDING, heart rate, respiratory rate, OXYGEN SATURATION, temperature and BLOOD SUGAR?'**

**WIPE and open: 'I hear you had a fall in the bathroom overnight — is it alright if I sit down and we go through what happened?'** Then **acknowledge: 'that must have been frightening. LET'S FIND OUT WHAT'S HAPPENING TOGETHER.'**

**SIGNPOST AND SET THE AGENDA: 'I'll ask about the blackout itself, then about your heart, lungs and medications, then I'll explain what I think is going on. IS THERE ANYTHING PARTICULAR WORRYING YOU THAT YOU'D LIKE ME TO COVER?'**

**TRUE LOC: 'DID YOU BLACK OUT COMPLETELY, OR DID YOU FALL AND STAY AWARE THE WHOLE TIME? What's the last thing you remember?'** Then **HOW LONG WERE YOU OUT, WAS ANYONE WITH YOU · has anything like this happened before?**

**CONTEXT: what exactly were you doing just before · had you been standing a while · WERE YOU IN A LOT OF PAIN · DID IT HAPPEN WHILE YOU WERE PASSING URINE OR OPENING YOUR BOWELS, OR STRAINING · WAS THE BATHROOM HOT AND STEAMY?**
**BEFORE: any warning — light-headed, sweaty, sick in the stomach, ringing in the ears, vision closing in · ANY CHEST PAIN OR RACING HEART · any strange smell or taste?**
**DURING: did anyone see you · were you told you SHOOK OR STIFFENED, BIT YOUR TONGUE, OR WET YOURSELF · WERE YOU PALE?**
**AFTER: when you came round, WERE YOU CONFUSED OR DROWSY, AND FOR HOW LONG · how quickly did you feel normal · DID YOU INJURE YOURSELF — DID YOU HIT YOUR HEAD?**
**CNS: any headache before or since · blurred or double vision, slurred speech, weakness or numbness · any fever, neck stiffness or rash?**

**THE CVS AND RESPIRATORY SCREEN — ASK EVERY ONE EVEN THOUGH ALL ARE NEGATIVE, because THE EXAMINER IS WATCHING FOR THE SCREEN, NOT THE ANSWERS: any chest pain or tightness · heart racing or skipping · ANY SHORTNESS OF BREATH, EVEN JUST ON MOVING · any cough or BLOOD IN YOUR PHLEGM · ANY PAIN, SWELLING OR REDNESS IN EITHER CALF?**
**GI: nausea or vomiting · tummy pain · BLACK STOOLS OR BLOOD. METABOLIC: are you diabetic · when did you last eat and drink · have you been drinking enough?**

**DRUGS, and this block is marked: WHAT ARE YOU ON FOR PAIN — ANY STRONG PAINKILLERS, OR A NERVE TABLET LIKE PREGABALIN · ANY BLOOD-PRESSURE TABLETS RESTARTED THIS MORNING · HAVE YOU HAD A BLOOD-THINNING INJECTION SINCE THE OPERATION — WHICH ONE, AND WERE ANY DOSES MISSED · any alcohol or other substances?**

**PSYCHOGENIC: breathing very fast beforehand · anything particularly stressful? VTE RISKS: EVER HAD A CLOT IN THE LEG OR LUNG · ANY CANCER · long flights or drives recently · ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH CLOTTING PROBLEMS · any liver trouble?**

**SADMA, PAST AND FAMILY HISTORY: smoking, alcohol, drugs, medications, allergies · heart disease, diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy, previous VTE · FAMILY SUDDEN DEATH UNDER 40, the one family item never to skip in a syncope station.**

**DELIVER THE EXPLANATION — Version A or Version B script — IN PLAIN WORDS, and name the differentials: the simple faint, a heart attack, and a drop in blood pressure from blood loss and strong painkillers.**

**TO THE EXAMINER, EACH TEST TIED TO ITS DIFFERENTIAL: oxygen, IV access and monitoring · 12-LEAD ECG and BEDSIDE GLUCOSE · FBE, UEC, TROPONIN, coagulation, group and hold · AND AN URGENT CT PULMONARY ANGIOGRAM.**

**Say the D-dimer sentence explicitly.** Then **empirical anticoagulation DISCUSSED WITH THE ORTHOPAEDIC TEAM while awaiting the scan, and escalation to your senior and the MET team if he deteriorates.**
pefe: **Do now: repeat full vitals INCLUDING LYING AND STANDING BP; continuous SpO2 and cardiac monitoring · 12-LEAD ECG · BEDSIDE BSL · OXYGEN TITRATED TO SpO2 94–98% · TWO LARGE-BORE IV CANNULAE · POST-FALL NEUROLOGICAL OBSERVATIONS · INSPECT WOUND, DRAINS AND DRESSINGS FOR BLOOD LOSS · REVIEW THE MEDICATION CHART.**

**Do next: CT PULMONARY ANGIOGRAPHY — SAY THESE WORDS. Check eGFR and contrast allergy first; if contrast is contraindicated, V/Q SCAN · FBE for a haemoglobin drop, UEC with pre-contrast renal function, TROPONIN, coagulation profile, GROUP AND HOLD, CRP, magnesium and calcium · CXR, USUALLY NORMAL IN PE but excludes collapse, effusion, pneumothorax, pneumonia · ABG or VBG if hypoxic, where HYPOXIA WITH HYPOCAPNIA SUPPORTS PE · CT HEAD if head strike, unwitnessed LOC, anticoagulation or persisting confusion · BEDSIDE ECHO if hypotensive, where RV DILATATION SUPPORTS HIGH-RISK PE.**

**Awaiting CTPA with high suspicion: DISCUSS IMMEDIATE EMPIRICAL ANTICOAGULATION WITH THE SURGICAL TEAM — BALANCE CLOT AGAINST A FRESH ARTHROPLASTY WOUND. ENOXAPARIN 1 mg/kg SUBCUTANEOUSLY 12-HOURLY, or 1 mg/kg DAILY IF CrCl BELOW 30; or an UNFRACTIONATED HEPARIN INFUSION when bleeding risk is high or thrombolysis may be needed, BECAUSE IT IS SHORT-ACTING AND REVERSIBLE WITH PROTAMINE.** VERIFY.

**Confirmed and stable: RIVAROXABAN 15 mg TWICE DAILY FOR 21 DAYS THEN 20 mg DAILY, or APIXABAN 10 mg TWICE DAILY FOR 7 DAYS THEN 5 mg TWICE DAILY, once the surgeon accepts the bleeding risk. MINIMUM THREE MONTHS FOR A PROVOKED PE.** VERIFY.

**HIGH-RISK PE WITH SHOCK: MET CALL, ICU, senior and orthopaedic input. THROMBOLYSIS IS RELATIVELY CONTRAINDICATED WITHIN 3 WEEKS OF MAJOR SURGERY — CATHETER-DIRECTED THERAPY OR SURGICAL EMBOLECTOMY IS PREFERRED. IVC FILTER ONLY IF ANTICOAGULATION IS ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED.**

**Do not miss: PE WITH A COMPLETELY NORMAL RESPIRATORY HISTORY — THIS IS THE WHOLE STATION · SILENT PERI-OPERATIVE MI, TROPONIN NOT REASSURANCE · OCCULT SURGICAL OR GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING · INTRACRANIAL BLEED AFTER A HEAD STRIKE, especially with prophylaxis on board · HYPOGLYCAEMIA in a patient fasted for theatre.**

**Avoid: D-DIMER · a shotgun screen unlinked to differentials · reassuring him that a normal chest examination or ECG excludes PE · MOBILISING HIM AGAIN UNSUPERVISED before the cause is known.** **Supportive: analgesia review, APERIENTS TO STOP STRAINING, mechanical prophylaxis, supervised mobilisation with physiotherapy, falls precautions, call bell and toilet assistance, incident report.** **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33; do not delay empirical anticoagulation awaiting transfer.**

stem: James Whitfield, 60, has come in complaining of dizziness. Reception note: 'dizzy spells, 5 days'. HR 78 reg · BP 132/80 sitting, 128/78 standing · RR 14 · SpO2 98% RA · T 36.7 · BGL 5.8 · GCS 15.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history
Ask the examiner for the examination findings you require
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the patient
Outline your management plan to the patient
findings: ONE WORD, THREE STATIONS

SYNCOPE (transient LOC) · RECURRENT FALLS (no LOC, repeated falls) · DIZZINESS/VERTIGO. THE STEM WORD NEVER DECIDES YOUR STRUCTURE — THE PATIENT'S DEFINITION DOES. AMC RE-LABELLED THE FALLS STEM 'DIZZINESS' SPECIFICALLY TO PUNISH RECALL MEMORISATION
QUESTION ONE — the whole station

'DIZZINESS MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE. DO YOU MEAN A SPINNING SENSATION — THE ROOM GOING ROUND? OR DO YOU FEEL LIGHT-HEADED, AS IF YOU'RE ABOUT TO FAINT? OR IS IT MORE THAT YOU FEEL OFF-BALANCE AND UNSTEADY?' Then TWO MORE INSIDE 90 SECONDS: ANY FAINTING OR BLACKING OUT · ANY FALLS?
THE SINGLE NAMED FINDING CANDIDATES LOSE

If you say 'CRANIAL NERVES THREE, FOUR AND SIX — EYE MOVEMENTS', THE CARD WILL SAY EYE MOVEMENTS NORMAL AND YOU WILL NEVER BE TOLD ABOUT THE NYSTAGMUS. SAY THE WORD: 'IS THERE ANY NYSTAGMUS, AND IF SO WHAT DIRECTION, AND DOES IT FATIGUE?' And name DIX–HALLPIKE by name
THE VERSION A FINDINGS CARD

Alert, well, not pale · BP 132/80 lying, 128/78 standing, NO POSTURAL DROP · pulse 78 regular · GAIT NORMAL, ROMBERG NEGATIVE · cranial nerves intact, fundi normal, NYSTAGMUS PRESENT ON POSITIONAL TESTING · limbs normal · OTOSCOPY NORMAL BOTH EARS, RINNE POSITIVE, WEBER CENTRAL · heart sounds dual · DIX–HALLPIKE POSITIVE · BGL 5.8 · ECG sinus rhythm
READ THE CARD ALOUD AS EVIDENCE, NOT AS A FORMALITY
EVERY NORMAL ON THAT CARD IS A REASON YOU ARE ALLOWED TO SAY 'BENIGN'
THE HIGHEST-YIELD SINGLE QUESTION
'DOES A CHANGE OF POSITION SUCH AS ROLLING OVER IN BED SET IT OFF?' — IT IS THE ONE POSITIONAL CHANGE NOBODY CAN AVOID. Ask it directly if nothing is volunteered about triggers
VERSION B — same word, completely different station

MARGARET DOYLE, 74, DIZZINESS AND TWO FALLS IN A MONTH. PERINDOPRIL, INDAPAMIDE, TAMSULOSIN, SERTRALINE. LIVES ALONE. BP 138/82 LYING, 106/64 STANDING. 'I GO LIGHT-HEADED WHEN I STAND UP AND MY LEGS GIVE WAY' → POSTURAL HYPOTENSION AND FALLS. Medication review, postural BP, home safety, gait
THE DELIBERATE MISDIRECTION
'I HAD A FALL TEN DAYS AGO — I'M ON APIXABAN.' → NON-CONTRAST CT HEAD URGENTLY, AND SAY THE WORDS SUBDURAL HAEMATOMA OUT LOUD. He may volunteer the fall ONLY IF ASKED DIRECTLY
SOURCE CORRECTION — nystagmus direction

The source describes HORIZONTAL nystagmus on Dix–Hallpike. POSTERIOR-CANAL BPPV PRODUCES BRIEF UPBEATING, TORSIONAL NYSTAGMUS, LATENCY 1–5 SECONDS, LASTING UNDER 60 SECONDS, FATIGUING ON REPETITION. PURELY HORIZONTAL SUGGESTS THE LATERAL CANAL VARIANT — supine roll test, LOG-ROLL (Lempert) manoeuvre, not an Epley
The patient is frightened

60-YEAR-OLD MEN WITH NEW DIZZINESS ARE USUALLY THINKING STROKE OR BRAIN TUMOUR. A bare 'it's nothing serious' READS AS DISMISSAL AND LOSES THE RAPPORT MARKS. If he asks 'AM I HAVING A STROKE?' → 'THAT'S EXACTLY WHAT I NEED TO RULE OUT, AND I'M GOING TO CHECK FOR IT CAREFULLY'

dx: **BENIGN PAROXYSMAL POSITIONAL VERTIGO, POSTERIOR SEMICIRCULAR CANAL — brief recurrent episodes of TRUE ROTATIONAL VERTIGO lasting SECONDS TO UNDER A MINUTE, provoked by A CHANGE OF HEAD POSITION, with NO hearing loss, tinnitus or aural fullness, NO neurological deficit, and a NORMAL EXAMINATION BETWEEN EPISODES.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: YOU ARE ASKED TO AWARD THE WORD 'BENIGN', AND YOU MUST SHOW YOU EARNED IT. Every candidate can say 'BPPV'. THE STATION SEPARATES PEOPLE ON WHETHER THE LABEL IS JUSTIFIED OUT LOUD.**

**THERE ARE EXACTLY TWO GROUNDS, AND THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR BOTH. ONE — IT IS POSITIONAL AND BRIEF: short spells triggered by a change of head position, settling when still. TWO — THE RED FLAGS ARE ABSENT: no hearing loss, no tinnitus, no vomiting, no headache, no weakness, no numbness, no speech or vision change, no head injury, NORMAL NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION.**
**MISS THE EAR QUESTIONS AND YOU HAVE NOT EARNED THE LABEL — THE EXAMINER WILL FAIL YOU EVEN IF THE WORD 'BPPV' CAME OUT OF YOUR MOUTH.**

**THE SECONDARY DISCRIMINATOR IS THE OPENING DEFINITION QUESTION — the difference between running the right structure and running a memorised one. Candidates who skip it and launch into ear questions ON A VERSION B PATIENT FAIL BEFORE MINUTE TWO.**

**REASSURANCE MUST BE ITEMISED: NAME EACH SERIOUS THING YOU LOOKED FOR AND SAY WHY IT IS NOT PRESENT. 'Your hearing is normal, there's no ringing in your ears, no headache, no weakness or numbness, your speech and vision are fine, and your neurological examination is completely normal. THAT'S WHAT MAKES ME CONFIDENT THIS IS THE BENIGN TYPE.'**

**BPPV is A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS confirmed by a positive Dix–Hallpike — THERE IS NO BLOOD TEST OR SCAN THAT MAKES IT.** **Review in 1–2 WEEKS; refer to vestibular physiotherapy or ENT if it fails after TWO OR THREE ATTEMPTS.** **Prognosis: most settle within weeks; ROUGHLY HALF RECUR within a few years — recurrence is NOT a sign something was missed, but IS a reason to teach the home manoeuvre.**

dx: **MULTIFACTORIAL RECURRENT FALLS. RECURRENT means TWO OR MORE FALLS IN 12 MONTHS.** **A FALL is unintentionally coming to rest on the ground, NOT caused by an overwhelming external force or a major intrinsic event.** **A FALL WITHOUT LOSS OF CONSCIOUSNESS IS NOT SYNCOPE — ESTABLISH THIS IN THE FIRST MINUTE.**
**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: NAMING EVERY CONTRIBUTING CAUSE — INCLUDING THE ONES THE EXAMINATION DID NOT CONFIRM — AND NEVER COLLAPSING THE CASE INTO A SINGLE LABEL.**
**CANDIDATES FAIL IN TWO WAYS. They ANCHOR ON THE RECALL THEY MEMORISED AND STOP LOOKING, or they GO QUIET WHEN THE EXAMINER SAYS 'EXAMINATION IS NORMAL', BECAUSE THEY HAVE NOTHING LEFT TO SAY.**
**THE PASS IS A NUMBERED LIST OF PLAUSIBLE REASONS, EACH ANCHORED TO SOMETHING THE PATIENT ACTUALLY TOLD YOU, delivered warmly and in plain English.**

**THE FRAME, USED IN EVERY VERSION: 'falls at your age ALMOST NEVER HAVE ONE SINGLE CAUSE — they're usually SEVERAL SMALL THINGS STACKING UP, and that's actually GOOD NEWS, BECAUSE EACH ONE WE CAN DO SOMETHING ABOUT. I'VE FOUND FOUR THINGS IN YOUR CASE. Let me take them one at a time.'**

**THEN FOR EACH CAUSE, THE SAME THREE-PART MOVE: NAME IT IN PLAIN ENGLISH — 'you have an infection in your water' · GIVE THE MEDICAL NAME ONCE — 'we call this a urinary tract infection' · LINK IT TO THE FALLS — 'and that's why you've been rushing to the toilet at night, WHICH IS WHEN YOU FELL.' Then PAUSE: 'does that make sense so far?'**

**POSTURAL HYPOTENSION WITH A NORMAL TEST STILL GETS NAMED — BUT SAY WHY, DO NOT JUST ASSERT IT: 'your blood pressure was steady when we checked TODAY, but you're on two tablets that can lower it, and THAT DROP DOESN'T HAPPEN EVERY TIME — it can happen at home when you get up quickly.' A SYSTOLIC DROP UNDER 20 mmHg MAKES IT LESS LIKELY BUT DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT — IT IS INTERMITTENT.**

**ALCOHOL HITS THREE SYSTEMS, NOT ONE: NERVES — alcoholic sensory neuropathy · CEREBELLUM — alcoholic cerebellar degeneration, VERMIS, SO GAIT IS AFFECTED MORE THAN LIMBS · NUTRITION — and the sedation on top. Say all of them, WITHOUT SHAMING.** **NHMRC: NO MORE THAN 10 STANDARD DRINKS A WEEK AND 4 IN ANY ONE DAY.**

**SOURCE CORRECTION — the source says tricyclics are no longer used in Australia and mirtazapine is used instead. THAT OVERSTATES IT. AUSTRALIAN FIRST-LINE IS AN SSRI; MIRTAZAPINE IS CHOSEN WHEN SEDATION OR APPETITE STIMULATION IS WANTED; TRICYCLICS ARE STILL USED, MOSTLY FOR NEUROPATHIC PAIN AND MIGRAINE PROPHYLAXIS.** Say: **'AMITRIPTYLINE IS BEST AVOIDED IN AN OLDER PERSON AT RISK OF FALLS; I'd review the indication with her GP or psychiatrist RATHER THAN STOP IT ABRUPTLY.'**

**The storyline that holds every risk factor: the older man with PROSTATE ENLARGEMENT who gets up FOUR TIMES A NIGHT, has the TOILET DOWNSTAIRS, POOR LIGHTING, A DOG UNDERFOOT, OSTEOARTHRITIC KNEES, weakness and NUMBNESS IN THE LEGS after a stroke, believes wine is good for the heart so has THREE GLASSES EACH EVENING, and takes A TABLET TO SLEEP. RUN THAT PICTURE AND YOU WILL NEVER LEAVE A DOMAIN OUT.**

**THE NUMBERED-REASONS SCRIPT: the frame, then each cause with plain English, the medical name once, and the link to the falls — pausing to check understanding.**

**THE DIFFERENTIALS YOU ARE KEEPING IN MIND: a drop in blood pressure on standing, heart rhythm problems, the nerves in the legs, the balance centre, low salt levels, and anything at home that's easy to trip on.** Then **SAFETY-NET, REVIEW INTERVAL, AND WHO TO CALL — plus ONE SENTENCE EACH on BONE HEALTH AND DRIVING.**

stem: A 70-year-old man has come to see you about three falls over recent months; on one occasion he struck his head and was taken to hospital. Observations are normal.
tasks: Take a relevant focused history (about 5 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
findings: The examination card

SENSORY LOSS IN BOTH LEGS, and in one recall LOSS OF PROPRIOCEPTION · GLUCOSE NORMAL · NO POSTURAL DROP. Everything else normal. THE NORMAL GLUCOSE DOES NOT EXCLUDE AN OVERNIGHT DROP ON ONE MEAL A DAY
THE FOUR ANSWERS THAT CHANGE THE CASE

'I HAVE NUMBNESS IN BOTH LEGS' · 'ONE TIME I HIT MY HEAD AND THEY TOOK ME TO HOSPITAL' · 'I HAVE A FULL BOTTLE OF WINE EVERY NIGHT, ALWAYS HAVE' · 'I ONLY EAT ONE MEAL A DAY — I CAN'T BE BOTHERED COOKING AND THERE'S NO ONE TO HELP.' Plus 'MY FAMILY ARE ALL INTERSTATE'
THE HEAD STRIKE IS NOT A DETAIL

HE WAS TAKEN TO HOSPITAL. ASK: ANY ANTICOAGULANTS OR ANTIPLATELETS · WAS HE IMAGED · ANY ONGOING HEADACHE, DROWSINESS OR CHANGE IN THINKING SINCE. SUBDURAL HAEMATOMA IN AN OLDER PERSON CAN FOLLOW A TRIVIAL STRIKE WEEKS EARLIER
QUANTIFY, THEN CONVERT OUT LOUD
A 750 mL BOTTLE OF WINE IS SEVEN TO EIGHT STANDARD DRINKS. NHMRC GUIDANCE IS NO MORE THAN TEN IN A WHOLE WEEK AND FOUR IN ANY ONE DAY. 'Do you drink?' — 'yes' — AND MOVING ON IS A FAIL
ALCOHOL HITS THREE SYSTEMS, PLUS SEDATION

NERVES → ALCOHOLIC SENSORY NEUROPATHY, and when you CANNOT FEEL THE GROUND YOU FALL. CEREBELLUM → ALCOHOLIC CEREBELLAR DEGENERATION, which affects the VERMIS SO GAIT IS AFFECTED MORE THAN LIMBS. NUTRITION → hypoglycaemia and deficiency. AND THE DROWSINESS AT NIGHT ON TOP
THE SOCIAL SCREEN IS WHERE THIS VERSION IS WON
LIVES ALONE · FAMILY FAR AWAY · ONE MEAL A DAY. Cutting the social screen for time loses the missed meals IN CONTEXT, the fear of falling, and the driving question
ADDED — the two screens this version needs

ELDER ABUSE OR NEGLECT, where isolation appears: 'DO YOU FEEL SAFE AT HOME? IS ANYONE MANAGING YOUR MONEY OR MEDICINES FOR YOU?' And a MOOD AND SAFETY question — a recently bereaved man living alone, drinking a bottle a night, barely eating
What the examiner is listening for on the neurology

GLOVE-AND-STOCKING SENSORY LOSS · ABSENT ANKLE JERKS · IMPAIRED VIBRATION AND PROPRIOCEPTION · A POSITIVE ROMBERG, WHICH MEANS SENSORY ATAXIA AND SENDS YOU TO B12 · WIDE-BASED GAIT AND HEEL–SHIN DYSMETRIA for the cerebellar component
THE TONE THE STATION IS MARKING
'I'M NOT HERE TO LECTURE YOU, BUT I DO NEED TO BE STRAIGHT WITH YOU, BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS THREE OF THE FOUR THINGS I'VE FOUND.' NAME EVERY MECHANISM WITHOUT SHAMING HIM
TWO THINGS YOU MUST NOT DO
DO NOT ADVISE ABRUPT CESSATION — STOPPING SUDDENLY ON THAT AMOUNT CAN BE DANGEROUS. And GIVE THIAMINE BEFORE ANY GLUCOSE

dx: **MULTIFACTORIAL RECURRENT FALLS, ALCOHOL-DRIVEN. Name FOUR causes: ALCOHOLIC SENSORY NEUROPATHY · ALCOHOLIC CEREBELLAR DEGENERATION · HYPOGLYCAEMIA FROM ONE MEAL A DAY · AND NOCTURNAL SEDATION FROM THE ALCOHOL ITSELF.** Plus **the unsafe home and absent supports underneath all of them.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: LINKING THE ALCOHOL TO THREE SEPARATE MECHANISMS, NOT ONE — AND DOING IT WITHOUT SHAMING HIM.** **Naming the neuropathy and stopping there is the commonest way to lose this version.**

**THE SCRIPT: 'a bottle of wine is AROUND SEVEN OR EIGHT STANDARD DRINKS — the national guidance is NO MORE THAN TEN IN A WHOLE WEEK. I'm not here to lecture you, but I do need to be straight with you, BECAUSE IT EXPLAINS THREE OF THE FOUR THINGS I'VE FOUND.'**

**ONE: 'the NUMBNESS AND LOSS OF FEELING IN YOUR LEGS comes from DAMAGE TO THE NERVES — alcoholic neuropathy. WHEN YOU CAN'T FEEL THE GROUND PROPERLY, YOU FALL.' TWO: 'alcohol also affects THE BALANCE CENTRE AT THE BACK OF THE BRAIN — cerebellar degeneration — and it makes you UNSTEADY ON YOUR FEET.' THREE: 'you're eating ONE MEAL A DAY, so your BLOOD SUGAR CAN DROP LOW OVERNIGHT.' FOUR: 'the alcohol itself MAKES YOU DROWSY AT NIGHT, which adds to all of it.'**

**THE HEAD STRIKE NEEDS ITS OWN THREE QUESTIONS: WAS HE ON AN ANTICOAGULANT OR ANTIPLATELET · WAS HE IMAGED AT THE TIME · ANY ONGOING HEADACHE, DROWSINESS, GAIT DETERIORATION OR COGNITIVE CHANGE SINCE.** **A SUBDURAL HAEMATOMA IN AN OLDER PERSON FOLLOWS A TRIVIAL STRIKE, OFTEN WEEKS EARLIER, AND THE THRESHOLD FOR A CT HEAD IS LOW.**

**THE PROPRIOCEPTIVE VERSION OF THE CARD MATTERS: LOSS OF PROPRIOCEPTION WITH A POSITIVE ROMBERG IS SENSORY ATAXIA — DORSAL COLUMN OR LARGE-FIBRE NEUROPATHY — AND IT SENDS YOU TO B12 AS WELL AS ALCOHOL. Say both.**

**TREATMENT SEQUENCE THAT MUST NOT BE REVERSED: THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE IN ANY HEAVY DRINKER. THIAMINE 100 mg ORALLY DAILY FOR PREVENTION; PARENTERAL THIAMINE AND URGENT REFERRAL IF WERNICKE ENCEPHALOPATHY IS SUSPECTED.** VERIFY.

**DO NOT ADVISE STOPPING SUDDENLY — STOPPING ABRUPTLY ON THAT INTAKE CAN BE DANGEROUS. Offer a PLANNED WITHDRAWAL: 'I'd like to talk about CUTTING DOWN SAFELY, because stopping suddenly on that amount can be dangerous.'** **BRIEF INTERVENTION USING THE 5 As; Drug and Alcohol Services SA; dietitian; LFTs.**

**THE SOCIAL LAYER IS PART OF THE DIAGNOSIS, NOT A COURTESY: 'I'd also like to arrange SOME HELP WITH MEALS AND SOME COMPANY, BECAUSE DOING THIS ALONE IS MAKING EVERYTHING HARDER.'** **MY AGED CARE 1800 200 422 for meals, personal care and social support; consider a PERSONAL ALARM for someone living alone.**

**FRAME IT AS ALWAYS: 'falls at your age ALMOST NEVER COME FROM ONE SINGLE THING — they're several small things STACKING UP, and that's GOOD NEWS, BECAUSE EACH ONE IS SOMETHING WE CAN DO SOMETHING ABOUT. I'VE FOUND FOUR.'** Then **each cause in plain English, the medical name once, and the link to the falls.**
plan: **Say the observations out loud, WIPE, open question.** Then **acknowledge, SIGNPOST THE LONG LIST, and ask the agenda question: 'was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'**
**FALL OR FAINT, SECOND ALWAYS: did you BLACK OUT, EVEN FOR A SECOND · do you REMEMBER HITTING THE FLOOR · any SHAKING OR JERKING, TONGUE BITING, WETTING YOURSELF?**

**CHARACTERISE: HOW MANY AND WHEN DID THEY START · TALK ME THROUGH EACH ONE, what were you doing · any WARNING · DID YOU HURT YOURSELF IN ANY OF THEM · COULD YOU GET YOURSELF UP, OR WERE YOU ON THE FLOOR A WHILE?**
**CHASE THE HEAD STRIKE PROPERLY: were you ON ANY BLOOD THINNERS AT THE TIME · DID THEY SCAN YOUR HEAD · ANY HEADACHE, DROWSINESS OR TROUBLE THINKING SINCE THEN · has your WALKING GOT WORSE since?**

**ORGANIC SCREEN, rapid: NUMBNESS OR PINS AND NEEDLES IN YOUR LEGS · weakness · slurred speech · trouble with vision · headache · any SPINNING · chest pain, palpitations, breathlessness · vomiting, diarrhoea, BLACK OR BLOODY MOTIONS · ARE YOU EATING REGULARLY, OR SKIPPING MEALS?**

**When the numbness comes, CHASE THE CAUSE rather than recording it: how long, BOTH LEGS, how far up, any WEAKNESS with it — and then ALCOHOL, DIABETES AND B12 as the three causes you are thinking of.**
**PAST HISTORY, the four questions for anything he names, then MEDICATIONS INCLUDING ANYTHING FOR SLEEP, FOR PAIN, OR FROM THE CHEMIST, and allergies.**

**THE SIX RISK DOMAINS IN ORDER. HOME: rugs, cords, steps, LIGHTING AT NIGHT, where's the toilet. URINARY: frequency, urgency, nocturia, burning. MSK: joint pain, stiffness, balance, feet, WHAT SHOES INDOORS. SENSES: eyes and hearing last checked, BIFOCALS.**
**DRUGS, then ALCOHOL — AND QUANTIFY: 'do you drink? HOW MUCH, AND HOW OFTEN?'** Then **CAGE if the intake is heavy, and CONVERT IT OUT LOUD: 'that's around seven or eight standard drinks a night.'**

**GERIATRIC AND SOCIAL SCREEN — WHERE THIS VERSION IS WON: WHO'S AT HOME · who helps if you need it · DESCRIBE A TYPICAL DAY'S MEALS · managing showering, dressing, shopping, cooking, money and medicines · any MEMORY trouble · HOW HAS YOUR MOOD BEEN · weight loss · STILL DRIVING · HAVE THE FALLS MADE YOU AFRAID TO MOVE ABOUT?**
**Where isolation and neglect appear, add the two screens: DO YOU FEEL SAFE AT HOME, IS ANYONE MANAGING YOUR MONEY OR MEDICINES FOR YOU · and a MOOD AND SAFETY question.**

**ASK THE EXAMINER IN ORDER: general appearance, hydration, BRUISING OR EVIDENCE OF INJURY · GAIT AND TIMED UP AND GO · vitals with LYING AND STANDING BP AT ONE AND THREE MINUTES and PULSE RHYTHM · BEDSIDE GLUCOSE.**

**Then LOWER LIMB NEUROLOGY — tone, power, reflexes, SENSATION INCLUDING VIBRATION AND PROPRIOCEPTION, and CEREBELLAR SIGNS WITH ROMBERG, HEEL–SHIN AND TANDEM WALKING · visual acuity and fundoscopy · cardiovascular for a MURMUR OF AORTIC STENOSIS · lower limb joints and FOOTWEAR · abdomen and urine dipstick.**
**THE FRAME, THEN FOUR NUMBERED CAUSES — nerves, cerebellum, sugar, sedation — each in plain English with the link to the falls, pausing to check he is following.**

**ANSWER HIS CONCERN DIRECTLY, then the differentials you are still checking: heart rhythm, B12 and diabetes as other causes of the leg numbness, low salt levels, anaemia, AND THE POSSIBILITY OF A SLOW BLEED AFTER THE HEAD INJURY.**

**THE PLAN: THIAMINE TODAY, BLOODS, ECG · CUTTING DOWN SAFELY RATHER THAN STOPPING SUDDENLY · MEALS AND COMPANY THROUGH MY AGED CARE · OT home assessment with LIGHTING · podiatry and safe footwear.** Then **RED FLAGS, A REVIEW DATE, AND TEACH-BACK: 'can you tell me back the two things you'll change this week?'**
pefe: **Do now: BEDSIDE GLUCOSE — if below 4.0 and conscious, 15 g FAST CARBOHYDRATE and RECHECK AT 15 MINUTES, BUT THIAMINE FIRST IN A HEAVY DRINKER · lying and standing BP at 1 and 3 minutes · AN ECG IN EVERY FALLS PATIENT · INJURY SURVEY including head, hips and wrists · medication review on the spot.**
**CT HEAD with a low threshold given the earlier head strike — and MANDATORY if he was anticoagulated, or if there is any headache, drowsiness, gait deterioration or cognitive change.**

**Bloods: FBE, UEC, CALCIUM, MAGNESIUM, PHOSPHATE, LFTs, TSH · VITAMIN B12 AND FOLATE, which the proprioceptive loss makes essential · fasting BGL and HbA1c · vitamin D · DXA, because A FALLER WITH OSTEOPOROSIS IS A HIP FRACTURE WAITING TO HAPPEN.**
**MRI only if there is diagnostic doubt about the cerebellar signs. A COGNITIVE SCREEN — RUDAS where English is a second language or in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients.**

**Alcohol management: BRIEF INTERVENTION USING THE 5 As · THIAMINE 100 mg ORALLY DAILY FOR PREVENTION, PARENTERAL AND URGENT REFERRAL IF WERNICKE IS SUSPECTED · DIETITIAN · LFTs · A PLANNED WITHDRAWAL, NEVER ABRUPT CESSATION · Drug and Alcohol Services SA.** VERIFY.

**Do not miss: SUBDURAL HAEMATOMA AFTER THE HEAD STRIKE · CARDIAC SYNCOPE, so get an ECG · HYPOGLYCAEMIA, where FOUR IS THE FLOOR · B12 DEFICIENCY behind the proprioceptive loss · OCCULT HIP OR WRIST FRACTURE · ELDER ABUSE OR NEGLECT · OSTEOPOROSIS, because THE FALLS PLAN IS ONLY HALF THE JOB · DEPRESSION in a bereaved man living alone.**

**Avoid: LECTURING · advising abrupt cessation · GLUCOSE BEFORE THIAMINE · labelling it all 'old age' · reassuring without a plan · discharging without addressing BONE HEALTH AND DRIVING.** **SA and the NT are the jurisdictions where the doctor has a LEGAL DUTY TO REPORT an unfit driver to the Registrar; TELL THE PATIENT BEFORE YOU REPORT.** **Balance-challenging exercise is THE SINGLE BEST-EVIDENCED INTERVENTION.**
