dx: **INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS — ACUTE EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS INFECTION. Fever, exudative pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy with POSTERIOR CERVICAL prominence, PROFOUND FATIGUE, splenomegaly in roughly half; peak age 15–25.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — TWO HARMS YOU CAN PREVENT IN ONE CONSULTATION: FIRST, THE SPLEEN — a 19-year-old who feels better in ten days and goes back to rugby is THE PERSON WHO RUPTURES; the restriction must be given WITH A REASON AND A TIMEFRAME, plus the shoulder-tip warning. SECOND, THE ALLERGY LABEL — 'penicillin allergy' today commits him to DECADES OF SECOND-LINE ANTIBIOTICS for a rash caused by the virus. CANDIDATES WHO EXPLAIN THE SEROLOGY BEAUTIFULLY AND DO NEITHER HAVE MISSED THE POINT.**

**THE RESULTS, ONE AT A TIME: 'your blood count shows a high number of LYMPHOCYTES that look ATYPICAL — THAT SOUNDS ALARMING AND IT ISN'T; it's the classic appearance of a body fighting this virus. Your LIVER TESTS ARE MILDLY RAISED — the virus irritates the liver a little; it settles, and it's why I'll ask you to lay off alcohol. The virus test has three parts — two positive, and ONE CALLED EBNA IS NEGATIVE. THAT NEGATIVE ONE IS THE MOST USEFUL, because EBNA only appears SIX TO TWELVE WEEKS AFTER YOU CATCH IT — so this is A RECENT, CURRENT INFECTION.'**

**UN-LABELLING THE ALLERGY: 'I gather you've been told you're allergic to penicillin — AND I DON'T THINK YOU ARE. People with glandular fever who take AMOXICILLIN — that class specifically — come out in a widespread rash BECAUSE OF THE INFECTION, NOT AN ALLERGY. IF "PENICILLIN ALLERGY" GOES ON YOUR RECORD, FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE YOU'D GET SECOND-CHOICE ANTIBIOTICS. So I'M RECORDING IT AS AN AMOXICILLIN RASH IN THE SETTING OF ACUTE EBV, NOT A TRUE ALLERGY — and please tell any doctor who asks that it was a rash with glandular fever.' An allergy specialist can confirm formally if it ever matters.**

**THE SPLEEN, VERBATIM: 'this virus makes THE SPLEEN SWELL — an organ under your ribs on the left. When it's enlarged it's FRAGILE, and A KNOCK CAN MAKE IT RUPTURE — serious internal bleeding and a surgical emergency. Rare, but when it happens IT'S USUALLY IN SOMEONE WHO FELT FINE AND WENT BACK EARLY. So: NO CONTACT OR COLLISION SPORT, NO HEAVY LIFTING, NOTHING WHERE YOU COULD TAKE A HIT TO THE ABDOMEN, FOR AT LEAST FOUR WEEKS FROM WHEN THIS STARTED — longer if you're still unwell. Light exercise is fine. If you get SUDDEN SEVERE PAIN IN THE UPPER LEFT TUMMY, PAIN AT THE TIP OF YOUR LEFT SHOULDER, OR FEEL FAINT — CALL AN AMBULANCE; DON'T DRIVE YOURSELF.' Then TEACH-BACK.** VERIFY — guidance varies 3–4 weeks; give the more cautious interval.

**THE HIV OFFER — ROUTINE, NOT ALARMING: 'one last thing, and I ASK THIS OF EVERYONE WHO PRESENTS LIKE YOU HAVE — it isn't about anything you've told me. A small number of infections cause exactly this picture — fever, sore throat, swollen glands, a rash. ONE OF THEM IS THE EARLY STAGE OF HIV. It's uncommon, VERY TREATABLE WHEN FOUND EARLY, and it's a simple blood test. I'd like to include it — is that alright?' ACUTE HIV SEROCONVERSION IS CLINICALLY IDENTICAL, AND A POSITIVE EBV SEROLOGY DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT.**

**THE HONEST ANSWER ABOUT FATIGUE: 'the sore throat and fevers usually settle over one to two weeks. THE TIREDNESS IS THE BIT THAT DRAGS — several weeks for most, A FEW MONTHS FOR SOME. NOTHING SHORTENS IT, AND PUSHING THROUGH TENDS TO PROLONG IT. A GRADUAL, STEPPED RETURN. With exams in three weeks, I'd rather we were realistic now — I CAN WRITE YOU A MEDICAL CERTIFICATE AND SUPPORT SPECIAL CONSIDERATION OR DEFERRAL.'** **Never promise a recovery date.**

**MANAGEMENT: SUPPORTIVE — rest as needed, fluids, regular paracetamol and an NSAID if tolerated, gargles · NO ANTIBIOTICS — if strep is ever proven, PHENOXYMETHYLPENICILLIN, NEVER AMOXICILLIN OR AMPICILLIN · NO ALCOHOL WHILE LFTs ARE DERANGED; recheck at review · SALIVA TRANSMISSION — no kissing or sharing drinks, cutlery, toothbrushes while symptomatic · NO EXCLUSION from uni or work — shed for months, isolation pointless; NOT NOTIFIABLE · review 1–2 weeks.**

**STEROIDS ONLY FOR AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION, SEVERE HAEMOLYSIS OR SEVERE THROMBOCYTOPENIA — NOT FOR SORE THROAT OR FATIGUE. Routine ultrasound to 'check the spleen' before clearing sport doesn't reliably predict rupture — clinical judgement and time.** VERIFY local practice. **Monospot can be falsely negative in the first week; EBV-specific serology is more reliable.**

**DIFFERENTIALS BY BUCKET: INFECTION — ACUTE HIV SEROCONVERSION (the must-not-miss), CMV, toxoplasmosis, GAS pharyngitis (swab negative; co-infection possible), viral hepatitis, adenovirus, influenza · HAEMATOLOGY — ACUTE LEUKAEMIA OR LYMPHOMA; atypical lymphocytes are not blasts — check the film comment and red flags · DRUGS — DRESS, SJS/TEN — facial swelling, mucosal involvement, blistering · OTHER — thyroiditis, post-viral fatigue as a diagnosis over time.** **SA: a certificate stating DATES AND IMPACT — vague ones get rejected; SA Health sexual health services and headspace for a 19-year-old.**

findings: THE WORD THAT DECIDES THE STATION — 'IMMEDIATE'

THE TASK DOESN'T SAY 'MANAGEMENT', IT SAYS IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT. THE EXAMINER WANTS THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION MADE IN THE FIRST SENTENCE OF TASK 3 — NOT A GENERAL COPD LECTURE WITH ANTIVIRALS BOLTED ON AT 7:50
THE COMORBIDITIES ARE NOT SCENERY — THEY ARE THE ELIGIBILITY

dx: **COVID-19 LOWER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION CAUSING A VIRAL EXACERBATION OF COPD — SAY BOTH. The stem hands you the positive test and tells you the cough and sputum are increasing on a COPD background; NAMING ONLY ONE LOSES MARKS.**

**THE DISCRIMINATOR: RECOGNISE THAT THE COMORBIDITIES EXIST TO MAKE HER ELIGIBLE FOR AN ORAL ANTIVIRAL, AND START IT — WHILE EXPLICITLY DECLINING ANTIBIOTICS AND STEROIDS WITH A STATED REASON. A candidate who runs a flawless history, names both diagnoses, and delivers THE STANDARD COPD PACKAGE OF PREDNISOLONE PLUS AMOXICILLIN HAS ANSWERED A DIFFERENT QUESTION.**

**TASK 2, BOTH HALVES: 'your test confirms COVID-19, and it has gone down into your chest — A LOWER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION. COVID usually settles on its own. But there's A SECOND PART: because you have COPD, your airways are already narrowed, and the inflammation the virus causes makes that worse. So ON TOP OF THE COVID YOU'RE HAVING A FLARE-UP OF YOUR COPD — that's why the cough and phlegm are increasing.'**

**TASK 3 OPENS WITH THE ANTIVIRAL: 'because you have COPD and diabetes, YOU'RE AT HIGHER RISK OF BECOMING SERIOUSLY UNWELL — AND THAT MAKES YOU ELIGIBLE FOR AN ANTIVIRAL TABLET. It works best started early, WITHIN THE FIRST FIVE DAYS, and you're on day three, so I'D LIKE TO START IT TODAY. I'm sending a script to your pharmacy now.'** **Eligibility, said aloud: 70+ · 50–69 WITH 2 RISK FACTORS · Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander 30+ with 1 · 18+ moderately–severely immunocompromised.** VERIFY current PBS criteria.

**CORRECTION — WHICH ANTIVIRAL: Australian guidance favours NIRMATRELVIR–RITONAVIR (PAXLOVID) FIRST-LINE WHERE SAFE, with MOLNUPIRAVIR (LAGEVRIO) as the alternative when Paxlovid is contraindicated by interactions or renal impairment — its efficacy evidence is weaker. 'I'd normally use nirmatrelvir–ritonavir, but it has EXTENSIVE INTERACTIONS — including statins and some antihypertensives — and needs renal dose adjustment. I'D CHECK HER FULL MEDICINE LIST; if there's a significant interaction, MOLNUPIRAVIR — 800 mg BD FOR 5 DAYS — is the safer choice.' Molnupiravir: nausea; contraindicated in pregnancy.** VERIFY.

**DECLINING THE ANTIBIOTIC: 'I know more phlegm feels like it should mean antibiotics. Two things make this different. FIRST, WE KNOW WHAT'S CAUSING IT — the test is positive and antibiotics do nothing to a virus. SECOND, THE TRIGGER FOR ANTIBIOTICS IN COPD IS WHEN YOUR BREATHLESSNESS GETS WORSE AND THE PHLEGM INCREASES OR CHANGES COLOUR — and your breathing hasn't changed. If that changes, I want to know immediately.'** **'Wouldn't you cover for secondary infection?' — 'Prophylaxis isn't recommended; I'd give A CLEAR TRIGGER to start the amoxicillin from her action plan and review in 24–48 hours.'**

**DECLINING THE STEROID: 'I'm also not giving you steroid tablets. We give those when a COPD flare-up is making you SIGNIFICANTLY MORE BREATHLESS, and yours isn't. They also LOWER YOUR IMMUNITY AND PUSH YOUR SUGARS UP — with your diabetes and an active infection, a trade I don't want to make unless we have to.'** **'Dexamethasone helps in COVID' — 'IN PATIENTS REQUIRING SUPPLEMENTAL OXYGEN. She isn't hypoxic and is being managed at home.'**

**THE REST OF IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT: INCREASE THE RELIEVER — SALBUTAMOL 4–8 PUFFS VIA SPACER EVERY 3–4 HOURS · CONTINUE HER PREVENTERS · THE SICK-DAY PLAN — the point most candidates walk past: CHECK SUGARS MORE OFTEN, NOT LESS; keep fluids up; STOP THE SGLT2 INHIBITOR (EUGLYCAEMIC KETOACIDOSIS) AND WITHHOLD METFORMIN IF NOT EATING AND DRINKING; WITHHOLD ACE INHIBITOR/ARB AND DIURETIC IF DEHYDRATED; NO NSAIDs — the triple whammy; INSULIN IS NEVER STOPPED · paracetamol, fluids, rest · isolation advice per SA Health.**

**THE DIFFERENTIALS AND THE SAFETY DECISION: BACTERIAL PNEUMONIA — fever with rigors, pleuritic pain, rapid deterioration → face-to-face, CXR · QUINSY · INFLUENZA OR RSV CO-INFECTION · HEART FAILURE OR PE — orthopnoea, swelling; pleuritic pain with sudden breathlessness · DIABETIC DECOMPENSATION — vomiting, drowsiness, SGLT2 inhibitor · AKI. MUST NOT MISS: SILENT HYPOXIA — comfortable at rest with a low saturation; ASK ABOUT FUNCTION, NOT JUST SYMPTOMS.**

**SAFETY NET, THEN TEACH-BACK: 'ring us straight away, or call 000, if you become SHORT OF BREATH AT REST OR MORE THAN YOUR USUAL, CAN'T DO YOUR NORMAL ACTIVITIES, get CHEST PAIN, COUGH UP BLOOD, become CONFUSED OR VERY DROWSY, CAN'T KEEP FLUIDS DOWN, or your sugars keep running high. Overnight, healthdirect is 1800 022 222. I'LL RING YOU MYSELF TOMORROW. Can you tell me back the two things that would make you call an ambulance?'** **SA: ring the local pharmacy before she does, ARRANGE DELIVERY so she doesn't leave isolation · Country Health Connect in-home support · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 from Wallaroo · TIS National 131 450 offered before the history.**

findings: THE DIAGNOSIS IS NOT THE TEST — THE STRUCTURE IS

AMC NOW SWITCHES THE FINDINGS WITHOUT CHANGING THE STEM. A — CLASSIC: heat intolerance, diarrhoea, weight loss, sweating, palpitations → THYROTOXICOSIS. B — MIXED: add irregular periods, mood swings, headaches, poor sleep → THYROTOXICOSIS AND PERIMENOPAUSE. C — PSYCHIATRIC: SAME STEM, but PANIC ATTACKS, AVOIDANCE, A NAMED TRIGGER, OR LOW MOOD → RUN THE PSYCHIATRIC STRUCTURE
THE TWO WAYS PEOPLE FAIL

1 NO DIFFERENTIAL LIST AT ALL — THE COMPLAINT IS VAGUE, SO THEY WANDER FOR SIX MINUTES AND NEVER NAME ANYTHING. 2 THEY REMEMBER THE RECALL, WALK IN, ANNOUNCE 'HYPERTHYROIDISM', AND RULE NOTHING OUT. AN EXAMINER WILL NOT PASS EITHER
DEFINE THE WORD FIRST
'CAN YOU DESCRIBE WHAT YOU MEAN BY SOMETHING WRONG WITH YOUR NERVES? DO YOU MEAN FEELING ANXIOUS AND ON EDGE, YOUR HEART RACING, SHAKING, OR SOMETHING ELSE AGAIN?'
WHY PSYCHOLOGICAL GOES FIRST HERE

In a chest pain station you rule out organic causes first because the complaint is physical. HERE THE COMPLAINT ITSELF IS PSYCHOLOGICAL, SO THE WEIGHTING REVERSES — LEAD WITH THE PSYCHOLOGICAL SCREEN, BUT FINISH THE ORGANIC LIST BEFORE YOU NAME ANYTHING. dx: **Acute inferior myocardial infarction** — territorial ST elevation in **II, III and aVF** with **reciprocal ST depression in aVL**.

**Part of the score is explicitly the reciprocal change.** Pointing out the elevation alone is not a passing interpretation, however confidently you name the territory — and **the reciprocal is also what distinguishes infarction from pericarditis, so naming it does two jobs at once.**

**Inferior = II, III, aVF — the triangle at the bottom. Lateral = I and aVL — the oblique pair at the top left. Anterolateral = V1–V6, taken as one group; you do not need to subdivide septal, anterior and lateral.** **Reciprocal rule: inferior elevation → look at I and aVL. Anterolateral elevation → look at II, III and aVF. IGNORE aVR.**

**Never pattern-recognise.** A formal step-by-step interpretation is expected every time — **recognising an inferior infarct at a glance is not the skill being tested; a reproducible method is, because that is what protects you on the tracing you cannot recognise.**

**Two extras worth naming in an inferior infarct: right ventricular involvement — request V4R — and bradycardia or heart block, which are common.** **If the right ventricle is involved, AVOID NITRATES: those patients are preload dependent and nitrates can drop the blood pressure profoundly. Give fluid instead.**

Management: **aspirin 300 mg CHEWED · a second antiplatelet and anticoagulation per protocol · analgesia · oxygen ONLY if hypoxic · reperfusion — primary angioplasty, or thrombolysis and urgent transfer if angioplasty is not promptly available · continuous monitoring for arrhythmia and heart block · urgent cardiology.**

plan: **Five seconds of silence first, in your head only: what is the most obvious abnormality, and does it map to a territory?** Then speak the steps. **Do not merge the two** — the examiner needs the structure, not your first impression. **No housekeeping: name, date, calibration and paper speed score nothing.**

**Step 1, rate: 'there are about X large squares between R waves, so the rate is around Y.'** Regular → **300 ÷ large squares** (1→300 · 2→150 · 3→100 · 4→75 · 5→60 · 6→50). Irregular → **count the complexes across the whole 10-second strip and multiply by 6**.
**Step 2, regularity: 'the R-R intervals are equal throughout, so the rhythm is regular.'** March them out with paper or fingers if you need to.

**Step 3, P waves: 'there is a P wave before every QRS, so this is sinus rhythm'** — or **'I cannot see P waves; the deflection after each QRS is the T wave.'** Look in **lead II and V1**. **A P and a T must both be present and separate.**

dx: **Hyperkalaemia on the ECG — a medical emergency, treated before the level is repeated.** In a patient with **chronic kidney disease and a recently increased medication**, that is the whole story.
**Tall, peaked, narrow-based ‘tented’ T waves** across the leads are the earliest and most characteristic change.
Then in order as the potassium rises: **P waves flatten and disappear · the PR interval lengthens · the QRS widens progressively.** The late change is a **broad sine-wave pattern**.

The impression, in one sentence: **‘an ECG consistent with hyperkalaemia, which in this patient with chronic kidney disease and a recent medication increase I would treat as a medical emergency without waiting for a repeat level.’**

Management in three moves: **calcium (gluconate or chloride) to protect the myocardium → insulin with glucose ± nebulised salbutamol to shift it intracellularly → a potassium binder or dialysis to remove it.** VERIFY
**Stop the offending drug** — most often a **potassium-sparing diuretic, an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker**.

To the patient, no lead names: **‘the potassium level in your blood is too high, and I can see its effect on your heart tracing. At high levels it interferes with the heart’s electrical activity, which can be dangerous. We’re going to treat it straight away, and stop the tablet that is contributing.’**

The seven steps, always in this order: **rate → regular? → P waves? → PR interval → QRS duration → ST segments and T waves → one overall impression.** Two of the seven are rhythm, which is why some people count six.
Numbers: **small square 0.04 s (1 mm) · large square 0.20 s (5 mm) · full strip 10 seconds · normal rate 60–100 · PR 0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares) · QRS under 0.12 s (under 3 small squares).**

If the label will not come, **describe before you label**: **‘a [regular/irregular], [narrow/broad] complex rhythm at [rate], with [P waves present / no visible P waves], and [ST changes described]’** — the description alone earns most of the mark.
plan: Five seconds silently first: **what is the most obvious abnormality, and does it map to a territory?** Here it does not — the abnormality is in the **T waves**. Then start the steps out loud. Do not merge the silent look with the spoken read.
**Rate**, with its method stated: **‘there are about X large squares between R waves, so the rate is around Y.’**
**Rhythm — regular?** ‘The R-R intervals are equal throughout.’ **Rhythm — P waves?** Here they are **flattened and difficult to identify**. Say that; do not invent one.
**PR interval — prolonged.** If the P waves have gone: **‘the PR interval is not measurable, as there is no P wave.’**
**QRS duration — widened.** Normal is **under 3 small squares (0.12 s)**.
**The T waves — tall, peaked and narrow-based, tented, seen across the leads.** This is the striking abnormality, and it is the step the whole tracing turns on.
**One overall impression, no hedging** — hyperkalaemia, **treated as an emergency without waiting for a repeat level**, in a patient with CKD and a recent medication increase.
Task 2 — to the patient. **Name it → say what it means in one sentence → say what happens next.** No lead names, no ‘ST elevation’, no ‘QRS’.

Task 3 — **‘what do you do first?’** → **calcium to protect**, then **shift**, then **remove**, then **stop the offending drug**. Reading the ECG and then carrying on with the history is a fail — an acute tracing changes the station.
pefe: **There is no physical examination task** — the tracing is handed over and the station is the readout. What must be requested is the **structured interpretation**, not findings.
**The ECG is the confirmation, not the screening test.** Treat on the tracing; **do not wait for a repeat potassium level.**
The history that belongs with this tracing is a **renal and medication history**, not a chest pain history: **chronic kidney disease, and which drug was recently increased.**
Housekeeping earns nothing and burns the time you need: **name, date, calibration, paper speed, axis, R wave progression.** Go straight to rate.
If the tracing is deliberately poor quality, say so **once** — **‘the tracing quality is limited, but in the leads I can read clearly…’** — then work with the readable leads and do not stall.
If challenged on what you left out: **‘I can assess the axis — but I prioritised rate, rhythm, intervals and ST segments as the findings that change management here.’**

**NAME THE STEM'S FINDING AND WHAT IT MEANS: 'there is a MIDLINE STERNOTOMY SCAR consistent with his bypass surgery, with drain scars below, and I cannot see a device box below the left clavicle.' **THE SIX-STEP CONVERSATION: 1 BRIDGE — report the six negatives IN HIS WORDS · 2 STATE — 'the treatment has worked; the fluid has gone, the heart condition hasn't' · 3 ASK — 'what's pulling you home today?' THEN STOP TALKING · 4 SOLVE — whatever he just told you · 5 RISK — SPECIFIC, not apocalyptic: the diuretic is only just back to tablet form with renal function unchecked, and the precipitant is unresolved · 6 RESPECT — it is his decision, with a medication list, bloods, GP within the week, and red flags.**

**THREE DECISIONS AT THE DOOR: SIXTY SECONDS on the film — two findings, one caveat, one conclusion · EVERY SENTENCE GETS AN EXPECTATION — doing, expecting, why · and NEVER ASSERT A FINDING, because there is nothing inside a mannequin.**

**THE FILM IN ORDER OF IMPORTANCE: one sentence of orientation (AP film of a young child, trachea central, adequate inspiration), then the STRIKING ABNORMALITY — CARDIOTHORACIC RATIO WELL OVER 0.5, CARDIOMEGALY — then SECOND, blunted costophrenic angles, PLEURAL EFFUSIONS — then increased interstitial markings from CONGESTION. Always go to the costophrenic angles second; your eye is drawn only to the heart.**

**CONCEDE THE LIMITATION, THEN COMMIT: an AP projection magnifies the heart and a young child tolerates a higher ratio, up to about 0.55 — but at this degree, in a breathless child, it is genuine. Name PERICARDIAL EFFUSION as the alternative for a globular silhouette and an URGENT ECHOCARDIOGRAM to separate them.** **Then STATE THE DIAGNOSIS before you are asked.**
**TAKE CONSENT FROM THE MOTHER AND WARN HER YOU WILL NARRATE ALOUD — the last clause is what makes talking over a child professional rather than rude.**

**NAME THE NORMAL POSITION BEFORE THE ABNORMAL ONE, or 'displaced' means nothing: apex beat normally in the fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line — I WOULD EXPECT IT DISPLACED LATERALLY AND INFERIORLY TOWARDS THE AXILLA, because of the cardiomegaly.** **Offer the JVP with the paediatric caveat — raised, but unreliable at five, so you lean on the LIVER EDGE instead.**

**CARDITIS IS PANCARDITIS, SO LISTEN FOR ALL THREE LAYERS — bell at the apex first: a GALLOP RHYTHM (decompensation) · an APICAL PANSYSTOLIC MURMUR of MITRAL REGURGITATION, possibly an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation · a CAREY COOMBS MURMUR — the short mid-diastolic murmur of acute mitral valvulitis · and a PERICARDIAL FRICTION RUB.**

**THE TASK SAYS CHEST EXAMINATION, NOT AUSCULTATION — so all five respiratory steps, anterior, each with its expectation. And TWO LUNG FINDINGS WITH TWO CAUSES: REDUCED BREATH SOUNDS AND STONY DULLNESS at both bases FROM THE EFFUSIONS, and BIBASAL CREPITATIONS FROM PULMONARY OEDEMA.**

**ABDOMEN: I would expect HEPATOMEGALY with the edge well below the costal margin from hepatic congestion — a centimetre or two is normal at this age, so it is the degree and any tenderness that matter — and a SUSTAINED rise on hepatojugular reflux. In a child, look for FACIAL AND PERIORBITAL PUFFINESS rather than ankle oedema.**

**CLOSE ON THE OTHER JONES FEATURES AND THE PLAN: migratory arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules — then an ECHOCARDIOGRAM IN ANY CASE (subclinical carditis is itself a major criterion), streptococcal serology and throat swab, ESR, CRP, an ECG for the PR interval, URINALYSIS for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, admission, penicillin, heart failure treatment, NOTIFICATION AND REGISTRATION, and SECONDARY PENICILLIN PROPHYLAXIS FOR AT LEAST TEN YEARS.**

dx: **PULMONARY EMBOLISM, PROVISIONAL — a 40-year-old woman two days after a flight from New York, on the COMBINED PILL, with breathlessness and PLEURITIC chest pain. The examination is NORMAL, and that does not exclude it.** **This is a REASONING station wearing a chest examination: the examiner is watching for the moment your provisional diagnosis changes what your hands do next.**

**THE THREE SENTENCES THAT CARRY THE STATION: 'THE PAIN IS PLEURITIC, SO MY CORE EXAMINATION IS RESPIRATORY' · 'BECAUSE I SUSPECT A PULMONARY EMBOLISM, I WANT TO EXAMINE THE LOWER LIMBS FOR THE SOURCE OF THE CLOT' · 'THERE IS NO SIGNIFICANT SIZE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE CALVES.'**

**THIRTY-SECOND WIPE WITH A CHAPERONE OFFER — 'I will keep you covered in between, and I can offer you a chaperone' — then MOVE HER TO THE FAR END OF THE BED, which buys the access to inspect from above and reach behind. Candidates who panic at inspection skipped this.**

dx: **VERSION A — ECTOPIC PREGNANCY, or an INTRAUTERINE PREGNANCY WITH AN ADNEXAL PROBLEM, and ONE FINDING SEPARATES THEM.** Jane Kelleher, 27: a week of right lower quadrant pain, now constant at 6/10, vomited twice, a period about two weeks late, a faint home pregnancy test, brown spotting.

**THE UTERINE SIZE IS THE FORK. A NORMAL-SIZED UTERUS with a positive test, CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS and RIGHT ADNEXAL TENDERNESS → ECTOPIC PREGNANCY: 'the pregnancy is not where it should be.' A UTERUS ENLARGED TO ABOUT TEN WEEKS → an INTRAUTERINE pregnancy with a SEPARATE adnexal problem.**
**ASK FOR THE TEMPERATURE — in a young woman with pelvic pain, FEVER moves pelvic inflammatory disease up the list.**

**COMPLETE THE WHOLE ACUTE ABDOMEN STRUCTURE FIRST, in forty seconds for the peripheral survey and inspection: hands, face, CULLEN and GREY TURNER, bend down to look. Rushing this to reach the pelvis costs four scored steps.**

**PALPATION: cough (she points to the right lower quadrant), superficial palpation of all nine regions away from the pain — no tenderness — then DEEP: right lower quadrant tender. REBOUND IN ONE MOVEMENT — press, hold, warn, release. Version A: rebound NEGATIVE.** **Lifting off and coming back to test rebound separately inflicts the same pain twice.**
**PERCUSS THE SORE AREA for tenderness, auscultate below the umbilicus, and REQUEST the groins and a DRE — asking is the mark, even when the examiner skips it.**

**THE PELVIC EXAMINATION, OFFERED UNPROMPTED WITH ALL ITS ITEMS: INSPECTION — bleeding, discharge, rash, swelling · SPECULUM — cervix, tissue at the os, vaginal wall · BIMANUAL — CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS, UTERINE SIZE, uterine tenderness and contour, ADNEXAL masses or tenderness · plus a URINE PREGNANCY TEST and dipstick.**

**WHY A BIMANUAL WHEN YOU SUSPECT AN ECTOPIC: 'the examination is the tool I use to reach the diagnosis, not to confirm one I already hold. Without it I cannot tell an ectopic from an intrauterine pregnancy with an adnexal problem, from PID, or from torsion — and I have no bedside ultrasound. I would be gentle, and stop if she asked.'**

**FINDINGS SET 1 → ECTOPIC: send a serum β-hCG, arrange an URGENT TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND, involve gynaecology NOW. FINDINGS SET 2 → an adnexal problem in an intrauterine pregnancy — ovarian cyst, haemorrhagic cyst or its rupture, OVARIAN TORSION, salpingitis, and rarely HETEROTOPIC PREGNANCY — urgent ultrasound and gynaecology review.**

**A FOUR-BUCKET DIFFERENTIAL, not fifteen GI diagnoses: GASTROINTESTINAL — appendicitis, IBD, mesenteric adenitis, strangulated hernia · O&G — ectopic, torsion, cyst or rupture, PID · URINARY — ureteric colic, UTI, pyelonephritis · MUSCULOSKELETAL — septic arthritis of the hip, rectus sheath haematoma.**

BP 110/70 with no postural drop — HR 80 — RR 12 — T 36.9. The pain started yesterday around the umbilicus and has moved to the right lower quadrant; no appetite.

dx: **VERSION B — ACUTE APPENDICITIS WITH LOCALISED PERITONITIS.** Jane Kelleher, 27: pain that began around the umbilicus yesterday and MOVED to the right lower quadrant, anorexia, bowels normal today, last period three weeks ago. **The absent pregnancy makes this an appendicitis station — but it does NOT excuse you from the pelvic examination.**
**VITALS WITH THE TEMPERATURE: afebrile and haemodynamically stable here, and SAY SO.**
**THE FULL ACUTE ABDOMEN STRUCTURE BEFORE ANY SPECIAL TEST: peripheral survey, inspection with Cullen and Grey Turner, the COUGH — she localises to the right lower quadrant.**

**PALPATION: superficial of all nine regions starting away from the pain, RLQ last — no tenderness — then DEEP: right lower quadrant tender. Keep your hand where it is, then release: REBOUND POSITIVE — 'ow, that was worse.'**
**PERCUSS THE SORE AREA: TENDERNESS ON PERCUSSION supports LOCALISED PERITONITIS. Then bowel sounds, the groins, and the DRE with consent and chaperone.**

**THE PELVIC EXAMINATION IS STILL OFFERED, with every item — inspection, speculum, bimanual (CMT, uterine size, tenderness and contour, adnexae) — plus a URINE PREGNANCY TEST AND DIPSTICK. Here they are all normal and the test is negative, which is exactly what licenses the appendicitis diagnosis.**

**ONLY THEN THE SPECIAL TESTS, from her right side. ROVSING: press the LEFT lower quadrant → pain felt on the RIGHT. OBTURATOR: flex the right hip and knee and internally rotate by moving the ankle outwards → pain low down.** **If the bell goes here in Version A you have lost the diagnosis; nobody fails for omitting an obturator sign.**

**PSOAS if asked: roll her onto the left side and extend the right hip; pain suggests a RETROCAECAL appendix — omitted because it means repositioning a patient in pain. McBURNEY'S POINT: one third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus, palpated as part of the RLQ rather than as a separate test.**

**EXPLAIN IN PLAIN WORDS: the appendix is a small pouch where the small bowel joins the large bowel, low on the right; hers looks inflamed because it hurt when pressed, hurt MORE when released, and both extra tests brought the pain back to that spot. The usual treatment is an operation — most likely today — with bloods, a scan and the surgical team now.**

**THE FOUR-BUCKET DIFFERENTIAL: GASTROINTESTINAL — IBD, mesenteric adenitis, strangulated hernia · GYNAECOLOGICAL — ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion or cyst, PID · URINARY — ureteric colic, UTI · MUSCULOSKELETAL — septic arthritis of the hip.**

stem: Medical outpatient clinic. A 55-year-old man referred with abdominal swelling over the past three months. He drinks heavily. He is not acutely unwell and his observations are stable and afebrile.
tasks: Perform an abdominal examination, with a running commentary to your examiner
Explain your findings, your diagnosis and your differentials to the examiner

dx: **DECOMPENSATED CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE WITH ASCITES AND PORTAL HYPERTENSION — most likely ALCOHOL-RELATED CIRRHOSIS.** A 55-year-old heavy drinker with three months of abdominal swelling, NOT acutely unwell. **This is the examination the acute abdomen station FORBIDS.**

**THREE ITEMS ARE THE STATION: the LIVER SPAN measured in centimetres in the mid-clavicular line · the FLUID THRILL · SHIFTING DULLNESS. A candidate who names twenty peripheral signs and never measures a span has failed; one who names six and does all three has passed.**
**EXPOSE FROM THE CHEST DOWN TO THE HIPS — you need the chest for spider naevi, gynaecomastia and loss of body hair. Exposing only to the umbilicus loses them.**

**THE FLAPPING TREMOR IS HELD 15–30 SECONDS: arms out, wrists back 'as if stopping traffic', fingers spread. A flap tested for three seconds is a flap you will not see. It indicates HEPATIC ENCEPHALOPATHY — and also occurs in CO2 retention and uraemia.**

**THE PERIPHERAL SIGNS CANDIDATES OMIT: LEUKONYCHIA · PROXIMAL MYOPATHY ('lift both arms above your head') · PAROTID ENLARGEMENT (in front of and below the ears) · CONSCIOUS LEVEL. Plus palmar erythema, Dupuytren's, SPIDER NAEVI COUNTED (more than FIVE is abnormal, blanching from the centre), scleral icterus, gynaecomastia, loss of body hair, the left supraclavicular fossa. Finish the peripheries by 3:30.**

**THE LIVER SPAN, NARRATED: from the right iliac fossa up on each expiration with the RADIAL BORDER OF THE INDEX FINGER — edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, firm, smooth, non-tender — then PERCUSS DOWN FROM ABOVE THE NIPPLE in the mid-clavicular line for the upper border — dull at the fifth intercostal space — SPAN 15 cm, enlarged; normal 8 to 12.** **If you cannot feel the edge, SAY SO, use the costal margin as the lower border, and still give a number.**

**SPLEEN FROM THE RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA — a large spleen can reach it, and starting at the umbilicus palpates straight over it. Roll to the right lateral position to confirm, percuss CASTELL'S POINT (dull on inspiration supports splenomegaly), and ballot both kidneys.**

**SHIFTING DULLNESS IN FOUR STEPS: percuss from the umbilicus out to the flank until dull · KEEP YOUR FINGER ON THAT SPOT · roll him TOWARDS you · WAIT ABOUT THIRTY SECONDS and re-percuss the same point — now resonant. FLUID THRILL: the PATIENT'S OWN HAND edge-down in the MIDLINE to stop the wave travelling through fat, then flick one side and feel the other.**

**Shifting dullness is MORE SENSITIVE and detects smaller volumes; a fluid thrill is MORE SPECIFIC and suggests a large volume. Ultrasound beats both — but the bedside tests are what tell you to order it.**

**CLOSE WITH THE THREE OFFERS AND AN AETIOLOGY SCREEN: legs for pitting oedema · external genitalia for TESTICULAR ATROPHY with consent and chaperone · DRE for melaena · a formal encephalopathy assessment. Then the diagnosis, the differentials beyond alcohol (HBV, HCV, fatty liver, haemochromatosis, autoimmune, HCC) and for the ascites itself (malignancy, right heart failure, nephrotic syndrome), and the plan.**

stem: Emergency department. A 60-year-old man with abdominal pain and constipation — no bowel motion for two days, vomiting. He had an appendicectomy in his twenties. Observations are stable. Inside the room: a mannequin torso on the bed and a person seated in a chair. An abdominal X-ray is on the wall or handed to you.
The recall variant: the person in the chair is the patient's SON, and the patient is the mannequin.
tasks: Perform an abdominal examination
Explain your findings and your diagnosis to the examiner
Interpret the abdominal X-ray provided

dx: **SIMPLE SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION, MOST LIKELY ADHESIONAL** — a 60-year-old with two days of absolute constipation, green vomiting and distension, an APPENDICECTOMY in his twenties, a soft non-tender abdomen, and a film showing dilated central small bowel loops. **A mannequin on the bed, a person in the chair, and a film to read.**

**CLARIFY THE ROOM IN THE FIRST FIVE SECONDS: 'am I examining the model on the bed, and is this gentleman the patient?' In one recall the person in the chair is the SON and the patient is the mannequin — candidates who rehearsed only one script freeze.**

**THE SON VARIANT IS A SMALL CHANGE: consent, explanation and history questions go to the SON · the examination goes to the MANNEQUIN · 'does that hurt?' goes to the EXAMINER · and ONE sentence — 'I would confirm the patient's own consent for the examination and for discussing his care with his son.'** **Refusing to speak to the son on confidentiality grounds, or never mentioning consent, both fail.**

**THE HISTORY WHILE YOU WORK, and flatus is the question: last bowel motion · HAS HE PASSED ANY WIND SINCE (no) · the vomiting — how often and what COLOUR (green, six or seven times) · distension · weight loss or blood · PREVIOUS OPERATIONS. ABSOLUTE CONSTIPATION = no faeces AND no flatus.**

**INSPECT THE MANNEQUIN PROPERLY: no Cullen, no Grey Turner, a RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA SCAR consistent with an open appendicectomy, symmetrical generalised DISTENSION, no visible peristalsis — and bend down to look across.**

**DO NOT INVENT FINDINGS: superficial and deep palpation — no tenderness, guarding or mass; 'as there is no tenderness, rebound cannot meaningfully be assessed'; RESONANT throughout, consistent with gaseous distension. Bowel sounds PRESENT — report present or absent; if abnormal, describe the character: HIGH-PITCHED AND TINKLING in mechanical obstruction, ABSENT in ileus or a late obstruction.**

**GROINS AND RECTUM ARE CAUSES YOU CAN FIND AT THE BEDSIDE: inguinal regions and scrotum for an OBSTRUCTED HERNIA · DRE — empty or loaded, a mass, blood. An EMPTY rectum supports a proximal mechanical obstruction; a LOADED rectum points to faecal impaction, managed very differently.**

**THE FILM, SYSTEMATICALLY: supine AXR, identity and date — MULTIPLE DILATED LOOPS, CENTRALLY PLACED, with folds crossing the FULL WIDTH — VALVULAE CONNIVENTES — so SMALL BOWEL, over 3 cm · NO GAS IN THE RECTUM · no free gas, no abnormal calcification · bones and lung bases unremarkable. Small bowel obstruction.**
**NAME A CAUSE, NOT JUST 'OBSTRUCTION': adhesions from the appendicectomy. The soft, non-tender abdomen suggests a SIMPLE rather than strangulated obstruction.**

**EXPLAIN AND MANAGE: rest the bowel, drip, nasogastric tube — 'quite often it settles by itself over a day or two' — surgical team, transfer if it does not settle or the blood supply is threatened. To the examiner: nil by mouth, IV fluid, NG tube, catheter, bloods with LACTATE, erect CXR and CT abdomen and pelvis, surgical referral, MedSTAR if rural.**

**HISTORY while you work: last motion · FLATUS · vomiting frequency and colour · distension · weight loss and blood · OPERATIONS.**
**INSPECT THE MANNEQUIN: Cullen, Grey Turner, the RIF SCAR, distension, peristalsis — bend down to look.**
**Palpation of nine regions superficial and deep — NON-TENDER, reported plainly. Ask the examiner about tenderness if the patient is the mannequin.**
**Percussion — RESONANT throughout. Bowel sounds PRESENT, with the character answer ready.**
**GROINS and scrotum for a hernia. DRE — empty or loaded, mass, blood — and INTERPRET IT.**
**THE FILM: systematic read — small versus large bowel, gas in the rectum, free gas.**

pefe: **Given on request: no hernia · rectum EMPTY, no mass, no blood. Observations stable.**
**Film: dilated central loops with VALVULAE CONNIVENTES, >3 cm, no rectal gas, no free gas → SMALL BOWEL OBSTRUCTION.**

**Numbers: small bowel dilated >3 cm · colon >6 cm · caecum >9 cm · adhesional obstruction may be managed conservatively for about 48 hours without peritonism · examination finished by 6:00, film read by 7:00.** VERIFY.
**Large versus small bowel: LARGE bowel is PERIPHERAL, with HAUSTRA that do NOT cross the full width; small bowel is CENTRAL with valvulae conniventes crossing it.**

**OPERATE IMMEDIATELY FOR: peritonism, fever, tachycardia, a RISING LACTATE, FREE GAS on the erect film, a STRANGULATED HERNIA, or a CAECUM beyond about 9 cm — any of these means it is no longer a simple obstruction.**

**VARIANT — COFFEE-BEAN FILM: a single massively dilated loop with a dense central line, arising from the PELVIS and pointing to the LEFT UPPER QUADRANT = SIGMOID VOLVULUS → resuscitate, flexible sigmoidoscopic decompression with a flatus tube; theatre if ischaemia is suspected; elective sigmoid colectomy discussed. Arising from the RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA = CAECAL VOLVULUS in a younger patient → operative management.**

**VARIANT — FAECAL LOADING FILM: mottled faecal material to the rectum with rectal gas and no dilated small bowel, matching a LOADED rectum → review opioids and anticholinergics, suppositories or enema, manual evacuation if needed, then a regular bowel regimen.**

stem: Version A: Emergency department. A 35-year-old man with abdominal pain, fever, vomiting and diarrhoea for two days; observations in the notes. Lying BP 118/76, pulse 92; standing 96/64, pulse 112 — RR 16 — T 37.8.

Version B (February 2026 recall): Emergency department. A patient with vomiting and diarrhoea. Your ONLY task is to assess hydration status and report your findings — same eight minutes for a quarter of the work.
tasks: Assess his hydration status
Perform a focused abdominal examination
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the examiner

dx: **ACUTE INFECTIVE GASTROENTERITIS WITH MODERATE DEHYDRATION — a 35-year-old with two days of crampy abdominal pain, fever, vomiting and watery diarrhoea, two workmates affected, a roadhouse meal, dizziness on standing, and a soft non-tender abdomen.** **Three tasks, and hydration is scored SEPARATELY from the abdomen.**
**HYDRATION IS A FULL, STRUCTURED EXAMINATION IN ITS OWN RIGHT — not two sentences before the abdomen.**

**ASK FOR THE LYING AND STANDING BLOOD PRESSURES, AND ASK AGAIN IF FOBBED OFF: 'may I specifically have the standing blood pressure? A normal lying pressure does not exclude significant volume depletion.'** **Here: lying 118/76, pulse 92 → standing 96/64, pulse 112 — a drop of 22 systolic and 12 diastolic with a rise in pulse = POSTURAL HYPOTENSION.**

**SAY THE TECHNIQUE: rest supine five minutes · SYSTOLIC BY PALPATION FIRST, then confirm by auscultation, to avoid an AUSCULTATORY GAP · stand him and repeat at ONE AND THREE MINUTES with the pulse · ask whether he feels dizzy.**

**THE PERIPHERAL SURVEY, each sign named: alert and orientated · CAPILLARY REFILL prolonged at three seconds · TURGOR reduced, the fold tents · LOW-VOLUME radial pulse · warm dry peripheries · SUNKEN EYES · 'could you OPEN YOUR MOUTH for me?' — DRY mucous membranes, no pooled saliva.**

**ASK FOR THE CHARTS, THEN GRADE IT: fluid balance chart, urine output and a recorded weight → 'postural hypotension, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, reduced turgor, sunken eyes, dry mucosa and reduced urine output — MODERATE DEHYDRATION, and he needs INTRAVENOUS rather than oral rehydration.'**

**DO THE WHOLE ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION EVEN THOUGH YOU EXPECT IT TO BE NORMAL — and report the normal result as a finding, not an apology: it is what removes APPENDICITIS, OBSTRUCTION and DIVERTICULITIS from the top of the list. Include the groins and a DRE looking specifically for BLOOD.**

**CHOOSE ONE DOMINANT COMPLAINT rather than hunting for one diagnosis that explains all four symptoms: 'I will take ABDOMINAL PAIN as the dominant complaint.' Gastroenteritis is then offered as a diagnosis of exclusion with the dangerous mimics named.**

**THE TWO OTHERS THAT EXPLAIN ALL FOUR SYMPTOMS ARE NAMED FIRST: APPENDICITIS and INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE. Then by system — GI (diverticulitis, pancreatitis, obstruction, C. DIFFICILE, bowel cancer), URINARY (pyelonephritis, calculus, UTI), O&G in a woman (ectopic, PID, torsion), METABOLIC (DKA).**

**VERSION B — ONE TASK ONLY, hydration: candidates finish in three minutes and stand in silence. USE THE TIME — the full postural technique, every peripheral sign with its normal value, the JVP from the sternal angle, the charts and a weight, the grading, what the grade changes, and the bedside tests: capillary GLUCOSE AND KETONES, urine dipstick, and a PREGNANCY TEST in a woman.**
plan: **Vitals — AND THE LYING AND STANDING BLOOD PRESSURES. Ask again if told 'stable'.**
**Name the POSTURAL DROP and the compensatory tachycardia. Describe the technique: supine 5 min, palpatory then auscultatory, 1 and 3 minutes.**
**WIPE: hydration then abdomen explained, exposure, wash hands, analgesia.**
**HYDRATION: consciousness · capillary refill · turgor · pulse volume · peripheries · sunken eyes · OPEN THE MOUTH — mucous membranes and saliva.**
**Ask for the FLUID BALANCE CHART, URINE OUTPUT and a WEIGHT. GRADE IT — moderate — and say it means IV rehydration.**
**Abdomen: Cullen, Grey Turner, scars, distension — bend down. Cough. Superficial and deep palpation — soft, generalised crampy discomfort only.**
**Percussion, bowel sounds, groins, DRE for BLOOD.**
**Plain-language explanation — a tummy bug, the concern is the fluid lost — drip, antiemetic, bloods, and red-flag return advice.**
**ONE DOMINANT COMPLAINT, then gastroenteritis as most likely, appendicitis and IBD named, then the system-based list.**
**Plan: bloods with lactate, glucose and ketones, IV sodium chloride, antiemetic — and NO ROUTINE ANTIBIOTICS.**
pefe: **Vitals: lying BP 118/76, pulse 92 · STANDING BP 96/64, pulse 112 · RR 16 · T 37.8 °C. Fluid balance negative by about 1.5 L, urine output poor, no weight available. Groins normal, DRE normal, no blood.**

**Numbers: POSTURAL DROP ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes · capillary refill <2 s · supine rest 5 min before the lying reading · moderate dehydration 5–10% of body weight · resuscitation bolus 20 mL/kg sodium chloride 0.9% · C. difficile oral vancomycin 125 mg QID for 10 days · food handlers excluded until 48 hours symptom-free.** VERIFY.

**Rehydration: MILD — oral rehydration solution in small frequent volumes (the glucose and sodium matter; water or soft drink is not equivalent). MODERATE to SEVERE or persistent vomiting — IV sodium chloride 0.9%, a bolus of about 20 mL/kg if shocked, then REASSESS; check electrolytes before adding potassium; reassess the postural BP and urine output rather than working to a fixed volume.** VERIFY.

**Why turgor misleads: elasticity falls with age, so an older patient can tent without being dry, and an obese patient can have normal turgor while depleted — weight the POSTURAL BP, URINE OUTPUT and MUCOUS MEMBRANES more heavily.**

**Three easy misses: DIABETIC KETOACIDOSIS (capillary glucose and ketones) · ECTOPIC PREGNANCY in any woman (β-hCG) · SEPSIS in an older patient, where the only signs may be confusion and a postural drop.**
**Safety net: come back if unable to keep anything down, if there is BLOOD, if the pain becomes severe or moves to one spot, or if he STOPS PASSING URINE.**
**Antibiotics are NOT routine. Stool sample for blood, prolonged symptoms, recent antibiotics or hospitalisation, travel, or public-health reasons.**

stem: Hospital ward. A 54-year-old man admitted after a brief episode of feeling weak and clumsy down one side, which has now resolved. He is alert and comfortable; vital signs stable.
tasks: Perform a basic neurological physical examination with running commentary
State your findings and where you would localise any abnormality

dx: **A RIGHT PRONATOR DRIFT — the only abnormality in an otherwise normal four-limb screen — in a 54-year-old man after a brief, resolved episode of right-sided weakness and clumsiness. That LOCALISES TO THE LEFT CEREBRAL HEMISPHERE, and in this history means a TRANSIENT ISCHAEMIC ATTACK until proven otherwise.**

**DECODE AND DECLARE IN THE FIRST FIFTEEN SECONDS: 'I will perform a SCREENING neurological examination of ALL FOUR LIMBS — inspection, tone, power, reflexes, screening sensation and coordination — COMPARING BOTH SIDES THROUGHOUT, with gait at the end if safe.' 'Basic' means screening — not one limb exhaustively, and not cranial nerves. Declaring it makes brevity read as design rather than omission.**
**THE GLOBAL LOOK IS FREE MARKS: alert and comfortable, SPEECH FLUENT, FACE SYMMETRICAL, no tremor or involuntary movement, no mobility aid at the bedside.**

**COMPARE LEFT AGAINST RIGHT MOVEMENT BY MOVEMENT — testing one whole arm and then the other hides asymmetry ninety seconds apart. Upper limbs C5 to T1: shoulder abduction C5, elbow flexion C5/6, extension C7, grip C8, finger abduction T1. Biceps, supinator, triceps.**

**THE TEST THAT MAKES THE STATION: 'hold both arms straight out, PALMS UP, and CLOSE YOUR EYES' — HELD FOR A FULL TEN SECONDS. The right arm slowly pronates and sinks. Omitting drift because power was 5/5 is the error: DRIFT DETECTS SUBTLE PYRAMIDAL WEAKNESS THAT FORMAL POWER TESTING MISSES, and it takes fifteen seconds.**

**NAME IT AND CHANGE FOCUS OUT LOUD: 'there is a pronator drift of the right arm. That is an UPPER MOTOR NEURON sign and the only abnormality so far. I will pay particular attention to the right side for the rest of the examination.'**

**LOWER LIMBS, WITH THE PYRAMIDAL SCREEN: tone and ANKLE CLONUS · hip flexion L2/3, knee extension L3/4, knee flexion L5/S1, dorsiflexion L4/5, great-toe extension L5, plantarflexion S1/2 · knee and ankle jerks · PLANTAR RESPONSES — 'this may feel unpleasant' — among the most informative ten seconds in a possible pyramidal lesion.**

**SCREENING SENSATION WITH AN ESCALATION RULE: light touch at C5, C6, C8, L3, L5 and S1, compared side to side — 'had any point been abnormal I would have mapped it fully and added vibration and proprioception.' That sentence converts brevity into a deliberate decision. When told 'assume sensation is normal', obey instantly and say what you are omitting.**

**COORDINATION AND A SAFE GAIT: finger-nose with the arm fully straight, rapid alternating movements, heel-shin — then 'HAVE YOU HAD ANY FALLS OR DIZZINESS?' before walking him to the wall, TURNING and back, WALKING BESIDE HIM.**

**LOCALISE BEFORE YOU DIAGNOSE, then act: 'a right pronator drift with no other sign localises to the LEFT CEREBRAL HEMISPHERE — the corticospinal pathway — and in this history my leading diagnosis is a TIA.' Time-critical even though he looks well: GLUCOSE now, ECG for AF, same-day TIA pathway with brain and carotid imaging, vascular risk factors, antithrombotic therapy with the stroke service — and NO DRIVING until assessed, documented.**
plan: **DECODE AND DECLARE the four-limb screen. WIPE, exposure of arms and legs, consent, ask about pain.**
**Global observation: alert, speech fluent, face symmetrical, no tremor, no aids.**
**Upper limbs: inspection, tone at wrist, elbow and shoulder, POWER C5–T1 compared movement by movement, biceps, supinator, triceps.**
**PRONATOR DRIFT — palms up, eyes closed, TEN FULL SECONDS. Name it, call it UMN, change focus aloud.**
**Lower limbs: inspection, tone, ANKLE CLONUS, POWER L2–S2, knee and ankle jerks, PLANTARS.**
**Screening sensation in six dermatomes with the ESCALATION RULE — or obey the skip and state the omission.**
**Coordination: finger-nose, rapid alternating movements, heel-shin.**
**FALLS QUESTION, then GAIT with a turn, walking beside him.**
**Summary with EXPLICIT NEGATIVES, then LOCALISE — left hemisphere — then DIAGNOSE — TIA.**
**Plan: glucose, ECG, same-day TIA pathway, imaging, risk factors, antithrombotics, no driving. Completion sentence: cranial nerves, full sensory, cardiovascular, cognition and speech.**
pefe: **Findings: no wasting, normal tone, NO CLONUS, power 5/5 throughout, symmetrical reflexes, DOWNGOING plantars, intact screening sensation, normal coordination and gait — and a RIGHT PRONATOR DRIFT that appears ONLY if tested.**

**Numbers: MRC 0–5 · GCS 3–15 in three components · >3 beats of clonus is sustained · drift held 10 seconds · C5–T1 upper limb, L2–S2 lower limb power, L1–S1 lower limb sensation · 128 Hz for vibration · biceps C5/6, triceps C7, knee L3/4, ankle S1/2.** VERIFY.

**The examiner interrupts three times — about 2 min 'assume the reflexes are normal', about 4 min 'assume sensation is normal, move on', about 5:30 'tell me your findings now'. Each time: 'thank you — I will move on to…', stop mid-movement if necessary, and say what remains. NEVER 'can I just finish this?'**

**IF THE DRIFT IS ABSENT: do not manufacture a finding — 'this is a normal screening neurological examination. A normal examination does not exclude a transient ischaemic attack — by definition the deficit has resolved — and the urgency of assessment is unchanged.' That sentence scores as well as finding the drift.**

**To the patient, without jargon: 'when you held your arms out with your eyes closed, the right one drifted a little, which suggests the signal from the brain to that arm is not quite getting through as it should.' Avoid 'pronator drift', 'upper motor neuron', 'pyramidal' in front of him.**

**VARIANT B — GIDDINESS ('relevant' means CHOOSE and JUSTIFY): cranial nerves with NYSTAGMUS and eye movements, cerebellar testing in upper and lower limbs, GAIT AND ROMBERG, a screening limb examination for focal deficit, and a LYING AND STANDING BLOOD PRESSURE — and ask whether it is spinning or light-headedness. A rote four-limb screen that never tests coordination, gait or postural BP chooses badly.**

**VARIANT C — CONSCIOUS STATE: open with GCS in three components (e.g. E3 V4 M5 = 12), pupils, and BSL immediately; rely on TONE, REFLEXES, PLANTARS and symmetry of response to a painful stimulus — trapezius squeeze or supraorbital pressure, not a sternal rub. Commercial driving: check the Austroads standards before quoting a timeframe.** VERIFY.

stem: Regional general practice. A 61-year-old carpenter with six weeks of right-sided neck pain radiating down the arm, tingling in the thumb and index finger, and a grip that feels weaker. Worse looking up or turning his head. Vital signs normal.
tasks: Perform an upper limb neurological examination with running commentary
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient

dx: **RIGHT C6 CERVICAL RADICULOPATHY** — a 61-year-old carpenter with six weeks of right neck pain radiating down the arm, tingling in the thumb and index finger, a grip that gives way, worse looking up or turning his head. **THREE AGREEING FINDINGS: weakness of right elbow flexion and wrist extension at 4/5 · REDUCED right biceps and supinator reflexes · REDUCED SENSATION in the right C6 dermatome.**

**THE TEMPTATION IS BUILT IN: 'my mate reckons it's carpal tunnel.' Acknowledge it and PARK IT — 'that is a very reasonable thought and I will come back to it once I have examined you.' Candidates who take the bait start palpating the wrist and testing Tinel's and never finish the examination they were asked for.**
**DECLARE THE SCAFFOLD AND EXPOSE BOTH ARMS TO THE SHOULDERS — the whole station is comparison, and you cannot compare through a sleeve.**

**INSPECT THE DORSUM AS WELL AS THE PALMS: interosseous guttering shows from the back, thenar wasting from the side. TONE in more than one plane, with SUPINATION AND PRONATION at the wrist, then PRONATOR DRIFT.**

**POWER C5–T1, MRC GRADED, SIDE BY SIDE MOVEMENT BY MOVEMENT: shoulder abduction C5 · ELBOW FLEXION C5/6 — 4/5 on the right · WRIST EXTENSION C6 — 4/5 on the right · elbow extension C7 · grip C8 · finger abduction T1. Testing one whole arm and then the other means a 4/5 never stands out against its partner.**

**REFLEXES WITH BOTH ARMS POSITIONED IDENTICALLY, AND REINFORCE BEFORE CALLING ONE REDUCED: biceps and supinator REDUCED on the right, triceps normal — 'please clench your teeth when I say' — still reduced.**

**SENSATION BY DERMATOME, demonstrated on the sternum first: C5 lateral upper arm, C6 THUMB, C7 MIDDLE FINGER, C8 little finger, T1 medial forearm. Reduced over the right thumb and lateral forearm — and NAME THE SPARED MIDDLE FINGER, because that single negative is what EXCLUDES THE MEDIAN NERVE.**

**ASSEMBLE, LOCALISE, THEN DIAGNOSE — and exclude three alternatives with reasons: CARPAL TUNNEL (dermatomal loss with a spared middle finger, neck pain, a depressed reflex) · CERVICAL MYELOPATHY (no upper motor neuron signs) · PANCOAST TUMOUR (no small-muscle wasting, no Horner's — but he smokes, so a chest X-ray).**

**ASK WHAT WORRIES HIM BEFORE EXPLAINING — 'whether I can keep working, I'm on the tools six days a week' — and let that shape the explanation. Never say 'C6 radiculopathy' to a carpenter: 'a nerve where it leaves your neck is being pinched.'**

**THE SENTENCE THAT ANSWERS THE MATE: 'carpal tunnel affects a nerve at the wrist and usually numbs the thumb, index and middle fingers. Your middle finger is completely normal, you have neck pain, and one of your reflexes is quieter on that side — that combination points to the neck, not the wrist.'** **Most settle in 6–12 weeks: keep working with modified overhead and heavy work, physiotherapy, a letter for the employer, ReturnToWorkSA if work-related, and a safety net.**
plan: **DECLARE the full upper limb scaffold. WIPE, BOTH ARMS EXPOSED to the shoulders. Park the carpal tunnel question in one sentence.**
**INSPECTION of palms AND dorsum: thenar and hypothenar wasting, guttering, fasciculation, posture, tremor, scars.**
**TONE in more than one plane including supination and pronation, both sides. PRONATOR DRIFT, ten seconds.**
**POWER C5–T1, MRC graded, side by side — find the 4/5 elbow flexion and wrist extension.**
**REFLEXES — arms positioned identically — biceps, supinator, triceps, with REINFORCEMENT.**
**SENSATION BY DERMATOME, sternum first, C5 to T1 — the C6 loss, and the SPARED MIDDLE FINGER named.**
**COORDINATION with the arm fully extended; rapid alternating movements.**
**Offer to complete: lower limbs and plantars, cervical spine with Spurling's, entrapment tests if indicated.**
**SUMMARY: three agreeing findings → right C6 root → radiculopathy, with three alternatives excluded.**
**Ask his worry, then the plain-English explanation, the answer to the mate, work advice, and the safety net.**
pefe: **Findings: no wasting or fasciculation, normal tone, no drift · power 4/5 right ELBOW FLEXION and WRIST EXTENSION, 5/5 elsewhere · right BICEPS and SUPINATOR reduced, triceps normal · reduced light touch over the right THUMB and LATERAL FOREARM, middle and little fingers normal · coordination normal.**

**The C-roots: C5 shoulder abduction, lateral upper arm · C6 elbow flexion and wrist extension, THUMB · C7 elbow extension, MIDDLE FINGER · C8 grip, little finger · T1 finger abduction, medial forearm. Biceps and supinator C5/6, triceps C7. Drift held 10 seconds.**
**Investigations: chest X-ray (smoker — Pancoast), glucose and TSH, and MRI of the cervical spine if weakness progresses or pain persists.**

That converts two omissions from gaps into judgement. The tendon hammer on the trolley is a distractor.**

Then the wound: open, bone visible, NO ACTIVE BLEEDING, dried blood, FOREIGN MATERIAL (glass), no dressing, deformed and swollen. Do not invent granulation tissue, muscle herniation or pulsatile bleeding.**

Say why no bony tenderness: a known fracture — pain without information.**

'I am UNABLE TO ASSESS active movements because of pain — I'd record the motor component as UNASSESSABLE RATHER THAN NORMAL, and repeat it once analgesia has taken effect.'**

Report your findings to the examiner
Explain to the patient what you have found and what will happen next

dx: **THE CORE THYROID EXAMINATION — the framework for every thyroid station.** **Jane Whitmore, 38, regional SA, four months of a front-of-neck swelling, feels well. Examine with a RUNNING COMMENTARY (no history) → report → explain.** **In the index version EVERY FINDING IS NORMAL — so the marks are entirely in TECHNIQUE, COMMENTARY and the EXPLANATION, not in spotting pathology.**

**SIX STEPS, IN ORDER: INSPECT → SIP AND SWALLOW → PALPATE → PERCUSS → AUSCULTATE → PEMBERTON'S.** **Palpation itself has FOUR PARTS FROM BEHIND (the gland, thrills, the second sip, the nodes) PLUS ONE FROM THE FRONT (the trachea).** **Hands in the LOWER HALF of the neck — the thyroid sits below the cricoid.**

**THE TRAP THAT FAILS CANDIDATES: PALPATING IN SILENCE, then saying ‘the thyroid feels normal, examiner.’ That is SIX SEPARATE MARKS COMPRESSED INTO ONE SENTENCE.** **Say all six key points aloud — SIZE · LOWER BORDER · CONSISTENCY · NODULARITY · TENDERNESS · MOBILITY — and ASK the patient about tenderness rather than declaring it.** **Generic commentary (‘looking for swelling, redness and rashes’) scores nothing; NAME THE FOUR SPECIFIC INSPECTION FINDINGS: visible mass, engorged veins, scars, the cricoid-to-notch contour.**

**THE WATER IS USED TWICE, AND THEY ARE SEPARATE MARKS — once LOOKING, once FEELING.** **And the instruction is sip → HOLD → get your eyes into position → ‘SWALLOW NOW’.** **‘Take a sip and swallow’ as one instruction means the swallow happens while you are still straightening up — the role-player is briefed to swallow immediately if you say it that way. Tell her to hold it, and she waits.**

**THE LOWER BORDER IS THE QUIET HINGE OF THE EXAMINATION.** **If you CAN feel it, the gland is confined to the neck. If you CANNOT, you must think RETROSTERNAL EXTENSION — which is exactly why percussion over the manubrium and Pemberton's follow.** **Percussion is 3–4 TAPS, SIDE TO SIDE ACROSS THE MANUBRIUM — a single tap, or percussing DOWN the sternum, is a named trap.**

**THE NODE SWEEP ENDS AT SUPRACLAVICULAR — the group that matters in malignancy.** **Stopping at the jugular chain is one of the three common traps.** **Eight groups: submental, submandibular, pre-auricular, post-auricular, occipital, anterior cervical, posterior cervical, supraclavicular.**

**THE SCRIPTED EXAMINER CHALLENGE — have this word for word**: *‘Would you perform Pemberton's sign if you had found the thyroid to be of normal size?’* → **‘No, Examiner — in CLINICAL PRACTICE I WOULDN'T, because the sign only becomes relevant when there is a GOITRE THAT MAY EXTEND RETROSTERNALLY. But FOR COMPLETENESS OF MY EXAMINATION IN THIS SETTING, I would still like to perform it.’** **Then DO IT. NAMING A MANOEUVRE AND SKIPPING IT IS WORSE THAN NEVER MENTIONING IT — it is an automatic fail.**

**APPROACH AND EXPOSURE ARE SCORED.** **Full WIPE · consent at EACH stage · WARN before standing behind · ask about tenderness.** **She wears a SCARF and keeps it on: raise it — ‘would you mind slipping that off for a couple of minutes so I can see the whole neck? I can pull the curtain across, and I'm happy to have a chaperone with us.’** **Examining through it is an automatic fail; reaching for it unasked is a conduct concern (she says ‘oh —’ and pulls back).**

**THE EXPLANATION — reassuring about the examination, honest about its limits**: **‘The thyroid is a small BUTTERFLY-SHAPED GLAND at the front of the neck, just below the Adam's apple. It makes the hormone that SETS THE SPEED YOUR BODY RUNS AT. Today I couldn't feel any lump or swelling, it wasn't tender, and there were no enlarged glands. Everything I could check was normal, which is reassuring. BUT AN EXAMINATION ON ITS OWN CAN'T TELL ME EVERYTHING, AND YOU HAVE DEFINITELY NOTICED SOMETHING — so I'd like a BLOOD TEST to check the gland is working at the right speed, and an ULTRASOUND, which looks far more closely than my fingers can.’** **Then the FNA pathway if the scan shows anything, and a safety-net.**

**THE HIDDEN AGENDA: HER AUNT HAD HER THYROID REMOVED FOR ‘A GROWTH’ THAT NOBODY EXPLAINED.** **She never volunteers worry; she raises ‘is it cancer?’ only if invited, or quietly at the very end.** **‘That's EXACTLY THE RIGHT QUESTION, and I'd rather you asked it than worried on your own. MOST NECK LUMPS LIKE THIS ARE NOT CANCER — the great majority are a benign nodule or a slightly enlarged gland. What I CAN'T do is PROMISE you that from an examination alone, and I DON'T WANT TO GIVE YOU A REASSURANCE I CAN'T BACK UP. That's exactly why we do the blood test and the ultrasound.’** **Blanket reassurance is the commonest way to lose Task 3 after perfect Tasks 1 and 2 — she pushes back: ‘how can you be sure without any tests?’**

**Inspection front and side — the four named findings and the cricoid-to-notch line — then the FIRST SIP: hold → position → ‘swallow now’ → ‘moves with swallowing’.** **Hands behind the patient by 1:30.**
**Warn, stand behind, palpate: displace the trachea LEFT to feel the RIGHT lobe, RIGHT to feel the LEFT, then the ISTHMUS below the cricoid. SAY THE SIX KEY POINTS, ASKING about tenderness.**

**Explain in plain words, INVITE CONCERNS, answer ‘is it cancer?’ honestly, answer ‘do I have to go to Adelaide?’ (possibly for the scan — PATS helps with travel), SAFETY-NET, commit to reviewing her yourself.**

My differential for the reported swelling would be a small multinodular goitre or a benign solitary nodule; I would want to exclude a thyroglossal cyst and thyroid carcinoma. My plan is a TSH and a neck ultrasound, with ultrasound-guided FNA if the ultrasound shows a suspicious nodule, and review with the results.’**

**VARIANT 1 — RETROSTERNAL GOITRE.** Lower-neck swelling, distended superficial veins, lost lateral contour, diffusely enlarged and firm, **CANNOT FEEL THE LOWER BORDER**, dull over the left manubrium, **PEMBERTON'S POSITIVE**. → **‘Jane, are you light-headed or short of breath?’** → **‘This indicates THORACIC INLET OBSTRUCTION. I'd want a CT NECK AND THORAX, a FLOW–VOLUME LOOP, an URGENT ENDOCRINE SURGICAL OPINION, and I'd ask about ORTHOPNOEA AND STRIDOR.’**

There's a firm lump in the gland, and one of the glands above your collarbone feels firmer than I'd like. I'm NOT ABLE TO TELL YOU TODAY WHAT IT IS — that needs a scan and a small needle sample. I'm going to arrange it URGENTLY, THIS WEEK, and I'll RING YOU MYSELF with a time. Is there someone who can come with you?’**

**VARIANT 3 — PAINFUL GLAND AFTER A VIRAL ILLNESS.** Diffusely enlarged, exquisitely tender. → **SUBACUTE (DE QUERVAIN) THYROIDITIS: TSH, fT4 and inflammatory markers; expect an EARLY THYROTOXIC PHASE followed by a HYPOTHYROID PHASE; treat symptomatically with simple analgesia and NSAIDs, CORTICOSTEROIDS RESERVED FOR SEVERE PAIN.** VERIFY dosing against Therapeutic Guidelines. **TENDERNESS IS A FINDING YOU ONLY OBTAIN BY ASKING.**

**THE SAFETY-NET, verbatim**: **‘Please come back sooner if the swelling GETS BIGGER QUICKLY, if your voice becomes HOARSE, if you have any TROUBLE SWALLOWING OR BREATHING, or if you feel a HARD LUMP in your neck.’** **Then: ‘Does that all make sense — and what questions do you have?’**

dx: **GRAVES' DISEASE — thyrotoxicosis with a DIFFUSE HYPERVASCULAR GOITRE (thrill and bruit) and ORBITOPATHY.** **Daniel Okafor, 42, regional SA, six weeks of tiredness and feeling ‘wound up’; TSH suppressed, fT4 raised. Examine for thyrotoxicosis with a running commentary (no history) → report and COMMIT to a diagnosis → explain and PRESCRIBE SAFELY.**

**NAME THE EXAMINATION IN THE FIRST FIFTEEN SECONDS: ‘EXAMINER, GIVEN THE BLOOD RESULTS I'M GOING TO PERFORM AN EXAMINATION FOR THYROTOXICOSIS.’** **If the stem says ‘nervousness and tremor’ (Version B), the words PULL candidates into a tremor or upper-limb neurological examination — which is an AUTOMATIC FAIL.** **And ask for ARMS, NECK AND SHINS uncovered in the WIPE — never asking for the shins makes pretibial myxoedema unreportable, and the role-player won't offer them.**

**THE SINGLE COMMONEST ACCURACY ERROR IN THE STATION: reporting ‘no lid lag’ from a MOTIONLESS FACE.** **LID RETRACTION is an INSPECTION sign; LID LAG is a MOVEMENT sign and CANNOT be commented on unless you move the eye DOWNWARDS.** **Four manoeuvres, four separate findings: FROM THE FRONT (retraction, proptosis, chemosis), FROM ABOVE AND BEHIND (proptosis), H-PATTERN (ophthalmoplegia, diplopia), DOWNGAZE (lag).**

**THE HANDS BLOCK HAS FOUR TRAPS**: **1 ‘looks unwell’ instead of NAMING THE FACIAL SWEATING · 2 SKIPPING THE PAPER — a fine tremor is often invisible on the hands alone · 3 LOOKING at the palms rather than FEELING them · 4 SILENTLY TIMING THE PULSE for thirty seconds — ESTIMATE the rate, then STATE THE RHYTHM, which is the marked finding (AF would change the plan).**

**PICK UP THE HAMMER.** **‘I would also check the reflexes’ earns nothing. Elicit ONE — the BICEPS — and give the DIRECTION: HYPER → BRISK, HYPO → SLOW-RELAXING.** **All four limbs is the opposite error and burns the clock.** **Test PROXIMAL MYOPATHY against resistance — arms out like wings, stop me pushing them down — and ask about rising from a chair or climbing stairs.**

**DO NOT ABANDON THE NECK BECAUSE THE DIAGNOSIS IS OBVIOUS.** **The gland gets a cursory feel and percussion, auscultation and Pemberton's are dropped — but the neck examination is MARKED IN FULL whatever you have already worked out.** **Here it is what CLINCHES the diagnosis: diffuse, symmetrical, smooth, firm, with a THRILL AND A BRUIT — a hypervascular gland.**

**COMMIT, WITH THREE REASONS — and be ready for the examiner's ‘why Graves' rather than a toxic multinodular goitre?’**: **‘Three reasons. The gland is DIFFUSE AND SYMMETRICAL rather than nodular; it is HYPERVASCULAR with a THRILL AND A BRUIT; and there is ORBITOPATHY, which occurs in GRAVES' DISEASE and not in a toxic multinodular goitre. I would confirm with TSH-RECEPTOR ANTIBODIES.’** **The three Graves'-only signs: ORBITOPATHY, ACROPACHY, PRETIBIAL MYXOEDEMA.**

**THE EXPLANATION — the accelerator pedal**: **‘You have a gland in the front of your neck called the thyroid, and it works like the ACCELERATOR PEDAL for your body: it sets the speed everything runs at. Yours is STUCK TOO FAR DOWN — it's making far too much hormone, and that's why you feel wound up, why your heart is racing, why your hands shake and why you're losing weight without trying. The reason is GRAVES' DISEASE — an AUTOIMMUNE condition where your immune system makes an ANTIBODY that SWITCHES THE GLAND ON AND WON'T LET IT SWITCH OFF. It's COMMON, VERY TREATABLE, and NOBODY'S FAULT. It's also what's causing the changes around your eyes.’**

**THE THREE-TIER PLAN**: **‘First, a BETA-BLOCKER to settle the racing heart and the shakes — you should feel better within a few days. Second, a tablet that TURNS THE GLAND DOWN. Third, once you're stable, a PERMANENT FIX — either a dose of RADIOACTIVE IODINE you swallow, or an OPERATION. You DON'T DECIDE THAT TODAY.’** **Before the second tablet: FBC, LIVER FUNCTION and (in a woman) a PREGNANCY TEST. Review in FOUR WEEKS with repeat thyroid tests.**

**THE SAFETY COUNSELLING — MUST BE SAID OUT LOUD, AND NAMING THE DRUG WITHOUT IT IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL**: **‘The tablet is called CARBIMAZOLE. It works well, but it has ONE RARE AND SERIOUS SIDE EFFECT: in about ONE PERSON IN THREE HUNDRED it can DROP THE WHITE CELLS THAT FIGHT INFECTION. So this is the rule, and it MATTERS MORE THAN ANYTHING ELSE I'VE SAID TODAY — if you develop a SORE THROAT, MOUTH ULCERS, a FEVER, or you just feel UNWELL AND FLUEY, STOP THE TABLETS AND GET A BLOOD TEST THE SAME DAY. Don't wait to see if it settles. Can you tell me back what you'd do if you woke up with a sore throat?’** **TEACH-BACK IS SCORED — don't assume it landed.** **If a drug is named with no warning, the role-player pushes once: ‘are there any side effects I should know about?’**
plan: **WIPE, check identity, explain the whole examination in one sentence (hands, eyes, pulse, shoulders, a reflex, the neck, the shins), ask for ARMS, NECK AND SHINS uncovered, sit him on the edge of the bed — and NAME THE EXAMINATION TO THE EXAMINER.**

**General appearance — ANXIOUS, RESTLESS, FACIAL SWEATING, THIN.** **Hands palms down (onycholysis, acropachy), then turn them and FEEL the palms (warm, sweaty).** **Arms out, fingers spread → coarse tremor → PAPER ON THE DORSUM → fine tremor.** **Radial pulse: estimate the rate, STATE THE RHYTHM, note the wide pulse pressure, ‘I'd confirm with an ECG’.**
**Proximal myopathy against resistance, plus the stairs question → PICK UP THE HAMMER, one biceps jerk → ‘brisk — hyperreflexia, consistent with thyrotoxicosis’.**

**THE EYES, whatever is unfinished: FRONT → FROM ABOVE AND BEHIND → H-PATTERN (‘tell me if you see double or if it hurts’) → DOWNGAZE for lid lag.** **If he volunteers WASHED-OUT COLOUR, reduced vision or pain on movement → possible OPTIC NEUROPATHY, say so, same-day referral.**

**THE NECK — the FULL thyroid sequence, all six key points, THRILL, second sip, nodes, trachea, percussion, BRUIT, Pemberton's.** **Then chest (gynaecomastia, heart sounds), SHINS, and ‘to complete: observations, weight, full cardiovascular examination’.** **Stop examining at 4:50.**

**The 45-SECOND SUMMARY — positives, relevant negatives, COMMIT TO GRAVES' with the three reasons, differentials with why they're less likely, then the plan: ECG, TRAb, FBC and LFTs; beta-blocker; carbimazole after baselines WITH the agranulocytosis rule; endocrinology for definitive treatment; ask about smoking.**
**Explain — accelerator pedal, autoimmune, common, treatable, nobody's fault, the eyes → the THREE TIERS → baselines → THE SAFETY COUNSELLING WITH TEACH-BACK.**
**ASK ABOUT SMOKING — he admits ten a day only if asked — and offer to help him stop: ‘smoking is the SINGLE BIGGEST THING that makes the eye changes worse.’** **Four-week review, invite questions.**
pefe: **THE 45-SECOND SUMMARY, verbatim**: **‘I examined a 42-year-old man with six weeks of fatigue and agitation, a suppressed TSH and a raised free T4. Positive findings: anxious and restless with visible facial sweating; a fine tremor amplified on paper; a resting tachycardia of around 105, regular, with a wide pulse pressure; a brisk biceps jerk; bilateral lid retraction, lid lag and mild proptosis with full eye movements; and a diffuse, smooth, symmetrical goitre with a palpable thrill and an audible bruit. Relevant negatives: no onycholysis or acropachy, no proximal myopathy, no ophthalmoplegia or diplopia, no lymphadenopathy, central trachea, resonant percussion, negative Pemberton's, no gynaecomastia, no pretibial myxoedema. My diagnosis is GRAVES' DISEASE — a diffuse hypervascular goitre with a bruit, together with orbitopathy, which occurs in Graves' and not in the other causes of thyrotoxicosis. Differentials: toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma, less likely with a diffuse rather than nodular gland, and thyroiditis, less likely with a non-tender gland. Plan: ECG for AF, TSH-receptor antibodies, baseline FBC and liver function; a beta-blocker; after those baselines, carbimazole with explicit counselling that a sore throat or fever means stopping it and an urgent blood count; endocrinology for radioiodine or surgery; and smoking, which worsens eye disease.’**

**HIS QUESTIONS.** *‘Will I be on tablets forever? Am I going to need an operation?’* → **‘Not necessarily. A beta-blocker now, a tablet to turn the gland down, and later a conversation about a permanent fix — radioactive iodine you swallow, or an operation. You don't decide that today.’** *‘Is the radioactive stuff dangerous to my kids?’* → answer honestly; there are temporary precautions after radioiodine, which endocrinology will go through with him in detail. VERIFY *‘Are my eyes going to stay like this?’* → the eye changes often improve, and **stopping smoking is the single biggest thing he can do to help them.** **His underlying fear — cancer, or an operation on his neck — is voiced ONLY if you invite concerns.**

**WITHHELD UNLESS ASKED**: **the SMOKING (ten a day) · the GRITTY EYES · the LOOSER BOWELS (three or four times a day) · the WEIGHT LOSS FIGURE (4 kg in six weeks, eating more) · his SISTER'S THYROID · the SHINS.** **Also ask about amiodarone, thyroxine, supplements and ‘fat burners’ — exogenous causes of thyrotoxicosis (all negative here).**

**VARIANT 1 — TOXIC MULTINODULAR GOITRE.** Pulse ~130, **IRREGULARLY IRREGULAR — ATRIAL FIBRILLATION**; **NO EYE SIGNS**; gland **asymmetrically enlarged with multiple discrete nodules, NO THRILL, NO BRUIT.** → **‘Thyrotoxicosis due to a toxic multinodular goitre rather than Graves' — nodular rather than diffuse, no bruit, no eye signs. I'd confirm with a RADIONUCLIDE UPTAKE SCAN showing PATCHY uptake. The AF CHANGES MY PLAN: RATE CONTROL, STROKE-RISK ASSESSMENT AND ANTICOAGULATION, and RADIOIODINE is usually the definitive treatment of choice.’**

**VARIANT 2 — SUBACUTE (DE QUERVAIN) THYROIDITIS.** **‘Daniel, is that painful?’** → diffusely enlarged and **EXQUISITELY TENDER**, no thrill, no bruit, no eye signs, after a viral illness. → **‘The thyrotoxicosis is DESTRUCTIVE — stored hormone is LEAKING OUT, so UPTAKE IS LOW, NOT HIGH, and inflammatory markers are raised. CRITICALLY, A THIONAMIDE WOULD NOT HELP — the gland is not overproducing. Simple analgesia and NSAIDs, a beta-blocker for symptoms, steroids for severe pain, and warn him to EXPECT A HYPOTHYROID PHASE before recovery.’** VERIFY

**VARIANT 3 — SIGHT-THREATENING ORBITOPATHY.** **Marked bilateral proptosis, CHEMOSIS and CONJUNCTIVAL INJECTION, RESTRICTED UPGAZE with DIPLOPIA, and COLOURS LOOK WASHED OUT.** → **‘Loss of colour vision raises COMPRESSIVE OPTIC NEUROPATHY. I would check VISUAL ACUITY and COLOUR VISION formally, look for a RELATIVE AFFERENT PUPILLARY DEFECT, and make a SAME-DAY OPHTHALMOLOGY REFERRAL. High-dose corticosteroids after specialist discussion; RADIOIODINE IS CONTRAINDICATED WHILE THE EYE DISEASE IS ACTIVE. Smoking cessation is the single most important modifiable factor.’**

**PREGNANCY — the other half of safe prescribing.** **In a woman of childbearing age, ask about PREGNANCY AND CONTRACEPTION BEFORE prescribing a thionamide.** **FIRST TRIMESTER → PROPYLTHIOURACIL rather than carbimazole** VERIFY. **Prescribing without asking is an automatic fail.**

**THE SCORING DOMAINS** (0/1/2 each): **APPROACH** — full WIPE, NAMED the examination as thyrotoxicosis, asked for arms/neck/SHINS, consent at each stage, chaperone offered · **TECHNIQUE** — specific general appearance including facial sweating, nails, FELT the palms, hands then PAPER, pulse rate AND RHYTHM, proximal myopathy against resistance, a reflex ACTUALLY ELICITED, eyes FOUR WAYS, a COMPLETE thyroid examination, gynaecomastia and heart sounds, shins exposed · **ACCURACY** — retraction and lag distinguished correctly, reflex direction correct, no movement sign reported from a still face · **DIAGNOSIS** — committed to Graves' with at least three reasons, differentials rejected with reasons, TRAb/ECG/FBC/LFTs · **MANAGEMENT AND COMMUNICATION** — three-tier plan in plain English, beta-blocker, thionamide WITH the agranulocytosis rule, TEACH-BACK, pregnancy asked in a woman, smoking raised, follow-up.

Helen Marchetti, 40 — four months of tiredness, poor concentration, constipation and 6 kg weight gain; her mother has Hashimoto's. Bloods: TSH 18 mIU/L, fT4 low.
