dx: **OVERT PRIMARY HYPOTHYROIDISM, MOST LIKELY HASHIMOTO THYROIDITIS.** **Helen Marchetti, 40, regional SA, four months of tiredness, poor concentration, constipation and 6 kg weight gain; her mother has Hashimoto's; TSH 18, fT4 low.** **‘Fewer signs, higher stakes — the clothing, the eyebrows, the reflex.’**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE OF THE WHOLE STATION IS EXPOSURE AND CONSENT — THE HIGHEST-WEIGHTED ITEM.** **She is in a jacket, cardigan and scarf in a warm February room.** **Three wrong moves, all common: EXAMINING AROUND THE FABRIC; asking AT MINUTE FOUR when there is no time left; or saying ‘I would like to expose the neck’ TO THE EXAMINER without ever asking the patient.** **CONSENT IS A SCORED INTERACTION BETWEEN YOU AND HER. Ask INSIDE THE WIPE. NEVER REACH FOR HER CLOTHING — LET HER UNCOVER HERSELF.**

**THE EXPOSURE CONVERSATION — she resists once (‘Do I have to? I'm freezing in here’), then agrees ONLY IF GIVEN A REASON**: **‘I understand, and that's ACTUALLY USEFUL FOR ME TO KNOW. Can I explain why I'm asking? The gland sits right at the front of the neck and I have to see it and feel it — THROUGH FABRIC I'D MISS THINGS THAT MATTER. I'll be quick, and you can put everything straight back on. Shall I turn the heater up first?’** **DO NOT REPEAT THE REQUEST LOUDER. Give a reason, ask ‘WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS EASIER FOR YOU?’, offer PRIVACY, a CHAPERONE or a FEMALE COLLEAGUE. The same words work whether the barrier is cold, modesty or religious observance.**

**THE CLOTHING IS ALSO THE FIRST CLINICAL SIGN — SAY IT**: **‘She is dressed in a jacket, cardigan and scarf, which is NOT APPROPRIATE FOR THE WEATHER today — this suggests COLD INTOLERANCE.’** **Commenting on it is scored under exposure AND under general appearance.**

**THE BEST PERIPHERAL SIGN: THE DELAYED RELAXATION OF THE REFLEX (WOLTMAN).** **The jerk LOOKS NORMAL IN SIZE, so candidates report ‘reflexes normal’ and lose the best sign in the station. THE ABNORMALITY IS IN THE RELAXATION, NOT THE CONTRACTION.** **Strike the biceps and KEEP WATCHING FOR A FULL SECOND.** **Say both terms: ‘HYPOREFLEXIA’ is accepted AMC wording; ‘DELAYED RELAXATION PHASE’ shows you understand it.** **The role-player counts ‘one-and-two’ before the arm settles.**

**WHERE THE DIAGNOSIS IS OFTEN WON: THE FACE, CLOSE UP.** **Step in and look DELIBERATELY at the LATERAL END OF EACH EYEBROW — LOSS OF THE OUTER THIRD, the SIGN OF HERTOGHE.** **In one recall it was SIMULATED WITH SKIN-TONED TAPE, and candidates who glanced from a metre away while talking to the examiner lost the diagnosis.** **Name XANTHELASMA (absent here) too — it links your finding to the HYPERCHOLESTEROLAEMIA you will test for.**

**DO NOT CLOSE EARLY ON THE NECK.** **By minute three you know the answer, and the temptation is to drop AUSCULTATION on the reasoning that a bruit is a Graves' sign — an AUTOMATIC FAIL. The station marks a COMPLETE thyroid examination whatever your differential.** **And INSPECT BEFORE PALPATING — or you miss a THYROIDECTOMY SCAR, which is the whole diagnosis in Variant 2.** **The gland here: firm, RUBBERY and LUMPY — the Hashimoto consistency.**

**THE EXAMINER'S ONE-TEST QUESTION** — *‘if you could order one blood test, what would it be?’* → **‘TSH, Examiner. A RAISED TSH with a LOW FREE T4 confirms OVERT PRIMARY HYPOTHYROIDISM. TSH tells me WHICH DIRECTION the gland is going; the FREE T4 tells me HOW FAR.’** **And if the TSH were LOW with a low fT4, think a SECONDARY, PITUITARY cause.**

**THE EXPLANATION, and the self-blame it must address**: **‘The thyroid works like the THERMOSTAT AND THE ACCELERATOR for your body. Yours is UNDERACTIVE — it isn't making enough hormone. That is why you're tired, why you're cold when everyone else isn't, why your bowels have slowed, why the weight has gone on and why your thinking has felt foggy. I want to be CLEAR about something. THAT IS NOT LAZINESS AND IT IS NOT IN YOUR HEAD. There is a REAL, MEASURABLE, PHYSICAL REASON for how you've been feeling, and it's ONE OF THE MOST TREATABLE CONDITIONS WE SEE. **LIE HIM DOWN ONCE, THEN PALPATE FAST: temperature, capillary refill, posterior tibial pulse · SEVEN LANDMARKS named as you go with ONE summary line — ASIS, iliac crest, PSIS (slide a hand under), JOINT LINE (outer half of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral pulse — TENDER), greater trochanter, quadriceps, adductor origin. **MOVEMENT, DEMONSTRATED NOT DESCRIBED (described-only makes him do it wrong): flexion · abduction — with your hand on the hip, 'EXAMINER, I AM FEELING FOR CREPITUS' · adduction · INTERNAL ROTATION (ankle OUT) · EXTERNAL ROTATION (ankle IN) · offer extension prone or on his side. **MEASURE — the step most candidates lose: TRUE length ASIS to medial malleolus, APPARENT length umbilicus to medial malleolus, both legs — equal, which makes fracture or AVN with collapse less likely.**

dx: **ACUTE RIGHT S1 RADICULOPATHY — L5/S1 DISC PROTRUSION — James, 40, a storeman, three days of back pain after lifting a heavy box, radiating down the right leg. **CONSENT UNDER PRESSURE: offer analgesia before touching him ('have you had anything for it?'). When he says 'can you do it? I can't let go of the desk' — 'of course — may I step behind you?' Ask, get the yes, act. Opening the gown without asking, or examining through fabric, both fail.**

**GENERAL APPEARANCE: obvious pain and distress, PROTECTIVE POSTURE, leaning forward onto the desk. Then OFFER GAIT AND DEFER IT OUT LOUD: 'I would normally assess gait including heel walking for L4/5 and toe walking for S1; I'm deferring it because he can barely stand and it wouldn't change management.' **THE ONE THING: SAY 'I CAN SEE', NEVER 'I AM LOOKING FOR'. On a real patient with visible disease, 'I'm looking for' is the sound of a candidate who can't identify what is in front of them. Expect the interruption — 'don't tell me what you're looking for, tell me what you see' — and answer by naming one finding at once, without apologising or restarting.**

**SET UP IN THE WIPE: both arms bare to the elbow on a PILLOW · ASK ABOUT PAIN BEFORE YOU TOUCH ('are your hands sore now — anywhere especially painful?') — scored, decent, and it earns permission to keep going when he winces · and SPOT THE TRAY — a KEY, a COIN, a PAPERCLIP and a small BOTTLE out of the line of sight. Finding them is part of the station.**

**INSPECTION IS WHAT DECIDES IT — dorsal then palmar, specific signs named, organised by disease: for OA — I can see NO Heberden's or Bouchard's nodes and no thumb-base squaring · for RA — ULNAR DEVIATION at the MCPs, mild RADIAL DEVIATION at the wrists, a Z DEFORMITY of the thumb, SWAN-NECK of the index and middle fingers; no boutonnière, no dactylitis · nails and nail folds (no pitting, vasculitis, splinters) · no rheumatoid nodules at the hands or ELBOWS · WASTING of the small muscles · MCPs and PIPs swollen but not red · palms: thenar and hypothenar wasting, no Dupuytren's, no palmar erythema.**
**Naming a negative sign is still specific — 'no Heberden's nodes' names a sign at a joint. The failing version names nothing.**

**PALPATE EVERY JOINT GROUP, SUPPORTING AND SQUEEZING GENTLY, and say what you're feeling for — 'TENDERNESS AND SYNOVITIS OR EFFUSION': DIPs, PIPs, thumb IP, MCPs 1–5, metacarpals, wrist, snuffbox, styloids → tenderness with a BOGGY, SOFT FULLNESS at the MCPs and PIPs; DIPs not tender. He winces — apologise, stay gentle, KEEP GOING: a palpation abandoned halfway tells the examiner nothing about DISTRIBUTION, which is the point. Offer the second hand; accept the skip and spend the time on function.**
**ACTIVE MOVEMENT of thumb, fingers and wrist with both hands — globally reduced, worst on making a fist.**

**PROTECT THE TIME FOR FUNCTION — if the bell comes before the key leaves the tray, you've failed it: GRIP (reduced, no palmar tendon crepitus) · then the FOUR OBJECTS, INSTRUCTED NOT DEMONSTRATED ('turn it as if you were opening a lock'): he holds the KEY IN THE PALM rather than a lateral grip, manages the coin slowly, CANNOT open the paperclip, opens the bottle with the whole hand. Demonstrating destroys the test — the abnormality is the grip he chooses unaided.**

**THUMB GRIND TEST: compress the thumb metacarpal towards the wrist while rotating → NEGATIVE — argues against first-CMC osteoarthritis and so supports an inflammatory picture. Report negatives with the same confidence as positives.**

**DIFFERENTIALS IN NAMED GROUPS, WITH A LEADING DIAGNOSIS: INFLAMMATORY — RHEUMATOID (MCP and PIP distribution sparing the DIPs, the named deformities, boggy synovitis), psoriatic, gouty, reactive · DEGENERATIVE — osteoarthritis, less likely with the DIPs and thumb base spared and a negative grind · CONNECTIVE TISSUE — SLE · NEUROLOGICAL AND SOFT TISSUE — carpal tunnel (which RA predisposes to), De Quervain's, cervical radiculopathy. Inflammatory markers, RF and anti-CCP, hand X-rays, URGENT RHEUMATOLOGY (outcomes depend on early DMARDs), analgesia and OT. His hidden agenda — his wife now does the jars and his buttons.**

dx: **A TRACTION INJURY TO THE LOWER TRUNK OF THE RIGHT BRACHIAL PLEXUS (C8 and T1) — Klumpke — in Max, 30, who fell from a tree grabbing a branch with his right hand. A FULL CLAW involving ALL FOUR FINGERS, C8 and T1 sensory loss, no demonstrable C8 or T1 power, ABSENT TRICEPS jerk with a preserved biceps; warm, well-perfused limb; no bony tenderness to the clavicle; no wasting; no Horner's.**

**IT'S A FALL FROM HEIGHT, SO START WITH STABILITY: 'may I confirm his observations are stable?' — before a single finger is laid on him. Then the WIPE, both arms exposed to the shoulder, on a pillow, palms up.**

**THE ONE LINE THE WHOLE STATION TURNS ON: 'on inspection I can see a full claw hand of the right hand INVOLVING ALL FOUR FINGERS' — MCPs hyperextended, IPs flexed in index, middle, ring and little. Without 'all four fingers' the examiner can't tell you've distinguished a LOWER PLEXUS lesion from an ULNAR palsy. Add NO WASTING — consistent with an acute injury, and it quietly excludes every chronic cause.**

**PALPATION: PERFUSION FIRST, THEN BONE, HAND TO NECK: temperature at three levels including the shoulders and neck base · capillary refill · both radial pulses (offer brachials and a bruit over the supraclavicular fossa) · then tenderness DISTAL TO PROXIMAL — phalanges up to the elbow — then 'I'm now examining the SHOULDER AND ROOT OF THE NECK, because the presentation is in the hand but I suspect the lesion is up here': AC joint, clavicle, SUPRACLAVICULAR FOSSA, cervical spinous processes — all non-tender.**

**HE REFUSES EVERY ACTIVE MOVEMENT because of pain. NEVER say 'let me move it for you' — an automatic fail on an un-imaged limb that can displace a fracture. ANNOUNCE the omission: 'as this is a traumatic limb in which I have not excluded a fracture, I am deliberately omitting passive movement. I'd like to give analgesia and reassess.'**

**MOTOR BY MYOTOME, DEMONSTRATED EVEN THOUGH HE WON'T MOVE: C5 abduction, C6 elbow flexion, C7 extension, C8 GRIP (firm on the left, NOTHING on the right), T1 finger abduction (none on the right). 'C5–7 cannot be assessed; C8 and T1 cannot be demonstrated.' Skipping the block because 'he can't move anyway' loses every motor mark; running Froment's and Tinel's is nerve testing in a root problem.**

**SENSATION, ONE MODALITY, FIVE POINTS, sternum first: C5 deltoid, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger present — C8 LITTLE FINGER and T1 MEDIAL FOREARM: COMPLETE SILENCE on the right. He will not say 'no'. Touch, pause one beat, ANNOUNCE THE ABSENCE and move on.**

**REFLEXES ON THE AFFECTED SIDE, AND THE FACE: biceps (C5/6) present · TRICEPS (C7/8) ABSENT, fitting C8 · supinator skipped (same roots as biceps). Then LOOK FOR HORNER'S — ptosis, miosis — because the sympathetic supply leaves with T1: Horner's means a PRE-GANGLIONIC ROOT AVULSION, which won't recover spontaneously and needs urgent referral. None present. Offer analgesia.**

**EXPLAIN IN PLAIN WORDS, WITH HONEST PROGNOSIS: nerves leave the neck and join a BUNDLE into the arm, which splits into three branches; when he grabbed the branch the arm was pulled too far and the LOWER branch was stretched. Reasons: all four fingers curled (the small hand muscles are all supplied by that branch) and he couldn't feel the little finger or inner forearm. Most stretch injuries recover, but in MONTHS, not weeks, and you can't promise how much. His agenda: self-employed fencing contractor, no income protection.**

**THE EXAMINER'S QUESTIONS: WHY NOT ULNAR? — an ulnar palsy claws only the ring and little fingers (index and middle lumbricals are median-supplied); here all four claw, so every intrinsic is out, and every intrinsic is C8/T1 · ULNAR PARADOX — the higher the lesion, the LESS the claw, because FDP to ring and little is lost too · THE SIGN THAT CHANGES MANAGEMENT TODAY — Horner's, or any pulse deficit (a vascular emergency).**

**INSPECTION — TWO KEY FINDINGS: NO PALLOR of the affected hand · a PRESERVED FLEXED RESTING CASCADE of the fingers, symmetrical. He asks 'do you want the bandage off?' → NO: 'I'll leave it exactly where it is — the surgical team will look underneath in a controlled setting.' If there is glass: don't remove it — it may be tamponading a divided vessel.**

**SAY BEFORE YOU MOVE ANYTHING: 'the tendons crossing a volar wound are the FLEXORS, so I'll test three flexor groups with FIVE isolated movements and name the tendon each one tests.' Count them off on your own fingers — it stops the thumb being forgotten.**

**MOVEMENTS 1–4: (1) WRIST FLEXION → FCR and FCU intact · (2) a tight FIST → superficialis and profundus combined — 'a SCREENING TEST ONLY; it does not exclude an isolated injury, so I'll separate them' (superficialis lies nearer the skin and is divided first, but an intact profundus still pulls every finger into a fist) · (3) block the PIPs, bend just the tips → isolates FDP · (4) three fingers held flat, middle one free, bend that finger → pure PIP flexion isolates FDS.**

**MOVEMENT 5 — THE FINDING: hold the base of the thumb, 'bend the tip of your thumb … and again' → it won't go → 'I am testing flexion at the INTERPHALANGEAL JOINT OF THE THUMB, which isolates FLEXOR POLLICIS LONGUS. The patient is unable to perform that movement, so I am concerned about an injury to that tendon.' Don't decide for him that a movement is too painful — attempt all five.**

**NEUROLOGY, NERVE BY NERVE — 'a laceration divides named peripheral nerves, not roots': thumb pointed at the ceiling against resistance → MEDIAN motor · pinch paper, thumb stays straight, FROMENT'S negative → ULNAR · wrist cocked back → RADIAL · sensation at the INDEX PULP (median), LITTLE FINGER PULP (ulnar), SNUFFBOX (radial), comparing sides. **EXPLAIN WITHOUT JARGON AND WITHOUT FALSE REASSURANCE: three things run through the front of the wrist — nerves, blood vessels and tendons (the cords that bend the fingers); vessels fine, nerves working, but the cord that bends the tip of the thumb has probably been cut. Repairable, but in theatre. 'It's only a small cut' is a fail sentence. His agenda — he's a chef: repaired tendons usually do well but need months of hand therapy and no promise of perfection; no driving; ReturnToWorkSA if at work; tetanus review and an X-ray for retained glass.**

dx: **AN OCCULT SCAPHOID FRACTURE — Jenny, 30, a head chef, fell on an outstretched right hand two hours ago; the X-ray is REPORTED AS NORMAL. Mild but definite tenderness in the ANATOMICAL SNUFFBOX and over the SCAPHOID TUBERCLE, and a POSITIVE AXIAL COMPRESSION test. If you had fifteen seconds: do the axial compression test, then leave.**

**NAME WHAT THE FILM DOESN'T EXCLUDE BEFORE YOU TOUCH HER: 'the radiograph shows no visible fracture line, but in a patient with this mechanism a normal film does not exclude a scaphoid fracture, so my examination is directed at that.' That sentence tells the examiner you understand what the station is testing.**

**USE THE PILLOW and comment on GENERAL APPEARANCE — posture and SLING, because in trauma versions they're positive findings. INSPECT PALMS AND BACKS, naming the three that change management FIRST: NO PALLOR, NO LACERATION OR OPEN FRACTURE, KNUCKLE CONTOUR PRESERVED — then the generic list (mild swelling on the radial side).**

**PALPATION IS WHERE THE DIAGNOSIS LIVES: temperature, capillary refill, radial pulses both sides · then the RIGHT hand only, ONE HAND, zone by zone: fingers and IP joints, metacarpals and MCPs, the wrist supported from below, then 'I am now palpating the ANATOMICAL SNUFFBOX — any pain?' and 'now the SCAPHOID TUBERCLE — just where I'd take your pulse — and there?', then the radial and ulnar styloids and shafts.**

**THE ROLE-PLAYER GIVES NOTHING UNLESS THE EXACT POINT IS PRESSED — which is why the same case produces opposite recalls on the same day. Announcing the snuffbox while pressing near it gets 'no, that's fine'. And MILD tenderness at either point is POSITIVE — don't wait for a scream.**

**MOVEMENT, ASKED NOT PRESUMED — fingers, thumb and wrist separately: present, pain at the extremes of wrist movement; since active is achievable, no passive — say so. Then 'because this is a distal injury my neurological screen is NERVE-WISE': median (thumb against resistance), ulnar (Froment's), radial (wrist extension), sensation at index pulp, little fingertip, snuffbox — all intact.**

**THE AXIAL COMPRESSION TEST — GRIP THE FIRST METACARPAL, NOT THE THUMB: support the wrist and compress in and out along the thumb ray → reproduces her pain: a positive scaphoid compression test. Gripping the phalanges lets the MCP joint flex and absorb the force, so a genuinely positive case gives a negative test.**

**EXPLAIN — AND HOLD THE LINE WHEN SHE PUSHES: 'the X-ray doesn't show a break, but I'm still concerned you have one. The SCAPHOID is well known for not showing on an X-ray for the first week or two.' When she says 'doesn't that mean it's just a sprain?' → its BLOOD SUPPLY COMES IN FROM ONE END ONLY, so a missed break can fail to heal — a much bigger problem than two weeks in a cast. 'Good news, nothing's broken' is the failure this station was built to catch.**

**DIFFERENTIALS TO HER, EACH WITH A REASON: distal radius fracture (no deformity or radial tenderness) · tendon damage (movements work) · nerve damage (feeling and power normal) · vascular injury (warm, good pulse).**

**THE PLAN IN FULL — CAST, SCAN, FALLBACK, SAFETY NET: analgesia · a below-elbow cast around the thumb ('the position you'd hold a can') · an MRI if available, otherwise keep the cast on and REPEAT THE X-RAY IN 10–14 DAYS · fracture clinic · return if pain worsens instead of improving, stops responding to painkillers, fingers numb, tingle, change colour or won't move (the sentence that generates the compartment syndrome station). Her agenda — a 90-person wedding on Saturday: she won't be cooking it; a work certificate written for capacity, and ReturnToWorkSA since it happened at work.**

A radiograph in the room shows a fracture of the MIDDLE THIRD of the right clavicle with minimal displacement.

dx: **A CLOSED, MINIMALLY DISPLACED FRACTURE OF THE MIDDLE THIRD OF THE RIGHT CLAVICLE — uncomplicated — in Jake, 25, a shearing-shed hand, after a fall onto his outstretched arm at footy. Four tasks in eight minutes, and one needs your hands: explain the film · examine · explain the diagnosis · apply the sling and give the plan. The only thing that will beat you is the clock — SLING IN YOUR HANDS BY 6:00.**

**OFFER ANALGESIA, DON'T ASK 'ARE YOU IN PAIN?' — he visibly is. Then EXPLAIN THE FILM IN FORTY SECONDS AND THREE SENTENCES: this is your collarbone and it's BROKEN · it's in the MIDDLE THIRD · the ends have shifted only SLIGHTLY — 'the good version of this injury.' Explaining it for two minutes costs the station.**

**EXPOSURE UNDER PRESSURE: 'are you able to slip the gown down?' → 'yeah, okay' (does nothing) → 'you do it' → 'may I undo the tapes on the shoulder and lower it for you? Only to your chest.' Ask, get the yes, act — thirty seconds. Undressing him unasked or examining through the gown are both automatic fails.**

**GENERAL APPEARANCE AND INSPECTION, EACH FINDING MAPPED TO A COMPLICATION: pain and distress, PROTECTIVE posture, no sling, and importantly NO RESPIRATORY DISTRESS · right shoulder sits LOWER · bruising and erythema over the middle third · SKIN INTACT — no laceration, no open fracture, NO TENTING · no pallor of either hand.**

**PALPATION: temperature over both clavicles and shoulders · both hands warm · CRT <2 s · both radial pulses — VOLUME compared, not rate · then SC joint, along the clavicle — 'I am DELIBERATELY SKIPPING THE FRACTURED SEGMENT, which is already confirmed radiologically' — AC joint, coracoid, acromion, humeral head, biceps tendon.**

**MOVEMENT: ask him to lift the arm → 'too sore' → 'as this is an acute traumatic limb, I am deliberately NOT attempting passive movement.' 'Alright, let me move it for you then' is an instant fail and can displace the fracture. Elbow and finger wiggle only.**

**NERVES BY ROOT, because you're looking for a BRACHIAL PLEXUS injury: C5, C6, C7 myotomes named as SKIPPED because of pain (a silent skip looks like forgetting) · C8 grip and T1 finger abduction preserved · DERMATOMES C5 badge, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T1 MEDIAL ELBOW — on the correct arm, which is folded across his chest — intact.**

**THE SPECIAL TEST IS THE LUNG: the clavicle overlies the lung apex, so exclude a PNEUMOTHORAX — his arms are locked across the front, so AUSCULTATE POSTERIORLY in six areas; percussion and vocal resonance omitted for time and offered if abnormal → equal air entry. Never picking up the stethoscope is an automatic fail.**

**EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS BY ADDING ONLY WHAT THE EXAMINATION TOLD YOU: the bone sits on NERVES, a MAJOR BLOOD VESSEL and the TOP OF THE LUNG — all three checked and normal — so it's UNCOMPLICATED; almost certainly no operation. Then APPLY THE SLING WHILE YOU TALK: elbow at a right angle, forearm across the chest, hand a touch higher than the elbow, fingertips visible, knot to the side of the neck with padding — then RE-CHECK the hand (pulse, warmth, movement, sensation), the line almost everyone misses.**

**THE PLAN, THE AGENDA, FIVE RED FLAGS: regular paracetamol and ibuprofen BY THE CLOCK, ice, rest, and PROP THE ARM ON A PILLOW AT NIGHT (lying flat the sling does nothing) · move fingers, wrist and elbow daily as soon as pain allows · physiotherapy once knitted · FRACTURE CLINIC IN 7–10 DAYS · ~6 weeks to heal, ~3 months to footy. His agenda — shearing starts in three weeks, paid by the day: he won't be shearing; certificate, ReturnToWorkSA if work-related, no driving in a sling. Red flags: LUNG (short of breath) · NERVE (pins and needles, weakness) · VESSEL (pale, blue, cold hand) · PAIN (uncontrolled) · SKIN (breaking down over the fracture).**

dx: **A REFRACTIVE ERROR, MOST LIKELY MYOPIA — Gary, 50, a storeman, six months of gradually blurred vision, no pain, redness or headache. The ONLY abnormality is a REDUCED ACUITY IN ONE EYE (6/18) FULLY CORRECTED BY A PINHOLE, with normal fields, movements, pupils and fundi.** **This is the EYE FRAMEWORK — pair 1 of 5 — and every other eye station builds on it.**

**A FORTY-SECOND WIPE IN FOUR VERBS — 'looking at your eyes, reading some letters, following my pen, and shining a light' — then to the examiner: 'my eye examination has EIGHT PARTS — inspection, acuity, fields, colour vision, movements, accommodation, pupils and fundoscopy — I'll nominate each.' Ninety seconds explaining all eight is where the clock is lost.**

**INSPECTION IN THREE NAMED GROUPS, not 'inspection is normal': LIDS (swelling, redness, discharge, PTOSIS) · GLOBE (exophthalmos, enophthalmos, redness, subconjunctival haemorrhage) · PUPILS AND ANTERIOR CHAMBER (round, regular, symmetrical; no HYPHAEMA — blood — or HYPOPYON — pus).**

**ACUITY CARRIES THE FINDING: patient on the cross, one eye covered with the PALM (no pressing, no peeking), START AT THE TOP LINE, at least two letters per line, each eye then BOTH together. The acuity is the LAST LINE READ, not the line he failed. 6/18 means a normal eye reads it at 18 m; this eye at 6 m.**

**THE PINHOLE, ONLY ON THE REDUCED EYE, WITH ITS REASON: 6/18 → 6/6 through the pinhole = REFRACTIVE, not media or retina. Pinholing a 6/6 eye shows you're following a ritual rather than a reason. Write the figures down if asked, Right and Left in words.**

**CONFRONTATION FIELDS — THE EXAMINER CAN SEE EVERY ERROR FROM ACROSS THE ROOM: bring a chair, sit facing at the SAME LEVEL, about an ARM'S LENGTH (1 m) · cover the MATCHING eye of your own · the pen EQUIDISTANT between your faces (~50 cm each), never beside your head · 'look at my nose, don't follow the pen; tell me the moment you see it, then tell me if it disappears' · temporal quadrants, then SWAP HANDS keeping the SAME eye covered for the nasal quadrants → four quadrants per eye, eight total.**

**STEPS 3–7 IN ~90 SECONDS, RUN WITHOUT PAUSING: colour vision (Ishihara or the chart's red and green bands) · movements — head still, H-pattern, ASK ABOUT DOUBLE VISION in each direction · accommodation (far wall, then the pen) · pupils direct and consensual both eyes plus a SWINGING TORCH (no RAPD) · fundoscopy — RIGHT EYE, RIGHT HAND, dial at zero. Expect a run of skips; every skipped step still had to be NAMED.**

**EXPLAIN WITHOUT JARGON: the right eye is normal; the left couldn't read as far — but through the card with holes it read the whole chart, so the eye is HEALTHY and just isn't focusing light in the right place — a refractive error, almost certainly short-sightedness, corrected with glasses; an optometrist to make a prescription. Never reassure before the pinhole result is known.**

**GROUPED DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH ITS EXCLUSION: EYE (presbyopia, astigmatism, cataract, glaucoma, macular degeneration) · VASCULAR/METABOLIC (diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy, vascular occlusion) · NEUROLOGICAL (optic neuritis, a chiasmal or post-chiasmal compressive lesion) · INFLAMMATORY (uveitis, keratitis) · DRUGS (hydroxychloroquine, ethambutol, amiodarone, steroids). Cataract and retinal causes less likely because the pinhole FULLY corrected it; neurological less likely because fields, pupils and colour were normal.**

**HIS HIDDEN CONCERN — 'my father went blind from pressure in the eyes' — answer it: nothing found points to anything serious, but a family history of GLAUCOMA matters, so the optometrist should check pressures and the optic nerve. Safety net for the same day: sudden vision loss, eye pain, FLASHES or FLOATERS, a CURTAIN, or double vision.**

dx: **A REFRACTIVE ERROR, MOST LIKELY MYOPIA — Raymond, 50, a forklift driver at a grain terminal, several months of blurred distance vision, never worn glasses. One eye reduced (6/12–6/18) and FULLY CORRECTED BY A PINHOLE; everything else normal.** **Pair 2 of 5 — the ACUITY station: task 1 is 'check the visual acuity', and four figures on paper are part of the answer.**
**ASK ABOUT GLASSES OR CONTACT LENSES BEFORE TESTING — a scored item. 'Only cheap readers from the chemist' opens a PRESBYOPIA thread.**

**DON'T SKIP INSPECTION BECAUSE THE TASK NAMED ACUITY FIRST: thirty seconds — lids, globe, pupils and anterior chamber — tells you the eye is quiet. The task says 'check the acuity', not 'do nothing else first'.**

**DISTANCE ACUITY, MONOCULAR THEN BINOCULAR: on the cross · cover with the PALM, 'don't press, and don't peek through your fingers' · from the TOP line, across, two letters per line · each eye, then both. Report the LAST LINE READ — not 6/12 because that's where he struggled; read the figure off the chart, don't estimate it.**

**THE PINHOLE, WITH THE REASON BEFORE YOU USE IT: 'if the vision improves the problem is one of FOCUS; if it doesn't, it's further back — MEDIA, RETINA or OPTIC NERVE.' 6/18 → 6/6. Never pinhole the 6/6 eye 'to be thorough' — there's nothing to improve.**

**NEAR VISION — OFFER IT GIVEN HIS AGE (print at ~30 cm), then THE WRITTEN RECORD, read aloud as you hand it over: 'Right 6/6 uncorrected. Left 6/18 uncorrected, 6/6 with pinhole. Near vision normal both eyes. Binocular 6/6.' Right and Left written in words.**

**THE REST OF THE EXAMINATION, RUN WITHOUT PAUSING, EVERY STEP NOMINATED: fields by confrontation (chair, arm's length, eight quadrants) · colour vision · movements asking about diplopia · accommodation · pupils with SWINGING TORCH · fundoscopy right eye right hand.**

**EXPLAIN IN TWO SENTENCES AND A REASSURANCE — he drives a forklift, so no lecture on axial length: the back of the eye, the side vision and the pupils are normal; the eye couldn't read as far but read the whole chart through the pinhole, so it's HEALTHY and just not focusing properly — short-sightedness; not a disease; glasses correct it; optometrist for a prescription.**

**HIS HIDDEN AGENDA — 'am I going to lose my forklift ticket?': answer honestly without quoting a threshold you're unsure of: there is a legal vision standard for driving and a work requirement, but his vision came back to NORMAL through the pinhole, so a lens should correct it; you'll go through the work paperwork together once he has the prescription. Quoting a specific legal threshold as fact when unsure is an auto-fail.**

**GROUPED DIFFERENTIALS AND A SAFETY NET: cataract and presbyopia, then glaucoma, macular degeneration and retinopathy — each less likely for its reason (the pinhole fully corrected it; fundi normal). **THE INSTRUCTION BEFORE YOU MOVE THE PEN: 'keep your head still, follow my pen with your eyes only; tell me STRAIGHT AWAY if you see double, and WHERE you're looking when it happens.' She won't volunteer it unless asked.**

**THE THREE CHECKS, A FULL BIG H TO THE EXTREMES EVERY TIME: (1) BOTH EYES OPEN — 'two of everything, worst looking left' · (2) LEFT EYE COVERED with her own palm — 'single' · (3) RIGHT EYE COVERED — 'single'. Don't shrink the H on checks two and three to save time — the finding may only appear at the extremes.**

**STATE THE CONCLUSION OUT LOUD: 'diplopia with both eyes open that RESOLVES with EITHER eye covered — BINOCULAR diplopia; each eye is normal alone, so this is a disorder of ocular MOVEMENT AND ALIGNMENT.' The separation is horizontal and worst on left gaze — REPORT it as an observation but DON'T LOCALISE to one nerve, 'because left gaze requires both the left lateral rectus (VI) and the right medial rectus (III).'**

**FINISH THE EXAMINATION — AND THE PUPILS ARE THE TRIAGE QUESTION: acuity 6/6 · fields full · colour and accommodation (take the skips) · PUPILS — direct, consensual, swinging torch — 'equal and briskly reactive, no RAPD; with no ptosis at rest, a compressive third nerve lesion is much less likely' · fundoscopy looking specifically for PAPILLOEDEMA. Skipping the pupils is an auto-fail: ptosis + a dilated pupil + pain = an ANEURYSM.**

**ASK THE FATIGABILITY AND BULBAR QUESTIONS: worse at any time of day? (much worse by the evening) · a droopy eyelid? (her husband says the left droops at night) · trouble chewing or swallowing, slurred speech, breathlessness, limb weakness? (none) · headache?**

Eye movement is controlled along a chain — BRAIN, the NERVES to the eye muscles, the JUNCTION where nerve meets muscle, and the MUSCLES. Evening worsening with a drooping lid points to that junction — MYASTHENIA GRAVIS, which is treatable — but you won't guess: scan and bloods, seen quickly. Her fear ('is it a stroke?') — nothing in the examination points that way today.**

Plus the bruise below the left eye with lid swelling, no subconjunctival haemorrhage, and PUPILS round and regular — a TEARDROP pupil means a RUPTURED GLOBE.**

**PALPATION — WARN, START ON THE UNINJURED SIDE, ONE SIDE AT A TIME, FIVE REGIONS: skull (temporal, parietal, occipital, vertex — no step, no bogginess) · right orbital rim · left orbital rim — superior, LATERAL WALL, and the INFERIOR RIM: 'definite tenderness and possibly a small step' · nasal bones · zygomatic arches · mandible and TMJ (bite normal). He won't volunteer it: 'any double vision looking UP?' → 'two of everything.' dx: **POSTMENOPAUSAL BLEEDING — THE PELVIC EXAMINATION FRAMEWORK. Jenny, 54, three weeks of spotting, no period for four years. Version A: the vaginal walls are THIN, PALE AND DRY — ATROPHIC VAGINITIS — but ENDOMETRIAL CANCER must still be ruled out. Three tasks: explain and consent · examine the model · explain the diagnosis and differentials to her.**

**INTRODUCE AND SAY WHY, IN HER WORDS, TIED TO HER COMPLAINT: 'I've been asked to examine your private parts today because of the bleeding you've been having, so we can work out what's causing it.' Launching into steps before the reason loses it.**

**EXPLAIN ALL THREE STEPS WITHOUT SOFTENING: LOOK at the private parts · pass a SPECULUM into the VAGINA to see the walls and the CERVIX, the opening of the womb · place TWO FINGERS into the vagina while the other hand presses on the lower tummy, to feel the WOMB and OVARIES · uncomfortable, not painful. 'A quick look down below' is not consent.**

**THE CONSENT SEQUENCE — SIX ITEMS AND CONSENT TWICE: CONSENT ① · PRIVACY to undress from the waist down with a SHEET and full exposure · POSITION (on your back, knees bent, let them fall to the sides) · STOP SIGNAL · CHAPERONE ('would you like me to arrange one?' — if yes, 'I'll arrange one now and we'll start when they're here'; if no, 'I'll note it was offered and declined') · CONSENT ② ('are you happy for me to begin now?').**

**HAND HYGIENE, GLOVES, GENERAL APPEARANCE — alert, comfortable, not pale, no cachexia. INSPECTION after warning her: vulva and perineum — no rash, redness, ulceration or warts, no lumps or visible prolapse, no bleeding or discharge.**

**THE SPECULUM, WARNED AT INSERTION AND REMOVAL: blades vertical, angled downward ~45°, rotate 90°, open and lock under direct vision, one hand on it throughout · the CERVIX — os closed, smooth, no polyp or growth, no bleeding or discharge · then ASK THE EXAMINER ABOUT THE VAGINAL WALLS — the model can't show atrophy and the examiner only volunteers it if you say you're looking → 'thin, pale and dry' → 'consistent with atrophic change.'**

**THE BIMANUAL, WARNED: cervical motion tenderness (any pain?) · supinate and palpate suprapubically for uterine SIZE, BORDER and TENDERNESS · if told it's ENLARGED, ask 'IS THE BORDER REGULAR OR IRREGULAR?' — the question that turns a finding into reasoning · right adnexa, left adnexa — masses or tenderness · warn on removal and COVER HER ('take your time sitting up').**

I WOULD REMOVE THAT NOW with SPONGE FORCEPS, because tissue retained in the canal causes continued bleeding and can cause CERVICAL SHOCK. THE OS IS OPEN — clearly open.' Saying 'I can see tissue' and moving on scores nothing — the mark is for the ACTION. Vaginal walls normal.**

**THE BIMANUAL: CMT none · uterus SIX WEEKS, regular, non-tender · adnexae normal → 'no adnexal mass or tenderness makes an ECTOPIC less likely, and a uterus smaller than dates is consistent with tissue already passed.' Warn on removal; COVER HER; 'come and sit with me when you're ready.'**

**THE SILENCE — 30 TO 40 SECONDS, EMPATHIC LINES ONLY: 'I'm so sorry. I wish I had better news today.' · 'Take all the time you need.' · 'THIS IS NOT YOUR FAULT.' Keep talking and she gets louder. When she asks 'was it because I lifted that box?' → absolutely not — most early miscarriages come from a problem in how the pregnancy formed at the very beginning; nothing she did caused it or could have prevented it.**

**ONLY NOW THE DETAIL: the opening of the womb was already open with pregnancy tissue in it — the miscarriage has started and some tissue has come away — an INCOMPLETE MISCARRIAGE; the rest usually passes over hours or days. Options later: wait, medication, or a short procedure. THEN the statistic — about ONE IN FIVE pregnancies, and most women go on to a normal pregnancy (said too early, statistics sound like brushing her off).**

**THE PLAN AND SAFETY NET: remove the tissue from the cervical canal now · an ultrasound for retained products · BLOOD GROUP (anti-D if Rh-negative) · FBC for anaemia · support information and follow-up. Return immediately for SOAKING A PAD AN HOUR, faintness, severe pain, fever or offensive discharge.**

TWO THINGS ARE SCORED: 'I CANNOT SEE THE THREADS' and FIBROID VERSUS CANCER, named in that order, as the explanation for the bulky uterus.**

**EXPLAIN AND CONSENT — WHY, THREE STEPS, CONSENT TWICE: 'I've been asked to examine your private parts because of the bleeding, so we can work out where it's coming from' · look · speculum to see the walls and cervix · two fingers with the other hand on the lower tummy · uncomfortable not painful · consent ① · privacy and sheet · position · stop signal · CHAPERONE · consent ②. If she asks about the coil, 'I'll check on that as I go' — six words, finish task one.**
**GENERAL APPEARANCE AND INSPECTION: alert, comfortable, not pale, no cachexia · vulva — no rash, redness, ulceration or warts; no lumps, swellings or prolapse; no bleeding or discharge.**

**THE SPECULUM — WHERE THE KEY POINT LIVES: blades vertical, 45° down, rotate, open, hold · the CERVIX — os closed, smooth, no polyp or growth, no bleeding or discharge · 'I CANNOT SEE THE THREADS OF THE INTRAUTERINE DEVICE' · vaginal walls normal. Reporting a normal cervix and moving on misses the entire point.**

**THE BIMANUAL AND THE QUESTION YOU MUST ASK: CMT · supinate, palpate suprapubically for size, border, tenderness → 'the uterus feels BULKY' → 'ROUGHLY WHAT SIZE, AND IS THE BORDER REGULAR OR IRREGULAR?' → about TEN WEEKS, IRREGULAR, non-tender · adnexae normal. 'Bulky' alone isn't a finding you can reason from. Warn on removal; COVER HER.**

**DIAGNOSIS 1 — THE UTERUS, IN HER WORDS: larger than it should be and uneven, with bleeding between periods and after sex → most likely a LUMP in the womb — commonly benign, a FIBROID — 'but there is a smaller chance a lump like this is a CANCER OF THE LINING OF THE WOMB, and I can't tell them apart by feeling. That's why I want a scan.' When she says 'I've got two kids at home': 'I'm not telling you that you have cancer — it's what I have to rule out first, quickly.'**

**DIAGNOSIS 2 — THE THREADS: sometimes they curl up inside and the device is fine; it may also have been EXPELLED unnoticed or moved out of position. Until the scan finds it you can't promise contraceptive protection — use CONDOMS, and mention unprotected sex in the last few days today. The device explains irregular bleeding; it does NOT explain a ten-week uterus.**

dx: **MENORRHAGIA WITH A TEN-WEEK REGULAR UTERUS — MOST LIKELY FIBROIDS, CANCER TO EXCLUDE — AND IRON-DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA. Samantha, 35, three months of heavy periods, tired and pale; mother had fibroids and a hysterectomy at 45. NO PELVIC MODEL in the room; a SPHYGMOMANOMETER on the trolley. Two systems: THYROID, then a pelvic examination by REQUEST.**

**THREE THINGS ARE SCORED: repeating CONSENT AND CHAPERONE when you request the pelvic examination · asking for a URINE PREGNANCY TEST · naming FIBROID AND CANCER and saying palpation can't separate them.**

**EXPLAIN BOTH EXAMINATIONS AND CONSENT TO BOTH — she must consent to the pelvic examination you're going to REQUEST: the neck first ('the thyroid can be a common and treatable cause of heavy periods'), then look, speculum, two fingers · consent · privacy and position · stop signal · CHAPERONE · consent again.**

**GENERAL, HANDS, BLOOD PRESSURE: alert, dressed appropriately, not flushed or sweaty, no cachexia · palms (pallor, erythema), nails together (clubbing) · pulse — ask for a TIMER; if none, 'I'd count for fifteen seconds' · arms out for tremor · 'MAY I CHECK HER BLOOD PRESSURE?' — the machine is there deliberately.**

**FACE AND EYES FOR BOTH SYSTEMS: exophthalmos, lid retraction, eye movements and lid lag (thyroid) · CONJUNCTIVAL PALLOR (anaemia) · gums and tongue — no hypertrophy or bleeding, glossitis or angular stomatitis.**

**THE THYROID, TAKING THE SKIPS WITHOUT ARGUMENT: front and SIDE inspection (the cricoid-to-notch line) · sip and swallow · palpate from behind, neck slightly flexed — SIZE, LOWER BORDER, consistency, nodularity, tenderness · nodes · trachea · offer percussion and a bruit → normal thyroid. If you can't feel the lower border, the words are 'retrosternal extension'.**

**CONVERT THE PELVIC EXAMINATION INTO A REQUEST, WITH CONSENT AND CHAPERONE SAID AGAIN: 'I'd now like to perform a pelvic examination, WITH THE PATIENT'S CONSENT AND WITH A CHAPERONE PRESENT — is there a model, or shall I ask you for the findings?' → 'Ask me.' Then ONE QUESTION AT A TIME, waiting for each answer: bleeding? discharge? rash or redness? lumps, swellings or prolapse? Firing them as one sentence gets you stopped — the exchange is the mark.**

**SPECULUM AND BIMANUAL BY REQUEST, THEN THE SENTENCE THAT PASSES THE STATION: vaginal walls, cervix (bleeding, discharge, polyp, growth) · CMT · uterine SIZE, BORDER, TENDERNESS · adnexae → uterus TEN WEEKS, REGULAR, non-tender · then 'AND BEDSIDE TESTS, PLEASE — A URINE PREGNANCY TEST' → negative. An enlarged uterus at 35 is pregnancy until proven otherwise, and it's an office test, so it belongs inside the examination.**

**EXPLAIN IN HER WORDS: pregnancy test negative · thyroid normal (a common treatable cause, excluded) · the womb is bigger than expected — most likely a benign FIBROID (especially with her mother's history), 'but I also have to consider a CANCER OF THE WOMB, and I can't tell them apart just by feeling, which is why I want a scan' — uncommon at 35 but not impossible. Other causes: polyp or hyperplasia, cervical causes, hormonal (thyroid, PCOS), infection, a bleeding disorder, medications. AND THE ANAEMIA — losing this much blood each month, her iron stores are likely low, which is why she's tired.**

**THE INVESTIGATIONS — THREE AND A HALF: TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND · FBC and FERRITIN (the best measure of iron stores) · serum βhCG to confirm · (and) TSH. 'Would you order a CA-125?' → NO — not a screening test, neither sensitive nor specific, more likely to mislead. Safety net: much heavier bleeding, faintness, dizziness or breathlessness. Her agenda: 'will I need my womb taken out? We wanted one more.'**

**THE ROOM: the manikin is on the bed, the man across the room — talk to the man, examine the manikin, and narrate the turn between them. Don't try to stand the manikin up; it tips, and has cost candidates three minutes.**

**THE SENSITIVE-EXAMINATION OPENING, IN DETAIL BEFORE TOUCHING: 'I'll need to examine your private parts — look at your penis and scrotum, feel each testicle gently, and at the end feel in your groin. Is that alright?' · privacy and a sheet · 'WOULD YOU LIKE A CHAPERONE PRESENT?' (declined → 'I'll document that I offered') · STOP SIGNAL · hand hygiene. 'I'm going to examine your testicles, okay?' is not a detailed explanation.**

**POSITION AND THREE INSPECTION BOXES, EACH WITH ITS SECOND MOVE: 'could you STAND up for me' (said aloud — the box is ticked even if he doesn't move) · SCROTUM, then LIFT it to see the under-surface · PENIS, then RETRACT THE FORESKIN — redness of the glans and inner foreskin — and REPLACE it · squeeze the tip for DISCHARGE · COUGH for a hernia. Don't call normal asymmetry abnormal — the left hangs lower.**

**PALPATION — BOTH SIDES BEFORE ANY CONCLUSION, GENTLY: TEMPERATURE with the backs of the fingers (left warmer) · each testis between thumb in front and two fingers behind — FRONT, BACK, and a SWEEP OF THE BORDER · then up each SPERMATIC CORD. dx: **ACUTE LABYRINTHITIS — James, 57, a long-haul truck driver, giddiness, nausea and a buzzing in both ears since yesterday, a head cold ten days ago; smoker, hypertensive. Horizontal nystagmus (fast phase left) with an otherwise entirely normal cranial nerve and limb examination and normal hearing tests. The station exists to make you EXCLUDE A POSTERIOR CIRCULATION (LATERAL MEDULLARY) STROKE.**

**OPEN WITH THE FRAMING SENTENCE: gloves, 'I've washed my hands', the plan in plain words, exposure of arms and legs · confirm observations and GLUCOSE · then to the examiner: 'because giddiness can come from the INNER EAR, the CEREBELLUM or the POSTERIOR CIRCULATION, I'll do a cranial nerve and limb neurological examination, with a complete ear examination inside cranial nerve eight.' Without it, your ENT-looking opening looks accidental.**

**GENERAL APPEARANCE WITH HORNER'S: alert, unwell, keeping very still, no abnormal posture, no facial asymmetry, 'I cannot see a HORNER SYNDROME — no ptosis and no miosis.' Then ASK HIM TO STAND AND WALK, and to stand feet together — he refuses both — and NARRATE: 'unable to stand, so I cannot assess gait, Romberg or a lying and standing BP.' Not asking loses the mark; asking and moving on silently looks like an omission.**

**CRANIAL NERVES I–VII, WITH THE PHRASES THAT UNLOCK FINDINGS: smell · II — fundoscopy for PAPILLOEDEMA, pupils (no Horner), acuity — nothing more · III, IV, VI — H-pattern: 'full, no diplopia, and I AM SPECIFICALLY LOOKING FOR NYSTAGMUS' → a video → 'HORIZONTAL nystagmus, fast phase to the LEFT, no vertical or rotatory component' — commit to a description · V — ask for PAIN sensation first ('I don't have a neurological pin'), then cotton wool, then masseter and temporalis, then OFFER JAW JERK AND CORNEAL REFLEX · VII — full.**

**CRANIAL NERVE VIII — THE COMPLETE EAR EXAMINATION: inspect and compare the ears, mastoid, discharge · palpate helix, tragus, lobule, mastoid, move the pinna · offer otoscopy · WHISPER test (block the other ear, whisper close then at arm's length) · RINNE with a 512 Hz fork — instruct FIRST, strike on your knee, base on the MASTOID, 'tell me when you stop hearing it', then in front · WEBER — louder left, right or the same · offer DIX–HALLPIKE (head 45°, extended below horizontal, watch 30–45 s).**

**STATE THE RULE BEFORE THE CONCLUSION — findings are rotated within a day: air better than bone means a NORMAL ear OR a SENSORINEURAL loss — which is why you did the whisper test · bone better than air = CONDUCTIVE loss · Weber lateralises TOWARDS a conductive loss and AWAY from a sensorineural loss. Here: whisper normal, Rinne air > bone both sides, Weber central → no significant hearing loss.**

**IX–XII AND THE LIMBS, PAIN AND TEMPERATURE FIRST: palate and uvula, cough, gag offered · trapezius and sternocleidomastoid · tongue · RESTATE 'no Horner syndrome' · limbs I-T-P-R-S-C — 'for sensation I'd like PAIN first, then TEMPERATURE' (both normal — 'that argues strongly against a lateral medullary infarct'), then light touch, vibration, joint position · coordination — finger-nose, rapid alternating movements, heel-shin → no cerebellar signs. Protect the last 75 seconds for the explanation.**

**EXPLAIN IN LAY TERMS: a small organ deep in the ear does two jobs — it hears, and it tells the brain which way up you are; it's become INFLAMED, usually after a virus, and sends the wrong balance signals — the giddiness, sickness and buzzing.**

**ITEMISED REASSURANCE — HIS FEAR IS A STROKE (his brother-in-law's began with dizziness): 'the reason I'm confident it's your ear and not your brain is that I looked specifically for the stroke signs — the feeling in your face, the reflexes in your eye and jaw, your pupils and eyelids, strength and sensation in your arms and legs, your coordination — and every one was normal.' A bare 'nothing serious' reads as dismissal.**

**DIFFERENTIALS BY SITE, EACH WITH A REASON: EAR — vestibular neuritis (but tinnitus involves the cochlea), Ménière's (single episode, not recurrent 20-min–12-h attacks with fullness), acoustic neuroma (gradual, unilateral) · BRAIN — posterior circulation/LATERAL MEDULLARY stroke (excluded by facial pain, jaw jerk and corneal reflex, no Horner's, normal crossed pain and temperature), cerebellar or CPA tumour (normal fundi and coordination), MS · drugs (aminoglycosides, furosemide, high-dose aspirin), B12 · NOT BPV — tinnitus and sustained nausea don't belong to it. Plan: antiemetic for ONLY a day or two (longer slows recovery), fluids, rest, audiometry, vestibular rehabilitation, NO DRIVING (he drives trucks — duty to notify if he remains unfit), safety net for headache, weakness, numbness, slurred speech, diplopia, sudden hearing loss. Imaging if asked: none for a clear peripheral cause; MRI with DWI, not CT, if any central feature.**

Reach for cotton wool first and this patient examines as normal.**

**VARIANT C — CONDUCTIVE LOSS: whisper reduced left, Rinne bone > air left, Weber lateralises left → a left CONDUCTIVE loss; want otoscopy and audiometry. If challenged ('labyrinthitis is inner ear'): classically sensorineural; Murtagh allows either with coexisting middle ear inflammation; the diagnosis rests on the symptom cluster, and audiometry will characterise it.**

**VARIANT D — VERTIGO AND TINNITUS WITHOUT NAUSEA: nausea is near-universal in an acute vestibular syndrome, so labyrinthitis is less likely — put ACOUSTIC NEUROMA higher (unilateral tinnitus, sensorineural loss, unsteadiness) — MRI internal auditory meati with gadolinium. VARIANT E — Dix–Hallpike allowed: warn, position so the shoulders reach the edge, head 45° to the tested ear, drop rapidly to supine with the head extended, watch 30–45 s, sit up slowly, repeat the other side.**

**The one sentence for every variant: 'whatever the findings, I will not call this benign positional vertigo — tinnitus and sustained nausea exclude it, and a positive Dix–Hallpike would not change that.'**

dx: **BILATERAL PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE (INTERMITTENT CLAUDICATION), WORSE ON THE LEFT — Ron, 68, bilateral calf pain on walking relieved by rest, at a FIXED ~200 m, worsening over six months, 25 a day for 45 years. The legs look and feel near-normal; distal PULSES PRESENT; Buerger's negative; no bruit; ABI LEFT 0.7, RIGHT 0.9. Version B: a 52-year-old diabetic with cotton wool and a neurotip on the trolley.**

**EXPOSURE IN UNDER 40 SECONDS: he's in shorts and won't undress further — ask once, then 'ideally I'd expose to the groin; I'll work with what we have.' Negotiating costs the time you need for Buerger's. This isn't a hip examination.**

**DECLARE THE STRUCTURE, THEN COMMIT DESPITE SILENCE: 'the history is pain on walking relieved by rest, so I'm treating this as CLAUDICATION — a lower limb examination for the two big causes, VASCULAR and NEUROGENIC, finishing with special tests.' The examiner says nothing until you ask for the ABI — silence isn't disapproval.**

**GENERAL APPEARANCE AND GAIT — PICK UP THE CLUE ALOUD: walks normally over a short distance → 'he bears weight fully, no antalgic gait — and the fact that STANDING STILL relieves it points to a VASCULAR rather than a NEUROGENIC cause' (neurogenic claudication is relieved by sitting or bending forward).**

**INSPECTION IN TWO NAMED LISTS, STANDING: ARTERIAL — pallor, hyperpigmentation (venous), shiny atrophic skin, HAIR LOSS over the lower shins, ulcers, gangrene · NEUROPATHIC — clawed toes, bunion, deformity, Charcot foot, ulceration over the metatarsal heads, wasting · then swelling, redness, scars, symmetry. Don't describe findings you can't see — 'hair distribution preserved' is a legitimate negative.**

**PALPATION IN FOUR STEPS, ON THE COUCH: TEMPERATURE at four levels looking for a DROP distally (a cold clammy foot) · CAPILLARY REFILL at the big toes · PULSES — posterior tibial behind the medial malleolus, DORSALIS PEDIS lateral to EHL — 'as you can feel on the patient' = PRESENT → 'present pulses DO NOT EXCLUDE mild disease — I'll need the ABI' · brief tenderness sweep. Check the SOLES when he lies down.**

**MOVEMENT BRIEF, THEN THE ANNOUNCEMENT THAT SAVES THE STATION: active ankle, knee and hip movement — full and pain-free — 'in the interest of time I've kept joint palpation and movement brief, because the stem describes claudication rather than joint pain; I'd like to move to the special tests.' A full joint survey eats Buerger's. Plan two phases: chair → gait → standing inspection → COUCH for everything else.**

**THE THREE B'S: BUERGER'S — lying down, raise the leg and wait for PALLOR (the Buerger's angle; <20° = severe), then hang it over the edge for REACTIVE HYPERAEMIA → negative (demonstrate one side for time, bilateral findings) · the FEMORAL BRUIT — diaphragm at the mid-inguinal point, one site only → none · and the ABI: 'the higher ankle Doppler pressure over the higher brachial pressure' → LEFT 0.7, RIGHT 0.9 → INTERPRET UNPROMPTED: normal is 0.91–1.30, so this confirms MILD-TO-MODERATE PAD, worse on the left, consistent with palpable pulses. Buerger's in a chair can't be done — and is remembered.**

**EXPLAIN SITTING AT EYE LEVEL, NO JARGON: the ARTERIES are pipes carrying blood to the leg muscles; years of smoking have furred up and narrowed them; at rest the muscles get enough, but walking needs far more, so they cramp — his 200 metres. Treatable: STOPPING SMOKING is the most powerful thing (patches, tablets, QUITLINE 13 7848), SUPERVISED WALKING through the discomfort lengthens the distance, and an ANTIPLATELET and a STATIN protect the heart and brain too. His fear — his father lost a leg: 'at this stage, no — mild reduction, healthy feet; the risk rises if the smoking continues, which is why I want to act now.'**

**GROUPED DIFFERENTIALS AND THE SAFETY NET: VASCULAR — PAD (most likely), chronic venous insufficiency, acute limb ischaemia (excluded: no sudden onset, pallor, pulselessness or paralysis) · NEUROGENIC — LUMBAR CANAL STENOSIS and radiculopathy (less likely: fixed reproducible distance, relieved by STANDING STILL not sitting or leaning forward) · JOINT/SOFT TISSUE — OA, inflammatory or gouty arthritis, tendinopathy, bursitis (no tenderness, full painless movement) · diabetic neuropathy in a diabetic; cauda equina if bilateral with sphincter change. Return urgently for REST PAIN, night pain, a non-healing sore or a toe changing colour. Arterial duplex to confirm.**

**AXILLAE, BOTH SIDES, FIVE NAMED POSITIONS: support the arm on your forearm so the muscles relax · APICAL (infraclavicular) · CENTRAL (chest wall) · ANTERIOR/PECTORAL · POSTERIOR/SUBSCAPULAR · LATERAL/HUMERAL. Daniel, 19, an apprentice electrician and footballer, a week of fever and sore throat; EBV IgM and IgG positive, platelets 118, atypical lymphocytes; on AMOXICILLIN since Tuesday. Findings: slightly dry mucosa · grossly enlarged exudative tonsils · tender cervical nodes, POSTERIOR most marked · HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY (liver 3 cm, spleen 2 cm).**

**STRUCTURE: a HAEMATOLOGICAL examination with an ENT insert at the face. The throat gets FIFTY SECONDS and FIVE NAMED TARGETS; ears, nose and sinuses get NOTHING. The liver and spleen are where the marks are — leave the throat by 3:35, hands on the abdomen by 4:45.**

**OPEN, WARN ABOUT THE MOUTH, DECLARE THE STRUCTURE: hands, arms, face, tummy; armpits (can be sensitive), neck, tummy; 'I'll also need to look inside your mouth and throat with a light' · sitting, then lying later · then to the examiner: 'the diagnosis is established on serology, so I'll examine for SEVERITY AND COMPLICATIONS — a haematological examination with a focused throat examination.'**

**GENERAL APPEARANCE — DEHYDRATION IS THE FINDING THAT CHANGES DISPOSITION: a week of fever and a painful throat limits intake — dry mucosa, turgor · PALLOR (EBV haemolytic anaemia) · JAUNDICE (EBV hepatitis) · periorbital oedema · hands and pulse. Reciting the CLL triad (cachexia, pallor, jaundice) misses the point.**

**SKIN — BOTH RASH TYPES, AND ASK ABOUT ANTIBIOTICS: a BLANCHING MACULOPAPULAR rash, which follows AMOXICILLIN or ampicillin in EBV — 'have you had any antibiotics this week?' ('amoxicillin on Tuesday') — and PURPURA/PETECHIAE, non-blanching, because the platelets are 118 → no rash of either type. Then EPITROCHLEAR both sides, and AXILLAE — five groups each (a partial survey is a failed survey).**

**THE THROAT — FIFTY SECONDS, FIVE TARGETS, THEN LEAVE: 'open wide and say ah' — TONSILLAR ENLARGEMENT · EXUDATE or membrane · PHARYNGEAL ERYTHEMA · PALATAL PETECHIAE · UVULAR DEVIATION (peritonsillar abscess), plus TRISMUS and a MUFFLED voice → grossly enlarged exudative tonsils, central uvula, no trismus → 'exudative tonsillitis consistent with EBV; central uvula and no trismus argue against a PERITONSILLAR ABSCESS. I won't examine the ears, nose or sinuses in this context.' Announcing the omission converts it into a decision. Eyes — no pallor or jaundice.**

**THE NECK — CHAINS, THEN STIFFNESS: warn, from behind — eight chains ending SUPRACLAVICULAR → tender bilateral lymphadenopathy, most marked POSTERIORLY → 'posterior chain involvement favours EBV over streptococcal pharyngitis' · then 'tuck your chin to your chest' — no NECK STIFFNESS, because MENINGITIS and ENCEPHALITIS are recognised complications (five seconds most candidates never spend).**

**THE ABDOMEN — BOTH ORGANS, THEN SAY IT BACK: lie flat, inspect · LIVER from the RIF with the radial border on each expiration · SPLEEN bimanually from the RIF, roll RIGHT · CASTELL'S (left anterior axillary line, inspiration and expiration) → liver 3 cm, spleen 2 cm → 'so there is HEPATOSPLENOMEGALY — consistent with EBV, and it matters because an enlarged SPLEEN CAN RUPTURE: no CONTACT SPORT or HEAVY LIFTING for at least FOUR WEEKS.' Don't palpate an enlarged spleen deeply and repeatedly once told.**

**CLOSE: offer the INGUINAL nodes with permission and a chaperone; cover him and thank him. SUMMARY: serologically confirmed acute EBV; exudative tonsillitis, tender posterior-predominant cervical nodes, hepatosplenomegaly; no quinsy or airway compromise, no neck stiffness, no rash despite platelets 118; mildly dry.**

**PLAN AND HIS AGENDA: supportive — analgesia and hydration · LFTs · no contact sport or heavy lifting for at least four weeks (longer while the spleen is palpable) · STOP THE AMOXICILLIN — aminopenicillins cause a widespread rash in EBV, and this is NOT a penicillin allergy · avoid sharing drink bottles and mouthguards · escalate for STRIDOR, DROOLING, or sudden LEFT UPPER QUADRANT or SHOULDER-TIP pain. His agenda — 'I've got footy Saturday, I'll be right?' → a firm NO, with the reason.**

A HAEMATOLOGICAL, NOT OBSTETRIC, examination — ALL FINDINGS NORMAL. Nine key points layered on the routine sequence; four differential groups, PREGNANCY FIRST.**

**WIPE WITH ONE EXPLANATION, THEN CONSENT: hands, eyes, mouth; glands at elbows, armpits, neck and top of the legs; listen to the heart; examine the tummy — sitting, then lying · pain? · CHAPERONE? · consent · HAND HYGIENE (no hand hygiene or no consent is a single-item fail). Bank her question — 'will it hurt the baby?' — to answer properly after examining.**

**GENERAL INSPECTION — NAME THE FOUR THINGS BEFORE ANSWERING: PALLOR · JAUNDICE · CACHEXIA · a RASH, thinking of DERMATITIS HERPETIFORMIS (coeliac) — none; no bruising. 'She looks well' scores nothing.**

**HANDS, NAILS, PULSE: clubbing (nails together) · pale palmar creases · looking specifically for KOILONYCHIA — the brittle spoon-shaped nail of iron deficiency · radial pulse — 'no TACHYCARDIA to suggest significant anaemia'. If she offers 'my nails have been brittle', say it back — it fits iron deficiency.**

**ARMS, EPITROCHLEAR, AXILLAE: scratch marks, purpura · EPITROCHLEAR — 'feeling just above the MEDIAL EPICONDYLE' (a named key point candidates skip) · warn, then AXILLAE — apical, central, pectoral, subscapular, humeral, both sides.**

**EYES AND MOUTH — THREE SEPARATE ASKS: conjunctival pallor, scleral jaundice · 'big smile' — gums · 'tongue out' — ATROPHIC GLOSSITIS and ANGULAR CHEILITIS (if she mentions a sore crack at the corner last month, 'that fits with angular cheilitis') · 'say ah' — tonsils, Waldeyer's ring.**

**NECK, BONE, JVP, HEART — ADAPTED, NOT ABANDONED: eight cervical chains with supraclavicular · press STERNUM AND CLAVICLES aloud (a named key point most forget) · JVP ideally at 45° · keep her covered: 'I can't inspect or palpate the apex without exposing the breast, so I'll AUSCULTATE AND ADAPT' — aortic, pulmonary, lower left sternal edge and apex from below — 'listening for an EJECTION SYSTOLIC FLOW MURMUR of anaemia' — none; lung bases clear, so no high-output failure.**

**THE ABDOMEN — THE HIGHEST-VALUE BLOCK, AND NO OBSTETRIC MANOEUVRES: lie flat, uncover ribs to above the underwear · 'at ten weeks the uterus is not palpable abdominally, so this is a STANDARD abdominal examination' (reassure her it's safe — the womb is behind the pubic bone) · nine regions soft · SPLEEN from the RIF, then ROLLED RIGHT · liver edge · CASTELL'S resonant. A fundal height, Leopold's or a speculum is a single-item fail. Hands off the abdomen by 4:50; inguinal nodes and legs (accept the skip); cover her and help her sit.**

Her real question: treated properly, a normal pregnancy and a healthy baby expected; untreated it can affect growth and leave her vulnerable at delivery — which is why we treat now. Iron tablet: empty stomach or with orange juice, two hours from tea, coffee, milk and antacids, BLACK STOOLS are harmless, constipation or nausea possible; iron-rich foods; repeat bloods in 2–4 weeks; safety net for breathlessness, dizziness, palpitations, bleeding.**

**THE DIFFERENTIALS ARE THE CAUSES OF IRON DEFICIENCY, IN FOUR GROUPS — WHERE THE STATION IS WON: (1) INCREASED DEMAND — the pregnancy itself · (2) BLOOD LOSS — heavy periods before conception, GI loss (peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, NSAIDs, haemorrhoids, IBD), urinary loss, surgery, blood donation · (3) MALABSORPTION — COELIAC classically at her age, H. pylori, IBD, gastric or bariatric surgery, long-term PPIs · (4) INADEQUATE INTAKE — low red meat, vegetarian or vegan. Only then, briefly, the other microcytic causes: THALASSAEMIA TRAIT (argued against by ferritin 8 — test the partner if present), anaemia of chronic disease.**

dx: **HENOCH–SCHÖNLEIN PURPURA (IgA VASCULITIS) — ONE PROCESS, FOUR ORGANS. Liam, 5, brought by his mother Jenny: an URTI two weeks ago, then a rash on the legs and COLICKY ABDOMINAL PAIN. No meningism; observations and BP normal; urine BLOOD 4+, PROTEIN 1+. The mother is the person you speak to; the MANIKIN is the thing you examine.**

**EVERY WORD OF THE WIPE GOES TO JENNY — she's the one who consents. If she asks 'is it meningitis?', ANSWER IMMEDIATELY: exactly the right thing to think about; Liam has no neck stiffness, he's alert, and his temperature, heart rate and blood pressure are normal; children with meningococcal infection are usually very unwell very quickly, and he isn't.**

**EXPLAIN THE RASH — FOUR FEATURES IN NINETY SECONDS, FINISHING WITH NON-BLANCHING — the photograph turned so she can see it: (1) TYPE — a PURPURIC rash, a small amount of bleeding under the skin · (2) SYMMETRICAL — both legs and both buttocks · (3) SITE — legs and bottom only, nothing on the tummy, chest or back · (4) NON-BLANCHING — the colour doesn't fade when pressed, so it's blood in the skin. Primary morphology and borders are noise to a mother.**

**CONSENT FROM JENNY, THEN NAME EVERY SIGN BEFORE TOUCHING THE MANIKIN: 'I appreciate this is a manikin, so I'll name each sign as I go' · level of consciousness, pallor, cachexia · the BP is given and normal — you'd otherwise measure it because HYPERTENSION marks RENAL involvement · hands — clubbing, palmar creases, tachycardia. If you weren't given it, you don't have it.**

**ARTHRITIS — THE DISCRIMINATING BLOCK — DONE EARLY, AT ~3:20: 'I'd now like to examine for arthritis, a feature of HSP' · the ANKLE, the joint most typically involved — inspect for swelling and redness, palpate for tenderness and PERI-ARTICULAR swelling, range of movement · and the knees, wrists, elbows, hips the same way → mild puffiness and tenderness around both ankles. It's the first casualty when a manikin station runs long. Don't describe deformity — that's chronic arthritis.**

**THE NODE SURVEY, NAMED EVEN ON PLASTIC: arms for purpura and scratch marks · epitrochlear both sides · axillae — five groups named · mouth — gums, glossitis, angular cheilitis, tonsils and Waldeyer's ring, palatal petechiae, and the THROAT given the recent infection · eyes · neck from the front (the manikin can't sit) — eight chains · bone tenderness over clavicles and sternum.**

**THE ABDOMEN — FIVE NAMED STEPS, BEYOND THE SPLEEN: inspection · SUPERFICIAL palpation (tenderness, guarding, rigidity) · DEEP palpation for masses — specifically INTUSSUSCEPTION · ORGANS — liver edge, spleen bimanually from the RIF, Castell's · BOWEL SOUNDS → soft, mildly tender centrally, no guarding or mass → 'fits the abdominal involvement of this condition rather than a surgical abdomen'. The gut is one of the four inflamed organs.**

**OFFER WHAT YOU WON'T DO: the INGUINAL nodes, and the SCROTUM — 'scrotal involvement occurs in HSP and must be distinguished from TESTICULAR TORSION.' Eight seconds; it's where the torsion mark lives.**

**EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS — ONE MECHANISM LINKING FOUR ORGANS: Henoch–Schönlein purpura, also called IgA vasculitis, the commonest condition of its type in children · the SMALL BLOOD VESSELS become INFLAMED, usually set off by an infection (the cold two weeks ago) · inflamed vessels in the SKIN leak blood (the rash), in the KIDNEYS (blood in the urine), in the BOWEL (the tummy pains), and in the JOINTS (the puffy ankles) · it isn't a bleeding disorder and isn't meningitis; most settle over a few weeks.**

**THE KIDNEYS AND THE FOLLOW-UP PLAN — the management of this condition: most children recover completely; because the kidneys can be involved, URINE AND BLOOD PRESSURE are checked regularly for SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS; bloods today (platelets and clotting) to confirm it isn't a bleeding problem. Blanket reassurance without follow-up is a missed management point. Her held-back fear — her niece's leukaemia — answer with evidence: no enlarged glands, spleen, bone tenderness or bleeding gums, not pale; the blood count will confirm.**

**SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT — LANDMARKS BEFORE THE TAPE: ULNAR BORDER from below the xiphisternum to find the FUNDUS · the upper border of the SYMPHYSIS · ZERO AT THE SYMPHYSIS, midline across the umbilicus → 36 cm, appropriate for 37 weeks (weeks ±2–3 cm), plotted on her customised chart. **IF YOU FEEL NOTHING, DON'T PRESS HARDER OR INVENT: commentate what each grip is assessing, and 'I'd confirm the lie and presentation with a bedside ultrasound.' Candidates have passed this examiner feeling nothing at all.**

**THE FETAL HEART — THE STEP HALF OF CANDIDATES FORGET: 'do I have a Doppler, or shall I use my stethoscope? May I have a timer?' · over the FETAL BACK, below the umbilicus on the left · count FIFTEEN SECONDS × 4 → 144 (normal 110–160) · palpate the MATERNAL RADIAL PULSE at the same time to confirm it's the baby's. Never guess — every candidate hears the same recording. Lost count? Ask for another fifteen seconds.**
**CLOSE AND COMPLETE: cover her and help her sit · offer a urine dipstick for protein, weight, plotting the SFH, and confirming the GROUP B STREP swab (35–37 weeks).**

**EXPLAIN IN PLAIN WORDS — SIZE, POSITION, HEARTBEAT: the tape measure says the baby is growing as expected · lying up and down with the head at the bottom and the back on her left — the ideal position for a normal birth — the head just starting to settle into the pelvis · heartbeat 144, normal · BP normal. Her hidden worry — 'my sister said I look small' — the measurement is right on track; more than ~3 cm off would simply mean a scan. Safety net: reduced movements, bleeding, fluid loss, abdominal pain, headache with blurred vision.**

**VERSION B — PROLONGED PREGNANCY (40+4): baby head-down and well, but she's close to 41 weeks — beyond it risks rise · CAUSES — usually none; check dates (certain); primigravida, family history, previous post-dates, a boy, older age, higher BMI · IMPLICATIONS — longer labour, instruments or caesarean, tears and PPH for her; macrosomia, SHOULDER DYSTOCIA, oligohydramnios and cord compression, MECONIUM aspiration and rising stillbirth risk for the baby · MANAGEMENT — CTG and ultrasound for liquor and growth · a speculum and the BISHOP SCORE · a MEMBRANE SWEEP now · INDUCTION offered from 41 weeks (ripen first if Bishop ≤6; ARM and oxytocin if ≥7) — HER DECISION; if she declines, TWICE-WEEKLY CTG and liquor checks and delivery by 42 weeks.**

**Numbers: 4 grips + fetal heart = 5 steps · grips 1–3 face the head, grip 4 faces the feet · SFH = gestation in weeks ±2–3 cm (34–40 cm at 37 weeks), plotted from 24 weeks · engagement 5/5 free → ≤2/5 engaged → 0/5 · FHR 110–160, count 15 s × 4 · tilt 15–30° left lateral · GBS swab 35–37 weeks.**

**VARIANT 1 — THE EMPTY MANNEQUIN ('tell me what you feel'): 'I'm not able to define a fetal pole here — I'll continue through the grips, tell you anything I feel, and confirm the lie and presentation with a bedside ultrasound.' Conclusion: SFH and FHR reassuring, but don't assume a cephalic presentation without imaging. To her: honest uncertainty plus a plan — never 'everything is completely fine' when you determined nothing.**

**VARIANT 2 — TRANSVERSE LIE: abdomen broader than long, no fundal pole, a hard ballottable mass in the flank, no presenting part at the brim → transverse lie at 37 weeks — scan for placenta and liquor, offer EXTERNAL CEPHALIC VERSION around 37 weeks, caesarean if it fails or she declines — and come in IMMEDIATELY by ambulance if the waters break or contractions start (CORD PROLAPSE risk).**

**VARIANT 3 — SHE DECLINES INDUCTION: completely her decision; acknowledge induced contractions can feel stronger (full pain relief available); weigh that against rising risk past 41 weeks — then give the concrete SURVEILLANCE plan (twice-weekly CTG and liquor scan) and the 42-WEEK LIMIT, plus the safety net. Never pressure; never simply agree and walk away.**

**The three-way triangle: before each step, turn your head to the woman and tell her what's coming; while your hands work, speak to the examiner. She'll say 'ow' loudly if you press hard — respond, then continue gently.**

dx: **PRE-ECLAMPSIA WITH SEVERE-RANGE HYPERTENSION AT 30 WEEKS — Sarah, 28, G1P0, a teacher, at a routine visit, feeling completely well. BP 158/98 then 162/102 four hours later; urine protein 3+. A MIXED station — a three-minute history, a rapid multi-system examination, and the explanation. It's a RACE: splits of history by 3:30, examination by 7:00, diagnosis by 7:45.**

**OPEN WITHOUT REASSURANCE OR ALARM: identity; 'your blood pressure is higher than we'd like and there's some protein in your urine — I'll ask some questions, examine you, then explain' · an open question about the pregnancy. If she asks 'is something wrong?' → 'it might be something we need to act on — let me ask and examine first.'**

**THE RED-FLAG BLOCK — WARN IT'S A LIST, THEN RUN IT FAST: 'most will be a no, but I need to check each one' — HEADACHE not settling with paracetamol · VISUAL change (blurring, flashing lights) · RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT or EPIGASTRIC pain · nausea or vomiting · chest pain · BREATHLESSNESS or cough · dizziness, confusion, drowsiness · SWELLING of legs, hands or face · SUDDEN WEIGHT GAIN · reduced urine · jaundice or easy bruising · fits. Positives (puffy ankles, 3 kg in a fortnight) are named as important, then the list continues.**
**THE BABY — NEVER SKIPPED: movements as usual? · any BLEEDING or FLUID loss? · any tightenings, contractions or abdominal pain? Three questions, always.**

**RISK FACTORS AND ANTENATAL CARE, BRIEFLY: previous hypertension, diabetes or kidney disease · FIRST PREGNANCY · singleton or twins · FAMILY HISTORY of pre-eclampsia (her mother) · autoimmune disease · IVF · booking bloods, scans and the GTT · smoking, medications, allergies. Nulliparity and family history are both positive — ask, so you can say 'two risk factors' later.**

**CONSENT AND EXPOSURE, THEN HEAD TO TOE ALOUD: eyes with a torch, heart and chest, tummy and baby, legs and reflexes · tummy and legs from the knee exposed · CHAPERONE · general appearance — alert, no PURPURA, petechiae or bruising · hands · MEASURE THE BP YOURSELF (162/102, severe range) · conjunctival pallor, scleral jaundice, periorbital oedema · 'may I have the OPHTHALMOSCOPE? — looking for PAPILLOEDEMA and hypertensive retinopathy' (no view? say so, and don't delay treatment).**

**HEART, CHEST, ABDOMEN, BABY: heart sounds · lung bases from behind for BIBASAL CRACKLES (PULMONARY OEDEMA) · abdomen — RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT tenderness, and UTERINE tenderness (ABRUPTION) — none · SFH 30 cm, appropriate · longitudinal, cephalic · Doppler and a timer — FHR 148.**

**LEGS, REFLEXES, URINE — DONE LAST, NOT OMITTED: 'is there OEDEMA — does it PIT, and to what LEVEL?' (one precise question extracts everything) → pitting to mid-shin · ANKLE JERK brisk · CLONUS — a sharp dorsiflexion held — no sustained beats · dipstick 3+. Cover her.**

**EXPLAIN — NAME IT, SAY IT'S SERIOUS, SAY WHAT HAPPENS NEXT, THEN STOP: 'I believe you have PRE-ECLAMPSIA' — second half of pregnancy, BP rises, kidneys leak protein, other organs and the baby's growth and blood supply can be affected · 'I know you feel completely well — that's very common — but it is SERIOUS for you and the baby, and it can CHANGE QUICKLY' · ADMIT TODAY — bloods, monitoring for the baby, a tablet to lower the BP, the obstetric team, STEROIDS for the baby's lungs at 30 weeks · the only cure is DELIVERY, so the team will weigh up timing — 'nothing is happening this minute.' Leading with fits and stillbirth loses the communication mark.**

**'CAN'T I JUST COME BACK TOMORROW?' — empathise, hold the line, solve the practical problem: feeling well doesn't tell us how you're doing; it can change over hours; sending you home would be a disservice — who can bring your things in? Her hidden fear — an early baby and a caesarean: today his heartbeat and growth are reassuring, babies at this stage do very well in a specialist unit and the steroid injection helps; you can't promise an outcome, only very close watching. To the examiner: admit, bloods, urine PCR, CTG, LABETALOL, BETAMETHASONE, consider MAGNESIUM SULFATE, obstetric registrar now.**

**The RED-FLAG BLOCK — warned, then run fast; name positives (swelling, weight gain) as important and continue.**

**'PRE-ECLAMPSIA' — serious, can change quickly — ADMIT TODAY; steroids; delivery is the cure. Hold the line on 'come back tomorrow'.**

**If the clock beats the history: 'in the interest of time I'll move to examining — I'd also review her booking bloods, growth scans and BP record.' The habit that saves the station: say what you're doing before you do it, and what you're looking for while you do it — a named step you ran out of time for scores better than silence.**

**VARIANT 1 — HEADACHE IN THE STEM (frontal, two days, unresponsive to paracetamol, flashing spots): explore 30–40 seconds, then back on the list — severe pre-eclampsia with NEUROLOGICAL features; MAGNESIUM SULFATE in the plan. Version C — swelling of legs and face: explore that complaint first.**

**VARIANT 2 — SUSTAINED CLONUS (>5 beats): CNS irritability — IMPENDING ECLAMPSIA, severe regardless of BP → obstetric registrar NOW, monitored area, MgSO4 4 g IV over 20 min then 1 g/h, control BP, betamethasone (<34 weeks), prepare for delivery once stable. To Sarah: honest, not frightening — a medication to protect her from a fit, the specialist team on the way.**

**VARIANT 3 — SHE REFUSES ADMISSION: respect autonomy but explain why you're firm (how she feels doesn't reflect how she is; fits and the baby's blood supply can change without warning); if she still declines — bloods and fetal monitoring before she goes, specific safety-netting (headache, visual change, RUQ pain, rapid swelling, reduced movements), review tomorrow morning, involve her partner with permission, and offer to talk with the OBSTETRIC CONSULTANT first.**
**Late pre-eclampsia can present up to 6 weeks postpartum. SADMA if asked: smoking, alcohol, drugs, medications, allergies.**

BEFORE YOU WALK IN, READ THE CHART: the op note (indication, elective versus emergency and category, incision, uterine closure, estimated blood loss, complications); the ANAESTHETIC chart (spinal, epidural or GA, intrathecal morphine, last top-up, block height); the DRUG chart (is VTE prophylaxis charted? Is analgesia regular or PRN only?); bloods (group and screen, ANTI-D STATUS, rubella and varicella immunity, pre- and post-op Hb); the BABY'S chart (weight, Apgars, vitamin K, hepatitis B, newborn exam); and the observation and MEOWS trend with fluid balance and urine output.
