FAIL — Announcing a score that was never derived, or a total without the E, V and M components — two patients with a GCS of 8 can have completely different injuries; give the number, the word and the BEHAVIOUR every time: 'his eyes were closed on my arrival and opened to my voice, not spontaneously — that is 3'; 'he made sounds but no identifiable word — incomprehensible sounds, 2'; 'his elbows flexed inwards and his hands never reached the source — abnormal flexion, 3'; 'E3, V2, M3 — a total of 8 out of 15' (★)

FAIL — Supraorbital pressure in a head injury, or nail-bed pressure, which produces spinal reflex withdrawal you cannot separate from M4 — the role-player breaks role to say the examiner would not permit it; use a TRAPEZIUS SQUEEZE or a sternal rub only (★)

FAIL — Never speaking to the patient, or firing all four COWS questions in one breath — each is a SEPARATE stimulus and you must see the answer to each, using his name throughout: 'James, can you hear me?' … 'James, open your eyes' … 'what is your name?' … then PLACE YOUR FINGERS IN HIS PALM and say 'squeeze my fingers', because asking for a squeeze from two metres away gets nothing, and even the faintest squeeze is M6 and ends the motor assessment (★)

FAIL — Saying 'Good Samaritan law' instead of the EMERGENCY DOCTRINE — the Good Samaritan provisions cover assistance given outside your employment, not a hospital doctor working in their own emergency department: 'Examiner, my patient is unconscious and cannot consent; I am proceeding under the emergency doctrine, because the assessment is necessary and cannot reasonably be delayed'; mention hand hygiene and gloves, and ask about injuries or precautions before you begin — and if the sanitiser has been removed from the room, say the words, take no action and move on (★)

SAY — Deliver the significance in THREE BLOCKS and stay OUT of management, because the task is significance and not a plan: WHAT IT IS, with its four properties — a standardised tool scored from 3 to 15 across eye opening, verbal response and best motor response, which is QUANTITATIVE (conscious level as a number), OBJECTIVE (a different doctor should reach the same score), a COMMON LANGUAGE (one figure handed over rather than a description) and REPEATABLE (it detects improvement or deterioration); THREE MANAGEMENT IMPLICATIONS phrased as what the score TELLS you to do — it grades severity (14–15 mild, 9–13 moderate, 3–8 severe), a score of EIGHT OR LESS means the airway is unlikely to be protected, and moderate or severe injuries need a CT head; and PROGNOSIS — the lower the score at presentation the worse the outcome, with the MOTOR component carrying most of the prognostic weight; then name THIS patient's trend, because a fall from 10 to 8 is a DETERIORATION that concerns you more than the absolute value; make the one-sentence offer of pupils, plantars and inspection for clear discharge from the nose or ears, and if told to stick to your task, stop INSTANTLY and thank them, because arguing costs marks; have the limitations ready as the commonest add-on question — poor inter-rater reliability for the verbal component, untestable in an intubated, aphasic or facially swollen patient, confounded by alcohol, drugs, sedation and hypoglycaemia, silent on brainstem reflexes and pupils, and the same total arising from very different component combinations; the components — E4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none; V5 orientated, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 sounds, 1 none; M6 obeys, 5 localises, 4 withdraws, 3 flexion, 2 extension, 1 none — with no zero, and GCS-P being the GCS minus a pupil score of 0, 1 or 2; variants — EXTENSION with pronated forearms is M2 and the more ominous of the two abnormal postures, suggesting a lower brainstem lesion and warranting escalation now; a hand CROSSING THE MIDLINE of the chest to push yours away is LOCALISING at M5; clear but disorientated speech is CONFUSED at V4, not 5 and not 3; and eyes already open as you walk in are SPONTANEOUS at E4, stated explicitly as not a response to your voice

setting: PROCEDURE AND BEREAVEMENT — palliative care ward overnight, THE SON IS ALREADY CRYING WHEN YOU OPEN THE DOOR. THREE WORDS CARRY THE STATION: SIT. SILENCE. RETURN. Four automatic fails: going to the bed before speaking to the son; examining without permission; NEVER USING THE WORD DIED; and never returning to him afterwards. No clinical vocabulary at the bedside — no painful stimulus, no sternal rub, no corneal reflex in front of the family.
stem: You are the HMO covering the wards overnight. The nurse in charge of the palliative care ward has called you: Mr Peter Vasilakis, 78, has been found unresponsive and she believes he has died. CONFIRM AND CERTIFY HIS DEATH. HIS SON IS AT THE BEDSIDE. In the room: a full-body manikin, a pen torch, a timer, gloves, TISSUES, WATER, and a form on the desk. 8 minutes.
Tasks: introduce yourself to the son and explain the examination; perform the examination to confirm death; complete the form.
tasks: Introduce yourself to the son and explain the examination you are going to perform
Perform a physical examination to confirm death
Complete the form provided
time: PULL UP A CHAIR AND SIT AT HIS LEVEL · never stand over him · and FIND OUT WHAT HE ALREADY KNOWS before you say anything · WARNING SHOT, then PLAIN WORDS, then FIVE FULL SECONDS OF SILENCE with the tissues slid across · condolence and support, and if he says 'I should have stayed', NAME IT rather than moving on · EXPLAIN THE EXAMINATION IN LAY WORDS AND ASK PERMISSION, offering him the choice to stay or wait outside · THEN THE EXAMINATION WITH COMMENTARY: IDENTITY BAND FIRST; general appearance and conscious state with COWS and a trapezius squeeze, GCS 3 OF 15; LOOK (no spontaneous movement, no respiratory effort), FEEL (no radial, no carotid over ONE MINUTE), LISTEN (precordium ONE MINUTE, both lung fields THREE MINUTES) · offering to observe or take the findings; THEN THE THREE REFLEXES · pupils ONE EYE AT A TIME because one hand holds the lid and one the torch, corneal with cotton wool, gag NAMED BUT NOT PERFORMED with a suction catheter rather than your finger; ECG rhythm strip offered as an ADDITIONAL assessment · THE FORM, spoken as you write, with FINDINGS AND DURATIONS in box 3, and THE TIME OF VERIFICATION, NOT THE TIME OF DEATH · THEN GO BACK AND SIT WITH HIM.

back.dx: VERIFICATION OF DEATH — findings consistent with death: identity confirmed by wristband; no response to verbal or central painful stimulus with a GCS OF 3 OF 15 (never zero); no spontaneous movement of any limb; no visible respiratory effort or chest wall movement; no central pulse palpable over ONE MINUTE; no heart sounds over ONE MINUTE; no breath sounds bilaterally over THREE MINUTES (VERIFY — many services use one continuous five-minute observation); pupils FIXED, DILATED AND UNREACTIVE bilaterally; corneal reflex absent bilaterally; gag reflex absent. Additional assessment: ECG rhythm strip showing asystole. THE FORM: box 1 the patient's details, with the AGE recorded if the band gives no date of birth, the place of death, and method of identification as the hospital band; box 2 your name, role, signature, date and THE TIME OF YOUR EXAMINATION, WHICH IS THE TIME OF VERIFICATION; box 3 the FINDINGS AND DURATIONS, not headings — 'look normal, feel normal, listen normal' tells the examiner nothing about whether you examined the patient. CAUSE OF DEATH if asked: part 1(a) the immediate cause, 1(b) and 1(c) 'due to', part 2 other significant conditions — so 'bronchopneumonia, due to metastatic prostate carcinoma', with ischaemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes in part 2. NOT cardiac arrest or old age, which are modes of dying. REPORTABLE FEATURES (a recent procedure, a fall) mean the CORONER rather than a certificate you complete yourself — said as 'that is not a suggestion anything was done wrong; it can delay the funeral by a few days'. Lodged with the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages; Coroners Act 2003 (SA); DonateLife SA; TIS National 131 450.
plan: SIT DOWN AND ASK WHAT HE KNOWS — walk past the bed to the chair: 'Mr Vasilakis? My name is Doctor -, I am one of the doctors here tonight. MAY I SIT WITH YOU FOR A MOMENT? The nursing staff asked me to come and see you about your father. BEFORE I GO ON — CAN YOU TELL ME WHAT THEY HAVE ALREADY SAID TO YOU?' → 'they rang me. They said he'd gone. I only went home for an hour.' (Standing up, talking over the crying, or opening with 'I'm here to confirm the death' — that is your task, not his need. And do not put the news in a question: 'you know your father has passed away?' puts the burden on him.)

WARNING SHOT, PLAIN WORDS, THEN SILENCE: 'I AM AFRAID I DO NOT HAVE GOOD NEWS FOR YOU TONIGHT. ... That is right. YOUR FATHER HAS DIED. I am so very sorry.' SLIDE THE TISSUES ACROSS AND SAY NOTHING FOR FIVE FULL SECONDS. Then, once he has settled: 'my condolences. TAKE ALL THE TIME YOU NEED — there is no rush at all. We are here to support you and your family, and if there is anything you need, practical, religious or cultural, my team and I will do our best to arrange it.' AND IF HE SAYS 'I SHOULD HAVE STAYED', DO NOT MOVE ON: 'YOU WERE NOT TO KNOW. Many families are not there at the moment it happens, and it does not mean you were not with him.' (Euphemisms — passed on, gone to a better place, we lost him — get you 'sorry, do you mean he's dead?')

EXPLAIN IN LAY WORDS AND ASK PERMISSION: 'I have been asked to examine your father now, so that I can formally confirm that he has died. I will CHECK HIS IDENTIFICATION BAND, LOOK at him, FEEL FOR A PULSE at his wrist and at his neck, LISTEN to his chest for any heart sounds or breathing, and SHINE A SMALL LIGHT IN HIS EYES. It will take a few minutes and I WILL BE GENTLE WITH HIM. Is that all right with you? YOU ARE VERY WELCOME TO STAY WITH HIM, OR TO WAIT OUTSIDE — whichever you would prefer.' (Skipping permission because the patient has died misses the point: you are still asking to touch his father.)

IDENTITY FIRST, THEN CONSCIOUS STATE: 'Examiner, before I begin I am going to CONFIRM THIS PATIENT'S IDENTITY. I am lifting the sleeve to check the IDENTIFICATION BAND. The name, age and record number match the notes.' Then: 'on general inspection he is pale, with no cyanosis and no obvious injury. I will check for any response. [QUIETLY, TO THE PATIENT] Peter, can you hear me? Open your eyes. [Fingers into the palm] Squeeze my fingers. [Trapezius squeeze, held two seconds.] Examiner, there is no response to voice or to a central stimulus. HIS GLASGOW COMA SCALE IS 3 OUT OF 15 — the minimum possible score.'

LOOK, FEEL, LISTEN, with the durations named: 'looking at him, there is NO SPONTANEOUS MOVEMENT of any limb, and NO VISIBLE RESPIRATORY EFFORT or chest wall movement. Feeling: there is NO RADIAL PULSE, and NO CAROTID PULSE PALPABLE OVER ONE MINUTE. Listening: I would AUSCULTATE THE PRECORDIUM FOR ONE MINUTE AND BOTH LUNG FIELDS FOR THREE MINUTES. WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO OBSERVE FOR THAT PERIOD, OR WILL YOU GIVE ME THE FINDINGS?' → 'no heart sounds and no breath sounds — you do not need to wait.'

THE THREE REFLEXES: 'I would now like to check three reflexes. First the PUPILS — I am opening ONE EYE AT A TIME, BECAUSE ONE HAND HOLDS THE LID AND ONE HOLDS THE TORCH. The pupils are DILATED, FIXED AND UNREACTIVE to light, and the same on the other side. Second, the CORNEAL REFLEX, which I would test with a wisp of cotton wool — absent bilaterally. Third, I would confirm an ABSENT GAG REFLEX, WHICH I WOULD CHECK WITH A SUCTION CATHETER RATHER THAN MY FINGER. If you would like, I would also record a three-lead ECG RHYTHM STRIP and expect asystole — I would record that as an ADDITIONAL ASSESSMENT rather than as part of the physical examination.' (Trying to open both eyes at once has failed candidates; and never put a finger in the manikin's mouth — name it, do not do it.) Then: 'Examiner, my findings are consistent with death, and I am verifying death at this time.'

THE FORM, SPOKEN AS YOU WRITE: box 1 — 'the patient's details: name, age — THE BAND GIVES AN AGE RATHER THAN A DATE OF BIRTH, SO I WILL RECORD THE AGE — sex, record number, and the place of death. Method of identification: hospital identification band checked.' Box 2 — 'my name, my role as hospital medical officer, my signature, and the date and time. I AM RECORDING THE TIME OF MY EXAMINATION, WHICH IS THE TIME OF VERIFICATION, NOT THE TIME OF DEATH.' BOX 3, word for word: identity confirmed by hospital wristband; no response to verbal or central painful stimulus, GCS 3 of 15; no spontaneous movement of any limb; no visible respiratory effort or chest wall movement; no central pulse palpable over one minute; no heart sounds over one minute; no breath sounds bilaterally over three minutes; pupils fixed, dilated and unreactive bilaterally; corneal reflex absent bilaterally; gag reflex absent; additional assessment — ECG rhythm strip, asystole.

RETURN TO THE SON AND SIT DOWN AGAIN — if you finish the form and do not come back, the role-player says nothing at all and lets the station end in silence, and marks it a fail: 'Mr Vasilakis — I have finished. I CAN CONFIRM THAT YOUR FATHER HAS DIED, and that he died peacefully. I am very sorry for your loss. The nursing staff will stay with you for as long as you would like to be with him, and our social worker can help with the practical arrangements when you are ready. IS THERE ANYONE I CAN CALL FOR YOU TONIGHT?' → and his second agenda, if you have made room for it: 'DID HE SUFFER?' → 'from everything the staff described, and from examining him, he was comfortable and he died peacefully. He was not alone.'

VARIANTS: THE RELATIVE IS THE WIFE — swap 'your father' for 'your husband' throughout, and only ask 'how long were you married?' if there is time AT THE END, never before the news. / NO MANIKIN, the examiner giving every finding as you name the step — DO NOT SHORTEN THE SEQUENCE: name every step and duration as if performing it. / A REPORTABLE FEATURE disclosed ('he had a scope this morning', 'he had a fall last week') → 'thank you for telling me — that is important. IN THESE CIRCUMSTANCES THE LAW REQUIRES ME TO REPORT THIS TO THE CORONER rather than complete the certificate myself. That is not a suggestion anything was done wrong; it can delay the funeral by a few days.' / 'CAUSE OF DEATH?' → 'part 1(a) bronchopneumonia, 1(b) due to metastatic prostate carcinoma. Part 2: ischaemic heart disease and type 2 diabetes. NOT cardiac arrest or old age — those are modes of dying.'

Numbers and facts: GCS 3, NEVER 0. Central pulse 1 minute, heart sounds 1 minute, breath sounds 3 minutes both sides — VERIFY, since many services use one continuous 5-minute observation. Pupils ONE EYE AT A TIME. Record the AGE if the band has no date of birth. THE RECORDED TIME IS THE TIME OF VERIFICATION. Part 1(a) immediate cause, 1(b) and 1(c) due to, part 2 other significant conditions. Lodged with the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Coroners Act 2003 (SA). DonateLife SA. pefe: Role-player: Mark Vasilakis, 46, schoolteacher. His father Peter, 78, has been on the palliative care ward eleven days with metastatic prostate cancer; Mark has been there every day for a week, went home for an hour tonight, and the ward rang him. Greek Orthodox; his mother died four years ago; his sister is driving down from Port Pirie. HE IS ALREADY CRYING WHEN THE DOOR OPENS — sits with his head down and does not look up until the doctor speaks to him. HIDDEN AGENDA: guilt at not being there — IF THE DOCTOR GIVES ANY SILENCE, he says 'I SHOULD HAVE STAYED WITH HIM'; if they never leave a gap he says it once anyway at about six minutes, AND MARKS THEM DOWN IF THEY MOVE STRAIGHT ON. Second agenda: whether his father suffered — asked ONLY IF THE DOCTOR RETURNS TO HIM AFTER THE EXAMINATION.

HOW TO PLAY IT: cry continuously for the first ninety seconds and speak through it — do not make it easy. THE ORDER IS THE ANSWER: BLOOD CULTURES, then EMPIRICAL IV ANTIBIOTICS WITH DEXAMETHASONE, plus ACICLOVIR — WITHOUT WAITING FOR IMAGING OR A LUMBAR PUNCTURE — then CT head before LP given his conscious state. CT before LP if there is a focal deficit, seizure, papilloedema, immunocompromise or reduced conscious state; also avoid the tap if coagulopathic, anticoagulated or shocked. AND BE HONEST ABOUT THE SIGNS: neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski are ALL INSENSITIVE, so a negative examination would not have excluded meningitis — which is exactly why you treat on suspicion. Base-of-skull fracture signs: raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea, haemotympanum. Kernig: hip flexed to 90 then extend the knee. Brudzinski: flex the neck, hips and knees flex. Meningococcal disease is URGENTLY NOTIFIABLE. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.

Lie supine, eyes closed, arms by the sides, breathing quietly, and GIVE NOTHING unless the exact stimulus is applied. EYES: closed, and DO NOT OPEN TO ANY VOICE however loud or however often — open them only to a SUSTAINED painful stimulus. VOICE: nothing to any question; to the painful stimulus, SHOUT ONE CLEARLY RECOGNISABLE SWEAR WORD — a single word, not a sentence, not a groan. MOVEMENT: nothing to any command including the hand squeeze; to the painful stimulus, bring the RIGHT HAND ACROSS THE MIDLINE and push their hand away — that is LOCALISING. THE NECK: when they put a hand under the head and try to flex it, KEEP THE NECK RIGID so the chin cannot reach the chest, LET THE UPPER BACK COME OFF THE BED with the head, grimace and groan, and AS THEY FLEX THE NECK LET THE HIPS AND KNEES BEND. NAME the corneal and oculocephalic reflexes and ASK for the findings rather than touching a live role-player's cornea or turning his head, either of which breaks role; use the EMERGENCY DOCTRINE rather than 'Good Samaritan law'; note the primary survey is complete without repeating it; and neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski are all INSENSITIVE, so their absence would not have excluded meningitis either — which is exactly why you treat on suspicion; variants — a non-blanching purpuric rash with hypotension is MENINGOCOCCAL SEPTICAEMIA, needing immediate antibiotics, fluid resuscitation, intensive care, urgent notification to the Communicable Disease Control Branch and clearance antibiotics for the flatmates; PINPOINT pupils with a respiratory rate of 6 and track marks make opioid toxicity leading, treated with airway support and titrated naloxone while still culturing and covering for meningitis; a GLUCOSE of 1.8 is treated immediately with intravenous glucose and rechecked, without abandoning meningitis; a UNILATERAL FIXED DILATED PUPIL with contralateral weakness suggests third nerve compression from uncal herniation — a neurosurgical emergency with airway protection, avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension, urgent CT and NO lumbar puncture; and if the cervical spine is NOT cleared, the collar stays on, you image first, and you have lost your only physical sign for meningism, so you treat empirically on suspicion

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — ED trauma, live role-player in a HARD COLLAR. THE FOUR-PART SENTENCE, said five times, IS THE STATION: 'Assessing [letter]... I am looking for [the life threat]... I have found [the finding]... therefore I would [the action]. Moving to [next letter].' FOUR AUTOMATIC FAILS: removing or opening the collar; asking the patient to move his neck; leaving a life-threatening finding unaddressed and moving to the next letter; and no analgesia offered despite a stated pain score. HE GREETS YOU AT THE DOOR — his voice has already given you Response and most of Airway, so USE IT AND SAY SO.
stem: Emergency department; you are the HMO. John Delaney, 25, RESTRAINED FRONT-SEAT PASSENGER in a motor vehicle collision two hours ago at highway speed, airbags deployed, ALERT ON ARRIVAL. HR 92, BP 148/88, RR 18, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.8, GCS 15. Live role-player in a gown and a HARD CERVICAL COLLAR. On the trolley: pen torch, timer, GCS chart, sphygmomanometer. 8 minutes.
tasks: Perform a primary survey
Give a running commentary to the examiner
Explain your findings to the examiner at the end
time: D, R AND S IN THIRTY SECONDS · no danger, he has ANSWERED YOU so he is alert on AVPU and his airway is patent, inform the registrar and consultant, NO CATASTROPHIC EXTERNAL HAEMORRHAGE · A: voice and stridor, face, MOUTH WITH A TORCH, then the neck for bruising, SURGICAL EMPHYSEMA and tracheal position, WITH THE COLLAR STAYING ON · B: look, feel, listen, then ASK FOR THE RESPIRATORY RATE OVER ONE FULL MINUTE AND THE SATURATION · and do NOT turn B into a respiratory examination, because percussion, fremitus and vocal resonance belong to the secondary survey · C: radial pulse with rate, rhythm AND VOLUME, a central pulse, capillary refill and perfusion, then ASK FOR THE BLOOD PRESSURE, name THE FIVE PLACES BLOOD HIDES, two large-bore cannulae and a group and hold · D: GCS IN THREE COMPONENTS, pupils with a swinging light test, gross limb movement, A BEDSIDE GLUCOSE, and A PAIN SCORE WITH ANALGESIA GIVEN · E: name full exposure with warming and dignity, and accept a refusal in ONE sentence · THEN THE CERVICAL SPINE: DISCUSS NEXUS, DO NOT DO IT, and say you are not removing the collar yourself · then the handover, letter by letter.

back.dx: A HAEMODYNAMICALLY STABLE TRAUMA PATIENT WITH A NORMAL PRIMARY SURVEY APART FROM CHEST WALL TENDERNESS IN A SEATBELT DISTRIBUTION AND MIDLINE NECK PAIN. Adjuncts: chest and pelvic X-ray and an eFAST; analgesia; CT CERVICAL SPINE; then a secondary survey including a log roll. THE FIVE PLACES BLOOD HIDES: chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones, and ON THE FLOOR. NEXUS, all five required to clear a spine clinically: NO MIDLINE CERVICAL TENDERNESS, no focal neurological deficit, normal alertness, no intoxication, and NO PAINFUL DISTRACTING INJURY — and here he has midline neck pain, so the spine is NOT clearable and the collar stays on pending imaging. THE ELEVATED BLOOD PRESSURE: in a 25-year-old with a GCS of 15 and a normal pulse, attribute it to PAIN AND ANXIETY with catecholamine release rather than rising intracranial pressure — a CUSHING RESPONSE is hypertension WITH BRADYCARDIA and an irregular respiratory pattern — treat the pain and recheck. And say you would TREND the numbers rather than accept one set, because a young adult compensates until they suddenly do not. THE DESTABILISING VARIANTS: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX in B — saturations 88% on 15 L, absent air entry, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins — 'I am not moving on and I am not waiting for imaging: immediate decompression, finger thoracostomy in the fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line or needle decompression, then an intercostal catheter, and reassess.' HAEMORRHAGIC SHOCK in C — 'in trauma I assume shock is haemorrhagic until proven otherwise: two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, activate the massive transfusion protocol, GIVE BLOOD RATHER THAN CRYSTALLOID, TRANEXAMIC ACID WITHIN THREE HOURS, and hunt the source.' A FALLING GCS — 'go back to the beginning: airway first, jaw thrust WITH MANUAL IN-LINE STABILISATION, suction, an oropharyngeal airway, call for anaesthetic support, then repeat the whole primary survey.' A SEATBELT SIGN on the abdomen — high risk of hollow viscus and mesenteric injury and an associated LUMBAR CHANCE FRACTURE, and an initially benign abdomen does not exclude it: eFAST, CT abdomen and pelvis, serial examination.
plan: D, R AND S IN THIRTY SECONDS, using the greeting he has already given you: 'Hello John, my name is Doctor -, I am one of the doctors here. I am going to examine you now to make sure nothing has been missed after the crash. TELL ME STRAIGHT AWAY IF ANYTHING HURTS. Is that all right?' Then: 'Examiner, there is NO DANGER to the patient, the team or myself. HE HAS ANSWERED ME, SO HE IS ALERT ON THE AVPU SCALE AND I KNOW HIS AIRWAY IS PATENT AT THIS MOMENT. I would ask the nurse to inform my registrar and consultant that I am assessing a trauma patient. I CAN SEE NO CATASTROPHIC EXTERNAL HAEMORRHAGE.' (Starting Response from scratch when he greeted you at the door wastes the free information; ninety seconds on danger and help wastes the station.)

A — AIRWAY WITH CERVICAL SPINE CONTROL, face then mouth then neck: 'assessing the airway. His VOICE IS NORMAL with no hoarseness and I hear NO STRIDOR. Inspecting the face: no injuries, no bleeding, no dental damage. John, can you open your mouth for me? [Torch] No foreign body, no loose teeth, no secretions — IF THERE WERE, I WOULD SUCTION UNDER DIRECT VISION. Moving to the neck: no bruising or wounds, NO SURGICAL EMPHYSEMA on palpation, and THE TRACHEA IS CENTRAL. THE COLLAR STAYS IN PLACE. The airway is patent and protected. Moving to breathing.' (NEVER open the collar single-handed. If you must inspect the front: 'I would ask a colleague to maintain MANUAL IN-LINE STABILISATION while the front of the collar is opened.')

B — LOOK, FEEL, LISTEN, THEN THE NUMBERS: 'assessing breathing. On inspection the chest expands symmetrically, there is no respiratory distress, NO BRUISING OR SEATBELT MARK and no flail segment. On palpation there is no tenderness and NO CREPITUS, which would suggest rib fractures or surgical emphysema.' → he winces: 'ah — yeah, there, where the belt was' → 'sorry. Examiner, there is TENDERNESS ACROSS THE LEFT ANTERIOR CHEST WALL IN A SEATBELT DISTRIBUTION, with no crepitus and no palpable step. On auscultation, air entry is equal and vesicular bilaterally with no added sounds. EXAMINER, MAY I HAVE THE RESPIRATORY RATE COUNTED OVER ONE FULL MINUTE, AND THE OXYGEN SATURATION?' → 18 and 98% → 'breathing is adequate, though THE CHEST WALL TENDERNESS WILL NEED A CHEST X-RAY AND ADEQUATE ANALGESIA TO PREVENT HYPOVENTILATION.' (Percussion, tactile fremitus and vocal resonance belong to a full respiratory examination and the secondary survey — if asked, say exactly that.)

C — AND WHERE BLOOD HIDES: 'assessing circulation. The RADIAL PULSE is present, regular and of GOOD VOLUME. I would also confirm a CENTRAL pulse. Capillary refill is under two seconds, and his peripheries are warm and well perfused with no pallor. EXAMINER, MAY I HAVE A BLOOD PRESSURE AND A PULSE RATE? I can see no external bleeding. I WOULD LOOK FOR CONCEALED BLEEDING IN FIVE PLACES — THE CHEST, THE ABDOMEN, THE PELVIS, THE LONG BONES AND ON THE FLOOR. I would site TWO LARGE-BORE CANNULAE and send bloods including a group and hold. Circulation is stable. Moving to disability.' → 'why is his blood pressure high?' → 'in a 25-year-old with a GCS of 15, I would attribute that to PAIN AND ANXIETY with catecholamine release rather than to a rising intracranial pressure. A CUSHING RESPONSE IS HYPERTENSION WITH BRADYCARDIA AND AN IRREGULAR RESPIRATORY PATTERN, and his pulse and respiratory rate are normal. I would treat his pain and recheck it.'

D — DISABILITY, including the two things candidates drop: 'John, squeeze my fingers for me. Examiner: his eyes are open spontaneously, that is 4; he is talking and orientated, that is 5; he obeys commands, that is 6 — A GCS OF 15 OUT OF 15. Pupils are equal at 3 millimetres, reactive directly and consensually, with an intact swinging light test. He moves all four limbs on command. I WOULD LIKE A BEDSIDE BLOOD GLUCOSE. John, ARE YOU IN ANY PAIN? Where is it, and out of ten? I WOULD GIVE HIM TITRATED INTRAVENOUS ANALGESIA NOW.' (Forgetting the glucose misses that a crash may have been CAUSED by hypoglycaemia; and no analgesia despite a stated pain score is an automatic fail.) If the torch is too close: 'not too close, please' — apologise and continue.

E — EXPOSURE, named and not argued: 'I would fully expose the patient to complete my assessment, KEEPING HIM WARM with a blanket and warmed fluids and PRESERVING HIS DIGNITY.' → 'no — please don't' → ONE SENTENCE: 'that is fine, John. Examiner, I will note that I WOULD expose him fully in a real resuscitation.' Then, if he asks about the driver: 'I do not have that information yet, and I PROMISE I WILL FIND OUT FOR YOU as soon as I can. Right now my whole job is you — is that all right?'

THE CERVICAL SPINE — DISCUSS, DO NOT DO: 'Examiner, I would now like to assess the cervical spine and decide whether it can be CLEARED CLINICALLY or whether he needs imaging. I would apply THE NEXUS CRITERIA: no midline cervical tenderness on palpation of the spinous processes, no focal neurological deficit, a normal level of alertness, no evidence of intoxication and no painful distracting injury. If all five were satisfied I would ask him to move his neck actively through a full pain-free range. HE HAS TOLD ME HIS NECK IS SORE, SO ON THE INFORMATION I HAVE HIS SPINE IS NOT CLEARABLE AND THE COLLAR STAYS ON PENDING IMAGING. I AM NOT GOING TO REMOVE THE COLLAR MYSELF.' → 'what imaging?' → 'CT cervical spine.'

THE HANDOVER, LETTER BY LETTER, then the plan: 'in summary, a haemodynamically stable trauma patient with a normal primary survey apart from chest wall tenderness in a seatbelt distribution and midline neck pain. I would like a CHEST AND PELVIC X-RAY AND AN eFAST as adjuncts, ANALGESIA, a CT CERVICAL SPINE, and then a SECONDARY SURVEY INCLUDING A LOG ROLL.' → 'why not do a secondary survey?' → 'the task was a primary survey, and I would not begin a head-to-toe assessment until the primary survey is complete and the adjuncts are under way. If there is time I am happy to outline it: head, neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, limbs, log roll and back, then the perineum.'

'Air entry is equal and vesicular with no added sounds.' / 'May I have the respiratory rate over one full minute, and the saturation?' / 'Chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and on the floor.' / 'Eyes 4, verbal 5, motor 6 — a GCS of 15 out of 15.' / 'I would like a bedside blood glucose.'

'I would expose him fully while keeping him warm and preserving his dignity.' / 'I am not going to remove the collar myself.' / THE FOUR-PART SENTENCE: 'Assessing [letter]... I am looking for [the life threat]... I have found [the finding]... therefore I would [the action]. Moving to [next letter].' Say it five times and the station is passed.

DESTABILISING VARIANTS: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX in B → immediate decompression, finger thoracostomy in the fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line or needle decompression, then an intercostal catheter — AND DO NOT MOVE ON OR WAIT FOR IMAGING. / HAEMORRHAGIC SHOCK in C (pulse 128, BP 88/54, refill 4 s) → two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, massive transfusion protocol, BLOOD RATHER THAN CRYSTALLOID, tranexamic acid WITHIN THREE HOURS, and hunt the source with an eFAST at the bedside. / GCS FALLS MID-SURVEY → 'his conscious state has deteriorated, SO I AM GOING BACK TO THE BEGINNING. Airway first — jaw thrust with manual in-line stabilisation, suction, an oropharyngeal airway, and anaesthetic support for a definitive airway. Then I repeat the whole primary survey.' / SEATBELT SIGN ON THE ABDOMEN → high risk of hollow viscus and mesenteric injury and an associated LUMBAR CHANCE FRACTURE; an initially benign abdomen does not exclude it.

THE EMOTIONAL INTERRUPTS: 'am I going to be all right?' → 'from what I have found so far, everything important is working well — you are breathing normally, your circulation is good and you are completely with it. I do want some scans because of the neck pain, and I will explain each one before we do it.' / 'What about the driver?' → 'I do not have that information yet, and I promise I will find out for you as soon as I can. Right now my whole job is you.' Numbers: capillary refill under 2 s; respiratory rate over ONE MINUTE; GCS 15 = E4 V5 M6; FIVE places blood hides; NEXUS all five; TRANEXAMIC ACID WITHIN 3 HOURS; the LETHAL TRIAD — hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy; two large-bore cannulae; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.
pefe: Role-player: John Delaney, 25, diesel mechanic, front-seat passenger when his mate's ute left the road on the way back from Kadina and hit a tree two hours ago; seatbelt on, airbag deployed, no loss of consciousness, remembers everything. Lie on the trolley in a gown and a hard collar, FULLY ALERT, co-operative and a bit frightened, answering normally in short sentences. FINDINGS: MIDLINE NECK SORENESS about six out of ten — say so if asked about pain, AND THIS IS THE FINDING THAT STOPS THE COLLAR COMING OFF; chest tender across the left side where the belt sat, about five out of ten, with 'ah, there' and a wince when palpated; mouth opens fully with mild jaw ache; everything else normal.

HOW TO PLAY IT: SAY 'HI DOCTOR' AS SOON AS THEY REACH YOU, BEFORE THEY START — and watch whether they use it. If they shine the torch close to your face: 'can you not shine that right in my eye' — they should apologise and continue. If they try to expose you: 'NO — PLEASE DON'T', and the examiner voice says 'that is fine' — they should accept it in ONE sentence, not argue. IF THEY TRY TO TAKE THE COLLAR OFF OR ASK YOU TO TURN YOUR HEAD, DO NOT MOVE — examiner voice: 'no' — AND MARK IT AS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL. At around minute five, ask 'WHAT ABOUT THE DRIVER?' and note whether they acknowledge it and return to the task. IF THEY NEVER ASK ABOUT PAIN, SAY NOTHING AND MARK IT DOWN. If they start palpating the abdomen or doing a full chest examination: 'your task is the primary survey.' If the summary is unstructured: 'can you structure that for me?'

Scored out of 20: introduced and gained assent; danger, response, send for help; excluded catastrophic haemorrhage; airway voice and stridor; airway face and mouth with a torch; airway neck, emphysema, trachea, COLLAR KEPT ON; breathing inspection, palpation and auscultation both sides; asked for respiratory rate and saturations; circulation pulse rate, rhythm and volume; capillary refill and perfusion; asked for blood pressure; NAMED THE FIVE SITES OF CONCEALED BLEEDING; GCS in three components; pupils and gross limb movement; ASKED FOR A BLOOD GLUCOSE; PAIN SCORE AND OFFERED ANALGESIA; named exposure and warming; and a handover structured letter by letter.
Everything else — Normal
Exposure — REFUSED — 'no, please don't'; accept it in one sentence

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner

FAIL — Leaving a life-threatening finding unaddressed and moving to the next letter — the FOUR-PART SENTENCE said five times is the station: 'assessing [letter]… I am looking for [the life threat]… I have found [the finding]… therefore I would [the action]. Moving to [next letter]'; a tension pneumothorax in B means you do not move on and you do not wait for imaging (★)

FAIL — No analgesia offered despite a stated pain score — ask where the pain is and out of ten, then act: 'thank you — I will give you something for that now; Examiner, I would give titrated intravenous analgesia'; and if you never ask about pain at all, he says nothing and it is marked down (★)

(★)

FAIL — Ignoring that he greeted you at the door and starting Response from scratch — his voice has already given you Response and most of Airway, so USE it and SAY so: 'he has answered me, so he is alert on the AVPU scale and I know his airway is patent at this moment'; and keep D, R and S to THIRTY SECONDS total (no danger to the patient, the team or yourself; ask the nurse to inform the registrar and consultant; no catastrophic external haemorrhage) rather than spending ninety on danger and help

SAY — Name the FIVE PLACES BLOOD HIDES in C — chest, abdomen, pelvis, long bones and ON THE FLOOR — with two large-bore cannulae and bloods including a group and hold; and do not accept one set of numbers in a young trauma patient, because a young adult compensates until they suddenly do not, so say you would TREND them; if asked why the blood pressure is high, 'in a 25-year-old with a GCS of 15 I would attribute that to pain and anxiety with catecholamine release rather than to a rising intracranial pressure — a CUSHING RESPONSE is hypertension with BRADYCARDIA and an irregular respiratory pattern, and his pulse and respiratory rate are normal; I would treat his pain and recheck it'; in D give the GCS in three components with reasons, check the pupils including a swinging light test, confirm movement in all four limbs, and ASK FOR A BEDSIDE GLUCOSE, because a crash may have been CAUSED by hypoglycaemia; destabilising variants — a TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX (saturations 88% on 15 L, absent air entry, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins) means immediate decompression by finger thoracostomy in the FIFTH intercostal space in the anterior axillary line or needle decompression, then an intercostal catheter and reassessment; HAEMORRHAGIC SHOCK means blood rather than crystalloid, a massive transfusion protocol, tranexamic acid and hunting the source; a FALLING GCS sends you back to the beginning with a jaw thrust under manual in-line stabilisation and anaesthetic support for a definitive airway; a SEATBELT SIGN carries a high risk of hollow viscus and mesenteric injury and an associated lumbar Chance fracture, so an initially benign abdomen does not exclude it and you arrange an eFAST, CT abdomen and pelvis and serial examination; and the emotional interrupts ('am I going to be all right?', 'what about the driver?') each get one warm sentence and a return to the task

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION AND VIVA — regional ED, ADVANCED LIFE SUPPORT MANNEQUIN, examiner reads the responses. THE MANNEQUIN GIVES YOU NOTHING: every observation you would have made must be SPOKEN, or it did not happen. SIX AUTOMATIC FAILS: a bare total with no components; a score of 8 with NO MENTION OF THE AIRWAY; THREE SEPARATE PAINFUL STIMULI; nail-bed pressure used to score the motor component; saying 'the motor scale is different in children'; and any mention of a GCS of zero.
stem: Emergency department, regional hospital; you are the HMO. THOMAS, 8 YEARS OLD, brought in by ambulance after being FOUND UNRESPONSIVE AT HOME. His mother is on her way and NO HISTORY IS AVAILABLE. Primary survey complete, on oxygen by mask, cervical spine immobilised AND CLEARED RADIOLOGICALLY. Full-body ALS mannequin; the examiner reads out the responses when you apply each stimulus. A GCS chart and pen on the trolley. 8 minutes.
tasks: Assess this child's level of consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale, explaining each step to the examiner
State his score with its components
Answer the examiner's questions
time: ENTRY, HAND HYGIENE, CONTEXT · and ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS INCLUDING THE BLOOD GLUCOSE, which is four extra words and the one reversible cause you can exclude at the bedside · GENERAL APPEARANCE BEFORE YOU TOUCH HIM, with NAMED NEGATIVES: no decorticate flexion, no decerebrate extension, not pale or cyanosed, no Cheyne-Stokes or Kussmaul pattern, no external injury, no scalp swelling, AND NO BRUISING IN UNUSUAL SITES · THE VERBAL SCREEN, four sentences with four pauses, then SAY WHAT IT WAS FOR · ONE PAINFUL STIMULUS, WARNED AND CENTRAL, a trapezius squeeze sustained up to ten seconds, which gives you all three components at once · THE ONE CLARIFYING QUESTION WORTH ASKING: did the arm cross the midline towards the stimulus, or move away from it · SCORE ALOUD COMPONENT BY COMPONENT WITH THE BEHAVIOUR JUSTIFYING EACH, and say WHICH SCALE YOU USED AND WHY · THEN THE AIRWAY SENTENCE IMMEDIATELY, the completion offers, the repeat at fifteen minutes, and THE SAFEGUARDING SENTENCE · then the six viva questions.

back.dx: E2 V2 M4 = 8 OUT OF 15, IN THE SEVERE RANGE — eyes did not open to voice but opened to pain (E2); an incomprehensible sound with no recognisable word (V2); the limb PULLED AWAY WITHOUT CROSSING THE MIDLINE, so WITHDRAWING rather than localising (M4). AND SAY WHICH SCALE: 'at eight years I have used the standard adult scale, SINCE THE PAEDIATRIC VERBAL MODIFICATION APPLIES BELOW FOUR.' THE AIRWAY SENTENCE MUST FOLLOW THE TOTAL: a GCS of 8 or less means he is unlikely to protect his own airway, so arrange airway protection NOW with anaesthetics and intensive care in parallel. THE SIX VIVA ANSWERS. (1) WHICH COMPONENT DIFFERS IN A CHILD: THE VERBAL RESPONSE, BELOW FOUR YEARS — under four, 5 is alert and babbling or words normal for age, 4 is fewer words than usual or a spontaneous irritable cry, 3 is crying only to pain, 2 is moaning to pain, 1 is none; the EYE column is identical at every age, and the motor column changes only at the top, where 6 becomes spontaneous purposeful movement and 5 becomes withdrawal to touch. (2) LOWEST SCORE: THREE, one per component, NO ZERO AT ANY AGE — a deceased patient still scores 3. (3) INTUBATED AND SEDATED: V1 WITH A T ANNOTATION — and say explicitly that sedation and paralysis invalidate the eye and motor components too, so the post-intubation score cannot be compared with the pre-intubation one, which is why documenting the score BEFORE intubation matters. (4) WHY NOT NAIL-BED PRESSURE: it is PERIPHERAL, producing a SPINAL REFLEX withdrawal rather than a brain-mediated response, so it cannot score the motor component — trapezius is central, reproducible and does not bruise; a sternal rub bruises and makes localisation harder to demonstrate; supraorbital pressure risks eye injury. (5) ASYMMETRY: score the BEST response on the BETTER side, so M5 — but REPORT THE ASYMMETRY SEPARATELY, because a difference between sides suggests a lateralised intracranial lesion and matters more than the total. (6) WHAT WOULD MAKE YOU DISTRUST THE SCORE: sedation or paralysis, intubation, PERIORBITAL SWELLING preventing eye opening (E1 with a C annotation), hypoglycaemia or hypothermia, a pre-existing developmental or speech disorder, and a language barrier — recording the limitation beside the score rather than presenting the number as clean.
plan: ENTRY AND THE GLUCOSE: 'Hello, my name is Doctor -, one of the doctors here in the emergency department. THOMAS, I AM GOING TO CHECK YOU OVER NOW. I WILL BE GENTLE AND I WILL TELL YOU BEFORE I DO ANYTHING.' [Sanitise hands.] 'Examiner, I note the primary survey is complete and the cervical spine has been immobilised and cleared. BEFORE I BEGIN, MAY I HAVE HIS OBSERVATIONS, INCLUDING HIS BLOOD GLUCOSE?' → 5.1 → 'thank you — the glucose is normal, SO I HAVE EXCLUDED HYPOGLYCAEMIA AT THE BEDSIDE.'

GENERAL APPEARANCE, BEFORE YOU TOUCH HIM, with named negatives: 'on general appearance he is lying still with NO ABNORMAL POSTURING — no decorticate flexion and no decerebrate extension. He is not pale and not cyanosed. His breathing is regular, with no CHEYNE-STOKES or KUSSMAUL pattern. I can see no obvious external injury, no scalp swelling and NO BRUISING IN UNUSUAL SITES.' → 'why do you mention bruising?' → 'BECAUSE IN A CHILD WITH AN UNEXPLAINED REDUCED CONSCIOUS STATE I HAVE TO CONSIDER NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY.' (On a mannequin, the named negatives are the only thing you can be marked for at this step.)

THE VERBAL SCREEN — four sentences, four pauses, then say what it was for: 'Thomas, can you hear me?' ... 'Thomas, open your eyes.' ... 'What is your name?' ... [fingers placed into his palm] 'Can you squeeze my fingers?' → no response → 'THOSE FOUR QUESTIONS SCREEN EYE OPENING TO VOICE, THE VERBAL RESPONSE AND MOTOR OBEDIENCE TO COMMAND, WITHOUT HURTING HIM. As there is no response to any of them, I now need a painful stimulus.' (Going straight to the sternum is both unkind and lower-scoring — the verbal screen is free and covers three components.)

ONE PAINFUL STIMULUS, WARNED AND CENTRAL: 'Examiner, I am going to apply A SINGLE CENTRAL PAINFUL STIMULUS. Thomas, I am going to squeeze your shoulder now, and it may be uncomfortable.' [Trapezius squeeze, firm, SUSTAINED UP TO TEN SECONDS.] → 'he opens his eyes; he makes a groaning sound with no recognisable words; his right arm pulls away from your hand but does not come across his body towards it.' (THREE SEPARATE STIMULI, ONE PER COMPONENT, IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL — one sustained stimulus gives you all three at once, and using three tells the examiner you do not understand the test.)

THE ONE CLARIFYING QUESTION WORTH ASKING: 'thank you. CAN I JUST CONFIRM WHETHER THE ARM CROSSED THE MIDLINE TOWARDS THE STIMULUS, OR MOVED AWAY FROM IT? THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN LOCALISING AND WITHDRAWING.' → 'it moved away; it did not cross the midline.' (Asking it once, precisely, shows you know the discriminator BEFORE you use it. Repeatedly asking the examiner to interpret findings for you is a different behaviour and scores badly.)

SCORE ALOUD, COMPONENT BY COMPONENT: 'on EYE OPENING, he did not open his eyes to voice but opened them to the painful stimulus, so that is E2. On BEST VERBAL RESPONSE, he made an incomprehensible sound with no recognisable word, so that is V2. On BEST MOTOR RESPONSE, he pulled the limb away from the stimulus without bringing it across the midline towards it, so he is WITHDRAWING RATHER THAN LOCALISING — M4. That gives a total GCS of 8 OUT OF 15, WHICH IS IN THE SEVERE RANGE. AT EIGHT YEARS I HAVE USED THE STANDARD ADULT SCALE, SINCE THE PAEDIATRIC VERBAL MODIFICATION APPLIES BELOW FOUR.' (A bare 'his GCS is 8' is an automatic fail — on a mannequin the commentary is the ONLY evidence you performed the assessment.)

THE AIRWAY SENTENCE IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE TOTAL, then the completion offers: 'A GCS OF 8 OR LESS MEANS HE IS UNLIKELY TO BE ABLE TO PROTECT HIS OWN AIRWAY, SO I WOULD ARRANGE AIRWAY PROTECTION NOW and involve anaesthetics and intensive care in parallel. To complete my neurological assessment I would examine his PUPILS for size, symmetry and the direct light reflex; perform FUNDOSCOPY looking for papilloedema and RETINAL HAEMORRHAGES; assess TONE, REFLEXES AND PLANTARS ON BOTH SIDES LOOKING FOR ASYMMETRY; look for signs of a BASE-OF-SKULL FRACTURE; assess for NECK STIFFNESS, since the cervical spine is cleared; and REPEAT THE SCORE IN FIFTEEN MINUTES, BECAUSE THE TREND MATTERS MORE THAN ANY SINGLE READING.' Then the parallel management if pushed: high-flow oxygen, IV access, bloods including a gas, electrolytes, liver and renal function, FBC and a TOXICOLOGY SCREEN, urgent CT head, empirical meningitis cover if febrile, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval.

THE SAFEGUARDING SENTENCE, said once and neutrally — not saying it at all is the more common error: 'I would also want a careful, NON-JUDGEMENTAL history from his mother about how he was found and what happened beforehand, BECAUSE IN A CHILD WITH AN UNEXPLAINED REDUCED CONSCIOUS STATE I HAVE TO ACTIVELY CONSIDER ACCIDENTAL INGESTION AND NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY.' IF THE MOTHER ARRIVES: 'hello, I am Doctor -, one of the doctors looking after Thomas. I am very glad you are here. Thomas is unconscious and we do not yet know why, so we are checking him thoroughly and getting the team ready to help him breathe safely. I am not going to guess at a cause until we have looked properly. CAN I ASK YOU TWO QUICK QUESTIONS THAT WILL HELP HIM RIGHT NOW — HOW WAS HE FOUND, AND IS THERE ANY MEDICINE IN THE HOUSE HE COULD HAVE REACHED?' (Two targeted questions from a parent are worth more than anything else in the room; reassuring her he will be fine, or making her wait, is the trap.)

THE SIX VIVA QUESTIONS (see dx), answered precisely. AND IF THE EXAMINER DISAGREES WITH YOUR SCORE — 'I would have called that M5' — neither argue nor collapse: 'THAT MAY WELL BE RIGHT, AND I WOULD BE HAPPY TO BE CORRECTED. My reasoning was that the arm moved away from the stimulus rather than crossing the midline towards it, which is the discriminator I use between withdrawal and localisation. IF IT DID CROSS THE MIDLINE THEN IT IS M5 AND THE TOTAL BECOMES 9.' State the discriminator, accept the correction, and RECOMPUTE THE TOTAL OUT LOUD.

ask: 'Thomas, I am going to check you over now. I will tell you before I do anything.' / 'May I have his observations, including his blood glucose?' / 'No bruising in unusual sites — because in a child I have to consider non-accidental injury.' / 'Those four questions screen eye, verbal and motor without hurting him.'

'I am going to apply a single central painful stimulus.' / 'Thomas, I am going to squeeze your shoulder and it may be uncomfortable.' / 'Can I confirm whether the arm crossed the midline towards the stimulus, or moved away from it?' / 'E2, V2, M4 — a total of 8 out of 15, which is in the severe range.' / 'At eight years I have used the standard adult scale, since the paediatric modification applies below four.'

'A GCS of 8 or less means he is unlikely to protect his own airway.' / 'I would repeat the score in fifteen minutes — the trend matters more than any single reading.' / 'The component that differs in a child is the verbal response, below four years of age.'

VARIANTS: THE SAME CHILD AT THREE — eyes open to voice is E3, unchanged; BABBLING WORDS NORMAL FOR HIS AGE is V5; pushing your hand away across the midline is M5; total 13 — 'and I would say explicitly that scoring the verbal response depends on KNOWING WHAT IS NORMAL FOR HIM, so I would ask his mother how many words he usually has.' / THE INFANT — the same paediatric scale, many charts printing a separate infant column, plus ASSESSING THE ANTERIOR FONTANELLE (tense or bulging suggests raised intracranial pressure) and weighting THE QUALITY OF THE CRY AND WHETHER HE IS CONSOLABLE BY HIS MOTHER. / NO RESPONSE AT ALL → 'E1, V1, M1 — a total of 3, the lowest possible score. THERE IS NO ZERO. This is a peri-arrest situation: confirm he has a pulse and is breathing, call a resuscitation team immediately, and secure the airway.'

THE DETERIORATING CHILD, fifteen minutes later — no eye opening, no sound, BOTH ELBOWS FLEX ONTO THE CHEST, pulse 48, BP 132/80 → 'E1, V1, M3 — ABNORMAL FLEXION, WHICH IS DECORTICATE POSTURING — a total of 5. THAT IS A FALL OF THREE POINTS, which is a significant deterioration in its own right. THE BRADYCARDIA WITH HYPERTENSION IS A CUSHING RESPONSE and indicates raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation. I would call for immediate senior help, secure the airway, avoid hypoxia and hypotension, NURSE HIM HEAD-UP AT THIRTY DEGREES, arrange an urgent CT head and speak to neurosurgery, AND I WOULD NOT PERFORM A LUMBAR PUNCTURE.'
pefe: Partner brief: THERE IS NO PATIENT ROLE — the patient is a mannequin (a pillow, a rolled towel, or a housemate lying still with eyes shut and instructed not to react). YOU ARE THE EXAMINER: stand beside the candidate, say nothing unless asked, and READ OUT THE FINDINGS ONLY WHEN THE CORRECT STIMULUS IS APPLIED, then ask the six questions. The correct answer is E2 V2 M4 = 8. Observations on request: HR 72, BP 108/64, RR 12, SpO2 97% on oxygen, T 36.4 — AND THE GLUCOSE 5.1 ONLY IF THEY ASK, never volunteered. On general appearance: 'that is all correct', then 'WHY DO YOU MENTION BRUISING?' To the verbal screen: 'there is no response to any of those.' To ONE warned central stimulus: 'he opens his eyes; he makes a groaning sound with no recognisable words; his right arm pulls away from your hand.' To a second or third stimulus: repeat the same findings AND MARK IT DOWN. To nail-bed or earlobe pressure: 'the arm pulls away', then ask question 4 early. Pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm; fundi normal; tone, reflexes and plantars normal and symmetrical; no neck stiffness.

THE THREE MOMENTS THAT DECIDE THE STATION: do they WARN THE CHILD before the painful stimulus? Do they GIVE THE COMPONENTS, or just the total — a bare '8' is a fail, and DO NOT PROMPT THEM, wait and let the silence sit. And do they SAY THE AIRWAY SENTENCE — a score of 8 without any mention of airway protection is the second automatic fail. Timing prompts: at 4 minutes, if they have not scored, 'please give me your score'; at 5 minutes start the six questions regardless of where they are; and throughout, if they ask you to interpret a finding more than once, say 'YOU TELL ME'.

Numbers: E 1-4, V 1-5, M 1-6, total 3-15, NO ZERO. This station E2 V2 M4 = 8. THE PAEDIATRIC VERBAL MODIFICATION APPLIES BELOW FOUR YEARS VERIFY. Verbal under 4: 5 alert or babbling normally, 4 fewer words than usual or irritable cry, 3 cries only to pain, 2 moans to pain, 1 none. Motor under 4: 6 spontaneous purposeful movement, 5 withdraws to touch; rows 4 to 1 unchanged. THE EYE COLUMN IS UNCHANGED AT EVERY AGE. M5 LOCALISES — crosses the midline, above the clavicle, reaches you; M4 WITHDRAWS — away, never reaches you. Severity mild 13-15, moderate 9-12, severe 8 or less VERIFY. A fall of 2 or more triggers senior review and re-imaging. One central stimulus, warned, up to 10 seconds. Best response, better side, then report asymmetry separately. Intubated V1 T; eyes swollen shut E1 C. Weight (age + 4) x 2 = 24 kg at eight. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, WCH paediatric retrieval, Poisons Information 13 11 26 VERIFY.
Verbal screen — NO response to any of the four questions
To ONE sustained central stimulus — He opens his eyes (E2) · a groaning sound with no recognisable words (V2) · the right arm pulls away without crossing the midline (M4)
Total — E2 V2 M4 = 8 — the SEVERE range
If you ask for extras — Pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm; fundi normal with no papilloedema or retinal haemorrhages; tone, reflexes and plantars normal and symmetrical; no neck stiffness

★ A score of 8 with no mention of the airway — the examiner has chosen 8 deliberately

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — A bare total with no components — on a mannequin the commentary is the ONLY evidence you did the assessment at all, and the examiner is briefed to say nothing and let the silence sit; give the behaviour justifying each component: 'he did not open his eyes to voice but opened them to the painful stimulus, so that is E2; he made an incomprehensible sound with no recognisable word, so V2; he pulled the limb away from the stimulus without bringing it across the midline towards it, so he is WITHDRAWING rather than localising — M4; a total GCS of 8 out of 15, which is in the SEVERE range' (★)

FAIL — A score of 8 with no mention of the AIRWAY — the examiner has chosen 8 deliberately, and the sentence comes IMMEDIATELY after the total: 'a GCS of 8 or less means he is unlikely to be able to protect his own airway, so I would arrange airway protection now and involve anaesthetics and intensive care in parallel with the rest of my assessment'; then offer to complete the neurological assessment — pupils for size, symmetry and direct light reflex; fundoscopy for papilloedema and RETINAL HAEMORRHAGES; tone, reflexes and plantars on both sides looking for ASYMMETRY; signs of a base-of-skull fracture; neck stiffness, since the cervical spine is cleared; and REPEAT THE SCORE IN FIFTEEN MINUTES, because the trend matters more than any single reading (★)

FAIL — Three separate painful stimuli, one per component, or nail-bed pressure used to score the motor response — ONE sustained central stimulus gives you all three at once, and using three tells the examiner you do not understand the test; WARN him first ('Thomas, I am going to squeeze your shoulder now, and it may be uncomfortable'), use a TRAPEZIUS squeeze because it is central, reproducible and does not bruise, and know why the alternatives are wrong: nail-bed pressure is PERIPHERAL and produces a SPINAL REFLEX withdrawal rather than a brain-mediated response, a sternal rub bruises and makes localisation harder to demonstrate, and supraorbital pressure risks eye injury (★)

FAIL — Saying 'the motor scale is different in children' — it is the VERBAL column, and it differs BELOW FOUR YEARS: under four, 5 is alert and babbling or using words normal for age, 4 is fewer words than usual or a spontaneous irritable cry, 3 is crying only to pain, 2 is moaning to pain, 1 is none; the EYE column is identical at every age, and the MOTOR column changes only at the top, where 6 becomes spontaneous purposeful movement and 5 becomes withdrawal to touch; and any mention of a GCS of ZERO is an automatic fail, because the minimum is THREE at every age, one point per component, with a maximum of 15 (★)

FAIL — Not asking for the BLOOD GLUCOSE, the one reversible cause you can exclude at the bedside in a child and four extra words — and do not skip the FREE VERBAL SCREEN, which is painless and screens three components at once ('Thomas, can you hear me?' … 'Thomas, open your eyes' … 'what is your name?' … fingers placed in his palm, 'can you squeeze my fingers?'), saying what it was for: 'those four questions screen eye opening to voice, the verbal response and motor obedience to command, WITHOUT HURTING HIM — as there is no response to any of them, I now need a painful stimulus' (★)

SAY — Give NAMED NEGATIVES on general appearance, because on a mannequin they are the only thing you can be marked for at that step: no abnormal posturing, meaning no DECORTICATE flexion and no DECEREBRATE extension; not pale and not cyanosed; regular breathing with no CHEYNE–STOKES or KUSSMAUL pattern; no obvious external injury, no scalp swelling, and NO BRUISING IN UNUSUAL SITES — because in a child with an unexplained reduced conscious state you have to actively consider NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY; add the safeguarding sentence once, neutrally, since not saying it at all is the commoner error ('I would want a careful, non-judgemental history from his mother about how he was found and what happened beforehand, because I have to consider accidental ingestion and non-accidental injury'); ask the ONE clarifying question precisely — 'can I just confirm whether the arm crossed the midline TOWARDS the stimulus, or moved AWAY from it? That is the difference between localising and withdrawing' — because asking it once shows you know the discriminator, while repeatedly asking the examiner to interpret findings for you scores badly; M5 LOCALISES by crossing the midline above the clavicle and reaching you, M4 WITHDRAWS away and never reaches you; score the BEST response on the BETTER side, then report any asymmetry SEPARATELY, because a difference between sides suggests a lateralised intracranial lesion and matters more than the total; if intubated, the verbal component is V1 with a T annotation, and sedation and paralysis invalidate the eye and motor components too, so the post-intubation score cannot be compared with the pre-intubation one; eyes swollen shut are E1 with a C annotation; things that make you distrust a score — sedation, paralysis, intubation, periorbital swelling, hypoglycaemia or hypothermia, a pre-existing developmental or speech disorder, and a language barrier — each recorded BESIDE the score rather than presented as though the number were clean; weight is (age + 4) × 2, so 24 kg at eight, and MedSTAR is 1300 13 12 33 for paediatric retrieval; variants — a fall of THREE points with BRADYCARDIA and HYPERTENSION is a CUSHING RESPONSE indicating raised intracranial pressure with impending herniation, needing immediate senior help, airway protection, avoidance of hypoxia and hypotension, nursing head-up at thirty degrees, urgent CT and neurosurgery, and NO lumbar puncture; if the examiner disagrees with your score, state the discriminator, accept the correction and RECOMPUTE THE TOTAL OUT LOUD rather than arguing or collapsing; and when the mother arrives mid-station, do not reassure her that he will be fine and do not make her wait — two targeted questions ('how was he found, and is there any medicine in the house he could have reached?') are worth more than anything else in the room

setting: Physical examination — ED, resuscitation mannequin, and the father is the only person in the room who can talk. One warm sentence to him inside the first fifteen seconds, then narrate the sequence out loud. Four AUTOMATIC FAILS: never naming a diagnosis; never speaking to the father at all; calling the child stable because the saturations are 98% on oxygen; and promising him the child will be fine. The three words that must be said: stridor, wheeze, anaphylaxis.
stem: Emergency department. A 2-YEAR-OLD BOY brought in by his father with SWOLLEN LIPS AND DIFFICULTY BREATHING; background of ATOPY (eczema and hay fever), a flu-like illness two weeks ago, and TODAY HE ATE PEANUTS AT A BIRTHDAY PARTY. Symptoms over the last 60 minutes. Full-body resuscitation mannequin, supine, OXYGEN MASK IN PLACE; the father is at the bedside and frightened. PAEDIATRIC CUFFS IN THREE SIZES, an aneroid sphygmomanometer, stethoscope, pulse oximeter and thermometer on the trolley. 8 minutes.
tasks: Measure the vital signs and explain the steps of measuring them
Perform an anterior chest examination
Give your diagnosis
time: HAND HYGIENE, THEN THE FATHER: 'I can see you are very worried, and I would be too... he is in safe hands', and permission in one sentence, because for a two-year-old CONSENT COMES FROM THE PARENT · THEN DRSABCD, EACH NUMBER INTERPRETED AGAINST THE CHILD'S AGE: general appearance and AIRWAY FIRST, looking for foreign body, vomitus and LIP AND TONGUE SWELLING · BREATHING: look, listen and feel, RESPIRATORY RATE OVER A FULL SIXTY SECONDS, and SATURATIONS BOTH WITH AND WITHOUT THE MASK · CIRCULATION: BRACHIAL pulse in a two-year-old, rate over sixty seconds with rhythm and volume, capillary refill centrally and peripherally · THE CUFF, justified by the 40% RULE and chosen from the labels rather than measured with a tape · BLOOD PRESSURE IN TWO STEPS, palpatory THEN auscultatory, naming K1 AND K5 · TEMPERATURE, which is one of the five AND does diagnostic work here · THEN THE ANTERIOR CHEST: inspect (naming the specific signs of distress and the skin), palpate expansion and trachea, percuss, auscultate side against side in three zones and the axillae · AND CONNECT THE TWO SOUNDS · then the diagnosis to the examiner and ONE PLAIN SENTENCE to the father.

back.dx: ANAPHYLAXIS, most likely to PEANUT, WITH AIRWAY INVOLVEMENT — a two-year-old with a background of atopy who developed swollen lips and difficulty breathing within an hour of eating peanut; tachypnoeic at 44, tachycardic at 168, normotensive at 88/54, afebrile at 36.9, and OXYGEN DEPENDENT at 98% on the mask and 91% off it; with STRIDOR indicating UPPER airway obstruction and WIDESPREAD EXPIRATORY WHEEZE indicating BRONCHOSPASM, plus lip swelling and urticaria. Differentials, all less likely given the acute onset after a known allergen, the lip swelling and THE ABSENCE OF FEVER: croup, epiglottitis, an inhaled foreign body, and acute asthma. MANAGEMENT even though not asked: INTRAMUSCULAR ADRENALINE IMMEDIATELY — 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 into the OUTER MID-THIGH, about 0.12 mL for an estimated 12 kg — KEPT LYING FLAT, oxygen continued, and senior paediatric and anaesthetic help called; repeat at five minutes; 20 mL/kg saline if hypotensive; observe at least four hours after the last dose. AND THE INTERPRETATIONS THAT CARRY THE MARKS: RR 44 is well above the normal 20-30 for a two-year-old; HR 168 is above the normal 90-140, and A SLOW HEART RATE WOULD WORRY YOU FAR MORE, because BRADYCARDIA IN A DISTRESSED CHILD IS A PRE-ARREST SIGN; 88 systolic is normal, with the threshold roughly 70 PLUS TWICE HIS AGE, about 74 — and HYPOTENSION IN ANAPHYLAXIS IS A VERY LATE SIGN, SO A NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE IS NOT REASSURING; and the absence of fever is what makes croup and epiglottitis less likely.
plan: HANDS, THEN THE FATHER — one warm sentence inside fifteen seconds: [sanitise hands] 'Hello, my name is Doctor -, I am one of the doctors here. Are you Jack's dad? I CAN SEE YOU ARE VERY WORRIED, AND I WOULD BE TOO. I am going to check him over now, find out what is going on, and give him the best treatment we have. HE IS IN SAFE HANDS. I will talk you through everything as I go. Is it all right with me to examine him?' (If he interrupts again mid-examination: 'THAT IS A REALLY IMPORTANT QUESTION AND I PROMISE I WILL ANSWER IT FULLY IN JUST A MINUTE. Right now the fastest way I can help Jack is to finish checking him over. STAY RIGHT WHERE HE CAN SEE YOU.' Acknowledge, promise, keep going — and NEVER say 'he will be fine'.)

GENERAL APPEARANCE AND AIRWAY FIRST: 'Examiner, on general appearance I am assessing whether Jack is ALERT AND RESPONSIVE — looking at me, reaching for his father, crying or resisting — and I am LISTENING FROM THE END OF THE BED for audible noisy breathing, stridor or wheeze. Moving to airway: I would look in the mouth for a foreign body or vomitus, and SPECIFICALLY FOR SWELLING OF THE LIPS AND TONGUE. May I have those findings?' → 'the airway is patent; the child has stridor; the lips are swollen' → SAY WHAT IT MEANS IMMEDIATELY: 'thank you — STRIDOR MEANS OBSTRUCTION OF THE UPPER AIRWAY, and in this context that is a serious sign that changes my urgency.' (Being handed the word stridor and not interpreting it is exactly what the examiner is testing.)

BREATHING — and ask for BOTH saturations: 'assessing breathing. I would LOOK for chest movement, and LISTEN AND FEEL for air at the mouth and nose. I would COUNT THE RESPIRATORY RATE OVER A FULL 60 SECONDS and measure the oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter on the finger or toe. Examiner, MAY I HAVE HIS RESPIRATORY RATE, AND HIS SATURATIONS BOTH WITH AND WITHOUT THE MASK?' → 44, and 98% with, 91% without → INTERPRET BOTH: 'a respiratory rate of 44 is well above the normal 20 to 30 for a two-year-old — he is TACHYPNOEIC. And HE IS ONLY MAINTAINING HIS SATURATIONS ON OXYGEN, so he is OXYGEN DEPENDENT and the mask stays on.' (Asking only for saturations on the mask, reporting 98% and calling the child stable is an automatic fail.)

CIRCULATION — pulse first, and the bradycardia line: 'assessing circulation. HE IS BREATHING AND HAS A PULSE, SO I AM NOT STARTING COMPRESSIONS. In a two-year-old I would use the BRACHIAL pulse, count the rate over 60 seconds and comment on rhythm and volume, and check capillary refill centrally and peripherally.' → HR 168, refill 2 s → '168 is above the normal 90 to 140 for his age — he is tachycardic, which fits distress and early shock. I WOULD BE FAR MORE WORRIED BY A SLOW HEART RATE IN A CHILD THIS UNWELL, BECAUSE BRADYCARDIA IN A DISTRESSED CHILD IS A PRE-ARREST SIGN.'

THE CUFF AND THE BLOOD PRESSURE IN TWO STEPS: 'before I take a blood pressure I want the correct cuff size. THE BLADDER WIDTH SHOULD BE ABOUT 40% OF THE MID-ARM CIRCUMFERENCE, and the length should encircle 80 to 100% of the arm. The paediatric cuffs are labelled, and IF TWO SIZES WOULD FIT, GUIDANCE IS TO TAKE THE LARGER. For a two-year-old I will take the small child cuff.' → 'what happens if the cuff is too small?' → 'IT OVER-READS the blood pressure; too large UNDER-READS.' Then: 'I would measure it in two steps. FIRST, PALPATORY: I palpate the brachial pulse, inflate until it disappears, then deflate slowly — the pressure at which the pulse returns is my estimated systolic. THAT STEP PREVENTS ME BEING CAUGHT BY AN AUSCULTATORY GAP. SECOND, AUSCULTATORY: stethoscope over the brachial artery below the cuff, inflate 20 to 30 mmHg above the palpated systolic, deflate slowly. THE FIRST KOROTKOFF SOUND IS SYSTOLIC; THE DISAPPEARANCE OF SOUND, THE FIFTH, IS DIASTOLIC.' → 88/54 → 'normal for his age — the threshold I would worry about is roughly 70 plus twice his age, about 74 — BUT HYPOTENSION IN ANAPHYLAXIS IS A VERY LATE SIGN, SO A NORMAL BLOOD PRESSURE IS NOT REASSURING.' (Measuring the mannequin's arm with a tape, or spending two minutes comparing cuffs, wastes the station: name the rule, read the label, choose.)

TEMPERATURE AND THE SUMMARY OF THE VITALS: 'finally I would take his temperature, ideally axillary or tympanic in a child of this age.' → 36.9 → 'so to summarise the vital signs: he is TACHYPNOEIC at 44, TACHYCARDIC at 168, NORMOTENSIVE at 88 over 54, AFEBRILE at 36.9, and OXYGEN DEPENDENT with saturations of 98% on the mask and 91% off. THE ABSENCE OF FEVER IS IMPORTANT — IT MAKES CROUP AND EPIGLOTTITIS LESS LIKELY.' (Forgetting the temperature is an automatic fail — it is one of the five, and here it also does diagnostic work.)

THE ANTERIOR CHEST, in order and with the specific signs named: '[to father] I am going to lift his top so I can see his chest. [To examiner] Inspecting the anterior chest. I am looking at chest movement in the upper and lower zones for symmetry, and for signs of respiratory distress: TRACHEAL TUG, INTERCOSTAL RECESSION, SUBCOSTAL RECESSION, PARADOXICAL ABDOMINAL MOVEMENT, ACCESSORY MUSCLE USE, NASAL FLARING, HEAD BOBBING AND GRUNTING. I am also looking at the skin for URTICARIA, flushing or swelling. Palpating for chest expansion, hands on the lateral chest with my thumbs toward the xiphisternum, comparing sides. Two fingers into the suprasternal notch — checking the trachea is central. Percussing both sides at the same level, comparing left with right down to the bases. Auscultating the same points, side against side, in the upper, mid and lower zones and out into the axillae — I would use a PAEDIATRIC DIAPHRAGM if available. I would also assess vocal resonance, ALTHOUGH A TWO-YEAR-OLD WILL NOT SAY NINETY-NINE ON REQUEST, so I would listen while he cries or talks.' (If tempted to roll the mannequin: 'THE TASK IS THE ANTERIOR CHEST, SO I AM NOT EXAMINING THE BACK.')

CONNECT THE TWO SOUNDS, THEN NAME IT: 'so he has STRIDOR, WHICH IS INSPIRATORY AND COMES FROM THE UPPER AIRWAY, and WIDESPREAD EXPIRATORY WHEEZE, WHICH COMES FROM THE LOWER AIRWAY. HE HAS OBSTRUCTION AT BOTH LEVELS.' Then the full diagnosis to the examiner with the differentials and the management sentence (see dx), and finally ONE PLAIN SENTENCE TO THE FATHER: 'Jack is having a SEVERE ALLERGIC REACTION, almost certainly to the peanuts. It is making his airways swell and tighten. WE HAVE A MEDICINE CALLED ADRENALINE THAT WORKS VERY QUICKLY, AND I AM GOING TO GIVE IT NOW.' (Describing the findings without ever saying the word ANAPHYLAXIS fails task 3; and a three-minute explanation of IgE and mast cells to a frightened father is the opposite error.)

'May I have his saturations both with and without the mask?' / 'He is only maintaining his saturations on oxygen — he is oxygen dependent.' / 'Bradycardia in a distressed child is a pre-arrest sign, not reassurance.' / 'The bladder width should be about 40% of the mid-arm circumference; if two would fit, take the larger.' / 'Too small over-reads; too large under-reads.' / 'First Korotkoff sound is systolic; disappearance, the fifth, is diastolic.'

'Stridor is upper airway and inspiratory; wheeze is lower airway and expiratory. He has obstruction at both levels.' / 'My diagnosis is anaphylaxis, most likely to peanut, with airway involvement.' / 'The task is the anterior chest, so I am not examining the back.' / To the father: 'Jack is having a severe allergic reaction... we have a medicine called adrenaline that works very quickly, and I am going to give it now.'

VARIANTS: HYPOTENSION AND COLLAPSE (BP 62/30, floppy and drowsy) → 'that systolic is well below the threshold for his age, roughly 70 plus twice his age, about 74. With drowsiness this is ANAPHYLACTIC SHOCK. He needs intramuscular adrenaline immediately, TO BE KEPT LYING FLAT WITH HIS LEGS RAISED — NEVER STOOD UP — high-flow oxygen, intravenous or intraosseous access and a 20 mL/kg normal saline bolus, with the adrenaline repeated at five minutes and an infusion considered if he does not respond.' / IT IS CROUP (T 38.6, barking cough, hoarse voice, no lip swelling or rash, three days of coryza) → 'the barking cough, hoarse voice, fever and gradual onset over days fit CROUP — laryngotracheobronchitis — and the absence of an allergen, lip swelling and urticaria argues against anaphylaxis. Keep him CALM ON HIS FATHER'S LAP, avoid upsetting him, and give ORAL DEXAMETHASONE, with nebulised adrenaline if the stridor is severe or at rest.' VERIFY / IT IS EPIGLOTTITIS (T 39.2, drooling, sitting forward, muffled voice, not fully immunised) → 'this is EPIGLOTTITIS until proven otherwise. I WOULD NOT EXAMINE HIS THROAT, WOULD NOT LIE HIM DOWN AND WOULD NOT DISTRESS HIM. Leave him on his father's lap, oxygen if tolerated, and call immediately for senior ANAESTHETIC AND ENT help for a definitive airway IN THEATRE, with intravenous antibiotics once the airway is secure.'

MORE: THE FOREIGN BODY (wheeze only over the right chest, no rash or lip swelling, violent coughing while eating) → 'unilateral wheeze after a choking episode makes an INHALED FOREIGN BODY the leading diagnosis. HE IS CURRENTLY ABLE TO BREATHE, SO I WOULD NOT PERFORM BLIND FINGER SWEEPS OR BACK BLOWS — keep him calm, give oxygen, and arrange urgent ENT or paediatric surgical review for bronchoscopy.' / 'WHY NOT ANTIHISTAMINE FIRST?' → 'because antihistamines DO NOT TREAT AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION OR HYPOTENSION, and delay in giving adrenaline is one of the recognised contributors to FATAL anaphylaxis. Adrenaline is first line and there is NO ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION. Antihistamines have a role for the skin symptoms afterwards, and I would avoid promethazine in a child this young.' / THE EXAMINER RUSHES YOU ('assume all the vital signs are normal') → 'thank you. FOR COMPLETENESS, the observations I would have wanted are the respiratory rate over sixty seconds, saturations on and off oxygen, heart rate, rhythm and volume, capillary refill, blood pressure with an appropriately sized cuff, and temperature. Moving to the chest.' / THE FATHER BREAKS DOWN ('is he going to die?') → 'he is very unwell, AND I AM NOT GOING TO PRETEND OTHERWISE. But this is something we treat every week and we have the medicine for it right here. I am giving it now. STAY WHERE HE CAN SEE YOU AND HOLD HIS HAND — THAT HELPS HIM.'
pefe: Partner brief — THEY PLAY BOTH THE FATHER AND THE EXAMINER. Sam Whitlock, 34, father of Jack, 2: an hour ago Jack was at a cousin's birthday party and ate something with peanuts — a satay skewer or a slice of cake. Within about twenty minutes his lips went puffy and he started making a noise breathing in, and Sam drove him straight here. Jack has ECZEMA AND HAY FEVER, had a bad cold two weeks ago, HAS NEVER HAD A REACTION LIKE THIS BEFORE and has never been told he is allergic to anything; THERE IS NO EPIPEN AT HOME. No regular medicines except a steroid cream, immunisations up to date, no choking, no vomiting or diarrhoea, and the father's SISTER HAS A NUT ALLERGY. HE IS FRIGHTENED: start standing, leaning over the trolley, IN THE DOCTOR'S WAY — not aggressive, just scared and asking questions. IF THE DOCTOR ACKNOWLEDGES THE FEAR SPECIFICALLY IN THEIR FIRST FEW SENTENCES, sit down, calm noticeably, and interrupt only twice more. IF THEY WALK STRAIGHT PAST TO THE MANNEQUIN, INTERRUPT EVERY THIRTY SECONDS — 'what are you doing?', 'is he getting worse?', 'why is nobody doing anything?' — until they address you. If they say 'he will be fine', accept it BUT MARK IT DOWN, because nobody can promise that. At about six minutes ask once: 'IS HE GOING TO DIE?' At the end: 'WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG WITH HIM?' — and they must answer in PLAIN ENGLISH, not 'anaphylaxis with airway involvement'.

EXAMINER FINDINGS, GIVEN ONLY WHEN ASKED: mouth — 'no foreign body, no vomitus, the airway is patent'; general appearance and audible sounds — 'the child has STRIDOR'; lips and tongue — 'the lips are swollen, the tongue is not'; respiratory rate 44; saturations '98% with the mask' — AND GIVE THE 91% ONLY IF THEY ASK ABOUT OFF OXYGEN; pulse 'present, 168, regular, good volume'; capillary refill 2 seconds; BLOOD PRESSURE 88/54 — BUT ONLY AFTER THEY HAVE DESCRIBED BOTH THE PALPATORY AND AUSCULTATORY STEPS; temperature 36.9; inspection — 'tracheal tug and intercostal recession, urticarial rash over the trunk'; expansion symmetrical, trachea central, resonant and equal; auscultation — 'widespread expiratory wheeze in all zones'; the back — 'the task is the anterior chest'; blood gas, chest X-ray or tryptase — 'not available. What is your diagnosis?' IF THEY NEVER ASK FOR OBSERVATIONS, SAY NOTHING AT ALL AND MARK IT DOWN. Prompts: at 4 minutes 'please move on to the chest examination'; at 6:30 'what is your diagnosis?'; if they name anaphylaxis, 'what would you give, and by what route?'; if they choose a cuff, 'what happens if the cuff is too small?'

Numbers: cuff bladder width about 40% of mid-arm circumference, length 80-100%, TAKE THE LARGER of two. BP palpatory THEN auscultatory, inflating 20-30 mmHg above the palpated systolic; K1 systolic, K5 diastolic (K4 muffling in young children). NORMAL AT 2 YEARS VERIFY: HR 90-140, RR 20-30, systolic 85-100, SpO2 95% or more on air, T 36.5-37.5. HYPOTENSION FOR AGE is roughly systolic under 70 + (2 x age), about 74 mmHg. WEIGHT (age + 4) x 2 = 12 kg. ADRENALINE 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 IM, OUTER MID-THIGH, max 0.5 mg, repeat every 5 minutes — about 0.12 mL here. Autoinjector 150 mcg for 7.5-20 kg, 300 mcg over 20 kg. Saline 20 mL/kg bolus if hypotensive. OBSERVE AT LEAST FOUR HOURS after the last dose. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450, WCH for paediatric retrieval. Scored out of 10, one point each, with the automatic fails listed on the front of this card.
