must: FAIL — Saying the child is stable because the saturations are 98% ON OXYGEN — ask for them BOTH WAYS, because the examiner gives 91% only if you ask about off the mask: 'may I have his saturations both WITH and WITHOUT the mask?' → 'he is only maintaining his saturations on oxygen, so he is OXYGEN DEPENDENT and the mask stays on' (★)

FAIL — Never saying the word ANAPHYLAXIS, or never speaking to the father at all — task 3 is the diagnosis, so NAME it: 'my diagnosis is ANAPHYLAXIS, most likely to peanut, WITH AIRWAY INVOLVEMENT', with differentials of croup, epiglottitis, an inhaled foreign body and acute asthma, all less likely given the acute onset after a known allergen, the lip swelling and the absence of fever; then ONE plain sentence to the father rather than three minutes on IgE and mast cells — 'Jack is having a severe allergic reaction, almost certainly to the peanuts; it is making his airways swell and tighten, and we have a medicine called adrenaline that works very quickly — I am going to give it now' (★)

FAIL — Promising the father he will be fine — nobody can promise that, and he is briefed to mark it down; ONE WARM SENTENCE inside the first fifteen seconds settles him for the rest of the station ('I can see you are very worried, and I would be too; I am going to check him over now, find out what is going on and give him the best treatment we have — he is in safe hands'), and if he interrupts again, ACKNOWLEDGE, PROMISE and KEEP GOING ('that is a really important question and I promise I will answer it fully in just a minute; right now the fastest way I can help Jack is to finish checking him over — stay right where he can see you'); when he asks 'is he going to die?' at about six minutes, be honest rather than dismissive: 'he is very unwell, and I am not going to pretend otherwise — but this is something we treat every week and we have the medicine for it right here; I am giving it now. Stay where he can see you and hold his hand, that helps him' (★)

FAIL — Being handed the word STRIDOR and not saying what it means, or reporting the wheeze without CONNECTING the two sounds — the examiner gives you stridor precisely to see whether you can interpret it: 'stridor means obstruction of the UPPER airway, and in this context that is a serious sign'; then after auscultation, 'so he has STRIDOR, which is inspiratory and comes from the upper airway, and widespread EXPIRATORY WHEEZE, which comes from the lower airway — he has obstruction at BOTH levels' (★)

FAIL — Reporting numbers without INTERPRETING them against the child's age, or forgetting the temperature, which is one of the five and here also does diagnostic work — a respiratory rate of 44 against a normal 20 to 30 is TACHYPNOEA; a heart rate of 168 against 90 to 140 is tachycardia fitting distress and early shock, with the added line that BRADYCARDIA IN A DISTRESSED CHILD IS A PRE-ARREST SIGN rather than reassurance; a systolic of 88 is normal, with the threshold at roughly 70 plus twice the age, about 74 — and HYPOTENSION IN ANAPHYLAXIS IS A VERY LATE SIGN, so a normal blood pressure is not reassuring; and afebrile at 36.9 makes croup and epiglottitis less likely (★)

SAY — Justify the CUFF with the rule rather than measuring the mannequin's arm or spending two minutes comparing cuffs: the bladder width should be about 40% of the mid-arm circumference and the length should encircle 80 to 100% of the arm, the cuffs are labelled, and IF TWO WOULD FIT, TAKE THE LARGER — with 'too small OVER-reads, too large UNDER-reads' ready; describe BOTH blood pressure steps, because the examiner withholds the number until you do — PALPATORY first (palpate the brachial pulse, inflate until it disappears, deflate slowly, and the pressure at which it returns is the estimated systolic, which stops you being caught by an AUSCULTATORY GAP), then AUSCULTATORY (stethoscope over the brachial artery below the cuff, inflate 20 to 30 mmHg above the palpated systolic, deflate slowly; the FIRST Korotkoff sound is systolic and the FIFTH, disappearance, is diastolic, with K4 muffling used in young children); run the chest in order — inspection naming the specific signs of distress (tracheal tug, intercostal and subcostal recession, paradoxical abdominal movement, accessory muscle use, nasal flaring, head bobbing, grunting) plus the skin for urticaria, flushing or swelling; palpation of expansion and a central trachea; percussion comparing sides; then auscultation side against side in three zones and into the axillae — and do NOT try to roll the mannequin, because 'the task is the anterior chest, so I am not examining the back' satisfies the examiner; sanitise hands and take consent from the PARENT in one sentence; then management even unasked — intramuscular ADRENALINE 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1000 into the OUTER MID-THIGH, about 0.12 mL for an estimated 12 kg by (age + 4) × 2, maximum 0.5 mg, repeated every five minutes, kept LYING FLAT with the legs raised and NEVER STOOD UP, oxygen continued, and senior paediatric and anaesthetic help called, with a 20 mL/kg saline bolus if hypotensive and observation for at least four hours after the last dose (autoinjector 150 mcg for 7.5–20 kg, 300 mcg above 20 kg); variants — a temperature of 38.6 with a BARKING COUGH, hoarse voice, no lip swelling and three days of coryza is CROUP, kept calm on his father's lap with oral dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline if the stridor is severe or at rest; 39.2 with DROOLING, sitting forward, refusing to lie down and a MUFFLED voice in an incompletely immunised child is EPIGLOTTITIS — do not examine the throat, do not lie him down, do not distress him, and call immediately for senior anaesthetic and ENT help for a definitive airway in theatre; UNILATERAL wheeze after a choking episode with no rash or lip swelling is an INHALED FOREIGN BODY, so no blind finger sweeps or back blows while he is still breathing, but urgent ENT or paediatric surgical review for bronchoscopy; and 'why not an antihistamine first?' is answered by saying antihistamines do not treat airway obstruction or hypotension, delay in giving adrenaline is a recognised contributor to fatal anaphylaxis, adrenaline is first line with no absolute contraindication, and promethazine is avoided in a child this young

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional GP, and THE STEM FORBIDS A CRANIAL NERVE EXAMINATION IN CAPITALS. THE STATION IS ONE SENTENCE: you will find the tender temporal artery early, AND FINDING THE SIGN AND STOPPING IS THE SINGLE COMMONEST FAIL — say out loud that you are completing a systematic examination before you commit. Six automatic fails: doing cranial nerves after the stem forbade it; stopping when you find the tenderness; OMITTING FUNDOSCOPY; OMITTING THE SHOULDER GIRDLE; reassuring her it is the jaw joint; and DELAYING STEROID FOR THE BIOPSY OR THE ESR.

BP 138/82 — pulse 84 — TEMPERATURE 37.4 — RR 16 — SpO2 98% — BGL 6.1. time: ASK FOR THE OBSERVATIONS FIRST, then WIPE · AND WARN HER ABOUT TENDERNESS BEFORE YOU TOUCH HER, because she is briefed to wince · GENERAL APPEARANCE naming CACHEXIA AND PTOSIS, the two systemic and neurological items you can still have without cranial nerves · INSPECTION of scalp and face, every negative a differential excluded aloud · SYSTEMATIC PALPATION starting at the OCCIPUT and working forward, so the tender temple is found in sequence rather than jabbed at · THEN THE SENTENCE: 'that is highly suggestive, BUT I AM GOING TO COMPLETE A SYSTEMATIC EXAMINATION BEFORE I COMMIT' · periorbital margins, zygoma, mandible, SINUSES, parotid and salivary glands, and the GLOBES OFFERED BUT NOT PRESSED · THE TWO KEY POINTS: FUNDOSCOPY for a swollen pale chalky white disc, and THE SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLES for polymyalgia, which overlaps in about one in five · EARS with the otoscope ASSEMBLED, nose, mouth, throat and nine node groups, each site NAMED · THE TMJ examined SEPARATELY with one finger · neck and shoulders · then diagnosis in lay words WITH THE EYE RISK NAMED, and differentials in lay words.

back.dx: GIANT CELL ARTERITIS (TEMPORAL ARTERITIS) — a 68-year-old with six weeks of right-sided headache, JAW CLAUDICATION (pain worse on chewing), scalp tenderness, weight loss and fatigue, with a THICKENED, TENDER, NON-PULSATILE right superficial temporal artery and overlying erythema, a low-grade temperature, and SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLE STIFFNESS WITH PRESERVED POWER suggesting overlapping polymyalgia rheumatica. TO THE PATIENT IN LAY WORDS: a blood vessel running up the side of your head has become inflamed and swollen; chewing hurts because those muscles need extra blood and the narrowed vessel cannot deliver it; your immune system has started attacking your own blood vessels. THEN THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS: THE SAME VESSELS SUPPLY THE EYE, AND UNTREATED IT CAN CAUSE PERMANENT LOSS OF VISION — which is why treatment starts TODAY, BEFORE THE TESTS COME BACK. Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily VERIFY; IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for three days if there is visual loss VERIFY; ESR and CRP; temporal artery biopsy with an adequate segment WITHIN ONE TO TWO WEEKS, which stays useful after steroids have started VERIFY — and WAITING IS THE ONE THING THAT COSTS PEOPLE THEIR SIGHT. DIFFERENTIALS IN LAY WORDS: the jaw joint itself (her joint was not sore), a tooth or gum infection, a sinus infection, a salivary gland problem which can hurt with eating, an ear infection spreading to the bone behind the ear, and the commoner headaches — migraine and neck-related headache — 'none of them fit as well, AND NONE OF THEM CAN TAKE YOUR SIGHT'. Safety-net: any change in vision — blurring, a shadow, double vision — straight to an emergency department. IMPORTANT PHRASING: report the girdle as LIMITED BY PAIN AND STIFFNESS WITH PRESERVED POWER; polymyalgia does not cause true weakness, and reporting 'proximal weakness' describes a myositis instead. And a NORMAL FUNDUS DOES NOT EXCLUDE THE DIAGNOSIS.
plan: OBSERVATIONS, WIPE, AND THE WARNING: 'Examiner, may I have this patient's vital signs before I begin?' Then: '...I have been asked to examine your head and face today. I will look at your head, feel over different parts of it, look in your ears, eyes and mouth, and finish with some special tests. PARTS OF IT MAY BE TENDER, SO PLEASE TELL ME THE MOMENT ANYTHING HURTS AND I WILL STOP. Is that all right? I will just clean my hands and put on gloves.' (She is briefed to wince — a candidate who never warned her looks careless when she does.)

GENERAL APPEARANCE AND INSPECTION, both spoken: 'on general appearance my patient is sitting comfortably, alert and orientated with a normal level of consciousness, and not in obvious pain or distress. THERE IS NO CACHEXIA, NO PTOSIS, no facial asymmetry, no tremor and no abnormal limb posture.' Then: 'on inspection of the scalp and face, ON THE RIGHT I CAN SEE A PROMINENT, THICKENED, TORTUOUS, CORD-LIKE TEMPORAL ARTERY WITH OVERLYING REDNESS. No temporalis wasting. No vesicular rash. No periorbital swelling, no proptosis, no red eye. No raccoon eyes or Battle sign. No parotid swelling.' (Cachexia and ptosis are the two the examiner is listening for, because they are the systemic and neurological items you can still have without cranial nerves. And inspecting in silence throws away every excluded differential.)

SYSTEMATIC PALPATION — START AT THE BACK: 'Mary, I am going to feel gently through your hair now. Tell me if anything is sore. Starting at the back of the head... over the top... and forward to the forehead.' → she pulls away: 'ooh, that's very tender' → 'I'M SORRY, I'LL BE GENTLER. Examiner, there is MARKED TENDERNESS OVER THE RIGHT TEMPORAL REGION. THE RIGHT SUPERFICIAL TEMPORAL ARTERY IS THICKENED, TENDER AND NON-PULSATILE; THE LEFT IS NORMAL AND PULSATILE. THAT IS HIGHLY SUGGESTIVE, BUT I AM GOING TO COMPLETE A SYSTEMATIC EXAMINATION BEFORE I COMMIT. Periorbital margins, zygomatic arch, along the mandible — all non-tender.' (SAY THE COMPLETION SENTENCE OUT LOUD so the examiner records the decision — finding the sign and stopping is the single commonest fail in this station.)

SINUSES, GLANDS, GLOBES: 'pressing up under the brow ridges for the FRONTAL sinuses — any pain? And up under the cheekbones for the MAXILLARY sinuses? No sinus tenderness. Now over both cheeks for the PAROTID glands, and I would like to perform BIMANUAL PALPATION OF ALL THE SALIVARY GLANDS. Examiner, I would also like to MENTION gently assessing the globes for a hard, stony eye suggesting ACUTE GLAUCOMA — I WILL NOT PERFORM IT.' (Offer it; never press on the eyes.)

THE TWO KEY POINTS — both are automatic fails if omitted: 'Examiner, two things specific to my working diagnosis. FIRST, FUNDOSCOPY, LOOKING FOR A SWOLLEN, PALE, CHALKY WHITE DISC and for papilloedema.' → normal → 'thank you — NOTING THAT A NORMAL FUNDUS DOES NOT EXCLUDE THE DIAGNOSIS. SECOND, THE SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLES, BECAUSE POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA OVERLAPS IN ABOUT ONE IN FIVE. Mary, lift both arms out to the side and hold them against my hands — and now stand up from the chair without using your arms.' → 'they've been stiff, especially first thing' → REPORT IT CORRECTLY: 'Examiner, SHOULDER GIRDLE MOVEMENT IS LIMITED BY PAIN AND STIFFNESS WITH PRESERVED POWER.' (Reporting 'proximal weakness' is wrong — polymyalgia does not cause true weakness, and if power really were reduced you would be describing a myositis.)

EAR, NOSE, MOUTH, THROAT, NODES — each site named, because each clears a differential: 'Examiner, I would like to examine the ears — MAY I ASSEMBLE THE OTOSCOPE?' [swap the heads] 'canals clear, drums intact, no bulging. Pressing behind the ears over the MASTOIDS — non-tender, no swelling. I would like to look inside the nose: septum central, no polyps, no discharge. Mary, open wide for me — I am looking for DENTAL CARIES OR AN ABSCESS, and for any ulcers or lesions in the mouth or throat. No caries, NO TENDER TOOTH ON PERCUSSION, no ulcers, no exudate. I will step behind you now for the neck glands: submental, submandibular, jugular chain, posterior triangle, pre- and post-auricular, occipital and supraclavicular. No lymphadenopathy.' (Asking to do 'an ENT examination' as one lump loses the marks that live in the individual sites.)

THE TMJ, EXAMINED SEPARATELY WITH ONE FINGER, then neck and completion: 'a finger just in front of each ear — any pain? Now open and close slowly, and pretend to chew.' → 'no, that bit's not sore — the sore part is higher up' → 'joints non-tender, no crepitus or clicking, no deviation, OPENING ADMITS THREE FINGERS.' Then: 'down the spinous processes and paraspinal muscles — no tenderness. Show me your neck movements — full and pain-free. Now the shoulders themselves, actively and then passively. To complete I would CHECK THE BLOOD PRESSURE IN BOTH ARMS, PALPATE ALL PULSES AND LISTEN FOR BRUITS, take a focused history for VISUAL SYMPTOMS AND JAW CLAUDICATION, and perform a full neurological examination if permitted.' (Pressing with a flat hand over the temple and the joint together and then calling the joint tender is the trap — one finger, named landmark.)

DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIALS IN LAY WORDS (see dx), with THE EYE RISK NAMED and treatment started today. She pushes once: 'shouldn't you wait and see what the tests say?' → 'it's a fair question, but no. WAITING IS THE ONE THING THAT COSTS PEOPLE THEIR SIGHT, and the biopsy stays useful for a week or two after we start.' Then the differentials in her words and the safety-net. HER HIDDEN AGENDA: 'last Tuesday everything went dark in my right eye for a couple of minutes' — IF SHE SAYS THIS, STOP EVERYTHING: 'thank you for telling me — THAT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING YOU HAVE SAID TODAY... Examiner, this is AMAUROSIS FUGAX in the context of suspected giant cell arteritis. I would treat this as a SIGHT-THREATENING EMERGENCY: intravenous methylprednisolone in the order of 500 to 1000 mg daily for three days, urgent ESR and CRP, and a SAME-DAY discussion with the on-call ophthalmology registrar. I will finish examining her, but I AM NOT WAITING FOR RESULTS BEFORE TREATING.' VERIFY (Filing it away and carrying on palpating converts a pass into a fail.)

'That is highly suggestive, but I will complete a systematic examination before I commit.' / 'I would like to MENTION assessing the globes rather than perform it.' / 'Fundoscopy, looking for a swollen, pale, chalky white disc.' / 'A normal fundus does not exclude the diagnosis.' / 'Girdle movement limited by pain and stiffness, WITH PRESERVED POWER.' / 'May I assemble the otoscope?'

VERSION B — SINUSITIS AT 35: out go the temporal artery key points, arteritis-framed fundoscopy and the shoulder girdle; IN come a fuller nose examination, throat, teeth, and the cervical and supraclavicular nodes — and TEMPERATURE BECOMES A LIVE FINDING rather than a formality. The finding: 'tenderness over both maxillary sinuses, the turbinates are oedematous and there is purulent postnasal discharge... I would like to MENTION sinus transillumination, THOUGH I WOULD NOT RELY ON IT.' To the patient: 'the air spaces in your cheekbones and forehead are inflamed — that is why leaning forward makes it worse, the pressure builds. MOST OF THESE ARE VIRAL and settle in a week or so with saline rinses, a steroid nasal spray and simple painkillers; ANTIBIOTICS USUALLY DO NOT HELP. But I want you back straight away if the skin around your eye becomes swollen or red, if your eye starts to bulge or you see double, or if you become drowsy or very unwell.' VERIFY

VARIANT — THE DECOY JOINT: she says 'it's sore right here, IN FRONT of my ear — and it clicks when I open wide' → 'the tenderness is ON THE JOINT ITSELF, immediately in front of the tragus, with palpable crepitus and clicking on opening. THE TEMPORAL REGION ABOVE IT AND THE TEMPORAL ARTERY ARE NORMAL AND PULSATILE. That moves me AWAY from giant cell arteritis and towards TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DYSFUNCTION. I would still send ESR and CRP given her age, and I would tell her exactly what visual symptoms would bring her straight back.' (Diagnosing arteritis anyway because of the age and the chewing is exactly what the variant tests — whether you examine or pattern-match.) / THE EXAMINER SHUTS YOU DOWN — 'stick to your task, doctor' → 'THANK YOU, EXAMINER', then move straight on: no justification, no second attempt, no visible irritation.
pefe: Role-player: Mary Whitfield, 68, retired schoolteacher in Kadina, still driving and doing the church flowers; polite, understated, slightly apologetic, not wanting to make a fuss. Six weeks of right-sided headache most of the day at 7/10, barely touched by paracetamol; JAW ACHES AFTER A FEW MOUTHFULS so she leaves the crusts and cuts up meat; THREE KILOGRAMS LOST without trying; SCALP SORE WHEN BRUSHING HER HAIR; shoulders and hips stiff for an hour every morning; feels drained and a bit warm at night. Perindopril and knee osteoarthritis, non-smoker, two wines on a Friday. HIDDEN AGENDA: LAST TUESDAY HER RIGHT EYE WENT COMPLETELY DARK FOR ABOUT TWO MINUTES and came back — she has told nobody, having decided it was the heat. She volunteers it ONLY if the doctor asks about her eyes or vision, looks into her eyes with the ophthalmoscope, or asks whether anything else is worrying her — AND IF NOTHING IS ASKED BY SEVEN MINUTES she says it anyway, quietly: 'doctor — is it silly to mention my eye went dark for a minute last week?'

HOW SHE PLAYS IT: THE WINCE — when the right temple is palpated, pull the head away and say 'ooh, that's very tender', AND ONLY FOR THE TEMPLE; nothing else hurts. THE JOINT — if the doctor presses in front of the ear, say clearly 'NO, THAT BIT ISN'T SORE — THE SORE PART IS HIGHER UP.' THE GIRDLE — lift the arms slowly and wince, BUT DO NOT GIVE WAY: she is STIFF, NOT WEAK. PUSH ONCE when steroids are mentioned: 'shouldn't you wait and see what the tests say?' Become emotional ONLY if the word blindness is used bluntly without warning — then go quiet: 'I look after my husband. I have to be able to drive.' If the doctor never speaks to her and only narrates to the examiner, SAY NOTHING AND LET THEM LOSE THE MARKS.

Numbers: 8-minute station, STOP EXAMINING AT 6:20. GCA essentially only over 50. Prednisolone 40-60 mg daily VERIFY; IV methylprednisolone 500-1000 mg daily for three days if visual loss VERIFY; BIOPSY WITHIN 1-2 WEEKS with an adequate segment VERIFY. PMR overlap about ONE IN FIVE. Acuity is 6/6, NEVER 20/20. Mouth opening THREE FINGERS. Sinusitis antibiotics only if severe or beyond 7-10 days VERIFY. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. Scored out of 14: observations first; full WIPE with consent, hand hygiene and gloves; WARNED ABOUT TENDERNESS; general appearance and inspection out loud; SYSTEMATIC skull palpation rather than a jab at the temple; commented on the artery pulse BOTH SIDES; KEPT EXAMINING AFTER FINDING THE TENDERNESS; sinuses, parotid and salivary glands; FUNDOSCOPY; SHOULDER GIRDLE; ears, mastoids, nose, mouth, throat, cervical nodes; TMJ examined SEPARATELY from the temple; diagnosis in words she understood WITH THE EYE RISK NAMED; and at least four differentials in lay language.
The temple — RIGHT TEMPLE MARKEDLY TENDER — the right superficial temporal artery is THICKENED, TENDER and NON-PULSATILE; the LEFT is normal and pulsatile
Skull, orbits, zygoma, mandible — All non-tender
Sinuses and salivary glands — Non-tender; parotid and salivary glands normal
TMJ — Non-tender, no crepitus, no deviation, opening admits three fingers
Hidden agenda — Two minutes of complete darkness in the RIGHT eye last Tuesday — given only if you ask about vision or concerns
fails: ★ Stopping the examination when you find the tenderness — the single commonest fail, and the completion sentence must be said out loud
★ Omitting fundoscopy, or omitting the shoulder girdle — both are automatic fails
Performing a cranial nerve examination when the stem forbade it in capitals
Delaying steroid for the biopsy or the ESR; or reassuring her it is the jaw joint

Never warning her about tenderness before touching a patient briefed to wince; pressing on the globes instead of offering; reporting 'proximal weakness' rather than stiffness with preserved power; asking for 'an ENT examination' as one lump; and filing away the two minutes of darkness in her right eye and carrying on palpating

Ears, nose, mouth, throat

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
must: FAIL — Stopping the examination when you find the tenderness — the single commonest fail, and the COMPLETION SENTENCE must be said aloud so the examiner records the decision: 'that is highly suggestive, but I am going to complete a systematic examination before I commit'; the palpation is SYSTEMATIC FROM THE OCCIPUT FORWARD — back of the head, over the top, forward to the forehead — after a warning, because she is briefed to wince and a candidate who never warned her looks careless, and then 'there is marked tenderness over the right temporal region; the right superficial temporal artery is thickened, TENDER and NON-PULSATILE, and the left is normal and pulsatile' (★)

FAIL — Omitting FUNDOSCOPY, or omitting the SHOULDER GIRDLE — both are automatic fails, and both are announced as specific to the working diagnosis: 'first, fundoscopy, looking for a swollen, pale, CHALKY WHITE disc and for papilloedema' — adding that A NORMAL FUNDUS DOES NOT EXCLUDE THE DIAGNOSIS — and 'second, the shoulder and hip girdles, because POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA overlaps in about one in five', with arms out against your hands and standing from the chair without using her arms; report it as 'girdle movement LIMITED BY PAIN AND STIFFNESS, WITH PRESERVED POWER', never 'proximal weakness', because polymyalgia does not cause true weakness and that wording describes a myositis instead (★)

FAIL — Performing a cranial nerve examination when the stem forbade it IN CAPITALS — read the card; and when the examiner shuts you down mid-task, say 'thank you, Examiner' and move straight on, with no justification, no second attempt and no visible irritation, because candidates lose more time arguing about visual acuity than the test would have taken (★)

FAIL — Reassuring her it is the jaw joint, or pressing with a flat hand over the temple and the joint together and then calling the joint tender — ONE finger, named landmark, IMMEDIATELY IN FRONT OF THE TRAGUS, with opening, closing and pretend chewing, and she is briefed to say 'no, that bit isn't sore — the sore part is higher up'; report the joint separately ('joints non-tender, no crepitus or clicking, no deviation, opening admits three fingers'); the decoy variant — tenderness ON the joint, palpable crepitus and clicking, and a NORMAL PULSATILE temporal artery — moves you to temporomandibular joint dysfunction, but you still send ESR and CRP given her age and still name the visual symptoms that would bring her straight back (★)

FAIL — Delaying steroid for the biopsy or the ESR — she pushes once with 'shouldn't you wait and see what the tests say?', and the answer is no: 'waiting is the one thing that costs people their sight, and the biopsy stays useful for a week or two after we start'; prednisolone 40–60 mg daily, or IV methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg daily for three days if there is visual loss, with biopsy within one to two weeks and an adequate segment (VERIFY); and if she volunteers AMAUROSIS FUGAX — 'everything went dark in my right eye for a couple of minutes last Tuesday' — STOP EVERYTHING, because filing it away and carrying on palpating converts a pass into a fail: 'that is the most important thing you have said today', then treat it as a sight-threatening emergency with intravenous methylprednisolone, urgent ESR and CRP, and a same-day discussion with the on-call ophthalmology registrar (★)

SAY — Give the diagnosis in LAY words with the MECHANISM attached: 'there is a blood vessel running up the side of your head, just here, and in your case it has become inflamed and swollen; that is why chewing hurts — the chewing muscles need extra blood and the narrowed vessel cannot deliver it; it happens because your immune system has started attacking your own blood vessels, and we call it GIANT CELL ARTERITIS' — then the eye risk named explicitly ('the same vessels supply the eye, and untreated it can cause permanent loss of vision, which is why I want to start treatment today, before the tests come back'); TASK 3 IS SEPARATELY MARKED AND WORTH THE SAME AS TASK 2, so give at least four differentials in LAY language each with the reason it was excluded — the jaw joint, but your joint wasn't sore; a tooth or gum infection, but your teeth looked healthy; a sinus infection, but no tenderness over the sinuses; a saliva gland problem, which can hurt with eating; an ear infection spreading to the bone behind the ear; and the commoner headaches, migraine and neck-related headache — closing with 'none of them fit as well, and NONE OF THEM CAN TAKE YOUR SIGHT'; ask for the VITAL SIGNS before you begin; on general appearance name CACHEXIA and PTOSIS specifically, because they are the two the examiner is listening for as the systemic and neurological items you can still have without a cranial nerve examination; inspect ALOUD, because every negative is a differential excluded (a prominent, thickened, tortuous, cord-like temporal artery with overlying erythema, no temporalis wasting, no vesicular rash, no periorbital swelling, proptosis or red eye, no raccoon eyes or Battle sign, no parotid swelling); OFFER assessment of the globes for a hard, stony eye suggesting acute glaucoma but NEVER press on them; ask to ASSEMBLE the otoscope, since the heads are supplied separately on purpose; name each ENT site individually rather than asking for 'an ENT examination' as one lump, because each is a differential being cleared; stop examining at 6:20; safety net — any change in vision, blurring, a shadow or double vision means going straight to an emergency department; and Version B, the 35-year-old with nasal congestion and headache worse leaning forward, drops the temporal artery key points, the arteritis-framed fundoscopy and the shoulder girdle, and adds a fuller nose, throat and teeth examination with cervical and supraclavicular nodes, with temperature now a live finding, transillumination offered but not relied on, and antibiotics reserved for severe disease or symptoms beyond 7 to 10 days

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — regional GP, cranial nerves. 'RELEVANT' DOES NOT MEAN PICK A FEW: with eight minutes you FINISH ALL TWELVE — it means you may drop colour vision, accommodation and the gag reflex OUT LOUD, and that you do NOT palpate the head, ears, sinuses or jaw joint. THE FIELDS ARE THE STATION, AND A BITEMPORAL DEFECT IS INVISIBLE WITH BOTH EYES OPEN — cover one of his eyes and the opposite one of yours, every time. START TALKING AT 7:10. And do not send him home to drive.
stem: Regional general practice, Copper Coast. Tim Halloran, 46, with HEADACHES AND DISTURBANCE OF HIS VISION. BP 132/80 — pulse 76 — T 36.8 — RR 14 — SpO2 99% — BGL 5.4. Equipment: ophthalmoscope, otoscope, torch, tongue depressor, cotton wool, SNELLEN CHART WITH A CROSS ON THE FLOOR, gloves. 8 minutes.

time: OBSERVATIONS, WIPE, and an explanation in PLAIN WORDS rather than a list of twelve nerves · APPEARANCE and NERVE I BY HISTORY · ACUITY IN NINETY SECONDS, on the cross, ONE EYE AT A TIME, reported as 6/6 AND NEVER 20/20 · FIELDS IN SIXTY SECONDS, an arm's length apart, HIS RIGHT EYE COVERED AND YOUR LEFT, four diagonals each ending at the centre, then swap · REPORT THE DEFECT BY EYE AND BY QUADRANT, then name it · PUPILS IN THIRTY SECONDS: direct, CONSENSUAL, and THE SWINGING LIGHT TEST, which is what separates a chiasmal lesion from an optic nerve lesion · FUNDOSCOPY, never omitted in a headache station · III, IV and VI with a wide H and the diplopia question, reporting OPHTHALMOPLEGIA FIRST rather than leading with nystagmus · V in four steps with the jaw jerk and corneal reflex OFFERED not performed · VII, then VIII with THE OTHER EAR MASKED, because an unmasked whisper test means nothing · IX to XII together in under a minute · then START TALKING AT 7:10: the defect, the localisation, the pituitary, the reassurance, the differentials, AND THE DRIVING.

back.dx: BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA FROM A PITUITARY MACROADENOMA COMPRESSING THE OPTIC CHIASM — upper and lower temporal fields impaired in BOTH eyes with nasal fields full, normal acuity, no RAPD and normal fundi, in a 46-year-old with four months of morning headaches plus fatigue, reduced libido and weight change. LOCALISE IT, DO NOT JUST SAY 'A BRAIN TUMOUR': the nerves from the two eyes cross at a junction sitting just above a small gland at the base of the brain, the PITUITARY, and the pattern lost tells you something is pressing on that junction FROM BELOW. Reassure honestly: these are almost always non-cancerous, they are treatable, and some shrink on tablets alone — but promise nothing before a scan. Plan: URGENT MRI BRAIN AND PITUITARY WITH CONTRAST, a full anterior pituitary panel, and referral to neurosurgery and endocrinology. DIFFERENTIALS in lay words: other things pressing in the same place; a problem further back in the brain (which THE PATTERN ARGUES AGAINST, because bitemporal means the chiasm and homonymous means behind it); raised pressure inside the head (which the normal eye examination argues against); and migraine, which comes and goes rather than staying. THEN THE TWO THINGS BEFORE HE LEAVES: NO DRIVING until his vision is formally tested, WITH THE DUTY TO NOTIFY THE LICENSING AUTHORITY ON HIM, because with this pattern he cannot see what is coming from either side; and an emergency safety-net — sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision or drowsiness means call an ambulance, do not wait for the scan. LOCALISING RULES: BITEMPORAL = CHIASM = PITUITARY; HOMONYMOUS = BEHIND THE CHIASM, OPPOSITE SIDE; superior quadrants = temporal radiation (Meyer loop); inferior quadrants = parietal radiation. Uvula deviates AWAY, tongue deviates TOWARDS. Head turned left tests the RIGHT sternocleidomastoid.
plan: OBSERVATIONS, WIPE, AND A PLAIN EXPLANATION: 'Examiner, may I have this patient's vital signs?' Then: '...I have been asked to examine the nerves that supply your face and head. MOSTLY THAT MEANS YOUR EYES: I will ask you to read some letters, shine a light in them, and look into the back of them. Then I will check the feeling on your face, ask you for some facial movements, and check your hearing. NOTHING WILL HURT. Happy to go ahead?' (Listing twelve nerves to the patient burns forty seconds and communicates nothing.) Then appearance and nerve I: 'sitting, alert and orientated, no ptosis, no facial asymmetry, no abnormal head posture, no obvious squint. Tim, any change in your sense of smell? CRANIAL NERVE ONE IS INTACT BY HISTORY.'

ACUITY IN NINETY SECONDS: 'Tim, stand on the cross for me, glasses on if you wear them for distance. Cover your left eye with your palm and read down from the top as far as you can. Good. Now swap and cover the right. Examiner: VISUAL ACUITY IS 6/6 IN THE RIGHT EYE AND 6/6 IN THE LEFT. AS ACUITY IS NORMAL THERE IS NOTHING FOR A PINHOLE TO IMPROVE.' (Saying 20/20 is the correction to make now — Australian charts are metric.)

THE FIELDS — the station, and the technique that makes it work: 'sit facing me, about an arm's length away. COVER YOUR RIGHT EYE AND I WILL COVER MY LEFT. Keep looking straight at my nose. TELL ME THE MOMENT YOU SEE THE PEN TIP APPEAR.' Four diagonals, each ending at the centre, then swap. THEN REPORT IT EXACTLY LIKE THIS: 'RIGHT EYE: UPPER AND LOWER TEMPORAL FIELDS ARE IMPAIRED, NASAL FIELDS FULL. LEFT EYE: UPPER AND LOWER TEMPORAL FIELDS ARE IMPAIRED, NASAL FIELDS FULL. EXAMINER, MY PATIENT HAS A BITEMPORAL HEMIANOPIA. I will finish with DOUBLE SIMULTANEOUS STIMULATION for visual inattention — none.' (Testing with both eyes open makes a bitemporal defect INVISIBLE, and the role-player is briefed to say 'now' immediately every time and let you find nothing.)

PUPILS AND FUNDI IN UNDER A MINUTE: 'pupils are equal, round and about four millimetres. Light into the right: DIRECT response present — AND CONSENSUAL on the left. Light into the left: direct present — and consensual on the right. SWINGING LIGHT TEST: NO RELATIVE AFFERENT PUPILLARY DEFECT. Examiner, I am performing FUNDOSCOPY, looking for PAPILLOEDEMA AND DISC PALLOR. In the interests of time I will not formally test colour vision or accommodation, though I will ask: Tim, does the red top of this pen look the same brightness to both eyes?' (Direct only, with no consensual and no swinging light, misses the test that separates a chiasmal lesion from an optic nerve lesion. And omitting fundoscopy in a headache station is an automatic fail.)

III, IV, VI — and name the movement, not the nystagmus: 'keep your head still and follow my pen with your eyes only — TELL ME IF YOU SEE DOUBLE.' Wide H, pausing at the extremes. 'Examiner: eye movements are full and conjugate, THERE IS NO OPHTHALMOPLEGIA, no diplopia, no nystagmus, no ptosis, and no pupil-involving third nerve palsy.' Then V IN FOUR STEPS: 'clench your teeth — masseter and temporalis bulk and tone normal and symmetrical. Open your jaw against my hand — no deviation. THIS IS COTTON WOOL; IT FEELS LIKE THIS ON YOUR CHEST. NOW CLOSE YOUR EYES and say yes each time you feel it' — forehead, cheek, jaw, left against right — 'ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions symmetrical. Examiner, I WOULD ALSO LIKE TO TEST THE JAW JERK AND CORNEAL REFLEX.' (Offer the corneal reflex; never perform it. And test sensation with his eyes CLOSED, after a demonstration.)

VII AND VIII, with the masking that makes the whisper mean something: 'copy what I do: raise your eyebrows; screw your eyes tight shut and don't let me open them; puff out your cheeks; show me your teeth. Facial movements full and symmetrical, UPPER AND LOWER FACE. Now your hearing.' [Stand behind, RUB THE TRAGUS OF THE OTHER EAR, breathe out fully, whisper.] 'Repeat what I said. Normal to whispered voice in both ears; AS THERE IS NO HEARING LOSS I WILL NOT PROCEED TO RINNE AND WEBER.'

IX TO XII TOGETHER, under a minute: 'open wide and say aah — now a cough. PALATE RISES SYMMETRICALLY, UVULA CENTRAL, COUGH NOT BOVINE; I would OFFER the gag reflex but not perform it. Shrug and stop me pushing down — trapezius five out of five. Turn your head left, stop me — and right. Tongue resting on the floor of your mouth: no wasting, NO FASCICULATION. Stick it out: no deviation. Examiner, that completes twelve nerves. To complete I would examine the limbs, arrange FORMAL AUTOMATED PERIMETRY, and take a focused history.'

START TALKING — the defect, the localisation, then the reassurance: 'Tim, I've found something and I want to explain it clearly. YOU'VE LOST THE OUTER HALF OF THE VISION IN EACH EYE. You may not have noticed, because your brain fills the gap in.' → 'actually — I nearly clipped a cyclist a fortnight ago. He came out of nowhere on my left' → 'thank you for telling me — that fits exactly, and it matters. THE NERVES FROM YOUR TWO EYES CROSS AT A JUNCTION SITTING JUST ABOVE A SMALL GLAND AT THE BASE OF THE BRAIN, THE PITUITARY. The pattern you've lost tells me something is pressing on that junction FROM BELOW, and the commonest cause is a growth on the pituitary gland. I know that word is frightening. THESE ARE ALMOST ALWAYS NON-CANCEROUS, THEY ARE TREATABLE, AND SOME SHRINK ON TABLETS ALONE.' → 'so it's a tumour. Is it going to kill me?' → 'most of these are benign and very treatable. But I CAN'T PROMISE YOU ANYTHING BEFORE A SCAN, so I'm arranging an urgent MRI and blood tests today, and referring you to the brain surgeons and the hormone specialists in Adelaide.' Then the differentials in lay words, and THE TWO THINGS BEFORE HE LEAVES: 'PLEASE DON'T DRIVE UNTIL YOUR VISION IS FORMALLY TESTED; with this pattern you can't see what's coming from either side, and YOU HAVE TO NOTIFY THE LICENSING AUTHORITY. Is there someone who can drive you home? And if you get a sudden severe headache, vomiting, double vision or feel drowsy, CALL AN AMBULANCE — don't wait for the scan.'

ask: 'I'll be examining the nerves that supply your face and head — mostly your eyes.' / 'Cranial nerve one is intact by history.' / 'Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left.' / 'Cover your right eye; I will cover my left. Keep looking at my nose.'

'Upper and lower temporal fields impaired; nasal fields full.' / 'That is a bitemporal hemianopia, which localises to the optic chiasm.' / 'Swinging light test — no relative afferent pupillary defect.' / 'Performing fundoscopy, looking for papilloedema and disc pallor.' / 'Eye movements are full and conjugate; there is no ophthalmoplegia.'

'This is cotton wool; it feels like this on your chest. Now close your eyes.' / 'I would also like to test the jaw jerk and the corneal reflex.' / 'Hearing is normal to whispered voice, so I will not proceed to Rinne and Weber.' / 'Something is pressing on that junction from below — a growth on the pituitary gland.' / 'PLEASE DON'T DRIVE UNTIL YOUR VISION HAS BEEN FORMALLY TESTED.'

VERSION A — RIGHT HOMONYMOUS HEMIANOPIA: 'RIGHT EYE: temporal field impaired, nasal field full. LEFT EYE: NASAL field impaired, temporal field full. Examiner, THE RIGHT HALF OF THE VISUAL FIELD IS LOST IN BOTH EYES — a right homonymous hemianopia. That localises BEHIND THE CHIASM ON THE LEFT SIDE: tract, radiation or occipital cortex.' And if the onset was SUDDEN: 'a sudden homonymous defect is A STROKE UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. I would activate the stroke pathway, arrange urgent non-contrast CT and CT angiography, check the blood glucose, and discuss with the on-call stroke service BEFORE HE LEAVES THE BUILDING.' VERIFY (Calling a homonymous defect a pituitary problem is the trap — only the chiasm gives bitemporal.) / A QUADRANTANOPIA: 'the defect is confined to the UPPER quadrants on the right in both eyes. Superior quadrants are carried in the TEMPORAL radiation, MEYER LOOP, so the lesion is in the left temporal lobe. If it were the LOWER quadrants I would be localising to the left PARIETAL radiation.'

MORE VARIANTS: PAPILLOEDEMA ('the discs are swollen with blurred margins bilaterally') → CHANGE GEAR: 'bilateral disc swelling means RAISED INTRACRANIAL PRESSURE. That converts this from an outpatient problem into a SAME-DAY one: urgent imaging today INCLUDING VENOUS IMAGING to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, discuss with neurosurgery before he leaves, and warn him that headache worse lying flat or on coughing, vomiting, or drowsiness means an emergency department immediately.' / PITUITARY APOPLEXY (thunderclap headache an hour ago, vomiting twice, pale) → 'a thunderclap headache with vomiting, ophthalmoplegia and a visual field defect in a patient with a probable pituitary lesion is PITUITARY APOPLEXY. This is an emergency: INTRAVENOUS HYDROCORTISONE, resuscitate, urgent imaging, urgent bloods including electrolytes and a CORTISOL, and speak to neurosurgery and endocrinology now — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval.' VERIFY / HE REFUSES TO STOP DRIVING ('I can't not drive, it's my whole job') → neither back down nor threaten: 'you couldn't see a cyclist on your left a fortnight ago, and next time it might not be a near miss. THE LAW PUTS THE DUTY TO NOTIFY ON YOU, and I have to tell you clearly that you are not currently safe to drive AND TO RECORD THAT I HAVE TOLD YOU. The good news is this is often reversible — if the pressure comes off the nerves, fields can recover and licences can be reinstated. In the meantime, who can drive you?' VERIFY
pefe: Role-player: Tim Halloran, 46, farm machinery sales rep in Kadina driving about 60,000 km a year; married with two teenagers; practical, a bit blunt, mildly impatient with work to get back to. Four months of dull headaches across the front and behind the eyes, WORSE FIRST THING IN THE MORNING, about 4/10 but constant. HIS VISION: he cannot describe it well — things 'come out of nowhere' at the sides, he has clipped the door frame twice and knocked a mug off the bench. If asked: FLAT AND TIRED for months, LIBIDO DROPPED OFF (put down to work), SHIRTS FEEL LOOSER, and he gets up once or twice at night to pass urine. No medications, non-smoker, four or five beers a week. HIDDEN AGENDA: A FORTNIGHT AGO HE NEARLY HIT A CYCLIST on the Copper Coast Highway who 'came out of nowhere on my left' — he has told nobody including his wife, because he is FRIGHTENED OF LOSING HIS LICENCE AND THEREFORE HIS JOB. He volunteers it only if told he has lost part of his vision, asked about driving, or asked whether anything else is worrying him — otherwise at the very end: 'doctor — would this explain nearly hitting a cyclist a couple of weeks ago?'

HOW HE PLAYS IT — THE FIELDS ARE THE WHOLE PERFORMANCE: when the doctor brings a pen in FROM THE OUTER SIDE of whichever eye is uncovered, DO NOT SAY 'NOW' UNTIL THE PEN IS ALMOST DIRECTLY IN FRONT; when it comes in FROM THE NOSE SIDE, say 'now' straight away. BOTH EYES, exactly the same. IF THE DOCTOR TESTS WITH BOTH EYES OPEN, SAY 'NOW' IMMEDIATELY EVERY TIME — AND LET THEM FIND NOTHING. Acuity: read the whole chart with each eye. Everything else is normal — do exactly what is asked and give no other findings. PUSH ONCE when the word tumour is used: 'so it's a tumour. Is it going to kill me?' PUSH AGAIN ON DRIVING: 'I can't not drive — it's my whole job', giving way only if the doctor is honest and offers a way forward. If the doctor never speaks to him and narrates only to the examiner, stay silent and let the marks go.

Numbers: 8-minute station, TALK FROM 7:10. Acuity 90 s, fields 60 s, pupils 30 s, fundi 15 s. 6/6, NEVER 20/20. Two letters per line to move down. FOUR QUADRANTS PER EYE, target midway. BITEMPORAL = CHIASM = PITUITARY; HOMONYMOUS = BEHIND THE CHIASM, OPPOSITE SIDE. Uvula deviates AWAY, tongue deviates TOWARDS. Head turned LEFT tests the RIGHT sternocleidomastoid. Tuning fork 512 Hz. MRI brain and pituitary WITH CONTRAST, urgent. MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. Scored out of 14, with the starred items: fields tested WITH ONE EYE COVERED and four quadrants each; the defect reported BY EYE AND QUADRANT and named bitemporal; FUNDOSCOPY requested; the lesion LOCALISED to chiasm and pituitary rather than called 'a brain tumour'; and DRIVING addressed with emergency safety-netting.
Version A variant — RIGHT temporal field impaired and LEFT NASAL field impaired = a right HOMONYMOUS hemianopia, localising behind the chiasm on the left
fails: ★ Testing the fields with both eyes open — a bitemporal defect is invisible that way, and the role-player will let you find nothing
★ Sending him home to drive, or backing down when he pushes on his licence
Running out of time inside the eye and never reaching nerves IX to XII, or sacrificing tasks 2 and 3 for them
Describing the defect in the wrong eye or the wrong quadrant; saying 'a brain tumour' without localising it to the chiasm and the pituitary

Omitting fundoscopy in a headache station; examining the head, ears, sinuses or jaw joint when this is a cranial nerve station; saying 20/20 instead of 6/6; whispering without masking the other ear; testing facial sensation with his eyes open; and pupils done as direct only with no consensual and no swinging light

back.dx: THE FRAMEWORK THAT CARRIES EVERY MEDICATION CHART STATION. FIVE BOXES BEFORE ANY DRUG: (1) ID FRONT — URN, family name, given names, address only if given, DOB, sex ticked, and THE PATIENT'S NAME PRINTED in 'first prescriber to print patient name' — writing your own name there is a fail, because the label is checked against the wristband; (2) ID BACK — turn the chart over IMMEDIATELY, same identifiers on the PRN page, patient's name printed again, with the year optional unless charting a PRN — MORE THAN HALF THE ROOM NEVER TURNS THE CHART OVER; (3) ALLERGIES AND ADR — a real entry (peanuts / anaphylaxis / 2002) or NIL KNOWN if the stem is silent, or UNKNOWN if the history could not be obtained — always initialled, signed, printed and dated, because A SILENT STEM MEANS TICK A BOX AND SIGN IT; (4) MEDICINES TAKEN PRIOR TO PRESENTATION — filled if the stem lists home medicines, left empty if not, and NEVER filled with today's inpatient orders; (5) VTE PROPHYLAXIS — completed on EVERY chart, ticked 'prophylaxis not required' with signature and date when nothing is needed. THEN THE ORDER: year, dated columns, and inside the box the date, generic name, route, ONE dose, frequency written IN FULL (never OD, never Q24H), indication, prescriber signature, printed name and contact, administration times in the grid — and, IF A DURATION WAS SPECIFIED, EVERY REMAINING COLUMN CROSSED OUT so the nurse knows it stops. HERE: ceftriaxone IV 1 g daily for pneumonia, 0800 on days 1-5, days 6-8 blocked. Any single dose in range passes — 1 g daily, 2 g daily, 1 g BD, 500 mg BD — but '1-2 g' is not a prescription. 'CAP' is accepted as the indication; 'pneumonia' is safer.
plan: DECIDE

Before you open the book: 'the stem says FOR FIVE DAYS. That is a REGULAR medicine with a FIXED DURATION — page 3, right-hand inside page.' Named indications carry their own doses; EVERYTHING ELSE TAKES THE GENERAL DOSE — so 'pneumonia isn't in the list, so I'll pick meningitis' is wrong. And never write the range: '1-2 g' is not a prescription and the nurse will ring you.
BOX 1

ID FRONT: URN as given, family name CITIZEN, given names JAMES, address only if given, DOB, sex ticked. FIRST PRESCRIBER TO PRINT PATIENT NAME: JAMES CITIZEN — THE PATIENT, NOT YOU. (Writing your own name there is a fail on its own.)
BOX 2

ID BACK — TURN THE CHART OVER NOW, immediately after box 1 and before the allergy box: same identifiers on the PRN page, patient's name printed again. The year on the PRN page is optional — fill it if you are charting a PRN. (More than half the room never turns the chart over.)
BOX 3

ALLERGIES AND ADR: medicine or other — PEANUTS; reaction, type and date — ANAPHYLAXIS 2002; initials; then SIGN, PRINT YOUR NAME AND DATE IT. If the stem gives no allergy, tick NIL KNOWN and sign; if the history could not be obtained — unconscious, no ID — tick UNKNOWN. A SILENT STEM MEANS TICK A BOX AND SIGN IT.
BOX 4

MEDICINES TAKEN PRIOR TO PRESENTATION: nothing here, because the stem lists no home medicines — leave it empty, and DO NOT put today's inpatient orders in it. (The opposite error is skipping this box when the stem DOES list home medicines.)
BOX 5

VTE PROPHYLAXIS: tick PROPHYLAXIS NOT REQUIRED, signature, date. Guidance is that this box is completed on EVERY chart even when nothing is needed — and the worse error is a THERAPEUTIC anticoagulant written into it.
THE BOOK

Back index, C, ceftriaxone, bold page number, FINGER IN THE INDEX. The page lists a general dose and specific doses for meningitis, cellulitis, meningococcal disease and influenza-type infection. PNEUMONIA IS NOT LISTED, SO THE GENERAL ADULT DOSE APPLIES: 1-2 g daily in one or two doses. 'I'll use 1 g daily.' Close the book.
THE ORDER

YEAR 2026 top-left. DATED COLUMNS across the top — exam date then the following days, seven or eight columns. Then the first regular box on the right-hand page: DATE 3/11/26 — MEDICINE ceftriaxone — ROUTE IV — DOSE 1 g — FREQUENCY daily (written in full, NEVER OD) — INDICATION pneumonia — PHARMACY left empty — SIGNATURE, PRINTED NAME, CONTACT — ADMINISTRATION TIMES 0800 in the first column and repeated across days 1 to 5 — THEN DAYS 6, 7 AND 8 CROSSED OUT, a cross through each box or the whole remaining area blocked. COUNT 1-2-3-4-5 ALOUD IN YOUR HEAD, THEN CROSS OUT: the critical error of this case is a specified duration with the later columns left open.
RE-CHECK

Say it in your head before you leave: 'ID front — done. ID BACK — done. Allergy — SIGNED. Prior — nil. VTE — ticked and signed. Year — yes. Dates — yes. Times — five of them. BLOCK-OUT — yes.' Only now leave. (Walking out at four minutes without re-checking is marked.)

ask: WRITE EXACTLY THIS: ceftriaxone — IV — 1 g — daily — pneumonia — 0800 — peanuts, anaphylaxis 2002 — 'Nil known' when no allergy is given — 'Prophylaxis not required' — and JAMES CITIZEN as the printed patient name.

Passing dose choices: 1 g daily, 2 g daily, 1 g BD, or 500 mg BD — any single dose inside the AMH general range. 'Daily' written in full, never OD or Q24H. Indication written — 'CAP' is accepted but 'pneumonia' is safer. Five days counted from today, with everything after day 5 blocked. BD means 0800 AND 2000, written with a blank square between them so the nurse's initials do not overlap.

Charting in the LOWER BOXES OF PAGE 2 is allowed — but the date row is far away and candidates forget it, so page 3 keeps the dates above the order. And if you ask the examiner 'is 1 g or 2 g better?', they will shrug and say nothing — AND NOTE THAT YOU ASKED.

VARIANTS: NO ALLERGY IN THE STEM → tick NIL KNOWN, sign, print, date; if the stem says the allergy history could not be obtained, tick UNKNOWN. / 'FOR SEVEN DAYS' → date EIGHT columns, 0800 in seven, cross out the eighth; if the chart has only seven columns, ALSO write 'for 7 days — review' on the indication line. / CEFTRIAXONE 2 g IN TWO DOSES → dose 1 g, frequency BD, times 0800 and 2000 in the same column WITH A BLANK SQUARE BETWEEN THEM; still five days, still blocked after. / A WEIGHT GIVEN WITH A PER-KG PAEDIATRIC LINE → in an adult stem, IGNORE the paediatric per-kg line, but WRITE THE WEIGHT IN THE ID BOX ANYWAY — it costs nothing.

THE OTHER RECALLS IN THIS SET, each testing one decision: 2B tramadol with oxycodone CEASED; 2C gentamicin as a STAT order; 2D pre-operative aspirin and HOME MEDICINES; 2E NSTEMI enoxaparin and aspirin; 2F asthma or COPD with prednisolone and salbutamol. The five boxes and the re-check are identical in all of them — what changes is WHICH BOX the drug belongs in and WHETHER THE COURSE IS BLOCKED.

back.dx: TWO ORDERS, ONE DECISION. ENOXAPARIN, THERAPEUTIC: AMH unstable angina / NSTEMI is 1 mg/kg subcut every 12 hours for 2-8 days, so at 60 kg that is 60 MG SUBCUT BD — written in the REGULAR box on page 3, with 0800 and 2000 entered in each of the chosen columns and every column after the course CROSSED OUT. The examiner may treat an unblocked specified duration as a CRITICAL ERROR. Write SUBCUT, not SC. Write 60 mg, NOT '1 mg/kg' — the calculation is yours to do. And the VTE box on page 2 is STILL ticked 'prophylaxis not required', because this is treatment, not prophylaxis. ASPIRIN: the AMH acute-conditions line is 150-300 mg initially with long term 100-150 mg daily, and NSTEMI is an acute coronary syndrome, so take the ACUTE line — 150 mg PO daily, indication NSTEMI, 0800 in EVERY column, OPEN-ENDED because aspirin continues and nothing is blocked. If challenged that Therapeutic Guidelines uses 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily: 'I USED THE AMH SUPPLIED IN THE STATION; A 300 MG LOADING DOSE WOULD FOLLOW LOCAL ACS PROTOCOL.' Frequency is written in full — 'daily', never OD, which nurses have read as QID; and BD rather than 'q12h' or '12/24', because BD is the regular-page convention. VARIANTS: WEIGHT 80 kg AND eGFR 25 — 80 mg per dose, but SEVERE RENAL IMPAIRMENT reduces enoxaparin to ONCE DAILY (1 mg/kg daily) below a CrCl of 30, so READ THE RENAL LINE ON THE PAGE AND CHART WHAT IT SAYS. 'CHART VTE PROPHYLAXIS' POST-OPERATIVELY — now it IS the VTE box: risk assessed yes, enoxaparin subcut 40 mg daily, indication VTE prophylaxis, signed with a prescribing plan, plus the mechanical prophylaxis line for stockings. 'CHART WARFARIN FOR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION' — warfarin has its OWN box on page 2: select brand, route PO, TARGET INR 2-3, indication AF, sign, then enter the day-one dose with your initials and 1600 as the time, with INR results and later doses entered day by day.

(A candidate asked in class whether OD was acceptable — it is not; nurses have read it as QID.)
ENOXAPARIN

The second regular box: DATE — MEDICINE enoxaparin — ROUTE SUBCUT (not SC) — DOSE 60 mg (the calculated number, NOT '1 mg/kg') — FREQUENCY BD (twelve-hourly means the same, but BD is the regular-page convention, and 'q12h' is marked amber) — INDICATION NSTEMI — sign, print, contact — TIMES 0800 IN THE TOP SQUARE AND 2000 TWO SQUARES BELOW IT, in each of eight columns, WITH A GAP so the nurse's initials do not overlap — THEN CROSS OUT THE REMAINING COLUMNS.
VTE BOX

Page 2 STILL reads: prophylaxis not required, signed, dated. This is a TREATMENT dose, and it belongs on page 3. Saying that to yourself as you tick the box is what stops the pen drifting to the wrong page.
RE-CHECK
'Enoxaparin on PAGE 3, not page 2 — yes. BLOCKED AFTER 8 — yes. SUBCUT — yes. Aspirin DAILY, not OD — yes. WEIGHT — yes. ID BACK — yes.' Only then leave.

If challenged on the aspirin dose: 'I USED THE AMH SUPPLIED IN THE STATION; a 300 mg loading dose would follow local ACS protocol.' Aspirin 300 mg daily also passes, being inside the AMH acute range; aspirin 100 mg is AMBER, because that is the long-term line in an acute case, and you would be asked to justify it.

THE MARKING TABLE. FAIL: charts enoxaparin in the VTE prophylaxis box (wrong box, wrong label); writes SC; writes '1 mg/kg' as the dose; chooses 8 days but blocks nothing after; misses the ID box on the back. AMBER: writes 'q12h' or '12/24'; writes aspirin 'OD'; omits the weight from the ID box; enters only 0800 for a BD order. PASS: aspirin 300 mg daily; ticking VTE 'prophylaxis not required'.

VARIANTS: WEIGHT 80 kg, eGFR 25 → 80 mg per dose, BUT severe renal impairment means the AMH reduces enoxaparin to ONCE DAILY (1 mg/kg daily) below a CrCl of 30 — READ THE RENAL LINE AND CHART WHAT IT SAYS; eGFR is given as the CrCl proxy. / 'CHART VTE PROPHYLAXIS' POST-OPERATIVELY → now it IS the VTE box: risk assessed yes, ENOXAPARIN SUBCUT 40 mg DAILY, indication VTE prophylaxis, sign, print, contact, prescribing plan, plus the mechanical prophylaxis line for stockings if asked. / 'CHART WARFARIN FOR AF' → warfarin has its OWN box on page 2: select brand (Marevan or Coumadin), route PO, TARGET INR 2-3, indication AF, sign; enter the day-one dose (for example 5 mg) with your initials and 1600 as the time; INR results and later doses go in day by day.

THE SIX RECALLS IN THIS SET: 2A ceftriaxone for five days (the framework); 2B tramadol with oxycodone CEASED; 2C gentamicin as a STAT order; 2D pre-operative aspirin with HOME MEDICINES; 2E this one, NSTEMI enoxaparin and aspirin; 2F asthma or COPD with prednisolone and salbutamol. The five boxes and the re-check never change — what changes is WHICH BOX and WHETHER THE COURSE IS BLOCKED.
pefe: How to run it: give the stem WITH THE TWO NUMBERS, a blank NIMC and the AMH, then say nothing. WATCH WHETHER THE PEN GOES TO PAGE 2 (the VTE box) OR PAGE 3 for the enoxaparin — that single movement is the station. Time eight minutes and note whether they re-checked before leaving. Every red item is a fail on its own; two amber items together also fail.

Numbers: ENOXAPARIN for UA/NSTEMI is 1 mg/kg subcut every 12 hours for 2-8 days, so 60 kg gives 60 mg BD at 0800 and 2000 for eight days, then blocked. ASPIRIN AMH acute 150-300 mg initially, long term 100-150 mg daily, so 150 mg PO daily. Therapeutic Guidelines uses 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily. WEIGHT 60 kg goes in the ID box. BD = 0800 and 2000, with a gap between them.

The internal script, start to finish: 'Therapeutic enoxaparin — regular box, not VTE. 1 mg/kg, 60 kg, 60 mg BD. Aspirin acute line. Weight in the ID box. Five boxes.' Then ID front with the weight, flip, ID back, allergy Nil known signed, prior medicines none, VTE prophylaxis not required signed and dated — 'treatment dose, not prophylaxis'. Then the book: aspirin acute 150, enoxaparin 60 mg BD for eight days. Then the two orders and the block-out. Then the re-check, out loud in your head.

FAIL — Choosing a duration and blocking nothing after it — an unblocked specified course may be treated as a CRITICAL ERROR; pick a number of days inside 2 to 8 (eight is taught, five or seven are fine), put 0800 in the top square and 2000 TWO SQUARES BELOW with a GAP, so the nurse's initials do not overlap, in each of the eight columns, then CROSS OUT the remaining columns (★)

FAIL — Missing the ID box on the BACK of the chart — more than half the room never turns it over, so do it IMMEDIATELY after the front box and before the allergy box, with the same identifiers and the patient's name printed again; and never write your own name in 'first prescriber to print patient name', because the label is checked against the wristband and it must be the PATIENT (★)

FAIL — Aspirin written as 'OD', which nurses have read as QID — write DAILY in full; take the dose from the AMH's ACUTE line, because NSTEMI is an acute coronary syndrome (initially 150 to 300 mg; long term 100 to 150 mg), and 150 mg sits in both ranges so it is the safe choice, while 100 mg is a long-term dose in an acute case and will be questioned; aspirin is OPEN-ENDED, with 0800 in every column and nothing blocked, because it continues; and if challenged on a loading dose, 'I used the AMH supplied in the station — a 300 mg loading dose would follow local ACS protocol'

SAY — Work the FIVE BOXES first, in order, before either drug: ID front (URN, family name, given names, address if given, date of birth, sex ticked, patient's name printed, and the WEIGHT); ID back; ALLERGIES AND ADR, ticking NIL KNOWN with initials, signature, printed name and date, because a silent stem means TICK A BOX AND SIGN IT rather than leaving it untouched; MEDICINES TAKEN PRIOR TO PRESENTATION, left EMPTY when no home medicines are listed and never filled with today's inpatient orders; and the VTE box; then the YEAR in the top-left and the DATED COLUMNS across the top before either order; each order carries date, generic medicine name, route, dose, frequency, INDICATION, signature, printed name and contact number, with the administration times entered; RE-CHECK before leaving — enoxaparin on page 3 rather than page 2, blocked after day 8, 'subcut' not SC, aspirin 'daily' not OD, weight recorded, ID box on the back done; the six recalls in this set are 2A ceftriaxone for five days (the framework), 2B tramadol with oxycodone CEASED, 2C gentamicin, 2D a PRN order, 2E this NSTEMI case and 2F a home-medicines stem; variants — at 80 kg the dose is 80 mg per dose, but with an eGFR of 25 the AMH REDUCES enoxaparin to once daily at a creatinine clearance below 30, so read the renal line on the page and chart what it says; a post-operative 'chart VTE prophylaxis' stem DOES use the VTE box, with risk assessed yes, enoxaparin subcut 40 mg daily, indication VTE prophylaxis, signature, printed name, contact and prescribing plan, plus the mechanical prophylaxis line for stockings; and warfarin for atrial fibrillation has its OWN box on page 2 — brand selected (Marevan or Coumadin), route PO, target INR 2 to 3, indication AF, with the day-one dose and 1600 as the time, and INR results and later doses entered day by day

setting: PROCEDURE — a specimen, a strip bottle, a timer, tissues, gloves and a bin. NO ROLE-PLAYER IN MOST VERSIONS: the examiner is your only audience. THE STRIP RESULT IS NEARLY THE SAME IN ALL FOUR STEMS — THE STEM IS THE WHOLE DISCRIMINATION, so read it twice and read it again while the pads develop. AND THE ONE BEHAVIOUR THAT SEPARATES A PASS FROM A FAIL: ATTACH THE PAD TO THE STEM, OUT LOUD, IN ONE SENTENCE. The waiting time between ninety seconds and four minutes is not dead time — it is when you write the list and re-read the stem.
stem: VARIANT A — BLOOD: a 24-year-old woman with chronic cough and shortness of breath (an older recall adds haemoptysis), AND A SECOND CONTAINER OF PINK, BLOOD-STAINED SPUTUM ON THE BENCH. Blood 4+, protein 1+.

VARIANT B — GLUCOSE: a 30-year-old man with treated hypertension AND A NORMAL BLOOD SUGAR LEVEL. Glucose 4+, everything else negative. A related recall: an insurance health check, on candesartan, BP 150/90, with a role-player tapping his foot and rubbing his eyes.

VARIANT C — PROTEIN, CHRONIC: a 50-year-old man with lower limb oedema extending to the knees, high blood pressure, no past history. Protein 3+, SG 1.010, pH 6. VARIANT D — PROTEIN, ACUTE: a 42-year-old man, TWO DAYS of sudden bilateral leg swelling with nocturia and new hypertension. Protein 3+, blood 1+.

Explain your findings to the examiner
Explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses — and, in some versions, your further investigations
time: 0:00-1:00 SET UP OUT LOUD: hand hygiene and gloves; TISSUES LAID OUT; the TIMER located and placed beside them; ONE strip out and THE BOTTLE CLOSED AGAIN because the strips are moisture-sensitive; then CHECK THE LABEL against the patient's name, date of birth and identification number · ASK ONCE AND THEN DROP IT · 1:00-1:30 INSPECTION: colour and clarity out loud, and SMELL · not frankly blood-stained, not cola-dark, not tea-coloured, no foul or sweet odour · 1:30-2:00 THE DIP: BEND THE STRIP AGAINST THE INNER WALL so every pad is submerged, one dip of about a second, then A HORIZONTAL TAP against the rim, never vertical, because a vertical tap runs the reagents from one pad onto the next · strip down on the tissue, pads up, TIMER STARTED IN THE SAME MOVEMENT · 2:00-4:00 THE WAITING, USED: write the ten analytes down the page in order, then RE-READ THE STEM SILENTLY and decide your answer BEFORE you read the abnormal pad · 4:00-5:30 READ AND REPORT PAD BY PAD at or near the printed times, NAMING THE NEGATIVES · dispose, degloved, hands · 5:30-8:00 the summary, the stem-linked diagnosis, GROUPED differentials, and tiered investigations ending with the definitive test.

back.dx: THE DISCRIMINATING SENTENCE, said out loud in every version: NOT 'there is protein, so this is chronic kidney disease', BUT 'PUTTING THE PROTEIN AT THREE PLUS TOGETHER WITH A 50-YEAR-OLD MAN WHO HAS OEDEMA TO THE KNEES AND HYPERTENSION AND NO PAST HISTORY, MY MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS IS NEPHROTIC SYNDROME.' That sentence is what tells the examiner you performed a CLINICAL ASSESSMENT rather than a laboratory test — and it is the only thing that changes between the four versions. VARIANT C — NEPHROTIC SYNDROME within the broader picture of chronic kidney disease, which you would then STAGE. Differentials in TWO GROUPS: for the PROTEINURIA — primary glomerular disease (membranous, FSGS), diabetic nephropathy, hypertensive nephrosclerosis, glomerulonephritis, myeloma light chains, and the benign causes (orthostatic, exercise-induced, fever, infection); for the OEDEMA — heart failure, chronic liver disease, protein-losing enteropathy or malnutrition, hypothyroidism, venous insufficiency or DVT, and medication, particularly a calcium channel blocker. Investigations: first morning urine ACR, UEC with eGFR, urine microscopy for DYSMORPHIC RED CELLS AND CASTS, serum albumin and lipids, glucose and HbA1c, FBE, calcium, phosphate and PTH, renal tract ultrasound — adding an immunology screen and SERUM FREE LIGHT CHAINS WITH ELECTROPHORESIS if nephrotic or unexplained — nephrology referral, and RENAL BIOPSY AS THE DEFINITIVE INVESTIGATION. VARIANT A — a PULMONARY-RENAL SYNDROME, leading diagnosis ANTI-GBM (GOODPASTURE) DISEASE, differentials the other pulmonary-renal causes (GPA, microscopic polyangiitis, EGPA, lupus nephritis), then the respiratory causes of haemoptysis alone and the renal causes of haematuria alone — and remember a positive blood pad can mean HAEMOGLOBINURIA OR MYOGLOBINURIA. TIME-CRITICAL: anti-GBM antibody, ANCA, ANA and complement, urgent renal function, chest X-ray, urine microscopy, and speak to the renal team TODAY about transfer, biopsy, corticosteroid, cyclophosphamide and plasma exchange. VARIANT B — GLYCOSURIA: confirm with fasting glucose and HbA1c, BUT ASK EXACTLY WHICH MEDICINES HE TAKES, because an SGLT2 INHIBITOR PRODUCES GLYCOSURIA WITH A NORMAL BLOOD GLUCOSE — then familial renal glycosuria and Fanconi syndrome — and if diabetes is confirmed, assess him whole: ACR and eGFR, lipids, absolute cardiovascular risk with an ECG, feet with pulses, monofilament and tuning fork, and retinal screening. VARIANT D — ACUTE NEPHRITIC SYNDROME from an acute glomerulonephritis: post-infectious, IgA nephropathy, vasculitis or lupus — ask about a sore throat or skin infection in the preceding two to three weeks, and send ASOT and anti-DNase B, complement C3 and C4, ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, hepatitis and HIV serology with same-day nephrology discussion.
plan: SET UP OUT LOUD: 'before I start I'll set myself up. I'm performing hand hygiene and putting on gloves. I'm laying out a few tissues here on the bench. I can see there is a timer, and I'll place it beside the tissues SO I CAN START IT THE MOMENT THE STRIP GOES DOWN. I'm opening the container of reagent strips, taking out ONE strip, AND CLOSING THE BOTTLE AGAIN — the strips are moisture-sensitive and I don't want to spoil the rest of them. Before I handle the sample: I would normally CHECK THE LABEL ON THE SPECIMEN against the patient's name, date of birth and identification number. May I confirm this is the correct patient's sample?' → 'yes' or 'there is no label; assume it is correct' → 'THANK YOU' and MOVE ON. (Arguing the point after the examiner has answered is a mark lost, not a mark gained.)

INSPECTION, including the smell: 'on inspection, the specimen is a pale, whitish-grey fluid and it is CLOUDY rather than clear. It is not frankly blood-stained, NOT DARK LIKE COLA, and NOT TEA-COLOURED. I'm removing the lid. There is NO FOUL OR OFFENSIVE SMELL to suggest infection, and NO SWEET OR KETOTIC SMELL. I'll replace the lid loosely and put it where it won't be knocked over.' (If challenged 'do you really smell urine samples in practice?': 'not deliberately — smell is an incidental observation rather than a manoeuvre, and I wouldn't inhale over a clinical specimen. I commented on it because an offensive or sweet smell is a genuine clinical finding and I didn't want to leave it unsaid.')

THE DIP — two technique points the examiner leans in for: 'I'm dipping the strip now. I'M BENDING IT AGAINST THE INNER WALL OF THE CONTAINER SO THAT EVERY PAD IS SUBMERGED — if the strip stays straight the upper pads sit above the fluid line and READ FALSELY NEGATIVE. One dip, about one second. Now A HORIZONTAL TAP against the rim to take off the excess. I TAP SIDEWAYS RATHER THAN DOWNWARDS, because a vertical tap runs the reagents from one pad onto the next and contaminates the colours. Strip down on the tissue, pads facing up — AND I'M STARTING THE TIMER NOW. Lid back on the specimen and out of the way.'

THE WAITING, USED — not silence: 'while the pads develop I'm writing the ten analytes down the page so that I report them in order and don't miss one: GLUCOSE, BILIRUBIN, KETONES, SPECIFIC GRAVITY, BLOOD, pH, PROTEIN, UROBILINOGEN, NITRITE, LEUCOCYTES. Each has its own reading time printed on the bottle — thirty, thirty, forty, forty-five, then sixty seconds for the next five, and TWO MINUTES FOR LEUCOCYTES.' THEN RE-READ THE STEM SILENTLY and decide your answer BEFORE you read the abnormal pad, so the reading CONFIRMS a hypothesis rather than replacing one.

READ AND REPORT PAD BY PAD, holding the strip beside the guide on the bottle and NAMING THE NEGATIVES: glucose negative — bilirubin negative — ketones negative — SPECIFIC GRAVITY 1.010, 'a mid-range, adequately concentrated sample, SO I CAN RELY ON THE OTHER PADS' — blood negative — pH six — PROTEIN 'strongly positive, THREE PLUS; it sits between the three and four plus blocks, so I would report it as AT LEAST three plus' — urobilinogen within the normal range — nitrite negative — leucocytes negative. Then: 'I'm wrapping the used strip in the tissue and disposing of it in the bin, removing my gloves and performing hand hygiene.' (Reporting only the abnormal pad and saying 'everything else was normal' loses marks; REPORTING A PAD YOU NEVER READ IS AN AUTOMATIC FAIL — if you missed one, SAY SO.)

THE SUMMARY, THEN THE STEM-LINKED DIAGNOSIS: 'to summarise my findings: a cloudy, pale urine with no abnormal smell, and on dipstick a SINGLE abnormality — protein at three plus, with a specific gravity of 1.010 and a pH of six. Glucose, bilirubin, ketones, blood, urobilinogen, nitrite and leucocytes were all negative.' Then THE SENTENCE: 'PUTTING THAT TOGETHER WITH THE HISTORY IN THE STEM — a 50-year-old man with oedema extending to the knees and a high blood pressure, with no past medical history — MY MOST LIKELY DIAGNOSIS IS NEPHROTIC SYNDROME: heavy protein loss in the urine, a low serum albumin, and oedema as a consequence. That sits within the broader picture of chronic kidney disease, WHICH I WOULD THEN STAGE FORMALLY.'

DIFFERENTIALS IN GROUPS, then investigations in TIERS ending with the definitive test (see dx). And if the examiner pushes back — 'I think the answer here is chronic kidney disease, not nephrotic syndrome' → 'I agree this sits within chronic kidney disease, and I'd want to confirm that with an eGFR and an ACR and stage it. I NAMED NEPHROTIC SYNDROME FIRST BECAUSE CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE IS A STAGING FRAMEWORK RATHER THAN A DIAGNOSIS — it tells me how bad the kidney function is, but not WHY this man's legs are swollen. The combination of heavy proteinuria and oedema is the syndrome I want to act on today.'
CHALLENGES

'The pad is for nitrates, isn't it?' → 'NITRATE is what comes in through the diet. Gram-negative uropathogens with nitrate reductase convert it to NITRITE, and the Griess reaction on the pad detects the nitrite.' / 'So a negative nitrite means no infection?' → 'no — nitrite is SPECIFIC BUT NOT SENSITIVE. It is negative when the urine has not been in the bladder long enough, roughly four hours, and when the organism does not reduce nitrate — ENTEROCOCCUS, STAPHYLOCOCCUS SAPROPHYTICUS AND PSEUDOMONAS. In a symptomatic patient I would treat and send a culture regardless.' / 'A negative protein pad excludes myeloma?' → 'NO. The pad measures ALBUMIN and is close to blind to immunoglobulin light chains — I'd ask for serum free light chains and serum and urine electrophoresis.' / 'How would you tell acute from chronic?' → repeat eGFR for the trajectory, previous results, KIDNEY SIZE AND ECHOTEXTURE on ultrasound (small echogenic kidneys mean chronic), and the markers of established disease: normocytic anaemia, low calcium, high phosphate, raised PTH. / 'Isn't this simply an acute kidney injury?' → 'AKI is DEFINED by a change in creatinine or urine output over a stated time — a rise of 26.5 micromol/L within 48 hours, or 1.5 times baseline within seven days, or under 0.5 mL/kg/hour for six hours VERIFY. What the two-day history describes is an ACUTE NEPHRITIC PRESENTATION, and I'd expect an AKI to accompany it.' / 'Goodpasture is a vasculitis?' → grouped with the small-vessel vasculitides, but the mechanism is an AUTOANTIBODY against the ALPHA-3 CHAIN OF TYPE IV COLLAGEN, shared by alveolar and glomerular basement membrane — which is why exactly those two organs bleed. / 'Wegener's?' → 'GRANULOMATOSIS WITH POLYANGIITIS — the eponym was retired in 2011.'

ask: 'I'm closing the bottle again — the strips are moisture-sensitive.' / 'May I confirm this is the correct patient's sample?' — then drop it. / 'Cloudy rather than clear, not cola-dark, not tea-coloured.' / 'I'm bending it against the inner wall so that every pad is submerged.' / 'A horizontal tap, because a vertical tap runs the reagents from one pad onto the next.'

'Specific gravity 1.010 — a mid-range, adequately concentrated sample, so I can rely on the other pads.' / 'At least three plus.' / 'Putting that together with the history in the stem...' / 'Chronic kidney disease is a staging framework rather than a diagnosis.'

THE FOUR STEMS AND THEIR CLOSING SENTENCES: VARIANT A — 'a young woman with chronic cough, breathlessness and haemoptysis, and haematuria at the same time. THAT COMBINATION IS A PULMONARY-RENAL SYNDROME, and my leading diagnosis is ANTI-GLOMERULAR BASEMENT MEMBRANE DISEASE... this is TIME-CRITICAL: untreated, anti-GBM disease can destroy renal function within days.' / VARIANT B — 'my most likely diagnosis is GLYCOSURIA. The commonest cause is diabetes, so I would confirm with a fasting glucose and HbA1c. BUT THE STEM TELLS ME HIS BLOOD SUGAR IS NORMAL AND HE IS ALREADY ON TREATMENT, so I would want to know EXACTLY WHICH MEDICINES HE TAKES: AN SGLT2 INHIBITOR PRODUCES GLYCOSURIA WITH A NORMAL BLOOD GLUCOSE, and in that case the pad is the drug working rather than a new diagnosis.' / VARIANT D — 'a two-day history of sudden bilateral swelling, nocturia and NEW hypertension: my leading diagnosis is an ACUTE NEPHRITIC SYNDROME due to an acute glomerulonephritis — post-infectious, IgA nephropathy, a vasculitis, or lupus nephritis.'

THE VARIANT B ROLE-PLAYER, when present, DOES NOT TALK — he TAPS ONE FOOT REPEATEDLY AND RUBS HIS EYES, and gives the answer only if asked: 'there's one for the blood pressure. And the doctor added another one last year — something for my heart and kidneys, she said. I'd have to check the box.' THAT IS THE WHOLE POINT OF THE VARIANT. If asked about his feet: 'a bit numb and tingly at night.' About his eyes: 'my vision's been a bit blurry when I read.' About thirst: 'I drink a lot of water and get up once or twice at night.'

PARTNER PRACTICE: set a bench with a cup of water and a splash of milk, a strip bottle, a phone timer, tissues, paper and a bin; your partner reads one of the four stems, starts eight minutes, hands over the result card AT THE MOMENT YOU READ THE PAD, then asks three challenges one at a time. Run the same variant twice — once slowly and correctly, once deliberately rushed — so you can feel the difference in how the reading goes. (LACTOSE-FREE MILK gives a positive glucose pad as well as protein, because the lactose has already been split into glucose and galactose.)
pefe: RESULT CARDS — read out when the candidate reads each pad. VARIANT A: glucose negative, bilirubin negative, ketones negative, SG 1.020, BLOOD 4+, pH 6, PROTEIN 1+, urobilinogen normal, nitrite negative, leucocytes negative; appearance CLOUDY, FAINTLY PINK; AND A SECOND CONTAINER OF PINK SPUTUM ON THE BENCH. VARIANT B: GLUCOSE 4+, everything else negative, SG 1.015, pH 6; appearance clear, pale. VARIANT C: PROTEIN 3+, everything else negative, SG 1.010, pH 6; appearance cloudy, pale. VARIANT D: PROTEIN 3+, BLOOD 1+, SG 1.020, pH 6.5, rest negative; appearance cloudy, pale. IF THE CANDIDATE ASKS FOR SOMETHING NOT PROVIDED — serum albumin, creatinine, a blood glucose, a chest X-ray — answer 'that is not available in this station — TELL ME WHAT YOU WOULD EXPECT AND WHY', and DO NOT INVENT NUMBERS: asking for them is correct behaviour and should be credited.

MARKING CHECKLIST: hand hygiene and gloves before touching anything; tissues laid out and timer placed ready; bottle opened, ONE strip removed, BOTTLE CLOSED; identification stated ONCE then dropped when answered; colour and clarity out loud; smell out loud; STRIP BENT SO ALL PADS SUBMERGED with one dip of about a second; HORIZONTAL tap, not vertical; strip on tissue and TIMER STARTED IN THE SAME MOVEMENT; WAITING TIME USED — list written, stem re-read, no silence; each pad read at or near its printed time; ALL TEN PADS NAMED INCLUDING THE NEGATIVES; strip and tissue disposed of, gloves off, hand hygiene; ABNORMAL PAD CORRECTLY IDENTIFIED AND GRADED; DIAGNOSIS EXPLICITLY LINKED TO THE STEM IN ONE SENTENCE; differentials as a GROUPED list; the not-to-miss diagnosis named for that variant; investigations in TIERS with the definitive test named; URGENCY stated where the variant demands it (A and D); and finished inside eight minutes without rushing the procedure.

AUTOMATIC FAILS: reporting a pad you never read — reciting ten results after one glance; misreading the abnormal pad, calling 4+ protein 'trace' or the blood pad negative in Variant A; a diagnosis with NO LINK TO THE STEM — naming diabetes in Variant C or chronic kidney disease in Variant D; MISSING THE SECOND CONTAINER in Variant A; and reading a contaminated strip after a vertical tap and reporting the results confidently. MARKS LOST BUT NOT FAILS: no gloves or disposal; bottle left open; no timer started; silence through the two-minute wait; reporting only the abnormal pad; pressing the identification question after it has been answered; one differential where a grouped list was asked for; and finishing in three minutes and standing there.

setting: PHYSICAL EXAMINATION — GP or ED. ONE-LINE STRATEGY: PROVE THERE IS A LOSS, PROVE IT IS SENSORINEURAL, THEN EXAMINE THE NEIGHBOURS OF THE EIGHTH NERVE — THE FIFTH AND THE SEVENTH — AND THE CEREBELLUM BEHIND THEM. WHISPER DECIDES WHETHER; RINNE AND WEBER DECIDE WHICH. Two structural fails: going straight to the tuning fork, because Rinne with air better than bone is BOTH the normal result AND the sensorineural result; and finishing at the tuning fork, when the whole point is a mass in the cerebellopontine angle. AND NOBODY TELLS YOU HOW FAST THE LOSS CAME ON — YOU HAVE TO ASK.
stem: General practice or emergency department. A 27-YEAR-OLD WOMAN with HEARING LOSS IN THE LEFT EAR and A BUZZING NOISE in the same ear. NO NAUSEA AND NO VOMITING. HER TYMPANIC MEMBRANES HAVE BEEN INSPECTED AND ARE NORMAL. Gloves, an otoscope and a 512 Hz TUNING FORK are available. 8 minutes.
