ask: 'Examiner, is my patient stable enough for me to proceed with the history?' / 'Can you tell me more about this rash?' / 'Where did it start, and is it spreading?' / 'Is it itchy, or is it painful?' / 'What were you doing in the day or two before it came up?' / 'Have you had any fevers, chills or shivering?'

'As this is an infective rash, may I have the full vital signs?' / 'Site, colour, primary morphology, secondary morphology, borders.' / 'A linear erythematous patch with well-defined borders, running proximally.' / 'Temperature with the backs of my fingers, on the rash, compared with the other side.' / 'I am pressing to check for blanching — I would expect this to blanch.'

'The rash crosses the elbow, so I want to exclude joint involvement.' / 'My special test is the epitrochlear node, then the axilla, affected side only.' / 'I've drawn a line at the top of the redness with today's date on it.' EXAMINER CHALLENGES: 'did the rash blanch?' → 'it did not blanch on my testing, BUT THE RASH HAS BEEN APPLIED TO THE SKIN, so I do not think that finding is interpretable. Clinically, lymphangitis blanches, and nothing else in the examination suggests a purpuric process.' / 'Why the epitrochlear node?' → 'it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE FOR THE FOREARM. A reactive node there supports a lymphatic infection, and involvement of the node itself is LYMPHADENITIS.' / 'How do you tell this from cellulitis?' → 'SHAPE. Cellulitis spreads laterally and gives an AREA with a poorly defined margin. Lymphangitis travels in a channel and gives a WELL-DEFINED LINE running toward the draining node.'

VERSION B — FEBRILE AND TACHYCARDIC: INTERRUPT YOURSELF. 'Examiner, I want to STOP AND FLAG that the temperature is 38.6 and the pulse is 108. I AM TREATING THIS AS SEPSIS FROM A SKIN AND SOFT TISSUE SOURCE. I would like large-bore intravenous access, BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, FBE, CRP, UEC, glucose and lactate, intravenous fluids, and INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS NOW. I would then complete my examination.' (Continuing a calm examination in the febrile, tachycardic variant without recognising sepsis is an automatic fail.)

THE PAIN-OUT-OF-PROPORTION MOMENT — ask, then escalate: 'Alex, IS THE PAIN MUCH WORSE THAN THE RASH LOOKS? Does the skin feel NUMB anywhere over it? And how fast has it changed — over days, or over HOURS?' → if yes, yes, hours → 'Examiner, PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION, ALTERED SENSATION OVER THE RASH AND SPREAD OVER HOURS make me concerned about NECROTISING FASCIITIS. THIS IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS AND A SURGICAL EMERGENCY — I would resuscitate, give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and CALL THE SURGICAL REGISTRAR IMMEDIATELY RATHER THAN ARRANGE IMAGING.' / THE NODULAR VARIANT, when the line is made of LUMPS and has evolved over WEEKS: 'the lesions are NODULES ARRANGED IN A LINE rather than a continuous streak. That pattern is NODULAR OR SPOROTRICHOID LYMPHANGITIS. I would ask specifically about ROSE THORNS AND SPHAGNUM MOSS, which points to SPOROTHRIX, and about FISH TANKS OR FISH HANDLING, which points to MYCOBACTERIUM MARINUM. It needs a BIOPSY WITH TISSUE CULTURE, and I would TELL THE LABORATORY WHAT I SUSPECT so the cultures are held long enough.'
pefe: Role-player: Alex Brennan, 32, works at the Wallaroo grain terminal, lives with his partner and a four-year-old, plays footy on Saturdays and almost never sees a doctor. Two days ago he noticed a red mark near his right wrist; it is now a RED LINE RUNNING HALFWAY UP THE FOREARM, SORE NOT ITCHY, hot, with nothing coming out of it. WHAT HE DID: on Sunday he spent the afternoon CUTTING BACK THE ROSES WITHOUT GLOVES and got scratched a few times, thinking nothing of it — ONLY VOLUNTEER THIS IF ASKED WHAT HE WAS DOING. No medications or allergies, non-smoker, six to eight beers a week; no eczema, hay fever or asthma in him or the family; no cannulas, injections or blood tests; no overhead work; no new soaps or creams; last tetanus probably at school. HIDDEN AGENDA: HIS MATE AT WORK TOLD HIM THIS WAS 'BLOOD POISONING' and that people lose arms from it — he is more worried than he is letting on. Raise it WHEN THE DOCTOR NAMES THE DIAGNOSIS, or in the last minute if they never ask about concerns, AND NOT IN THE FIRST THREE MINUTES. Practical, cheerful, slightly embarrassed to be here, not distressed.

THE MOST IMPORTANT CUE: IF THE DOCTOR PRESSES ON THE RASH, WINCE AND SAY IT IS TENDER — and IF THEY NEVER PRESS THE RASH, DO NOT PROMPT THEM. Move the elbow freely when asked: 'that's fine, no pain.' THREE MISTAKES ROLE-PLAYERS MAKE: VOLUNTEERING THE GARDENING — wait to be asked, because it is the single most discriminating question in the history; ANSWERING A BUNDLED QUESTION FULLY — if four questions arrive at once, ANSWER ONLY THE LAST, which is what a real patient does; and FORGETTING TO WINCE, when tenderness is a physical sign the candidate has to elicit and report.

Scored out of 20: washed hands, introduced, consented; ASKED THE EXAMINER ABOUT STABILITY FIRST; used an open question and let him answer; ASKED WHERE IT STARTED AND ESTABLISHED THE DIRECTION; asked itchy versus painful; ASKED WHAT HE WAS DOING BEFOREHAND; asked about scratches, thorns or bites; asked about cannulas or injections; ASKED ABOUT FEVER AND CHILLS; asked for the FULL VITAL SIGNS AND USED THE EQUIPMENT; described site, colour, primary and secondary morphology and borders; COMPARED TEMPERATURE WITH THE OTHER ARM; PRESSED THE RASH FOR TENDERNESS; commented on elevation and surface; HANDLED BLANCHING WITHOUT ASSERTING NON-BLANCHING; EXAMINED THE ELBOW by palpation and movement; EXAMINED THE EPITROCHLEAR NODE AND THE AXILLA; gave a shaped differential with reasons in plain words; and gave a safety net with named reasons to return. Numbers: capillary refill under 2 s; PATCH flat and 1 cm or more, MACULE flat and under 1 cm, PLAQUE raised and 1 cm or more, PAPULE raised and under 1 cm; VESICLE under 5 mm, BULLA 5 mm or more; epitrochlear node about 3 cm above the medial epicondyle; 5 axillary chains; flucloxacillin 500 mg PO six-hourly for 5 days or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly VERIFY; review 24-48 h; tetanus if over 5 years VERIFY; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.
Entry point — A small LINEAR ABRASION at the wrist

must: FAIL — Continuing a calm examination in the febrile, tachycardic variant without recognising SEPSIS — INTERRUPT YOURSELF: 'Examiner, I want to STOP AND FLAG that the temperature is 38.6 and the pulse is 108; I am treating this as SEPSIS FROM A SKIN AND SOFT TISSUE SOURCE — large-bore intravenous access, BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, FBE, CRP, UEC, glucose and lactate, intravenous fluids, and intravenous antibiotics now; I would then complete my examination' (★)

FAIL — Never asking about FEVER at all — it is the single most discriminating question in the history, and he is briefed to wait to be asked; if the three-minute prompt is coming, ASK FEVER FIRST and drop the atopy questions, because fever changes management and atopy does not (★)

FAIL — Never examining the JOINT the rash crosses: 'the rash crosses the elbow, so I want to exclude joint involvement' — palpate the joint line for tenderness and effusion, then active movement in both planes ('bend and straighten your elbow, and turn your palm up and down'), reporting 'full pain-free active movement with no joint-line tenderness, so no evidence of septic arthritis' (★)

FAIL — Asserting a NON-BLANCHING rash and then treating it as lymphangitis anyway — the rash has been APPLIED to the skin, so the finding is not interpretable and you must say so rather than claim it: 'I am pressing to check for blanching — I would expect this to blanch; the applied colouring limits my interpretation, so I am not relying on it', and if challenged, 'clinically, lymphangitis blanches, and nothing else in the examination suggests a purpuric process' (★)

FAIL — Sending him away with no REVIEW and no SAFETY NET, palpating landmarks and never once PRESSING THE RASH, or going to the axilla and skipping the EPITROCHLEAR node — that node sits about 3 cm above the medial epicondyle, it is the FIRST DRAINING NODE for the forearm, and it is the special test the examiner is waiting for ('a tender, mobile node is REACTIVE and consistent with infection; a hard, fixed or matted node would make me think about malignancy'); then antibiotics, a LINE DRAWN at the top of the redness WITH TODAY'S DATE, review in 24 to 48 hours, tetanus if it has been over five years, and named reasons to return — redness passing the line, fevers or shakes, pain much worse than it looks, or the elbow becoming painful to move (★)

SAY — Ask the examiner about STABILITY before the history ('is my patient stable enough for me to proceed with the history?'), then ONE QUESTION PER TURN, because bundling four into one breath gets you the last answer only and you lose the DIRECTION OF SPREAD, which IS the diagnosis: when it started, WHERE ON THE ARM it started, whether it is spreading and IN WHICH DIRECTION, ever before, itchy or painful, warm, any discharge; then find the PORTAL OF ENTRY, because 'I was gardening' is the CONTEXT and THE SCRATCH IS THE FINDING — ask specifically about cuts, scratches and thorn pricks, insect or spider bites, gloves, and recent injections, drips or blood tests in that arm; describe the rash in FIVE PARTS (site with dimensions and laterality; colour; PRIMARY morphology — flat and over a centimetre is a PATCH, in a LINEAR distribution; SECONDARY morphology, with no vesicles, scratch marks, erosions, discharge, scale or visible venous cord; and well-defined BORDERS), looking for the entry point as you go; on palpation compare TEMPERATURE with the backs of your fingers ON the rash against the same level on the other arm, check capillary refill and the radial pulse, then press gently ALONG the line for tenderness, which is the physical sign he is briefed to give you; name it and explain in ONE sentence ('under the skin there are small drainage channels called lymphatic vessels, and bacteria have got in through that scratch and are travelling ALONG one of those channels, which is why it looks like a LINE rather than a patch'); answer the BLOOD POISONING fear directly, because his mate told him people lose arms from it ('it's not blood poisoning, and it's very treatable with tablets — but it can turn into a more serious infection if it's left, which is exactly why I want to see you again in two days'); give the differentials in PLAIN WORDS and not a lecture, because meningococcaemia, Henoch–Schönlein purpura, ITP, lymphoma and viral exanthems frighten the patient for no clinical gain — cellulitis (the same infection spread over an AREA with a poorly defined margin rather than a line), inflammation of a vein (which usually gives a firm tender cord you can feel), a plant reaction (itchy and blistery rather than sore), an insect bite, and a clot in the deep veins of the arm (which swells the WHOLE arm, and his isn't swollen), offering to measure both forearms at the same level; flucloxacillin or cefalexin 500 mg six-hourly for five days (VERIFY); variants — PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION with altered sensation over the rash and spread over HOURS rather than days raises NECROTISING FASCIITIS, a CLINICAL diagnosis and a surgical emergency, so resuscitate, give broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and call the surgical registrar IMMEDIATELY rather than arranging imaging; and NODULES arranged in a line, evolving over WEEKS, is nodular or sporotrichoid lymphangitis, so ask specifically about ROSE THORNS AND SPHAGNUM MOSS for Sporothrix and about FISH TANKS OR FISH HANDLING for Mycobacterium marinum, arranging a biopsy with TISSUE CULTURE and telling the laboratory what you suspect so the cultures are held long enough

dx: **Acute viral gastroenteritis with 4–6% clinical dehydration in an 18-month-old. THIS IS THE FRAMEWORK DOCUMENT FOR THE WHOLE PAEDIATRIC BLOCK — the spine below fits every paediatric history: cough, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, rash, abdominal pain, poor feeding. Only blocks 2 and 3 change with the presentation.**

**★ THE SPINE, SIX BLOCKS: 1 OPEN QUESTION — let the parent run 30–45 seconds uninterrupted; half the case arrives free. 2 EXPLORE THE COMPLAINT. 3 RULE DIFFERENTIALS IN AND OUT — one or two targeted questions per differential; this is the clinical reasoning mark. 4 WELL-BABY QUESTIONS. 5 BINDSMA. 6 CONCERNS AND SUMMARY. Say the headings out loud so the examiner can tick them.**

**★ THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS, and their single purpose is DEHYDRATION: 1 APPEARANCE AND CONSCIOUS STATE — 'is he alert and active and playful as usual, or drowsy and not himself?' 2 INTAKE, DRINKING BEFORE EATING — 'is he drinking as he normally would? And what about eating?' 3 OUTPUT — 'have you noticed any drop in the number of wet nappies?' 4 BOWEL MOTIONS.** **Whatever the complaint, if the child is severely dehydrated nothing else you find changes the plan: that child goes to hospital.**

**★ THE COMMONEST SINGLE MARK LOST IN PAEDIATRICS: asking 'is he eating normally?' and stopping. Under six months there are no solids, and at any age it is FLUID, not food, that determines whether the child is safe at home. EXAMINERS ARE EXPLICITLY INSTRUCTED NOT TO AWARD THE POINT FOR AN INTAKE QUESTION THAT OMITS DRINKING.**

**BINDSMA — Birth, Immunisation, Nutrition, Development and growth, Social, Medication, Allergy — IS A SAFETY NET AT THE END, NOT A PLACE TO STORE IMPORTANT QUESTIONS. If a letter is central to the diagnosis — birth history in a neonate, nutrition in growth faltering, social history in a habit cough — ask it WHERE IT BELONGS, in detail, and leave only leftovers for the end.** **Reciting all of it in a healthy 18-month-old costs 90 seconds you need for tasks 3 and 4.**

**SOCIAL HISTORY SPLITS THREE WAYS — know which one you are in. 1 INFECTIVE presentations: you are looking for SICK CONTACTS, not child protection — unwell family, childcare, school. 2 NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY: who lives at home, who cares for the child, financial and housing stress, parental substance use, previous notifications. 3 PSYCHOGENIC — tension headache, functional abdominal pain, habit cough: school, friendships, bullying, family change, separation, bereavement. Here the social history IS the diagnosis.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: hydration must be established EXPLICITLY, EARLY, AND IN NUMBERS — and must then visibly drive the plan. 'He seems a bit dehydrated' scores NOTHING. 'He has lost 600 grams, that is a 5% deficit, which puts him in the clinical dehydration band' scores everything AND justifies the entire management plan in one sentence.**

**PARENTERAL DIARRHOEA — the pearl that prevents premature closure. In children almost ANY infection produces vomiting, diarrhoea and fever together: otitis media, tonsillitis, pneumonia, urinary tract infection. A child with vomiting and diarrhoea HAS NOT BEEN DIAGNOSED WITH GASTROENTERITIS until you have examined the EARS, THROAT, CHEST AND URINE and found no other source.** **That is how a toddler's UTI gets missed.**

**DEHYDRATION BANDS (Royal Children's Hospital): under 4% no clinical signs · 4–6% CLINICAL DEHYDRATION · 7% or more SHOCK. BLOOD PRESSURE FALLS LATE — a falling BP in a dehydrated child is PRETERMINAL, not an early warning. 1 kg lost = 1 L lost. Deficit for 4–6% ≈ 50 mL/kg over 4 hours. BOLUS 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride IV or IO. Maintenance 100/50/20 mL/kg/day. Ongoing losses 10 mL/kg per watery stool, 2 mL/kg per vomit. ORS 0.5–1 mL/kg every 5 minutes. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4–6 hourly, max 60 mg/kg/24 h.** VERIFY

**If an examiner challenges your percentages: 'I'm using the Royal Children's Hospital bands, which are the ones used in Australian paediatric practice. Other texts, including older Murtagh editions, use mild under 5%, moderate 5–10% and severe over 10% — but the clinical actions at each level are the same.'** SA: **MedSTAR paediatric and neonatal retrieval 1300 13 12 33** — ring early rather than late; **RFDS**; **Women's and Children's Hospital**; **PATS** — mention it before the family asks; **CaFHS**; **Pika Wiya Health Service** in the Port Augusta region; **Closing the Gap PBS**; **Poisons Information 13 11 26**; **Child Abuse Report Line 13 14 78**.
plan: **WIPE, ADAPTED FOR A PARENT AND CHILD — and acknowledge the child by name**: **'I'm Dr ___, one of the GP registrars. You must be Danielle — and this must be Riley. Hello, mate. I can see he's had a rough couple of days. I'd like to ask you some questions, then examine him, then we'll make a plan together. Is that all right?'**

**THE OPEN QUESTION — and do NOT interrupt for 30 seconds**: **'tell me, in your own words, what's been happening with Riley.'** *Vomiting since Thursday, diarrhoea since yesterday, hasn't eaten, hanging off her all morning, hasn't played.* **Half the case arrives free. Reflect it back in one line.**

**EXPLORE THE VOMITING**: how many in 24 hours · **'what does it look like — is any of it GREEN?'** · any blood · **'does it just come up, or does it shoot right out?'** · **'is it worse first thing in the morning?'** *Six or seven, yellowy curdled, no blood, not forceful.*
**If the colour answer is vague, DISAMBIGUATE**: **'green like grass or spinach, or yellow like curdled milk?'** **Green is malrotation until excluded, and it ends the outpatient conversation.**

**EXPLORE THE DIARRHOEA**: how many, how loose · **'any blood or mucus, anything that looks like jelly?'** · **'does he go pale and pull his knees up in episodes, then seem completely fine in between?'** **That last question is what separates gastroenteritis from intussusception at exactly this age, and it carries its own mark.**

**EXCLUSION BLOCK — signpost it**: **'a few quick questions to make sure nothing more serious is going on.'** Fever and measured · **any rash, and does it fade under a glass** · ear pulling, cough, working hard to breathe · offensive urine · **'has he been drinking and weeing FAR MORE than usual over the last week?'** (DKA) · **any access to medicines or chemicals.**
**★ WHEN THE EAR-PULLING COMES, DO NOT DISCARD IT**: **'that's worth knowing — I'll make sure I look in his ears, because an ear infection can cause vomiting and diarrhoea in a little one.'**

**★ THE WELL-BABY QUESTIONS — signpost them, all four, every case**: **'now some questions about how well Riley is in himself — these are the ones that matter most to me.'** **1 alert and active as usual, or drowsy? 2 IS HE DRINKING as he normally would — and what about eating? 3 how many wet nappies NORMALLY, and how many TODAY? 4 any other change in his bowel motions?**

**TARGETED BINDSMA ONLY — immunisation, social, medication, allergy**: **'are his immunisations up to date including his rotavirus doses? Is anyone else at home or at daycare unwell? Any medical problems, medicines or allergies?'** *Two children at daycare with the same thing.* **Skip birth history — it is worth almost nothing here.**

**★ CONCERNS — ask it and then WAIT**: **'before I examine him — was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?'** *She becomes tearful about her sister's son and 'I've left it too long.'*

**NAME THE EMOTION AND ANSWER IT DIRECTLY — this is a scored item, not a courtesy**: **'thank you for telling me — it sounds like that was frightening to watch. YOU HAVE NOT LEFT IT TOO LONG. He is alert and he is still taking fluid, and those are the two things that matter most.'**
**SUMMARISE BACK IN 20 SECONDS**: two days of vomiting then watery diarrhoea, daycare outbreak, alert but clinging, sips only, three or four nappies down to one. **'Have I missed anything?'**

**ASK THE EXAMINER — and the marks are for HYDRATION and the SEARCH FOR ANOTHER SOURCE**: **'weight undressed; full observations with CENTRAL capillary refill; hydration signs — eyes, mucous membranes, tears, turgor, fontanelle; full abdominal and hernial orifice examination; EARS, THROAT AND CHEST; full skin inspection for rash; BEDSIDE GLUCOSE AND KETONES; and a CLEAN-CATCH URINE.'**

**★ GRADE IT OUT LOUD**: **'dry mucous membranes, slightly sunken eyes and reduced turgor with a normal central refill and warm peripheries — that is clinical dehydration, not shock. With a 600-gram weight loss I'd put him at about five per cent.'**

**EXPLAIN, GOOD NEWS FIRST, THEN THE NAMED EXCLUSIONS IN LAY WORDS**: a tummy bug, a virus, the one going round daycare, settling over three to five days. **'If the vomit had been green that could have meant a blockage needing surgery — it isn't. If he'd been screaming in episodes and going pale, that could have been a telescoping bowel — he isn't. His ears, throat and chest are clear, and so is his urine, which matters because a urine infection in a toddler looks just like this. His sugar and ketones are normal, so it isn't diabetes, and there's no rash, so it isn't meningococcal.'**
**ANSWER THE ANTIBIOTIC QUESTION, THEN OFFER WHAT WORKS**: **'antibiotics work on bacteria; this is a virus, and they'd make the diarrhoea worse. What fixes it is fluid, given the right way.'**

**THE REHYDRATION TECHNIQUE — the examinable content is the METHOD, not the name**: **'Hydralyte or Gastrolyte, about a TEASPOON EVERY FIVE MINUTES by syringe. Tiny and often — a whole cup comes straight back. Four hours, then we re-weigh him here. NO juice, cordial, sports drinks or lemonade — too sugary, they make it worse. Keep breastfeeding or milk going, and let him eat as soon as he wants. If he can't manage by mouth the next step is a fine tube through the nose, NOT a drip.'**

**★ SAFETY-NET IN NUMBERS, NOT ADJECTIVES — six triggers, in writing**: **floppy or hard to wake · fewer than three wet nappies in a day · nothing kept down over six hours · the vomit turns GREEN · blood in the vomit or nappy · a rash that doesn't fade under a glass** — **'or you're simply worried; you know him better than I do.'** Then **review in 24 hours regardless**, and mention **PATS before she asks.**
pefe: **Weigh the child UNDRESSED and compare with the last recorded weight** — serial weight is the ONLY quantitative measure of deficit.
**Full observations including RESPIRATORY RATE BEFORE TOUCHING the child, and CENTRAL capillary refill.** Hydration signs: eyes, mucous membranes, tears, skin turgor, fontanelle.
**Search for another source in EVERY vomiting child: EARS, THROAT, CHEST AND URINE.** Do not use the word gastroenteritis until you have.
**BEDSIDE GLUCOSE AND KETONES in any unwell or vomiting child — it is a two-minute test.** 'Gastro that isn't improving' with wet nappies despite dehydration is DKA until disproven.
**CLEAN-CATCH OR CATHETER urine for dipstick, microscopy and culture. A BAG URINE IS NOT ADEQUATE FOR CULTURE.**

**ORS 0.5–1 mL/kg every 5 minutes, increasing as tolerated; replace the deficit over 4 hours (≈50 mL/kg for 4–6%), then reassess. If oral fails, GO TO NASOGASTRIC BEFORE INTRAVENOUS — safer, cheaper, better tolerated.**
**Shock: 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride IV or IO over 10–20 minutes, reassess, repeat. ISOTONIC maintenance only (0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose) — never hypotonic.**

**AVOID: antibiotics in uncomplicated viral gastroenteritis · LOPERAMIDE AND DIPHENOXYLATE, contraindicated in children · undiluted juice, cordial, sports drinks and flat lemonade · ibuprofen while dehydrated · routine bloods and stool cultures in a well-hydrated child · REFLEXIVE FLUID BOLUSES IF DKA IS SUSPECTED — discuss with paediatrics first.**
**ONDANSETRON: a single oral dose in children over 6 months when vomiting prevents oral rehydration — 8–15 kg 2 mg, 15–30 kg 4 mg, over 30 kg 6–8 mg.** VERIFY

**DISPOSITION: home if no clinical dehydration, tolerating fluids IN FRONT OF YOU, reliable carer and reasonable access · observe and rehydrate for 4 hours then RE-WEIGH if clinically dehydrated · admit or retrieve if shocked, failing nasogastric rehydration, unsafe social situation, or any diagnostic doubt · review at 24 hours regardless.**

stem: General practice, Wallaroo (nearest ED five minutes, the Women's and Children's in Adelaide two hours by road). NOAH, 18 MONTHS, brought for an urgent appointment by his father with FEVER AND VOMITING FOR 24 HOURS — and the father says he has been 'UNRESPONSIVE'.

Vitals on request: T 39.4 — HR 168 — RR 38 — SpO2 96% air — CAPILLARY REFILL 3 SECONDS — weight 11 kg. History six minutes with a prompt, then the examination card, then two minutes on investigations and management.
tasks: Take a history from the father (6 minutes — you will be prompted)
Read the examination findings, which are given on a card
Explain your immediate investigations and management to the father (2 minutes)
findings: ★ VITALS ON REQUEST — and READING THEM IS NOT THE MARK, INTERPRETING THEM IS

T 39.4 °C · HR 168 · RR 38 · SpO2 96% air · CRT 3 s · weight 11 kg. Say it out loud: 'HEART RATE 168 AND CAPILLARY REFILL 3 SECONDS ARE ABNORMAL FOR AN 18-MONTH-OLD' — RCH upper limits are HR 150 and RR 40 for 1–4 years
★ THE EXAMINATION CARD AT 6 MINUTES — the designed distractor

Drowsy, rousable, WHIMPERS ON HANDLING, POOR EYE CONTACT. Hot, flushed. MILD PHARYNGEAL ERYTHEMA, tonsils not enlarged, no exudate. Tympanic membranes normal. NO RASH. No neck stiffness. Fontanelle closed. Chest clear. Abdomen soft. DRY LIPS, REDUCED SKIN TURGOR, CRT 3 s. No joint swelling
What the card is FOR
The drowsiness sits in the HISTORY and the only positive on the card is a mildly red throat. THE CASE IS BUILT TO TEMPT 'viral URTI, go home'
The history he gives

Fever two nights, 39 on the ear thermometer, PANADOL HELPS FOR AN HOUR. Vomiting since yesterday, six times, MILKY THEN CLEAR — no green, no blood. NOTHING KEPT DOWN SINCE THIS MORNING. Floppy since about 6 am
★ 'UNRESPONSIVE' CLARIFIED
'SLEEPY AND FLOPPY. He wakes when I pick him up but he just cries and shuts his eyes.' GRADUAL over the morning. NO jerking, NO eye rolling, NO incontinence — so NOT post-ictal
The soft signs he gives
Runny nose a few days ago. NO drooling. HIS CRY HAS GONE WEAK AND SQUEAKY. No cough but HE'S BREATHING FAST. No rash. No diarrhoea. HE CRIES WHEN PICKED UP
★ THE WELL-BABY ANSWERS — only if you ask, and only in numbers
TWO WET NAPPIES SINCE LAST NIGHT. NOT DRINKING. Drowsy. 'Wees seem normal — but there haven't been many'
★ THE TEMPTING RED HERRING

'He had a FIT WITH A FEVER at 14 months — they said febrile convulsion.' Hearing this and switching to a febrile-convulsion spine is the named trap. NO SEIZURE FEATURES TODAY — say so out loud and stay on sepsis
Background
Term. FULLY IMMUNISED including the 18-month doses last month. Growing fine. No medicines, no allergies. Daycare three days a week. Lives with both parents and a 4-year-old sister
★ HIS HIDDEN AGENDA
He cannot get hold of his wife Jess and THE UTE IS LOADED FOR A JOB — so when the ambulance is raised he says 'I'LL DRIVE HIM, IT'S FIVE MINUTES.' He backs down if you explain WHY
His three scripted reactions
'Sepsis? HE'S ONLY GOT A COLD.' · 'CAN'T YOU JUST GIVE HIM ANTIBIOTICS HERE?' · 'IS HE GOING TO DIE?' And if you never mention fluids: 'He won't drink — what about that?'
If you say 'tonsillitis, go home'
He replies 'Okay… BUT WHY IS HE SO FLOPPY?' — and the station is marked a FAIL
VARIANT — purpuric spots on the legs
MENINGOCOCCAL DISEASE until proven otherwise. CEFTRIAXONE 50 mg/kg INTRAMUSCULARLY RIGHT NOW, before the ambulance; notify SA Health today; household contacts need prophylaxis
Other practice cards

Smelly urine and screaming at nappy changes → still sepsis, urosepsis likely, CATHETER urine · jerking for 3 minutes at 6 am then sleepy → a febrile convulsion, BUT drowsy four hours later with these vitals is sepsis or meningitis until proven otherwise · fever SIX days with red eyes, cracked lips and peeling fingers → KAWASAKI (needs ≥5 days), echo and IVIG · unimmunised → Hib, pneumococcal and meningococcal all back on the table, higher urgency

dx: **SEPSIS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE — fever plus altered conscious state plus tachycardia plus prolonged capillary refill plus dehydration, with NO adequate source. THE MILD RED THROAT IS THE DESIGNED DISTRACTOR.**

**★ THE PASS LINE, said to the father despite the card: 'A MILDLY RED THROAT DOES NOT EXPLAIN A DROWSY, TACHYCARDIC, POORLY PERFUSED CHILD. Fever with drowsiness is sepsis until proven otherwise, and I am sending him to hospital now.'** **Candidates who anchor on the card diagnose tonsillitis and send the child home with paracetamol — the critical error.**

**The second discriminator is ORDERING, named as ACTIONS: transfer → investigations → antibiotics → fluids → monitoring.** **Opening with 'I would refer to a paediatrician' is a named fail — the referral is HOW they happen, not WHAT you are doing.**

**DEFINITIONS: SEPSIS is suspected or proven infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction. SEPTIC SHOCK is sepsis with cardiovascular dysfunction — and HYPOTENSION IS LATE IN CHILDREN. Tachycardia, CRT over 2 seconds, cool or mottled peripheries and altered conscious state all come FIRST.**

**RCH AGE-ADJUSTED LIMITS, so you can say 'abnormal for age': HR under 1 yr 160 · 1–4 yr 150 · 5–11 yr 130. RR under 1 yr 50 · 1–4 yr 40 · 5–11 yr 30. CRT over 2 s is abnormal.** Noah at 168 and 3 seconds ticks every column except rash. VERIFY

**★ THREE THINGS THE LECTURE SKIPS THAT THE AMC MARKS: 1. FLUID INTAKE AND URINE OUTPUT IN NUMBERS — wet nappies in 12 hours. 2. IMMUNISATION STATUS including pneumococcal and meningococcal — an unimmunised febrile drowsy child changes the antibiotic AND the urgency. 3. A PREVIOUS FEBRILE CONVULSION, which tempts you to call this post-ictal. NO SEIZURE FEATURES TODAY = NOT POST-ICTAL, and saying that out loud is the mark.**

**THE DIAGNOSIS SENTENCE TO THE FATHER, in his words**: **'I am very concerned that Noah has SEPSIS — a serious infection that has spread into his blood and is affecting his whole body. The reasons are his high fever, that he is drowsy and floppy, his heart is racing, his circulation is slow, and he isn't drinking or passing much urine. The slightly red throat does not explain how unwell he is. This needs the hospital, NOW.'**

**THE FOUR-PART PLAN. ONE — my nurse is calling an ambulance now, I'll ring the emergency department so they're ready, and if he needs the children's hospital in Adelaide the retrieval team will come to him. TWO — blood count, infection markers and a BLOOD CULTURE, a urine sample, possibly a chest X-ray, and once he's stable possibly a lumbar puncture. THREE — ANTIBIOTICS STRAIGHT INTO A VEIN WITHIN THE HOUR, and IF THE AMBULANCE IS DELAYED I WILL GIVE THE FIRST DOSE HERE AS AN INJECTION, plus IV fluids because he is dry and can't drink, and paracetamol. FOUR — continuous monitoring by the paediatric team. MOST CHILDREN TREATED THIS EARLY DO VERY WELL.**

**DOSES: CEFTRIAXONE 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IV or IM once daily — 100 mg/kg (max 4 g) IF MENINGITIS IS SUSPECTED. Benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg IV if under 3 months, or if only penicillin is available for meningococcal disease. Vancomycin 15 mg/kg if septic shock or MRSA risk. Aciclovir 20 mg/kg 8-hourly if encephalitis is suspected. Fluid bolus 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride (10 mL/kg if cardiac concern) — 220 mL for Noah. Paracetamol 15 mg/kg, max 1 g.** VERIFY **ANTIBIOTICS WITHIN 60 MINUTES. LP is deferred if drowsy or unstable; ANTIBIOTICS ARE NEVER DEFERRED.**

**WHEN HE SAYS 'I'LL DRIVE HIM, IT'S FIVE MINUTES'**: **'I know it's close. If Noah gets worse in the car you'd be alone with him at the wheel; in the ambulance a paramedic is with him with oxygen and monitoring the whole way, and they can bypass the waiting room. Please let us do it this way — I'll ring the department now.'** **And when he asks 'is he going to die?': 'he is seriously unwell, but we've caught it and we're starting treatment now, which is what matters most.'** SA: **000 to Wallaroo Hospital (Yorke and Northern LHN)**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for retrieval advice and the WCH on-call paediatric consult; **RFDS**; **WCH PICU** is the tertiary destination; **notifiable — meningococcal, invasive pneumococcal and Hib — SA Health CDCB 1300 232 272**; **Aboriginal children have higher rates of invasive disease and rheumatic fever** — involve the ACCHS and Aboriginal Health Practitioner and check the extra NIP doses; **TIS National 131 450**; **Parent Helpline SA 1300 364 100**; **PATS**.
plan: **★ ASK FOR THE VITALS BEFORE YOU GREET ANYONE, AND INTERPRET THEM**: **'could I have Noah's observations, please? … 39.4, heart rate 168, breathing 38, oxygen 96, capillary refill 3 seconds. HIS HEART RATE AND CIRCULATION ARE ABNORMAL FOR HIS AGE, so I'll be efficient.'** **Reading them without comment loses the mark.**

**Then the father, briefly**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___ — you must be Noah's dad. I can see you're worried. Tell me what's been happening.'** *Fever and vomiting two days, now floppy, 'I think it's gastro, can you give him something?'*
**TIMING OF ALL THREE SYMPTOMS TOGETHER**: **'when did the fever, the vomiting and the floppiness each start — and is it getting worse?'** Two nights, yesterday, 6 am, and worse.
**FEVER**: **'have you measured it — how high? Have you given paracetamol or ibuprofen, and did it help?'** 39, Panadol works for an hour.

**VOMITING — three questions, and the colour one is non-negotiable**: **'what colour is it — ANY GREEN? Any blood? IS HE KEEPING ANYTHING DOWN?'** Milky then clear, no green, no blood, nothing since this morning.

**★ CLARIFY 'UNRESPONSIVE' — do not assume**: **'when you say unresponsive — is he SLEEPY AND HARD TO WAKE, FLOPPY AND NOT RESPONDING, or was he FITTING?'** Sleepy and floppy, wakes and cries then shuts his eyes.

**SUDDEN OR GRADUAL, THEN THE THREE SEIZURE QUESTIONS**: **'did it come on suddenly or gradually? Any jerking of the arms or legs? Eyes rolling up? Did he wet or soil himself?'** Gradual; no to all three.

**FEVER SPINE — ENT**: **'pulling at his ears? Runny nose? DROOLING? Any change in his voice or cry? Lumps in the neck?'** *Runny nose a few days ago; CRY WEAK AND SQUEAKY.* **Note that — it is a sepsis sign, not an ENT one.**

**RASH — ask for the glass test by name**: **'any rash at all — especially spots that DON'T FADE when you press a glass on them?'** None. **CHEST**: cough, noisy or fast breathing, sucking in under the ribs. *No cough but breathing fast.*
**CONTACTS AND GI**: anyone unwell at home or daycare, travel · diarrhoea, blood in the stool, drawing his legs up. **URINE**: **'crying or upset when he wees or at nappy changes? Smelly urine?'**

**MENINGITIS AND SEPSIS BLOCK**: **'does he dislike being handled or picked up? Does he dislike the light? Is his neck stiff? Is the soft spot bulging?'** *Cries when picked up.* **Neck stiffness is unreliable under 2 and the fontanelle is closed at 18 months — say so.**
**★ THE WELL-BABY QUESTIONS, IN NUMBERS**: **'is he drinking? HOW MANY WET NAPPIES IN THE LAST TWELVE HOURS? Bowels? Is he alert and active, or drowsy?'** **TWO wet nappies, not drinking, drowsy.**

**JOINTS AND KAWASAKI, ten seconds each**: swollen or red joints, limping or not weight-bearing · **red eyes, red cracked lips, swollen hands or feet** — and **Kawasaki needs five days of fever; he is on day two.**
**BINDSMA, TARGETED**: term birth · **immunisations up to date including the 18-month doses** · growing and developing well · medicines and allergies · **'has he ever had a fit?'** · who's at home.

**★ WHEN THE FEBRILE CONVULSION COMES, NAME IT AND DISMISS IT**: **'that fit last year was a febrile convulsion; there are NO seizure features today, so this is different.'** **Switching to a febrile-convulsion spine here is the named trap.**

**TAKE THE CARD AND READ IT BACK IN ONE LINE**: **'so he is drowsy, whimpers on handling, hot and dry with a capillary refill of three seconds; the ONLY source is a mildly red throat; no rash, no neck stiffness, chest and abdomen clear.'**

**★ THE SEPSIS SENTENCE, WITH ITS REASONS** — high fever, drowsy and floppy, racing heart, slow circulation, not drinking or passing urine — **'and the slightly red throat does not explain how unwell he is. This needs the hospital, now.'**

**Answer 'can't you just give him antibiotics here?'**: **'the antibiotics he needs go into a vein, with fluids and monitoring, and that needs the hospital team.'** Then **THE FOUR-PART PLAN, in order: ambulance and ring ahead · the sepsis work-up named · IV antibiotics within the hour, first dose here as an injection if the ambulance is delayed · IV fluids and paracetamol · continuous monitoring.**

**Handle the ambulance refusal, then close**: the paramedic, oxygen and monitoring, bypassing the waiting room. Answer **'is he going to die?'** honestly and calmly. Then **'could you ring his mum to meet you there? I'll stay with Noah until the ambulance arrives. Any questions?'**
pefe: **Ask for vitals FIRST and INTERPRET them against age-specific limits.** RCH: HR <1 yr 160 · 1–4 yr 150 · 5–11 yr 130; RR <1 yr 50 · 1–4 yr 40 · 5–11 yr 30; CRT over 2 s abnormal. **Hypotension is LATE.** VERIFY

**If there is no card (the online version): general appearance and conscious state with AVPU · vitals and capillary refill · FULL UNDRESS for a non-blanching rash · fontanelle, neck stiffness, Kernig's · ears and throat · work of breathing and air entry · heart sounds · abdomen and hernial orifices · joints and limbs · hydration — lips, turgor, eyes · BEDSIDE GLUCOSE and urine dipstick.**

**IN THE GP ROOM: say 'I am concerned about sepsis' · nurse calls 000 while YOU STAY with the child · oxygen if SpO2 under 92% · IV access, IO after two failed attempts · blood culture and glucose IF ACHIEVABLE WITHOUT DELAY · CEFTRIAXONE 50 mg/kg IV or IM — give IM if there is no IV · 20 mL/kg saline bolus if shocked, then reassess · paracetamol 15 mg/kg · continuous monitoring · ISBAR to ED.**

**IN ED: FBC, CRP, blood culture, BLOOD GAS AND LACTATE, electrolytes, glucose, urine MCS by CATHETER OR SUPRAPUBIC ASPIRATE in an unwell toddler, CXR if respiratory signs, LP when stable and no contraindication.** **If drowsy → CT or defer the LP — but DO NOT DEFER ANTIBIOTICS.**

**Empiric IV ceftriaxone ± vancomycin (shock or MRSA risk) ± aciclovir (encephalitis features). Maintenance plus deficit fluids for 5–7% dehydration. Hourly observations and fluid balance. Paediatric team and PICU discussion.**

stem: General practice, Mount Gambier; you are the GP registrar. LIAM DOYLE, 9, brought by his mother Sarah with RECURRENT COUGH AND WHEEZE. He is a KNOWN ASTHMATIC and is already on medication — THE STEM DOES NOT SAY WHICH.
Vital signs from the examiner on request; NO examination findings are provided beyond the vitals. 8 minutes, 2 minutes reading — about five minutes for the history.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother
Explain the condition to the mother
Explain your management steps
findings: ★ VITALS ON REQUEST — ask BEFORE you sit down

RR 20 · SpO2 98% room air · HR 92 · T 36.8. COMFORTABLE AT REST, SPEAKING IN FULL SENTENCES. This is a CONTROL station, not an exacerbation — but you do not know that until you have the numbers, and ASKING IS A SCORED ITEM
The cough
DRY, nothing comes up. Audible wheeze sometimes. WORST AT NIGHT — he wakes up coughing. HE HAS STOPPED GOING TO FOOTY TRAINING because he can't keep up. Tired at school because he isn't sleeping
★ KEY FINDING 1 — only if you ask whether he is TAKING it
'HONESTLY? I'M NOT SURE. I give it to him but I don't stand over him.' She does NOT volunteer this
★ KEY FINDING 2 — only if you ask about TECHNIQUE
'NO. NEVER.' HE HAS NO SPACER and puffs it straight into his mouth
The other two known-asthma answers
Diagnosed at about FOUR. Follow-up: 'not really — we just get the repeat prescription.' Admissions: ONE ED VISIT last year for a nebuliser, NEVER ICU
★ THE FOUR CONTROL ANSWERS — vague first, numbers only if you push

NIGHT: 'almost every night' · EXERCISE: 'he's given up footy' · DAYTIME: she says 'a fair bit' first, then 'MOST DAYS, FIVE OR SIX' · RELIEVER: 'quite often' first, then 'NEARLY EVERY DAY — that's why I'm always getting repeats.' HE FAILS ALL FOUR
★ THE PLANTED TRIGGER — only if asked
'HIS DAD DOES. IN THE KITCHEN, WITH THE WINDOW OPEN.' If you lecture her she becomes defensive: 'He's trying to cut down'
The other triggers
MOVED SIX MONTHS AGO to a house CARPETED THROUGHOUT. ONE INDOOR CAT. Eczema as a baby; his dad has hay fever
The two differentials she closes off
NO choking episode. NO recurrent chest infections, growing fine — so no foreign body and no chronic suppurative lung disease
Her scripted pushes

Around minute six: 'IS THAT A STEROID? I'm not sure about a child being on steroids' — she presses once if the answer is vague · If you finish early: 'how long before it works?' and 'will he be on it forever?' · If you use jargon: 'Sorry, what does that mean?'
VARIANT B — already on ICS, taking it properly

Orange preventer twice daily plus the blue one, done WITH her every morning and night, and the practice nurse CHECKED THE TECHNIQUE three months ago. NOTHING LEFT TO FIX — say so explicitly ('this is not anything you've done wrong'), then STEP 3: add MONTELUKAST nocte, with the BEHAVIOURAL COUNSELLING, and describe step 4
VARIANT C — a 4-year-old at step 3

On ICS and montelukast, still symptomatic. She asks for 'the purple combination one my niece is on.' STEP 4 DIFFERS UNDER SIX — REFER TO A PAEDIATRICIAN, do not start a LABA from general practice. But a referral alone is not a plan: re-check technique with a SPACER AND MASK, confirm the montelukast is given nightly, and revisit triggers while waiting
VARIANT D — the steroid-averse parent

'I've read about steroids… stunting their growth. I don't want him on them.' Give BOTH real options — low-dose ICS with the honest position that the growth effect is SMALL AT LOW DOSE, weighed against what uncontrolled asthma does; or MONTELUKAST, a bit less effective, with its own mood and behaviour caution — and let her choose
VARIANT — anaphylaxis, not asthma

Sudden wheeze at a party after cake containing nuts, WIDESPREAD RASH, HR 150, looks unwell. TREAT AS ANAPHYLAXIS FIRST — intramuscular adrenaline. It looks very like an asthma attack and killing time on the wrong diagnosis is fatal
VARIANT — inhaled foreign body

Cough three weeks and WORSENING, NO night or exercise pattern, WHEEZE ON THE RIGHT ONLY, was eating peanuts when it began. LOCALISED wheeze is one obstructed airway — chest X-ray and bronchoscopy. Ask about choking EVEN in a diagnosed asthmatic

dx: **POORLY CONTROLLED ASTHMA in a 9-year-old on reliever alone. NOT 'asthma' — the stem already told you that, and saying it back earns NOTHING. This is a KNOWN-CONDITION history, not a cough differential case: the stem names asthma deliberately, because it is there for you to EXPLORE, and the findings are inside it.**

**★ THE FOUR CONTROL QUESTIONS, VERBATIM — the stated pass/fail item. 1 'Does he have any symptoms at NIGHT — any coughing or wheezing?' 2 'Does he have any limitation or difficulty with EXERCISE because of his symptoms?' 3 'How many DAYS A WEEK does he have cough or wheeze during the day?' 4 'How many DAYS A WEEK does he need to use his Ventolin?'** **The threshold for 3 and 4 is TWO DAYS A WEEK. Questions 1 and 2 have NO threshold — any night symptoms and any exercise limitation count against control.**
**Good control = all four favourable. Partial = one or two adverse. Poor = three or four. TREAT PARTIAL THE SAME AS POOR — step up.** Liam fails all four.

**★ THE FOUR KNOWN-ASTHMA QUESTIONS — this block applies to ANY chronic condition a stem names. 1 DURATION: 'when was he diagnosed?' 2 TREATMENT, ADHERENCE AND TECHNIQUE: 'what is he on? … IS HE TAKING IT AS PRESCRIBED? … HAS ANYONE EVER CHECKED HIS TECHNIQUE?' — the highest-yield block, because a puffer not taken or taken badly is the commonest reason asthma looks uncontrolled. 3 FOLLOW-UP: 'is he having regular reviews?' 4 COMPLICATIONS: the control questions, plus 'has he ever been admitted to hospital, ED or INTENSIVE CARE?' — admission history is the single best marker of severity and future risk.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE HAS TWO SYMMETRICAL FAILURES. The first is answering the question the stem already answered — telling the mother her son has asthma, which she knew. The second is the opposite haste: correctly identifying poor control and reaching straight for a new drug WITHOUT establishing whether the current one is being taken, or taken properly. ESCALATING TREATMENT FOR A CHILD WHO IS NOT RECEIVING THE TREATMENT HE ALREADY HAS IS A CLINICAL ERROR.**

**BOTH HALVES IN ONE SENTENCE**: **'his asthma is poorly controlled — he's coughing most nights, he can't keep up at sport, and he has symptoms and needs his reliever on most days of the week. Before I add anything, I want to be sure he's actually taking what he's already got, and taking it properly — because if he isn't, a second medicine won't help either.'**

**THE LADDER, 6–11 YEARS: 1 SABA as required → 2 add LOW-DOSE ICS twice daily → 3 add MONTELUKAST → 4 ICS/LABA COMBINATION. 1–5 YEARS: steps 1 to 3 identical, but STEP 4 IS REFERRAL, NOT A LABA.** **NEVER a LABA alone, at any age. NEVER remove the reliever when adding a preventer.** **Walk the whole ladder from wherever the child sits — the task says management stepS, plural.**

**INHALER TECHNIQUE, because offering to check it and not knowing the steps is worse than not offering: SPACER FOR EVERY CHILD (mask under 4–5 years) · shake it · ONE PUFF INTO THE SPACER · four to six normal breaths · then repeat for the second puff · ONE PUFF AT A TIME, never two together · RINSE THE MOUTH after an ICS.**

**THE TWO INTERVALS, both said aloud: REVIEW 4–6 WEEKS after any step up, re-checking technique at every visit; THREE MONTHS of stable control before considering a step down — and step back up if control slips.** **DOSES: salbutamol 100 microgram/actuation, 1–2 puffs via spacer PRN · fluticasone low dose 100–200 microgram/day · budesonide 200–400 microgram/day · montelukast 4 mg (2–5 yr), 5 mg (6–14 yr), 10 mg (15+) nocte.** VERIFY

**TWO CAUTIONS THE SOURCE LECTURE OMITS. MONTELUKAST carries an Australian safety advisory for NEUROPSYCHIATRIC adverse effects — sleep disturbance, vivid dreams, anxiety, irritability, low mood and rarely suicidal thinking. If you offer it you MUST counsel the parent to stop it and contact you if behaviour or mood changes. And WHERE GUIDANCE DIVERGES: the Australian Asthma Handbook retains a short-acting reliever as step 1 for CHILDREN — give that in the exam. GINA has moved adults and adolescents toward anti-inflammatory reliever regimens.** VERIFY If challenged: **'I'm following the Australian Asthma Handbook for a six-to-eleven-year-old; I'm aware international guidance now favours anti-inflammatory reliever therapy, and in Australia that is established in adults and adolescents rather than this age group.'** SA: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for severe acute asthma; **WCH** paediatric respiratory referral for step 4 in a young child; **telehealth** respiratory clinics to avoid a Mount Gambier round trip; **PATS**; GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangements; **Closing the Gap PBS** when adding a second and third medicine; ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officers — **asthma prevalence and hospitalisation are higher in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.** VERIFY
plan: **★ ASK THE EXAMINER FOR VITALS BEFORE YOU SIT DOWN**: **'before I begin, could I have Liam's vital signs — respiratory rate and oxygen saturation particularly, plus heart rate and temperature.'** *RR 20, sats 98%, comfortable, full sentences.* **This is how you exclude an exacerbation before settling into a long-term conversation.**

**Introduce and open**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___. You must be Sarah, and this is Liam. What's been happening? … And is there anything in particular that's worrying you today?'** *Coughing for months, the puffer doesn't work, she wants something stronger.*

**EXPLORE THE COUGH — two minutes at most, weighted toward asthma features**: **'is it dry, or is he bringing anything up? Any wheeze or whistling? Is there a time of day it's worse — IS IT WORSE AT NIGHT? IS IT WORSE WHEN HE'S RUNNING AROUND OR PLAYING SPORT? And how is it affecting him at school and at home?'** **Do NOT run a croup/pertussis/reflux differential here.**

**★ SIGNPOST INTO THE KNOWN-CONDITION BLOCK**: **'the notes tell me he already has asthma, so I'd like to ask about that in some detail.'** Then **'when was he diagnosed?'** *Age four.* **'What treatment is he on at the moment?'** *'Just the blue one. Ventolin.'*

**★ DO NOT STOP AT THE DRUG NAME — the marks are in the next two questions**: **'and is he taking it as prescribed?'** *'Honestly? I'm not sure.'* → **'thank you for being straight with me — that's genuinely useful and it changes what I'd do next.'** Then **'has anyone ever watched him use his inhaler and checked his technique?'** *'No. Never.'*

**The remaining two**: **'is he having regular reviews, with a GP or a specialist?'** *Just repeats.* **'Has he ever been admitted to hospital, the emergency department, or INTENSIVE CARE because of his asthma?'** *One ED visit, never ICU.*

**★ SIGNPOST THE CONTROL BLOCK AND ASK ALL FOUR**: **'now four questions I ask everyone with asthma, to work out how well controlled it is.'** **Night symptoms · exercise limitation · HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK daytime symptoms · HOW MANY DAYS A WEEK reliever.**

**PUSH FOR NUMBERS — 'sometimes' is not an answer**: she offers 'a fair bit' and 'quite often'. **Ask again: 'how many days a week?'** *Five or six; nearly every day.* **Questions 3 and 4 have a threshold and the others do not — that is why the numbers matter.**

**TRIGGERS, four groups**: **'does anyone smoke at home?'** *Dad, in the kitchen.* **'Do you have pets, or carpet? Any recent change — a house move?'** *Moved six months ago, carpet throughout, indoor cat.* **'Does he have eczema or hay fever, and is there asthma or allergy in the family?'**

**THE TWO DIFFERENTIALS STILL WORTH EXCLUDING, ten seconds each**: **'has he ever had an episode of CHOKING?'** — ask it even in a diagnosed asthmatic — and **'has he had a lot of chest infections, or any concerns about his growth?'**
**Concerns and a short summary back**, then signpost the explanation: **'that's given me a clear picture. Let me tell you what I think.'**

**★ NAME THE CONDITION PROPERLY**: acknowledge she knows he has asthma and explain it in one line — narrowed, irritable breathing tubes — **'but the important thing I want to tell you today is that HIS ASTHMA IS CURRENTLY POORLY CONTROLLED. And I want to tell you exactly why I say that.'**

**THE FOUR REASONS, spoken as a list**: coughing at night almost every night · can't exercise normally, has given up football · symptoms on most days, well over two · reliever on most days, well over two. **Then the standard: 'well-controlled asthma means NO night symptoms, NO limitation on exercise, and symptoms and reliever use on no more than two days a week. He fails all four.'**

**★ ADHERENCE AND TECHNIQUE FIRST, AND SAY THE ORDER MATTERS**: **'two things have to happen, and the order matters. The first is making sure he's actually getting the medicine he already has. If the medicine isn't reaching his lungs, adding a second one won't help either. So I'd like to watch him use it right now, WITH A SPACER.'** Then **the technique in concrete steps** — shake, one puff in, four to six normal breaths, repeat, one puff at a time.

**STEP UP — and explain reliever versus preventer before naming a drug**: **'a reliever opens the airways when symptoms come, so it's used as needed. A preventer is taken every day whether he feels well or not, and stops the airways becoming narrowed in the first place.'** Then **add low-dose ICS morning and night — AND HE KEEPS THE VENTOLIN.**

**WALK THE LADDER BEYOND THE NEXT RUNG — the task says stepS**: **'if that isn't enough when I see him again, the step after is a tablet called montelukast at night on top of the preventer. And if that still isn't enough, a combination puffer containing both a preventer and a long-acting reliever. I'm telling you all of it so you can see there's a plan and a sequence.'**
**Answer 'is that a steroid?' honestly**: a very small dose straight into the lungs, quite different from steroid tablets; **rinsing the mouth deals with most local side effects.**

**THE LAST NINETY SECONDS ARE SEPARATELY MARKED — PROTECT THEM. SMOKING, without moralising**: **'smoking in the kitchen still fills the house. If Liam's dad can stop I'd love to help — and if that's not realistic, entirely outside would still make a real difference.'** **TRIGGERS**: vacuum the carpet, cat out of the bedroom. **EXERCISE**: **'I don't want him giving up football — not being able to play is a sign the asthma isn't controlled, not a reason to stop.'** **THEN: written ASTHMA ACTION PLAN, review in 4–6 WEEKS with technique re-checked, step down only after 3 months stable, and BOTH sets of red flags — acute (sudden worsening, can't speak in sentences, reliever not lasting, blue lips) and chronic (night symptoms returning, sport limited again, reliever more than two days a week).**
pefe: **Ask for RESPIRATORY RATE and OXYGEN SATURATION first, plus heart rate and temperature — and work of breathing and mental state.** This excludes an acute exacerbation, and asking is scored.
**WATCH HIM USE THE DEVICE, with a spacer.** Checking technique is not a question you ask — it is something you observe.
**SPACER FOR EVERY CHILD; MASK UNDER 4–5 YEARS. Shake · one puff into the spacer · four to six normal breaths · repeat · ONE PUFF AT A TIME · rinse the mouth after an ICS.**
**Grade control against the four questions and SAY THE GRADE OUT LOUD.**
**SPIROMETRY confirms the diagnosis from age six if it has never been done. Under 12 months it is NEVER asthma. At 1–5 years, response to treatment replaces spirometry.**

**Generalised wheeze = diffuse small-airway narrowing (asthma, or bronchiolitis in an infant). LOCALISED wheeze = one obstructed airway = FOREIGN BODY until proven otherwise.** **If an examiner offers 'wheeze' without qualifying it, ASK WHICH.**
**Step up from wherever the child sits. Written ASTHMA ACTION PLAN with green, amber and red zones. Annual influenza vaccination. Review 4–6 weeks; re-check technique every visit.**

**AVOID: a LABA alone, ever · starting a LABA under six in primary care · removing the reliever when adding a preventer · stepping up again the following week rather than at 4–6 weeks · ADVISING THE CHILD TO GIVE UP SPORT · stepping down before three months of stable control.**

**Non-drug measures are separately marked: smoking cessation or entirely outdoors and never in the car · vacuum carpets for dust mite, pets out of the bedroom · ENCOURAGE EXERCISE with a pre-exercise reliever if needed · reading material — RCH fact sheets, National Asthma Council, Lung Foundation.**

**MONTELUKAST requires behavioural counselling every time you offer it** — sleep disturbance, vivid dreams, anxiety, irritability, low mood, rarely suicidal thinking. Stop it and contact the doctor if any change appears.

findings: ★ VERSION A — the findings you ASK FOR

Well, afebrile, observations normal. RIGHT ARM PRONATED, SLIGHTLY FLEXED. NO swelling, bruising or deformity. NO TENDERNESS FROM CLAVICLE TO WRIST. DISTRESSED ON ATTEMPTED SUPINATION. Radial pulse present, capillary refill under 2 s, MOVING ALL FINGERS
★ VERSION B — the trap
'SWELLING OVER THE RIGHT ELBOW WITH SIGNIFICANT TENDERNESS; otherwise as above.' ANY CANDIDATE ALREADY DEMONSTRATING THE MANOEUVRE HAS FAILED
★ YOU GET EXACTLY WHAT YOU ASK FOR

Ask for 'an elbow examination' and THE CLAVICLE AND THE PULSE WILL NOT APPEAR. Ask for the WHOLE LIMB FROM COLLARBONE TO FINGERTIPS, plus radial pulse, capillary refill, hand colour and finger movement
The mechanism she gives
'He pulled towards the road, I YANKED HIM BACK UP BY THE HAND and he screamed.' About an hour ago. SHE FELT A LITTLE CLICK. NO fall, NO head knock — 'I had hold of him'
Arm use since
'NOT AT ALL. He just lets it hang.' And the discriminating detail: 'FINE IF YOU LEAVE IT. SCREAMS IF YOU BEND IT' — distress ONLY on movement, not at rest
The red-flag answers
No swelling, redness, bruising or deformity — 'it looks exactly like the other one.' 'HE LET ME HOLD IT IN THE CAR.' Hand normal, PICKING AT HIS SHOE WITH THE FINGERS. No fever
★ HER EMOTIONAL REGISTER AND HIDDEN AGENDA

GUILTY AND FRIGHTENED — convinced she has broken his arm and HALF-EXPECTING TO BE TOLD OFF. Tearful in the first minute. She asks 'SO I DID THIS TO HIM?' when you name it, and if concerns are never asked she volunteers 'WAS IT MY FAULT?' in the last minute
★ HER SCRIPTED PUSH
'DOES HE NEED AN X-RAY?' at about three minutes if you have not raised it, and she PRESSES ONCE: 'Wouldn't it be safer to just X-ray it?'
If you say 'dislocated' without explaining
She is ALARMED: 'DISLOCATED?! Shouldn't he be in hospital?' Say 'SLIPPED SLIGHTLY OUT OF PLACE' instead
If you grab the arm without explanation
She PROTESTS. Consent properly and warn her he will cry
Her closing questions
'Will it hurt him? … OK. CAN I HOLD HIM?' and 'Will it happen again? Was it because I picked him up wrong?'
VERSION C — no pull remembered

'I don't know — he was playing and just stopped using it.' ABOUT HALF HAVE NO PULL HISTORY. Broaden the limb examination, ask about a fall and a head knock, lower your threshold for X-ray — BUT REDUCTION IS STILL REASONABLE IF THE EXAMINATION IS CLEAN

dx: **PULLED ELBOW — radial head subluxation, 'nursemaid's elbow'. Sudden axial traction on a PRONATED, EXTENDED forearm lets the ANNULAR LIGAMENT slip over the radial head and become trapped between it and the capitellum. A SUBLUXATION — not a dislocation, not a fracture.**

**★ THE WHOLE STATION IN ONE LINE: confirm the pull, CLEAR THE WHOLE LIMB AND THE CLAVICLE, name it in plain words, reduce with your THUMB ON THE RADIAL HEAD, and wait for the high-five.** **This is the one station where you fix the problem in the room.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING BEHAVIOUR IS A DEMONSTRATION — on the examiner's arm, a manikin, or your own forearm — with your thumb over the radial head, AND stating in the same breath the two conditions under which you would NOT do it or would STOP: RED FLAGS BEFORE, TWO FAILURES AFTER.** **Say the red-flag rule BEFORE the findings arrive, so it is on record whichever version you get.**

**THE MANOEUVRE, WORD FOR WORD: 'he sits on Mum's lap facing me. I support the right elbow in my LEFT hand with my THUMB OVER THE RADIAL HEAD — outside of the elbow, just below the crease. Right hand on his wrist, elbow at NINETY DEGREES. I firmly HYPERPRONATE the forearm — palm down and beyond — in one smooth movement, feeling for a CLICK under my thumb. If that fails: SUPINATE fully, then FLEX the elbow completely, hand to shoulder. Then release, step back, and offer a toy above head height.'** **Hyperpronation first — higher first-attempt success and less painful in trials.**

**SUCCESS IS NORMAL USE WITHIN 5 TO 30 MINUTES — and you prove it: ask for a reach overhead and a high-five.** **If the injury is over 12 hours old, return of use may take 1–2 DAYS after a successful reduction — but two failed attempts still means X-RAY TODAY, not a two-day wait.** VERIFY
**RED FLAGS — STOP AND X-RAY: significant tenderness · swelling · deformity · bruising · a fall or direct blow · fever · a story that does not fit · TWO FAILED ATTEMPTS. NEVER a third attempt.**

**★ THE ELBOW-ONLY EXAMINATION IS THE CLASSIC WAY THIS STATION IS LOST. A child who 'won't use the arm' may have a CLAVICLE FRACTURE. Ask for the whole limb from collarbone to fingertips, every time — plus the radial pulse, capillary refill, hand colour and finger movement.** **Skipping vascular and neurological assessment because 'it's just a pulled elbow' is fifteen seconds that separate this from a supracondylar fracture.**

CORRECTION — **on analgesia. The source transcript says 'you can't give them painkillers'. RCH's actual wording is that analgesia is GENERALLY NOT REQUIRED because reduction relieves the pain — it is NOT prohibited.** **Paracetamol 15 mg/kg orally (about 180 mg for a 12 kg toddler) is entirely reasonable if you or the parent prefer. Offer it; do not present it as mandatory and do not claim it is forbidden.**

**EXPLAIN IT IN PLAIN WORDS, AND ANSWER THE GUILT BEFORE SHE ASKS**: **'one of the forearm bones, the radius, has a rounded head held in the elbow by a band called a ligament. A sudden pull on the hand stretches that band and the head SLIPS PARTLY OUT from under it — a small slip, not a true dislocation and not a broken bone. It only hurts when the elbow moves, which is why he keeps it so still. Thousands of children a year get this — it's a quirk of the joint until about five, NOT something you did wrong.'** **Saying 'dislocated' on its own alarms her.**

**NUMBERS AND CLOSING: age 6 months to 5 years, PEAK 1–4, rare after 5 as the ligament thickens · ABOUT HALF have NO pull history · RECURRENCE ABOUT 25% until the ligament matures · normal film but still not using it → collar-and-cuff or sling, paracetamol, review 24–48 hours, because spontaneous reduction is common · NO SLING once he is using it.** VERIFY **PREVENTION: lift under the arms, not by the hands; no swinging.** SA: reduce in the room at a regional GP or ED; **WCH orthopaedics via the on-call registrar** for a fracture or a failed reduction with an abnormal film; **PATS** for travel; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 ONLY for neurovascular compromise**; ACCHS and Aboriginal Health Practitioner; **TIS National 131 450**; **RCH Kids Health Info 'Pulled elbow' fact sheet**; **NAI is a mandated notification under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 — CARL 13 14 78.** VERIFY
plan: **WIPE — and greet the child without reaching for the arm**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the GPs here. You must be Sarah — and this is Oliver? Hi Oliver.'** *(crouch, smile, hands to yourself)* **'I can see you're worried about his arm. A few questions, then I'll take a look, and we'll work out what's going on together.'** *She is tearful: 'I think I've broken his arm.'*

**THE INCIDENT, exactly**: **'can you describe exactly how it happened — what were you doing, and how did you pull him? Which arm? When? Did you hear or feel a POP or a CLICK? Did he cry straight away and then settle? DID HE FALL, OR BUMP HIS HEAD at the time?'** *Yanked up by the hand, an hour ago, a little click, no fall.*
**★ DISARM THE GUILT EARLY — it runs the consultation otherwise**: **'that's a really common way for this to happen — it's not something you did wrong.'**

**ARM USE SINCE**: **'did he stop using it immediately, or later on? Is he not using it AT ALL, or on and off? How is he holding it? IS HE UPSET WHEN IT'S STILL, OR ONLY WHEN IT'S MOVED?'** *Not at all; fine if left, screams if bent.* **Distress at rest PLUS tenderness would make you think fracture.**

**RED-FLAG SCREEN — MSK**: **'any swelling, redness or bruising around the elbow? Does the elbow look different from the other side — any bend or deformity?'** Then the best question in the history: **'DOES HE LET YOU TOUCH THE ELBOW?'**

**VASCULAR, NEURO AND INFECTION — fifteen seconds that separate this from a supracondylar fracture**: **'has the hand changed colour — pale, blue or cold? Is he moving his fingers normally? Any fever?'**

**★ NAI SCREEN, NORMALISED**: **'can I ask a couple of questions about home, which I ask every family? Who was with him when it happened, and who's at home? How are things at home at the moment? Has he had any previous injuries, fractures or hospital visits? Has anything like this happened before?'**

**WELL-CHILD WRAP-UP**: **'is he alert and himself — not drowsy or vomiting?'** Then past history, medications, **allergies (you are about to offer paracetamol)**, immunisations, development, eating and drinking.

**★ ANSWER THE X-RAY QUESTION WITHOUT A FLAT NO**: **'if the examination is as I expect, we usually don't need one — and I'll explain exactly why. If anything doesn't fit, we will.'** **And say the rule NOW, before the findings arrive: 'if there's tenderness, swelling, bruising or deformity I won't reduce — I'll X-ray.'**

**★ ASK FOR THE EXAMINATION IN FULL — you get exactly what you ask for**: **'general appearance and observations, then the right upper limb: inspection for swelling, bruising or deformity; PALPATION OF THE CLAVICLE, humerus, elbow including the radial head, forearm and WRIST; resting posture and tolerated movement; and DISTAL NEUROVASCULAR STATUS — radial pulse, capillary refill, hand colour, finger movement.'**

**READ IT BACK**: arm pronated and slightly flexed, no swelling or deformity, **no tenderness from clavicle to wrist**, distressed only on attempted supination, **pulse present, refill under two seconds, moving all fingers.**

**EXPLAIN — good news first, then the mechanism in plain words**: **'the good news is I don't think anything is broken. This is a pulled elbow.'** Then the radius, the ligament, the small slip — **'not a true dislocation, not a fracture — and it only hurts when the elbow moves, which is why he keeps it so still.'**
**She says 'so I did this to him' — answer it properly**: **'thousands of children a year get this. It's a quirk of the joint at his age, not something you did wrong.'**

**CONSENT, AND WARN HER HE WILL CRY**: **'I can put it back right now — it takes a few seconds. I hold his elbow and turn his forearm in one quick movement. He'll probably cry for a moment, then within minutes to half an hour he should be using the arm normally. Painkillers usually aren't needed — the movement takes the pain away — but I can give paracetamol first if you'd prefer. Happy for me to go ahead?'**

**★ DEMONSTRATE, WORD FOR WORD, TO THE EXAMINER**: on Mum's lap facing you · **elbow supported in your left hand, THUMB OVER THE RADIAL HEAD, just below the crease on the outside** · right hand on the wrist, elbow at ninety degrees · **firm HYPERPRONATION, palm down and beyond, one smooth movement, feeling for the CLICK** · **second option: supinate fully, then flex completely, hand to shoulder.**
**RELEASE, DISTRACT, AND PROVE IT WORKED**: step back, offer a toy above head height, **'all done, mate — high five?'** **Success is normal use within five to thirty minutes.**

**THE TWO-ATTEMPT RULE, SAID ALOUD**: **'if he hadn't used it within half an hour I'd re-examine and try once more. After two goes, or if anything changes on examination, we X-ray.'** Add: **over twelve hours old it can take a day or two.**

**PREVENTION, SAFETY-NET AND CLOSE — all separately marked**: **recurrence about one in four while he's small, so LIFT UNDER THE ARMS, NOT BY THE HANDS, and no swinging** · **no sling once he's using it** · **RCH fact sheet** · **'come back, or go to hospital, if he isn't using it normally by tomorrow, if it swells, or if the hand goes pale or cold.'** Then a one-line summary and **'any questions?'**

**THE PEARL: ask the mother to feel the elbow while the child watches a screen.** If she can handle it freely and he keeps watching, there is no tenderness — you have your diagnosis, and you have modelled the examination without touching an unhappy toddler.
**NO IMAGING in a classic presentation with a clean examination.** Radiation, cost and delay — and the elbow may reduce during positioning anyway.
