stem: VERSION A: general practice. JACK, 5, with his mother Emma — 'a 5-year-old boy is brought in by his mother with RIGHT KNEE PAIN. He has been LIMPING AND REFUSING TO WALK for two days.' NO vitals given. History 4 minutes, examination findings from the examiner 2 minutes, explanation 2 minutes.

VERSION B (recalled March 2025): LIAM, 4 to 5, with his mother Jenny — 'a 4-to-5-year-old boy is brought to you because of LIMPING.' NO PAIN IN THE STEM. A PELVIS X-RAY IS IN THE ROOM, and some candidates were also handed a card reading 'reduced range of movement of the hip'. Tasks: history, EXPLAIN THE X-RAY, then diagnosis and differentials.
tasks: Take a history from the mother (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings (2 minutes) — or, in Version B, explain the X-ray to the mother
Explain the most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the mother (2 minutes)
findings: General, gait, vitals, growth
Alert, no rash. BEARS WEIGHT; ANTALGIC GAIT. TEMPERATURE 36.5 — the finding the examiner is holding for you — HR 96, BP normal for age. Growth chart normal, tracking the 50th centile
★ THE HIP — found ONLY if you examine the hip

KNEE AND ANKLE COMPLETELY NORMAL. Right hip: inspection and palpation normal; on movement, PAIN AND RESTRICTED RANGE, ESPECIALLY ABDUCTION AND INTERNAL ROTATION. TRUE LEG LENGTHS EQUAL. LOG ROLL POSITIVE on the right. Abdomen soft, dipstick normal
★ THE MOTHER INSISTS IT IS THE KNEE
'He only ever says his knee.' She will concede the hip only if asked directly. DO NOT ARGUE WITH HER — note it and EXAMINE THE HIP. Knee pain in a limping child is HIP PATHOLOGY until excluded
The limp and the pain

Since Saturday, two days. 'HE CAN STAND ON IT and walks a few steps, hobbles, then sits down — wouldn't walk to the car.' Same all day. 'PANADOL HELPED A LOT, he was brighter after it.' About 4/10, an ache, stays in the knee. SLEPT THROUGH BOTH NIGHTS
★ THE ONLY POSITIVE — never volunteered
'Yes, actually, he had a COLD ABOUT TWO WEEKS AGO — runny nose and a bit of a temperature for a day. That's gone.' Answered ONLY if you ask about recent viral illness
The red-flag answers
No swelling, redness, rash or stiffness. NO FEVER — she checked. Eating and playing. No weight loss, lumps, tiredness, pallor or bruising
★ THE SCRIPTED SHARP MOMENT
When you ask about weight loss and lumps she PAUSES, then asks 'WHY, WHAT ARE YOU THINKING?' She SOFTENS if you explain that you ask every child with leg pain these questions
The injury answer — testing your tone

'I'M NOT SURE IF HE FELL AT CHILDCARE, NOBODY SAID ANYTHING.' That is NOT an admission and not a red flag on its own — it tests whether you ask the social questions calmly. Home fine; loves childcare; soccer on Saturdays
The distractor
'My MUM HAS ARTHRITIS IN HER HANDS' — osteoarthritis, if asked about family history. It is irrelevant
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA

'IS IT SOMETHING IN THE BONE? A girl at work, her son had LEUKAEMIA.' Volunteered only if you ask what worries her — or in the last minute if you never do. She also wonders aloud about 'growing pains'
Her scripted pushes

If you say 'definitely synovitis' or 'just a virus': 'BUT HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T SOMETHING IN THE BONE?' · If there is no safety-net by the last 30 seconds: 'AND WHAT IF HE GETS WORSE TONIGHT?' · She asks about an X-ray if you have not raised imaging
★ VERSION B — PERTHES, with an X-ray in the room

Liam, 5, limping for WEEKS. 'He WON'T PUT HIS FOOT DOWN AT ALL now, I have to carry him.' Knee pain only on asking, 6–7/10. NO viral illness, NOTHING makes it better, everything else negative. AP pelvis: the femoral head on one side is FLATTENED, DENSE AND FRAGMENTED with a widened joint space and a short broad neck; the other side is a round ball in its socket. Some candidates get a card: REDUCED HIP RANGE OF MOVEMENT — that card IS the examination
Version B — her tearful question

After the word 'damaged': 'DID HE DO THIS AT CHILDCARE? IS IT MY FAULT?' — 'No. Perthes happens when the blood supply to the ball of the hip is interrupted for a time, and we don't know why. It isn't from a fall and it isn't anything you did or missed'
VARIANT — the hot hip

4-year-old, limp one day, WILL NOT STAND, TEMPERATURE 38.9, hip held FLEXED AND EXTERNALLY ROTATED, SCREAMS ON LOG ROLL. SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise — stop, same-day ED, bloods, ultrasound, aspiration. No analgesia-and-review
Other practice cards

Three weeks of leg pain WORSE AT NIGHT, tired, PALE, BRUISES EASILY, 'growing pains' → LEUKAEMIA until the FBE says otherwise — blood count TODAY · 2-year-old 'fell off the couch' three days ago, DELAY in presenting, bruises of DIFFERENT COLOURS on the back → NAI, skeletal survey, CARL 13 14 78 · 13-year-old, BMI 95th centile, knee pain after basketball, hip EXTERNALLY ROTATES ON FLEXION → SUFE, urgent non-weight-bearing and orthopaedics

dx: **VERSION A: TRANSIENT SYNOVITIS (irritable hip) of the right hip — a PROVISIONAL, HIGHER-PROBABILITY diagnosis, not a confirmed one. VERSION B: PERTHES DISEASE — avascular necrosis of the femoral head. ONE history structure for both, and SEPTIC ARTHRITIS IS RULED OUT IN EVERY VERSION.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: RULE OUT THE SEPTIC JOINT OUT LOUD, EVEN WHEN THE RECALL IS BENIGN. The examiner listens for four things in sequence: the FEVER QUESTION in the history · the TEMPERATURE as the FIRST vital sign · the WEIGHT-BEARING question · and septic arthritis NAMED IN THE EXPLANATION as the diagnosis you considered and excluded. Candidates who know the recall is transient synovitis skip these and fail — THE DIAGNOSIS WAS NEVER THE TEST.**

**THE LINE THAT SHOWS YOU EXCLUDED IT**: **'the most important thing I had to rule out today is an infection inside the hip joint. That is an emergency. Jack has no fever, his temperature is normal, he is well in himself, he can still put weight on the leg, and the joint is not hot or swollen — so I don't think that's what this is. But if any of those things change, I need to see him straight away.'**

**KNEE PAIN IN A LIMPING CHILD IS HIP PATHOLOGY UNTIL EXCLUDED.** Ask 'what about the hip?' in the history, and request 'lower limb examination: HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE' — the examiner will NOT volunteer the hip findings unless you examine the hip. **Asking for a knee examination only is an auto-fail.**

**WHY THE HISTORY ALONE CANNOT SEPARATE A FROM B. Both: a 4–10-year-old boy, limp, knee pain, restricted abduction and internal rotation, positive log roll. The differences are of DEGREE: Perthes gives more pain and more limp, often NO weight-bearing, WEEKS not days, NO viral prodrome, and Panadol does not fix it. The only confident discriminator is the X-RAY — normal in synovitis, flat, sclerotic, fragmented head in Perthes.** **So with no film: say 'transient synovitis is MORE LIKELY', never 'this is definitely synovitis'.**

**THE ORDERED HISTORY, ten blocks: explore the limp and WEIGHT-BEARING · PAIN, with 'what about the hip?' and NIGHT PAIN · general MSK screen (swelling, redness, rash, stiffness) · INFECTION · MALIGNANCY (weight loss, lumps, tiredness, pallor, bruising) · FRACTURE, accidental and NAI (falls, sport, home, childcare) · VIRAL ILLNESS · rheum, HSP and IBD (other joints, family history, rash, abdominal pain, bloody diarrhoea, waterworks) · abdomen and scrotum · birth, the SIX-WEEK CHECK (the DDH question), well-child.** **The viral question is number 7, not number 1 — but it MUST be reached.**

**THE EXPLANATION, VERSION A, with three reasons**: **'the knee pain is actually coming from the hip — in children hip problems often show up as knee pain. The LINING of the hip joint has become inflamed, usually because of a virus. Three things point me there: he can still stand and walk; he had that cold two weeks ago; and on examination the hip was the only sore spot, with a positive test we use for this.'** **Then 3–5 differentials, EACH WITH A REASON, in order: Perthes (only an X-ray excludes it), infection (no fever, well), blood or bone cancer (nothing points there), fracture or injury, childhood arthritis.**

**★ VERSION B — THE X-RAY, NORMAL SIDE FIRST. 'On an X-ray, white is bone, grey is soft tissue and black is air — today we're looking at the white shadows. This long bone is the thigh bone; at the top it has a rounded head that sits inside the hip bone, LIKE A BALL IN A SOCKET. Let's look at the NORMAL side first: the head is round, like a ball. Now the other side: the head is FLAT, it has lost its curve, and it doesn't match. That tells me it has been damaged.'** **Point at the abnormal hip first and the parent has no reference point. And never say 'sclerosis', 'epiphysis' or 'avascular necrosis' to her — 'Perthes disease' is enough.**

**MANAGEMENT. VERSION A: NO INVESTIGATIONS if there are no red flags, he bears weight with mild discomfort, and the working diagnosis is clear — say this to the examiner as a DECISION, not an omission. Rest; paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4–6-hourly (max 4 doses/24 h) and/or ibuprofen 10 mg/kg 8-hourly with food; REVIEW IN 24–48 HOURS; X-RAY AT TWO WEEKS if not resolved, or for a SECOND EPISODE. If any doubt at all: AP and FROG-LEG pelvis X-ray first, then ultrasound for effusion, FBE, CRP, ESR.** VERIFY **VERSION B: prompt paediatric orthopaedic referral; limit running and jumping; analgesia; crutches only on orthopaedic advice; better prognosis under 6.** VERIFY

**KOCHER CRITERIA for septic arthritis: T >38.5 · NON-WEIGHT-BEARING · ESR >40 · WCC >12.** VERIFY **If challenged — 'why not investigate every child?': 'septic arthritis must be excluded before diagnosing an irritable hip, but that exclusion is CLINICAL when the child is afebrile, well, weight-bearing and has no red flags. If any of those are absent, or there is doubt, I'd send him the same day for bloods, ultrasound and orthopaedic review.'** **Ultrasound shows an effusion but CANNOT distinguish synovitis from a septic joint.** SA: **WCH paediatric orthopaedics** via GP referral with **PATS**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** only if febrile or in severe pain; **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children carry higher rates of bone and joint infection (S. aureus) — lower your threshold for bloods and same-day review**; **CARL 13 14 78** for NAI — a mandatory notification under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **Open, and acknowledge the child**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the GPs here. You must be Emma, and this is Jack? Hi Jack. How can I help you both today?'** Then signpost the serious questions so they don't frighten her: **'a limp in a child is something I take seriously, so I'm going to ask quite a few questions — some about serious things I ask every parent.'**

**★ SEVERITY FIRST — two separate questions**: **'can he put any weight on the leg at all? IS HE STILL WALKING?'** *He stands and walks a few steps, then sits.* **Weight-bearing points toward synovitis; refusal points toward Perthes or something worse.**

**TIMING AND PATTERN**: when did it start · constant or on and off · getting worse · **worse in the morning or the end of the day, after rest or after activity** · anything that makes it better. *Same all day; PANADOL HELPED A LOT.* **Note the Panadol response — it becomes a reason in your explanation.**

**★ PAIN, AND ASK THE HIP BY NAME**: **'where exactly is the pain? Anywhere else — WHAT ABOUT THE HIP? The ankle?'** *'He only says his knee.'* **Do NOT argue — note it, and examine the hip.** Then severity out of ten, character, radiation, and **'does it WAKE HIM AT NIGHT?'** — the malignancy question.
**GENERAL MSK SCREEN in one breath**: **'any swelling in the leg or the joints? Any redness or rash? Any stiffness?'**
**★ INFECTION — the auto-fail block**: **'has he had any FEVER OR CHILLS? Is the joint hot, red or swollen? Has he been unwell in himself?'** *No fever — she checked.*

**MALIGNANCY — and handle the sharp moment**: **'any weight loss? Any lumps or bumps? Unusually tired or pale? Bruising easily?'** *(pause) 'Why, what are you thinking?'* → **'these are questions I ask every child with leg pain, to be sure I'm not missing something rare like a problem with the blood or the bones. Nothing you've told me points that way.'**

**FRACTURE AND NAI, calmly and routinely**: **'any falls, injuries or knocks to the leg? Does he play any sport? How are things at home at the moment? And childcare — how is that going, any problems?'** *'I'm not sure if he fell at childcare.'* **Not an admission — do not react to it.**

**★ THE VIRAL QUESTION — it must be reached**: **'any recent flu-like illness, a cold, or a virus?'** *A cold two weeks ago.* **'That's helpful.'** Then **rheum, HSP and IBD**: other joints, family history of arthritis, rash, tummy pain, diarrhoea or blood in the stool, waterworks. **Birth and the six-week check** in one line.

**PEFE IN A FIXED ORDER — general, gait, TEMPERATURE FIRST**: **'is he alert or drowsy? Any rash? Can he bear weight — if so I'd like to observe his gait. Vital signs: TEMPERATURE FIRST, then heart rate and blood pressure. May I see his growth chart?'**

**★ LOWER LIMB: HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE — look, feel, move, length, special test**: **'inspection: swelling, redness, rash, deformity or abnormal posture? Palpation: local warmth, tenderness? Movements, active and passive — pain and range, at the hip, knee and ankle? True leg length compared. LOG ROLL. And the abdomen, with a urine dipstick if available.'**
**READ IT BACK**: knee and ankle normal; **right hip painful and restricted, especially abduction and internal rotation; log roll positive**; leg lengths equal; afebrile; abdomen soft.

★ THE PEFE CARD AT 6 MINUTES

Alert, GCS 15. PUPILS EQUAL AND REACTIVE. Full neurological examination NORMAL, gait normal. NO NECK TENDERNESS. SMALL LEFT TEMPORAL SCALP HAEMATOMA, no laceration. Cardiovascular and respiratory normal. BSL 5.6
★ TREAT THE CARD AS INCOMPLETE — and say what you'd add

Pupils and FUNDOSCOPY · a look at the scalp for a BOGGY swelling · BEHIND THE EARS (Battle sign) · AROUND THE EYES (raccoon eyes) · the EARDRUMS for blood. BASE-OF-SKULL SIGNS ARE THE CLASSIC OMISSION
The incident
About an hour ago. Tackled, FELL HEAD-FIRST onto the ground and ANOTHER BOY LANDED ON TOP. Running flat out. Just his head. No neck pain
★ TWO EVENTS, TWO DURATIONS

LOC: 'COMPLETELY OUT, about a minute.' Then separately: ALL FOUR LIMBS JERKING, EYES ROLLED BACK, about a minute. No tongue bite, frothing or incontinence. Ask BOTH durations — hearing 'shaking' and stopping is the trap
The rest of the red-flag box

FELT SICK, HASN'T VOMITED · confused and groggy in the ambulance, CLEARER NOW · vision, strength, speech and walking all NORMAL · DOESN'T REMEMBER THE TACKLE · MILD HEADACHE, NOT WORSENING · no fluid from nose or ears
★ THE PLANTED CLUE — offered with guilt
'He SKIPPED BREAKFAST, we were running late. DOES THAT MATTER?' It is NOT the cause (BSL 5.6), but the examiner marks whether you asked and whether you checked the glucose
The other causes of a seizure — all negative

No warning before the tackle. No fever or rash — well all week. No medications, nothing in the house. No blood thinners, no easy bruising. NEVER had a seizure. Normal development. No family history of epilepsy
Home and school — ask anyway
Me, his dad and his little sister, things are fine. He loves school. Immunisations up to date. NOTHING about NAI is planted — YOU STILL ASK ABOUT HOME
★ HER FIXED QUESTION

'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?' — and if never asked about concerns, she volunteers at minute five: 'Is his brain bleeding? CAN'T YOU JUST SCAN HIM?' She wants BOTH a scan and to go home. If you say 'he's fine' she pushes: 'HOW DO YOU KNOW?'
Her closing questions
'What if he gets worse at home?' · 'When can he play again?' · 'SHOULD I KEEP HIM AWAKE TONIGHT?' — you can let him sleep; check on him every few hours and make sure he rouses normally VERIFY
★ VERSION B — the story that doesn't fit

4-year-old 'FELL OFF THE COUCH' YESTERDAY EVENING, presented this morning after a fit. Mother vague on timing; STEP-FATHER ANSWERS FOR HER. Vomited three times overnight. PEFE: BRUISING OF DIFFERENT AGES on back and upper arms, a BOGGY SCALP SWELLING, GCS 14. NAI until proven otherwise — urgent CT, admission, skeletal survey, MANDATORY NOTIFICATION. ★ VERSION C — the deterioration

PEFE shows GCS 13 and a RIGHT PUPIL 5 mm, SLUGGISH. Now a MODERATE head injury — immediate CT, neurosurgeon, MedSTAR, protect airway and neck. Continuing the history while the child deteriorates is the trap

dx: **POST-TRAUMATIC SEIZURE after a MILD HEAD INJURY (GCS 15) WITH RISK FACTORS — loss of consciousness and a seizure. Concussion. No focal deficit. Observe 4 hours, scan on triggers, neurosurgeon aware.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING SENTENCE — NAME THE SEVERITY CATEGORY BEFORE NAMING THE PLAN: 'this is a MILD head injury, because his GCS is 15, but WITH A RISK FACTOR, because he had a seizure and lost consciousness.'** **That one sentence justifies the observation, justifies not scanning immediately, and justifies the triggers for scanning. Candidates who say 'I'll do a CT' or 'he can go home' without it FAIL — regardless of which they chose.**

**SEVERITY IS GCS: 14–15 MILD · 9–13 MODERATE · 3–8 SEVERE (minimum 3, never 0). GCS ≤8 — protect the airway.** **RISK FACTORS (PREDICT/RCH) sort mild into 'home' or 'observe': loss of consciousness · post-traumatic seizure · vomiting (≥2) · severe headache · drowsiness or amnesia · focal deficit · signs of skull fracture · DANGEROUS MECHANISM (fall >1 m or 5 stairs, high-speed MVA, high-impact object, no bike helmet) · anticoagulation or a bleeding disorder · age under 1 · suspected NAI.** VERIFY

**★ THE FOUR-BOX HISTORY, and BOX 2 IS PASS/FAIL. 1 THE INCIDENT — when, direct blow or fall onto head or neck (give options), how hard, OTHER INJURIES, NECK PAIN. 2 AFTER: THE RED-FLAG BOX — LOC and how long · seizure features and how long · tongue bite, frothing, incontinence · VOMITING · confused or drowsy, better or worse · VISION, WEAKNESS, NUMBNESS, SPEECH, WALKING · AMNESIA · HEADACHE, worsening · FLUID OR BLOOD FROM NOSE OR EARS. 3 BEFORE: CAUSES OF THE SEIZURE — what was he doing, any warning, MISSED MEALS, FEVER OR RASH, MEDICATIONS. 4 BACKGROUND — blood thinners, previous seizures, development, home, school, family history, immunisations.**

**★ WHY THE LECTURE FAILS CANDIDATES HERE: two red flags asked and then a leap to management · only seizure questions, with no vomiting, headache, deficit, amnesia or neck · calling it moderate or severe with a GCS of 15 · FORGETTING THAT A HEAD INJURY CAN BE THE RESULT OF A SEIZURE OR COLLAPSE, so the 'before' box is skipped · announcing 'I'll do a CT' with no reasoning about severity.**

**EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS, THE CATEGORY, AND WHAT YOU EXCLUDED — three moves**: **'Liam has had a seizure caused by his head injury — a burst of abnormal electrical activity that a knock can set off. The jerking of all four limbs, the eyes rolling and the drowsiness afterwards tell me it was a seizure. We grade head injuries by how awake a child is; he's fully alert, so this is MILD — but because he was knocked out and had a fit, we count those as RISK FACTORS. I've also checked for other reasons a child might fit: his sugar is normal, no fever, no medicines, no previous seizures, and his examination is normal.'**

**★ ANSWER 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?' HONESTLY — without promising**: **'I can't promise that yet — that's exactly why we watch him. But everything I can see right now is reassuring.'** **'His brain isn't bleeding' before the four hours are up is inappropriate reassurance.** **And 'is it epilepsy?': 'no — this was a one-off fit triggered by the knock. A small number of children have another fit in the first week, which is one more reason we keep an eye on him.'** VERIFY

**★ THE PLAN IS OBSERVATION WITH STATED TRIGGERS, NOT A YES/NO ON CT. OBSERVE 4 HOURS with neuro observations — RCH: HALF-HOURLY FOR 2 HOURS, THEN HOURLY.** VERIFY **'We don't scan every child, because a CT is RADIATION TO A GROWING BRAIN and most children with a mild injury don't need one. We WILL scan if he becomes DROWSY or hard to wake, VOMITS REPEATEDLY, or his HEADACHE GETS WORSE.'** **Plus senior review and a discussion with WCH paediatric neurosurgery. CT is the acute imaging — NOT MRI.**

**DRUGS: paracetamol 15 mg/kg oral (max 1 g); ibuprofen 10 mg/kg if no contraindication; ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg oral (max 8 mg) if vomiting; SEIZURE >5 MINUTES = TREAT — midazolam 0.15 mg/kg IM/IN/buccal (max 10 mg); ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV if meningitis is suspected.** VERIFY **Cervical collar until cleared. Bloods only if indicated — BSL, UEC if vomiting, coagulation if a bleeding history. ECG if a collapse could have PRECEDED the injury. AVOID sedation that masks the GCS.**

**DISCHARGE after 4 hours if GCS 15, no vomiting, headache settling, normal examination, a RESPONSIBLE ADULT overnight, and the family can return. WRITTEN head-injury advice — return immediately for repeated vomiting, worsening headache, drowsiness or difficulty waking, confusion, seizure, weakness, unequal pupils, fluid from nose or ears. Concussion: rest 24–48 h, graded return to school then sport; NO CONTACT SPORT until symptom-free and cleared. GP in 2–3 days.** VERIFY SA: **WCH paediatric neurosurgery**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for retrieval and neurosurgical advice; **RFDS**; **PATS** if transferred; **TIS National 131 450**; **suspected NAI → mandatory notification to CARL 13 14 78** under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 — **you notify on reasonable suspicion, you do not investigate**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer or local ACCHS early.
plan: **★ TO THE EXAMINER BEFORE YOU SIT**: **'may I confirm the primary survey is complete, and have his vital signs, GCS — and a BEDSIDE BLOOD GLUCOSE?'** *BSL 5.6.* **The glucose is given only if asked.**

**WIPE, and reassure her the child is safe**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the doctors in the emergency department. You must be Liam's mum — is it all right if I call you Lily? Liam is safe with our nurses. Can you tell me what happened?'** *'He went down head-first… then he started shaking all over. I thought he was dying.'*

**ADDRESS THE FEAR BEFORE THE QUESTIONS**: **'that sounds absolutely terrifying, and you did the right thing calling the ambulance. I'm going to ask a series of questions to work out how serious this head injury is, because that's what decides what we do next. Then I'll explain everything.'**

**BOX 1 — THE INCIDENT, giving options**: **'when did this happen? Was it a DIRECT BLOW to the head, or did he FALL onto his head or neck? How hard — was he running at full pace? Apart from his head, any other injuries or pain anywhere? ANY NECK PAIN?'**
**★ BOX 2 — THE RED-FLAG BOX, and you cannot leave it until it is finished. Signpost it**: **'that tells me about the injury itself; now I need to ask what happened afterwards.'**

**LOC and SEIZURE as TWO EVENTS**: **'when he hit his head, did he lose consciousness COMPLETELY, or was he awake and aware? How long?'** Then **'AND SEPARATELY, the shaking — were his arms and legs jerking, all four limbs or one side? Eyes rolling up? Tongue bite? Frothing? Did he wet himself? How long did the shaking last?'**

**The rest of the box**: **'any vomiting since — how many times? Was he confused or drowsy when he woke — BETTER NOW, OR WORSE? Any problems with vision, weakness, numbness, speech or walking? Does he REMEMBER what happened? Is he complaining of headache — getting worse? Any FLUID OR BLOOD FROM HIS NOSE OR EARS?'**

**★ BOX 3 — BEFORE: THE CAUSES OF THE SEIZURE. Signpost it**: **'I've asked about after; now a few things about before.'** **'What was he doing just before? Did he complain of anything — sick, dizzy, funny — before the tackle? HAD HE MISSED ANY MEALS? Any FEVER OR RASH in the last few days? Is he on any MEDICATIONS, or could he have taken anything?'**
**When the skipped breakfast comes — answer her guilt and link it to the glucose**: **'it can matter, because a low sugar can cause a fit — that's why I checked it, and it's normal.'**

**BOX 4 — BACKGROUND**: **'any BLOOD THINNERS, or does he bruise or bleed easily? Ever had a seizure before? Any concerns about his development? How are things at home — who lives there, any stress? I'd add PUPILS AND FUNDOSCOPY, and check BEHIND THE EARS, AROUND THE EYES and the EARDRUMS for signs of a skull-base fracture.'**

**NAME IT**: **'Liam has had a seizure caused by his head injury — a burst of abnormal electrical activity set off by the knock. The jerking of all four limbs, the eyes rolling and the drowsiness afterwards tell me it was a seizure.'**

**★ SHE ASKS 'IS HIS BRAIN BLEEDING?' — then THE SEVERITY SENTENCE**: **'I can't promise it isn't yet — and that's exactly why he's staying with us. But everything I can see is reassuring. He's fully alert, so this is a MILD head injury. Because he was knocked out and had a fit, we treat those as RISK FACTORS — so it's MILD WITH RISK FACTORS. That means we don't send him home yet.'**

**OBSERVE, and the nurses' checks**: **'he stays at least four hours, and the nurses check him regularly — how awake he is, his pupils, his strength — because we're watching for bleeding inside the head that can show up over the first few hours.'**

**★ SHE ASKS 'SHOULDN'T YOU JUST DO A SCAN?' — observation plus three triggers**: **'a CT is radiation to a growing brain, and most children with a mild injury don't need one. We WILL scan him if he becomes DROWSY or hard to wake, VOMITS REPEATEDLY, or his HEADACHE GETS WORSE. And I'll let the children's neurosurgeon at the Women's and Children's know about him.'** Then **paracetamol, and his neck protected until it's fully checked.**

**DISCHARGE CRITERIA AND SAFETY-NET — the plan never ends without them**: **if he stays well, home tonight with a WRITTEN SHEET of warning signs** — repeated vomiting, worsening headache, hard to wake, confusion, another fit, weakness, fluid from nose or ears — **'come straight back or call 000.'** **Someone with him overnight; GP in two to three days; NO FOOTBALL OR CONTACT SPORT until symptom-free and cleared.** Then a one-line summary and **'is there anything else you're worried about?'**

stem: GP clinic, metropolitan Adelaide, late afternoon. A 4-MONTH-OLD BOY brought by his mother JENNY for EXCESSIVE CRYING. NO physical examination is given; the role-player holds a doll, cradled as she would hold her baby.

History about five minutes, then diagnosis and management in about three. 8 minutes. VERSION B (online): the same stem with WRITTEN examination findings replacing the doll — multiple bruises OF DIFFERING AGES on the cheeks, buttocks and inner thighs, child otherwise alert with normal vitals.
tasks: Take a history from the mother (5 minutes)
Explain your diagnosis to the mother
Explain your management plan
findings: ★ THE CUE — nobody will point it out

The role-player CRADLES A DOLL with THREE VISIBLE BRUISES ON THE FACE AND CHEEK — the same doll used in the neonatal examination station. NO physical examination is given. IF YOU DO NOT LOOK AT THE DOLL, YOU WILL NOT FIND THE CASE. Note it silently in the first ten seconds; do not comment yet
Vitals on request
HR, RR, temperature and saturations ALL NORMAL; he is ALERT. Asking before you sit down is a scored item
The crying
About THREE WEEKS, worst in the evenings, sometimes hours. Rocking, feeding, driving him around — nothing works. 'I'M EXHAUSTED, I've hardly slept'
The medical screen — all negative

No fever, cold, ear pulling, nappy pain, urine smell or rash. Posits a little after feeds, NOTHING GREEN, no blood, no groin or scrotal lump, no hair tourniquet, no red eye. Formula every three hours, nappies fine. Weighed 'a while ago'; thinks immunisations are DUE
★ THE ACCIDENTAL DOOR — offered ONLY when asked about falls
'MY PARTNER DROPPED HIM the other day while changing his nappy.' Off the change table onto FLOORBOARDS. He screamed, seemed alright after. 'I WASN'T IN THE ROOM — my partner told me'
★ THE PIVOT — offered ONLY if you ask whether it has happened before
'A couple of times. THREE OR FOUR, MAYBE. He's not very careful.' Said CASUALLY, as if it were clumsiness. DO NOT REACT VISIBLY — keep your voice level and keep going
★ THE HOUSEHOLD — each offered only on a direct question

Lives with her partner. HE IS NOT THE BIOLOGICAL FATHER — 'we split before the baby came' — AND 'HE'S BEEN ASKING ABOUT THAT, ACTUALLY.' Arguing. HE GETS FRUSTRATED — 'he says he can't think with the noise'
The stressors
Both students, MONEY VERY TIGHT. Her own mood: 'FLAT, I CRY A LOT.' HE DRINKS MORE THAN HE USED TO. Safe at home: 'No, I'm fine' — SAID QUICKLY, and moved past
The third-person question
'NO. NEVER.' Expect the denial — the mark is for asking it SAFELY, in the third person
★ HER REACTION WHEN ABUSE IS RAISED

DEFENSIVE — 'WE'D NEVER DO THAT, WE'RE NOT THOSE KIND OF PEOPLE' — PULLS THE DOLL CLOSER, looks away, goes quiet. She SOFTENS and becomes tearful and cooperative ONLY with non-accusatory, safety-focused language. If you ask 'DID YOUR PARTNER HIT HIM?' she SHUTS DOWN COMPLETELY and answers in one word
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA — the marked moment
She is frightened of LOSING THE BABY and won't raise it until child protection is mentioned. Then: 'WILL THEY TAKE MY BABY AWAY?' — answer it BEFORE she has to ask
If you never mention the head injury
She asks at the end: 'SO WE JUST GO HOME?' — the second-commonest reason candidates fail this station
VERSION B — the online recall

Same stem, but WRITTEN findings replace the doll: MULTIPLE BRUISES OF DIFFERING AGES on the cheeks, BUTTOCKS AND INNER THIGHS; child alert, vitals normal. Occasionally an older walking child — the point is identical: bruises in sites unexpected for that developmental stage
Other practice cards

18 months, 'fell off the couch', bruises to BOTH EARS and buttocks, presents THREE DAYS later → EARS ARE NEVER ACCIDENTAL · 9 months, arm swelling, 'rolled off the bed', X-ray: acute SPIRAL HUMERAL fracture plus TWO HEALING RIB fractures → skeletal survey, notify · 2-year-old, BOTH FEET SYMMETRICALLY RED TO THE ANKLES → IMMERSION BURN · 3 months, VOMITING AND FLOPPY after 'a fall from the change table' → ABUSIVE HEAD TRAUMA, emergency transfer · 3-year-old, bruised shins and forehead, active, consistent story → NOTHING — do not notify reflexively

dx: **NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY — bruising in a NON-MOBILE 4-month-old, presenting as excessive crying, in a household with multiple stressors. In a baby who cannot roll, cruise or crawl, ANY BRUISE IS ABNORMAL. 'THOSE WHO DON'T CRUISE RARELY BRUISE.'**

**★ WHAT THE EXAMINER IS ASSESSING, in five parts: do you NOTICE THE NON-VERBAL CUE without being told · do you STILL EXCLUDE THE MEDICAL DIFFERENTIALS — a separately scored task, and skipping it fails you EVEN IF YOU NAME THE ABUSE · can you raise a safeguarding concern WITHOUT ACCUSING, keeping the mother in the room and on side · do you know the NOTIFICATION IS MANDATORY, and can you explain what child protection actually does BEFORE she asks · and do you TREAT THE ACUTE INJURY FIRST.**

**THE ORDER IS NOT NEGOTIABLE: ACUTE INJURY → SUSPICION → NOTIFICATION → PAEDIATRIC ED → DOCUMENTATION.** **One-line strategy: 'rule out the medical causes, then raise SAFETY — not blame — treat the head first, notify because I must.'**

**★ ASK IN THIS ORDER — the guarded-psychiatry principle: bank the easy information BEFORE the atmosphere changes. The crying and how she's coping → INFECTION screen → GI AND SURGICAL screen → feeding and growth (neglect) → the ACCIDENTAL question → RECURRENCE → household and BIOLOGICAL FATHER → the THIRD-PERSON QUESTION → finances, mood, substances, family-violence screen.** **Going to abuse at 60 seconds is a named error.**

**THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION, VERBATIM**: **'looking after a baby who cries for hours is really hard, and some parents get so frustrated that they shake or smack the baby. Has that ever happened with you or your partner?'** **Never 'did your partner hit him?' — you are NOT the investigator.**

**TEN-4-FACESp (validated, under 4 years): TORSO, EAR, NECK bruising in a child 4 or under · ANY bruise in an infant under 4.99 months · FRENULUM, ANGLE OF JAW, fleshy CHEEK, EYELID, SUBCONJUNCTIVA · any PATTERNED bruise.** **The developmental test: COULD THIS CHILD HAVE CAUSED THIS INJURY?** **Red flags beyond bruising: symmetrical burns, fractures of different ages, a torn frenulum, delayed presentation, a story that changes or does not fit development.**

**★ RAISING IT — SIX STEPS. 1 EXCLUDE OUT LOUD so she hears you were thorough ('an infection like an ear or urine infection, a problem in the tummy like reflux or a blockage — I haven't found anything to suggest those'). 2 RAISE SAFETY, no label yet ('what I am concerned about is his SAFETY… bruises like that on the face of a baby who isn't yet rolling are unusual… I'm worried about the possibility of a non-accidental injury'). 3 THE RESCUE LINE. 4 THE NOTIFICATION, framed as LAW. 5 ANSWER THE REMOVAL QUESTION BEFORE SHE ASKS. 6 THE ACUTE INJURY — which is why you go today.**

**THE THREE SENTENCES TO OWN: 'I WOULD NEVER ACCUSE YOU or your partner of doing such a thing. My job is simply to make sure your son is safe.' · 'I am LEGALLY REQUIRED to let the child protection service know — every doctor in South Australia has to do this; it isn't a choice about you, and it isn't a punishment.' · 'That DOESN'T MEAN anyone is taking your baby away. What they do is a FULL ASSESSMENT — most of the time children stay with their family and services are put in place.'** **Say 'safe' or 'safety' AT LEAST FOUR TIMES. And never GUARANTEE the outcome: 'I can't promise you what they'll decide.'**

**★ THE ACUTE INJURY — the second-commonest reason candidates fail: 'because he has bruises on his face and he's been crying, I'm worried about the possibility of an INJURY OR BLEEDING INSIDE HIS HEAD. That has to be checked TODAY, so I'm sending you both to the children's emergency department now.'** **Do NOT send home to await CPS. ED work-up: full examination and body map, SKELETAL SURVEY, CT/MRI head, FUNDOSCOPY, FBC and COAGULATION SCREEN, bone profile.** VERIFY **The coagulation screen is part of the same work-up — never an ALTERNATIVE to notification: 'a normal screen wouldn't remove my concern, and an abnormal one wouldn't explain the site of these bruises.'**

**THE MOTHER MAY BE A VICTIM TOO — screen her mood and her safety, and support her: 'if you ever can't cope, put him down somewhere safe like his cot, walk out of the room, and ring someone.' Ask about SIBLINGS and name them in the notification. DOCUMENT her account VERBATIM with a body map. AVOID: accusing or interrogating · promising confidentiality or no removal · photographing injuries outside local policy · delaying urgent care for a CPS response · confronting the partner, or asking her to.** **If the partner is in the room: 'would it be alright if I speak with Jenny on her own for a few minutes? I do that with every parent.'** SA: **Child Abuse Report Line 13 14 78, 24 hours** — mandatory for medical practitioners; **suspicion on reasonable grounds is enough; you do not need proof, and you are protected if the assessment finds nothing**; **an unexplained injury in an infant under 12 months — including a bruise in a non-mobile baby — is a SERIOUS CONCERN that must be PHONED, not submitted via e-CARL** VERIFY; **CaFHS 1300 733 606**; **Parent Helpline 1300 364 100**; **1800RESPECT 1800 737 732**.
plan: **LOOK AT THE ROLE-PLAYER AND WHAT SHE IS HOLDING — in the first ten seconds, every station.** The doll has three facial bruises. **Note it silently; say nothing yet.**
**BEFORE YOU SIT DOWN**: **'could I have his observations, please?'** *All normal; alert.* **You are confirming the baby is stable before spending five minutes talking.**

**A DELIBERATELY WARM OPENING**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___. You must be Jenny — and this is your little one. I can see he's been having a hard time. Constant crying is exhausting and it can be really overwhelming. Is it alright if I ask some questions so I can work out why he's crying, and then we'll make a plan together?'**

**THE CRYING, AND HOW SHE IS COPING — a question that earns marks twice**: **'when did it start? Constant or in episodes? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse? What have you been doing to settle him — AND HOW ARE YOU COPING WITH IT?'** *Three weeks, evenings, hours; exhausted.*
**INFECTION SCREEN**: **'any fever? Runny nose or cough? Pulling at his ears? Does he cry when you change his nappy — any smell to his urine? Any rash? Feeding normally? More sleepy than usual?'**

**GI AND SURGICAL SCREEN**: **'any vomiting — any GREEN in it? Does he arch his back with feeds? Any blood or redcurrant-jelly in his stools? Constipated? Any lump in the groin or scrotum? Any HAIR wrapped round a finger or toe? A red, watery eye?'**

**FEEDING AND GROWTH — the neglect screen**: **'breast or formula? How much, how often? Plenty of wet nappies? Has he been weighed — is he gaining as expected?'** *Formula three-hourly; weighed a while ago.*

**★ OPEN THE INJURY DOOR — START WITH ACCIDENTAL**: **'has he had any falls, knocks or head injuries lately?'** *'My partner dropped him changing his nappy.'* → **'that must have been frightening. Tell me exactly what happened — how far did he fall, what did he land on, did he cry straight away, was he floppy afterwards, any vomiting or drowsiness?'** **That last part is the head-injury symptom screen.**
**★ THE PIVOT — keep your voice level**: **'has anything like that happened before?'** *'A couple of times. Three or four, maybe.'* **Do not react visibly. Keep going.**

**HOUSEHOLD, asked neutrally, as routine**: **'can I ask who lives at home with you? … Is he your son's BIOLOGICAL FATHER? … How are things between you two at the moment? How is he coping with the crying?'** *Not the father; arguing; frustrated.*

**★ THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION, VERBATIM**: **'Jenny, looking after a baby who cries for hours is really hard, and some parents get so frustrated that they shake or smack the baby. Has that ever happened with you or your partner?'** *'No. Never.'* **The mark is for asking it safely.**

**FAMILY CONTEXT AND SAFETY — all of them**: **'how are things financially? How has your own mood been? Does anyone at home use alcohol or other drugs? Who supports you? And — DO YOU EVER FEEL UNSAFE AT HOME?'** *Students, tight; flat and tearful; he drinks more; 'no, I'm fine' — said quickly.*

**★ STEP 1 — EXCLUDE OUT LOUD**: **'Jenny, let me tell you what I've been thinking. I was looking for causes of the crying — an infection like an ear or urine infection, a problem in the tummy such as reflux or a blockage — and I haven't found anything today to suggest those.'**

**STEP 2 — RAISE SAFETY, NO LABEL FIRST**: **'what I am concerned about is his SAFETY. You've told me about the falls, you've told me how hard things have been at home, and I can see the bruises on his cheek. Bruises like that in a baby who isn't yet rolling over are unusual, and I have to take them seriously. I'm worried about the possibility of a non-accidental injury — an injury that wasn't caused by an accident.'**

**STEP 3 — SHE PULLS THE DOLL CLOSER AND LOOKS AWAY. Slow down, lower your voice, DO NOT RETREAT FROM THE CONCERN**: **'Jenny, I would never accuse you or your partner of doing such a thing. I can see how overwhelming things have been for you. My job is simply to make sure your son is SAFE, and to make the safest decisions in his best interest. That's all this is.'**

**STEPS 4 AND 5 — THE LAW, THEN THE REMOVAL QUESTION BEFORE SHE ASKS IT**: **'because of that concern, I am LEGALLY REQUIRED to let the child protection service know. Every doctor has to do this — it isn't a choice I make about you, and it isn't a punishment. And it doesn't mean anyone is taking your baby away. What they do is a full assessment — they'll talk with you, see him, speak with your family and look at what supports you need.'** **Then honestly: 'I can't promise you what they'll decide, but removal isn't what a notification automatically means.'**

**★ STEP 6 — THE ACUTE INJURY, WHICH IS WHY YOU GO TODAY**: **'there's one more thing that's just as important. Because he has bruises on his face and he's been crying, I'm worried about the possibility of an injury or bleeding inside his head. That has to be checked today — I'm sending you both to the children's emergency department now. They'll examine him and may do a scan, and the child protection team can talk with you there. I'll ring ahead.'**

**SUPPORT HER, DOCUMENT, SUMMARISE**: **'and I haven't forgotten you — what you're doing is exhausting, and it's normal to feel frustrated. If you ever can't cope, PUT HIM DOWN SOMEWHERE SAFE, WALK OUT OF THE ROOM AND RING SOMEONE.'** Then the **Parent Helpline and CaFHS**, a review of her own mood, **'I'll write down what you've told me in your own words and record where the bruises are,'** and a one-line summary with **'do you have any questions?'**

stem: General practice, Wallaroo. HARRY, 7 DAYS OLD (also recalled at three weeks), brought by his mother PRIYA, who is concerned about YELLOW DISCOLOURATION OF HIS SKIN. A bilirubin result is provided: TOTAL BILIRUBIN 200, CONJUGATED 60. NO physical examination will be given. History six minutes, then diagnosis, differentials and management. 8 minutes.

VERSION B: emergency department, 7 days, YELLOW, FEBRILE AND DROWSY, and the mother's late-pregnancy swab was POSITIVE FOR 'THE STREP BUG'. VERSION C: three weeks old, STILL YELLOW BUT WELL, breastfed and thriving, with normal urine and stools.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother (6 minutes)
Explain the most likely diagnosis and the differential diagnoses to the mother
Outline your management
findings: ★ THE RESULT IN THE STEM — calculate it OUT LOUD

TOTAL BILIRUBIN 200 µmol/L, CONJUGATED 60 µmol/L. 60 of 200 = 30% CONJUGATED. Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia is >10% (RCH) to >20% (RACGP) of total, or conjugated >25 µmol/L VERIFY — and it is ALWAYS pathological
Vitals on request — ask FIRST
Temperature 36.8, HR 140, RR 40, ALERT. Sepsis is on every jaundice list, and an unwell neonate is sepsis first
The jaundice
NOT on day one — DAY THREE. Face first, now CHEST, TUMMY AND THIGHS, NOT the palms. CONSTANT, WORSE EVERY DAY
★ THE FIVE-STAR ANSWER — offered ONLY if you ask about urine or stools

'Yes — actually yes. The WEE'S A DARK YELLOW-BROWN in the nappy, and the POOS WENT PALE — LIKE PUTTY — over the last three or four days.' If never asked, she volunteers at the end: 'Is it normal that his poos have gone so pale?' — by which point the mark is gone
★ THE WEIGHT
Born 3.4 kg; the nurse weighed him yesterday — 3.1 kg — 'SHE SAID HE SHOULD BE CLIMBING BACK BY NOW.' Up to 10% loss in week one is normal, regained by day 10–14
Pregnancy and birth — all normal

No infections. GBS NEGATIVE, no antibiotics. No diabetes or high BP. Vitamins only. Scans normal. A POSITIVE, NO ANTIBODIES. 39 weeks, normal vaginal delivery, four hours, no instruments, NO BRUISING, cried straight away. HEEL-PRICK day 3, normal. VITAMIN K given
Feeding and the well-baby screen

Breastfed, about EIGHT FEEDS a day, 15 minutes each side, no pain, seems satisfied. No fever, no rash, ALERT, 6–7 wet nappies. No dry skin or hoarse cry. No family thyroid disease, prolonged jaundice or blood disorder
Her questions
FRIGHTENED, TEARFUL: 'IS IT MY FAULT? Did I do something in pregnancy?' · 'IS IT BECAUSE OF MY MILK?' · 'WILL HE NEED SURGERY?' when biliary atresia is mentioned
★ IF YOU SAY PHYSIOLOGICAL OR BREAST-MILK JAUNDICE
'So I don't need to do anything? BUT HE'S GETTING WORSE.' Either label with a 30% conjugated fraction and pale stools is an AUTO-FAIL
★ VERSION B — the ED neonate

Temperature 38.4, HR 180, RR 60, CAPILLARY REFILL 4 s, DROWSY. Hot since last night, so sleepy, hardly fed, TWO WET NAPPIES. Mother's swab was POSITIVE 'for the strep bug' — antibiotics given but the birth was quick; waters broke six hours before. NEONATAL SEPSIS (late-onset GBS) — say the word, STOP THE HISTORY, and escalate
★ VERSION C — three weeks, still yellow, well

'YOU SAID IT WOULD GO AWAY by now. IS IT MY MILK? SHOULD I STOP BREASTFEEDING?' Normal urine and stool colour, eight feeds, gaining weight, heel-prick normal. Card: active, well hydrated, tracking the 50th centile, MILD JAUNDICE OF FACE AND SCLERAE ONLY, no hepatosplenomegaly, urine dipstick normal. BREAST-MILK JAUNDICE — NOT physiological, because it is past 14 days
Other practice cards

Yellow at 18 HOURS, mother O NEGATIVE, pale, splenomegaly → ABO/Rh HAEMOLYTIC DISEASE, DAT, nomogram, IVIG/exchange · day 4, 12% WEIGHT LOSS, three wet nappies, sore nipples → DEHYDRATION/insufficient feeding, lactation support, NOT 'stop breastfeeding' · 5 weeks, sleepy, constipated, HOARSE CRY, 'they never called' about the heel-prick → CONGENITAL HYPOTHYROIDISM · 10 days, vomiting, lethargy, CATARACTS, E. coli sepsis → GALACTOSAEMIA, stop lactose · forceps, BOGGY SCALP SWELLING not crossing sutures → CEPHALHAEMATOMA

dx: **CONJUGATED HYPERBILIRUBINAEMIA — 30% of the total — BILIARY ATRESIA UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE; neonatal hepatitis and choledochal cyst are the alternatives. Three versions of one station: A biliary atresia, B late-onset GBS SEPSIS, C BREAST-MILK JAUNDICE.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING QUESTION — the examiner's own words: ASK IT AND PASS, FORGET IT AND FAIL: 'have you noticed his wee being dark, or his poos being pale, white or chalky?'** **Dark urine plus pale stools = CONJUGATED, OBSTRUCTIVE jaundice. Ask it SECOND, right after onset, so it is never forgotten — and ask again under 'bowel motions' if you did forget. When she answers, SAY IT BACK: 'that's the most important thing you've told me — it tells me the bile isn't getting through.'**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ACT DIFFERS BY VERSION. A: name conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, most likely biliary atresia, give THREE REASONS, and REFER TODAY. C: call it BREAST-MILK jaundice, NOT physiological, and say 'there is nothing wrong with your milk — keep breastfeeding'. B: say the word SEPSIS and STOP the consultation to escalate.**

**DEFINITIONS. PHYSIOLOGICAL: unconjugated, onset day 2–3, peak day 3–5 term (5–7 preterm), GONE BY 14 DAYS TERM / 21 PRETERM. PROLONGED: beyond those limits. JAUNDICE IN THE FIRST 24 HOURS IS ALWAYS PATHOLOGICAL — haemolysis or sepsis. CONJUGATED jaundice is ALWAYS pathological.**

**THE HISTORY — BINDSMA with ISOIMMUNISATION as the I. Explore the jaundice (onset, day-one, ZONES cephalocaudally, constant, worsening) → THE PATTERN QUESTION → PREGNANCY (infections, GBS swab and intrapartum antibiotics, diabetes, BP, medicines, antenatal bloods) → DELIVERY (term, mode, long or instrumental, bruising or a scalp lump) → AFTER (HEEL-PRICK, resuscitation, VITAMIN K) → BLOOD GROUP (O mother with A or B baby; Rh-negative with antibodies) → FEEDING in detail (type, frequency, duration, problems, supply) → WEIGHT → sepsis and well-baby → thyroid and family.** **A one-line feeding history and a one-line birth history are named traps.**

**EXPLAIN THE RESULT, THEN PLAIN WORDS**: **'bilirubin is the yellow pigment made when old red blood cells break down. The liver processes it and sends it out in the bile into the bowel. Harry's total is 200, and 60 of that — NEARLY A THIRD — is the processed type. That means the bile isn't draining out of the liver properly, and the pale poos and dark wee say the same thing.'**

**THE DIAGNOSIS WITH THREE REASONS**: **'the condition I'm most concerned about is BILIARY ATRESIA — a blockage of the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the bowel. Three things point to it: the PALE POOS AND DARK WEE, the WEIGHT NOT CLIMBING, and the HIGH PROCESSED FRACTION. It could instead be inflammation of the liver itself, or a cyst on the bile duct. Nothing you did caused this.'**

**THE DIFFERENTIAL IN ORDER — CONJUGATED FIRST, THEN UNCONJUGATED, PHYSIOLOGICAL LAST. Conjugated: biliary atresia · neonatal hepatitis (TORCH, idiopathic) · choledochal cyst · galactosaemia · alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency · CF · sepsis. Unconjugated: sepsis · hypothyroidism · haemolysis (ABO/Rh, G6PD, spherocytosis) · cephalhaematoma or bruising · dehydration from insufficient feeding · breast-milk jaundice · PHYSIOLOGICAL, LAST.** CORRECTION — **an O mother cannot have an AB baby.** CORRECTION — **the source transcribes 'hyperthyroidism'; it is HYPOthyroidism that causes prolonged jaundice.**

**★ MANAGEMENT: TREAT THE BILIRUBIN, AND TREAT THE CAUSE — and REFER TODAY WITH THE KASAI CLOCK IN MIND. KASAI HEPATOPORTOENTEROSTOMY IDEALLY BEFORE 60 DAYS; success falls sharply after 100.** VERIFY **Confirm a SPLIT SERUM bilirubin — TRANSCUTANEOUS bilirubin is a screening tool only for well babies >35 weeks and DOES NOT MEASURE THE CONJUGATED FRACTION. Check vitamin K was given — cholestasis brings coagulopathy. Tertiary work-up: LFT with GGT, coagulation, FBC and film, group and DAT, TFT, urine MCS and reducing substances, TORCH, alpha-1 antitrypsin, FASTING ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND (absent or atrophic gallbladder, triangular cord sign), HIDA, biopsy, intra-operative cholangiogram. Fat-soluble vitamins and MCT feeds while cholestatic. PHOTOTHERAPY IS NOT FOR CONJUGATED JAUNDICE — bronze baby, and it treats nothing.**

**VERSION B — THE UNWELL NEONATE. CORRECTION — the source lists a 'tachycardic, HYPERtensive, febrile' child. Sepsis produces tachycardia, fever or HYPOthermia, poor perfusion and HYPOtension — a LATE, ominous sign, not a marker of stability. Full septic screen INCLUDING A LUMBAR PUNCTURE (meningitis is common in late-onset GBS), IV BENZYLPENICILLIN + GENTAMICIN, adding CEFOTAXIME if meningitis is suspected, glucose, fluid bolus if shocked.** VERIFY **VERSION C — breast-milk jaundice is a DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION after a split SBR, TFT, urine and FBC/DAT; recheck in 1–2 weeks; expect resolution by 12 weeks.** VERIFY SA: **in Wallaroo the referral is a PHONE CALL to the WCH paediatric registrar today — not a fax, not a letter**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for an unwell baby; **PATS** for family travel; **TIS National 131 450**; **ACCHS and the Aboriginal Maternal and Infant Care program**; **AVOID sunlight 'therapy', water or glucose top-ups, and 'wait a week to see' with pale stools.**
plan: **★ VITALS BEFORE ANYTHING**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___. You must be Priya, and this is Harry. Before we start, may I have his observations — temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, and is he alert?'** *36.8, 140, 40, alert.* **An unwell neonate is sepsis first — this is how you'd catch Version B.**

**Open and address the fear**: **'tell me what's been worrying you.'** *Tearful: yellow since day three, spreading, 'I'm scared it's his liver.'* → **'you've done exactly the right thing. A yellow baby is something we look into carefully, and I'll explain the blood test.'** Then signpost: **the colour, then the pregnancy and birth, his feeding and weight, and a few questions to rule out infection.**

**EXPLORE THE JAUNDICE**: **'when did you first notice it — WAS IT THERE ON HIS FIRST DAY?'** *Day three.* **'Which parts are yellow now — face, chest, tummy, arms, legs, palms?'** *Face, chest, tummy, thighs.* **'Constant, or coming and going? Getting worse?'** *Constant, worse daily.*

**★ THE PATTERN QUESTION — SECOND, not last**: **'have you noticed his wee being dark, or his poos being pale, white or chalky?'** *Dark yellow-brown wee; pale, putty-coloured poos for three or four days.* **SAY IT BACK: 'that's the most important thing you've told me — it tells me the bile isn't getting through. I'll come back to it.'**

**PREGNANCY**: **'any infections or fevers in the pregnancy? Did you have the group B strep swab — and antibiotics in labour? Any high blood sugar or blood pressure? Any medicines, alcohol or drugs? Were your antenatal tests and scans normal?'**

**ISOIMMUNISATION**: **'do you know your blood group, and whether you had any antibodies? Are you Rh negative — did you have the anti-D injection? Do you know Harry's group?'** *A positive, no antibodies.*

**DELIVERY AND AFTER**: **'born at term — how many weeks? Vaginal or caesarean? A long labour, forceps or vacuum? Any bruising or a lump on his head? Did he need help to breathe? Was the HEEL-PRICK test done and normal? Was VITAMIN K given?'**

**★ FEEDING — six questions, not one**: **'breast or formula? How many feeds in 24 hours? How long on each side? Any pain, attachment problems or cracked nipples? Do you feel you have enough milk — is he satisfied?'** Then **'what was his birth weight, and what is he now?'** *3.4 to 3.1 — the nurse said he should be climbing.*

**SEPSIS AND WELL-BABY**: **'any fever, or feeling hot or cold? Any rash? Alert and active, or drowsy and hard to wake? Fewer wet nappies? Any change in his bowel motions besides the colour?'** **The bowel-motions question is your last chance at the pale stools if you'd forgotten.**

**THYROID AND FAMILY**: **'any dry skin, a hoarse cry, constipation or unusual sleepiness? Thyroid problems in the family? Anyone jaundiced for weeks as a baby, or with a blood disorder like G6PD or spherocytosis?'** Then a short summary back.

**★ READ THE RESULT ALOUD, THEN THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS**: bilirubin, the yellow pigment from old red cells; the liver processes it and sends it into the bowel in bile; **'Harry's total is 200, and 60 of that — nearly a third — is the processed type. That means it isn't draining out of the liver, and the pale poos and dark wee say the same thing.'**

**★ NAME IT, WITH THREE REASONS**: **'the condition I'm most concerned about is biliary atresia — a blockage of the tubes that carry bile from the liver to the bowel. Three things point to it: the pale poos and dark wee, the weight not climbing, and the high processed fraction.'** Then **'it could instead be inflammation of the liver, or a cyst on the bile duct. NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS.'**

**THE FULL DIFFERENTIAL, IN ORDER**: infection, a rare sugar-processing problem, then the unprocessed causes — thyroid, blood-group mismatch, bruising, not enough milk. **'Ordinary newborn jaundice and breast-milk jaundice are common and harmless — but they don't cause pale poos or this pattern, so they're at the BOTTOM of the list.'**

**★ SHE ASKS 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' — and this is where the Kasai clock goes**: **'if it's biliary atresia, yes — the Kasai operation connects the bowel directly to the liver so bile can drain, and it works best BEFORE ABOUT TWO MONTHS OF AGE. That's why I'm ringing the Women's and Children's Hospital NOW so you go TODAY.'**

**TREAT THE BILIRUBIN AND TREAT THE CAUSE**: liver and clotting bloods, an ultrasound, a bile scan and possibly a small liver sample; **lights if the level is over the line for his age.** Then the line she needs: **'PLEASE KEEP BREASTFEEDING — there is nothing wrong with your milk.'**

**SAFETY-NET AND CLOSE**: **'come back or call 000 if he becomes DROWSY, feeds poorly, has a FEVER, or the yellow reaches his PALMS AND SOLES.'** Travel support arranged, written down, then **'to summarise: the blocked-drainage type; most worried about biliary atresia; Adelaide today for tests and possibly early surgery; keep breastfeeding. What questions do you have?'**

stem: General practice, regional South Australia. ETHAN, 12, brought in by his mother SHARON with LIMPING AND KNEE PAIN FOR TWO WEEKS, which started while he was playing BASKETBALL. Afebrile, NO TRAUMA RECALLED. He is a keen basketballer.
The examiner will give you physical examination findings ON REQUEST, and TWO X-RAYS — KNEE AND HIP. 8 minutes. The mother mentions 'the hip is a bit sore too' ONLY IF ASKED.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother and from Ethan (3 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain the X-rays, knee and hip, to the mother
Explain the diagnosis and your management plan to the mother
findings: ★ THE EXAMINATION — you get only what you name

Well, in pain when walking, no rash. BMI 30 — THE MARKED ITEM. Afebrile, vitals normal. ANTALGIC GAIT, LEFT FOOT OUT-TOED, reluctant to weight-bear. No swelling, NO tenderness at the knee or tibial tuberosity, KNEE RANGE AND STABILITY NORMAL. LEFT HIP: INTERNAL ROTATION, ABDUCTION AND FLEXION RESTRICTED AND PAINFUL; ON FLEXION THE HIP ROTATES EXTERNALLY. Left leg 1.5 cm SHORTER. Log roll positive. Abdomen and scrotum normal
★ THE TWO X-RAYS — and the knee film is a decoy

KNEE X-RAY NORMAL. HIP X-RAY (AP pelvis): a line along the superior femoral neck — KLEIN'S LINE — should intersect the femoral head; on the abnormal side the head lies BELOW it. The FROG-LEG LATERAL shows the slip earliest: the head has fallen POSTERIORLY off the neck
What Ethan says

'It just started hurting during a game. I DIDN'T FALL.' Mostly the knee — and ONLY IF ASKED about the hip, groin or thigh: 'THE HIP'S SORE TOO, now you ask.' Worse walking, getting worse. 'TODAY I CAN HARDLY PUT WEIGHT ON IT'
★ THREE THINGS NEVER VOLUNTEERED

The HIP PAIN (only if you ask hip, groin or thigh) · the FOOT POINTING OUT (only if you ask about the foot or leg) · a SORE HIP TWO MONTHS AGO THAT WENT AWAY (only if you ask about previous episodes) — that last one is the acute-on-chronic slip
The screen — all negative
No fever, well. No falls, home and school fine. Sleeps fine, 'EATING WELL — TOO WELL.' No other joints, rash or eye problems. No tummy pain. Ethan, embarrassed: no testicular pain
The growth history

Normal birth, vaccines done. 'He's ALWAYS BEEN BIG — he's PUT ON A LOT THIS YEAR AND SHOT UP.' No medical problems, no medications, no thyroid or kidney history, no family hip problems. Basketball THREE TIMES A WEEK
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA
FINALS IN THREE WEEKS. She is hoping for 'rest and physio.' If not asked what she's hoping for, she asks at about 6:30: 'CAN HE PLAY IN THE FINALS?'
★ THE TRAP SHE IS BRIEFED TO SPRING

If you offer CRUTCHES or 'rest and review', she ACCEPTS HAPPILY — THAT IS THE FAIL. When you say wheelchair and ambulance she pushes back ONCE: 'CAN'T WE JUST DRIVE HIM?' When you say 'operation': shocked, then tearful — 'TODAY? CAN'T HE JUST REST IT?'
If you use jargon
Klein's line or 'epiphysis' unexplained → she looks blank: 'What does that mean?'
★ VERSION B — Osgood–Schlatter, one finding changed

History identical. Examination: TENDER, SWOLLEN TIBIAL TUBEROSITY, pain on RESISTED KNEE EXTENSION; HIPS NORMAL; BMI 19. Both X-rays normal, or fragmentation of the tuberosity. Activity modification, ice, simple analgesia, quadriceps and hamstring stretches, reassurance that it settles with skeletal maturity — and it stays on the list ONLY until the hip has been examined
VARIANT — the unstable slip

'He hasn't been able to put ANY weight on it since yesterday.' UNSTABLE SLIP — AVN risk up to ~50%. He stays exactly where he is; ambulance and the orthopaedic registrar now; MedSTAR Kids if any delay; nil by mouth
Other practice cards

Temp 38.8, hip held FLEXED AND EXTERNALLY ROTATED, won't let you move it, CRP high → SEPTIC ARTHRITIS · six weeks of thigh pain WAKING HIM AT NIGHT, swelling above the knee, 3 kg weight loss → OSTEOSARCOMA, X-ray today · 9-year-old, SHORT FOR AGE, BOTH HIPS stiff, bilateral slips → ATYPICAL SCFE, endocrine screen · sudden severe GROIN AND THIGH pain in basketball, vomited, hips move fully, 'won't let me look down there' → TESTICULAR TORSION

dx: **SLIPPED CAPITAL FEMORAL EPIPHYSIS (SCFE/SUFE) of the LEFT hip. The femoral head (epiphysis) slips POSTERIORLY AND INFERIORLY off the femoral neck through a weakened growth plate — typically an OVERWEIGHT BOY aged 10–16 during the GROWTH SPURT. It presents as hip, thigh OR KNEE pain with a limp and out-toeing. STABLE = can walk (with or without crutches); UNSTABLE = cannot, with a much higher risk of AVASCULAR NECROSIS.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — REFUSING THE KNEE. The stem is built to anchor you on a basketball knee injury. The pass mark has THREE PARTS: in the HISTORY you ask about the hip, groin and thigh and about weight-bearing · in the EXAMINATION you request BMI, BOTH hips and their rotation, and the SCROTUM · and in MANAGEMENT the first two sentences are 'stop weight-bearing — a wheelchair now' and 'urgent referral to orthopaedics for surgery.'** **Candidates who explain the X-ray beautifully and then run out of time before the wheelchair FAIL.**

**WHY THE KNEE HURTS: REFERRED PAIN. The OBTURATOR and FEMORAL nerves supply both the hip capsule and the medial thigh and knee, so a hip problem presents as knee pain. That is why the knee X-ray in this station is normal, and why the hip must be examined.** **Say the pivot OUT LOUD when she mentions the hip: 'knee pain with hip pain at your age makes me think about the hip joint itself.'**

CORRECTION — **say the rotation the RIGHT WAY ROUND. The source lecture says hip movements are 'restricted EXCEPT for internal rotation'. In SCFE the head slips posteriorly and inferiorly, so the leg lies in EXTERNAL rotation — the movements LOST are INTERNAL ROTATION, ABDUCTION AND FLEXION, and attempting flexion forces the hip into OBLIGATORY EXTERNAL ROTATION (the DREHMANN SIGN). External rotation is preserved or increased.** **If challenged: 'the slip leaves the leg externally rotated, so internal rotation is what's lost; the classic sign is external rotation on flexion.'**

**THE X-RAY SCRIPT — KNEE FIRST, THEN THE HIP, NORMAL SIDE FIRST**: **'bone is white, soft tissue grey, air black. This is the knee — COMPLETELY NORMAL, so the knee isn't the problem. This is his hip — a ball-and-socket joint. On the RIGHT, the round head of the thigh bone sits neatly on top of its growth plate. On the LEFT, the head has SLIPPED OFF THE GROWTH PLATE — it's sitting lower and further back. That's what's causing the pain and the limp.'** **Never 'Klein's line' or 'epiphysiolysis' to the mother.**

**NAME IT IN PLAIN LANGUAGE, AND REMOVE THE BLAME**: **'this is called a slipped capital femoral epiphysis — a slipped hip growth plate. In growing boys, particularly around Ethan's size and during the growth spurt, the growth plate is weaker and the head can slip off it. IT'S NOT BROKEN, and BASKETBALL DIDN'T CAUSE IT — it just showed up during the game.'**

**★ THE TWO BULLET POINTS, VERBATIM, BEFORE ANY DETAIL**: **'two things straight away. FIRST, Ethan must not walk on that leg at all from now — I'm getting him a WHEELCHAIR, NOT CRUTCHES, and NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK until the surgeon has seen him. SECOND, I'm PHONING the children's orthopaedic team at the Women's and Children's now — this needs an OPERATION, SOON, to pin the head of the bone in place.'**

**WHY NOT CRUTCHES — the answer if challenged**: **'with crutches he'll still put some weight through it, and if this is an unstable slip that's the difference between a good hip and a dead femoral head. The safest thing is NO WEIGHT AT ALL.'** **And why the rush: 'every step risks the head slipping further and damaging its blood supply, which can permanently damage the joint — that's why it's a wheelchair and an AMBULANCE, not the car.'** **UNSTABLE: AVN risk up to ~50%.**

**AFTER THE TWO BULLETS: IN-SITU PINNING with a single cannulated screw across the growth plate; unstable slips may be gently positioned by the surgeon ONLY — never reduced or put in traction in general practice. THE OTHER HIP: BILATERAL IN ~20–25% — about ONE IN FIVE — and the second slip is often silent, so PROPHYLACTIC PINNING is considered, especially if young, an endocrine cause, or remote follow-up. Post-op: crutches ~6 weeks, physio, NO SPORT UNTIL CLEARED, serial X-rays to physeal closure; later, weight management.** VERIFY **Complications: AVN, chondrolysis, early osteoarthritis.**

**ATYPICAL PATIENT → ENDOCRINE SCREEN: age UNDER 10 or OVER 16, SHORT STATURE, underweight, or BILATERAL slips — TSH and free T4, renal function, and consider the GH axis (hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, renal osteodystrophy).** **When she asks about the finals: 'not until the surgeon clears him — walking on it now can damage the hip permanently.' Promising a return date is a named error.** SA: **SA Ambulance from Wallaroo/Kadina to WCH Emergency (~2 h) with the orthopaedic registrar expecting him — NOT PATS or the family car for an acute slip**; **MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33** for advice or retrieval if unstable or remote; **RFDS** fixed-wing from Yorke Peninsula; **WCH paediatric orthopaedics — SCFE admitted same day, theatre usually within 24 h** VERIFY; **Country Health Connect** for physio; **PATS** for outpatient reviews; ACCHS; **CARL 13 14 78** if NAI suspected.
plan: **WIPE — and address Ethan directly; he's 12**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___. Sharon, and you must be Ethan. I'll just clean my hands. Ethan, I hear your knee's been sore and you've been limping — tell me what's been happening.'** *'It just started hurting during a game. I didn't fall.'*

**Acknowledge and agenda**: **'two weeks of limping when you love basketball — that's frustrating, and I can see it's worrying you both. I'll ask some questions, examine you, and we'll look at the X-rays together. Anything you want to make sure we cover?'**

**★ THE MECHANISM — and when there isn't one, widen to the hip**: **'was there a specific moment — a twist, a landing, a fall — or did it just start hurting?'** *Just started hurting.* **Gradual, activity-related pain with no real injury in an overweight adolescent is SCFE until the hip is proven normal.**

**★ THE SITE QUESTION, AND THE PIVOT OUT LOUD**: **'where exactly — can you point? Is it in the knee only, or the THIGH, the GROIN or the HIP as well?'** *'The hip's sore too, now you ask.'* → **'that's important — knee pain with hip pain at your age makes me think about the hip joint itself.'** **The examiner needs to hear you pivot.**

**★ WEIGHT-BEARING — stable or unstable**: **'is it there all the time or with activity? Getting worse? CAN YOU PUT WEIGHT ON IT AND WALK? Has there been a time you couldn't walk on it at all?'** *Hardly weight-bearing today.* **That changes the urgency and the transport.**

**THE THREE HIDDEN ITEMS**: **'have you noticed his FOOT TURNING OUT, or that leg looking SHORTER? Any swelling, redness, clicking or locking? Any EARLIER EPISODES — a limp or hip ache that came and went?'** *Foot points out; a sore hip two months ago.* **That last one is acute-on-chronic.**

**THE DIFFERENTIAL SCREEN in one run**: **infection** — fever, unwell, recent cold or gastro · **trauma and NAI** — falls, who was there, home and school · **malignancy** — night pain, weight loss, tiredness, bruising, lumps · **rheumatological** — other joints, morning stiffness, rash, eyes · **abdomen and testes** — tummy pain, vomiting, **'Ethan — any pain or swelling in the testicles?'**

**BINDS, GROWTH AND WEIGHT**: pregnancy, birth, immunisations · **'tell me about his diet and weight — has he put on weight recently? Had his growth spurt? Growing like his classmates?'** · medications, **thyroid or kidney problems**, family hip problems, how much basketball.

**SUMMARISE AND TRANSITION**: **'so: two weeks of left knee and hip pain with a worsening limp and no injury, in a boy who has grown and gained weight this year; no fever, night pain or other joints. I'd like to examine him.'**

**★ THE EXAMINATION REQUEST — the examiner gives nothing you don't name**: **'general appearance — well, in pain, any rash? His HEIGHT, WEIGHT AND BMI, please. TEMPERATURE and vital signs. Can he stand and walk — ANTALGIC, OUT-TOED, Trendelenburg? Inspection of BOTH legs, and how the leg lies at rest. Palpation — warmth, tenderness, the TIBIAL TUBEROSITY, the knee joint lines.'**

**The hip, by name, and the end of every limp examination**: **'movement of BOTH hips, active and passive — specifically INTERNAL ROTATION, ABDUCTION AND FLEXION, and whether FLEXION FORCES THE HIP INTO EXTERNAL ROTATION; knee range and stability. TRUE LEG LENGTH. Log roll. The ABDOMEN, and inspection and palpation of the SCROTUM.'**

**PRESENT THE FINDINGS BACK BEFORE ASKING FOR THE FILMS**: **'BMI 30, afebrile, out-toed antalgic gait, knee normal, painful restricted internal rotation, abduction and flexion of the left hip with obligatory external rotation, and a shorter leg — THIS IS A HIP PROBLEM, NOT A KNEE PROBLEM. Could I see the X-rays?'**

**★ THE X-RAYS — KNEE FIRST, then the hip NORMAL SIDE FIRST**: three shades; **'the knee is completely normal, so the knee isn't the problem'**; the ball and socket; **'on the right the round head sits neatly on top of its growth plate — on the left it has slipped off.'**
**NAME IT AND REMOVE THE BLAME**: a slipped hip growth plate; weaker in growing boys around Ethan's size; **'it's not broken, and basketball didn't cause it.'**

**★ THE TWO BULLET POINTS — SAY THEM BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE**: **FIRST — no weight on that leg from now, a WHEELCHAIR NOT CRUTCHES, NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK. SECOND — I'm PHONING the children's orthopaedic team now; this needs an OPERATION, SOON.** **Steps 1 and 2 are the pass marks; everything after is extra.**

**She says 'today? Can't we just drive him down?' — push back, with the reason**: **'I know that's a shock. Every step on it risks the head slipping further and damaging its blood supply, which can permanently damage the joint — so he goes by AMBULANCE, with the orthopaedic team expecting him.'**

**The operation and the other hip**: **'a small operation — a screw across the growth plate to hold the head where it is. Because this happens on the other side in about ONE IN FIVE children, they may suggest pinning the other hip too.'** Then **pain relief now.**

**★ 'CAN HE PLAY IN THE FINALS?' — honest, no promise**: **'not until the surgeon clears him.'** Then **crutches for about six weeks after, physio, X-rays until the growth plates close, and later we'll work on his weight together.** Close with a written summary and **'any questions?'**
pefe: **Request BMI BY NAME — it is the marked examination item. Ask it SECOND, straight after general appearance.**
**TEMPERATURE** — the septic-hip screen in every limping child.
**GAIT: antalgic? OUT-TOED? Trendelenburg? Can he weight-bear at all?** Unable to weight-bear = UNSTABLE slip.

**BOTH HIPS, not just the painful one: INTERNAL ROTATION, ABDUCTION and FLEXION — LOST in SCFE — and OBLIGATORY EXTERNAL ROTATION ON FLEXION (Drehmann sign). External rotation is preserved or increased.**
