stem: VERSION A (master): general practice, Wallaroo. EMILY, 9, brought by her mother KAREN, with HEADACHES FOR SIX MONTHS. NO vitals on the card; growth chart available on request; the mother answers for Emily. History FOUR MINUTES ONLY, then examination findings from the examiner, then diagnosis, differentials and management. 8 minutes.

THE OTHER FOUR RECALLS: (B) 9 years, months of headache WITH WEIGHT LOSS, BLURRED VISION AND MORNING VOMITING. (C) 16 years, brought by her father, ON DOXYCYCLINE FOR ACNE, with blurred vision and buzzing, overweight, BP high, FUNDI NOT ON THE CARD. (D) 9 years, EPISODIC right-sided throbbing with nausea and flashing lights, mother has migraine. (E) 6 years, a few days of dull headache all over WITH FEVER AND A SORE THROAT.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother (4 minutes only)
Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differentials to the mother
Outline your management to the mother
findings: Vitals — request BEFORE you sit down
All within normal limits in Version A. Asking for BP, pulse, RR and temperature even in a SIX-MONTH history is a scored item — the Cushing response lives in the BP and pulse
★ VERSION A — THE PEFE

Alert, well, no rash, normal posture. Vitals normal. CRANIAL NERVES NORMAL, FUNDOSCOPY NORMAL, limbs normal. ENT, sinuses and teeth normal. Neck supple, no lymphadenopathy. Growth chart tracking the 50th centile
★ FUNDOSCOPY — ask for it BY NAME
'Cranial nerves normal' HAS BEEN GIVEN WHILE PAPILLOEDEMA WAS ON THE CARD. Fundoscopy is part of the optic nerve examination, but if you don't name it, you won't be told
The headache itself

Six months, RIGHT SIDE MOSTLY, SOMETIMES BOTH. 5–6/10. SOMETIMES THROBBING, SOMETIMES SQUEEZING. On and off, not worse, doesn't spread, Panadol does nothing. SHE STILL PLAYS THROUGH IT. Missing nearly a day of school a week. The recall DELIBERATELY MIXES site and quality — do not diagnose from 'right side, throbbing'
★ THE WEEKEND QUESTION
'Does she get them on weekends and in the holidays too?' → (pauses) 'NO. NOW THAT YOU SAY IT — IT'S ONLY EVER SCHOOL DAYS.' She hasn't noticed until asked
The eight red flags — all negative

No night waking, no morning headache or vomiting, not worse on coughing or sneezing, no blurred or double vision, no weakness, no numbness, no head injury. Eating well, weight fine, no lumps. Marks have slipped a little — 'she's been missing school'
The migraine five — all negative
No nausea, no light or noise sensitivity, no flashing lights or buzzing, no family migraine. Triggers: 'STRESS, I SUPPOSE'
★ THE REAL STORY — offered ONLY when you ask about school

(quieter) 'There's a GROUP OF GIRLS. It started about six months ago — leaving her out, saying things. SHE CRIES ABOUT IT. I told the teacher once; nothing changed.' She's SADDER, DREADS MONDAYS, sleeps okay, has never talked of hurting herself. Ask about home first and she says home is fine
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA — named in her opening

'Our NEIGHBOUR WAS JUST DIAGNOSED WITH A BRAIN TUMOUR and honestly, doctor, I can't sleep for worrying about it.' If you never come back to it: 'SO YOU DON'T THINK IT'S A TUMOUR?' at the end. If you reassure before asking the red flags: 'BUT HOW CAN YOU BE SURE?'
★ VERSION B — the brain tumour

Red flags POSITIVE: 'she has LOST SOME WEIGHT… her VISION ISN'T GOOD… she doesn't get the headache in the morning BUT SHE VOMITS IN THE MORNING.' PEFE: BP 150/90, PULSE 54 — a CUSHING RESPONSE — cranial nerves and limbs normal, PAPILLOEDEMA, weight down a centile
★ VERSION C — benign intracranial hypertension

16-year-old, brought by her father. 'DOXYCYCLINE for her acne, about four months.' Blurred vision, BUZZING IN THE EARS, nausea. Overweight, BMI 95th centile, BP 135/85. FUNDOSCOPY IS NOT ON THE CARD — ask for it: bilateral disc swelling
★ VERSION D — migraine

Right-sided throbbing; SHE FEELS SICK WITH IT; SEES FLASHING LIGHTS; 'I GET MIGRAINES'; 'STRESS SETS IT OFF.' Home and school fine. Examination normal. STRESS HERE IS A MIGRAINE TRIGGER — one diagnosis, never 'migraine and tension'
★ VERSION E — URTI

6-year-old, a few days, all over, dull, 5/10. 'She's been HOT. Sore throat, yes.' No earache, runny nose or rash; NECK MOVES FINE. PEFE: mildly dehydrated, TEMP 38.3, fundi normal, NO NECK STIFFNESS, enlarged RED TONSILS, red pharynx, NO EXUDATE, RED TYMPANIC MEMBRANES, cervical nodes. She asks for antibiotics
VERSION E-HARD — meningococcal
Fever 39.2, vomiting, DROWSY, dislikes the light, PURPURIC SPOTS on the legs, NECK STIFF. Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IM or IV NOW, MedSTAR, do NOT wait for a lumbar puncture

dx: **ONE STRUCTURE, FIVE RECALLS: A TENSION-TYPE HEADACHE · B BRAIN TUMOUR / space-occupying lesion with raised ICP · C BENIGN (IDIOPATHIC) INTRACRANIAL HYPERTENSION · D MIGRAINE · E UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION. THE STEM NEVER TELLS YOU WHICH ONE YOU'RE IN — THE PARENT'S ANSWERS DO.**

**★ THE UNFORGIVABLE DIFFERENTIAL IS A BRAIN TUMOUR. Every version is passed or failed on the same three things: ask the RED FLAGS OUT LOUD · request FUNDOSCOPY BY NAME · then commit to ONE diagnosis and tell the parent WHY IT IS NOT A TUMOUR.** **Candidates who decide 'tension' at the door miss the morning vomiting in Version B; candidates who decide 'tumour' at the door frighten the mother in Version A.**

**★ THE EIGHT RED FLAGS, as a fixed block, every version: NIGHT WAKING · EARLY-MORNING HEADACHE OR VOMITING · worse on COUGH, SNEEZE OR STRAIN · BLURRED OR DOUBLE VISION · WEAKNESS · NUMBNESS · a change in SCHOOL WORK, speech or walking · HEAD INJURY.** **Plus weight loss, appetite, tiredness, lumps. The examiner is listening for the WORDS, not the intent.**

**THE SPINE: vitals → concern → SICORA plus the paediatric second A (IMPACT at home and school) → RED FLAGS → MEDICATIONS (the BIH drugs) → THE MIGRAINE FIVE (nausea, photo/phonophobia, aura, family history, triggers) → home and school → infections, ENT, dental, neck, rash → vision and injury → well-child → BINDSMA → PEFE by system, fundoscopy by name → one diagnosis with reasons.**

**★ THE THREE SENTENCES THAT PASS EVERY VERSION: 'Most likely she has ___.' → 'My reasons are ___.' → 'I know you were worried about a brain tumour; I think that is unlikely because ___.'** **Candidates fail by HEDGING, by a diagnosis WITHOUT REASONS, or by never closing the tumour question.**

**VERSION A — TENSION-TYPE**: **'most likely Emily has a condition called tension-type headache — a stress-related headache from tightening of the muscles around the head and neck. My reasons: there's real stress at school with the bullying, the headaches only happen on SCHOOL DAYS, she still plays and eats through them, and her examination is completely normal. I don't think this is a tumour: no night headaches, no morning vomiting, no weight loss, no weakness or numbness, and the back of her eyes and her nerves are normal.'** **Never the word 'PSYCHOGENIC' to the parent.** **Depth rule: once bullying appears, go DEEP — what, since when, told the school, mood, sleep, AND SELF-HARM.**

**VERSION B — THE TUMOUR, broken gently**: **'headaches can have many causes. In Emily's case, I am concerned about the possibility of a GROWTH IN THE BRAIN.'** *(pause — let her react)* **Then the reasons: weight loss, vision, morning vomiting; BP HIGH and PULSE SLOW, which happens when pressure around the brain rises; and SWELLING AT THE BACK OF HER EYES.** **No tumour types.** CORRECTION — **the source says no indication for ED, just urgent MRI and neurosurgical referral. Give that — but a 9-year-old with BP 150/90, pulse 54 and papilloedema has a CUSHING RESPONSE. In Wallaroo there is no same-day MRI: 'I'd arrange urgent MRI and neurosurgical referral today, and because she has a Cushing response with papilloedema, in a rural setting I'd phone the on-call paediatrician at WCH now and transfer through MedSTAR.'**

**VERSION C — BIH**: the medication (doxycycline, minocycline, isotretinoin, the OCP, steroid withdrawal), blurred vision, pulsatile tinnitus, and weight. **But EXCLUDE A TUMOUR FIRST — urgent MRI ± MR venography, THEN LP with opening pressure; STOP THE DRUG; URGENT OPHTHALMOLOGY because untreated papilloedema CAN CAUSE PERMANENT VISUAL LOSS.** CORRECTION — **it is now termed IDIOPATHIC intracranial hypertension; use either, but never call it 'benign' without saying it can threaten sight.** **Acetazolamide is a specialist decision.** VERIFY

**VERSION D — MIGRAINE**: nausea, flashing lights, a throbbing pain she can't play through, and it runs in the family — **'stress here is a TRIGGER for her migraine, NOT a separate condition.'** **Ibuprofen 10 mg/kg at onset (or paracetamol 15 mg/kg), a dark quiet room, a trigger diary; nasal sumatriptan in adolescents per paediatric neurology.** VERIFY CORRECTION — **'dilation of the blood tubes' is the source's explanation and it passes; current understanding is NEUROVASCULAR (trigeminovascular activation; cortical spreading depression for aura). If pressed: 'a disorder of brain nerve signalling that changes blood flow — I keep it simple for parents.'** **VERSION E — URTI**: name the CLUSTER, most likely VIRAL (redness without pus, 38.3); **exclude meningitis FIRST** — neck soft, no rash, alert; **no antibiotics for a viral picture, and NEVER amoxicillin if EBV is possible**; strep swab only with exudate, high fever, no cough, tender nodes.

**IMAGING: NONE in A, D or E without red flags. MEDICATION-OVERUSE HEADACHE — analgesics on 15+ days a month for 3 months — so paracetamol only occasionally.** **Frontal sinusitis does not occur in young children — the frontal sinuses develop from about 7. Cluster headache is an adolescent diagnosis.** **Paracetamol 15 mg/kg 4–6-hourly, max 4 doses/24 h · ibuprofen 10 mg/kg 8-hourly · ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (max 2 g).** VERIFY SA: **Women's and Children's Hospital** paediatric neurosurgery and neurology; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **RFDS**; **PATS** for MRI and specialist travel — **distance must not delay imaging for a rural or Aboriginal child**; **Country Health Connect**; **ACCHS**; **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**; **SA Department for Education wellbeing leader and anti-bullying policy**, with the parent's consent.
plan: **VITALS BEFORE YOU SIT, even in a six-month history**: **'examiner, before I begin, could I have her blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?'** *All normal.* **The Cushing response lives in the BP and pulse.**

**Open, and let her talk**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the GPs here. Karen, tell me about Emily's headaches from the beginning.'** *Six months, Panadol does nothing — and the neighbour with the brain tumour.*

**★ NAME THE FEAR, AND PROMISE TO RETURN — do NOT reassure yet**: **'that must be frightening, especially with what happened next door. I'm going to ask a lot of questions — some specifically about the serious causes — and at the end I'll tell you exactly what I think and why.'** **Reassuring now, before the red flags, earns 'but how can you be sure?'**

**SICORA**: **'where does she say it hurts — always that side, or sometimes both? Out of ten? Throbbing, or dull and pressing? On and off, or all the time — getting worse? Does it spread to the face or neck? Anything that makes it better or worse — is it worse when she runs around?'** **Children's migraine is often bilateral — don't close on site or quality.**

**★ THE PAEDIATRIC SECOND A — IMPACT**: **'how is it affecting her at home and at school?'** *Missing nearly a day a week.* **Then the moment school problems appear: 'does she get the headaches on weekends and in the holidays too?'** *'No — only school days.'*

**★ THE RED FLAGS — signposted, all eight, in words**: **'now some important questions I ask every child with headaches. Does it WAKE HER AT NIGHT? Any headache or VOMITING FIRST THING IN THE MORNING? Worse when she COUGHS, SNEEZES or strains? Any BLURRED OR DOUBLE VISION? WEAKNESS in an arm or leg? NUMBNESS or pins and needles? Any change in her SCHOOL WORK, speech or walking? Any HEAD INJURY, even months ago? Losing weight, off her food, tired, any lumps?'**

**MEDICATIONS — the BIH question**: **'is she on any regular medicines — anything for skin or acne, vitamin A treatments, the pill, steroids?'** *Nothing.* **(Version C: doxycycline for four months.)**

**THE MIGRAINE FIVE**: **'when she has the headache, does she feel sick or vomit? Is she light and noise sensitive? Does she see sparkling or flashing lights before it, or hear buzzing? Does anyone in the family get migraines? Does it come on with certain foods, missed meals, poor sleep or stress?'** *No to all — 'stress, I suppose.'*

**HOME, THEN SCHOOL — and go deep when it turns abnormal**: **'how are things at home?'** *Fine.* **'And school? Any bullying you're aware of? How is her performance?'** *The group of girls, six months, crying, teacher told once.*

**★ THE DEPTH RULE — once bullying appears**: **'I'm sorry — that's hard for both of you. Has it affected her mood, her sleep, her wanting to go to school? HAS SHE EVER SAID ANYTHING ABOUT HURTING HERSELF?'** *Sadder, dreads Mondays, nothing like that.*

**INFECTION, VISION, WELL-CHILD, BINDSMA in one run**: fever, sore throat, earache, toothache, **stiff neck**, rash, lumps · trouble seeing the board · alert, eating, drinking, weeing, pooing · growth, development, immunisations. **Development and medications are the two BINDSMA items that carry marks here.**

**★ THE PEFE REQUEST — by system, FUNDOSCOPY BY NAME**: **'general appearance — alert or drowsy, dehydration, rash, limb posture, PTOSIS. Vital signs. Neurological: cranial nerves and SPECIFICALLY FUNDOSCOPY; upper and lower limbs for power, sensation and reflexes. ENT: eardrums, nose, throat for redness, swelling or exudate, sinus tenderness, TEETH. Neck: stiffness, pain on movement, lymph nodes. And the GROWTH CHART.'**
**Read it back in one sentence, fundoscopy named**: vitals normal, **cranial nerves and fundoscopy normal**, limbs normal, ENT and neck normal, growth on the 50th centile.

**★ ONE DIAGNOSIS, WITH REASONS**: **'Karen, most likely Emily has a condition called tension-type headache — a stress-related headache from tightening of the muscles around the head and neck. My reasons: real stress at school with the bullying, headaches only on school days, she still plays and eats through them, and a completely normal examination.'**

**★ CLOSE THE TUMOUR QUESTION — explicitly, with negatives**: **'I know your neighbour's diagnosis has been on your mind, so let me answer that directly: I don't think Emily has a brain tumour. No night headaches, no morning vomiting, no weight loss, no weakness or numbness, no vision problems, and the back of her eyes and her nerves are normal today.'**

**THE OTHER DIFFERENTIALS, each with its reason**: migraine — no nausea, light sensitivity, flashing lights or family history · infection in the ears, throat, sinuses or teeth — no fever, all normal · eye strain — vision fine.

**She asks 'are you sure she doesn't need a scan?'**: **'a scan wouldn't help her and isn't needed with a normal examination — and I'll tell you what would change that.'** **Then: 'what WILL help is dealing with the bullying. With your permission I'll write to the school's wellbeing leader — every SA school must act on bullying.'**

**THE REST OF THE PLAN AND THE SAFETY-NET**: a child psychologist or school counsellor · regular sleep, meals, water, less screen time · **Panadol only now and then — daily use causes headaches of its own** · a headache diary · review in two weeks · **'come straight back or call 000 for night or morning headache, vomiting, vision change, weakness or drowsiness.'** Then **'anything else worrying you?'**
pefe: **VITALS FIRST — BP, pulse, RR, temperature.** BP UP + pulse DOWN in a child is the CUSHING RESPONSE — raised ICP (rarely with irregular breathing).

**FUNDOSCOPY BY NAME.** Papilloedema = raised ICP, tumour or BIH: bilateral disc swelling, blurred margins, lost cup, obscured vessels. **'Neurological examination normal' is NOT the same as 'cranial nerves and fundoscopy normal.'**
**General appearance: alert or drowsy, dehydration, rash, abnormal limb posture, PTOSIS. Limbs: power, sensation, reflexes; gait.**
**ENT: tympanic membranes, nasal discharge, throat for redness, swelling or exudate, sinus tenderness, and a DENTAL check for caries. Neck: stiffness, pain on movement, lymph nodes.**
**GROWTH CHART — weight, height, and HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE if young enough.** A rising head circumference = hydrocephalus. **BMI** in the adolescent (BIH).
**Fever + NECK STIFFNESS, drowsiness or a non-blanching RASH = MENINGITIS until proven otherwise — assess it BEFORE the ENT findings.**

**Imaging: NONE in tension-type, migraine or URTI with no red flags and a normal examination.** **Brain tumour → urgent MRI brain (CT only if MRI unavailable).** **BIH → MRI ± MR venography FIRST, then LP with opening pressure.**
**If Cushing triad plus drowsiness or persistent vomiting = acute raised ICP → MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
**Medication-overuse headache: analgesics on 15+ days a month for 3 months.** Keep analgesia occasional; use a diary.

**AVOID: imaging in tension-type or migraine · daily analgesics · the label 'psychogenic' · opioids · antibiotics for a viral picture · amoxicillin if EBV is possible · calling BIH 'benign' without the sight risk · reassurance or 'wait and see' in Version B · explaining tumour types to a frightened parent.**

dx: **Two recalled versions, ONE structure, ONE QUESTION DECIDES. VERSION A — BRUE, a brief resolved unexplained event: nothing preceded it. VERSION B — BREATH-HOLDING SPELL: a jammed finger and a scream preceded it. The lecturer builds the structure TO THE STEM, not the recall — a trigger means breath-holding; no trigger means BRUE.**

**★ THE TRIGGER QUESTION — both versions share every question EXCEPT ONE: 'did anything hurt or upset him just before?' Ask it in every unresponsive-infant station, with stars beside it. Without it, Version B is mislabelled a BRUE — the single-item fail.**

**★ THE SECOND DISCRIMINATOR IS THE DIAGNOSIS STATEMENT. The examiner is NOT marking the word 'BRUE' or 'breath-holding' — they are marking THE LIST OF SERIOUS CONDITIONS YOU SAY YOU HAVE EXCLUDED. A candidate who says 'it was a breath-holding spell, nothing to worry about' WITHOUT the list fails a station a weaker candidate passes.**

**BRUE (AAP 2016; REPLACES 'ALTE'): an infant UNDER 12 MONTHS · SUDDEN · UNDER 1 MINUTE · RESOLVED TO BASELINE · with ≥1 of cyanosis or pallor, absent or irregular breathing, marked tone change, or altered responsiveness — AND NO EXPLANATION after history and examination.** **It is reached ONLY BY EXCLUSION — never the first word out of your mouth.**

**BREATH-HOLDING SPELL: involuntary apnoea after a PROVOKING CRY (pain, anger, fright), with colour change ± brief loss of tone or stiffening; 6 MONTHS TO 5 YEARS; BENIGN. The sequence: pain or fright → CRY → apnoea → pale or blue → floppy → seconds → SUDDEN FULL RECOVERY. CYANOTIC type (anger, pain) versus PALLID type (fright, vagal).** **The mother must give you the TRIGGER and the CRY BEFORE the colour change — a seizure has neither.**

**ONE-LINE STRATEGY: 'BEFORE, DURING, AFTER — then the EXCLUSION LIST out loud — then the NAME.' Reconstruct the event: DURING (timing, duration, first time, THREE SEIZURE QUESTIONS, colour, breathing, tone, choking) · BEFORE (what he was doing, the TRIGGER, missed feeds, fever, head injury, ingestion) · AFTER (sudden or gradual, drowsy or himself). Then the buckets: infection · GI · social/NAI · cardiac family history · CNS/trauma · metabolic/drugs · well-baby and BINDSMA.**

**VERSION B — THE DIAGNOSIS, WITH THE EXCLUSIONS**: **'the most likely explanation is a breath-holding spell. When a young child gets a sudden pain or fright, they cry hard, and at the end of the cry the breath catches — they stop breathing for a few seconds, go pale or blue, and go limp. It looks dreadful, but it is a REFLEX; it is NOT DANGEROUS, it does NOT HARM THE BRAIN, and children grow out of it by school age. I've made sure it was NOT A SEIZURE — no jerking, alert straight afterwards — NOT A SERIOUS INFECTION, NOT A BOWEL PROBLEM, A HEAD INJURY, A HEART RHYTHM PROBLEM OR LOW SUGAR, and his examination is completely normal.'**

**VERSION A — BRUE, SAID AS THREE WORDS**: **'BRIEF — it lasted seconds. RESOLVED — he came back to normal on his own. UNEXPLAINED — after asking about seizures, infection, bowel problems, injury, heart problems and low sugar, and examining him, we have found no cause. It is a diagnosis we reach only after ruling out the serious things, and he is in the LOWEST-RISK GROUP.'** **Never the acronym alone — she asks 'what does that mean?'**

**LOWER-RISK BRUE: age >60 DAYS · born ≥32 WEEKS and ≥45 weeks corrected · FIRST event · UNDER 1 MINUTE · NO CPR · no concerning features. Plan: nothing mandatory; consider a 12-lead ECG and pertussis PCR; brief oximetry observation 1–4 h optional; shared decision; INFANT CPR EDUCATION; review 24 h; NO HOME APNOEA MONITOR. HIGHER-RISK (under 60 days, ex-preterm, recurrent, >1 min, CPR needed, concerning findings): admit, continuous oximetry, ECG, FBC, glucose, electrolytes ± gas, pertussis PCR, consider CXR, sepsis screen if febrile, senior review.**

**BREATH-HOLDING PLAN: FBC AND FERRITIN — IRON DEFICIENCY makes spells more likely and is easy to fix · ECG if PALLID, ATYPICAL, EXERTIONAL, or a FAMILY HISTORY of sudden death · what to do if it recurs: lay him on his side, stay calm, don't shake him, nothing in the mouth, it stops by itself · 000 if no recovery within a minute, fever, drowsiness or jerking.** **When she says 'it's my fault': ONE SENTENCE OF COMFORT — 'this was an accident, and what happened next is a known reflex, not damage' — then CONTINUE THE SCREEN.** **AVOID: home apnoea monitors · routine bloods, EEG or imaging in lower-risk BRUE · anticonvulsants for breath-holding · telling a parent to ignore or punish spells.** SA: **WCH paediatric registrar** for higher-risk BRUE from a rural ED; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unstable or recurrent apnoea; **PATS**; **CARL 13 14 78** for child-protection concerns (mandatory notifier); **Poisons Information 13 11 26**; GP within 24–48 h; **Country Health Connect** child health nurse; **Parent Helpline SA 1300 364 100**; RCH fact sheets; **ACCHS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **★ OBSERVATIONS BEFORE YOU SIT**: **'could I have Oliver's observations first, please?'** *All normal, alert and smiling.* **'Heart rate, breathing, temperature and oxygen levels are all normal and he looks well — that's reassuring.'** **That is reassurance about NOW — not a diagnosis.**

**Open, empathise, signpost the structure**: **'Mary, I'm Dr ___. This must have been terrifying. Tell me what happened.'** *'He went floppy and wasn't breathing… I thought he was dead.'* → **'I'm so sorry. He's well right now, which is the most important thing. I'm going to ask a lot of small questions about the seconds BEFORE, DURING AND AFTER, because that's how we work out what it was.'**

**DURING — timing, then the THREE SEIZURE QUESTIONS**: **'when did it happen, how long did it last, and has it ever happened before? While he was floppy, was there any JERKING of his arms or legs? Did his EYES ROLL UP? Did he WET OR SOIL himself?'** *Twenty seconds, first time, no to all three.*

**DURING — colour, breathing, tone, choking**: **'did he go pale, or blue around the lips? Did his breathing change or stop? Floppy or stiff? Any choking, gagging or coughing — anything he could have swallowed?'** *White then bluish, not breathing, floppy like a doll, no choking.*

**★ BEFORE — THE TRIGGER, the question that decides the station**: **'what was he doing in the seconds just before? DID ANYTHING HURT OR UPSET HIM JUST BEFORE — a bump, a fright, a jammed finger?'** *(tearful) 'I shut his fingers in the car door. He screamed, and then it happened. It's my fault.'*

**ONE SENTENCE OF COMFORT — then do NOT stop the screen**: **'that was an accident, Mary, and what happened next is a known reflex in some children, not an injury to his brain. I'll explain it properly in a moment. A few more questions first.'**

**The rest of BEFORE**: **'had he missed any feeds? Any fever, rash or illness this week? Any falls or bumps to the head, or anything he could have got into?'** *Fed an hour before; a snuffle last week; no falls, no medicines in reach.*

**AFTER — the post-ictal question**: **'when he came round, was it SUDDEN or GRADUAL? Was he DROWSY afterwards, or straight back to himself?'** *Sudden, smiling, not drowsy.* **Sudden complete recovery argues against seizure.**

**INFECTION and GI**: **'any cough, snuffles, vomiting or diarrhoea? Anyone at home coughing? Immunisations up to date?'** Then **'any GREEN vomit, BLOOD in the poo, DRAWING HIS LEGS UP, or lumps in the tummy or groin?'** **The pertussis and intussusception screens.**

**★ SOCIAL HISTORY — the NAI bucket, which must not be empty**: **'how are things at home? Who lives with you? Who was with him today? Any stresses? Does he go to childcare?'** *Mary, Dave and Oliver; she was with him; fine; no childcare.*

**CARDIAC FAMILY HISTORY and CNS**: **'has anyone in the family DIED SUDDENLY or young, FAINTED WITH EXERCISE, or been DEAF from childhood? Any seizures in the family?'** **That is the long-QT screen.** Then **well-baby and BINDSMA**: alert, feeding, wet nappies, term, growing and developing, medicines, allergies.

**★ THE EXAMINATION, BY SYSTEM — including the NAI and cardiac items**: **'general appearance — alert, interactive? Hydration? Any rash, and ANY BRUISING ANYWHERE, including BEHIND THE EARS? Temperature. Growth chart. Fontanelle, FUNDOSCOPY, pupils, tone in all four limbs, symmetry, REFLEXES. Chest. HEART SOUNDS, MURMUR, FEMORAL PULSES. Abdomen — distension, MASS, hernias. And a BEDSIDE GLUCOSE.'**

**Read it back**: alert, no bruising, fundi normal, tone and reflexes normal, heart and femorals normal, no mass, glucose 4.8. **If told 'you can't do reflexes in a baby': 'I would still assess tone, symmetry and reflexes.'**

**★ THE NAME, IN PLAIN WORDS**: **'Mary, the most likely explanation is a breath-holding spell. When a young child gets a sudden pain or fright, they cry hard, and at the end of the cry the breath catches — they stop breathing for a few seconds, go pale or blue, and go limp. It looks dreadful, but it's a reflex — not dangerous, it does not harm the brain, and children grow out of it by school age.'**

**★ THE EXCLUSION LIST, OUT LOUD — this is what's actually marked**: **'I've made sure it was NOT A SEIZURE — no jerking and he was alert straight afterwards. NOT A SERIOUS INFECTION — no fever and he's well. Not a BOWEL problem, a HEAD INJURY, a HEART RHYTHM problem or LOW SUGAR, and his examination is completely normal. So it isn't the unexplained kind of event we sometimes see in babies — this one has a clear explanation.'**

**She asks 'will it happen again? What do I do?'**: **'it may — more likely after a fright or a bump. Lay him on his side, stay calm, don't shake him and don't put anything in his mouth; it stops by itself.'**

**THE PLAN AND THE ECG TRIGGERS**: **'I'll check his blood count and iron today, because LOW IRON makes spells more common and is easy to fix. If a spell ever happens WITHOUT a trigger, lasts MORE THAN A MINUTE, happens WITH EXERCISE, or comes with jerking, a fever or drowsiness — come straight back or call 000.'**

**Answer the hidden agenda, then close**: **'it isn't epilepsy, and you didn't hurt his brain — you did exactly the right thing bringing him in.'** Then **GP in two days, the RCH fact sheet**, and **'any questions?'**

**DEFINITIONS: bowel (in GIRLS often the OVARY) trapped in a PATENT PROCESSUS VAGINALIS at the deep inguinal ring — in infants almost always INDIRECT. INCARCERATED = IRREDUCIBLE (the words are synonyms). STRANGULATED = the BLOOD SUPPLY IS COMPROMISED — tense, exquisitely tender, RED OR DUSKY skin, a TOXIC child, obstruction.** **Say: 'an incarcerated inguinal hernia — irreducible and tender — which is a surgical emergency because it CAN strangulate.' Only call it strangulated if there is skin colour change, peritonism or systemic toxicity.**

**NUMBERS THE EXAMINER LIKES: inguinal hernia in 1–5% of term infants, UP TO 30% OF VERY PREMATURE infants (he was born at 34 weeks); 60% RIGHT-SIDED (later descent of the right testis); INCARCERATION RISK HIGHEST IN THE FIRST YEAR (10–20% in infants) — which is why infant hernias are REPAIRED SOON AFTER DIAGNOSIS rather than watched.** VERIFY

A LOOP OF BOWEL HAS SLIPPED INTO THAT POUCH AND GOT STUCK, which is why he's in pain and vomiting. I'm confident because the lump CAN'T BE PUSHED BACK and it's PAINFUL TO TOUCH.'** **Then SIX OR SEVEN SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIALS, grouped: intussusception · a twisted testicle · reflux disease · a tummy bug like his brother's · a urine or ear infection or a serious infection · food allergy · a knock to the head · and colic AT THE BOTTOM.** **'Intussusception, gastro, colic' scores 2.**

stem: Emergency department. A 5-YEAR-OLD BOY, RYAN, with A RASH ON HIS FACE AND CHEST AFTER HAVING BREAKFAST, brought in by his father. ON ARRIVAL HIS VITAL SIGNS ARE STABLE.
Observations: HR 112 — RR 22 — BP 100/68 — SpO2 98% on room air — T 36.9. 8 minutes: history, then examination findings from the examiner, then diagnosis, then immediate management.
tasks: Take a focused history from the father
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis to the father
Explain your immediate management
findings: ★ THE OBSERVATIONS — interpret them OUT LOUD

HR 112, RR 22, BP 100/68, SpO2 98% room air, T 36.9. ALL NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD. Every sitting produces candidates who see a number that is not 120/80, ANNOUNCE SHOCK, and diagnose anaphylaxis on it. Say: 'those observations are normal for a five-year-old'
★ SATURATIONS — the vital sign of this station
98% on room air. It is the one candidates forget, and the one that matters most here. Temperature matters least — ask it, then move on
The examination card

ALERT and interactive. NO stridor, no audible wheeze. RAISED ERYTHEMATOUS RASH on the face and upper chest WITH WELL-DEFINED MARGINS. NO lip or tongue swelling. NO hoarseness. Chest clear, equal air entry. Heart sounds normal. Abdomen soft, non-tender
The rash

About HALF AN HOUR after breakfast; started 15–20 minutes after eating, on his CHEEKS, now his CHEST — spreading. 'Raised. Bumpy.' VERY ITCHY — he keeps scratching. Urticaria itches; a painful rash points elsewhere
★ 'ON HIS FACE' IS NOT AN ANSWER
Ask 'on his face?' and he says 'yes, his face' and WAITS. Only if you ask WHERE on the face: 'HIS CHEEKS. NOT HIS LIPS.' Eyes are reassuring; lips make you look at the tongue
★ THE SIX RED FLAGS — all negative, but only if asked INDIVIDUALLY

Ask 'any other symptoms?' as one vague question and he answers 'no' — making you ask each one. Lips/tongue normal · no drooling · breathing sounds normal · 'he's been RUNNING AROUND' · voice the same · no vomiting · 'COMPLETELY WITH IT'
★ THE PLANTED SECOND TRIGGER

'Oh — I put a NEW SUNSCREEN on his face and chest this morning.' Offered ONLY if you ask about creams or anything new on the skin — and it went on EXACTLY WHERE THE RASH IS. You aren't required to solve it; you are required to FIND IT
The rest of the trigger hunt
TOAST WITH PEANUT BUTTER — 'now you mention it, the FIRST TIME he's had it.' No medicines. No stings he knows of. Never happened before
The distractors

BRONCHIOLITIS as a baby (overnight admission). Mother has HAY FEVER, sister has ASTHMA. No food allergies in the family. Otherwise well, no regular medicines, immunised. Atopy slightly raises background risk — it does NOT escalate the label
★ HIS HIDDEN AGENDA
'A boy at his school has an EPIPEN. SHOULD RYAN HAVE ONE?' — raised after the diagnosis, or at about seven minutes if never invited. Refuse WITH A REASON AND A PATHWAY, never a flat no
★ HIS SCRIPTED REACTIONS

Early: 'IS IT SERIOUS?' — if you diagnose before examining, he presses 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW ALREADY?' · If you say 'anaphylaxis': 'IS THAT THE ONE THAT KILLS PEOPLE?' · If you promise he'll be fine: 'CAN YOU GUARANTEE THAT?' · Close: 'so what do I do if it happens again?'
VERSION B — the bee sting

Same structure. The STING IS STILL IN THE SKIN — flick or scrape it out sideways, DON'T SQUEEZE the venom sac. The catch: for INSECT VENOM, PERSISTENT ABDOMINAL PAIN OR VOMITING COUNTS AS ANAPHYLAXIS — which it does NOT for food. Three vomits and cramping after a sting = adrenaline, even with no airway sign
VERSION C — the wheezing asthmatic

Known asthmatic, 7, WHEEZING after a new chocolate bar, no urticaria. You cannot separate asthma from anaphylaxis, so you don't try: TREAT AS ANAPHYLAXIS — ADRENALINE FIRST, then salbutamol, then oxygen. Adrenaline treats both; withholding it and being wrong can kill
Other practice cards

Father adds his VOICE HAS GONE CROAKY in the last ten minutes → STOP the history, anaphylaxis, IM adrenaline now, lie flat · 4-year-old, urticaria THREE DAYS into amoxicillin → probable drug reaction, often NOT IgE-mediated — don't mislabel him penicillin-allergic for life · 'it happened six months ago, his LIPS SWELLED' → today unchanged, but mark the allergy referral URGENT with a request for autoinjector risk assessment

dx: **MILD TO MODERATE IgE-MEDIATED ALLERGIC REACTION TO FOOD, presenting as acute URTICARIA — skin only, NO respiratory, cardiovascular or neurological involvement. THIS IS NOT ANAPHYLAXIS, AND THE WORD MUST NOT APPEAR IN YOUR ANSWER.**

**This is a SEVERITY-ASSESSMENT station wearing the COSTUME OF A RASH station. The examiner is not testing whether you can recognise urticaria — the stem hands you that. He is testing whether you will ask EVERY anaphylaxis red flag before you commit, and then whether you will COMMIT CLEANLY TO ONE LABEL instead of hedging between two.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — COMMIT TO ONE LABEL, AND DO NOT SAY THE OTHER WORD. Every candidate who fails this station fails it the same way: a competent history, a proper examination, and then 'I think this is an allergic reaction, BUT IT COULD ALSO BE ANAPHYLAXIS.' THAT SENTENCE IS THE FAIL. Anaphylaxis is the severe form, so a reaction cannot be both — offering both tells the examiner you did not do the severity assessment. Historically this case has essentially NEVER been anaphylaxis — it exists to catch candidates who OVER-CALL it.**

**ONE-LINE STRATEGY: PROVE IT IS ALLERGIC, THEN PROVE HOW SEVERE IT IS NOT, USING NAMED NEGATIVES. Everything else is decoration.** **And skip your usual rash structure — say once: 'the TIMING makes infective and autoimmune causes very unlikely' — you do not catch an infection from breakfast in thirty minutes. Then spend the eight minutes inside the allergy box, where the marks are.**

**★ THE SIX RED FLAGS, AS A NAMED BLOCK — signpost them, then all of them: 'I'm going to run through a short list of specific things. Just yes or no.' LIPS OR TONGUE swelling · DROOLING or trouble swallowing · NOISY breathing — wheeze or stridor · DIFFICULTY breathing · VOICE or cry change · NAUSEA or vomiting · DIZZY, FLOPPY, DROWSY or collapse.** **THREE OUT OF SIX IS A FAIL — asking them as a named block is what makes it audible as a SYSTEM rather than as luck.** **Eyelid and lip swelling alone sit in the mild column; tongue, throat, voice and drooling do not.** VERIFY against the current ASCIA wording.

**★ HUNT THE TRIGGER — THE SENTENCE THAT BUYS THE WHOLE SECTION: 'before I settle on the food, I want to make sure I haven't missed something else — because children often get a MEDICINE with food, and a NEW CREAM goes on exactly where this rash is.'** **And CAKE IS NOT AN ALLERGEN — egg, milk, wheat and nut all live inside a cake, and that is why allergy testing is worth doing at all.**

**THE EXPLANATION, WITH NAMED NEGATIVES**: **'Ryan has had a MILD ALLERGIC REACTION to something he had at breakfast — most likely the peanut butter, though I'm keeping the new sunscreen in mind, because it went on exactly where the rash is. I want to tell you why I'm confident it's the mild kind. I was deliberately looking for the signs of a severe reaction: swelling of the tongue, tightness in the throat, a change in his voice, noisy or difficult breathing, drooling, dizziness or drowsiness. He has NONE of them. His oxygen is normal, his blood pressure and heart rate are normal for a five-year-old, and his chest is clear.'**

**WHEN HE ASKS 'ARE YOU SURE?' — answer with the PLAN, not a hedge: 'I'm confident on what I can see now, and that is EXACTLY WHY I want to keep him here and watch him rather than send him home.'** **If the examiner pushes 'could this become anaphylaxis?': 'any allergic reaction can progress, which is exactly why I'm observing him and have given the father specific red flags — but on the findings in front of me this is mild to moderate, and I would not give adrenaline.'**

**MANAGEMENT — FOUR THINGS NOW: a NON-SEDATING ANTIHISTAMINE (cetirizine 5 mg or loratadine 5 mg for 2–5 years) VERIFY · OBSERVE FOR A FEW HOURS with repeat observations, because reactions can come back (BIPHASIC) · SPECIFIC RED FLAGS in plain words to the father · STOP THE TRIGGERS — no peanut butter, no more of that sunscreen. Then home with an ALLERGY ACTION PLAN (ASCIA, green) — NOT an anaphylaxis action plan; the word choice is scored — avoidance and label reading, PAEDIATRIC ALLERGY REFERRAL for skin-prick testing or allergen-specific IgE, dietitian if a staple, GP review, and CHECK HIS ASTHMA CONTROL — uncontrolled asthma is the biggest risk factor for a future severe reaction.**

CORRECTIONS carried from the transcript: **RAST is the superseded name — say skin-prick testing or allergen-specific IgE · CORTICOSTEROIDS have no proven benefit in acute allergic reactions and are no longer routine · no PROMETHAZINE in a young child · autoinjectors are 150 microgram for 7.5–20 kg and 300 microgram over 20 kg — the transcript's '0.5 mg EpiPen' and '0.3 mg junior for a 30 kg child' are both wrong · onset is usually within 30 minutes, up to 2 hours, not the transcript's four · and in anaphylaxis you lay the child flat because you fear HYPOtension, not 'hypertension'.** **THE AUTOINJECTOR REFUSAL: 'adrenaline pens are for children who have had a SEVERE reaction, or whom the ALLERGY SPECIALIST decides are at high risk. If I gave one to every mild reaction, almost every family would have one and it would STOP MEANING ANYTHING. I'm referring him to the allergy clinic, and if they find he needs one, they'll prescribe it.'** SA: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** early for any rural child given adrenaline; paediatric allergy at the **Women's and Children's Hospital** with **PATS**; **TIS National 131 450**; schools need the ASCIA plan; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.
plan: **WIPE, ACKNOWLEDGE, SIGNPOST — before any question**: **'good morning, I'm Dr ___, one of the doctors in the emergency department. Are you Ryan's dad? Hi Ryan. I can see the rash and I can see you're worried — you were right to bring him straight in. I'm going to ask some questions to work out how serious this is, then examine him, then explain what I think and what we'll do.'**

**If he interrupts with 'is it serious?' — don't diagnose yet**: **'that's exactly what I'm working out right now, and I'll tell you honestly in a couple of minutes.'** **Diagnosing before examining earns 'how can you know already?'**

**EXPLORE THE RASH — pin the interval IN MINUTES**: **'tell me what happened. When did he have breakfast, and HOW LONG AFTER that did the rash come up? Is it spreading?'** *Half an hour; started 15–20 minutes after; cheeks then chest.*

**★ WHERE ON THE FACE — and morphology**: **'whereabouts on his face — near the EYES, or the LIPS? Is it raised or flat? Itchy or painful?'** *Cheeks, not lips; raised and bumpy; very itchy.* **Accepting 'on his face' loses the chance to establish the lips are spared.**

**★ THE SIX RED FLAGS — signpost, then all six, individually**: **'I'm going to run through a short list of specific things I need to check. Just yes or no. Any swelling of his LIPS or his TONGUE? Any DROOLING, or trouble swallowing his saliva? Any NOISY BREATHING — a wheeze, or a harsh sound breathing in? Any DIFFICULTY breathing? Has his VOICE or his cry changed? Any NAUSEA or VOMITING? Has he been DIZZY, FLOPPY or DROWSY, or passed out?'**

**Acknowledge the negatives**: *No to all — running around, chatting the whole time.* **'Good — that's really helpful.'** **The examiner is counting; a vague 'any other symptoms?' gets 'no' and scores nothing.**

**★ THE TRIGGER HUNT — and don't assume the food**: **'now I want to work out exactly what set this off, and I don't want to assume it was the food. What exactly did he eat? Was that the first time? Any new medicine, even one dose? Any chance of an insect sting? ANYTHING NEW ON HIS SKIN — soap, body wash, cream, sunscreen? Has this ever happened before?'**

**When the sunscreen appears, put it on the list OUT LOUD**: *'I put a new sunscreen on his face and chest this morning.'* → **'that's useful, thank you — that went on exactly where the rash is, so it goes on my list too.'**

**ATOPY, FAMILY, WELL CHILD — food allergy by name FIRST**: **'does anyone in the family have FOOD ALLERGIES OR ANAPHYLAXIS? Does Ryan or anyone have asthma, eczema or hay fever? Is he normally well — any medical problems or regular medicines? Immunisations up to date? Behaving normally for him?'** **Note the distractors — they change nothing today.**

**★ THE EXAMINATION — in a scored order, SATURATIONS included**: **'general appearance and level of consciousness — alert or drowsy? Any audible stridor or wheeze? Full vital signs, INCLUDING OXYGEN SATURATION. Is the rash RAISED with well-defined margins? Any lip or tongue swelling? Any hoarseness? Respiratory — air entry, added sounds? Heart sounds? Abdomen — any tenderness?'**
**★ INTERPRET THE VITALS OUT LOUD**: **'thank you — and those observations are NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD.'** **A heart rate of 112 and BP of 100/68 are not shock at this age.**

**★ ONE LABEL, NAMED NEGATIVES — and do NOT say the other word**: **'Ryan has had a MILD ALLERGIC REACTION, most likely to the peanut butter, with the new sunscreen also on my list. I'm confident it's the mild kind because I looked specifically for the severe signs — tongue swelling, throat tightness, voice change, noisy or difficult breathing, drooling, dizziness — and he has none of them, his oxygen is normal and his chest is clear.'**

**★ HE ASKS FOR AN EPIPEN — refuse with a REASON and a PATHWAY**: **'not from today, and let me explain why rather than just say no. Adrenaline pens are for children who've had a severe reaction, or whom the allergy specialist decides are at high risk. Ryan has had a mild one. If I gave a pen to every child with a mild reaction, almost every family would have one and it would stop meaning anything. I'm referring him to the allergy clinic — if they find he needs one, they'll prescribe it.'**

**MANAGEMENT NOW — four things**: **an antihistamine, cetirizine** · **we keep him here for a few hours, because reactions can occasionally come back** · **no peanut butter, no more of that sunscreen** · and the red flags: **'tell us immediately if his TONGUE swells, his VOICE changes, his breathing gets NOISY or difficult, he DROOLS, or he goes FLOPPY.'**

**BEFORE HE GOES HOME — and say 'allergy action plan', not 'anaphylaxis action plan'**: **an ALLERGY ACTION PLAN, the allergy clinic referral for testing — 'cake and biscuits can contain egg, milk, wheat and nut at once' — and a GP review.** When he asks **'what do I do if it happens again?'**: **'I can't promise it will never happen again, but I can tell you exactly what to do if it does.'**

**SATURATION is the vital sign of this station.** Forgetting it, then trying to add it after the examiner has moved on, is a named error.

**Interpret paediatric vitals against AGE-SPECIFIC RANGES, out loud.** 5–12 yr roughly HR 70–120, RR 18–25, SBP 95–120 — and a 5-year-old at HR 112, BP 100/68 is normal. VERIFY against your hospital's paediatric chart.
**Ask ONE question about the rash itself: 'is it raised?'** Morphology makes the diagnosis, colour does not.
**NON-SEDATING ANTIHISTAMINE: cetirizine 5 mg or loratadine 5 mg (2–5 years).** VERIFY **OBSERVE A FEW HOURS — biphasic reactions.**

**ALLERGY ACTION PLAN (green), avoidance and label reading, paediatric allergy referral for skin-prick testing or specific IgE, dietitian if a staple, GP review, and CHECK ASTHMA CONTROL.**

DEVELOPMENTAL MILESTONES ACHIEVED · GROWTH CHART NORMAL · NO DYSMORPHIC FEATURES. The whole station is the history

'The school rang — Ethan HIT ANOTHER BOY. And we've been worried about his SPEECH for a long time.' She LEADS WITH THE SCHOOL and adds the speech as an AFTERTHOUGHT. Choosing one and forgetting the other is the named trap

Slapped a boy who TOOK HIS SEAT; a couple of smaller incidents before. BEHIND IN READING AND WRITING. No bullying that they know of

'Yes — he LASHES OUT AT HOME TOO when things don't go his way.' Home 'fine — close family'; NOT CLOSE TO HIS SISTER, 'she finds him hard.' NOBODY in the family with similar problems. Ask the relationship question even after 'fine at home' — it is where abuse and stress surface
Speech
Can talk, but 'WHEN HE WANTS SOMETHING HE CAN'T GET IT OUT.' REPEATS THE SAME WORDS AND PHRASES over and over. Understands IF YOU KEEP IT SIMPLE. NEVER LOST WORDS — no regression
ASD — social and repetitive
'He LOOKS PAST YOU.' 'HATES CUDDLES — always has.' 'He'd RATHER BE ALONE.' 'THE CURTAIN — he'll play with it FOR HOURS.' 'If we MOVE ANYTHING in the house HE SCREAMS'

'No, he'll SIT FOR HOURS with the curtain.' Finishes homework IF HE LIKES IT; remembers instructions. 'NOT IMPULSIVE — it's WHEN THINGS CHANGE.' Skipping ADHD because the answers already say autism is the trap

'He WON'T TAKE NO — but it's that he CAN'T COPE, not that he's defiant.' Follows instructions if they're clear. Refusal ≠ forgetting (ADHD) ≠ not understanding (ASD, hearing)

dx: **POSSIBLE AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER (Version A) — a neurodevelopmental condition affecting how a person PROCESSES INFORMATION, BEHAVES AND SEES THE WORLD, with persistent differences in social communication and interaction and restricted, repetitive behaviours, present from early childhood. The lecture's teaching triad — SOCIAL · SPEECH · REPETITIVE BEHAVIOUR — maps onto the two DSM-5 domains. VERSION B is ADHD; VERSION C is sleep apnoea.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — YOU PASS FOR THE HISTORY, NOT FOR THE ANSWER. The handbook says it in plain words: the case is written to SUGGEST a diagnosis, and the mark is for whether the candidate approaches the problem LOGICALLY, EXPLORING ALL THE OTHER POSSIBILITIES BEFORE CONCLUDING. Candidates who recognise the recall, fire six autism questions and announce ASD HAVE BEEN FAILED WITH THE RIGHT ANSWER.**

**The discriminating behaviour is a VISIBLE, ORDERED EXCLUSION: say the component headings out loud, ONE QUESTION PER COMPONENT, and in the explanation give the examiner A REASON FOR EACH CONDITION YOU SET ASIDE.** **The pivot line: 'some of my next questions will sound unrelated to what happened at school — they help me rule out other reasons for a child to behave this way, and that matters before anyone uses a diagnosis.'**

**ONE-LINE STRATEGY: complaint → school → HOME → speech → ASD → ADHD → ODD → organic/sleep/senses → BINDS → 'a POSSIBILITY'.** **The examiner ticks COMPONENTS, not conditions: ASD — social · communication · repetitive. ADHD — hyperactive · inattentive · impulsive. ODD — anger · refusal. One good question each, every component covered.** **The organic screen is where candidates run out of time — keep one question per item and budget sixty seconds.**

**THE TWO-SETTINGS RULE — 'any similar behaviour at home?' early, and always the RELATIONSHIPS question even after 'fine at home'.** **FAMILY HISTORY is a marked item: 'anyone in the family with similar problems — siblings, parents, even YOURSELVES AS CHILDREN?'** **And HEARING is the commonest missed cause of a speech concern — audiology is MANDATORY with any speech complaint, even after a normal school screen.**

**THE DIAGNOSTIC FRAMES, IF CHALLENGED. ADHD (DSM-5): SIX OR MORE symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity for ≥6 MONTHS, several present BEFORE AGE 12, in TWO OR MORE SETTINGS, impairing function. ASD: persistent social-communication deficits across contexts PLUS restricted, repetitive patterns, from early development, needing a MULTIDISCIPLINARY assessment across settings (paediatrician, psychologist, speech pathologist; ADOS-2 / ADI-R) — never one consultation. ODD: angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behaviour, vindictiveness, ≥6 months, with someone not a sibling; CONDUCT DISORDER if aggression to people or animals, destruction, deceit or serious rule violation.**

CORRECTION — **the lecture says ADHD requires symptoms in 'more than two settings'. The criterion is TWO OR MORE.** **If challenged: 'symptoms must be present in at least two settings — typically school and home.'**

**THE EXPLANATION — THE POSSIBILITY, DEFINED, THEN THE REASONS**: **'I want to be careful and honest with you. Putting everything together, there is a POSSIBILITY that Ethan has a condition called autism spectrum disorder — a developmental condition that affects how a person processes information, behaves and sees the world. It shows as difficulty with social interaction, difficulty with communication, and repetitive behaviours, and it's a SPECTRUM, so it looks different in every child. I'm raising it because he avoids eye contact and cuddles and prefers his own company; his speech is limited and repetitive; he plays only with the curtain and is distressed by change; and it's happening BOTH AT SCHOOL AND AT HOME.'**

**★ THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH ITS REASON FOR BEING LESS LIKELY: ADHD — he isn't hyperactive or impulsive and concentrates on things he likes · ODD — his outbursts come with CHANGE, not defiance · SLEEP APNOEA — no snoring · HEARING OR VISION — school checks normal, but I'd still like a formal hearing test · head injury, seizures, thyroid — nothing in the history · low mood, anxiety, or stress at school or home — frustrated rather than sad, home settled.** **Then: 'nobody should use the word autism until a proper assessment has been done — a children's specialist with a psychologist and speech pathologist, more than once, in more than one setting, with information from school.'** **'Is it our fault?' — ONE SENTENCE: 'no — it is not caused by anything you've done.'**

**★ NAME BOTH COMPLAINTS BACK, AND ADDRESS THE CONCERN**: **'so there are two things — what happened at school, and his speech. I'll go through both. I understand how worrying that call from the school must have been. I'm going to ask quite a few questions to understand him properly, and then we'll make a plan together.'**

**THE EVENT — the step most candidates skip**: **'can you describe exactly what happened? Is this the first time, or have there been other episodes?'** *Slapped a boy who took his seat; a couple of smaller things.*

Does he understand instructions? HAS HE EVER LOST WORDS HE USED TO HAVE?'** *Can't express wants; repeats words; understands if simple; never gone backwards.*

**★ ADHD — all three components, even though the answers already say autism**: **'is he very ENERGETIC and hard to slow down? Can he WAIT in a line for his turn? Does he FINISH HIS HOMEWORK? Remember instructions? Does he ACT WITHOUT THINKING?'** *Sits for hours; finishes if he likes it; not impulsive — it's change.*
**ODD**: **'any ANGER outbursts or temper tantrums? Does he REFUSE to follow instructions?'** *Can't cope with no — not defiant.* **Refusal is not forgetting, and not failing to understand.**

**THE ORGANIC SCREEN — one question each, sixty seconds**: **'any concerns about his development or growth? His VISION OR HEARING? How is his SLEEP — any snoring or gasping? Any HEAD INJURY? Any STARING SPELLS or seizures? How is his MOOD — sad, worried?'** *Slow to talk; school screen fine; sleeps well; no injuries; frustrated, not sad.*

**BINDS, then a one-line summary**: **'any problems in the pregnancy or delivery? Vaccines up to date? Other medical problems, medicines or allergies?'** *Normal, term, done.* **'Thank you. Let me summarise what you've told me.'**

**★ THE POSSIBILITY, DEFINED — never a label**: **'I want to be careful and honest with you. Putting everything together, there is a POSSIBILITY that Ethan has a condition called autism spectrum disorder — a developmental condition that affects how a person processes information, behaves and sees the world. It shows as difficulty with social interaction, communication, and repetitive behaviours — and it's a spectrum.'**

**THE REASONS, mapped to the three components, plus two settings**: avoids eye contact and cuddles, prefers his own company · speech limited and repetitive · plays only with the curtain, distressed by change · **'and it's happening both at school and at home.'**

**★ THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH WITH A REASON**: **ADHD** — not hyperactive or impulsive · **ODD** — outbursts with change, not defiance · **sleep apnoea** — no snoring · **hearing or vision** — 'school checks normal but I'd still like a formal hearing test' · **head injury, seizures, thyroid** — nothing in the history · **low mood or stress** — frustrated rather than sad, home settled.

**'IS IT OUR FAULT?' — one sentence, then the plan**: **'no. It is not caused by anything you've done. And nobody should use the word autism until a proper assessment is done — a children's specialist with a psychologist and a speech pathologist, seeing him more than once and getting information from school. I'll arrange that and a hearing test today, connect you with speech therapy, school support and a parent support service, and see you back in a few weeks.'**

stem: General practice or emergency department. A 3-YEAR-OLD CHILD brought in after A BURN WHICH HAPPENED AT HOME. Observations: HR 138 — RR 28 — BP 96/58 — T 36.4 — ALERT AND CRYING.

History 5 minutes, then YOU ARE HANDED A PHYSICAL EXAMINATION CARD, then explain your management plan. 8 minutes. FOUR VERSIONS: 8% going home, 12% admitted, 10% BROUGHT BY AN UNCLE, and 20% INVOLVING THE FACE.
tasks: Take a history (5 minutes)
Read the physical examination card you are handed
Explain your management plan
findings: ★ THE CARD CHANGES BY VERSION — the history does not

VERSION A: 8% anterior trunk and right arm → HOME. VERSION B: 12% same sites → ADMIT. VERSION C: EXACTLY 10%, brought by the UNCLE → ADMIT + NOTIFY. VERSION D: 20% INCLUDING THE FACE → AIRWAY AND EYES FIRST. Candidates who memorise '8%, send home' get destroyed by the 12% version — PRACTISE ARRIVING AT SIX MINUTES WITHOUT HAVING DECIDED ANYTHING
Version B card, read aloud

12% TOTAL BODY SURFACE AREA, anterior trunk and right arm. BLISTERED, MOIST, PINK — superficial to mid dermal. NO facial, perineal or circumferential involvement, NO airway concern. Observations normal for a three-year-old (HR 138, RR 28, BP 96/58, T 36.4, CRT 2 s)
★ READ THE TOTAL — do not recalculate it

The chart arrives MARKED AND TOTALLED. Say DEPTH and SIZE as TWO SEPARATE SENTENCES, name what is ABSENT, then say the sentence that decides the station: 'THAT IS ABOVE TEN PERCENT.' SIMPLE ERYTHEMA IS NOT COUNTED. Never grade the whole burn in one word like 'second degree'
The mechanism

About AN HOUR AGO. Soup on the table to cool; she TURNED TO THE SINK for a few seconds; he REACHED UP AND PULLED THE BOWL OVER HIMSELF. Down his FRONT and RIGHT ARM. Chicken soup, straight off the stove. A PULL-OVER SCALD — splashes and runs downwards, deepest at the top — the commonest true accident at this age
★ THE FIRST-AID DURATION — only if you ask how long

'I got his top off and ran it under the cold tap.' Stop there and she says 'yes' and waits. Only on 'FOR HOW LONG?': 'TWO OR THREE MINUTES — he was screaming so I stopped.' Then a wet tea towel. Her mum said BUTTER; she didn't. PANADOL half an hour ago. Twenty minutes is the standard — and at one hour you can STILL COOL NOW (worthwhile up to 3 hours)
The five red flags

BLISTERS on his tummy — YES. No other burn or injury, ever. NOT the face, eyes or private parts. Nothing around the mouth. Breathing fine — 'he's just been crying.' 'ANY OTHER INJURY?' is the one question that opens BOTH the trauma door and the safeguarding door
Tetanus and past history
All immunisations up to date. Healthy, no medicines, no allergies, NEVER in hospital. Ask it even though he's covered — the version where the family declines vaccination is why it exists
★ THE HOME SCREEN — defensive if not normalised

Ask without normalising and she becomes defensive: 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ME THAT? AM I IN TROUBLE?' Normalise first and she answers openly: her, her husband, Charlie and his 6-year-old sister; her mum ten minutes away; no stresses, no alcohol or drugs; SHE WAS SUPERVISING HIM
★ HER EMOTIONAL REGISTER AND HIDDEN AGENDA

GUILTY, TEARFUL, apologises twice, QUIETLY FRIGHTENED OF BEING REPORTED. She wants to be told it's NOT HER FAULT — 'IS THIS MY FAULT?' after the plan, or at seven minutes. If you LECTURE HER ABOUT KITCHEN SAFETY while she's crying, she goes quiet and STOPS COOPERATING
Her scripted traps

'IS HE GOING TO BE SCARRED?' — if you say he DEFINITELY WON'T, she looks relieved AND MARKS YOU DOWN · If you never say whether he's being admitted: 'SO IS HE STAYING IN, OR CAN I TAKE HIM HOME?' — mark lost
★ VERSION C — the uncle, exactly 10%

Darren, 34, the uncle: his sister 'WASN'T UP TO IT — SHE'D BEEN DRINKING.' She lives with a BOYFRIEND WHO IS NOT CHARLIE'S FATHER. He doesn't know exactly how it happened. Volunteers the drinking ONLY if asked why the mother didn't come. ADMIT (10% is at the line; in a 3-year-old you admit) PLUS CHILD PROTECTION NOTIFICATION — establish who has parental responsibility and who can consent
★ VERSION D — 20% and the face

Before anything else: AIRWAY — burns around the mouth and nose, SINGED NASAL HAIRS, SOOT, HOARSENESS, stridor; involve ANAESTHETICS EARLY because swelling can close an airway over hours. Then the EYES — fluorescein, ophthalmology. Admit for size AND site. No NG tube through a badly burnt nose
Other practice cards

BOTH FEET burnt TO THE SAME LEVEL with a SHARP MARGIN; 'he ran into the bathroom himself' → IMMERSION PATTERN inconsistent with the history, admit and notify · mother put ICE AND BUTTER on it → correct kindly; ice DEEPENS the burn by vasoconstriction · the unrun versions: CIRCUMFERENTIAL (escharotomy), CHEMICAL (brush off dry, irrigate long, never neutralise), ELECTRICAL (ECG, entry and exit wounds), UNDER ONE (refer everything)

dx: **SCALD BURN in a 3-year-old. THERE IS NO DIAGNOSTIC PUZZLE. The station is decided by DEPTH, PERCENTAGE, SITE, MECHANISM and WHO IS AT HOME — and by whether you screen the home situation WITHOUT BEING ASKED TO. The history is identical in all four versions; a single number on a card and a single sentence from the parent flip the management completely.**

**WHY CHILDREN'S BURNS ARE DIFFERENT — three sentences everything else follows from: a child's skin is THINNER, so the same insult burns DEEPER · the SURFACE-AREA-TO-WEIGHT RATIO is higher, so they lose FLUID AND HEAT faster and dehydrate sooner · and the body PROPORTIONS differ enough that ADULT NINES WILL MISLEAD YOU.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — LEAD WITH THE DISPOSITION, AND JUSTIFY IT WITH THE NUMBER. Candidates fail in two directions: the first list every dressing, analgesic and follow-up detail and NEVER SAY WHETHER THE CHILD IS BEING ADMITTED; the second say 'we'll admit him' and CANNOT SAY WHY. The pass is a single opening sentence: THE DECISION, THEN THE REASON, THEN THE LIST.**

**★ THE SECOND DISCRIMINATOR IS QUIETER, AND IT IS THE ONE THE EXAMINER IS REALLY WATCHING: did you screen the home situation BEFORE YOU WERE GIVEN A REASON TO? In Version C the concern is handed to you. In A, B and D it isn't there at all — and the candidate who only asks when prompted has shown they would MISS THE CHILD WHOSE UNCLE NEVER SAYS ANYTHING.** **Five minutes of history for a burn is deliberately long — the candidates who finish in two are the ones who never asked.**

**THE SENTENCE THAT PROTECTS YOU IN EVERY VERSION, said before the home screen**: **'most burns in three-year-olds are exactly what they look like — a moment's inattention with something hot. I ask these questions of every family, not because I think anything is wrong here.'** **It lets you ask hard questions without the role-player becoming defensive, and the examiner hears you managing the relationship as well as the burn.**

**THE FIVE RED FLAGS — any positive means this child is NOT going home, and SAY THAT OUT LOUD in management so the questions are seen to be doing work: BLISTERS · ANY OTHER BURN OR INJURY, even an old one · FACE, EYES OR PRIVATE PARTS · AROUND THE MOUTH · NOISY BREATHING or a change in voice or cry.** **Plus special sites: hands, feet, perineum, genitalia, CIRCUMFERENTIAL burns, and a DELAYED PRESENTATION or a story that doesn't fit the child's development.**

**THE DISPOSITION SENTENCES. VERSION A (8%): 'the good news first: Charlie DOESN'T need to stay in hospital. The burn covers about eight percent, it's not on his face or private parts, his breathing is normal, and there's nothing else going on — so we can look after this as an outpatient.' VERSION B (12%): 'the most important thing I need to tell you is that Charlie DOES need to come into hospital. The burn covers about twelve percent, and in small children, once a burn is over about TEN PERCENT, they lose fluid and body heat much faster than adults and can become dehydrated. He needs a drip and careful monitoring, which we can't do at home.'**

**THE NUMBERS: 20 MINUTES of cool running water, STILL WORTHWHILE UP TO 3 HOURS · 10% TBSA is the admission and referral line · CHILD: head 18%, each arm 9%, each leg 13.5%, trunk 18% FRONT + 18% BACK, perineum 1% · Lund and Browder head 19% at birth, 17% at 1–4 years, 13% at 5–9 · PALM INCLUDING FINGERS = 1% · MODIFIED PARKLAND 3–4 mL/kg per % TBSA of Hartmann's over 24 h FROM THE TIME OF THE BURN, half in the first 8 h, PLUS MAINTENANCE in a child · urine output ~1 mL/kg/h · review 24–48 h; healing beyond 3 weeks predicts scarring.** VERIFY

CORRECTIONS carried from the transcript: **the risk from exposure is HYPOthermia, not 'hyperthermia' — keep the child warm · the child's TRUNK is 18% FRONT AND 18% BACK, not 18% total · a fully immunised Australian child has had FIVE tetanus-containing doses (2, 4, 6, 18 months, 4 years), not twenty — the threshold is a dose within 5 years for a tetanus-prone wound.** VERIFY **Silver sulfadiazine is now less favoured — it obscures depth assessment and is avoided in small infants.**

**MANAGEMENT, EVERY VERSION: ANALGESIA FIRST (paracetamol 15 mg/kg, ibuprofen 10 mg/kg; intranasal fentanyl 1.5 microgram/kg if severe) · COOL if within 3 hours · WARM THE CHILD · clean the wound and surrounding skin · NON-ADHERENT DRESSING (silicone or hydrocolloid) — never plain gauze on a moist burn · PHOTOGRAPHS WITH CONSENT · push oral fluids if going home · tetanus booster if over 5 years. ADD IF ≥10% OR A SPECIAL SITE: ADMIT · IV Hartmann's by modified Parkland plus maintenance · strict fluid balance and catheter · FBE, UEC, glucose, VBG, group and hold · NBM initially, NG for ileus · burns unit discussion.** VERIFY **AVOID: ice · butter, toothpaste, creams · circumferential cling film · de-roofing blisters in primary care · prophylactic antibiotics · deciding it can't be abuse because the family seems nice.** **SCARRING, answered honestly: 'burns at this depth usually heal in about two weeks without much scarring, but deeper patches can scar — and BURNS DECLARE THEMSELVES over the first day or two, which is why we review him.'** SA: **mandated notifiers under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017; CARL 13 14 78; REASONABLE SUSPICION, not certainty, is the threshold** · paediatric burns at the **Women's and Children's Hospital** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** from a country site · **PATS** · **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **WIPE, ACKNOWLEDGE, AND OPEN WITH ANALGESIA — a free mark**: **'good morning, I'm Dr ___. Are you Charlie's mum? Hi Charlie. I can see he's been burnt, and I can see how upsetting this is — it happens incredibly fast with three-year-olds. Before anything else — HAS HE HAD SOMETHING FOR THE PAIN?'** *Panadol half an hour ago.* → **'good — we'll give him something stronger shortly.'**

**Signpost**: **'I'm going to ask you exactly what happened, then look at the examination findings, then talk you through the plan.'** **Opening with analgesia buys goodwill from a mother who is expecting to be judged.**

**EXPLORE THE BURN — mechanism is where a story first stops fitting**: **'when did it happen? How did it happen — tell me exactly what he was doing? What did he burn himself with — hot water, soup, a hot surface, electricity, a chemical? Where on his body?'** *An hour ago; soup; turned to the sink; front and right arm.*

**★ FIRST AID — and ask FOR HOW LONG**: **'what did you do straight afterwards — did you get his clothes off, and did you run it under water? FOR HOW LONG? Did you put anything on it?'** *Two or three minutes; wet towel; nearly butter.*

**CORRECT IT KINDLY, AND ACT ON THE THREE-HOUR WINDOW**: **'that was exactly the right instinct. The recommendation is twenty minutes of cool running water, and because it's only been an hour, we can still do some of that here — it's worth it up to three hours after a burn. And good that you didn't use butter — butter and ice both make burns worse.'**

**★ THE FIVE RED FLAGS — signpost as a block**: **'I'm going to ask a few specific things that change how I treat this. Are there any BLISTERS? Is there ANY OTHER BURN OR INJURY anywhere on him, even an old one? Any burn to his FACE, his EYES or his PRIVATE PARTS? Anything around his MOUTH? Any NOISY BREATHING, or a change in his voice or his cry?'** *Blisters on his tummy; nothing else.*

**TETANUS AND PAST HISTORY — ask it though he's covered**: **'is he up to date with his immunisations, particularly tetanus? Any medical problems, regular medicines or allergies? Has he been in hospital before?'** *All up to date; healthy; never.*

**★ NORMALISE, THEN THE HOME SCREEN — every version**: **'I ask everybody this next bit, so please don't read anything into it. Most burns at this age are exactly what they look like. How are things going at home generally? Who lives with you? Do you have support around you? Any stresses — money, housing, anyone unwell? Who was looking after him when it happened?'**

**She asks 'am I in trouble?' — answer it**: **'not at all. Pulling something hot down is one of the commonest accidents there is at this age, and you brought him straight in, which is the important part.'**

**★ READ THE CARD — depth and size as two sentences, absences named**: **'the chart shows a 12% total body surface area burn to the anterior trunk and right arm. It's blistered, moist and pink, so superficial to mid dermal. There's no facial, perineal or circumferential involvement and no airway concern, and his observations are normal for a three-year-old.'** **Do NOT recalculate.**

**★ THE DISPOSITION — FIRST SENTENCE, WITH THE NUMBER**: **'the most important thing I need to tell you is that Charlie DOES need to come into hospital. The burn covers about twelve percent of his body, and in small children, once a burn is over about ten percent, they lose fluid and body heat much faster than adults do. He needs a drip and careful monitoring, and that isn't something we can do at home.'**

**She asks 'is he going to be scarred?' — honest, never 'definitely not'**: **'I'll be honest rather than reassuring: burns at this depth usually heal in about two weeks without much scarring, but the deeper patches can scar, and we won't know exactly how deep it is for a day or two, because burns declare themselves. That's one of the reasons we watch it closely.'**

**THE PLAN, AFTER THE DECISION**: stronger pain relief now · clean the burn and **a special non-stick dressing — ordinary gauze sticks and hurts coming off** · **photographs with your permission** · a drip, **fluids in and out measured**, bloods · **we keep him WARM** · discussion with the burns team · **you can stay with him the whole time.**

**★ 'IS THIS MY FAULT?' — answer the guilt, DEFER the prevention advice**: **'no. This is the single commonest way a three-year-old gets burnt, and it happens in careful households every day. When he's better I'll give you a couple of practical things — hot bowls back from the edge, kettle cords tucked away — but that's for later, not now.'** **Lecturing her while she cries ends the cooperation.**

**VERSION A instead — the sentence flips**: **'the good news first — he doesn't need to stay in hospital,'** then clean, dress, regular paracetamol and ibuprofen, **push fluids**, photos, keep warm, **review in 24 to 48 hours**, and red flags: **fever, drowsiness, not drinking, increasing pain, or a smell from the dressing.** **Do not admit him.**
pefe: **READ THE TOTAL off the chart — it arrives marked and added up. DEPTH and SIZE as SEPARATE sentences. Name the ABSENT features — face, perineum, circumferential, airway.**
**SIMPLE ERYTHEMA (epidermal burn) IS NOT COUNTED in TBSA. At the bedside, the child's own PALM INCLUDING FINGERS ≈ 1%.**
**Why not adult nines: the child's HEAD is proportionally larger and the LEGS smaller** — use Lund and Browder or paediatric proportions.
**One wound, several depths — describe rather than grade.** A white waxy centre won't heal without grafting; a moist pink edge heals in two weeks.
**ANALGESIA FIRST · COOL if within 3 hours (20 min cool running water) · WARM THE CHILD · non-adherent dressing · PHOTOGRAPHS WITH CONSENT.**

**≥10% or a special site: ADMIT · modified Parkland 3–4 mL/kg/% Hartmann's over 24 h FROM THE TIME OF THE BURN, half in 8 h, PLUS MAINTENANCE · catheter, urine ~1 mL/kg/h · FBE, UEC, glucose, VBG, group and hold · NBM, NG for ileus · burns unit.** VERIFY

★ THE X-RAY — Version A
A ROUND RADIO-OPAQUE DISC in the LOWER THIRD OF THE OESOPHAGUS, MIDLINE, seen FACE-ON, uniform density, NO HALO. Lungs normal, TRACHEA INTACT. A single smooth disc — most consistent with a COIN

The disc at the level of the ARCH with a DOUBLE RIM — a HALO. That is a BUTTON BATTERY. On the lateral, a STEP-OFF between the two faces. If you see the halo, SAY BATTERY WITH CONFIDENCE

The oesophagus is a FLATTENED tube in the coronal plane, so a disc lies FLAT and is seen FACE-ON. The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings, so a coin there lies EDGE-ON and appears as a LINE on the AP. An object this size rarely passes the cords anyway

At the grandparents'. Alone in the lounge with his 4-year-old brother for ABOUT AN HOUR. Found drooling and screaming about half an hour before arrival — 'SO AN HOUR AND A HALF AGO AT MOST.' No one saw it. His brother said he COUGHED ONCE. The clock runs from INGESTION, not arrival — SAY IT ALOUD

**★ ONE QUESTION DECIDES THE STATION: 'WHAT DID HE SWALLOW, AND IS THERE ANY CHANCE IT WAS A BUTTON BATTERY OR A MAGNET?' Candidates fail by ACCEPTING 'A COIN' AND MOVING ON. The examiner has scripted the mother to volunteer a coin; the battery is hidden in the ORNAMENT, the CABINET or the TOY. The behaviour marked is a DELIBERATE, NAMED RISK ASSESSMENT OF THE OBJECT — and letting the answer CHANGE YOUR URGENCY.**

**THE SCRIPT, VERSION A (coin, no battery mentioned): 'you've said it might be a coin. I need to ask two specific questions. Is there any possibility it was a small round battery, the kind in toys, remotes or hearing aids? And could it have been a magnet, or more than one? I ask because those two things need much faster treatment than a coin.' VERSION B/C: 'because there were batteries within his reach, I'm going to TREAT THIS AS A POSSIBLE BATTERY UNTIL WE PROVE OTHERWISE. A battery in the food pipe can burn the wall within two hours, so we act now rather than watching and waiting.'**

**THE HIGH-RISK OBJECTS — name the first two unprompted: BUTTON BATTERY — caustic injury within 2 HOURS, perforation, AORTO-OESOPHAGEAL FISTULA · MAGNETS — TWO OR MORE (or magnet + metal) can trap bowel between them · LARGE objects — over 6 cm long or 2 cm wide (the pylorus and C-loop are the bottlenecks) · SHARP objects · expanding water beads, usually invisible on X-ray.** **The HIGH-RISK CHILD: prior oesophageal or bowel surgery, atresia repair, stricture, fundoplication — objects impact where a normal child's would pass.**

**★ THE X-RAY IN THREE COLOURS, LANDMARKS BEFORE THE ABNORMALITY**: **'this is an X-ray of his neck, chest and tummy. Three colours: WHITE is bone, GREY is soft tissue like muscle and organs, BLACK is air. Down the middle is his spine, these curved lines are his ribs, these two dark areas are his lungs and they look normal. His WINDPIPE is here and it is OPEN. This bright white circle is a METAL OBJECT sitting in his FOOD PIPE, the lower part — it hasn't gone into the stomach yet. IT IS NOT IN HIS WINDPIPE.'** **Say 'food pipe, not windpipe' explicitly — her fear is the lungs. Never 'radio-opaque'.**

**THEN THE SENTENCE THAT DEPENDS ON THE FILM. A: 'a single smooth disc, most consistent with a coin. I've looked carefully for the DOUBLE EDGE a battery shows and I can't see one — but because I can't be certain, we manage it carefully.' B: 'around the edge I can see a SECOND RING, A HALO. That is the sign of a button battery. I'm now certain enough to treat this as a battery, which means we act IMMEDIATELY.'**

Mohammed is 15 months, so it applies. DO NOT DELAY TRANSFER FOR IT.** VERIFY **Battery in the stomach in a well child: some guidelines allow observation with a repeat film at 48 h if under 20 mm and over 5 years — for the exam, say THE GASTROENTEROLOGIST DECIDES and it is treated as urgent.** VERIFY

tasks: Counsel Jenny about SIDS — what it is, the risk factors, and how to reduce the risk
Address her concerns

dx: **SIDS / SUDI SAFE SLEEP COUNSELLING — a structured counselling station with ALMOST NO CLINICAL REASONING. It is FAILED BY GIVING A LIST OF TWO. Small counselling stations are PASS–FAIL ON COMPLETENESS: candidates who say 'on his back, nothing in the cot' and stop have failed, however warm they were.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: THE COMPLETE LIST, DELIVERED KINDLY — position AND environment AND smoking AND breastfeeding. The examiner's checklist is the RED NOSE SIX PLUS THE TWO 'IFS'. Make the structure AUDIBLE — 'there are six things: one… two… three…' — and end with the sentence that names the aim: 'OUR GOAL IS TO PREVENT SIDS BY REMOVING THE RISKS WE CAN CHANGE.'**

CORRECTION — **the definition. SIDS is SUDDEN INFANT DEATH SYNDROME — the 'S' is SYNDROME, not 'sleep' (the source expands it as 'sudden infant death during sleep'). It is the sudden, unexpected death of an infant under 1 year that REMAINS UNEXPLAINED after a FULL INVESTIGATION including autopsy, death-scene examination and history review. SUDI — Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy (source: 'SUTI') — is the UMBRELLA term for ALL sudden unexpected infant deaths, explained and unexplained; SIDS is the unexplained subset.** **If challenged: 'SIDS is a diagnosis of exclusion within SUDI; the S is syndrome.'**

**THE DEFINITION IN HER WORDS, including the Coroner without alarming her**: **'SIDS stands for sudden infant death syndrome. It means a baby who seemed well dies suddenly and unexpectedly, almost always during sleep, and even after a full investigation — which every family goes through with the Coroner — no cause is found. Sometimes a cause IS found — an infection, a heart rhythm problem, or something in the cot blocking breathing — and then it isn't called SIDS. It isn't about blame.'** **When she asks 'was it something they did?': 'we can't know, and it isn't for us to judge. What we do know is which sleep practices make it much less likely.'**

**RISK FACTORS, IN THREE BOXES — the modifiable column IS the consultation. NON-MODIFIABLE, said once, not dwelt on: premature or small babies · boys · age 2–4 MONTHS (Max's age) · families with fewer supports — 'we can't change those, and they don't mean it will happen.' MODIFIABLE, all FOUR by name: sleeping on the TUMMY OR SIDE · an unsafe SLEEP ENVIRONMENT — soft surfaces, pillows, loose bedding, sharing a bed or couch · SMOKING in pregnancy or the home · NOT BREASTFEEDING. PROTECTIVE: breastfeeding, immunisation, a dummy at sleep time.** **Peak 2–4 months; ~90% under 6 months; higher in preterm, low-birth-weight and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander infants, and where smoking and unsafe sleeping co-exist.**

**★ THE RED NOSE SIX, IN FULL, COUNTED ALOUD: ONE — always on his BACK, day and night; once he rolls BOTH WAYS by himself you don't need to turn him back. TWO — HEAD AND FACE UNCOVERED; no hats or hoods indoors (the BEANIE), nothing that can ride up. THREE — SMOKE-FREE pregnancy, home and CAR. FOUR — a SAFE COT meeting the Australian standard; FIRM FLAT mattress with no gaps; fitted sheet; FEET AT THE FOOT OF THE COT; blankets TUCKED FIRMLY NO HIGHER THAN THE CHEST, or a sleeping bag with fitted neck and armholes and NO HOOD; NO pillows, doonas, bumpers, soft toys or sheepskins; a comfortable room, DON'T OVERHEAT. FIVE — his OWN COT IN YOUR ROOM, beside your bed, for the first 6–12 MONTHS. SIX — BREASTFEED if you can.** VERIFY

**CO-SLEEPING HARM REDUCTION — realistic, scored under 'address concerns', and never a lecture**: **'the safest place is his own cot pushed right up against your side of the bed, so he's within reach. findings: The stem

Jenny, 28, mother of Max, 4 months, WELL. Her NEIGHBOUR'S 3-month-old son DIED SUDDENLY IN HIS SLEEP LAST WEEK. She has come to ask what SIDS is and how to prevent it in Max. Tasks: counsel her about SIDS — what it is, the risk factors and how to reduce the risk — and address her concerns
Her opening
Voice shaking: 'My neighbour's baby died last week. Cot death. He was three months old. I can't stop thinking it could be Max. I GET UP TEN TIMES A NIGHT to check he's breathing'
★ HIDDEN AGENDA 1 — co-sleeping

'…He sleeps IN OUR BED most nights. I know you're not supposed to.' Disclosed ONLY if asked whether anything else worries her — or volunteered after the six steps: 'but he sleeps in our bed…' He sleeps under HER DOONA. There's a cot in the nursery, UNUSED
★ HIDDEN AGENDA 2 — smoking

'I smoke — ONLY OUTSIDE, never near him.' Five a day. Disclosed when smoking is mentioned. Her husband doesn't smoke — but smoke on clothes and hair still raises the risk, AND IT MAKES BED-SHARING HIGHER RISK
★ HIDDEN AGENDA 3 — the monitor and the dummy
Her husband bought an UNDER-MATTRESS BREATHING MONITOR — 'is it enough?' Not using a dummy yet — 'should I?' She raises both HERSELF during the 'ifs'
★ HIDDEN AGENDA 4 — her own state
EXHAUSTED, ON EDGE, CRYING A LOT. Disclosed ONLY if you ask how SHE is. If never asked, at the end: 'SORRY, I'M A MESS — I HAVEN'T SLEPT IN A WEEK'

The nursery is WARM and he wears a BEANIE AT NIGHT — step two (head and face uncovered) and overheating, both, in one answer
Background
Term, WELL, BREASTFED AND THRIVING — feeding going well. Sleeps ON HIS BACK, but in their bed. Immunisations up to date. Husband supportive but 'THINKS I'M OVERREACTING.' Would come back with him
