Anxious, guilty, grateful when treated kindly. She asks 'SO WAS IT SOMETHING THEY DID?' herself. She BRISTLES IF LECTURED: 'I know, I know'

19, Aboriginal, 6-week-old daughter. 'She only sleeps ON MY CHEST ON THE COUCH. And I smoke — MY PARTNER TOO, INSIDE. My nan says that's how we always did it.' Culturally safe harm reduction: offer an Aboriginal health worker first, keep her CLOSE AND SAFE, a cot or bassinet beside where she sleeps, AMIC and Red Nose can help with a safe sleep space, Quitline and patches FREE THROUGH CLOSING THE GAP — and never forget the partner's smoking

dx: **TRISOMY 21 SUSPECTED ON CLINICAL FEATURES — UNCONFIRMED until the karyotype (or rapid FISH / QF-PCR) returns. A breaking-bad-news counselling station with NO history task and NO examination task.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — 'IT IS NOT CONFIRMED', SAID EARLY, SAID PLAINLY, SAID AGAIN. The lecturer would fail any candidate who counsels as though the diagnosis were established. The line must come BEFORE the explanation of chromosomes, and AGAIN BEFORE MANAGEMENT: 'IF the result confirms it, this is what we do.'**

**THE SECOND DISCRIMINATOR IS EMOTIONAL PACING: empathy at the OPENING, AGAIN after her disclosure, and AGAIN at the close — EMPATHY SHOWN TWICE, NOT ONCE. A candidate who delivers a perfect complications list to a mother who is still sobbing HAS NOT PASSED.** **The honest line when she asks you to guess: 'likely enough to test, not confirmed' — BOTH HALVES. 'He probably has it' to seem honest is a trap.**

**THE ONE-LINE STRATEGY: 'NOT CONFIRMED, here is what it would mean, here is what we would do, here is who will help, and children with Down syndrome live long, full lives.' The order: emotional containment → not confirmed → condition → cause → screening → features → complications → care plan → supports → family meeting → hopeful close.**

**CONDITION AND CAUSE IN HER WORDS**: **'our genes come packed in bundles called chromosomes — 23 pairs. In Down syndrome there is an extra copy of chromosome 21, three instead of two. It happens by chance at the moment the egg and sperm join. NOTHING YOU DID OR DIDN'T DO caused it — not the wine at the wedding, not stress, not work. The only known risk factor is the mother's age, and it happens at every age — most babies with Down syndrome are born to younger mothers simply because more younger women have babies.'** CORRECTION — **the lecture says 'an extra PAIR of the 21st chromosome'. It is an extra COPY — three in total.**

**THE MECHANISMS, if an examiner asks: 95% FREE TRISOMY from non-disjunction · 3–4% ROBERTSONIAN TRANSLOCATION — which CAN BE INHERITED, so the parents may need testing · 1–2% MOSAIC. 1 in ~1,100 Australian births; 1:1,000 at 30, 1:100 at 40. Recurrence ~1% for free trisomy.** **SCREENING vs DIAGNOSIS: 'our screening tests are very good, but they estimate a RISK; they can't rule it out. That's why the chromosome test, which is DEFINITE, is being done now.'**

**★ THE COMPLICATIONS — the part most candidates under-deliver, and THYROID AND COELIAC CARRY THE MARKS: heart problems in about HALF (40–50%, AVSD commonest) — a heart scan BEFORE DISCHARGE · bowel problems in the first days (duodenal atresia 2–5%, Hirschsprung) · hearing and vision · an underactive THYROID · COELIAC disease · chest infections · snoring with pauses (OSA) · leukaemia 10–20× · learning difficulties, which vary a great deal — 'most children learn to walk, talk, read and make friends, at their own pace.' THEN THE SENTENCE THAT MATTERS: 'WE LOOK FOR EVERY ONE OF THESE EARLY, AND TREAT THEM AS WE FIND THEM.'** CORRECTION — **coeliac disease is AUTOIMMUNE, not a 'gluten allergy': 'the immune system reacts to gluten and damages the bowel lining' — tTG-IgA plus total IgA, not an IgE allergy.**

**CORRECT THE GOOGLE BELIEF WITH THE NUMBER AND THE REASON**: **'what you read is out of date. Because we now screen for these problems from birth and treat them as we find them, people with Down syndrome live long lives — the average is now AROUND 60 YEARS, and many live well beyond. Most go to MAINSTREAM SCHOOL WITH SUPPORT, many finish school, work, and live semi-independently. A child with Down syndrome can enjoy a long, happy and healthy life.'** VERIFY — **median ~60 in high-income countries, up from ~25 in the 1980s, largely from early cardiac surgery and thyroid and coeliac surveillance.**

**THE CARE PLAN — conditional, then concrete: 'let's wait for the result. IF it confirms Down syndrome, Leo will have a team' — paediatrician; GP as coordinator; cardiology, audiology, ophthalmology; physiotherapy for the floppiness; speech pathology for feeding now and speech later; later psychology and the school. SURVEILLANCE: ECHO before discharge · TSH at birth, 6 and 12 months, then YEARLY · hearing 6–12-monthly to 5 years · vision by 12 months then 1–2-yearly · COELIAC serology once on gluten (~2–3 years) · SLEEP STUDY by 4 years · growth on a Down syndrome chart · NIP immunisation plus annual influenza.** VERIFY

**SUPPORTS — NAMED, not 'there are services available': DOWN SYNDROME SA (information, and parents who've been exactly where she is) · the NDIS, which funds early therapy FROM THE MOMENT OF DIAGNOSIS · CENTRELINK Carer Allowance and Carer Payment · RCH and Down Syndrome Australia fact sheets · and a FAMILY MEETING with her, TOM and the paediatrician when the result is back.** **Close on hope: 'you're in safe hands. Whatever the result, Leo has a team, and you have us.'** **AVOID: 'mongol', 'suffers from', 'Down's child' · listing complications with no plan attached · promising outcomes · reciting frequencies you don't know.** SA: **Women's and Children's Hospital** — paediatric cardiology, the **SA Clinical Genetics Service**, audiology; **PATS**; **Country Health Connect**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if the baby deteriorates; ACCHS and Aboriginal Health Practitioner; **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **ENTER, INTRODUCE, SIT — and break the ice**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the ward doctors. The nurses said you wanted to see someone. Is it Janna? … Is it all right if I sit down here?'** *She nods, crying: 'I'm just so sad, doctor.'*

**★ EMPATHY 1 — NAME IT, OFFER HELP, AND WAIT. Do NOT ask a second open question**: **'I can see that. I'm sorry. I'm here to help you, and I'm not in a rush. When you feel ready, tell me what's worrying you most, and I promise my team and I will do everything we can.'** *Long pause.*
**The statement comes**: *'They told me Leo has Down syndrome. I looked it up last night. It said they only live a few years.'*

**★ EMPATHY 2, THEN PERMISSION**: **'I'm so sorry. Hearing that word about your own baby, and then reading things like that at night on your own — that's a frightening, overwhelming thing to go through. Would it be okay if I gave you some accurate information, and then we go through anything you've read?'** *'Yes. Please.'*

**★ NOT CONFIRMED — BEFORE ANY EXPLANATION**: **'the first thing, and the most important: Down syndrome has NOT been confirmed. The doctor saw some features that can go with it, so a blood test called a karyotype was sent to look at Leo's chromosomes. Until it comes back — a few days, sometimes faster — we don't know. Right now it's a possibility, not a diagnosis.'**

**She says 'the doctor seemed so sure'**: **'I understand why it came across that way, and I'm sorry. What she saw was enough to TEST — that's different from knowing. Can I explain what the test looks for?'**

**CONDITION AND CAUSE — lay words, 'not your fault'**: chromosomes, 23 pairs, **an extra copy of number 21, three instead of two**, by chance when egg and sperm join — **'nothing you did or didn't do caused it.'**

**★ THE CHAMPAGNE**: *'I had a glass of wine at my sister's wedding. Before I knew.'* → **'that did not cause this. Truly. It had already happened — or not — on the day Leo was conceived. The only known risk factor is the mother's age, and it happens to women of every age.'** **Never 'it's probably because of your age' — she's 31.**

**THE SCREENING QUESTION**: **'did you have the screening test in early pregnancy — the 12-week blood test and scan, or the NIPT?'** *'The 12-week one. Low risk. So how is this happening?'* → **'a fair question. Those tests are very accurate, but they're screening tests — they estimate a risk, and a small number of babies are missed. That's why the chromosome test, which is definite, is being done now.'**

**THE FEATURES — and honour her 'he looks perfect'**: **'he is beautiful. The features are subtle: eyes that slant slightly upward with a little fold at the inner corner, a flatter nose bridge, small ears, a single crease across the palm, a gap between the first two toes, and muscles that feel a bit floppy. Some healthy babies have one or two of these. When several are together, we test.'**

**★ THE COMPLICATIONS — WITH THE SENTENCE THAT CARRIES THE MARK**: **'if it's confirmed, some health problems are more common — and I want to be clear that WE LOOK FOR EVERY ONE OF THEM EARLY.'** Heart in about half, **so a heart scan before he goes home** · bowel problems in the first days · hearing and vision · **an underactive THYROID** · **COELIAC disease, where the immune system reacts to gluten** · chest infections · snoring with pauses · learning difficulties that vary a lot.

**★ 'AND THEY DIE YOUNG' — correct it with the number and the reason**: **'no. That's the part of the internet I want to put right. Because we now screen from birth and treat things as we find them, people with Down syndrome live long lives — around SIXTY years on average, and many well beyond. Most go to mainstream school with support. Many adults work and live semi-independently.'** *She stops crying: 'Sixty. Okay.'*

**'Will he go to a normal school?' — hope with honesty, no promise**: **'most children go to mainstream school with support — the family, the GP and the school plan it together.'** **Never 'he'll be fine.'**

**★ THE PLAN — CONDITIONAL AGAIN**: **'first we wait for the result. IF it confirms Down syndrome, Leo has a team'** — paediatrician, GP coordinating, heart, hearing and eye specialists, physio, speech pathology, later psychology and school. **Concretely: heart scan before discharge, thyroid test now and regularly, hearing and vision checks through childhood, a coeliac test when he's older, growth on a special chart.**

**SUPPORTS — NAMED**: **'for you and your family: Down Syndrome SA, who have information and parents who've been exactly where you are; the NDIS, which funds his therapy from diagnosis; and Centrelink's Carer Allowance and Carer Payment. I'll give you fact sheets.'** *'I didn't know there was anything like that.'*

**THE FAMILY MEETING — and it unlocks the hidden agenda**: **'I'd like to set up a family meeting with you, your partner and the paediatrician when the result is back.'** *'My husband Tom — he's gone quiet. Can you talk to him too?'* → **'of course — that's exactly what the family meeting is for, and I can see him today if he'd like.'**

**OTHER CONCERNS, THEN THE HOPEFUL CLOSE — empathy a third time**: **'is there anything else worrying you that we haven't covered? … You're in safe hands. Whatever the result, Leo has a team, and you have us. I'll come back this afternoon, and the nurses can call me any time.'**
pefe: **No history task and no examination task — the marks are empathy, the not-confirmed statement, a plain explanation, the complications with their plan, the life-expectancy correction, named supports and a family meeting.**
**KARYOTYPE (sent). Rapid FISH / QF-PCR if available — an answer in 24–72 h.**
**ECHOCARDIOGRAM and cardiology review BEFORE DISCHARGE — AVSD may have NO MURMUR early.**
**FBC — transient myeloproliferative disorder, polycythaemia. TSH via the newborn screen. RED REFLEX (cataract). Feeding assessment and weight. Hearing screen.**

**NOT-TO-MISS NOW: BILIOUS VOMITING or no meconium (duodenal atresia, Hirschsprung) · murmur or cyanosis · absent red reflex · hypotonia affecting feeds.** Green vomit on day 2 = duodenal atresia until proven otherwise — NBM, NG, AXR double bubble, surgical referral.
**Genetics counselling — a TRANSLOCATION means PARENTAL KARYOTYPES; recurrence ~1% for free trisomy; NIPT offered early in a next pregnancy.**

**SURVEILLANCE: TSH birth, 6 mo, 12 mo, then yearly · hearing 6–12-monthly to 5 yr · vision by 12 mo then 1–2-yearly · coeliac serology once on gluten (~2–3 yr) · sleep study by 4 yr · Down syndrome growth chart · NIP plus annual influenza.** VERIFY
**Paediatrician follow-up at 2 weeks. NDIS early childhood referral. Down Syndrome SA. Centrelink. Family meeting. GP care plan with the surveillance schedule.**
**Screen BOTH parents for depression. Atlanto-axial instability symptoms and leukaemia signs belong on the long-term list.**

findings: The stem

Postnatal ward. Janna, 31, term boy LEO born 14 hours ago, 3.1 kg, Apgars 8 and 9. The paediatric registrar saw: UPWARD-SLANTING PALPEBRAL FISSURES, FLAT NASAL BRIDGE, LOW-SET SMALL EARS, SINGLE TRANSVERSE PALMAR CREASE, HYPOTONIA. A KARYOTYPE HAS BEEN SENT AND IS PENDING. Baby pink, feeding, sats 97% air. Tasks: counsel her, address her concerns, answer her questions
★ THE FIRST MINUTE — SILENCE IS THE TEST
She is CRYING HARD and will NOT answer your first open question — only 'I'M JUST SO SAD.' Asking 'how can I help?' a SECOND TIME is the trap. NAME THE FEELING, OFFER HELP, AND WAIT
★ HER OPENING STATEMENT — only after you name her feelings

'They told me Leo HAS DOWN SYNDROME. I GOOGLED IT. THEY ONLY LIVE A FEW YEARS.' She heard 'he HAS it' when the registrar said 'some features.' She read a 2 a.m. forum thread saying 'they don't live past their teens'
★ THE NOT-CONFIRMED MOMENT

'BUT THE DOCTOR SOUNDED SO SURE' — then 'SO HE MIGHT NOT HAVE IT?' She CALMS NOTICEABLY when told it isn't confirmed. If you say 'HE HAS DOWN SYNDROME' AS FACT she sobs 'SO IT'S DEFINITE?' — MARKED AS A FAIL
★ HER HIDDEN GUILT

'I had ONE GLASS OF CHAMPAGNE at my sister's wedding BEFORE I KNEW.' She secretly blames herself — raised after you say 'not your fault', or late if never asked about concerns. And if you say 'IT'S BECAUSE OF YOUR AGE': 'I'M THIRTY-ONE!'
The screening answer
'The 12-WEEK ONE. IT SAID LOW RISK. SO HOW IS THIS HAPPENING?' — screening estimates a risk; it can't rule it out
★ THE COMPLICATIONS LIST — two scripted reactions

List them WITHOUT saying each is screened and treated early → she CRIES HARDER: 'SO HE'LL BE SICK HIS WHOLE LIFE?' List them WITH early screening → 'AND THEY DIE YOUNG?' Never mention THYROID or COELIAC → she does NOT prompt, and marks it missing
★ THE LIFE-EXPECTANCY MOMENT
Give the modern figure and she STOPS CRYING: 'SIXTY. OKAY.' Then 'WILL HE GO TO A NORMAL SCHOOL?' — accept 'mainstream with support.' If you say 'HE'LL BE FINE': 'YOU CAN'T KNOW THAT'
The baby now
'He's feeding okay. He's A BIT FLOPPY when I hold him'
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA
Her husband TOM has 'GONE SILENT and is sitting in the CAR PARK.' 'CAN YOU TALK TO TOM?' — volunteered when the family meeting is offered, or late if never asked about concerns
If you use jargon
Trisomy, hypotonia, AVSD, serology → 'WHAT DOES THAT MEAN?'
Variants

The FATHER ARRIVES ANGRY: 'WHO MISSED THIS? THE SCAN WAS NORMAL!' — acknowledge, no blame, screening limits · 'WILL OUR NEXT BABY HAVE IT?' — about 1 in 100 for free trisomy; translocation higher, so parental karyotypes and genetics · the RESULT RETURNS POSITIVE during the station — 'the test has confirmed Down syndrome. I'm sorry'
Other practice cards

Baby VOMITS GREEN on day 2 → DUODENAL ATRESIA until proven otherwise: NBM, NG tube, AXR (DOUBLE BUBBLE), surgical referral · Aboriginal family from Port Augusta → ACCHS in the meeting, PATS to WCH, extended family, Closing the Gap

stem: General practice, regional South Australia. RILEY, 18 MONTHS, brought by his mother JENNY. THE CHILD HEALTH NURSE HAS REFERRED HIM because of AN ABNORMAL WEIGHT found when his growth was plotted at his routine check. YOU HAVE NOT YET SEEN THE GROWTH CHART. She says: 'the nurse told me he's not putting on weight like he should, and I'm worried.'

Afebrile, immunisations up to date, no medications, no known allergies. History FIVE MINUTES, then THE CHART IS HANDED TO YOU, then diagnosis and differentials, then management. VERSION B is COELIAC; VERSION C has A COMPLETELY NORMAL CHART.
tasks: Take a focused history for five minutes
Interpret the growth chart and explain it to the mother in plain English
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differentials, with your reasons
Outline your immediate management
findings: ★ THE CHART — Version A

Tracked the 50TH CENTILE TO ABOUT 8 MONTHS, then FLATTENED AND DRIFTED DOWN, crossing the 15th and now ON OR JUST BELOW THE 3RD. TWO MAJOR CENTILE LINES CROSSED — act. Length and head circumference PRESERVED
★ THE CHART — Version C, the trap

COMPLETELY NORMAL — ON THE 50TH AT EVERY VISIT. Examination normal. Identical opening, and she volunteers 'HE'S A FUSSY EATER.' Candidates fail by PATTERN-MATCHING THE RECALL and diagnosing faltering growth WITHOUT LOOKING AT THE CHART
The chart is only given at five minutes
The examiner CUTS YOU OFF EXACTLY AT FIVE MINUTES of history, then hands it over. You have NOT seen it while taking the history
The complaint, clarified

Two months ago 'a bit low'; this time 'dropping.' 'NOT LOSING. Just not putting it on. And he IS SMALL next to the others at playgroup.' The LOSING / NOT-GAINING / SMALL question is a MARKED ITEM because it changes the differential
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA — offered if you ask her ideas
'I think it's because HE'S A FUSSY EATER. He won't eat what I give him.' Her explanation for everything
★ THE INTAKE — vague unless pushed with specifics

'HONESTLY? I'M NOT REALLY SURE what he eats. He picks at things.' An open question gets an open, unhelpful answer. Pushed: breastfed to 4 months then bottles · 'FOUR OR FIVE BOTTLES OF MILK a day — HE'LL ALWAYS TAKE MILK' · solids at 6 months, FRUIT AND TOAST, WON'T TOUCH MEAT OR VEGGIES · a SIPPY CUP OF JUICE HE CARRIES ROUND ALL DAY · EATS IN FRONT OF THE TELLY. She CANNOT describe what he ate yesterday — VAGUENESS IS THE FINDING
Absorption and utilisation — all negative, and that is the point

Two or three NORMAL nappies, nothing greasy, NO BLOOD. No vomiting, arching or rash. No family bowel disease. The odd cold, nothing needing antibiotics. NOT blue, sweaty or breathless on feeds — 'he just doesn't want much'
The well-baby sweep

Active, into everything, WALKS, SAYS A FEW WORDS, plays fine. Nappies unchanged. Born at term, 3.4 kg, heel-prick and six-week check normal. Mother an average-sized child. NORMAL DEVELOPMENT and BIRTH WEIGHT push AWAY from genetic or antenatal causes, towards an ACQUIRED, POSTNATAL INTAKE problem
★ THE PSYCHOSOCIAL BOX — warn her first

Just her and Riley; SPLIT WITH HIS DAD IN PREGNANCY; he's not involved. Mum in QUEENSLAND, no friends nearby. MONEY 'REALLY TIGHT — some weeks I don't know how I'll do the shop.' A glass of wine some nights, no drugs, nobody she's frightened of. Guarded and a little defensive — she ALREADY FEELS JUDGED
★ THE MOOD DISCLOSURE — the auto-fail pivot

ONLY if asked directly about her own mood: quiet, close to tears — '[pause] NOT GOOD. I've been pretty down. I'M NOT IN A GOOD HEADSPACE.' If never asked, at about 4:30: 'IT'S BEEN REALLY HARD, ACTUALLY.' Carrying on with the checklist after this IS A FAIL ON ITS OWN. On the safety question: 'no, nothing like that. I just feel flat and tired'
Her pushes

'SO THERE IS SOMETHING WRONG WITH HIM' after the chart · crying, 'SO IT'S MY FAULT?' when her situation is linked to his weight · 'WILL THEY TAKE HIM OFF ME?' when notification is mentioned — settles if answered warmly and specifically. If you're JUDGEMENTAL she closes down: 'I DO MY BEST'
★ VERSION B — coeliac

SIX loose motions a day, FOUL, HARD TO CLEAN OFF. Breastfed to 4 months; solids with good variety; the FATHER'S SIDE has bowel problems. Card: PALE child, MILD ABDOMINAL DISTENSION. COELIAC DISEASE WITH IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA; IBD second, but no blood and 18 months is early. The mark most candidates drop: 'PLEASE DON'T TAKE GLUTEN OUT OF HIS DIET YET'
Other practice cards

Weight, length and head circumference ALL on the 3RD SINCE BIRTH, BOTH PARENTS SHORT, well, developing normally → CONSTITUTIONALLY SMALL — normal; mid-parental height, reassure, plot in three months · length and head circumference ALSO falling → not simple faltering growth; severe or long-standing disease

dx: **VERSION A: FALTERING GROWTH (SLOW WEIGHT GAIN) FROM INADEQUATE INTAKE, in the setting of NEGLECT OF FEEDING — a form of child abuse — with psychosocial factors driving it. VERSION B: coeliac disease with iron deficiency. VERSION C: NORMAL GROWTH. One line to hold: THE CHART TELLS YOU WHETHER THERE IS A PROBLEM; THE HISTORY TELLS YOU WHICH OF FOUR BOXES IT IS IN; THE PSYCHOSOCIAL BOX IS THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE STATION.**

**★ THE SENTENCE THAT DECIDES THIS STATION — say it before anything else about the chart: 'I AM NOT LOOKING AT ONE POINT — I AM LOOKING AT THE TREND ACROSS ALL HIS VISITS.' In Version A it earns you the diagnosis; in Version C it is the only thing that stops you INVENTING A DISEASE IN A HEALTHY CHILD. Then: 'he started on the 50th line and he is now on the 3rd — that is a fall of TWO MAJOR CENTILE LINES.'**

**DEFINITION: a SUSTAINED FALL ACROSS TWO OR MORE MAJOR CENTILE LINES on serial weights, or weight persistently well below expected on a plotted trend. ONE DOT IS NEVER A DIAGNOSIS. Major lines: 3rd · 15th · 50th · 85th · 97th. Order of loss: WEIGHT, THEN LENGTH, THEN HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE.** CORRECTION — **the transcript's first definition, 'weight below expected for age and sex', should be REJECTED OUT LOUD — it labels every constitutionally small child. Examiners reward saying so.** VERIFY the centile-space thresholds (1, 2 or 3 spaces by birth centile; below 0.4th at any age) against current RCH guidance.

**LANGUAGE RULE: say 'SLOW WEIGHT GAIN' or 'FALTERING GROWTH' to the parent. 'Failure to thrive' has been retired by RCH and most Australian services because parents hear it as a VERDICT ON THEM.** **And 'slow weight gain is a DESCRIPTION, NOT A CAUSE' — stopping there as though it were the diagnosis is a named auto-fail.**

**★ THE FOUR BOXES — tick every one OUT LOUD; the examiner is marking coverage, and it is usually more than one: 1 NOT ENOUGH IN — inadequate or unbalanced intake, feeding difficulty, excess milk or juice, GORD. 2 NOT ABSORBED — coeliac, cow's milk protein allergy, giardia or chronic gastro, cystic fibrosis, liver disease. 3 BURNT TOO FAST — congenital heart disease, recurrent infection, chronic lung disease. 4 THE FEEDER — parental mental illness, drugs, alcohol, poverty, isolation, neglect. Psychosocial factors are the commonest significant contributor and sit UNDERNEATH the other three.** **The rule: EIGHT TO TEN questions in box 1, ONE OR TWO in boxes 2 and 3 — coverage beats depth.**

CORRECTION — **hypothyroidism does NOT belong in the high-demand box.** Untreated hypothyroidism causes poor LINEAR growth with RELATIVE WEIGHT PRESERVATION; the high-metabolic-demand entry is HYPERthyroidism, rare at this age. **Keep hypothyroidism on the list — but for SHORT STATURE, not for burning calories.**

**THE INTAKE BLOCK IS THE LONGEST AND HIGHEST-SCORING — budget 90 seconds and if you haven't asked about milk volume and juice by 3:00, you're behind: breast or formula → solids and age → VARIETY, including an iron source → COW'S MILK IN CUPS A DAY (aim UNDER ABOUT 500 mL/day at this age — more fills him and drives IRON DEFICIENCY) → juice, cordial, lollies, snacks → how long a meal takes and WHERE he eats → who feeds him, childcare.** VERIFY **Accepting 'he eats fine' or 'he's fussy' as an answer is a trap — IF SHE CANNOT TELL YOU WHAT HE ATE YESTERDAY, THAT GOES IN YOUR SUMMARY AS EVIDENCE.**

**EXPLAIN THE PERCENTILE WITH A WORKED EXAMPLE, TRACING THE LINE WITH A FINGER**: **'this chart compares his weight with other boys the same age. If we lined up 100 boys his age, being on the 50th line means he's heavier than 50 of them and lighter than the other 49 — right in the middle. From birth to about eight months he sat right on that line. From around nine months he comes away from it and crosses two of the main lines. He's now on the 3rd line, which means only two or three of those hundred boys would be lighter than him.'**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — HOW YOU SAY THE WORD 'NEGLECT'. Every candidate finds the low mood and the money problems. The pass is decided by what you do with them IN FRONT OF THE MOTHER.** CORRECTION — **the source goes straight to 'I'm concerned he is being neglected for feeding'. Formulating it that way TO YOURSELF is correct; saying it to her in those words LOSES RAPPORT and, in real practice, LOSES THE FAMILY. Deliver it in FIVE STEPS: 1 NAME THE CHILD'S PROBLEM ('slow weight gain') → 2 NAME THE MECHANISM, NOT THE PERSON ('he isn't taking in enough energy and variety') → 3 NAME THE PRESSURES WITHOUT BLAME ('you're doing this on your own, money is tight, your mood has been low — all three together would floor anybody') → 4 OFFER HELP FIRST → 5 BE HONEST ABOUT THE OBLIGATION ('I'm required to let the child protection service know… I'd rather tell you than do it behind your back. It is not about taking him away').**

**MANAGEMENT: measure and plot yourself; get EVERY previous point (the Blue Book, CaFHS) — THE TREND IS THE INVESTIGATION · examine UNDRESSED for bruising or injury · a THREE-DAY DIET DIARY and an OBSERVED FEED · NO SHOTGUN BLOODS in a well child with a clear dietary cause — investigate only what the history points to · intake: energy-dense food, 3 meals + 2–3 snacks, family meals at a table, food BEFORE milk, cap cow's milk, DIETITIAN · psychosocial: TREAT HER DEPRESSION, income and housing support, CaFHS HOME VISITS — THIS IS THE TREATMENT in Version A · NOTIFY CARL · REVIEW 1–2 WEEKS ON THE SAME SCALES.** VERIFY **Version B: tTG-IgA + total IgA WHILE STILL ON GLUTEN, then gastroenterology for biopsy — never remove gluten first.** **Version C: 'he's been on the 50th line since birth and he's still on it today. His weight is completely normal' — NO TESTS — then treat the mealtime battle (division of responsibility, 10–15 neutral offers, 20–30-minute meals at a table, no grazing, never force or bribe).** SA: **mandated notifiers under the Children and Young People (Safety) Act 2017 — REASONABLE SUSPICION, not proof** · **CARL 13 14 78** · **CaFHS 1300 733 606** · **Parent Helpline 1300 364 100** · WCH paediatrics with **PATS** · Country Health Connect dietitian · **TIS 131 450** · ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**. **Never promise secrecy.**
plan: **WIPE, SIT AT HER LEVEL, don't take the child**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the doctors here. Are you Jenny? And this is Riley — hello, mate. Is it all right if I ask you some questions about him and how he's feeding? Before I look at anything — tell me in your own words what's worrying you.'** *The nurse said his weight was dropping; she got scared.*

**THE CONCERN STATEMENT — don't reassure yet**: **'that's a very reasonable thing to be frightened about, and I'm glad she sent you in. We'll work through it together.'** **'I'm sure he's fine' in the first thirty seconds is an early, avoidable loss.**

**★ EXPLORE — including the marked question**: **'when did you first become concerned?'** *Two months ago, a bit low; now dropping.* **'And when you say he isn't gaining — do you mean he's LOSING weight, not gaining as fast as expected, or that he's SMALL compared with other children?'** *Not losing; not putting it on; small at playgroup.*
**HER IDEA — this unlocks the hidden agenda**: **'is there anything in particular you're worried might be causing it?'** *(looking down) 'I think he's just a fussy eater.'*

**★ INTAKE — WARN HER, THEN GO FORENSIC**: **'I'm going to ask quite a lot of detail about food — more than you might expect. Talk me through a typical day from when he wakes up.'** *'Honestly? I'm not really sure. He picks at things.'* **Vagueness is the finding — don't move on.**

**Quantify, don't accept adjectives**: **'roughly how many cups or bottles of cow's milk a day?'** *Four, maybe five.* **'Was he breastfed? Solids — when, and is he getting meat, vegetables, fruit and cereals?'** *Breastfed to four months; fruit and toast; no meat or veggies.* **'Any juice, cordial, lollies or snacks between meals? Where does he eat, and who feeds him?'** *A sippy cup of juice all day; in front of the telly.*

**ABSORPTION — one or two questions, OUT LOUD**: **'how many nappies a day? Are the stools pale, greasy or foul-smelling, hard to clean off? Any blood? Any rash around his mouth after milk? Does he vomit or arch with feeds? Any coeliac or bowel problems in the family?'** *All normal.* **Negatives only earn marks if the examiner HEARS the question.**
**UTILISATION**: **'any long-standing cough, chest infections, urine infections? Does he go BLUE, SWEATY OR BREATHLESS when he feeds, or stop to rest?'** *No — he just doesn't want much.*

**THE FAST SWEEP — under a minute**: **'is he alert and active? Any drop in wet nappies? Is he WALKING, SAYING WORDS, playing with other children? Pregnancy, birth weight, heel-prick and six-week check? Were you or his dad small as children?'** *Walks, words, term, 3.4 kg, all normal.*

**★ THE PSYCHOSOCIAL BOX — WARN HER FIRST**: **'the next few questions I ask every family who comes in about a child's growth — they're not about you personally. How are things at home, and who lives with you? Do you have support nearby? Are money or housing a struggle at the moment? And how has YOUR OWN MOOD been since he was born?'**

**★ THE DISCLOSURE — STOP THE CHECKLIST**: *(quiet, close to tears) 'Not good. I've been pretty down. I'm not in a good headspace.'* → **'thank you for telling me — that took something to say. How low has it got? Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or of harming Riley?'** *'No — I just feel flat all the time.'* **Carrying on here is a fail on its own.**

**★ THE CHART — the trend sentence FIRST, then explain it to her**: **'I'm reading the trend across all his visits, not a single point.'** Then **the 100-boys picture, tracing the line with a finger — the 50th to about eight months, then crossing two of the main lines to the 3rd.** **In Version C, this sentence is what stops you inventing a disease.**

**She says 'so there IS something wrong with him' — step 1 and 2**: **'there's something we need to fix, yes. It has a name — slow weight gain. But that's a description, not a cause. The most likely reason is that he isn't taking in enough energy, and not enough variety — he's filling up on milk and juice, which leaves no room for food.'**

**STEP 3 — THE PRESSURES, WITHOUT BLAME**: **'and I can see exactly why that's happened. You're doing this on your own, money is very tight, and your mood has been low. Any one of those makes feeding a toddler hard. All three together would floor anybody.'** *Crying: 'so it's my fault.'* → **'this is not about blame. You brought him in and you told me the truth — that's exactly what he needed.'**

**THE DIFFERENTIALS, OUT LOUD, EACH WITH A REASON**: absorption problems — coeliac, cow's milk allergy, a gut infection — **but his nappies are normal**; burning too many calories — cystic fibrosis, infections, a heart problem — **but no cough, no infections, no colour change on feeds**; feeding difficulty — **he feeds mechanically well**; something he was born with — **normal birth weight, screening and development.**

**★ STEP 4 — HELP FIRST, THEN STEP 5 — THE HONEST OBLIGATION**: **'the plan is about supporting you, not judging you: cut the milk right back and give food first, a dietitian, the child health nurse visiting at home, and I want to see you about your own mood — treating that will do more for his weight than anything else. I also have to be straight with you: when a child's growth is affected because he isn't getting enough food, I'm required to let the child protection service know. I'd rather tell you than do it behind your back.'**

**'Will they take him off me?' — warm and specific, then the safety-net and teach-back**: **'that's not what this is for — it's to get you support, and I'll keep seeing you both.'** Then **weigh again in a week on these same scales**, and **'come back sooner, or go to ED, if he's very sleepy or floppy, stops drinking, has fewer wet nappies, vomits repeatedly, or there's blood in his nappy. What will you do differently this week?'** *'Cut the milk down and give him food first.'*
pefe: **The chart is handed over at five minutes. SAY THREE THINGS BEFORE COMMITTING: 'I'm looking at the trend across all his visits' · 'he started on the [x] line and is now on the [y] line' · 'that is a fall of [n] major centile lines.'** Trace the line with a finger.

**Measure and plot yourself: WEIGHT, LENGTH AND HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE on the WHO chart; calculate weight-for-length. Get EVERY previous point — the Blue Book (My Health and Development Record) and CaFHS records.**
**If length and head circumference are ALSO falling, it is NOT simple faltering growth — severe or long-standing disease.**
**EXAMINE FULLY UNDRESSED: alertness, hydration, WASTING and loose skin folds, abdomen, heart and chest, mouth (cleft, tongue-tie), dysmorphism — and BRUISING OR INJURY.**
**A THREE-DAY WRITTEN DIET DIARY, and an OBSERVED FEED — worth more than any blood test.**

**NO PANEL OF BLOODS in a well child with a clear dietary cause. If a cause IS suspected: FBC and film, iron studies, UEC, LFT, calcium and phosphate, TSH, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA), CRP/ESR, urine MCS; stool MCS and giardia PCR; calprotectin if IBD, faecal elastase if pancreatic insufficiency; targeted sweat test, echo, CXR, microarray if dysmorphic.**

**COELIAC: test WHILE STILL ON GLUTEN — serology sent after gluten is removed is falsely negative.** Positive tTG → gastroenterology before removing gluten; lifelong GFD; screen first-degree relatives.
**Microcytic anaemia → CUT THE MILK VOLUME and treat iron deficiency.** Cow's milk under about 500 mL/day. VERIFY

**RED FLAGS — ESCALATE TODAY: weight below the 0.4th centile or visible wasting · dehydration, lethargy, too weak to feed · falling length AND head circumference · bruising in a non-mobile child, frozen watchfulness · blood in the stool, persistent vomiting, systemically unwell.**
**Review 1–2 weeks, SAME SCALES, then monthly — weighing more often than weekly produces noise, not information.** VERIFY **Mid-parental height if constitutional smallness is possible.**

dx: **INFANTILE COLIC — recurrent, prolonged crying in an otherwise WELL, THRIVING infant with NO identifiable cause. A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION.** **Wessel 'rule of 3s': crying >3 h/day, >3 days/week, >3 weeks, in a thriving baby. Rome IV drops the 3-week requirement; the diagnosis stays clinical.** VERIFY

**★ THE PASS/FAIL HINGE: colic is a NORMALISING diagnosis, and the temptation is to REASSURE AND STOP. The candidate who passes does THREE THINGS the reassurer does not: SAYS THE EXCLUSIONS OUT LOUD · gives EXPLICIT RED FLAGS WITH AN OPEN DOOR · and NAMES THE SHAKEN-BABY RISK WITH A CONCRETE ALTERNATIVE BEHAVIOUR.**

**The one-line strategy: 'NAME IT, NORMALISE IT, EXCLUDE IT ALOUD, RED-FLAG IT, SETTLE IT, AND LOOK AFTER HER.'** **The communication challenge: giving a 'nothing is wrong' diagnosis to an exhausted parent WITHOUT SOUNDING DISMISSIVE — she must leave feeling BELIEVED, not brushed off.**

**THE STEM TELLS YOU HER MENTAL HEALTH IS NORMAL — that is the examiner RULING OUT POSTNATAL DEPRESSION AS THE DIAGNOSIS, NOT PERMISSION TO IGNORE HER.** **Marks sit in asking 'how are you coping?' ONCE, early, and in the support you build into the plan.**

**PURPLE, TRANSLATED INTO WHAT SHE IS SEEING — not recited: P, it PEAKS around two months · U, it's UNEXPECTED, comes and goes for no reason · R, he RESISTS SOOTHING — you can do everything right and he may still cry · P, a PAIN-LIKE FACE, which is why parents worry he's hurting, though usually he isn't · L, LONG LASTING — more than three hours a day is still within colic · E, worse in the EVENINGS.** **'Some people now call it PURPLE crying' — RCH prefers it because 'colic' implies a gut cause we cannot demonstrate.** VERIFY

**THE LEGS BELIEF — correct it, never agree: 'lots of babies with colic draw their legs up, and it's very natural to read that as tummy pain — but there's NO GOOD EVIDENCE it's coming from his bowel. It's part of the crying, not a sign of a bowel problem.'** **THE NATURAL HISTORY IS THE ACTUAL REASSURANCE: 'it usually starts around six to eight weeks, is at its worst around two months, and settles by three to four months. That's the part I most want you to hold on to — IT DOES END.'**

**CAUSES — HONEST UNCERTAINTY, AND NOT HER FAULT: 'we're not certain what causes it. The two things that seem to trigger it, and that we can work on, are HUNGER AND TIREDNESS — which is why the plan focuses on feeding and sleep. It isn't caused by anything you've done, it isn't because of how you're feeding him, and colic happens to babies with very good parents.'**

**★ THE EXCLUSIONS — THE SINGLE MOST-MARKED SENTENCE IN THE STATION: 'before I settled on this I wanted to be sure there wasn't something else. I EXAMINED HIM TODAY and he's completely normal, and I've CHECKED HIS GROWTH CHART and he's growing beautifully. That makes REFLUX DISEASE AND COW'S-MILK ALLERGY very unlikely — with those we'd expect his growth to suffer, and usually a rash or blood in his stools. And there's nothing to suggest an INFECTION or a BLOCKAGE. Because of that, he doesn't need any blood tests or scans.'** **REASSURANCE WITHOUT STATED EXCLUSIONS IS UNSAFE REASSURANCE.**

**MEDICINES — BE DIRECT, WITHOUT SHAMING: simeticone (Infacol), gripe water and over-the-counter colic drops DO NOT WORK. PPIs are NOT indicated for crying without reflux disease — 'it's not a harmless medicine to give without a reason.' Probiotics (L. reuteri) have some evidence in exclusively breastfed infants but are NOT routine Australian practice — mention only if pushed, badged uncertain.** VERIFY **THE MILK: 'there's nothing wrong with your milk, and I wouldn't change anything at this stage. If he had a milk allergy I'd expect a rash, blood or mucus in his stools, or problems with his growth — and he has none of those. If any of that appeared, we'd look at it properly with a dietitian rather than guessing.'**

**★ THE NEVER-SHAKE SCRIPT — SAID EVERY TIME, UNIVERSALLY: 'one last thing, and I say this to EVERY PARENT, not because of anything about you. Hours of crying is genuinely hard, and it's normal to feel frustrated or even angry. If you ever get to that point, PUT HIM DOWN SOMEWHERE SAFE like his cot, WALK OUT OF THE ROOM, and take a few minutes — he'll be fine crying in his cot for five minutes. What you must NEVER do is SHAKE HIM. Shaking can cause bleeding around the brain and permanent damage, and it happens to ORDINARY PARENTS AT THE END OF THEIR ROPE. Ring me, the Parent Helpline, or someone you trust instead.'** **When she says 'I'd never do that': 'I know. I tell everyone, so that if the moment ever comes you already know what to do instead.'** **ESCALATE rather than counsel if she describes thoughts of harming the baby or herself, has handled him roughly, has no support, there's family violence or substance use, growth or examination isn't actually normal, or there's ANY BRUISE in a non-mobile baby — that is the NAI station.** SA: **CaFHS 1300 733 606** · **Parent Helpline 1300 364 100** · **PANDA 1300 726 306** VERIFY · Purple Crying website · Raising Children Network · **CARL 13 14 78** if NAI.
plan: **WIPE — LET HER SPEAK FIRST**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___, one of the GPs here. You must be Sarah — and this is the little man. From the notes I can see he's been crying a great deal. Before I tell you what I think is happening, tell me how things have been at home.'** *'Awful. Hours every evening. Nothing works. I feel like I'm doing something wrong.'*

**★ ANSWER THE GUILT, THEN THE ONE QUESTION ABOUT HER**: **'that sounds exhausting, and I want to say straight away that you're not doing anything wrong. How are you coping with it — are you getting any sleep?'** *'Not really. My partner works nights.'* → **'that's a lot to carry on your own. Let's go through what I think is going on and what will help.'** **Do NOT re-take the history.**

**NAME IT**: **'what your son has is a condition called infantile colic — long, excessive crying in a baby who is otherwise completely well. Some people now call it purple crying, and each letter describes something you'll recognise. Can I take you through it?'**

**PURPLE, LETTER BY LETTER, TRANSLATED**: **peaks around two months · unexpected, comes and goes · resists soothing, so you can do everything right and he may still cry · a pain-like face, though usually he isn't hurting · long lasting — over three hours is still colic · worse in the evenings.** *'That is exactly him.'*

**★ SHE PUSHES THE LEGS — correct it**: *'But he pulls his legs right up — isn't that pain?'* → **'lots of babies with colic do that, and it's completely natural to read it as tummy pain — but there's no good evidence it's coming from his bowel. It's part of the crying rather than a sign of a bowel problem.'**

**THE NATURAL HISTORY — the actual reassurance**: **'the bit I most want you to hold on to is the timeline: it usually starts around six to eight weeks, is worst around two months, and settles by three to four months. It does end.'** *'So it's not forever.'* → **'it's not forever.'**

**CAUSES — honest, then not her fault**: **'we're not certain what causes it. The two things that seem to trigger it, and that we can work on, are hunger and tiredness — which is why the plan focuses on feeding and sleep. It isn't caused by anything you've done.'**

**★ THE EXCLUSIONS, OUT LOUD — the most-marked sentence**: **'before settling on this I wanted to be sure there wasn't something else. I examined him today and he's completely normal, and his growth chart is normal. That makes reflux disease and cow's-milk allergy very unlikely — with those we'd expect his growth to suffer and usually a rash or blood in his stools. There's nothing to suggest an infection or a blockage either. So he doesn't need any blood tests or scans.'**

**SHE RAISES DAIRY — no dietary change without indication**: *'My sister said I should cut out dairy.'* → **'I wouldn't, at this stage. If he had a milk allergy I'd expect a rash, blood or mucus in his stools, or problems with his growth — and he has none of those. If any of that appeared, we'd look into it properly with a dietitian rather than guessing.'**

**★ THE RED FLAGS AND THE OPEN DOOR — the safety core**: **'now the important part. Bring him straight back, or go to the emergency department, if he develops a FEVER, starts VOMITING repeatedly or the vomit is GREEN, if there's BLOOD in his nappy or his stool looks like REDCURRANT JELLY, if he becomes DROWSY or FLOPPY or won't feed, if he gets a RASH or trouble BREATHING, or if the CRYING SUDDENLY CHANGES. And if you're just worried, that's reason enough — I'd rather see him.'**

**THE DIARY AND THE ROUTINE**: **'keep a sleep–cry diary for a week — when he cries, when he sleeps. Once we see the pattern we can put him down for a nap BEFORE the crying usually starts. And keep his feeds to a regular pattern so hunger isn't part of it.'**

**SETTLING TECHNIQUES**: **'in the evenings, keep things calm — dim lights, less noise, less handling and passing around. Soft music, carrying and walking, rocking, patting his back, a gentle massage or a warm bath all help some babies. Sucking is comforting, so a dummy or a bottle is fine, and a pram or car ride works for some.'**

**★ THE INFACOL — direct, without shaming**: *'I've been giving him Infacol. Should I keep going?'* → **'I'll be straight with you — the colic drops and gripe water don't work. They're harmless, so you haven't done any damage, but I'd rather you put your energy into the things that do help.'**

**SUPPORT — 'it's part of the treatment'**: **'now the part about you. Please get help — your partner, family, a friend — take it in turns so you can rest. Nobody does hours of this on their own.'** *'I don't like asking.'* → **'I know. Ask anyway — it's part of the treatment.'**

**★ THE NEVER-SHAKE SCRIPT — universal, with the alternative**: **'I say this to every parent, not because of anything about you: it's completely okay to feel frustrated, even angry. If you ever reach that point, put him down somewhere safe like his cot, walk out of the room and take a few minutes. What you must never do is shake him — it can cause bleeding around the brain and permanent damage, and it happens to ordinary parents at the end of their rope. Ring me, the Parent Helpline, or someone you trust instead.'** *'I'd never do that.'* → **'I know. I tell everyone.'**

**RESOURCES, REVIEW, SUMMARY, CHECK**: **the Purple Crying website, the Raising Children Network, the child health nurse, and a visit together with her partner — then 'I'd like to see you both again in a week or two, partly for him and partly to see how you're going.'** Summary: **colic; well and growing; peaks at two months, settles by three to four; diary, naps, regular feeds, calm evenings; skip the drops; come back for the warning signs; never shake him. 'How does that sound?'**
pefe: **The examination and growth chart are GIVEN as normal — don't redo them. STATE WHAT THEY RULE OUT, out loud.**
**NO INVESTIGATIONS in a well, growing infant with a normal examination.** Ordering tests to seem thorough is a named error.

**RED FLAGS — six, plus an open door: fever · repeated or BILE-STAINED vomiting · BLOOD or REDCURRANT stool · drowsy, floppy, poor feeding · rash or breathing difficulty · poor weight gain · a SUDDEN CHANGE in the character of the cry.**
**SLEEP–CRY DIARY → plan naps BEFORE the predicted crying window. Regular feeding pattern; check attachment and volume.**

**Reduce stimulation; carrying, rocking, patting, massage, warm bath, music; a dummy; pram or car ride. Wrapping and skin-to-skin help some — with SAFE SLEEPING (back, face uncovered, own cot, smoke-free).**
**DO NOT WORK: gripe water, simeticone (Infacol), colic drops. PPIs NOT indicated for crying alone. Probiotics (L. reuteri) — uncertain, not routine.** VERIFY
**NO dairy exclusion or formula change WITHOUT allergy features or faltering growth — and then dietitian-supervised.**
**Look after the parent: 'how are you coping?', practical support, rest, mood — and the NEVER-SHAKE message with a concrete alternative.**
**Review in 1–2 weeks; RE-WEIGH AND RE-PLOT at review.** Sooner — THIS WEEK — if she says she can't cope.

**DO NOT MISS: intussusception, incarcerated hernia, testicular torsion (surgical emergencies that present as crying) · NON-ACCIDENTAL INJURY — check the child, not just the story · otitis media, UTI, meningitis · faltering growth (if growth is off, the diagnosis is wrong) · the mother's mental health and the risk of abusive head trauma.**

findings: ★ THE RESULTS — the diagnosis is handed to you
HAEMOGLOBIN LOW · MCV LOW · MCH LOW · MCHC LOW · FERRITIN LOW. Iron deficiency anaemia is ALREADY ESTABLISHED — THE STATION IS THE CAUSE. White cells and platelets normal — don't explain them
★ THE TRAP BUILT INTO THE STEM

A URTI a week ago — the reason he was seen. Ask ONCE: 'has he recovered from the chest infection?' — 'yes, completely, ten days ago.' Keep asking fever, cough, sore throat and she KEEPS SAYING HE'S BETTER and does not help you. CHASING THE FLU is an AUTO-FAIL
Pallor and anaemia symptoms
The doctor noticed it last week; 'now you mention it, he DOES look washed out.' About the same. A bit tired, sleeps a lot. 'He's only little, doesn't run around much.' A bit GRIZZLY lately
★ THE NUMBER — the single question that unlocks the diagnosis

Cow's milk since twelve months — 'A FEW GLASSES A DAY' and she STOPS. The current recall no longer volunteers the number, and ONE OR TWO IS ALSO 'A FEW.' Only on 'HOW MANY GLASSES IS A FEW?' — unhurried — does she say: 'um… SEVEN OR EIGHT, probably. He asks for the bottle all day'

Ask 'is his diet healthy?' and she says 'YES, HE EATS WELL.' Breastfed to six months, then formula; 'HE LOVES HIS MILK.' 'He doesn't really like solids — BISCUITS, CHIPS, bits of fruit.' The loss and absorption boxes — all negative in Version A
No rash round the mouth after milk. No bleeding, no surgery, NO BLOOD IN THE STOOL. No greasy stools, no diarrhoea, no rash. No family history of anaemia, coeliac or bowel inflammation
Well child
Alert and active. Growth FINE ON THE BLUE BOOK CHART. Development normal. Immunised, no medicines or allergies

'HAVE I DONE SOMETHING WRONG?' — raised after the cause is explained. 'He just loves his bottle, I couldn't stop him.' If you never ask about red meat: 'SO IS IT JUST THE MILK?' If you give only iron and no diet: 'SO THE MEDICINE FIXES IT?' — MARKED DOWN. Also 'WILL HE NEED A TRANSFUSION?'

Same stem, same iron-deficient picture. Asked about stools: 'yes, ALL THREE — they STICK TO THE PAN, FLOAT, and I have to FLUSH TWICE. My SISTER HAS COELIAC DISEASE.' Management not asked in the recall — be ready anyway. The single most examinable point: KEEP GLUTEN IN
Why NO thalassaemia questions

The FERRITIN IS LOW — not the thalassaemia pattern, which gives a microcytic anaemia with NORMAL OR HIGH ferritin. Asking ethnicity and family history here wastes time; if challenged, EXPLAIN THE FERRITIN LOGIC

dx: **IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA — already established by the results. THE DIAGNOSIS IS HANDED TO YOU; THE STATION IS ABOUT THE CAUSE. VERSION A: EXCESSIVE COW'S MILK PLUS LOW DIETARY IRON — NAME BOTH. VERSION B (the 5-year-old, 2025 recall): COELIAC DISEASE.**

**★ THE PASS/FAIL LINE — TWO THINGS, BOTH EASY TO HALF-DO. FIRST, the diagnosis IS THE CAUSE — 'iron deficiency anaemia' is the result, not the answer. SECOND, management has TWO COMPONENTS — the SUPPLEMENT fixes TODAY'S DEFICIT, the DIET fixes TOMORROW'S. A candidate who names one cause or one treatment has HALF THE STATION.**

**One-line strategy: 'has he recovered from the flu?' → pale and tired → INTAKE, LOSS, ABSORPTION → four numbers in sixty seconds → BOTH causes → iron AND diet.** **Four tasks are hidden inside three in Version A — history, investigations, diagnosis and management.**

**THE THREE CAUSE BOXES — intake is where the recall lives and most of your time goes; ABSORPTION is the box that changes the diagnosis in the older child. INTAKE: late or poor iron-rich solids, no red meat, excessive cow's milk, a vegetarian or vegan family diet. LOSS: bleeding, surgery, occult gut loss from cow's milk protein allergy. ABSORPTION: coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease.** **Ask box 3 in EVERY version — it costs 30 seconds and it is the entire diagnosis in the older child.**

**★ THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT DECIDE THE STATION: 1 'HOW MANY GLASSES?' — the role-player no longer volunteers 'eight glasses'; the current recall answer is a controlled 'A FEW GLASSES', and one or two is also 'a few'. YOU MUST ASK THE NUMBER. 2 'INCLUDING RED MEAT?' — because 'a variety of solids' can mean mashed fruit and vegetables with no iron in them at all.**

**WHY COW'S MILK CAUSES IT — the lecture asks for the first two; the third is worth one sentence if the rash or stool clue appears: IT FILLS HIM UP so he won't eat solids · IT HAS ALMOST NO IRON · and in cow's milk protein allergy it causes OCCULT GUT BLOOD LOSS.** **The ceiling: ONE TO TWO GLASSES (about 500 mL) A DAY.**

**THE FOUR NUMBERS IN SIXTY SECONDS, one sentence each**: **'red blood cells carry oxygen using a substance called HAEMOGLOBIN, and its main building block is IRON. His haemoglobin is LOW. The MCV — the SIZE of the red cells — is low, so they're smaller than they should be. The MCH and MCHC — HOW MUCH HAEMOGLOBIN IS INSIDE EACH CELL — are also low. And his FERRITIN, the IRON STORE, is low. Together we call that iron deficiency anaemia.'** **Asked about the other numbers: 'they were all normal — the red cells are the part that matters today.'** **Ferritin is an ACUTE-PHASE REACTANT — a normal ferritin with a high CRP doesn't exclude deficiency.**

**THE 'BOTH CAUSES' SENTENCE, THEN 'NOT YOUR FAULT'**: **'there are two things going on together. Cow's milk has ALMOST NO IRON in it, and seven or eight glasses a day FILLS HIM UP so he isn't hungry for solids. And the solids he does eat — biscuits and chips — have no iron either; there's NO RED MEAT in his diet. Between those two, he isn't taking in enough iron to build haemoglobin. I did consider blood loss and absorption problems like coeliac disease, but there's nothing to suggest those.'** **Then: 'this is extremely common at his age, and it's fixable — a toddler who loves his bottle is completely normal.'**

**★ THE 'TWO TREATMENTS' SENTENCE. plan: **★ INTRO, AND CLOSE THE FLU IN ONE QUESTION**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___. Your colleague arranged a blood test for Jack last week and the results are back — we'll go through them together. First though: has he recovered from that chest infection?'** *'Yes, completely. Ten days ago.'* → **'good, we can set that aside.'**

**If she volunteers more about the flu, redirect**: **'that sounds like it has settled — today I want to focus on the blood test.'** **Every further respiratory question is a wasted second and signals you haven't recognised the case.**

**PALLOR AND ANAEMIA SYMPTOMS**: **'does he look pale to you? When did you first notice — or was it the doctor who mentioned it? Has it got worse? Would you say he's tired? Does he get short of breath or struggle when he's active?'** *Washed out; a bit tired; he's little.*

**BOX 1 — INTAKE, OPEN FIRST, THEN LET HER TALK**: **'please describe his diet for me.'** *'Breastfed till six months, then formula. He loves his milk.'* **Don't accept 'he eats well' if she offers it.**

**★ SOLIDS, AND RED MEAT BY NAME**: **'have you started solids? And is he getting a variety of solids — INCLUDING RED MEAT?'** *'He doesn't really like solids. Biscuits, chips. No, he won't touch meat.'*

**★ THE COW'S MILK — AND THE NUMBER**: **'is he drinking cow's milk?'** *'Yes — since he turned one. A few glasses a day.'* → *(unhurried)* **'HOW MANY GLASSES IS A FEW?'** *'Um… seven or eight, probably. He asks for the bottle all day.'* → **'thank you.'** **Take 'a few' at face value and you've missed the diagnosis.**
**The allergy clue**: **'any rash around his mouth after cow's milk?'** *No.*
**BOX 2 — LOSS**: **'any bleeding episodes recently? Any recent surgery? Any blood in his stools?'** *No to all.*

**BOX 3 — ABSORPTION, IN EVERY VERSION**: **'have you noticed GREASY stools — ones that STICK TO THE PAN, FLOAT on the water, and are HARD TO FLUSH? Any diarrhoea? Any rash? Any blood in the stool?'** **Older child: tummy pain, joint pains, mouth ulcers, limping.** *Version A: bowels normal.*

**FAMILY HISTORY**: **'any family history of anaemia — or of coeliac disease or bowel inflammation?'** *Not that she knows.* **(Version B: 'my sister has coeliac.')** **Do NOT ask the thalassaemia questions — the ferritin is low.**

**WELL CHILD AND BINDSMA LEFTOVERS**: **'is he alert and active, eating and drinking, passing urine normally? Are you happy with his GROWTH and weight gain? Any concerns with his DEVELOPMENT or behaviour? Birth, immunisations, medicines, allergies?'** *Active; fine on the blue book chart; a bit grizzly.*

**★ THE FOUR NUMBERS IN SIXTY SECONDS, results turned so she can see**: **red cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin, built from iron · haemoglobin LOW · MCV — size — LOW, so smaller cells · MCH and MCHC — haemoglobin inside each cell — LOW · ferritin — the iron store — LOW. 'Together we call that iron deficiency anaemia.'** **No white cells, no platelets.**

**★ NAME THE CONDITION, THEN BOTH CAUSES**: **'so the condition is iron deficiency anaemia — but the more important question is WHY, and here there are TWO THINGS TOGETHER.'** **Cow's milk has almost no iron AND fills him up · the biscuits and chips have no iron either, and there's no red meat.** Then **'I considered blood loss and absorption problems like coeliac disease — nothing suggests those.'**

**'Have I done something wrong?' — no blame**: **'not at all — a toddler who loves his bottle is completely normal, and this is one of the commonest problems we see. It's very fixable.'** **Do not let the explanation become an accusation.**

**★ PLAN PART 1 — THE IRON**: **'two parts to the plan. First, an iron syrup dosed on his weight. It can cause CONSTIPATION, it turns the stools BLACK — that's harmless — and it can STAIN THE TEETH, so give it through a STRAW and brush afterwards. Give it with ORANGE JUICE rather than milk. We'll repeat the blood test IN A MONTH to check it's working, and keep going for at least THREE MONTHS after his count is normal.'** *'Will he need a transfusion?'* → **'no — the syrup does it.'**

**★ PLAN PART 2 — THE DIET, 'just as important'**: **'second — and this matters just as much, because if we only top him up the stores empty again — cut the cow's milk to ONE OR TWO GLASSES a day; I'M NOT ASKING YOU TO STOP IT. Get RED MEAT and other iron-rich foods in, with a good variety, and fewer biscuits and chips. Toddler diets are genuinely hard, so I'll refer you to a DIETITIAN. I'll see you both in a month with the repeat test.'** *'He'll scream if I take the bottle away.'* → **'cutting back, not taking away — the dietitian will help with how.'**

dx: **HEREDITARY SPHEROCYTOSIS — a red-cell MEMBRANE DEFECT causing SPHERICAL, RIGID cells that are destroyed in the SPLEEN (extravascular haemolysis). Autosomal dominant in about 75%. VERSION B: spherocytosis TOP OF THE LIST, but a THREE-WAY DIFFERENTIAL that cannot be closed without a film.**

**★ THE PASS/FAIL LINE — THE LIST IS THE MARK, NOT THE DIAGNOSIS. The examiner already knows the answer. What separates candidates is whether the five-minute history VISIBLY SCREENED ALL SIX GROUPS, and whether the diagnosis came with REASONS and a RANKED DIFFERENTIAL. In Version B the honest sentence — 'MOST LIKELY, BUT I CANNOT CONFIRM IT WITHOUT A BLOOD FILM, AND I CANNOT EXCLUDE LEUKAEMIA WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST TODAY' — IS the mark.**

**★ THE SIX DIFFERENTIAL GROUPS, in the order the lecture asks them — every box asked even when you already suspect the answer, ONE SIGNPOST EACH: 1 IRON DEFICIENCY — red meat, cow's milk quantity · 2 THALASSAEMIA — family history, ethnicity · 3 BLOOD LOSS — surgery, medicines, bleeding · 4 MALABSORPTION — greasy stools, IBD features, family history · 5 HAEMOLYSIS — jaundice, dark urine, triggers, family jaundice/gallstones/splenectomy · 6 MALIGNANCY — weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats, bruising, bone pain, fever. Then well-child and BINDSMA leftovers.**

**THE TIME BUDGET: 30 s intro · 30 s pallor and anaemia symptoms · 3.5 MINUTES ON THE SIX GROUPS · 30 s leftovers — then the card, a 60-second explanation, 90 s diagnosis.** **Spending three of five minutes on the pallor itself is a named auto-fail.**

**WHY ETHNICITY AND BROAD BEANS: THALASSAEMIA clusters in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, South and South-East Asian families; G6PD DEFICIENCY (X-linked) in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, African and South-East Asian families, triggered by OXIDANT STRESS — FAVA BEANS, sulfonamides, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, naphthalene mothballs, infection. Ask ethnicity WITH PERMISSION: 'may I ask your family's ethnic background?'**

**★ THE 60-SECOND EXPLANATION — THREE MOVES, SHAPE → SPLEEN → RETICULOCYTES, with a drawing: 'red blood cells carry oxygen. Normally they're shaped like a DOUGHNUT. In your son's blood film many are shaped like a BALL — a sphere. Those round cells can't squeeze through the tiny vessels in the SPLEEN, so they get TRAPPED AND BROKEN DOWN there — which is why the spleen is enlarged, and why he went yellow after his cold. To keep up, the bone marrow pumps out YOUNG red cells called RETICULOCYTES, and we can see a high number. Overall the haemoglobin is low — that's anaemia.'** **No white cells, no platelets, no 'extravascular haemolysis with reticulocytosis'.**

**VERSION A — CLOSING LINE, WITH REASONS AND RANKED DIFFERENTIALS: 'your son has SPHEROCYTOSIS — hereditary, because it runs in families, which fits your father-in-law's spleen operation. My reasons: pale and tired, yellow after a cold, an enlarged spleen, sphere-shaped cells on the film, and high young red cells. I also considered IRON DEFICIENCY — his diet is good; THALASSAEMIA — no family history and the film doesn't fit; BLEEDING — none; ABSORPTION problems like coeliac — normal bowels; other red-cell breakdown like G6PD; LEUKAEMIA — no weight loss, lumps, bruising or fevers, and no abnormal white cells on the film; and B12 or folate deficiency.'**

**★ VERSION B — THE HONEST THREE-WAY LIST: 'three things are at the top of my list, and I want to be honest that I CAN'T CONFIRM ANY OF THEM WITHOUT A BLOOD TEST. Most likely is SPHEROCYTOSIS — because of the paleness, the yellow episode and your father-in-law's history. I also have to consider OTHER RED-CELL BREAKDOWN like G6PD — though no dark urine after a trigger; and LEUKAEMIA — though no weight loss, lumps, bruising or fevers. Because the spleen is enlarged I want the BLOOD TEST DONE TODAY, and I'll speak to the children's hospital.'** **Order doesn't matter; LEAVING ONE OUT DOES.** **'Is it cancer?' — 'it's on my list and I take it seriously, which is why the test is today. The pattern fits an inherited red-cell condition much better, and that is not cancer.'**

**INVESTIGATIONS: SAME-DAY FBE, FILM AND RETICULOCYTES in ANY child with splenomegaly · the haemolysis screen — UNCONJUGATED BILIRUBIN, LDH, HAPTOGLOBIN, DAT (negative in HS) · ferritin with CRP · LFT, U&E · spherocytosis confirmation by EMA-BINDING FLOW CYTOMETRY (preferred) or osmotic fragility.** VERIFY **AVOID serum iron/TIBC (ferritin is enough) and IRON 'JUST IN CASE' — haemolytic patients can overload.** CORRECTION — **haemolysis does not raise transaminases.**

**MANAGEMENT: WCH paediatric haematology · GENETIC COUNSELLING and testing of parents and siblings · DAILY FOLIC ACID for chronic haemolysis VERIFY · ultrasound for PIGMENT GALLSTONES from school age · SPLENECTOMY only for severe disease, ideally AFTER AGE 6, with pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination BEFOREHAND and lifelong penicillin prophylaxis VERIFY · avoid contact sport if the spleen is large · THE SAFETY-NET: 'sudden severe paleness after a viral illness is an EMERGENCY — his marrow can briefly stop' (parvovirus aplastic crisis, reticulocytes LOW).** **Anaemia cut-offs: Hb <110 (6 m–5 y), <115 (5–11 y), <120 (12–14 y) g/L.** VERIFY SA: SA Pathology same-day FBE — phone the lab for an urgent film · **WCH Michael Rice Centre** for haematology and oncology · **PATS** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for the unwell or pancytopenic child · ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officer.
