findings: ★ THE GROWTH CHARTS — the trend IS the diagnosis

HEIGHT tracking the 50TH CENTILE throughout. WEIGHT and BMI on the 50th until ~10 years, NOW ABOVE THE 97TH. Height normal + BMI crossing 50th → >97th in two years = EXOGENOUS OBESITY until proven otherwise
The stem

Sophie, 12, brought by her father MARK. KNOWN ASTHMA, WELL CONTROLLED — her respiratory physician reviewed her recently and is happy (ICS/LABA preventer + salbutamol reliever). SOPHIE IS IN THE WAITING ROOM. Five minutes of history, then explain the chart and the plan
The timeline
About 68 kg. 'Maybe 15 KILOS SINCE SHE WAS TEN. Before that she was a NORMAL SIZE.' Always big or recent? — RECENT
★ THE DIET — the summary first, the detail only when pushed

He opens with 'SHE EATS JUNK.' Pushed: cereal · whatever's at the CANTEEN · CHIPS AND A COKE after school · pasta or TAKEAWAY 2–3 nights · BISCUITS OR CHIPS while gaming. Not big on veggies; an apple sometimes. COKE MOST DAYS
★ THE HIDDEN AGENDA — only when asked about exercise or barriers

Screens: the PLAYSTATION FOUR OR FIVE HOURS after school. Exercise: 'HONESTLY, NONE. I DON'T LET HER DO SPORT — I'M WORRIED IT'LL SET OFF HER ASTHMA.' He stopped her two years ago after a flare during a school run. If you never address it in management, he asks at the end: 'SO CAN SHE DO SPORT WITH HER ASTHMA?'
Medications — ask them early
SERETIDE morning and night, the blue one if needed. PREDNISOLONE ONCE, TWO YEARS AGO. Nothing for mood or sleep. 'The specialist says she's well controlled'
The organic screen — all negative
'She's ONE OF THE TALLEST.' No cold intolerance, constipation or dry skin. NO pink stretch marks, round face, bruising or dark velvety neck patches
★ THE COMPLICATIONS — the point of the case

No hip, knee or groin pain, NO LIMP. 'She's been A BIT QUIET, to be honest.' Sleep OK. Home fine. 'A COUPLE OF GIRLS HAVE SAID THINGS. She doesn't want to talk about it.' No bingeing or vomiting that he knows of. SNORES A BIT, always has, not sleepy. Not drinking or weeing more
The family history — only if asked
His FATHER HAS TYPE 2 DIABETES; he's 'a bit overweight' himself
★ HIS REACTIONS

Worried; DEFENSIVE if he feels blamed. After the chart: 'IS THIS OUR FAULT?' If 'OBESE' is used as a LABEL rather than explained: 'THAT'S A HORRIBLE WORD.' Quiet and defensive if you say 'FAT.' When the asthma point is explained: 'I DIDN'T KNOW SHE WAS ALLOWED. I THOUGHT I WAS PROTECTING HER'
★ VERSION B — 2023 online, the striae

8-year-old boy, mother, after a URTI. PE supplied: BMI >97th, PINK STRIAE ON THE ABDOMEN, thyroid normal, no acanthosis, BSL normal. The striae turn this into OBESITY PLUS A CUSHING SCREEN — 'a gland above the kidney making too much of a stress hormone.' Late-night salivary cortisol, overnight dexamethasone suppression, or 24-hour urinary free cortisol → paediatric endocrinology if abnormal
★ VERSION C — 2025 face-to-face, plot it yourself

A blank BMI-for-age chart and serial numbers: BMI 6 y 15.5 · 7 y 15.5 · 8 y 16 · 10 y 16.5 · 11 y 24 · 12 y 25.5 — FOUR MINUTES. READ THE AXIS UNITS (kg vs cm) BEFORE THE FIRST DOT; plotting weight on the height grid is a named error. 'Implications' = complications + possible causes + the need to manage

dx: **EXOGENOUS (LIFESTYLE) OBESITY in a child with WELL-CONTROLLED ASTHMA — BMI ≥ 95th centile, height tracking the 50th. BMI ≥ 85th = OVERWEIGHT; ≥ 95th = OBESE (CDC charts 2–18 y; WHO 0–2 y). In children BMI is read against AGE AND SEX AS A CENTILE, never against an adult cut-off.** VERIFY

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — REVERSING THE ASTHMA EXERCISE BAN. The father's fear is the hidden agenda, and it must be DISMANTLED IN MANAGEMENT with correct asthma advice: 'when we say her asthma is WELL CONTROLLED, that means there is NO LIMITATION ON EXERCISE — being active is actually one of the BEST THINGS FOR HER LUNGS and her weight. If she gets a bit tight when she runs, TWO PUFFS OF HER BLUE RELIEVER THROUGH THE SPACER ABOUT FIFTEEN MINUTES BEFORE SPORT prevents it. And I'll link you with an EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST who can build a plan she enjoys.'** VERIFY **When he says 'I thought I was protecting her': 'you were doing what any parent would — now you have the right information.'**

**'BUT SHE COUGHS WHEN SHE RUNS': 'cough or wheeze with exercise in someone on a preventer can mean the asthma ISN'T AS CONTROLLED AS WE THINK — so I'd review her technique and adherence, use the reliever before sport, and loop back to her respiratory physician. It's a REASON TO CHECK THE ASTHMA, NOT A REASON TO STOP THE EXERCISE.'**

**THE THREE BOXES — SAY THE HEADINGS OUT LOUD: LIFESTYLE → CAUSES → COMPLICATIONS. Block 0 is the WEIGHT ITSELF (now, how much, over what period, always big or recent — RECENT AND RAPID pushes organic causes up). Block 1 LIFESTYLE: a typical day, then SPECIFICS REGARDLESS OF THE ANSWER — veg and fruit, chips and takeaway, SOFT DRINKS, snacks; exercise; SCREEN HOURS; 'IS ANYTHING STOPPING HER BEING ACTIVE?' Block 1B MEDICATIONS, early: which puffers, PREDNISOLONE TABLETS AND HOW OFTEN, antipsychotics or valproate.** **The asthma is PARKED — the stem says it's controlled; a full asthma history for four minutes is a named error.**

**BLOCK 2 — ORGANIC CAUSES, two or three questions each: THYROID (cold, constipation, dry skin, tiredness — AND 'HAS HER HEIGHT KEPT UP?') · CUSHING (pink or purple striae, round face, bruising) grouped with ACANTHOSIS (dark velvety patches — insulin resistance). THE FORK IS HEIGHT: exogenous obesity children are TALL OR NORMAL; hypothyroid and Cushing children are SHORT AND SLOWING.** VERIFY

**★ BLOCK 3 — COMPLICATIONS, THE POINT OF THE CASE. Signpost it — 'now the effects of the weight on her body and mood' — and run SIX: HIP, KNEE OR GROIN PAIN, OR A LIMP (SCFE) · MOOD and SLEEP · HOME and SCHOOL — ANY TEASING OR BULLYING · BINGE (a large amount, can't stop) and PURGE (vomiting, laxatives) — two questions · SNORING, gasping, tired or headachy mornings (OSA) · THIRST AND URINE (type 2 diabetes). Missing the complications box entirely is the common fail; asking only about diet is a fail.**

**THE CHART, EXPLAINED WITHOUT SHAME: ORIENT ('BMI is a number from her weight and height together — a better guide to body size than weight alone') → DEFINE A PERCENTILE ('IF YOU LINE UP 100 TWELVE-YEAR-OLD GIRLS, the 90th percentile means her number is higher than 90 of them') → WALK THE TREND ('her HEIGHT has sat on the 50th — that tells me this is about WEIGHT, NOT A GROWTH PROBLEM; her BMI was in the middle until ten, then CLIMBED THROUGH THE LINES and now sits above the 97th') → CONCLUDE ('we classify this as obesity, which just means ABOVE THE HEALTHY RANGE for her age and height — IT'S ABOUT THE NUMBER, NOT ABOUT SOPHIE, and at twelve it's very treatable').** **Never 'standard deviations'. 'Is this our fault?' → 'No — lots of things add up; what matters is what we do from here, together.'**

**MANAGEMENT — FAMILY-BASED, MULTIDISCIPLINARY: 'the main treatment at her age is changes to everyday habits, done AS A FAMILY, with A TEAM helping.' DIET: more veg and fruit, less takeaway and chips, WATER OR MILK INSTEAD OF COKE, healthier snacks, family meals, no food as reward → DIETITIAN. ACTIVITY: ≥ 60 MINUTES A DAY moderate–vigorous, SCREENS ≤ 2 HOURS, 9–11 h sleep (Australian 24-hour movement guidelines, 5–17 y) → EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST, asthma-safe. TEAM: GP Management Plan + Team Care Arrangement; paediatric weight-management service. SCREEN: HbA1c or fasting glucose, LIPIDS, LFTs (NAFLD); BP with a CORRECTLY SIZED CUFF; TSH only if short or slow; hip X-ray if limp; sleep study if OSA. REVIEW 4–6 WEEKS, re-plot each visit — and 'I'd like to see SOPHIE HERSELF next time so she has a say.'** VERIFY

**AVOID: CALORIE-RESTRICTION DIETS, skipped meals, WEIGHT-LOSS TARGETS in a growing child — aim for WEIGHT MAINTENANCE WHILE SHE GROWS INTO IT · PHARMACOTHERAPY or BARIATRIC talk in a GP consult — specialist territory, don't raise it · blame, the word 'fat', singling the child out with a separate diet · banning exercise for asthma · routine TSH or cortisol on every obese child — target them.** **'Should I put her on a diet?' → 'no strict diets — we want her weight to stay steady while she grows.' 'Medication or an operation?' → 'not at her age from me — this is about habits and a team, and it works.'**

**SAFETY-NET — THE COMPLICATIONS ARE THE REASON FOR FOLLOW-UP: 'extra weight can strain HIPS AND KNEES, affect BREATHING AT NIGHT, raise DIABETES risk, and really affect MOOD, especially with teasing — bring her back if she LIMPS or has hip or knee pain, SNORES AND IS TIRED, DRINKS A LOT, or seems LOW, isn't sleeping, or has trouble with eating.' SCFE = no weight-bearing, frog-leg lateral X-ray, SAME-DAY orthopaedics.** **VERSION B — THE STRIAE: 'everything about food, activity and the team still stands. Because of the stretch marks and the rapid gain, I want to rule out CUSHING SYNDROME — a gland above the kidney making too much cortisol. It's uncommon but worth ONE EXTRA TEST: a bedtime saliva sample, or a tablet at night and a blood test next morning, or a 24-hour urine. If abnormal, the children's hormone specialists.'** VERIFY SA: WCH paediatric clinic / weight-management service VERIFY · **Country Health Connect** dietitian and EP in regional SA · GPMP/TCA Medicare items · **CaFHS 1300 733 606** · ACCHS · **TIS 131 450**.

HYPERTONIA with PERSISTENT PRIMITIVE REFLEXES (Moro, ATNR) beyond the age they should have gone. Moro should be gone by ~6 MONTHS, ATNR by 6–7 MONTHS; persistence is an UPPER MOTOR NEURONE sign exactly as hyperreflexia is. BOTH CARDS SAY UMN

HYPOTONIA, REDUCED OR ABSENT REFLEXES, wasting, possibly a HOARSE CRY and CONSTIPATION. LOWER MOTOR NEURONE or MUSCLE: neuromuscular disease, spinal cord lesion, or HYPOTHYROIDISM — the treatable one you must not miss. TSH, free T4, chase the heel-prick, CK, inspect the back

Noticed MONTHS AGO, more obvious since he's been trying to walk. ALL THE TIME. 'He BARELY USES IT.' 'It's STIFF — it doesn't hang down like the other one.' Right side fine — 'HE DOES EVERYTHING RIGHT-HANDED.' NO PAIN when it's moved

The four domains — only one is abnormal

GROSS MOTOR: pulls up on the sofa, CAN'T STAND ALONE, SHUFFLES rather than crawls, sits fine, head control always fine. FINE MOTOR: the RIGHT HAND IS BRILLIANT — scribbles, picks up peas — but THE LEFT IS ALWAYS IN A FIST. COMMUNICATION: mama, dada and two more; understands 'no' and 'come here.' SOCIAL: loves peekaboo, very smiley

She looks away: 'I had a FEVER AROUND FIVE MONTHS. I felt awful for a few days. I NEVER WENT TO THE DOCTOR — I thought it was just a virus.' About three days of aches and temperature. dx: **SPASTIC HEMIPLEGIC CEREBRAL PALSY. Cerebral palsy is a group of PERMANENT disorders of movement and posture causing activity limitation, attributed to a NON-PROGRESSIVE disturbance in the developing fetal or infant brain. 'NON-PROGRESSIVE' is the load-bearing word: the picture evolves as the child grows, but SKILLS ARE NEVER LOST. REGRESSION MEANS IT IS NOT CEREBRAL PALSY.**

**★ THE TWO SENTENCES THAT DECIDE THIS STATION: 1 'The tone is INCREASED and the reflexes are BRISK — that is an UPPER MOTOR NEURONE pattern, which LOCALISES the problem to the BRAIN OR SPINAL CORD.' 2 'He has NEVER LOST A SKILL he once had — which is what allows me to call this CEREBRAL PALSY rather than a PROGRESSIVE CONDITION.' The first earns the diagnosis. The second is the one ALMOST NOBODY SAYS — the difference between a pass and a good pass.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — LOCALISE BEFORE YOU LABEL, AND EXCLUDE IN THE SAME BREATH. Most candidates get to 'cerebral palsy'. The pass is decided by: UMN said in those words BEFORE the diagnosis · 'NEVER LOST A SKILL' excludes a progressive condition · 'LONG-STANDING AND PAINLESS' excludes infection, fracture and NAI · 'the OTHER THREE DOMAINS are normal' makes global delay and a genetic syndrome much less likely.** **Don't diagnose from the stem — it says 'unilateral motor problem', not CP.**

**THE HISTORY — FOUR DOMAINS, THEN BIRTH, THEN CAUSES; if you haven't started the birth history by 2:30 you'll run out of time. PIN THE COMPLAINT FIRST: when noticed · constant or intermittent · LESS, or NOT AT ALL · STIFF OR FLOPPY · right side normal · PAIN · and REGRESSION. Decide ACUTE vs LONG-STANDING, UNILATERAL vs BILATERAL, STIFF vs FLOPPY in the first minute — it splits the whole differential.** **THE FOUR LADDERS — open, then step down on each 'no': GROSS MOTOR (stands alone → with support → crawls → sits → HEAD CONTROL, always) · FINE MOTOR, on the NORMAL side (scribbles → pincer → passes hand to hand → reaches → HANDS ALWAYS CLENCHED?, always) · COMMUNICATION · SOCIAL — plus 'does he COUGH OR CHOKE on food?' (bulbar).**

**RED-FLAG AGES — 9, 12, 18 MONTHS; a 15-month-old is judged against the 12-MONTH column (nothing between 12 and 18): 12 m — stands holding on, babbles phrases, pincer grip, peekaboo. 18 m — walks alone, one clear word, scribbles, plays with others. HAND PREFERENCE BEFORE 12 MONTHS IS ABNORMAL — the EARLIEST SIGN OF HEMIPLEGIA.** **THE BIRTH HISTORY IN THREE PHASES — the block the examiner is waiting for: PREGNANCY (BP, diabetes, INFECTIONS OR FEVERS, drugs, scans) · DELIVERY (term, mode, PROLONGED, FORCEPS OR VACUUM, weight) · AFTER BIRTH, THE RICHEST (CRIED AND BREATHED STRAIGHT AWAY? RESUSCITATION or OXYGEN? NEONATAL SEIZURES? heel-prick? JAUNDICE and treatment? feeding? HOW LONG IN HOSPITAL?).** **'Was the birth normal?' and moving on is a named trap.**

CORRECTION — **the source leans hard on the birth history. A NORMAL birth history does NOT exclude CP, and only about 10% of cases are attributable to INTRAPARTUM HYPOXIA — most are ANTENATAL. In a TERM baby with a purely HEMIPLEGIC pattern, the commonest single cause is a PERINATAL ARTERIAL ISCHAEMIC STROKE — and neonatal seizures in a term baby are its classic marker.** **If challenged 'the birth was difficult, so it's hypoxic?': 'it may have contributed, but only around one in ten is attributable to intrapartum events — in a term baby with a hemiplegic pattern I'd be looking for a perinatal stroke on MRI.'** **Kernicterus causes DYSKINETIC, not spastic, CP.**

**THE CAUSE LIST, BUILT ANATOMICALLY — say the levels BEFORE naming a disease: BRAIN (CP; acquired injury — meningitis, encephalitis, head injury, haemorrhage, prolonged seizure, kernicterus; congenital or genetic syndromes) · NERVE / CORD (hereditary neuropathy — CHARCOT–MARIE–TOOTH; spinal cord lesion; spina bifida) · MUSCLE (Duchenne, congenital myopathies) · JOINT AND BONE (DDH, club foot, fracture, NAI) · THYROID across the whole track · plus BRACHIAL PLEXUS injury for an arm alone.** CORRECTION — **congenital HYPOTHYROIDISM is usually SILENT AT BIRTH (that's why the heel-prick exists) and shows as prolonged jaundice, HOARSE CRY, CONSTIPATION, umbilical hernia, large fontanelle and HYPOTONIA — not 'cold intolerance' in an infant.**

**★ THE EXPLANATION — THE WORDS IN ORDER: 1 NAME IT — 'Mason most likely has a condition called cerebral palsy.' 2 WHAT IT IS — 'a movement and posture disorder caused by an INJURY TO THE DEVELOPING BRAIN — the part that sends signals to the muscles. The injury ISN'T GETTING WORSE; it happened once. But as he grows, the way it shows changes.' 3 WHEN — pregnancy, around birth, or the first couple of years. 4 LINK TO HER HISTORY, CAREFULLY — 'two things MAY HAVE CONTRIBUTED: the fever in pregnancy, and the difficult delivery when he didn't breathe straight away — and we often CAN'T PIN IT TO ONE THING.' 5 THE QUESTION SHE HASN'T ASKED — 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS, and there's nothing you could reasonably have done to prevent it.' 6 REFUSE THE PROGNOSIS, OFFER THE PLAN.**

**'SO IT WAS THE FEVER — I SHOULD HAVE GONE': 'most people don't see a doctor for three days of fever, and we can't say the fever caused it — only that it's one of several possibilities.' 'WILL HE WALK?': 'I CAN'T TELL YOU THAT TODAY, and I'M NOT GOING TO GUESS. Children with his pattern have a wide range of outcomes. What I can tell you is that STARTING THERAPY EARLY MAKES A REAL DIFFERENCE.'** **When she says she's scared, stop the checklist for one sentence — 'that's a very natural thing to feel, and I'm going to tell you everything I know' — five seconds, and a marked item.**

**INVESTIGATIONS AND MANAGEMENT: CP is a CLINICAL diagnosis — imaging looks for the CAUSE and anything treatable; a normal MRI doesn't unmake it. MRI BRAIN (pattern and timing) · TSH AND FREE T4 and confirm the heel-prick · CK if floppy or wasted · microarray and metabolic screen if dysmorphic or MRI normal · EEG if seizures · VISION AND HEARING · plot growth · HIP SURVEILLANCE (AP pelvis — children with CP SILENTLY DISLOCATE). REFER TODAY — developmental paediatrics, PHYSIO, OT, SPEECH — 'WE DON'T WAIT FOR THE SCAN TO START THERAPY'; orthoses, constraint-induced movement therapy, botulinum toxin (specialist-led); NDIS EARLY CHILDHOOD APPROACH (under 9, no formal diagnosis needed to start).** VERIFY **Safety-net: losing skills, fits, unwell.** **AVOID: prognosis on the day · stating the delivery caused it · waiting for MRI before therapy · calling it CP if any skill was lost · assessing tone in a crying toddler.** SA: **Novita** · **WCH Child Development Unit** · Country Health Connect allied health · **CaFHS 1300 733 606** · **PATS** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** · **CARL 13 14 78** if injury is unexplained · ACCHS · **TIS 131 450**.

stem: VERSION A (current online format): general practice. An 11-YEAR-OLD BOY brought by his mother with A LUMP IN THE NECK. NO examination task and NO vitals. Her concern: 'HIS COUSIN HAD LYMPHOMA AND IT STARTED WITH A LUMP IN THE NECK.' History 6 minutes, then diagnosis and differentials in 2.

VERSION B (face-to-face): a 4-YEAR-OLD BOY with A LATERAL LUMP, present THREE WEEKS, with A FLU-LIKE ILLNESS A MONTH AGO that resolved untreated — and the cousin's lymphoma stated up front. History about 4 minutes, THEN ASK THE EXAMINER FOR THE EXAMINATION FINDINGS in 2, then diagnosis and management in 2.
tasks: Take a history from the mother (6 minutes in Version A, about 4 in Version B)
In Version B, ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differentials — and in Version B, your management plan
findings: ★ THE SITE — vague until you ask the right question
'IT'S IN THE NECK.' The role-player is instructed to stay vague until you ask MIDDLE OR SIDE. Then: 'IN THE MIDDLE, JUST BELOW HIS CHIN.' Midline vs lateral HALVES THE DIFFERENTIAL
Timing
About TEN DAYS. FIRST TIME. SAME SIZE — not growing
★ CHARACTER — asked as history, because there's no examination

Size: 'A GRAPE.' Hard or soft: 'I'M NOT SURE — SOFT-ISH?' Painful: 'YES, WHEN I PRESS IT.' Mobile: 'I DON'T KNOW.' Skin: 'A BIT PINK.' Warm: 'YES, WARM.' Candidates who skip these because 'you can't ask a mother' LOSE THE FINDINGS THAT MAKE THE DIAGNOSIS. Ask every one and ACCEPT 'NOT SURE'
★ THE TWO MOVEMENT QUESTIONS — the discriminator

Swallowing: 'YES — IT GOES UP when he swallows.' Tongue, asked separately: 'I THINK SO — I've seen it move when he POKES HIS TONGUE OUT.' THYROID moves on swallowing; a THYROGLOSSAL CYST moves on BOTH. Skipping the tongue question because swallowing was positive is the trap
Thyroid symptoms — negative
No heat or cold intolerance. Bowels normal
The infection screen — one positive
No fever. 'He had A COLD TWO WEEKS AGO.' Nothing now — no sore throat, runny nose, ear pain, cough, rashes. Teeth fine. No travel, sick contacts or pets
★ The malignancy screen — the questions she's waiting for

No weight loss — 'EATING LIKE A HORSE.' No other lumps. Not tired; PLAYING FOOTY, doing fine at school. No night sweats, bone pain or bruising. Growing well. Alert, eating, drinking, passing urine normally. Normal pregnancy, immunised, no medicines
★ HER FEAR — acknowledge it early, answer it late

'His COUSIN HAD LYMPHOMA and it STARTED WITH A LUMP IN THE NECK — I'M TERRIFIED it's the same.' (Oliver's cousin, 14, Hodgkin lymphoma last year.) Frightened, a little clipped; SOFTENS WHEN THE COUSIN IS ACKNOWLEDGED. 'I'm sure it's nothing' at the door is the trap
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA AND LAST-MINUTE PUSH

She's been googling and thinks he needs tests: 'SHOULDN'T HE HAVE A BLOOD TEST TODAY?' — volunteered if asked about concerns, otherwise late. If you NEVER MENTION CANCER at the end: 'BUT ARE YOU SURE IT'S NOT CANCER?' — and not closing it is the single-item auto-fail
★ VERSION B — the 4-year-old, lateral, WITH an examination

Lateral, THREE WEEKS, unchanged, first time; FLU A MONTH AGO, resolved untreated; everything else negative. Card: a SINGLE left cervical node ~2 cm, NORMAL CONSISTENCY, MOBILE, NON-TENDER, skin normal; NO OTHER NODES; NO hepatosplenomegaly; NO BONE TENDERNESS; no pallor, bruising or SCRATCH MARKS; ENT, teeth, skin, thyroid, chest, heart normal; GROWTH NORMAL. → POST-VIRAL (REACTIVE) LYMPHADENOPATHY — observe to six weeks total, no tests today
Version B red-flag card

'The node is HARD AND FIXED, and the SPLEEN is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.' → changes the plan: check pallor, bruising, all node groups; FBE and film TODAY; speak to WCH paediatric oncology now — 'I'm not saying it's cancer; I'm saying it needs looking at properly and quickly'
Other practice cards

Fever 38.9, RED TENDER lump under the jaw, sore throat with exudate → BACTERIAL LYMPHADENITIS: antibiotics, review 48 h, drain if fluctuant · painless lump SEVEN WEEKS, GROWING, tired, pale, BRUISES ON SHINS, spleen tip palpable → LEUKAEMIA: same-day FBE and film · tender axillary and neck node, NEW KITTEN, a scratch on the forearm → CAT-SCRATCH DISEASE, Bartonella serology · non-tender lump two months, PURPLISH SKIN, unimmunised → ATYPICAL MYCOBACTERIA: specialist, EXCISION NOT INCISION · fever ≥ 5 DAYS + node ≥ 1.5 cm + rash, red eyes, lips → KAWASAKI, same-day paediatrics

dx: **VERSION A: INFECTED THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST — the thyroid forms at the BASE OF THE TONGUE and DESCENDS to the front of the neck; if part of that track stays open it forms a MIDLINE SAC that may inflame or infect — presenting for the FIRST TIME, often AFTER A URTI, as a WARM, TENDER MIDLINE LUMP that RISES ON TONGUE PROTRUSION AND SWALLOWING. The commonest midline congenital neck mass. VERSION B: POST-VIRAL (REACTIVE) CERVICAL LYMPHADENOPATHY — a node enlarged by a viral infection that stays palpable for weeks after the illness; normal characteristics, no red flags, self-limiting.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE — ASK THE EXAMINATION AS HISTORY (A); EXAMINE FOR LEUKAEMIA, NOT FOR A LUMP (B); THEN ANSWER THE MOTHER'S REAL QUESTION. A: with no examination task, candidates who skip character questions lose the findings that make the diagnosis — WARM, PAINFUL, MIDLINE, MOVES ON SWALLOWING. The script: 'some of these are things I'd normally check by examining him — BUT YOU KNOW THE LUMP BETTER THAN ANYONE.' B: THE LUMP IS THE EXCUSE; THE EXAMINATION IS A HAEMATOLOGICAL ONE. BOTH: finish by NAMING THE FEAR.**

**THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT SPLIT THE NECK: MIDLINE OR LATERAL · and does it MOVE ON SWALLOWING / ON TONGUE PROTRUSION. Midline lumps are THYROID-FAMILY (thyroglossal cyst, goitre, nodule, ECTOPIC THYROID) or DERMOID; lateral lumps are LYMPH NODES or a BRANCHIAL CLEFT CYST.** CORRECTION — **the lecture says tongue protrusion 'doesn't make much difference'. IT IS THE DISCRIMINATOR: the thyroid moves on swallowing; a thyroglossal cyst moves on BOTH (a dermoid moves on neither). Ask both.**

**THE ONE-LINE STRATEGY: concern → WHERE EXACTLY → timing → CHARACTER (size · hard/soft · painful · mobile · skin · warm) → THYROID (heat/cold, bowels, the two movements) → INFECTIONS BY REGION (ENT · CHEST · SKIN · DENTAL · TRAVEL / CONTACTS / ANIMALS — cats for cat-scratch) → CANCER (weight, appetite, other lumps, tired / school, sweats, BONE PAIN, BRUISING, growth) → well-child → BINDSMA (congenital lumps → pregnancy; immunisation matters for infection and TB).** **Acknowledge the cousin the moment it's mentioned: 'I can understand how frightening that is — it's a very fair worry, and we'll work it out together.'**

**VERSION A — NAME IT, LAY MECHANISM, WHY NOW, REASONS: 'most likely Oliver has a THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST. The thyroid is a gland at the front of the neck. Before birth it forms at the BASE OF THE TONGUE and MOVES DOWN to the lower neck. Sometimes part of that path STAYS OPEN and forms a small SAC. It can sit quietly for years, then gets INFLAMED OR INFECTED — often after a cold, like his — and becomes bigger, warm and sore, which is why you've only noticed it now. It fits because it's EXACTLY IN THE MIDLINE, it MOVES UP WHEN HE SWALLOWS AND WHEN HE POKES HIS TONGUE OUT — that's the giveaway — and it's WARM AND SORE, which is the inflammation.'**

**★ SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIALS — 'infections' alone SCORES NOTHING: OTHER THYROID problems (goitre, nodule, ECTOPIC thyroid) · LYMPH GLANDS swelling with EAR INFECTIONS, TONSILLITIS, a runny nose, DENTAL infection, SKIN infections like school sores, a CHEST infection, or a gland that stays up AFTER A VIRUS · because of her worry, LEUKAEMIA AND LYMPHOMA — rare in children · and at the bottom, a BRANCHIAL CYST (side of the neck) and a DERMOID CYST.** **Plus: EBV/CMV, cat-scratch, atypical mycobacteria/TB, KAWASAKI (fever ≥ 5 days + node ≥ 1.5 cm).**

**★ CLOSE THE CANCER CONCERN — EXPLICITLY, WITH REASONS, BEFORE SHE ASKS: 'I know you were worried about lymphoma. I DON'T THINK THAT'S WHAT THIS IS, and here's why: the lump is IN THE MIDDLE, it MOVES WITH HIS TONGUE, it's SORE AND WARM rather than painless and hard, he has NO WEIGHT LOSS, TIREDNESS, SWEATS, BRUISING OR OTHER LUMPS, and he's GROWING WELL.'** **'It's definitely not cancer' without reasons — or leaving the word unsaid — both fail.** **RED-FLAG NODE: > 2 cm · HARD · FIXED · MATTED · SUPRACLAVICULAR · GROWING · persisting beyond 6 WEEKS — plus B symptoms, pallor, bruising, bone pain, hepatosplenomegaly.**

**VERSION A — MANAGEMENT: examine when you can (midline cyst rising on tongue protrusion; CONFIRM THE THYROID IS PALPABLE IN ITS NORMAL POSITION; temperature) · ULTRASOUND NECK (the cyst, and A NORMAL THYROID IN THE NORMAL PLACE) · TSH · oral antibiotic for the infected cyst (amoxicillin–clavulanate or cefalexin per Therapeutic Guidelines) VERIFY · analgesia · review in 48 HOURS · refer paediatric ENT / surgery for a SISTRUNK PROCEDURE (cyst, tract and mid-hyoid) ONCE SETTLED — recurrence is high if only the cyst is removed.** **NEVER INCISE OR DRAIN a thyroglossal cyst, or excise it during infection — and never before imaging, because an ECTOPIC 'cyst' may be the child's ONLY THYROID TISSUE.** **'Shouldn't he have a blood test?' → 'the ultrasound and thyroid test answer the question this lump is asking; a leukaemia test isn't needed on what I've found — but if anything changes, we do it straight away.'**

**VERSION B — THE HAEMATOLOGICAL EXAMINATION, requested aloud: 'Examiner, because the family is worried about lymphoma, I'd like to look for SIGNS OF A BLOOD CANCER as well as at the lump' — general appearance: PALLOR, BRUISES/PETECHIAE, rashes, SCRATCH MARKS · vitals and GROWTH CHART · ENT, TEETH, head-and-neck skin · the node's size, consistency, mobility, tenderness, skin · the THYROID · ALL NODE GROUPS (occipital, pre/post-auricular, submandibular, SUPRACLAVICULAR, axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal) · SPLEEN AND LIVER · BONE TENDERNESS · chest and heart.** **Forgetting the thyroid, the spleen or the full node survey are named errors.**

**VERSION B — MANAGEMENT: 'lymph nodes are glands in the neck, part of the immune system; they get bigger fighting an infection — his flu a month ago — and it's normal for them to STAY UP FOR A FEW WEEKS after the infection has gone.' REASSURE; NO BLOODS TODAY in a well child with a normal examination (RCH says 'consider', not 'do') VERIFY; NO ANTIBIOTICS for a non-tender post-viral node; REVIEW AT 3 WEEKS (6 weeks total); WRITTEN RED FLAGS — still there at 6 weeks, growing, new lumps, weight loss, tiredness, pallor, fever, night sweats, bruising. If persisting or any red flag: FBE and film, ESR/CRP, EBV serology, LFTs, LDH, CXR, ultrasound; biopsy if suspicious.** SA: paediatric ENT, surgery and oncology at the **Women's and Children's Hospital** · **PATS** · **Country Health Connect** · ACCHS · **TIS 131 450** · airway emergency (stridor, drooling, trismus, toxic) → 000 / **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**.
plan: **WIPE, OPEN — then acknowledge the cousin the moment it's named**: **'hello, I'm Dr ___. You've brought Oliver in — how can I help today?'** *'A lump in his neck. His cousin had lymphoma and it started with a lump — I'm terrified.'* → **'I can understand how frightening that is, with what happened to his cousin. It's a very fair worry and we'll work it out together. Let me ask some questions so I understand exactly what's going on.'** **Never 'I'm sure it's nothing'.**

**★ SITE — don't accept 'in the neck'**: **'where exactly is it — can you show me? Is it in the MIDDLE of the neck, or OFF TO ONE SIDE?'** *'In the neck' → 'the middle, just below his chin.'* **Point to your own neck if she's still vague.**
**TIMING**: **'when did you first notice it? Is this the first time he's had a lump there? Is it getting bigger?'** *Ten days; first time; same size.* **Growth over time is the worry question.**

**★ CHARACTER — the examination, asked as history**: **'some of these are things I'd normally check by examining him, but you know the lump best. How big — a pea, a grape, a walnut? Hard or soft? Painful when you touch it? Does it move freely, or feel stuck? Any redness or skin change? Is it warm?'** *A grape; not sure; yes, sore; don't know; a bit pink; warm.* **Ask every one — accept 'not sure'.**

**★ THYROID — BOTH MOVEMENT QUESTIONS**: **'does he feel the heat or cold more than others? Any diarrhoea or constipation? Does the lump move when he SWALLOWS? And when he STICKS HIS TONGUE OUT?'** *No; no; 'it goes up'; 'I think so — when he pokes his tongue out.'* **The tongue question is the discriminator.**

**THE INFECTION SCREEN, REGION BY REGION**: **'any fever or chills? Any recent flu-like illness? Sore throat, runny nose, ear pain? Cough or breathlessness? Rashes or skin infections on the head, neck or scalp? Toothache? Any travel, sick contacts, or animals — cats?'** *No fever; a cold two weeks ago; nothing else.*

**★ THE MALIGNANCY SCREEN — signpost it for her**: **'now the questions that matter for what you're worried about. Any weight loss? Loss of appetite? Any other lumps or bumps? More tired than usual — any drop at school? Night sweats? Bone pain, bleeding or bruising easily? Any concerns about his growth?'** *'No — eating like a horse, playing footy, fine at school.'*

**WELL-CHILD AND BINDSMA**: **'is he alert and active? Eating, drinking, passing urine normally? Any infections, high blood pressure or diabetes in the pregnancy? Immunisations up to date? Other medical problems, medicines, allergies? Anything else in the family?'** *All normal — just the cousin.*

**HER CONCERNS — this surfaces the hidden agenda early**: **'is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd do today?'** *'Shouldn't he have a blood test?'* → **'I'll come to exactly what tests make sense in a moment.'** Then **'thank you — let me tell you what I think.'**

**★ NAME IT, THE LAY MECHANISM, WHY NOW**: **'most likely Oliver has a thyroglossal duct cyst. The thyroid forms at the base of the tongue before birth and moves down to the lower neck. Sometimes part of that path stays open and forms a small sac. It can sit quietly for years, then gets inflamed or infected — often after a cold, like his — which is why you've only noticed it now.'**

**THE REASONS, THEN SPECIFIC DIFFERENTIALS**: **'it fits because it's exactly in the middle, it moves up when he swallows and pokes his tongue out — that's the giveaway — and it's warm and sore.'** Then **other thyroid problems · glands swelling with ear, throat, nose, dental, skin or chest infections, or after a virus · leukaemia and lymphoma, rare in children · a branchial or dermoid cyst.**

**★ CLOSE THE CANCER CONCERN — BEFORE SHE ASKS, WITH REASONS**: **'I know you were worried about lymphoma. I don't think that's what this is: the lump is in the middle, it moves with his tongue, it's sore and warm rather than painless and hard, he has no weight loss, tiredness, sweats, bruising or other lumps, and he's growing well.'**

**THE PLAN — and answer the blood-test request**: **'I'll examine him today, arrange an ultrasound of the neck and a thyroid blood test, start an antibiotic with pain relief, see him again in two days, and refer him to a children's ear, nose and throat surgeon — the usual treatment is a small operation to remove the sac once the infection settles, so it doesn't keep coming back. A leukaemia blood test isn't needed on what I've found — but if anything changes, we do it straight away.'**

setting: HISTORY, EXAMINATION REQUEST, DIAGNOSIS WITH REASONS AND DIFFERENTIALS — ED or GP. TREAT IT AS AN EYE COMPLAINT UNTIL THE URINE TELLS YOU OTHERWISE. NAME THE THREE BUCKETS OUT LOUD IN THE FIRST THIRTY SECONDS — THE EYE ITSELF, ALLERGY, OR FLUID — then ask ONE EYE OR BOTH, AND ONE LID OR BOTH, which deletes most of the differential in ten seconds. back.dx: VERSION A — NEPHROTIC SYNDROME. TO THE FATHER, IN PLAIN WORDS: 'THE KIDNEYS WORK LIKE A VERY FINE FILTER — THEY LET WASTE OUT AND KEEP PROTEIN IN. In this condition THE FILTER BECOMES LEAKY AND PROTEIN ESCAPES INTO THE URINE. PROTEIN IS WHAT HOLDS FLUID INSIDE THE BLOOD VESSELS, so when it drops THE FLUID SEEPS OUT INTO THE TISSUES — AND IT SHOWS FIRST WHERE THE SKIN IS THINNEST, AROUND THE EYES.' Never say albumin, oncotic pressure or proteinuria to a parent — the role-player looks blank and says 'sorry, I didn't follow that'. THE REASONS, WHICH THE TASK EXPLICITLY DEMANDS: A LARGE AMOUNT OF PROTEIN AND NO BLOOD on the dipstick; the swelling is BILATERAL AND WORSE IN THE MORNING; there is FLUID IN THE ABDOMEN AND AT BOTH LUNG BASES; and THE BLOOD PRESSURE IS NORMAL, WHICH ARGUES AGAINST THE OTHER KIDNEY CONDITION. THE DIFFERENTIALS IN THREE GROUPS, NOT AS A LIST: (1) THE EYE — ORBITAL CELLULITIS, excluded because the eye is white with FULL PAINLESS MOVEMENTS and he is afebrile; PRESEPTAL CELLULITIS, for the same reasons; and a STYE OR CHALAZION, which would be ONE LID, NOT FOUR. (2) ALLERGY — a reaction or ANGIOEDEMA, against which there is NO TRIGGER, NO ITCH AND NO RASH, and you screened for anaphylaxis. (3) FLUID RETENTION — renal, and within that NEPHROTIC SYNDROME, POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS and IgA NEPHROPATHY; then CARDIAC FAILURE, CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE, HYPOTHYROIDISM and PROTEIN-LOSING ENTEROPATHY. MANAGEMENT AND REASSURANCE: 'IT ISN'T ANYTHING YOU DID. It is serious enough that HE NEEDS TO COME INTO HOSPITAL, but the common form in four-year-olds — ABOUT NINE IN TEN — USUALLY RESPONDS WELL TO STEROID TREATMENT.' Confirm with a URINE PROTEIN:CREATININE RATIO on a first-morning sample, SERUM ALBUMIN and bloods, with nephrology involved today. VERSION A2 — POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS: 'after a throat infection with a particular bacterium, THE IMMUNE SYSTEM MAKES ANTIBODIES, and A COUPLE OF WEEKS LATER those can INFLAME THE FILTERS in the kidney. That's why there's BLOOD in the urine, why he's PASSING LESS, why his BLOOD PRESSURE IS UP, and why he's swollen.' Investigations: urine microscopy for RED CELL CASTS, electrolytes, C3 LOW WITH NORMAL C4, ASOT or anti-DNase B, throat swab. Management: SALT AND FLUID RESTRICTION, DAILY WEIGHTS, blood pressure monitoring, a diuretic if overloaded — most children recover fully, and RECHECK C3 AT EIGHT WEEKS. VERSION B — ORBITAL CELLULITIS: 'I'm concerned about AN INFECTION IN THE TISSUES BEHIND THE EYE. It usually STARTS IN THE SINUSES AND SPREADS THROUGH A VERY THIN PIECE OF BONE into the eye socket. The reasons are that it is ONLY ONE EYE, the eye itself is RED, he has A FEVER, and ABOVE ALL IT HURTS HIM TO MOVE IT — THAT IS WHAT TELLS ME THE INFECTION IS BEHIND THE EYE RATHER THAN IN THE LID.' Admit; IV ANTIBIOTICS STARTED NOW, NOT AFTER THE SCAN; urgent CT ORBITS AND SINUSES WITH CONTRAST; blood cultures and inflammatory markers; ophthalmology and ENT today; HOURLY ACUITY, COLOUR VISION AND PUPIL CHECKS; and surgery for an abscess or no improvement at 24-48 hours. VERSION B-MINUS — PRESEPTAL: 'this is an infection of THE EYELID TISSUE IN FRONT OF THE EYE, NOT BEHIND IT. I can say that because HIS EYE MOVES FREELY AND IT DOESN'T HURT HIM TO MOVE IT, his vision is normal and THE EYE ITSELF ISN'T RED' — oral antibiotics, review tomorrow, NO SCAN, and return sooner if it spreads, the eye becomes red or painful to move, vision changes, or he becomes febrile. BEING ABLE TO SEPARATE THOSE TWO OUT LOUD, WITH THE REASON ATTACHED, IS THE HIGHEST-VALUE THIRTY SECONDS IN THE STATION.
plan: FRAME THE THREE BUCKETS — it costs eight seconds: 'I can see his eyes are puffy. SWELLING AROUND A CHILD'S EYE COMES FROM ONE OF THREE PLACES — A PROBLEM IN THE EYE OR THE EYELID ITSELF, AN ALLERGIC REACTION, OR FLUID THE BODY IS HOLDING ONTO — so I'm going to ask about each of those in turn, then examine him, then tell you what I think.'

CHARACTERISE, AND ASK LATERALITY BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: 'when did it start? Has it happened before? Is it getting worse? IS IT ONE EYE OR BOTH? IS IT ONE EYELID OR BOTH EYELIDS? IS IT WORSE AT ANY PARTICULAR TIME OF DAY?' → both eyes, all four lids, WORST FIRST THING IN THE MORNING and better by the afternoon. (Taking a full history without ever establishing laterality is the first trap — those two questions delete most of the differential in ten seconds.)

BUCKET 1, THE EYE — NEVER SKIPPED: 'any blurring of his vision, or bumping into things? ANY PAIN IN THE EYE? ANY PAIN WHEN HE MOVES HIS EYE OR LOOKS AROUND? Any redness — IN THE LIDS, AND IN THE EYE ITSELF? Any discharge, or stuck shut in the mornings? Are they itchy? ANY FEVER OR CHILLS? Any blocked nose, headache or pain in the face?' (Skipping straight to the kidney is what examiners have watched candidates do for years — and in the orbital cellulitis version it is the difference between a pass and a miss.)

BUCKET 2, ALLERGY — forty-five seconds that buy you an explicit anaphylaxis screen AND one of the three differential groups: 'what was he doing just before it started? Any new food or medicine? ANY INSECT BITE OR STING? Any known allergies, asthma, eczema or hay fever? Any rash anywhere? ANY SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE? ANY NOISY BREATHING?'

BUCKET 3, FLUID — RENAL FIRST, AND ASKED PRECISELY: 'any change in HOW MUCH WEE he's passing? IS IT FROTHY OR BUBBLY? IS IT DARK, OR BLOODY — LIKE COLA OR TEA? Has he had A SORE THROAT OR ANY SKIN SORES recently — AND HOW LONG BEFORE THE SWELLING STARTED? Did he see a doctor or take antibiotics for it?' → he is going less, AND IT'S BEEN REALLY BUBBLY — given only because you asked. (Accepting 'his wee's a funny colour' without splitting FROTHY from DARK is the named trap: frothy is protein and nephrotic, cola is blood and glomerulonephritis — different diseases, different treatments.)

THE REST OF BUCKET 3: 'any swelling of his legs or feet? Any chest pain or breathlessness when he runs and plays? DOES HE EVER GO BLUE? Any yellowing of his eyes or skin? Any pale stools or dark urine? Is he bothered by the cold? Constipated? Dry skin? Any tummy pain, vomiting or diarrhoea? HAS HIS TUMMY LOOKED SWOLLEN?' → ankles puffy in the evening, AND HIS TUMMY HAS LOOKED BLOATED FOR A FEW DAYS — the second withheld finding.

THE EXAMINATION, AND THE ORDER IS THE POINT: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, any rash, ANY STRIDOR, and his growth? ALL THE VITAL SIGNS, PARTICULARLY THE BLOOD PRESSURE AND THE TEMPERATURE. I'D LIKE TO EXAMINE THE EYE FIRST: any redness, any discharge, ANY PROPTOSIS? VISUAL ACUITY? Pupils? ARE THE EYE MOVEMENTS FULL, AND IS THERE PAIN ON MOVEMENT? Thyroid. Respiratory — equal air entry, added sounds, ANY DULLNESS AT THE BASES? Cardiovascular. Abdomen — distension, tenderness, organomegaly, ballotable kidneys, SHIFTING DULLNESS? Lower limbs for PITTING OEDEMA. AND A URINE DIPSTICK.' → 'WHAT WERE YOU LOOKING FOR ON THE DIPSTICK?' → 'TWO THINGS: PROTEIN AND BLOOD.' (Asking for the abdomen before the eye, or reciting every dipstick pad, both lose marks. And missing the blood pressure leaves you unable to separate nephritic from nephrotic.)
THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS, WITH SUPPORTING AND EXCLUDING REASONS (see dx) → 'IS THAT SERIOUS? IS IT SOMETHING WE DID?' → no, and the hospital admission with the nine-in-ten steroid response.
THE DIFFERENTIALS IN THREE GROUPS, NOT AS A LIST (see dx), each with the reason it is excluded. → and late, if never invited: 'SHOULD I HAVE BROUGHT HIM IN EARLIER?'

VERSION A2 — PSGN: 'this is a different kidney condition. After a throat infection with a particular bacterium, THE IMMUNE SYSTEM MAKES ANTIBODIES, and a couple of weeks later those can INFLAME THE FILTERS in the kidney. That's why there's BLOOD in the urine, why he's passing less, WHY HIS BLOOD PRESSURE IS UP, and why he's swollen.' Investigations: urine microscopy for RED CELL CASTS, electrolytes, C3 AND C4, ASOT or anti-DNase B, throat swab. Management: SALT AND FLUID RESTRICTION, DAILY WEIGHTS, blood pressure monitoring, diuretic if overloaded, and RECHECK C3 AT EIGHT WEEKS. TIMING: PSGN follows a sore throat by 1-2 WEEKS and a skin infection by 3-6 WEEKS — whereas IgA NEPHROPATHY gives haematuria 1-2 DAYS INTO THE ILLNESS, so calling a two-day post-viral haematuria post-streptococcal is wrong.

VERSION B — ORBITAL CELLULITIS: 'THIS CHANGES THINGS' — then the explanation (see dx), then ADMIT, IV ANTIBIOTICS NOW NOT AFTER THE SCAN, urgent CT ORBITS AND SINUSES WITH CONTRAST, blood cultures, ophthalmology and ENT today, HOURLY ACUITY, COLOUR VISION AND PUPIL CHECKS, and surgery for an abscess or no improvement at 24-48 hours. / VERSION B-MINUS — PRESEPTAL: oral antibiotics, review tomorrow, NO SCAN, with return criteria. / IF ASKED FOR INVESTIGATIONS INSTEAD OF DIFFERENTIALS, ANSWER THE WHOLE CHILD: 'bedside — urine dipstick, A URINE PROTEIN:CREATININE RATIO ON A FIRST-MORNING SAMPLE, microscopy and culture. Bloods — electrolytes and creatinine, SERUM ALBUMIN, full blood count, lipids, C3 AND C4, ASOT or anti-DNase B, liver function, TSH, AND HEPATITIS AND VARICELLA SEROLOGY BEFORE ANY STEROID. Imaging — renal ultrasound if there is renal impairment or an atypical picture. AND A KIDNEY BIOPSY IS NOT FIRST-LINE IN A TYPICAL FOUR-YEAR-OLD — it is for atypical features or steroid resistance, and that decision belongs with nephrology.'
pefe: Role-player: Daniel, 36, works in logistics; partner at home with the baby; father of Sam, 4. He has brought Sam in because HIS EYES HAVE BEEN PUFFY FOR ABOUT A WEEK AND THE CHILDCARE CENTRE COMMENTED ON IT. REGISTER: CALM, COOPERATIVE, SLIGHTLY PUZZLED RATHER THAN FRIGHTENED — HE HALF EXPECTS TO BE TOLD IT IS AN ALLERGY, and becomes concerned ONLY WHEN THE DOCTOR MENTIONS HOSPITAL. HIDDEN AGENDA: he is quietly worried he missed something, because it has been a week and he did not come sooner — raised late: 'SHOULD I HAVE BROUGHT HIM IN EARLIER?'

THE DETAILS HE HOLDS BACK — THE TWO FINDINGS THAT MAKE THE CASE: THE BUBBLY URINE AND THE BLOATED TUMMY. DO NOT VOLUNTEER EITHER. Give the urine detail ONLY if asked whether it is FROTHY OR BUBBLY; give the tummy ONLY if asked about ABDOMINAL SWELLING OR TUMMY PAIN. IF ASKED A VAGUE 'ANYTHING ELSE?', SAY NO. If asked 'is his urine normal?', say 'I THINK SO' — and only if they ask frothy or bubbly do you say yes. Background: Sam is otherwise well, MILD ECZEMA, immunised, no medicines or allergies, growing normally, NO family history of kidney disease; he had a runny nose and cough a fortnight ago, NO sore throat, NO skin sores.

HOW TO PLAY IT: answer only what is asked, and answer briefly. IF THEY ASK ABOUT THE EYE AT ALL, BE CLEARLY REASSURING — no pain, no redness, normal vision, normal movements. IF THEY NEVER ASK A SINGLE QUESTION ABOUT THE EYE ITSELF, SAY NOTHING AND MARK THEM DOWN. IF THEY USE WORDS LIKE ALBUMIN, ONCOTIC PRESSURE OR PROTEINURIA, LOOK BLANK AND SAY 'SORRY, I DIDN'T FOLLOW THAT.' When they mention hospital, become worried: 'HOSPITAL? IS IT SERIOUS?' Ask 'IS IT SOMETHING WE DID?' once the diagnosis is given, and close with 'WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?' MARK OUT OF 10: framed the history naming the three groups; ONE EYE OR BOTH AND ONE LID OR BOTH; AT LEAST FOUR EYE QUESTIONS INCLUDING PAIN ON EYE MOVEMENT; asked whether THE EYE ITSELF was red, separately from the lids; screened allergy INCLUDING LIPS, TONGUE AND NOISY BREATHING; ASKED WHETHER THE URINE WAS FROTHY AND FOUND IT; ASKED ABOUT ABDOMINAL SWELLING AND FOUND IT; asked for THE EYE EXAMINATION FIRST plus blood pressure and temperature; asked for a dipstick AND NAMED PROTEIN AND BLOOD; and gave the diagnosis WITH REASONS AND EXCLUDED THE ALTERNATIVES OUT LOUD. AUTOMATIC FAIL: asked nothing about the eye itself; never asked for a urine dipstick; named a diagnosis with no supporting reasons; or in Version B, did not recognise orbital cellulitis or sent the child home on oral antibiotics.
The preceding illness — A runny nose and cough a fortnight ago — no sore throat, no skin sores

The two findings the father withholds — THE URINE IS REALLY BUBBLY IN THE TOILET, given ONLY if you ask frothy or bubbly; and HIS TUMMY HAS LOOKED BLOATED FOR A FEW DAYS, given ONLY if you ask about abdominal swelling

setting: HISTORY AND EXPLANATION — regional GP. THE DIAGNOSIS IS NOT THE POINT; THE SCREEN IS. TWO ITEMS ARE REQUIRED TO PASS: EXPLORING THE DIARRHOEA PROPERLY, and LINKING IT TO THE THRUSH AND NAMING THE SCREEN. The mother volunteers NEITHER the loose stools NOR her own sore nipples unless asked — and if you start explaining without asking about bowels she says at the end 'HE'S ALSO HAD RUNNY POOS FOR A WHILE — IS THAT CONNECTED?' and marks it a miss. TREAT MOTHER AND BABY TOGETHER. And never ask 'do you have HIV?' cold — USE THE ANTENATAL-SCREEN ROUTE.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. A 6-MONTH-OLD BOY brought in by his mother, WORRIED ABOUT A RASH IN HIS MOUTH. A PHOTOGRAPH shows CREAMY-WHITE PLAQUES ON THE TONGUE, PALATE AND CHEEKS. HE IS AFEBRILE AND FEEDING.

Take a focused history from the mother, then explain the most likely diagnosis AND YOUR REASONING. 8 minutes. back.dx: ORAL CANDIDIASIS — oral thrush — with chronic pale greasy diarrhoea that must be linked and screened. Explain it in plain words: 'Sam most likely has oral thrush. It's a yeast called candida that lives harmlessly in most people's mouths; in babies it sometimes overgrows because their immune system is still maturing. The creamy patches that don't WIPE off, with a red base, are typical. It's common, it's not caused by anything you've done — it's not about cleanliness — and it's treatable.' then the two additions that carry the station. First, treat both: 'Thrush passes back and forth between a baby's mouth and mum's nipples, so I'd treat you both.' Second, link and screen — and the examiner's checklist item reads links the thrush to the chronic diarrhoea and names the screen: 'And this is why I asked so many questions. Thrush is more likely when the body's defences are a little lower. He's had loose, greasy stools for a month; with the thrush, I'd like to check his gut is absorbing food properly and his immune system is working: confirm his newborn screening result, a sweat test for cystic fibrosis, and some blood tests. Most babies I check are completely fine.' On its own the diarrhoea would be watched — together with the thrush it is checked. When she asks 'Cystic fibrosis — isn't that really serious?': 'It is serious, which is exactly why I'd rather check than assume; his normal heel-prick makes it unlikely, but the test isn't perfect, and the check is simple.' Note that coeliac cannot be assessed yet, because he started solids only last week. The plan: antifungal drops or gel after feeds for one to two weeks, continued a couple of days past clearing; antifungal cream for her nipples after each feed; antifungal cream for the nappy rash; boil the dummy daily and sterilise teats; and keep breastfeeding. Review in two weeks — sooner if he stops feeding, has a fever, is drowsy or has fewer wet nappies — and if it keeps returning or his weight drops, refer to the children's hospital. Version B — antibiotics and no diarrhoea: 'That's the likely trigger — antibiotics knock back the friendly bacteria and let the yeast overgrow. His bowels are normal, he's growing well, no unusual infections, so I'm not concerned about his immune system' — treat, sterilise the teats, review in two weeks. Harder variant — growth has dropped: 'That changes things. I'll weigh him today, arrange the sweat test and bloods this week, and phone the paediatric team today.' and if she declines the tests — 'He's fine, I just want the cream': 'You'll have the treatment today regardless; the tests are simple, and if they're normal we can both stop worrying.'
plan: OPEN, ADDRESS THE CONCERN, AND SIGNPOST: 'I can see that's worrying. Let me ask some questions about the patches, THEN ABOUT HIS HEALTH GENERALLY, and then I'll explain what I think is going on.' Then the patches: how long, first time, spreading, DO THEY WIPE OFF, IS IT RED UNDERNEATH, feeding, fever, dribbling, unusual crying. → two weeks, spread from tongue to cheeks, DOESN'T WIPE OFF AND LOOKED RED AND RAW UNDERNEATH. (Stopping to explain after three questions is the trap — THE DIAGNOSIS IS NOT THE POINT, THE SCREEN IS.)

SOURCE AND OTHER SITES: 'any other rashes or white patches — NAPPY AREA, NECK FOLDS? Breast, bottle or both? ANY PAIN, CRACKING, SHININESS OR WHITE PATCHES ON YOUR NIPPLES? Dummy or bottle teats? Any thrush or discharge around the time of his birth?' → a nappy rash that won't clear, fully breastfed, AND — only because you asked — 'MY NIPPLES HAVE BEEN STINGING AFTER FEEDS AND LOOK SHINY.' (Treating the baby and not the mother is the named trap, and the role-player mentions the nipples ONLY if asked.)
DRUGS: 'any antibiotics recently — FOR HIM OR FOR YOU WHILE BREASTFEEDING? Any steroid creams, puffers or medicines? Any regular medicines at all?'

THE IMMUNE SCREEN — THE PASS/FAIL BLOCK, PREFACED SO IT MAKES SENSE: 'I'd like to ask about his general health, BECAUSE THRUSH SOMETIMES SHOWS UP WHEN THE BODY'S DEFENCES ARE LOWER. HOW ARE HIS BOWEL MOTIONS?' → 'he's actually had LOOSE POOS FOR ABOUT A MONTH.' → THEN EXPLORE IT PROPERLY: 'how long has that been going on? Every day or on and off? Getting worse? WHAT DO THEY LOOK LIKE — WATERY, GREASY, PALE, BULKY, SMELLY? Any blood or mucus? How many a day?' → four or five a day, PALE AND GREASY, quite smelly, no blood. (Hearing 'loose poos for a month' and moving on is the fail — THE MARKS ARE IN EXPLORING IT AND LINKING IT.)

THE REST OF THE SCREEN: 'WAS HIS HEEL-PRICK TEST DONE AND NORMAL? Has he had MANY INFECTIONS, OR ANY THAT WERE SERIOUS? Has he STARTED SOLIDS — ANYTHING WITH WHEAT? Any lumps or bumps, pale colour, easy bruising?' → heel prick fine, one cold, rice cereal started last week.

WELL-BABY, ANTENATAL AND GROWTH: alert and active, drinking, wet nappies; 'ANY INFECTIONS IN THE PREGNANCY? WERE ALL YOUR ANTENATAL BLOOD TESTS AND SCREENING NORMAL?'; term, special care; immunisations and development; 'IS HE GAINING WEIGHT AS EXPECTED ON THE GROWTH CHART?'; family history of immune problems, cystic fibrosis, coeliac or bowel disease; and who is at home and how she is coping. (Asking 'DO YOU HAVE HIV?' COLD is the trap — USE THE ANTENATAL-SCREEN ROUTE, and if she asks why, explain honestly.)

setting: History, examination findings and explanation — regional GP. Age adaptation must be audible: no pain questions to a 15-month-old — the mother looks puzzled and says 'He can't tell me, he's one'. The timing question replaces pain: has the limp been there since his very first steps. And the AUTO-FAIL is the birth history: she says 'A caesarean' and will not say breech unless you ask — then breech must chain immediately to hip ultrasound, the six-week check and family history. stem: General practice, regional South Australia. JAYDEN, 15 MONTHS, brought in by his mother KELLY: 'HE'S NOT WALKING PROPERLY — HE LIMPS.' Well child, afebrile, immunisations up to date. He PULLED TO STAND AT 12-13 MONTHS and took INDEPENDENT STEPS ABOUT A MONTH AGO, AND SHE HAS NOTICED THE LIMP SINCE HE STARTED WALKING.

History FIVE MINUTES, then the examiner HANDS YOU A CARD OF EXAMINATION FINDINGS AND AN X-RAY, then explain the most likely diagnosis WITH YOUR REASONS to the mother. 8 minutes. IN THE FACE-TO-FACE FORMAT you ask the examiner for the findings instead.

Read the card of physical examination findings and the X-ray — or, face to face, ask the examiner for the findings
Explain the most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, to the mother
time: WIPE, open and acknowledge without reassuring · do not agree with grandma, because a limp from first steps in a well child is a structural hip until proven otherwise · explore the limp: can he stand and bear weight on both legs, which leg does he favour, when did he pull to stand and take his first steps, has the limp been there since those very first steps or did it start later, is it getting worse, anything better or worse · then what she sees and the septic-hip screen: swelling or redness at hips, knees or ankles; deformity, a foot turning in, a leg that looks shorter; does he cry when you change his nappy or move the leg; fever; has there ever been a time he wouldn't weight-bear at all; recent illness · then the birth history, signposted and deep: 'Because this has been there since his first steps, I need to go back to when he was born' · pregnancy, medications, delivery, forceps or vacuum, was he breech, was he your first, term, special care, was he swaddled tightly, did he have his six-week check and was anything said about his hips, did he ever have a hip ultrasound, and anyone in the family with hip problems as a child · then the other three domains in thirty seconds: pincer grip, babble and words, stranger awareness and peekaboo, plus floppy or stiff as a baby and when he sat · then trauma, NAI, growth and binds · then summarise, read the findings aloud and translate them, and explain ball and socket with the normal side first.

back.dx: Developmental dysplasia of the left hip. Read the findings aloud and translate them: 'The left leg is 2 centimetres shorter, the thigh creases are asymmetric and left hip abduction is restricted, in an afebrile child with no warmth or tenderness. On the x-ray the right hip is normal; on the left the ball sits high and outside a shallow socket, and the smooth curve we call Shenton's line is broken.' then explain it, normal side first, in plain words: 'The hip is a ball-and-socket joint — the round TOP of the thigh bone sits in a cup in the pelvis. In Jayden's left hip the cup didn't form deeply enough, so the ball has slipped up and out of it. That's why his left leg is shorter, why the skin folds on his thighs don't match, and why that hip doesn't open out as far — and it's why he LIMPS.' The reasons and the blame removed: 'Being breech, being a first baby and having a family history all make it more likely — none of that is anything you did. It's called developmental because the hip can look normal early on and slip out later as the baby grows, so it can be missed at six weeks even by a careful examiner. What matters is that we've found it now, while treatment is still straightforward.' What happens next, with honest expectations: x-ray today, phone the children's orthopaedic team so he is seen quickly, and PATS for travel. 'At his age the usual treatment is to put the ball back into the socket under a short anaesthetic and hold it there with a plaster cast for a few months; sometimes an operation is needed' — never 'He'll grow out of it' and never 'The brace will fix it', because a 15-month-old is past the brace window. Safety-net: 'If he gets a fever, stops walking on the leg, or the hip becomes hot or swollen, bring him straight in — that would be something different and urgent.' then offer to write it down for his father. Variants: bilateral DDH in a waddling girl — 'Because both hips can be affected, symmetrical creases don't reassure me': ask whether abduction is restricted on both sides, whether there is a waddling gait with a pronounced lower-back curve, and x-ray both hips — 'Both sockets are shallow, so both balls sit out of place, which is why she rocks from side to side rather than limping on one leg.' The examiner pushes on the x-ray: 'A horizontal line through the growth cartilage of the pelvis and a vertical line from the edge of the socket — a normal head sits in the lower-inner quadrant; here it's upper-outer. And Shenton's line, the curve from the femoral neck to the pubic bone, is broken on the left. I'm not measuring angles — that's for orthopaedics.' Febrile and refusing to weight-bear — the case flips: 'A febrile toddler who won't bear weight has a septic hip until proven otherwise' — temperature, the position he holds the hip in, warmth and tenderness, same-day bloods and ultrasound, phone the orthopaedic registrar, and MedSTAR kids if he is unwell. And when she says her mother told her not to fuss: 'I understand — and a family history of hip problems actually makes it more likely, not less. This is one where waiting makes the treatment bigger.'
plan: WIPE, OPEN, ACKNOWLEDGE — AND DO NOT AGREE WITH GRANDMA: 'that does sound worrying, especially when he's only just started walking. I'll ask you a number of questions, INCLUDING ABOUT HIS BIRTH AND DEVELOPMENT, and then we'll work out what's going on.' (Reassuring before the history is the first trap — and if you do, she pushes back: 'SO WHY IS THE LEG SHORTER?')

EXPLORE THE LIMP: 'can he stand and put weight on both legs? WHICH LEG DOES HE FAVOUR? When did he first pull to stand, and when were his first steps? HAS THE LIMP BEEN THERE SINCE THOSE VERY FIRST STEPS, OR DID IT START LATER? Is it getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse?' → left, FROM THE VERY FIRST STEPS, unchanged. (Asking 'where does it hurt?' or 'is the pain sharp or dull?' of a 15-month-old is what the examiner listens for — THE TIMING QUESTION REPLACES PAIN.)

WHAT SHE SEES, AND THE SEPTIC-HIP SCREEN: 'any swelling or redness around his hips, knees or ankles? ANY DEFORMITY — A FOOT TURNING IN, A LEG THAT LOOKS SHORTER? DOES HE SEEM IN PAIN — CRYING WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY OR MOVE THE LEG? ANY FEVER? HAS THERE EVER BEEN A TIME HE WOULDN'T PUT WEIGHT ON THE LEG AT ALL? Has he been unwell recently?' → the left leg does look shorter when she changes him.

THE BIRTH HISTORY — SIGNPOSTED, EARLY AND DEEP, AND THIS IS THE AUTO-FAIL BLOCK: 'because this has been there since his first steps, I NEED TO GO BACK TO WHEN HE WAS BORN. How was the pregnancy? Any medications, alcohol or drugs? The delivery — was it long, forceps or vacuum, WAS HE BREECH? WAS HE YOUR FIRST? Born at term? Any special care? WAS HE SWADDLED TIGHTLY? DID HE HAVE HIS SIX-WEEK CHECK — WAS ANYTHING SAID ABOUT HIS HIPS, AND DID HE EVER HAVE A HIP ULTRASOUND? ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH HIP PROBLEMS AS A CHILD?' → BREECH, caesarean, first baby, swaddled, six-week check normal, NO SCAN, AND HER SISTER WORE A BRACE. (Hearing 'breech' and not chaining to the ultrasound, the six-week check and the family history is the fail — and hearing 'normal six-week check' and dropping DDH is the other one, because A NORMAL EARLY CHECK DOES NOT EXCLUDE A DEVELOPMENTAL DISLOCATION.)

THE OTHER THREE DOMAINS IN THIRTY SECONDS: 'walking is one part of his development — a few quick questions on the rest. Can he pick up small things like A SULTANA WITH HIS THUMB AND FINGER? Does he babble, any words? Does he notice strangers, play peekaboo, roll a ball back? AS A BABY WAS HE FLOPPY OR STIFF? WHEN DID HE SIT?'

TRAUMA, NAI, GROWTH AND BINDS — fifteen seconds that are marked even though the mother seems lovely: 'any falls or injuries to the legs — DID ANYONE SEE THEM HAPPEN? Any bruises you couldn't explain? How are things at home? WHO LOOKS AFTER HIM — does he go to childcare? Any stress at home lately? Is he growing and gaining weight as expected? Any pallor, or waking at night crying? Immunisations, other problems, medicines, allergies?'

SUMMARISE AND TRANSITION: 'so: A PAINLESS LIMP ON THE LEFT SINCE HIS FIRST STEPS A MONTH AGO, in a well boy who was BREECH AND FIRST-BORN, with a normal six-week check BUT NO HIP SCAN, other development on track, no injury or fever. I'd like to examine him now.'

THE CARD AND THE X-RAY — READ THEM ALOUD AND TRANSLATE (see dx). IN THE FACE-TO-FACE VERSION, REQUEST BY NAME: general appearance, temperature and growth chart; WATCH HIM STAND AND WALK — weight-bearing, and is the gait A LIMP, A WADDLE OR OUT-TOEING; inspection of both legs INCLUDING WHETHER THE THIGH AND GLUTEAL CREASES ARE SYMMETRICAL; palpation for warmth or tenderness; movement, SPECIFICALLY HIP ABDUCTION WITH HIPS AND KNEES FLEXED; TRUE LEG LENGTH, ASIS TO MEDIAL MALLEOLUS; BARLOW AND ORTOLANI, NOTING THEY ARE UNRELIABLE AFTER THREE MONTHS; tone and reflexes; and the spine for a dimple or hair tuft. (A generic 'lower limb examination' request gets 'normal' and loses creases, length and abduction — THE THREE MARKED FINDINGS.)

NAME IT, BALL AND SOCKET, NORMAL SIDE FIRST, THEN THE REASONS AND THE BLAME REMOVED (see dx) → 'IS THAT BECAUSE HE WAS BREECH? DID I DO SOMETHING WRONG?' and 'WHY DIDN'T THEY PICK IT UP AT THE CHECK?' (Become tearful at the words 'developmental dysplasia' if no plain-language explanation follows within fifteen seconds.)

THE PLAN, THE HONEST EXPECTATIONS AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → it depends on what the specialist finds: cast, sometimes an operation — NOT A BRACE. Then offer to write it down for his father.

pefe: Role-player: Kelly, 27, part-time hairdresser who stopped work when Jayden was born; partner Dean drives trucks and is away a lot; money is tight. JAYDEN: FIRST CHILD, BREECH, ELECTIVE CAESAREAN AT 39 WEEKS, 3.4 kg, home day 3, SWADDLED, breastfed then formula, immunisations up to date, no illnesses except a cold two months ago. Sat 7 months, crawled 9, stood 12-13 months, FIRST STEPS 4-5 WEEKS AGO — AND HE LIMPED ON THE LEFT FROM THE FIRST STEP. NO pain, NO fever, NEVER REFUSED TO WALK. HIS LEFT LEG LOOKS SHORTER WHEN SHE CHANGES HIM — volunteer only if asked about deformity or leg length. SIX-WEEK CHECK 'NORMAL', NO HIP ULTRASOUND. HER SISTER WORE A HIP BRACE AS A BABY — volunteer only when family history is asked. No falls, no bruises. HER MOTHER AND DEAN BOTH SAY 'DON'T FUSS'.

How to play it: answer only what is asked. If the doctor asks 'Any problems with the birth?', say 'No, it was a caesarean' — do not volunteer breech unless they ask about breech or why the caesarean. If pain questions are asked, look puzzled: 'He can't tell me, he's one.' if the doctor reassures early — 'Probably nothing' — push: 'So why is the leg shorter?' Become tearful at 'Developmental dysplasia' if no plain-language explanation follows within fifteen seconds. Hidden agenda: you fear he will need surgery and that you caused it by swaddling or by the breech birth — raise it late as 'Did I do something wrong?' Unless the doctor asks what worries you most; if never asked, at 6:30 say 'Will he need an operation? Was it the swaddling?' Register: anxious, slightly defensive — 'I'm not overreacting' — and visibly relaxing when the doctor explains without blame.

Score them on: WIPE and concern acknowledged; 'SINCE FIRST STEPS?' The other three domains — ALL NORMAL — pincer grip, a few words, shy with strangers and loves peekaboo, sat at 7 months
Her hidden agenda — She fears he will need surgery and that she caused it by swaddling or by the breech birth — raised late as 'Did I do something wrong?' Unless you ask what worries her

DO — Read the findings aloud and translate them — shorter leg, asymmetric creases, restricted abduction means the ball has slipped up and out of a shallow socket — normal side first

setting: History, examination request, diagnosis and differentials — regional GP. The pass mark is the order: ask infection and malignancy before trauma, even though the stem smells of fracture — and ask the NAI questions fully, framed as routine. The mother becomes briefly defensive — 'Why are you asking about home?' — and settles when told it is routine, but if you never ask who was there she never volunteers it. Name the film precisely — spiral, undisplaced, distal tibia, fibula intact — and never say 'Normal'. Management is not a task: one sentence if asked, and do not skip the differentials.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. NOAH, 3 YEARS, brought by his mother EMMA. PAIN IN HIS RIGHT LEG SINCE YESTERDAY AND REFUSING TO WALK. OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL.

History about 3 minutes, then ask the examiner for the examination findings; investigations have been ordered and are handed to you at the end of the examination — no need to ask for them and no need to explain the film to the mother. Then explain the diagnosis and differentials to her. Further management is not asked. 8 minutes.

back.dx: AN UNDISPLACED SPIRAL FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL TIBIA — a toddler's fracture. Name the film precisely to the examiner: 'A fine spiral lucency in the distal third of the tibial shaft, undisplaced, fibula intact.' Do not explain the film to the mother — it is not a task — and never say 'Normal'. To the mother, in plain words: 'Noah has a broken bone: a fine spiral crack in the lower part of his shin bone, the tibia. The bone hasn't moved out of place. We call it a toddler's fracture because it happens in children his age who are new walkers, from a twist of the leg, often on a slide or when a foot gets caught, and very often nobody sees it. So please don't feel you missed something.' then the differentials, each excluded with its reason — the task says diagnosis and differentials, so this half is not optional: 'An infection in the bone or joint — he has no fever, he's well, his hip moves freely, so that doesn't fit. A blood problem like leukaemia — good colour, no bruising, no night pain, so no. An irritable hip after a cold — no recent cold, and the hip is fine. Joint inflammation — no rash or swollen joints. And, as I ask every family, nothing about how this happened worries me.' when she asks 'Did his sister push him?': 'Nothing suggests that; a twist on the slide is enough. His sister didn't do anything wrong either.' Management is not a task — one sentence if asked: 'Pain relief and a plaster from above the knee for some weeks, with the bone doctors reviewing him. Children's bones heal fast and completely; he will walk normally again.' then summarise and close with 'What is worrying you most?' → 'Just that I didn't see it' → 'That's the usual story with this fracture. You brought him in within a day, which is exactly right.' Version B — the film is reported normal: 'The x-ray doesn't show a break, but a well child who is tender over the shin bone and won't bear weight has a toddler's fracture until proven otherwise; the crack is often invisible for the first week or two. We treat it as a fracture with a plaster and repeat the x-ray in ten to fourteen days, when the healing bone shows.' Version C — febrile with a hip held still, and the station stops: 'Emma, I'm going to stop here. A fever with a hip he won't let anyone move is an infection in the joint until we prove otherwise, and that can damage the joint within hours. He needs blood tests, an ultrasound of the hip and the bone doctors today; I'm arranging that now' — and name the Kocher criteria. The pale child: 'Pale, tired and now leg pain is a combination I never leave: we do a blood count today, before anything else.' Bruises of different ages on the back: 'Bruises on the back at different ages in a three-year-old are unusual. I'll ask the children's team to see him today and do a full check of his bones; I'm required to speak with the child protection service, and I'll keep you informed.'
plan: VITALS INCLUDING TEMPERATURE, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE: 'Examiner, may I have his vital signs INCLUDING TEMPERATURE?' → 36.9, HR 110. Then: 'Emma, tell me what's been happening with his leg.' → 'since yesterday afternoon HE WON'T WALK. NOBODY SAW HIM FALL, and now I'm worried something's really wrong.' → 'THAT'S FRIGHTENING WHEN THERE'S NO OBVIOUS REASON, AND IT'S EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING TO BRING HIM IN.'

DEFINE THE LIMP: 'when you say he won't walk — CAN HE PUT ANY WEIGHT ON IT AT ALL, OR DOES HE WALK WITH A LIMP? When did it start, and was it sudden? Is it getting better or worse? Worse in the morning or the evening? Anything that helps?' → NO WEIGHT AT ALL, sudden at about 3 pm, same or a bit worse, happy sitting. (NON-WEIGHT-BEARING IS A KOCHER CRITERION — register it. And do NOT suggest a mechanism yet.)

THE PAIN AND THE MUSCULOSKELETAL SWEEP: 'WHERE IS THE PAIN — HIP, THIGH, KNEE, SHIN, ANKLE OR FOOT? CAN HE POINT? Constant or does it come and go? Does it go anywhere? DOES IT WAKE HIM AT NIGHT? How bad? Any swelling, redness, warmth, bruising or change in the shape of the leg? ANY OTHER JOINTS SORE OR SWOLLEN?' → lower shin, sometimes the ankle, slept okay, nothing visible. (KNEE PAIN IS HIP PAIN UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE, so at least ask where — and NIGHT PAIN WOULD MOVE MALIGNANCY UP THE LIST.)

THE DIFFERENTIALS IN ORDER — THE PASS MARK. INFECTION: 'any fever? Is he unwell, off his food? ANY RECENT COLD, EAR INFECTION OR SKIN INFECTION?' BLOOD PROBLEMS: 'has he been PALE, TIRED, BRUISING EASILY, LOSING WEIGHT, SWEATING AT NIGHT?' ONLY THEN INJURY, AND OPEN FIRST: 'WHAT WAS HE DOING YESTERDAY? Any fall, twist, jump, trampoline, SLIDE, FOOT CAUGHT IN A COT OR A FENCE? WHO WAS WITH HIM? Any injuries or broken bones before?' IRRITABLE HIP: 'any cold or tummy bug in the last couple of weeks?' JOINT INFLAMMATION: 'any rash, red eyes, swollen joints, STIFF IN THE MORNINGS?' (Asking trauma first because the stem smells of fracture is exactly what this station tests.)

THE NAI BLOCK, FRAMED AS ROUTINE BEFORE SHE CAN TAKE IT PERSONALLY: 'and AS I ASK EVERY FAMILY: WHO WAS LOOKING AFTER HIM YESTERDAY? Who lives at home? Any brothers or sisters? Any stresses at the moment? Does he go to childcare?' → 'WHY ARE YOU ASKING ABOUT HOME?' → 'BECAUSE WHEN A CHILD HAS AN INJURY THAT NO ONE SAW, I ASK EVERY FAMILY THE SAME QUESTIONS. IT PROTECTS HIM, AND IT'S ROUTINE.' Then: walking on time, growth and development, birth and WERE HIS HIPS CHECKED, immunisations, medicines, allergies, AND ANY HIP OR BONE PROBLEMS IN THE FAMILY.

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST — HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE EVERY TIME: 'general appearance — well or unwell, alert, colour, growth chart? WILL HE STAND OR WEIGHT-BEAR? With BOTH LEGS EXPOSED: any swelling, redness, bruising, deformity, rash, OR BRUISES ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY? FEEL: the hip, the knee, the ankle, THEN BONE BY BONE ALONG THE TIBIA, AND THE SOLE OF THE FOOT; any warmth? MOVE: hip range of movement AND A LOG ROLL TEST; knee; ankle? Leg lengths equal? Spine and abdomen? LYMPH NODES, PALLOR, BRUISING?' (A candidate who palpates the tibia only has not run the limping examination — and SAY 'LOG ROLL' BY NAME.)
The film, named precisely to the examiner (see dx) — trace the distal tibia and say spiral, undisplaced, distal tibia, fibula intact.
THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS, WITH THE BLAME REMOVED (see dx) → 'DID HIS SISTER PUSH HIM?' → nothing suggests that, and a twist on the slide is enough.

THE DIFFERENTIALS, EACH EXCLUDED WITH ITS REASON (see dx) — infection, leukaemia, irritable hip, joint inflammation, and 'nothing about how this happened worries me'. Then ONE SENTENCE OF MANAGEMENT IF ASKED, a summary, and 'WHAT IS WORRYING YOU MOST?'

pefe: Role-player: Emma, 29, works part-time at the supermarket; partner Dan is a farmhand; daughter Ruby is 5. NOAH, 3: walked at 13 months, normal birth, HIPS CHECKED, fully immunised, no medicines, no allergies, well, eating normally. YESTERDAY AFTERNOON he was playing in the backyard with Ruby, RUNNING AND USING THE SLIDE, while she hung washing. AROUND 3 PM HE SAT DOWN CRYING AND HAS REFUSED TO STAND SINCE. NO ONE SAW A FALL. HE POINTS TO THE LOWER SHIN. He slept normally. No fever, not pale, no bruising or weight loss, no recent colds, no rash or stiff joints, no previous fractures, no family bone problems.

Register: anxious and a little guilty — 'I didn't see it' — briefly defensive when asked about home — 'Why are you asking about home?' — and settling if told it is routine; relieved at the end. Hidden agenda: she is afraid ruby pushed him and that she will be blamed for not watching. Only ask 'Did his sister push him?' after the diagnosis. If the doctor never asks who was there or about home, do not volunteer it. If pushed on stresses, add 'Dan's been working long hours with harvest.' Close by asking 'Will he need a cast? Will he walk again?'

Mark them against: ASKED FOR VITALS INCLUDING TEMPERATURE and acknowledged the fear; DEFINED THE LIMP — no weight-bearing, onset, pattern; full pain history INCLUDING SITE AND NIGHT PAIN; swelling, redness, bruising, deformity, other joints; INFECTION AND MALIGNANCY ASKED BEFORE TRAUMA — the pass mark; AN OPEN QUESTION ABOUT YESTERDAY BEFORE SUGGESTING A MECHANISM, AND WHO WAS THERE; recent viral illness, rash, eyes, morning stiffness; HOME, SIBLINGS, STRESS AND CHILDCARE, FRAMED AS ROUTINE; walking age, growth, birth and hip check, immunisations, family history; EXAMINATION — general, weight-bearing, look, HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE, TIBIA BONE BY BONE, SOLE, LOG ROLL, LEG LENGTH; NAMED THE FILM — SPIRAL, UNDISPLACED, DISTAL TIBIA, FIBULA INTACT, AND DID NOT SAY NORMAL; and explained in plain words, SAID NO ONE IS BLAMED, LISTED THE DIFFERENTIALS EXCLUDED WITH REASONS, summarised, and asked what worries her most.
The rest — Leg lengths equal; spine and abdomen normal; NO NODES, NO PALLOR, NO BRUISING

HE HAD A FALL LAST NIGHT, WITNESSED BY THE FATHER, and is complaining of PAIN IN HIS LEFT WRIST AND FOREARM. HE HAS A HISTORY OF A LEFT ARM FRACTURE FOUR MONTHS AGO, WITNESSED BY THE MOTHER. Observations normal. AN X-RAY OF THE FOREARM HAS BEEN TAKEN.
