back.dx: A BUCKLE (TORUS) FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL RADIUS. EXPLAIN THE FILM WITH THE NORMAL LANDMARKS FIRST, POINTING ON BOTH VIEWS: 'this is an X-ray of Oliver's forearm FROM THE FRONT AND THE SIDE. WHITE IS BONE, GREY IS SOFT TISSUE, BLACK WOULD BE AIR, AND THERE'S NONE HERE. The hand, finger and wrist bones ALL LOOK NORMAL. These are the two forearm bones: THE ULNA on the little-finger side, WHICH IS FINE, and THE RADIUS on the thumb side. Just above the wrist on the radius you can see A SMALL BULGE, A BUMP IN THE EDGE OF THE BONE, HERE ON BOTH PICTURES. THAT'S THE INJURY.' When he says the nurse thought it looked normal: 'IT'S EASY TO MISS.' NEVER SAY 'NORMAL' AND NEVER SAY 'STRESS FRACTURE'. THEN THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN WORDS: 'this is called A BUCKLE FRACTURE. When he landed on his outstretched hand, THE SOFT BONE JUST ABOVE THE WRIST WAS SQUASHED AND BUCKLED OUTWARDS, LIKE A DENT IN A CAN, RATHER THAN SNAPPING. It's THE MILDEST AND ONE OF THE COMMONEST FRACTURES IN CHILDREN, because THEIR BONES ARE SOFTER THAN OURS. IT HASN'T MOVED AND IT DOESN'T NEED TO BE PUT BACK INTO PLACE. IT HEALS IN ABOUT THREE WEEKS.' THEN ANSWER THE TWO THINGS HE IS ACTUALLY ASKING: 'NOTHING YOU'VE TOLD ME SUGGESTS WEAK BONES OR ANYTHING YOU DID WRONG: TWO WITNESSED FALLS IN AN ACTIVE FOUR-YEAR-OLD, NORMAL GROWTH, NO BONE PAIN. TWO BREAKS IN FOUR MONTHS WITH A GOOD STORY EACH TIME IS NOT UNUSUAL.' MANAGEMENT IS NOT A TASK — one sentence if he asks: 'pain relief, and A SPLINT OR A HALF-PLASTER ON THE BACK OF THE ARM FOR ABOUT THREE WEEKS, with a GP check-up. HE WON'T NEED ANOTHER X-RAY unless something changes — and come back sooner if his fingers go PALE OR NUMB or the pain gets worse in the splint.' Then summarise and CLOSE WITH A CONCERN CHECK: 'is there anything worrying you?' THE EXAMINATION EXPLAINED TO THE FATHER, IN LAYMAN'S TERMS AND UNDER TWO MINUTES — do NOT list radial, median and ulnar nerves to a parent: 'I'll LOOK at both hands and forearms for swelling, bruising, cuts and any difference in shape. I'll GENTLY FEEL them: compare the warmth, CHECK THE PULSE AT THE WRIST, PRESS THE NAILS TO CHECK THE BLOOD FLOW, and press along each bone to find where it's sore. I'll ask him to MOVE his fingers, wrist and elbow. Then I'll CHECK THE NERVES with a piece of cotton wool and a few hand shapes. I'll wash my hands first.' VERSION C — THE STORY CHANGES: 'James, I NEED TO BE HONEST. THE STORY HAS CHANGED A LITTLE BETWEEN TELLINGS, and IT'S BEEN TWO DAYS, and THIS IS HIS SECOND FRACTURE IN FOUR MONTHS. FOR EVERY CHILD IN THAT SITUATION I'M OBLIGED TO LOOK FURTHER. I'M NOT ACCUSING YOU. The children's doctors will see him TODAY and may do EXTRA X-RAYS AND BLOOD TESTS TO CHECK HIS BONES, and I'LL BE SPEAKING WITH THE CHILD PROTECTION TEAM, WHICH IS MY LEGAL DUTY. I'll keep you informed.' 'HE BRUISES EASILY': 'WHERE, AND HOW OFTEN? Any NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, or FAMILY BLEEDING PROBLEMS? I'll examine his skin all over and CHECK A BLOOD COUNT.' A DEFORMITY ON THE FILM — AN ANGULATED GREENSTICK RATHER THAN A BUCKLE: 'THIS ONE HAS BENT AND CRACKED ON ONE SIDE; IT NEEDS TO BE STRAIGHTENED UNDER SEDATION AND PUT IN A PLASTER BY THE BONE DOCTORS TODAY.'
plan: OPEN, REASSURE, SIGNPOST: 'I can see you're worried about Oliver's arm. HIS OBSERVATIONS ARE NORMAL AND HE'S HAD SOME PAIN RELIEF. I'd like to hear exactly what happened, then LOOK AT THE X-RAY WITH YOU. Tell me what happened.' (The father starts standing and anxious, and sits once reassured.)

THE INJURY IN DETAIL — and the lecture's own phrase is THE MORE QUESTIONS YOU ASK ABOUT THE INJURY, THE HAPPIER THE EXAMINER: 'can you take me through it STEP BY STEP? What was he doing, HOW DID HE FALL, AND HOW DID HE LAND? WAS HIS HAND OUT FLAT, AND WAS THE WRIST BENT BACK? HOW HIGH WAS HE, AND ONTO WHAT SURFACE? YOU SAW IT YOURSELF? WHAT TIME WAS IT, AND WHAT DID YOU DO THEN?' (A one-line fall is not a history — and TIMING MATTERS, because a story that fits, promptly presented, IS the first NAI screen.)

Head and other injuries — before the pain questions, because head injury outranks the wrist: 'Did he hit his head? Did he lose consciousness at all, even briefly? Has he vomited since? Any other injuries — swelling, redness, bruises anywhere else on his body? Is he limping, or complaining of pain anywhere else?'

THE PAIN AND ALL THREE SYSTEMS — BONES, BLOOD SUPPLY, NERVES: 'where exactly is the pain — the wrist or further up? How bad is it, and IS HE USING THE HAND AT ALL? Does it go anywhere else? HAVE YOU NOTICED ANY DIFFERENCE IN SHAPE COMPARED WITH THE OTHER ARM? Any pain or difficulty moving the arm, the wrist, the fingers? ANY CHANGE IN COLOUR OF THE HAND — PALE, BLUE, BLOTCHY? IS IT COLD? ANY PINS AND NEEDLES, or not using his fingers?' (A selective SOCRATES — site, severity, radiation only — is the trap, and DEFORMITY MEANS DISPLACEMENT AND A DIFFERENT FILM.)
The previous fracture, explored: 'The notes say he broke the same arm four months ago. Can you tell me more about that? What happened, who saw it, where was the break and what treatment did he have?'

Home and bone, framed as routine — and 'Happy family' is scripted to see whether you stop: 'Tell me about home: who lives with you? Any siblings? Any recent stresses or problems at home — work, money, relationships? Does he go to childcare or kindy — any concerns there? Who else looks after him?' → 'We're a happy family, doctor. Why all the questions?' → 'When a child has had two breaks in a few months I ask every family these questions; sometimes the reason is in the bones, and it protects him.' then: 'Any concerns about his growth or weight? Has he ever complained of bone pain, or does anyone in the family break bones easily?' → 'My brother has brittle bones, he's broken heaps. Does that matter?' (Given only if you ask — and it is his hidden worry.)
The x-ray — normal landmarks first, then point on both views (see dx) → 'I thought the x-ray was normal, the nurse said it looked fine' → 'It's easy to miss.'
THE EXAMINATION EXPLAINED IN LAYMAN'S TERMS, UNDER TWO MINUTES (see dx) — look, gently feel, move, check the nerves, hands washed first.

THE DIAGNOSIS — A DENT IN A CAN, SOFTER BONES, HASN'T MOVED, HEALS IN THREE WEEKS — THEN ANSWER THE WEAK-BONES AND THE FAULT QUESTIONS (see dx), one sentence of management if asked, a summary, and a concern check.

back.dx: HERPETIC GINGIVOSTOMATITIS IN AN IMMUNOCOMPETENT CHILD WITH MILD DEHYDRATION — supportive care, no antivirals, and the reason said aloud. Explain it: 'Liam has herpetic gingivostomatitis: a viral infection, the herpes simplex virus, in his mouth, on his gums and tongue and around his lips. It's very common in young children, this first episode is always the worst, and it runs its course over about one to two weeks. Antibiotics don't work on viruses. The treatment is pain relief so that he can drink.' The pain ladder, which is the whole point: paracetamol every four to six hours, no more than four times a day; ibuprofen with food; and a numbing gel, lignocaine, dabbed on the sores with a cotton bud about ten minutes before he drinks or eats. Then fluids: small sips often, cool drinks, icy poles, oral rehydration like Hydralyte, water or milk rather than juice, which stings. Then the antiviral decision in one sentence with its reason: 'There is an antiviral, but because Liam has no condition and no medicine that weakens his immune system, he doesn't need it; his own immune system will clear this, and the tablets make little difference in a healthy child. If he were on steroids or had diabetes, I'd give it.' then exclusion and hygiene: home from school until the sores have dried, wash hands, no sharing cups, and no kissing the baby. Review in a day or two. The red flags, including a measurable urine-based one: 'Come straight back or go to the emergency department if he becomes drowsy or hard to wake, complains of headache, vomits, has a fit, gets a red or sore eye or blisters on the eyelid, or if he stops drinking or has no wee for eight hours. Count the wees: fewer than three a day, or none for eight hours, or too drowsy to drink — bring him straight in and we'll give fluids through a tube or a drip.' then summarise and ask what worries her most. Version B — prednisolone or another immunocompromising condition: 'Because Liam is on prednisolone his immune system is weaker, so this infection can spread further and last longer. I'm going to start an antiviral, aciclovir, five times a day for a week, and I'll speak to the children's team today. If he can't keep fluids down he needs to come in.' Version C — the whitlow: 'The blister on his thumb is the same virus, spread from his mouth when he sucks it. It's painful but it heals by itself; we don't cut it. Keep it covered and wash hands, so it doesn't spread to his eyes.' The red eye: 'A red, sore eye with this infection can be the virus on the surface of the eye. That needs an eye specialist today, with a dye test and antiviral drops. Please don't use any leftover eye drops at home.' Drowsy and vomiting: 'Drowsiness and vomiting with this infection can mean the virus has reached the brain. I'm stopping here and arranging the emergency department now; he'll need a drip and an antiviral through the vein.'
plan: VITALS, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE AND PROMISE: 'Examiner, may I have Liam's vital signs?' → 38.4, HR 118. Then: 'I've read that Liam has a herpes infection in his mouth AND I CAN SEE HOW SORE IT IS. I'd like to ask how he's been, examine him, and then go through the plan.' → 'he's screaming when he eats, he's not sleeping, and now he won't drink either. CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' → 'THAT SOUNDS MISERABLE FOR BOTH OF YOU, AND YES, THERE'S A LOT WE CAN DO FOR HIS PAIN. Let me ask a few things first.' (She wants a prescription now — acknowledge, promise, and keep moving. And do NOT spend the four minutes re-deriving a diagnosis you were given.)

THE LESIONS: 'when did you first notice the sores? IS THIS THE FIRST TIME? Getting worse? WHERE EXACTLY — gums, tongue, lips, the skin around the mouth? WERE THERE BLISTERS FIRST? Any pus or discharge? Painful, or itchy?'

GENERAL FEATURES AND SOURCE: 'any fever or chills? Did you give anything, and did it help? Is he tired or flat? ANY RASH ANYWHERE ELSE, ON HIS HANDS OR FINGERS? Any lumps in his neck? Anyone at home or at school with cold sores or something similar?' (A NEGATIVE CONTACT HISTORY IS NORMAL — most sources shed without symptoms — so do NOT chase the source at the cost of the immune block.)

The immune block — the pass mark: 'Now some questions about his general health, because they change how I treat this. Does he have any long-term medical conditions? Does he get infections more often than other children, or take a long time to get over them? Is he on any regular medicines, particularly steroids like prednisolone, or anything for his immune system? Any concerns about his growth or weight? Any diabetes, kidney or blood problems?'

THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN, BY SYSTEM AND BY NAME: 'HIS BRAIN: any headache? Is he DROWSY OR HARD TO WAKE? Vomiting? Blurred vision or unusual behaviour? ANY FITS? HIS EYES: any RED EYE? SPOTS ON THE EYELIDS? Discharge? DOES LIGHT BOTHER HIM? HIS CHEST: any cough or fast breathing? HIS SKIN: DOES HE HAVE ECZEMA, AND IS IT FLARING?'

HYDRATION, WITH NUMBERS: 'is he DROOLING? HOW MUCH IS HE DRINKING COMPARED TO NORMAL? HOW MANY WEES TODAY? Bowels? Alert and playing, or flat?' → drooling, half of normal in small sips of juice, TWO WEES TODAY. (JUICE STINGS — swap to water, milk, oral rehydration or icy poles. And TWO WEES IN A DAY IS YOUR MEASURABLE MARKER TO HAND BACK TO HER AS A RED FLAG.) Then birth and development, immunisations, allergies, home and school.

THE EXAMINATION, IN ORDER: 'general appearance — is he alert, and how does he look? HYDRATION — mucous membranes, tears, skin turgor, CAPILLARY REFILL? Growth chart? MOUTH — site of the ulcers, any blisters, any discharge, tonsils? CERVICAL LYMPH NODES? EYES — conjunctival redness, LID VESICLES, discharge, visual acuity, fundi? NEUROLOGICAL — conscious level, NECK STIFFNESS, cranial nerves, limbs, gait? CHEST — air entry, added sounds? SKIN AND HANDS — ANY VESICLES OR ECZEMA?' (Do not lead with a urine dipstick or blood sugar; if you mention ketones, do it last.)

MANAGEMENT: the virus explained, ANTIBIOTICS DON'T WORK, the pain ladder with LIGNOCAINE GEL TEN MINUTES BEFORE DRINKS, and fluids in small sips WITHOUT JUICE (see dx) → 'SO NOTHING TO MAKE IT GO AWAY?'

THE ANTIVIRAL DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE WITH ITS REASON, THEN EXCLUSION, REVIEW AND THE RED FLAGS (see dx) → 'HOW DO I KNOW IF HE'S GETTING DEHYDRATED?' → COUNT THE WEES. Then summarise and ask what worries her most. ('We could give aciclovir' with no decision has not answered the task.)

pefe: Role-player: Mary, 34, WORKS IN THE LOCAL PHARMACY, so she knows Panadol and WANTS 'SOMETHING STRONGER'. Liam is her only child, in reception. Normal birth, fully immunised, no allergies, NO MEDICAL CONDITIONS, NO MEDICINES (VERSION B: ON PREDNISOLONE FOR NEPHROTIC SYNDROME — SAY IT ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT MEDICINES OR CONDITIONS). Her husband works away on a mine roster and SHE HAS HAD THREE NIGHTS WITHOUT SLEEP. THE STORY: three days of sores on the gums, inside the lips, a few on the tongue and crusty bits on the lip, WITH LITTLE BLISTERS FIRST; no pus; painful enough that he screams; FEVER UP TO 39 with Panadol helping for a few hours; flat but played a bit this morning; no other rash; NECK LUMPY BOTH SIDES; no known cold-sore contacts.

REGISTER: FRAYED AND A LITTLE SHARP AT THE START — 'CAN'T YOU JUST GIVE HIM SOMETHING?' — softening when the doctor promises to deal with the pain, and TEARFUL ONCE when asked what worries her most. HIDDEN AGENDA: SHE IS FRIGHTENED HE IS DEHYDRATED BECAUSE HE HAS ONLY DONE TWO WEES TODAY, BUT SHE DOES NOT SAY THE NUMBER UNLESS ASKED ABOUT WEES OR DRINKING — AND IF NOT ASKED BY 3:30 SHE VOLUNTEERS 'HE'S HARDLY WEED TODAY'. UNDERLYING BELIEF: that ANTIBIOTICS would fix it faster — push once, then accept a clear explanation. Ask 'ISN'T THERE A TABLET TO KILL IT?' after the antibiotic answer, and 'HOW DO I KNOW IF HE'S DEHYDRATED?' if no urine-based red flag has been given.

back.dx: VULVOVAGINITIS — non-specific vulval erythema — in a well, happy 4-year-old, with no feature of abuse on history or examination. Explain it: 'Jenny, I completely understand why you were worried. Having gone through everything with you and examined Mia, I believe the likely cause is a condition called vulvovaginitis — an inflammation of the skin of the private parts. It's very common in young girls, because the skin there is thin and sensitive and gets irritated easily by moisture, urine, soaps and bubble bath.' then give the reasoning before she asks for it — this is a required item: 'Let me tell you why I don't think this is abuse. The skin is simply red — there is no bruising, no tears, no discharge, no blisters or sores, and those are the things I specifically look for. She's happy, sleeping well and keen to see her dad. And the pattern fits the daily bubble bath and the leggings. I did consider other skin irritations and infections, and I found nothing else.' The management, and in mild cases no tests are needed: keep the area clean and dry; WIPE front to back; wash with water or a soap-free cleanser; stop the bubble bath and any scented WIPEs; about half a cup of white vinegar in a shallow bath for ten minutes; loose cotton underwear, no leggings for now, and nothing at night; a mild moisturiser and a zinc barrier cream to the red skin; and if she is itchy or it is not settling, a thin layer of one-percent hydrocortisone twice a day for about a week. Sort out the constipation. Review in one to two weeks. Safety-net: 'If anything changes — bruising, discharge, bleeding, or a change in how she's behaving — I want to see her straight away.' and when she says 'How can you be sure?' — re-explain once, then offer the pathway, never argue: 'I can't give you a guarantee, but I've looked specifically for every sign of abuse and found none, and she's happy in herself. If you still have concerns, we can involve the child protection team at the women's and children's for a more complete assessment. I expect they'll say the same, but I'd rather you felt sure. Would you like me to make that call?' The variant — the card shows blisters and inner-thigh bruising: 'Jenny, what I found on examination concerns me. There are blisters and bruising, and I'm not able to call this a simple skin irritation. I need to involve the child protection team at the women's and children's today so Mia is properly assessed and kept safe. I am required to report this, and I will support you through every step. Please don't question Mia about it yourself — the team are trained to do that gently.' Notify CARL on 13 14 78, involve the women's and children's child protection service, document verbatim, and do not perform a forensic examination in general practice.

NEW SOAPS, BODY WASH, BUBBLE BATH, WIPES, MOISTURISER? Swimming? WHO WIPES AFTER THE TOILET, AND WHICH WAY? Eczema in her or the family? THE CHILD'S BEHAVIOUR — AND DO NOT SKIP IT BECAUSE THE SOCIAL ANSWERS WERE REASSURING, BECAUSE THE SYMPTOMS OF ABUSE ARE BEHAVIOURAL: 'how is she behaving these days? Withdrawn, clingy, angry? back.dx: BALANITIS — inflammation of the skin at the tip of the penis and the foreskin, with a non-retractile foreskin that is normal for age and a negative dipstick. Explain it: 'Liam has a condition called balanitis. In plain words, it's inflammation of the skin at the tip of the penis and the foreskin. That skin is thin and sensitive, and under a nappy it sits in moisture and urine; bubble bath and WIPEs irritate it further, and sometimes a yeast joins in. It's the boy's version of nappy rash, and very common.' then kill the UTI idea explicitly: 'It hurts when he wees because urine stings the irritated skin — it doesn't mean he has a urine infection, and his dipstick is clear.' then the foreskin: 'His foreskin not pulling back is normal at his age — please don't force it; it loosens by itself over the next few years.' Management, conservative and specific: keep it clean and dry — change nappies often, nappy-free time, wash with water or a soap-free cleanser, and stop the bubble bath and scented WIPEs; a warm salt-water bath once or twice a day, then Pat dry; a mild steroid cream with an antifungal — hydrozole from the pharmacy — a thin layer two or three times a day for up to a week; and paracetamol if he's sore. Review in three to five days. The red-flag safety-net, which is a required item: 'Come back straight away if he can't pass urine, if the tip swells or goes dark, if the redness spreads up the shaft with fever, or if he becomes unwell.' The three questions he will ask: 'Is it because I pulled it back?' → 'That may have added a little irritation, but this happens in boys who've never been touched — please just don't force it again.' 'Does he need antibiotics?' → 'No — antibiotics don't help skin inflammation; the cream does.' 'Should he be circumcised?' → 'No. Circumcision is only considered for repeated problems or a scarred, tight foreskin that doesn't respond to cream.' Variants: febrile at 38.8 with redness onto the shaft, warmth and pus at the meatus — 'This is more than balanitis — a cellulitis, and I must exclude a urine infection. Urine culture first, oral antibiotics today, review in twenty-four hours; drowsy, vomiting or not improving means the children's hospital.' VERIFY the foreskin stuck back with a purple tip — 'That's paraphimosis and it's urgent — the foreskin is acting like a tight ring and cutting off the blood supply. I'll give him pain relief and try to reduce it now; if I can't, he goes to the children's surgeons today.' The changed social history — a new partner, weekends with his mother, bedwetting again and nightmares: go deeper on supervision, who bathes him, bruising and disclosures, then 'Thank you for telling me. I'd like advice from the child protection team at the women's and children's — a routine step to make sure Liam is safe.'
plan: OPEN AND ADDRESS THE CONCERN, THEN SITE AND MORPHOLOGY BOTH: 'you're Liam's dad? I can see you're concerned about his penis — TELL ME MORE... I understand the worry. Let me ask a few questions, then examine him, then explain. WHERE EXACTLY IS THE REDNESS — TIP, FORESKIN, SHAFT, OR THE GROIN CREASES? JUST RED SKIN, OR BLISTERS, SPOTS OR SORES? Painful? Itchy? ANY DISCHARGE FROM THE TIP? Other rashes anywhere?' (Site and morphology are what separate dermatitis from herpes and cellulitis — ASK BOTH.)

TIMING, TRIGGERS AND DERMATITIS RISK FACTORS: 'when did you first notice it? First time? Getting worse? Anything making it better or worse — BATHS, BUBBLE BATH, MOISTURISER? STILL IN NAPPIES? Any NEW SOAP, BODY WASH, WIPES? ECZEMA IN HIM OR THE FAMILY? AND HAS ANYONE BEEN PULLING THE FORESKIN BACK TO CLEAN IT?' → worse after the bubble bath, still in nappies, new wipes last month, and 'I TRIED TO PULL IT BACK ONCE TO CLEAN UNDERNEATH AND HE SCREAMED, SO I STOPPED.'

INFECTION, AND THE REAL UTI QUESTIONS — a required item: 'any fever or chills? Drowsy or off his food? DOES IT HURT WHEN HE PASSES URINE?' → 'yes — he cries when he wees. IS IT A URINE INFECTION?' → SAY IT OUT LOUD: 'IT CAN BE, BUT IRRITATED SKIN AT THE TIP STINGS WHENEVER URINE TOUCHES IT, SO I'LL CHECK PROPERLY.' Then: 'ANY DIFFICULTY PASSING URINE — STRAINING, DRIBBLING, A POOR STREAM, OR THE FORESKIN BALLOONING? FOUL-SMELLING URINE? VOMITING?' → good stream, no smell, no vomiting. (Answering 'yes, a urine infection' and reaching for antibiotics is the fail the father is briefed to mark.)

The foreskin question, asked as routine — the second required item: 'One question I ask every dad: are you able to gently pull his foreskin back, and has it ever got stuck?' → 'It doesn't really go back — it never has. Never stuck.'

THE SOCIAL AND ABUSE SCREEN, FRAMED AS ROUTINE: 'some routine questions I ask FOR EVERY CHILD WITH A PROBLEM IN THIS AREA. How are things at home? Who lives with you? Any stressors? ANY BRUISES ON HIS PRIVATE PARTS OR ELSEWHERE? ANY CHANGE IN HIS BEHAVIOUR — SAD, WITHDRAWN, NOT SLEEPING, NEW FEARS? How are things at childcare?' Then well-child and BINDSMA: alert and active, eating, drinking, wet nappies, term, immunisations, development and toilet training, medicines, allergies.

CONSENT AND CHAPERONE, THEN THE EXAMINATION REQUEST WITH RETRACTABILITY AND THE DIPSTICK NAMED: 'WITH DAD'S CONSENT AND A CHAPERONE PRESENT, I'd examine Liam. General appearance — alert or drowsy, hydration, any other rash? Temperature and heart rate? Inspecting the penis: WHERE IS THE REDNESS — foreskin, glans, shaft, groin? Blisters, ulcers, discharge, bruising, swelling? On palpation — warm, tender, fluctuant? INGUINAL LYMPH NODES? IS THE FORESKIN RETRACTABLE, WITHOUT FORCING, AND IS THERE ANY SCARRING OR A TRAPPED RING? Scrotum and testes? AND A URINE DIPSTICK.' (Forgetting consent and chaperone, or forgetting retractability, are the two traps here.)
Explain balanitis in plain words, kill the UTI idea with the dipstick, and say the foreskin is normal for age (see dx) → 'Is it because I pulled it back?' → answer it without blame.

THE CONSERVATIVE PLAN AND THE RED FLAGS — the third required item (see dx): clean and dry, nappy-free time, soap-free wash, STOP THE BUBBLE BATH AND SCENTED WIPES, SALT-WATER BATHS, HYDROZOLE THINLY TWO OR THREE TIMES A DAY FOR UP TO A WEEK, paracetamol, NO ANTIBIOTICS, review in three to five days, and 'COME BACK STRAIGHT AWAY IF HE CAN'T PASS URINE, IF THE TIP SWELLS OR GOES DARK, IF THE REDNESS SPREADS UP THE SHAFT WITH FEVER, OR IF HE BECOMES UNWELL.' → 'WILL HE NEED TO BE CIRCUMCISED?' → only for repeated problems or a scarred tight foreskin that does not respond to cream.

back.dx: VERSION A — ACUTE OTITIS MEDIA in a 9-month-old, and the station is about EXCLUDING THE OTHERS ALOUD. NAME IT WITH REASONS: 'your son has a condition called OTITIS MEDIA — AN INFECTION IN THE MIDDLE EAR, BEHIND THE EARDRUM. He has a fever, HE'S PULLING HIS EARS, and when I looked in, THE EARDRUM IS RED AND BULGING.' THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS BY GROUP, QUICKLY, WITH COLIC LAST — never a fifteen-item list: 'I was also thinking about OTHER INFECTIONS — a urine infection, a joint infection, a chest infection; PROBLEMS IN THE TUMMY — reflux, A HERNIA IN THE GROIN, INTUSSUSCEPTION, constipation; INJURIES, INCLUDING BLEEDING INSIDE THE HEAD; and things like A SCRATCH ON THE EYE OR A HAIR WRAPPED ROUND A TOE. NORMAL EXCESSIVE CRYING — COLIC — IS AT THE BOTTOM OF MY LIST, AND I ONLY CONSIDER IT ONCE EVERYTHING ELSE IS EXCLUDED.' MANAGEMENT, VERSION-SPECIFIC: OTITIS MEDIA — 'PAIN RELIEF FIRST, paracetamol or ibuprofen AT THE RIGHT DOSE FOR HIS WEIGHT. BECAUSE HE IS UNDER TWO AND QUITE UNWELL, I'll start AMOXICILLIN FOR FIVE DAYS. Most ear infections settle on their own; the antibiotic shortens it and reduces complications.' UTI — 'I'll collect A CLEAN URINE SAMPLE TO SEND TO THE LAB BEFORE STARTING THE ANTIBIOTIC, start ORAL CEFALEXIN today, and arrange A KIDNEY ULTRASOUND AFTER THIS FIRST INFECTION.' INTUSSUSCEPTION, HERNIA, SEPTIC JOINT OR NAI — 'THIS NEEDS THE CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL TODAY. I'm arranging transfer BY AMBULANCE, NOTHING TO EAT OR DRINK, and I'll speak to the surgeons now.' THE SAFETY-NET, EVERY VERSION: 'come back or go to the emergency department straight away if he becomes DROWSY OR FLOPPY, has FEWER WET NAPPIES, VOMITS REPEATEDLY OR GREEN VOMIT, PASSES BLOOD, DEVELOPS A LUMP, STOPS MOVING AN ARM OR LEG, or you're worried. I'll see you in 48 HOURS. AND IF YOU EVER FEEL YOU CAN'T COPE, PUT HIM SAFELY IN THE COT AND WALK AWAY FOR A FEW MINUTES — and call the Parent Helpline or me.' AND NAME THE PATHWAY, BECAUSE 'REFER TO HOSPITAL' WITHOUT A ROUTE LOSES MARKS: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval, the Women's and Children's for surgery, CARL 13 14 78 for a child-protection notification. THE NAI VERSION, AFTER THE DISCLOSURE: 'THANK YOU FOR BEING HONEST WITH ME — THAT TOOK COURAGE. BABIES' HEADS ARE FRAGILE AND SHAKING CAN CAUSE BLEEDING AROUND THE BRAIN, so he needs to be CHECKED IN HOSPITAL TODAY — A SCAN AND X-RAYS. I AM REQUIRED BY LAW TO NOTIFY THE CHILD PROTECTION SERVICE; THAT IS NOT ABOUT PUNISHING YOU, IT'S ABOUT KEEPING HIM SAFE AND GETTING YOU SUPPORT. I'LL STAY WITH YOU THROUGH THIS.' To the examiner: ADMIT VIA MedSTAR, DO NOT DISCHARGE, DOCUMENT VERBATIM, NOTIFY CARL, involve the paediatric team and social work, AND SCREEN THE MOTHER FOR DEPRESSION AND DOMESTIC VIOLENCE. THE COLIC VERSION: 'everything is normal. This is INFANT COLIC — EXCESSIVE CRYING WITHOUT A CAUSE. It peaks around two months and settles by three to four. IT'S NOT YOUR FAULT.' Feed on demand, rocking, white noise or a carrier, the safe-cot line, the child health nurse, review in two weeks, sooner for fever, drowsiness, vomiting, fewer wet nappies or blood.
plan: VITALS AND TEMPERATURE, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE BEFORE THE FIRST CLOSED QUESTION: 'may I have the vital signs, INCLUDING THE TEMPERATURE?' Then: 'how can I help you today?' → 'he's been crying for four hours and NOTHING SETTLES HIM. I'm exhausted.' → 'I CAN HEAR HOW STRESSFUL AND OVERWHELMING THIS IS. Let me ask you some questions so we can find out what's going on, and then we'll make a plan together.' (Opening with 'babies cry at this age' signals premature closure in the first twenty seconds, and she answers 'SO YOU'RE NOT GOING TO CHECK HIM?')

EXPLORE THE CRYING — INCLUDING THE QUESTION THAT OPENS EVERY DOOR: 'when did it start? IS IT ON AND OFF, OR CONTINUOUS? Getting worse? Anything that makes it better or worse — feeding, nappy changes, picking him up? AND WHAT HAVE YOU TRIED TO CALM HIM DOWN?' (That last one is what produces GRIPE WATER in the colic version and 'WE SHOOK HIM' in the NAI version — ask it every time and LISTEN TO THE ANSWER.)

THE INFECTION BLOCK: 'any fever? PULLING HIS EARS? Discharge? Vomiting? Diarrhoea? Anyone else unwell? Travel? ANY RASH, REDNESS, OR A RED SWOLLEN JOINT? CRYING WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY? SMELLY URINE? Nappy rash? Runny nose, cough, DROOLING?' Then THE FOUR WELL-BABY QUESTIONS: 'is he ALERT AND ACTIVE, OR DROWSY? Eating and drinking as usual? FEWER WET NAPPIES?'

THE GASTROINTESTINAL BLOCK: 'ANY LUMP OR SWELLING IN THE GROIN? DOES HE GO PALE WHEN HE CRIES? ANY RED, JELLY-LIKE STOOL? Recent viral illness or vaccination? Refusing feeds? ARCHING HIS BACK? Constipation or blood in the stool?' → 'I HAVEN'T LOOKED IN THE GROIN — HE'S HAD THE NAPPY ON.' (A 'no' to the groin question DOES NOT RULE OUT A HERNIA — the mother has not looked, so THE EXAMINATION REQUEST MUST NAME THE INGUINAL AREA.)

INJURY AND THE SEVEN SOCIAL QUESTIONS — asked even in the versions where nothing is planted: 'any falls or bumps to the head? Any bruises? IS HE MOVING BOTH ARMS AND LEGS? HOW HAVE YOU BEEN COPING WITH THE CRYING? How are things at home — who do you live with, IS YOUR PARTNER SUPPORTIVE? How has your mood been? Any financial worries? Do you or your partner use drugs or alcohol?' AND IF THE VIBE IS THERE, THE THIRD-PERSON QUESTION: 'SOME PARENTS GET SO FRUSTRATED THEY SHAKE OR HURT THE BABY — HAS THAT HAPPENED WITH YOU OR YOUR PARTNER?' THEN SILENCE. (Asking 'do you hit him?' closes the parent. And if you never ask it in the NAI version, YOU FAIL THE STATION. If you never ask about coping at all, she becomes tearful at the end and says 'I FEEL LIKE A BAD MOTHER'.)

THE REST: red eyes or discharge; breast or formula, how much and how often, solids, rash after solids; immunisations; development and growth; medical problems, medicines, allergies; AND 'DID ANYONE IN THE FAMILY CRY A LOT AS A BABY?'

THE EXAMINATION REQUEST, HEAD TO TOE AND UNDRESSED, NAMING WHAT THE EXAMINER WILL OTHERWISE WITHHOLD: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? FONTANELLE? Any rash or bruising ANYWHERE? Temperature? EYES — red, discharge, FLUORESCEIN? EARS — tympanic membranes? Throat? Chest — air entry, added sounds? ABDOMEN — distension, masses, tenderness, rigidity, bowel sounds? INGUINAL AREA — ANY LUMP? IF SO, IS IT REDUCIBLE AND IS IT TENDER? JOINTS AND LIMBS — swelling, redness, warmth, IS HE MOVING ALL FOUR LIMBS? FINGERS, TOES AND GENITALIA — ANY HAIR TOURNIQUET? Nappy area? AND A URINE DIPSTICK, PLEASE.'

back.dx: A MILD LOCAL REACTION TO A BEE STING — NOT ANAPHYLAXIS. NAME IT: 'Liam has had A MILD LOCAL REACTION TO A BEE STING. That means HIS BODY HAS REACTED TO THE VENOM ONLY WHERE THE STING WENT IN — the redness, the swelling and the pain are all in that one spot.' THEN THE NEGATIVES, SAID OUT LOUD, WHICH IS WHAT TURNS A LABEL INTO REASONING: 'I say that because I'VE SPECIFICALLY CHECKED FOR THE THINGS THAT WOULD MAKE THIS A SEVERE REACTION, AND HE HAS NONE OF THEM: NO RASH ANYWHERE ELSE ON HIS BODY, NO SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE, NO CHANGE IN HIS VOICE, NO NOISY BREATHING OR WHEEZE, NO VOMITING OR TUMMY PAIN, AND HE HASN'T BEEN DROWSY, FLOPPY OR FAINT. His breathing, his heart rate and his blood pressure are ALL NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD.' WHEN HE ASKS 'SO HE'S NOT ALLERGIC TO BEES?': 'NOT IN THE DANGEROUS SENSE. ALMOST EVERYONE SWELLS AND GOES RED WHERE A BEE STINGS THEM — THAT'S THE VENOM, AND IT'S NORMAL. A DANGEROUS ALLERGY IS WHEN THE REACTION SPREADS BEYOND THE STING. ONE LOCAL REACTION LIKE THIS DOESN'T TELL US HE HAS THAT.' THE PLAN: the sting already removed BY SCRAPING SIDEWAYS — 'I'M SCRAPING IT OUT RATHER THAN SQUEEZING IT, BECAUSE THE VENOM SAC KEEPS EMPTYING WHILE IT'S IN'; wash it; A COLD PACK FOR TEN TO FIFTEEN MINUTES; PARACETAMOL FOR THE PAIN, because a sting hurts more than it itches; A NON-DROWSY ANTIHISTAMINE for the itch and swelling; and a period of observation before home. NO ADRENALINE, NO STEROIDS, NO ANTIBIOTICS — 'the redness today is the venom, not an infection.' AND DO NOT INVENT AN OBSERVATION RULE: 'THERE'S NO FIXED NUMBER OF HOURS FOR A REACTION LIKE THIS' — four hours is the ANAPHYLAXIS observation, not this. THE PEN QUESTION, WHICH IS THE AUTO-FAIL: 'it's a fair question, AND THE HONEST ANSWER IS NO — AND I WANT TO EXPLAIN WHY RATHER THAN JUST SAY IT. AN ADRENALINE PEN IS FOR A CHILD WHOSE REACTION GOES BEYOND THE STING SITE: breathing trouble, swelling of the tongue or throat, a rash all over, collapse. LIAM'S REACTION STAYED EXACTLY WHERE THE STING WAS. CARRYING A PEN WOULDN'T MAKE HIM SAFER, AND IT WOULD MEAN LABELLING HIM WITH A SEVERE ALLERGY HE HASN'T SHOWN ANY SIGN OF.' THEN GIVE HIM THE TRIGGER, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THE REFUSAL SAFE: 'WHAT MATTERS FAR MORE IS THAT YOU KNOW WHAT TO WATCH FOR. IF HE IS EVER STUNG AGAIN AND REACTS AWAY FROM THE STING — A RASH ON HIS BODY, SWELLING OF HIS LIPS OR TONGUE, NOISY BREATHING, VOMITING — THAT IS A DIFFERENT SITUATION. CALL AN AMBULANCE, AND HE'LL THEN NEED AN ALLERGY SPECIALIST AND VERY LIKELY A PEN.' SAFETY-NET AND CLOSE: six red flags — lip or tongue swelling, voice change, noisy breathing or wheeze, a rash anywhere else, vomiting, or going pale, floppy or faint — plus 'if in two days the redness is spreading AND he has a fever, that would be an infection'; then avoidance advice, a written sheet, AND TEACH-BACK: 'CAN YOU TELL ME TWO OF THE THINGS THAT WOULD BRING YOU BACK?' And speak to Liam: 'you were very brave.' THE FOUR SENTENCES THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR: those observations are normal for a five-year-old; there is nothing away from the sting site and no airway, breathing or circulation involvement; this is a mild local reaction, not anaphylaxis; and he does not need adrenaline or a pen — AND HERE IS EXACTLY WHEN HE WOULD. IF YOU RUN SHORT OF TIME, drop the avoidance advice and the immunisation question — NEVER DROP THE SYSTEMIC SCREEN, THE STING REMOVAL, OR THE RED FLAGS.
plan: VITALS FIRST, BECAUSE THE STEM OMITS THEM ON PURPOSE — THEN INTERPRET THEM: 'examiner, could I have his vital signs, please: heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, saturations and temperature?' → 90/60, 125, 26, 98%, 36.9. → 'thank you — THOSE ARE ALL NORMAL FOR A FIVE-YEAR-OLD, SO HE'S STABLE, and I'll take a history. THANK YOU FOR BRINGING HIM STRAIGHT IN. Tell me what happened.' (The examiner is marking THE INTERPRETATION, not the request.)

THE STING AND THE SITE: 'when exactly did it happen, and WHERE ON HIS BODY? Do you know WHAT STUNG HIM — A BEE, A WASP, AN ANT? WAS HE STUNG MORE THAN ONCE? Is there swelling or redness around the sting? IS IT GETTING BIGGER? Is it painful or itchy? And has anything been done to it already?' (Stopping here and giving a diagnosis is THE COMMONEST FAIL — the marks are in the next block.)

The anaphylaxis screen, as a block: 'I need to run through some specific things. Has he come up in any rash, hives or welts anywhere else on his body? Any swelling of his face or eyes? Any swelling of his lips or tongue? Any drooling? Has his voice or his cry sounded different? Has he said his throat feels tight? Any noisy breathing, wheeze, cough or trouble getting his breath? Any vomiting or tummy pain? Has he been drowsy, floppy or pale at any point? Did he faint or go blank?' (Skipping the gut is the named trap: after an insect sting, persistent vomiting or abdominal pain is anaphylaxis, not an upset tummy — and it is the feature examiners add to turn this into version B.)

BACKGROUND, ATOPY AND FAMILY: 'any new food or new medicine today? HAS HE EVER BEEN STUNG BEFORE, AND WHAT HAPPENED THAT TIME? Does he have any known allergies, or has he ever had a severe allergic reaction? Does he have ASTHMA, ECZEMA OR HAY FEVER? Any regular medicines? Immunisations up to date? ANY FAMILY HISTORY OF ALLERGY OR ANAPHYLAXIS? And has he been eating, drinking and passing urine normally?' → 'MY SISTER CARRIES ONE OF THOSE PENS FOR BEES, ACTUALLY.' (If he says Liam has asthma, SAY OUT LOUD THAT THIS RAISES THE STAKES IF HE EVER REACTS SYSTEMICALLY.)

WHAT WAS WORRYING YOU MOST? → 'HONESTLY — THAT HE'D STOP BREATHING. MY SISTER ENDED UP IN INTENSIVE CARE.' → ACKNOWLEDGE IT WITHOUT LETTING IT BECOME LIAM'S DIAGNOSIS: 'I can hear how frightening that is with your sister's history behind it. Let me go through it carefully and then I'll tell you exactly where Liam stands.'

THE EXAMINATION, NAMING THE AIRWAY STRUCTURES AND THE STING SITE: 'general appearance and conscious state; the observations again INCLUDING CAPILLARY REFILL; THE LIPS AND TONGUE, ANY DROOLING, THE VOICE, AND ANY STRIDOR; THE WHOLE SKIN for hives or swelling AWAY FROM THE SITE; THE STING SITE — the size of the erythema and swelling, warmth and tenderness, AND IS THE STING STILL VISIBLE, AND MAY I REMOVE IT? The chest for work of breathing and wheeze; heart sounds and peripheral perfusion; and the abdomen.' THEN REMOVE IT: 'I'M SCRAPING IT OUT SIDEWAYS RATHER THAN SQUEEZING IT, BECAUSE THE VENOM SAC KEEPS EMPTYING WHILE IT'S IN.' (Asking for 'a general examination' gets you a general answer and no marks — and the sting removal is THE ONE PROCEDURAL MARK IN THE STATION.)
The diagnosis with the negatives said out loud (see dx) → 'So it's not an allergy?' / 'So it's not like my sister?'

THE PLAN, THEN THE PEN DECLINED WITH THE FUTURE TRIGGER (see dx) → 'MY SISTER CARRIES AN EPIPEN. SHOULDN'T WE HAVE ONE FOR LIAM?' — asked at least once, and AGAIN IF FOBBED OFF. Then the six red flags, the infection line at 48 hours, avoidance advice, a written sheet, AND TEACH-BACK: 'CAN YOU TELL ME TWO OF THE THINGS THAT WOULD BRING YOU BACK?' Then a one-paragraph summary, and a word to Liam.

You are frightened Liam will stop breathing, and you want a pen for him. You will not say this until the doctor asks what worries you — or, if they never ask, raise it yourself once they start explaining the plan. HOW TO PLAY IT: ANSWER ONLY WHAT IS ASKED. DO NOT VOLUNTEER THE SYSTEMIC NEGATIVES AS A LIST — MAKE THE DOCTOR ASK EACH ONE. PUSH ONCE AT MINUTE SIX: 'SHOULDN'T YOU GIVE US ONE OF THOSE PENS?' back.dx: INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS — EBV — with the aminopenicillin rash; the second differential is amoxicillin hypersensitivity and the third is scarlet fever. To the father: 'Noah most likely has glandular fever — an infection with a virus called Epstein-Barr, EBV. It causes exactly this: a very sore throat with white patches, glands at the back of the neck, tiny red spots on the roof of the mouth, and it can make the spleen — an organ under the left ribs — swell. The rash is the important part: when someone with this virus takes amoxicillin, most of them come out in exactly this kind of rash. So it is the virus and the antibiotic together, which is why I am confident about the diagnosis.' then the two differentials, each with its reason: 'A genuine allergy to the amoxicillin — less likely because the rash isn't hives, it came on days in, and there's no swelling or wheeze; and scarlet fever — less likely because his rash is smooth rather than rough and his tongue is normal.' The allergy question, answered properly: 'A true allergy gives hives, swelling of the lips or face, sometimes wheeze, usually within an hour of a dose. Noah's rash is flat and smooth, came on two days in, no swelling, no breathing trouble. I'll record it as a rash with amoxicillin during glandular fever, so nobody wrongly labels him allergic.' then the three things the task does not ask for but the mark sheet contains: stop the amoxicillin today — 'It isn't treating a virus and it's driving the rash'; the spleen rule — 'It can swell with this virus and a knock can tear it, so no football, rugby, trampolines or rough play for at least four weeks and until he is completely well. If he gets pain under the left ribs or in the left shoulder, or goes floppy or pale, that is an ambulance'; and the red flags — 'Bring him straight back if he can't swallow his own saliva, breathes noisily, stops drinking, goes yellow, or gets a rash that doesn't fade when you press a glass on it.' then a blood test to confirm, review in two days, and teach-back: 'Can you tell me the two things you'll watch for?'
plan: HAND HYGIENE STATED, AND THE FATHER ADDRESSED FIRST: 'I've read that Noah was here two days ago with a sore throat and started amoxicillin, and now he has a rash. I'm going to go through his examination with the examiner, examine his tummy, and then explain what I think is going on.' → 'IT'S EVERYWHERE — IT CAME UP OVERNIGHT. IS IT THE ANTIBIOTIC?' → 'THAT'S A VERY SENSIBLE QUESTION AND I'LL ANSWER IT PROPERLY ONCE I'VE EXAMINED HIM.'

GENERAL APPEARANCE — and the airway words are what make it a paediatric assessment: 'is Noah alert or drowsy? Any signs of dehydration — sunken eyes, dry mouth? IS HE DROOLING? ANY STRIDOR OR NOISY BREATHING? HAS HIS VOICE CHANGED? Is he toxic-looking? IS THERE A RASH?'

THE RASH IN NINE PARTS — and stopping at 'yes there is a rash' is the first trap: 'ON INSPECTION: what is the PRIMARY MORPHOLOGY — macular, papular, petechial, purpuric, urticarial? WHERE is it and WHAT COLOUR? Any discharge or scratch marks? ON PALPATION: is it WARM, TENDER, BLANCHING OR NON-BLANCHING, AND WHAT IS THE SURFACE LIKE?' (SURFACE IS THE ONE THAT REMOVES SCARLET FEVER.)

VITALS, ENT AND NODES: 'temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, saturations, capillary refill. Ears — red or bulging drums? Nose — discharge? Mouth and throat — are the TONSILS swollen, red, WITH EXUDATE? IS THERE A STRAWBERRY TONGUE? ANY PETECHIAE ON THE PALATE? Any PERIORAL PALLOR? Sinus tenderness? CERVICAL NODES — WHICH CHAIN, tender, mobile, how big? Neck stiffness?' ('Yes there are nodes' then 'thank you' loses it — POSTERIOR TRIANGLE IS THE EBV CHAIN, and the examiner has it on the card waiting for you.)

THE FULL CHEST AND HEART — not a two-second version because 'it's EBV': 'respiratory — symmetrical movements, trachea central, percussion note, air entry, added sounds, vocal resonance? Cardiovascular — S1 and S2, any murmur? ANY PALLOR, BRUISING OR JAUNDICE ELSEWHERE?' (You have five minutes to spare; a brief chest reads as a candidate who has stopped thinking.)

THE MANNEQUIN, EXAMINED AS A CHILD: 'I'd wash my hands, EXPLAIN TO NOAH AND DAD, expose from nipples to groin and have him flat. INSPECTING FROM THE LEVEL OF THE ABDOMEN for symmetrical movement, distension, scars, masses, bruising — AND I'M NOTING NO BRUISING IN THE FLANKS OR AROUND THE UMBILICUS. SUPERFICIAL PALPATION OF ALL NINE REGIONS, WATCHING HIS FACE for tenderness, guarding or rigidity. DEEP PALPATION OF ALL NINE REGIONS.' (Announcing that the mannequin is not breathing, or doing nothing but the left upper quadrant, are the two traps — SAY WHAT YOU SKIP AND WHY.)

LIVER, THEN SPLEEN, WITH THE TECHNIQUE NARRATED: 'the LIVER: from the right iliac fossa up to the costal margin WITH EACH BREATH IN, feeling for an edge. The SPLEEN: MY LEFT HAND BEHIND HIS LEFT LOWER RIBS, RIGHT HAND FROM THE RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA MOVING DIAGONALLY to the left costal margin with each inspiration, FEELING FOR A NOTCHED EDGE... not felt — I'D ROLL HIM ONTO HIS RIGHT SIDE AND REPEAT. I'd PERCUSS TRAUBE'S SPACE AND CASTELL'S POINT ON INSPIRATION. Auscultating for bowel sounds. I WOULD NOT PERFORM A RECTAL EXAMINATION — NOT INDICATED IN THIS CHILD. And I'd finish the LYMPH NODE SURVEY: axillary, epitrochlear, inguinal, supraclavicular.'

Turn fully to the father, give the diagnosis with its three reasons and the two differentials (see dx) — and keep EBV despite the absent spleen: 'Half of children with glandular fever have no palpable spleen.' → 'So is he allergic to penicillin?'

THE ALLERGY ANSWER, STOPPING THE AMOXICILLIN, THE SPLEEN AND SPORT RULE, THE RED FLAGS, THE BLOOD TEST, REVIEW AND TEACH-BACK (see dx) → 'HE'S GOT FOOTBALL ON SATURDAY' — held until the end. (The task says DIAGNOSIS — but leaving without stopping the amoxicillin, answering the allergy question and giving the spleen rule leaves marks on the table.)

'Left hand behind the ribs, right hand from the right iliac fossa.' / 'I'd roll him onto his right side and repeat.' / 'Traube's space and Castell's point on inspiration.' / 'I would not perform a rectal examination — not indicated.' / 'Half of children with glandular fever have no palpable spleen.'

'It's the virus and the antibiotic together — not a true allergy.' / 'A true allergy gives hives, swelling, sometimes wheeze, usually within an hour.' / 'I'll record it as a rash with amoxicillin during glandular fever, so nobody wrongly labels him allergic.' / 'Stop the amoxicillin today.' / 'No contact sport for at least four weeks and until he's well.' / 'Pain under the left ribs is an ambulance.'

VARIANT A — URTICARIAL WITHIN THE HOUR: 'urticarial, itchy, lip swelling, forty minutes after a dose — THIS IS A TRUE HYPERSENSITIVITY UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. Any wheeze, stridor, hypotension? Then STOP THE AMOXICILLIN, oral antihistamine, observe, ADRENALINE 10 MICROGRAM/KG IM if any airway, breathing or circulation involvement. I'll DOCUMENT A PENICILLIN ALLERGY and refer for allergy assessment. HE MAY STILL HAVE GLANDULAR FEVER UNDERNEATH — the examination for that continues.' VERIFY / VARIANT B — SCARLET FEVER: 'a ROUGH, SANDPAPER-TEXTURED blanching rash with A STRAWBERRY TONGUE and PERIORAL PALLOR — this is scarlet fever, streptococcal. The amoxicillin will be covering it, BUT THE RECOMMENDED DRUG IS PHENOXYMETHYLPENICILLIN FOR TEN FULL DAYS, and he's excluded from childcare UNTIL 24 HOURS AFTER THE FIRST DOSE. I'd still check for a spleen.'

VARIANT C — DROOLING AND A MUFFLED VOICE: 'drooling with a muffled voice in a child with huge tonsils IS AN AIRWAY EMERGENCY. I'll stop the routine examination, keep him UPRIGHT ON DAD'S LAP, give oxygen, NOT EXAMINE THE THROAT WITH A SPATULA, and call MedSTAR Kids on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the Women's and Children's. Steroids for tonsillar airway compromise on specialist advice.' VERIFY / VARIANT D — THE SPLEEN IS 3 cm BELOW THE COSTAL MARGIN: 'thank you — A PALPABLE SPLEEN SUPPORTS EBV. I'd confirm with percussion, check for tenderness, AND THE ADVICE BECOMES STRICTER: no contact sport, NO HEAVY LIFTING, seat-belt and rough-play warnings, and I'd RE-EXAMINE AT EACH REVIEW UNTIL IT HAS GONE DOWN. Sudden left-sided pain or faintness is an emergency.'
pefe: Role-player: Mark, 36, A MECHANIC IN KADINA, father of Noah, 4, his only child. Two days ago the practice saw A SORE THROAT WITH BIG TONSILS and prescribed AMOXICILLIN LIQUID; NOAH HAS HAD EVERY DOSE — FOUR SO FAR. THIS MORNING HE WOKE COVERED IN A PINK RASH that came up overnight, ABOUT TWO DAYS AFTER STARTING. He is grizzly but playing, EATING LITTLE, DRINKING OKAY, weeing normally, VERY TIRED — SLEPT FOURTEEN HOURS. Fever 38 this morning, paracetamol helps. The rash is A LITTLE ITCHY but he is not scratching much; NO lip or face swelling, no wheeze, no vomiting, no tummy pain. No known allergies; immunisations up to date; A CHILD AT KINDY HAD 'TONSILLITIS'.

Register: worried, holding the medicine box, and slightly annoyed that 'The antibiotic made him worse'. Hidden agenda, three questions: (1) is he allergic to penicillin — raise this as soon as the doctor pauses, and again if not answered; (2) should he keep taking it; (3) can he play under-6s football on Saturday — hold this until the end. Become sharper if the doctor rushes the examination or brushes off the allergy question. Soften when they explain the virus-plus-drug rash clearly.
Why surface matters — SMOOTH REMOVES SCARLET FEVER, which is rough and sandpapery — and it is given only if you ask
Why that does not change the diagnosis — About half of children with EBV have no palpable spleen — absence does not exclude it
Variant A — Urticarial, itchy, lip swelling, forty minutes after a dose — true hypersensitivity
Variant B — Rough, sandpaper rash with a strawberry tongue and perioral pallor — scarlet fever
Variant C — DROOLING WITH A MUFFLED VOICE — an airway emergency, and the routine examination stops
Variant D — 'THE SPLEEN IS 3 cm BELOW THE COSTAL MARGIN' — which SUPPORTS EBV and makes the advice stricter
fails: ★ Stopping at 'yes there is a rash' — the five inspection and four palpation questions are the marks, and SURFACE is what removes scarlet fever
★ Accepting 'yes there are nodes' without asking the chain — posterior triangle is the EBV chain and the examiner is waiting for it
Dropping EBV because the mannequin gives nothing — about half of children with EBV have no palpable spleen
Leaving without stopping the amoxicillin, answering the allergy question, or giving the spleen and sport rule

A two-second chest because 'it's EBV', when you have five minutes to spare; announcing that the mannequin is not breathing, or doing nothing but the left upper quadrant; and forgetting to decline the rectal examination with a reason
numbers: Splenomegaly in about 50% of EBV, hepatomegaly about 10% · rash in most children given an aminopenicillin, several days in VERIFY · illness 2-4 weeks, fatigue longer · no contact sport for at least 4 weeks and until well VERIFY · monospot unreliable under 4 years and in week one

Serology: VCA IgM POSITIVE, IgG POSITIVE, EBNA NEGATIVE = ACUTE; EBNA APPEARS AT 6-12 WEEKS · TRUE ALLERGY IS MINUTES TO HOURS AND URTICARIAL · scarlet fever: PHENOXYMETHYLPENICILLIN FOR 10 DAYS, exclusion until 24 hours after the first dose · Kawasaki: fever 5 days or more, IVIG within 10 days · NINE ABDOMINAL REGIONS, TWICE · MedSTAR Kids 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450

setting: History, examination request and explanation — general practice, and the recall notes say 'Precocious puberty'. The examiner is waiting for the candidate who knows that nine is normal — and who shows the exclusion process before saying so. Three AUTOMATIC FAILS: labelling it precocious puberty or ordering hormone or bone-age tests; reassuring before any screen or examination; and using the word 'Smelly' in front of the child. Ask the puberty questions last, deliberately, so the examiner sees the exclusion process before the answer.
stem: General practice, Kadina, South Australia. ELLA, 9 YEARS AND 4 MONTHS, brought by her mother because of A NEW, UNPLEASANT BODY ODOUR OVER THE PAST TWO MONTHS. ELLA IS IN THE ROOM, well, sitting quietly.

Vitals on request: HR 84 — RR 18 — T 36.7 — BP 98/62. Weight 31 kg (50th-75th), height 136 cm (50th-75th), TRACKING HER PREVIOUS CENTILES. History from the mother 5 minutes, EXAMINATION FINDINGS ON REQUEST, then explain your diagnosis and differentials to the mother.
tasks: Take a history from the mother (5 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and differentials to the mother

I'll ask some questions that MAY SEEM UNRELATED so we can be sure about the cause. Ella, okay if I ask Mum about you? back.dx: NORMAL PUBERTY — NOT PRECOCIOUS. GIVE IT WITH THREE REASONS: 'the most likely cause of the new smell is NORMAL PUBERTY. My reasons: Ella has EARLY BREAST DEVELOPMENT AND THE BEGINNINGS OF HAIR GROWTH, which are exactly the first normal signs of puberty at her age; HER GROWTH CHART IS NORMAL; and I HAVE CHECKED FOR THE OTHER CAUSES — thyroid, diabetes, rare inherited conditions, skin problems and diet — AND FOUND NOTHING. PUBERTY STARTING AT NINE IS NOT EARLY; WE ONLY CALL IT EARLY IF IT BEGINS BEFORE EIGHT.' THEN THE MECHANISM IN PLAIN WORDS: 'in puberty the body starts making NEW HORMONES. They SWITCH ON A SECOND TYPE OF SWEAT GLAND in the armpits and groin, and THE BACTERIA THAT NORMALLY LIVE ON OUR SKIN ACT ON THAT SWEAT and produce the adult-type smell. IT IS THE SAME SWEAT EVERYONE GETS — IT'S JUST NEW FOR ELLA.' THEN SIX DIFFERENTIALS NAMED: 'whether it was MAINLY ELLA who felt she smelled, WHICH CAN HAPPEN WITH ANXIETY — but you and Dad noticed it; AN OVERACTIVE THYROID; DIABETES; BEING OVERWEIGHT; RARE CONDITIONS LIKE PKU, CYSTIC FIBROSIS OR COELIAC DISEASE that change the smell of sweat; SKIN INFECTIONS; and SPICY FOODS OR MEDICINES. NONE OF THOSE FIT.' MANAGEMENT AND SAFETY-NET: 'NO TESTS ARE NEEDED. Practical things: A DAILY WASH WITH SOAP, DRYING WELL, BREATHABLE COTTON CLOTHES, SPORTS GEAR WASHED AFTER EACH USE, AND A MILD DEODORANT OR ANTIPERSPIRANT — THEY'RE SAFE AT HER AGE. I'll give Ella A GOOD BOOK ON PUBERTY AND THE ROYAL CHILDREN'S HOSPITAL FACT SHEET so she knows what's coming. About the comment at school — if it happens again, LET THE TEACHER OR WELLBEING LEADER KNOW. I'd like to see Ella in THREE TO SIX MONTHS to check that puberty is progressing normally, and SOONER IF SHE GROWS VERY QUICKLY, GETS ACNE OR A DEEP VOICE, DRINKS OR WEES MUCH MORE, OR SEEMS LOW OR WORRIED.' THEN TURN TO THE CHILD: 'Ella — any questions for me?' → 'CAN I STILL PLAY NETBALL?' → 'ABSOLUTELY. Just wash the uniform.' THE VARIANTS. THE MOTHER INSISTS ON HORMONE TESTS AND A SPECIALIST: 'I understand — you want to be certain. HORMONE TESTS AND BONE-AGE X-RAYS ARE FOR CHILDREN WHO START PUBERTY BEFORE EIGHT, or who are growing unusually fast or have signs like a deep voice or severe acne. Ella has none of those, SO THE TESTS WOULD NOT CHANGE ANYTHING AND WOULD ONLY WORRY HER. What I WILL do is see her again in three months and measure her; IF ANYTHING CHANGES, I'LL REFER HER TO THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S THAT DAY.' 'NOBODY ELSE CAN SMELL IT — SHE SHOWERS FIVE TIMES A DAY AND WON'T GO TO SCHOOL': 'THAT TELLS ME THE WORRY ITSELF IS THE PROBLEM, NOT THE SMELL. Ella, can I ask you a few questions on your own for a minute?' — then a HEADS assessment with a mood and self-harm screen. 'This is a recognised kind of anxiety; it responds well to talking therapy, and I'd like to involve a psychologist and the school wellbeing leader.' A SEVEN-YEAR-OLD WITH THE SAME FINDINGS: 'at seven, breast development IS EARLIER THAN WE EXPECT, so I DO want tests: A BONE-AGE X-RAY, HORMONE BLOODS, A PELVIC ULTRASOUND, and a PAEDIATRIC ENDOCRINOLOGIST at the Women's and Children's. Most causes are benign, and early puberty is treatable if needed.'
plan: GREET ELLA FIRST AND GET HER PERMISSION, THEN NORMALISE WITHOUT REASSURING: 'you must be Ella — hi. Mum, what's brought you both in?' → 'about two months ago we noticed SHE SMELLS — LIKE AN ADULT. She showers every day. I'm worried something's wrong, OR THAT IT'S PUBERTY FAR TOO EARLY.' → 'that's VERY COMMON FOR PARENTS TO NOTICE AROUND THIS AGE AND IT'S SENSIBLE TO CHECK. I'll ask some questions that may seem unrelated so we can be sure about the cause. ELLA, OKAY IF I ASK MUM ABOUT YOU? JUMP IN ANY TIME.' (Saying 'smelly' or 'body odour problem' with Ella in the room is an automatic fail — SAY 'THE NEW SMELL MUM HAS NOTICED'. And reassuring before any screen earns 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW WITHOUT CHECKING?')

THE COMPLAINT, WITH TWO DISCRIMINATING QUESTIONS: 'when did you first notice it? All the time or on and off? Worse? Anything that makes it worse — sport, hot days, foods? IS SHE SWEATING MORE THAN BEFORE, OR A NORMAL AMOUNT THAT SMELLS DIFFERENT? Where — armpits, feet, everywhere? AND HAVE OTHER PEOPLE NOTICED IT, OR IS IT MAINLY ELLA WHO SAYS SO?' → normal sweat, new smell, armpits, and BOTH PARENTS NOTICED WHILE ELLA IS NOT FUSSED.

IMPACT AND MIND, INCLUDING ONE DIRECT QUESTION TO THE CHILD: 'has anyone at school said anything — teasing, bullying? How is her mood? Sleep? How are things at home, school, friends?' Then: 'ELLA — ANYTHING BOTHERING YOU?' → 'I don't care. Mum does.'

THE ORGANIC SCREEN — ONE PLAIN QUESTION EACH, NO EXPLANATIONS, KEEP MOVING: washing and clothes, and is the netball gear washed each time; 'does she prefer heat or cold — HEAT INTOLERANCE, SHAKY HANDS, RACING HEART, WEIGHT LOSS? PASSING LOTS OF URINE, DRINKING LOTS, LOSING WEIGHT? Any recent WEIGHT GAIN? WAS HER NEWBORN HEEL-PRICK TEST NORMAL? Ongoing DIARRHOEA, GREASY POO, TUMMY PAIN, CHESTY COUGH, SALTY SKIN? YELLOW EYES, ITCH, DARK URINE, SWELLING? Rash in the armpits or groin, any discharge?' (Asking these as a lecture — 'I need to exclude phenylketonuria' — is the trap.)

Puberty last, deliberately: 'May I ask about puberty changes? Any breast development? Hair under the arms or in the private area? Any bleeding?' → 'Breast buds for about six months — I thought that was too early too. A little hair under the arms and down below. No bleeding.' (The lecturer wants this asked last so the examiner sees the exclusion process before the answer.)

DIET, DRUGS, FAMILY AND WELL-CHILD: 'any medicines or supplements? Lots of GARLIC, ONION, CURRY OR SPICES? HOW OLD WERE YOU WHEN YOUR PERIODS STARTED? Anyone in the family with thyroid problems, diabetes OR VERY EARLY PUBERTY? Is she alert and active, eating and drinking normally? Born at term, immunised, developing normally?'

THE EXAMINATION, ASKED BY NAME: 'general appearance — sweaty, flushed, dressed appropriately? Vitals. THE GROWTH CHART — height, weight, BMI, ANY CENTILE CROSSING? TANNER STAGING — BREAST STAGE, PUBIC HAIR STAGE, AXILLARY HAIR. THYROID — goitre, tremor, eye signs. SKIN — intertrigo, acne, hirsutism, acanthosis. Chest, heart, abdomen for masses. BLOOD GLUCOSE AND URINE DIPSTICK.'
The diagnosis with three reasons and the 'Not early' sentence, then the mechanism in plain words (see dx) → 'So it's normal? I really thought nine was too young.'

SIX DIFFERENTIALS, THEN MANAGEMENT WITH NO TESTS, THE SCHOOL COMMENT, REVIEW AT THREE TO SIX MONTHS AND THE RED FLAGS (see dx) → 'DO WE NEED BLOOD TESTS?' — and if you never mention tests, she asks it late. Then turn to Ella for her question.

ask: 'That's very common to notice around this age, AND SENSIBLE TO CHECK.' / 'MORE SWEAT, OR THE SAME SWEAT SMELLING DIFFERENT?' / 'HAVE OTHER PEOPLE NOTICED IT, OR MAINLY ELLA?' / 'ELLA — ANYTHING BOTHERING YOU?' / 'May I ask about puberty changes — breast development, hair, bleeding?'

'TANNER STAGING — BREAST AND PUBIC HAIR — AND THE GROWTH CHART, PLEASE.' / 'Was her newborn heel-prick test normal?' / 'Any greasy poo, chesty cough, salty skin?' / 'How old were you when your periods started?'

'NORMAL PUBERTY — THREE REASONS: THE SIGNS, THE GROWTH CHART, AND THE NEGATIVE SCREEN.' / 'PUBERTY AT NINE IS NOT EARLY; BEFORE EIGHT IS EARLY.' / 'New hormones SWITCH ON A SECOND TYPE OF SWEAT GLAND, and skin bacteria make the smell.' / 'NO TESTS NEEDED.' / 'Review in three to six months — sooner if rapid growth, acne, a deep voice, thirst or low mood.'

THE MOTHER INSISTS ON HORMONE TESTS: 'I understand — you want to be certain. HORMONE TESTS AND BONE-AGE X-RAYS ARE FOR CHILDREN WHO START PUBERTY BEFORE EIGHT, or who are growing unusually fast, or have a deep voice or severe acne. Ella has none of those, SO THE TESTS WOULD NOT CHANGE ANYTHING AND WOULD ONLY WORRY HER. What I will do is see her again in three months and measure her; IF ANYTHING CHANGES, I'LL REFER HER TO THE WOMEN'S AND CHILDREN'S THAT DAY.' / 'NOBODY ELSE CAN SMELL IT — SHE SHOWERS FIVE TIMES A DAY AND WON'T GO TO SCHOOL': 'THAT TELLS ME THE WORRY ITSELF IS THE PROBLEM, NOT THE SMELL. Ella, CAN I ASK YOU A FEW QUESTIONS ON YOUR OWN for a minute?' — then HEADS, mood and a self-harm screen. 'This is a recognised kind of anxiety; it responds well to talking therapy, and I'd like to involve a psychologist and the school wellbeing leader.'

A seven-year-old with the same findings — and the answer flips: 'At seven, breast development is earlier than we expect, so I do want tests: a bone-age x-ray, hormone bloods, a pelvic ultrasound, and a paediatric endocrinologist at the women's and children's. Most causes are benign, and early puberty is treatable if needed.' Numbers: precocious is under 8 in girls and under 9 in boys (4 mL testes) — delayed is 13 in girls and 14 in boys — menarche about 2 to 2.5 years after breast buds, mean 12.5-13 — tanner 2 is the bud — zero tests needed in this case.
pefe: Role-player: SARAH HARTLEY, 38, PRIMARY TEACHER, mother of Ella (9 years 4 months) and Jack (6). ELLA IS WELL, plays netball, loves school. TWO MONTHS AGO you noticed AN ADULT-TYPE SWEATY SMELL FROM HER ARMPITS, WORSE AFTER NETBALL — A NORMAL AMOUNT OF SWEAT. YOU AND HER FATHER BOTH NOTICE IT; ELLA GENUINELY IS NOT BOTHERED. She showers daily; the netball uniform is washed after each game. BREAST BUDS FOR ABOUT SIX MONTHS, a little axillary and pubic hair, NO PERIODS. No thyroid symptoms, no thirst or polyuria, weight steady, HEEL-PRICK NORMAL, no gut symptoms, no rash or discharge, no medicines, normal diet. YOU STARTED PERIODS AT 12. ONE GIRL AT SCHOOL MADE A COMMENT and Ella was upset for a day.

Register: slightly embarrassed, protective, convinced nine is 'Way too early' — and you relax when the doctor gives reasons. Hidden agenda: you have read about precocious puberty and want to ask 'Does she need hormone tests?' — volunteer it late if not addressed. Play Ella too: shrug, 'I don't care, mum does', and at the end 'Can I still play netball?' if the doctor says 'Precocious puberty' or orders hormone tests: 'So it is early? Is something wrong with her?' — and mark it a fail. If they say 'Smelly' or 'Body odour problem' in front of Ella, glance at her and look uncomfortable. If they reassure before asking anything: 'How can you know without checking?'

SCORE — ONE POINT EACH, 12 OF 17 TO PASS: greeted Ella and asked permission; normalised WITHOUT reassuring prematurely; timing, pattern and triggers; SWEAT VOLUME VERSUS SMELL; DO OTHERS NOTICE IT; impact — teasing, mood, sleep, home, school; ONE DIRECT QUESTION TO ELLA; hygiene; thyroid, diabetes, weight, heel-prick, gut and cystic fibrosis, liver, skin — one each; PUBERTY ASKED LAST; diet and drugs; maternal menarche and family history; ASKED FOR THE GROWTH CHART AND TANNER STAGING BY NAME plus thyroid, skin, systems and BSL; DIAGNOSIS = NORMAL PUBERTY WITH THREE REASONS AND 'NOT EARLY — BEFORE EIGHT IS EARLY'; the mechanism in plain words; SIX DIFFERENTIALS NAMED; management — hygiene, antiperspirant, a resource, the school, review at 3-6 months with red flags; and NO UNNECESSARY TESTS.
The complaint — Two months, most days, worse after netball — a normal amount of sweat that smells different — armpits — and both parents have noticed, while Ella is not fussed
Why that matters — If it were mainly Ella who said she smelled, that would point to anxiety — so ask who noticed
The puberty answer, asked last — BREAST BUDS FOR ABOUT SIX MONTHS — 'I THOUGHT THAT WAS TOO EARLY TOO' — a little axillary and pubic hair, NO BLEEDING

Organic screen — ALL NEGATIVE — gear washed, no thyroid or diabetes symptoms, weight steady, HEEL-PRICK NORMAL, no gut or chest symptoms, no rash or discharge, no medicines, normal diet; the mother's menarche was at TWELVE
The impact — ONE GIRL MADE A COMMENT and Ella was upset for a day; mood, sleep and school otherwise fine
fails: ★ Labelling it precocious puberty, or ordering hormone or bone-age tests — nine is normal, and before eight is early
★ Reassuring before any screen or examination, which earns 'how can you know without checking?'
Saying 'smelly' or 'body odour problem' in front of Ella — say 'the new smell Mum has noticed'
Asking the puberty questions first, when the examiner needs to see the exclusion process before the answer

Never asking whether the sweat volume changed or who noticed the smell — if it were mainly Ella, that would point to anxiety; running the organic screen as a lecture instead of one plain question each; never speaking directly to Ella; and giving the diagnosis without the three reasons
numbers: Precocious puberty: under 8 in girls, under 9 in boys (4 mL testes) · delayed: 13 in girls, 14 in boys · tanner 2 is the breast bud · menarche about 2 to 2.5 years after the buds, mean 12.5-13

Zero tests needed in this case · review at 3 to 6 months · red flags: rapid growth, acne, a deep voice, thirst or polyuria, low mood · the seven-year-old version needs a bone-age x-ray, hormone bloods, a pelvic ultrasound and paediatric endocrinology

setting: History, diagnosis and counselling — rural hospital, and she is crying when you walk in. Four empathy points are scored separately: at the opening, before the diagnosis, before management, and at the end — so it is not one warm sentence, it is four. And there are three forgotten management points that decide the station: investigations then antibiotics, surfactant as an option, and transfer to a tertiary NICU because a rural hospital cannot provide the care. 'He is stable and this is a condition we treat' is honest — 'He'll be fine' is not.
stem: You are the hospital medical officer at a rural hospital in Wallaroo. Jane, 26, has just delivered a baby boy at 32 weeks. Delivery was uncomplicated, but immediately after birth he developed respiratory distress and was placed in a headbox with 40% oxygen; he is now stable. This is her second pregnancy — the first ended in miscarriage. She is crying and asking to speak to a doctor.

8 minutes: take a focused history from the mother (3 minutes), explain the most likely diagnosis, then explain your immediate management AND COUNSEL HER, ADDRESSING HER CONCERNS. VERSION B: COUNSELLING ONLY, NO HISTORY. VERSION C: she volunteers AN E. COLI URINARY INFECTION AT 14 WEEKS and RUPTURE OF MEMBRANES EIGHT HOURS BEFORE DELIVERY.

May I ask a few questions, then explain?' · THE BREATHING: IS HE COUGHING, IS IT NOISY, OR IS HE WORKING HARD AND STRUGGLING; did it start STRAIGHT AFTER BIRTH or was he fine at first; constant or on and off; worse with feeding or position · PREGNANCY: INFECTIONS OR FEVERS, PARTICULARLY URINE INFECTIONS; high blood sugar or blood pressure; DID YOUR WATERS BREAK EARLY AND HOW LONG BEFORE HE WAS BORN; medicines, alcohol, drugs; tests and scans; AND WERE YOU GIVEN STEROID INJECTIONS BEFORE THE BIRTH · DELIVERY AND AFTER: how many weeks, vaginal or caesarean, complications, DID HE CRY STRAIGHT AWAY AND DID THEY NEED TO HELP HIM BREATHE, ANY MENTION OF A BOWEL MOTION INSIDE THE WOMB, VITAMIN K, ANY DROOLING OR FROTHY SALIVA, ANY TURNING BLUE, alert or sleepy, HAS HE PASSED URINE OR A BOWEL MOTION · THEN THE MOTHER HERSELF: how are you feeling right now, IS ANYONE HERE WITH YOU, and how are you physically · bleeding, pain · THEN THE DIAGNOSIS WITH THE SURFACTANT EXPLANATION AND THE BLAME REMOVED · then TESTS THEN ANTIBIOTICS, oxygen to CPAP to intubation, fluids and expressing, SURFACTANT AS AN OPTION, AND THE TRANSFER FRAMED AS BEST CARE · then PATS, her own fitness to travel, written information, a family meeting with Sam, and a summary ending in empathy.
findings: The breathing
Started straight after birth — grunting with the chest sucking in, oxygen low — constant
Gestation and delivery
32 WEEKS, quick normal vaginal delivery, no forceps — HE CRIED BRIEFLY THEN WENT GRUNTY; RUBBED AND GIVEN OXYGEN, NO TUBE

back.dx: NEONATAL RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME — SURFACTANT DEFICIENCY OF PREMATURITY at 32 weeks. NAME IT AND EXPLAIN SURFACTANT CORRECTLY: 'your son most likely has a condition called RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME — it's VERY COMMON IN PREMATURE BABIES. INSIDE THE LUNGS ARE MILLIONS OF TINY AIR SACS, AND THEY'RE COATED WITH A SOAPY SUBSTANCE CALLED SURFACTANT THAT STOPS THEM STICKING SHUT AT THE END OF EACH BREATH. BABIES MAKE MOST OF THEIR SURFACTANT IN THE LAST FEW WEEKS OF PREGNANCY, so a baby born at 32 weeks DOESN'T HAVE ENOUGH YET; the air sacs PARTLY COLLAPSE WITH EVERY BREATH and he has to work hard to breathe — THAT'S THE GRUNTING AND THE PULLING-IN OF HIS CHEST.' The 'chest-wall lubricant' explanation is wrong and is a named trap. THEN REMOVE THE BLAME AND REASSURE AGAIN: 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS, AND THE MISCARRIAGE ISN'T CONNECTED. BEING BORN EARLY IS THE REASON — and that happens to many women who did everything right. We can treat this, AND MOST PREMATURE BABIES WITH IT DO WELL.' THEN THE MANAGEMENT, AND THE THREE FORGOTTEN POINTS ARE THE STATION. ONE — INVESTIGATIONS, THEN ANTIBIOTICS: 'first, some tests — blood tests INCLUDING A BLOOD CULTURE, a check of his oxygen and sugar levels, and A CHEST X-RAY. THE MAIN REASON FOR THE TESTS IS TO MAKE SURE THERE'S NO INFECTION, BECAUSE INFECTION CAN LOOK EXACTLY LIKE THIS — and given the urine infection and your waters breaking early, WE TAKE THAT SERIOUSLY. SO AS SOON AS THE SAMPLES ARE TAKEN, WE'LL START HIM ON ANTIBIOTICS THROUGH A DRIP, AS A PRECAUTION, AND STOP THEM IF THE TESTS COME BACK CLEAR.' TWO — RESPIRATORY SUPPORT AND FLUIDS, WITH SURFACTANT NAMED AS AN OPTION: continuous oxygen monitoring; 'if his breathing gets harder we can help him in two ways: A SMALL MASK THAT GIVES A GENTLE CONTINUOUS FLOW OF AIR TO HOLD THE AIR SACS OPEN — CALLED CPAP — or, if needed, A TUBE INTO HIS WINDPIPE with a machine to breathe for him. Because breathing is hard work, HE WON'T FEED BY MOUTH YET — fluids and sugar through the drip, AND I'D ENCOURAGE YOU TO START EXPRESSING MILK so it's ready when he can take it. THERE IS ALSO A TREATMENT WHERE THE SPECIALISTS GIVE HIM SURFACTANT — THE VERY SUBSTANCE HE'S SHORT OF — DOWN A THIN TUBE INTO THE LUNGS. It's an option they'll consider, and OFTEN THE TRANSPORT TEAM GIVES IT BEFORE HE TRAVELS.' THREE — TRANSFER, FRAMED AS BEST CARE: 'THE MOST IMPORTANT THING I NEED TO TELL YOU: this condition needs CLOSE, CONTINUOUS MONITORING IN A NEONATAL INTENSIVE CARE UNIT, and it usually takes DAYS TO WEEKS to improve. WE DON'T HAVE THAT UNIT HERE IN WALLAROO. So I'm arranging for the specialist neonatal retrieval team — MedSTAR — to take him to the Women's and Children's Hospital in Adelaide. THAT IS NOT BECAUSE HE'S GETTING WORSE; IT'S SO HE GETS THE BEST POSSIBLE CARE.' THEN HER: 'we'll do everything to keep you together' — travel with him where possible, otherwise as soon as she is fit, with PATS TRAVEL AND ACCOMMODATION SUPPORT for her and Sam; CHECK HER OWN BLEEDING AND BLOOD PRESSURE so she is well enough to go; WRITTEN INFORMATION from the Women's and Children's; A FAMILY MEETING WITH SAM BEFORE THE TEAM ARRIVES; and 'any question, at any hour, ask the nurses to get me.' CLOSE WITH THE SUMMARY AND THE FOURTH EMPATHY POINT: 'a treatable lung condition of prematurity; he's stable; tests, antibiotics as a precaution, support for his breathing, and the specialists may give surfactant; and he's going to the intensive care nursery in Adelaide for the best care, with you close by. I'M SO SORRY YOU'RE GOING THROUGH THIS — YOU'VE DONE NOTHING WRONG.'
plan: EMPATHY, REASSURANCE, PERMISSION — THE FIRST OF FOUR SCORED EMPATHY POINTS: [sit close, hand the tissues] 'Jane, I'm Dr -, the doctor looking after you and your son. I'M SO SORRY THIS IS HAPPENING — IT MUST BE TERRIFYING SO SOON AFTER THE BIRTH.' → [crying] 'he can't breathe properly. WHY IS THIS HAPPENING? I LOST THE FIRST ONE — IS HE GOING TO DIE?' → 'I can only imagine what you're going through. I want you to know first that HE IS STABLE RIGHT NOW, HE'S IN SAFE HANDS, and we're giving him the very best care. May I ask a few questions, and then I'll explain exactly what's happening and what we're doing?' (Launching into questions without empathy, or answering 'HE'LL BE FINE', are the two traps — 'HE IS STABLE AND THIS IS A CONDITION WE TREAT' is the honest version.)

THE BREATHING: 'when you say he's having trouble — IS HE COUGHING, IS IT NOISY, OR IS HE WORKING HARD, STRUGGLING? Did it start STRAIGHT AFTER BIRTH or was he fine at first? Constant, or on and off? Worse with anything — feeding, lying a certain way?'

PREGNANCY — AND THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT CARRY MARKS: 'any infections or fevers in the pregnancy — URINE INFECTIONS? High blood sugar or blood pressure? DID YOUR WATERS BREAK EARLY — HOW LONG BEFORE HE WAS BORN? Any medicines, alcohol or drugs? Were your tests and scans normal? WERE YOU GIVEN STEROID INJECTIONS BEFORE THE BIRTH?' → an E. coli urine infection at 14 weeks, WATERS BROKE ABOUT EIGHT HOURS BEFORE, and NO STEROIDS BECAUSE THERE WASN'T TIME. (Not asking about antenatal steroids, or not linking the UTI and early rupture to infection risk, are both named traps.)

DELIVERY AND AFTER: 'how many weeks were you? Vaginal or caesarean, any complications? DID HE CRY STRAIGHT AWAY — DID THEY NEED TO HELP HIM BREATHE? Did they mention HE'D PASSED A BOWEL MOTION INSIDE THE WOMB? Has he had VITAMIN K? Any DROOLING OR FROTHY SALIVA, any TURNING BLUE? Is he alert or sleepy? HAS HE PASSED URINE OR A BOWEL MOTION YET?'

THE MOTHER HERSELF — a scored item candidates drop: 'and HOW ARE YOU FEELING RIGHT NOW, Jane? IS ANYONE HERE WITH YOU? How are you physically — bleeding, pain?' → 'terrified. My partner Sam is parking the car. I'm sore but OK.'

The diagnosis — empathy again first, then surfactant in plain words (see dx) → 'Is it because of the infection I had? Because I lost the first one?' / 'Did I do something wrong?' → 'No. Nothing you did caused this, and the miscarriage isn't connected.' then reassure again — the second scored empathy point sits right here.

Management, point one and two: tests then antibiotics, then oxygen, CPAP, intubation, fluids, expressing, and surfactant named as an option (see dx) → 'Can't you just give the surfactant now?' / 'Will he be on the machine for long?'

MANAGEMENT, POINT THREE — THE TRANSFER, FRAMED AS BEST CARE (see dx) → [panicking] 'TRAVELS? WHERE?' / 'WHY ADELAIDE — IS IT THAT BAD?' / 'CAN I GO WITH HIM?' → 'we'll do everything to keep you together' — then PATS, and checking she is well enough to travel. ('We'll keep him here and see' is the fail, and if you never mention transfer she asks 'SO HE'LL STAY HERE WITH ME?')

SUPPORT, SUMMARY AND THE FOURTH EMPATHY POINT (see dx): written information, a family meeting with Sam before the team arrives, 'any question at any hour', then the five-part summary ending 'I'M SO SORRY YOU'RE GOING THROUGH THIS — YOU'VE DONE NOTHING WRONG.'

'A SOAPY SUBSTANCE CALLED SURFACTANT THAT STOPS THE AIR SACS STICKING SHUT.' / 'Babies make most of it in the last few weeks — at 32 weeks he doesn't have enough yet.' / 'NOTHING YOU DID CAUSED THIS — BEING BORN EARLY IS THE REASON.' / 'The miscarriage isn't connected.'

'As soon as the samples are taken we'll start antibiotics as a precaution.' / 'CPAP — a gentle continuous flow of air to hold the air sacs open.' / 'Surfactant is an option the specialists will consider.' / 'We don't have a neonatal intensive care unit here — so he's going to the women's and children's, not because he's worse, but for the best care.' / 'We'll arrange travel and accommodation for you both.' / 'I'd encourage you to start expressing milk.'

VERSION B — COUNSELLING ONLY, NO HISTORY: open with empathy and stability, THEN THE AGENDA QUESTION, WHICH IS WHAT THIS VERSION SCORES: 'before I explain, CAN I CHECK WHAT YOU'VE BEEN TOLD SO FAR, AND IS THERE ANYTHING YOU'RE MOST WORRIED ABOUT?' → 'nobody's told me anything. IS HE GOING TO DIE? IS IT MY FAULT?' Then the diagnosis and surfactant as above, then: 'THREE THINGS WE DO NOW, AND ONE BIG THING. Tests then antibiotics as a precaution; oxygen, with CPAP or a breathing tube if he needs it, and fluids through a drip; and the specialists may give him surfactant into the lungs. THE BIG THING: he needs an intensive care nursery, WHICH WE DON'T HAVE HERE, so the retrieval team will take him to the Women's and Children's — FOR THE BEST CARE, NOT BECAUSE HE'S WORSE.'

VERSION C — THE POSITIVE FINDINGS: 'I had a urine infection at 14 weeks — E. coli — and my waters broke eight hours before he came. DID THAT CAUSE THIS?' → 'thank you for telling me — BOTH ARE IMPORTANT. The infection was treated, and eight hours is not a long time for the waters to be broken, SO NEITHER OF THESE CAUSED HIS LUNGS TO BE SHORT OF SURFACTANT; BEING BORN AT 32 WEEKS DID. BUT BOTH MAKE INFECTION SOMETHING WE TAKE EVEN MORE SERIOUSLY — which is exactly why we'll take blood tests and start antibiotics straight away, rather than waiting for results.' And to the examiner, if asked whether it changes management: 'NO — IT STRENGTHENS THE CASE FOR EMPIRICAL ANTIBIOTICS AFTER CULTURES, and I would ADD A LUMBAR PUNCTURE IF HE SHOWED ANY SIGNS OF SEPSIS; the diagnosis, respiratory support, surfactant option and transfer are unchanged.' (Saying the findings 'DON'T MATTER' is the trap — they do not change the plan, but they MUST be acknowledged and linked to sepsis risk.)
pefe: Role-player: JANE, 26, A SCHOOLTEACHER IN WALLAROO. You have just delivered your son AT 32 WEEKS after a quick labour; YOUR WATERS BROKE ABOUT EIGHT HOURS BEFORE. YOUR FIRST PREGNANCY ENDED IN MISCARRIAGE AT 10 WEEKS LAST YEAR. You had AN E. COLI URINARY INFECTION AT 14 WEEKS, treated with antibiotics. No diabetes, no blood pressure problems, normal scans, NO STEROID INJECTIONS — NO TIME. The baby CRIED BRIEFLY, THEN GRUNTED; the midwives rubbed him and gave oxygen through a headbox; NO TUBE. HE HAS NOT FED. Your partner SAM IS PARKING THE CAR.

Emotional register: crying, frightened, guilty. Ask early: 'Is he going to die?' and 'Is it my fault — the infection? I lost the first one.' when transfer is mentioned, panic: 'Why Adelaide? Is it that bad? Can I go with him?' if the doctor never mentions transfer, ask at the end: 'So he'll stay here with me?' if they never mention antibiotics or infection, ask: 'Could the infection I had have got into him?' if they never mention surfactant, ask: 'Is there any medicine for his lungs?'

Score the doctor: EMPATHY AT THE OPENING; reassurance — STABLE, SAFE HANDS; explored the breathing and its onset; pregnancy infections, PROM, diabetes AND STEROIDS; delivery, resuscitation, meconium; feeding, drooling, blue, alert, urine and stool; ASKED HOW YOU ARE; NAMED RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME; SURFACTANT EXPLAINED AS AN AIR-SAC LINING AND LINKED TO PREMATURITY; 'NOT YOUR FAULT'; EMPATHY AGAIN BEFORE MANAGEMENT; tests INCLUDING BLOOD CULTURE AND CHEST X-RAY; ANTIBIOTICS AFTER CULTURES; oxygen to CPAP to intubation; IV fluids, nil by mouth, EXPRESSING; SURFACTANT AS AN OPTION; TRANSFER TO NICU FRAMED AS BEST CARE; PATS, travel AND YOUR OWN CARE; written information and a family meeting; AND A SUMMARY WITH FINAL EMPATHY.
The baby now — STABLE, IN A HEADBOX WITH 40% OXYGEN — not blue on oxygen, a bit alert, HAS NOT FED, nothing passed yet
Antenatal steroids — NONE — 'THERE WASN'T TIME, IT ALL HAPPENED SO FAST'. Given only if you ask, and not asking is the named trap
The infection risk — An E. Coli urinary infection at 14 weeks, treated with antibiotics — and the waters broke about eight hours before delivery
What those two mean — Neither caused the surfactant deficiency — but both raise the weight you give to sepsis, and you must say so
The rest of the pregnancy — No diabetes or hypertension, no medicines, alcohol or drugs, SCANS NORMAL
Meconium, vitamin K, drooling — NO meconium mentioned — VITAMIN K GIVEN — NO drooling or frothy saliva
Her own history — FIRST PREGNANCY ENDED IN MISCARRIAGE AT 10 WEEKS LAST YEAR — and she believes it may be connected
The mother now — TERRIFIED, CRYING, GUILTY — partner SAM IS PARKING THE CAR — she is sore but physically okay
What she will ask — 'Is he going to die?' — 'Is it my fault — the infection? I lost the first one' — and when transfer is mentioned, 'Why Adelaide? Is it that bad? Can I go with him?'

What she asks if you omit it — No transfer mentioned: 'SO HE'LL STAY HERE WITH ME?' — no antibiotics: 'COULD THE INFECTION I HAD HAVE GOT INTO HIM?' — no surfactant: 'IS THERE ANY MEDICINE FOR HIS LUNGS?'
