time: Ask for the observations first · the examiner has them on a card and marks whether you asked · then address the concern and signpost: 'A few rashes look alike early on and one or two are serious, so I'm going to ask a set of questions, some about things that may seem unrelated' · the rash: when first noticed, where it started and where it is now, spreading, what colour, raised, are some of them blisters, any pus or weeping, warm or painful, itchy and worse at night or after a bath · group 1, infective: has he had a fever, and when in relation to the rash; immunisations; anyone at home or childcare unwell, anyone with chickenpox; travel; coryzal symptoms; vomiting or diarrhoea; recent antibiotics; and the well-baby questions · alert, drinking, normal wet nappies · group 2, autoimmune: blood in the stool, greasy stool, sore joints, sore or red eyes, mouth ulcers, cracked lips · group 3, allergic: family asthma, hay fever or eczema; new soaps, creams, sunscreen, foods, medicines or bites; noisy breathing or lip swelling · group 4, purpuric: easy bruising, nosebleeds, bleeding gums, pale, tired, weight loss, lumps · then BINDSMA and the social history, which is the NAI screen and is scored in every rash station · then the examination in structure, ending with spleen and lymph nodes.

back.dx: VERSION A — VARICELLA (CHICKENPOX). 'A common virus that causes A FEVER AND THEN VERY ITCHY SPOTS that turn into little blisters and then scabs — THE MIX OF NEW SPOTS, BLISTERS AND SCABS TOGETHER IS WHAT MAKES ME CONFIDENT. His cousin's illness two weeks ago fits exactly.' DIFFERENTIALS NAMED: a cold-sore-type virus (HSV), HAND-FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE, and SCHOOL SORES (impetigo) — 'the pattern and the sites don't fit those. And importantly, HE'S ALERT, DRINKING, THE SPOTS FADE WHEN PRESSED AND HE HAS NO BRUISING, so I'm not worried about the serious rashes.' MANAGEMENT: no specific medicine in a healthy child; PARACETAMOL, AND AVOID IBUPROFEN AND ASPIRIN IN CHICKENPOX; cool baths, calamine, SHORT NAILS, loose cotton clothes; EXCLUSION FROM CHILDCARE UNTIL EVERY BLISTER HAS SCABBED, ABOUT FIVE DAYS. THEN THE QUESTION THAT MUST BE ASKED: 'IS ANYONE PREGNANT, A NEWBORN, OR ON TREATMENT THAT WEAKENS THE IMMUNE SYSTEM IN YOUR CIRCLE? THEY SHOULD RING THEIR DOCTOR TODAY' — and if she is not immune, ZOSTER IMMUNOGLOBULIN CAN PROTECT HER IF GIVEN EARLY, WITHIN 96 HOURS AND UP TO 10 DAYS. SAFETY-NET: come straight back or call 000 if he becomes DROWSY, STOPS DRINKING, HAS TROUBLE BREATHING, or ANY SPOT BECOMES RED, SWOLLEN AND PAINFUL, or THE FEVER RETURNS AFTER A FEW DAYS. Give it in writing, and notify SA Health as routine. VERSION B — HENOCH-SCHONLEIN PURPURA: 'inflammation of small blood vessels after a viral infection. IT USUALLY SETTLES, but I need A BLOOD COUNT TODAY to be sure her platelets are normal, and because IT CAN AFFECT THE KIDNEYS we'll CHECK HER URINE AND BLOOD PRESSURE REGULARLY FOR SIX MONTHS.' Emergency return for SEVERE TUMMY PAIN, BLOOD IN THE STOOL, OR A SWOLLEN PAINFUL TESTICLE. Ask: does it blanch, blood in the urine, nosebleeds or bleeding gums, pale or tired, any lumps — and request BLOOD PRESSURE AND A URINE DIPSTICK FOR BLOOD AND PROTEIN by name. VERSION C — ROSEOLA INFANTUM (HHV-6): 'THE TELL-TALE SIGN IS THE FEVER BREAKING JUST AS THE RASH APPEARS.' No treatment, childcare when well — and the one thing to add: THE HIGH FEVER CAN OCCASIONALLY TRIGGER A BRIEF FEBRILE SEIZURE, so lie him on his side, nothing in the mouth, and call 000 if it lasts more than five minutes. THE TRAP IN VERSION C IS CALLING IT MEASLES — he is immunised, there is no cough, coryza or conjunctivitis, AND THE FEVER HAS GONE — or ordering tests on a well, blanching child.
plan: VITALS FIRST, THEN OPEN AND SIGNPOST — skipping the observations because the child 'looks well' is the first trap, and the examiner marks whether you asked. 'A few rashes can look alike early on and ONE OR TWO ARE SERIOUS, so I'm going to ask a set of questions, some about things that may seem unrelated, then examine Liam and tell you what I think.' (Jumping to 'it's chickenpox' in the first minute earns 'ARE YOU SURE? HOW DO YOU KNOW IT ISN'T SOMETHING WORSE?')

THE RASH: onset, WHERE IT STARTED AND WHERE IT IS NOW, spreading, colour, RAISED OR FLAT, ARE SOME OF THEM BLISTERS, pus or weeping, warm or painful, itchy and worse at night or after a bath. (NOT ASKING ABOUT BLISTERS AND STAGES IS THE TRAP — THE MULTIPLE-STAGE DESCRIPTION IS THE DIAGNOSIS.)

GROUP 1, INFECTIVE — with the two marked items: 'HAS HE HAD A FEVER? WHEN, IN RELATION TO THE RASH?' then immunisations, CONTACTS INCLUDING CHICKENPOX, travel, coryza, vomiting or diarrhoea, recent antibiotics, AND 'IS HE ALERT, DRINKING NORMALLY, NORMAL WET NAPPIES?' (Both the fever-rash timing and the drowsy/drinking/nappy questions are separately marked.)

GROUPS 2, 3 AND 4, RUN AS BLOCKS: AUTOIMMUNE — blood in the poo, greasy poo, sore joints, sore or red eyes, mouth ulcers, cracked lips. ALLERGIC — family atopy, NEW SOAPS, CREAMS, SUNSCREEN, FOODS, MEDICINES OR BITES, NOISY BREATHING OR LIP SWELLING. PURPURIC — EASY BRUISING, NOSEBLEEDS, BLEEDING GUMS, pale, tired, weight loss, lumps.

BINDSMA AND THE SOCIAL HISTORY — and omitting it because the diagnosis is obvious is a named trap, because IT IS THE NAI SCREEN AND IS SCORED IN EVERY RASH STATION: 'born at term, any problems? Growing and developing well? Regular medicines or allergies? AND I ASK EVERY FAMILY THIS — who's at home with you, how are things going, any stresses? How is childcare — any concerns?'

THE EXAMINATION, IN STRUCTURE AND ENDING WITH THE LAST TWO BOXES: 'general appearance and hydration; THE RASH — distribution, whether the lesions are MACULES, PAPULES OR VESICLES, WHETHER THEY ARE AT DIFFERENT STAGES, any crusting or discharge; WHETHER THEY BLANCH; warmth and tenderness; the throat and mouth, ears, chest, heart, ABDOMEN FOR LIVER AND SPLEEN, joints, AND A FULL LYMPH NODE EXAMINATION.' (Stopping after the rash is the trap — LYMPH NODES AND SPLEEN ARE THE LAST TWO BOXES.)
Diagnosis in plain words with the stages as the reason, then the differentials and the reassuring negatives (see dx).

MANAGEMENT, THE PREGNANT-CONTACT QUESTION AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'MY SISTER'S 30 WEEKS PREGNANT AND SHE WAS HERE YESTERDAY.' Then written information, notification, and a summary. (Ibuprofen, the wrong exclusion period, no pregnant-contact question, or reassurance without safety-netting are the four management traps.)

It usually settles, BUT I NEED A BLOOD COUNT TODAY to be sure her platelets are normal, and BECAUSE IT CAN AFFECT THE KIDNEYS we'll check her urine and blood pressure REGULARLY FOR SIX MONTHS. SEVERE TUMMY PAIN, BLOOD IN THE POO, OR A SWOLLEN PAINFUL TESTICLE needs the emergency department.'

VERSION C — ROSEOLA: the winning question is 'SO THE RASH APPEARED AS THE FEVER DISAPPEARED?' Then alert and drinking, does it blanch, immunisations. 'This is ROSEOLA — a common, harmless virus in toddlers. THE TELL-TALE SIGN IS THE FEVER BREAKING JUST AS THE RASH APPEARS. No treatment, childcare when he feels well. The one thing to know is that THE HIGH FEVER CAN OCCASIONALLY TRIGGER A BRIEF FEBRILE SEIZURE — lie him on his side, DON'T PUT ANYTHING IN HIS MOUTH, and call 000 if it lasts more than five minutes.' (Calling it measles in an immunised child with no cough, coryza or conjunctivitis and a settled fever, or ordering tests on a well blanching child, are the two traps.)

THE FOUR GROUPS, AS A CHECKLIST FOR ANY PAEDIATRIC RASH: INFECTIVE — fever and its timing, immunisations, contacts, travel, coryza, gut symptoms, antibiotics, and the well-baby questions. AUTOIMMUNE — bowel, joints, eyes, mouth and lips. ALLERGIC — atopy, new exposures, and the anaphylaxis screen. PURPURIC — bruising, bleeding, pallor, fatigue, weight loss and lumps. THEN BINDSMA AND THE SOCIAL SCREEN.

back.dx: IRRITANT NAPPY DERMATITIS — IRRITANT CONTACT DERMATITIS — triggered by the diarrhoea three weeks ago, WITH A MOTHER WHO IS NOT COPING. EXPLAIN IT: 'when WEE AND POO SIT AGAINST THE SKIN for a while, ESPECIALLY AFTER DIARRHOEA, the skin gets OVER-WET AND INFLAMED, and wiping makes it sting. SOMETIMES A YEAST CALLED CANDIDA GROWS ON TOP; I DON'T SEE SIGNS OF THAT TODAY, but it's common and easy to treat if it appears.' THE FOUR-PART PLAN, GIVEN AS A TEAM PLAN: CHANGE — every two hours by day, AT EVERY NIGHT FEED, and straight after every poo; CLEAN — warm water and a soft cloth or fragrance-free wipes, PAT DRY, NO SOAP; BARRIER — A THICK ZINC CREAM AT EVERY SINGLE CHANGE, THICK ENOUGH THAT YOU CAN'T SEE SKIN THROUGH IT, AND LEAVE THE OLD LAYER ON; AIR — nappy off on a towel a few times a day. THEN THE ESCALATION RULE: 'IF THE REDNESS SPREADS INTO THE CREASES OR YOU SEE LITTLE RED DOTS AROUND THE EDGE, WE ADD AN ANTIFUNGAL CREAM UNDERNEATH.' WHEN SHE ASKS 'IS IT MY FAULT? BECAUSE I DON'T CHANGE HIM ENOUGH?' — NEVER SAY YES: 'RASHES LIKE THIS HAPPEN TO LOTS OF BABIES AFTER DIARRHOEA. MORE FREQUENT CHANGES WILL HELP IT HEAL — AND I WANT TO MAKE THAT EASIER FOR YOU, NOT JUST TELL YOU TO DO IT.' THEN THE SUPPORT, WHICH IS THE PART THAT PASSES THE STATION: a HOME VISIT FROM THE CHILD AND FAMILY HEALTH NURSE this week; THE PANDA LINE for parents feeling overwhelmed; 'could your mum come up for a week?'; when the partner is home, HE DOES THE NIGHT CHANGES; and THE 6-WEEK CHECK AND IMMUNISATIONS booked for next week so the rash, the weight and the mother are all reviewed together. SAFETY-NET: come straight back if he has A FEVER, IS SLEEPY OR FEEDING POORLY, or the rash develops SORES, PUS OR BLISTERS, or HASN'T IMPROVED IN A WEEK — and write it all down. VERSION B — ECZEMA: 'the skin barrier is leaky and the immune system over-reacts, so it's dry, inflamed and itchy in cycles; it runs with asthma and hay fever.' TWO THINGS WORK: A THICK MOISTURISER OVER THE WHOLE BODY AT LEAST TWICE A DAY, EVERY DAY, FLARING OR NOT; and A STEROID CREAM — hydrocortisone on the face, slightly stronger on the body — ONCE OR TWICE DAILY UNTIL THE FLARE IS COMPLETELY CLEAR, usually one to two weeks, THEN STOP. ANTIHISTAMINES DON'T HELP THIS ITCH. Soap-free wash, short lukewarm baths, cotton clothes, a WRITTEN ACTION PLAN, review in two weeks — sooner if it WEEPS, CRUSTS, or he has COLD-SORE-LIKE BLISTERS AND IS UNWELL. (The traps are 'steroids are dangerous, use for a week only', prescribing an antihistamine, and not specifying moisturiser frequency.) VERSION C — SEBORRHOEIC DERMATITIS: 'the oil glands are over-active and inflamed, producing GREASY YELLOW SCALE ON A PINK BASE. IT ISN'T ITCHY, ISN'T INFECTIOUS AND ISN'T CAUSED BY ANYTHING YOU'VE DONE; it settles by itself, USUALLY BY SIX TO TWELVE MONTHS.' Soften with baby oil or white soft paraffin, leave an hour, mild shampoo, lift gently with a soft brush; 1% HYDROCORTISONE for a few days if the skin underneath is red and sore; an antifungal shampoo if it persists. THE DIFFERENCE FROM ECZEMA: ECZEMA IS ITCHY, COMES AND GOES, AND RUNS IN FAMILIES. VERSION D — ERYTHEMA INFECTIOSUM: take the abuse concern seriously and DO THE SOCIAL AND NAI SCREEN AND THE INJURY EXAMINATION FIRST — 'any concern that a child has been hurt is something I take seriously and will look into properly.' Ask about fever and coryza this week, alertness, immunisations, OTHER RASH ON THE ARMS OR TRUNK, sick contacts at daycare, home and daycare history. Then: 'BRIGHT SYMMETRICAL ERYTHEMA OF BOTH CHEEKS SPARING THE MOUTH, a RETICULAR RASH ON THE ARMS, NO BRUISING, NO FINGER MARKS, no other injuries' — 'this is SLAPPED CHEEK DISEASE, PARVOVIRUS: a few days of fever and a runny nose, THEN BRIGHT RED CHEEKS — THERE ARE NO MARKS OF A HAND. No treatment; HE CAN GO BACK TO DAYCARE BECAUSE HE'S NO LONGER INFECTIOUS ONCE THE RASH IS OUT. ONE IMPORTANT THING: IS ANYONE IN YOUR FAMILY OR CLOSE CONTACTS PREGNANT? THEY SHOULD SEE THEIR DOCTOR FOR A BLOOD TEST.'
plan: VITALS, OPEN, AND CATCH THE TIREDNESS: 'may I have Oscar's observations — temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, and is he alert and feeding?' Then: 'Emma, tell me what's been happening.' → 'he's had this rash for three weeks. IT'S NOT GOING AWAY WHATEVER I PUT ON IT. I'M JUST SO TIRED — HE DOESN'T LET ME SLEEP.' → 'THAT SOUNDS EXHAUSTING — a rash that won't settle plus broken nights, six weeks in. Let me work out what's driving this rash, AND WE'LL SORT IT OUT TOGETHER.' (Ignoring the tiredness comment is the first trap — NOTE IT NOW AND RETURN TO IT.)

THE RASH: 'where exactly is it — IS IT ANYWHERE ELSE, LIKE HIS SCALP, FACE OR NECK FOLDS? When did it start, is it spreading? Just redness, or any BLISTERS, RAW AREAS OR SORES? Any discharge or WHITE MATERIAL? Warm to touch? Is he more irritable, ESPECIALLY AT CHANGES? First time? What have you tried?' ('Anywhere else?' is a marked question even though the photograph shows the site.)

THE THREE KEY QUESTIONS — and the second one is where the station turns: 'HAS HE HAD ANY DIARRHOEA RECENTLY? HOW OFTEN DO YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY — DURING THE DAY, AND OVERNIGHT? ANY NEW WIPES, BODY WASH, CREAM, OR A NEW BRAND OF NAPPY?' → 'three or four times a day. At night, ONCE, WHEN I REMEMBER — I'M SO TIRED.' → NO CHANGE IN TONE: 'THANK YOU FOR BEING HONEST WITH ME — THAT REALLY HELPS.' (Reacting with a lecture here loses the station; come back to it in the social history.)

THE OTHER GROUPS: other rashes — scalp, behind the ears, neck; FAMILY ATOPY; fever, alert or sleepier, feeding and wet nappies; sick contacts; IMMUNISATIONS; AND 'ANY WHITE PATCHES IN HIS MOUTH OR ON HIS TONGUE?' Then feeding, weight gain, blood or greasy stools, rash after feeds, vomiting, birth, heel-prick, medicines and allergies.

The social and mood block — the discriminating one, asked warmly and not as an accusation: 'Emma, you've mentioned a couple of times how tired you are. Who's at home with you? How much sleep are you getting? Over the last two weeks, have you often felt down, depressed or hopeless — or had little interest or pleasure in things? Do you have anyone who can help with night changes and feeds?' → tearful: 'Not depressed exactly. Flat. Overwhelmed. Some days I don't know if I'm doing any of it right.' → 'That is a very normal thing to feel six weeks in with no sleep and no help — and it's something I can actually do something about.' (Two screening questions plus a support question, warmly, is the pass.)

THE EXAMINATION, WITH THE TWO DECIDING ITEMS NAMED: 'general appearance, hydration and temperature, AND HIS WEIGHT ON THE GROWTH CHART. The rash: DISTRIBUTION — CONVEX SURFACES OR INTO THE FOLDS — ANY SATELLITE SPOTS, PUSTULES, EROSIONS OR DISCHARGE. THE MOUTH FOR THRUSH. Scalp, face, neck folds and behind the ears, and the rest of the skin. Abdomen for liver and spleen, and lymph nodes.' (Not asking about the folds and satellites is the trap — THAT IS WHAT DECIDES WHETHER YOU ADD AN ANTIFUNGAL.)
The diagnosis in plain words and the four-part plan — change, clean, barrier, air — with the escalation rule (see dx) → 'Is it because I don't change him enough? Is it my fault?' → never yes.

THE SUPPORT, THE 6-WEEK CHECK AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx): the child health nurse home visit, PANDA, asking about her mother coming up, the partner doing night changes when home, immunisations next week, and the return criteria — written down. Then summarise.

setting: History, examination request and explanation — regional ED. And the examiner will not volunteer the olive — if you do not ask for a mass and its site, the diagnostic finding never enters the room. back.dx: Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Explain it as a gateway: 'At the bottom of the stomach there's a ring of muscle — a gateway — that lets milk into the bowel. In this condition that muscle gets thick and the gateway narrows, so milk can't get through. The stomach squeezes hard against it and the milk comes back up with force.' then four reasons: 'One, his age — it shows up at two to eight weeks, and he's three weeks. Two, the vomiting is forceful. Three, he's hungry straight after and takes another feed. Four, the vomit is milky, not green, which tells me the blockage is at the stomach exit, not lower down. And when I examined him I felt the thickened muscle as a small lump and saw the stomach squeezing' — plus the family history, because it runs in families. Then the two things she is waiting for: 'Nothing you've done — the formula, the feeding — caused this' and 'Reflux is a fair thought, but reflux babies dribble milk without force and often go off their feeds; Oliver is the opposite.' Differentials: reflux; a blockage or twist lower in the bowel, which usually gives green vomit; a trapped hernia in the groin; an infection — urine, chest or blood; a knock to the head; and a rare salt-losing gland condition — congenital adrenal hyperplasia — that we check for on his bloods. Management, in order, and never 'Surgery tonight': stop the feeds; a drip to rehydrate and replace the salts he's lost, with bloods to check them; an ultrasound to confirm; then the children's surgeons. 'The treatment is a small operation that opens up the gateway — it's curative, and most babies feed within hours and go home in a day or two. It isn't done tonight: we get his salts right first because that makes the anaesthetic safer.' Safety-net: tell the nurse straight away if he vomits green, becomes floppy or drowsy, or stops weeing. Version B — the bloods: 'These show what the vomiting has done. He has lost a lot of the acid and salt from his stomach, so his chloride and potassium are low and his blood has become slightly alkaline. He's also dry — that's the raised urea. This pattern actually supports the diagnosis. We correct it before any operation: a drip with salt water, sugar and potassium, recheck every few hours, and the surgeons operate once the numbers are back in range — usually within a day or two.' and if the examiner asks why not operate now: 'Uncorrected alkalosis is associated with post-operative apnoea; correction to a chloride above 100 and bicarbonate below 30 is standard before anaesthesia.' Version C — the green vomit: 'Green vomit changes things — it means the blockage may be below the stomach, and one cause is a twist of the bowel that needs the surgeons urgently. Is his tummy swollen or sore? Any blood in the nappy? I'm going to examine him now and call the surgical team straight away.' Do not continue down the HPS pathway once the vomit is bilious — malrotation with volvulus is the diagnosis to exclude first.
plan: VITALS AND HYDRATION BEFORE YOU SIT, THEN OPEN: 'could I have the vital signs AND HYDRATION STATUS, please?' Then introduce, signpost, and 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'he keeps throwing up his feeds. It started two days ago and IT'S GETTING WORSE — IT COMES FLYING OUT OF HIM. MY MATERNAL NURSE SAID IT'S PROBABLY REFLUX but he's not keeping anything down.' → 'that sounds frightening, AND YOU'VE DONE THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM IN.' (She has handed you 'reflux' — TAKE IT AS A HIDDEN AGENDA TO ADDRESS LATER, NOT AS THE DIAGNOSIS.)

THE VOMIT: 'how many times a day? EVERY FEED? Getting worse? WHAT COLOUR — MILKY, YELLOW, GREEN — ANY BLOOD? How much — a mouthful, or the whole feed? DOES IT COME OUT WITH FORCE, UNDER PRESSURE? How soon after the feed? Does lying him down or his position change it?' (Do not accept 'a small amount' as reassurance, and DO NOT SKIP FORCE BECAUSE SHE SAID REFLUX.)

The hungry question — the one that separates it from reflux: 'After he vomits, is he still hungry? Does he take another full feed?' → 'He's starving.' then: 'Have you ever felt a lump in his tummy, or seen a rippling movement across it after a feed?'

THE GI BLOCK: last bowel motion, wind, diarrhoea, BLOOD IN THE NAPPY, distension; ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN WHEN HE CRIES; SCREAMING EPISODES WITH LEGS DRAWN UP, GOING PALE, RED-JELLY STOOL; then the GORD block — refuses feeds, ARCHES HIS BACK, laid flat after feeds, burping; AND IS HE GAINING WEIGHT? → he had STOPPED GAINING at the last weigh.

INFECTION, WELL-BABY AND NEURO: fever, contacts, travel, cough, runny nose, DROOLING, crying on weeing or smelly urine, rash; ALERT OR DROWSY; feeding as usual; HOW MANY WET NAPPIES TODAY → 'ONLY THREE — USUALLY SIX OR SEVEN' → SAY IT OUT LOUD: 'THAT'S FEWER THAN I'D LIKE — IT TELLS ME HE'S GETTING DRY.' Then falls or knocks to the head, and who else looks after him.

BIRTH AND FAMILY — AND LEAVE TWENTY SECONDS FOR THE LAST QUESTION, WHICH IS THE FINAL MARK: pregnancy complications, medicines, alcohol, smoking; delivery; FIRST BOWEL MOTION, HEEL-PRICK, JAUNDICE; breast or formula and how much; antibiotics; AND 'ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WHO VOMITED A LOT AS A BABY OR HAD A TUMMY OPERATION AS A BABY?' → THE BROTHER. Then: 'is there anything you're particularly worried about?' → 'IS IT MY FORMULA? IS IT REFLUX LIKE THEY SAID? WILL HE NEED SURGERY?'

THE EXAMINATION, AND YOU MUST ASK FOR THE MASS: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, DEHYDRATION, rash, jaundice? Vital signs? Throat and ears? Chest — air entry, added sounds? ABDOMEN: DISTENSION, SCARS, VISIBLE PERISTALSIS? ON PALPATION — ANY MASS, WHERE, TENDERNESS, GUARDING? Bowel sounds? GROIN AND SCROTUM? Urine dipstick and glucose?' — and INTERPRET THE DEHYDRATION ALOUD as about five per cent.
NAME IT, THE GATEWAY EXPLANATION, THEN THE FOUR REASONS (see dx) → 'WHY DO YOU THINK IT'S THAT AND NOT REFLUX?' → the four reasons plus the family history.
THE TWO ANSWERS SHE NEEDS AND THE DIFFERENTIALS (see dx) → 'DID I CAUSE IT WITH THE FORMULA?' → 'NO. Nothing you've done caused this.' Then the six differentials, each dismissed against the findings.

MANAGEMENT IN ORDER AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx) → 'WILL HE NEED AN OPERATION?' → yes, curative, feeds within hours, home in a day or two — BUT NOT TONIGHT, AND SAY WHY. Then summarise. (She becomes tearful at the word OPERATION and settles once you say it is curative and not tonight.)

Everything else: stool this morning, wind yes, no fever, rash, cough or contacts, ALERT BUT ONLY THREE WET NAPPIES TODAY, no falls, no groin lump, no screaming episodes. back.dx: VERSION A — gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. 'In babies, the gateway at the bottom of the food pipe is immature and doesn't close properly, so some of the stomach contents come back up and he brings up his milk — that's reflux. When it starts to cause problems — inflammation in the food pipe, arching and distress, and most importantly trouble gaining weight, which his chart shows — we call it reflux disease.' Version B — physiological GOR: 'The good news is this is reflux — physiological reflux — not a disease. I'm confident because it's only milk, it's effortless, it's always after feeds, and most importantly he's happy, well hydrated and growing beautifully on his chart. It settles as the gateway matures — most babies by their first birthday.' The differentials, long and specific in both versions: cow's milk protein allergy; a narrowing at the stomach outlet — pyloric stenosis; a bowel blockage or hernia; infections including a urine infection; a metabolic condition; and pressure inside the head — 'Nothing points to those.' Management, four things, and education comes before any drug: one — positioning: 'After each feed hold him upright against your shoulder for twenty to thirty minutes and burp him before you lie him down; he still sleeps flat on his back.' Two — thickening: 'Express some milk and add a feed thickener from the pharmacy; keep breastfeeding, there's no need for a special formula.' Three — smaller feeds more often, with a lactation consultant or child health nurse review of how he feeds. Four — red flags: 'If he starts refusing feeds, arching and screaming, stops gaining weight, or the vomit is ever green or has blood in it, or he's feverish or drowsy, come straight back.' Review in two weeks with a weight. In version A only, the drug comes after the education in the same breath: 'First we change how we feed him, and I'll also start a four-week trial of an acid-suppressing medicine, omeprazole, to let the food pipe heal' — plus referral to the paediatrician and consideration of cow's milk protein in the mother's diet. 'It's safe as a short course; we avoid long-term use because of side effects, which is why the feeding changes come first.' In version B, when she pushes for medicine: 'I understand why you'd want that. Medicine doesn't fix an immature gateway and has side effects, so for a baby who's growing well we don't use it. The feeding changes work — and if he ever stops gaining or starts refusing feeds, I'll see him straight away and refer him to the paediatrician, and we'd talk about medication then.' The other variants: blood or mucus in the stool with eczema — 'This makes me think of an allergy to cow's milk protein, which can come through breast milk. Cut all dairy from your diet for two weeks and we'll see whether the vomiting and the stools settle; then we reintroduce it to check' — with a paediatrician and dietitian to keep her diet safe. A 2-month-old with forceful vomiting — ask 'Is it projectile? Is he hungry straight after? Losing weight?' and if the examiner gives an olive and visible peristalsis, it is pyloric stenosis and he goes to the women's and children's today. Green vomit on a reflux background — 'Green means bile, which means a blockage until proven otherwise — this is not his reflux', emergency department now, ring ahead, MedSTAR kids. Head circumference crossing upward — ask about a bulging fontanelle and prominent scalp veins, and arrange an urgent scan and paediatric review today.
plan: VITALS, THEN THE EMPATHY STATEMENT — A MARKED BOX, DONE ONCE AND PROPERLY: 'Examiner, the vital signs please.' Then: 'tell me what's been going on.' → 'he's been vomiting for two months. I'VE SEEN THREE DOCTORS AND THEY ALL SAY IT'S NOTHING. I'm exhausted and I'M SICK OF BEING TOLD IT'S NOTHING SERIOUS.' → 'I'M REALLY SORRY YOU'VE HAD THAT EXPERIENCE. Two months of this is exhausting, and IT'S ABSOLUTELY RIGHT TO WANT IT LOOKED AT PROPERLY. Let's go through it carefully together.' (Launching into 'how many times?' costs the communication mark — and if you never acknowledge it, SHE CUTS IN AT MINUTE TWO WITH 'YOU'RE JUST LIKE THE OTHERS'. Do it once, then move on.)

THE VOMIT: how long, how many a day, most days, worse; WHAT COLOUR, ANY BLOOD, IS IT JUST THE MILK HE'S HAD; how much; DOES IT SHOOT OUT WITH FORCE; smell; better or worse; ANY POSITION; related to feeds or food. (You now know it is reflux — THE MARK IS IN CONTINUING THE STRUCTURE ANYWAY.)

The GI bucket and the reflux block: last bowel motion, wind, diarrhoea, blood or mucus in the nappy, bloated. Then: 'Does it always happen after a feed? Do you lie him down straight after feeding? Do you burp him? Does he arch his back? Does he refuse feeds? Is he gaining weight as expected on his growth chart? Does he sleep well? How much and how often is he feeding?' (Ask the growth question in those words — 'Any concerns about his growth?' Gets 'Not really'.)
The three exclusions: 'Any lump in the groin? Screaming episodes — does he go pale? Ever a forceful, projectile vomit?'

INFECTION, WELL-BABY, NEURO, ALLERGY, BIRTH AND IMMUNISATION, run fast: fever, travel, contacts, coryza, cough, DROOLING, ear-pulling, crying with nappy changes, smelly urine, rash; alert or drowsy, drinking, WET NAPPIES; falls or head knocks; how are things at home; solids started, RASH ROUND THE MOUTH WITH A FOOD; pregnancy and birth, HEEL-PRICK, FIRST POO, immunisations.

THE EXAMINATION, WITH THE CHART REQUESTED BY NAME: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? Dehydration? Rash? COULD I SEE HIS GROWTH CHART — WEIGHT, LENGTH AND HEAD CIRCUMFERENCE? ENT: throat, drums? Chest: air entry, added sounds? Abdomen: distension or visible mass, then mass, tenderness, rigidity or organomegaly, and bowel sounds. INGUINAL REGION — ANY LUMP? FONTANELLE — BULGING? AND A URINE DIPSTICK.' THEN READ THE TREND ALOUD: 'his weight HAS CROSSED TWO CENTILE LINES DOWNWARD while his head and length are tracking — THAT IS FALTERING GROWTH' or 'weight, length and head circumference are ALL TRACKING NORMALLY.'
The label with its reason, the gateway explanation, and the long specific differential list (see dx) → 'So it is something. Why did nobody say?' / 'Is it serious?'

MANAGEMENT — EDUCATION FIRST, ALWAYS (see dx): positioning with the twenty to thirty minutes upright and STILL FLAT ON HIS BACK TO SLEEP; thickening with breastfeeding continued; smaller feeds more often with a lactation review; then in Version A only, THE FOUR-WEEK OMEPRAZOLE TRIAL IN THE SAME BREATH AS THE FEEDING CHANGES, plus paediatrician referral. → 'CAN'T YOU GIVE HIM SOMETHING TO STOP IT?' / 'SHOULD I STOP BREASTFEEDING AND TRY A SPECIAL FORMULA?'

RED FLAGS AND REVIEW: refusing feeds, arching and screaming, stopping gaining, GREEN OR BLOODY VOMIT, fever or drowsiness — and REVIEW IN TWO WEEKS WITH A WEIGHT. Then check the plan feels right to her.

pefe: Role-player: JANE, 31, a teacher on maternity leave in Wallaroo. Her son is 6 MONTHS (Version A) or 4 MONTHS (Version B), her first, EXCLUSIVELY BREASTFED, NO SOLIDS. He has brought up milk TWO OR THREE TIMES A DAY, MOST DAYS, FOR TWO MONTHS — whitish, JUST MILK, a mouthful or two, NEVER FORCEFUL, NEVER GREEN, NO BLOOD. IT ALWAYS HAPPENS AFTER A FEED, ESPECIALLY WHEN YOU LAY HIM STRAIGHT IN THE COT; YOU DON'T REALLY BURP HIM. Feeds are TWO-HOURLY AND LONG. Bowels normal, no blood or mucus. No groin lump, no screaming fits, no pallor. No fever, cold, cough, ear-pulling, nappy-change crying, rash. Alert, drinking, six or seven wet nappies. No falls; HOME IS FINE BUT YOU ARE EXHAUSTED. Normal pregnancy, term, heel prick normal, meconium day one, immunised.

Version A only: he sometimes arches and cries after feeds, wakes often, and the child health nurse said he has 'Slipped down the chart'. Version B: no arching, sleeps well, the nurse is happy with his weight. Register: frustrated, near tears at the start — you have seen three doctors. You soften only if the doctor acknowledges this before asking questions; if they don't, stay clipped and say 'That's what the last doctor asked' once — and cut in at minute two with 'You're just like the others'. Hidden agenda: you fear something is being missed and want to know if it's serious — volunteer it at the diagnosis if never asked. In version B, push for medicine once and be satisfied by a reasoned answer.

back.dx: VERSION A — FEBRILE URINARY TRACT INFECTION in a 9-month-old. GIVE IT WITH THREE REASONS: 'most likely David has A URINARY TRACT INFECTION — AN INFECTION IN THE BLADDER AND THE URINARY TUBES. I'm saying that because HE HAS A FEVER AND VOMITING, WHICH TELL ME THERE'S AN INFECTION; HE CRIES WHEN YOU CHANGE HIS NAPPY AND HIS URINE SMELLS STRONG; and WHEN I EXAMINED HIM I COULDN'T FIND ANOTHER SOURCE — HIS THROAT, EARS AND CHEST ARE CLEAR — BUT THE URINE TEST SHOWS SIGNS OF INFECTION.' THEN A FIVE-SECOND DIFFERENTIAL LIST: a blockage in the bowel, reflux, a hernia, a tummy bug, other infections — throat, ears, chest — AND A SERIOUS BLOOD INFECTION — 'none of those fit.' DO NOT SAY CYSTITIS OR PYELONEPHRITIS: THEY ARE NOT SEPARABLE CLINICALLY IN INFANTS, AND A FEBRILE INFANT UTI IS TREATED AS UPPER TRACT. TASK 4, AND THE FIRST WORDS MATTER: 'TO CONFIRM IT I NEED TO SEND A URINE SAMPLE FOR MICROSCOPY, CULTURE AND SENSITIVITY. We'll collect it BY CLEAN CATCH — clean his genitals and catch the urine in a sterile jar as it comes. THE MOST RELIABLE WAY, WHICH WE USE IF A BABY IS UNWELL OR IN HOSPITAL, IS A SUPRAPUBIC ASPIRATE — drawing urine directly from the bladder with a fine needle — OR A SMALL CATHETER.' ANY ANSWER THAT STARTS WITH 'FBE, CRP, ULTRASOUND' HAS SPENT THE MARK. THEN: oral antibiotics for SEVEN DAYS once the sample is taken, small frequent fluids, KEEP BREASTFEEDING, and REVIEW IN 48 HOURS WITH THE RESULT. 'HE DOESN'T NEED AN ULTRASOUND FOR A FIRST INFECTION unless it's severe, doesn't respond in two days, or comes back.' SAFETY-NET: come straight back or call 000 if he becomes DROWSY, WON'T DRINK, HAS NO WET NAPPY FOR SIX HOURS, GETS A RASH, OR KEEPS VOMITING THE MEDICINE. VERSION B — VIRAL PHARYNGITIS: 'most likely he has PHARYNGITIS — an infection in the throat. He has fever, he's vomiting, YOU TOLD ME HE'S DROOLING, and when I examined him HIS THROAT IS RED.' Then the same broad differential list — bowel obstruction such as intussusception or a hernia, reflux, gastroenteritis, pneumonia, middle-ear infection, urine infection, SEPSIS, and problems in the head. 'URTI' IS NOT SPECIFIC ENOUGH WHEN YOU HAVE BEEN HANDED A RED PHARYNX. AND WHEN DROOLING IS REVEALED, CLEAR THE AIRWAY FIRST: 'is he BREATHING NOISILY OR WORKING HARD TO BREATHE? CAN HE SWALLOW HIS SALIVA? IS HE SITTING FORWARD OR HOLDING HIS NECK STILL?' — 'good, that fits A SORE THROAT RATHER THAN ANYTHING BLOCKING HIS AIRWAY.' MANAGEMENT, FOUR THINGS: PARACETAMOL, and ibuprofen with food if he's drinking well; ONDANSETRON — A WAFER THAT MELTS UNDER THE TONGUE — as a SINGLE DOSE; PUSH FLUIDS in small sips, Hydralyte or Gastrolyte, icy poles fine; and RED FLAGS — if he keeps vomiting, the fever climbs, he becomes DROWSY, has TROUBLE BREATHING OR SWALLOWING, or gets A RASH, come straight to hospital. NO BLOOD TESTS. Home from childcare until well. STARTING WITH 'I WOULD DO SOME BLOOD TESTS' FAILS A VIRAL PHARYNGITIS. THE OTHER VARIANTS: A CLEAR OTHER FOCUS — exudative tonsils or a red drum — means 'BECAUSE I'VE FOUND THE SOURCE OF THE FEVER, I DON'T NEED TO COLLECT URINE TODAY; if the fever hasn't settled in 48 hours we'll re-look and test the urine.' AN INFANT UNDER 3 MONTHS WITH A FEBRILE UTI: 'AT THIS AGE A URINE INFECTION CAN SPREAD TO THE BLOOD, so he needs HOSPITAL FOR INTRAVENOUS ANTIBIOTICS and a full check including A SUPRAPUBIC SAMPLE AND AN ULTRASOUND' — call the Women's and Children's and MedSTAR Kids. MODERATE DEHYDRATION OR NOT TOLERATING ORAL: nasogastric or intravenous fluids and IV antibiotics until he keeps them down. RECURRENT UTI: a KIDNEY ULTRASOUND — not urgent — and a paediatrician referral; PREVENTIVE ANTIBIOTICS ARE NOT ROUTINE.
plan: VITALS AT THE DOOR, THEN ONE OPEN QUESTION AND THE CONCERN STATEMENT: 'Examiner, before I begin, could I have the vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate and temperature?' Then: 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'he's been vomiting for two days and he's really hot. I'M WORRIED, DOCTOR.' → 'I can see how worrying this is. Let's work through it together — I'll ask some specific questions and then we'll examine him.' (Asking three open questions in a row is the trap — THE ROLE-PLAYER ANSWERS ONE, THEN WAITS FOR SPECIFICS.)

THE VOMIT AND THE FEVER: when it started, how many times since, on and off or continuous, getting worse, WHAT COLOUR, ANY BLOOD, large or small, IS IT FORCEFUL, any foul smell, anything better or worse, any position, related to feeds or a food. Then: 'HAVE YOU MEASURED THE FEVER? GIVEN ANYTHING? DOES IT WORK?'
THE GI BUCKET: last bowel motion, passing wind, DIARRHOEA, BLOOD IN THE STOOL, bloated tummy, ANY LUMP IN THE GROIN, ANY EPISODES OF SCREAMING.

Every infection — and two questions here are the diagnosis: travel; sick contacts; runny nose, drooling, cough; pulling at his ears; 'Does he cry or seem irritable when you change his nappy or he passes urine? Does the urine smell unusual?'; any rash. → 'He screams every time I change his nappy' and 'It does smell strong.' (The cousin's cold or the brother's tummy bug is bait — no diarrhoea plus nappy-change crying keeps you on UTI.)

WELL-BABY, NEURO AND BINDSMA: alert or drowsy, drinking as usual, FEWER WET NAPPIES, falls or knocks to the head, how are things at home, immunisations, gaining weight as expected. → SLEEPIER, A BIT FLOPPY, DRINKING LESS, TWO FEWER AND DARKER NAPPIES.

THE EXAMINATION, HEADLINED, WITH DEHYDRATION FIRST AND THE DIPSTICK REQUESTED WITHOUT DEBATE: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy? ANY SIGN OF DEHYDRATION — capillary refill, mucous membranes, skin turgor, sunken eyes? Any rash? ENT — throat red, any exudate, tympanic membranes red or bulging? Respiratory — air entry equal, added sounds? Abdomen — distension or visible mass, then mass, tenderness or rigidity, and bowel sounds. INGUINAL REGION — ANY LUMP OR SWELLING? A URINE DIPSTICK PLEASE — AND IS THE ANTERIOR FONTANELLE BULGING?' (Do NOT ask for cervical nodes, hepatosplenomegaly or a full neurological examination — there is no time and no marks.)

The diagnosis with three reasons, then the five-second differential list (see dx) → 'A urine infection? He doesn't seem to have trouble weeing.' / 'Could it be meningitis?' if you never asked what worries her.

TASK 4 IN ONE SENTENCE, STARTING WITH THE RIGHT WORDS: 'TO CONFIRM IT I NEED TO SEND A URINE SAMPLE FOR MICROSCOPY, CULTURE AND SENSITIVITY' — then clean catch, and the suprapubic aspirate or catheter as the reliable method in an unwell baby. Then oral antibiotics for seven days, fluids, KEEP BREASTFEEDING, review at 48 hours, and no ultrasound for a first infection. → 'DOES HE NEED A SCAN OF HIS KIDNEYS?'
THE SAFETY-NET AND CLOSE: drowsy, won't drink, NO WET NAPPY FOR SIX HOURS, a rash, or vomiting the medicine — come back or call 000. Then invite questions.

Register: anxious, tired; you settle once the doctor explains a plan. Hidden agenda: you are worried it is meningitis because a friend's baby had it — volunteer this at the diagnosis only if the doctor never asks what you are worried about. Become tearful if the doctor lists differentials without reassurance. Push once: 'Shouldn't he have a scan?' and ask 'How do you get wee from a baby?'

setting: History, examination request, x-ray explanation and management — postnatal ward. back.dx: OESOPHAGEAL ATRESIA WITH A TRACHEO-OESOPHAGEAL FISTULA. EXPLAIN THE FILM BY DESCRIBING BEFORE NAMING: 'three colours: WHITE IS BONE — her ribs and spine; GREY IS SOFT TISSUE — her heart is this shadow; BLACK IS AIR, in her lungs. You saw us pass a thin tube through her nose. IT WAS SUPPOSED TO GO DOWN HER FOOD PIPE INTO HER STOMACH. ON THE X-RAY IT HASN'T GONE THROUGH — IT HAS CURLED UP AT THE TOP OF HER CHEST. That tells me HER FOOD PIPE HASN'T FORMED PROPERLY: IT COMES TO A BLIND END, so nothing she swallows can get down, AND IT SPILLS INTO HER WINDPIPE — which is why she splutters and goes dusky. AND THERE IS AIR IN HER TUMMY HERE; THE ONLY WAY IT CAN GET THERE IS THROUGH A SMALL CONNECTION BETWEEN HER WINDPIPE AND THE LOWER FOOD PIPE.' To the examiner, the same finding is 'COILED IN THE UPPER POUCH AT T2-T4 WITH GAS BELOW THE DIAPHRAGM'. THEN NAME IT WITH FOUR REASONS: 'OESOPHAGEAL ATRESIA — THE FOOD PIPE HASN'T JOINED UP — and in most babies it comes with a connection to the windpipe, which THE AIR IN HER TUMMY tells me she has. I think this because SHE'S BEEN FROTHY AND CHOKING WITH FEEDS SINCE BIRTH, SHE WENT DUSKY WITH A FEED, YOU HAD TOO MUCH FLUID AND A SMALL STOMACH ON THE SCANS, AND THE TUBE COULDN'T PASS.' AND LINK THE POLYHYDRAMNIOS ALOUD WHEN SHE GIVES IT: 'IF THE FOOD PIPE IS BLOCKED THE BABY CAN'T SWALLOW THE FLUID, SO IT BUILDS UP, AND THE STOMACH STAYS SMALL.' DIFFERENTIALS, EACH DISMISSED: A LARYNGEAL CLEFT letting milk into the windpipe — but THE TUBE WOULD HAVE PASSED; CHOANAL ATRESIA — but THE TUBE WENT THROUGH HER NOSE; A HEART PROBLEM, which can go with this — no murmur, BUT SHE WILL HAVE A HEART SCAN; ASPIRATION PNEUMONIA, which she may already have; and SEPSIS — the swab was negative and she is alert. A BLOCKAGE LOWER IN THE BOWEL WOULD GIVE GREEN VOMITING, AND HERS ISN'T. MANAGEMENT, AND THE FOUR SPECIFICS ARE THE MARK: NO FEEDS, so nothing more goes into her lungs; A SPECIAL SUCTION TUBE — A REPLOGLE — SITTING IN THE TOP OF THE FOOD PIPE ON CONTINUOUS LOW SUCTION TO KEEP THE SALIVA CLEARED; NURSE HER HEAD UP AT 30 TO 45 DEGREES; AND THE CHILDREN'S SURGEONS. Plus A DRIP for fluids and sugar; ANTIBIOTICS for the milk already in her lungs; AND THE ASSOCIATED-ANOMALY SCREEN — A HEART SCAN, A KIDNEY SCAN AND SPINE X-RAYS, 'BECAUSE THESE CAN GO TOGETHER'. Transfer to the Women's and Children's with the retrieval team, THE MOTHER GOING WITH HER, AND 'MOST BABIES DO VERY WELL'. If pushed, ADD 'NO BAG-MASK OR CPAP IF WE CAN AVOID IT', because it inflates the stomach through the fistula. AND ANSWER HER TWO QUESTIONS: 'IT'S NOT YOUR MILK — THIS FORMED IN THE FIRST WEEKS OF PREGNANCY' and 'YOU DIDN'T DO ANYTHING'. VERSION B — A GASLESS ABDOMEN: 'a gasless abdomen with a coiled tube means THERE IS NO CONNECTION BETWEEN THE AIRWAY AND THE LOWER OESOPHAGUS — A PURE OESOPHAGEAL ATRESIA, TYPE A. That usually means A LONG GAP between the two ends, so the surgeons MAY NOT BE ABLE TO JOIN THEM STRAIGHT AWAY: she'd have A FEEDING TUBE PLACED DIRECTLY INTO THE STOMACH AND A STAGED REPAIR over weeks to months, with the suction tube and head-up nursing continuing meanwhile. THE IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT IS OTHERWISE THE SAME.' VERSION C — THE ASSOCIATIONS VIVA: 'THE VACTERL ASSOCIATION — VERTEBRAL anomalies on a spine film, ANORECTAL malformation on inspection, CARDIAC defects AND THE SIDE OF THE AORTIC ARCH on echocardiogram, RENAL anomalies on ultrasound, and RADIAL OR LIMB anomalies on examination; plus a chromosomal check if she's dysmorphic. AROUND HALF OF THESE BABIES HAVE AT LEAST ONE, AND THE ECHO CHANGES THE OPERATIVE SIDE' — say ECHO BEFORE THEATRE and RIGHT-SIDED ARCH, which are the two details examiners reward.

THE VOMIT: every feed and between, getting worse; MILKY, FROTHY, YELLOW, GREEN, ANY BLOOD; the whole feed, how soon, forceful; WORSE LYING FLAT. → milky and frothy LIKE BUBBLES, never green, the whole feed WITHIN SECONDS, not forceful.

The four TOF questions — and they are the diagnosis: 'Does she cough or choke when she feeds? Is she frothy or bubbly at the mouth — drooling a lot? Is her breathing noisy or fast? Has she gone blue or dusky?' → yes, yes, yes, and dusky with the first feed. Then say it immediately, mid-history: 'That's important — I'm going to ask that she has no more feeds until we've checked her food pipe.'

THE BOWEL BLOCK AND FEEDING: 'has she PASSED HER FIRST BOWEL MOTION? Passing wind? Any blood? IS HER TUMMY SWOLLEN? Any lump or movement? IS SHE ATTACHING AND SUCKING, OR REFUSING — WAS A BOTTLE TRIED? Any groin swelling?' → meconium passed, tummy A BIT ROUND, and SHE SUCKS A FEW TIMES THEN CHOKES, bottle the same.

THE NEONATAL INFECTION SET — and the maternal questions are what make it neonatal: fever or cold to touch, rash, alert or drowsy, wet nappies; 'ANY INFECTIONS OR COMPLICATIONS IN THE PREGNANCY? ANY RASHES OR SORES ON YOUR PRIVATE PARTS BEFORE DELIVERY? THE SWAB TEST AT 36 WEEKS — WHAT WAS THE RESULT?' → GBS NEGATIVE.

NEURO, DELIVERY, AND THE ANTENATAL QUESTION THAT HANDS YOU THE ANSWER: 'any swelling or redness on her head? Was the delivery long or complicated — FORCEPS OR VACUUM?' Then: 'high blood pressure or sugar? Medicines, alcohol, smoking? ON THE SCANS, WERE YOU TOLD THERE WAS TOO MUCH FLUID — OR ANYTHING ABOUT HER STOMACH?' → 'YES — TOO MUCH FLUID FROM 30 WEEKS, AND AT ONE SCAN THEY COULDN'T SEE THE STOMACH PROPERLY.' → LINK IT ALOUD: 'IF THE FOOD PIPE IS BLOCKED THE BABY CAN'T SWALLOW THE FLUID, SO IT BUILDS UP, AND THE STOMACH STAYS SMALL.' Then heel prick, family history, and 'anything you're particularly worried about?' → 'CAN I TRY FEEDING HER AGAIN? IS IT MY MILK?'

THE EXAMINATION, ENDING WITH THE TUBE: 'general appearance — alert, SECRETIONS AT THE MOUTH OR NOSE, colour, dehydration, rash? Vitals and saturations? Respiratory — work of breathing, STRIDOR, air entry, CRACKLES? Abdomen — DISTENDED OR SCAPHOID, mass, tenderness, bowel sounds? Groin? IS THE ANUS PATENT? Scalp and fontanelle? SPINE, LIMBS AND THUMBS, ANY MURMUR — A VACTERL SCREEN? AND MAY I PASS A NASOGASTRIC TUBE?' → 'THE TUBE STOPS AT ABOUT 10 cm. HERE IS THE X-RAY.'
THE X-RAY, DESCRIBED BEFORE IT IS NAMED (see dx) — three colours, the tube curled at the top of the chest, the blind end, the spill into the windpipe, and THE AIR IN THE TUMMY MEANING A CONNECTION.
Name it with four reasons, then the differentials each dismissed (see dx) → 'What is it called? Did I do something?' → 'You didn't do anything; this forms in the first weeks of pregnancy.'

Management — no feeds, suction tube, head up, surgeon — plus drip, antibiotics, and the heart, kidney and spine screen (see dx), then transfer with the retrieval team, the mother going too, 'Most babies do very well', and a summary. → 'Does she need surgery?' / 'Is something wrong with her heart?'

pefe: Role-player: JENNY, 27, first baby, cafe manager. EIGHT HOURS POST-PARTUM, EXHAUSTED, TEARFUL, HOLDING THE BABY; partner has gone to move the car. THE MIDWIFE TOLD YOU SHE WAS 'JUST A MUCOUSY BABY' AND YOU HALF BELIEVE IT — QUOTE THAT LINE EARLY. PREGNANCY: POLYHYDRAMNIOS FROM 30 WEEKS, and at one scan 'THEY COULDN'T SEE THE STOMACH PROPERLY' and they said they'd look again — REVEAL ONLY IF ASKED ABOUT FLUID OR SCANS. No infections, no genital sores, GBS SWAB NEGATIVE, no blood pressure or sugar problems, no medicines, alcohol or smoking. Normal vaginal delivery, five hours, no instruments, term, 3.2 kg.

THE 'VOMITING': since birth, CONSTANT FROTHY, BUBBLY MILKY STUFF FROM MOUTH AND NOSE, even between feeds; the whole feed comes back WITHIN SECONDS; not forceful; NEVER GREEN; no blood; WORSE LYING FLAT. COUGHS AND SPLUTTERS WITH EVERY FEED. DRIBBLY AND BUBBLY ALL THE TIME. NOISY, FAST BREATHING. WENT DUSKY AROUND THE MOUTH ONCE WITH THE FIRST FEED. FEEDING: attaches, SUCKS A FEW TIMES, THEN CHOKES — the midwife tried a bottle and it was the same, AND YOU WANT TO TRY AGAIN. Small sticky MECONIUM passed, wind yes, no blood, TUMMY A BIT ROUND, no groin swelling, no fever or rash, alert, ONE WET NAPPY, no head swelling, heel prick not done, no family history.

HIDDEN AGENDA: 'CAN I TRY FEEDING HER AGAIN? IS IT MY MILK?' — volunteer at three and a half minutes if not asked. After the diagnosis, if scans are mentioned: 'IS SOMETHING WRONG WITH HER HEART?' HOW TO PLAY IT: quote the midwife's 'mucousy' line early; BECOME TEARFUL AT 'OPERATION' and settle if told most babies do well and that you can go with her; PUSH ONCE: 'DID I DO SOMETHING?' Mark them on: vitals INCLUDING SATURATIONS; colour asked and NON-BILIOUS established; COUGH AND CHOKE, DROOL, NOISY BREATHING AND DUSKY; STOPPED FEEDS DURING THE HISTORY; meconium, wind, distension; feeding, attachment and groin; fever, rash, alert and nappies; MATERNAL INFECTIONS, SORES AND THE SWAB; scalp swelling and delivery; POLYHYDRAMNIOS AND THE STOMACH ON THE SCAN; examination covering secretions, chest, abdomen, ANUS, VACTERL AND PASSING THE TUBE; the X-RAY WITH COLOURS, THE CURLED TUBE, THE BLIND END AND GAS MEANING FISTULA; NAMED OESOPHAGEAL ATRESIA WITH FISTULA AND THREE OR MORE REASONS; differentials including heart, aspiration and sepsis; MANAGEMENT — NO FEEDS, SUCTION TUBE, HEAD UP, DRIP, SCANS, SURGEON, TRANSFER; answered 'my milk' and 'did I do something'; and safety-netted.

Gas in the abdomen = fistula; a gasless abdomen = pure atresia with a long gap · Replogle tube on continuous low suction · head up 30-45 degrees · avoid bag-mask and CPAP if possible · echo before theatre, and look for a right-sided aortic arch · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33

back.dx: Duodenal atresia. Explain the film first, pointing at both circles and without saying 'Atresia' yet: 'Three colours: white is bone — the spine; grey is soft tissue; black is air, which is what matters. What I can see is two black circles — here, and here. That's air trapped in the stomach and in the very first part of the bowel. We call it the double bubble sign, and it is a sign of a blockage in the first part of the small bowel, the duodenum. There's no air beyond it, so the block is complete.' then name it: 'Duodenal atresia — the duodenum hasn't formed properly before birth, so there's a narrowing and a block, and nothing can get past it.' Four reasons: 'He's been vomiting since his first day and the vomit is green — bile — which means the block is below the stomach; his tummy is flat, not swollen, which fits a block high up; you had extra fluid in the pregnancy, which happens when the baby can't swallow the fluid because the bowel is blocked; and the x-ray shows the two bubbles.' The differentials, with volvulus named first as the one that cannot wait: 'A twist of the bowel — that's the one we must rule out quickly, because it can cut off the blood supply; a block further down the small bowel; hirschsprung disease, where the nerves at the end of the bowel are missing; meconium ileus — very thick first stool blocking the bowel, which can be a sign of cystic fibrosis; an imperforate anus — I've checked and his is normal; oesophageal atresia — but he isn't drooling or choking; sepsis, though your swab was negative and he's alert; and intracranial bleeding from the birth, unlikely after a normal delivery.' then answer her three questions honestly: 'Some babies with this blockage do have down syndrome — I haven't seen any signs, and the surgical team will check his heart and do a chromosome test to be sure.' 'Nothing you did caused it; it happens in the first weeks of the pregnancy.' 'Yes — this is fixed with an operation, and babies do very well after it.' Management, in order: stop the feeds; a nasogastric tube to let out the air and fluid, which stops the vomiting; a drip for fluids and sugar; bloods — salts and a blood gas; and the surgical team now. Add, if there is time, that the surgeons will check his heart and, if needed, do a dye test to make sure there's no twist. In a country hospital, transfer to the women's and children's with the mother going too. Safety-net: tell the nurse straight away if he becomes floppy, cold, or his tummy swells or looks sore. Variant — distal gas beyond the bubbles: 'Yes, that changes things. Gas beyond the duodenum means the obstruction is incomplete — a duodenal stenosis or web — or that this is malrotation with volvulus, which is a surgical emergency. I'd ask for an urgent upper GI contrast study to look for the position of the duodeno-jejunal flexure and a corkscrew sign, and I'd speak to the paediatric surgeon immediately rather than waiting for a planned repair.' Double bubble does not equal atresia if there is distal gas — say the word volvulus. Variant — the sibling with hirschsprung: 'That's very important — hirschsprung disease can run in families, so I'll make sure the surgical team knows. In hirschsprung the tummy is usually swollen and the first bowel motion is late — has he passed meconium? Whichever it turns out to be, the first steps are the same: no feeds, a tube, a drip, and the surgeons.' Do not change the diagnosis to match the sibling — add it to the differential and let the film decide.

The neonatal bowel block — four questions: 'Has he passed his first bowel motion — the meconium? Is he passing wind? What did the meconium look like — any blood? Is his tummy swollen?' → a sticky black poo this morning, wind yes, and the tummy looks a bit flat.

THE MALFORMATION QUESTIONS: any lump or movement across his tummy; DOES HE COUGH OR CHOKE WITH FEEDS, IS HE DROOLING A LOT, ANY NOISY OR DIFFICULT BREATHING; is he feeding normally or refusing, were you shown how to attach and burp him; ANY SWELLING IN THE GROIN?

The neonatal infection set — and it is maternal: 'Any fever, or has he been cold to touch? Any rash? Is he alert or drowsy? Wet nappies? Did you have any infections or complications during the pregnancy? Any rashes or sores on your private parts before or around the delivery? Did you have the swab test at 36 weeks — from the vagina and back passage — and what was the result?' (Travel, contacts and runny nose are the wrong questions here — the infection comes from the mother.)

NEURO, DELIVERY AND THE ANTENATAL MARK: 'any swelling or redness on his head? Was the delivery long or complicated — FORCEPS OR A VACUUM CUP? Any high blood pressure or sugar problems? Medicines, alcohol, drugs, smoking? ON YOUR SCANS, WERE YOU EVER TOLD THERE WAS TOO MUCH FLUID AROUND THE BABY?' → 'YES — AT THE 32-WEEK SCAN.' → LINK IT ALOUD: 'BABIES WHO CAN'T SWALLOW THE FLUID BECAUSE THE BOWEL IS BLOCKED CAUSE EXTRA FLUID.' Then heel prick and FAMILY HISTORY OF NEWBORN VOMITING OR A BOWEL OPERATION. Then: 'is there anything you're particularly worried about?' → 'IS IT MY MILK? SHOULD I KEEP FEEDING HIM?' → 'PLEASE STOP FEEDING HIM FOR NOW — I'LL EXPLAIN WHY. IT'S NOT YOUR MILK.'

THE EXAMINATION: 'general appearance — alert, dehydration, rash, jaundice? Chest? ABDOMEN — DISTENDED OR SUNKEN, visible loops or mass? On palpation — mass, tenderness? Bowel sounds? Groin? IS THE ANUS PATENT? Scalp swelling, fontanelle? ANY FEATURES OF DOWN SYNDROME, ANY MURMUR?' → SCAPHOID abdomen, anus patent, no dysmorphism, no murmur — and the X-ray is handed over.
The x-ray — point to both circles, say 'Double bubble' once, and do not say atresia yet (see dx).

NAME IT WITH FOUR REASONS, THEN THE DIFFERENTIALS WITH VOLVULUS FIRST (see dx) → 'DID I DO SOMETHING?' → no, this happens in the first weeks of pregnancy. → 'DOES HE HAVE DOWN SYNDROME?' → some babies with this blockage do; no signs seen, and the team will check his heart and do a chromosome test.

MANAGEMENT IN ORDER AND THE SAFETY-NET (see dx): STOP FEEDS, NASOGASTRIC TUBE, DRIP, BLOODS, SURGEONS — then transfer with the mother, and 'if he becomes floppy, cold, or his tummy swells or looks sore, tell the nurse straight away.' Then summarise.

No infections, NO GENITAL SORES, GBS SWAB AT 36 WEEKS NEGATIVE, no blood pressure or sugar problems, no medicines, alcohol or smoking. back.dx: NEONATAL LOW BOWEL OBSTRUCTION — say 'Obstruction', then list the causes. The x-ray, explained without naming a cause: 'Three colours: white is bone, grey is soft tissue, black is air — the important one. I can see many black bubbles all over his tummy. Each is a loop of bowel that has filled with air because it is stretched and blocked. When the block is low down, all the loops above it swell like this. So the x-ray tells me his bowel is obstructed — but not exactly what's causing it.' For the examiner's mark, the same finding is 'Multiple dilated loops with a soap-bubble pattern on the right'. The diagnosis with four reasons: 'He has a blockage low in the bowel. I think this because he's vomiting green, which is bile from below the stomach; he hasn't passed his first stool or wind; his tummy is swollen with loops I can feel; and the x-ray shows the swollen loops.' then the five causes, in plain words — this is the list the station is built on: 'One: the first stool — the meconium — is so thick and sticky it blocks the bowel; that can be a sign of cystic fibrosis, which we test for. Two: the nerves that make the last part of the bowel move are missing — that's hirschsprung disease, the condition his brother had, and it can run in families. Three: the bowel didn't settle in the right position before birth and has twisted — that's the one we move fastest for. Four: the back passage hasn't formed — I've checked, and his is normal. Five: part of the bowel didn't form properly. The surgeons and a dye test from the back passage will sort out which.' when she asks whether it is hirschsprung like his brother, be honest rather than definite: 'It may well be, given his brother — but I don't want to guess when a test can tell us. Most of these need an operation; some, like the sticky stool, can sometimes be cleared with the dye test itself.' Management, in order: stop the feeds; a nasogastric tube to let out the air and fluid, which stops the vomiting; a drip for fluids and sugar; bloods — salts, a blood gas and an infection screen, with antibiotics if there is any concern; the children's surgeons now; and transfer to the women's and children's by the retrieval team, with the mother going too. Safety-net: tell the nurse immediately if his tummy becomes sore or discoloured, or he becomes floppy or cold. Version B — the nurse: work from the charts, and her three specific questions are has he been examined since the vomiting started, was the anus specifically seen to be patent, and does he look dehydrated — fontanelle, mouth, skin, weight against birth weight, nappies. Also ask what the mother's notes say: GBS swab, fever in labour, labour length, delivery, instruments, Apgars and liquor. And give instructions before you hang up — management inside the history is a mark: 'Please stop feeds now, keep him warm, and bring mum when she wakes — I need to ask her about the pregnancy and family. I'm coming to examine him and pass an NG tube, and I'll order an abdominal x-ray.' then the same content in professional register: 'Multiple dilated loops — low obstruction — causes are meconium ileus, hirschsprung, atresia, imperforate anus (Excluded) and malrotation with volvulus — nil by mouth, NG, IV fluids, bloods, surgeon, transfer.' Variant — the tender abdomen: 'That changes the urgency: a tender, discoloured abdomen with bilious vomiting means ischaemic bowel or perforation — most likely volvulus or a complicated meconium ileus. I'd start IV antibiotics now, resuscitate, and ask the surgeon to see him immediately for theatre rather than waiting for a contrast study.' Tenderness moves the surgeon from 'Next' to 'Now' and removes the enema.

The three bowel questions — and say the link out loud: 'Has he passed his first bowel motion — the meconium? Is he passing wind? Is his tummy swollen?' → nothing, no wind, swollen and tight. → 'No stool, no wind and a swollen tummy — that tells me there's a blockage low in the bowel.'

THE MALFORMATION QUESTIONS: any lump or movement across his tummy; cough or choke with feeds, drooling, noisy breathing; feeding normally, shown how to attach and burp; ANY SWELLING IN THE GROIN? → 'IT FEELS LUMPY ON THE RIGHT.'

The neonatal infection set: fever or cold to touch, rash, alert or drowsy, wet nappies; infections or complications in pregnancy; rashes or sores on your private parts before delivery; the swab test at 36 weeks and its result.

DELIVERY, SCANS AND FAMILY: swelling or redness on his head; long or complicated delivery, FORCEPS OR VACUUM; blood pressure, sugar, medicines, alcohol, smoking; TOO MUCH FLUID ON THE SCANS; heel prick; AND 'ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WHO VOMITED A LOT AS A NEWBORN OR NEEDED A BOWEL OPERATION? ANYONE WITH CYSTIC FIBROSIS?' → THE BROTHER WITH HIRSCHSPRUNG. → 'THAT'S IMPORTANT — IT CAN RUN IN FAMILIES — I'LL TELL THE SURGEONS.' (Do NOT switch the diagnosis to Hirschsprung on the film.) Then concerns: 'IS IT THE SAME AS HIS BROTHER? WILL HE NEED THE OPERATION?'

THE EXAMINATION: 'general appearance, dehydration, rash, jaundice? Chest? ABDOMEN — DISTENDED? VISIBLE LOOPS OR MASS? On palpation — mass, TENDERNESS, GUARDING? BOWEL SOUNDS? Groin? IS THE ANUS PATENT? Scalp swelling, fontanelle?' → distended and tense with visible loops, a doughy right-sided fullness, HIGH-PITCHED BOWEL SOUNDS, anus patent.
THE X-RAY — MANY BUBBLES, OBSTRUCTED, CAUSE UNKNOWN (see dx). Do not name a cause here.
The diagnosis with four reasons, then the five causes in plain words (see dx) → 'Is it hirschsprung like his brother?' → 'It may well be — but I don't want to guess when a test can tell us.'

MANAGEMENT AND TRANSFER (see dx): stop feeds, tube, drip, bloods with an infection screen, the surgeons now, and retrieval to the Women's and Children's with the mother going too. Then the safety-net — A SORE OR DISCOLOURED TUMMY, FLOPPY OR COLD — and a summary.

back.dx: DISTAL INTESTINAL OBSTRUCTION SYNDROME — a bowel obstruction of cystic fibrosis. The x-ray, described in three colours and two findings: 'White is bone — the spine; grey is soft tissue; black is air, which is what matters today. The first thing I see is a collection of stool at the end of the small bowel, here on the right, and it has blocked the bowel. The second is air trapped in the bowel above the block — these black shadows with flat TOPs, which we call air-fluid levels; several of them tells us the bowel is blocked. So overall, the bowel is obstructed.' Never describe stool you cannot see. Name it with both names: 'Most likely max has a blockage of the bowel — in cystic fibrosis this kind of blockage is called distal intestinal obstruction syndrome. It's common in children with CF: their stool is thick and sticky, and it builds up at the end of the small bowel and blocks it.' Five reasons: 'He's vomiting, but more importantly he hasn't passed a bowel motion for two days and isn't passing wind; he has cystic fibrosis and had a blockage as a newborn, which makes this more likely; you've just started solids; his tummy was distended and I felt a lump in the right lower part, which is the stool that has collected; and the x-ray shows the block.' The three best differentials first, then the rest: 'A trapped hernia in the groin — his groin is normal; scar tissue bands from his operation as a baby, which can also block the bowel — the surgeons will keep that in mind; and intussusception, where the bowel telescopes into itself, which is a bit more common in CF — but he hasn't had the screaming episodes or jelly stools. Also simple constipation, a twist in the bowel, a chest infection or another infection making him vomit, and less likely a bump to the head.' when she asks whether the enzymes caused it, answer without a false promise: 'Starting solids and the enzyme change probably contributed, but it's a known problem in CF, not something you did wrong — we'll get the dietitian to sort the doses. Most of these settle without surgery.' Management, and the order is the mark: 'Our job today is to reopen the blocked bowel. First, nothing by mouth, and a tube from his nose to his stomach to let out the air and fluid — that also stops the vomiting. A drip for fluids, because he's dry and can't drink; blood tests for his salts and a blood gas. Then we use medicine to soften and wash out the stool — a laxative through the tube, or an enema from the back passage, done in the x-ray department. If that doesn't clear it, the surgeons would need to open the blockage in theatre. I'll involve the children's surgeons and the CF team now', plus the dietitian for the enzyme doses with solids. Fluids and NG before the laxative; surgeon as the escalation, not the opening line. Safety-net: tell the nurse straight away if he vomits green again, his tummy becomes painful, or he becomes drowsy. Variant — the film with no visible stool: describe only what is there — 'Air trapped in the bowel, several air-fluid levels, so the bowel is blocked. The x-ray doesn't show me exactly what is blocking it, but with his cystic fibrosis, no stool and no wind, and the lump I felt on the right, the most likely cause is a build-up of thick stool.' Bowel obstruction as the diagnosis with DIOS as the most likely cause passes. Variant — the management push: 'After IV rehydration and NG decompression, for an incomplete obstruction I'd start an osmotic washout — macrogol by nasogastric tube, or diluted oral Gastrografin per the CF protocol — with the CF team. For a complete obstruction I'd ask for a Gastrografin enema under fluoroscopy, which is diagnostic and therapeutic. I'd operate — with paediatric surgery — if there is peritonism, bilious vomiting with a tender abdomen, or failure of two attempts at washout; the operation is decompression and washout through an enterotomy, not resection.' Naming the escalation criteria is the mark.

ABDOMEN ON INSPECTION — DISTENSION, SCARS, VISIBLE PERISTALSIS OR MASS? ON PALPATION — ANY MASS, AND WHERE? TENDERNESS, GUARDING, RIGIDITY? BOWEL SOUNDS? Groin and scrotum? NAME IT WITH BOTH NAMES AND FIVE REASONS, THEN THE THREE BEST DIFFERENTIALS AND THE REST (see dx) → 'IS IT BECAUSE I GOT THE ENZYMES WRONG WITH THE SOLIDS?' → contributed, but a known problem of CF, and the dietitian will sort the doses.

back.dx: A SINGLE UNPROVOKED SEIZURE — not epilepsy, and not a febrile convulsion. Name it and define it: 'Ethan has had what we call an unprovoked seizure. A seizure is a sudden burst of abnormal electrical activity in the brain. The jerking of all four limbs, the eyes rolling back, wetting himself and being confused afterwards are all typical of a seizure.' then the reasons — and the reasons are the excluded causes, said one by one in plain words: 'When a child has a seizure we always look for a reason. He hasn't had a head injury. He hasn't had a fever, so I'm not worried about an infection of the brain like meningitis. He'd eaten, so a low sugar is unlikely — and his sugar here is normal. He's not on any medicines. He hasn't had the long-standing headaches or morning vomiting that would make me think of a growth in the brain. And there's nothing to suggest stress is behind it. When we look and find nothing, we call it unprovoked.' then her three questions, answered in order: 'The fits he had as a baby were with fevers, which is a different thing and very common; today there was no fever. Epilepsy means repeated unprovoked seizures, and Ethan has had one. His dad's single seizure is worth knowing but doesn't mean Ethan has epilepsy. Most children who have one seizure don't go on to have epilepsy, though some do have another — that's why he'll be seen by the children's specialists. And no — nothing you did caused this.' Differentials, briefly: 'I've also considered other things that can look like a fit — a faint, a heart rhythm problem, a stress-related episode, a severe migraine — and none of them fit what happened today.' then stay inside the task: 'I'm not going to go into tests today; the specialists will decide about those. What's your biggest worry?' → 'That it'll happen at school again and no one will know what to do' → the written plan: 'Stay calm, nothing in his mouth, protect him from injury, don't hold him down, roll him on his side when it stops, and call 000 if it lasts more than five minutes or he doesn't wake up.' Variant B — the 15-year-old accused of shoplifting: ask whether her eyes were open or closed, whether she wet herself, and whether she remembers all of it. Then: 'What happened to you was real and frightening, and you didn't fake it. Because you could hear everything, your eyes were closed, you were breathing very fast beforehand and it came on at a moment of intense stress, I think this was your body's response to overwhelming stress rather than an electrical seizure. It's called a non-epileptic seizure. It's treatable, and it doesn't need epilepsy medicines.' then the safety and mood screen, including thoughts of self-harm. Never say 'Fake' or 'Pseudo'; never dismiss the shoplifting accusation, which is the stressor; and do not make the reverse error of calling a genuine seizure psychogenic because a teenager was upset — an ECG and a proper history still apply. Variant C — right arm only, seven minutes, three weeks of morning vomiting: 'Three things concern me: the jerking was on one side only, it went on for seven minutes, and he has been vomiting in the mornings with headaches for weeks. Together those make me want to look at his brain today rather than wait — a scan, and the children's neurologist. These are the signs we never leave for later.' Examine the fundi and gait. 'Unprovoked seizure, first seizure clinic in six weeks' is the fail here. Variant D — the 12-month-old with a febrile convulsion: 'A simple febrile convulsion. I call it simple because all four limbs were involved, it lasted under fifteen minutes, it only happened once, and she woke up straight away — and because she has no history of fits without fever and no developmental problems. I've also checked the things that matter: no rash, no vomiting, she's alert, wet nappies normal — so I'm not worried about meningitis. Because it's simple, she needs no tests today — no scan, no blood test.' Find and treat the source of the fever, paracetamol for comfort, fluids. 'It can happen again with another fever, and paracetamol doesn't prevent that, but most children grow out of it and it is not epilepsy.' then the same first-aid plan. The traps there are saying 'Febrile convulsion' without first ruling out the source, ordering an EEG, and promising it will not recur.

ANY HEAD INJURY OR FALL RECENTLY? HAD HE MISSED ANY MEALS — DID HE HAVE BREAKFAST?' Then: 'any fever or rash in the last few days? Is he on any medicines — COULD HE HAVE GOT INTO ANYTHING AT HOME? Sleeping badly? Any stress? A lot of screens or flashing lights?'

After: 'When he woke, was he confused and drowsy — how long for? Did he wake straight away or gradually? Does he remember it? Any weakness on one side afterwards?' → fifteen minutes, gradual, no memory, no weakness.

THE SCREENS, WHICH BELONG HERE AND NOT EARLIER: neurological — headaches, blurred vision, weakness, numbness, speech; CARDIAC — chest pain, racing heart, breathlessness; gastrointestinal; THE TUMOUR QUESTIONS — LONG-STANDING HEADACHES, VOMITING IN THE MORNINGS, WEIGHT LOSS; then home, who lives there, stress, school and bullying, AND 'WAS HE BREATHING FAST BEFORE IT STARTED?' (Running the symptom screens BEFORE the four before-questions is the ordering trap — the checklist is INCIDENT, BEFORE, AFTER, THEN SCREENS.)

BACKGROUND: 'any concerns about his development? Any other medical problems? Immunisations up to date? ANY FAMILY HISTORY OF SEIZURES OR EPILEPSY — YOU MENTIONED HIS DAD? ANYONE WHO DIED SUDDENLY YOUNG, OR DROWNED?' → the father's single seizure at 19 after heavy drinking, never repeated.
Name it and define it, then give the excluded causes one by one as the reasons (see dx). (A diagnosis with no reasons fails — and so does 'It's epilepsy' or 'It's just a febrile fit'.)

Her three questions, the brief differentials, and staying inside the task (see dx) → 'But he had fits as a baby, and his dad had one — is it epilepsy?' → the febrile fits were different, epilepsy means repeated unprovoked seizures and he has had one. Then: 'What's your biggest worry?' → the school → the written first-aid plan, and a summary.

VARIANT B — THE 15-YEAR-OLD AFTER A SHOPLIFTING ACCUSATION: ask 'WERE YOUR EYES OPEN OR CLOSED? DID YOU WET YOURSELF? DO YOU REMEMBER ALL OF IT?' → closed, no, yes. → 'WHAT HAPPENED TO YOU WAS REAL AND FRIGHTENING, AND YOU DIDN'T FAKE IT. VARIANT C — RIGHT ARM ONLY, SEVEN MINUTES, MORNING VOMITING FOR THREE WEEKS: 'THREE THINGS CONCERN ME: THE JERKING WAS ON ONE SIDE ONLY, IT WENT ON FOR SEVEN MINUTES, AND HE HAS BEEN VOMITING IN THE MORNINGS WITH HEADACHES FOR WEEKS. Together those make me want to LOOK AT HIS BRAIN TODAY RATHER THAN WAIT — a scan, and the children's neurologist in Adelaide. I'm not saying it is anything serious yet, BUT THESE ARE THE SIGNS WE NEVER LEAVE FOR LATER.' Examine the fundi and gait. ('Unprovoked seizure, first seizure clinic in six weeks' is the fail.)

VARIANT D — THE 12-MONTH-OLD, SIMPLE FEBRILE CONVULSION: 'I call it SIMPLE because ALL FOUR LIMBS WERE INVOLVED, IT LASTED UNDER FIFTEEN MINUTES, IT ONLY HAPPENED ONCE, AND SHE WOKE UP STRAIGHT AWAY — and because she has no history of fits without fever and no developmental problems. I've also checked the things that matter: NO RASH, NO VOMITING, SHE'S ALERT, WET NAPPIES NORMAL — so I'm not worried about meningitis. BECAUSE IT'S SIMPLE, SHE NEEDS NO TESTS TODAY — NO SCAN, NO BLOOD TEST.' Find and treat the fever source; paracetamol 15 mg/kg for comfort and fluids. pefe: Role-player: AMANDA, 36, Ethan's mother, works at the council office; married to Dave, a fitter at the port; daughter Mia, 4. ETHAN is a healthy, happy Year 2 boy — NO medications or allergies, immunised, NORMAL DEVELOPMENT, doing well at school, no bullying, sleeps well. HE HAD TWO BRIEF FEBRILE CONVULSIONS AS A BABY at 6 and 12 months, both simple. DAVE HAD ONE SEIZURE AT 19 AFTER A NIGHT OF HEAVY DRINKING — investigated, no treatment, never recurred. NO SUDDEN DEATHS IN THE FAMILY.

YOU HAVE THE TEACHER'S NOTE — read it out or hand it over when asked about the event. From the teacher you know: ALL FOUR LIMBS JERKED, EYES ROLLED BACK, ABOUT A MINUTE, WET HIMSELF, PALE NOT BLUE, NO TONGUE BITE SEEN, SLEEPY AND CONFUSED FOR FIFTEEN MINUTES then normal. HE SAID 'I FEEL SICK' JUST BEFORE. He had WEET-BIX for breakfast, NO fever or illness this week, NO head injury, nothing in the house he could have taken. MILD HEADACHE AFTERWARDS, now gone. No vomiting, no chest symptoms, NO MORNING VOMITING, no weight loss, no weakness.

REGISTER: anxious, controlled, factual. YOUR HIDDEN QUESTION IS 'IS IT EPILEPSY LIKE HIS DAD?' — RAISE IT ONCE WHEN ASKED ABOUT FAMILY HISTORY, AND AGAIN IF THE DOCTOR NAMES THE DIAGNOSIS WITHOUT EXPLAINING. IF NEVER ASKED ABOUT CONCERNS, VOLUNTEER AT MINUTE FIVE: 'WHAT IF IT HAPPENS AT SCHOOL AGAIN?' Score them on: vitals and glucose; concern addressed; USES THE NOTE AND ASKS WHAT IS MISSING; all four limbs versus one side; tongue, frothing, incontinence; previous events; FEVER TODAY; activity before; WARNING; HEAD INJURY; MISSED MEALS; fever and rash; medications and ingestion; sleep, stress and lights; POST-ICTAL CONFUSION; memory; the neurological screen; the cardiac screen; the gastrointestinal screen; THE TUMOUR QUESTIONS; home, school and hyperventilation; development; FAMILY HISTORY INCLUDING SUDDEN DEATH; SAYS 'UNPROVOKED SEIZURE'; DEFINES SEIZURE; THE REASONS ARE THE CAUSES EXCLUDED ONE BY ONE; handles 'febrile' and 'epilepsy' correctly; offers differentials; STAYS WITHIN THE TASK with no investigation lecture; and invites questions. AUTOMATIC FAIL: NO CAUSES-OF-SEIZURE QUESTIONS; LABELS IT EPILEPSY OR FEBRILE CONVULSION.

The teacher's note — '10:30 am, in class. Ethan said HE FELT SICK. He fell off his chair and had JERKING OF HIS ARMS AND LEGS, EYES ROLLED BACK, LASTED ABOUT 1 MINUTE. HE WET HIMSELF. SLEEPY AND CONFUSED FOR ABOUT 15 MINUTES afterwards, then back to normal. NO FEVER, no injury that we saw'

The gaps, filled — ALL FOUR LIMBS — NO tongue bite seen, no frothing — PALE, NOT BLUE — and nothing like it before

The planted history — 'He had fits with fevers when he was a baby, at six months and a year' — and the reply is to ask about fever today: no fever, completely well this week. Age 7 and afebrile is not a febrile convulsion
