back.dx: Complete Kawasaki disease. Explain it: 'Jack most likely has a condition called Kawasaki disease. In this condition there is inflammation in the blood tubes — the blood vessels — caused by the immune system working abnormally. It is not an infection he caught, and it is not something you missed.' then the reasons — and the reasons are the criteria, or the diagnosis is not credited: 'His fever for more than five days that is not settling with paracetamol, the rash including his palms and feet, his red eyes, his cracked lips and red tongue, his swollen peeling hands, and the glands in his neck.' The differentials must be conditions, never organisms — no EBV, no streptococcus, no adenovirus: 'A throat infection called scarlet fever, which can look similar; a serious blood infection or meningitis; measles and other viral rashes; and the usual infections of the ears, chest, tummy, urine, joints and skin, which I could not find on examination.' Her three questions: 'Is it dangerous?' → 'It is serious mainly because it can affect the small blood vessels of the heart, which is why we treat it early.' 'Did the other doctor miss it?' → 'Two days ago it would have looked like a virus; the signs that make it clear have appeared since' — never blame the previous doctor. 'Is it contagious?' → no. Management: 'Jack needs to go to hospital today — the women's and children's. I'll ring the paediatric team now and arrange transport. In hospital they will give him intravenous immunoglobulin, which settles the immune system and reduces the inflammation. He will start a low dose of aspirin to protect the blood vessels of the heart, and he will have an echocardiogram — now, at two weeks and at six weeks — to look at the coronary arteries. The team will keep him on aspirin until the scans are clear. There is a small risk with aspirin during chickenpox or flu, so they'll talk about the flu vaccine, and his next live vaccines will be delayed for about eleven months after the immunoglobulin.' and the aspirin question answered honestly: 'You're right that we avoid aspirin for ordinary fevers; Kawasaki disease is one of the few conditions where the benefit clearly outweighs the small risk, and it is given under specialist supervision.' PATS for travel and accommodation. Saying 'Let's do some blood tests and see' is a fail — the IVIG window is ten days from fever onset and you are on day five. The variants: an infant under 12 months with six days of fever, CRP 90 and only conjunctivitis and rash — 'He does not meet the full criteria, but babies under one often show fewer features and carry the highest risk to the heart. I'm treating this as incomplete Kawasaki disease and arranging an echocardiogram and paediatric review today, not in a week.' Tonsils with white exudate — 'Exudate with a strawberry tongue and a rash makes scarlet fever my leading diagnosis. I'd confirm with a throat swab, start phenoxymethylpenicillin for ten days, and still review the other features carefully — if the fever persists beyond five days despite penicillin I would reconsider Kawasaki disease.'
plan: VITALS FIRST — NONE ARE GIVEN — THEN THE CONCERN WITHOUT BLAME: 'Examiner, could I have the vital signs please?' → 39.2, HR 130. Then: 'he's been burning up for five days — THE OTHER DOCTOR SAID IT'S A VIRUS BUT HE'S GETTING WORSE. I JUST WANT SOMEONE TO TAKE THIS SERIOUSLY.' → 'I can hear that, and five days of fever in a little one is frightening. WHAT YOU WERE TOLD ON MONDAY WAS REASONABLE AT THE TIME — MOST FEVERS ARE VIRAL — BUT A FEVER STILL THIS HIGH AT DAY FIVE NEEDS A FRESH LOOK, AND THAT IS WHAT WE'LL DO TOGETHER NOW.' (Do NOT comment on the previous GP — if you criticise him she pushes with 'SO HE GOT IT WRONG?')

EXPLORE THE FEVER: 'have you measured it? How high? Is it there all the time? Getting worse? WHAT HAVE YOU GIVEN HIM — AND IS IT HELPING? Any shivers?' → 39, constant, AND PARACETAMOL DOES NOTHING. → SAY IT ALOUD: 'THAT TELLS ME THIS IS MORE THAN A SIMPLE VIRUS' — then KEEP HUNTING.

THE EIGHT-GROUP SOURCE HUNT, SIGNPOSTED: 'I'M GOING TO GO THROUGH THE PLACES AN INFECTION CAN HIDE.' EARS AND THROAT — ear pain, runny nose, sore throat, DROOLING, VOICE CHANGE, NECK LUMPS, RASH. CHEST — cough, difficulty breathing, noisy breathing. TUMMY — vomiting, diarrhoea, pain. WATERWORKS — smelly urine, crying when he wees. JOINTS AND SKIN — SWOLLEN RED JOINTS, LIMPING, rash. MENINGITIS — headache, sore neck, BOTHERED BY LIGHT. THE WELL-BABY THREE — alert or drowsy, eating and drinking, WET NAPPIES. (The role-player volunteers the rash ONLY if asked — AND A CANDIDATE WHO STOPS AT 'RED THROAT' WALKS OUT WITH SCARLET FEVER AND FAILS.)

EXPLORE THE RASH WHEN SHE GIVES IT: 'where did it start? IS IT ITCHY? Does it hurt him? DOES IT FADE WHEN YOU PRESS IT? ANY PEELING?' → chest two days ago, not itchy, BLANCHING, maybe a little peeling at the fingertips.

The Kawasaki questions and CIST: 'Have his eyes been red? Are his lips dry or cracked? Any glands or lumps in his neck? Any peeling on his palms or feet?' then travel, sick contacts, immunisations. → both eyes red for two days without discharge, cracked bleeding lips, a lump on the right side of the neck.

THE EXAMINATION IN NINE STEPS, THEN THE FIVE KAWASAKI POINTS BY NAME: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, DEHYDRATION, and THE RASH — SITE, COLOUR, WARM, TENDER, SURFACE? Vitals. ENT — ANY EXUDATE? Chest — air entry, added sounds. Heart — S1, S2, murmur. Abdomen. A FULL JOINT EXAMINATION. A FULL LYMPH NODE EXAMINATION — SIZE AND TENDERNESS. NECK STIFFNESS. URINE DIPSTICK. And specifically: STRAWBERRY TONGUE? CRACKED LIPS? CONJUNCTIVITIS — BILATERAL, ANY DISCHARGE? RED OR SWOLLEN HANDS AND FEET? DESQUAMATION?' (If you never say 'full joint examination', 'full lymph node examination', 'neck stiffness', or ask the Kawasaki points, THE EXAMINER WILL NOT VOLUNTEER THEM.)

The diagnosis with the criteria as the reasons, then differentials as conditions (see dx) → 'Kawasaki? I've never heard of it. Is it dangerous?' / 'Did the other doctor miss it?' / 'Is it contagious — my daughter is at home.'

MANAGEMENT AND CLOSE (see dx): hospital TODAY, ring the paediatric team now, IVIG, LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN, and ECHO NOW, AT TWO WEEKS AND AT SIX WEEKS — plus the flu vaccine discussion, live vaccines delayed eleven months, PATS, and practice follow-up. → 'ASPIRIN? I THOUGHT CHILDREN CAN'T HAVE ASPIRIN.' → answer it honestly. (If you offer blood tests and review tomorrow she says 'CAN'T WE DO SOMETHING TODAY?')

JACK HAS HAD A FEVER SINCE FRIDAY — TODAY IS WEDNESDAY. You saw the GP on Monday, WHO SAID IT WAS VIRAL. You give paracetamol every four hours AND IT HARDLY HELPS. He is MISERABLE BUT AWAKE, DRINKING VERY LITTLE, TWO WET NAPPIES YESTERDAY. He has A BLOTCHY RED RASH ON HIS CHEST AND TUMMY SINCE MONDAY, RED PUFFY HANDS AND FEET, BOTH EYES RED FOR TWO DAYS WITHOUT DISCHARGE, CRACKED BLEEDING LIPS, AND A LUMP ON THE RIGHT SIDE OF HIS NECK. His throat looked red on Sunday. No cough, vomiting, diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, limp, headache or neck pain. No travel; colds at kindy.

Hidden agenda: you are angry that Monday's doctor 'Fobbed you off' and terrified something serious has been missed. Register: anxious, tearful when the word 'Heart' is used, relieved when the doctor is calm and specific. How to play it: volunteer only the fever and the Panadol failure. Mention the rash, the eyes and the lips only if asked directly. If the doctor criticises Monday's GP, say 'So he got it wrong?' and push. If the doctor has not asked what worries you by minute five, say 'Is this something bad?'. If the doctor suggests blood tests and review tomorrow, say 'Can't we do something today?'

Why surface matters — SMOOTH, NOT ROUGH — which is what separates it from scarlet fever

The five Kawasaki points, asked by name — A photograph of a strawberry tongue — lips dry and cracked — bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge — hands red and swollen — early peeling at the fingertips
The fever — 39 on the ear thermometer, constant, five days — paracetamol every four hours and it does nothing — shivers at night
Why that matters — PARACETAMOL DOING NOTHING IS THE SEVERITY MARKER — say aloud that this makes you think beyond a simple virus, THEN KEEP HUNTING rather than jumping to Kawasaki

'Has he coughed at all?' Is the discriminator — no cough is the finding, so say 'That's important' so the examiner hears you register it. And the order of management is the mark: airway and help before antibiotics — leading with IV antibiotics misses the point.
stem: Emergency department of a regional hospital. OLIVER, 4 YEARS, brought in by his mother EMMA with DIFFICULTY BREATHING AND NOISY BREATHING THAT BEGAN THIS AFTERNOON. HE LOOKS UNWELL, IS SITTING UP ON HIS MOTHER'S LAP AND DOES NOT WANT TO LIE DOWN.

Vitals on request: T 39.6 — HR 150 — RR 36 — SpO2 94% ON ROOM AIR — CRT 2 s. THE CHILD IS NOT IN THE ROOM — ALL EXAMINATION FINDINGS COME FROM THE EXAMINER. History 3-4 minutes, examination findings, diagnosis and differentials to the mother, then immediate management. VARIANTS: A LATERAL NECK X-RAY; THE STRIDOR GOING QUIET; a sore-throat door; and A FULLY IMMUNISED CHILD.

Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings

EXAMINER CARD

ONLY GIVE A FINDING IF ASKED FOR BY NAME. Obs: T 39.6, HR 150, RR 36, SpO2 94% RA, CRT 2 s. General: IRRITABLE, TOXIC, DRY LIPS, DROOLING, TRIPOD, SOFT STRIDOR AT REST, MILD SUPRASTERNAL RECESSION, NO CYANOSIS. IF ASKED TO EXAMINE THE THROAT, EARS OR NOSE: ASK 'WOULD YOU LIKE TO LOOK AT HIS THROAT?' ONCE; IF THE CANDIDATE INSISTS, GIVE 'THE CHILD CRIES, THE STRIDOR WORSENS' AND MARK THE FAIL. Chest: equal air entry, TRANSMITTED NOISE, no wheeze or crackles. Heart: tachycardic, no murmur. Abdomen and neck: 'DEFERRED' IS ACCEPTABLE. If asked for an X-ray: 'WOULD YOU SEND HIM TO X-RAY NOW?' Score: vitals requested; fear acknowledged; noise versus struggle; noise character, timing, better or worse; COUGH ASKED AND ITS ABSENCE NOTED; fever explored; throat, ear, nose; DROOLING, VOICE, SWALLOWING, LUMPS, RASH; POSITION ASKED; asthma, foreign body, croup, pertussis and pneumonia screens; well-baby; IMMUNISATION; general appearance with drooling, position and stridor; THROAT EXAMINATION DECLINED WITH A REASON; chest and heart; EPIGLOTTITIS NAMED WITH FOUR OR MORE REASONS; croup plus three other differentials; NO BLAME; UPRIGHT AND MINIMAL HANDLING; OXYGEN; AIRWAY TEAM AND MedSTAR; NIL BY MOUTH; IV ANTIBIOTICS AFTER THE AIRWAY; intubation explained; notification, contacts and catch-up; her questions answered; and a summary.

back.dx: ACUTE EPIGLOTTITIS — supraglottitis — with impending upper-airway obstruction. Explain it slowly and in short sentences: 'Oliver most likely has a condition called epiglottitis. The epiglottis is a small flap of tissue at the back of the throat that acts like a lid over the windpipe. It has become infected and swollen, and that's why he can't swallow, is dribbling, sounds muffled and is breathing noisily.' Five reasons: 'The high fever that came on over hours, the drooling, the change in his voice, the trouble swallowing, the way he's sitting to keep his airway open — and because there's no cough, which we'd expect with croup. The fact that some of his vaccines were missed also fits, because the germ that usually causes this is one we vaccinate against.' The differentials: 'Croup, which usually comes with a barking cough and a cold; a swallowed object, which comes on suddenly in a well child; an abscess at the back of the throat; and a severe allergic reaction. His picture fits epiglottitis best, and it's the one we treat as an emergency until proven otherwise.' and when she asks whether it is her fault: 'This isn't about blame — right now it's about getting him safe, and we'll sort the vaccines out later.' Management, and the order is the mark: one — 'He stays exactly where he is, upright on your lap; we won't lay him down or upset him, and nobody will look in his mouth.' Two — 'Oxygen — I'll ask you to hold the mask near his face.' Three — 'I'm calling the senior doctor and the anaesthetist now, and our retrieval service, MedSTAR kids, because the safest place for him is the children's hospital intensive care with a team that can protect his airway. If his breathing gets worse they will put a tube into his windpipe under anaesthetic to keep it open — that's a planned, safe step, not a last resort.' Four — 'Once his airway is safe he'll have a drip with strong antibiotics into the vein, fluids because he's dry, and medicine for the fever. Nothing to eat or drink.' then her three questions: 'Can I stay with him?' → 'Yes — you staying calm with him is part of the treatment.' 'Will he need an operation?' → 'The tube isn't an operation; it's done by the anaesthetist and usually comes out in a day or two once the swelling settles.' 'What about his sister?' → 'If tests show it's the germ we think, the public health unit will be told and the family may need a short course of antibiotics to protect her, and we'll catch up everyone's vaccines.' The variants. A lateral neck x-ray: 'This shows a swollen epiglottis — the thumb sign — with thickened aryepiglottic folds. It confirms epiglottitis. I would not have sent him for this film before securing his airway; if it has been taken, he must have been accompanied by an airway-capable doctor, and the plan is unchanged.' The stridor going quiet with drowsiness: 'Quietening stridor with drowsiness is impending complete obstruction, not improvement. I'm calling the arrest team, the most senior airway operator intubates now — gas induction, upright — with a surgical airway kit open at the bedside. Two-person bag-mask with jaw thrust until then.' VERIFY a sore-throat door: same station, explore the sore throat first, and the red flags land in the same place. A fully immunised child: 'Immunisation makes Hib unlikely but does not exclude epiglottitis — pneumococcus, group A strep and Staph cause it in vaccinated children. The clinical picture decides; the management is the same.'
plan: VITALS, THEN THE FEAR ACKNOWLEDGED WITHOUT TOUCHING THE CHILD: 'Examiner, may I have his observations first?' → 39.6, HR 150, SpO2 94%. Then, at her level: 'I can see he's working hard AND I CAN SEE YOU'RE FRIGHTENED. HE'S IN THE RIGHT PLACE and the nurses are with him. Tell me what's happened.' → 'he was fine at lunch. About three hours ago he started sounding funny and HE WON'T LIE DOWN. IS HE GOING TO STOP BREATHING?' → 'WE ARE GOING TO LOOK AFTER HIS BREATHING — THAT'S MY WHOLE FOCUS.'

The complaint and the discriminator: 'Is it mainly a noise, or is he struggling for breath? What does the noise sound like — a harsh sound when he breathes in, or a rattle? Is it getting worse? Anything better or worse — lying down, moving about? Has he been coughing at all?' → 'No, he hasn't coughed at all.' → say it: 'No cough — that's important.'

FEVER AND ENT, THEN THE THREE RED FLAGS ASKED TOGETHER: 'has he had a fever — did you measure it, any chills, did you give anything? Sore throat? Ear pain? Runny nose? NOW THREE IMPORTANT ONES: IS HE DROOLING OR DRIBBLING? HAS HIS VOICE CHANGED — MUFFLED, LIKE SOMETHING HOT IN HIS MOUTH? IS HE REFUSING TO SWALLOW — SPITTING OUT SALIVA? Any lumps in the neck? Any rash? HOW IS HE SITTING?' (Once you have drooling, STOP AND ASK THE OTHER RED FLAGS TOGETHER — drifting back to 'any vomiting?' before finishing them reads as not recognising the emergency.)

THE QUICK SCREENS AND THE HIDDEN CLUE: wheeze, night cough, puffers; A CHOKING EPISODE WHILE EATING OR PLAYING; coughing fits or vomiting after coughing; grunting; tummy symptoms; IS HE HIS NORMAL SELF OR FLOPPY AND SLEEPY, DRINKING, LAST WEE. Then: 'ARE HIS IMMUNISATIONS UP TO DATE?' → she looks down: 'HE HAD THE SIX-MONTH ONES. THEN WE MOVED AND IT DIDN'T HAPPEN.' → NOTE IT ALOUD: 'SO THE TWELVE- AND EIGHTEEN-MONTH ONES WERE MISSED. THAT'S USEFUL TO KNOW.' Then medical problems, medicines, allergies, sick contacts.

The examination — general appearance first, then the refusal: 'General appearance: is he alert or drowsy? Does he look toxic? Dehydration? Is he drooling? What position is he in? Is there audible stridor? Any recession, tracheal tug or cyanosis?' then: 'Saturations 94% on room air. I am not going to examine his throat, ears or nose — I'm concerned about epiglottitis and I don't want to precipitate obstruction. Chest, with minimal handling: air entry, added sounds? Heart sounds? I'll defer the abdomen and neck.' → the examiner tests you: 'Would you like to look at his throat?' → 'No. In a drooling, toxic child with stridor, the throat is examined by the airway team in a controlled setting.'

The diagnosis in short sentences with five reasons, then the differentials (see dx) → 'Is it because we missed his needles? Is this my fault?' / 'Isn't it just croup?' → 'This isn't about blame — it's about getting him safe.' (If you blame her she becomes defensive and stops answering freely.)

MANAGEMENT IN ORDER — UPRIGHT AND UNDISTURBED, OXYGEN, THE AIRWAY TEAM AND MedSTAR, THEN ANTIBIOTICS ONCE THE AIRWAY IS SAFE (see dx). (Leading with 'IV antibiotics' and forgetting the airway team has missed the point.)

HER THREE QUESTIONS AND THE SUMMARY (see dx): staying with him, the tube not being an operation, and the sister's prophylaxis and vaccine catch-up. Then to the examiner: 'an UNDER-IMMUNISED 4-year-old with ACUTE EPIGLOTTITIS AND IMPENDING AIRWAY OBSTRUCTION. Upright, minimal handling, oxygen, airway team and MedSTAR Kids, nil by mouth, IV CEFTRIAXONE ONCE THE AIRWAY PLAN IS MADE, PICU, notification and contact prophylaxis. QUIETENING STRIDOR OR DROWSINESS MEANS IMMEDIATE INTUBATION.'

pefe: Role-player: EMMA, 29, a hairdresser in Kadina, SOLE PARENT of Oliver (4) and MIA (18 months). Oliver was WELL AT LUNCH; over THREE HOURS he became feverish, started DRIBBLING, SOUNDS MUFFLED, REFUSES TO SWALLOW and makes A HARSH NOISE BREATHING IN. HE WILL NOT LIE DOWN AND SITS LEANING FORWARD. NO COUGH. You gave paracetamol WITH NO EFFECT. He is on your lap throughout — THE CHILD IS NOT PLAYED.

Immunisations: he had the 2-, 4- and 6-month vaccines; then you moved towns after a relationship breakdown and the 12- and 18-month ones never happened. You are ashamed of this and will only volunteer it if asked directly. If the doctor blames you, become defensive and stop answering freely; if the doctor says it is not about blame, soften. Hidden agenda: 'Is he going to stop breathing?' Asked early; 'Can't you just look in his throat, or give him something?' Pushed once after the doctor declines; and 'Can I stay with him? What about Mia?' At the end. Register: frightened, fast-talking, tearful at the vaccine question.
What 94% means — OXYGEN NOW — say it aloud
The story — Well at lunch, then three hours of noisy breathing and fever — mainly the noise, a harsh sound on breathing in — worse in the last hour and much worse lying down
The discriminator — 'No — he hasn't coughed at all.' A barking cough would make this croup
The three red flags — Dribbling everywhere — voice thick and muffled — he spits everything out and won't drink — and he sits leaning forward with his chin out
Fever — 39.5 AT HOME AND PARACETAMOL DID NOTHING — throat hurts badly, no earache or runny nose
The hidden clue — 'He had the six-month ones. Then we moved and it didn't happen' — so the twelve- and eighteen-month vaccines were missed. She is ashamed and volunteers it only if asked directly
Everything else — No wheeze or puffers, NO CHOKING EPISODE, no coughing fits, no tummy symptoms — QUIET AND SCARED, NOT HIMSELF, WON'T DRINK, LAST WEE AT MIDDAY — no allergies, nobody sick at home
fails: ★ Examining the throat, ears or nose before the airway is secure — the examiner offers it once, and insisting makes the child cry, worsens the stridor and is marked a fail
★ Leading management with IV antibiotics instead of airway and help first — the order is upright, oxygen, airway team and retrieval, then antibiotics once the airway is safe
Not asking about cough, or not saying aloud that its absence matters — a barking cough would make this croup
Blaming the mother for the missed vaccines, which makes her defensive and stops the history

Drifting back to routine screens before finishing the three red flags once drooling is disclosed; never asking about immunisations, which is the hidden clue; and sending the child to X-ray unaccompanied before the airway is secured

back.dx: FEBRILE NEUTROPENIA — emergency department now, cultures, and IV antibiotic within 60 minutes, whatever the card shows. Explain it in context: 'Liam looks well, and I can see why you might wonder if this is just a cold from his sister. But my main concern is a situation we call febrile neutropenia. Liam has leukaemia, which is a cancer of the white blood cells, and last week's chemotherapy pushes the number of infection-fighting white cells — the neutrophils — right down; eight days after a cycle is when they're lowest. So right now his body has very little to fight an infection with, and it also can't show us how bad an infection is — it can't make the pus and swelling that usually tell us. That means a fever, even in a child who looks well, has to be treated as a possibly serious infection until the tests prove otherwise. The red ear and throat may be where it's started, but I can't rely on them to tell me it's mild.' and answer the relapse question honestly: 'Nothing today suggests that — this is about infection while his counts are low, and his team will check his blood.' Management: 'Liam needs to go to the emergency department now — I'll ring ahead and speak to his oncology team so they're expecting him. In hospital the very first thing is to take blood for cultures from his Port and from a vein, and then, within the hour and without waiting for any results, give him strong antibiotics straight into the vein. After that a full examination and a sepsis work-up: a full blood count to see how low his white cells are, inflammatory markers, urine, and if needed a chest x-ray, a nose and throat swab, or a lumbar puncture. Paracetamol for the fever — not ibuprofen, because his platelets may be low. He'll be admitted under his oncology team, who will decide about transfer, and they'll review him at 48 hours with the results. PATS can help with travel and accommodation, and I'll give you a letter.' Refuse the two requests: 'Can't you just give him antibiotics here and we go home?' → 'I understand the appeal, but tablets aren't enough here — he needs them into a vein, in hospital, with blood tests taken first, and someone watching him overnight. If he were to get sicker, that can happen quickly with low white cells.' and if the examiner asks 'Isn't it better to check the neutrophil count and then decide?' → 'No — I assume he's neutropenic; the count confirms it but doesn't change the first hour.' (The role-player is briefed to look relieved if you say check the bloods first, and let you fail.) version B — the shocked child: 'He's drowsy with a four-second capillary refill and a heart rate of 150 — this is septic shock. I'm calling MedSTAR and the emergency department now, getting IV or intraosseous access, giving oxygen and a 20 mL/kg bolus, and, if we stock it, IV ceftriaxone after cultures on oncology advice.' VERIFY the adult equivalent, worth knowing: an adult on carbimazole with a sore throat and fever — 'Same rule: stop the carbimazole, urgent full blood count today, and if the neutrophils are low he goes to ED for IV antibiotics.'
plan: VITALS INCLUDING CRT AND SATURATIONS, THEN NAME THE CONTEXT AND VALIDATE HER: 'Examiner, the vital signs please, INCLUDING CAPILLARY REFILL AND SATURATIONS?' → 38.6, HR 118, CRT 2 s. → 'he's FEBRILE AND A LITTLE FAST, BUT PERFUSED.' Then: 'I CAN SEE HE'S BEING TREATED FOR LEUKAEMIA. Tell me what's been happening.' → 'the hospital told us if he ever gets a fever WE HAVE TO GET HIM SEEN STRAIGHT AWAY. He seems okay in himself, but they said not to wait.' → 'YOU DID EXACTLY THE RIGHT THING.'

THE FEVER: 'how high has it been? Since when? All the time or on and off? Have you given anything — AND DOES IT HELP? ANY SHIVERING OR SHAKING, ESPECIALLY AFTER HIS PORT HAS BEEN FLUSHED?' → paracetamol helps for a few hours. (A GOOD PARACETAMOL RESPONSE IS THE REASSURANCE BAIT — IT CHANGES NOTHING.)

The leukaemia block — nine questions: 'When was he diagnosed? What treatment is he on, and which phase? When exactly was the last chemotherapy? Does he have a Port or central line? Were his last blood counts low? Any transfusions? Is he on preventive medicines like co-trimoxazole? Any steroids this cycle? Who is his oncology team, and did they give you a fever plan or card?' → eight days ago. → say it: 'That puts him right at the point his white cells are lowest.' and ask for the fever card — it usually names the antibiotic and the number to call.

THE SEVEN GROUPS PLUS THE EXTRA SITES: ear pain, runny nose, sore throat, MOUTH ULCERS, drooling, voice change, neck lumps, rash; cough, breathlessness, noisy breathing; vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain, PAIN AROUND THE BOTTOM; burning or frequency passing urine; swollen or red joints, limping, red skin, ANY REDNESS AROUND THE PORT; headache, stiff neck, photophobia. → ONLY POSITIVES: A RUNNY NOSE AND A SCRATCHY THROAT. (The examiner is watching whether you RUN THE WHOLE STRUCTURE OR STOP AT 'IT'S A COLD'.)

WELL-CHILD AND CIST: alert or drowsy, eating and drinking, passing urine as usual; travel; anyone unwell at home or school; AND 'IMMUNISATIONS — AND WHICH ARE ON HOLD?' → his sister had a cold, and NO LIVE VACCINES DURING TREATMENT.

THE EXAMINATION CARD WITH THE NEUTROPENIA SWEEP: general appearance INCLUDING BRUISING, PALLOR AND MOUTH ULCERS; vitals with CRT and saturations; ENT including the mouth; chest; heart; abdomen with liver and spleen; FULL JOINT EXAMINATION; FULL LYMPH NODE EXAMINATION; neck stiffness; urine dipstick; AND THE PORT SITE — REDNESS, TENDERNESS, DISCHARGE — THE SKIN AND NAIL FOLDS — AND THE PERIANAL AREA ON INSPECTION ONLY.

back.dx: SEPTIC ARTHRITIS OF THE KNEE — hospital today, cultures before antibiotics. Version A: 'Tom most likely has a condition called septic arthritis in his right knee. Put simply, that is an infection inside the joint. The reasons I think this are the fever, which tells me there is an infection; the swelling you noticed; and when I examined the knee it was red, warm and painful to touch, and he won't put weight on it.' Version B: '...most likely has osteomyelitis — an infection in the bone just below the knee. The reasons are the fever, the swelling and redness, and that when I examined him the most painful spot was on the bone rather than the joint itself. The infection can spread into the joint, so septic arthritis is my second concern.' The differentials, with osteomyelitis and cellulitis named before the group list: 'An infection in the bone next to the joint, called osteomyelitis; an infection in the skin over the knee, called cellulitis; an irritable joint after a cold, which is usually milder than this; and an injury. I have also checked for the usual infections of the ears, throat, chest, tummy and urine, and for meningitis, and I didn't find any.' Never give organisms — not Staph, not Kingella — as differentials. His questions: 'How did he get that?' → 'Usually bacteria from a small skin break or from the bloodstream settle in the joint; it isn't anyone's fault.' 'Can't you just give him antibiotics?' → 'Antibiotics are essential, but they need to go into a vein in hospital, and the joint usually needs to be washed out so the infection doesn't damage the cartilage.' 'Will he walk properly?' → 'Treated quickly, most children walk normally afterwards — which is why we act today.' and the couch fall: 'That may well be part of it, and I'll ask the hospital to x-ray the leg. But a hot, swollen joint with a fever of 39 has to be treated as an infection until the tests prove otherwise — waiting would risk the joint.' Management if asked: 'Tom needs to go to the women's and children's hospital today. I'll ring the orthopaedic and paediatric teams now and arrange the ambulance. Please don't give him anything to eat or drink from now, in case he needs a short anaesthetic to take fluid from the knee. In hospital they will take blood tests and blood cultures first, do an ultrasound, and then start antibiotics through a drip and wash out the joint.' PATS for travel, and practice follow-up. No oral antibiotics from the surgery. The variants: a freely mobile joint in a child who has just walked across the room — 'A freely mobile joint with spreading skin redness makes cellulitis more likely than septic arthritis. I'd still check inflammatory markers today and arrange review within 24 hours, and I would refer if he stops weight-bearing or the fever persists.' The well-baby answers turning bad — floppy, mottled, CRT 4 seconds: 'This is now sepsis until proven otherwise. I'm calling MedSTAR for retrieval, gaining IV access, taking cultures and giving the first dose of IV antibiotics here before transfer.'
plan: VITALS, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE: 'Examiner, the vital signs please?' → 39.0, HR 150, CRT 2 s. → 'he is FEBRILE AND HIS HEART RATE IS UP, BUT HE IS PERFUSING WELL.' THE FEVER: measured, since when, constant or on and off, getting worse, what have you given and does it help, ANY SHIVERING. → paracetamol helps for a few hours, AND HE SHIVERED LAST NIGHT. (A helpful antipyretic response IS THE NORMAL PATTERN AND DOES NOT MAKE THE CHILD SAFE.)

THE SOURCE HUNT, GROUPS ONE TO FOUR: ears and throat — pulling at his ears, runny nose, DROOLING, CHANGE IN HIS CRY, neck lumps, rash; chest — cough, difficulty breathing, noisy breathing; tummy — vomiting, diarrhoea, DRAWING HIS LEGS UP; nappies — smelly wee, crying at changes. → all negative, BUT: 'HE DOES SCREAM WHENEVER I PICK HIM UP, THOUGH. The examination — general first, then inspect, palpate, locate: 'General appearance: alert or drowsy? Dehydration? Rash? Is he holding a leg still? Vitals. ENT. Chest. Heart. Abdomen. Neck stiffness. Dipstick. Lymph nodes. Now the joints: on inspection, is any joint swollen or red, and which? On palpation, is it warm to touch and tender to touch? Where is the tenderness — across the joint line or over the tibial tuberosity? Effusion? Other joints and the hip on that side?' (Asking to move the knee wastes twenty seconds; not asking where it is tender loses version B.)
The diagnosis with its reasons, then osteomyelitis and cellulitis before the group list (see dx) → 'An infection in the joint? How did he get that?' / 'Can't you just give him antibiotics?'

back.dx: SCARLET FEVER — group A streptococcal pharyngitis with the toxin rash. Name it and explain it: 'I'm confident Liam has an infection called scarlet fever. It's a throat infection caused by a common bacterium called streptococcus — the same one that causes strep throat — and in some children the bug makes a toxin that produces this particular rash.' Five reasons: 'The sore throat and fever, his tonsils inflamed with white patches, the rash rough like sandpaper that fades when pressed, the pale ring around his mouth, and the red bumpy strawberry look of his tongue.' Say both names if you like — 'Scarlet fever, a strep throat infection with its rash' — but the marking scheme says scarlet fever. Then the concern, answered with three reasons rather than reassurance: 'I don't think this is meningococcal disease, for three reasons. Children with meningococcal are very unwell and drowsy — Liam is alert and playing. Their rash is dark and doesn't fade under pressure — Liam's fades and is rough, which is the strep pattern. And his heart rate, breathing and circulation show no sign of a body-wide infection. Nothing in medicine is one hundred per cent, so I'll give you exactly what to watch for.' Management: check the allergy first — 'Does Liam have any allergies, particularly to penicillin?' then: 'Because the strep bug is already showing on his skin, this is one throat infection we do treat with antibiotics — to clear it and, importantly, to protect his heart and kidneys from the rare complications of strep. Phenoxymethylpenicillin syrup, twice a day, for ten full days. He'll feel better in two or three days — please keep going to the end of the bottle; the length of the course is what does the protecting.' The swab question: 'A swab takes a few days to come back and wouldn't change what we do — the picture is clear enough to treat today.' then comfort, fluids and exclusion: paracetamol or ibuprofen with food; small drinks often, icy poles, soft food; and home from school until 24 hours after the first dose and he feels well. The safety-net has two HALVEs, and the late half is what the examiner is listening for: tonight — drowsy or hard to wake, new spots that don't fade under a glass, stops drinking or passing urine, drooling or noisy breathing; and in the next few weeks — dark or cola-coloured urine, puffy eyes, painful swollen joints, chest pain or breathlessness. Review in two to three days, a fact sheet, and teach-back: 'What will you do if he seems worse tonight?' The variants: the toxic child — 'This child is drowsy with a non-blanching rash and delayed capillary refill. I am treating this as meningococcal septicaemia. I'm calling for help, giving high-flow oxygen, obtaining IV or intraosseous access for a 20 mL/kg bolus, giving ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg intramuscularly if access is delayed, and calling MedSTAR kids for retrieval. I will notify SA health.' VERIFY a declared penicillin allergy — 'What happened when he had penicillin? A rash a few days in, no swelling or breathing trouble — that's a non-severe reaction, so I'll use cefalexin twice daily for ten days. If it had been swelling or breathing difficulty I would use azithromycin once daily for five days.' VERIFY an Aboriginal child at high rheumatic fever risk — 'Children in your community have a higher chance of a strep throat going on to affect the heart — rheumatic fever — so this one we definitely treat, and finishing the course matters even more. If the twice-daily syrup for ten days will be hard, a single injection of long-acting penicillin today does the same job. Would it help if I linked in with the Aboriginal health service for the follow-up? The medicine is covered under closing the gap.'
plan: VITALS, THEN ACKNOWLEDGE THE FEAR IN THE FIRST MINUTE: 'Examiner, may I have Liam's observations?' Then: 'tell me what's been happening.' → 'he's had fevers for two days and I READ ABOUT THAT BOY WITH MENINGOCOCCAL — I JUST WANT TO KNOW IT ISN'T THAT.' → 'THAT'S A FRIGHTENING THING TO HAVE HEARD, AND YOU'VE DONE THE RIGHT THING BRINGING HIM IN. I'll ask some questions, examine him, AND THEN I'LL ANSWER THAT WORRY DIRECTLY.' (If you have not acknowledged it within the first minute, SHE INTERRUPTS WITH 'BUT IS IT MENINGOCOCCAL?')
THE FEVER: measured, highest, what have you given and how much, DOES IT HELP, when it started, constant or on and off, any shivering.

ENT AND THE FIVE RED FLAGS: 'any ear pain or pulling at his ears? Runny nose? SORE THROAT? IS HE DROOLING? HAS HIS VOICE CHANGED? ANY TROUBLE SWALLOWING? NOISY BREATHING? LUMPS IN THE NECK?' → the throat really hurts, and a small lump under the jaw.

The rash — and two of these questions are the whole diagnosis: 'Has he got any rash anywhere? Where did it start and where is it now? Spreading? What colour? Itchy? Painful? Warm? Any weeping? When you run your hand over it, is it smooth or rough? Anything about his face or tongue? Does it fade if you press a glass on it?' → 'Rough, like fine sandpaper' and 'His cheeks are red but he looks pale around his mouth.' (She will not say 'Sandpaper' unless you ask the surface, and will not mention the mouth unless you ask about the face — ask both.)

CLUSTERS, SEPSIS SCREEN AND BACKGROUND: cough or fast breathing; vomiting, diarrhoea, tummy pain; pain passing urine; sore or swollen joints, limping; HEADACHE, STIFF NECK, BOTHERED BY LIGHT; IS HE ALERT AND PLAYING BETWEEN FEVERS, DRINKING, PASSING URINE; ANY RED EYES, CRACKED LIPS, SWOLLEN HANDS; immunisations, travel, ANYONE UNWELL AT SCHOOL, past illnesses, medicines, ALLERGIES.

THE EXAMINATION — THE FOUR SIGNS BY NAME, THEN MOVE: 'general appearance — alert or drowsy, dehydration, toxic? IS THERE A RASH — where, what morphology, warm or painful, BLANCHING OR NON-BLANCHING, AND WHAT IS THE SURFACE LIKE? Vital signs? Ears? Nose? Throat — TONSILS SWOLLEN, RED, EXUDATE? IS THERE A STRAWBERRY TONGUE? PALLOR AROUND THE MOUTH? PALATAL PETECHIAE? CERVICAL NODES — which chain, tender, mobile? NECK STIFFNESS? Chest, heart, abdomen, joints, AND ANY PEELING OF HANDS OR FEET?' (Stopping at 'there is a rash', or running a complete systems examination that EATS TASKS 3 AND 4, are the two traps.)

NAME IT WITH FIVE REASONS, THEN ANSWER THE CONCERN WITH THREE REASONS (see dx) → 'SCARLET FEVER? I THOUGHT THAT WAS SOMETHING FROM THE OLDEN DAYS.' → 'IT IS A VERY OLD NAME, BUT IT'S COMMON AND TREATABLE.' (She stays tense if only told 'don't worry', and relaxes visibly once given reasons.)
Management — allergy check first, then the ten-day course with its reason, and the swab declined (see dx) → 'Ten days is a lot. Can't you just do a swab to check it's really strep?'

COMFORT, FLUIDS, EXCLUSION, THE TWO-PART SAFETY-NET AND TEACH-BACK (see dx): tonight's red flags AND the late complications — dark urine, puffy eyes, sore joints, chest pain — then review in two to three days, a fact sheet, and 'WHAT WILL YOU DO IF HE SEEMS WORSE TONIGHT?'

pefe: Role-player: SARAH, 34, a teacher's aide in Kadina. LIAM IS 5, her only child, previously well, FULLY IMMUNISED, no medicines, NO KNOWN ALLERGIES. A BOY AT A NEARBY SCHOOL WAS ADMITTED WITH MENINGOCOCCAL DISEASE LAST WEEK AND IT WAS ON THE LOCAL NEWS. YOU HAVE NOT SLEPT.

Register: anxious and talkative at the start; you interrupt once with 'But is it meningococcal?' if the doctor has not acknowledged it within the first minute. You relax visibly once given reasons; you stay tense if only told 'Don't worry'. Hidden agenda: you want a clear yes-or-no on meningococcal with reasons, and you privately believe a swab or blood test would settle it — if the doctor never asks whether you have concerns, raise the swab during the management task.

How to play it: volunteer only the fever at first. Give the sore throat only when asked ENT questions. Mention the pale ring around his mouth only when asked about the face, and the rough texture only when asked about the surface. Push back once on ten days of antibiotics. Score them on: vitals requested; concern acknowledged early; fever explored; the ENT cluster; all five red flags; asked about the rash unprompted; asked the surface; asked the face and tongue; the other clusters and sepsis screen; immunisation, contacts and allergy; the examination with blanching and surface, tongue, perioral pallor, nodes, chest and heart; named scarlet fever with reasons; three reasons it is not meningococcal; allergy check; phenoxymethylpenicillin for ten days; declined the swab with a reason; fever and fluid advice; exclusion for 24 hours; red flags including the late complications; and review with teach-back.

Neck and the rest — TENDER, MOBILE ANTERIOR CERVICAL NODES BILATERALLY — NO NECK STIFFNESS — chest clear, heart normal, abdomen soft, joints normal, NO PEELING
The fever — 38.4 this morning and 38.9 last night — paracetamol twice today, works for a few hours then it climbs back

The sepsis screen — SLIGHT COUGH ONLY — no vomiting, normal urine, no joint pain, NO HEADACHE OR NECK STIFFNESS — PLAYING WHEN THE FEVER IS DOWN, DRINKING WELL — no red eyes, cracked lips or swollen hands
Background — Immunised, no travel, a boy in his class had a sore throat, no known allergies

The face, only if you ask — 'His cheeks are red but he looks pale around his mouth' — and the tongue is 'A bit red'. She has not tried the glass test

back.dx: VERSION B — recurrent viral upper respiratory tract infections at a normal frequency, with immunodeficiency excluded on history and examination. 'Archie is having recurrent upper respiratory tract infections — colds. For a two-year-old at childcare, eight to twelve a year is normal — roughly one a month, more in winter.' The differentials are marked one by one, so name four with reasons: 'Allergies in the nose, which his examination doesn't show; a long-standing sinus infection; something stuck up his nose, which gives a one-sided smelly discharge; and conditions that weaken the immune system — cystic fibrosis, coeliac disease, very rarely a blood cancer, or medicines that suppress immunity. Nothing in his story or examination points to any of those.' Stopping at 'Colds' loses the task. When she pushes: 'It's the number that frightens you, and I understand that. What tells me his immune system is working is how he gets sick: short, mild colds, over in a few days, never in hospital, never needing antibiotics, and growing beautifully in between. Children with a weak immune system look very different.' The two refusals, each with reasons: antibiotics — 'Not today, because this cold is viral and antibiotics don't work on viruses. But it isn't never: each time he's unwell, bring him in; if he has signs of a bacterial infection — high fever, ear infection, chest signs — we'll treat it.' Blood test — 'Not today either, for three reasons: no warning signs in his history, he's growing well with a normal examination, and these are the mild colds we expect at childcare. A normal blood count in a well child wouldn't change anything.' then say what would change your mind — the red flags: 'More than ten to twelve a year, infections that drag on or are severe — pneumonia, joint or skin infections, needing hospital — poor weight gain, lumps, or thrush that won't go. If any of those happen we test straight away.' Management, four things, and the first is the only one that will actually reduce the colds: 'The biggest one is the smoke: children in smoking households get more and longer colds and more ear infections. Smoking outside helps; stopping helps most, and I can refer you both to Quitline on 13 7848 or start you on something today.' then the flu vaccine each Autumn, free under five; for each cold fluids, rest, saline drops, paracetamol if uncomfortable, and no cough-and-cold medicines under six; and a fact sheet with review in a month to check his growth. And when she says she didn't want to be fobbed off: 'You're not being fobbed off — you've asked the right question and I've looked for the answer properly. The door is open.' Version A — allergic rhinitis: 'Most likely Noah has allergic rhinitis — an allergic reaction in the lining of the nose to things he breathes in, like dust or pollen — and I think that because the discharge is clear and constant, the lining of his nose looks the way allergy looks, and he mouth-breathes. He doesn't have the sneezing or itchy eyes some children get; many his age don't.' and when the father offers 'So it's just childcare then?': 'Childcare certainly spreads colds, but colds come and go with fevers and coughs, and Noah's nose runs clear every day even when he's well. I want to look at his nose before I tell you what it is.' The two other variants: the history reveals the package — two pneumonias, one needing a drip, and weight down two centile lines: 'That changes things. I'm not reassured, and I'm going to test today: a full blood count and film, immunoglobulin levels, an HIV test with your consent, a sweat test for cystic fibrosis and coeliac antibodies, and I'll speak to the paediatric immunologists.' A green, one-sided discharge: 'A smelly discharge from one nostril in a toddler usually means something has been pushed up there. I'm going to look now with a TORCH. If I can see it and it's soft we can try the parent's kiss technique; if not, he needs ENT the same day — and if there's any chance it's a button battery, that's an emergency.'
plan: Vitals, acknowledge, and ask the agenda question early: 'What's been worrying you?' → 'He just gets sick all the time. Cold after cold. I'm worried something's wrong with him.' → 'That sounds exhausting and worrying, and I'm glad you've come. Was there something in particular you were hoping for today?' → 'Antibiotics to knock it on the head, and a blood test to make sure his immune system is ok.' → 'Noted — I'll come back to both once I understand what's been happening.'

THE COMPLAINT IN SEVERITY TERMS, NOT COUNT: 'HOW MANY COLDS IN THE LAST TWELVE MONTHS? HOW LONG DOES EACH ONE LAST? HAS HE EVER BEEN ADMITTED TO HOSPITAL FOR AN INFECTION? EVER NEEDED ANTIBIOTICS? ANYTHING THAT WASN'T JUST A COLD — CHEST, EARS, JOINTS, SKIN? What does a typical one look like? Is he having one now?' → THEN SAY IT ALOUD: 'SO THEY'RE SHORT AND MILD.' ('Eight' is not the finding — the duration, the absent admissions and the absent antibiotics are.)

The immunodeficiency box, before anything else — this order is the concept of the case: 'Any infections during the pregnancy — were HIV and hepatitis tested? Born at term? Was the newborn heel-prick done and normal? Any long-term diarrhoea or greasy, pale stools? Any concerns about his growth or weight gain? Any lumps or bumps, or unusual bruising? Anyone in the family with a weak immune system? Any regular medicines — steroids? Any thrush in his mouth that won't clear?' → and when the sister comes up, one question only: 'Has she ever been admitted, or been given a diagnosis?' then move on.

Allergic rhinitis, then immunisation and childcare: itchy nose or rubbing, sneezing, red itchy watery eyes, wheeze, itchy rashes; mouth breathing, dark shadows under the eyes; snoring or gasping at night, daytime tiredness, ear infections, hearing or speech worries; anyone smoke at home or in the car, carpets, pets, dust, asthma, eczema or hay fever in the family; immunisations, childcare, eating, drinking, wet nappies. → 'We both smoke — inside, yes.' → register it neutrally.

THE CARD — READ IT ALOUD IN ONE SENTENCE AND SAY WHAT THE GROWTH CHART MEANS: 'normal ENT examination, clear chest, no nodes or thrush, AND A NORMAL GROWTH CHART — THAT'S THE MOST REASSURING FINDING.' (Silence while you read is wasted marks.)

Name it, give the normal frequency, then four differentials each with a reason (see dx) → 'But eight colds — that can't be normal. His sister was never this bad.' → answer with how he gets sick, not how often.
The two refusals with reasons, then the red flags that would change your mind (see dx). (Refusing flatly earns 'So you're fobbing me off'.)

MANAGEMENT — FOUR THINGS, SMOKE FIRST (see dx): the smoke addressed WITHOUT BLAME and with Quitline or medication offered; the FLU VACCINE, free under five; cold care with NO COUGH-AND-COLD MEDICINES UNDER SIX; and a fact sheet with review in a month. → 'I JUST DIDN'T WANT TO BE FOBBED OFF.' → 'YOU'RE NOT. YOU ASKED THE RIGHT QUESTION AND WE'VE LOOKED PROPERLY. THE DOOR IS OPEN.' Then summarise.

pefe: Role-player (Version B): JANE, 31, works part-time at the IGA; partner Dean drives trucks. Two children: ARCHIE (2) and RUBY (5). ARCHIE GOES TO CHILDCARE THREE DAYS A WEEK. In the last year he has had ABOUT EIGHT COLDS, each a runny nose, a bit of a cough, maybe a bit warm, OVER IN TWO OR THREE DAYS. NEVER IN HOSPITAL, NEVER HAD ANTIBIOTICS, NEVER ANYTHING WORSE THAN A COLD. Mild runny nose today. Eats and sleeps well, GROWING FINE. Normal pregnancy with all tests normal, term, HEEL PRICK NORMAL, immunised. Normal stools, no lumps or bruising, NO THRUSH, no medicines or allergies. YOU AND DEAN BOTH SMOKE, MOSTLY INSIDE — you know you shouldn't and WILL GET DEFENSIVE IF LECTURED, BUT WILL ENGAGE IF OFFERED HELP. RUBY 'GETS CHEST INFECTIONS' — if asked: two courses of antibiotics for bronchitis last winter, NEVER ADMITTED, NO DIAGNOSIS.

Agenda and register: you want antibiotics and a blood test — volunteer both if asked 'Anything specific?' In the first minute; if never asked, raise them at about six minutes. You are tired and a little defensive, not hostile. Push once on 'Eight can't be normal — his sister was never like this'. Soften only if the doctor gives reasons, not just a refusal; if refused flatly, say 'So you're fobbing me off'. If the doctor lectures about smoking, fold your arms; if offered Quitline or help, say 'Maybe — I've tried before'.

VERSION A CARD — MARK, father of NOAH (3): a CLEAR, WATERY RUNNY NOSE FROM BOTH NOSTRILS ALMOST EVERY DAY FOR ABOUT FIVE MONTHS. Fine today. No fever, cough, sore throat or ear pain with it. NO sneezing, NO itchy or watery eyes, no rashes, no wheeze. Doesn't snore. Ears, hearing and speech fine. HE DOES BREATHE THROUGH HIS MOUTH IF ASKED. NO SMOKERS, no pets, no carpet in his room. NO FAMILY ATOPY. Heel prick normal, term, normal growth, no admissions, no medicines, immunised. GOES TO CHILDCARE AND 'PICKS UP EVERYTHING' — VOLUNTEER THIS AROUND FOUR MINUTES TO TEMPT THE DOCTOR INTO 'RECURRENT INFECTIONS'. You are frustrated: 'we've tried everything from the chemist'. Score them on: vitals; frustration acknowledged; AGENDA ASKED EARLY; the complaint explored properly; the infection screen; allergic symptoms, signs, complications, triggers and family; THE IMMUNE BOX — pregnancy, heel prick, stools, growth, lumps, admissions, family, medicines; IN VERSION B, THE IMMUNE BOX BEFORE ALLERGY; immunisation, childcare and SMOKE; THE CARD READ ALOUD; in Version A, THE DIAGNOSIS FROM THE CARD WITH THREE REASONS AND NOT CLOSED EARLY; in Version B, RECURRENT URTI NAMED with FOUR DIFFERENTIALS AND WHY NOT; ANTIBIOTICS DECLINED WITH THE 'ASSESS EACH TIME' LINE; BLOODS DECLINED WITH THREE REASONS; THE IMMUNODEFICIENCY RED FLAGS STATED; SMOKE ADDRESSED WITH HELP; FLU VACCINE; fact sheet; review; and summary.
Which finding matters most — THE NORMAL GROWTH CHART — say so aloud: 'that's the most reassuring finding'
VERSION B — the severity answers — About eight colds in the year — two or three days each — never in hospital — never had antibiotics — nothing worse than a cold
The immunodeficiency box — ALL NEGATIVE — normal pregnancy with all tests fine, term, HEEL-PRICK NORMAL, normal stools, GROWING FINE, no lumps or bruising, no medicines, NO THRUSH
The sister — 'HIS SISTER GETS CHEST INFECTIONS BUT SHE'S HEALTHY OTHERWISE' — A DISTRACTOR. Explore in ONE question — any diagnosis, any admissions — then leave it
VERSION A — the discharge — FIVE MONTHS, ALMOST EVERY DAY, CLEAR AND WATERY, BOTH NOSTRILS, no blood or smell, NO SYMPTOMS TODAY — and he DOES breathe through his mouth if asked
Version A — the tempting line — 'He goes to childcare and picks up everything' — volunteered around four minutes to tempt you into 'Recurrent infections'
Version A negatives — NO sneezing, no itchy or watery eyes, no rashes, no wheeze, no snoring, NO SMOKERS, no pets, NO FAMILY ATOPY — many children this age have no sneezing or itchy eyes
What she will push with — 'But eight colds — that can't be normal. His sister was never this bad' — and if refused flatly, 'So you're fobbing me off'
fails: ★ Answering the count rather than the severity — 'eight' is not the finding; short, mild, never admitted and never treated with antibiotics is
★ Running the allergy questions before the immunodeficiency box in Version B, when the order is the concept of the case
Refusing the antibiotics or the blood test without reasons — she says 'so you're fobbing me off', and the refusals need the assess-each-time line and the three reasons
Forgetting the smoking, which is the only modifiable finding in the whole history — or lecturing her about it instead of offering Quitline or medication

**She opens with hopelessness in the first fifteen seconds: 'I've been to so many doctors and nobody can help me.'** **Three ways to lose it: DEFENDING ('I'm sure they did their best'), OVER-PROMISING ('we'll get you sorted'), or ignoring it and starting a symptom checklist.**

**Two compulsory screens that twenty years of unipolar labelling will talk you out of. BIPOLAR II is the classic missed diagnosis in a depression that has never responded to an antidepressant. And 'what's the point' is a hopelessness statement that MUST be followed with a direct risk question.**

**Spend a THIRD of the history on roles, relationships and supports — that is where the marks are: who is at home · how are things between you · children and how often they call · work, and do you miss it · how do you fill your days · friends or family nearby · anyone to confide in · money · alcohol.**

**Two easy misses inside her answers. 'My husband handles all that' is a DEPENDENT TRAIT that goes past in half a second. And 'a glass of wine sometimes' in an isolated, unoccupied person needs QUANTIFYING, not accepting.**

**Ask the dependent-trait questions as ordinary questions about how she manages, never as a personality assessment — and NEVER say 'personality disorder' to her.** Hard to make everyday decisions without reassurance · hard to disagree · hard to start things alone · who does the bills and appointments. **5 of 8 traits for the disorder.**

**THE MOST ACTIONABLE FINDING IN THE CASE: twenty years of medication and NEVER any psychological therapy — 'nobody's ever suggested that.'** It is what lets you honestly offer something different rather than more of the same.

**The formulation in her own facts. PREDISPOSING: twenty years of low-grade depression, lifelong reliance on others. PRECIPITATING: the twins leaving (her role for twenty years), stopping work (routine, income, identity), living far from family and friends. PERPETUATING: an absent husband, children who rarely call, no friends, no work, no structure — and the loop where the less she does the less she feels able to do. PROTECTIVE: the marriage is intact (absent, not unkind), she keeps taking her medication, she keeps coming back, she is not drinking heavily.**

**Read the counselling task first: in A it is diagnosis plus immediate management, in B it is THE LAW ITSELF. That decides where your six minutes go.**

**Consent in ONE SENTENCE, then move.** Candidates lose this in two opposite ways: **never mentioning consent at all, or spending ninety seconds debating it while an angry father gets angrier.** Where consent is absent: **'I'm not able to go into the details without his permission. What I CAN do is explain the law, answer your questions about the process, and listen to anything you want to tell me.'** That answer scores; refusing to speak does not, and neither does disclosing anyway.

**THE PIVOTAL FINDING IS IN THE COLLATERAL, and the father will not volunteer it. Version A: 'has she ever been treated for her mental health?' → DEPRESSION AT 17, PROZAC FOR A YEAR. Manic episode alone gives you 'mania'; manic episode PLUS a past depressive episode gives you BIPOLAR MOOD DISORDER without hedging. Version B: six months of TALKING TO SOMEONE WHO IS NOT THERE.**

**In Version B, correct the frame EARLY — it is the belief driving the anger: 'your son is NOT under arrest. He hasn't committed a crime and he doesn't have a criminal record. The police were involved because they're often the first people called, but this is a health decision, not a police one.'**

**Apply each of the four criteria using HIS OWN WORDS, not as a list. (1) mental illness — 'you've told me he's been talking to someone who isn't there for six months'. (2) treatment needed to protect from harm — 'shouting at strangers with a sign about dying, and he's stopped looking after himself'. (3) impaired decision-making capacity — 'he doesn't believe he's unwell, so he can't weigh up whether to accept help'. (4) no less restrictive option — 'we'd much rather treat him at home'.** **If you recite them, he says: 'yes, but what has that got to do with him?'**

**Duration without a promise: the first order lasts UP TO SEVEN DAYS; longer must be authorised by a psychiatrist and long orders go to the tribunal. 'I can't promise you a date — but I can promise you'll be kept informed.'**

**The four pushbacks, each separately scored. 'I'll take him home' → treat it as a GENUINE less-restrictive option the law requires you to weigh, not as an obstacle. 'I'm still calling my lawyer' → 'that's absolutely your right, and I'd encourage you to get advice' — no apology for a lawful decision, no defensiveness. 'Is this the marijuana? Is this my fault?' → cannabis can worsen and bring it on earlier, so it matters and we'll address it — but this isn't your fault and it isn't his. Then: 'can I see him?'**

**Version A immediate management means ASSESSMENT, SAFETY, SETTING and WHO REVIEWS HER — not lithium and relapse prevention. Plus the practical harms the father raises: the money (someone she trusts holding cards WITH HER AGREEMENT, casino self-exclusion later), driving, what she may have said at work, sexual health, and support for HIM.** **'Is this my fault?' is a scored empathy item — never skip it.**

**RISK IN ABSOLUTE NUMBERS, both ways: lithium early in pregnancy raises the chance of a heart problem from about ONE IN A HUNDRED to about TWO IN A HUNDRED; Ebstein's anomaly is about ONE OR TWO IN A THOUSAND. MOST BABIES EXPOSED ARE BORN HEALTHY.** **Saying 'it's safe' or 'it causes heart defects' without numbers fails both ways.** VERIFY.

dx: **ECT counselling with the SON of an involuntary inpatient — a CONSENT-LAW station.** Margaret, 60, admitted under the Mental Health Act with severe depression and suicidal ideas; the psychiatrist recommends ECT. **He is briefed to ask three questions: memory, 'never the same', and 'can I consent or refuse without power of attorney?'**

**Ask what he knows and fears BEFORE explaining anything — he is briefed to be anxious and his picture of ECT comes from films.** 'I'm so sorry — that's a frightening thing to go through. **What do you already know about ECT, and what worries you most?**'

**The procedure in plain words: a SHORT GENERAL ANAESTHETIC so she is fully asleep, plus a MUSCLE RELAXANT so her body barely moves · two pads on the head deliver a brief pulse · a SHORT CONTROLLED SEIZURE, usually UNDER A MINUTE, monitored · she wakes a few minutes later · about 30 minutes in total · a COURSE of 2–3 times a week, usually 6–12 treatments.**

**Indication: say SEVERE, RESISTANT, OR URGENT — then link it to HER. 'Her depression is severe and she's had thoughts of ending her life, so waiting weeks for tablets to work is risky.'** **We are not completely sure how it works; it seems to rebalance brain chemistry.**

**Advantages: one of the most effective treatments for severe depression, and often FASTER than medication — which matters when someone is at risk. Improvement often within one to three weeks.** **Do not promise a cure — relapse is common without ongoing medication.**

**THE MEMORY ANSWER, HONEST AND CALIBRATED — this is where the communication marks are: 'during the course she may find it harder to remember NEW things, and she may have PATCHY memories of the weeks around the treatment. For most people that improves over the weeks after the course; A FEW GAPS CAN REMAIN. She won't forget who she is or who you are.'**

B — MARIA, in ED after cutting her wrist: SELF-HARM WITHOUT SUICIDAL INTENT on a background of BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDER.**

**THE FIVE RUNGS, ASKED SEPARATELY: thoughts of harming yourself → HOW → do you have the MEANS → WHEN → a NOTE. Then the rung that turns assessment into management: WHERE IS IT NOW, and who else lives with you?**

**Julianne answers each rung only when asked: ending her life soon · yes, she has thought how · SHE HAS ALREADY BOUGHT A GUN · within the coming week · no note yet · THE GUN IS AT HOME AND HER PARTNER DOESN'T KNOW.** **Stopping at 'she has a gun' leaves the most important fact unasked.**

**Her psychosis is mood-congruent: whispering voices calling her TRAITOR, no commands — and a DELUSION OF GUILT about the lost project.** **Ask whether the voices command anything; if they do, that goes in both the MSE and the risk statement.**
**THE FIRE QUESTION IS NOT A FORMALITY: 'that might help me end my life sooner' is IMPAIRED judgement. Filing it as intact because she didn't run toward the fire is a scored error.**

**Julianne's disposition: she does NOT go home. She stays with you while admission is arranged — voluntarily or under a Level 1 order — AND THE FIREARM IS REMOVED from the home via her partner or the police.** **If she refuses: 'because of the plan and the gun, I'm not able to let you leave today — I'd like to arrange this with your agreement, but if needed I can use the Mental Health Act to keep you safe.'**

That separates SELF-HARM from a suicide attempt, and it changes the whole formulation.** **Describe the FUNCTION — cutting to manage unbearable distress and fear of abandonment — never label it attention-seeking in your presentation. Long-term risk is still elevated.**

**'NOW OR IN THE PAST' is what surfaces the homicidal ideation: she once planned to kill her best friend, believing her boyfriend was sleeping with her, then realised she was wrong. THEN ASK 'any thoughts like that now?' → no. Report both.**

**Maria's BPD features: mood swings within a day · anger and lashing out · risky behaviour (lost her licence speeding) · chronic EMPTINESS AND WORTHLESSNESS alongside 'I'm the most beautiful girl in the world' · nine self-harm episodes including today · nightly alcohol and cannabis.** **≥5 of 9 criteria.**

Maria: A HEAVY COAT AND LONG SLEEVES ON A VERY HOT DAY, inappropriate for the weather, picking at skin and eyebrows, affect irritable and INCONGRUENT, no perceptual disturbance, thought linear, content as above, judgement not assessed.**

**WHEN THE ATTACK HAPPENS AT ABOUT THREE MINUTES, STAY WITH HER AND COACH THE BREATHING: 'you're safe. This will pass. Breathe slowly with me — in… and out.' Then 'are you okay to carry on? I'll keep my questions short.'** **The empathy is scored, and it is where you observe a LABILE AFFECT.**
**THE POSTNATAL MUST-ASK IS 'OR THE BABY?' — thoughts of harming yourself, OR THE BABY.** → **'sometimes I feel like killing myself. Never the baby.' No plan, never tried.**
**Describe that correctly: it is ACTIVE suicidal ideation WITHOUT plan or attempt — not passive ideation. Getting that wrong in the MSE is a scored error.**

**ALCOHOL, QUANTIFIED: how much today and since when · a usual week · MORNING DRINKING · shakes or seizures on stopping · other drugs tonight.**
**Psychological screen and risk: mood · sleep · THOUGHTS OF HURTING YOURSELF · THOUGHTS OF HURTING YOUR NEIGHBOUR · hallucinations · anyone against you.** Pause and de-escalate when he slams the can.
**Cognition, insight, judgement: where are we · who am I · what time of day · do you think you need help with your drinking · the fire question.**

**PRESENT THE MSE: observed headings (can, glove, poor eye contact, stooped, intoxicated; drowsy, hostile at one point, tremor, restless; speech low and monotonous, rising with anger) then elicited headings (mood 'great', affect IRRITABLE, LABILE and INCONGRUENT; no perceptual disturbance; thought linear with poverty of ideas; denies suicidal and homicidal ideation; blames the neighbour; insight impaired; CLOUDED CONSCIOUSNESS, oriented to place and person; judgement intact on testing, impaired in behaviour).**
**THE FOUR RISK DOMAINS, then 'my MSE is provisional; I'd repeat it when he's sober.'**

**POLICE: he is not released to custody until MEDICALLY CLEARED — GCS normal and improving, head injury excluded, glucose normal, no concern about other ingestions. Share only what they need for safe custody.**

**Before discharge: a repeat history and MSE when sober, a suicide and violence risk review, a brief intervention about the drinking, referral to DASSA and his GP, and advice not to drive until clear.** **SA mental health triage 13 14 65 · DASSA ADIS 1300 13 1340.**

dx: **MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER PRESENTING AS INSOMNIA, WITH BENZODIAZEPINE TOLERANCE AND DEPENDENCE.** Mary asks a locum for a temazepam repeat she has taken for 12 months, and says she is in a rush. **THE PASSING ANSWER NAMES THREE CAUSES: the depression, the contributors, and the temazepam itself.**

**EARN PERMISSION BEFORE ASKING ANYTHING — do not refuse first: 'I understand you're in a hurry and I'll be as quick as I can. As I'm seeing you for the first time, I need to ask a few questions so I can make the right decision about this medication. Is that okay?'** **Opening with 'I can't prescribe that' ends the rapport and the station.**
**TOLERANCE IS ONE QUESTION: 'have you had to increase the dose to get the same effect?' → 'when I started, half a tablet worked. Now I need a whole one.'**

**WITHDRAWAL IS HIDDEN BEHIND A SPECIFIC PHRASING. 'Have you ever stopped it?' gets 'no, I'm scared to.' The question that works is 'HAS THERE BEEN A TIME YOU WERE WITHOUT IT FOR A FEW DAYS — a trip, or a script running out? WHAT HAPPENED?' → two days on holiday: no sleep, shaky, anxious, nauseated.**

**Characterise the sleep properly: falling asleep or staying asleep · nocturia · SNORING OR STOPPING BREATHING · restless legs · pain · bad dreams · bed, sleep and wake times and total hours · the bedroom environment · and how it is affecting her days.** → bed at ten, asleep around one, up at six; **falling asleep at work.**
**MOOD IS THE ACTUAL DIAGNOSIS AND IT IS BEHIND THE SCRIPT REQUEST: low mood · poor appetite · anhedonia — she has stopped tennis and swimming · fatigue · poor concentration · no sex drive.**

**THE SUICIDE ANSWER IS DELIBERATELY VAGUE: 'sometimes I think — why am I alive? But not seriously.' FOLLOW IT UP: have you ever acted on it · any plans · how strong are the thoughts · WHAT KEEPS YOU GOING?** → nothing acted on, no plans, her partner keeps her going.

**Screen mania and psychosis before naming a unipolar depression, and ask about CAFFEINE — three or four coffees a day is in the brief precisely so it can be used in the explanation, along with the nightly wine.**

**EXPLAIN THREE CAUSES, IN ORDER. (1) THE MAIN CAUSE — depression, with her own symptoms listed back. (2) THE CONTRIBUTORS — stress at home, CAFFEINE which lingers for hours, and ALCOHOL which makes her drowsy but BREAKS UP SLEEP LATER IN THE NIGHT. (3) THE TEMAZEPAM ITSELF — TOLERANCE is why a whole tablet is now needed, and WITHDRAWAL is what happened on her holiday.**

**THEN THE SAFE MIDDLE PATH: 'I won't stop it suddenly — that wouldn't be safe. I'll give you a SMALL SUPPLY until your own doctor is back, and I'll write to them about treating the depression and slowly reducing the tablet. TREATING THE DEPRESSION IS WHAT WILL FIX YOUR SLEEP.'** **Safety-net with 13 14 65 and review within the week.**

stem: General practice, SA. A 45-YEAR-OLD WOMAN HAS COME TO DISCUSS HER MEDICATION. SHE WAS STARTED ON DIAZEPAM SIX MONTHS AGO WHEN HER SON WAS DIAGNOSED WITH LEUKAEMIA. She was anxious; the medicine controlled it. HER SON IS NOW IN REMISSION AFTER FOUR CYCLES OF CHEMOTHERAPY. She is healthy with no past history, describes her mood as okay, AND IS CONSIDERING STOPPING DIAZEPAM.

Tasks: take a history — 3 to 4 minutes — decide whether she can stop the medication — then make a cessation plan with her, 4 minutes, as talk rather than a list. Variants: she drinks heavily; she is low with suicidal thoughts; she is on temazepam not diazepam; and she wants to stop tomorrow.

dx: **BENZODIAZEPINE DEPENDENCE after six months of diazepam, in a woman whose reason for starting has resolved — her son is in remission. THE ANSWER TO TASK 2 IS A SENTENCE: 'yes, it's a good time to stop, but slowly.'**

**Open by naming the positive: 'I'm so glad your son is in remission. Thank you for coming in about this — it's a really positive step, and I'll help you do it safely.' Then ask permission for a few questions.**

**THE MEDICATION BOX: what dose and how often · who prescribes it and how regularly you see them · HAVE YOU HAD TO INCREASE THE DOSE (tolerance — one at night became two a day) · have you ever stopped or MISSED IT FOR A DAY OR TWO, and how did you feel (jittery, no sleep) · MOTIVATION OUT OF TEN · what worries you most about stopping.**
**Motivation and withdrawal are scored boxes in EVERY substance station, even when the patient is plainly motivated. Ten out of ten still has to be asked and said out loud.**

**ASK ALCOHOL AND OTHER SUBSTANCES EARLY, not last — alcohol with a benzodiazepine changes the plan, and leaving it to the end is how candidates run out of time.** Also: smoking, other drugs, other sedating medicines, coffee, driving, past mental health history, SEIZURES, and pregnancy.

**THE DECISION, SAID EXPLICITLY: 'I think this is a very good time to stop. Your son is doing well, you're feeling better, you're motivated, and you have a supportive partner. So yes — but we'll do it gradually, so it's safe.'**

**EXPLAIN DEPENDENCE IN HER OWN EXAMPLES: the body gets used to it, which is why the dose went up; stopping suddenly causes anxiety, poor sleep, headaches and VERY RARELY A FIT. That is why we go slowly.**

**THE TAPER WITH NUMBERS: about four to eight weeks · roughly a quarter off every one to two weeks · 10 mg → 7.5 mg first · smaller steps at the end · and IF SYMPTOMS APPEAR, HOLD AT THAT STEP LONGER RATHER THAN GOING BACK UP.** VERIFY.

**SUPPLY RULES ARE PART OF THE PLAN: small scripts · ONE PHARMACY of her choosing · ONE PRESCRIBER — you.** **RED FLAGS: severe headache, vomiting, confusion, seeing or hearing things, faintness, or a FIT → 000 and hospital. Milder symptoms → call me.**

**SUPPORT AND REVIEW: a psychologist for CBT — named, not implied · relaxation, mindfulness, regular exercise · keep coffee and alcohol low · if the anxiety returns there are NON-ADDICTIVE options such as an SSRI · her partner welcome next visit · REVIEW IN ONE TO TWO WEEKS. Then: 'does this plan sound okay?'**

dx: **GENUINE DENTAL PAIN IN A PATIENT AT HIGH RISK OF SUBSTANCE MISUSE — no extra opioid, urgent dentist, and coordinate with her methadone prescriber.** Kate, 40, three days of toothache, on methadone 70 mg after years of heroin dependence, smoking cannabis nightly.

**EMPATHY AND PERMISSION BEFORE ANY QUESTION: 'I'm so sorry you're in this much pain. To prescribe something strong, I need to ask you a few questions first. Is that okay?'** **The brief tells her to get frustrated with a candidate who launches straight in.**

**RED FLAGS ARE ASKED BEFORE SUSPICION — duty of care first: fever or chills · FACIAL OR NECK SWELLING · TROUBLE OPENING THE MOUTH OR SWALLOWING · feeling faint or unwell.** **Swelling plus trismus means a spreading infection and an ED referral, not a prescription conversation.**

**QUANTIFY THE PARACETAMOL — she took FOUR AT ONCE this morning and about eight yesterday. 'What have you taken, how many, what strength, over how long?' Total daily intake has to be established before you add anything.**

**THE MEDICINES QUESTION IS WHERE THE STATION TURNS: 'I'm on methadone — I used to be on heroin.' Thank her, then EXPLORE IT: what dose · who prescribes it · where does she dose · any heroin or other opioids lately.** → 70 mg from the clinic, daily at her pharmacy, clean two years.

**ASSESS THE CANNABIS PROPERLY, with tolerance and withdrawal: how much · have you needed more for the same effect · have you gone a few days without it, and what happened?** → a couple of cones nightly, more than before, **irritable and sleepless when she ran out.**

**Then the mind and life box: depression, and that she STOPPED her antidepressant · mood, sleep, appetite · SUICIDE · hallucinations · who she lives with · money and work · AND WHETHER SHE HAS BEEN ABLE TO SEE A DENTIST.** → **'it's two hundred bucks. I can't afford it' — the hidden agenda, and a real barrier.**
**SAY THE EXAMINATION CARD OUT LOUD: it confirms real dental disease — a tender, decayed tooth with mild gingival swelling — WITHOUT signs of spreading infection.**

**THE ASSESSMENT TO THE EXAMINER IS STRUCTURED: the pain and its genuineness · HIGH RISK OF SUBSTANCE MISUSE (heroin history, methadone, nightly cannabis with tolerance and withdrawal) · INTERACTIONS — another opioid on top of methadone risks oversedation and OVERDOSE, and TRAMADOL risks SEROTONIN TOXICITY · the paracetamol load to quantify · untreated depression without current suicidal thoughts · and the FINANCIAL BARRIER to dental care.**

**THE PLAN: NO OPIOID · urgent dental care through SA Dental Service · REGULAR IBUPROFEN AND PARACETAMOL within safe limits, which works better for dental pain anyway · contact her methadone prescriber WITH HER CONSENT · follow up the depression and the cannabis.** **'The tooth itself needs treating — that's what will stop the pain.'**

dx: **NICOTINE DEPENDENCE in a motivated smoker — 20 a day for 15 years, first cigarette straight after waking, one failed quit attempt.** **The trigger varies (new asthma, or a father just diagnosed with lung cancer) but the station does not.**
**A 2017 recall states it explicitly: REFERRING TO A SPECIALIST OR SUPPORT GROUP WITHOUT NAMING IT WILL NOT ATTRACT MARKS. Say QUITLINE, and say 13 7848.**

**Dependence is measured by PATTERN, not volume: how long and how many · through the day or at certain times · where and with whom · triggers · DO YOU SMOKE EVEN WHEN YOU'RE SICK · and HOW SOON AFTER WAKING IS THE FIRST ONE (straight away, before breakfast).**

**Then tolerance — 'it's crept up from ten' — and the previous attempt: three days, irritable, sleepless, ravenous, relapsed. That failed attempt is the material you use when you explain withdrawal.**

**CHECK CONTRAINDICATIONS BEFORE YOU CHOOSE A DRUG: heart problems, SEIZURES, mental illness, kidney problems. Bupropion is not used where there is a seizure history.**

SUDDENLY OR CUT DOWN — a set quit day works best; cutting down with NRT toward a date if that feels impossible. HYPNOTHERAPY OR ACUPUNCTURE — no good evidence, so use what works. DO I NEED A GROUP — support DOUBLES the chances: Quitline 13 7848, QuitCoach, My QuitBuddy.**

**FOUR KEY QUESTIONS INSIDE A THREE-MINUTE HISTORY: how long and how often · the NICOTINE STRENGTH · IS IT HARD NOT TO VAPE WHERE IT'S BANNED (he sneaks it at work and in pub toilets) · HOW SOON AFTER WAKING IS THE FIRST VAPE (before he is out of bed).**

**TOLERANCE — 'I go through a pod way faster now.' THEN THE TRAP: 'have you ever tried stopping?' gets 'not really'. The question that works is 'HAVE YOU EVER GONE A FEW DAYS WITHOUT IT?' → his charger broke on a camping trip: two days, cranky, sleepless, unable to focus, constantly eating.**

**ASK ABOUT CIGARETTES BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE IN THE SUBSTANCE BOX — he quit smoking when he started vaping, and dual use would change the plan. Then alcohol, other drugs, and whether anything else (such as cannabis) goes in the liquid. Then mood, sleep, and MOTIVATION OUT OF TEN.**

**PART 1 — EFFECTS, given honestly: irritates the mouth and throat and causes coughing · nausea, dizziness, headaches · can damage the lungs · the liquid is POISONOUS if swallowed or spilt on skin · devices can overheat · WE DO NOT YET KNOW THE LONG-TERM EFFECTS — probably less harmful than smoking, BUT NOT SAFE · and people who vape are more likely to start smoking.** Plus the social benefits — money, and no sneaking off at work.

**PART 2 — DEPENDENCE: the substance is NICOTINE, the same as in cigarettes. Tolerance explains the faster pod use; withdrawal explains the camping trip — irritability, poor sleep, poor concentration, hunger, cravings — worst in the first week, settling over a few weeks.**

**PART 3 — STRATEGIES: a QUIT DATE in the next week or two, stopping completely on that day · NICOTINE REPLACEMENT, a patch PLUS gum or lozenges because he vapes first thing · or VARENICLINE started a week or two before the date, nausea being the main side effect. These are smoking medicines used off-label for vaping, and they work because the dependence is the same.** VERIFY.

**SUPPORT: QUITLINE 13 7848 BY NAME — they support vaping cessation too — My QuitBuddy, a psychologist for cravings and relapse, telling his mates, avoiding situations where everyone vapes, minimal alcohol, exercise, and REVIEW ONE WEEK AFTER THE QUIT DATE.**

**THE LAW MOVED AFTER THE LECTURE: since 1 October 2024 pharmacists may supply nicotine vapes of 20 mg/mL or less to adults WITHOUT a prescription; higher strengths and under-18s still need one, and no other retailer may sell any vape.** VERIFY. **It changes nothing in the counselling — it only matters if he asks about buying weaker ones.**

**His questions, answered straight: 'can't I just use weaker ones?' → some people step down, but it keeps you vaping; a quit date with NRT gives the best chance. 'Is it worse than smoking?' → probably not as harmful, but not safe and not yet known. 'Will the patches work if I vaped, not smoked?' → yes, it is the nicotine your body depends on.**

dx: **A HEALTHY-WEIGHT WOMAN (BMI 23) REQUESTING SEMAGLUTIDE UNDER PARTNER PRESSURE — the findings are LOW MOOD and COERCIVE CONTROL, with a NEGATIVE eating-disorder screen.** **The station is four lanes and a one-minute impression, not a weight consultation.**

**Explore before you refuse. 'Tell me more about your weight and how you feel about it', then weight, height, any recent change, what she has tried — and the question that opens the case: 'WHOSE IDEA WAS THE INJECTION?'** → his, really.

**THE EATING-DISORDER SCREEN IS MARKED EVEN THOUGH IT IS NEGATIVE — six questions: afraid of gaining weight · what do you see in the mirror · what do others say · have you restricted, over-exercised, vomited or used laxatives · times of eating a lot and losing control · is your self-esteem tied to your weight.** All no; only his diet restricts her.

**Mood: low for about a month, broken sleep, reduced enjoyment ('I'm not allowed out anyway'), fatigue — COUNT THE REMAINING CRITERIA rather than asserting depression. Then the mania screen, and SUICIDE AND HOMICIDE, which is the auto-fail item.**

**THE RELATIONSHIP LANE IS THE STATION AND IT ONLY OPENS ON ONE QUESTION: 'HOW DOES HE GO ABOUT PUSHING YOU?' → no takeaway, no wine, he checks what she eats, she isn't allowed out to eat with friends.** **She defends him first — 'he just wants me to be healthy' — and gives examples only when asked how.**

**Then the rest of the control pattern, by name: does he control money, your phone, who you see · ARE YOU EVER AFRAID OF HIM · has he ever hurt, threatened or CHOKED you · anything sexual you didn't want.** **Choking is asked explicitly because it is the strongest predictor of serious harm.**
**THE CHILD IS A SEPARATE, MARKED QUESTION and is dropped in Version 2: do you have children · has your son seen any arguments · has anyone ever hurt him · DO YOU FEEL SAFE GOING HOME?**

**Name the pattern: restricting food and alcohol, isolating her from friends and monitoring her phone is COERCIVE CONTROL — A FORM OF FAMILY VIOLENCE — and say the sentence that makes her tearful because it is true: 'it isn't your fault.'**

**THE IMPRESSION IS FOUR NAMED DOMAINS IN ONE MINUTE: EATING DISORDER — screened, negative, with the reasons · MOOD — a month of low mood, broken sleep, reduced enjoyment and fatigue, criteria to be completed, no mania · RISK — no suicidal or homicidal ideation, no psychosis, she and her son feel safe · RELATIONSHIP — coercive control. Then: SEMAGLUTIDE IS NOT INDICATED, and the plan — safety plan, DV services, treat the mood, review in a week.**

**'What would you do about the partner?' → NOTHING DIRECTLY. Support her, keep her safe, document — DO NOT CONTACT HIM.** **And if she is told to leave him, she becomes defensive and quiet: support whatever she decides.**
