dx: **SEVERE SELF-NEGLECT in a homeless 40-year-old with an ULCER HE CANNOT SEE — brought in after a fall while a dog chased him.** **Every psychiatric screen is NEGATIVE: mood fine, sleep fine, no suicidal or homicidal thoughts, no hallucinations, no delusions, oriented, recalls three words. The abnormality is that a man has a large leg ulcer he was unaware of.**

**SELF-NEGLECT IS A PRESENTATION, NOT A DIAGNOSIS. Go looking for the cause: schizophrenia · depression · dementia or alcohol-related brain damage · delirium · head injury · PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY, most often diabetic.**
**'WHICH WOUND?' IS THE FINDING. Do not move past it — pause and say it out loud: 'there's a large wound on your lower leg. YOU WEREN'T AWARE OF IT?' → no, and he doesn't know how he got it.**

**SCREEN COGNITION even though this is framed as a psychosocial history: today's date, where we are, three words to recall later, and any memory trouble. He gets all of it right — which is itself a finding, because it points away from dementia and delirium and toward neuropathy or neglect.**

**THE PSYCHOSOCIAL CORE: where are you living · WHERE DO YOU SLEEP · how long · HOW DO YOU GET MONEY AND FOOD · any family or friends · what do you do in the day?** → no place, parks, a few years, Centrelink, **eats what he finds**, no one, walks around.
**HEALTH NEGLECT IS A SEPARATE BOX: any medical problems · tablets · WHY DID YOU STOP THEM ('I feel OK') · when did you last see a GP (years) · any diabetes · NUMB FEET · alcohol, drugs, smoking.**

**Then the full psychiatric screen with the negatives stated: mood · sleep · SUICIDE AND HARM TO OTHERS · hallucinations · anyone trying to harm you. Saying the negatives out loud is what shows you looked.**
**TEST INSIGHT PROPERLY, because 'I'm OK, doc' is not insight: 'WHY DO YOU THINK THE WOUND GOT THIS BAD?' · 'do you think you need treatment?' · 'IF YOU WENT BACK OUT TODAY, WHAT WOULD HAPPEN?'**

**THE PLAN NAMES THE THREE PROBLEMS AND ADMITS HIM: a serious wound he was unaware of · stopped antihypertensives · no safe place to live. Then: daily cleaning and dressing · BLOODS INCLUDING INFECTION MARKERS AND DIABETES · a test of the leg circulation (ABI) · an X-ray if deep · restart the blood pressure treatment · A MENTAL HEALTH REVIEW · and a SOCIAL WORKER for housing, money and food.**

**HANDLE 'I DON'T WANT TO STAY' WITHOUT THREATENING: 'I hear you, and I don't want to keep you here against your will. But I'm really worried this wound could become badly infected. COULD YOU STAY TONIGHT so we can make a start? If you tried to leave, I'd need to talk with the team about how to keep you safe — sometimes that means using the Mental Health Act for a short time, and a psychiatrist would review that quickly.'** **He agrees to 'tonight' only if you are warm and explain why.**

stem: A four-minute video of a 30-year-old man. Background: a motor vehicle accident five years ago with two weeks in a coma, prolonged neurological rehabilitation, he stopped working, and he now drinks five beers a day. He presents after a fight in a pub, triggered by someone calling him 'Psycho'.

Tasks: talk to his father and explain why he has had this change in behaviour. You are explicitly told not to give a diagnosis or management — the marks are the predisposing, precipitating and protective factors. Variants: the angry father; the guilty father; 'Is he going to be charged?'; and the online format, where a history comes first and the formulation goes to the examiner.

dx: **A FORMULATION STATION, NOT A DIAGNOSIS STATION. You are told explicitly NOT to give a diagnosis or a management plan — the marks are PREDISPOSING, PRECIPITATING and PROTECTIVE factors, explained to the father in plain words.** A 30-year-old man five years after a motor vehicle accident with two weeks in a coma, now drinking five beers a day, after a pub fight triggered by being called 'psycho'.

**LEARN THE FRAMEWORK, NOT THE CASE. The five Ps: PRESENTING (the complaint) · PREDISPOSING (the past) · PRECIPITATING (the trigger) · PERPETUATING (what keeps it going) · PROTECTIVE (the strengths). Any station can ask for the formulation.**

**CONFIRM THE RELATIONSHIP AND THE PERMISSION BEFORE A SINGLE CLINICAL DETAIL: 'can I confirm your name and your relationship to him? He has agreed that I can talk with you about his care — is that your understanding?'**

**START FROM HIM, NOT FROM YOU: 'what have you been told so far?' and 'WHAT HAS WORRIED YOU MOST about the changes you've seen in him?' Talking for two minutes before asking a question loses the communication marks.**

**TAKE COLLATERAL — it is where the formulation's evidence comes from: when did you first notice the change · WHAT'S HE LIKE ON A GOOD DAY · how much do you think he's drinking · has anything like this happened before?** → about a year after the accident, 'the old him' on a good day, a carton lasting two days, never violent before.

**PREDISPOSING, IN PLAIN WORDS AND NO JARGON: a severe head injury with two weeks in a coma — 'an injury like that can change how the brain manages MEMORY, MOOD AND TEMPER', which the father has seen as forgetfulness and a short fuse · not working since, which removes routine, income and confidence · and heavy daily drinking, which makes all of it worse.** **Never say 'frontal disinhibition', 'organic' or 'cognitive deficits'.**

**PRECIPITATING: the beliefs he currently holds that people are against him or talking about him, and then the insult — 'someone called him psycho, and TO HIM THAT WASN'T JUST A RUDE WORD, IT FELT LIKE A THREAT. That, with the alcohol, was the spark.'**

**PROTECTIVE FACTORS ARE MARKED AND ARE THE MOST COMMONLY OMITTED: he has a father who cares and came straight in · he WORKED HARD AT REHABILITATION BEFORE, so we know he can engage with help · and he has no other serious illness.** **Name the father explicitly.**

**WHEN HE PRESSES FOR THE DIAGNOSIS — and he will, twice — neither invent one nor stonewall: 'that's exactly the right question, and the psychiatry team will answer it properly once they've assessed him. What I CAN tell you today is what seems to have contributed — the head injury, the alcohol, losing his work, and the beliefs he's having at the moment.'**

**CHUNK AND CHECK TWICE, AND SAY IT ISN'T ANYONE'S FAULT — not his, and not the father's.** **'Will he get better?' → no promises and no guesses before assessment, but people do improve with support, and cutting back the drinking makes a real difference to memory and temper.**

stem: General practice. A community disability worker attends to discuss his client and to collect a repeat prescription. The client, Travis, has epileptic seizures and takes carbamazepine and sodium valproate. He had a motor vehicle accident at age 12 resulting in an acquired brain injury. The worker reports a recent change in behaviour.

Tasks: take a history from the disability worker — the bulk of the station — then explain the possible causes of the change in behaviour, and explain your supportive management. Variants: the carer discloses a concern about another staff member; a toxicity picture; and the friend who moved out.

dx: **A CHANGE IN BEHAVIOUR IN A MAN WITH ACQUIRED BRAIN INJURY AND EPILEPSY — and the station does NOT ask for a diagnosis. The marks are the BREADTH of the differential and the decision to INVESTIGATE AND SEE HIM.**

**CONFIRM THE LEGAL CARER AND CONSENT BEFORE ANY CLINICAL DETAIL: 'can I confirm that you are Travis's legal carer and have consent to discuss his health with me?' Discussing him first is an auto-fail.**

**A NEW BEHAVIOUR HAS A NEW CAUSE. Describe it properly: what do you mean by a change · when did it start · constant or intermittent · getting worse · WERE THERE ANY EVENTS OR CHANGES BEFORE IT STARTED · HOW IS IT AFFECTING HIS USUAL LEVEL OF FUNCTION · anything better or worse?** → six weeks, worse, **his housemate Joe moved out last month**, and he now needs prompting to dress.

**EPILEPSY AND MEDICATION: is he taking his tablets regularly (REFUSING THEM FOR WEEKS) · when was his last seizure (a fortnight ago, first in a year) · any long vacant or confused episodes · dose changes or new medicines · drowsiness, unsteadiness, tremor · recent WEIGHT GAIN.**

**THE SYSTEMIC SCREEN IS THE STATION, BECAUSE HE CANNOT REPORT SYMPTOMS: pain — TEETH, ears, tummy (he rubs his jaw) · weight loss, lumps, low energy · fever, chills, rash · pain or smell on passing urine · CONSTIPATION (he strains) · DRINKING OR PASSING MORE URINE (he's been drinking a lot of water) · weather preference · falls or injuries.**

**THEN THE ABUSE QUESTION, ASKED PLAINLY AND WITHOUT ACCUSING: 'I ask this of everyone — is there any chance he could have been physically or sexually harmed, by anyone at the house, another resident or a visitor?' → the carer hesitates, then mentions A NEW CASUAL WORKING NIGHTS.** **If he takes it personally: 'I'm not suggesting anything about you or your team — you're the one who noticed and brought him in.'**

**PSYCHIATRIC SCREEN IN THIRD-PARTY PHRASING: mood · sleep, with the type · appetite and weight · still enjoying what he used to (he has STOPPED HIS MUSIC and his garden program) · HAS HE EVER HARMED HIMSELF OR ANYONE ELSE · does he seem to see or hear things that aren't there.**

**SOCIAL: family visits (mother and sister interstate, not for over a year) · FRIENDS AT THE HOUSE AND WHETHER ANYONE HAS MOVED OUT · how he gets on with his carers · work or programs · alcohol, drugs, smoking.**

**GIVE THE CAUSES AS A LIST, NOT A GUESS, and never as 'the brain injury': PHYSICAL — dental or other pain, urinary or dental infection, constipation, thyroid disease, DIABETES (fits the weight gain and thirst) · MEDICATION — he has stopped his anticonvulsants, which affects seizures, mood and thinking · SOMETHING THAT HAS UPSET OR FRIGHTENED HIM, including being hurt or treated badly · MENTAL HEALTH — depression or anxiety, which in someone who cannot explain himself shows as behaviour, especially with no family visits and Joe gone.**

**MANAGEMENT IS TEST, SEE HIM, AND SAFEGUARD: bloods — FBE, CRP, UEC with sodium, LFT, TSH, glucose or HbA1c, AND ANTICONVULSANT LEVELS — plus urine · SEE AND EXAMINE TRAVIS THIS WEEK (teeth, ears, chest, abdomen, skin) · restart medication with support and involve neurology about the seizure · psychologist for mood, psychiatry advice before any new medicine · a video meeting with his mother and sister · AND ADDRESS THE SAFETY QUESTION ABOUT THE NIGHT STAFF.** **Do the repeat scripts, but do not let them be the only thing that happens.**

stem: The four history steps: introduction under 45 seconds — explore the pain with CICORA, finished — the differential sweep, one specific question each — then a good closure. Step 3 is the only thing that separates you: everyone does an open question, CICORA and a closure.

The order within step 3: your provisional diagnosis first, with every key point — five or six questions over two minutes, no apology — then the space-occupying lesion red flags in full — then the rest of the list, one question each. Do not run a head-to-toe list of associated symptoms: an examiner marking forty candidates a day recognises it instantly, and a medical student can do it.

dx: **One headache structure for every headache station** — acute or chronic, adult or adolescent. The context of the case makes minor changes; it does not make a second structure.

**Three things pass this station: differentials, structure, key points.** ‘Infections’ earns nothing — **meningitis, sinusitis, dental abscess** earns three ticks. As many as you can, as specific as you can, and all of them good.
**Step 1 — intro, under 45 seconds.** Vitals at the door (**blood pressure, pulse, temperature, respiratory rate**), open question then **stop talking**, acknowledge the concern once, promise a plan.

**Step 2 — CICORA, finished**: **site · intensity out of ten · character · onset, pattern and progression · radiation · aggravating and relieving · affect on life.** In **nine out of ten** headache stations the provisional diagnosis falls out here. The exception is **giant cell arteritis**, where CICORA gives you nothing.

**Step 3 is the only thing that separates you** — everyone does an open question, CICORA and a closure. Order within it: **provisional diagnosis key points first** (five or six questions, **two minutes, no apology**) → **space-occupying lesion red flags in full** → the rest of the list, **one specific question each**.

**Step 4 — closure**: past medical history then family history; **SADMA last and least.** If you run out of time before SADMA you have lost nothing — anything in it that mattered was already asked as a key point.

**The thirteen, in memorised order**: **space-occupying lesion · migraine · tension-type · cluster · trigeminal neuralgia · subarachnoid haemorrhage · other intracranial haemorrhage · benign intracranial hypertension · meningitis, encephalitis, abscess · sinusitis · dental · cervicogenic · glaucoma.** Plus **TMJ dysfunction, medication-overuse headache**, and **giant cell arteritis only if over 50**.

**Glaucoma, not refractive error.** By the time you reach the eye you have asked about vision four times — for tumour, aura, arteritis and deficit. **‘Have you had a red eye?’** is a question you have not asked, and it is specific.

**Diagnosis in 90 seconds, three moves**: name it, explain it in five seconds, **reason it from your key points** → **answer the stated concern by name, with the negatives** → reason three or four differentials, then **list the rest until the bell.** Every named condition is a tick; an eloquent explanation of differential two is two ticks you did not collect.

**Context switches**: over 50 → add giant cell arteritis · sudden and severe → subarachnoid to the top · fever → meningitis and encephalitis · young woman, raised BMI, acne treatment → benign intracranial hypertension · any fall at any age → intracranial haemorrhage, chronic subdural in the elderly · under 25 → drop arteritis.

**‘Examiner, before I start — can you tell me the blood pressure, pulse rate, temperature and respiratory rate?’** One sentence, before you sit down.
**‘Hello, I’m one of the doctors here. How can I help you today?’** Then **stop talking** and let the opening statement land.

Address the concern — this is where approach-to-patient is scored: **‘I understand why that is worrying you. Let me ask you some questions, examine you, and we’ll work out the cause together and make a plan. Does that sound alright?’** Then **‘are you in any pain now?’** — almost always no.

**CICORA, finished.** **‘Show me where it is — one side or both?’ · ‘Out of ten, ten being the worst pain of your life?’ · ‘Throbbing or pulsating, or dull, or sharp?’ · ‘How long? On and off or constant? Getting worse?’ · ‘Does it travel anywhere?’ · ‘Anything make it better or worse?’ · ‘How is it affecting your life?’** The **progression** question is the one that gets skipped.
**Key points of the provisional diagnosis** — five or six questions, two minutes, **no apology for the depth**. Knowing the recall is not the same as asking the key points.

**Space-occupying lesion red flags, probing depth, every one**: **‘Any weight loss? Loss of appetite? Lumps or bumps? Feeling tired?’ · ‘Does the pain wake you at night?’ · ‘Any early-morning headache with vomiting?’ · ‘Any blurring of vision? Weakness? Numbness or pins and needles? Trouble walking?’ · ‘Is it worse when you cough, sneeze or bend forward?’**

**The sweep — one specific question each.** Tension: **home and work separately**. Meningitis: **fever, sore neck, rash**. Subarachnoid: **sudden onset, worst ever**. Cluster: **watery eye or runny nose on that side**. Trigeminal: **set off by talking, smiling, shaving, touching the cheek**. Sinusitis: **secretions down the back of the throat**. Dental: **toothache, last dentist**. BIH and overuse: **medications, painkiller days a month**. Haemorrhage: **injury, trauma or fall**. Glaucoma: **red eye**. Cervicogenic: **neck pain**.

PMHx, then FHx, **SADMA last**. Never ask SADMA twice — under stress it becomes a comfort ritual, and those are the seconds that were meant for the aura question.
Bell → +2:00

**PEFE, hard stop at 2:00.** General appearance → **all four vitals** → cranial nerves → **fundoscopy asked separately** → limbs → neck → **ENT and dental** → chest and heart in ten seconds. A thin examination does not fail; running past the bell does.
Last 90s

**Name it and reason it → answer the stated concern with its negatives → three reasoned differentials, then list the rest.** Never two diagnoses, never a scan to reassure, never ‘infections’ as a differential.

**Headache core = neurological examination + ENT + neck.** Most candidates forget the ENT.
General appearance in a headache case: **alert or drowsy · any rash · any ptosis · if over 50, a visible or thickened temporal artery.**

Cranial nerves, in these words: **‘are the pupils symmetrical and the light reflexes normal? Are the eye movements full? Is sensation over the three divisions of the face normal? Are the facial movements symmetrical?’** — pupils, III/IV/VI together, trigeminal, facial. Skip the rest.

**Fundoscopy, always, and asked separately: ‘do I see any papilloedema?’** The single highest-yield request in the cluster. Asked inside ‘cranial nerves’ you will simply be told ‘normal’ and lose the finding.
Limbs: **power in the myotomes, sensation, and the reflexes.** Reflexes and coordination if time; **skip tone and inspection**.
Neck: **tenderness over the spinous processes or paraspinal muscles · painful movements · neck stiffness** — cervicogenic, spondylosis, metastasis, and meningism.

**ENT and dental — the part almost everyone drops**: **‘any dental caries, or redness and swelling of the gums? Any post-nasal drip? Is there sinus tenderness?’** Three questions, fifteen seconds, three differentials closed.
Office tests: **blood glucose and dipstick are not relevant and earn ‘unavailable’ and no marks.** A **urine pregnancy test** is defensible in a woman of reproductive age.

**Conditional add-ons only on a positive finding** — meningism → **Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s**; over 50 → **temporal tenderness, thickened or pulseless artery, girdle tenderness**; raised pressure → fundoscopy, then **blood pressure and pulse again for a Cushing response**. CORRECTION — polymyalgia rheumatica is often taught as ‘proximal myopathy’. It causes **pain-limited movement with preserved power**, not true weakness. If pressed: **‘I would expect tenderness and restriction from pain, with power preserved — true weakness would make me think of an inflammatory myopathy instead.’**

dx: **Migraine with aura in a 30-year-old woman** — recurrent unilateral throbbing headache, **4–72 hours** untreated, worse on routine activity, with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia, relieved by sleep in a dark quiet room, triggers and a family history. VERIFY

**The stem is deliberately bare** — no timeline, no severity, nothing acute or chronic — precisely so the whole diagnosis has to come out of your history. **Build the history, do not chase the recall.**

**Aura is present in around one third** of migraine sufferers; typically **5–60 minutes**, resolving as the headache begins. VERIFY Do not let the aura answer contaminate the red-flag vision answer — **clarify which one she means.**

The reasoning sentence: **‘Most likely you have migraine, and specifically migraine with aura. It happens because of changes in the blood vessels and nerves of the brain. I’m saying that because your headache is one-sided and throbbing, you get flashing lights before it starts, you’re sensitive to light and noise, you feel sick with it, wine sets it off, and your mother had the same thing.’**

**Aura plus the combined oral contraceptive pill is the management point of the whole station** — migraine with aura raises ischaemic stroke risk and the combined pill compounds it. **Stop the pill today** and replace the method. VERIFY

Acute attack: **aspirin or ibuprofen or paracetamol, taken early and at an adequate dose**, plus an **antiemetic — metoclopramide or an ondansetron wafer**, which also improves absorption of the analgesic. If that fails, a **triptan (sumatriptan, rizatriptan)** as tablet, wafer or nasal spray. VERIFY

**Avoid opioids and codeine-containing compounds** — they worsen nausea and drive overuse. **Cap acute analgesia below roughly 15 days a month** (10 for triptans or combination analgesics) to prevent medication-overuse headache. VERIFY

**No imaging, and say why**: **‘a scan wouldn’t tell us anything your story and examination haven’t already told us. If any of those warning signs appear, we scan the same day.’** Ordering an MRI to reassure teaches her the scan, not your assessment, is the answer.

Non-drug and prevention: **headache diary — date, duration, what she ate, what she was doing, medication taken**; identify and avoid the triggers it actually shows; dark quiet room, ice pack, gentle neck stretches; **sleep regularity, meals, hydration, graded aerobic exercise**. Prevention at roughly **4 or more disabling attacks a month**: **propranolol, amitriptyline, candesartan or topiramate**. VERIFY

**The commonest headache in the population, and the commonest headache the AMC dresses up as something frightening.** At most **one** of photophobia or phonophobia, and **no vomiting** — or it is not tension-type. VERIFY
**The discriminating issue is answering the brother out loud, with reasons, before he asks.** Reassurance without reasons is not reassurance; it is a guess the patient is asked to trust.

The sentence that wins it: **‘Jacob, you came in worried about a brain tumour, so let me answer that directly. I do not think you have one, and these are my reasons: the headache doesn’t wake you at night, you have no early-morning headache or vomiting, no weight loss or appetite change, no weakness, numbness or change in vision, and it doesn’t get worse when you cough or bend. Your neurological examination is completely normal, and I looked into the back of your eyes — the pressure signs we’d expect with a tumour are not there.’**

Then commit: **‘What I think you do have is a tension-type headache — a stress-related headache, where the muscles of the scalp and neck tighten up. I’m saying that because it’s on both sides, it’s a dull tightening ache rather than a throbbing one, it’s four or five out of ten, it runs down into your neck, paracetamol helps, and it started when work got very stressful.’**

**Name the trigger as the treatment target — the work stress, not the headache.** Address the stressor: workload, hours, and **the bullying if it is disclosed**. Screening for it and then not acting on it is worse than never asking.

Management: **simple analgesia used sparingly** VERIFY · sleep, regular meals, hydration, aerobic exercise, **screen and posture breaks** · **physiotherapy or neck and shoulder stretching** if there is a postural component · **psychological therapy and a mental health treatment plan** if indicated VERIFY · **cap analgesia below roughly 15 days a month** VERIFY · **review in 4–6 weeks with a headache diary**.

**No imaging, and justify it**: a normal neurological examination, no red flags and no papilloedema. **‘A scan wouldn’t tell us anything your story and examination haven’t already told us, and a normal scan wouldn’t stop the headaches.’**
**Never the word ‘just’.** ‘It’s just tension’ dismisses six months of real pain, and reads as dismissal to both the patient and the examiner.

**Four tasks in eight minutes: roughly 4:00 history · 1:30 examination · 1:15 diagnosis and differentials · 1:15 management.** The station is failed by the clock, not by the medicine — **if you never say the word ‘hospital’, the first three tasks do not matter.**
**AMC role-players rarely say ‘I have a fever’. They say ‘I’ve been feeling hot’.** The moment you hear it, move straight into the meningitis block.
**Exclude the bleed first — two questions and ten seconds**: not sudden in onset, not the worst headache of her life. **Saying that out loud is a mark.**

Management, **starting with the disposition**: **‘Amanda, I’m not able to let you go home. **Notifiable.** Invasive meningococcal and pneumococcal disease are notifiable in South Australia; **clearance antibiotics for household and intimate contacts are arranged through the public health unit.** VERIFY Audiology follow-up after pneumococcal meningitis. VERIFY

dx: **Delirium caused by viral encephalitis — herpes simplex until proven otherwise.** **Name both layers.** The syndrome the father watched is **delirium: an acute change in mental state with confusion and disordered behaviour.** The cause is **encephalitis — inflammation of the brain tissue itself.** Saying only ‘encephalitis’ leaves him without a name for what he actually saw.

**This looks like an infectious-diseases case and is scored as a communication case.** The medicine is straightforward; the marks are in **consent, pacing, plain language, checking understanding, and honesty about implications without minimising or catastrophising.**

**The one-sentence explanation: ‘Meningitis is the covering of the brain. Encephalitis is the brain tissue itself. That’s why his neck isn’t stiff.’** Explain the absent neck stiffness rather than ignoring it.

**IV aciclovir empirically — started now, not when the PCR returns.** VERIFY Say it early and unprompted: **‘we’ve already started the antiviral — we haven’t waited for the final virus test, because starting early makes a real difference to the outcome. If the test comes back negative, we’ll stop it.’**

Add **empirical antibacterial cover until bacterial meningitis is excluded** if there is any doubt. VERIFY **Blood cultures, FBC, UEC, LFT, glucose, coagulation profile.** Manage the seizure: **airway, oxygen, a benzodiazepine if it recurs, a loading antiepileptic if seizures continue.** VERIFY

Translating the CSF rather than reciting it: **‘there are more white cells than there should be, and nine out of ten are the type that go up with a virus rather than a bacterium. The sugar is normal and the protein only slightly raised — again a viral picture.’** Bacterial CSF by contrast is **neutrophil-predominant with low glucose and markedly raised protein.** VERIFY

**The guilt and contagion questions, answered directly and before he has to ask twice**: **‘This is a very rare complication of an extremely common virus. It isn’t anyone’s fault, he didn’t catch it from you, and encephalitis itself isn’t passed from person to person. Your other children are not at risk from him.’**

Implications, **honestly**: **‘Most people recover well — around six in ten with no lasting problems** VERIFY **. But some are left with difficulties with memory, concentration, speech, personality or mood, and some develop seizures needing long-term treatment. I can’t tell you today which group he’ll be in.’** Then what is in his favour, and **the rehabilitation team — occupational therapy, speech therapy, neuropsychology.**

**Quote prognosis as a range with uncertainty, not a single number** — outcome in HSV encephalitis turns on **how quickly aciclovir was started.** Untreated HSV encephalitis is far worse than the general viral-encephalitis figure.

**Driving**: he must not drive after a seizure — **Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive** and the reporting duty under the **Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)**. VERIFY SA — from a rural site this needs a metropolitan centre: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, and **give the first dose of aciclovir before transfer**. **TIS 131 450**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer early for families facing metropolitan transfer.
plan: **Introduction and role**: **‘Hello, are you Mark? I’m one of the doctors in the emergency department and I’m looking after your son today.’**

**Consent — the box almost everyone misses, and it takes six seconds**: **‘Before we start — your son isn’t well enough to take this in himself at the moment. Is it alright with you if I go through his results with you? Are you his next of kin?’**

**‘Can I ask what you’ve been told so far, and what you understood from it? That way I won’t repeat things or leave gaps.’** Then acknowledge, once and genuinely: **‘That must have been terrifying to watch.’**
**Warning shot and signpost**: **‘Some of what I’m going to say is serious, and I’ll go through it slowly. I’ll cover what we found, what we think it is, and what it means. Stop me at any point.’**

**Task 1 — findings, one at a time, pausing.** Mild temperature · confused and disorientated, speech not making sense · **‘his neck was not stiff — I’ll come back to why that matters’** · drowsy after the fit. Then bloods · normal glucose and biochemistry · **the CT: ‘no abscess, no bleed, no tumour — but it doesn’t show inflammation itself’** · the spinal fluid. **Pause after the scan and after the fluid** — the father cannot absorb five results in one breath, and the examiner is watching for whether you noticed.

**Task 2 — the diagnosis in two layers.** **‘What you’ve been watching has a name — delirium, a sudden change in how the brain is working. Delirium always has a cause, and we think his cause is encephalitis — inflammation of the brain tissue itself, almost always from a virus, most commonly the cold sore virus.’** Then **the neck-stiffness explanation**, then **the contagion and guilt answer before he asks twice**.

**Differentials — name them, do not lecture.** Bacterial meningitis (soft neck, mild fever, viral CSF pattern) · abscess, tumour, bleed (**excluded by the normal CT**) · metabolic causes — low sugar, sodium, liver or kidney failure (**excluded by the bloods**) · drugs, alcohol or withdrawal · prolonged post-ictal state · **autoimmune encephalitis, neurosyphilis, HIV if the PCR is negative.**

**Task 3 — implications, two minutes, and it is a third of the marks.** **Treatment already started, first.** Then the honest proportions, then **‘I can’t tell you today which group he’ll be in’**, then what is in his favour, then **the rehabilitation team by name**.

**The practical one**: **‘because he’s had a seizure, he won’t be able to drive for a period, and that will be reviewed by the specialists. I know that’s a small detail today, but it’s better you hear it from me now.’**
**‘Is that making sense so far? What questions do you have?’** Pause after each block rather than talking for eight minutes straight — **no check of understanding is its own fail risk.**

**The findings you are given**: mild temperature (**not the 39–40°C of bacterial meningitis**) · confused, disorientated, inappropriate speech · **no neck stiffness** · post-ictal after a witnessed seizure · no rash, no focal deficit.

**The investigations you are given**: raised WCC, ESR and CRP; **normal glucose and remaining bloods**; **normal CT brain**; **CSF with raised white cells, 90% lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly elevated protein.**
**The normal CT excludes abscess, bleed and tumour — and nothing else.** ‘Good news, the scan is clear’ is a fail risk; it does not show the inflammation.

**A repeat lumbar puncture may be needed if the first was taken very early and is normal** — a normal CSF does not exclude encephalitis.

**Version C — mosquito exposure**: recent time in rural south-eastern Australia, camping near waterbirds, or work around piggeries adds **Japanese encephalitis virus** — notifiable, vaccine for at-risk groups, **no specific antiviral, management supportive** VERIFY . **Aciclovir is still started empirically until HSV is excluded.** Also consider Murray Valley and West Nile/Kunjin.

dx: **Benign intracranial hypertension (idiopathic intracranial hypertension, pseudotumour cerebri) in a 16-year-old girl** — raised CSF pressure **without a mass lesion**. The package: **young, female, raised BMI, on acne treatment, headache with visual symptoms and nausea.**

**It is called pseudotumour because it behaves exactly like a tumour** on history and examination — chronic headache, blurred and double vision, visual obscurations, tinnitus, papilloedema — **and then the scan comes back normal.**

**The pivot is the medication question.** **Doxycycline, minocycline, isotretinoin, vitamin A derivatives, the combined pill and corticosteroids all cause it**, and combining them multiplies the risk — **which is why isotretinoin and doxycycline are not given together.** VERIFY

**Correct the word ‘benign’ explicitly**: **‘Benign only means there’s no tumour. If this isn’t treated, the pressure can permanently damage her sight. That’s why I want her eyes examined properly within a day or two, not in a few weeks.’**

**The order of investigation, said out loud**: **‘We’ll do a scan of her brain first, including the veins, to be certain there’s nothing there. Only after that would we measure the pressure with a needle in the back — doing it the other way round can be dangerous if there turns out to be something pressing on the brain.’**

**Same-day or next-day ophthalmology: visual acuity, formal visual fields and documented fundoscopy. Vision is what is at stake.** Then serial visual field monitoring, and **surgical options — optic nerve sheath fenestration, shunting, venous stenting — if vision deteriorates.** VERIFY

stem: Your next patient is a 55-year-old man who presents to your general practice complaining of difficulty in walking, which has been getting worse. He has a specific concern: he is worried he is having a stroke. Tasks: take a very complete six-minute history — this is the predominant assessment area — then explain your diagnosis, and explain your differentials.

A gait stem carries one of the widest differential lists in the whole exam — brain, cord, nerve, muscle, cerebellum, vestibular apparatus, joints, eyes and drugs. The station appeared in 2022 and 2023 and very few candidates passed it even knowing the recall, because the marks are in the breadth of the list rather than the diagnosis. Variants: no trauma at all with a normal CT; and a new focal deficit appearing.

dx: **Chronic subdural haematoma in a 55-year-old man** — a fall three months ago, apparently trivial at the time, with **a slow venous collection that only became symptomatic weeks later.**

**The trap is arithmetic.** Candidates hear ‘three months ago’ and strike intracranial haemorrhage off, reasoning that a bleed would have declared itself on the day. **That is exactly how chronic subdurals are missed in real practice.** Symptoms may not appear for weeks, and when they do they are **vague, fluctuating and non-focal**: headache, lightheadedness, unsteadiness, cognitive change, seizures.
**Risk factors: age, alcohol, cerebral atrophy and anticoagulation — and a ‘trivial’ fall is the usual history.** CT appearance: **a crescentic collection, often hypodense, ± midline shift.**

Explaining the mechanism when he disbelieves you: **‘It sounds wrong, and it’s exactly how this one behaves. A small vein tears when you hit your head, and it bleeds very slowly — so slowly that nothing happens for weeks. Then the collection gets big enough to press on the brain. Being on a blood thinner makes it a good deal more likely, because the bleeding doesn’t stop as readily.’**

**Answering the stroke concern by name, with reasons**: **‘I don’t think this is a stroke. A stroke comes on suddenly, usually in minutes, and then stays the same or improves. Yours has come on gradually over a month, is getting worse, and varies from day to day — and you’ve had no slurred speech, no weakness down one side, no numbness and no loss of vision.’**
**Urgent CT head — today, not next week.** Then **bloods: FBC, UEC, LFTs, coagulation profile and INR, glucose and B12.** Assess and document any focal deficit and conscious state.

**Review the anticoagulant with the treating team** — it will likely need to be withheld or reversed depending on the findings, and **reversal is discussed with the receiving team before any agent is given.** VERIFY **Neurosurgical referral if a collection is confirmed — many chronic subdurals are drained via burr holes, with good outcomes.** VERIFY

**If the CT is normal**: MRI cervical spine for **myelopathy** and MRI brain, plus the metabolic screen. **Cervical myelopathy is easily missed and a common real cause of gait change at this age** — neck pain, clumsy hands, bladder symptoms.

**He should not drive until this is sorted** — a progressive gait disturbance of unknown cause. VERIFY Then **physiotherapy and occupational therapy assessment, a gait aid, a home falls-hazard review, a medication review (sedatives, antihypertensives) and a postural blood pressure.**

SA — **CT from an MM5 site means the regional hospital, arranged today rather than as an outpatient**; discuss with the **neurosurgical registrar** at the receiving metropolitan unit and arrange transfer, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if he deteriorates; **PATS** for travel; community physio and OT through **Country Health Connect**; **My Aged Care 1800 200 422** if he needs home supports; driving under the **Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)** and **Austroads — document the advice you give**; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS.
plan: **Vitals are optional here** — there is no subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis on a gait list. Asking costs ten seconds and is never penalised; **skipping it to buy differential time is also defensible.** Then the open question.

Acknowledge the stated fear **and make a mental note to answer it**: **‘I understand why a stroke is on your mind — that’s a reasonable thing to worry about. Let me ask you some questions and I’ll tell you directly what I think by the end.’**

**‘Tell me what you mean by difficulty walking — is it weakness, stiffness, balance, pain, or your legs not doing what you tell them?’** **Weakness, imbalance, stiffness and pain lead to four different groups, and the answer redirects the whole history.** Then: how long · getting worse · does it come and go · have you fallen because of it · **‘is it worse at the end of the day when you’re tired?’** · effect on life.

**Group 1 — upper motor neuron.** The deficit block, which does double duty for everything in this group: **blackouts or fainting · slurred speech · blurring of vision · weakness in arms or legs · numbness or pins and needles.** Then tumour: **long-standing headaches · early-morning headache or vomiting · weight loss.**

**The question over the right time frame**: **‘Have you had any trauma, injury or fall — not just recently, but at any point over the last few months?’** **‘Any recent falls?’ invites a no, because three months does not feel recent to the patient.**

**The fall, explored — do not move on.** **‘Describe the fall for me — what happened, and what did you hurt? Did you hit your head? Did you lose consciousness, even briefly? Did you vomit afterwards? Did you see a doctor at the time — did you have a scan?’** Then **‘Are you on any blood thinners — aspirin, warfarin, apixaban, clopidogrel?’** and **‘How much alcohol do you drink?’**

**Groups 2–3 — lower motor neuron, muscle, extrapyramidal.** Parkinson’s: **shakiness in the hands · taking longer to do things.** Myasthenia: **the end-of-day question, plus drooping eyelids, double vision, difficulty chewing or swallowing.** Neuropathy causes: **diabetes, alcohol.** Myopathy: **rising from a chair, stairs, thyroid, statin.** Cord: **back or neck pain · numbness around the back passage · bowel or bladder control.**

**Groups 4–5 — cerebellar and vestibular.** **Balance overall · difficulty saying some words · shakiness reaching for things** · then **hearing loss · buzzing or ringing · spinning · nausea with it.**

**Group 6 — antalgic and the non-neurological risk factors.** **Pain in legs, hips, knees or feet on walking · vision and hearing · sleeping tablets or sedatives, new blood pressure medications · dizziness on standing · other recent falls.** Then closure: PMHx, FHx, smoking, alcohol.

Then **CT today, not next week**, and **don’t drive.**

She is worried because she cannot walk properly, cannot get to work, and it is not improving. Tasks: take a six-minute history — physical examination given on a card or from the examiner — then explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient.

The card gives: swelling and bruising over the posterior thigh; tenderness over the ischial tuberosity; lower limb neurology with normal tone, sensation and reflexes but power reduced and limited by pain, therefore not formally assessable; decreased range of movement at the hip; and no leg-length discrepancy, with true lengths equal. dx: **Pelvic fracture in a 26-year-old footballer — most consistent with an injury involving the ischium**, given **tenderness over the ischial tuberosity, posterior thigh bruising, restricted hip movement and equal true leg lengths.**

**Why not ‘hip fracture’?** The hip is a joint built from **the acetabulum (ilium, ischium and pubis) and the femur**, so ‘hip fracture’ does not tell the examiner what you think is broken. **A proximal femoral fracture classically shortens and externally rotates the leg** — **here the true lengths are equal**, which points away from the femur and towards the pelvis.

**Your differential list is built for the complaint, not for what you find.** You make the list for ‘difficulty walking’ **before you know anything**. The history then **reorders** it — acute and traumatic pushes fracture and infection up, degenerative causes down — **but the list itself does not change, and you still rule the others out.**

**This case appeared two months after the chronic subdural gait station.** Candidates walked in expecting a bleed, heard ‘I had a fall’, and stopped thinking — **then a full page of musculoskeletal findings arrived on the card.**

**Read the card correctly, out loud**: **‘The power is reduced, but the card tells me that is limited by pain rather than true weakness — and with normal tone, sensation and reflexes I would not call that a neurological deficit.’**

**When an AMC role-player volunteers a paragraph, it is scripted, and it is the answer.** Here: **pushed from the left, landed on the right hip, unable to walk properly since.** Mine it — direction of force, landing point, **could she get up, could she weight-bear at the time.**

Naming it precisely: **‘Most likely you have a fracture in your pelvis — the ring of bone your hip joint sits in. I’m saying pelvis rather than hip because there is bruising at the back of your thigh and tenderness right over the sitting bone, your hip doesn’t move through its full range, and importantly both your legs are the same length — a break in the top of the thigh bone usually makes one leg shorter.’**

**Pelvic X-ray today, with CT pelvis if the plain film is equivocal or a ring injury is suspected.** VERIFY **Analgesia; non-weight-bearing until imaging is reviewed, with crutches and instruction.** **Assess haemodynamic stability — an unstable pelvic ring injury can bleed litres.** VERIFY **Orthopaedic referral — same day if she cannot weight-bear or the ring may be involved.**

**Most isolated, stable pelvic fractures are managed conservatively**: analgesia, protected weight-bearing, physiotherapy. **Unstable ring injuries or displaced acetabular fractures require operative fixation.** VERIFY **VTE prophylaxis if mobility is significantly reduced** VERIFY ; work certificate and modified duties; **if it turns out to be a hamstring avulsion, surgical repair is time-sensitive.** VERIFY

**Skip the geriatric falls assessment** — vision, hearing, home hazards and polypharmacy belong to the 65-year-old with recurrent falls, not a 26-year-old tackled at football. **Say so if challenged; it shows you are reasoning, not reciting.** SA — plain films locally, **CT pelvis at the regional centre with PATS travel**; discuss with the **orthopaedic registrar** before sending her; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unstable; community physio via Country Health Connect; **ReturnToWorkSA** only if it happened at work; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS.
plan: Open question, then the framing line that works for any gait case: **‘I’m going to ask about quite a few different systems — walking involves the brain, the nerves, the muscles, the joints and the balance organs, so some questions will sound unrelated.’**

**‘Tell me what you mean by difficulty walking — is it pain, weakness, stiffness, balance, or your leg not doing what you tell it?’** → **pain**. Then: how long · getting worse · **can you weight-bear at all** · better or worse · worse at the end of the day · effect on life.

**Vascular and infective, asked EARLY in an acute presentation** — **before** the trauma answer arrives. **Calf pain on walking that eases with rest · swelling, warmth or pain in one calf · on the pill, long flights, recent immobility · fever or chills · rash on the legs · any hot, swollen, red joint.** **Skipping the fever question because the story is obviously traumatic is how a septic hip gets missed.**

**The head-injury screen that follows EVERY fall**: **‘Did you hit your head? Did you lose consciousness or faint, even for a few seconds? Did you vomit afterwards? Any headaches since? Did anyone look at you at the time — a trainer, a doctor? Any imaging?’** **The marks for asking are there whether or not the answer is positive.**

**Neurological deficit, head to toe, after any injury**: **blurring of vision · slurred speech · weakness moving the leg · numbness or pins and needles · headaches since · weight loss** (intracranial haemorrhage and tumour are still on the list).

**The cauda equina screen — two questions, ten seconds, and it belongs in every acute gait case**: **‘Any back or neck pain since the injury? Any numbness around the back passage or inner thighs? Any change in bowel or bladder control?’**

**Groups 4–6, asked anyway** — because the examiner is marking whether you rule out differentials **for the complaint**. Cerebellar: **balance, difficulty saying words.** Vestibular: **hearing loss, buzzing, spinning, nausea.** Myopathy and endocrine: **thyroid, rising from a chair, statin.** Drugs: **any medications including the pill, sleeping tablets.**

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to your general practice concerned about shakiness in his hands. In the opening statement he tells you he is worried he has Parkinson's disease. Tasks: take a comprehensive six-minute history — explain your diagnosis to the patient — and explain your differentials.

No examination task. Variants: a rest tremor with slowness, which is Parkinson's; drug-induced parkinsonism from an antipsychotic, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or valproate; and an acute tremor of days with sweating and agitation, which is withdrawal or thyrotoxicosis.

dx: **Benign essential tremor in a 50-year-old man who is frightened he has Parkinson’s** — a **kinetic or postural tremor, present on action, not at rest**, typically bilateral, often involving **head, voice and legs**, **worse with stress, better with alcohol**, with a **strong family history**.

**Tremor was always a physical examination case until it became a history case. That change is the whole difficulty**: everything you would normally look for in Parkinson’s — **bradykinesia, rigidity, gait, arm swing** — you now have to ask about.

**Bradykinesia, verbalised**: **‘Have you noticed your movements becoming slower? Does it take you longer to do things than it used to? Has your handwriting got smaller? And any change in your sense of smell?’** Plus **balance, walking and falls · constipation · acting out dreams · dizziness on standing · mood.**

CORRECTION — **essential tremor can produce a rest component, and Parkinson’s can have a postural component.** If pressed: **‘the classical distinction is rest versus action, though there is overlap — which is why I would also assess bradykinesia, rigidity and gait.’** **Gait is the most useful discriminator.**

Answering the concern by name: **‘I don’t think this is Parkinson’s. In Parkinson’s the shaking happens at rest and settles when you use the hand — yours is the opposite. People with Parkinson’s also become slower at everything, their handwriting shrinks, their sense of smell fades, and their walking changes — small steps, less arm swing. You have none of that. And Parkinson’s doesn’t usually shake the voice or the head, or improve with alcohol, or run in families the way yours does.’**

**The honest caveat, which reads as competence**: **‘I can’t give you a blood test or a scan that proves it either way — there isn’t one for Parkinson’s. What I can do is check the reversible causes today, and see you again in a couple of months. If anything changes — slowness, stiffness, changes in your walking — we reassess.’**
**The alcohol line, said before he does**: **‘The fact that a drink settles it is a clue for me, not a treatment for you. I’m not going to suggest you use alcohol to manage it.’**

**Bloods to exclude the reversible systemic causes: TSH, LFTs, UEC, FBC, glucose** VERIFY , plus a **full medication review including anti-nausea and psychiatric drugs** — **metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, antipsychotics and valproate cause a reversible drug-induced parkinsonism.** **No imaging for a typical bilateral action tremor with a family history — and say why.**

**Propranolol is first-line when treatment is needed; primidone is the alternative.** VERIFY CORRECTION — **do not use benzodiazepines, despite older texts**: dependence, falls and cognitive effects. VERIFY Reduce caffeine. **Occupational therapy: weighted cutlery, wide-grip pens, two-handed technique.** **Review in 6–8 weeks**, and reassess if it becomes **unilateral, rapidly progressive, or acquires new features.**

**Do not let ‘benign’ be the whole message.** It is not dangerous, **but it can be socially and occupationally disabling** — he is a self-employed electrician who has stopped going out for meals. **Ask about the impact and take it seriously.** SA — neurology by telehealth via Country Health Connect with **PATS** for in-person review; **Austroads** and the **Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)** if it affects driving safety VERIFY ; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap** co-payment; **Parkinson’s SA** if the diagnosis turns out to be Parkinson’s.

Acknowledge **and promise an answer — do not reassure yet**: **‘Thank you for coming in to get it looked at properly. Let me ask you some questions and we’ll work out the cause together, and I’ll tell you directly what I think about Parkinson’s by the end.’** **Premature reassurance is scored as poorly as ignoring the concern.**
**Explore the tremor — four components.** Timing: **how long · on and off or constant · getting worse.** Pattern: **‘one hand or both?’** then **‘any shakiness in any other part of your body?’**

**The question that decides the case, with both options offered**: **‘Does the shakiness mainly happen when you’re resting — hands in your lap — or when you’re doing a task, like writing, using a knife and fork, or holding a glass?’** **An open ‘when does it happen?’ gets a vague answer; the contrast is what pulls the diagnostic reply out.**

**Modifiers and impact**: better or worse with anything · **how is this affecting your life?** He spilled wine at a work dinner, has stopped going out for meals, and fine work is getting hard. **Come back to that.**

**The four essential-tremor key points**: **‘Any shakiness in your voice when you talk?’ · ‘Does your head shake or nod? Any shakiness in your legs when you walk?’ · ‘Is it worse when you’re stressed or anxious?’ · ‘Is it better when you drink alcohol?’ · ‘Does anyone in your family have shaky hands?’**

**Parkinson’s, asked because you cannot look**: **slowness and time taken · handwriting smaller · sense of smell · balance, walking, falls · constipation · acting out dreams · dizziness on standing · mood.** **These negatives are what let you answer his concern — without them you have nothing to reassure him with.**

**Structural and cerebellar**: **long-standing headaches · weight loss · blurring of vision, weakness, numbness or pins and needles** (also screens MS) · **balance and walking · difficulty saying some words.**

**The systemic sweep — one or two questions each, and do not skip liver, kidney and lung because they feel unlikely.** Thyroid: **heat intolerance, diarrhoea.** Liver: **jaundice, itch, dark urine.** Lung: **long-standing cough, wheeze.** Kidney: **urine output, itch.** Phaeo: **episodes of racing heart, headache and sweating together.** Anxiety: **mood, stress at home and work** — and it is a diagnosis made **after** organic exclusion, not before.

**Stimulants and drugs**: **coffee or tea · smoking · alcohol · recreational drugs · any medications — and have you stopped any recently?** Then the small geriatric screen: **memory problems · falls**, and PMHx and FHx. **He forgets the blood pressure tablet unless asked twice.**

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to your general practice complaining of double vision. He is a known case of diabetes and hypertension and is on treatment for both. Tasks: take a six-minute history — explain your diagnosis to the patient — and explain your differentials.

No examination task. Variants: fatigable diplopia with evening ptosis, which is ocular myasthenia; a pupil-involving third nerve palsy, which is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise; and diplopia after facial trauma, which is an orbital floor fracture with entrapment.

dx: **Binocular diplopia from a diabetic cranial mononeuropathy in a 50-year-old man** — a microvascular palsy of the third, fourth or sixth nerve in a man with **poorly controlled, poorly followed-up diabetes.**

**Say the diagnosis in two layers.** First the mechanism — **‘binocular diplopia, meaning the two eyes are not moving together’**. Then the cause — **‘most likely because high blood sugar has damaged the nerve that moves the eye’**. **Naming only ‘diabetic neuropathy’ skips the reasoning the examiner wants to hear.**

**Resolves with either eye covered = binocular** — each eye is normal alone, so this is **alignment: brain, nerve, junction, muscle.** **Persists with one eye covered = monocular** — the problem is **inside that eye: cornea, lens, retina.**

CORRECTION — **do not name a single cranial nerve from the direction of gaze.** Left gaze needs the **left lateral rectus (VI) and the right medial rectus (III)**. **Say the level, not the nerve**, unless the pattern is unambiguous. Localising questions that do cost five seconds: **horizontal versus vertical separation · worse for distance (VI) or near (medial rectus) · a compensatory head tilt (IV).** VERIFY

**AUTO-FAIL — the aneurysm.** **A painful third nerve palsy with ptosis, a down-and-out eye and a dilated, poorly reactive pupil is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise**, and it can rupture. **Diabetic third nerve palsies usually spare the pupil; compressive ones do not.** Urgent CT and CT or MR angiography today, neurosurgical discussion, **no outpatient pathway.** VERIFY

**The four chronic-disease questions are the diagnosis, not scenery**: **when were you diagnosed · what treatment · are you taking it regularly and having follow-up and blood tests · any other complications.** His answers — **not taking the tablets, no GP for two years, numb feet** — **are your diagnostic reasoning.**

The reasoning said aloud: **‘The most likely cause is damage to one of the nerves that moves the eye, from your diabetes. I’m saying that because you haven’t been taking your tablets regularly, you haven’t seen your GP or had blood tests for a long time, and you’ve got numbness in your feet — which is the same process affecting a different nerve.’**

**Driving is not negotiable**: **‘You shouldn’t drive while you’re seeing double. It isn’t safe, and there’s a legal standard as well. Is there someone who can pick you up?’** VERIFY Covering one eye at roundabouts is not a solution.

**Most microvascular palsies improve over weeks to a few months** VERIFY — **a temporary eye patch or occlusive tape gives symptomatic relief** — **but diabetes control is the treatment.** **Review at 4–6 weeks and refer if not improving or if new signs appear.** Prisms or strabismus surgery only if the deviation persists beyond about six months. VERIFY

SA — ophthalmology via **RAH, Flinders or TQEH** with **PATS** travel; **a pupil-involving third nerve palsy is a same-day transfer conversation**, **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unwell; **Austroads** and the **Motor Vehicles Act 1959 (SA)** — **document the advice** VERIFY ; diabetes review with a **GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangements**, diabetes educator and podiatry via Country Health Connect, **NDSS** for supplies; **TIS 131 450**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap** co-payment, with attention to the much higher burden of diabetes complications.
plan: Open question, acknowledge — then **the first substantive question, in the first thirty seconds, because it decides which half of the list you work from**: **‘When you cover one eye, does the double vision go away? And does it go away whichever eye you cover?’**

**Explore the diplopia — timing and pattern.** When first noticed · on and off or constant · getting worse · **‘are the two images side by side, or one above the other?’** · **‘worse looking in any particular direction?’** · **‘worse for things far away or close up?’** · **‘is there a position you hold your head in that makes it better?’**

**‘Is it worse at the end of the day?’** — the fatigability question · **‘any pain in or around the eye, or on moving it?’** — painful ophthalmoplegia has its own list · **‘how is this affecting your life — are you driving?’** He drove here.

**Level 1 — the brain.** Headaches · **vomiting, particularly in the morning** · weight loss · weakness · numbness or pins and needles · balance or walking · slurred speech · **‘any history of migraine, or migraine in the family?’**

**Level 2 — the nerve, and the diabetes worked up properly.** The four chronic-disease questions, then **‘any other complications — numbness in your feet, kidney or eye problems, any ulcers?’**, then the hypertension: **‘any chest pain? What’s your blood pressure usually running at?’**
**The aneurysm question**: **‘Did the double vision come with pain, and has anyone noticed a difference in the size of your pupils, or a droopy eyelid?’**

**Level 3 — the neuromuscular junction.** Worse at the end of the day · **drooping eyelids, particularly in the evening** · difficulty making facial expressions · **‘any trouble chewing, swallowing, or with your speech as a meal goes on? Any shortness of breath?’** — **the bulbar and respiratory screen is the life-threatening part** · arm weakness after repeated use.

**Level 4 — muscle and orbit.** Thyroid: **problems, heat intolerance, weight change, palpitations, diarrhoea, ‘has anyone said your eyes look more prominent, or that you stare?’** · **‘any injury to your face or eye?’** — orbital floor fracture with entrapment · swelling, pain on eye movement, redness.

**The monocular list, asked even though he is binocular — skipping it is the commonest reason this station is failed.** Cataract: **haloes, faded colours, night glare.** Macular: **trouble seeing faces, wavy lines, changing lanes.** Glaucoma, phrased functionally: **‘when you’re driving, do you have to turn your head to see the signs at the side?’** Refractive: **last eye test, glasses.**

dx: **An infection in or around the eye — and you name TWO: orbital cellulitis and endophthalmitis.** Marked lid swelling almost closing the eye, redness, pain, feeling hot and cold, headache, **and a scratch from a branch while gardening.**

**Candidates fail this station by trying to be certain.** The stem withholds the one finding that would settle it — **you are on the telephone, and the pain-on-movement answer was never recalled.** **The task is not ‘name the diagnosis’; it is ‘explain the most likely diagnosis and differentials, and your initial management’.**

Naming both, with a reason for each: **‘I’m worried about two things in particular. Endophthalmitis — an infection inside the eyeball itself — because you scratched your eye with a branch, which is the worst kind of injury for getting an infection into the eye. And orbital cellulitis — an infection in the tissues around the eye — because your lid is so swollen it’s almost closing, the eye is red and painful, and you’ve been feeling hot and cold.’**

**Pain on eye movement is the question that separates orbital from preseptal cellulitis.** Ask it anyway, then say plainly: **‘that’s the question we’ll answer when you’re seen.’** **Ethmoid sinusitis is the usual route into the orbit, through the thin lamina papyracea** — which is why the sinus questions belong in a sore-eye history.

**‘Go to the emergency department’ is not an answer — say what will happen there.** **‘First they’ll examine your eye properly with a slit lamp — a microscope for the eye — which is the thing I can’t do over the phone. The most important thing they’ll check is whether moving your eye is painful. If it is, that points to infection behind the eye, and they’ll do a CT of your eye socket and sinuses and start antibiotics through a drip. If it looks like the infection is inside the eye, they’ll start antibiotics and the eye specialist will see you straight away.’**

**Refusing the drops, with the reason**: **‘Drops won’t touch an infection behind or inside the eye, and giving them would waste the hours that matter.’** **Never give steroid drops for an undiagnosed red eye — catastrophic in herpes simplex keratitis.**

**AMC role-players say ‘I’ve been feeling hot and cold’, not ‘I have a fever’.** Take it as fever and act on it. **The scratch is given only to a direct question about injury or trauma** — ask it early, before you have committed to a diagnosis.

back.dx: LYMPHOMA — reached through a head and neck examination rather than a systemic one. The warning shot, the word, then the reasons: 'David, thank you for waiting. I am afraid what I have found does concern me.' Pause. 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' Pause and let it land. 'The lump you can feel is an enlarged gland, and there are three of them. They feel rubbery, they do not move, and they are not sore — and glands from an infection are usually tender and move freely. I also found your spleen is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks on your skin. Your thyroid gland is normal, so this is not a thyroid problem.' The euphemism and the reassurance are both AUTOMATIC FAILS here — 'Probably just a gland' and 'Let's try another course of antibiotics' — and so is delivering a differential list instead of a diagnosis. When he asks if it is the smoking: 'Smoking causes several cancers of the head, neck and lungs, and those are on my list — but lymphoma is not usually caused by smoking. Either way, stopping now would be the single best thing you could do for whatever we find, and I will help you with that.' then the three groups with named members, because group names with no members score nothing and the rule is specificity. Thyroid problems — a cancer, a nodule or a cyst, or a goitre; less likely, because the gland felt normal and this lump does not move on swallowing. Infections — in the skin, such as impetigo or cellulitis; in the teeth; in the throat and ears, such as tonsillitis; and longer-standing infections like glandular fever, tuberculosis and HIV, which need blood tests and his permission. Other cancers — skin cancers on the head and neck, cancers of the nose, mouth or throat, of the food pipe or stomach, and lung cancer. 'That is why I looked at so many areas today.' The investigations, in order of priority and delivered slowly: one, full blood examination. Two, blood film. Three, an excisional biopsy of one of the cervical nodes, because lymphoma is classified on nodal architecture. Four, PET-CT for staging, or CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis. Then for the other differentials: TSH and a neck ultrasound for the thyroid group; nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for a pharyngeal or laryngeal primary; a chest x-ray; gastroscopy if there is any dysphagia; and ESR, CRP with EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, HIV and syphilis serology and an IGRA for the infective group. The answer that separates you, when the examiner asks why not a fine-needle aspirate: 'Suspected lymphoma means excisional biopsy, because we need nodal architecture and tissue for immunophenotyping — an aspirate gives cells without architecture. Suspected metastatic squamous cell carcinoma means fine-needle aspiration plus nasendoscopy to find the primary, and I would avoid an open biopsy of the neck before ENT assessment.' The safety-net: 'I will organise the blood tests today and speak to the specialist myself. Come back or go straight to hospital if you develop difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, trouble swallowing, swelling of your face or neck, or a fever. I will phone you with the blood results personally. Cancer council SA on 13 11 20 can help with information and with travel. Is there someone at home with you?' The variants. A stony hard fixed node with a non-healing lateral tongue ulcer and referred ear pain in a smoker over forty: metastatic squamous cell carcinoma is the leading diagnosis, not lymphoma — urgent ENT referral for nasendoscopy and fine-needle aspiration, CT neck and chest, and no open neck biopsy first. A midline lump that rises both on swallowing and on tongue protrusion: movement on tongue protrusion is the discriminator, so it is a thyroglossal duct cyst — ultrasound and TSH to confirm normal thyroid tissue elsewhere before any excision. And a temperature of 38.3 with a tender mobile node, red overlying skin and a broken molar with gingival swelling: reactive cervical lymphadenitis from dental sepsis — urgent dental review and drainage, antibiotics, and review in 48 hours; and if the node has not settled once the dental source is treated, it still needs investigating.

Declare the three groups, which license everything that follows: 'Examiner, this man has a lump in the neck, so my differentials fall into three groups — thyroid disease, infection, and malignancy of the head, neck and chest. My examination follows those.' then general appearance and vital signs, temperature first.
HANDS AND FACE: clubbing, scratch marks, ecchymoses; gum hypertrophy or bleeding.
The ENT examination, region by region and as four separate asks (see PEFE) — and then say it out loud: 'Those negatives make the infective group and an oral primary much less likely.'

'A full lymph node examination, all chains over the whole body — cervical and supraclavicular, axillary, epitrochlear and inguinal.' Wait. Then the four characters: 'Consistency? Mobile or fixed? Tender — I'm asking to separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy? And is the overlying skin normal?'

'Separately, I would like a full thyroid examination' — with the follow-up loaded for 'What are you looking for?': inspection for a visible mass and engorged veins, palpation for size, nodularity and tenderness, and percussion over the manubrium for retrosternal extension. (Sip-and-swallow, tongue protrusion, auscultation and Pemberton's are all correct and all optional — if the first three are normal, stop, because you need the time for the skin check.)

Chest and abdomen, each with its reason said aloud: 'Air entry equal, any added sounds? I'm asking because lung cancer is on my list.' 'Inspection for swelling, distension or redness; then tenderness, masses, and hepatomegaly or splenomegaly? I'm asking because gastric carcinoma is on my list.'
The skin check: 'Finally, a full skin check — are there any suspicious skin lesions or moles on the head and neck?'
Stop asking. Turn the chair fully towards him and lower your voice — then the warning shot, the word lymphoma, a pause, and the reasons from what you found (see dx).
The three groups with named members (see dx) — then the investigations in order of priority, the excisional-versus-fna answer ready, and the safety-net with someone at home confirmed.

ask: The thirteen lines, one to seven: 'With a lump in the neck my differentials fall into three groups — thyroid, infection, and malignancy.' / 'Vital signs, and the temperature first.' / 'A full ENT examination, and I will go region by region.' / 'Any caries, and any swelling or redness of the gums?' / 'A full lymph node examination, all chains, over the whole body.' / 'Consistency, mobility or fixation, tenderness, and the overlying skin.' / 'Separately, I would like a full thyroid examination.'

Eight to thirteen: 'Inspection, palpation, and percussion for retrosternal extension.' / 'A full skin check — any suspicious skin lesions or moles on the head and neck?' / 'I am afraid what I have found does concern me.' / 'I am concerned about the possibility of a cancer of the lymph glands, called lymphoma.' / 'Your thyroid gland is normal, so this is not a thyroid problem.' / 'Suspected lymphoma: excisional. Suspected metastatic squamous cell carcinoma: fine-needle aspiration plus nasendoscopy.'

If the examiner asks 'Do you need to examine them separately?' — this is a check that you understand the anatomy: 'Yes — I asked for the lymph nodes specifically and the thyroid specifically, because a neck lump is one or the other. The answers tell me this is a node.'

The discriminators to hold: a neck lump is one of two structures, lymph node or thyroid — movement on swallowing means thyroid, and movement on tongue protrusion means a thyroglossal duct cyst — four node characters, four ENT sub-requests, three differential groups — and tender and mobile is lymphadenitis while rubbery, fixed and non-tender is a malignant pattern.

The first four investigations in order: full blood examination, blood film, excisional biopsy of a cervical node, and PET-CT for staging. Cancer council SA 13 11 20 — TIS National 131 450 — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.
pefe: The ENT examination as four separate asks, because a summary request invites 'What are you looking for?': 'Throat — any redness or exudate? Are the tonsils enlarged? Mouth — any ulcers? Dental — any caries, and any swelling or redness of the gums? Nose — any discharge, or any abnormal growth in the nasal cavity?'

Role-player: David Nowak, 45, a grain handler at the Wallaroo terminal, living with his partner with two adult children. Twenty-five a day since he was twenty, six to eight beers on Friday and Saturday, no regular medications, no allergies. A lump on the right side of his neck for about three months, slowly bigger, painless, unchanged by two courses of antibiotics. Weight loss with his belt two holes tighter and a poor appetite. Itching all over for weeks with scratching in his sleep. No sore throat, toothache, dysphagia, hoarseness, cough beyond a smoker's morning cough, or noticed night sweats — though his wife says he is hot at night. He is outdoors all day and has never had his moles checked.

How to play it: stoic, understated, slightly gruff, minimising everything — 'It's probably nothing.' You are mostly a witness for the first five minutes while the doctor talks to the examiner; do not interrupt, but watch them. One interruption is allowed — at around four minutes, if they have not looked at you once, say 'Are you going to tell me what it is?' when the word cancer is said, go still, then flatly: 'Cancer? I've had two lots of antibiotics for this. Nobody said cancer.' Push once with 'Is it because I smoke?' Become emotional only if they rush past your reaction without a pause — then go quiet and say 'My dad had throat cancer.' if they use jargon, say 'In English, doc?' Do not volunteer the itching, the weight loss, the smoking or your father unless asked.

Score them out of ten: did they greet you before turning to the examiner (1); ask for cachexia and the temperature (1); ask the ENT regions separately — throat, mouth, dental, nose (2); ask for all four node characters (1); ask for the thyroid as a separate examination (1); ask for a full skin check of the head and neck (1); say the word lymphoma to you (1); give differentials in three groups with named members (1); and give investigations in order (1).
The four characters — Rubbery — fixed — non-tender — largest about 3 cm, with normal overlying skin. That is a malignant pattern, and say so
Why you ask about tenderness — To separate lymphadenitis from lymphadenopathy — say the reason aloud as you ask

The best line in the station — The full skin check — no suspicious lesions, with scratch marks over the trunk and limbs. Melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck drain to exactly these nodes, almost nobody asks, and it costs eight seconds

What he tells you — Three months, slowly bigger from a PEA to a grape, never painful — two courses of antibiotics that made no difference — his belt two holes tighter without trying — and itching all over for weeks, scratching himself raw in his sleep. 25 a day since he was twenty

His hidden agenda — 'My dad died of throat cancer at fifty-eight. I watched it happen. I've been telling myself this is just a gland' — given only if you ask what he is worried about, or after you say the word cancer

What he does in the room — He is a witness for the first five minutes while you talk to the examiner — and at about four minutes, if you have not looked at him once, he says 'Are you going to tell me what it is?' if you use jargon he says 'In English, doc?'
