findingsLabel: What the examiner gives back, and what he never volunteers
must: FAIL — Opening with 'a full lymph node examination' instead of DECLARING THE THREE GROUPS — that is the previous case's sequence, and the groups are what LICENSE every unusual request that follows: 'Examiner, this man has a lump in the neck, so my examination is built around THREE GROUPS — thyroid disease, infection, and malignancy of the head, neck and chest; may I have the general appearance, cachexia, pallor and scratch marks, and the vital signs, TEMPERATURE FIRST?' (★)

FAIL — Softening it into 'probably just a gland' or offering another course of antibiotics — both are automatic fails here, and so is delivering a DIFFERENTIAL LIST instead of a DIAGNOSIS; warning shot, the word, then the reasons, pausing after each: 'David, I am afraid what I have found does concern me… I am concerned about the possibility of a CANCER OF THE LYMPH GLANDS, called LYMPHOMA… the lump you can feel is an enlarged gland, and there are three of them; they feel RUBBERY, they do NOT MOVE, and they are NOT SORE — and glands from an infection are usually tender and move freely; I also found your spleen is bigger than it should be, and I noticed the scratch marks on your skin; your thyroid gland is normal, so this is not a thyroid problem' (★)

FAIL — Asking for the ENT examination as a SUMMARY rather than FOUR SEPARATE REGIONS, which invites 'what are you looking for?' and burns the clock — THROAT (any redness or exudate, and are the tonsils enlarged), MOUTH (any ulcers), DENTAL (any caries, and any swelling or redness of the gums — never 'tell me the dental hygiene') and NOSE (any discharge, or any abnormal growth in the nasal cavity); every answer comes back negative, and every negative is a differential you exclude out loud later (★)

FAIL — Group names with no members — 'infections' scores nothing, while 'skin infections such as impetigo or cellulitis, dental infection, and ENT infections such as tonsillitis' scores the item, and the rule is SPECIFICITY; the three groups given to the PATIENT are thyroid problems (a cancer, a nodule or a cyst, or a goitre — less likely, because the gland felt normal and this lump does not move when you swallow), infections (in the skin, in the teeth, in the throat and ears, and the longer-standing ones: glandular fever, tuberculosis and HIV, which need blood tests and his permission) and other cancers (skin cancers on the head and neck, cancers of the nose, mouth or throat, of the food pipe or stomach, and lung cancer) — closing with 'that is why I looked at so many areas today' (★)

FAIL — Never asking for the FULL SKIN CHECK of the head and neck — the best line in the station, because melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck drain to EXACTLY these nodes, almost nobody asks, and it costs eight seconds; likewise ask for the THYROID as a SEPARATE examination with the follow-up already loaded, because the examiner is likely to ask 'what are you looking for?' first ('on inspection, a visible mass and any engorged veins; on palpation, the size of the gland, any nodularity and any tenderness; and PERCUSSION over the manubrium for RETROSTERNAL EXTENSION') — but do not gold-plate it, because sip-and-swallow, tongue protrusion, auscultation and Pemberton's sign are all correct and all OPTIONAL, and if inspection, palpation and percussion are normal you stop, since you need the time for the skin check; ask for all FOUR NODE CHARACTERS after the chains (consistency, mobile or fixed, tender — 'I am asking about tenderness to separate LYMPHADENITIS from LYMPHADENOPATHY' — and the overlying skin), and stop asking for findings at 5:15

SAY — Give the investigations IN ORDER and slowly: FULL BLOOD EXAMINATION, BLOOD FILM, an EXCISIONAL BIOPSY of one of the cervical nodes, and PET–CT for staging (or CT of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis) — then, for the other differentials, TSH and a neck ultrasound; nasendoscopy and laryngoscopy for a pharyngeal or laryngeal primary; a chest X-ray; gastroscopy if there is any dysphagia; and ESR, CRP with EBV, CMV, toxoplasma, HIV and syphilis serology and an IGRA; the answer that separates you is WHY — 'suspected LYMPHOMA means an EXCISIONAL biopsy, because lymphoma is classified on NODAL ARCHITECTURE and an aspirate gives cells without architecture, and an excised node also provides tissue for immunophenotyping; suspected METASTATIC SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA means FINE-NEEDLE ASPIRATION plus NASENDOSCOPY to find the primary, and I would avoid an open biopsy of the neck before ENT assessment'; the discriminators to hold — a neck lump is one of TWO STRUCTURES, LYMPH NODE OR THYROID; movement ON SWALLOWING means thyroid, and movement ON TONGUE PROTRUSION means a THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST; and asking for the nodes and the thyroid SEPARATELY is what lets you say which; ask for the chest ('lung cancer is on my list') and the abdomen ('gastric carcinoma is on my list') with the reason attached; GREET the patient before you turn to the examiner, and turn the chair fully towards him when you name it, because he is briefed to ask 'are you going to tell me what it is?' at about four minutes if you have not looked at him once; answer 'is it because I smoke?' honestly ('smoking causes several cancers of the head, neck and lungs, and those are on my list — but lymphoma is not usually caused by smoking; either way, stopping now would be the single best thing you could do for whatever we find, and I'll help you with that'); translate every piece of jargon, because he will say 'in English, doc?'; his father died of throat cancer at 58 and he watched it, which he will not volunteer unless you ask what he is worried about; safety net — difficulty breathing, noisy breathing, trouble swallowing, swelling of the face or neck, or a fever — with Cancer Council SA on 13 11 20, a personal phone call with the results, and 'is there someone at home with you?'; variants — a STONY HARD fixed node with a non-healing lateral tongue ulcer and referred ear pain in a smoker over forty makes METASTATIC SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA the leading diagnosis rather than lymphoma; a MIDLINE lump rising on BOTH swallowing and tongue protrusion is a THYROGLOSSAL DUCT CYST, needing an ultrasound and a TSH to confirm normal thyroid tissue elsewhere before any excision; and a TENDER, MOBILE node with red overlying skin, a temperature of 38.3 and a broken molar with gingival swelling is REACTIVE CERVICAL LYMPHADENITIS FROM DENTAL SEPSIS — urgent dental review and drainage, antibiotics, review in 48 hours, and if the node has not settled once the dental source is treated, it STILL needs investigating

stem: Your next patient is a 32-year-old man who has come to you complaining of low back pain. Tasks: take a focused history for six minutes — at six minutes you are handed a card with the physical examination findings, which you do not perform and do not read aloud — then explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient. 8 minutes total.

The clock rule: still exploring the pain at three minutes? Stop and move to the red flags. You can pass with an incomplete SICORA. You cannot pass having never asked about saddle numbness. Variants: the card shows no deficit, which is non-specific mechanical back pain; and he volunteers a cauda equina symptom at about three minutes.

Read the physical examination card silently at six minutes

findings: Inspection
Normal
Palpation
Normal, or mild PARASPINAL tenderness — muscle, not midline bone

Straight leg raise

40° ON THE RIGHT, 60° ON THE LEFT. That is a CROSSED STRAIGHT LEG RAISE — raising the unaffected leg reproduces pain on the affected side. Less sensitive, considerably MORE SPECIFIC for a disc-related radiculopathy. Read it as CONFIRMATION, not confusion. Positive window 30–60° VERIFY
Reflexes
KNEE JERK ABSENT — or ankle jerk reduced on the affected side VERIFY
Sensation
REDUCED OVER THE MEDIAL CALF AND FOOT — or over the sole

Normal, or mild weakness
How the card is handed over

At six minutes, and you DO NOT EXAMINE and DO NOT READ IT ALOUD. Ten seconds, silent, take what you need and move on. Recall variation: some recalls report the LEFT leg — take the side from the role-player and stay consistent
VARIANT A — the card shows NO deficit

Tender over the paravertebral muscles, movements restricted by pain, NEUROLOGY NORMAL, SLR NEGATIVE → non-specific mechanical low back pain. THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST IS IDENTICAL — do not shorten it because the diagnosis is benign
VARIANT B — he volunteers a cauda equina symptom

‘I’ve been wetting myself a bit for two days, and the inside of my thighs feels odd when I wipe.’ STOP THE HISTORY. Same-day MRI and neurosurgical referral; MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and the RAH spinal service from MM5. DELAY HERE IS THE AUTOMATIC FAIL

dx: **Lumbar radiculopathy from a disc protrusion in a 32-year-old storeman** — **pain, sensory change or weakness in the distribution of a single lumbosacral nerve root**, caused by compression or irritation of that root as it leaves the spinal canal.

**Say radiculopathy, not sciatica.** ‘Sciatica’ names a symptom; **radiculopathy names the mechanism.** Use the correct term with the examiner and **plain English with the patient**: **‘one of the nerves that leaves your spine and runs down your leg is being squeezed.’**

**Nobody fails for missing the diagnosis — it is written on the card.** They fail because **the differential list is short, generic, or delivered as an undifferentiated stream.** ‘Fractures’ scores nothing; **‘osteoporotic and pathological vertebral fractures’ scores.** **Name the group before its members**, and **aim for fifteen names.**
**The four groups, every back and neck station in this cluster**: **red flags · spinal · arthritis · referred** — and inside red flags, **cancer · cauda equina · infection · myeloma.**

**The three planted distractors — statin, past kidney stones, father's aneurysm — do not change the diagnosis.** They exist so you can **name each and dismiss it with a reason**, which is exactly where the marks sit: **‘You’re on a cholesterol tablet and those can cause muscle aching — but yours is focal and runs into one leg, not a general ache. You’ve had kidney stones — but no burning, no blood in the urine, no fever. And your father’s aneurysm — a swelling of the main blood vessel in the tummy can cause back pain, so I’ll examine your tummy, but nothing in your story suggests it today.’**

**Three reasons drawn from this patient — one from the pain, one from the history, one from the card**: **the sharp radiating pain below the knee is nerve pain not muscle pain · the same leg feels numb, so the nerve is under pressure rather than irritated · lifting the leg reproduced the pain and one reflex was absent.**

**Management: regular paracetamol ± NSAID if not contraindicated** VERIFY **· stay active, advise against bed rest · physiotherapy and graded return · a Work Capacity Certificate with SPECIFIC RESTRICTIONS — no heavy lifting — rather than blanket unfitness · review at 4–6 weeks.** Most improve substantially within **six weeks, with leg pain often the last to go.**

**No imaging in the first six weeks of an uncomplicated radiculopathy — and say so out loud; it is a mark, not an omission.** **‘It does not change management, frequently shows incidental findings, and plain films expose him to unnecessary gonadal radiation and will not show a disc. I would image for red flags, a progressive deficit, or failure of conservative care.’** **Avoid bed rest, opioids first-line, and surgical referral without a progressive deficit.** Evidence for **pregabalin and gabapentin in radiculopathy is weak and Australian guidance has moved away from routine use.** VERIFY

**The safety net, verbatim and named**: **‘Come back immediately, or go to an emergency department, if you get numbness around your back passage or private parts, if you can’t pass urine or start leaking, if the leg becomes weak, or if you develop fevers.’** **Four named symptoms — ‘any questions?’ is not a safety net.**

SA — suspected cauda equina from MM5: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** and spinal services at the **Royal Adelaide Hospital**; **PATS** for metropolitan appointment travel; a work-related injury goes to **ReturnToWorkSA** with a Work Capacity Certificate carrying specific restrictions; **ACCHS** and Aboriginal Liaison Officer with **Closing the Gap** PBS co-payment; **TIS National 131 450.**
plan: **WIPE, open question FIRST** — the role-player is briefed to deliver **two free lines only in response to an open question.** Ask a closed question first and you never get them, **and the examiner watched you not ask.** Then acknowledge and reassure.

**The analgesia offer — eight seconds, not a consultation.** **‘Are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it? I’ll organise some now, and we can keep talking while it’s being arranged.’** No allergies, no what-have-you-tried, no doses.

**SICORA.** **Point to exactly where · out of ten · dull ache or SHARP AND STABBING · when did it start, constant or intermittent, getting worse, IS THIS THE FIRST TIME · does it TRAVEL anywhere, into the buttock, down either leg · anything better or worse · WORSE SITTING OR STANDING · WORSE WHEN YOU COUGH OR SNEEZE · how is it affecting work, sleep and daily life.**

**Pattern of the pain, and the MSK screen — fifteen seconds.** **Night pain, does it wake you · worse in the morning or at the end of the day · worse after resting or after being active · any swelling, any RASH over the back, any stiffness, any injury.** **The rash question is not a throwaway — shingles causes severe unilateral back pain for two to three days before the rash appears.**

**Group 1 — red flags, the block you never sacrifice.** Malignancy and myeloma: **weight loss · appetite · lumps or bumps · more tired · ever treated for a cancer, or anyone in the family · repeated infections · unusually thirsty.**

**The two you never skip**, normalised: **‘Two questions I ask everyone with back pain. Any numbness or pins and needles in your private parts, around the saddle area? And any loss of control of your bladder or your bowels?’** Then infection: **‘Any fevers, chills or night sweats?’**

**Group 2 — spinal, the most commonly dropped questions.** **‘Any numbness or pins and needles in your legs? Any weakness — does the leg give way, or do you catch your toe?’** **You cannot claim a nerve root is under pressure if you never asked whether anything is numb or weak.** Then **occupation and heavy lifting**, and **‘any leg pain when you walk that eases when you stop or lean forward?’**

**Group 3 — arthritis, four questions in one breath**: other joints · family history of arthritis · **rashes, scaly patches on elbows, knees or scalp** · painful red eye · **recent diarrhoea or blood in the stools** · **recent discharge** — reactive arthritis follows a urogenital or GI infection by **one to four weeks.**

**Group 4 — referred; drop this group first if you are behind.** **Burning passing urine · going more often · blood in the urine · tummy pain · nausea or vomiting.** Then **one question, three differentials**: **‘Are you on any medications? In particular any blood thinners, any steroids, or a cholesterol tablet?’** — retroperitoneal haemorrhage, osteoporotic fracture and spinal infection, statin myopathy.
6:00 — card

**Read it silently.** Then **thirty seconds maximum** on the diagnosis in plain English, **three reasons**, **the three distractors named and dismissed**, **the grouped list**, then **plan and the four named return symptoms.** **Over-explaining the disc is how candidates lose the larger mark.**
pefe: **You do not examine — the findings arrive on a card at six minutes, and you must not read it aloud.** Ten seconds, silent.

**The crossed straight leg raise is the line that panics candidates.** ‘SLR 40° right, 60° left’ is **not** bilateral radiculopathy and **not** canal stenosis: **raising the unaffected leg reproduces pain on the affected side.** If asked: **‘it is less sensitive than the standard test but considerably more specific for a disc-related radiculopathy, so it strengthens the diagnosis rather than confusing it.’**

**Root patterns worth recognising**: **L3/L4 — medial calf, knee jerk · L5 — dorsum and big toe, reflexes normal · S1 — sole, ankle jerk.** VERIFY You are **not required to announce a nerve root level** — but recognising that **the deficit matches the symptomatic leg** converts ‘I think it’s a disc’ into a defended diagnosis.

**What you would examine yourself**: **cauda equina screen — saddle sensation, bladder and bowel function, and if concerned anal tone and post-void residual** · **full lower limb neurology — tone, power, reflexes, sensation, gait, plantars** · **abdominal examination including the aorta and the renal angles**, given the distractors in this history.

**Investigations**: **MRI lumbosacral spine** for red flags, progressive deficit or failed conservative care — **the test of choice for cauda equina and for infection.** **FBE, CRP, ESR** if infection or malignancy is suspected; **calcium, ALP, EUC, LFT, EPG and free light chains** for myeloma; **urine dipstick and MSU** given the stone history; **CK only if statin myopathy is genuinely in play** — diffuse aching, not focal back pain.

**Do not miss**: **progressive or bilateral neurological deficit · saddle anaesthesia · urinary retention with overflow · fever with focal midline tenderness · a pulsatile abdominal mass.** **Any one of these turns the station from a consultation into an emergency transfer.**

dx: **One stem, two patients.** **Version A — a 32-year-old with a lifting injury: non-specific mechanical low back pain. Version B — a 65-year-old: spinal malignancy.** What separates them is **one answer on history — unintentional weight loss — and one line on the examination card — where the tenderness is.**

**Version A is not an easier station. It is the same station with a reassuring answer, and it is only reassuring because you asked.** **Run the full six-minute structure for both; let the answers, not the patient's age, decide which diagnosis goes on top.**

**A ‘yes’ is the start of a question, not the end of one.** Every positive red flag gets the follow-up ladder: **how many kilos · over what period · were you trying to.** Here: **four to five kilograms over the last few months, unintentional, at 65.**

**The prostate questions move forward in version B.** In a 65-year-old man with weight loss and back pain, **prostate is one of the three commonest primaries to metastasise to bone** — so **stream, nocturia and dribbling** go inside the red flag block rather than waiting for referred pain at the end, **which in a six-minute history you may never reach.** His answer — **up twice a night, poor stream** — turns the list from a recital into **‘prostate first, because of what you told me about your waterworks.’**

**The six primaries, plus myeloma**: **breast · lung · prostate**, then **thyroid · kidney · melanoma**, plus **multiple myeloma — a primary marrow cancer, not a metastasis.** Name all of them; **‘cancer, infection, fracture’ scores nothing.**

**Breaking it — four moves, thirty seconds. Signpost, warn, say it, justify, then stop talking and let him speak.** **‘I’ve asked you a lot of questions and examined your back, and I’ve been thinking about a number of causes. I’m afraid what I have to say isn’t straightforward.’** [pause — two full seconds] **‘I’m concerned there may be a cancer in your spine, or a cancer somewhere else in the body that has spread to it.’**

**Answering ‘are you sure?’**: **‘I’m not certain, and that’s an honest answer. What I am certain of is that this needs sorting out quickly, and I’m not prepared to wait and see. The tests will tell us.’** Then **two reasons**: **the four to five kilos lost without trying, and the tenderness over one particular bone, which points at the bone itself rather than the muscles.**

**Version A — reassure with a timeframe, not a shrug.** ‘It’s nothing to worry about’ is dismissal. **‘What you have is non-specific mechanical back pain — the muscles and small joints beside your spine have been strained and are in spasm. Three things tell me that: the pain stays in your back and doesn’t run down your leg; there’s no numbness or weakness; and the tenderness was in the muscles beside your spine, not on the bones. It is the commonest cause of back pain and most people are much better within four to six weeks.’** **Three negatives are a positive finding — say all three out loud.**

**Version B plan**: **full examination looking for the primary — breast, chest, abdomen, lymph nodes, skin, thyroid, and prostate on rectal examination** · **assess for cord compression — any neurology, any bladder or bowel change** · bloods as above · **MRI whole spine** · **CT chest, abdomen and pelvis** · **urgent referral to a service that can biopsy and stage, telephoned today rather than posted.** Then: **‘Is there someone at home with you — would you like your wife to come in so we can go through this together?’**

**The cord compression safety net, verbatim**: **‘If you develop any weakness or numbness in your legs, any numbness around your back passage, or you can’t pass urine or start leaking — go straight to an emergency department, day or night. Do not wait for the scan.’** **Metastatic spinal cord compression converts an urgent referral into a same-day emergency: MRI whole spine within hours, dexamethasone, and immediate oncology or neurosurgical discussion.** VERIFY SA — **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for time-critical transfer, **PATS** for planned appointments, tertiary oncology and spinal services at the **RAH** and **Flinders**; **ACCHS** and Aboriginal Liaison Officer with **Closing the Gap** co-payment; **TIS National 131 450.**

**Version B is the one candidates fail — and they fail it AFTER getting the diagnosis right.** They worked out renal colic and were then asked what examination they would perform, and **asked only for the abdomen and kidneys.** **It is still a back pain presentation. Ask for one and you land on a three.**

**Version A — ankylosing spondylitis.** A chronic seronegative spondyloarthropathy causing **inflammatory back and buttock pain with progressive restriction of spinal movement, typically beginning before 45.** **Ten years of recurrent back pain in a young man is chronic inflammatory disease until proven otherwise — chronicity is the clue, not the comfort.**

**The inflammatory pattern, asked in full**: **worse in the morning · how long before you loosen up (over 30 minutes) · worse after resting or sitting still · better with exercise · buttock pain that swaps sides · wakes him in the second half of the night.** **Night pain is not one thing** — in A it is inflammatory and **improves once he gets up and moves**; in C it is a red flag, **unremitting and not relieved by position.** **Ask what happens when he gets up.**

**Version A management: exercise IS the treatment, not an adjunct** — daily spinal extension and mobility work, and physiotherapy experienced in spondyloarthritis — **with regular NSAIDs first-line.** VERIFY Bloods **FBE, CRP, ESR, HLA-B27** (supports, does not confirm — common in healthy people and absent in a minority); **sacroiliac X-ray first, MRI SIJ if the X-ray is normal and suspicion is high, because radiographic change lags years behind symptoms.** Biologics for inadequate response. **Smoking cessation — smoking accelerates radiographic progression, Quitline 13 7848.** **Safety net: a painful red eye with blurred vision or photophobia is acute anterior uveitis and needs same-day ophthalmology, not chloramphenicol.**

**Version B — renal (ureteric) colic.** Four minutes only, so **the order must change.** **Say the redirect out loud**: **‘The way you’ve described that — one-sided, coming in spasms, and travelling to your flank and groin — makes me want to ask about your waterworks first.’** That tells the examiner you reshuffled **deliberately** rather than by accident.

**Version B management**: **analgesia is the priority — an NSAID first-line unless contraindicated**, opioid if insufficient VERIFY · antiemetic · **urine dipstick and MSU; FBE, EUC, CRP, calcium and urate** · **non-contrast CT KUB is the first-line imaging test** (ultrasound first in pregnancy and children) · **strain the urine and send any stone for analysis.** **Urgent urology — do not manage in the community: fever with obstruction, a solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral obstruction, acute kidney injury, or pain not controlled by adequate analgesia.**

**Version C — the grey zone.** **The most defensible top diagnosis is lumbar radiculopathy, with osteoporotic vertebral fracture a strong second — and any of several answers passes provided it is reasoned.** **‘I can’t say without examining her’ fails. So does four diagnoses with equal weight.**

**Version C's extra block, which nobody asks**: **‘When did you have your last period? Any flushes or sweats around that time? Have you ever taken hormone replacement? Ever had a bone density scan, or been told your bones are thin? Have you lost any height? Any steroid tablets, ever? Do you smoke?’** **A post-menopausal woman who never took HRT, whose pain began as she stood up from gardening, is the classic candidate for an osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture — minimal force, sudden onset.**

**Committing, the script**: **‘Back pain can come from a number of different places, and I want to be honest with you that I can’t be certain today. But if you ask me what I think is most likely, it is a lumbar radiculopathy — a nerve leaving the lower spine that is being irritated or pressed on. I say that because the pain travels down one leg, and that pattern is typical of a nerve rather than a muscle.’** Then **name and dismiss the rest — the standing-up mechanism and post-menopausal bone loss, the past kidney stones, the mother's breast cancer with her own normal mammograms.**

**Version A — the answer that should change your track in the first sentence**: **‘On and off for about ten years now — it's nothing new for me.’** **Stop racing through SICORA and move the arthritis group forward.**

stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. James Bennett, 42, a storeman, with low back pain for ten days after lifting pallets at work. Pain across the lower back, worse on bending and by the end of the day, eased by lying down. No leg pain, numbness or weakness. No trauma, fever, weight loss, bladder or bowel change, or cancer history. Tasks: explain the most likely diagnosis to the patient — and discuss your management with the patient.

Examination: afebrile with normal observations, lumbar paraspinal tenderness with painful restriction of flexion, negative straight leg raise and normal lower limb neurology. Variants: lumbar radiculopathy; six weeks on and still off work; and the cauda equina emergency.

dx: **The seven bullets, in order: reassure · stay active · pain relief · physiotherapy · NO IMAGING, and say why · work with modified duties · review at 2–4 weeks with a named safety net.** **Ninety seconds. Bullets five and six are the two candidates omit, and they are the two the examiner is waiting for.**

**THE discriminating issue: never say ‘rest’ without ‘but keep doing your usual daily activities’ in the same breath.** **‘Rest from the thing that set it off — so no heavy lifting for now — but I want you up and moving and doing your usual day-to-day things.’** **Practise the two halves as one unbreakable sentence so they cannot be separated under pressure.**

**Reassurance is the treatment, not the preamble.** **‘The problem is in the muscles, ligaments and small joints of your back — it is not a problem with the bones, and I've specifically checked for and ruled out the serious causes. Backs are strong. HURTING IS NOT THE SAME AS HARMING. And this will get better.’** **Never ‘it's JUST a muscle strain’** — *just* is heard as dismissal by a man in pain who is frightened for his job.

**The two clocks, not to be mixed**: **mechanical — conservative 4–6 weeks before reassessing. Radiculopathy — conservative 6–8 weeks before considering surgical referral. BOTH — review the patient at 2–4 weeks regardless.** Escalate immediately at any point for a **progressive deficit or cauda equina symptoms.**

**Drugs**: **NSAID first line — ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food, short course** VERIFY (check renal function, blood pressure, peptic ulcer disease and asthma). **Paracetamol optional — Australian randomised evidence found no benefit over placebo in acute low back pain**, so offer it but do not present it as effective. VERIFY **Heat is cheap, safe and modestly effective — recommend it.**

**AVOID opioids — Australian randomised evidence found them no better than placebo for acute low back and neck pain, with more harm.** VERIFY **AVOID pregabalin and gabapentin — no benefit over placebo in sciatica with substantial adverse effects.** VERIFY **Muscle relaxants rarely: limited evidence, sedation, dependence risk.** If he asks for something stronger: **‘there's good Australian research showing opioids are no better than a dummy tablet for back pain like yours, and they cause drowsiness, constipation and dependence. What actually shifts this is keeping moving and the physio.’**

**CORRECTION on certificates — the source teaches a medical certificate and time off at home, which contradicts the stay-active advice given in the same breath.** **Time away from work is one of the strongest predictors of long-term disability in back pain, and the risk rises with the duration of absence.** The evidence-based instrument is **a work capacity certificate specifying what he CAN do**, not a sickness certificate. **Total incapacity is reserved for jobs that cannot be modified at all, and then for days.**

**The safety net is a marked item, not a formality**: **‘Come back the same day, or go to the emergency department, if you get numbness between your legs or around your back passage; trouble passing urine, or not feeling when you need to go; any loss of control of your bowels; weakness in both legs; a fever; or if the pain suddenly becomes much worse.’** **Cauda equina is the one outcome here where a delay of hours produces permanent bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction.**

**Five versions, same seven bullets, differently loaded.** **B — radiculopathy: same plan, 6–8 weeks, add an image-guided epidural corticosteroid injection as an option and name the spinal surgical service as the escalation.** **C — demands a scan: the incidental-findings explanation, then the criteria that would change your mind.** **D — not better at six weeks: re-check red flags, screen yellow flags, address fear-avoidance, graded return to work, and only now consider imaging.** **E — the red flag: cauda equina. Immediate transfer, urgent MRI, emergency surgical referral, nil by mouth.** VERIFY

SA — **ReturnToWorkSA**: a lifting injury at work is a claim; complete a work capacity certificate specifying **capacity, not incapacity**, and engage the employer's return-to-work coordinator early. **SafeWork SA** if the workplace manual handling is generating injuries. **MM5: MRI is not available locally — book through the regional service or refer to Adelaide with PATS; suspected cauda equina is a TRANSFER, not a booking — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.** CORRECTION — **both neurosurgical and orthopaedic spinal services manage lumbar disc disease in Australia; refer to whichever spinal service your region uses rather than assuming one specialty.** **ACCHS** and Aboriginal Liaison Officer with **Closing the Gap** co-payment; **TIS 131 450.**
plan: **The diagnosis first, 25 seconds — as a MECHANISM, not as ‘just a strain’.** Muscles, ligaments and small joints; not the bones; serious causes specifically checked for and ruled out; **hurting is not the same as harming**; and it will get better.
**Bullet 1 — signpost.** **‘Let me tell you what I'd like to do about it — there are a few parts to the plan.’** Signposting buys you structure and stops the task becoming a lecture.

**Bullet 2 — STAY ACTIVE, one unbreakable sentence.** Rest from the trigger, **but keep doing your usual day-to-day things — walking, the shopping, getting out. Not lying in bed or on the couch.** Then defend it when he pushes: **‘It's the opposite of what most people expect, and it used to be what doctors said. Lying still stiffens you up, weakens the muscles that support your back and prolongs the pain. Moving hurts a bit at first — that's expected, and it isn't doing damage.’**
**Bullet 3 — pain relief.** **NSAID with food, short course** · paracetamol as an option **with the honest caveat** · **heat** · and **decline anything stronger with the reason**, not just a refusal.

**Bullet 4 — allied health.** Physiotherapy for **stretching, strengthening and the confidence to move** — **the part with the best evidence, both for getting better and for preventing recurrence.** Massage or manual therapy is reasonable **alongside the exercise, not instead of it.**

**Bullet 5 — NO IMAGING, said OUT LOUD.** **‘If we scanned the backs of everyone in this waiting room — including the people with no pain at all — we'd find bulging discs, worn joints and little tears in nearly all of them. It's a normal part of getting older, a bit like grey hair. So a scan would very likely show something, that something probably wouldn't be causing your pain, and it wouldn't change what we do — but it might leave you frightened of your own back.’** Then **name what WOULD make you scan.**

**Hold the line when he pushes**: **‘How do you know mine isn't serious without looking?’** → **‘Because of what you've told me and what I found examining you. The things that would worry me are a fever, weight loss, a history of cancer, numbness between the legs, trouble with your waterworks or weakness in your legs. You have none of them, and your nerve examination is completely normal.’**

**Bullet 6 — work.** **‘I'd rather keep you at work than sign you off, because staying at work is part of getting better.’** A certificate for **modified duties — no heavy lifting, the chance to change position — for the next couple of weeks.** If the employer can't manage it, review. **And the ReturnToWorkSA claim, done today.**

**The hidden agenda.** His father **hurt his back at the abattoir and never worked again**, and he is frightened the same thing is happening. **Ask what is worrying him — or he volunteers it after the work discussion.** Then **separate his situation from his father's**: no nerve damage, no serious cause, and **the single best thing for keeping him in work long term is staying in it now, in some form.**

**Bullet 7 — review at 2–4 weeks, then the safety net in plain English, then STOP.** **‘Does that all make sense — anything you'd like me to go over?’** Write it down for him. **Running over means losing the safety net, and the safety net is the marked item.**

**The rule, in one paragraph**: **do not image mechanical, non-specific low back pain — not an X-ray, not a CT, not an MRI.** It does not improve outcomes, delivers radiation for no benefit with plain films and CT, and **reliably produces findings that are present in asymptomatic people of the same age.**

**Do not image lumbar radiculopathy early either.** If the history and examination have established a root lesion, **an early scan does not change management, which is conservative for six to eight weeks.** **Image when surgery is genuinely on the table** — the scan is then a **surgical planning tool rather than a diagnostic one.**

**When you DO image**: **any red flag** — suspected cauda equina, malignancy, infection or fracture · **a progressive or severe neurological deficit** — a worsening foot drop, not a stable patch of numbness · **failure of conservative management at the end of the window**, where the patient would accept surgery or an injection · **diagnostic uncertainty that genuinely changes the plan.**

**The honest test**: **what would I do differently on Monday if the scan were abnormal? If the answer is nothing, it is not an investigation.** **MRI is the modality where imaging is indicated**, because it shows the disc, the root and the cord; **CT is the alternative where MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, and is the test for suspected fracture.**

**The reassessment at 4–6 weeks is not just ‘extend the certificate’.** **Re-check the red flags — they were negative ten days ago, they are not negative forever; a malignancy or an infection can declare itself between visits.** Then **screen the yellow flags formally — they predict chronicity better than any imaging finding, and they are treatable.**

**Version B adds an image-guided epidural corticosteroid injection** for persisting severe radicular pain — short-term benefit, referred and performed under image guidance. VERIFY **Surgery comes late, for specific indications, and most people never need it — do not promise it.**

dx: **Acute right C6 cervical radiculopathy, most likely a lateral disc protrusion at C5/6**, in a 40-year-old teacher two days after a weekend painting ceilings overhead. **The label follows the deficit, not the recall.**

**The premature-closure trap this case was built to punish**: old recalls record the answer as ‘cervical spondylosis’, and candidates say it even when the card in their hand describes **a numb thumb and weak elbow flexion.** CORRECTION — **spondylosis is simply osteoarthritis of the spine and is a fine diagnosis for mechanical neck pain with normal neurology. It is the WRONG diagnosis when there is an objective root-level deficit.** If challenged: **‘degenerative change may well be present and may even be the underlying cause of the foraminal narrowing, but the diagnosis I have to act on is the radiculopathy, because that is what the sensory loss over the thumb and the weak elbow flexion demonstrate.’**

**Localise the root — the only table you need.** **C5 lateral shoulder · shoulder abduction · biceps jerk. C6 THUMB · ELBOW FLEXION and wrist extension · BICEPS AND SUPINATOR. C7 middle finger · elbow extension and wrist flexion · triceps. C8 little finger · finger flexion · no reliable reflex. T1 medial upper arm · finger abduction.** **The sentence that scores is the one that joins them: ‘those two findings belong to the same single nerve root.’**

**Radicular versus referred**: radicular pain **travels below the elbow in a band and comes with numbness, tingling or weakness.** Referred pain from a facet joint or muscle is **a diffuse ache over the shoulder and upper arm with no neurological symptoms and no clear border.** **Naming that distinction out loud is worth more than any single question.**

**THE discriminating issue: screen for cervical myelopathy OUT LOUD, then cite the negative when you explain.** It is **the neck equivalent of saddle anaesthesia in low back pain**, it costs fifteen seconds, and **its absence is visible to the examiner twice — when you fail to ask, and again when your differential cannot say why myelopathy is unlikely.**

**Three corrections to how myelopathy is usually taught**: **(1) it is usually NOT acute and usually NOT a disc** — the commonest cause is **degenerative cervical myelopathy** developing over months to years; **(2) the legs are usually numb and clumsy, NOT painful** — leg pain is a radiculopathy or claudication feature; **(3) LOSS OF HAND DEXTERITY is the earliest and most useful symptom, earlier than bladder involvement, which is a LATE sign.** **Asking only about bladder and bowel will miss the diagnosis you are screening for.**

**Explaining it to her, plain English first**: **‘One of the nerves that leaves your spine in the neck and runs down your arm is being squeezed. The usual cause is a small tear in one of the cushions between the bones — a disc — where some of the softer centre bulges out and presses on the nerve as it comes out. Two days of painting with your head back is exactly the sort of thing that sets it off.’** **Never say the jargon version to Jenny — that is a sentence for the examiner.**

**Management**: **analgesia offered at minute one, not at the end** · **NSAID, ibuprofen 400–600 mg up to three times daily with food, shortest effective course** VERIFY · **keep the neck moving rather than resting it** · **NO COLLAR — it relieves briefly, then deconditions** · physiotherapy and graded return · **review at two weeks.** **AVOID pregabalin and gabapentin — Australian randomised evidence found no benefit over placebo in radicular pain with substantial adverse effects.** VERIFY **Most are much better within about six weeks; the great majority settle within three months without an operation.** VERIFY

**No imaging in the first six weeks without red flags or a progressive deficit — say it out loud, it is a marked point.** **‘A scan now would show wear and tear that nearly everyone over forty has. It wouldn't change what we do, and it can leave people frightened of a picture rather than reassured by how they're feeling.’** **MRI cervical spine is the test if imaging becomes indicated** — red flags, progressive or severe deficit, myelopathic features, or failure at six weeks. **Plain films only for suspected fracture, instability, or before manipulation in rheumatoid arthritis.**

**The hidden agenda: her mother's breast cancer went to her bones and her neck.** **Answer it with the specific negatives you elicited, not with blanket reassurance**: **‘Nothing you've told me points that way — no weight loss, no lumps, no pain waking you at night, and you've never had cancer yourself. A relative's breast cancer doesn't cause a spread in you.’** **Never ‘it's definitely not cancer’ — say that and add a review date.** SA — **MM5: MRI not available locally, book through the regional service or refer to Adelaide with PATS; urgent MRI means transfer, not a waiting list.** Cord compression → **RAH neurosurgical service, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.** **Significant upper limb weakness affects vehicle control — advise against driving and document it** (Motor Vehicles Act 1959 SA). **ACCHS**, Closing the Gap, **TIS 131 450.**
plan: **WIPE and open question**, then **acknowledge the distress before questioning.** **Then the analgesia offer — ten words, one mark, and it changes the tone of the whole consultation**: **‘Before we start — are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it?’**

**SICORA, SITE FIRST — ‘is it at the FRONT of your neck or the BACK?’** **The answer changes the entire differential structure**, and in version C this one question saves the station. Then severity, character, onset and what she was doing, constant or intermittent, getting better or worse, ever before.

**The question that makes the diagnosis**: **‘Does the pain travel anywhere — into your shoulder, your arm, your hand? WHICH FINGERS? Any pins and needles, numbness or weakness in that arm?’** **‘My hand tingles’ localises nothing. ‘Thumb and index’ is C6 and it makes the diagnosis for you.**

**Pattern of pain — three questions, never skipped**: **wakes you at night · worse in the morning or the end of the day · worse with activity or worse after rest · morning stiffness and how long.** Then **say what you just learned**: **‘so it's worse with activity and eases with rest, and the stiffness is short — that fits a mechanical pattern.’** The examiner hears you reasoning, not collecting.

**General MSK screen, four quick questions**: swelling · redness or rash · **stiffness AND ITS DURATION — the highest-yield of the four, separating mechanical from inflammatory in one question** · any injury, even minor.

**Red flag block one — malignancy.** Weight loss · appetite · lumps · unusually tired · **ever diagnosed with any cancer, anyone in the family** · cough or haemoptysis · **tailored: ‘ever had a breast lump, or been called back from a mammogram?’** · smoking. CORRECTION — in a man ask about **a known prostate diagnosis or a previous PSA**, not nocturia, which is non-specific BPH.

**Red flag block two — infection, then meningitis in the same breath.** Fevers, chills, night sweats · recent infections, skin infections, dental work · diabetes · steroids · injecting drug use. Then **headache, nausea or vomiting, photophobia, rash.** **Neck stiffness is not neck pain — meningitis gives painful resistance to passive flexion with fever and systemic illness.**

**Red flag block three — CERVICAL MYELOPATHY, four questions word for word.** **‘Have you had any problems with your walking — any unsteadiness or falls? Any loss of control of your bladder or bowel? Have your hands become clumsy — buttons, keys, handwriting, dropping things? When you bend your neck forward, do you get any electric-shock feeling down your back?’** If she asks why: **‘there's a more serious condition where the pressure is on the spinal cord itself rather than a single nerve, and your answers tell me that isn't what's happening.’**

**Spine group, then arthritis, then referred.** Occupation, desk or overhead work, **anything out of the ordinary in the last week** — *she painted the ceilings, so repeat it back so the examiner hears you registered it.* Then other joints, family arthritis, scaly rash and nail changes, diarrhoea or blood in stools, dysuria or discharge. Then **headaches and stress, EXERTIONAL CHEST PAIN OR BREATHLESSNESS, shoulder and hip girdle stiffness.**

**SADMA, then ideas concerns and expectations — this is where the hidden agenda lives.** **You will not run out of time in this station**: neck pain has a shorter differential than low back pain and most candidates finish the nine blocks at about 5:30. **Spend the spare thirty seconds on ‘anything you were particularly worried this might be?’** Then at 6:00 **ask for the card, read it silently, and say what it MEANS before you say what it IS.**
pefe: **Ask for the findings specifically, not generically** — inspection, palpation of spinous processes and paraspinal muscles, active movements, **Spurling's test**, full upper limb neurology **including the supinator reflex**, and **a myelopathy screen (Hoffmann, gait, plantars).** **Once the card is handed over the history is closed** — turning back to the patient gets you ‘you have what you have.’

**Read the card out loud before you speak to her, and say the meaning first**: **‘a sensory deficit in the thumb and weak elbow flexion — the same nerve root.’** Candidates who skim the card and announce a diagnosis lose the reasoning mark.

What I won't do is leave you struggling meanwhile — let's sort your painkillers today, and I'll get the physiotherapist to look at a walking aid.’** *‘I've waited fourteen months’* → pause → **‘I'm sorry — that matters and I'm not dismissing it. The hip isn't off the table; it's waiting until we know what we're treating.’**

**TWO CORRECTIONS that protect the patient.** (1) **Treatment is NOT ‘just symptom relief’** — the source says surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy in metastatic prostate cancer are only palliative. **That is wrong and saying it to a patient is a serious error.** **Androgen deprivation, commonly with an androgen-receptor pathway inhibitor or docetaxel, is DISEASE-MODIFYING and prolongs survival, often by years**; bone-targeted agents reduce skeletal events; radiotherapy to a painful deposit is analgesic and locally disease-modifying. VERIFY (2) **Palliative care is not the end of the road** — it is **symptom-focused care delivered ALONGSIDE active anticancer treatment**, and early referral improves quality of life. **Say ‘supportive care’, and say ALONGSIDE, not instead of.** To him, verbatim: **‘If it is prostate cancer that has spread, I want to be straight with you: it wouldn't be curable. But it is very treatable — HORMONE TREATMENTS work well and can control it for a long time, and targeted RADIOTHERAPY is very good for bone pain. We'd bring in a supportive care team alongside that treatment, not instead of it.’** **Never a survival figure, and never a timeframe for the results** — *‘I'll chase these and ring you as soon as I have anything’* is a promise you can keep; *‘we'll know by Friday’* is not.
plan: **There is no presenting complaint, so BUILD THE BRIDGE YOURSELF in fifteen seconds.** **‘I do have your x-ray report and I do have an answer for you. Before we go through it, would it be all right if I asked you a few questions first? It will help me explain what it means. Is there anything in particular that's been on your mind?’** **The agenda question is the only door his hidden concern walks through** — his daughter's wedding in March, volunteered at seven minutes if never asked.

**Symptoms of the lesion — FOUR QUESTIONS AND MOVE, not four minutes of SOCRATES.** **‘Have you had any back pain? Whereabouts, and how long?’** (one line of character and duration) **‘Does it wake you at night?’** **‘Any numbness, pins and needles or weakness in your legs?’** **‘Any change in your waterworks or bowels — trouble holding on, or numbness around the back passage?’** **If any are positive the station changes — say so: ‘that combination needs an urgent MRI today, not next week.’**

**The general cancer screen.** Signpost first: **‘I'm going to ask about a few different parts of the body. Some questions will seem unrelated — there's a reason and I'll explain at the end.’** Then **weight loss — and QUANTIFY it even when he explains it away** · appetite · tiredness, night sweats, fevers · **‘any lumps or bumps anywhere?’** (he hesitates, then gives the left neck lump — **acknowledge it, date it, add it to the plan**) · **ever been told you had a cancer · ever had radiotherapy.**

**The sweep, seven groups, two or three questions each.** **Prostate** — nocturia and how many times, difficulty starting, weak stream, dribbling, incomplete emptying, haematuria. **Lung** — cough or breathlessness beyond baseline, haemoptysis, **smoking in pack-years (here 20 a day for 30 years = 30 PACK-YEARS, quit 12 years ago)**, **and occupation now AND before retirement** — on Yorke Peninsula that earns its keep: **the Moonta and Wallaroo copper mines and smelters, farm chemicals, asbestos in older sheds, silos and fibro housing.** Add **‘were you ever around asbestos or dust at work?’**

**Thyroid** — neck swelling, voice change, trouble swallowing, heat or cold intolerance. **Kidney** — haematuria, loin pain. **Skin** — a changing mole, a skin cancer cut out, sun exposure. **Bowel** — pain, change in habit, blood or black motions, **the screening kit.** **Blood** — bone pain elsewhere, recurrent infections, **thirst, constipation, confusion** (hypercalcaemia).

**Background, only if the clock allows — thirty seconds.** **‘Your COPD and anaemia — when were you diagnosed, what treatment, who reviews them, any admissions?’** **They are not scenery**: unexplained anaemia with a bone lesion points at **marrow infiltration, myeloma, or occult GI blood loss**, and **a COPD patient can still develop lung cancer** with breathlessness blamed on the wrong disease for years. **If you are behind, skip it and tell the examiner you would have taken it.**
**Task 2 — explain the report.** Name the test, then the finding, in plain words. Then **warning shot → pause → the word → ‘this is not a diagnosis’ → stop talking.**
**Task 3 — the most likely diagnosis with THREE REASONS, then the differentials in plain English**, including **at least one benign and one infective cause.**

**Task 4 — the operation FIRST, with two reasons and a pain plan.** Then **how we confirm it and what each test is for**: today — examination including DRE and the neck lump, bloods including **PSA, calcium and a myeloma screen**; this week — **MRI spine, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan**; then **a sample, most likely from the neck lump.** Then **urgent urology and medical oncology, and an MDT.**

**The last thirty seconds carry marks.** **Red flags** — leg weakness or numbness, trouble passing urine or holding on, saddle numbness, **a band of pain around the chest** → same day. **Written information with the practice number and Cancer Council SA 13 11 20** · **PATS for Adelaide** · **‘is there someone you'd like with you next time? I'm happy to go through it again with Beryl’** (*‘I haven't told her anything yet’* → **‘then let's do it together’**) · **review in a week.** **And no moralising about the smoking.**
pefe: **No film and no examination findings are given — the report is on the desk.** What is scored is **what you would examine and what you would order**, and both must look for **spread**.

**Examine: the cord compression screen first** — power, sensation, reflexes, plantars, **saddle sensation and anal tone** — then **for the primary**: DRE, **cervical and supraclavicular nodes**, breasts, **full skin survey including the back**, chest, abdomen, testes.

**CORRECTION — do not overclaim the neck node.** The source concludes from a left-sided node that this is prostate. **A left supraclavicular (Virchow) node classically drains the abdomen and chest — stomach, pancreas, lung, lymphoma — and only uncommonly prostate.** If challenged: **‘I used the node as evidence of systemic malignancy rather than of prostate specifically. A left supraclavicular node would push me to look hard at the abdomen and chest as well — and it is the most accessible site to biopsy.’**

**Analgesia today** — regular paracetamol, add an opioid for significant bone pain; **avoid NSAIDs by reflex in an anaemic, comorbid 72-year-old.** And **cancel the theatre booking and tell the surgical unit yourself.**

**Do not miss**: **metastatic spinal cord compression** (new weakness, a sensory level, sphincter change or band-like pain = **same-day MRI and same-day discussion with neurosurgery or radiation oncology**, with high-dose corticosteroid on specialist advice VERIFY ) · **hypercalcaemia of malignancy** — corrected calcium today · **impending long-bone fracture** — ask about hip and thigh pain, a painful femoral deposit may need prophylactic fixation · **infection dressed as tumour** — fever and rigors mean **blood cultures before antibiotics.**

**If the examiner pushes**: *‘why not do the hip and investigate afterwards?’* → **‘an undiagnosed malignancy raises anaesthetic and thrombotic risk, the T5 lesion is a hazard during positioning, and treatment may need to start before the joint is addressed.’** *‘What if the PSA is normal?’* → **‘that makes prostate less likely but does not exclude it, and does not remove the need for tissue. I'd broaden the search, not stop it.’** VERIFY

**If the role-player gives you nothing** — some briefs are written with every answer negative — **do not invent a primary**: **‘I haven't found a clear source today, which happens. We then look with scans, and if we still can't find it we take a sample from the abnormal area itself.’** **Then still answer the operation question — that decision does not depend on knowing the primary.**

SA — Wallaroo is **Yorke and Northern LHN, MM5**: imaging beyond plain film and specialist review mean travel, so **arrange PATS at this visit, not later**; tertiary referral to **RAH, TQEH or FMC** by unit; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** and the RFDS for retrieval; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**; **TIS 131 450**; Aboriginal Liaison Officer or ACCHS and Closing the Gap. Advance care planning is right to raise **later, once a diagnosis exists** — in SA that is an **Advance Care Directive under the Advance Care Directives Act 2013.**

stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. Daniel Hartley, 38, presents complaining of headache and neck pain. Temperature 36.7, heart rate 74, BP 132/84, respiratory rate 14, saturations 99 per cent — and he looks tired. Tasks: take a history for six minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings on a card, with no further questions afterwards — then explain your diagnosis and differentials to the patient.

8 minutes. Variants: a thunderclap episode three days ago, which is subarachnoid haemorrhage; sudden one-sided neck pain with a droopy eyelid after chiropractic manipulation, which is arterial dissection; daily Nurofen plus, which is medication-overuse headache; and a woman over 50 with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, which is giant cell arteritis.

findings: What to ASK FOR, by name

Blood pressure AND FUNDOSCOPY — both free, both marked, both routinely omitted · cranial nerves · limbs and gait · TEMPORAL ARTERIES · and for the neck: RANGE OF MOVEMENT, PARAVERTEBRAL AND TRAPEZIUS TENDERNESS, and WHETHER PRESSURE OVER THE UPPER CERVICAL SPINE REPRODUCES HIS HEADACHE. After the card, NO FURTHER QUESTIONS to the patient

Cranial nerves
Normal

Temporal arteries
NORMAL AND PULSATILE. He is 38 — in the 68-year-old version this row reads THICKENED, TENDER AND PULSELESS
Neck
FULL RANGE OF MOVEMENT with discomfort at end range · MARKED TENDERNESS OF THE PARAVERTEBRAL AND TRAPEZIUS MUSCLES BILATERALLY · NO MIDLINE BONY TENDERNESS · no lymphadenopathy · NO MENINGISM
Interpret the card BEFORE you name the diagnosis

‘So the only abnormality is tender neck muscles. The fundi, cranial nerves, limbs and gait are all normal, and there is no meningism and no bony tenderness. That combination excludes the serious causes and points to a muscular origin.’
THE OTHER FOUR VERSION CARDS

B — NECK STIFFNESS, PHOTOPHOBIA, DROWSY BUT ROUSABLE, no focal deficit → subarachnoid haemorrhage. C — PTOSIS AND MIOSIS on the painful side, NO ANHIDROSIS, otherwise normal → internal carotid dissection. D — normal examination with mild paravertebral tenderness → medication-overuse headache. E — THICKENED, TENDER, PULSELESS TEMPORAL ARTERY with proximal girdle tenderness → giant cell arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica

dx: **Tension-type headache** — bilateral, **pressing or tightening**, mild to moderate, **not aggravated by routine physical activity**, without vomiting, with **at most one of photophobia or phonophobia.** **Pericranial muscle tenderness is the physical sign, and it is exactly what the card describes.**

**A simple diagnosis wrapped in a deliberately awkward stem. The marks are not in the answer — almost everyone says tension headache — they are in whether you worked BOTH lists.** The neck pain was added because the plain headache version was too easy.

**The two complaints are not coincidental; they are the same problem seen from two ends.** **Cervicogenic headache is a GROUP, not a diagnosis — every cause of neck pain sits inside it** — and tension-type headache **arises from sustained contraction of the very neck muscles you are being asked about.**

**SAY THE WORD CERVICOGENIC OUT LOUD.** It is **the single word that tells the examiner you understood why both complaints were in the stem.** The patient-facing differential run, serious first: **‘a bleed around the brain — that comes on like a thunderclap, yours builds up slowly; a tear in one of the arteries in the neck — sudden one-sided neck pain and often a droopy eyelid, you have neither; an infection of the lining of the brain — but you have no fever, rash or light sensitivity; pressure inside the head, from a growth for example — that would be worse on waking or coughing, with vomiting or a change in vision, and the backs of your eyes are normal.’** Then **‘migraine, which throbs, worsens with activity and makes you feel sick; and cluster, which sits around one eye and makes it water.’** Then **‘headaches coming from the neck itself — we call those cervicogenic: wear and tear in the neck joints, arthritis, a trapped nerve. Your neck moves fully, no other joints are involved and you have no arm symptoms — but the muscular cause I've described sits at the mild end of that same group.’**

**The two red flags that live in the overlap.** **(1) Subarachnoid haemorrhage** — headache with neck pain is its signature, because blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges. **CORRECTION — the source drops SAH from this list because tension headache is likelier. Likelihood is not safety. It stays on the list.** **(2) Cervical artery dissection** — sudden unilateral neck pain with headache after minor trauma, heavy lifting or **neck manipulation**, with **Horner syndrome on the painful side.** It is **a leading cause of stroke in the under-fifties.**

**One question decides whether this is a GP problem or an emergency**: **‘How quickly did it come on — how long from feeling normal to the worst it got?’** **Duration tells you the pattern; SPEED OF ONSET is what finds the bleed.** **Severity alone does not do it — plenty of tension headaches are described as the worst ever.** If asked about severity: **‘the question is the speed of onset. If that is under a minute I would treat it as a subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.’**

**The three questions that separate the primary headaches**: **worse on routine activity?** yes → migraine, no → tension-type · **vomiting?** → migraine, raised pressure or an emergency, not tension-type · **worse on coughing, straining or bending?** → raised intracranial pressure.

**The explanation IS the treatment, and ‘it's just stress’ undoes it** — *just* is heard as ‘there's nothing wrong with you’. Give the mechanism: **‘When we're under pressure, and when we sit for hours with the head held forward and still, the muscles at the back of the neck and across the shoulders hold a low-grade contraction all day. Those muscles get tender — which is exactly what I found when I pressed on them — and the pain from them is felt as a tight band around the head. So your two complaints are one problem: THE NECK IS WHERE IT COMES FROM, THE HEAD IS WHERE YOU FEEL IT.’**

**Answer the brain tumour fear with your FINDINGS, not with comfort**: **‘The features that would make me worry about something inside the head are a headache worse first thing in the morning or on coughing, vomiting, a change in vision, weakness, numbness or fits — and swelling at the backs of the eyes. You have none of them and your examination is normal. That is why I'm not scanning you today, and I'll tell you exactly what would change my mind.’**

**Management**: **address the stressor** — hours, workload, sleep, desk breaks, and ask what he can actually change · **physiotherapy, posture and workstation review** (*‘those screens being low is worth fixing’*), stretching, regular aerobic exercise · **simple analgesia for individual bad days with an EXPLICIT cap, in these words: ‘no more than a couple of days a week — painkillers most days turn an occasional headache into a daily one’** VERIFY · **headache diary** — days affected, medication days, triggers · **relaxation or CBT, and a GP Mental Health Treatment Plan with sessions with a psychologist** where stress or mood is the driver · **low-dose amitriptyline nocte** as the usual first preventive for frequent or chronic tension-type headache VERIFY · **review at four weeks with the diary.** SA — **SafeWork SA** duties if the workload is a workplace hazard, **ReturnToWorkSA** for a psychological injury claim, and **a certificate for modified duties rather than blanket time off**; **MM5: CT is at the base hospital but MRI and angiography mean transfer — suspected dissection or SAH is a transfer, not an outpatient booking, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **TIS 131 450.**
plan: WIPE, open question, acknowledge, **offer analgesia** — then **SIGNPOST THE SPLIT, the cheapest structural mark in the station**: **‘You've mentioned two things, so I'm going to ask about the headache first and then about the neck, and then some questions to make sure I'm not missing anything serious.’**

**SICORA of the headache — ONSET FIRST.** **‘How quickly does it come on — how long from feeling normal to the worst it gets?’** Then side, character, severity, duration and frequency, radiation, **‘worse when you move about, climb stairs, bend over or cough?’**, aggravating and relieving. **If the answer to onset is seconds to a minute, STOP — you are in version B and the station is now a subarachnoid haemorrhage.**

**SICORA of the NECK, separately — do not blend the two into one muddled account.** Front or back · **‘which came first, the headache or the neck pain?’** · out of ten · dull or sharp · **radiation into the shoulder or down the arm, pins and needles, numbness** · wakes you at night · morning or end of day · worse with activity or after rest · **stiffness and how long** · any injury.

**Say what you have learned — the examiner hears you reasoning**: **‘So the neck ache and the headache rise together through the day, and neither wakes you — that fits a muscular, mechanical pattern rather than anything inflammatory or sinister.’** **Neck pain PRECEDING and provoking the headache points to cervicogenic; rising together points to tension-type.**

**The overlap red flags, one block.** **Thunderclap** — a single episode, worst ever, maximum within a minute, anything on exertion or straining. **Dissection** — sudden one-sided neck pain · **any injury, heavy lifting, or neck manipulation — a chiropractor or physiotherapist** · **drooping eyelid, double vision or blurring** · weakness, numbness or difficulty speaking down one side.

**Meningitis and raised pressure** — fevers, chills, rashes · nausea or vomiting **particularly first thing in the morning** · bright lights · **worse lying down or on waking** · vision, weakness, numbness, fits, **personality change others have noticed.** **Malignancy and the neck-specific ones** — weight loss, appetite, lumps, previous cancer · **unsteadiness or falls, and loss of bladder or bowel control.** **Say out loud that one neurological screen covered brain tumour, dissection, myelopathy and radiculopathy together.**

**The headache group.** **‘How are things at work and at home — any particular pressures at the moment? How is your sleep, and your mood?’** **DO NOT POUNCE.** The moment the boss is mentioned the temptation is *‘so it's stress then’* — **the stressor is the answer, but the EXPLORATION is the mark**: hours, sleep, mood, alcohol, home, plus **two depression screening questions.** Then **migraine** — aura, nausea, light and noise, family history — and **cluster** — watering or red eye, blocked or running nostril.

**THE NECK BLOCK — the block that decides the station, and it costs twenty seconds.** **‘What do you do for work, and how is your desk and screen set up? How many hours a day is your head forward and still? Any unaccustomed activity, a new pillow, an awkward sleeping position? Any pain or swelling in other joints? Any family history of arthritis, any scaly rashes, any recent diarrhoea or urinary symptoms? Any pain or stiffness across the shoulders in the morning?’**

**Analgesia frequency — almost always dropped.** **‘What have you been taking, and HOW MANY DAYS IN A TYPICAL MONTH? Anything with codeine? How much coffee, tea or energy drink — and does a missed coffee give you a headache?’** Then closure: PMHx **particularly blood pressure**, medicines, allergies, smoking, alcohol, and **‘is there anything you were particularly worried this might be?’** — the agenda arrives here, or is volunteered at 5:30 regardless.

**Ask for the card, naming fundoscopy and blood pressure.** Then **interpret it before you name the diagnosis** → **the diagnosis linking both complaints** → **the four reasons** → **both differential lists, serious first, and say CERVICOGENIC** → **decline imaging with the reason, cap the analgesia frequency, and give the safety net.**
pefe: **Ask for blood pressure and fundoscopy BY NAME.** Both are free, both are marked, and both are routinely omitted. **Add the temporal arteries**, and for the neck: **range of movement, paravertebral and trapezius tenderness, and whether pressure over the upper cervical spine reproduces his headache.**

**Read the card and interpret it before naming anything.** The only abnormality is tender neck muscles; everything that would indicate a serious cause is normal — **and saying that combination out loud is what converts a guess into a defended diagnosis.**

**Investigations: NONE in a typical tension-type headache with a normal examination.** **CT head only for thunderclap onset, focal deficit, seizure, papilloedema, immunosuppression, or a headache that has changed character.** **CT or MR angiography if dissection is suspected.** **ESR and CRP in ANY patient over 50 with a new headache.** **Blood pressure in everyone.**

**The scripted imaging answer**: **‘I would not image him. His headache has no warning features, his neurological examination and fundoscopy are normal, and imaging in that setting does not change management. It also has a real cost: an incidental finding in a worried man becomes a second problem. I would review him in four weeks, and I would image if the pattern changed, if he developed any neurological sign, or if the headache became worse on waking, coughing or straining.’**
**Never manipulate the neck where dissection is possible.** In version C: **‘please don't have your neck manipulated again.’**

**Separating tension-type from cervicogenic, if challenged**: **‘Cervicogenic headache is typically side-locked, preceded by neck pain, and reproduced by neck movement or upper cervical pressure. His is bilateral and rises WITH the neck ache rather than after it. In practice they overlap, and the management — posture, physiotherapy and the stressor — is much the same.’**

**Version D — medication overuse**: acute headache medication on **10–15+ days a month for three months or more** turns an episodic headache into a daily one, and **no preventive works until the offending drug is withdrawn.** VERIFY Simple analgesics have the higher threshold; **opioid, combination and triptan preparations the lower.** **Warn about 1–2 weeks of rebound and that the rebound is expected, not evidence you are wrong.** It is **the single most treatable cause of chronic daily headache in Australian general practice, and almost no candidate asks.**

**Version E — over 50 with a new headache**: add **scalp tenderness on brushing hair, jaw claudication on chewing, transient visual change, and girdle stiffness.** **Start corticosteroid immediately — do not delay for the biopsy** — with urgent ESR and CRP, temporal artery biopsy and same-day ophthalmology. VERIFY **And the household question once: carbon monoxide, if everyone at home has a headache that is better away from the house.**

The key differential is discoid eczema, which is itchier, more exudative and less sharply defined; I would also consider tinea corporis, which is annular with an active scaly edge and a clearing centre — a skin scraping would exclude it.' One well-argued differential beats a list of five with no reasoning. If asked what the auspitz sign is: 'Pinpoint bleeding when a psoriatic scale is lifted, because the thinned epidermis over dilated dermal capillaries is torn. It supports psoriasis; it is not needed for the diagnosis.' The focused examination for associated features: nails for pitting, onycholysis, oil-drop discolouration and subungual hyperkeratosis; scalp, hairline and behind the ears; knees, umbilicus and natal cleft; joints for swollen tender small joints, dactylitis and back stiffness; feet and flexures for the tinea and eczema differentials; and weight and blood pressure, because psoriasis carries cardiometabolic risk. Do not run a full musculoskeletal screen and run out of time. The explanation in plain words: 'This looks like psoriasis — a common, non-contagious condition where the skin renews itself too quickly and builds up into scaly patches. It tends to come and go. It's not caused by anything you've done, and we can control it well.' and to the hidden concern: 'It is not infectious at all — you cannot pass it to anyone. If a mate comments, the honest answer is that it's a skin condition like eczema.' Management: emollient with a potent topical corticosteroid once daily for four weeks, with or without calcipotriol; screening for psoriatic arthritis and cardiovascular risk; review in six weeks; and dermatology through PATS if it fails to respond or covers more than ten per cent of his skin. The safety net: come back sooner if it spreads quickly, becomes red all over, pus spots appear, or the joints swell or stiffen. Version B is henoch-schonlein purpura — IgA vasculitis — with early renal involvement. The examination, and why: 'The systems HSP involves, and the alternatives I must exclude. Abdomen for tenderness, a mass or intussusception; testes in a boy; joints — ankles and knees for swelling; blood pressure and a urine dipstick for nephritis; mouth and gums for mucosal bleeding; lymph nodes, liver and spleen and pallor for leukaemia; neck stiffness and conscious state for meningococcal disease; and a full skin survey for bruises of different ages in unusual sites, because non-accidental injury must be considered.' then: 'She is well and afebrile, so meningococcaemia is unlikely, but I'll send an FBC and film to exclude thrombocytopenia and leukaemia, U&E and a formal urine protein-creatinine ratio.' The thing we watch is the kidneys, so we'll check her urine and blood pressure weekly for a month and then monthly until six months. Bring her straight back — or call 000 — if she gets a fever with the rash spreading, severe tummy pain or vomiting, blood in the stool, swelling, or if she becomes drowsy. If there is protein in the urine or the pressure rises, she'll see the paediatric team at the women's and children's.' stem: The repeatable skeleton behind every gynaecology station: the opening, the five Ps in their adult, menopausal and teenage versions, the differential spine by complaint, and the word-for-word physical examination request. Learn this once and every later station becomes the same history with a different set of key points squeezed in.

The six station types: a period problem — heavy, painful, absent or between periods. A bleeding problem — post-coital, postmenopausal, or on a mirena. A discharge or vulval problem — discharge, itch, a lump down below, pain on sex. A urinary problem — leaking, frequency, retention. A counselling station — a result, a device, a hormone, a vaccine or a screening programme, with no history or a short one. And a result interpretation — her screening test, hormone profile or ultrasound handed to you.

findings: SAY THIS BEFORE ANY PELVIC REQUEST — the single most reliably scored sentence in gynaecology

‘I would like to perform a pelvic examination. I would EXPLAIN IT, obtain her CONSENT, and have a CHAPERONE present.’ Examining without consent or chaperone is treated as a PROFESSIONALISM BREACH, not a knowledge gap — AUTOMATIC FAIL. And HEADLINE every step: NAME THE MANOEUVRE, THEN ASK FOR THE FINDING — an examiner who does not hear the step will not give you the finding, and a finding you were never given cannot be used in your diagnosis
GENERAL AND ABDOMEN — NOT OPTIONAL

General appearance: LEVEL OF CONSCIOUSNESS, PALLOR, CACHEXIA, BMI · vital signs WITH A POSTURAL BLOOD PRESSURE · ABDOMEN — two questions only: TENDERNESS and MASS; then THE LOWER-BORDER QUESTION. The uterus is barely palpable abdominally when normal, which is exactly why a palpable mass matters — A MASS WHOSE LOWER BORDER YOU CANNOT REACH IS ARISING FROM THE PELVIS. Candidates rush to the speculum and skip this
INSPECTION — three fixed boxes, every time

‘On inspection of the vulva and perineum — any SKIN CHANGES such as redness, rash or ulcers? Any LUMPS OR SWELLINGS? Any DISCHARGE OR BLEEDING?’ Listening for: Bartholin swelling, PROLAPSE AT THE INTROITUS, lichen sclerosus, warts, an ulcer
SPECULUM — THE CERVIX AND THE VAGINAL WALLS

‘On speculum — is the CERVIX normal? Specifically any lesion, mass or abnormal growth, any CONTACT BLEEDING or discharge from the os? And can you describe the VAGINAL WALLS?’ Cervical cancer = an IRREGULAR, FRIABLE, BLEEDING lesion. ECTROPION = a SMOOTH RED RING around the os — the AMC's favourite finding. THE VAGINAL WALL QUESTION IS WHAT UNLOCKS ATROPHIC VAGINITIS: thin, pale, dry walls are ONLY GIVEN IF YOU ASK
BIMANUAL — and what each finding means

‘On bimanual — is there CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS? The UTERUS: size, and if enlarged is the border smooth or irregular, and is it tender? The ADNEXA: any mass or tenderness?’ CMT = PID in gynaecology, ECTOPIC in obstetrics · BULKY IRREGULAR uterus = FIBROIDS · BULKY TENDER SMOOTH uterus = ADENOMYOSIS · adnexal MASS = ovarian pathology · adnexal TENDERNESS = PID. Uterine size is described IN WEEKS, as in pregnancy
OFFICE TESTS
‘URINE DIPSTICK — blood, leucocytes, nitrites, glucose — and a URINE PREGNANCY TEST.’ NEVER SKIP THE PREGNANCY TEST IN A REPRODUCTIVE-AGE WOMAN
CORRECTION — PREGNANCY IS NOT OPTIONAL

The lecture treats the urine pregnancy test as a habit you may keep or drop. DO NOT DROP IT. In any woman of reproductive age with abnormal bleeding, pelvic pain or amenorrhoea, a urine or serum β-hCG is REQUIRED, because A STATED LAST MENSTRUAL PERIOD DOES NOT EXCLUDE AN ECTOPIC. Challenge — ‘her period was last week’ → ‘A reported recent bleed can occur with an ectopic pregnancy, so I would still confirm with a β-hCG before I move on.’
THE WHOLE REQUEST IN ONE BREATH — drill it without notes

‘Examiner, I would like the general appearance — level of consciousness, pallor, cachexia and BMI; vital signs with a postural blood pressure; a brief abdominal examination for tenderness and any mass, and if there is a mass, whether the lower border is palpable. I would then perform a pelvic examination WITH CONSENT AND A CHAPERONE: on inspection, skin changes, lumps and discharge; on speculum, the cervix for any lesion AND THE VAGINAL WALLS; on bimanual, cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, border and tenderness, and the adnexa. And a urine dipstick with a urine pregnancy test.’
