**Part A — frame it, then the three changes.** **'Your mum is right that it used to be called a pap smear. A few years ago the programme changed, and what we do now is better at picking up risk early. Let me take you through the three differences.'**

**Change 1 — age**: was 18, now **25 to 74**. Cervical cancer is very rare under 25, young immune systems clear the virus on their own, and testing that age group never reduced the number of cancers. **Change 2 — interval**: was two years, now **five**.

**Change 3 — the main one, and it answers her question directly**: **'your mum's test looked at the CELLS under a microscope, and sometimes by the time the cells looked abnormal the changes were well advanced. This test looks first for the virus — human papillomavirus, or HPV. The sample goes into a bottle of LIQUID, and if the virus is found, the laboratory automatically goes back to the same sample and checks the cells — that part is called CYTOLOGY. So it's one sample and one visit.'**

**When she says five years sounds like a long gap** — that is the cue for the **10–15 year** explanation. **When she asks about HPV and her boyfriend** — normalise it without blame, in the terms above.

**Part B — the procedure, in the order it happens to her**: privacy to undress with a sheet · lie on her back, knees bent and falling outwards · **offer a chaperone, and that she may bring someone** · speculum inserted gently and opened to see the cervix · **a small soft brush, a bit like a tiny broom, rotated against the cervix** · **'it shouldn't be painful — most women describe pressure or mild discomfort. Tell me at any point and I'll stop.'** · the brush rinsed into the bottle, light spotting afterwards is normal.

**Part C — self-collection, offered as a real choice**: the swab, **2–3 cm, rotated 20–30 seconds**, anyone who has used a tampon can do it, **equally good at detecting the virus** — **and then the limitation: a vaginal sample can be tested only for the virus, not the cells, so if the virus is found and it isn't one of the two highest-risk types she comes back for a cervical sample.** **'Which would you prefer?'**

**Close with the extras, in priority order**: **safe sex and an offer to screen for other infections at the same time**, and **the symptom safety-net** — **'a normal result is reassuring, but it isn't a guarantee: if you ever get bleeding after sex, bleeding between periods, or an unusual discharge, come back to me whatever your last result said.'**

dx: **HPV 16 positive with normal cytology — the first time the AMC handed candidates a pending result and asked them to explain it.** The whole station turns on two things: **the explanation is built BEFORE the result is dropped**, and **management is a TRIAD, not a referral.**

**The explanation structure, in this order: build understanding → bad news → good news → check.** **'Before I give you the details, can I explain briefly what this test looks for?'** Cervical cancer, the cervix, HPV as a very common virus most sexually active people pick up and clear, and **the two-part test — virus first, then the cells on the same sample if the virus is found.** **Then** the result.

**The bad news, plainly**: **'your test has found the virus, and it is type 16, which is one of the two highest-risk types.'** She will ask whether that means cancer. **The good news is the second half of the same breath**: **'no — because the virus was found, the laboratory checked your cells, and there are NO changes at all. That means we have found this virus early, before it has done anything to the cells, which is exactly what this test exists to do.'**

**A frightened woman who is told she has a high-risk cancer virus and nothing else has been given bad news badly.** The normal cytology is real good news and she is entitled to hear it, framed as **early detection**.

**MANAGEMENT IS A TRIAD AND THIS IS THE DISCRIMINATOR. Candidates say 'colposcopy' and stop. The stem deliberately contains multiple partners, no condoms and no vaccination — three findings that exist to be managed.** **Colposcopy · safe sex · vaccination, every time.** Plus smoking, plus the safety-net.

**Colposcopy, explained with the detail that earns the mark**: same kind of examination as the screening test, speculum, same position — **the difference is a magnifying camera, AND THE CAMERA STAYS OUTSIDE THE BODY. Nothing larger goes in.** That is the thing patients most commonly fear. Then: a dye that makes abnormal areas show up, possibly a small biopsy, and **they may treat it at the same visit — laser, freezing, or removing a small area**. **About 15 minutes, home the same day.** VERIFY

**Safe sex, with the reason**: **'having this virus does not mean protection stops mattering. There are many strains, and you do not want to pick up another one — and if your body clears this one, you do not want it back.'** Condoms **reduce rather than remove** the risk.

**Vaccination, and do NOT decline it because she already has HPV**: **'the current vaccine protects against nine strains — you have one of them, so it can still protect you against the other eight.'** It works best before any exposure, so it will be **less effective now, but still worthwhile**. VERIFY current funding — free through the school programme and catch-up criteria, otherwise a private cost. **Address the needle fear rather than dropping the offer: numbing cream, lying down, not looking.**

**ADDED — smoking, and say why. It impairs local immune clearance, so smokers are more likely to have persistent infection and high-grade change.** **'Stopping smoking would genuinely help your body clear this virus — it is one of the few things you can do yourself that changes the odds.'** **Quitline 13 7848.** Few candidates say it.

CORRECTION — **the percentage. The lecture quotes 60–80% of cervical cancers as caused by types 16 and 18. Australian guidance quotes approximately 70%, with the nine-valent vaccine covering types responsible for around 90%.** VERIFY. **If unsure in the room, say 'the great majority' and move on.** SA: colposcopy at a metropolitan gynaecology or dysplasia clinic with **PATS** — **say the travel out loud, because for a Yorke Peninsula patient the trip is the main barrier to attendance**; **National Cancer Screening Register**; **SHINE SA**; **Quitline 13 7848**; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**.

findings: THE TWO SENTENCES, IN EVERY DISCHARGE STATION

ONE: ‘Examiner, DOES SHE HAVE A FEVER, and IS THERE CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS?’ — how you find PID. TWO: ‘Because this discharge is UNEXPLAINED AND PERSISTENT, I would also take a CO-TEST to exclude a cervical cause.’ IF THE EXAMINER DOES NOT HEAR THESE TWO, YOU DO NOT PASS
General, vitals, abdomen
‘General appearance, and all four vital signs — PARTICULARLY THE TEMPERATURE.’ FEVER IS THE PID DISCRIMINATOR. ‘Lower abdominal tenderness, GUARDING, any MASS?’ — peritonism; a tubo-ovarian abscess
Inspection — with consent and a chaperone

‘Skin changes — redness, FISSURES, ulcers, white plaques; any lumps or swellings; VISIBLE DISCHARGE AND ITS CHARACTER.’ Looking for candidal erythema and fissuring, lichen sclerosus, Bartholin swelling, herpetic ulcers
Speculum

‘The CERVIX — any lesion or mass, any MUCOPURULENT DISCHARGE FROM THE OS, any CONTACT BLEEDING? The VAGINAL WALLS? Any visible FOREIGN BODY?’ Cervicitis · carcinoma · retained tampon · a STRAWBERRY cervix (punctate haemorrhages) in trichomoniasis
Bimanual — THE THREE SIGNS OF PID

‘CERVICAL MOTION TENDERNESS? UTERINE TENDERNESS? ADNEXAL TENDERNESS OR MASS?’ The three signs of PID — and A MASS MEANS ABSCESS. Office: URINE PREGNANCY TEST (it changes the drugs) and a URINE DIPSTICK (UTI)
THE TWO SWABS ARE NOT THE SAME SWAB

SWAB 1 — ENDOCERVICAL (or FIRST-VOID URINE, or a SELF-COLLECTED VAGINAL swab) FOR NAAT: CHLAMYDIA AND GONORRHOEA. A DIFFERENT swab from the cervical screening pack and from a plain HVS — you CANNOT take a chlamydia sample with the broom or the jumbo swab. Add THROAT and RECTAL swabs if the sexual history indicates. SWAB 2 — HIGH VAGINAL SWAB FOR MCS: returns CANDIDA, CLUE CELLS (bacterial vaginosis) and TRICHOMONAS, plus the vaginal pH
The rest of the work-up

CO-TEST (not a screening test) if the discharge is UNEXPLAINED AND PERSISTENT or the cervix looks abnormal · FULL STI SCREEN where risk is present — syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B and C · BLOOD GLUCOSE or HbA1c if candida is RECURRENT · PELVIC ULTRASOUND only to look for an ABSCESS or exclude other pathology — IT DOES NOT DIAGNOSE PID
DEMONSTRATION CASE — the card

Tara Nguyen, 27: AFEBRILE, observations normal. Abdomen soft, non-tender. Vulva normal, NO ERYTHEMA OR FISSURING. THIN GREY HOMOGENEOUS DISCHARGE coating the vaginal walls. Cervix normal, no contact bleeding. NO cervical motion tenderness, no uterine or adnexal tenderness. Pregnancy test negative → BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS
THE DISCHARGE TABLE — a GUIDE, NEVER A DIAGNOSIS ON ITS OWN

CANDIDA: thick white curdy, NO smell, INTENSE ITCH, erythema and fissuring · BV: thin grey homogeneous, FISHY, worse after sex, NO ITCH AND NO INFLAMMATION (the discriminator from candida) · TRICHOMONAS: FROTHY yellow-green, offensive, itch, strawberry cervix · GONORRHOEA: purulent yellow-green, often asymptomatic · CHLAMYDIA: mucopurulent OR NONE — the reason you SWAB rather than rely on the story · ATROPHIC: thin watery, dryness, pale walls · FOREIGN BODY: FOUL BROWN, a ‘lost’ tampon · CERVICAL CANCER: watery, blood-stained, offensive, with post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding · PHYSIOLOGICAL: clear or white, varies with the cycle, no itch, no soreness
THE NUMBERS VERIFY

Candida: clotrimazole 1% × 6 nights, 2% × 3, 10% × 1; FLUCONAZOLE 150 mg stat · BV: METRONIDAZOLE 400 mg BD × 7 DAYS · Trichomonas: METRONIDAZOLE 2 g STAT · Chlamydia: DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD × 7 DAYS, RETEST AT 3 MONTHS · Gonorrhoea: CEFTRIAXONE 500 mg IM + AZITHROMYCIN 1 g · PID: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat + DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg BD + METRONIDAZOLE 400 mg BD, both for 14 DAYS · BV pH >4.5, clue cells

dx: **VAGINAL DISCHARGE — THE STRUCTURE, THE SWABS, THE TREATMENTS.** **The framework document for the whole discharge cluster (Documents 11–14).** **A framework card with a demonstration case: Tara Nguyen, 27, bacterial vaginosis.** **TWO DIAGNOSES DECIDE EVERY STATION IN IT — PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE and CERVICAL CANCER. Everything else on the list is worth marks. THESE TWO ARE WORTH THE STATION.**

**PID — THE UPPER TRACT INFECTION YOU TREAT BEFORE YOU HAVE PROOF, because it SCARS TUBES AND BECOMES SEPSIS.** **Fever + pelvic pain + discharge in a sexually active woman is PID UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE.** **The cost of missing it is TUBAL DAMAGE, ECTOPIC PREGNANCY, INFERTILITY AND SEPSIS.** **Treat EMPIRICALLY TODAY — and if she REFUSES a pelvic examination, STILL TREAT: inability to examine does not change the provisional diagnosis.**

**CERVICAL CANCER — unexplained, persistent vaginal discharge is ONE OF ITS CARDINAL SYMPTOMS, and the test is a CO-TEST, NOT A SCREENING TEST.** **‘The screening test was normal last year’ DOES NOT COVER IT.** **Watery, blood-stained, offensive discharge with post-coital or intermenstrual bleeding, weight loss or a visible friable lesion → speculum, co-test, and colposcopy referral if a lesion is seen.**

**WORK INSIDE TO OUTSIDE**: **UPPER TRACT (PID) → CERVIX (cervicitis, carcinoma) → LOWER TRACT (candida, BV, trichomonas, atrophic) → SKIN (dermatitis, lichen sclerosus) → the things that are NOT INFECTIONS AT ALL (foreign body, physiological).**

**THE HISTORY BLOCKS.** **EXPLORE THE DISCHARGE: colour · thick or thin, watery or curdy · how much (does she need a liner?) · SMELL.** **ASSOCIATED: itch or soreness (→ candida) · burning passing urine (→ candida, herpes, gonorrhoea) · pain during sex · BLEEDING after sex or between periods (→ cervix).** **TIMING AND TRIGGERS: when, before, RECENT ANTIBIOTICS (→ candida), new soaps, washes or DOUCHING (→ dermatitis, BV), new contraception.** **FOREIGN BODY: ‘Do you use tampons — is there any chance one has been left in?’ — a foul brown discharge with a retained tampon is A COMPLETE DIAGNOSIS AND A COMPLETE CURE.**

**THE PID BLOCK — ASK IT IN EVERY DISCHARGE STATION**: **‘Any FEVER or chills? Any LOWER TUMMY PAIN? Any nausea or vomiting? Any DEEP PAIN DURING SEX? Any bleeding after sex or between periods?’** **Then the risk factors: ‘any NEW PARTNER in the last few months? Has a partner been DIAGNOSED WITH AN INFECTION? Any RECENT PROCEDURE — a COIL inserted, a TERMINATION, a MISCARRIAGE?’**

**THIS IS ONE OF THE FEW GYNAECOLOGY STATIONS THAT NEEDS A COMPLETE SEXUAL HISTORY, NOT A SCREEN — it determines WHICH SITES YOU SWAB.** **‘Are you sexually active? Partners in the last three to six months, and were they male, female or both? Do you use condoms? Any ORAL OR ANAL SEX? Have you or a partner ever been diagnosed with an STI? Any travel or partners overseas?’** **Then the standard five Ps with ‘any chance you could be PREGNANT?’ (pregnancy changes every treatment) and cervical screening (overdue raises the cervix).** **And the host factors: DIABETES, STEROIDS, IMMUNOSUPPRESSION, recent antibiotics — the recurrent-candida work-up, asked prospectively; plus weight loss, appetite, lumps and tiredness for cervical and vulval carcinoma.**

**CORRECTION — THE TWO LABELS THE LECTURE LEAVES UNSETTLED.** **TRICHOMONIASIS IS A SEXUALLY TRANSMITTED INFECTION: treat the patient, TREAT THE PARTNER, offer a FULL STI SCREEN, and ABSTAIN until both are treated. Uncommon in metropolitan Australia but SUBSTANTIALLY MORE PREVALENT IN SOME REMOTE COMMUNITIES — which matters in rural practice.** **BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS is classically an OVERGROWTH OF VAGINAL ANAEROBES rather than an infection acquired from a partner, but it is STRONGLY ASSOCIATED WITH SEXUAL ACTIVITY, and recent Australian-led trial evidence supports TREATING MALE PARTNERS in recurrent cases. The defensible answer: ‘TRADITIONALLY NOT CLASSIFIED AS AN STI, BUT SEXUALLY ASSOCIATED — and partner treatment is now part of the conversation in recurrent disease.’** VERIFY

**CORRECTION — PREGNANCY CHANGES TWO OF THE TREATMENTS.** **ORAL FLUCONAZOLE IS AVOIDED IN PREGNANCY — use an intravaginal imidazole, typically for 7 NIGHTS rather than the shorter courses, because candidiasis in pregnancy is harder to clear.** **BV in pregnancy is associated with PRETERM BIRTH and LATE MISCARRIAGE, so symptomatic women are treated.** **DOXYCYCLINE IS CONTRAINDICATED IN PREGNANCY — chlamydia in pregnancy is treated with AZITHROMYCIN instead.** **Challenge — ‘she is 12 weeks pregnant’ → ‘Then I would avoid oral fluconazole and doxycycline and use topical imidazole or azithromycin as appropriate.’** VERIFY all against current Therapeutic Guidelines.

**THE DEMONSTRATION EXPLANATION — bacterial vaginosis, verbatim**: **‘Tara, the pattern here — a thin grey discharge with a fishy smell, NO ITCH AND NO INFLAMMATION — fits BACTERIAL VAGINOSIS. That is not a sexually transmitted infection in the usual sense: it is an IMBALANCE in the normal bacteria that live in the vagina, where one type overgrows. It is common, and IT IS NOT YOUR FAULT.’** **‘What causes it?’ → ‘Anything that disturbs the balance — SCENTED WASHES are a classic one, so I'd stop that. Douching does the same. It's also more common around a CHANGE OF PARTNER, which is why I've taken swabs for other infections at the same time. The treatment is METRONIDAZOLE, 400 mg twice a day for a week. Avoid ALCOHOL while you're taking it and for a day afterwards, or you'll feel quite sick. It can also give you a METALLIC TASTE.’**

**THE STIs AND PID** VERIFY: **TRICHOMONIASIS — metronidazole 2 g orally stat; TREAT THE PARTNER, full STI screen, abstain until both treated.** **CHLAMYDIA — doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days; contact tracing; ABSTAIN 7 DAYS; RETEST AT 3 MONTHS; notifiable.** **GONORRHOEA — ceftriaxone 500 mg IM (in 2 mL of 1% lidocaine) PLUS azithromycin 1 g orally; RESISTANCE IS THE REASON FOR DUAL THERAPY; contact tracing; test of cure as advised; notifiable.** **PID (non-severe) — ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD 14 days; EMPIRICAL, START BEFORE RESULTS.** **ATROPHIC VAGINITIS — vaginal moisturisers and lubricants; topical vaginal oestrogen where appropriate.**

**THE PARTNER QUESTION, answered honestly**: *‘Does my partner need treating?’* → **‘Traditionally we've said no for BV, but that is changing — there's now good evidence that TREATING MALE PARTNERS REDUCES RECURRENCE, so if this comes back we'll discuss it. Your swabs will also tell us whether there's CHLAMYDIA OR GONORRHOEA, and if so, your partners DO need treating and we'd help you let them know, CONFIDENTIALLY.’**

dx: **Non-severe pelvic inflammatory disease in a 25-year-old — and the station is not testing whether you can recognise it. The findings are handed to you. It is testing whether you will COMMIT TO EMPIRICAL TREATMENT and say so explicitly.** **Candidates who say 'I'll send the swabs and review her when the results are back' have failed a station they otherwise understood.**

**PID is infection of the UPPER genital tract — cervicitis, endometritis, salpingitis, sometimes oophoritis, and at the severe end tubo-ovarian abscess and pelvic peritonitis. It is POLYMICROBIAL.** Chlamydia is the commonest identified cause, then gonorrhoea — **but in a substantial proportion no organism is found and the infection is the woman's own vaginal flora ascending.**

**The diagnosis is CLINICAL. No test confirms it.** The threshold to treat is deliberately low because untreated PID causes **tubal scarring, and therefore infertility and ectopic pregnancy; chronic pelvic pain; and progression to tubo-ovarian abscess and sepsis.**

**Say why it matters, in one sentence — it justifies the antibiotics, the follow-up, and the whole consultation**: **'left alone this can scar the tubes, which can make it harder to get pregnant later and raises the risk of a pregnancy growing in the tube.'**

**The three reasons for the diagnosis, delivered as a set: 1. symptoms — yellow smelly discharge, lower abdominal pain, hot and shivery. 2. examination — a temperature, tenderness on moving the cervix, tenderness on both sides. 3. history — unprotected sex with more than one partner and a previous chlamydia.**

**Doses worth memorising: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat in 2 mL of 1% lidocaine · doxycycline 100 mg BD × 14 days · metronidazole 400 mg BD × 14 days. Compare: chlamydia alone is doxycycline 100 mg BD × 7 days; bacterial vaginosis is metronidazole 400 mg BD × 7 days. Review at 48–72 hours.** VERIFY all against current Therapeutic Guidelines.

**Counsel the drugs briefly: doxycycline** — full glass of water, stay upright 30 minutes, **sun sensitivity so use sunscreen, and not in pregnancy**. **Metronidazole** — **avoid alcohol** during and for a day after; metallic taste is common. **Ceftriaxone** — one injection, it stings, which is why it is mixed with local anaesthetic.

**Who goes to hospital: haemodynamic instability — hypotension with tachycardia, or drowsiness · severe pain or high fever with systemic upset · a MASS, meaning tubo-ovarian abscess · vomiting, so oral therapy will not stay down · pregnancy · failure to improve after 48–72 hours · a suspected surgical diagnosis.**

**The IUD question: if she has a device and develops PID, TREAT FIRST AND LEAVE THE DEVICE IN.** Removal is considered only if she has not improved after **48 to 72 hours** of appropriate antibiotics — and if removed, she needs contraceptive cover, with emergency contraception considered if there has been recent unprotected sex.

**ADDED — two things the lecture omits and an examiner might ask. Fitz-Hugh–Curtis syndrome**: perihepatitis from ascending chlamydial or gonococcal infection — **right upper quadrant pain with PID**, from adhesions between the liver capsule and the abdominal wall. Worth naming if the stem puts right upper quadrant pain in a young woman with discharge. And **the other causes of acute pelvic pain must still be excluded — above all ectopic pregnancy, which also produces cervical motion tenderness. That is why the pregnancy test is not optional.** SA: **SHINE SA** for sexual health and contact tracing, with anonymous partner notification through **Let Them Know** and **Better to Know**; **chlamydia and gonorrhoea are notifiable** to SA Health; deterioration to the nearest emergency department with **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if unstable; gynaecology review with **PATS**; ACCHS, Aboriginal Health Worker, **Closing the Gap PBS**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.
plan: WIPE, **open question**. She says she has had a discharge for a week, it smells awful, there is pain low down, and **'I feel disgusting.'** **She is embarrassed and expects to be judged — answer that first**: **'I'm glad you came in — this is very common, it's nothing to be ashamed of, and it's treatable.'**

**Explore the discharge**: **'when did it start? Is it getting worse? Is this the first time?'** Then **'what colour is it? Is it watery, thick and cheesy, or like pus? Any blood in it? How much — do you need a liner, and is it soaked? Any smell?'** **Blood in the discharge sends you to cancer. A cyclical pattern sends you to physiological. Recurrence sends you to candida.**

**General vaginal symptom block, asked early because half your differentials share it**: **'any itch? Any soreness or irritation? Any rash, redness, blisters or ulcers? Any burning when you pass urine?'** **Dysuria here is not necessarily a urinary infection — external dysuria comes from anything inflaming the skin.**

**Red flag block 1 — cervical cancer**: **'any weight loss, loss of appetite, lumps or unusual tiredness? Any bleeding after sex, or pain during sex? Are you up to date with cervical screening? Did you have the HPV vaccination?'** **Unexplained persistent discharge is a cardinal symptom of cervical cancer.** Deep dyspareunia is the reward answer.
**Red flag block 2 — PID, the block that makes the diagnosis**: **'any fever or chills? Any lower tummy pain — where exactly? Any nausea or vomiting? Have you felt generally unwell or tired?'**

**Introduce the sexual history properly — you are going deeper than a screen, so earn it first**: **'I need to ask you some sensitive questions about your sex life so I can work out what's going on and what to test for. Is that alright? Everything we discuss is confidential.'**

**Partners**: **'are you in a stable relationship? Have you had more than one partner — and how many in the last six months? Are your partners male, female, or both?'** **Ask about multiple partners even if she says she is in a stable relationship. Partner gender changes the risk profile and the testing.**

**Method**: **'do you practise safe sex and use condoms? And what kind of sex do you have — vaginal, oral, anal?'** **This determines which sites you swab — pharyngeal gonorrhoea is managed differently, and you will not find it if you do not swab the throat.**

**Risk**: **'have you or a partner ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection? Has sex ever happened under the influence of alcohol or drugs? What do you do for work?'** The last two identify higher-risk groups **without judgement**.

**Remaining differentials in one run**: **'any dryness in the vagina? Any skin conditions — eczema, psoriasis, lichen — in you or the family? Do you use tampons, and could one have been left in? Are you on the pill?'**

**The two prescribing questions, and they close the history**: **'when was your last period, is there any chance you could be pregnant, and do you have any allergies — particularly to antibiotics?'** **If you forget the allergy question here, ask it before you name a drug — you still get the mark.**

**PEFE, temperature first**: **'is she alert or drowsy? Any dehydration? Pallor or cachexia? Her TEMPERATURE first, then blood pressure, pulse and respiratory rate.'** Then **abdomen — tenderness, guarding, rebound, any mass.**

**The pelvic request with consent and a chaperone**: inspection for skin changes, lumps, and the character of any discharge; **speculum — the cervix for a lesion, ectropion or polyp, any mucopurulent discharge from the os, and the vaginal walls**; **bimanual — cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, border and tenderness, and adnexal tenderness or mass.**

**SAY 'SWABS' AT THE SPECULUM, NOT LATER**: **'I'd take a high vaginal swab and an endocervical swab at the same examination, with a urine pregnancy test and a dipstick.'** **Candidates leave swabs to the management section and run out of time — ask here and the mark is banked even if the bell beats you.**

**The diagnosis in plain words, then the three reasons, then five seconds of differentials**: an infection that has travelled up from the vagina into the womb, the tubes and the area around them; most often from a sexually transmitted infection, though not always. Then symptoms, examination, history. Then **'I did also consider a cancer of the neck of the womb, dryness or a skin condition, and the simpler infections like thrush — but this fits an infection higher up.'**
**Say why it matters**, in the one sentence about tubal scarring, infertility and ectopic pregnancy. **It justifies everything that follows.**

**Management block 1 — swabs and empirical treatment TODAY, and say the sentence**: **'I'm starting treatment today without waiting for those results, because the picture is typical and this isn't an infection we wait on.'** Confirm no allergies, then **ceftriaxone injection today, doxycycline and metronidazole twice daily for two weeks**, with the counselling points.
**Block 2 — safe sex and partners**: abstain until she has finished treatment and any partner has been treated; **contact tracing with confidential and anonymous options**; condoms from here on.

**Block 3 — safety net and review**: **review in 48 to 72 hours** and again when the results are back. **Deterioration triggers: severe pain, vomiting so tablets will not stay down, feeling faint or drowsy — straight to the emergency department.** Check understanding.

**Abdomen: lower abdominal tenderness, guarding, rebound, and any mass.** **A mass means tubo-ovarian abscess** and changes the destination to hospital.

I'd take what swabs she consents to, start empirical antibiotics, and review her in 48 to 72 hours.'**
**Review at 48–72 hours.** Failure to improve by then is a hospital referral — and, if she has an IUD, the point at which removal is considered.

dx: **Bacterial vaginosis — and the stem solves itself if you read it. Doxycycline failed, so it is not chlamydia. An antifungal failed, so it is not candida. Three months without fever or systemic upset, so it is not PID. What remains is decided by the smell.**

**You are given NO examination and NO investigations. The history has to do all the work** — which is why the discharge must be re-characterised in full even though the stem already told you the colour. **The answer is greyish, not white.**

**THE REPORTED CRITICAL ERROR: telling the patient this is a sexually transmitted infection**, and triggering a full STI screen off the back of it. **Taking swabs here is LOOKING FOR THE CAUSE of an undiagnosed discharge, which is a different thing — and worth saying in those words**: **'I'm taking swabs to find out what's causing this, not because I think you have a sexually transmitted infection.'**

**The explanation**: **'normally the vagina has a balance of bacteria, mostly one friendly type that keeps things slightly acidic. In bacterial vaginosis that balance is upset and other bacteria overgrow — particularly one called Gardnerella. It is common, it is not something you have caught from someone, and it is not your fault.'**

**The three reasons — and the second and third are the design of the stem**: the discharge is **thin and greyish with a fishy smell**; there is **no itch or soreness**, which you would expect with thrush; and **she has already had an antibiotic covering chlamydia and a treatment for thrush, and neither worked.** **'The fact that neither treatment worked is itself a clue.'**

**The honest caveat, which is a strength rather than a weakness**: **'I can't be completely certain without the swab, and I'll test for gonorrhoea and chlamydia as well. But the pattern points most strongly to bacterial vaginosis.'**

**Amsel criteria — three of four: 1. thin, homogeneous, grey-white discharge · 2. vaginal pH greater than 4.5 · 3. positive whiff test, a fishy odour on adding potassium hydroxide · 4. clue cells on microscopy.** Clue cells are vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria so the cell border becomes indistinct. **If you have thirty spare seconds, this is the thing to say.**
**Dose: metronidazole 400 mg BD for 7 days.** Compare: **PID 14 days · trichomonas 2 g stat.** **Avoid alcohol during and for a day after** — metallic taste is common. VERIFY

**The douching and scented washes are a genuine cause AND a management item** — they strip out the protective flora and make it worse. **'Plain water is all that area needs.'** She volunteers this only if asked.

**Three things worth knowing: do not treat asymptomatic BV** outside pregnancy or before gynaecological instrumentation · **in pregnancy BV is associated with preterm birth and late miscarriage, and symptomatic women are treated** (VERIFY the preferred regimen) · **recurrence within 6–12 months is common — say so in advance, so a relapse brings her back rather than convincing her the diagnosis was wrong.** **The wider picture, if the examiner asks**: BV is strongly associated with sexual activity, and recent Australian trial evidence supports **treating male partners** to reduce recurrence in recurrent disease — **but that is not the same as calling it an STI.** SA: **SHINE SA**, pathology through **Country Health Connect**, ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**, **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.
plan: WIPE, open question. She is at her wits' end after three months and two failed treatments. **'That sounds frustrating, and three months is a long time to put up with it. Let me go through it properly and I think we can sort this out.'**
**Timing**: when did it start, constant or intermittent, getting worse, first time or has she had it before. Three months, constant.

**CCCVO — re-confirm the colour even though the stem gave it**: **'what colour is it? Any blood in it? Is it watery, or thick and cheesy? How much — do you need liners, and are they soaked? Any smell?'** **Greyish, thin, no blood, strong fishy odour.**

**Modifiers and cycle**: **'anything that makes it better or worse? Does it change around mid-cycle or before your period?'** **Worse after sex and after periods — not a physiological cyclical pattern.**

**General vaginal symptoms — and the negative here is diagnostic**: **'any itch? Any soreness or irritation? Any rash, redness, blisters or ulcers? Any burning when you pass urine?'** **No itch at all — which is why the thrush cream surprised her.**
**Red flag block 1, cervix**: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness; bleeding after sex; pain during sex; cervical screening up to date and normal; HPV vaccination. All negative.
**Red flag block 2, PID — this is how you exclude it without an examination**: **'any fever or chills? Lower tummy pain? Nausea or vomiting? Feeling unwell in yourself?'** All negative.

dx: **Atrophic vaginitis — and the station turns on TWO questions, one in the history and one in the examination.** **'Since your periods stopped, have you had any bleeding or spotting at all?'** converts this into a cancer work-up. **'And can you describe the vaginal walls?'** is the diagnosis, and **it is never offered unprompted.**

CORRECTION — **the modern name is the genitourinary syndrome of menopause**, because oestrogen deficiency affects the bladder and urethra as well as the vagina — **urgency, frequency, dysuria and recurrent urinary tract infections** alongside dryness, discharge and dyspareunia. Using the newer term **and asking the urinary questions** shows you understand the whole syndrome. If asked why she keeps getting urinary infections: **'the same oestrogen deficiency affects the urogenital epithelium, which is why vaginal oestrogen also reduces recurrent urinary tract infection.'**

**THE TRAP IS THE WORD BROWN. A brown discharge in a woman eleven years past menopause is OLD BLOOD until excluded, and any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhoea is postmenopausal bleeding — endometrial cancer until proven otherwise.** Ask about blood explicitly, twice if necessary.

CORRECTION — **do not close the case on the vaginal walls alone. Atrophic vaginitis is the commonest benign cause of postmenopausal discharge and bleeding, and finding it does not exclude cancer. Both coexist — and an atrophic vagina is exactly the setting in which an endometrial carcinoma bleeds.** If challenged — 'her walls are atrophic, isn't that your answer?' — **'it's the most likely cause, but atrophy and endometrial cancer coexist, and postmenopausal bleeding is investigated on its own account.'**

**The closing sentence that passes the station**: **'the most likely explanation is atrophic vaginitis, but because there may be blood in this discharge I'm not going to stop there — I'll arrange a co-test, an ultrasound to measure the lining of the womb, and a sample of the lining if it's thickened.'**

**The explanation and its three reasons**: oestrogen falls after the periods stop, the vaginal lining becomes thinner, drier and more fragile, and a thin lining gets irritated and produces a discharge sometimes containing old blood. **Reasons: periods stopped eleven years ago with flushes at the time · she feels dry and sex has become painful · the walls are thin, pale and dry on examination.**

**What changes in an older woman: P1 becomes 'when did your periods stop, and have you had ANY bleeding since?' · P2 is STILL a full sexual history — older women have sex and acquire sexually transmitted infections — plus dryness and pain with sex · P3 becomes hormone replacement and tamoxifen · P4 adds urinary leakage and prolapse, because some women describe leakage as discharge · P5 is cervical screening AND mammogram. Do NOT ask about Gardasil — she was well past school age when the programme began — and skip tampons.**

**Management. Non-hormonal first: vaginal moisturisers used regularly, lubricants for sex, avoid soaps and scented products. Topical vaginal oestrogen — cream or pessary — is the effective treatment, systemic absorption is low, and it also reduces recurrent urinary tract infections. Systemic menopausal hormone therapy is NOT needed for isolated vaginal symptoms, particularly when the flushes settled years ago. In a woman with a history of breast cancer, topical oestrogen is a specialist decision, particularly on an aromatase inhibitor.** VERIFY
**Do not forget lichen sclerosus** — common in this age group, **white plaques, fissures, loss of labial architecture — and a vulval cancer risk** requiring treatment and follow-up.

**Numbers: menopause = 12 months of amenorrhoea · postmenopausal endometrium greater than 4–5 mm → sample · around 1 in 10 women with postmenopausal bleeding has endometrial cancer · cervical screening to age 74, and symptomatic women get a CO-TEST, not a screening test · BreastScreen invitations 50–74.** VERIFY. SA: transvaginal ultrasound and gynaecology with **PATS**; pathology through **Country Health Connect**; **National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66**; **BreastScreen SA** for the mammogram she has let slip; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.

**Explore, and ask about blood EXPLICITLY**: **'when did it start? Constant or intermittent? Getting worse? What colour — and is there any blood, any streaks, any clots? Watery or sticky? How much? Any smell?'** Brownish, watery, small amount, no smell. **'That's important and I'll come back to it.'**

**General vaginal symptoms, INCLUDING the urinary block — it belongs to the syndrome**: **'any itch, soreness or irritation? Any rash, redness, blisters or ulcers? Any burning when you pass urine, urgency, or frequency?'** Sore; going more often; **two urinary infections this year.**

**The question that separates a benign station from a cancer station**: **'when exactly did your periods stop? And since then, have you had ANY bleeding or spotting at all?'** Eleven years; no frank bleeding apart from the brownish discharge.
**Menopausal symptoms**: **'any hot flushes or night sweats, now or in the past? How is your sleep and mood?'** Flushes for a few years, settled — **which confirms she is postmenopausal.**

**Atrophy — the history half of the diagnosis, and a reward answer**: **'do you feel dry down below? Are you sexually active — and if so, is sex uncomfortable or painful because of it?'** Very dry; sex has become painful so they have largely stopped.
**Full sexual history — do NOT skip it because of her age**: partners, stable or multiple, gender, condoms, type of sex, previous STI, **and any bleeding after sex**.

**Red flag block 1, cancer**: **'weight loss, loss of appetite, lumps, unusual tiredness? Cervical screening up to date? Mammogram? Any family history of cancer of the womb, ovary, breast or bowel?'** **The mammogram has slipped — note it, you will arrange it.**

**Red flag block 2, PID**: fever, lower tummy pain, nausea or vomiting. **Uncommon after menopause but not impossible.** Then **hormones and skin**: **'have you ever used hormone replacement therapy? Any tamoxifen? Any skin conditions — eczema, psoriasis, lichen?'**
**Continence and prolapse**: **'are you leaking urine? Have you noticed a lump or bulge down below?'** A little leaking when she coughs. **Some women describe urinary leakage as discharge.**

**PEFE ladder**: general appearance with pallor and cachexia, all four vital signs; abdomen for tenderness, any mass and its lower border; **pelvic with consent and a chaperone** — inspection for skin changes, **white plaques, fissures or ulcers, and any loss of the labial architecture**, lumps, visible discharge or bleeding.

**The speculum request, and the one question that makes the diagnosis**: **'the cervix — any lesion, ectropion or polyp? Any bleeding from the os? AND CAN YOU DESCRIBE THE VAGINAL WALLS?'** Thin, pale and dry. Then bimanual, then **swabs — high vaginal and endocervical — and a urine dipstick. Her age does not exempt her from swabs.**

**Name it and explain the mechanism**, tying in the bladder: **'the same hormone change affects the bladder, which is very likely why you've been going more often and had those water infections.'** Then **the three reasons.**

**She will ask 'so it's just the change of life?' — and this is where the station is won or lost**: **'it's the most likely explanation... but I want to be honest with you. Because the discharge is brownish and that may be old blood, and because any bleeding after menopause has to be taken seriously, I'm not going to stop here.'**

**When she asks 'you think it's something worse?'**: **'I don't think so, and the examination is reassuring. But thinning of the lining and a cancer of the womb can exist together, and the only way to be sure is to look.'** Then the work-up: **co-test, ultrasound for endometrial thickness, and a sample of the lining if it's thicker than it should be.**

**Treatment for the dryness, which you CAN start today**: moisturisers regularly, lubricant for sex, **topical low-dose vaginal oestrogen — very little absorbed, and it helps the bladder symptoms too.** **Arrange the overdue mammogram.** Safety-net: **frank bleeding, pain, or feeling unwell — come back sooner.**

**Inspection matters as much as the speculum here**: skin changes, **white plaques, fissures or ulcers**, and **any loss of the labial architecture** — that is lichen sclerosus, common in this age group and a vulval cancer risk.

dx: **Recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis with newly suspected diabetes — and the diagnosis is HANDED to you in the stem. Everything you are scored on sits behind it: why does a healthy 32-year-old get four episodes in three months?** **A candidate who takes a beautiful discharge history and then says 'I'll give you fluconazole' has answered the wrong question.**
**Definition: four or more symptomatic episodes in twelve months, with at least some microbiologically confirmed.** She meets it several times over. VERIFY

**The cause hunt IS the history, and it runs in this order: drugs (antibiotics, steroids, immunomodulators) · oestrogen (a new or changed pill, pregnancy) · diabetes · malignancy and HIV · the organism species · and LAST, weight and local factors.** **Leading with tight clothing is the named error — it is real but least important, and organic causes come first.**

**This patient has THREE contributors and gives two of them only if asked**: **antibiotics for a chest infection four months ago · started the combined pill around the same time · and thirst, nocturia, tiredness, weight gain and a father with type 2 diabetes.** **The diabetes answers are the reward questions.**

**ADDED — the cause the lecture does not mention. Non-albicans Candida, particularly Candida glabrata, causes a meaningful minority of recurrent cases and responds POORLY to fluconazole.** That is why the swab must be **a culture with SPECIATION, not just microscopy** — and why a woman failing standard therapy needs the species known before the next prescription. If challenged — 'she's completed six months of weekly fluconazole and it's back' — **'I'd culture and speciate. If it's a non-albicans species such as glabrata, azoles are often ineffective and it needs specialist advice on alternative topical treatment.'**

**TWO SETS of investigations, and saying 'two sets' out loud is the structure the task is asking for. Set 1, for the discharge: high vaginal swab for microscopy, culture AND SPECIATION · endocervical NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea · CO-TEST (HPV plus cytology), because this is a persistent unexplained discharge in a symptomatic woman · urine pregnancy test.**

**Set 2, for an underlying cause: blood glucose and HbA1c · full blood examination · HIV serology with consent · coeliac serology if supportive features · ESR and CRP if systemic illness is suspected · iron studies and thyroid function if the history suggests them.**

**Management: induction fluconazole 150 mg on days 1, 4 and 7, THEN 150 mg weekly for SIX MONTHS.** **The six-month maintenance course is the single most commonly omitted item in this station — say the dose, the days and the duration.** Simple single episode by comparison: **clotrimazole 1% × 6 nights, 2% × 3 nights, or 10% stat; or fluconazole 150 mg stat.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **two prescribing points. Nystatin is second line and now little used; it is less effective than the azoles, and the fact that she was given it is part of the case design. And oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy** — if she is or may be pregnant, use a **topical imidazole for 7 nights**, since candidiasis in pregnancy is harder to clear.

**ADDED — the partner question, said BEFORE she asks: routine partner treatment is not indicated. Treat a male partner only if he has symptomatic candidal balanitis.** Then the advice, last and briefly: plain water only, no washes or scented products, cotton underwear, out of gym gear and wet swimwear promptly. **And address the cause — if diabetes is confirmed, treating it will do more than any cream; and discuss whether the oestrogen-containing pill is contributing, since there are options without oestrogen.** SA: pathology through **Country Health Connect**; HIV testing with pre- and post-test discussion, **SHINE SA**; **Diabetes SA**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; gynaecology or sexual health with **PATS** if she fails maintenance.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'This is the fourth time in three months and I'm sick of it.'** Answer with the station's own thesis: **'that's genuinely wearing, and four episodes in three months is not something to just keep treating — I want to work out WHY it keeps coming back.'**

**Explore briefly — confirm the picture is still candida**: **'when did the first episode start? How many altogether? What is the discharge like — colour, consistency, any smell? Any itch?'** White, thick, curdy, no smell, **unbearable itch**. **A change of pattern would mean a change of diagnosis.**

**The treatment history — four questions, and the commonest reason for apparent 'recurrence' is inadequate treatment**: **'what treatment were you given each time? Did you complete the full course? Did it work, and for how long? Have you had any follow-up?'** Creams twice, then **nystatin** — second line and less effective than an azole.

**Cause hunt 1 — DRUGS**: **'have you had any antibiotics recently — even short courses? Any steroids, in any form — tablets, inhalers, creams? Any medications for arthritis, bowel disease or any immune condition?'** Antibiotics for a chest infection four months ago.
**Cause hunt 2 — OESTROGEN**: **'have you started the contraceptive pill recently, or changed it? Any chance you're pregnant?'** Started the pill four months ago — **one of the recalled positives.**

**Cause hunt 3 — DIABETES, and this is where the station is won**: **'have you ever been told your blood sugar was high? Any diabetes in the family? Are you passing more urine than usual, or drinking more, or losing weight?'** Father has diabetes; thirsty; up at night. **She gives all of this only if asked.**

**Cause hunt 4 — MALIGNANCY AND HIV**: **'any weight loss, loss of appetite, lumps or bumps, unusual tiredness? Any night sweats? Any recurring infections, mouth ulcers, or thrush in the mouth?'** **Night sweats and oral candidiasis are the additions that mark you out.**

**Cause hunt 5 — weight and local factors, asked LAST**: **'any recent weight gain? Do you wear tight or synthetic underwear or gym clothes for long periods? Do you use soaps, washes, douches or scented products?'**

**Full sexual history — it is still a vaginal discharge case**: partners, condoms, type of sex, previous STI. Then **cervical cancer**: **'any bleeding after sex? Pain during sex? Cervical screening up to date and normal?'** — **a previous candida swab does not immunise her against a cervical lesion.** Then **PID**: fever, lower tummy pain, nausea, vomiting.
**PEFE — short and mostly confirmatory, but two items carry it**: **'height, weight and BMI. Any pallor, cachexia, lymphadenopathy, or ORAL CANDIDIASIS?'** Then all four vital signs and the abdomen.

**Pelvic with consent and a chaperone**: inspection for **vulval erythema, swelling, fissuring, excoriation, satellite lesions**, white plaques or ulcers, and the character of the discharge. Speculum for the cervix, **the vaginal walls, and any adherent white plaques**. Bimanual as usual.

**The office tests, and ask for glucose BY NAME**: **'swabs, a urine pregnancy test, and a urine dipstick — INCLUDING FOR GLUCOSE.'** Glucose ++. **Glycosuria hands you the diagnosis, and you only get it if you asked.**

**Name it, then pivot immediately to the why**: **'you have recurrent thrush. But the important point today is that healthy people don't usually get four episodes in three months, so I've been looking for a reason — and I think I've found more than one.'**

**Give the reasons as a set**: **sugar in the urine, plus thirst, nocturia, tiredness, her father's diabetes and recent weight gain — which makes me suspect diabetes, and high blood sugar is one of the commonest reasons thrush keeps returning.** **On top of that, antibiotics four months ago and the pill started around the same time, both of which encourage thrush.**

**Say 'two sets of tests' and name them.** Set 1 about the discharge — **swab to confirm AND identify which type, because some types don't respond to the usual tablets**; chlamydia and gonorrhoea; a test from the cervix. Tasks: take a history for six minutes — explain your diagnosis and your differentials to the patient. 8 minutes. This is the structure behind every 'Lump down below' stem, and behind the Bartholin and prolapse stations that follow.

findings: THE THREE BEHAVIOURS THAT DECIDE THE STATION

ONE — LOCATE IT FIRST: vagina, back passage or groin; everything after that question is cheaper. TWO — ASK FOR VALSALVA TWICE: on inspection AND again at the speculum; prolapse does not exist at rest and an examiner will not volunteer it. THREE — RED FLAGS OUT LOUD: weight, appetite, tiredness, GROIN NODES, ulceration, bleeding. The recall diagnosis is usually benign; THE MARKS ARE IN HAVING EXCLUDED THE ONE THAT IS NOT
General and vitals
‘BMI, any CACHEXIA or wasting, any PALLOR?’ — obesity for prolapse, cachexia for malignancy. ‘All four vital signs, particularly the TEMPERATURE’ — abscess and systemic sepsis
Abdomen AND THE INGUINAL REGIONS — the extra branch in this cluster

‘Tenderness, any mass, and can I feel the LOWER BORDER? And an examination of the INGUINAL REGIONS — any masses or LYMPHADENOPATHY?’ The inguinal nodes are the DRAINAGE FIELD OF THE VULVA and are STAGED IN VULVAL CANCER. Missing them is a listed fail risk
Inspection — with consent and a chaperone

‘Any SKIN CHANGES — redness, rash, ULCERS, WHITE PLAQUES, LOSS OF THE NORMAL ARCHITECTURE? Any lumps or swellings, and WHERE EXACTLY? Any discharge or bleeding?’ Describe what you see: SITE, SIZE, COLOUR, SURFACE, EDGE, BASE
VALSALVA — THE FIRST ASK
‘On VALSALVA, or straining down — do I see any lump APPEAR OR DESCEND?’ PROLAPSE IS INVISIBLE AT REST: IF YOU DO NOT ASK FOR STRAINING, YOU WILL BE TOLD THE INSPECTION IS NORMAL
The cough test
‘If I ask her to COUGH, do I see any LEAKAGE OF URINE?’ — the bedside COUGH STRESS TEST for stress incontinence
SPECULUM — VALSALVA, THE SECOND ASK, and the Sims fallback

‘The cervix and vaginal walls — and AGAIN ON VALSALVA, do I see any descent of the ANTERIOR WALL, POSTERIOR WALL or CERVIX?’ If the answer is still no and the history is typical, ask for a SIMS SPECULUM IN THE LEFT LATERAL (SIMS) POSITION — AN OLD EXAM GAVE THE FINDING ONLY THEN
Bimanual and office
‘Cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and tenderness, adnexa. And a URINE DIPSTICK’ — dipstick if urinary symptoms; add a POST-VOID RESIDUAL if she describes incomplete emptying
DESCRIBING A LESION SO THE EXAMINER CAN HEAR YOU THINKING

‘A FIRM, 2 cm, NON-TENDER swelling at the POSTERIOR INTROITUS ON THE LEFT, with OVERLYING ERYTHEMA and NO ULCERATION.’ Site, size, consistency, tenderness, skin, edge — FIVE SECONDS, and it is the difference between a candidate who examined and a candidate who guessed. And describing a prolapse: ‘a STAGE 2 ANTERIOR COMPARTMENT PROLAPSE reaching the introitus on Valsalva, with a positive cough stress test’ — THAT SENTENCE IS WORTH MORE THAN ANY LIST
THE NUMBERS AND TERMS VERIFY

PROLAPSE STAGES 1–4: stage 1 well ABOVE the hymen · stage 2 AT OR NEAR the hymen · stage 3 BEYOND the hymen · stage 4 COMPLETE EVERSION = PROCIDENTIA · formal grading POP-Q · COMPARTMENTS: ANTERIOR (bladder — CYSTOCELE), POSTERIOR (rectum — RECTOCELE), APICAL (uterus or VAULT), ENTEROCELE · BARTHOLIN GLANDS sit at the 4 AND 8 O'CLOCK positions of the posterior introitus

dx: **A LUMP DOWN BELOW — THE VULVAL LUMP STRUCTURE.** **The framework behind Documents 16 and 17 and any ‘lump down below’ stem; the typical stem is a 52-YEAR-OLD WOMAN with a lump in her private parts — six minutes of history, then explain your diagnosis AND YOUR DIFFERENTIALS.** **A framework card: an AGELESS structure — LOCATE the lump, CHARACTERISE it, then run PROLAPSE and DERMATOLOGICAL causes in whichever order the AGE dictates.**

**WHY THIS CLUSTER HAS A HIGH FAILURE RATE — two reasons.** **1 Candidates recognise the recall — PROLAPSE in an older woman, BARTHOLIN ABSCESS in a younger one — reach the RIGHT diagnosis, and STILL FAIL, because they NEVER SHOWED THE EXAMINER A DIFFERENTIAL LIST. The task says ‘and your differentials’ for exactly that reason.** **2 ANATOMICAL NARROWNESS: ‘DOWN BELOW’ INCLUDES THE GROIN AND THE BACK PASSAGE. A hernia, an inguinal node, a perianal abscess, a thrombosed haemorrhoid and a rectal prolapse are all lumps in a woman's private parts.**

**THE GROUP HEADINGS — you do not name everything in the room; you name the HEADINGS and ONE OR TWO from each, and the examiner hears a structure**: **PROLAPSE · BARTHOLIN · SKIN BENIGN · SKIN INFECTIVE · SKIN MALIGNANT · GROIN · BACK PASSAGE.**

**EXPLORING THE LUMP — the questions that narrow everything.** **1 WHERE — ASK THIS FIRST; it deletes two thirds of the list in one answer.** **2 WHEN — intermittent and posture-related → prolapse or hernia; steadily enlarging → cyst or tumour; days with pain → abscess.** **3 PAINFUL? — the single most discriminating character question: painful → abscess, thrombosed haemorrhoid, herpes; painless → cyst, prolapse, hernia — AND CANCER.** **4 SKIN CHANGES — redness and heat → infection; ULCERATION OR SURFACE BLEEDING → MALIGNANCY.** **5 CAN YOU PUSH IT BACK IN? — reducible → prolapse, hernia, haemorrhoid.** **6 ‘Is it WORSE STANDING AND BETTER LYING DOWN?’ — the prolapse and hernia question, MORE USEFUL THAN ASKING ABOUT COUGHING.** **7 IMPACT — prolapse is treated according to BOTHER, NOT SIZE.**

**PROLAPSE — URINARY AND BOWEL SYMPTOMS ARE NOT A SIDE ISSUE: they are HOW PROLAPSE PRESENTS, and how you SEPARATE ANTERIOR FROM POSTERIOR COMPARTMENT.** **Ask: a DRAGGING OR HEAVY sensation · pain during sex · difficulty passing urine (straining, weak or stop-start stream, incomplete emptying) · LEAKING urine when you cough or laugh · difficulty passing stools or incomplete emptying — ‘DO YOU EVER HAVE TO PRESS TO HELP IT OUT?’ · recurrent UTIs.** **Risk factors: OBSTETRIC (how many pregnancies, vaginal or caesarean, and the bad-history questions — ‘any LARGE BABIES? A LONG LABOUR? FORCEPS OR VACUUM? Any TEARS OR STITCHES?’) · MENOPAUSE (oestrogen deficiency) · previous pelvic surgery, especially HYSTERECTOMY (vault prolapse) · RAISED INTRA-ABDOMINAL PRESSURE (chronic cough, constipation, heavy lifting, obesity) · connective tissue disorders and family history.**

**THE RED FLAGS — THE BLOCK THAT FAILS CANDIDATES, and the one almost everyone forgets**: **‘Have you lost any WEIGHT? Any change in APPETITE? Are you unusually TIRED? Have you noticed any LUMPS IN YOUR GROIN?’** **Note the wording of the last one — ‘lumps and bumps’ is a SILLY QUESTION in someone who has come about a lump, so MAKE IT SPECIFIC TO THE GROIN.** **Then SKIN (redness, rash, ulcers, blisters, BLEEDING, discharge, ITCHING — AND FOR HOW LONG; long-standing itch raises LICHEN SCLEROSUS, itself a VULVAL CANCER RISK) · INFECTION (fever, chills, unwell) · a SEXUAL HISTORY SCREEN (warts, herpes, syphilis) · BOWEL (pain, blood, discharge — perianal abscess, fistula, haemorrhoids, anal carcinoma) · HOST FACTORS (DIABETES for abscesses and hidradenitis; SMOKING and IMMUNOSUPPRESSION for vulval carcinoma) · the five Ps by age.**

**CORRECTION — THE VULVAL LUMP THAT HAS BEEN TREATED FOR MONTHS.** **Vulval cancer is characteristically DIAGNOSED LATE, because a lump or an ulcer gets treated as THRUSH, DERMATITIS OR IRRITATION, REPEATEDLY, FOR MONTHS.** **THE RULE THAT PREVENTS THIS: ANY VULVAL LUMP OR ULCER THAT PERSISTS, THAT DOES NOT RESPOND TO TREATMENT, OR THAT OCCURS IN A POSTMENOPAUSAL WOMAN, NEEDS A BIOPSY — NOT ANOTHER CREAM.** **Challenge — ‘her GP has given her three lots of antifungal already’ → ‘That is EXACTLY THE PATTERN IN WHICH VULVAL CANCER IS MISSED. I would examine it and refer for biopsy rather than prescribe again.’**

**PUTTING IT TOGETHER BY AGE — OLDER WOMAN, PAINLESS LUMP**: **start with PROLAPSE — symptoms, then bowel and urinary, then obstetric and pressure risk factors → then SKIN, with the RED FLAGS → then the MENOPAUSAL five Ps.** **Most likely: PROLAPSE. NEVER LEAVE OUT: VULVAL CARCINOMA, LICHEN SCLEROSUS, HERNIA.** **The 52-year-old gets the MENOPAUSAL version of the five Ps.**

**PUTTING IT TOGETHER BY AGE — YOUNGER WOMAN, PAINFUL LUMP**: **start with DERMATOLOGICAL causes — RED FLAGS FIRST, then skin changes, then fever and systemic features → then RUN PROLAPSE ANYWAY (it is quick, and it collects your bowel and urinary questions) → then the standard five Ps.** **Most likely: BARTHOLIN ABSCESS. NEVER LEAVE OUT: BARTHOLIN CARCINOMA, PERIANAL ABSCESS, MALIGNANCY.**

**‘PAINLESS’ IS NOT REASSURING — CANCER IS CLASSICALLY PAINLESS.** **Assuming a painless lump is benign is a listed fail risk.** **Other fail risks: not asking WHERE the lump is (first question, every time) · forgetting VALSALVA (inspection AND speculum; Sims position if still negative) · missing the INGUINAL NODES (the vulval drainage field) · skipping BOWEL AND URINARY symptoms (they are how prolapse presents).**

findings: The photograph
A TENSE UNILATERAL SWELLING at the lower part of the vaginal opening on the LEFT, about 3 cm, with ERYTHEMA of the overlying skin. NO ulceration, NO surface bleeding
Location — and why it matters

Posterior introitus, left. The Bartholin glands sit at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions of the posterior vaginal introitus — so this is exactly where they are. NOT the labium majus proper, not the groin, not perianal
Skin over it
Red and shiny. Not reducible — she would not dare push it
Systemic features
Shivery last night, probably febrile — this is what separates an ABSCESS from a cyst
Red flags
Weight, appetite, tiredness and groin nodes ALL NEGATIVE — and that is precisely WHY you asked them. A confident benign diagnosis is only defensible once they are negative
If the skin is dark

ERYTHEMA MAY NOT BE VISIBLE AT ALL. One exam used a photograph of a woman with dark skin and candidates were thrown. Describe the SWELLING and the ASYMMETRY, and rely on warmth, tenderness and fluctuance — a cultural-safety mark as well as a clinical one

dx: **Bartholin gland abscess — and this is the most reliably failed station in the gynaecology block, for a documented reason: candidates reach the right diagnosis with no differentials and no red flags.** They walk in with one diagnosis in mind, take a competent history, say 'Bartholin abscess', and fail. **Being right is not the same as being safe, and the marking sheet tests the second thing.**

**The three Bartholin diagnoses, because candidates are asked. CYST — the duct outlet is blocked, secretions accumulate, NOT infected: a smooth, PAINLESS swelling, no redness, no fever, often noticed incidentally. BARTHOLINITIS — infection of the gland WITHOUT a collection: tender, enlarged, no fluctuant swelling and no pus to drain. ABSCESS — the obstructed gland becomes infected and fills with pus: painful, tense, red, hot; she often cannot sit; fever and malaise. This is the recalled case.**

**Anatomy you must be able to state: the Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands sit at the 4 o'clock and 8 o'clock positions of the posterior vaginal introitus, with ducts opening just outside the hymenal ring, secreting mucus for lubrication.** So the expected swelling is at **the lower part of the vaginal opening, to one side.**

**The explanation**: two small glands at the lower part of the vaginal opening, one each side, that make fluid for lubrication; **if the outlet of one becomes blocked, fluid builds up, and if that becomes infected it forms an abscess — a sac full of pus.** **Reasons: the lump is exactly where those glands sit, it is very painful, the skin over it is red, and she has had a fever.**

**The differentials, said in this order, six minimum, grouped**: **Bartholin cyst without infection** (painless) · **Bartholin gland carcinoma — rare, but the reason we take a persistent lump seriously** · a boil or skin abscess · a perianal abscess · herpes or warts · a sebaceous or epidermoid cyst · hidradenitis suppurativa · vulval skin cancer · and less likely, a hernia, a thrombosed haemorrhoid, or a prolapse.

**DRAINAGE IS THE TREATMENT.** **'An abscess does not settle on tablets alone, because antibiotics do not get into pus well.'** Local anaesthetic, a small incision, let the pus out — **she should feel dramatically better almost immediately** — then **a WORD CATHETER, a small tube with a tiny balloon, left in for 2–4 weeks so a new outlet forms and it does not simply refill.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **antibiotics are not the reflex answer.** The lecture says 'definitely give antibiotics'. **For an uncomplicated, adequately drained abscess in a well, non-pregnant, non-diabetic woman, drainage alone is often sufficient.** The better answer: **'drainage is the treatment; I would add antibiotics if there is surrounding cellulitis, systemic features, pregnancy, diabetes or a positive swab.'**

CORRECTION — **where drainage happens.** The lecture routes every abscess to the emergency department. **In practice a Bartholin abscess is frequently drained under local anaesthetic in general practice, and Word catheter insertion is a GP-level skill.** Say what you actually mean: **'this needs to be drained today. I can do that here under local anaesthetic with a Word catheter, or if that isn't available I'll arrange it at the hospital — but it is not something to wait on.'** **Refer if she is septic, if the anatomy is unclear, or if malignancy is suspected.**

**Swab the pus for microscopy and culture, AND take chlamydia and gonorrhoea swabs** — gonorrhoea can occasionally be involved. **Analgesia and warm baths.** **For recurrence: marsupialisation**, where the edges are stitched open so the gland drains permanently.

**THE OVER-40 RULE: biopsy any Bartholin-area mass in a woman over about 40**, or any persistent mass. **A painless Bartholin-area swelling present for months in an older woman is not an abscess — it is a biopsy.** That rule is what connects this version to Version B. SA: drainage locally where possible; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if septic; gynaecology or gynae-oncology with **PATS**; **SHINE SA** for sexual health swabs; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**.

dx: **Vulval carcinoma, or rarely a Bartholin gland carcinoma — and this version exists to prove why the red flags in Version A are not optional. In Version A the red flags make a confident benign diagnosis defensible. HERE THEY ARE THE DIAGNOSIS. The same four questions carry both.**

**What the stem gives you, and what each item means: a lump around the vagina getting WORSE over four months — progressive, not self-limiting · PAIN present in some recalls and absent in others — painlessness is NOT reassuring · BROWNISH DISCHARGE — old blood · SPOTTING — surface bleeding from a friable lesion · and a photograph of an irregular, ugly lesion with superficial bleeding.**

**You are not expected to recognise the photograph.** The candidates who sat this case could not match it to any image they had seen. **That is the point. You are expected to know that irregular plus bleeding plus progressive equals cancer until biopsied.**

**How to say it — concern, honesty, reasons, urgency, and no false certainty**: **'I need to be honest with you about what I'm thinking. When I look at this area I can see an irregular growth with some bleeding on its surface, and it has been getting worse rather than better. That combination makes me concerned about the possibility of a cancer — either a skin cancer of the vulva, or, rarely, a cancer of the Bartholin gland itself.'**

**Then the sentence that keeps you honest**: **'I want to be clear that I cannot tell from looking. The only way to know is to take a small sample of it, and I am going to arrange that urgently with a specialist.'**

**Give your reasons**: the appearance, the progression over four months, the bleeding and the discharge, **the painlessness if that is the version you have**, and the red flags she gave you — **the weight loss and the tiredness.**

**ADDED — what you should know about vulval cancer. Mostly squamous cell carcinoma. TWO PATHWAYS: HPV-related (younger women, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, smoking, immunosuppression) and NON-HPV related (older women, arising in LICHEN SCLEROSUS).** Her **two-year unresolved itch is the lichen sclerosus clue**, and recognising it is on the marking sheet.
**It spreads FIRST to the INGUINAL LYMPH NODES** — which is why you examine the groin and why 'any lumps in your groin?' is in the history at all.
**Diagnosis is by BIOPSY. Management is surgical, by a gynaecological oncology service, with sentinel node assessment or groin node dissection. Referral is URGENT.** VERIFY

**And whichever version you get, the task says 'and your differentials'. Say six of them, grouped, before you move to management** — Bartholin cyst or abscess, Bartholin gland carcinoma, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, lichen sclerosus, a chronic ulcer from herpes or syphilis, hidradenitis, and a sebaceous cyst. **Naming them is scored even when you are confident.** SA: **urgent** gynae-oncology referral with **PATS**; **BreastScreen SA** and **National Cancer Screening Register** if screening has lapsed; ACCHS, Aboriginal Health Worker, **Closing the Gap PBS**; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**; **TIS National 131 450**.

**Explore the lump, location first**: **'where exactly — around the vagina, the back passage, or the groin? When did you notice it? Is it getting bigger? Is it painful to touch? Any change in the skin over it? Can you push it back in?'** Four months, enlarging, **not particularly painful.**
**Do NOT be reassured by the painlessness — say so to yourself and keep going.** Malignancy is classically painless until late, and this is where a candidate running the abscess script goes wrong.

**RED FLAGS, asked first and in full — here they ARE the diagnosis**: **'have you lost any weight? Any change in appetite? Are you unusually tired? Any lumps in your groin?'** **About four kilos without trying, and tired.** She gives these only if asked.

**Skin — and the last question in this block opens the second pathway**: **'any redness or rash? Any ulcers or blisters? Any bleeding from it? Any discharge? ANY LONG-STANDING ITCH?'** **An itch for two years that creams have not fixed — possible lichen sclerosus.**

**Characterise the discharge and the spotting**: colour, amount, any smell, and **'is there any blood — streaks, or spotting on your underwear?'** Brownish, with spotting. **In a 61-year-old, that is postmenopausal bleeding as well as a lesion.**

**Infection block, to be thorough**: fever, chills, feeling unwell, nausea. **Then the prolapse block quickly** — dragging, urinary symptoms, bowel symptoms or bleeding — which also covers the perianal differentials.

**Sexual history and screening**: sexually active, pain during sex, bleeding after sex, **cervical screening up to date and normal**, previous STI, smoking. **Smoking and immunosuppression sit on the HPV pathway.**
**Before you go further**: **'when did your periods stop? Any hormone therapy? Any medical conditions or medications — anything affecting your immune system? Any allergies?'**

**Ask to see the photograph and DESCRIBE IT OUT LOUD, without pretending to recognise it**: **'there is an irregular, raised, ulcerated lesion beside the vaginal opening with an uneven edge and superficial bleeding on the surface.'**
**Ask for the groin**: **'and can I have the inguinal nodes — are there any palpable nodes in either groin?'** **Vulval cancer spreads there first.**

**The honest conversation — concern first, in her words**: the irregular growth, the surface bleeding, the fact it has been getting worse rather than better, **'and that combination makes me concerned about the possibility of a cancer — either a skin cancer of the vulva, or, rarely, a cancer of the gland itself.'**

**Then the limit of what you can say**: **'I want to be clear that I cannot tell from looking. The only way to know is to take a small sample of it, and I'm going to arrange that urgently with a specialist.'** **Do not over-reassure, and do not claim certainty.**

**When she asks 'is it cancer?'**: **'I don't know, and I'm not going to guess. What I can tell you is that it needs to be looked at properly and quickly, and that I'm arranging that today.'** Pause. Let her react.
**Give your reasons**: the appearance, the four months of progression, the bleeding and the discharge, the painlessness, **and the weight loss and tiredness she told you about.**

**The differentials, six, grouped — the task asks for them even here**: Bartholin cyst or abscess (against — not painful, not tense, and four months is too long), Bartholin gland carcinoma, vulval intraepithelial neoplasia, **lichen sclerosus, which her two-year itch may represent**, a chronic ulcer from herpes or syphilis, hidradenitis, a sebaceous cyst.

**The plan**: **urgent referral to gynaecology or gynae-oncology for biopsy**; explain that management, if it is a cancer, is surgical and may involve assessing the glands in the groin; **arrange the travel support**; ask who is at home with her and whether she would like someone with her at the appointment. Safety-net: **heavy bleeding, severe pain, or fever — come back sooner.**

**Ask for the INGUINAL NODES in both groins.** Vulval cancer spreads first to the inguinal lymph nodes, and this is the examination step that connects the red-flag question to the anatomy.
**Full vulval inspection**: the lesion's site, size and edge; **white plaques, fissuring and loss of the labial architecture** (lichen sclerosus); any second lesion; discharge or bleeding.

**Speculum and bimanual** — she has spotting and brownish discharge at 61, so **postmenopausal bleeding must be worked up in its own right**: co-test, transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness, and endometrial sampling if thickened.
**BIOPSY is the diagnostic test.** Nothing else settles it, and no appearance excludes malignancy.
**Referral is URGENT, to gynaecology or gynaecological oncology.** Management is surgical, with **sentinel node assessment or groin node dissection**. VERIFY

**The over-40 rule applies here too: biopsy any Bartholin-area mass in an older woman, and any persistent mass at any age.**

dx: **Stage 2 uterine prolapse with stress incontinence. Two abbreviations decide this whole cluster: RF for RISK FACTORS of prolapse — obstetric history, menopause, surgery, raised intra-abdominal pressure — and RF for RED FLAGS of skin cancer — weight loss, appetite, tiredness, groin nodes, ulceration, bleeding. These two are the most commonly omitted blocks in the entire cluster, and between them they account for most of the failures.**

**VALSALVA IS THE STATION.** If you ask only for inspection, the examiner says 'inspection is normal' and keeps saying it. **Ask 'on Valsalva, do I see any lump appear or descend?' — then ask again at the speculum — then Sims position with a Sims speculum if it is still unclear.**

**The explanation**: **'you have a condition called uterine prolapse. The womb has dropped down towards the opening of the vagina — in your case far enough to come through it. That happens when the muscles and ligaments that hold it up, the pelvic floor, become weakened or stretched.'**

**Then the reasons, drawn ENTIRELY from her own history**: three vaginal deliveries including **a long labour, a forceps delivery and a 4.5 kg baby** · **a smoker's cough and constipation**, which push down repeatedly · **heavy lifting** as a cleaner · **BMI 32** · and **lower oestrogen since menopause**, making the tissues thinner. **Plus the examination: descent on bearing down, and leakage on coughing.**
**Name the second diagnosis too — stress incontinence.** The cough stress test is positive and it is a separate problem with its own management.

**The differentials, grouped, in fifteen seconds: other prolapses — bladder, bowel, or a rectal prolapse from the back passage · skin causes — a cyst, a boil, warts, and importantly a SKIN CANCER OF THE VULVA · Bartholin cyst or abscess · groin — a hernia or an enlarged gland · back passage — haemorrhoids or a perianal abscess.**

**Why the red flags belong in a prolapse station: a painless lump in a 52-year-old could be a vulval cancer.** Ask weight, appetite, tiredness, groin nodes, ulceration and bleeding — **and then say out loud that you asked them, and why.**
**Staging and terms: stages 1–4, where stage 4 is procidentia. Compartments: anterior, posterior, apical, and enterocele. Best demonstrated in the SIMS POSITION with a SIMS SPECULUM.** VERIFY

**Management ladder, and ask about future children and her wishes BEFORE recommending anything: pelvic floor physiotherapy first — it genuinely works for this degree and for the leaking · treat the constipation · address the cough, which means discussing smoking · weight and lifting · vaginal oestrogen for the tissues · then a PESSARY · then surgery.**

**'We treat this according to how much it bothers you, not by how it looks.'** **Treating by stage instead of by bother is a named error.** SA: pelvic floor physiotherapy and continence services — **National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66**; gynaecology and pessary fitting with **PATS** from a rural site; **Quitline 13 7848** for the cough; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'I've got a lump down below. It's embarrassing and it's been getting worse.'** **'Thank you for coming in — this is far more common than people realise, and it is treatable.'**

**Explore the lump, location first**: **'where exactly — around the vagina, around the back passage, or up in the groin?'** Then **'when did you notice it? Is it constant or does it come and go? Getting bigger? Painful to touch? Any skin change over it? Can you push it back in? IS IT WORSE STANDING AND BETTER LYING DOWN?'**
**Impact — it decides the management later**: **'how is it affecting your day-to-day life?'** Self-conscious, avoids intimacy, uncomfortable at work.

**Prolapse symptoms**: **'any dragging or heaviness down below? Pain during sex? Difficulty passing urine — straining, weak stream, incomplete emptying? DO YOU LEAK URINE, especially when you cough? Difficulty or incomplete emptying with your bowels? Any recurrent urine infections?'**

**RF block 1 — obstetric risk factors, in detail**: **'how many pregnancies? Vaginal or caesarean? Any large babies? A long labour? Any forceps or vacuum? Any tears or stitches?'** Three vaginal, one long labour, one forceps, one 4.5 kg.
**RF block 2 — pressure**: **'any chronic cough? Constipation? Do you lift heavy things at work or at home? What do you weigh — has it changed?'** Smoker's cough, cleaner, overweight.

**RF block 3 — SURGERY, and this single question is Version 2**: **'have you had any operations down below, or on the womb — including a hysterectomy?'** **Miss this and the examination will ambush you.**

**RED FLAGS — asked even though she is not in pain**: **'any weight loss? Appetite change? Unusually tired? Any lumps in your groin?'** Then **skin and infection**: **'any redness, rash, ulcers, blisters, bleeding or discharge? Any fever or chills?'** All negative.

**Menopausal five Ps — your safety net for anything forgotten**: **'when was your last period? Any hot flushes? And since your periods stopped, have you had ANY bleeding or spotting at all?'** Then dryness, dyspareunia, post-coital bleeding, hormone therapy, **cervical screening AND mammogram**.

dx: **Vaginal vault prolapse after hysterectomy — and the station is built to punish anyone who skipped the surgical question.** The history is identical to Version 1. **The only difference is one question you either asked or did not.**

**What happens if you skipped it**: you proceed to the examination, the examiner notes **a scar** on the abdomen and says nothing more, and then at the speculum tells you **'the patient has no cervix.'** **Candidates have described going blank at this point.**

**It is not a trick. She has had a hysterectomy.** The recovery is one sentence: **'do I see a vaginal vault prolapse on Valsalva?'** — and you will be told yes. **Ask it and the station is salvaged; freeze and it is not.**

**The explanation**: **'when the womb is removed, the surgeon closes off the inner end of the vagina, and that closed top end is called the vaginal vault. Because the vault no longer has the womb and its ligaments supporting it, it can itself drop down towards the opening of the vagina. That is what has happened here, and we call it a vaginal vault prolapse.'**

**The reasons are the same risk factors as Version 1 — three vaginal deliveries with a long labour, a forceps delivery and a 4.5 kg baby; a smoker's cough; constipation; heavy lifting as a cleaner; BMI 32; postmenopausal tissue change — PLUS the hysterectomy itself, and the examination finding of descent on straining.**

**ADDED — the follow-up an examiner may put to you: 'can a woman without a uterus have a prolapse?'** → **'Yes. Removing the uterus removes the APICAL SUPPORT; the vaginal vault can then descend, and an ENTEROCELE — small bowel herniating into the vaginal space — is also common after hysterectomy. Repair is apical, by SACROSPINOUS FIXATION or SACROCOLPOPEXY.'** VERIFY

**The two RFs still decide the station: RISK FACTORS of prolapse — obstetric history, menopause, SURGERY, raised intra-abdominal pressure — and RED FLAGS of skin cancer — weight loss, appetite, tiredness, groin nodes, ulceration, bleeding. Surgery is the one that matters here, and it is the one most often dropped.**

**The differentials are unchanged and still required: other prolapses — bladder, bowel, or rectal · skin causes including a VULVAL CANCER · Bartholin cyst or abscess · groin — hernia or enlarged node · back passage — haemorrhoids or perianal abscess.** **Add ENTEROCELE explicitly in this version**, because it is the post-hysterectomy companion diagnosis.

**Management ladder is the same — physiotherapy, constipation, cough and smoking, weight and lifting, vaginal oestrogen, pessary, surgery — but the SURGERY is different: apical repair rather than hysterectomy.** **Ask about her wishes and manage by bother, not by stage.**

**Terms: stages 1–4, stage 4 is procidentia · compartments anterior, posterior, apical, enterocele · best demonstrated in the SIMS POSITION with a SIMS SPECULUM.** VERIFY. SA: pelvic floor physiotherapy and **National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66**; gynaecology, pessary fitting and apical repair with **PATS**; **Quitline 13 7848**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
