stem: General practice or the hospital ward, rural South Australia. Your patient is a 60-year-old woman who was involved in a motor vehicle accident and underwent a CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis. There are no internal injuries. The report describes an incidental mass in the left breast.
Tasks: explain the scan report to the patient — explain your management plan. 8 minutes. The same station has run as an adrenal incidentaloma and, most recently, as an incidental thyroid nodule.
tasks: Open with a question rather than a statement, and find out what she has been told
Frame the scan, give the good news, deliver the finding, and pause
Explain the differentials and the triple test slowly, closing both branches

dx: **A PURE EXPLAINING STATION — no history to take, no examination to ask for. Just a scan report, a frightened patient, and four or five minutes to walk her through the triple test slowly enough that she understands it.** The commonest failure is **rushing**: candidates deliver the whole pathway in fifteen seconds and then stand there.

**The second failure is skipping the emotion. She came in after a car accident and is being told she may have breast cancer. PAUSE after the finding. Acknowledge it — 'I know this is not what you expected to be talking about today' — then continue.** The role-player is briefed to go quiet and give short answers if you do not.

**Do NOT open by talking at her. Open with a question and let her speak first**: **'how are you feeling now after the accident? And can you tell me what's happened so far, so I know what you've already been told?'** Then **seek permission**: **'I have the results of your scans here. Is it alright if we go through them together?'**

**Then the three-part delivery: FRAME the reason for the scan → GOOD NEWS first → THE FINDING.** **'After your accident we scanned your chest, abdomen and pelvis to make sure there were no injuries to the organs inside. The good news is that there are no injuries at all. There is one other thing on the scan I need to tell you about, because it's important and because it's not related to the accident. On the pictures of your chest, there's a lump in your left breast.'** **Then pause.**

**ADDED — two questions worth asking even in a no-history station: 'have you ever had a breast lump before, or are you aware of this one?' and 'have you been having your mammograms?'** She may be under surveillance for a known fibroadenoma, or overdue for screening. **Both change what happens next and both take ten seconds.** **If she volunteers symptoms, take them — and escalate.**

**The differentials, given gently: a CYST — a fluid-filled sac · a FIBROADENOMA — a benign solid lump · FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE — lumpiness of the breast tissue itself · FAT NECROSIS — scar tissue after a knock, worth mentioning given she has just been in an accident · and BREAST CANCER.** **'I can't tell from a CT scan which of those it is — and the reason we investigate every breast lump properly is to make sure it isn't a cancer.'**

CORRECTION — **the CT does not count as your imaging.** **CT is a poor test for breast soft tissue; it was performed to look for trauma, not to characterise a breast lesion, and it cannot tell you whether a lump is cystic or solid, or describe its margins and microcalcification.** If challenged — 'she's already had a CT, why another scan?' — **'CT isn't designed to assess breast tissue. She needs a mammogram and an ultrasound, which are the imaging components of the triple test.'**

**The triple test, explained SLOWLY. 1 CLINICAL — 'I examine you; how big, how firm, whether it moves, and I'll feel under your armpit and in your neck for glands. I'll arrange a CHAPERONE and explain each step.' 2 IMAGING — 'at your age, a MAMMOGRAM usually together with an ULTRASOUND — they look at the shape and edges of the lump and at any tiny specks of calcium.' 3 SAMPLE — 'a needle, usually with the ultrasound guiding it. Solid → a CORE BIOPSY. Fluid-filled → we draw the fluid off, a FINE NEEDLE ASPIRATION. Local anaesthetic, home the same day.'** **Naming both biopsy techniques and when each is used is a mark.**

**Close BOTH branches — this is what makes it a complete counselling answer. Benign: 'if it's a cyst or a fibroadenoma we usually just monitor it with a repeat scan to make sure it isn't changing; it doesn't always need removing.' Concerning or discordant: 'I'll refer you to a breast surgeon.' Malignant: 'treatment is with a surgeon and usually involves surgery, sometimes with other treatments afterwards.'**

**THE THYROID VARIANT — the newest version, and everything about the opening, framing, good news and emotional handling is identical. What changes is the pathway AND the reassurance you can honestly offer, because incidental thyroid nodules are very common and the great majority are benign. 1. History and examination — hoarseness, swallowing or breathing difficulty, rapid growth, neck nodes, childhood neck irradiation, family history of thyroid cancer; a fixed hard nodule. 2. TSH — if SUPPRESSED, the nodule may be autonomously functioning and a RADIONUCLIDE SCAN comes next rather than a biopsy. 3. Dedicated thyroid ULTRASOUND. 4. FINE NEEDLE ASPIRATION where features or size meet criteria. 5. Endocrinology or endocrine surgery.** VERIFY current size and sonographic thresholds. SA: mammography and ultrasound with **PATS** from a rural site; **BreastScreen SA** to catch up the missed screening; breast surgeon or endocrinology by referral; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**.
plan: **Open with a QUESTION, not a statement** — stations with no history task feel strange and candidates launch straight into results: **'how are you feeling now after the accident?'** Sore and shaken.

**'Can you tell me what you've been told so far?'** Only that they wanted to check nothing was damaged inside. **Then seek permission**: **'I have the results here. Is it alright if we go through them together?'**
**FRAME the reason for the scan**: chest, abdomen and pelvis, to make sure there were no injuries to the organs inside.
**GOOD NEWS FIRST**: **'there are no injuries at all — nothing damaged, nothing bleeding.'** Let her have the relief.

**THE FINDING, clearly, and flagged as unrelated**: **'there's one other thing on the scan I need to tell you about, because it's important, and because it's not related to the accident. On the pictures of your chest, there's a lump in your left breast.'**

**PAUSE. She says 'a lump? I had no idea. Is it cancer?'** **Answer honestly rather than reassuringly**: **'I don't know yet, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. What I can tell you is that a lump like this can be several different things, and the scan we did can't tell us which.'**

**The two quick questions**: **'have you ever had a breast lump before, or been aware of this one? And have you been having your mammograms?'** No previous lumps; **she has missed the last two mammograms.** **'That's alright, and we'll sort that out as part of this.'**

**The differentials, gently and in full**: a cyst · a fibroadenoma · fibrocystic change · **fat necrosis, worth mentioning given the accident** · and a breast cancer. **'The reason we investigate every breast lump properly is to make sure it isn't that.'**

**She will ask 'but you've just done a scan — can't you tell from that?'** **'Unfortunately not. The CT was done to look for injuries, and it isn't a good test for breast tissue — it can't tell us whether a lump is solid or fluid, or describe its edges properly. You need imaging designed for the breast.'**

**Frame the triple test and say WHY all three**: **'every breast lump is assessed the same way, with three tests together — what we call the triple test. We do all three even when one or two look reassuring, because together they're far more reliable than any one alone.'**

**Step 1, clinical — and do not omit the chaperone or the nodes**: **'the first step is that I examine you. I'll look at and feel the breast, checking how big the lump is, how firm, whether it moves — and I'll also feel under your armpit and in your neck for glands. I'll have a chaperone present and I'll explain each step as I go.'**

**Step 2, imaging, age-appropriate**: **'at your age that means a mammogram — an X-ray of the breast — usually along with an ultrasound. They look at the shape and edges of the lump and at any tiny specks of calcium, which help tell a harmless lump from a concerning one.'**

**Step 3, the sample, naming BOTH techniques**: **'a needle, usually with the ultrasound guiding it so it goes exactly to the right place. If the lump is solid we take a small piece of tissue — a core biopsy. If it's a fluid-filled cyst we draw the fluid off. Either way it goes to the laboratory. Local anaesthetic, and you go home the same day.'**

**Close the BENIGN branch first**: **'once all three are back we'll know what we're dealing with. If it's benign — a cyst or a fibroadenoma — we usually just keep an eye on it with a repeat scan to make sure it isn't changing; it doesn't always need removing.'**

**Then the concerning and malignant branches**: **'if any of the three raises concern, or if they don't agree with each other, I'll refer you to a breast surgeon. dx: **TWO DIAGNOSES, IN ORDER, WITH REASONS. The station hands you a deliberately messy history — bilateral lumps, brown discharge, a family history and a trauma, all at once — and asks you to RANK them. The trick is not picking one answer; it is giving two, in the right order, with reasons. Picking one and ignoring the rest fails either way.**

**DIAGNOSIS ONE — fibrocystic change**: **'the breast tissue develops multiple small cysts — little sacs of fluid — along with some thickening of the tissue around them, and that causes pain and lumpiness.'** **Reasons: MANY small lumps rather than one · in BOTH breasts · and TENDER. That is the typical pattern.**

**DIAGNOSIS TWO — the possibility of a breast cancer, and say it honestly**: **'your mother had breast cancer at 50, which raises your own risk, and you have some nipple discharge. Even though I think fibrocystic change explains most of what you're describing, one lump among many can still be something different, and I'm not prepared to assume.'**
**Six minutes of history and NO examination means the history has to do everything — so the role-player is briefed to answer examination-type questions about her lumps.** Ask them.

**How to weigh what she gives you. Two years, both sides, intermittent → benign, hormonal or fibrocystic. Many small bilateral tender lumps → the signature of fibrocystic change; it would be extraordinary for twenty of them to be cancers. 'Irregular' borders → concerning in a SINGLE lump, much less so across twenty small bilateral ones. Brown bilateral multi-duct discharge on expression with no blood → typical of DUCT ECTASIA. Mother with breast cancer → the finding that stops you settling. Trauma → raises fat necrosis, real and worth naming.**

**DISCHARGE, DECODED. Reassuring: bilateral · several ducts · only on expression · green, brown or milky · no blood. Concerning: unilateral · single duct · spontaneous · blood-stained · clear and watery · with a lump. Milky in a non-lactating woman → check PROLACTIN and think of a prolactinoma.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **fibrocystic change is not simply 'lots of cysts'. It is a SPECTRUM of benign change — cysts, fibrosis and adenosis — occurring in response to cyclical hormones, and it is common enough to be regarded as a NORMAL VARIANT rather than a disease.** **Important for the patient: ORDINARY FIBROCYSTIC CHANGE DOES NOT ITSELF INCREASE BREAST CANCER RISK. Only certain proliferative lesions with atypia do, and those are diagnosed on biopsy.** VERIFY

**ADDED — the reassurance you are entitled to give. Breast pain ALONE is an uncommon presentation of breast cancer, and the great majority of women with pain, no lump, no skin change and normal imaging have a benign cause.** That does not excuse you from assessing — **but your closing can be genuinely reassuring rather than evasive**: **'pain on its own is rarely the way breast cancer shows itself — but because you also have lumps and a family history, I'm not going to leave it there.'** VERIFY

**The rest of the differential, said out loud**: infection in the breast (no fever or redness) · **fat necrosis after the netball knock** · hormonal causes including the pill · cyclical breast pain · **and pain from outside the breast altogether — ribs, chest wall or spine — which her story does not suggest.** **Naming the non-breast group is what separates this from a lump station.**

**Management, if asked: any DOMINANT or PERSISTENT lump still gets a TRIPLE TEST. Multiple bilateral tender lumps in a 27-year-old are usually imaged with ULTRASOUND, and the brown discharge is documented and reviewed. For the pain itself: a well-fitted supportive bra — including for exercise and at night if severe · simple analgesia or a topical anti-inflammatory · a PAIN DIARY against the cycle to establish whether it is cyclical · reassurance, which is itself effective treatment · and review.** Evening primrose oil is widely used with weak evidence; **danazol or tamoxifen are reserved for severe refractory mastalgia under specialist care.** VERIFY. SA: breast ultrasound and surgeon with **PATS**; **BreastScreen SA** does not apply at 27; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **Cancer Council SA 13 11 20**.
plan: WIPE, open question. **'I've had pain in my breasts for ages and it's getting worse. I'm worried about it.'** Acknowledge, then characterise.

**Site — which breast, and where**: **'is it in one breast or both?'** Both. **'Whereabouts exactly — nearer the nipple, or out towards the armpit? Or is it more over the ribs?'** **Bilateral points to hormonal or fibrocystic; pain over the costal margin suggests chest wall.**

**Severity, quality, onset, course**: **'how bad out of ten? What sort of pain — aching, burning, sharp? When did it start? Is it there all the time or does it come and go? Is it getting worse?'** **Two years of intermittent bilateral ache is a different story from two weeks of unilateral sharp pain.**

**RADIATION — the question that opens the non-breast differentials**: **'does the pain go anywhere else — into the arm, the back, the neck?'** **Radiation to the arm or through to the back is not breast tissue.**

**CYCLICAL — the single most useful discriminating question**: **'is there anything that makes it better or worse? In particular — is it worse in the days before your period?'** **Bilateral premenstrual pain that settles with the period is cyclical mastalgia.**

**THE LUMP QUESTION — and the whole case turns on the answer**: **'can you feel any lumps?'** Yes, lots. **Then characterise them exactly as you would a single lump**: **'how many, one side or both? How big? Are they painful? Do they feel hard, or soft and rubbery? Is the edge smooth or irregular? Do they move?'**

**THE DISCHARGE, in full**: **'any discharge from the nipple? What colour — and is there any blood in it? From one side or both? From one spot or several? Does it come on its own, or only when squeezed?'** **Brown, no blood, bilateral, expressed only — the reassuring pattern.**
**Skin and nipple**: **'any change in the skin — dimpling, puckering, redness, an orange-peel look, a rash? Any difference between the nipples — pulling in, ulceration, eczema?'**

**Family history, BOTH cancers with ages**: **'any family history of breast or ovarian cancer — who, and at what age?'** **Mother, 50. This is the finding that stops you settling on a benign answer.**

**General cancer questions — AFTER the specific breast ones**: **'weight loss? Appetite? Unusual tiredness? Any lumps in your armpit?'** Then **infection**: **'are you breastfeeding? Any fever or chills? Any redness, heat or swelling? Any cracked nipples?'** — **mastitis occurs in non-lactating women too, so ask regardless.**

**TRAUMA — the reward answer**: **'any injury or knock to the breast? Any previous breast surgery?'** *'Actually yes — I took an elbow at netball a few months ago.'* **She gives it only if asked, and it raises fat necrosis.**

**OUTSIDE THE BREAST — the block that separates this station from a lump station**: **'any back or neck pain? Any cough or shortness of breath? Is the pain worse when you move or press on the ribs?'**

**Hormones and the five Ps, briskly**: **'have you started the pill recently, or any hormone treatment? Any other medications?'** Then **'when was your last period? Any chance you could be pregnant? Is your cervical screening up to date?'** **Breast tenderness is an early sign of pregnancy and it is a two-second question.**
**DIAGNOSIS ONE, with its three reasons**: fibrocystic change — many small lumps rather than one, in both breasts, and tender. **'It's very common and it isn't a disease as such.'**

**She will ask 'so it's nothing to worry about?' — and this is the ranking moment**: **'mostly, yes — but I want to be honest about my second concern, which is the possibility of a breast cancer.'** Then the two reasons: **her mother at 50, and the nipple discharge.** **'One lump among many can still be something different, and I'm not prepared to assume.'**

**'What else could it be?' — the rest of the list**: infection (no fever or redness) · **fat necrosis after the netball knock** · hormonal causes including the pill · cyclical breast pain · **and pain from outside the breast — ribs, chest wall or spine.**

**'And the discharge?' — decode it for her**: **'brown discharge from both sides, from several spots, only when you squeeze, with no blood in it, is usually a benign condition of the milk ducts called duct ectasia. The pattern that worries us is discharge from one spot on one side that appears on its own and has blood in it — and that's not what you have.'**

**The plan**: **ultrasound of both breasts, and if there is a lump that stands out from the rest, a full triple test on that one.** Then the practical advice — **a well-fitted supportive bra and simple analgesia genuinely help** — and the safety net: **a new lump that feels different, any blood in the discharge, or any change in the skin or nipple.**

**Evening primrose oil is widely used with weak evidence.** **Danazol or tamoxifen are reserved for severe refractory mastalgia under specialist care.** VERIFY

dx: **Lymphoedema after mastectomy with axillary node clearance. The diagnosis is handed to you in the stem and the photograph — the station is won on the EXPLANATION of why it happens and on a management plan that is ENTIRELY NON-PHARMACOLOGICAL.**

**The stem tells you the scans are clear and there is no recurrence. That is deliberate: it removes the diagnostic uncertainty so the station can test explanation and management. You should STILL NAME recurrence as a differential — but you do not need to chase it.**

**The mechanism, word for word**: **'your body has a drainage system alongside the blood vessels, carrying fluid called lymph. That fluid travels up the arm and passes through glands — lymph nodes — in the armpit. When the breast was removed, some of those glands were taken as well, and the drainage channels were disturbed. Because that route is damaged, the fluid can't get away as easily, so it collects in the arm.'** **Add the radiotherapy sentence only if she had it — she did not.**

**The differentials: 1. LYMPHOEDEMA — the diagnosis · 2. VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY · 3. DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS of the arm, particularly with a previous port or line · 4. CELLULITIS, which both causes and complicates lymphoedema · 5. TUMOUR RECURRENCE obstructing lymphatic drainage — ALWAYS named, even with clear scans · 6. SYSTEMIC causes — heart, kidney, liver failure, hypothyroidism — but those cause BILATERAL or generalised swelling, not one arm.**

**TWO SENTENCES SHE NEEDS TO HEAR. The honest one: 'this is a lifelong condition. We cannot cure it, but we can control the swelling and the symptoms well.'** Candidates who imply it will resolve are setting her up to lose faith in the plan. **The infection one: 'if the arm becomes red, hot or painful, or you develop a fever, come straight back — infections in this arm need treating quickly.'**

**THE FIVE COMPONENTS, and there are NO TABLETS in any of them. 1 EDUCATION — lifelong, controllable, reading material, support group. 2 SKIN CARE — moisturise daily because dry skin cracks and cracks let infection in; treat any cut or scratch promptly; gloves for gardening and washing up; avoid sunburn, tight jewellery, and heat including very hot days and saunas. 3 EXERCISE — graded and supervised, plus elevation on a pillow at night. 4 MANUAL LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE — by a practitioner, plus self-massage. 5 COMPRESSION — a MEASURED and FITTED garment. Together: COMPLEX DECONGESTIVE THERAPY. Last resort: surgery.**

CORRECTION — **EXERCISE IS TREATMENT, NOT A RISK.** Women were historically told to avoid lifting and exertion with the affected arm. **That advice has been reversed: supervised, graded resistance and aerobic exercise is safe and improves lymphoedema, and deconditioning makes it worse.** If challenged — 'should she avoid using that arm?' — **'no. Graded exercise under a lymphoedema physiotherapist improves lymphatic flow. What she should avoid is skin injury, infection and overheating.'** VERIFY
**DIURETICS DO NOT WORK for lymphoedema and should not be offered.** Say so explicitly — **'the things that work are not tablets; in fact water tablets don't help this at all.'**

**The clinical-procedure advice, said explicitly**: **'one practical thing to tell any health worker who sees you: use the other arm. No blood pressure cuffs, no blood tests, no drips, no injections and no vaccinations on the affected side, and take care with any skin procedure on that arm.'** VERIFY — **this is long-standing, widely taught precautionary advice; the evidence for absolute avoidance is weaker than its reputation, and some services now individualise it. In the exam, say it. In practice, say it and understand the caveat.**

**Investigations are mostly to exclude the differentials, because the diagnosis is CLINICAL: venous Doppler ultrasound for DVT and venous insufficiency · FBC, ESR and CRP for infection · thyroid, renal and liver function if the picture is not clearly unilateral · imaging of the axilla and chest if recurrence is suspected clinically, whatever the last scan showed · and arm circumference measurements or bioimpedance for objective monitoring.** VERIFY. **ASK FOR THE HIDDEN CONCERN — and this is the question the station turns on**: **'before I explain — is there anything else in particular you're worried about?'** *'Honestly? I'm worried the cancer is back.'* **'Thank you for telling me, and I'm going to address that directly.'**
**Onset and course**: **'when did the swelling start, and has it come on gradually or suddenly?'** Gradually, over months, getting worse. **Gradual is lymphoedema; sudden is a DVT.**
**Infection features**: **'is the arm painful, red or hot? Have you had any fever or felt unwell?'** Heavy and tight rather than painful; no redness, no fever.
**Recurrence red flags, and the scan date**: **'any weight loss, new lumps anywhere, bone pain or breathlessness? And when were your last scans?'** All negative; scans three months ago and clear.

**Clarify the treatment history**: **'tell me about the surgery — was it a mastectomy, and were glands taken from the armpit? Did you have radiotherapy as well?'** Mastectomy with axillary clearance, chemotherapy, tamoxifen, **no radiotherapy — so do not include it in the mechanism.**

**Name it, then answer her fear FIRST, with reasons**: **'what you have is called lymphoedema, and it's a common complication of breast cancer surgery.'** Then: **'your scans are clear, you have no weight loss, no new lumps and no other symptoms, and the swelling has come on gradually in exactly the arm and the way we'd expect after your surgery. So no — I don't think this is the cancer coming back. I'll still keep an eye out for it, and I'll tell you what to watch for.'**

**The mechanism in plain words** — the second drainage system, the lymph, the glands in the armpit taken at surgery, the disturbed channels, the fluid collecting. **No jargon until after the plain version.**

**The differentials, when she asks 'could it be anything else?'**: a problem with the veins not draining · **a clot in the arm, though that usually comes on suddenly and is painful** · an infection, which would make it red, hot and sore · **a recurrence blocking the drainage, which I've talked about** · and general causes such as heart, kidney or thyroid problems — **but those cause swelling in both arms and both legs, not one arm.**

**The honest sentence, before the plan**: **'lymphoedema is a lifelong condition. We cannot cure it. But we can control the swelling and the symptoms well — and the things that work are not tablets. In fact water tablets don't help this at all.'**
**Component 1 — EDUCATION**: reading material and a referral to a lymphoedema association for information and support.

**Component 2 — SKIN CARE, and say why it matters more than it sounds**: **'moisturise that arm every day, because dry skin cracks and cracks let infection in; treat any cut or scratch promptly; wear gloves for gardening and washing up; avoid sunburn, tight jewellery, and very hot days or saunas, because heat makes the swelling worse.'**

**Component 3 — EXERCISE, framed as beneficial**: referral to a lymphoedema physiotherapist for **graded exercises** — **'and to be clear, using the arm is GOOD for it; the old advice to rest it was wrong.'** Plus **elevation on a pillow at night.**
**Component 4 — MANUAL LYMPHATIC DRAINAGE**: a specific light massage that moves fluid toward working lymph glands, done by the practitioner and taught to her for self-massage.

**Component 5 — COMPRESSION**: measured and fitted with a compression sleeve. **Then name the package**: **'put together, that has a name — complex decongestive therapy — but it's just those things done properly.'**

**'And if none of that works?'** — **'if the swelling stays severe despite all of it, there are surgical options and I'd refer you to a surgeon to discuss them. That's a last resort rather than a starting point.'**

**THE CELLULITIS SAFETY NET — the most important part, and the red flag the examiner is listening for**: **'because the drainage in that arm is poor, it's prone to infection, and each infection makes the lymphoedema worse. So if the arm becomes red, hot or newly painful, if the swelling increases suddenly, or if you get a fever or chills — come straight back. We treat those infections quickly and we don't wait.'**

dx: **Both recalled versions are solved in the first ninety seconds of the differential sweep, in the block most candidates leave until LAST: HOW OFTEN, and WHEN.** Candidates run out of time having spent five minutes on the hypothalamus, and never reach the two questions that carry the station.

**Definitions you must be able to state. INFERTILITY — failure to conceive after 12 months of REGULAR UNPROTECTED intercourse in a woman under 35, or 6 months at 35 or over.** VERIFY. **The words that matter are REGULAR and UNPROTECTED. A woman who sees her partner three days a month and has intercourse twice has not met the definition however long she has been trying — and that is the entire point of Version A.** **PRIMARY — never conceived. SECONDARY — previously conceived, now unable.**

**ADDED — say the figure: about 40% of causes are MALE.** Roughly a third to 40% male, a third female, the remainder mixed or unexplained. VERIFY. **That single statistic justifies everything else: the male partner is investigated AT THE SAME TIME, not afterwards, and a semen analysis is the cheapest, quickest and least invasive test in the whole work-up.** If challenged — 'why are you asking about him? She's your patient' — **'because infertility is a problem of the couple, and around 40% of causes are male. Investigating both together avoids putting her through invasive tests for a problem a semen analysis would have found in a week.'**

**DO NOT TELL HER SHE IS INFERTILE.** Saying 'you have infertility' to a woman who has been trying for a year is unkind and unhelpful. **Phrase it around the CAUSE OF NOT CONCEIVING YET**: **'I think the most likely reason you haven't conceived so far is that you're having sex relatively infrequently, and not at the time in your cycle when the chance of pregnancy is highest. That's a very fixable thing, and it doesn't mean anything is wrong with either of you.'**

**The fertile window, explained with HER cycle length: the egg is released about halfway through — for a 30-day cycle, around day 15, counting the first day of bleeding as day one. Sperm survive several days, so the fertile window is roughly the FIVE DAYS BEFORE ovulation plus the day itself.** **Tracking: a calendar or phone app is simplest; OVULATION PREDICTOR KITS — urine tests — are the most accurate; temperature and mucus changes are described but not reliable enough to plan around.**

**ADDED — the advice that removes the timing problem altogether: intercourse EVERY TWO TO THREE DAYS throughout the cycle.** That covers the fertile window without anyone calculating anything, **and it avoids turning sex into a scheduled task, which is itself a common source of distress.** Also worth saying: **most lubricants impair sperm motility — use a fertility-friendly product if one is needed.**

**Female investigations: confirm ovulation with a MID-LUTEAL PROGESTERONE, taken about 7 DAYS BEFORE the expected period (day 21 of a 28-day cycle) · FSH and LH early follicular, days 2–5 · TSH · prolactin · AMH with the caveat below · pelvic ultrasound · chlamydia testing and cervical screening · rubella and varicella immunity · FBC and ferritin · androgens if PCOS is suspected · tubal patency testing — hysterosalpingogram or HyCoSy, usually arranged by the specialist.**

Ordering it at the FIRST visit, rather than after months of investigating her, is a mark of good practice and an easy thing to say aloud.** If abnormal: repeat, then hormonal assessment and urology or andrology review.

CORRECTION — **what AMH does and does not tell her. AMH is a marker of OVARIAN RESERVE and predicts response to ovarian stimulation in assisted reproduction. dx: **The station changes shape in the first ten seconds.** The stem reads like infertility and you will walk in with an infertility structure. **Then she tells you she has had three miscarriages. She is conceiving; she is not carrying.** **The switch happens on one question you already ask in an infertility history — 'have you ever been pregnant before?' — so ask it early and the case declares itself.**

**Say the re-orientation OUT LOUD — that single sentence tells the examiner you have switched**: **'so the difficulty is not falling pregnant; it is that the pregnancies are not continuing. That is a different problem and I want to look at it differently.'**

**Definition: RECURRENT PREGNANCY LOSS — two or more pregnancy losses before 24 weeks.** The older threshold was three; most current guidance uses two. VERIFY. **Guidelines moved deliberately from 'recurrent miscarriage' to 'recurrent pregnancy loss' because of how the word lands on women living it. Use 'pregnancy loss' with the patient — and NEVER say 'failed pregnancy', 'incompetent cervix' or 'abortion' to her face.**

**The gestation of each loss changes the entire differential. FIRST TRIMESTER → chromosomal and endocrine causes. SECOND TRIMESTER → antiphospholipid syndrome, uterine anomaly and cervical insufficiency.** She has both, so you need both lists.

**THREE THINGS SHE NEEDS TO HEAR, and the examiner wants to hear. 1. About HALF remain unexplained even after a complete work-up — saying it IN ADVANCE prevents normal results from feeling like a failure. 2. THE PROGNOSIS IS BETTER THAN SHE FEARS — most women with unexplained recurrent pregnancy loss go on to have a successful pregnancy, and that is evidence-based, not kindness. 3. AGE IS THE STRONGEST SINGLE FACTOR — at 37 after four years, that argues for REFERRAL rather than further waiting.** VERIFY

**The task is not 'list tests'. It is INVESTIGATIONS WITH REASONS, so every line has the shape: 'Because I am thinking about ___, I would do ___.' Said in that order, the examiner hears your differential list and your investigation list at the same time.**

**GENETIC — one of you may carry a balanced translocation without being affected: KARYOTYPING OF BOTH PARTNERS, and GENETIC TESTING OF THE PRODUCTS OF CONCEPTION if there is a future loss. Testing the tissue is MORE informative than testing the parents and is done first where available.** An abnormal result leads to genetic counselling. **Her sister's losses make this more relevant.**

**UTERINE — fibroids, a differently shaped womb, or scarring inside it following her curettage: TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND first, with three-dimensional ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, hysteroscopy or MRI if an anomaly is suspected.** **ENDOCRINE — TSH plus THYROID PEROXIDASE ANTIBODIES (thyroid autoimmunity is associated with loss even when the TSH is normal) · HbA1c or fasting glucose · prolactin · androgens and ultrasound if PCOS is suspected.** **GENERAL — FBC, ferritin, coeliac serology where suggested, and RUBELLA AND VARICELLA IMMUNITY, corrected BEFORE the next pregnancy.**

**ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME is the one clearly treatable cause and the reason her clot matters: LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT, ANTICARDIOLIPIN and ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I antibodies, requiring a POSITIVE RESULT ON TWO OCCASIONS AT LEAST 12 WEEKS APART. Treatment is ASPIRIN PLUS LOW MOLECULAR WEIGHT HEPARIN in the next pregnancy, which substantially improves live birth rates.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **do NOT order a routine inherited thrombophilia screen.** The lecture lists factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene, protein C and S alongside antiphospholipid antibodies. **Separate them: antiphospholipid syndrome is an accepted, testable, treatable cause screened for in everyone. Inherited thrombophilia screening is NOT recommended routinely in recurrent first-trimester loss — the association is weak, treatment based on it does not improve live birth rates, and a positive result creates anxiety and unnecessary anticoagulation.** Reserve it for a personal or strong family history of VTE, or second-trimester loss, preferably with specialist input. **And routine TORCH screening is not recommended — infection causes sporadic loss, rarely recurrent loss, because a single infection does not usually recur.** SA: recurrent pregnancy loss clinic or EPAS, metropolitan with **PATS**; **SA Clinical Genetics Service**; **Red Nose Grief and Loss 1300 308 307** and **SANDS**; counselling under a **Mental Health Treatment Plan**; **SHINE SA**; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **Empathic opening — this is a station about loss, and tone is scored**: **'I understand how stressful this must be for both of you, and I'm here to help.'** Then she gives the opening statement.

**ACKNOWLEDGE IT FIRST, before any question**: **'I'm very sorry. Three losses is a great deal to have gone through, and I want you to know I'm taking this seriously.'** **If you launch into questions instead, she answers flatly and withholds the clot and her sister's history.**

**RE-ORIENT OUT LOUD**: **'so the difficulty is not falling pregnant; it is that the pregnancies have not continued. That is a different problem, and I want to look at it differently. Can I ask you some questions so we can work out why?'**

**Number and GESTATION — the most useful question in the history**: **'how many pregnancy losses have you had? And at what stage of pregnancy did each one happen?'** Eight weeks, nine weeks, **and sixteen weeks.**

**How each presented**: **'how did each one happen — bleeding and pain, or was it found on a scan? Did you need a procedure afterwards, such as a curettage?'** First two bleeding and cramping; **the third was fluid loss, very quick, very little pain** — and **a curettage after the second.** **Both details matter and say so.**
**Tissue testing**: **'was any testing done on the tissue — the products of the pregnancy?'** No. **The single most informative test, and it was not done.**

**Any successful pregnancy ever**: **'have you ever carried a pregnancy to term and delivered a baby?'** Never — **primary recurrent loss.** Then **other surgery**: **'any surgery on your womb, cervix or abdomen — a cone biopsy, fibroid removal, anything else?'**

**IMPACT — support matters here as much as pathology**: **'how is all of this affecting you, and your relationship?'** *'It's been devastating. I'm frightened to try again.'* **'That's completely understandable, and it's something I want to help with as well, not just the medical side.'**

**Periods**: last period, cycle length, regularity, heavy bleeding or excessive pain, bleeding between. **Heavy painful periods raise fibroids and adenomyosis; irregular cycles raise PCOS.** Then **partner**: stable and supportive, previous STIs, pain with sex, bleeding after.

**ENDOCRINE — the largest single group, in one run**: **'any preference for hot or cold weather, weight or bowel change, thyroid problems in the family? Any acne, excessive hair growth or weight gain? Any headaches, vision changes or milky nipple discharge? Any diabetes — or increased thirst and passing more urine?'**

**IMMUNE AND THROMBOPHILIA — and the two reward answers are here**: **'any joint pains or rashes? Have you ever had a clot in your leg or lung? Has anyone in your family had clots — or recurrent pregnancy losses?'** **A calf clot after a long flight six years ago, and a sister with two losses. Both only if asked.**

**Lifestyle — given more weight in pregnancy loss than in infertility**: smoking, alcohol, other drugs, **caffeine**, stress at home and work. **Close**: medical conditions, medications including over-the-counter and herbal, **pets** (toxoplasmosis — ask if you like, but do not build a plan around it), cervical screening.

**Name it and give the two honest statements BEFORE the test list**: **'what you have is what we call recurrent pregnancy loss — two or more losses before 24 weeks.'** Then **'even after a full set of tests, in about half of couples we never find a specific cause'** and **'most women in your position do go on to have a successful pregnancy. That's not me being kind; it's what the evidence shows.'**

**Now the tests, each in the required shape. GENETIC**: **'because I'm thinking about a genetic cause — where one of you carries a rearrangement of chromosomes without being affected by it — I'd arrange chromosome testing for both of you. Your sister's losses make that more relevant. And if there's ever a future loss, I'd want the tissue tested, because that's the most informative test of all.'**

**UTERINE**: **'because I'm thinking about the shape and structure of the womb — fibroids, a differently shaped womb, or scarring inside it, which can follow a curettage like the one you had — I'd arrange a transvaginal ultrasound, and if that raises a question, a more detailed scan or a look inside with a small telescope.'**

**ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID — the most important one, and connect it to HER clot**: **'because I'm thinking about an immune condition called antiphospholipid syndrome, which causes clots and also causes pregnancy loss by affecting the placenta, I'd test for three specific antibodies. Your clot in the calf and your later loss both point that way. It matters enormously because it's treatable — aspirin and heparin injections in the next pregnancy substantially improve the chance of a live birth. The test has to be repeated twelve weeks later to confirm it.'**

**ENDOCRINE AND GENERAL, briskly**: thyroid including antibodies, blood sugar, prolactin — **'because hormone problems can all cause this'** — and **rubella and varicella immunity, 'because if you're not immune we need to vaccinate you BEFORE you conceive, not during.'**

**Raise CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY for the sixteen-week loss**: **'a loss at that stage, with fluid loss and very little pain, can be due to the neck of the womb opening early. It can't be tested for now, but in a future pregnancy it means we watch the cervical length on scans, and there are treatments including a stitch.'** Then **referral at 37 after four years, preconception care, and — not as an afterthought — supportive care in early pregnancy and bereavement counselling.**
pefe: **No examination task.** The whole task is investigations, **each paired with the differential it is chasing.**

**KARYOTYPING OF BOTH PARTNERS** for a balanced translocation, **and GENETIC TESTING OF THE PRODUCTS OF CONCEPTION at any future loss — more informative than testing the parents, and done first where available.** An abnormal result leads to **genetic counselling**.

**TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND first for uterine causes** — fibroids, congenital anomaly, Asherman after her curettage. **Three-dimensional ultrasound, saline infusion sonography, hysteroscopy or MRI if an anomaly is suspected.**

**ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID ANTIBODIES IN EVERYONE: lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I — POSITIVE ON TWO OCCASIONS AT LEAST 12 WEEKS APART.** Treatment: **aspirin plus low molecular weight heparin** in the next pregnancy. VERIFY

**TSH AND THYROID PEROXIDASE ANTIBODIES** — thyroid autoimmunity is associated with loss **even when the TSH is normal.** **HbA1c or fasting glucose** — poorly controlled diabetes raises loss; well-controlled diabetes does not. **Prolactin.** **Androgens and ultrasound if PCOS is suspected.**
**FBC, ferritin, coeliac serology where suggested, and RUBELLA AND VARICELLA IMMUNITY — corrected BEFORE the next pregnancy, not during it.**

**Do NOT order a routine inherited thrombophilia screen** — factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene, protein C and S. **Reserve it for a personal or strong family history of VTE, or second-trimester loss, preferably with specialist input.** If challenged: **'not routinely. I'd screen for antiphospholipid syndrome in everyone, but inherited thrombophilia screening hasn't been shown to change outcomes.'**
**Routine TORCH screening is not recommended.** Infection causes sporadic loss, rarely recurrent loss, because a single infection does not usually recur.

**CERVICAL INSUFFICIENCY is diagnosed from the HISTORY, not a test** — painless dilatation, ruptured membranes, rapid delivery without contractions. Managed with **cervical length surveillance** in the next pregnancy and consideration of a **cervical suture**. **Naming it for an 18–22 week loss is a strong answer.**

**Refer rather than observe: at 37 after four years, age is the strongest single factor** and further waiting is not the right plan. **Supportive care in early pregnancy — early scans and a team who know her history — genuinely improves outcomes, and it is the step candidates omit.**

dx: **The recall has been endometriosis almost every time — which is exactly why the station is failed. Candidates arrive with the answer, hear 'painful periods', and never exclude anything.** **The marking sheet rewards FOUR key differentials — ENDOMETRIAL CANCER · FIBROIDS · PELVIC INFLAMMATORY DISEASE · ENDOMETRIOSIS — and the red flags that separate them. Name all four even when you are confident of the last one.**

**The whole case turns on ONE question in the history and ONE request at the end of the examination.** The question: **does the pain start before the bleeding and ease, or worsen once bleeding starts and drag on?** That is **primary versus secondary**, and it is the spine of the case. **Primary: starts before bleeding, lasts 2–3 days, eases. Secondary: worsens once bleeding starts, lasts 7–8 days or longer.**

**THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT LINE: 'I would also like to perform a RECTAL EXAMINATION, to feel the uterosacral ligaments and the pouch of Douglas for tenderness and nodularity.'** **The pelvic examination in this station is NORMAL. Endometriotic deposits sit on the uterosacral ligaments and in the pouch of Douglas — behind the uterus, where a vaginal examination reaches poorly and a rectal examination reaches well. Ask, say why, and the examiner gives you tenderness and nodularity. Stop at the bimanual and you leave with nothing.**

**RANZCOG red flags in dysmenorrhoea: weight loss · rectal bleeding · new-onset pain, particularly in an older woman · pain after menopause · a palpable pelvic mass · post-coital bleeding · and SUICIDAL IDEATION from the burden of chronic pain.** Each changes the urgency. VERIFY

CORRECTION — **endometriosis and adenomyosis are related, not identical. ENDOMETRIOSIS — deposits OUTSIDE the uterus, on the ovaries, uterosacral ligaments and pouch of Douglas; classically a YOUNGER woman with dysmenorrhoea, dyspareunia, dyschezia and subfertility. ADENOMYOSIS — endometrial tissue WITHIN THE MYOMETRIUM; classically an OLDER, PAROUS woman with a BULKY, GLOBULAR, TENDER uterus and heavy painful periods; suggested on ultrasound, best characterised on MRI. They frequently coexist.**

**The four endometriosis question sets that make the diagnosis: cyclical DYSURIA and HAEMATURIA (deposits on the bladder) · cyclical DYSCHEZIA and RECTAL BLEEDING (deposits on the bowel) · DEEP dyspareunia — the second cardinal symptom · and SUBFERTILITY.** She has all four, **and gives three of them only if asked.**

CORRECTION — **laparoscopy is no longer required to diagnose endometriosis.** The lecture presents it as the diagnostic endpoint. **Current guidance has moved: a NORMAL ULTRASOUND DOES NOT EXCLUDE endometriosis, and EMPIRICAL MEDICAL TREATMENT may be started on clinical grounds without laparoscopic confirmation.** **This matters because the average diagnostic delay has been around SEVEN YEARS, much of it spent waiting for surgery.** Saying **'I'd start treatment now rather than make her wait for a laparoscopy to confirm what the history already shows'** is a strong, current answer. **And CA125 is NOT a diagnostic test** — it is raised in endometriosis, fibroids, PID, pregnancy and menstruation, and is not ordered routinely.

**Investigations, two, in this order: 1. TRANSVAGINAL ULTRASOUND — endometriomas, fibroids, adenomyosis, ovarian masses, and far more accurate than transabdominal. 2. LAPAROSCOPY — visualises deposits directly and allows excision or ablation in the same procedure, diagnostic and therapeutic together.** Guided by the differential: **swabs if PID is possible · a pregnancy test · midstream urine · hysteroscopy for suspected adhesions · MRI for deep disease or adenomyosis.**

**ADDED — the management the lecture does not cover. FIRST LINE: NSAIDs — mefenamic acid or ibuprofen — started BEFORE the pain begins rather than once it is established, which works far better; plus simple analgesia and heat. HORMONAL: the combined pill continuously or in extended cycles, often to skip withdrawal bleeds; a levonorgestrel intrauterine system; oral progestogens. Specialist: GnRH analogues with add-back. SURGICAL: laparoscopic excision or ablation; hysterectomy only in carefully selected cases with completed childbearing. ALONGSIDE ALL OF IT: pelvic floor physiotherapy, a chronic pain approach, and psychological support.** VERIFY

**ASK ABOUT HER PREGNANCY PLANS FIRST — hormonal treatment is contraceptive, so a woman trying to conceive needs a different plan and EARLIER specialist referral.** She has been trying for a year. SA: transvaginal ultrasound locally where available; gynaecology and laparoscopy with **PATS**; persistent pelvic pain services and pelvic floor physiotherapy are metropolitan — consider telehealth; **Endometriosis Australia** and **QENDO**; the **National Action Plan for Endometriosis** has funded specialist clinics; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **Empathic opening — chronic pain stations weight communication heavily, and these women are commonly dismissed before they reach you**: **'I'm sorry you've been going through this — severe period pain is exhausting and it's often not taken seriously. Let me ask some questions, find the cause, and we'll make a plan together.'**

**The pain, SOCRATES — standard, but not what decides the case**: site, severity out of ten, character, **when the painful periods started and whether they are getting worse**, radiation, and modifiers. Started three years ago after normal teenage periods, steadily worse.

**THE BLOCK THAT SEPARATES PRIMARY FROM SECONDARY — all four questions**: **'does the pain start before the bleeding or after it? Does it get WORSE once the bleeding starts? How many DAYS does it last? Do you get pain at other times of the month? And what painkillers have you tried — do they help?'** Worse once bleeding starts, seven or eight days, dragging ache between, analgesia barely touches it.

**IMPACT — scored, and days off work is itself a measure of severity**: **'how is this affecting your life — work or study, your relationship, your mood?'** Two or three days off every month; her manager has commented.

**P1 Periods**: last period, cycle length, days of bleeding, **heaviness — clots, flooding, changing protection hourly — and any bleeding or pain BETWEEN periods.** **Heavy and painful raises fibroids and adenomyosis; intermenstrual bleeding raises the cancers.**

**P2 Partner — and the second cardinal symptom lives here**: sexually active, multiple partners, previous STI, condoms, **'any pain during sex?'** — *deep inside, not at the entrance* — **and bleeding after sex.**

**P3 Pills**: **'are you using any contraception — including a coil?'** **A copper device causes heavier, more painful periods.** **P4 Pregnancy**: ever pregnant, surgery on womb or cervix, termination — **and 'are you hoping to become pregnant in the near future?'** She has been trying for a year. **P5 Screening.**

**KEY DIFFERENTIAL 1 — CANCER**: **'any weight loss? Change in appetite? Unusual tiredness? Any lumps or bumps? Any family history of cancer — womb, ovary, breast or bowel?'** All negative — **and asking is what lets you diagnose endometriosis safely.**
**KEY DIFFERENTIAL 2 — FIBROIDS**: **'any pressure or heaviness in your lower tummy? Any abdominal swelling? Any urinary frequency or constipation from pressure?'**

**KEY DIFFERENTIAL 3 — ENDOMETRIOSIS, the question set that makes the diagnosis**: **'any pain on passing urine, or on opening your bowels — particularly around your period? Have you noticed any BLOOD in your urine or your stools?'** **Yes to both — and both only if asked.**

**KEY DIFFERENTIAL 4 — PID**: **'any fever or chills? Any unusual vaginal discharge? Any nausea or vomiting?'** **The commonest missed differential in this cluster.** Then, if time: **bloating that does not settle, change in bowel habit, urinary symptoms, back pain.**

**PEFE**: **'general appearance for cachexia and pallor; all four vital signs, PARTICULARLY THE TEMPERATURE; abdomen for tenderness, any mass and its lower border.'** Then **pelvic with consent and a chaperone** — inspection; **speculum for the cervix, the vaginal walls AND the posterior fornix**; **bimanual for cervical motion tenderness, uterine size, border, tenderness and MOBILITY, and adnexal mass or tenderness.**

**THEN THE REQUEST THE STATION IS BUILT AROUND**: **'and I would also like to perform a rectal examination, to feel the uterosacral ligaments and the pouch of Douglas for tenderness and nodularity.'** **Tenderness and nodularity — the only positive finding in the case.**

**Name it and explain the mechanism in plain words**: tissue very similar to the lining of the womb growing outside it — on the ligaments behind the womb, the ovaries, sometimes the bladder or bowel — **'that tissue responds to your hormones each month just as the lining does, which is why the pain follows your periods.'**

**The reasons, as a set**: **severe, lasts seven or eight days rather than two or three, worse once bleeding starts, analgesia not touching it · deep dyspareunia · cyclical dyschezia and haematuria suggesting deposits near bowel and bladder · a year of trying without success · and tenderness and nodularity behind the womb.**

**The four differentials named explicitly**: cancer of the womb or ovary — **'which is why I asked about weight, appetite and family history, and nothing pointed that way'** · fibroids · pelvic infection — no fever or discharge · adenomyosis · **and less likely, bowel, urinary or referred back pain.**

**Investigations and treatment, with the two current points**: **transvaginal ultrasound first — 'and a normal scan does NOT rule this out' — then laparoscopy, which can treat at the same time.** **'But I don't want you waiting months in this much pain for a test to confirm what your history already shows, so we can start treatment now.'** Then **NSAIDs started a day or two BEFORE the pain begins**, and **the fertility caveat — hormonal options are contraceptive, so for her it is NSAIDs plus earlier specialist referral.** Offer **pelvic pain physiotherapy, support organisations and counselling.**

dx: **THE TRAP IS KNOWING THE ANSWER. The recall is vaginismus, and both vaginismus and vulvodynia are DIAGNOSES OF EXCLUSION — so naming either before working through cervical cancer, the pelvic masses, infection and endometriosis announces that you memorised the case.** **The examination card and the investigations are handed to you NORMAL precisely so you can exclude comfortably — which only works if you did the excluding.**

**SUPERFICIAL OR DEEP is the organising question and it splits the differential in half. SUPERFICIAL — at the entrance, on entry: vaginismus and vulvodynia · vaginal dryness (atrophic, lactational, hormonal contraception, reduced arousal, anti-oestrogen therapy) · dermatological (contact or allergic dermatitis, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, psoriasis) · infection (candidiasis, herpes, vulvovaginitis) · Bartholin cyst or abscess · trauma (perineal tear, episiotomy, surgery, female genital cutting) · vulval carcinoma.** **DEEP — on deep penetration: endometriosis and adenomyosis, the commonest organic cause · PID · pelvic masses — fibroids, ovarian cysts, ovarian and uterine carcinoma · cervical carcinoma and cervicitis · adhesions · retroverted uterus · interstitial cystitis and irritable bowel.**

**THE FOUR QUESTIONS THAT PLACE HER. 1. Beginning or deeper inside? — superficial versus deep. 2. Does the pain continue AFTER sex stops, or at other times? — the AFTER-SENSATION, which points to vulvodynia rather than vaginismus. 3. Is penetration possible at all — a tampon, a finger? Is it painful just to TOUCH? — severity, and touch-provoked pain again suggests vulvodynia. 4. Since she first had sex, or new? Same with previous partners? — lifelong versus acquired, generalised versus situational.**

**VAGINISMUS versus VULVODYNIA, and why they blur. VAGINISMUS — involuntary pelvic floor spasm on attempted penetration; triggered by penetration only; light touch usually NOT painful; NO after-sensation; FEAR prominent, in a fear-avoidance cycle. VULVODYNIA — chronic vulval pain of at least three months without identifiable cause, a pain-regulation disorder; provoked OR spontaneous; light touch of the vestibule IS painful; after-sensation PRESENT; fear less central.** **Vaginismus is widely regarded as a form of localised provoked vulvodynia — which is exactly why they overlap.**

**ADDED — the classification, and the answer that cannot be marked wrong. DSM-5 merged vaginismus and dyspareunia into GENITO-PELVIC PAIN/PENETRATION DISORDER. Gynaecological classification still separates them and describes vulvodynia on three axes: localised or generalised · provoked or spontaneous · primary (lifelong) or secondary (acquired).** VERIFY. **Say: 'this is a chronic vulval pain condition. Given that the pain occurs only on attempted penetration, stops when intercourse stops, and there's a clear fear component, I'd call it vaginismus — which is generally regarded as a localised, provoked form of vulvodynia. Both are diagnoses of exclusion and both are managed the same way.'** That names both, explains the relationship, and commits.

**VALIDATE BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN. Women with chronic pelvic and vulval pain report, consistently, being disbelieved and dismissed. If your explanation lands as 'the pain is in your mind', you have lost the patient and the station.** **The first sentence after the diagnosis is: 'I want to be clear about something. YOUR PAIN IS REAL. I'm not telling you it's imagined. It's caused by the muscles in that area tightening involuntarily, and by the nerves there becoming oversensitive — and both of those are treatable.'**

**The reasons, as a set: the pain is right at the START rather than deep inside · it stops completely when intercourse stops · touching the area is NOT painful · and she describes tensing up and dreading it beforehand — anticipating pain tightens the muscles, which causes pain, which increases the fear.**

CORRECTION — **adapt the investigations to what she can tolerate.** The reflex answers are transvaginal ultrasound and endocervical swabs; **neither is realistic in a woman who cannot tolerate a speculum.** Use **a TRANSABDOMINAL pelvic ultrasound — less sensitive but achievable — and a SELF-COLLECTED vaginal swab or FIRST-VOID URINE for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, which perform well and need no speculum.** Add a co-test when she is due and able. **Say it explicitly: 'because an internal examination is painful for her, I'd use a scan through the tummy and a self-collected swab rather than insisting on a speculum.'**

**MANAGEMENT IS NOT MEDICATION. Three strands. 1. THE MUSCLES — pelvic floor physiotherapy: where those muscles are and, importantly, how to RELAX them, then graded retraining. 2. VAGINAL TRAINERS — a graded set of smooth inserts, starting very small, used by HER, at HER pace, ENTIRELY IN HER CONTROL. 3. THE FEAR CYCLE — psychology for CBT, and a sex therapist who can work with her and her partner together if they both wish. Adjuncts only: lubricants, topical local anaesthetic gel, plain water and no soaps, and neuropathic agents later if needed.**

**Ask about sexual abuse — sensitively, after confidentiality is established, and with a supportive response ready.** If she discloses: **respond supportively, do NOT interrogate for detail, affirm it was not her fault, and offer support and referral rather than returning to the checklist.** SA: pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy are largely metropolitan — telehealth from a rural site; psychology under a **Mental Health Treatment Plan**; **SHINE SA** for sexual health and counselling; gynaecology with **PATS**; **1800RESPECT 1800 737 732** and **Yarrow Place** if assault is disclosed; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **Open carefully — this is a sensitive-topic station**: **'thank you for sharing this with me — I know it's not an easy thing to bring up. It must be distressing, and I'm here to help. I'll need to ask some sensitive questions so we can work out what's causing it. Everything we discuss is confidential. Is that alright?'**
**Discriminator 1 — superficial or deep**: **'does the pain happen right at the beginning, as penetration starts — or deeper inside?'** Right at the beginning, **'like hitting a wall.'**
**Discriminator 2 — the after-sensation**: **'does the pain carry on after sex stops? Do you get pain when you're not having sex at all?'** No to both — **which points away from vulvodynia.**

**Severity, quality, onset and course**: out of ten; **burning or deep dull ache** (burning suggests superficial or neuropathic, a deep ache suggests a pelvic cause); when it started, every time or intermittent, **same with previous partners**, getting worse.

**Discriminator 3 — modifiers**: **'do lubricants help? Is it painful just to TOUCH the area, or to insert a tampon? Is it worse in particular positions?'** **Lubricant failing argues against simple dryness; touch-provoked pain suggests vulvodynia; positional variation suggests a pelvic mass.**
**IMPACT — scored, central, and asked EARLY so you do not run out of time**: **'how is this affecting you, and your relationship?'** *'I feel broken… I've started avoiding it altogether.'*
**RED FLAGS FIRST — all the cancers. General**: weight loss, appetite, tiredness, lumps, family history of cancer.

**CERVIX — the red flag of this station**: **'any bleeding after sex? Any unusual vaginal discharge? Is your cervical screening up to date?'** **Direct contact with the cervix during intercourse is exactly how cervical cancer causes pain and bleeding.** At 22 she is not yet due — say so rather than skipping it.

**UTERUS AND OVARY**: **'any heavy periods, or bleeding between periods? Any pressure or heaviness in your lower tummy? Any bloating or change in your bowels?'** — **this block covers your urinary and bowel questions too.**

**ENDOMETRIOSIS — the commonest organic cause of deep dyspareunia**: **'are your periods very painful? Any pain passing urine or opening your bowels, especially around your period? Any blood in your urine or stools?'**

**PID plus a screening sexual history**: **'any fever? Any unusual discharge? Any lower tummy pain between periods?'** then **'stable relationship? Condoms? Multiple partners? Ever diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection?'**

**DRYNESS**: **'do you feel dry down there? Are you breastfeeding? Are you on any contraception or hormones?'** — **hormonal contraception reduces lubrication.** **SKIN**: **'any rash or redness? Any ITCHING? Any ulcers, blisters, splits or cracks? Any lump or swelling?'** — **a long-standing itch raises lichen sclerosus.**
**TRAUMA**: **'any recent pregnancy or delivery — any tear, stitches or episiotomy? Any surgery or procedure down there?'**

**ONLY NOW — the diagnosis of exclusion. Penetration**: **'is penetration possible at all? Can you insert a tampon, or a finger?'** **FEAR — the core of vaginismus and the target of treatment**: **'do you feel anxious or fearful about sex — do you find yourself tensing up beforehand?'** *Yes, completely.*

**PSYCHOSOCIAL, sensitively, confidentiality already established**: **'are there stresses in the relationship? How is your mood and sleep? And I need to ask sensitively, because it's relevant and it's common — has sex ever been forced, or have you ever experienced sexual abuse?'** **Have the supportive response ready.**

**Read the card**: abdomen normal; **vulva entirely normal**; **speculum not possible because of pain — and that refusal is itself a finding**; self-collected swabs and transabdominal ultrasound normal. **Say you adapted the investigations to her tolerance.**

**She will say 'so there's nothing wrong?' — and this is the scored moment**: **'there IS something wrong, and it has a name. But before I explain it, I want to be clear about one thing. Your pain is real. I'm not telling you it's imagined or in your head. It's caused by the muscles in that area tightening involuntarily, and that's a real, physical thing — and it's treatable.'**

**Name it with the relationship to vulvodynia**, then **the three reasons** — pain at the start, stops when you stop, touch is not painful — **and the fear cycle in her own words.** Then **the differentials in five seconds**: **cervical cancer, pelvic infection, endometriosis — 'and nothing in your history or examination points to any of them'** — plus dryness and skin conditions.

**Management, three strands**: **pelvic floor physiotherapy — where the muscles are and how to RELAX them** · **vaginal trainers, 'you use them yourself, at your own pace, entirely in your control'** · **CBT and sex therapy, with her partner if they both want that.**

**Adjuncts and close**: continue lubricants, **a local anaesthetic gel beforehand**, **plain water only — no soaps or washes**, and neuropathic agents later if needed — **'but I'd start with the physiotherapy and the therapy, because those treat the cause.'** Review in a few weeks.

**COTTON-SWAB TEST: gently touch the vestibule with a moistened cotton swab to map where the pain is and whether LIGHT TOUCH provokes it.** **Positive in provoked vestibulodynia — localised tenderness with a normal-looking vulva.** VERIFY
**If a speculum is not possible, that refusal IS a finding.** Do not press and do not force. Record it and adapt.
**Bimanual and rectal only if tolerated** — cervical motion tenderness, uterine size and mobility, adnexa, and **tenderness and nodularity for endometriosis.** Often not possible in this station.
**Pelvic floor tone, if she tolerates a single finger** — **increased tone in vaginismus.**

**ADAPT THE INVESTIGATIONS: a TRANSABDOMINAL pelvic ultrasound rather than transvaginal, and a SELF-COLLECTED vaginal swab or FIRST-VOID URINE for chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT.** Both perform well and need no speculum. **Say this explicitly — recognising the limitation and working around it is a mark of good practice.**
**Add a co-test when she is due and able** — at 22 she is not yet due for cervical screening, and saying so is better than skipping the question.
**Treatment is physiotherapy, trainers and therapy — NOT medication.** Management that is only drugs is a named failure.
**Vaginal trainers are hers**: graded, smooth, starting very small, **used by her, at her pace, entirely in her control.** Framing it that way matters as much as prescribing it.

**Adjuncts: lubricants continued even though they have not solved it · topical local anaesthetic gel before intercourse · plain water and no soaps or washes · neuropathic agents later if needed.** VERIFY

No cachexia. NO RASHES ELSEWHERE; MOUTH NORMAL — lacy white striae on the buccal mucosa would point to lichen PLANUS instead

If you ask only 'is there a rash?'

If you ask for COLOUR, SITE AND DISTRIBUTION, and MORPHOLOGY

dx: **A short differential list, which sounds easy and is not — if the list does not come to mind in the room, there is nothing to fall back on. TWO GROUPS and ONE RED FLAG. INSIDE points to VAGINITIS. OUTSIDE points to DERMATITIS. That single answer halves your list and tells you which version you are in.**

**Everyone asks about thrush; almost nobody asks about cancer.** The red flags in a chronic vulval itch: **weight loss, appetite change, tiredness, lumps IN THE GROIN, any lump, ulcer or sore that does not heal, bleeding from the skin, and any postmenopausal vaginal bleeding — which is never explained away by an itch.**

**WHY THE AMC KEEPS SETTING LICHEN SCLEROSUS: nobody dies of eczema or contact dermatitis. Lichen sclerosus is different — chronic inflammation scars the vulval skin, and a proportion of women develop VULVAL SQUAMOUS CELL CARCINOMA on that background.** VERIFY the quoted lifetime risk. **That single fact drives the whole management answer: treat it properly, and watch it for life.**

CORRECTION — **lichen sclerosus and lichen planus are not interchangeable. LICHEN SCLEROSUS SPARES THE VAGINA — vulval and perianal skin only. EROSIVE LICHEN PLANUS INVOLVES THE VAGINA, causing erosions, adhesions and a purulent discharge, and often the mouth as well — look for lacy white striae on the buccal mucosa.** Both carry a squamous cell carcinoma risk and both are treated with potent topical steroids, **but a woman with vaginal involvement and oral lesions has lichen planus.**

**READING THE PHOTOGRAPH. Candidates expect chalk white and are thrown when it is not. Look for PALLOR AND SHINE rather than pure white · a WRINKLED, CRINKLED or 'cigarette paper' TEXTURE · and the FIGURE-OF-EIGHT distribution encircling the vulva and the anus.** **In darker skin the pallor may be subtle or appear as hypopigmentation — rely on the TEXTURE, the DISTRIBUTION and the LOSS OF ARCHITECTURE.** **Fissures, purpura and bruise-like areas are part of the condition, not evidence of trauma, and should not distract you.**

**The explanation**: **'you have a condition called lichen sclerosus. It's an autoimmune condition — your own immune system is attacking the skin in that area and causing long-term inflammation. That inflammation is what causes the itch, the change in the skin, and over time the scarring.'**

**FOUR REASONS, and two of them are the failed creams**: **the appearance and distribution of the rash · the intense, long-standing itch · the pain with sex from scarring · and the fact that BOTH an antifungal AND an oestrogen cream failed, which rules out the two things she was treated for.** **Plus her Graves disease, because autoimmune conditions cluster.**

CORRECTION — **hydrocortisone will not treat this, and UNDER-TREATMENT is the usual error.** The instinct in genital skin is to reach for the mildest steroid because thin skin atrophies. **In lichen sclerosus that instinct is wrong: an inadequate steroid leaves the inflammation active, and it is the UNTREATED INFLAMMATION — not the steroid — that scars the skin and carries the cancer risk.** **Patients commonly under-apply out of fear, so say it explicitly**: **'people often worry about steroid creams thinning the skin. In this condition it's the opposite — using it properly protects the skin, and using too little is what causes damage.'**

**TREATMENT: CLOBETASOL PROPIONATE 0.05% ointment nightly for about 12 WEEKS, then reduce to 2–3 times a week long term.** VERIFY. **Plus plain water and a soap substitute only — no soaps, wipes or scented products · a simple moisturiser as a barrier · loose cotton underwear.** **And say it is CONTROLLED, NOT CURED — or she will stop the maintenance once the itch settles and return years later with scarring.**

**DIAGNOSIS AND SURVEILLANCE. The diagnosis is clinical in a typical case; a PUNCH BIOPSY is taken when the appearance is atypical, when it does not respond to adequate treatment, or when any lesion looks suspicious. In the exam, offering one is reasonable and safe. What is NOT done: routine repeat biopsies as surveillance — surveillance is CLINICAL EXAMINATION every 6–12 MONTHS, with biopsy of anything that changes.** **ADDED: it also occurs in PREPUBERTAL GIRLS, presenting with vulval itch, soreness, splitting and constipation — and the bruise-like purpura has been mistaken for injury.** SA: dermatology or vulval clinic for atypical or refractory disease with **PATS**; **urgent gynae-oncology for any suspicious lesion**; potent topical steroids are PBS-listed — check authority requirements; **National Continence Helpline 1800 33 00 66** for the contact dermatitis cases; ACCHS and **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450**.

**THE ORGANISING QUESTION**: **'can you describe what you mean — is the itch on the skin OUTSIDE, or does it feel like irritation INSIDE the vagina? And if outside, whereabouts — near the opening, on the lips, in the groin, around the back passage?'** **Perianal involvement in a figure-of-eight is characteristic of lichen sclerosus.**

**Timing**: **'how long? Constant or intermittent? Getting worse? Is it worse at night?'** **Constant and progressive suggests a dermatosis; intermittent suggests infection or irritant exposure. Night-time itch raises scabies and threadworm.**

**MODIFIERS AND TREATMENTS TRIED — critical, and the case design**: **'anything that makes it better or worse? Have you tried any creams — and did they help?'** **An antifungal that failed argues against candida; an oestrogen cream that failed argues against atrophy. She has tried both.**
**Impact**: **'how is it affecting your life — sleep, work, your relationship?'** Severe vulval itch wakes people and dominates their day.
**RED FLAGS FIRST, before anything else. General**: **'any weight loss? Change in appetite? Unusual tiredness? Any lumps or bumps — particularly IN THE GROIN?'**

**Skin lesion — the question that finds a vulval cancer**: **'have you noticed any lump, ulcer, sore or skin change that does not heal? Any bleeding from the skin?'** Also ask about **past skin cancers and family history.**
**Bleeding**: **'any spotting or vaginal bleeding — and since your periods stopped, any bleeding at all?'** **Postmenopausal bleeding is never explained away by an itch.**

**DERMATITIS GROUP — characterise the rash the way you characterise a discharge**: **'is there a rash or redness? What COLOUR? Where exactly? Any discharge from it? Any ulcers, blisters, splits or cracks? And is it ITCHY or PAINFUL?'** **Colour matters — most rashes are red; a PALE, WHITE, SHINY one is lichen sclerosus.**

**Atopy**: eczema, asthma or hay fever, in her or the family. **Contact**: **'any new soap, body wash, wipes, pads, laundry powder or underwear? Do you douche? Are you leaking urine onto the skin?'** — **incontinence is a common, fixable cause.**

**VAGINITIS GROUP. Discharge**: colour, consistency, blood, amount, smell. **Infection**: fever, lower abdominal pain, nausea. **Sexual history screen**: stable relationship, multiple partners, condoms, previous STI — **itch is a presentation of chlamydia as well as of thrush.**

**Atrophy — where Version 2 is won**: **'do you feel dry inside? Any pain during sex? Any burning passing urine, or going more often?'** **Host factors**: **'do you have diabetes? Any recent antibiotics or steroids?'**

**Menopausal five Ps, briskly**: last period, hot flushes, **any bleeding since they stopped**, dyspareunia and post-coital bleeding, hormone therapy, pregnancies and deliveries, **leaking urine and lump down below**, cervical screening and mammogram.

**PEFE. General**: **'any cachexia? And are there RASHES ELSEWHERE — elbows, knees, scalp, wrists or MOUTH?'** — **rashes elsewhere reframe the whole case: psoriasis, eczema, lichen planus.** **Vitals, temperature in particular. Abdomen, and the INGUINAL REGIONS for lymphadenopathy.**

**INSPECTION IN THREE LAYERS, with consent and a chaperone — and the third is the one nobody asks**: **'first, any rash or erythema? Second, any ulcers, blisters, fissures or excoriation? THIRD, any SUSPICIOUS LESION SUGGESTIVE OF MALIGNANCY — irregular, raised, bleeding? And is there any LOSS OF THE NORMAL ARCHITECTURE?'** **Resorption of the labia minora or burying of the clitoris is specific for lichen sclerosus.**

**DESCRIBE THE RASH — ask for all three, because 'is there a rash?' gets you 'yes' and nothing else**: **'can you describe its COLOUR, its SITE AND DISTRIBUTION, and its MORPHOLOGY — plaque or patch?'** White, shiny, wrinkled, figure-of-eight, perianal extension.

**Speculum — and ask for the walls by name**: **'the cervix — and can you describe the VAGINAL WALLS?'** **Version 2 is handed over here and nowhere else. And normal walls here confirm lichen sclerosus rather than lichen planus.** Then bimanual, swabs, and a **urine dipstick including glucose.**

**Name it, explain the autoimmune mechanism, and give the four reasons** — including both failed creams and her Graves disease. **Then say why it matters**: **'if the inflammation is left untreated over years it scars the skin, and a small number of women develop a skin cancer on that background. That's the reason we treat it properly and keep an eye on it, rather than just settling the itch.'**

**Treatment, and pre-empt the steroid fear she will raise**: punch biopsy to confirm and exclude anything worrying · **clobetasol nightly for about three months, then two or three nights a week long term** · **'it's the untreated inflammation that damages the skin; using too little is the common mistake'** · skin care · **'we control it rather than cure it'** · **review every 6–12 months**, and come back sooner for **a new lump, a non-healing sore, bleeding from the skin, or if the cream stops working.**
pefe: **Ask the THREE-LAYER inspection, because the third layer is the one nobody asks: rash or erythema → ulcers, blisters, fissures, excoriation → ANY SUSPICIOUS LESION SUGGESTIVE OF MALIGNANCY, and any LOSS OF ARCHITECTURE.**
**Ask for the rash by COLOUR, SITE AND DISTRIBUTION, and MORPHOLOGY.** Ask 'is there a rash?' and you get 'yes'. **Newer examiners give findings only on specific request.**
**Ask for RASHES ELSEWHERE, including the MOUTH.** Psoriasis, eczema and lichen planus all reframe the case, and **oral lacy white striae mean lichen planus, not sclerosus.**
**Ask for the INGUINAL NODES** — the drainage field of the vulva, and the red-flag examination.

**Ask for the VAGINAL WALLS by name.** Version 2 (atrophic vaginitis) is handed over there and nowhere else — **and normal walls in Version 3 are what confirm lichen sclerosus rather than lichen planus, which involves the vagina.**
**Swabs, and a urine dipstick INCLUDING GLUCOSE** — undiagnosed diabetes drives recurrent candidiasis.

**Diagnosis of lichen sclerosus is CLINICAL in a typical case.** **PUNCH BIOPSY when the appearance is atypical, when it fails adequate treatment, or when any lesion looks suspicious.** Offering one to confirm is reasonable and safe.
**CLOBETASOL PROPIONATE 0.05% nightly for about 12 weeks, then 2–3 times weekly long term.** VERIFY. **Hydrocortisone is inadequate and under-treatment is the usual error.**
**Skin care: plain water and a soap substitute only, a simple moisturiser as a barrier, loose cotton underwear.**

**SURVEILLANCE IS CLINICAL EXAMINATION EVERY 6–12 MONTHS, with biopsy of anything that changes. Routine repeat biopsies are NOT done.** Omitting lifelong surveillance is a named failure — it is the cancer plan.

setting: The sentence the examiner is waiting for is 'This is mild croup — which is why…'. Grade the child out loud, then let the grade choose the drug. Naming prednisolone without grading is a guess, and it is marked as one. Ask for the observations in the first fifteen seconds, because the examiner is holding them and without a saturation you will choose a treatment with no severity behind it.
stem: Your general practice, regional South Australia. Noah Whitfield, 15 months, is brought in by his mother Kate, concerned about a cough that keeps coming back and now noisy breathing. Weight 10 kg. Vital signs and examination findings are available from the examiner on request.

Tasks: take a focused history from the mother, 5 minutes — read and interpret the examination card, about 30 seconds — explain your diagnosis and differentials to the mother, about 90 seconds — explain your management plan, about 1 minute.
