Given: transvaginal ultrasound — single live fetus, cephalic, normal growth, normal liquor, normal fetal heart, placenta praevia grade 4 completely covering the internal os · previous caesarean in her first pregnancy · blood group O negative · BP 118/74, HR 84, afebrile. Tasks: explain the ultrasound findings — explain the other tests and investigations — explain your diagnosis — explain your management plan until the end of the pregnancy. 8 minutes.
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings
Explain the other tests and investigations
Explain your diagnosis
Explain your management plan until the end of the pregnancy
findings: What she opens with

'A big bleed this afternoon, bright red, NO PAIN. My husband rushed me in. It's stopped now, but I'm really worried about the scan.' Painless and bright red is praevia; constant pain would be abruption
After the normal findings
'Is the baby all right?' Then, after the praevia: 'WILL IT MOVE? Is it because of my caesarean?' — at 34 weeks and COMPLETELY covering the os, it will NOT move. Say so plainly
After the Kleihauer explanation
'I had the anti-D injection at 28 weeks — do I need another one?' YES. The 28-week dose is ROUTINE PROPHYLAXIS; a bleed is a separate sensitising event and needs its own dose, sized by the Kleihauer
When you mention hysterectomy
TEARFUL: 'Remove my womb? Is that likely?' Pause and reassure WITHOUT RETRACTING the information — most women with praevia do not need it, and you are saying it so the next scan looks for accreta
TRAP 1 — if you say 'you can go home'
She says 'GREAT' and STOPS ASKING. The role-player is briefed to accept it quietly and mark you down
TRAP 2 — if you say 'we'll admit you here for observation'
She ACCEPTS IT QUIETLY. Same trap, opposite direction. A level 4 hospital has an adult ICU but no neonatal intensive care and no round-the-clock obstetric theatre
Her hidden agenda — raised at management, and she pushes TWICE
'Can't I just go home now it's stopped? The kids are at home.' Then: 'Why can't I stay here — you have an ICU?'
Her later questions

'So I'll be in hospital till then?' · 'Is the steroid safe for the baby?' · 'What happens if it has grown in?' · 'What if I bleed in the car on the way down?' · 'Can Ben come with me? Who looks after the kids?'
What she forgot
Her 20-week scan said 'placenta low — rescan later' and she forgot about it. First birth was an EMERGENCY CAESAREAN for fetal distress
VARIANT 1 — bleeding continues

HR 118, BP 92/60. Two drips, fluids and blood, oxygen, continuous CTG, call retrieval and the obstetrician — and if the bleeding cannot be controlled, CAESAREAN AS SOON AS IT IS SAFE, here with the surgeon if she cannot be moved in time
VARIANT 2 — low-lying at 32 weeks, Rh POSITIVE

Edge about 15 mm from the os, small bleed, stopped. Admit, bloods, CTG, steroids — MANY LOW PLACENTAS MOVE UP, so rescan at 36 weeks. If still low, caesarean at 38–39 weeks; vaginal birth discussable if the edge moves beyond 10 mm. NO anti-D — she is Rh positive
VARIANT 3 — accreta confirmed

Placenta has grown into the scar. Birth at the level 6 unit with a full MDT — obstetrician, anaesthetist, blood bank, sometimes urologist and interventional radiologist. CAESAREAN 34–36 weeks, and be honest that there is a REAL chance the womb must be removed
VARIANT 4 — she refuses transfer

Respect the right to refuse, but ensure she is deciding with the full picture. SOLVE THE BARRIERS — social work for the children, PATS for cost, Ben with her. If she still declines: document it, keep her on the ward with blood cross-matched, and keep retrieval informed
VARIANT — the 5 cm placenta with pain
33 weeks, DARK bleeding, CONSTANT pain, tender hard uterus, placenta 5 cm from the os. That is ABRUPTION, not praevia — 5 cm is a normal position

dx: **Major (grade 4) placenta praevia with a resolved antepartum haemorrhage at 34 weeks, in a Rh-negative woman with a previous caesarean — therefore also at risk of PLACENTA ACCRETA.** **This was a station 'everyone used to fail' until candidates learnt the TRANSFER DECISION and the KLEIHAUER/ANTI-D PAIR.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS THE DISPOSITION. The case designer built in two critical errors. Discharge = FAIL — she may bleed at home 250 km away. Keeping her 'for observation' at the LEVEL 4 hospital = FAIL — if she bleeds at 3 am you cannot deliver a 34-week baby safely. SHE GOES TO A LEVEL 6 UNIT NOW.** Discharge is discussed later, from the metropolitan unit, after 24 hours without bleeding, to accommodation nearby.

**THE SECOND CRITICAL ERROR: the Rh-negative bleed. 'You're O negative' triggers BOTH the Kleihauer AND the anti-D, every time.** And when she says she had anti-D at 28 weeks: **'that's a routine prophylactic dose. A bleed is a separate sensitising event and needs its own dose, sized by the Kleihauer.'**

**FOUR EXPLAIN TASKS, no history task. TASK 1 — the ultrasound: NORMAL FINDINGS FIRST (fluid, heartbeat, growth, cephalic), THEN the placenta as a BRIDGE that normally sits at the top, hers at the bottom COMPLETELY COVERING THE OPENING — placenta praevia — with the previous caesarean as the likely cause. TASK 2 — three groups of tests, KLEIHAUER FIRST. TASK 3 — the diagnosis and its three risks. TASK 4 — six boxes, and SAY THE NUMBER OUT LOUD: 'there are six things in the plan.' The examiner is counting.**

**THE SIX BOXES. ONE — TRANSFER to a level 6 metropolitan unit today, by retrieval: blood bank, theatre around the clock, and a neonatal intensive care unit. TWO — at least 24 HOURS of monitoring for bleeding, contractions and the baby; then, if no bleeding, she may leave hospital but STAYS NEAR THE CITY, not 250 km away. THREE — planned CAESAREAN at 36–37 WEEKS, earlier if bleeding returns, because vaginal birth is impossible. FOUR — BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg IM today, second dose in 24 hours. FIVE — ANTI-D 625 IU, dose guided by the Kleihauer. SIX — REPEAT ULTRASOUND every 2–3 weeks, and ASK THE RADIOLOGIST SPECIFICALLY TO LOOK FOR ACCRETA.** Then red flags and family support.

**The three risks, and do not soften them into 'a low placenta' — the risks are what justify the transfer: SEVERE BLEEDING · often a need for TRANSFUSION · and in the severe form, the placenta growing into the wall of the womb, especially into a caesarean scar, which can mean HYSTERECTOMY to stop the bleeding.** Rare, but you plan for it.
**★ NEVER a digital vaginal examination with a praevia — it can provoke torrential bleeding.** Speculum only, and only if needed, by the senior clinician.

**Numbers: praevia = placenta OVER the internal os; LOW-LYING = edge within 20 mm. Grade 4 = complete. Anti-D 625 IU IM within 72 hours for any sensitising event from 12 weeks; Kleihauer after 20 weeks quantifies the bleed and guides extra doses (625 IU covers about 6 mL fetal red cells). Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM × 2, 24 hours apart — routine under 35 weeks, considered to 36+6 when a planned caesarean is likely. Caesarean at 36+0 to 37+0 for uncomplicated praevia; 34–36 with recurrent bleeding; 38–39 for a persistent low-lying placenta, where vaginal birth may be considered if the edge is over 10 mm and there has been no bleeding.** VERIFY

**ACCRETA: about 3% with praevia and no previous caesarean, 10–25% with ONE, up to 40–60% with THREE OR MORE.** VERIFY. **Ultrasound features to ask for: LOSS OF THE HYPOECHOIC RETROPLACENTAL CLEAR ZONE and irregular PLACENTAL LACUNAE; MRI if equivocal.** **Previous caesarean + praevia = accreta spectrum until proven otherwise, and it needs a level 6 unit with the full team.**

**When she asks to go home — the fail line — be kind and firm, and solve the barriers rather than arguing**: **'I completely understand, and I'm sorry. But I can't safely send you home, and I can't safely keep you here either. Today's bleed was a warning. If it happens again it could be heavy and sudden, and you'd need a hospital that can transfuse blood, do an urgent caesarean and care for a premature baby, all within minutes.'** Then **social work for the children, PATS for travel and accommodation, and Ben comes with her.** SA: call the on-call obstetrician at the receiving unit and **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for road or RFDS retrieval; **send the blood group, Kleihauer sample and crossmatch with her**; level 6 = **Women's and Children's Hospital** and **Flinders**, with **Lyell McEwin** (level 5) taking many northern-country transfers VERIFY; **PATS**, **Country Health Connect**, social work, **TIS National 131 450**, Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and AMIC worker; **SA Perinatal Practice Guideline on placenta praevia and accreta spectrum**, and RANZCOG.
plan: **WIPE — and STILL open with a question even though the task is 'explain'**: **'how are you feeling now, Jess? Can you tell me what's happened so far?'** Then pick it up: **'I have your results. Let's go through them together.'**

**SIGNPOST THE FOUR TASKS**: **'I'll explain the scan, the tests we need, what's going on, and the plan from now until the baby is born.'** **Do not turn this into a history — an examiner will say 'stick to your task'.**
**TASK 1 — NORMAL FINDINGS FIRST**: **'the fluid around the baby is normal, the heartbeat is normal, the baby is growing well and is head down.'** Let her have that before anything else.

**Then the placenta, as a bridge**: **'the placenta is a piece of tissue — like a bridge — that connects the baby to your womb; the baby's oxygen and food come across it. Normally it sits at the TOP of the womb. In your case it has formed at the BOTTOM, and it is COMPLETELY COVERING THE OPENING — the exit the baby would come through. We call this placenta praevia. Our biggest concern is severe bleeding — which is what happened today — and especially at the time of birth.'**

**The cause, and it is not her fault**: **'the most likely reason is your previous caesarean — the placenta tends to attach near the scar, low in the womb.'** Smoking, other uterine surgery, older age and more pregnancies also contribute. **When she asks 'will it move?' — 'at 34 weeks and completely covering the opening, it will not move out of the way.'** Do not promise migration.

**TASK 2 — three groups, and KLEIHAUER IS NUMBER ONE**: **'you're O negative. When you bleed in pregnancy, a little of the baby's blood can mix with yours, and your body can become sensitised to the baby's blood group — that can cause serious problems in a FUTURE pregnancy. We prevent it with an anti-D injection. But I need to know how much mixing has happened so I can give the right dose, so we do a blood test called a Kleihauer.'**

**Then the second and third groups**: **full blood count and iron studies** for anaemia and to prepare her in case she bleeds again, plus **group and cross-match** so blood is available; and **a CTG** to check the baby is not distressed.
**Answer the anti-D question when it comes**: **'yes. The 28-week dose is a routine one; a bleed is a separate event and needs its own dose, sized by the Kleihauer.'**

**TASK 3 — the diagnosis and the three risks, unsoftened**: placenta praevia; **vaginal birth is impossible — the baby cannot come out past the placenta without severe bleeding**; and the risks are **severe bleeding · often a transfusion · and in severe cases the placenta growing into the wall of the womb, especially into the scar, which can mean an operation to remove the womb.**

**When she becomes tearful at 'remove my womb' — PAUSE and reassure WITHOUT retracting**: **'it's uncommon, and most women with praevia don't need it. I'm telling you so we can look for that problem on your next scan and plan the birth in the right hospital.'**

**TASK 4 — announce the number: 'the plan has six parts.' BOX ONE, TRANSFER**: **'because there's a risk of severe bleeding and a risk we may need to deliver early, we need to transfer you to a more equipped hospital in the city — a level 6 unit with a blood bank, surgeons and theatre around the clock, and an intensive care unit for premature babies. We'll arrange the retrieval team.'**

**BOX TWO — 24 hours**: monitored for bleeding, contractions and the baby. **'If there's no bleeding for 24 hours you may be able to leave the hospital — but we'd prefer you to stay CLOSE to the city hospital, not 250 km away.'**

**BOX THREE — the caesarean**: **'a vaginal birth is impossible, so the plan is a caesarean, at 36 to 37 weeks — a little early, to get in before any more bleeding. If bleeding comes back or contractions start, it may be done sooner.'**

**BOX FOUR — steroids today**: **'an injection of corticosteroids, two doses 24 hours apart, which speeds up the maturing of the baby's lungs in case the baby needs to be born before 37 weeks.'** **BOX FIVE — the anti-D, dose guided by the Kleihauer.**

**BOX SIX — serial scans WITH accreta named**: **'repeat ultrasounds every two to three weeks to check the baby and the placenta — and I'll ask the radiologist SPECIFICALLY to look for placenta accreta, where the placenta grows into the caesarean scar.'**

**She will ask to go home, and she pushes TWICE.** Answer the first with the kind, firm no and the warning-shot framing. **Answer the second — 'why can't I stay here, you have an ICU?' — with: 'we have an adult ICU, but not the newborn intensive care or the round-the-clock obstetric surgical team a 34-week baby with this condition would need. It's safer to move you now while you're stable than in an emergency.'**
**Solve the barriers rather than arguing**: social work for the children, **PATS** for travel and accommodation, Ben travels with her.

**RED FLAGS TO THE END OF THE PREGNANCY — this is the online-exam wording and the third discriminator**: **'any bleeding, any pain or tightenings, fewer movements, feeling faint — straight back to hospital, call 000.'** Add **no sexual intercourse until after the birth**, then a one-line summary and written information.
pefe: **No history task and no examination task — four EXPLAIN tasks. Drifting into history-taking is noted by the examiner.**
**DO NOW: ABC, two large-bore IV cannulae, observations, and NO DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION** — speculum only if needed, by the senior clinician.
**KLEIHAUER, group and antibody screen, CROSS-MATCH 2–4 UNITS, FBC, ferritin, and a coagulation profile if the bleed is heavy.**
**CTG now and repeated.** **Anti-D 625 IU IM within 72 hours, with extra doses per the Kleihauer.** **Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now, second dose in 24 hours.**
**Call the tertiary obstetric registrar and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval — with an escort, and blood available for the transfer.**
**Admit at level 6 for at least 24 hours**: bleeding, contractions, CTG twice daily, FBC. **Discharge only to accommodation near the tertiary unit.**
**Transvaginal ultrasound is SAFE in praevia and is the accurate way to define the relationship to the os.** Repeat every 2–3 weeks **with specific accreta assessment**; MRI if equivocal.
**Treat anaemia: oral iron, or IV iron if ferritin is low or haemoglobin is under 100.**

**Plan the caesarean at 36–37 weeks by a senior obstetrician with blood and cell salvage available. If accreta is suspected: a multidisciplinary plan — obstetrics, anaesthetics, urology, interventional radiology, blood bank, NICU.**

**AVOID: digital vaginal examination · discharging her because the bleeding stopped · tocolytics for praevia bleeding · promising a vaginal birth for a complete praevia · taking a history when the task says explain.**

findingsLabel: Her scripted interruptions, the two traps, and the variants
must: FAIL — **Discharging her home**, OR **keeping her at the level 4 hospital.** Not home, not here — she goes to a **level 6** unit.
FAIL — **No Kleihauer and no anti-D** in a Rh-negative woman with a bleed. A critical-error item however good the rest was.
FAIL — **No steroids at 34 weeks**, or **no accreta assessment** in a woman with a caesarean scar.
FAIL — **Mentioning a digital vaginal examination**, or **taking a history** when all four tasks say *explain*.
FAIL — **Ending at transfer.** The task says **until the end of the pregnancy** — timing, serial scans, accreta, red flags, where she lives.

stem: You are the HMO in a rural hospital. You receive a call from the birth suite. The midwife tells you a 29-year-old woman delivered by normal vaginal delivery 15 minutes ago, a 3.7 kg baby, is having severe vaginal bleeding, and has already lost 1.5 litres of blood. You are five minutes away from the birth suite.

There is a telephone in the middle of the station. Pick it up and begin. Tasks: talk to the midwife and take a history, which here includes asking her for examination findings — advise her on the management steps to take between now and your arrival. 8 minutes.
tasks: Talk to the midwife and take a history, including examination findings
Advise her on the management steps to take before you arrive
findings: Her opening statement

'Doctor, I've got a 29-year-old, first baby, normal delivery fifteen minutes ago, 3.7 kilos. She's bled about a litre and a half and it's not stopping. I need you to come.' LET HER FINISH — opening with 'check her blood pressure' reads as panic and loses the rapport marks
Is she alert
'Awake and talking, but PALE AND CLAMMY'
Observations
BP 80/50 · PULSE 120 · sats 98%. SAY THE NUMBERS BACK — naming the shock out loud is a mark, and it explains why you are activating the MTP
The bleeding
BRIGHT RED and POURING, not settling. A couple of clots. 'I don't know if it's clotting' — ask her to WATCH IT, and say WHY you are asking
Blood group
O POSITIVE — so anti-D does not arise in this version
The delivery history
Labour about EIGHTEEN HOURS. NO instruments, NO episiotomy. Single baby. No previous caesarean or uterine surgery. No bleeding disorder, no blood thinners
The placenta
Delivered about ten minutes ago. 'I've checked it — it's COMPLETE and normal'
THE UTERUS
At the UMBILICUS, about twenty weeks' size. LAX AND SOFT. NOT tender. Size tells you it is not empty; tenderness would raise rupture
★ SET-PIECE 1 — the perineum
'The perineum's intact, doctor — DO YOU STILL WANT A SPECULUM?' A PASS ANSWER SAYS YES AND EXPLAINS WHY. This is the named critical error of the handbook case
★ SET-PIECE 2 — the tranexamic acid
'Should I wait for the coags before the tranexamic acid?' THE ANSWER IS NO — it works best within three hours of the bleeding starting
If you are vague
'Which medication, doctor?' — she will ask. 'Some medication to help the uterus contract' does not pass this station
At about six minutes
If theatre has not been mentioned she asks: 'Do you want me to prepare her for theatre?' — the fifth T, prompted because you missed it
At the end
If you never mention the woman herself she asks: 'What shall I tell her and her husband?'
VERSION B — the snapped cord

Controlled cord traction, the cord snapped, the placenta is still inside. THE MARKS MOVE TO THE TEN MINUTES BEFORE THEATRE: speculum to see the cord, CLAMP IT — that alone slows the bleeding — then gentle traction on the clamp; if it does not deliver, manual removal in theatre. AND STILL ALL FOUR T'S, because a retained placenta is itself a risk factor for atony
VARIANTS that change the answer

CONTRACTED uterus with continuing bleeding → TRAUMA until proven otherwise · SHOCKED with little visible blood, previous caesarean, tender abdomen → RUPTURE or broad ligament haematoma, urgent laparotomy, do not wait for imaging · blood NOT clotting and oozing from the cannula site → DIC · fundus NOT PALPABLE with a mass at the introitus and vagal bradycardia → UTERINE INVERSION, replace it first and HOLD the uterotonics until it is back

dx: **Primary postpartum haemorrhage, most likely uterine atony — but THE DIAGNOSIS IS NEARLY GIVEN TO YOU, so it is not what separates a pass from a fail. THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS THIS: you must manage ALL FOUR T'S OUT LOUD even though the findings point to only one.**

**The midwife hands you a LAX UTERUS and a COMPLETE PLACENTA. The temptation is to say 'this is atony' and spend three minutes on uterotonics. That is the failure — the handbook records the two critical errors as FAILING TO CONSIDER TRAUMA and FAILING TO CONSIDER RETAINED PRODUCTS, in the very case where the uterus feels lax.**

**THREE PHASES, ANNOUNCED OUT LOUD: 1 RESUSCITATE → 2 GATHER INFORMATION → 3 MANAGE ALL FOUR T'S.** **Candidates do not fail for forgetting carboprost. They fail for starting on drugs, jumping back to airway, remembering the catheter, and running out of time before the speculum. Say the phase name as you enter it and the examiner can follow you.**

**The transition sentence, scripted**: **'the most likely cause here is uterine atony, because the uterus is lax. But I'm going to treat all four causes together, because I can't exclude the others down a telephone.'** **If asked 'what exactly is the diagnosis?', the marked answer is not a single confident word — it is that honest sentence.**

**THE REASONING LINE THAT SHOWS YOU ARE THINKING: 'A CONTRACTED uterus with continuing bleeding is TRAUMA until proven otherwise. A SOFT uterus with continuing bleeding is ATONY or RETAINED TISSUE. SHOCK OUT OF PROPORTION to what you can see is CONCEALED — rupture, haematoma, or inversion.'**

**Definitions: primary PPH = blood loss ≥ 500 mL from the genital tract within 24 hours of birth (≥ 1000 mL after caesarean). MAJOR > 1000 mL. MASSIVE > 1500 mL or bleeding with shock — which is why 1.5 litres in the stem means ACTIVATE THE MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL.** VERIFY

**DOSES, and name the drug first and the dose second: OXYTOCIN 5 IU IV slowly or 10 IU IM, then an infusion of 40 IU in 1 L over 4 hours · ERGOMETRINE 250 mcg IM — NOT in hypertension or pre-eclampsia, and give an antiemetic with it · MISOPROSTOL 800–1000 mcg PR · CARBOPROST 250 mcg IM every 15 minutes, max 8 doses — NOT in asthma, and NEVER intravenously · TRANEXAMIC ACID 1 g IV early, best within 3 hours.** VERIFY against Therapeutic Guidelines. **If you can only remember two, remember oxytocin and tranexamic acid.**

**BLOODS, in this order of importance: GROUP AND CROSS-MATCH — name it FIRST; forget it and you have forgotten the most important test · FULL BLOOD EXAMINATION · COAGULATION SCREEN with INR, APTT and FIBRINOGEN · UEC and a venous gas for lactate.** **O-negative blood until the cross-match is back, and KEEP HER WARM — hypothermia worsens coagulopathy.**

CORRECTION — **do not say a speculum is contraindicated.** Some notes claim this; it is wrong here. **'I don't agree with that. I have a clear indication — I need to see the cervix and vaginal walls, because a tear there is a treatable cause I would otherwise miss.'** **Other AVOIDs: ergometrine in hypertension · carboprost in asthma or IV · waiting for the coagulation screen before tranexamic acid · crystalloid alone past about 2 L, or packed cells alone — she needs plasma and platelets too.**

**ADDED — anti-D matters, but it is NOT the emergency. Once she is stable, if she is Rh D negative with an Rh-positive baby, give anti-D ideally within 72 hours with a Kleihauer to size the dose — AFTER the four T's.** VERIFY. SA: at an MM5 site without on-site obstetrics or a blood bank, **call MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 EARLY for advice and retrieval**, alert the on-call obstetrician and anaesthetist by phone, **check the emergency O-negative stock held on site**, keep bimanual compression going while waiting, and work to the **SA Health Perinatal Practice Guidelines PPH pathway**; Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and Aboriginal Liaison Officer where relevant; **TIS National 131 450**; **debriefing and a formal incident review afterwards are part of good care.**
plan: **Open the call like an ISBAR in reverse**: **'Hello, this is Dr ___, I'm the HMO. Who am I speaking with?'** then **'thanks for calling. Can you tell me what has happened so far?'** **Let her finish — she is scripted to add detail beyond the stem, and opening with 'check her blood pressure' loses the rapport marks.**
**Announce the structure**: **'I'm going to do three things: resuscitate first, then ask you some questions, then give you a full plan. First, resuscitation.'**

**DRSABC through the midwife. R** — is she alert and responsive? **S — 'please SEND FOR HELP now, and call the obstetric registrar and the consultant. Tell them we have a postpartum haemorrhage.'** **A/B** — airway patent, breathing, **high-flow oxygen**.

**C** — **'blood pressure, pulse and saturations please, and I want them monitored continuously.'** 80/50, pulse 120. **SAY THE NUMBERS BACK**: **'eighty over fifty with a pulse of a hundred and twenty — she is shocked, and with 1.5 litres this is a massive obstetric haemorrhage.'**

**The rest of the resuscitation, as instructions**: **two large-bore cannulas, bloods as you go, warmed normal saline immediately · indwelling catheter with urine output measured · 'she has lost more than 1500 mL, so please activate the MASSIVE TRANSFUSION PROTOCOL and get O-negative blood up while we wait for the cross-match' · and keep her warm.**

**'Now let me gather some information.' The bleeding**: bright red or dark · clots · pouring or oozing · **'is the blood clotting on the floor? I'm asking because if it isn't, I'm thinking about a coagulopathy'** · and her blood group.

**The delivery history — and EACH QUESTION IS A T. Say the link out loud once**: **how long was the labour and how big the baby → TONE · any instruments or episiotomy → TRAUMA · single or multiple → TONE · any previous caesarean or uterine surgery → RUPTURE · has the placenta delivered and is it complete → TISSUE · any bleeding disorder or blood thinners → THROMBIN.**

**THE EXAMINATION YOU ASK THE MIDWIFE TO PERFORM — this is the part candidates forget. You are talking to a health professional; you may ask for FINDINGS, not just history.** **The uterus first**: **'please feel the fundus. What size is it? Is it firm or lax? Is it tender?'** At the umbilicus, lax and soft, not tender.
**The perineum**: **'please inspect the perineum — any tears or lacerations? Is the episiotomy bleeding?'** She replies that it is intact and asks whether you still want a speculum.

**★ THE SET-PIECE. Answer: 'YES please — an intact perineum does NOT exclude a cervical or vaginal tear, and I need to know before she goes to theatre.'** Then **'please lay the placenta out and check the cotyledons AND the membranes are complete.'**

**'Now the management.' State the working diagnosis HONESTLY**: **'the most likely cause is uterine atony, because the uterus is lax and soft, and she had a long labour and a big baby. But I can't exclude the others down a telephone, so I'm going to ask you to treat all four causes together.'**

**TONE**: **empty the bladder with the catheter, remove clots, RUB UP THE FUNDUS. Oxytocin 5 units IV slowly or 10 IM, then an infusion of 40 units in a litre over four hours. If bleeding continues, ergometrine 250 micrograms IM — she is not hypertensive — with an antiemetic. Then prepare misoprostol or carboprost. If still uncontrolled, BIMANUAL COMPRESSION and keep it on until I arrive.**

**TISSUE**: **'you've checked the placenta — thank you. Please lay it out again and run the MEMBRANES through your fingers as well. If anything is missing, or if the bleeding continues, she'll need manual removal and uterine exploration under anaesthesia.'**

**THE FIFTH T — THEATRE, before she has to prompt you**: **'please tell the registrar and consultant that this woman is likely to need theatre for examination under anaesthesia and uterine exploration, and ask them to prepare her now. Let the anaesthetist know.'**
**The person, not just the problem**: **'and please explain to her and her partner what is happening — tell her I'm on my way.'**

TEMPERATURE 38.5 °C · BP 110/70 · pulse 88 · RR 16 · sats 99. Asking for the temperature before you greet her hands you the case at TWENTY SECONDS, which lets you steer the whole history toward infection while still covering the other four causes
General
Alert, not pale, uncomfortable. No dehydration
ABDOMEN
Lower abdominal tenderness, a SUPRAPUBIC MASS, and THE LOWER BORDER CANNOT BE FELT. A mass you cannot get below arises from the pelvis — it is the uterus
Pelvic — inspection
Episiotomy HEALING, no bleeding from it
SPECULUM
THE OS IS OPEN, with blood coming through it. No tears or lesions of the cervix or vaginal walls. The os closes within 1–2 days — OPEN AT DAY TEN IS ABNORMAL

She is EMBARRASSED and will ONLY mention it if asked DIRECTLY: 'Yes — it smells awful. I was too embarrassed to say.' IF YOU NEVER ASK, SHE NEVER OFFERS IT. That is the whole point of the station
The bleeding
Started three days ago, constant, getting heavier. BRIGHT RED, a few clots, some discharge. FIVE OR SIX pads a day, SOAKED THROUGH

Light-headed on standing. EXHAUSTED. A dragging ache low down. Hot and cold, and SHE HAD THE SHIVERS LAST NIGHT
The afterbirth
'I wasn't watching. Nobody said there was a problem.' SHE WILL NOT HELP YOU — and that is why retained products cannot be excluded on history

dx: **Endometritis at the bedside, with retained products still on the list. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage = abnormal or excessive bleeding from the genital tract from 24 HOURS TO 12 WEEKS after birth — and unlike primary PPH there is NO agreed volume threshold; the judgement is clinical.**

**Ask for the observations, temperature first, BEFORE you greet her.** The examiner hands you **38.5 °C** and the case is effectively given away in the first twenty seconds — **which is exactly why the history is five minutes long and not two. You already have the diagnosis; the remaining four minutes are how you EARN the differentials mark.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: name it, justify it with FOUR FINDINGS, then give FOUR DIFFERENTIALS. Candidates who say 'endometritis' and stop do not pass.** **The four reasons, said back to her in plain English: 1. 'You have a fever.' 2. 'Your womb is bigger than I'd expect ten days after birth.' 3. 'It is painful when I press on it.' 4. 'The opening of the womb is still open, and it should have closed by now.'**

**THE FIVE BUCKETS — four pregnancy-related and one not. ENDOMETRITIS · RETAINED PRODUCTS · TRAUMA (episiotomy breakdown, missed laceration, haematoma) · COAGULOPATHY · and NOT PREGNANCY-RELATED (fibroid, cervical polyp, cervical cancer — and the first period returning, which can come early and heavy once breastfeeding stops).** **The last bucket is the one people forget.**
**Timing splits the list: bleeding in the FIRST WEEK leans coagulopathy; at DAY TEN it leans infection or retained tissue.**

**Why endometritis and not retained products? Because endometritis can be diagnosed AT THE BEDSIDE and retained products cannot. Fever plus a bulky tender uterus plus an open os is a complete clinical picture; retained products needs an ultrasound.** **And they are not rivals — every suspected retained product requires antibiotic cover, because there is always an element of endometritis with tissue sitting in the uterus. So you treat for infection either way, and the scan decides whether she also needs theatre.**

**★ DO NOT WAIT FOR THE ULTRASOUND BEFORE STARTING ANTIBIOTICS. This is the single most common wrong order in this station.** Cultures and swabs first if they do not delay the dose — **then antibiotics, then the scan, then theatre if products are seen.**

**The involution yardstick: fundus at the UMBILICUS immediately after birth, descending about one finger-breadth a day · BEHIND THE SYMPHYSIS and impalpable abdominally by DAY 10–14 · normal size by six weeks. A uterus of 10 weeks' size at day 10 is infected, or still holding tissue.** **And the OS closes within 1–2 days.** **Normal lochia runs red for a few days, then brown, then pale, over two to six weeks — FOUL-SMELLING IS NEVER NORMAL.**

CORRECTION — **do not quote an antibiotic regimen you are unsure of. 'Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines' is a complete answer.** If pressed, a typical Australian regimen combines **amoxicillin or ampicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole intravenously.** VERIFY. **And do not say a speculum is contraindicated — you need to see the os and the vaginal walls.**

CORRECTION — **anti-D is not a priority in the first minutes, but it is NOT optional. If she is Rh D negative with an Rh D positive baby, give anti-D within 72 hours of the sensitising event, with a Kleihauer to size the dose.** Routine antenatal prophylaxis is at 28 and 34 weeks. VERIFY. If challenged: **'I'd address it once she is stable and I have worked through the causes — but before she leaves, and within 72 hours.'** **She is O positive here.** SA: bloods and swabs to SA Pathology, **first dose of IV antibiotics locally**, discuss with the on-call obstetric or gynaecology team; **PATS** if she must transfer for ultrasound or theatre; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if she becomes septic and unstable; **Country Health Connect**; **TIS National 131 450**; Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and Liaison Officer; **Closing the Gap PBS**; postnatal mood support **PANDA 1300 726 306**.
plan: **Sanitise your hands where the examiner can see you, then ask for the observations BEFORE you greet her**: **'Examiner, before I start — may I have her observations, including her temperature?'** 38.5 °C.

**Then the patient**: **'Hello Mary, my name is Dr ___, I'll be looking after you today. How can I help?'** She gives the bleeding. **'That sounds worrying, and you were right to come in. Let me ask some questions, examine you, and we'll work out what's causing it together.'** **Signpost: the bleeding, then the delivery, then the other causes.**

**Block 1 — explore the bleeding**: when did it start · constant or on and off · getting worse · bright red or dark · any clots · any discharge as well · **how many pads a day, and are they FULLY SOAKED.**

**★ THE SMELL QUESTION, in plain words — ask it explicitly, do not hide it inside 'any discharge?'**: **'does it have a bad smell?'** *'Yes — it smells awful. I was too embarrassed to say.'* **Then name the significance out loud: 'that's important, because an offensive smell points towards an infection.'**
**Red flags**: **'are you feeling dizzy or light-headed? Are you unusually tired, or short of breath climbing stairs?'** Light-headed on standing, exhausted.

**Block 2 — the delivery history**: vaginal or caesarean · at term or early · **was it a long labour** · any instruments · **'did they have to make a cut? IS IT HEALING WELL?'** — do not skip the episiotomy because it is in the stem · one baby or more · first pregnancy.

**The afterbirth question, phrased so she can answer it**: **'were you aware of any problems delivering the afterbirth — did the cord break, or did it come away late?'** *'I wasn't watching.'* **She was not looking, and that is exactly why retained products cannot be excluded on history.** Then **'did you bleed heavily straight after the birth?'**

**Block 3 — endometritis symptoms**: **'any tummy pain with the bleeding? Any fever, chills or shakes? Any vaginal discharge, and does it smell? Any burning passing urine, or breast pain?'** Then **risk factors**: **'have you started having sex again? Are you using tampons? Has anything been put inside, like a coil?'**

**Block 4 — coagulopathy**: **'do you bruise easily? Any frequent nosebleeds? Were your periods heavy before pregnancy? Any family history of a bleeding problem? Are you on any blood thinners?'** **Heavy periods raise coagulopathy AND fibroid at once.**

**The non-pregnancy bucket, and closing**: **'are you up to date with your cervical screening? Do you know your blood group?'** Then **'how is the baby doing — feeding well? And how are you coping with motherhood?'** — **the wellbeing mark hidden in an obstetric case.**
**Task 2 — ask the examiner, ABDOMEN BEFORE PELVIS. General**: alert or drowsy, pale, in pain, signs of dehydration. **Then a postural blood pressure.**

**Abdomen — inspection then palpation**: distension, scars, movement with respiration; then **'is there tenderness? Is there a mass? AND CAN I FEEL THE LOWER BORDER OF THAT MASS?'** **Everyone rushes to the pelvis. The uterus is found in the abdomen, and the lower-border question is what turns a mass into a diagnosis.**
**Pelvic with consent and a chaperone — inspection**: **'is the episiotomy healing, or is it bleeding? Any discharge, swelling, redness or bruising?'**
**SPECULUM — and say the os FIRST**: **'IS THE OS OPEN OR CLOSED? Is there blood or tissue coming through it? Any tears or lesions of the cervix or vaginal walls?'** Open, with blood through it.
**BIMANUAL**: **'is there cervical motion tenderness? What size is the uterus, is it tender, is the border regular? Any adnexal tenderness or masses?'** CMT present, uterus 10 weeks' size and tender.

**Task 3 — name it in PLAIN ENGLISH**: **'Mary, I think the most likely cause is a condition called endometritis — an infection of the lining of the womb.'** **If you say 'endometritis' alone she will ask what it means.**

**THE FOUR REASONS, drawn from her own history and examination**: the fever of 38.5 · the womb larger than expected at ten days, when it should have shrunk behind the pubic bone · tender when you press · **and the opening of the womb still open, when it should have closed within a day or two. 'The bad smell fits with that too.'**

**THE FOUR DIFFERENTIALS, in plain English, forty seconds**: **retained tissue — a small piece of the afterbirth or its membranes left behind, 'and we can only really tell with a scan'** · **a tear — in the neck of the womb or the vagina, or the cut bleeding again** · **a clotting problem** · **and causes nothing to do with the pregnancy — a fibroid, a polyp, rarely a cancer — 'and your first period coming back can also be early and heavy, especially if you've stopped breastfeeding.'**

**If a management task is added**: **admit · bloods, blood cultures and swabs · IV ANTIBIOTICS STRAIGHT AWAY, 'we don't wait for the scan, because if there's tissue left behind there's almost always infection with it' · then ultrasound · then a short procedure in theatre if tissue is seen.** Answer her two questions: **'can I still breastfeed?' — yes, with antibiotics safe in breastfeeding; 'is my baby at risk?' — no, but someone needs to be with him while she is in hospital.**

'Sarah, the midwife. I've got a 32-year-old who delivered 20 minutes ago. Her BP is 190 over 100 and I'm worried. She had gestational hypertension from 39½ weeks and was induced. She's lost about 250 mL.' THEN NOTHING MORE until you ask
Resuscitation answers
Awake, talking, holding the baby · airway fine, RR 18, sats 98% · pulse 88, temp 37.1 · TWO readings five minutes apart, 190/100 and 186/102 · IV cannula already in from the induction
The pregnancy

Uncomplicated until 39½ weeks — BP 150/95 at a clinic visit, started on ORAL LABETALOL and booked for induction. PRE-ECLAMPSIA SCREEN NEGATIVE: urine protein negative, kidney and liver bloods and platelets normal. First baby
The delivery
Normal vaginal at 40 weeks after a FOURTEEN-HOUR INDUCTION. No instruments, no episiotomy — a SECOND-DEGREE TEAR, not yet sutured
★ IF YOU ASK 'ANY MEDICATIONS?' VAGUELY
'The usual for the third stage' — AND SHE WAITS. The midwife answers what you ask. She knows what an NSAID is; NAME THE DRUGS
★ IF YOU NAME THEM
'SYNTOMETRINE at the birth — and I gave her DICLOFENAC about ten minutes ago for the tear.' Both raise blood pressure
★ IF YOU NEVER ASK ABOUT DRUGS BY 4:30
She prompts: 'Do you want to know what she's had?' — you have already lost the mark
The fluid, the pain, the bleeding
About 2.5 LITRES of IV fluid with the Syntocinon · pain 6/10 from the tear and afterpains, 'a bit shaky' · bleeding HAS STOPPED, uterus FIRM and contracted below the umbilicus
The baby
3.5 kg, APGARS 9 AND 9, skin to skin. A reassuring Apgar closes the box in ten seconds
Symptom sweep — all negative
No headache, no visual problems, no dizziness, no chest pain, no breathlessness, no right upper quadrant pain, no nausea

Fully alert · no rash or bruising · 'I CAN'T DO FUNDOSCOPY, sorry' — an acceptable answer, say you will do it on arrival · no RUQ tenderness · uterus firm, not tender · REFLEXES NORMAL, NO CLONUS · dipstick when she next passes urine

'Her head is pounding and she's seeing flashing lights. Reflexes brisk, THREE BEATS OF CLONUS.' PRE-ECLAMPSIA WITH SEVERE FEATURES — magnesium sulfate NOW, 4 g over 20 min then 1 g/h, labetalol as planned, hourly reflexes/RR/urine output, calcium gluconate at the bedside, consultant and MedSTAR

Community midwife: BP 165/105 with a headache. DAYS 3–6 IS THE PEAK WINDOW for postpartum pre-eclampsia. She comes to hospital NOW — by ambulance if the headache is severe or there are visual symptoms. Do NOT manage it by phone

**THE DISCRIMINATING BEHAVIOUR IS A PAIR OF QUESTIONS THAT ORDINARY HYPERTENSION HISTORY-TAKING DOES NOT CONTAIN: 'what medication has she had — was she given ergometrine? Any NSAIDs?' and 'how much IV fluid has she received?'** — **asked BY NAME, to a midwife who knows what they are, and followed by 'is she in pain?' and 'has the bleeding stopped?'** **Candidates who run the antenatal pre-eclampsia script and never ask these explain the blood pressure wrongly and manage only half of it.**

**Three phases, ANNOUNCED: RESUSCITATE → GATHER (pregnancy, delivery, baby, symptoms) → MANAGE.** The source calls this case 'a mess' unless you divide it — and the spine is identical to the primary PPH telephone station with the content swapped.
**Thresholds: hypertension ≥140/90 on two readings. SEVERE ≥160 systolic AND/OR ≥110 diastolic. Target once treated around 110–140 / 80–85.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **SOMANZ defines severe as ≥160 systolic and/or ≥110 diastolic, NOT 160/100. Her 190 systolic puts her there.** If challenged: **'the severe threshold is 160 or 110; her systolic of 190 puts her there.'**

CORRECTION — **the uterotonic that raises blood pressure is ERGOMETRINE (and Syntometrine, which contains it). 'Ergotamine' is a migraine drug.** If challenged: **'the third-stage drug I'm asking about is ergometrine; it causes vasoconstriction and is avoided in hypertensive women.'**

**Keep POSTPARTUM PRE-ECLAMPSIA on the list and screen for it. The same definition applies after birth — hypertension plus proteinuria or organ involvement — and signs first appear postpartum in a significant minority of cases, most often DAYS 3–6 but up to six weeks.** VERIFY the quoted percentages; **say 'a significant minority' unless you have checked them.** Screen with **symptoms, reflexes, clonus, dipstick and bloods.**

**The causes, named MOST LIKELY FIRST: exacerbated gestational hypertension · pain · ergometrine or Syntometrine · NSAIDs · fluid overload with the loss of pregnancy vasodilation · postpartum pre-eclampsia or HELLP, not excluded · and, in one sentence at the END, phaeochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis and renal disease.** **Opening with phaeochromocytoma is a named error.**

**MANAGEMENT WITH NAMES AND DOSES. Bloods: UEC, creatinine, eGFR · FBE with platelets and haemoglobin · LFT · urine protein (dipstick now, spot PCR). LABETALOL 20 mg IV over 2 minutes, then 40, then 80 at 10-minute intervals, max 300 — or HYDRALAZINE 5–10 mg IV repeated every 20 minutes — or oral NIFEDIPINE 10–20 mg if no IV. PARACETAMOL 1 g for the pain. STOP the ergometrine, WITHHOLD NSAIDs until renal function and platelets are known, and repair the tear with good local anaesthetic. Call the CONSULTANT. Discuss MAGNESIUM SULFATE — 4 g IV over 15–20 min then 1 g/hour — which becomes mandatory if she develops headache, visual symptoms or clonus.** VERIFY

**Monitoring and follow-up: BP every 15 minutes until below 160/110, then half-hourly · neuro observations · strict fluid balance with NO further boluses · fundus and lochia checks · baby stays with her.** **Oral maintenance once controlled: labetalol 100–200 mg tds, nifedipine XR 20–30 mg daily, or enalapril — all compatible with breastfeeding.** **Before discharge: written safety-net — headache, visual disturbance, RUQ pain, breathlessness, swelling, fits. Community BP check within 3–7 days, GP at 6 weeks. Long term, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy roughly double later cardiovascular risk.** SA: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for retrieval to a level 5–6 unit if uncontrolled or severe features develop; **Country Health Connect**; ACCHS and Aboriginal Family Birthing Program; **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **Open the call**: **'Hello, this is Dr ___, the doctor on duty. Who am I speaking with?'** then **'thanks for calling, Sarah. Can you tell me what has happened so far?'** **Do not launch into drugs — the opening earns rapport and the detail she is scripted to add.**
**Announce the three phases**: **'I'm going to do three things: make sure she's safe right now, then ask you some questions, then give you a plan. First — is she alert and responsive?'**

**Phase 1, in order**: **'please send for help — notify the obstetric registrar and the consultant'** · airway patent, breathing, **respiratory rate and saturations** · **pulse and temperature** · **'how many times has the blood pressure been checked? Please repeat it now, correct cuff size'** · **'does she have an IV line? No fluids for the moment.'**

**Say the number back**: **'so this is severe hypertension — 190 systolic.'** Then signpost into the history: **'she's stable for now — can I ask about the pregnancy first, then the delivery, then the baby?'**

**Box 1, PREGNANCY**: complications — blood pressure, sugars, kidneys · **'when was the hypertension diagnosed, and was she TREATED?'** · **'was she investigated for pre-eclampsia — urine protein, kidney function, liver tests?'** · **'any previous pregnancies, and any high blood pressure in them, especially AFTER the birth?'**
**Box 2, DELIVERY — where the special questions live**: route, term, **how long was the labour**, instruments, cuts or tears.

**★ THE TWO SPECIAL QUESTIONS, BY NAME**: **'what medications has she had? Was she given ERGOMETRINE or SYNTOMETRINE for the third stage? Any NSAIDs — ibuprofen, diclofenac?'** and **'HOW MUCH IV FLUID has she received?'** **Asking 'any medications?' gets 'the usual' and nothing more.**

**Then the two that complete the box**: **'is she in pain right now? Is she anxious or worried about anything?'** and **'you said 250 mL — HAS THE BLEEDING STOPPED? Is the uterus firm?'** **Say it out loud: 'so this is not a haemorrhage — I'm treating the pressure.' 250 mL is below the 500 mL PPH threshold.**
**Box 3, BABY — ten seconds**: **'how is the baby doing? What was the Apgar? Weight? Is the baby with her?'** 3.5 kg, Apgars 9 and 9.

**Box 4, SYMPTOM SWEEP — brain, heart, lungs, liver in one breath**: **'headache, blurred vision, dizziness? Any chest pain or shortness of breath? Any abdominal pain, particularly under the right ribs? Nausea?'**

**DIRECTED EXAMINATION — six things, not a systems review**: **'is she fully alert? Any rash, bruising or petechiae? Are you able to do fundoscopy — if not that's fine, I'll do it when I arrive. Please check for right upper quadrant tenderness, and the uterus — firm and contracted, tender? Please check her REFLEXES and for ANKLE CLONUS. And a dipstick for protein when she next passes urine.'**
**The five-second addition**: **'and she's O negative — please send the cord blood group. If the baby is Rh positive she'll need anti-D within 72 hours.'**

**TASK 2 — the causes, MOST LIKELY FIRST**: **'she already has gestational hypertension, and it has become severe. The most likely reasons it has spiked now are pain after a long labour and a tear, the fluid she had in labour, and — if she had them — ergometrine or anti-inflammatories, which both push the blood pressure up.'**

**Keep pre-eclampsia open, explicitly**: **'I can't yet exclude pre-eclampsia developing after the birth — it can show up for the first time postpartum — which is why we're checking symptoms, reflexes, urine and bloods.'** Then **one sentence at the end**: thyroid or adrenal causes are possible but much less likely today.

**TASK 3 — bloods first**: **'please take bloods from the cannula: electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR; full blood count with platelets and haemoglobin; liver function. And a spot urine protein as well as the dipstick.'**

**The IV antihypertensive, BY NAME AND DOSE**: **'labetalol 20 mg IV over two minutes; if still above 160 over 110 after ten minutes, 40 mg, then 80 mg. If labetalol isn't available or she's asthmatic, hydralazine 5 to 10 mg IV every 20 minutes. Aiming initially below 160 over 110, then towards 110–140 over 80–85.'**

**Treat the CAUSE as well as the number**: **'paracetamol 1 gram now, oral or IV. No NSAIDs until we have her kidney function and platelets, and no ergometrine. Get that tear repaired with good local anaesthetic.'** **No further fluid boluses; start a fluid balance chart.**

**The consultant, and magnesium**: **'I'm calling the consultant now. I'll discuss magnesium sulfate with them — with a pressure this high it may be indicated even without pre-eclampsia features, and it becomes mandatory if she develops headache, visual symptoms or clonus.'**

**Monitoring and the closed loop**: **BP every 15 minutes until below 160/110 then half-hourly, neuro obs, strict fluid balance, fundus and lochia checks, baby stays with her.** Add **MedSTAR if it cannot be controlled or severe features develop.** Then **'can you read that back to me?'** and **'please tell her what we're doing and why — I'm on my way.'**

dx: **Three stems, one spine: THE POSTPARTUM B'S. Version A is the six-week check with gestational diabetes, sometimes with a fever. Version B is a breast lump in a woman who only admits to breastfeeding IF YOU ASK — and cancer stays on top. Version C is mastitis management.**

**THE B'S, in order: BREAST and BABY · BLUES · BIRTH CANAL · BLADDER · BOWEL · BREATHING · BLOOD · BIRTH CONTROL.** **But explore the DELIVERY and the PREGNANCY FIRST — without the GDM history you cannot earn the OGTT mark.**

**VERSION A'S MARKED ITEM: the 75 g OGTT at 6–12 WEEKS for every woman who had gestational diabetes, then HbA1c or OGTT every 1–3 years and before any future pregnancy.** **NOT fasting glucose, and NOT HbA1c at this point.** If challenged — 'why not an HbA1c, it's easier?' — **'HbA1c is unreliable in the weeks after pregnancy and blood loss, and it misses impaired glucose tolerance; guidelines specify the OGTT at six to twelve weeks. HbA1c is fine for the ongoing one-to-three-yearly checks.'** VERIFY

**VERSION A'S OTHER AUTO-FAIL: the safety question, asked of a happy-looking mother. Script it — 'I ask every new mum this: have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or the baby?'** **EPDS ≥13, or ANY positive answer to question 10, needs action.** **Red flag: thoughts of harming self or baby, confusion or hallucinations — postpartum psychosis is an emergency.**

**If there is a FEVER in Version A, the station becomes a deliberate hunt for THREE infections: ENDOMETRITIS (offensive lochia, uterine tenderness — swabs, blood cultures, amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 bd) · MASTITIS or ABSCESS · UTI (urine MCS — 'cheap, and UTI is common postpartum').** Plus wound infection, DVT/PE and pneumonia.

**VERSION B IS THE HARDER, NEWER CASE, AND THE ORDER IS DELIBERATE: characterise the LUMP → RED FLAGS → then breastfeeding → then infection.** **Asking 'are you breastfeeding?' first and then taking a mastitis history is the trap.** **The stem no longer says postpartum, and the top diagnosis is CANCER UNTIL EXCLUDED.**

**Say it kindly but say it**: **'you're breastfeeding, and a lump ten weeks after birth is often something simple — a milk-filled cyst, or the start of an infection. But you have a lump, it isn't behaving like an abscess — no fever, not very painful — and your mum had breast cancer. So my first job is to make sure this is not a breast cancer. It probably isn't — but I'm not willing to guess.'** **The failing sentence is 'it's probably a blocked duct, let's see how it goes.'**

**The lump plan: examine both breasts and axillae today · ULTRASOUND as first imaging (under 35 and lactating — dense tissue; MAMMOGRAM if 35 or over, or suspicious) · CORE BIOPSY of any solid or indeterminate lesion, which completes the TRIPLE TEST — positive if ANY component is abnormal · ASPIRATION for a cyst or galactocele, which is diagnostic and therapeutic (milk versus pus).** **Feeding continues through ultrasound, mammography (feed or express first) and biopsy.** **Never send a SYMPTOMATIC woman to BreastScreen.**

**VERSION C — MASTITIS IN FIVE MOVES: 1. FLUCLOXACILLIN or dicloxacillin 500 mg orally 6-hourly for AT LEAST 5 DAYS. 2. Paracetamol and ibuprofen (safe in breastfeeding); WARM pack BEFORE a feed to let the milk down, COLD pack AFTER to reduce swelling; rest and fluids. 3. KEEP THE BREAST EMPTY — continue feeding from the affected side, STARTING on it; express by pump if too painful; the milk is safe. 4. FIX THE TECHNIQUE — observe a feed, lactation consultant or child health nurse, ABA helpline. 5. REVIEW AT 48 HOURS.** **ULTRASOUND HAS ONLY TWO TRIGGERS: a lump on presentation, or no response at 48 hours.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **penicillin allergy in mastitis. The lecture says 'don't worry about allergies'. Know the answer: NON-SEVERE allergy → CEPHALEXIN 500 mg 6-hourly; SEVERE or immediate allergy → CLINDAMYCIN 450 mg 8-hourly.** VERIFY. CORRECTION — **combined pill timing. 'At least six weeks after delivery' is correct for a BREASTFEEDING woman. For a non-breastfeeding woman with no VTE risk factors it can start from DAY 21; with risk factors (caesarean, BMI >30, smoking, PPH, pre-eclampsia) wait until 6 weeks.** **Safe wording: 'no oestrogen before six weeks while breastfeeding; progestogen-only methods — Implanon, Mirena, the mini-pill — can start straight away.'** SA: breast clinic at **TQEH, RAH or FMC** with **PATS**; **McGrath breast care nurse**; familial cancer clinic for ≥2 first-degree relatives or young onset; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if septic; **ABA 1800 686 268**, **PANDA 1300 726 306**, **CaFHS 1300 733 606**, **TIS 131 450**.

Before we go through everything — how are you finding motherhood so far?'** **If she says 'harder than I expected', note it and follow it up under BLUES, not now.**
**Signpost — one sentence buys structure marks**: **'I'm going to go through the areas we check at six weeks: your recovery, bladder and bowels, the baby and feeding, your mood, and contraception.'**

**EXPLORE THE DELIVERY AND PREGNANCY FIRST**: **'was it a vaginal delivery or a caesarean? Any tears, or a cut, or heavy bleeding?'** then **'during the pregnancy, did you have high sugars, high blood pressure, or any other problem? What treatment did you have for the diabetes — and was it stopped after the birth?'**
**BLOOD and PAIN**: **'are you feeling more tired than you'd expect? Any breathlessness, racing heart, dizziness?'** (anaemia) · **'any pain in the tummy or down below?'**
**BIRTH CANAL**: **'are you still bleeding? Any discharge — what colour, any smell? Any fever or chills? Is the tear healing well? Do you feel any lump or bulge down below?'**

**BLADDER, BOWEL, BREATHING**: **'do you leak urine, especially when you cough, sneeze or laugh? Any burning?'** · **'any constipation? Lumps around the back passage? ANY LEAKING OF STOOL OR WIND you can't control?'** — **a targeted question, because third- and fourth-degree tears involve the anal sphincter** · **'any shortness of breath, or more coughs and colds than usual?'**

**BABY AND BREAST**: **'how is the baby doing? Any concerns with his weight gain? Breastfed or formula? WERE YOU SHOWN HOW TO ATTACH HIM PROPERLY? Any pain, redness or swelling in the breasts? Any cracked nipples? Pain while feeding?'**

**BLUES — and do not stop at 'mood OK'**: **'how has your mood been? How is your sleep — when the baby sleeps, can you? How are things at home, is your partner supportive, who else helps?'** Then, scripted and non-negotiable: **'I ask every new mum this: have you had any thoughts of harming yourself, or the baby?'** Then **alcohol or drugs since the birth.**

**BIRTH CONTROL AND SCREENING**: **'have your periods come back? Have you started having sex again — any pain or discomfort? What are your thoughts about contraception? When was your last cervical screening test?'**

**Ask for the findings you need**: general appearance and pallor, BP, temperature, abdomen for **uterine size and tenderness**, the perineum or caesarean wound, **both breasts**, thyroid, urine dipstick.

**VERSION A investigations, with the OGTT said by name**: **FBC and iron studies** — anaemia is expected after pregnancy and blood loss · **the 75 g OGTT at 6–12 weeks, 'because fasting glucose and HbA1c are not adequate here'** · **urine MCS given the temperature** · TSH if thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes or symptoms · **cervical screening if due**, deferred from the third trimester · **EPDS**.
**VERSION B — open by naming the fear**: **'I understand you've found a lump — that's a frightening thing to find, and you've done the right thing coming in. Tell me what you noticed.'**

**Characterise the lump**: when first noticed · first lump ever · getting bigger · how many and how big · painful to touch · any redness or swelling over it · **hard or soft** · **does it move freely.**

**RED FLAGS — BEFORE you ask about feeding**: **'have you lost weight, or your appetite? Any lumps in the armpit or the neck? Any discharge from the nipple, and what colour? Any change in the nipple — pulled in, a rash, an ulcer, different from the other side? Any family history of breast or ovarian cancer — WHO, and AT WHAT AGE?'**

**When the mother's breast cancer comes out, SAY THAT IT CHANGES YOUR PRIORITY** — and ask about other relatives and ovarian cancer. **Then the breastfeeding, discovered by you**: **'are you breastfeeding? When was the baby born?'** Then **the abscess questions**: fever, chills, feeling unwell, attachment technique, cracked nipples.

**The other differentials and the brief five Ps**: trauma or a knock (fat necrosis) · does the lump change with periods (fibrocystic) · smoking, alcohol, previous breast surgery, biopsies or chest radiation · **how many pregnancies** (the second safety net) · contraception · cervical screening.

**Explain with cancer FIRST, kindly** — the galactocele and infection framing, then **'so my first job is to make sure this is not a breast cancer'** — then the plan: **examine both breasts and axillae today, ultrasound this week, core biopsy if solid, and 'you can keep feeding through all of that.'**

**VERSION C in three moves, if that is the task**: **antibiotics · pain relief with warm before and cold after · and KEEP FEEDING FROM THE SORE SIDE.** **'There is nothing wrong with your breast or your milk. Stopping is the worst thing to do — the breast fills, and that's how an abscess forms.'** Feeding review, and **review in two days.**
pefe: **Version A findings to request: general appearance and pallor · BP and temperature · abdomen for UTERINE SIZE AND TENDERNESS · the perineal tear or caesarean wound · BOTH breasts · thyroid · urine dipstick.**
**75 g OGTT at 6–12 weeks after GDM — not fasting glucose, not HbA1c. Then HbA1c or OGTT every 1–3 years and before any future pregnancy.** Roughly a 50% lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes. VERIFY
**FBC and iron studies** — anaemia is expected after pregnancy and blood loss. **TSH** if pre-existing thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes or symptoms — **postpartum thyroiditis peaks at 2–6 months.**

**If febrile: FBC and CRP; blood cultures if ≥38 °C or unwell · high vaginal and endocervical swabs (MCS, chlamydia and gonorrhoea PCR) for endometritis · breast examination with ultrasound if a lump · urine MCS · wound check · legs and chest for DVT and PE.**
**TRIPLE TEST for any discrete lump: examination + imaging + core biopsy of a solid lesion. Positive if ANY component is abnormal.**
**Ultrasound is first imaging under 35 and in lactating women (dense tissue); mammogram if 35 or over or suspicious — and mammography is SAFE while breastfeeding; feed or express beforehand.**
**Aspiration decides between a galactocele and an abscess — milk versus pus — and is both diagnostic and therapeutic. A solid component is biopsied.**

**Mastitis is a CLINICAL diagnosis. The only two triggers for ultrasound are A LUMP ON PRESENTATION, or NO RESPONSE AT 48 HOURS.** Abscess → aspiration if small, incision and drainage if large, **keep expressing, continue antibiotics.**

dx: **Arrest of the active phase of the first stage of labour — and the whole station is NAMING IT IN THREE KEYWORDS and then REFUSING TO AUGMENT.** **A candidate who takes a beautiful history and says 'protracted labour, I'll rupture the membranes and start oxytocin' FAILS. A candidate with a merely adequate history who says 'this is an arrest in the active phase of the first stage — she needs a caesarean' PASSES.**

**Definitions, said cleanly. FIRST STAGE — onset of contractions to full dilatation at 10 cm; LATENT phase to about 4–5 cm, ACTIVE phase beyond. SECOND STAGE — full dilatation to delivery. THIRD STAGE — delivery of the placenta.** **Expected active-phase progress at least 0.5 cm per hour; LESS THAN 2 cm IN 4 HOURS IS A DELAY.** **ARREST — 6 cm or more, with or WITHOUT ruptured membranes, and NO cervical change for 4 hours with adequate contractions (or 6 hours with inadequate contractions despite oxytocin).**

CORRECTION — **the two wrong labels in circulating recalls. CEPHALOPELVIC DISPROPORTION (the 2024 recall) is wrong** — CPD is a problem of the PASSAGE, and here the estimated weight is 3 kg with no CPD concern. **ARREST OF THE SECOND STAGE is wrong** — the second stage begins only at FULL DILATATION; she is 8 cm, still the first stage, **and ruptured membranes do not move a woman into the second stage.** **If an examiner offers you either label, decline it politely and give the reason.**

**The stem hands you the proof that every lever has already been pulled: contractions 4 in 10 (POWERS adequate) · 3 kg baby (PASSENGER normal) · no CPD (PASSAGE normal) · membranes already ruptured.** **So oxytocin has nothing to add and there is nothing left to rupture.**

**Say it exactly like this**: **'this is an arrest — an arrest in the active phase of the first stage of labour. She is beyond 6 centimetres, her membranes are ruptured, and there has been no cervical change at all in ten hours despite contractions of 4 in 10. That is not a delay. A DELAY IS SLOW PROGRESS; THIS IS NO PROGRESS. She will most likely need a caesarean.'** **Hedging — 'possibly some sort of prolonged labour' — scores nothing.**

CORRECTION — **speculum or fingers? Dilatation, effacement, consistency, cervical position and station are DIGITAL findings, from a vaginal examination, not a speculum.** A speculum is for LOOKING — liquor, blood, a visible cord or lesion. **And with membranes ruptured for ten hours, vaginal examinations should be MINIMISED: ask for the findings of the examination already done; do not order a fresh one for curiosity.**

CORRECTION — **'contraction stress test' is an ANTENATAL test in which contractions are provoked in a woman NOT in labour.** A woman contracting 4 in 10 in established labour is simply on **continuous CTG** — use that term. **And the Bishop score is strictly a PRE-INDUCTION tool for cervical favourability, not a labour-progress score; here it is just a tidy checklist of what to ask — say so if challenged. Only DILATATION defines progress: not effacement, not consistency, not position.**

**ADDED — ten hours of ruptured membranes is the block almost everyone forgets. Rupture beyond 18 HOURS is PROLONGED and raises the risk of chorioamnionitis and early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis. Ask: temperature and maternal pulse · fetal baseline tachycardia · uterine tenderness and offensive liquor · GBS STATUS from the 35–37 week swab · how many vaginal examinations have been done.** **If GBS positive or unknown with prolonged rupture, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated** — VERIFY benzylpenicillin 3 g IV then 1.8 g 4-hourly until birth.

**MANAGEMENT. DO NOW: notify the obstetric registrar or consultant, saying the diagnosis out loud · continuous CTG and continuous monitoring of contractions and maternal observations INCLUDING TEMPERATURE · two large-bore cannulas with FBE and group and hold · nil by mouth and maintenance fluids · EMPTY THE BLADDER with an indwelling catheter · alert theatre, the anaesthetist and the neonatal team · document the diagnosis and the time.**

**CATEGORY 2 caesarean here — maternal or fetal compromise that is not immediately life-threatening, target decision-to-delivery within 75 MINUTES. If the CTG becomes abnormal it is CATEGORY 1 — 30 MINUTES.** VERIFY. **Consent covers bleeding and transfusion, infection, VTE, injury to bladder, bowel or ureter, rarely hysterectomy, and the implications for future pregnancies including VBAC and placenta accreta spectrum.** **Cefazolin 2 g IV before skin incision; antacid prophylaxis; postoperative VTE prophylaxis.** SA: many MM5 sites have no 24-hour obstetric theatre, **and a woman at 8 cm in established labour cannot be safely transferred by road — call MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 immediately for retrieval advice, for the neonate as much as the mother**; escalate through **Country Health Connect**; **in-utero transfer is an antenatal decision, not one for the active phase — say so if challenged**; **TIS National 131 450**; Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and Liaison Officers.
plan: **Open the call properly — do NOT bark for a blood pressure**: **'Hello, I'm Dr ___, the HMO covering the birth suite. Who am I speaking with?'** then **'before anything else — is the mother stable, and is the baby's heart rate normal?'** then **one open question: 'tell me what has happened so far and what is worrying you.'**

**Signpost the three boxes**: **'I'm going to ask you about the mother first, then the baby, then the pelvis, and then I'll give you a plan.'** **Say the headings out loud so the examiner can hear the structure.**

**MOTHER — obstetric history and contractions**: first pregnancy · complications — high blood pressure, high sugars, a large baby on any growth scan · when exactly labour started · **'is she contracting? HOW MANY IN TEN MINUTES? How long is each one lasting? Are the intervals shortening, and are they getting stronger?'** **Do not accept 'yes, she's contracting' and move on.**

**MOTHER — the symptoms block, four questions in the same order every time**: **'have the membranes ruptured, and when? IS THE LIQUOR MECONIUM STAINED? Any vaginal bleeding? Is she still feeling the baby move?'** Then **'has she passed urine, or does she have a catheter?'** — a full bladder obstructs descent — and **'what analgesia has she had, and is she exhausted or dehydrated?'**

**MOTHER — observations, and the temperature is not optional after ten hours of ruptured membranes**: **'please give me her observations — blood pressure, pulse, TEMPERATURE, respiratory rate and saturations.'** **Say why: 'that matters, because her membranes have been ruptured ten hours and I need to know she isn't febrile.'**

**Abdominal palpation, all four by name**: **'please do Leopold's. Tell me the LIE, the PRESENTATION, the POSITION and the ENGAGEMENT IN FIFTHS.'** 3/5 palpable — **say back that the head is still high and has not descended.**

**Vaginal examination — from the one already performed**: **'how many centimetres dilated? What is the effacement, the consistency, the position of the cervix, and the station of the head?'** Then the question the station turns on: **'AND HOW MANY HOURS SINCE THAT DILATATION LAST CHANGED?'**

**'That's the mother — now the baby.'** **'Are you running a CTG? What is the baseline and the variability? ARE THERE ANY DECELERATIONS — EARLY, LATE OR VARIABLE? Any accelerations?'** **'Is the CTG normal?' is not the question; the mark is for the type.** Then **'do we have an ultrasound estimate of fetal weight?'**
**'Last area — the pelvis.'** **'Has she been assessed for cephalopelvic disproportion, and is there any concern about the pelvis?'** No concerns — **say back that the passage is not the issue.**

**THE DIAGNOSIS, in three keywords and one sentence**: **arrest · active phase · first stage.** Then the evidence: beyond 6 cm, membranes ruptured, no cervical change at all in ten hours despite 4 in 10.

**Then the sentence that refuses the augmentation before she offers it**: **'that is not a delay. A delay is slow progress; this is no progress. Because the contractions are already adequate, oxytocin has nothing to add, and because the membranes are already ruptured, there is nothing to rupture. She will most likely need a caesarean.'**

**When she asks 'should I start some oxytocin while you come over?' — refuse and explain**: **'no, please don't. With contractions already at four in ten and no change in ten hours, oxytocin will not deliver this baby, and it risks hyperstimulation and fetal compromise — and if there were unrecognised obstruction, uterine rupture.'**

**PLAN, ESCALATION FIRST**: **'please notify the obstetric registrar and consultant NOW, and tell them I've diagnosed an arrest in the active phase of the first stage. Please also let the anaesthetist and theatre know, and give the neonatal team a heads-up. I'm coming to see her now.'**

**MONITORING**: **continuous CTG** — 'I'm concerned about a baby that has been stuck for ten hours' · **continuous monitoring of the contractions, tell me if they weaken** · **maternal observations including temperature every 15 to 30 minutes** · **and please do NOT do extra vaginal examinations, her membranes have been ruptured ten hours.**

**PREPARE FOR THEATRE**: **two large-bore cannulas, FBE and group and hold · nil by mouth and maintenance fluids · INDWELLING CATHETER, 'I want the bladder empty and I want urine output' · and prepare her for an EMERGENCY CAESAREAN SECTION.**

**Name the category and the clock**: **'this is a Category 2 — I want her in theatre well within 75 minutes. If the CTG changes it becomes Category 1 and the target is 30 minutes.'** Then **'I'll consent her myself when I arrive and explain it to her and her partner.'**

**THE CLOSED LOOP — free marks sitting there**: **'could you read that plan back to me?'** Then the safety-net for her: **'call me immediately if the CTG changes, if she spikes a temperature, or if she develops constant abdominal pain.'** Then the 40-second summary if the examiner asks for it.
pefe: **You are talking to a COLLEAGUE, not a patient — medical jargon is expected, and you may ask for EXAMINATION FINDINGS, not just history.** ISBAR in, closed loop out.

**Ask for the four Leopold's findings BY NAME: lie · presentation · position · engagement in fifths.** **Engaged = 2/5 or less palpable; 3/5 at station −1 means the head has neither engaged nor descended.**

**Ask for the five vaginal-examination findings: dilatation · length or effacement · consistency · position of the cervix · station.** **These are the Bishop components — a tidy checklist here, not a progress score. ONLY DILATATION DEFINES PROGRESS.**

dx: **Request for a planned VBAC after one previous lower-segment caesarean. YOU NEVER SAY YES AND YOU NEVER SAY NO. Candidates fail this station by ANSWERING THE QUESTION — 'yes you can' and 'no you can't' both fail.**

**The pass behaviour: explore WHY she wants it · ask the three eligibility questions · give both sides of BOTH options · say 'about 1 in 200' out loud · build the EMERGENCY CAESAREAN into the plan for a vaginal birth · and give a timeline with reading material.**

**Say the one-line strategy near the start and again at the end**: **'it is YOUR decision, not mine. My job is to tell you what is good and what is bad about both options, make sure nothing rules a vaginal birth out, and support you whatever you choose.'**

**THE THREE DECIDING QUESTIONS. 1. 'Why was the caesarean done last time?' — breech, fetal distress or praevia are NON-RECURRING and favour VBAC; failure to progress, failed induction or CPD MAY RECUR and lower success. 2. 'Is the scar on your tummy horizontal or vertical?' — SHE CANNOT TELL YOU THE UTERINE INCISION, so ask about the skin scar and then say 'I'll request the OPERATION REPORT so we know exactly what type of cut was made in the womb.' 3. 'Have you ever had any other surgery on your womb — fibroids removed — or been told your womb tore or ruptured?' — either is a contraindication.** **ADDED: 'have you ever had a vaginal birth?' — the STRONGEST single predictor of success.**

**THE NUMBERS, said plainly. UTERINE RUPTURE with one lower-segment scar in spontaneous labour: about 1 IN 200 — half a percent. Higher with oxytocin, higher again with PROSTAGLANDIN induction (about 1–2%); a CLASSICAL scar is 2–9%. SUCCESS: about 3 IN 4 (60–80%; RANZCOG and SA data around 72–75%), rising to 85–90% after a previous vaginal birth. INTRAPARTUM CAESAREAN: about 1 IN 4 of planned VBACs.** VERIFY

**CONTRAINDICATIONS, given as a structure: a CLASSICAL (vertical upper-segment) or T/J incision · previous UTERINE RUPTURE · a myomectomy that BREACHED THE CAVITY · TWO OR MORE previous caesareans (usually advised against, individualised) · and anything in THIS pregnancy that needs a caesarean — placenta praevia, malpresentation, fetal compromise.** **An interval under 18 MONTHS from caesarean to birth increases rupture risk.**

**Counsel BOTH options fairly. VBAC BENEFITS: shorter stay, faster recovery — 'you'd be on your feet sooner with a toddler at home' · avoids major surgery and its infection, bleeding, bladder or bowel injury, anaesthetic risk and clots · better chance of establishing breastfeeding · makes future vaginal birth more likely.** **ELECTIVE REPEAT CAESAREAN: PREDICTABLE — a date, no labour, almost no scar-rupture risk, less pelvic floor damage. BUT it is surgery — slower recovery, bleeding, infection, clots, and EACH CAESAREAN MAKES THE NEXT PREGNANCY RISKIER because the placenta can sit low or grow into the scar. stem: Emergency department of your country hospital, rural South Australia. Mary Doherty, 27, is 32 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. She has presented today because she is worried that her baby is moving and kicking less than usual.
Tasks: take a focused history from Mary — counsel her regarding your assessment and further management. 8 minutes. VERIFY the task wording on the door.
