dx: **★ THE RULE THIS STATION IS BUILT AROUND: 'maternal concern about fetal movement requires clinical assessment, and this OVERRIDES a low-risk pregnancy status or any other factor.'** **Overrides means exactly what it says — it does not matter that the pregnancy is low risk, that the scan was normal, that it is 3 a.m., or that you are busy.**
**And it does not matter which direction the change is in: FEWER movements — assess. WEAKER — assess. ABSENT — assess urgently. MORE than usual — assess. A CHANGE IN CHARACTER — assess.**

**The commonest explanation is a FETAL SLEEP CYCLE or a mother too busy to notice. What you are actually excluding, in order, is INTRAUTERINE FETAL DEATH first, then FETAL COMPROMISE — placental insufficiency, growth restriction, abruption, infection, fetomaternal haemorrhage.** **One-line strategy: WARN, NORMALISE, THEN INVESTIGATE ANYWAY — in that order.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS THE ORDER OF THE COUNSELLING, and there are TWO SYMMETRICAL FAILURES. The candidate who opens with 'it's probably just the baby sleeping' has REASSURED BEFORE ASSESSING and cannot recover the mark. The candidate who opens with growth restriction, placental failure, infection and preterm birth has TERRIFIED a frightened woman with no counterweight.**

**FOUR STEPS. 1 ACKNOWLEDGE AND COMMIT. 2 THE WARNING, before any reassurance: 'when a mother tells us her baby is moving less, we always take it seriously, because reduced movements can be a sign the baby isn't doing as well as we'd like. That's why we never brush it off, and it's why you were right to come in.' 3 NORMALISE: the sleep cycle, 20–40 minutes and sometimes up to an hour, and the busy day. 4 THE CONCERNS — FOUR CLAUSES, no lectures: a growth problem · a problem with the placenta · less fluid around him · an infection in the womb · occasionally early labour.**
**'You did the right thing coming in' is the single most valuable sentence in this station** — she is braced to be told she is being silly, and it settles her in one line.

**Ask 'WHEN DID YOU FIRST BECOME CONCERNED?', not 'when did it start?' — she cannot know when it started, only when she noticed.** And **make her describe the change: 'fewer, or none at all?', then quantify BEFORE and NOW.**

**THE BLOCK CANDIDATES FORGET IS THE CURRENT PREGNANCY — because 'it's just a baby not kicking'. Growth restriction, hypertension, diabetes and placental problems all live there, and they are the very things that reduce movement.** Booking bloods · dating scan · screening · **the 18–20 week scan, growth AND placental site** · the GTT · hypertension or diabetes · **and WEIGHT GAIN, a proxy for growth restriction and low liquor that almost nobody asks about.**

**THE PATHWAY, IN ORDER, AND EACH TEST ANSWERS A DIFFERENT QUESTION. HAND-HELD DOPPLER — is the baby ALIVE? Do it first and immediately. CTG / non-stress test — is the baby currently DISTRESSED? At least 20 minutes, extended to 40 if unreactive; a reactive trace needs at least TWO ACCELERATIONS of 15 bpm lasting 15 seconds in 20 minutes. ULTRASOUND — is the baby GROWING, plus liquor volume and placental appearance; DO IT EVEN IF THE CTG IS NORMAL. UMBILICAL ARTERY DOPPLER — is the placenta working; absent or reversed end-diastolic flow means urgent tertiary referral.** **Baseline 110–160, variability 5–25 bpm, SFH = gestation ±2–3 cm.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **the test is the KLEIHAUER–BETKE, not the 'Clay-Howard'. It detects fetal red cells in the maternal circulation and so identifies a FETOMATERNAL HAEMORRHAGE. It is NOT routine — consider it when the CTG is abnormal or fetomaternal haemorrhage is suspected, and to size the anti-D dose in a Rh-negative woman.** CORRECTION — **KICK CHARTS ARE NOT RECOMMENDED.** VERIFY. **Formal counting has not been shown to reduce stillbirth and it DELAYS presentation — do not offer one as your management plan.** SA: a CTG may be available locally but **a growth ultrasound with Doppler frequently is not — say so, arrange the scan where it can be done, use PATS, and do not let a two-day wait for imaging become the reason a non-reassuring CTG goes unactioned**; a non-reassuring CTG at 32 weeks needs an obstetric unit with a neonatal nursery, so **arrange IN-UTERO TRANSFER rather than retrieving a compromised newborn afterwards — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women carry a substantially higher burden of stillbirth** — Aboriginal Family Birthing Program, Liaison Officer, local ACCHS, **Closing the Gap PBS**; **TIS National 131 450, never the partner**; **and ask about transport and childcare BEFORE you say 'come straight back'** — for a woman fifty minutes away who does not drive, that instruction needs a practical plan attached.
plan: **WIPE, sit at eye level, unhurried.** She opens frightened: **'my baby isn't moving like he normally does. Something's wrong, I know it.'**

**The sentence that earns the mark**: **'I'm really glad you came in, Mary — that was exactly the right thing to do, and we always take this seriously. I understand how frightening this is.'** Then signpost and commit: **'can I ask you some questions, and then I'll examine you and tell you exactly what we're going to do? My team and I will take good care of you and your baby.'** **Never open with 'try not to worry' or 'it's probably fine'.**

**DESCRIBE IT — the block candidates skip**: **'can you describe what you mean by kicking less? Specifically — is he moving LESS than usual, or is there NO movement at all?'** Still moving, much less.
**QUANTIFY IT**: **'how many times would he normally kick or move in an hour? And how many now?'** Ten to fifteen, down to once every few hours.

**TIME IT, with the right question**: **'when did you first become CONCERNED about this? Has it been constant, or has he had spells of moving normally? And is this the FIRST time this has happened in this pregnancy?'**

**THE MOTHER'S DAY**: **'tell me about your day today — what have you been doing? Has anything kept you especially busy?'** Then **'have you smoked today? Any medications, including anything to help you sleep? Any alcohol or other drugs? Any fever, or felt unwell?'**

**Say to yourself what you must not say aloud as a conclusion**: sedatives, opioids, alcohol, nicotine and illicit drugs all genuinely reduce fetal movement, and a busy mother may simply not have noticed — **but a plausible explanation NEVER cancels the assessment.**

**THE CURRENT PREGNANCY — the forgotten block**: **'were the booking bloods normal? The dating scan? The Down syndrome screening? The 18 to 20 week scan — were they happy with the baby's GROWTH and with the PLACENTA? The sweet drink test at 26 to 28 weeks?'**
**Then the three that matter most here**: **'any high blood pressure or high blood sugars in this pregnancy? And has your WEIGHT GAIN been what they expected?'**

**★ THE THREE SYMPTOMS THAT MUST BE ASKED**: **'have you had any vaginal bleeding? Any leaking of fluid? Any abdominal pain, or has your tummy felt tender or tight?'** **Placental abruption presents exactly like this, and missing all three is an automatic fail.** Add nausea and vomiting.

**THE PRE-ECLAMPSIA SET, in one run**: headaches · visual change — blurring, flashing lights, spots · dizziness · swelling of legs, hands or face · chest pain or breathlessness · **passing less urine than usual.**

**PREVIOUS PREGNANCIES, asked gently**: first pregnancy? Anything like this before? Complications in the pregnancy or the delivery? **And the humane phrasing: 'DID YOU DELIVER A HEALTHY BABY?'** **If the answer is that she lost a baby, STOP and acknowledge it properly — previous stillbirth is a major risk factor and lowers your threshold for admission and obstetric review.**

**ASK WHAT SHE IS WORRIED ABOUT — this is where the cousin comes out**: **'is there anything in particular you're worried about?'** *'My cousin's baby died at 36 weeks.'* **Acknowledge it directly. If you never ask, she raises it at the end.**

**Request the findings**: **blood pressure and TEMPERATURE · abdominal examination for FUNDAL HEIGHT, UTERINE TENDERNESS and uterine activity · and the FETAL HEART RATE on hand-held Doppler.** Then say the sentence: **'the heart rate is present and normal, which tells me the baby is ALIVE — it does not yet tell me he is WELL, and that's what the CTG is for.'**

**COUNSELLING STEP 1 and 2 — acknowledge, then WARN before any reassurance**: reduced movements can be a sign the baby isn't doing as well as we'd like; that's why we never brush it off, and why she was right to come in. **She may say 'so there IS something wrong.'**

**STEP 3 — NORMALISE, with a duration**: **'one of the commonest reasons is simply that the baby is asleep. Babies have sleep cycles, usually 20 to 40 minutes and sometimes up to an hour, and during those they move much less. And it's very common for a mother who's been flat out all day — as you have — not to notice movements that were actually happening.'**

**STEP 4 — the concerns, FOUR CLAUSES and then stop**: a growth problem in the baby · a problem with the placenta, 'the tissue that connects you to him and carries his oxygen and food' · less fluid around him · an infection in the womb · occasionally early labour.

**THE PLAN, numbered. The CTG explained properly**: **'we'll put you on a monitor for about twenty minutes. What we want to see is at least TWO RISES in his heart rate, because a baby's heart rate goes up when he moves — so those rises tell us he's moving and coping well. If we don't see them in the first twenty minutes, that often just means he's asleep, so we'll simply run it longer.'** **Then the ULTRASOUND today: growth, fluid, placenta.**

**When she asks 'is my baby going to be all right?' — DO NOT PROMISE**: **'I can't promise you an outcome, and I won't pretend to. What I can tell you is exactly what we're going to do to find out, and that we're doing it now rather than waiting. Most babies in your situation turn out to be completely fine.'** **And when she asks 'and if it's not normal?' — have the next step: urgent ultrasound and the obstetric team straight away.**

**Follow-up and safety-net — and NO kick chart**: **'if both are normal, I'll see you in a week and give you a fact sheet. And this matters: if it happens again, come straight back — EVERY time. Don't wait, don't sit at home counting, and don't ever worry you're bothering us.'** **Attach a practical plan to that instruction if she lives far away and does not drive.**
pefe: **HAND-HELD DOPPLER FIRST AND IMMEDIATELY — alive or not is the first question.** **'A present fetal heart tells me the baby is alive. It does NOT tell me the baby is well — that is what the CTG is for.'**
**Blood pressure for pre-eclampsia and TEMPERATURE for intrauterine infection.** Both by name.

**Abdominal examination: inspect for scars and bruising; palpate for UTERINE TENDERNESS (abruption) and UTERINE ACTIVITY (contractions); SYMPHYSIO-FUNDAL HEIGHT, plotted** — small for dates points to growth restriction and oligohydramnios. **Say the abruption sentence out loud: 'a tender, woody uterus would make me think of placental abruption.'**

Longitudinal, cephalic
FETAL HEART RATE
PRESENT, 144 bpm. Say it out loud: 'a present heartbeat tells me the baby is ALIVE. It does NOT tell me the baby is WELL — that is what the CTG is for'

None; no protein
The change — she answers 'less' unless you press
'He's still moving. Just MUCH LESS.' Normally 10–15 an hour, most in the evening. NOW about ONCE EVERY FEW HOURS. One short burst around lunchtime. FIRST time this pregnancy
Her day
On her feet at work since seven, NON-STOP. Non-smoker, only a pregnancy vitamin, no alcohol or other drugs, NO fever
The pregnancy
Booking bloods, dating scan, screening all normal · 20-week scan FINE with a NORMALLY SITED placenta · GTT normal · no hypertension or diabetes · WEIGHT GAIN FINE
All negative
No bleeding, no fluid loss, no abdominal pain or tenderness. No headache, visual change, dizziness, swelling, breathlessness or reduced urine output. First pregnancy, no medical problems
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA

Her COUSIN had a STILLBIRTH AT 36 WEEKS two years ago, and it is all she has thought about since this morning. SHE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER IT — only if you ask what she is worried about, or near the end if you never ask: 'my cousin's baby died at 36 weeks. Is that what's happening?'
★ HOW SHE IS BRIEFED

She half expects to be told she is being silly, and is BRACED FOR IT. If you say she did the right thing coming in, she VISIBLY RELAXES. If you open with 'try not to worry' or 'it's probably nothing', she becomes MORE anxious: 'but how do you know?'

'Is my baby going to be all right?' — if you promise he will be fine she looks unconvinced: 'HOW CAN YOU KNOW THAT?' · 'And if it's not normal?' after you mention the CTG — testing whether you have a next step · and if offered a kick chart or told to come back tomorrow: 'so I just go home and wait?'

Nothing since yesterday morning, and the FETAL HEART IS NOT AUDIBLE. Do NOT say 'I'm sure it's fine' and do NOT leave her alone — immediate ultrasound, obstetric team now, and ask who she would like called to be with her

Third visit in a fortnight, two previous normal CTGs, fundal height 31 cm at 35 weeks. RECURRENT reduced movements is a different and more serious animal — GROWTH SCAN with liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler, and OBSTETRIC REVIEW, not another reassuring CTG

dx: **Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (the 2025 version) — and the whole topic hangs on ONE QUESTION asked in the first minute: IS THERE A RASH? Ask it early and the rest of the history writes itself; ask it at minute four and you have invested questions in the wrong arm.**

**RASH → the skin arm: polymorphic eruption, pemphigoid gestationis, atopic eruption, contact dermatitis, urticaria, scabies, tinea, psoriasis. NO RASH → LOOK AT THE LIVER.** **Say it out loud: 'no rash moves me away from the skin conditions and towards the liver.'** **And EXCORIATIONS ARE SECONDARY — they do not make this a skin disease.**
**The site is not a formality — it is most of the diagnosis. PALMS AND SOLES, worse at night, third trimester, no rash = cholestasis until the bile acids say otherwise.**

**SERUM BILE ACIDS is the single test that makes the diagnosis. Say that word BEFORE you say 'LFTs'. Diagnostic at ≥10 µmol/L; ≥40 moderate; ≥100 severe, with the steepest rise in stillbirth risk.** VERIFY

CORRECTION — **do not wait for jaundice or a raised bilirubin. Jaundice is UNCOMMON in cholestasis and the bilirubin is usually NORMAL.** 'Bilirubin is normal so this isn't the liver' is a named failure.

CORRECTION — **do not read the raised ALP as biliary obstruction. ALKALINE PHOSPHATASE RISES 2–4 FOLD IN NORMAL PREGNANCY from PLACENTAL isoenzyme, and GGT does not.** A raised ALP with a NORMAL GGT points to a **placental rather than a biliary source** — naming that is what separates a strong candidate. Do not scan for gallstones on it.

**THE MANAGEMENT SENTENCE THAT DECIDES THE STATION**: **'the important part is what this means for the baby rather than for your skin. Cholestasis carries a small but real increase in the risk of STILLBIRTH, and it goes up as the bile acid level goes up. The only thing that cures it is DELIVERING THE BABY. So we monitor your blood tests and the baby closely, and we PLAN the birth rather than waiting for labour to start on its own — usually around 36 to 37 weeks, and the obstetric team will set the exact timing from your bile acid levels.'** VERIFY **A candidate who explains cholestasis beautifully, prescribes ursodeoxycholic acid and antihistamines, and never mentions planned birth FAILS.**

CORRECTION — **ursodeoxycholic acid improves MATERNAL ITCH, but the PITCHES trial found NO improvement in perinatal outcomes. Do not offer it as something that protects the baby.** VERIFY. Say it honestly: **'it makes you more comfortable, but the evidence doesn't show it reduces the risk to the baby — the thing that does that is planning the birth.'**

**VERSION A — POLYMORPHIC ERUPTION OF PREGNANCY. Urticarial papules and plaques arising ON THE ABDOMINAL STRIAE with PERIUMBILICAL SPARING; primigravida, late third trimester, multiple pregnancy, high weight gain. NAME THE SPARING — it is the whole diagnosis.** **Benign, harmless to mother and baby, resolving within days to weeks of delivery. Mild to moderate topical corticosteroid, generous emollients, and a second-generation antihistamine — loratadine or cetirizine.** VERIFY **DELIVERY IS NOT INDICATED — that is the difference from cholestasis.** **The eczema and gestational diabetes in the stem exist to make you anchor: ask 'is this the same as your usual eczema, or different?'**

**PEMPHIGOID GESTATIONIS is the one that is NOT PEP: tense vesicles and bullae on urticarial plaques INVOLVING the umbilicus rather than sparing it. Biopsy with direct immunofluorescence (linear C3 at the basement membrane), dermatology referral, and CLOSER FETAL SURVEILLANCE for growth restriction and preterm birth.** CORRECTION — **pre-eclampsia is new hypertension AFTER 20 WEEKS**, not the first trimester as the source lecture states. SA: bile acids and LFTs through SA Pathology — **check turnaround, because a send-away result can take days and you must not wait passively before involving the obstetric team**; planned birth at 36–37 weeks needs an obstetric unit with a nursery, so arrange **in-utero transfer — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **PATS** for the extra monitoring visits; **scabies is associated with household CROWDING, not hygiene — treat all contacts, provide the treatment rather than a prescription where cost is a barrier, and say so without moralising**; ACCHS, Aboriginal Family Birthing Program, **Closing the Gap PBS**, **TIS National 131 450**.
plan: **WIPE and a SHORT acknowledgement — twenty seconds, then move. This station's marks are in the structure, not a communication crisis**: **'that sounds miserable — itching that stops you sleeping is genuinely exhausting. Let me ask you some questions so I can work out what's causing it, then I'll explain what I think and what we do about it.'**
**Timing and course**: **'when did the itching start? Is it constant or does it come and go? Is it getting worse? Have you ever had anything like this before — eczema, hives, any skin condition?'**

**★ THE RASH QUESTION, IN THE FIRST MINUTE**: **'have you noticed any rash, or any redness of the skin? Any blisters?'** *'No rash at all. Just the marks where I've been scratching.'* **Say what it means out loud, and name the excoriations as SECONDARY.**
**SITE — and react to the answer**: **'where exactly do you feel itchy?'** *Palms and soles.* **Say it back to her: that combination, with no rash, is the diagnosis.**

**Night, hot shower, contacts, web spaces — the scabies block folded in**: **'is it worse at night? Does it wake you? Is it worse after a hot shower? Is anyone else at home itchy? Any itching between your fingers?'**
**Secondary infection, two questions, once**: **'any fever? Any weeping, crusting or discharge from the skin where you've scratched?'** **Every itchy condition can become secondarily infected.**

**★ THE PRE-ECLAMPSIA SET — forty seconds, asked even though this is an itch stem**: **'now a set of symptoms we check in every pregnancy at this stage. Any headaches? Any change in your vision — blurring, flashing lights, spots? Any dizziness? Any swelling of your legs, hands or face? Any chest pain or shortness of breath? Are you passing less urine than usual?'**

**THE CHOLESTASIS BLOCK**: **'any pain in your tummy, particularly up under the ribs on the right? Any nausea or vomiting? How is your appetite — has it dropped off?'** A right-sided ache, off her food.

**The tiredness, in ONE question — do not open a tiredness workup**: **'you mentioned tiredness — can you describe it? Do you feel sleepy, or low in energy?'** **The context tells you this is itch with tiredness, not tiredness with itch.**

**THE LIVER QUESTIONS**: **'any yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes? Have you noticed dark urine or pale stools? Any past history of liver problems or gallstones? And does anyone in the family have liver problems, or did anyone have ITCHING IN PREGNANCY?'** **The mother is the buried clue — cholestasis runs in families and recurs.**

**NON-PREGNANCY CAUSES — four short blocks, ninety seconds, demonstrating you thought about them rather than working each one up. Scabies and fungal**: recent travel, close contact with anyone itchy, pets at home. **Contact**: any new cream, soap, body wash, laundry detergent or perfume.
**Urticaria**: new medicines or foods; **wheeze, or swelling of the lips or tongue.** **Atopy and psoriasis**: eczema, asthma or hay fever in her or the family; psoriasis or any other skin condition.

**OBSTETRIC HISTORY**: booking bloods · dating scan · screening · **the 18–20 week scan, baby and placenta** · the GTT · the 35–37 week swab. Then **never omit**: **'is the baby kicking as much as usual? Any bleeding or leaking of fluid?'** Then the previous pregnancy and **whether she itched then.**

**Name your investigations BEFORE the results are handed over**: **'serum bile acids and liver function tests, full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, a coagulation profile, her blood pressure and urine dipstick — and a CTG.'**

**READ THE RESULTS ALOUD IN THIS ORDER**: **the raised BILE ACIDS are the diagnostic result** · the mildly raised transaminases fit · **the normal bilirubin does NOT argue against it, because most women with cholestasis are never jaundiced** · **and interpret the ALP cautiously, because it rises two to fourfold in normal pregnancy from placental isoenzyme, and her GGT is normal.**

**Name it, and give the differentials you excluded**: pre-eclampsia and acute fatty liver — on symptoms, blood pressure and biochemistry · PEP, pemphigoid and atopic eruption — **by the absence of a rash** · scabies — no burrows, no web-space itch, no itchy contacts.

**Explain it in plain words**: the itch is on palms and soles, worse at night, no rash — **'that combination points away from a skin problem and towards your liver.'** Then **the mechanism: the liver makes bile, which normally drains into the gut; pregnancy hormones slow that drainage, so the salts build up in the bloodstream, and those salts make the skin itch.** **She will say 'my liver? I don't drink' — answer that it has nothing to do with drinking.**

**THE HONEST ANSWER ABOUT THE BABY — and she becomes tearful here**: the itch is miserable but not dangerous to her; **the reason we take it seriously is the baby — a small but real increase in stillbirth risk that rises with the bile acid level.** Then **the cure is birth, so we PLAN it, around 36 to 37 weeks — 'you're 36 weeks now, so this is a conversation about the next week or two.'** **Do not offer false reassurance; she is briefed to stay frightened if you are vague.**

**The rest of the plan and the safety-net**: same-day obstetric referral · serial bile acids and LFTs · fetal surveillance · symptom relief — nails short, loose cotton, cool compresses, emollients, menthol in aqueous cream — and **ursodeoxycholic acid with the honest caveat.** Safety-net: **reduced fetal movements, bleeding or fluid loss, contractions, jaundice, headache, visual change or rib pain.**
pefe: **SERUM BILE ACIDS — the single test that makes the diagnosis. Name it FIRST, before liver function tests.** ≥10 µmol/L diagnostic; ≥40 moderate; ≥100 severe. VERIFY

**LFTs alongside for the pattern and a baseline · blood pressure and urine dipstick, because you are still excluding pre-eclampsia · FBC, UEC and a coagulation profile if the picture is at all unclear.**
**Assess the fetus: movements, fetal heart rate, and a CTG.** **Refer to the obstetric team the SAME DAY — this is not a condition managed alone in general practice.**
**ALP rises 2–4 fold physiologically from placental isoenzyme; GGT does not.** A raised ALP with a normal GGT is placental, not biliary — **do not order a gallstone scan on it.**

**Repeat bile acids and LFTs to track severity — the level drives the timing of birth.** **Exclude other liver disease if the picture does not fit: hepatitis serology, liver ultrasound, autoimmune screen.**

**Symptom relief: emollients, cool compresses, loose cotton, nails short; menthol in aqueous cream is widely used and safe.** VERIFY **Ursodeoxycholic acid improves maternal itch — PITCHES showed no perinatal benefit.**
**VITAMIN K if there is steatorrhoea or prolonged cholestasis** — fat-soluble vitamin absorption falls, and this is a bleeding risk at delivery.
**PLAN THE BIRTH — typically around 36–37 weeks, earlier if bile acids are very high, with timing individualised by the obstetric team to the level.** VERIFY

**PEP management: mild to moderate topical corticosteroid, generous emollients, loratadine or cetirizine; a short course of oral prednisolone occasionally for severe disease. NO increase in fetal risk — say so explicitly. DELIVERY IS NOT INDICATED.** VERIFY

**Do not miss: pre-eclampsia and acute fatty liver hiding behind 'itch' · reduced fetal movements mentioned in passing · PUSTULAR PSORIASIS OF PREGNANCY, where fever, systemic upset and sheets of sterile pustules is an obstetric emergency · and pemphigoid gestationis mistaken for PEP.**

TWO SHALLOW ULCERS on the LEFT LABIUM MAJUS with surrounding redness. GROUPED, UNILATERAL, and the bases look SOFT rather than indurated. DESCRIBE IT BEFORE YOU CONCLUDE
The symptom
Left side. BURNING and STINGING, now painful. Two little sores. Started three days ago
★ THE PRODROME
'Yes — the tingling came a day or two BEFORE the sores.' NOTHING ELSE IN THE DIFFERENTIAL DOES THIS
★ THE URINARY SPLIT
'It stings ON THE OUTSIDE as it comes out.' And NO, not going more often. NO fever. External stinging without frequency = urine over broken skin, NOT cystitis
★ THE QUESTION THE CASE TURNS ON

'I think I had something like this about THREE YEARS AGO. It went away on its own. I never saw anyone — I was too embarrassed.' SHE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER IT. This converts the case from a first episode to a RECURRENCE, and the neonatal risk from 30–50% to 0–3%

'I'm with my partner now, but I've had A FEW PARTNERS over the last couple of years.' Condoms SOMETIMES, not always. Never had a sexual health check. IF YOU REACT AT ALL — a pause, repeating the number back — she looks uncomfortable and gives SHORTER ANSWERS for the rest of the station

dx: **Recurrent genital herpes simplex infection in pregnancy at 20 weeks. ALL THREE PARTS MATTER. RECURRENT, because she describes a similar episode three years ago — and recurrent versus primary is the single fact that drives the neonatal risk and the birth plan. GENITAL HERPES, because of the prodromal tingling followed by painful shallow ulcers. AT 20 WEEKS, because the management hangs on how far she is from delivery.**

**THE TRAP BUILT INTO THIS STATION: the diagnosis is easy and almost everybody says it. MOST PEOPLE STILL FAIL, because when asked for differentials they give THREE MORE INFECTIONS. The examiner is waiting for a SYSTEMS-BASED differential — and the NEUROLOGICAL bucket, with CAUDA EQUINA inside it, is what distinguishes a pass.**

**THE FIVE SYSTEMS, name the heading then one or two examples — forty seconds. INFECTIVE: thrush, syphilis, other STIs, urinary infection. DERMATOLOGICAL: eczema, lichen sclerosus. NEUROLOGICAL: a trapped or irritated nerve in the lower back, CAUDA EQUINA, sacral shingles. TRAUMATIC OR IRRITANT: shaving, friction, soaps and wipes. STRUCTURAL: a Bartholin cyst.**

**WHY CAUDA EQUINA BELONGS IN A HERPES STATION: she is describing altered sensation in the PERINEUM — a sensory disturbance in the S2–S4 dermatomes, and there is a diagnosis in that territory you cannot afford to miss. Saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg pain or weakness, and bladder or bowel dysfunction, usually with back pain — a SURGICAL EMERGENCY.** **In this woman it is very unlikely, but the examiner wants to hear that you asked and that you know why.** **The same territory gives you SACRAL SHINGLES, a genuine mimic of a first herpes episode.**

**THE WARNING SHOT IS A SCORED COMMUNICATION ITEM**: **'some of my next questions are quite personal, and they are about your sexual health. I ask everybody these, and whatever you tell me stays confidential. Is that all right?'** **Ask the intimate questions without it and you lose the rapport marks even with a perfect differential — and she is briefed to say 'do I have to answer that?'**

**DESCRIBE THE PHOTOGRAPH, THEN CONCLUDE**: **'there are two shallow ulcers on the left labium majus with surrounding redness. They are grouped and unilateral, and the bases look soft rather than indurated.'** **The features that make it herpes: PAINFUL (syphilis is painless) · MULTIPLE AND GROUPED (the chancre is single) · SHALLOW, preceded by vesicles (not indurated) · UNILATERAL and in the same site as before (herpes recurs in one dermatome) · PRODROME of tingling (no other genital ulcer does this) · EXTERNAL DYSURIA WITHOUT FREQUENCY.**

**CONFIRMING IT: HSV PCR SWAB from the base of a deroofed vesicle or the ulcer — the confirmatory test. TYPE-SPECIFIC HSV SEROLOGY (IgG) — this is what classifies primary versus non-primary versus recurrent. Plus a FULL STI SCREEN: chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, syphilis serology, HIV, hepatitis B.** **Type-specific IgG takes 2–12 WEEKS to appear, so a negative IgG in the first days of a genuine first episode does not exclude recent infection.** VERIFY
CORRECTION — **do NOT delay treatment for the result.** The PCR takes days and the serology longer. **Treat on clinical grounds and let the tests classify the episode afterwards.**

**TREATMENT: ACICLOVIR 400 mg three times daily for 5 days, or VALACICLOVIR 500 mg twice daily for 5 days — both used in pregnancy. TREAT RECURRENCES AS WELL AS FIRST EPISODES — shorter symptoms and shorter shedding. SUPPRESSION FROM 36 WEEKS: aciclovir 400 mg tds until birth.** VERIFY. **Symptom relief: paracetamol, salt baths and gentle drying, pass urine in a warm bath or pour water while passing urine, loose cotton, avoid soaps and wipes.** VERIFY topical lidocaine locally — some notes avoid it in pregnancy, many Australian sources permit short-term use.

Active lesions → caesarean. A PRIMARY episode within about 6 weeks of delivery → caesarean even without lesions, because there has been no time to make protective antibodies.** **Avoid fetal scalp electrodes and instrumental delivery.** **Neonatal risk: 0–3% recurrent · 30–50% primary near term.** **And the public-health answer: NOT NOTIFIABLE, NO CONTACT TRACING — but encourage partner disclosure, no sex while lesions are present, condoms reduce but do not abolish transmission, and avoid touching the lesions then the eyes.** SA: swabs and serology to **SA Pathology**; **SHINE SA** for sexual health advice, partner information and free or low-cost testing; **document the diagnosis in her pregnancy record so the birth suite sees it**; from an MM5 site discuss the delivery plan with the receiving obstetric unit early; **PATS**, **Country Health Connect**, **TIS National 131 450**, Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and ACCHS, **Closing the Gap PBS** for her antivirals.

**THE FIVE SYSTEMS, heading then example**: other INFECTIONS — thrush, syphilis, other STIs, a urine infection · SKIN conditions — eczema, lichen sclerosus · **NERVE causes — a trapped or irritated nerve in the lower back, or shingles in that area, 'which is why I asked about your back and your waterworks'** · IRRITATION or injury — shaving, friction, soaps and wipes · **STRUCTURAL — a Bartholin cyst.**

**Treatment and comfort**: **aciclovir 400 mg three times a day for five days, safe in pregnancy** · salt baths, paracetamol, loose cotton underwear, **and pour warm water over the area while you pass urine so it doesn't sting.**

What changes is that we write this in your pregnancy record so the birth team knows. From 36 weeks we'll offer you a daily antiviral to make an outbreak around the birth less likely.'**

stem: Antenatal clinic, rural South Australian general practice. Aisha Rahman, 26, is 15 weeks pregnant in her second pregnancy, attending a routine visit. Her booking bloods are back.

Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115–155) · MCV 72 FL (80–100) · MCH 24 pg (27–32) · red cell count 4.1 (3.8–5.2) · white cells and platelets normal · ferritin not provided. Tasks: take a focused history from Aisha — explain the blood results in language she understands — give your diagnosis, differential and management plan. 8 minutes.

dx: **Iron deficiency anaemia — the commonest cause of microcytic anaemia in pregnancy by a very wide margin, and everything in her history points to it. BUT YOU CANNOT SAY THAT YET, BECAUSE YOU HAVE NOT BEEN GIVEN A FERRITIN. The station rewards the candidate who names the diagnosis as MOST LIKELY, names THALASSAEMIA TRAIT as the alternative, and names the ONE TEST that separates them.**

**★ THE SENTENCE THE STATION IS BUILT ON: PHYSIOLOGICAL ANAEMIA OF PREGNANCY IS NORMOCYTIC. Plasma volume rises about 50% while red cell mass rises about 25%, so the haemoglobin falls by DILUTION — but the cells stay a NORMAL SIZE. A LOW MCV IS THEREFORE NEVER PHYSIOLOGICAL. It always has a cause, and in pregnancy that cause is iron until a ferritin says otherwise.**
**Anaemia in pregnancy: Hb <110 g/L in the first and third trimesters, <105 in the second. MCV <80 = microcytic. MCH <27 = hypochromic.** VERIFY

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE HAS TWO FAILURES. The candidate who says 'you're anaemic, which is common in pregnancy, take iron' has skipped the reasoning, missed the thalassaemia fork, and given a woman of Bangladeshi background iron she may not need. The candidate who reasons perfectly but explains it as 'microcytic hypochromic indices with a raised RDW' has failed the communication task, which here carries as many marks as the diagnosis.**

**THE EXPLANATION LADDER, one sentence per rung. 1. The NUMBER — haemoglobin 96, and we'd want above about 105 at this stage. 2. The MEANING — haemoglobin carries oxygen around your body and to your baby, which is why you're exhausted. 3. ★ THE SIZE — 'the test also measures how big your red cells are, and yours are SMALLER AND PALER than they should be. Pregnancy on its own drops the count a little because you make more fluid and it dilutes things — but that kind of anaemia leaves the cells a NORMAL SIZE. Yours are small. So this isn't just the pregnancy.' DO NOT SKIP RUNG 3 — nothing that follows makes sense without it. 4. THE TWO CAUSES. 5. THE ONE TEST. 6. CONNECT IT TO HER LIFE. 7. THE PLAN, AND THE COST.**

**Connect it to her, because this is where it lands**: **'your periods were always heavy. You bled heavily after your daughter and never really replaced what you lost. She's only 14 months, so you've had two pregnancies close together and you're still breastfeeding — three separate demands on your iron at once. And you don't eat meat, so what you take in is harder to absorb.'** **Non-haem (plant) iron is far less well absorbed than haem iron — a vegetarian diet needs MORE iron, not the same amount.**

**ONE SPECIFIC, PRACTICAL THING: the tea with dinner. Tannins in tea and coffee INHIBIT iron absorption; vitamin C ENHANCES it.** Move the tea between meals and add lemon, capsicum or fruit at dinner. **And the ice: 'you're not going mad — it's called pica, a recognised sign of low iron, and it usually stops once the iron is replaced.'**

**WHY THE PARTNER MATTERS, and this is what converts a blood result into antenatal genetic counselling: if she carries a trait, the risk to the baby depends ENTIRELY on whether he does too. TWO CARRIERS = 1 IN 4 RISK of a severely affected child in EACH pregnancy. At 15 weeks there is still time for prenatal diagnosis.**

**WHAT YOU ARE NOT GIVEN AND SHOULD ASK FOR: ★ SERUM FERRITIN — the single most useful test · CRP, because FERRITIN IS AN ACUTE-PHASE REACTANT and rises with inflammation, which can MASK deficiency · reticulocyte count · RDW · blood film · iron studies if the ferritin is equivocal · haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC if thalassaemia is suspected · B12 and folate if the picture is mixed · coeliac serology if there are gut symptoms.** **MENTZER INDEX = MCV / RBC: >13 favours iron deficiency, <13 favours thalassaemia trait.**

**MANAGEMENT: start oral iron EMPIRICALLY rather than waiting — the pretest probability is high and a rise in haemoglobin is itself confirmatory. Recheck FBC and ferritin at 4 WEEKS. Reticulocytes rise in about a week; haemoglobin by roughly 10 g/L over 3–4 weeks; continue for 3 MONTHS after normalisation to refill stores.** VERIFY. **If ferritin is NORMAL OR HIGH → electrophoresis, test the partner, genetic counselling. If no response after a month of genuine adherence → RE-DIAGNOSE, do not escalate.** **IV iron is generally avoided in the first trimester — she is 15 weeks, so it is available.** **And FLAG HER PREVIOUS POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE: correcting anaemia before birth reduces the consequences of another one, so ensure active management of the third stage.** SA: **ask for the ferritin to be ADDED TO THE EXISTING SAMPLE rather than recalling her — she has a toddler and no car**; **the affordability problem IS the clinical problem** — cheapest effective PBS-listed preparation, **Closing the Gap PBS** relief if eligible, and check she can physically reach a pharmacy, because **a perfect iron regimen she cannot buy is not a plan**; IV iron may need a day unit in a larger centre — **PATS**; thalassaemia partner testing and genetic counselling are metropolitan, **and at 15 weeks a rural referral must not delay prenatal diagnosis**; **TIS National 131 450 — never the partner, never a child, and a carrier-status conversation is exactly the one that needs a professional interpreter**; ask about dietary and religious practice before advising on meat.
plan: **WIPE, sit beside her, and ASK BEFORE YOU ANNOUNCE**: **'your booking blood tests are back and I'd like to go through them with you. Before I do — how have you been feeling in yourself?'** **Do NOT open with 'you're anaemic' — she stops listening and you lose the history that gives you the cause.**

**Signpost honestly without dumping the result**: **'there is something on the tests I want to talk about, and it's something we can treat. Before I explain it, can I ask you some questions so I can work out the cause? Then I'll take you through the results properly and we'll make a plan together.'**

**Symptoms, functionally**: **'tell me about the tiredness — how long, and what can't you do because of it? Are you short of breath — on exertion or at rest? Any palpitations, chest pain, dizziness or faints? Any headaches? Do you feel the cold more than you used to?'**

**★ THE TWO NOBODY ASKS**: **'this will sound like an odd question — do you ever crave anything unusual? Ice, dirt, chalk, uncooked rice? And do you get restless, crawling feelings in your legs at night?'** *'I chew ice constantly. I thought I was going mad.'* **Both are classical, the role-player is briefed to give them, and almost nobody asks.**
**BLOOD LOSS — the highest-yield block. Gynaecological**: **'before this pregnancy, were your periods heavy? How many days, and how many pads or tampons on the worst day? Any flooding or clots?'**

**★ THE OBSTETRIC QUESTION — the single biggest item in the history**: **'how much bleeding did you have after your last delivery — did anyone say you bled more than expected, or did you need a transfusion?'** *A drip and an extra day.* **'Thank you — that's a very important piece of information.'**

**Gut and urinary, briskly**: blood in the stool or black tarry stools · indigestion or heartburn · blood in the urine · anti-inflammatories or aspirin · **weight loss or night sweats.** **In a non-pregnant or postmenopausal patient a microcytic anaemia is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise — say that if the examiner asks.**

**INTAKE — a real dietary history, not 'do you eat well?'**: **'talk me through what you eat in a typical day. Do you eat red meat, chicken or fish? What about beans, lentils, leafy greens, eggs? AND DO YOU DRINK TEA OR COFFEE WITH YOUR MEALS?'**
**ABSORPTION**: **'any tummy problems — bloating, loose stools, or has anyone mentioned coeliac disease? Any previous stomach or bowel surgery? Do you take antacids or reflux medicines regularly?'**

**DEMAND**: **'how old is your first child? Are you still breastfeeding? Is this a single pregnancy? And have you been taking your pregnancy vitamins and folic acid?'** *(quietly)* **'I stopped — I couldn't afford them.'**

**RESPOND WITHOUT JUDGEMENT — this is scored**: **'thank you for telling me — that's very common and it isn't a criticism at all. Cost is a real problem and there are ways around it. Let's sort that out today.'** **NOT 'it's really important you take them.'**

**★ THE THALASSAEMIA BLOCK — the one that keeps the fork open**: **'can I ask about your background — where is your family from? Has anyone in your family been told they have a blood condition, or thalassaemia? Has anyone needed regular blood transfusions? Have you ever been told you were anaemic before, or that your count was low even when you felt well?'**
**AND THE PARTNER — do not raise thalassaemia and then drop it**: **'and your partner — where is his family from? Has he ever been tested?'**

**Close the history**: medical problems, regular medicines, allergies · any bleeding or pain in this pregnancy · booking scan and other tests. **At 15 weeks do NOT ask about fetal movements — asking suggests you have not read the gestation.**

**LADDER RUNGS 1–2**: the haemoglobin of 96 against a target above about 105; **and what haemoglobin does — carries oxygen around her body and to the baby, which is why she is exhausted and puffed on the stairs.**

**★ RUNG 3 — THE SIZE, AND DO NOT SKIP IT**: the cells are smaller and paler than they should be; pregnancy dilution leaves cells a NORMAL size; **'yours are small. So this isn't just the pregnancy — there's a reason, and we should find it.'**

**RUNGS 4–5 — the two causes and the one test**: iron deficiency, commonest by a long way; **thalassaemia, inherited, more common in families from South Asia, the Mediterranean, the Middle East, Africa and South-East Asia — 'not something you catch; you're born with it'** · then **'one extra blood test tells us which. It's called a ferritin, and I've asked the lab to add it to the sample they already have, so you won't need another needle.'**

**Answer 'would the baby have it?' properly**: **'carrying the trait causes very little trouble for you — a permanently slightly low blood count and not much else. It only matters for a baby IF BOTH PARENTS CARRY IT. So if your ferritin comes back normal we'd confirm it and test your partner. You're 15 weeks, so we have plenty of time. But I want to be clear: I think the iron is far more likely.'**

**RUNG 6 — connect it to her life**, all four drains named together. **When she says 'so it's my fault for not eating properly' — do NOT agree and do NOT lecture**: **'not at all. Pregnancy roughly doubles what your body needs, and you've had two close together while feeding a toddler. Almost anyone would be low in that situation.'** Then **the tea and vitamin C, and the explanation for the ice.**

**RUNG 7 — the plan, the side effects, the cost, and the next birth**: start iron today rather than wait; **recheck FBC and ferritin at four weeks** · **anticipate constipation and dark stools, and offer alternate-day dosing** · **'I'll prescribe the cheapest option that works, and I'd like our nurse to check whether you're eligible for extra help. Please don't stop it because of money without telling me first'** · **and 'because you bled heavily last time and you're anaemic now, I want your count properly corrected before you deliver.'**
pefe: **★ SERUM FERRITIN — the single most useful test, and the one deliberately withheld. Ask for it on the EXISTING sample.**
**CRP alongside it — ferritin is an ACUTE-PHASE REACTANT and rises with inflammation, so a normal ferritin in an unwell patient can mask true deficiency.**
**Reticulocyte count · RDW · blood film.** Iron studies (serum iron, transferrin, transferrin saturation) **if the ferritin is equivocal.**

**HAEMOGLOBIN ELECTROPHORESIS or HPLC if the ferritin is normal or high.** Plus **B12 and folate if the picture is mixed** — a long-standing vegetarian may have coexisting B12 deficiency producing a misleadingly normal MCV — **and coeliac serology if there are gut symptoms.**

**MENTZER INDEX = MCV / RBC. >13 favours iron deficiency; <13 favours thalassaemia trait.** **Thalassaemia trait: normal or high ferritin, HIGH red cell count, normal RDW, target cells and basophilic stippling. Iron deficiency: fewer cells of very unequal size, raised RDW.**

**Start oral iron EMPIRICALLY — a rise in haemoglobin is itself confirmatory.** **Reticulocytes rise in about 1 week; haemoglobin by roughly 10 g/L over 3–4 weeks; continue 3 months after normalisation.** VERIFY **Recheck FBC and ferritin at 4 weeks.**

**Take it on an empty stomach with vitamin C; expect constipation and dark stools; alternate-day dosing is often as effective and better tolerated.** VERIFY **Do not improvise milligram figures — name the preparation and the principles.**

**IV IRON if she cannot tolerate or absorb oral iron, if the anaemia is severe, or if gestation is advanced — generally avoided in the first trimester.** VERIFY **Transfusion is reserved for haemodynamic compromise or very severe anaemia close to delivery.**

**NON-RESPONSE AFTER A MONTH OF GENUINE ADHERENCE = RE-DIAGNOSE, NOT MORE IRON.** Check the reticulocyte count — a flat count means no response at all. Reconsider coexisting trait, ongoing blood loss, coeliac disease, anaemia of chronic disease — **and ask HOW she is taking it, because iron with tea or with food absorbs poorly.**

**AVOID: giving iron indefinitely to a non-responder · iron overload from prolonged unnecessary iron in thalassaemia trait · blaming her diet or her adherence when she has told you she could not afford the tablets.**

findingsLabel: The blood results, and the three clues she will not volunteer
findings: THE RESULTS HANDED TO YOU
Haemoglobin 96 g/L (115–155) · MCV 72 fL (80–100) · MCH 24 pg (27–32) · red cell count 4.1 · white cells and platelets NORMAL · FERRITIN NOT PROVIDED
★ THE MISSING FERRITIN IS THE ENTIRE DESIGN OF THE STATION
You cannot call it iron deficiency yet. Name it as MOST LIKELY, name THALASSAEMIA TRAIT as the alternative, and name the ONE TEST that separates them
Symptoms
Exhausted for MONTHS, even before this pregnancy. Puffed carrying washing upstairs, not breathless at rest. Dizzy on standing. No chest pain
★ THE TWO NOBODY ASKS
PICA — 'I chew ice. All the time. I thought I was going mad' (embarrassed, and ONLY if you ask about unusual cravings) · RESTLESS LEGS at night. Both classical of iron deficiency
★ BURIED CLUE 1 — the periods
'Seven days. FLOODING on the worst two.' Only if you quantify
★ BURIED CLUE 2 — the biggest item in the history
'I bled a lot after my daughter. They put a drip up and kept me an extra day. Nobody really explained it.' SHE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER THE POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE — it must be asked for
★ BURIED CLUE 3 — the cost
(quietly, looking down) 'I stopped the vitamins. I couldn't afford them on top of everything.' IF YOU LECTURE HER — 'it's really important you take them' — SHE GOES QUIET AND DISENGAGES
Diet and absorption
VEGETARIAN for years — rice, lentils, vegetables. TEA ALL DAY, usually WITH DINNER. No bloating, no coeliac, no gut surgery, no antacids
Demand
First child is FOURTEEN MONTHS and STILL BREASTFED AT NIGHT. Single pregnancy. Pregnancy, then lactation, then pregnancy again — FOUR DRAINS ON IRON AT ONCE
The thalassaemia block
Family from BANGLADESH. 'My mum's always been told she's anaemic.' Nobody needed transfusions. 'A bit low in my last pregnancy, I think.' PARTNER IS BANGLADESHI TOO AND HAS NEVER BEEN TESTED
Her three moments

'Is that bad?' when told the haemoglobin · ALARM at thalassaemia: 'WOULD THE BABY HAVE IT?' · and she BLAMES HERSELF ONCE: 'so it's my fault for not eating properly.' If you agree or lecture, she disengages; if you reframe it kindly, she warms up
Her closing question
'What if the tablets don't work?'
VARIANT — the ferritin comes back NORMAL

Ferritin 84, red cell count 5.8, Mentzer index UNDER 13. BETA THALASSAEMIA TRAIT — STOP THE IRON, request haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC, TEST THE PARTNER, refer for genetic counselling. At 15 weeks there is still time for prenatal diagnosis
VARIANT — the non-responder

24 weeks, iron daily for eight weeks, Hb still 94, MCV 71, insists she has taken every tablet. RE-DIAGNOSE, do not escalate the dose — coexisting trait, ongoing loss, coeliac disease, anaemia of chronic disease, or taking it with tea or food
VARIANT — severe and late

35 weeks, Hb 78, MCV 69, ferritin 4, breathless on one flight. INTRAVENOUS IRON rather than tablets, obstetric discussion, group and antibody screen available, active management of the third stage, and deliver where blood products are available
VARIANT — the wrong patient
68-year-old man, Hb 92, MCV 70. COLORECTAL CANCER UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE — say the sentence and refer for endoscopy

findings: The scan report
LOW-LYING PLACENTA, edge WITHIN 2 cm of the internal os — NOT covering it. Fetal anatomy NORMAL. Liquor NORMAL. Observations normal, first pregnancy, no bleeding, no pain
★ THE HIDDEN AGENDA

'I'm really scared of the pain. My friends said it's horrendous, and that a caesarean hurts less.' SHE VOLUNTEERS IT ONLY WHEN ASKED WHY. If you never ask, she says at minute 5: 'I just can't face the pain'
★ AND THE SECOND HALF OF THE AGENDA
'What do you know about pain relief in labour?' → 'NOTHING, REALLY.' The examiner ticks 'explores reason for request' and 'assesses knowledge of pain relief' as TWO SEPARATE ITEMS
★ THE TRAP SHE IS BRIEFED TO SPRING
If you say 'you'll probably need a caesarean anyway because of the placenta', she looks RELIEVED and says 'GREAT, SO WE'LL BOOK IT.' You have closed the decision prematurely — nine in ten resolve
Her history — all negative

Booking bloods normal, O POSITIVE, dating and screening scans normal. NO bleeding. NO pain or tightenings. FLUTTERS THIS WEEK. First pregnancy, NO caesarean or womb surgery, no termination or curette. Non-smoker. No headaches, vision change or swelling. Partner Mark supportive, mood fine, feels safe at home. Nothing in the past that makes birth frightening — 'just the stories'
Her scripted interruptions

'Is the baby OK?' — if you start with the placenta before giving the normal findings · 'So does that mean I need a caesarean anyway?' after the explanation · 'Does an epidural hurt? Can it paralyse you?' — if you list epidural WITHOUT side effects · and she PUSHES ONCE at minute 7: 'So can I have the caesarean or not?'
If you never mention pain relief
At minute 6 she asks: 'So how bad is the pain, honestly?'
Her register
Anxious, a little defensive. SOFTENS once the fear is acknowledged and the options are explained
VARIANT — the placenta is 5 cm from the os
That is a NORMAL position. Say so plainly, set it aside, and move to the request — 'the placenta doesn't affect how you give birth'
VARIANT — previous caesarean plus low placenta
Ask the sonographer to check for ACCRETA at 32 weeks — the placenta growing into the old scar. Uncommon, but it would mean birth in a large hospital with the full team
VARIANT — bleeding at 30 weeks, Rh-negative
HOSPITAL TODAY, not the clinic. Observations, SPECULUM but NO internal examination, CTG, KLEIHAUER and ANTI-D, and at 30 weeks STEROIDS for fetal lung maturity
VARIANT — previous traumatic birth

Validate it as a reasonable response, not a weakness. Three things: obstetric referral to discuss BOTH options with a birth plan · PERINATAL MENTAL HEALTH so the fear itself is treated · and CONTINUITY OF MIDWIFERY CARE. The decision stays hers
VARIANT — 'my mother says epidurals paralyse you'
Misinformation about one specific option. Be honest and specific about the real risks, offer the other rungs, and refer to the ANTENATAL ANAESTHETIC CLINIC

dx: **Low-lying placenta at 20 weeks, with a maternal request for caesarean driven by FEAR OF LABOUR PAIN. TWO THINGS MUST BOTH BE DONE OR YOU FAIL: counsel the low-lying placenta, AND find and address the hidden agenda with the full menu of pain-relief options. EITHER HALF ALONE FAILS.**

**And there is NO YES AND NO NO. This is a patient-centred station. Candidates do 'everything' and still fail because they never get the concept across: you explain, you give both sides, you give time — the decision is hers.**

**The one-line strategy, said out loud**: **'my job is to give you the pros and cons of every option so that YOU can make an informed decision — and it's too early to decide today, because the placenta itself may settle the question.'**

**DEFINITIONS AND NUMBERS. LOW-LYING = placental edge WITHIN 2 cm (20 mm) of the internal os. PRAEVIA = placenta OVER the os. 5 cm from the os = NORMAL. About 5% of 20-week scans show a low-lying placenta, and roughly 9 IN 10 RESOLVE by term as the lower segment forms — higher if the edge is more than 10 mm away. RESCAN TRANSVAGINALLY AT 32 WEEKS; again at 36 if persistent. Persistent low-lying → planned caesarean usually 38–39 WEEKS; praevia → 36–37 weeks. Vaginal birth may be considered with an edge over 10 mm and no bleeding.** VERIFY
**TRANSVAGINAL, not transabdominal, is the accurate way to measure the edge-to-os distance — and it is SAFE.**

**EXPLAIN THE SCAN WITH THE NORMAL FINDINGS FIRST, then the placenta as a BRIDGE**: **'the baby has formed well — brain, heart, spine, kidneys and limbs all normal, and the fluid is normal. Now the placenta. It's a piece of tissue, like a bridge, connecting the baby to your womb; the baby's oxygen and food come across it. Normally it sits towards the TOP. In your case it's in the LOWER part, within about two centimetres of the opening the baby comes out through. We call that a low-lying placenta. It is NOT covering the opening, and at 20 weeks it's common.'** **Jargon — 'internal os', 'placental edge distance', 'accreta', 'neuraxial' — is a named failure.**

**THE CAESAREAN, BOTH SIDES, FAIRLY. PROS: no labour pain, a known date, fewer tears or cuts to the birth canal, less later bladder leakage or prolapse. CONS: it is MAJOR SURGERY — bleeding, infection, injury to bladder or bowel, clots, anaesthetic problems, a very small increase in the risk of death or of losing the womb · MORE pain afterwards and a slower recovery, 4–6 WEEKS rather than days · and it affects FUTURE pregnancies — a low placenta again, the placenta growing into the scar, or the scar tearing in labour. For the baby: more breathing trouble in the first hours and a slightly higher rate of asthma later.** **The line that answers her friends: 'LESS PAIN DURING THE BIRTH, BUT MORE PAIN AND A SLOWER RECOVERY AFTER.'**

**★ THE FIVE-RUNG PAIN LADDER, IN THIS ORDER, AND THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR ALL FIVE. 1. BREATHING and relaxation, moving about, position changes, warm shower or bath, massage, a support person. 2. TENS — a small device with sticky pads on the back giving gentle pulses felt as tingling. 3. NITROUS OXIDE — the gas, through a mask with each contraction, takes the edge off and wears off in seconds. 4. MORPHINE injection — works in 20–30 minutes; used less because it can cause nausea and make the baby sleepy. 5. EPIDURAL — a fine tube in the lower back next to the spinal cord, numb from the waist down, the MOST EFFECTIVE. TWO CAVEATS THE EXAMINER WANTS: it can DROP THE BLOOD PRESSURE, so she'd have a drip, and it occasionally causes a HEADACHE — and the baby's heart is MONITORED CONTINUOUSLY.**

CORRECTION — **a maternal-request caesarean is booked AT OR AFTER 39 COMPLETED WEEKS, not before.** The source says 'before 39'; RANZCOG and NICE specify **not before 39 completed weeks**, because of neonatal respiratory morbidity. VERIFY. **RANZCOG position: after full counselling the doctor may agree, or refer for a second opinion.**

**DO NOT MISS what may sit behind the request: TOKOPHOBIA, a previous traumatic birth, PAST SEXUAL TRAUMA, FAMILY VIOLENCE, or perinatal anxiety — so ask about mood and safety. And PREVIOUS CAESAREAN + LOW PLACENTA = ASK FOR ACCRETA on the rescan.** **AVOID a digital vaginal examination with a low placenta — speculum only, and only if bleeding.** SA: the 32-week scan through the regional imaging service or tertiary unit; if it stays low, birth at a unit with a **blood bank and theatre**, accommodation nearby **from 37 weeks**, **PATS** for travel; bleeding at home — **call 000**, retrieval by **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**; **TIS National 131 450**; **Aboriginal Family Birthing Program**; **Pregnancy Birth and Baby 1800 882 436**; **1800RESPECT 1800 737 732** and **SA DV Crisis Line 1800 800 098** if violence is disclosed.
plan: **WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, open question.** *'I'm here for the scan results — and I want a caesarean. I don't want to go through labour.'*

**★ FIND THE AGENDA BEFORE THE SCAN — going straight to the report is the named trap**: **'thank you for coming in; I have the report and we'll go through it. Before we do — is there a particular concern about the birth you'd like to talk about? Can you tell me WHY you'd prefer a caesarean?'** *'I'm scared of the pain. My friends said a caesarean hurts less.'*

**★ THE SECOND, SEPARATELY SCORED QUESTION**: **'that's a very common and understandable worry, and I'm glad you told me. How much do you know about the options we have for PAIN RELIEF in labour?'** *'Nothing, really.'* **'Then we'll definitely cover that.'**
**This pregnancy**: booking bloods normal and blood group · dating scan · Down syndrome screening · and now the 20-week scan.

**THE SYMPTOM QUESTIONS — and bleeding is the most important, easy to skip because 'the scan already told me'**: **'have you had ANY vaginal bleeding at all? Any spotting after sex? Any tummy pain or tightenings? And have you started to feel the baby move?'** *Flutters this week — and 20 weeks is the threshold in a first pregnancy.*

**Risk factors for a placenta staying low or being stuck**: **'is this your first pregnancy? Any previous caesarean? Any other surgery on the womb — fibroids? Any previous terminations or curettes? Do you smoke?'**

**Pre-eclampsia screen as habit, then psychosocial**: headache, visual change, swelling · **'is your partner supportive? How's your mood? Has anything happened in the past that makes the idea of a vaginal birth frightening? Do you feel safe at home?'** **That last block is where tokophobia, past trauma or violence would surface.**
**TASK 2 — EXPLAIN THE SCAN, NORMAL FINDINGS FIRST**: the baby has formed well, brain, heart, spine, kidneys and limbs all normal, fluid normal. **Let her have that before anything else.**

**Then the placenta as a bridge**: normally at the top; hers in the lower part, **within about two centimetres of the opening** — a low-lying placenta — **not covering it, and common at 20 weeks.** **No jargon.**
**She asks 'so does that mean I need a caesarean anyway?' — and this is the trap. DO NOT SAY YES**: **'not necessarily, and that's the key thing.'**

**COUNSELLING HALF 1 — the placenta plan, with the numbers**: **'we repeat the scan at about 32 weeks. As the womb grows the lower part stretches and the placenta is carried up and away — in NINE OUT OF TEN women it's no longer low. In ONE IN TEN it stays low, and then there's a higher risk of heavy bleeding at the birth, so we'd usually recommend a planned caesarean at around 38 to 39 weeks.'**
**THE BLEEDING RED FLAG**: **'between now and then — if you have ANY bleeding, or tummy pain or tightenings, go STRAIGHT to the hospital. Don't wait for an appointment.'**

**COUNSELLING HALF 2A — the caesarean, both sides**: the pros, then **major surgery, bleeding, infection, bladder or bowel injury, clots, anaesthetic risks, a very small risk of death or losing the womb; more pain afterwards and four to six weeks' recovery; and the effect on future pregnancies.** Then the baby: breathing trouble at first, a little more asthma.

**Answer the friends directly**: **'they're right that you don't feel the birth itself. But afterwards there's a wound to recover from — so usually MORE pain in the days after and a slower recovery, weeks rather than days.'**

**★ COUNSELLING HALF 2B — acknowledge, then ALL FIVE RUNGS. Budget 90 seconds and do not let the caesarean risks eat it**: **'I understand the pain of labour can feel scary — that's a very normal worry. What I want you to know is that you would NOT be left to cope alone: there's a whole menu, and you can move up it as you need.'** Then one to five, **with the epidural's blood pressure and headache caveats and continuous monitoring.**

**Answer 'does an epidural hurt? Can it paralyse you?'**: **'a small sting of local anaesthetic first, then pressure. Serious nerve injury is extremely rare — the common side effects are a drop in blood pressure, which we treat with fluids, and occasionally a headache. The anaesthetist can see you in a clinic before the birth to talk it through.'**

**She pushes once: 'so can I have the caesarean or not?' — and the answer is not a verdict**: **'I hear that you're frightened, and I'm not going to dismiss that. I also won't tell you what to choose — it's your body and your birth. What I can promise is that whichever way you go, you'll have good pain relief and a team around you.'**

**CLOSE — too early, reading, partner, review**: **'it's too early to decide today, and the placenta may decide it for us. Here's reading on the low placenta, on caesarean, and on pain relief. Let's book a longer visit — bring your partner — and we'll go through it again. If you still want a caesarean then, we'll discuss it with the obstetrician. And remember: any bleeding, come straight in. Whatever you decide, I'll support you.'**

stem: General practice, Wallaroo. Sarah Whitlock, 33, married, a primary-school teacher. 'Sarah has come to see you because she and her husband have been trying for a baby for six years without success. She is otherwise well. Vital signs normal. BMI 27.'

What the stem does not say: she has conceived four times and lost every pregnancy at 7, 9, 8 and 11 weeks, and she only volunteers this to an open question. dx: **Recurrent pregnancy loss, cause to be established — and the station NEVER REACHES A DIAGNOSIS. It rewards a STRUCTURED SEARCH for one. Say 'recurrent pregnancy loss, cause to be established' and give the bucket list.**

**★ THE PIVOT IS THE WHOLE STATION, AND IT HAPPENS IN THE FIRST THIRTY SECONDS. The stem says infertility. Ask an open question, and the moment she says 'I keep losing them', SAY IT BACK**: **'so you are able to fall pregnant, but the pregnancies aren't continuing — that is a DIFFERENT PROBLEM from infertility, and it needs a different set of questions.'** **That sentence tells the examiner you have re-framed. Candidates who miss it take an ovulation-and-semen history and fail — and the role-player is briefed NOT to correct them.**

**DEFINITION: TWO OR MORE pregnancy losses before 24 WEEKS. Older texts said three consecutive; current RANZCOG, ESHRE and RCOG (2023) use two.** If challenged: **'the newer guidelines lowered the threshold to two so that investigation starts earlier.'**

**★ THE SIX BUCKETS, and the history must visibly walk them: UTERINE · ENDOCRINE · IMMUNE AND CLOTTING · INFECTION · GENETIC · ENVIRONMENT.** **Signpost them out loud — 'now some questions about hormones… about the immune system and clotting…' — or the examiner cannot see the structure.**

**★ THE GESTATION RULE — the most discriminating fact in the station: losses UNDER 10 WEEKS cluster with CHROMOSOMAL causes; losses AT OR OVER 10 WEEKS, stillbirth and early severe pre-eclampsia point to ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID SYNDROME and UTERINE causes.** **So use it: 'the early losses point toward a chromosomal cause; the eleven-week loss with a heartbeat and the curettage make me also consider antiphospholipid syndrome and the uterine cavity.' That sentence is task 2 done well.**

**KINDER WORDING THAT IS SCORED: 'have you ever COMPLETED A PREGNANCY?' — not 'do you have children?' to a woman with four losses.** **And the curettage question earns the Asherman follow-up: 'have your periods become LIGHTER since?'**

**THE INVESTIGATION LIST, IN THIS ORDER, KARYOTYPE FIRST: 1. KARYOTYPE OF BOTH PARENTS (peripheral blood). 2. PRODUCTS OF CONCEPTION for cytogenetics at the next loss. 3. UTERINE ASSESSMENT — transvaginal, ideally 3D, ultrasound; HSG or hysteroscopy for the cavity. 4. ANTIPHOSPHOLIPID ANTIBODIES — anticardiolipin, LUPUS ANTICOAGULANT, ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I, repeated at 12 weeks. 5. TSH ± TPO antibodies. 6. HbA1c or OGTT; prolactin. 7. Thrombophilia screen ONLY with a personal or family clot history. 8. Baseline FBC, UEC, LFT, STI screen, rubella IgG, blood group.**

**WHY KARYOTYPE BOTH — the examiner asks: 'a balanced translocation can sit in EITHER parent, gives a phenotypically NORMAL person, and only shows up as an unbalanced conceptus. Testing both is the standard.' Carrier in about 2–5% of RPL couples.**

CORRECTION — **do NOT order a routine TORCH screen.** The lecture lists TORCH 'apparently' as a cause. **Current RANZCOG, ESHRE and RCOG guidance does not recommend routine TORCH serology in RPL: these infections cause SPORADIC loss, not recurrence.** Ask the cat question, then say: **'infection is low yield; I'd do an STI screen and rubella immunity rather than a full TORCH panel unless the history suggests it.'** CORRECTION — **do NOT measure progesterone.** Luteal-phase testing is unreliable and not recommended. **What IS evidence-based (PRISM): vaginal micronised progesterone 400 mg twice daily for women with BLEEDING in early pregnancy AND one or more previous miscarriages, continued to 16 weeks.** VERIFY — **inherited thrombophilia screening is not recommended routinely; antiphospholipid testing is.**

**HONEST HOPE, NOT A PROMISE: in about HALF of couples NO CAUSE IS FOUND — and even then the live birth rate next pregnancy is around 60–75%.** **Say both. 'We'll definitely find the cause' earns 'you promise?'** **And name the supportive-care finding: care in a dedicated early pregnancy or RPL clinic itself improves live birth.** **APS treatment: aspirin 100 mg pre-conception plus enoxaparin 40 mg daily once pregnancy is confirmed. TSH target under 2.5 pre-conception. Caffeine under 200 mg/day — about two instant coffees. Folate 0.5 mg, or 5 mg if diabetes, BMI over 30 or a prior neural tube defect.** VERIFY. SA: **WCH Recurrent Pregnancy Loss / early pregnancy service**, or **Fertility SA / Repromed** — **PATS** for travel from Wallaroo; early scan at **6–7 weeks** next pregnancy; **Red Nose Grief and Loss 1300 308 307**; **Pregnancy, Birth and Baby 1800 882 436**; GP mental health plan; **TIS National 131 450**; ACCHS and Aboriginal Maternal Infant Care worker; **Closing the Gap PBS**.
plan: **WIPE, then an OPEN question — this is the pass or fail moment**: **'I understand you and your husband have been trying for a baby for some time — can you tell me what has been happening?'** *'Six years. I fall pregnant, but I keep losing them. Four times now. Nobody has told me why.'*

**★ ACKNOWLEDGE — eight seconds, and skipping it because 'there isn't time' is a named failure**: **'I'm so sorry. Four losses is a lot to carry, and I can hear how frightening the next attempt feels.'**

**★ SAY THE PIVOT BACK**: **'so you ARE able to fall pregnant, but the pregnancies aren't continuing — that's a different problem from infertility, and it has its own checklist of causes. Can I ask you some detailed questions, and then we'll talk about the tests?'**
**THE LOSSES — number, then gestation**: **'how many miscarriages altogether? AT WHAT STAGE OF PREGNANCY did each one happen?'** *Seven, nine, eight, and eleven — the last with a heartbeat.*
**Tissue and completed pregnancies**: **'was the tissue from any of them sent to the laboratory for testing?'** *No — nobody offered.* **'Have you ever COMPLETED a pregnancy?'** *No.*

**Uterine surgery, and the Asherman follow-up**: **'have you had any procedures down below — a curette after a miscarriage, a termination, or any surgery on the womb?'** *A D&C after the second.* **Then later in the period block: 'have your periods become LIGHTER since?'**

**PERIOD — this block rules the uterine bucket in or out, and it is 45 SECONDS, no more**: last period · regular · unusually heavy or painful · any bleeding or pain between · **and lighter than they used to be.**

**PARTNER AND SCREENING, briskly**: **'is your husband supportive through all of this?'** · ever diagnosed with an STI · bleeding after sex or pain with sex · cervical screening up to date. **Do NOT ask about contraception — she is conceiving, and asking tells the examiner you are on autopilot.**

**Respond to it properly, and screen safety**: **'that sounds exhausting, and I don't want to gloss over it — can I come back to how you're coping before you leave? Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself?'** Then **smoking, alcohol, coffees and energy drinks, recreational drugs, medications and FOLATE.**

**Answer 'is it my fault? Is it the coffee?' without blame**: **'no. Caffeine is worth reducing — under about two coffees a day — and stopping the wine while you're trying, but none of this is your fault.'**

IMMUNE AND CLOTTING — antiphospholipid syndrome, given the eleven-week loss with a heartbeat. UTERINE — septum, fibroid or adhesions after the curette; the lighter periods make adhesions worth excluding. ENDOCRINE — thyroid, PCOS, diabetes, prolactin, none suggested. INFECTION — low yield. ENVIRONMENT — caffeine and alcohol, modifiable.**

**Close with disposition and support**: review in two to three weeks with results · **referral to a recurrent pregnancy loss clinic** · **early scan at 6–7 weeks next pregnancy** · psychological support and **Red Nose 1300 308 307**. **And if asked for management: 'find the cause and treat it — and for the half where nothing is found, supportive care in a dedicated clinic, which itself improves live birth rates.'**

findingsLabel: What the stem hides, and how Sarah is briefed to play it
findings: The stem as written

'Sarah has come to see you because she and her husband have been trying for a baby for SIX YEARS without success. She is otherwise well. Vital signs normal. BMI 27.' NO examination. Tasks: history 6 min, then differentials with reasons, then investigations
★ WHAT THE STEM DOES NOT SAY
She has CONCEIVED FOUR TIMES and lost every pregnancy — at 7, 9, 8 and 11 WEEKS. She volunteers this ONLY when you ask an OPEN QUESTION
★ THE SAFETY NET if she does not volunteer it
'In those six years, have you ever had a positive pregnancy test?'
The losses

Seven, nine, eight, and the last at ELEVEN WEEKS — and THAT ONE HAD A HEARTBEAT on a nine-week scan. NO tissue ever sent to the lab: 'nobody offered.' NEVER completed a pregnancy. D&C AFTER THE SECOND because it would not come away
Periods
Regular 28–30 days. 'Maybe a bit LIGHTER SINCE THE D&C' — the adhesions clue, and only if you ask whether they have become lighter
The family history
'My SISTER had two miscarriages before her boys.' Mum, not sure
Everything negative

No thyroid, diabetes, PCOS or prolactin symptoms. No joint pains, rash, mouth ulcers, clots or stroke. A DOG, no cats, no fevers. No STI, no post-coital bleeding, cervical screening normal last year. Husband Tom supportive but quiet
Modifiable factors
Non-smoker. WINE MOST NIGHTS. FIVE OR SIX COFFEES a day. STOPPED THE FOLATE after the last loss. No medications
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA

She fears it is HER FAULT — the coffee, the wine, working too hard — and she is LOW: 'it's taken over everything. I avoid friends with babies. Some days I don't want to get out of bed.' No thoughts of self-harm. SHE VOLUNTEERS 'IS THIS BECAUSE OF THE COFFEE? IS IT ME?' only if you ask how she is coping — or at about 5 minutes if you never do
★ HOW SHE IS BRIEFED TO PUNISH THE WRONG SCRIPT

If you ask INFERTILITY questions — ovulation, timing, semen analysis — she answers briefly and LOOKS PUZZLED, and does NOT correct you. If you never acknowledge the losses she becomes FLAT AND MONOSYLLABIC. If you say 'we'll definitely find the cause' she asks: 'YOU PROMISE?'
★ VERSION B — the investigation card

After the history the examiner hands you: FBC normal · TSH 1.8 · HbA1c 5.3% · prolactin normal · anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant NEGATIVE · pelvic ultrasound NORMAL. 'Everything is normal. What is missing?' THE ANSWER IS ONE WORD: KARYOTYPE
Version B — the second half of the answer

These are SINGLE-TIME-POINT antiphospholipid tests, and ANTI-β2-GLYCOPROTEIN I IS MISSING. The syndrome requires TWO positive results TWELVE WEEKS APART, so one negative set does not exclude it. And the ultrasound does not define the CAVITY after her curette
If she asks for a tablet to stop it happening
'Without a specific cause, aspirin and heparin DON'T help and I wouldn't start them.' EMPIRICAL ANTICOAGULATION FOR UNEXPLAINED RPL IS AN EXAMINER TARGET

stem: Your general practice, rural South Australia, routine antenatal clinic. Karen Whitmore, 37, is 36 weeks pregnant, gravida 3 para 2, attending a scheduled visit. Presenting complaint: swelling of both legs. Antenatal care has been uncomplicated and today's observations are on the card in the room.

Tasks: take a focused history from Karen, six minutes — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings — explain your diagnosis and differential diagnoses to Karen. 8 minutes. No investigation task and no management task.
