findings: Blood pressure — READ THIS FIRST
118/76 — NORMAL. The single most important number on the card, and it does most of the work of excluding pre-eclampsia
Pulse and temperature
88 regular · 36.7 °C
Legs
BILATERAL PITTING OEDEMA TO THE MID-THIGH, SYMMETRICAL. Varicose veins both calves. CALVES SOFT, NON-TENDER, NO ASYMMETRY — which argues strongly against a clot
Vulva and perianal
OEDEMATOUS with VULVAL VARICOSITIES. HAEMORRHOIDS. Both NORMAL — same mechanism
Reflexes
ANKLE CLONUS — ONE BEAT. NORMAL. Sustained clonus means MORE THAN THREE BEATS
Abdomen
SFH 35 cm, longitudinal, cephalic, FHR 142
Urine dipstick
NOT PROVIDED — deliberately withheld so you feel you are missing something. With a normal blood pressure you do not need it to exclude pre-eclampsia
★ THE SCRIPTED OPENING LINE
She speaks BEFORE you ask anything: 'I just want this pregnancy to be over. I CAN'T TAKE THIS ANY MORE.' Arms folded, flat tone. THIS IS A COMMUNICATION MARK, NOT A SYMPTOM
★ HOW SHE IS BRIEFED
If you acknowledge how she feels in your first or second sentence she SOFTENS NOTICEABLY and cooperates. If you go straight to questions she stays CLIPPED AND SHORT until you do
★ THE PIVOTAL ANSWER — she will NOT offer it unless asked directly
'NO — it's much better in the MORNINGS. It builds up through the day and by evening it's terrible.' Physiological oedema is GRAVITATIONAL; swelling that persists overnight is not
The other sites
'Around my private parts. It's swollen and embarrassing' — she lowers her voice. And piles. But FACE, EYES AND HANDS NORMAL — 'my rings still fit'
★ HER HIDDEN AGENDA

Her SISTER had pre-eclampsia and was rushed in for an emergency caesarean at 34 weeks. She is frightened this is the same thing but WILL NOT SAY SO unless asked about her concerns — or she volunteers it late: 'Is this that pre-eclampsia thing? My sister had it'
Her second agenda, and her pushback
She wants to be INDUCED and raises it once near the end. And when told it is normal: 'NORMAL? Have you seen my legs!' She accepts a good explanation and stays unhappy with a dismissive one
VERSION C — one parameter moved

BP 156/98 on repeat · CLONUS FOUR BEATS, SUSTAINED · swelling PRESENT ON WAKING and in the FACE AND HANDS · headache and visual flashes on direct questioning. PRE-ECLAMPSIA WITH SEVERE FEATURES — hospital now, and at 36 weeks the treatment is delivery
Other variant cards

LEFT CALF 4 cm larger, warm and tender → DVT until proven otherwise; compression ultrasound today, and D-DIMER IS USELESS IN PREGNANCY · breathless lying flat, waking gasping, basal crackles → PERIPARTUM CARDIOMYOPATHY · intense itch of PALMS AND SOLES at night with no rash → intrahepatic cholestasis · one leg hot and red with a spreading edge and fever 38.2 → CELLULITIS

dx: **Physiological oedema of late pregnancy — NOT pre-eclampsia. Write that at the top of your page before you start, because the case is built to push you towards it.**

**ONE MECHANISM, FOUR FINDINGS: the gravid uterus compresses the pelvic veins and the inferior vena cava. That single thing produces the leg oedema, the vulval swelling and varicosities, the leg varicose veins and the haemorrhoids. Naming the single cause is what makes the explanation convincing, and it is explicitly what the case rewards.**

**Definition worth saying out loud: physiological oedema is BILATERAL, DEPENDENT, GRAVITATIONAL lower-limb swelling — worse on standing, worse by evening, and SETTLING OVERNIGHT. It affects the majority of women in the third trimester.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE HAS TWO HALVES AND YOU MUST DO BOTH: confidently NORMALISE, but only after you have been HEARD TO EXCLUDE pre-eclampsia — and without dismissing an exhausted woman.** **Candidates who ask a beautiful pre-eclampsia history and then hedge ('it might be pre-eclampsia, we'll need tests') fail on diagnosis. Candidates who correctly say 'this is normal' without having asked fail on safety. Candidates who do both but deliver it flatly to a woman who opened the station in distress lose the communication domain.**

**THE TWO TRAPS, NAMED. 1. OVER-CALLING PRE-ECLAMPSIA. The case supplies clonus — a genuine pre-eclampsia sign — but at ONE BEAT, which is normal. It supplies dramatic-sounding findings (vulval swelling, haemorrhoids, varicose veins, swelling to the thigh) which are ALL NORMAL. And it WITHHOLDS THE DIPSTICK so you feel you are missing something. 2. PANICKING AT THE LEVEL of the swelling — the red flag is PERSISTENCE ON WAKING, not how far up the leg it goes.**

CORRECTION — **do NOT name 'pelvic congestion syndrome'.** When this case first appeared, candidates searched the finding cluster online and returned it. **It is a CHRONIC NON-PREGNANT condition — six months or more of pelvic pain, worse on standing and after intercourse, with dyspareunia and ovarian and pelvic varices.** If an examiner raises it: **'pelvic congestion syndrome is a chronic pelvic pain disorder of non-pregnant women; it does not explain acute third-trimester dependent oedema, and her presentation is fully explained by physiological venous compression.'**

**THE EXAMINER'S CHALLENGE, and the answer that passes the station**: *'She has clonus. Isn't that pre-eclampsia?'* → **'Clonus only becomes a sign of cortical irritability when it is SUSTAINED — more than three beats. One or two beats occurs in normal people and in normal pregnancy. Combined with a normal blood pressure and no neurological or hepatic symptoms, I do not think this is pre-eclampsia.'** And on the missing dipstick: **'with a normal blood pressure I can exclude it clinically — though I'd still dipstick her today, because it is free and part of every antenatal visit.'**

**TWO NUANCES THAT SHOW REASONING. ORTHOPNOEA IS UNRELIABLE AT 36 WEEKS — a term uterus splints the diaphragm and reflux is near-universal, so ASK WHY she props herself up and say you are interpreting it cautiously. And on bilateral DVT: 'bilateral deep vein thrombosis is rare and this swelling is symmetrical — but pregnancy is itself a prothrombotic state, so I'm looking for a SECOND risk factor that would make it likely.'**

CORRECTION — **the Woltman sign in hypothyroidism is DELAYED RELAXATION of the ankle reflex, not hyperreflexia.** CORRECTION — **proteinuria is NO LONGER REQUIRED for the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia under current SOMANZ / ISSHP criteria: new hypertension after 20 weeks PLUS maternal organ or uteroplacental involvement.** VERIFY

**MANAGEMENT IS PRACTICAL, AND TWO THINGS ARE FORBIDDEN: left lateral rest, elevate the legs when sitting, avoid prolonged standing, GRADUATED COMPRESSION STOCKINGS, supportive footwear, normal fluids. For the haemorrhoids: fibre, fluids, a stool softener, a topical preparation safe in pregnancy.** VERIFY **NEVER diuretics — they reduce plasma volume and placental perfusion. NEVER salt restriction — no evidence, and not benign in pregnancy.** SA: bloods and urine through SA Pathology, **spot protein-creatinine ratio preferred to a 24-hour collection**; for Version C, **in-utero transfer via MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** rather than a country hospital bed; **PATS**; **Country Health Connect**; Aboriginal Family Birthing Program and ACCHS; **TIS National 131 450**; **Closing the Gap PBS** — and note she does six-hour shifts on checkouts with a partner away all week, **so make the leg-elevation advice fit her life rather than reciting it.**
plan: **WIPE, sit at eye level, and offer her comfort first**: **'before we start — are you comfortable sitting like that, or would you rather lie a little on your left side?'** **She then delivers the scripted line before you have asked anything.**

**★ ADDRESS IT — 30 to 40 seconds, and the role-player visibly softens, which is the signal the mark is awarded**: **'I'm really sorry you're feeling like that, Karen. Thirty-six weeks is genuinely hard work, and you're doing a great job carrying this baby. I'm here to help. Tell me what's been troubling you most, and I promise we'll go through it properly and make a plan together.'**
**Explore the swelling**: when did it start · constant or intermittent · getting worse · **one leg or both** · how far up.

**★ THE RED FLAG QUESTION, AS ITS OWN QUESTION**: **'this one matters — when you wake up in the morning, is the swelling still there?'** *'No — much better in the mornings.'* **Say what it means: 'that's a genuinely reassuring answer and I'll explain why shortly.'** Then **worse standing, better lying down.**

**THE OTHER SITES**: **'have you noticed swelling anywhere else on your body?'** *The vulval swelling, said with embarrassment.* **Take it matter-of-factly: 'thank you for telling me — that's important and it's nothing to be embarrassed about.'**

**★ THE NON-DEPENDENT CHECK**: **'and what about around your eyes or your face, or your hands and fingers?'** *'No — my rings still fit.'* **That is what turns 'she has swelling' into 'DEPENDENT swelling'.** Then **painful · itchy · any rash or redness · bulging veins · anything around the back passage** — four questions screening cellulitis, dermatitis, urticaria and venous insufficiency.

**★ THE PRE-ECLAMPSIA SET — forty seconds, asked HERE and not at five minutes**: **'now a group of symptoms we check in every pregnancy at this stage. Any headaches? Any change in your vision — blurring, flashing lights, spots? Any dizziness? Any pain in your tummy, especially up under the ribs on the right? Any nausea or vomiting? Any chest pain or shortness of breath? Are you passing less urine than usual?'**

**If she interrupts with 'is it pre-eclampsia?'**: **'that's exactly what I'm checking for, and it's the right thing to be worried about. Give me two more minutes of questions and I'll be able to answer you properly.'**

**CLOTTING**: calf pain or tenderness · long travel or bed rest · recent surgery · **personal or family history of a clot in the leg or lung** · cough or haemoptysis. **Say the reasoning aloud rather than box-ticking.**

**THE FOUR ORGAN FAILURES. CARDIAC** — exertional breathlessness beyond what you'd expect, chest pain, **breathless lying flat or waking at night gasping, and ASK WHY she props herself up.** **RENAL** — less urine, frothy urine, known kidney problem. **HEPATIC** — jaundice, itch, dark urine, pale stools. **THYROID** — cold intolerance, weight change beyond the pregnancy.

**One medication question and stop**: **'any medications, including anything for blood pressure? Any allergies?'** **A pregnant woman with a normal blood pressure is not on amlodipine — do not spend time here.**
**OBSTETRIC HISTORY — the stem gives permission to be quick, NOT to omit**: booking bloods · dating scan · screening · **the 18–20 week scan, baby and placenta** · the GTT · **the 35–37 week swab.**

**THE TWO THAT ALWAYS SCORE**: **'is the baby kicking as much as usual? Any bleeding, or any leaking of fluid?'** Then **previous pregnancies: 'any problems in the previous two — any high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia?'** **Her 'no' is a relevant negative — quote it back.**

**ASK FOR THE CARD BY NAMING FINDINGS, NOT REGIONS**: **'blood pressure first, repeated after rest; pulse and temperature; is the oedema pitting, symmetrical, how far does it extend, is either calf tender or asymmetrical; varicose veins, vulval swelling, haemorrhoids; reflexes, and specifically IS THERE ANKLE CLONUS AND HOW MANY BEATS; symphysio-fundal height, lie, presentation, fetal heart rate; and a urine dipstick for protein.'**

**READ IT BACK OUT LOUD**: **'her blood pressure is normal — that's the most important thing here. The oedema is bilateral, pitting and symmetrical with soft non-tender calves, which argues against a clot. One beat of clonus is within normal limits. Fundal height and fetal heart rate are normal.'**

**BRACKET THE NEWS BEFORE YOU GIVE IT**: **'Karen, before I explain — I can see how uncomfortable and worn down you are, and nothing I'm about to say means this isn't real or that it doesn't matter. The good news is that everything I've found today is normal for this stage of pregnancy.'** **When she pushes back: 'I'm not saying nothing is wrong — I'm saying nothing is DANGEROUS.'**

**THE MECHANISM IN ONE BREATH, then the clonus before anyone else raises it**: the heavy uterus pressing back on the big vessels, blood from the legs working harder, pressure backing up, fluid pushed into the tissues — **'that one thing explains all four of your problems, and it's why it's worse by evening and better by morning: gravity.'** Then: **'one beat is normal. It only concerns us beyond three beats.'**

**THE DIFFERENTIAL IN 22 SECONDS — one clause each, no explanations**: pre-eclampsia, excluded on a normal blood pressure and no symptoms · kidneys · heart · liver, including a liver condition specific to pregnancy · underactive thyroid · a clot in the leg that can travel to the lung · an infection in the skin. **Then the practical measures — left lateral rest, feet up, compression stockings, no diuretic, no salt restriction — and SAFETY-NET: morning swelling, face or hands, headache, flashing lights, rib pain, bleeding or fluid loss, reduced movements.** Close: **'normal doesn't mean you have to just put up with it — and you have five weeks to go, not fifteen.'**
pefe: **BLOOD PRESSURE FIRST, repeated after five minutes of rest, correct cuff size, arm at heart level, left lateral tilt. Everything turns on it.**

**Ask for the NUMBER OF BEATS of clonus** — asking that is what shows you know the threshold exists. **Sustained = MORE THAN THREE beats. One or two is normal in normal people and in normal pregnancy.**
**Name findings, not regions.** 'I'd like to examine the cardiovascular system' repeatedly is a named error — hunt the specific finding.
**Is the oedema PITTING and SYMMETRICAL, and are the CALVES tender or asymmetrical?** Calf circumference both sides if there is any asymmetry. **Temperature if the leg is red or painful.**
**Symphysio-fundal height plotted, lie, presentation and fetal heart rate** — SFH = gestation ±2–3 cm; FHR 110–160.
**Urine dipstick for protein — it is withheld, so ask for it.** If refused, say a normal blood pressure excludes pre-eclampsia clinically.

**If ANY red flag is present: spot URINE PROTEIN-CREATININE RATIO (not a 24-hour collection) · FBC, UEC, LFTs, LDH, urate, coagulation profile · CTG and ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler.**

**Practical measures: left lateral rest, elevate the legs when sitting, avoid prolonged standing, GRADUATED COMPRESSION STOCKINGS, supportive footwear, normal fluids.** Haemorrhoids: fibre, fluids, stool softener, a topical preparation safe in pregnancy. VERIFY **Vulval varicosities: reassurance, a supportive garment, side-lying rest — they usually resolve after birth.**
**NEVER diuretics (they reduce plasma volume and placental perfusion) and NEVER salt restriction.** Both are named errors.

**Thresholds: hypertension ≥140/90 on two readings four hours apart; severe ≥160/110; BP target once treated under 135/85, NOT 120/80; significant proteinuria PCR ≥30 mg/mmol; aspirin prophylaxis started before 16 weeks.** VERIFY. **D-dimer is useless in pregnancy — it is physiologically raised.**

dx: **Not a diagnosis station — a COUNSELLING station. The 'finding' is a woman with TWO PREVIOUS RETAINED PLACENTAS and a POSTPARTUM HAEMORRHAGE, traumatised by hospital care, who has chosen home birth as the way to stop it happening again — in a place where a repeat would be hard to manage.**

**★ THREE THINGS, ALL THREE, OR THE STATION IS NOT PASSED. 1. FIND THE AGENDA — the candles are not the agenda; two retained placentas and a haemorrhage are. 2. NAME HER TWO SPECIFIC RISKS, EARLY — the source says 'I do this very, very early because this is the reason people are failing.' 3. STAY PATIENT-CENTRED — neither 'no' nor 'yes'. If you give the risks and then tell her 'go and do a home birth' or 'don't', that is not a pass.**

**THE WARM OPENING IS A MARK. Candidates who answer 'I want candles' with a concern lose the room in the first thirty seconds.** Respond to a wish with enthusiasm and an offer of partnership: **'that's a really exciting decision, Karen. I want you to know I'm here to support you to make the best decision about your birth.'** THEN dig.

**THE TWO CONCERNS, IN HER WORDS. CONCERN ONE: 'because you've had difficulty delivering the placenta TWICE, there is a higher chance we will face difficulty delivering the placenta this time.' CONCERN TWO: 'you live in a rural area, and the services at our hospital might be insufficient to deal with a severe bleed or a stuck placenta — we may not be able to do an urgent operation here, and we are 400 kilometres from the tertiary centre.'**

**WHEN SHE SAYS 'I WANT IT TO COME BY ITSELF' — answer the belief, gently**: **'we usually expect the placenta to deliver by itself. If it doesn't, we can gently pull on the cord to remove it. Sometimes that can cause bleeding and other complications — and I think that is what happened to you.'** **Never promise the placenta will come by itself.**

**WHEN SHE SAYS 'SO YOU'RE SAYING I CAN'T' — the patient-centred close**: **'no — I'm saying in your specific case I have two concerns, and I want you to decide with all the facts.'** **And never argue a point twice: acknowledge, inform, move to the next box.**

**ELIGIBILITY, said as criteria rather than as a refusal: a SINGLE pregnancy · CEPHALIC near the birth · TERM (37–42 weeks) · NO previous caesarean or uterine surgery · NO previous complications · a SAFE HOME · TWO AHPRA-REGISTERED MIDWIVES · and a WRITTEN TRANSFER PLAN.** **Karen fails the 'no previous complications' criterion, and that is the entire point of the station.**

**THE EVIDENCE, FOR LOW-RISK WOMEN — give three pros and two cons and stop. PROS: lower risk of tears, less use of instruments, lower chance of an urgent caesarean, and the risk to the baby is the SAME as in hospital. CONS: transfer may be challenging — someone has to drive her, at whatever hour, on whatever road — and some pain relief, notably an EPIDURAL, is not available at home.**

**ADDED — the clinical spine. The Australian College of Midwives National Midwifery Guidelines for Consultation and Referral treat PREVIOUS PPH and PREVIOUS MANUAL REMOVAL OF THE PLACENTA as indications for consultation or referral, and publicly funded home-birth programs apply strict low-risk criteria and would be expected to decline her.** VERIFY **A LEVEL 2 service provides planned birthing for low-risk women at term with midwifery and GP care, with NO on-site caesarean capability and no 24-hour theatre — so a retained placenta with haemorrhage means RETRIEVAL, not a walk down the corridor.** VERIFY **Her third stage, wherever she births: ACTIVE MANAGEMENT — oxytocin 10 IU IM with the birth and controlled cord traction — plus IV access in labour, group-and-hold, and tranexamic acid and uterotonics ready. Retained placenta at 30 minutes despite active management → manual removal under anaesthesia in theatre.**

**THE SAFER MIDDLE PATH, offered rather than imposed: a BIRTH CENTRE OR BIRTHING SUITE CLOSE TO THE TERTIARY HOSPITAL — 'very similar to home; your family can be there, you can have your music — but help is minutes away.'** **And the timeline: it is TOO EARLY at 20 weeks; the final plan is made at 36 WEEKS, the same visit as the GBS swab, with a hospital visit in the third trimester and a home visit at 36 weeks.** SA: retrieval **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, RFDS for fixed-wing; **PATS** funds travel to a metropolitan birth centre; **Aboriginal Family Birthing Program** and ACCHS if she identifies as Aboriginal; **TIS National 131 450**; **Country Health Connect** for postnatal home support; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.

**★ RESPOND TO THE WISH WITH WARMTH, NOT A 'BUT'**: **'that's a really exciting decision, Karen. I want you to know I'm here to support you to make the best decision about your birth.'** Then signpost: **'is it OK if I ask you a few questions, and then we can talk through the plan together?'** *She softens.*
**AGENDA, LAYER 1**: **'can I ask why you've decided to deliver at home?'** *'I just want to, doctor.'* **This question is DESIGNED to be deflected — do not stop here.**
**LAYER 2**: **'do you have any concerns or worries about the delivery itself?'** *'I just don't want to be in a hospital.'*

**LAYER 3 — the one that opens it**: **'have you had any bad experiences with previous births — with the hospital, or with doctors or midwives?'** *'Yes. I had problems in my previous pregnancies. That's why I don't want any doctors or midwives involved.'*

**ACKNOWLEDGE BEFORE ASKING ANYTHING ELSE**: **'I'm so sorry to hear that. I can imagine how difficult that experience must have been.'** Then transition: **'thank you for telling me. Is it OK if I ask a few questions about this pregnancy and your previous ones?'**

**CURRENT PREGNANCY**: **'how is this pregnancy going? Booking bloods and dating scan? Down syndrome screening? And the 18-to-20-week scan — any problems, ESPECIALLY WITH THE POSITION OF THE PLACENTA? Have you started feeling the baby move?'** **A low-lying placenta would end the discussion, and the exam drops one in often enough to ask every time.**

**★ PREVIOUS PREGNANCIES — the block that finds the story**: **'tell me about your previous pregnancies. How many? Was each a vaginal birth or a caesarean? Any problems during the pregnancies — blood pressure, sugars? AND ANY PROBLEMS WITH THE BIRTH ITSELF — a long labour, instruments, bleeding afterwards, ANY TROUBLE WITH THE PLACENTA?'**

**Follow the story properly when it lands**: **'that sounds frightening. Did you need a blood transfusion? Did they take you to theatre to remove it?'** *Blood after the second.* Then **past medical, medications, allergies** in one line.

**THE HOME — the source's 'last important thing'**: **'because you're planning to give birth at home, can you describe your home situation for me? Who do you live with? Are they supportive? Any stress or problems at home? How are you coping with the pregnancy?'**

**The questions that turn 'home situation' into a TRANSFER PLAN**: **'how far is the nearest hospital from your house, and how long does it take at night? Do you have a reliable car and someone who could drive? Is your phone reception good at home?'** *Forty minutes, a ute, patchy reception.* **Each answer is a line you quote back in the counselling.**

**BOX ONE — ACKNOWLEDGE, AND DO IT STRONGLY**: **'Karen, first of all I want to tell you that I fully support your decision, and I understand how difficult your previous births have been — and how that has made this a bad experience for you. I'd like to talk a bit more about home birth, so you can make an informed decision based on the pros and cons.'**

**★ BOX TWO — THE TWO CONCERNS, SAID EARLY**: **'overall, I have two main concerns in your case.'** Then **concern one, the placenta**, and when she says she wants it to come by itself, **answer the belief** — the cord traction, the bleeding, 'and I think that is what happened to you.'

**Concern two — the stem said back to her**: rural area, services here may be insufficient for a severe bleed or a stuck placenta, **'we may not be able to do an urgent operation here, and we're 400 kilometres from the tertiary centre.'** *'So you're saying I can't.'* → **'no — I'm saying in your specific case I have two concerns, and I want you to decide with all the facts.'**

**BOX THREE — PROS AND CONS, THREE AND TWO, THEN STOP**: lower risk of tears, less use of instruments, lower chance of an urgent caesarean, **and the risk to the baby is the same as in hospital** · transfer may be challenging, and **an epidural is not available at home.**

**'TOO EARLY' — the timeline**: **'you're 20 weeks, and it's a little early to finalise. We usually make the delivery plan around 36 weeks. If any complication arises — the placenta lying low, the baby breech, the heart rate abnormal — we may need to deliver in hospital, possibly by caesarean.'**

**BOX FOUR — ELIGIBILITY AS CRITERIA, AND THE TRANSFER PLAN**: **'if you decide to proceed, we can do this for a single pregnancy, with no previous caesarean or womb surgery, with the baby head down close to the birth. And we'd need a transfer plan — who drives you and how long it takes.'** Then **two AHPRA-registered midwives, and an offer to introduce her to one: 'you can hear them out, and then decide.'**

**THE SAFER MIDDLE PATH, offered not imposed**: **'I'd recommend a birth centre or birthing suite close to the tertiary hospital. They're very similar to home — your family can be there, you can have your music — but help is minutes away.'**

**CLOSE, and the last sentence of the station is HERS**: reading material · a second meeting with her partner · an obstetrician or midwife if she wants · **'whatever you decide, it is your decision, and I'll support you. Let's book the next visit.'** **Never end with 'so I really think you should…'**

The numbers: bedside glucose 18 to 19 · dipstick glucose 4+ and ketones 3+, with blood ketones 4.2 · DKA is glucose over 11 plus ketones 3 or more plus a pH under 7.3 or bicarbonate under 15 · severity is pH under 7.3 mild, under 7.2 moderate, under 7.1 severe · fluids are 10 mL/kg of 0.9% saline only if shocked, with the deficit replaced over 48 hours and potassium at 40 mmol/L · insulin is 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h started an hour after fluids, with no bolus · cerebral oedema occurs 4 to 12 hours in · and MedSTAR kids is 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the women's and children's VERIFY all. If the examiner asks for immediate management: 'IV access; venous gas, glucose, blood ketones, electrolytes and full blood count; weigh him; call the paediatric team and MedSTAR kids. If he is shocked, 0.9% saline 10 mL/kg over 30 to 60 minutes; otherwise rehydrate over 48 hours with potassium added once I have a level; insulin infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units per kilo per hour starting an hour after fluids, no bolus; hourly glucose and neuro observations for cerebral oedema.' The variants. Version B hides the diabetes — the stem says only vomiting and diarrhoea, and it appears in past history if you ask: 'Does Liam have any medical conditions, or take any regular medicines?' → 'He's diabetic — on insulin' → and you pivot: 'That's very important, so let me ask about it properly' and run all four questions plus polyuria and polydipsia. Examiner: consciousness, breathing pattern, capillary refill, blood glucose and ketones first' — and the explanation shortens to one line: DKA, serious, retrieval. If the examiner challenges the abdomen — 'Vitals are stable and you know it's DKA, do you really need it?' → 'Yes. Vomiting with abdominal pain in a child can be appendicitis, intussusception or a strangulated hernia, and DKA can mask or mimic them — so a full abdominal examination and the groin, and I'd re-examine after treatment starts.' and if the father asks to go home — 'I understand; hospital with a small child is hard. They were camping at the weekend, ran out of insulin, and he missed the last two doses; his cousin had a vomiting bug there.

He answers only what is asked, in short answers. He raises 'So this is my fault?' when the trigger is named, pushes once for going home with fluids, and becomes quiet and looks at the floor if blamed. If the doctor is doing well but has not asked by 3:30 he says 'His tummy's been sore too.'

Chronic-diarrhoea questions on a two-day history waste time

That's what's causing the vomiting, the tummy pain, the thirst and the tiredness.' A pancreas lecture, or naming only one layer, is the trap

'Before I ask you anything, could I have his observations, please — temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, blood pressure, oxygen level and today's weight?' → version A: temp 37.4, HR 165, RR 40, BP 82 systolic, sats 98%, weight 7.3 kg. If the examiner says 'We'll come to the examination later', reply 'Thank you — I'll ask again after the history': asking early still scores the hydration-awareness mark
The weight loss is the diagnosis of severity

'It is significant — that's about ten per cent of his body weight in a week, which tells me how much fluid he's lost, and it's something I'll factor into his treatment. Thank you for weighing him.' Saying 'That's just fluid, nothing to worry about' is the trap — 10% is severe by definition

back.dx: GASTROENTERITIS WITH DEHYDRATION IN A 6-MONTH-OLD — severe in version A, mild to moderate in version B — where the marks are in committing to a grade with reasons and giving the fluid ladder in order. The numbers: normal heart rate at 6 months is up to about 160 to 170 with a systolic of about 70 to 105 · capillary refill 2 seconds or less is normal, 3 seconds is moderate to severe, and over 3 seconds is shock · dehydration is mild under 4%, moderate 4 to 6%, and severe at 7% or more — so 8.1 kg falling to 7.3 kg is 10% and severe by definition · ondansetron is 0.15 mg/kg, which is 2 mg for 8 to 15 kg, 4 mg for 15 to 30 kg and 8 mg above 30 kg, and it is used from 6 months · oral rehydration is 5 mL every one to two minutes, or 50 mL/kg over 4 hours, plus 10 mL/kg per stool and 2 mL/kg per vomit · a shock bolus is 20 mL/kg of 0.9% saline · rotavirus vaccine is given at 6 weeks and 4 months · exclusion is 24 hours, or 48 in an outbreak · review at 24 hours · and MedSTAR kids is 1300 13 12 33 VERIFY all. Her three questions and their answers: 'Should I stop breastfeeding?' → no, keep going · 'Can I give him juice or lemonade?' → no, sugary drinks make the diarrhoea worse; Hydralyte is the right one · 'Do we need antibiotics?' → no, this is a virus. And when she pushes back in version A — 'Can't we just do the Hydralyte thing at home? That's what they did with his sister' → 'For his sister, who was alert and drinking, that was right. Liam is drowsy and not keeping fluids in, and at this level a baby can get worse very quickly.' The variants. The ED setting → 'Supervised oral rehydration now: ondansetron, then 5 mL of ORS every minute by syringe with the nurses recording it; if he is not tolerating that within an hour we move to a nasogastric tube at 50 mL/kg over four hours; I'd check a glucose and electrolytes, and if he is shocked at any point, a 20 mL/kg bolus of normal saline. Reassess and REWEIGH at four hours.' The unvaccinated version — 'He hasn't had any vaccinations' → 'Thank you for telling me. Unvaccinated babies can get more severe rotavirus gastro, which fits with today. Once he's better I'd like to talk about catch-up immunisation — the rotavirus drops have an age limit, so we'll check what's still possible. Is there something that's held you back that I can help with?' Do not lecture: note it, link it to severity, and offer the conversation later — judgement here is an approach-to-patient mark. And her hidden agenda is guilt — she believes she gave him the bug by not washing her hands after looking after his sister, and she mentions it only if asked how she is coping, or at the end. The six red flags she leaves with, given as numbers: drowsy or floppy · no wet nappy for six hours · green vomit · blood in the stool · refusing all fluids · a rash that does not fade.

back.dx: TESTICULAR TORSION IN A 13-YEAR-OLD PRESENTING AS GROIN PAIN — twisting of the spermatic cord on its axis, cutting venous then arterial supply, with a peak incidence at 12 to 18 years and a second peak in neonates, affecting about 1 in 4,000 males under 25. The bell-clapper deformity, where the tunica vaginalis completely surrounds the testis, predisposes to it and is usually bilateral — which is why both sides are fixed at surgery. Pain is often felt in the groin or lower abdomen, and the AMC gives 'Groin' deliberately. The numbers: onset two hours ago against a window of about six · salvage about 90% under 6 hours and under 10% beyond 24 · an absent cremasteric reflex is the most useful sign but is preserved in 10 to 30% of torsions, so it does not exclude · Doppler sensitivity is about 85 to 95% · intranasal fentanyl 1.5 mcg/kg to a maximum of 100 mcg, or IV morphine 0.1 mg/kg · manual detorsion is 'Open book', medial to lateral · consent covers orchidopexy plus or minus orchidectomy with contralateral fixation · and MedSTAR is 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval to the women's and children's VERIFY all. The red flags in any groin-pain history: sudden severe pain in a teenager with nausea or vomiting · onset with exertion, sleep or cold · previous brief episodes that resolved, which is intermittent torsion · pain that has improved after hours, which may be infarction rather than recovery · and any groin pain in a boy where the scrotum has not been examined. Version B is the harder one: ten hours of lower abdominal and groin pain that woke him at 3 am, two vomits, and previous self-limiting episodes months ago — intermittent torsion — with an embarrassed adolescent minimising in front of his father. The opening that works: 'I can see this is uncomfortable to talk about, and I'll keep it quick. Sometimes a problem with the testicle is felt in the tummy — so I need to ask: is there any pain or swelling in the testicles or scrotum? And has this ever happened before, even for a few minutes, and then gone away?' → 'Yeah. It's the right one. It happened twice before, a few months ago — it went away after about half an hour, so I didn't say anything.' The harder explanation: 'It sounds like it has twisted briefly before and untwisted itself. This time it hasn't. Because it's been about ten hours, the chance of saving it is lower than it would have been at two hours, but not zero, and the only way to know is for the surgeon to look. Even if it can't be saved, the other one will be stitched so it can never twist, and one testicle is enough. You did nothing wrong by not mentioning the earlier episodes — but from now on, pain there is something to tell someone straight away.' The examination card in that version adds scrotal oedema and erythema with a reactive hydrocele, and a horizontal lie on the left too — the bell-clapper. And the investigation principle does not change: surgery now, a Doppler only if the surgeon wants it and it does not delay theatre, bloods for the anaesthetist on the way.

back.dx: OSMOTIC DIARRHOEA — chronic non-specific diarrhoea of childhood, or 'Toddler's diarrhoea' — loose stools in a thriving one- to five-year-old driven by excess fructose and sorbitol from juice, cordial and lollies, often with low fat and high fluid intake. Three weeks sits between acute, which is under 14 days, and chronic, which is usually over four weeks — so both acute and chronic causes stay on the list. The management, if asked, is six numbered items: juice, cordial and soft drink down to less than half a cup a day or none, with water to drink · whole fruit instead · a bit more fat — full-cream milk and yoghurt, cheese, avocado — and restart the dairy, since it was not the milk · total drinks to about a litre a day · a barrier cream for his bottom · and review in two weeks with a note of how many motions a day, coming sooner for blood, night-time motions, stopping eating or drinking, or seeming unwell. The numbers: two glasses at three meals is about six cups and over a litre a day · the juice ceiling is about 120 mL a day at 1 to 3 years, with total fluid about a litre · the four fs are fat up, fluid down, fruit juice out, fibre normal · review at two weeks · Rome IV functional diarrhoea is four or more stools a day for over four weeks between 6 and 60 months · and C. Difficile is treated with oral vancomycin and not tested under 12 months VERIFY all. Version B adds a recent antibiotic course, and the examiner is checking that the differential list did not change and that both findings were used: 'Two things are contributing. The juice is still the main driver — the sugar-and-water mechanism — but antibiotics can cause diarrhoea in two ways: as a side effect on their own, or by upsetting the balance of bugs in the bowel and letting an infection called Clostridioides difficile take hold, which is uncommon in children his age. He's finished the course, he's well, there's no blood or fever, so I'd expect it to settle with the juice change. If it doesn't, or if blood or fever appear, we'll send a stool sample for that bug and treat it if it's there.' Omitting the antibiotic when the mother has handed it to you is a missed finding — and so is dropping the juice because the antibiotic is 'More medical'. Her two hidden agendas: her mother-in-law has said she is 'Not feeding him properly' and she is braced to be blamed, which is why the no-blame framing is a mark rather than a courtesy · and she privately fears coeliac disease because a friend's child has it, raised only if you ask what she is worried about, or at the end. back.dx: NON-ORGANIC — functional — abdominal pain, which Rome IV calls 'Functional abdominal pain, not otherwise specified': episodic or continuous pain at least four times a month for at least two months, not explained by another condition. The red flags that would have changed everything, all absent here: pain waking the child from sleep or nocturnal stooling · weight loss, growth faltering or delayed puberty · blood in stool, persistent or bilious vomiting, chronic diarrhoea · dysphagia or odynophagia · fever · urinary symptoms · pain localised away from the umbilicus or perianal disease · extra-intestinal features — ulcers, rash, joint pain or limp, eye redness · pallor, bruising, lumps or tiredness suggesting leukaemia or lymphoma · and a family history of IBD, coeliac disease or peptic ulcer. If screening is wanted the set is full blood count, CRP or ESR, coeliac serology, urinalysis and possibly faecal calprotectin — offered for peace of mind, not because the findings demand it. Review at two weeks. Supports: kids helpline 1800 55 1800, parent helpline SA 1300 364 100, CARL 13 14 78, WCH via PATS, TIS 131 450 VERIFY all. The variants. Role-player: Karen, 38, a primary-school teacher. Ellie is 8, in year 3, with a brother Tom aged 5 and a farmer father Dan. Six months of pain — all over, dull, 4 to 5 out of ten, on and off, never at night, never worsening, nothing helps. About 20 days of school missed, some mornings she will not get out of bed, and weekends are better — which Karen only notices when asked.

How she plays it: frustrated and brisk at the start, softening when the doctor examines carefully and says the pain is real, and tearful when her mother is mentioned. Two doctors have said 'Probably stress' and she felt they were calling her daughter a liar — so if the doctor says 'Just stress' without explanation she asks 'That's what the others said — so she's making it up?'

She volunteers the grandmother only if asked openly about recent stress — and in version B, if asked 'Has her grandmother died?', she says 'No — why would you ask that?' Her hidden agenda is a fear of leukaemia after a colleague's child, raised only if invited, plus guilt that her own grief has made her less available to Ellie. The child is in the room, and speaking to her — 'Ellie, you're not making it up' — is part of the explanation.

The open stress question — and the recall question that fails — 'Has there been any stress in the family in the last six months or so — illness, a death, a move, separation?' → a pause, then the grandmother. Ask it by 3:15, because the psychosocial screen is what runs out of time

The two timing questions that discriminate — 'DOES IT EVER WAKE HER FROM SLEEP?' → NEVER — SHE SLEEPS FINE · 'DOES SHE GET IT ON WEEKENDS AND HOLIDAYS AS MUCH AS SCHOOL DAYS?' → '…NOW YOU MENTION IT, WEEKENDS ARE BETTER.' Both must be asked by name — she does not notice the weekend pattern until asked

The pain and its functional impact — 'Can she point with one finger, or is it all over?' → all over, sometimes here, sometimes there · 4 or 5 out of ten · dull · on and off for six months and not worsening · no radiation · nothing makes it better or worse, including food, dairy, position and opening her bowels · and the impact: about twenty days of school missed, some mornings she will not get out of bed, and she has stopped netball

The red-flag block, asked as a block — 'Some quick important questions' — weight loss or stopped growing · blood in her poo · vomiting, any green · persistent diarrhoea · fever · pain or difficulty swallowing · mouth ulcers, rashes, sore joints or limping, red eyes · pale, bruising easily, lumps in the neck or tummy, unusually tired · pain passing urine. All negative — and that is the point

Ask constipation properly — How often does she open her bowels, are they hard, does she strain, any soiling → daily, normal, no straining, no soiling. 'Bowels okay?' Misses the commonest organic cause of chronic abdominal pain in a child

The rest of the GI group, by name — Bloating and wind · travel or sick contacts · greasy stools that float or stick · anyone in the family with coeliac disease, Crohn's or colitis, or stomach ulcers · any lump in the groin · heartburn, or pain when hungry or after meals · and does dairy or any food set it off, with any rash around the mouth

Home, school and mood — 'I'd like to ask about things outside her tummy, because they matter for tummy pain in children' · how are things at home, who lives with her, how does she get on with everyone · then the stress question · then school — friends, teachers, any bullying · does she seem worried, sad or tearful · how is she sleeping → school fine and no bullying, but clingier, quieter, and broken sleep

What she tells you, and how to receive it — Version B: 'My mum was diagnosed with cancer about six months ago. She's still with us, but she's having chemo. She was very close to her. She cried a lot when we told her, and she's been quieter since' · version A: 'My mum died six months ago. They were very close' · the response: 'Thank you for telling me — I'm sorry about your mum; that's a lot for the whole family, and for her especially. That's very relevant to what's going on, and I'll come back to it'

The diagnosis — name it, and say the pain is real — 'I've examined her carefully and asked about all the warning signs, and I'M CONFIDENT THERE IS NO DISEASE OR STRUCTURAL PROBLEM in her bowel, her stomach or anywhere else. What she has is called NON-ORGANIC ABDOMINAL PAIN — some doctors say functional or stress-related pain. I WANT TO BE VERY CLEAR: THE PAIN IS REAL. SHE IS NOT MAKING IT UP. THE NERVES IN THE GUT AND THE BRAIN ARE CLOSELY CONNECTED, and when a child is under emotional strain THE GUT'S NERVES BECOME OVER-SENSITIVE AND SEND PAIN SIGNALS EVEN THOUGH NOTHING IS DAMAGED' · THEN THE SIX REASONS: PAIN ALL OVER RATHER THAN IN ONE PLACE · NEVER WAKES HER · BETTER ON WEEKENDS · GROWING NORMALLY · EXAMINATION NORMAL · NO WARNING SIGNS · AND IT BEGAN AT THE SAME TIME AS A BIG UPSET IN THE FAMILY

Differentials by group, then the plan — Bowel — a lingering gut infection, constipation, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, ulcers or reflux, a hernia, and food problems like lactose intolerance or allergy · urinary — infection or stones · gynaecological — she has not started her periods, but some girls have pain from a blockage before their first period · musculoskeletal — hip or spine problems referring pain · malignancy — leukaemia or lymphoma, with no pallor, bruising, lumps or weight loss · and abdominal migraine · then the plan: school every day with a letter you write, regular meals, sleep and sport, a chance to talk about her grandmother at home and with the school counsellor, a child psychologist, and review in two weeks

The examination request — say pallor, rash and lymph nodes — General appearance — alert, comfortable, pallor, bruising, rash, mouth ulcers · vitals and growth chart · lymph nodes — cervical, axillary, inguinal · abdomen — distension, masses, tenderness, guarding, faecal loading, liver and spleen, bowel sounds, hernial orifices, perianal inspection · hip and spine screen · urine dipstick and finger-prick glucose. findings: The four risks of the undescended testis

One, it can be injured in the groin · two, it can twist on itself, which is painful and an emergency · three, the groin is warmer than the scrotum, and a testicle needs to be cool to work properly, so fertility can be affected · four, over a lifetime there is a higher risk of testicular cancer. 'Bringing it down early lowers that risk — not to zero — and it also lets the testicle be checked easily later on.' Naming only fertility, or promising no cancer risk after surgery, is the trap

back.dx: Three diagnoses in one well 7-month-old: a 1.5 cm umbilical hernia, a right indirect inguinal hernia, and a right undescended — canalicular — testis. The definitions that keep the explanation plain: a hernia is a sac of abdominal contents protruding through a weakness in the wall · an umbilical hernia goes through the navel ring and closes spontaneously in most · an infant inguinal hernia is indirect, through a patent processus vaginalis, does not close, and needs surgery · an undescended testis has not reached the scrotum by term and cannot be brought down. The key differentials: a retractile testis can be milked into the scrotum and stays, which is normal and needs no surgery · a hydrocele transilluminates, you cannot get above it, and it usually resolves by 12 to 18 months · an ectopic testis · and bilateral impalpable testes, especially with hypospadias, which is a disorder of sex development and urgent. The numbers: the 6-2 rule is under 6 weeks to 2 days, 6 weeks to 6 months to 2 weeks, and over 6 months within 2 months · orchidopexy at 6 to 12 months and before the first birthday, with descent not expected after about 6 months · the umbilical hernia is observed to 4 years with about 95% closing by 2 to 3, and its 1.5 cm size does not change the plan · four testicular risks, one operation, two weeks to review · and TSH with free T4 VERIFY all. Supports: WCH paediatric surgery, PATS for over 100 km, MedSTAR kids 1300 13 12 33, TIS 131 450. The variants. Version B, where she is angry and asks whether to complain — 'I understand why you'd ask, and you're entitled to. At six weeks a testicle can be genuinely hard to feel, and some that were in the scrotum move up later, so I honestly can't tell you it was missed. What I can promise is that we're inside the best window now. If you'd like to raise it, I can note your concern and the practice manager can talk it through with you — and I'll make sure today's plan isn't delayed by any of that.' A three-week-old with an inguinal hernia sits in the first band of the rule — 'The surgeons want to fix this within about two days; the younger the baby, the more likely a hernia is to get stuck. I'm phoning the paediatric surgical registrar now.' if she returns at ten days with a hard red groin lump, vomiting and screaming — 'This is the trapped hernia we talked about. I'm not going to push on it. Hospital today: nil by mouth, a drip, pain relief, and MedSTAR kids for retrieval. The surgeons will try to settle it under sedation and repair it within a day or two — or operate straight away if the bowel is at risk.' if neither testis is palpable, or there is hypospadias with an impalpable testis — 'That changes the plan. This needs urgent review today by the children's hormone and surgical teams, and an ultrasound is not the answer': the disorder-of-sex-development pathway, where you do not reassure, do not circumcise, and check for a salt-losing crisis. And if the TSH comes back high — congenital hypothyroidism, very treatable with a daily tablet, seen by paediatric endocrinology that week, and the surgery still goes ahead. Her hidden agenda is that she secretly fears the missed finding means he will be infertile — raised only if you invite concerns, and otherwise at 6:30 as 'So will he be able to have kids?'

Role-player: Jenny, 29, a teacher's aide in Wallaroo with a partner working FIFO. Noah, 7 months, is her first baby, born at term, breastfed and thriving. She came about the belly-button lump that pops out when he cries; her mother says it is harmless and to tape a coin over it. She did not know about anything in the groin.

How she plays it: calm at first, with a flash of anger at 'Nobody told me' about the six-week check — settling to a no-blame explanation and escalating to 'Should I complain?' if the other doctor is blamed. She becomes tearful if cancer is mentioned bluntly, pushes once on the two-month timing, and asks about the coin if it is not pre-empted. She expects a named source for the reading material, and her secret fear is infertility, raised at 6:30 if never invited.

Open, then do not take a history — 'What brought you in today?' → THE BELLY-BUTTON LUMP THAT POPS OUT WHEN HE CRIES · 'I understand — a swelling on your baby is stressful. I'VE EXAMINED HIM CAREFULLY AND I'LL EXPLAIN EXACTLY WHAT I FOUND, WHAT IT MEANS, AND WHAT WE'LL DO. IS THERE ANYTHING SPECIFIC YOU WERE WORRIED IT MIGHT BE?' → whether it is dangerous, and whether he needs an operation. SLIDING INTO HISTORY — 'any vomiting? was he premature?' — GETS 'PLEASE STICK TO YOUR TASK'

The navel first, because it is her concern — 'That swelling is an umbilical hernia. A hernia is when a small sac from inside the tummy pokes out through a weak spot in the tummy wall. Here the weak spot is the ring at the belly button, which hasn't fully closed yet. It's very common, it's soft, it goes back in easily and it is not dangerous.' Explaining the groin before the navel is the trap — as is an anatomy lecture on direct versus indirect and the processus vaginalis

'Nobody told me at the six-week check' — 'I can hear that's upsetting. A testicle can be hard to feel at six weeks, and some move up later, so I can't say it was missed. What matters is we've found it now — and seven months is still the ideal time to fix it. Nothing has been lost for Noah.' Blaming the other doctor makes her ask 'Should I complain?' and keep pushing

'Cancer?! He's a baby' — 'I know that's a frightening word. THE RISK IS IN ADULT LIFE, IT'S SMALL, AND TREATING IT NOW IS EXACTLY HOW WE REDUCE IT. WITH ONE NORMAL TESTICLE AND THE OTHER BROUGHT DOWN EARLY, MOST BOYS HAVE NORMAL FERTILITY.' She becomes tearful if cancer is mentioned bluntly without this softening

The umbilical plan — and pre-empt the coin — 'For the belly button WE DO NOTHING EXCEPT WATCH. ABOUT 95% CLOSE ON THEIR OWN BY TWO TO THREE YEARS, SO WE'RE HAPPY TO WAIT UNTIL HE'S FOUR. If it's still there at four, A SIMPLE DAY-SURGERY CLOSES IT. IT MAY LOOK A BIT BIGGER OVER THE NEXT FEW MONTHS AS HE GROWS — THAT'S EXPECTED. And please: NO TAPE, NO COINS, NO STRAPPING — IT DOESN'T HELP AND CAN HURT THE SKIN.' Her mother has told her to tape a coin on it, and she will ask if you do not pre-empt it

The 6-2 rule, as reasoning not a memorised date — 'Surgeons time hernia repair by age: under six weeks, within about two days; six weeks to six months, within two weeks; over six months — Noah — within the next two months. That doesn't mean we wait two months; it means we have a little breathing room and the surgeon books the youngest babies first.' She pushes once: 'Two months seems a long time if it can get stuck'

One operation fixes both — 'The groin hernia and the testicle both need an operation — and it's one operation, in the groin, that fixes both. For the testicle the best window is six to twelve months, so seven months is ideal — both are done together, before his first birthday.' and yes, a general anaesthetic, usually day surgery, with the surgeon going through it

Referral, red flags, the thyroid drop, and the close — Refer today to the paediatric surgeons at the women's and children's, who will re-examine and set the date, with PATS organised for the travel · red flags to the emergency department: the groin lump bigger, hard, red or won't push back, or screaming, vomiting, or not passing poo or wind · then the drop: 'When I see more than one hernia together with an undescended testicle, I like to check the thyroid, a gland in the neck that controls growth. He had the heel-prick as a newborn — that's a screen; a simple blood test today confirms it' · and close with the Royal children's hospital fact sheets named, review in two weeks, and 'What questions do you have?'

The inguinal hernia — 'I also found TWO OTHER THINGS I NEED TO EXPLAIN. The first is A SECOND, SMALLER HERNIA IN THE GROIN — AN INGUINAL HERNIA. It forms in or around a little passage called THE INGUINAL CANAL, WHICH RUNS FROM THE TUMMY DOWN TO THE SCROTUM. That passage is MEANT TO SEAL BEFORE BIRTH; in Noah it has stayed open, so a small sac can slip into it. UNLIKE THE BELLY-BUTTON ONE, IT WON'T CLOSE BY ITSELF'

The undescended testis, with the descent story — 'I can feel only one testicle in the scrotum. The other is sitting up in the groin — an undescended testis. Before birth the testicles form inside the tummy and, near birth, travel down that same canal into the scrotum. Sometimes one doesn't finish the journey and gets stuck in the canal.' and when she asks whether it will come down: 'At seven months it won't come down on its own — after about six months we don't expect it to'

Incarceration — and the weighting is the mark — 'With any hernia the worry is that a loop of bowel slips into the sac and gets trapped — an incarcerated hernia — and if the blood supply is cut off, a strangulated hernia. The baby gets very upset, vomits, and the lump goes hard, tender and red. This is much more likely with the groin hernia and very rare with the belly-button one — which is why we treat them differently.' if she asks how she would know, park it: 'I'll give you the exact signs before you go'

The numbers: tramadol IV or IM 50 to 100 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 600 mg in 24 hours — so 50 mg IV 6 hourly PRN with 600 mg as the maximum · oxycodone subcut 7.5 to 12.5 mg every 2 hours for this age band — so 10 mg subcut 2 hourly PRN, maximum 120 mg, or 7.5 mg giving 90 mg · paracetamol, in the older version of this case, is 1 g orally 6 hourly with a maximum of 4 g in 24 hours, and never 'Qid' in the hourly-frequency box · and the sedation score runs 0 alert, 1 easy to rouse, 2 rousable but cannot stay awake, 3 difficult to rouse — with the dose held at 2 VERIFY all against the AMH and local protocol. The marking brief is blunt about what fails outright: ceasing only the PRN tramadol while the regular entry stays live · ceasing with a scribble that obliterates the order · omitting the reason, date or signature on either cease · writing 'Sc' for the route · charting the opioid as a regular order · and writing a range such as '7.5–12.5 mg' instead of one dose. Amber items, two of which together also fail: 'D/c' instead of ceased · 'Tds' in the hourly-frequency box · an empty maximum for the oxycodone · and dates written into the PRN administration record, which is the nurse's column. Choosing morphine passes, because the stem allowed either. The habit being trained, and separately noted by the marker, is the re-check before leaving: both tramadol entries ceased, reason and date and signature on both, route written as subcut, and a maximum in the box. The variants: if tramadol is charted in only one place, cease that one — but still open every face and say to yourself 'One entry only' · if the stem says 'Regular oxycodone', it becomes a page 3 order with a frequency word and times from the margin guide, which is the only time an opioid leaves the PRN box · and if you chart the new opioid in the wrong box, you cease it as 'Written in error' and re-chart rather than obliterating. The deeper point this card is worth remembering for: a chart is a legal document read by people who are not in the room. Everything that fails here fails because a nurse at 3 am could not tell what was intended — an order still live on another page, a word that might mean discharge, an abbreviation that might mean something else, or a maximum nobody set.

The administration record stays empty — NOTHING GOES IN THE ADMINISTRATION GRID — THE NURSE WRITES IT WHEN A DOSE IS GIVEN. For a REGULAR order you date the columns; FOR A PRN THE DOCTOR WRITES NO DATES AT ALL. Writing today's date in the record is the trap

Ceasing — the six things, in both places — One diagonal line through the order box, so the original stays legible · two lines crossing the administration grid · the word 'Ceased' — not D/C, not 'Stopped' · the reason · the date · and your signature. Then repeat it exactly on the other page. 'D/c' is ambiguous between discharge and discontinue, which is why ceased is the recommended word

Never obliterate, never overwrite — Scribbling the order out is a fail, and so is changing the dose on TOP of an existing order. If you needed a different dose you would cease and re-chart. The same applies to your own mistakes: one line, two lines, 'Ceased — written in error', date, sign, and re-chart in the correct box — the examiner sees a correct correction

The oxycodone PRN box — Date · medicine oxycodone · route subcut — written out, because 'Sc' is a non-approved abbreviation and a fail, even though the AMH itself abbreviates it · dose 10 mg · hourly frequency 2 hourly · max PRN dose 120 mg · indication pain · signature, print, contact · and fill the year on the PRN page. The AMH band for this age is 7.5 to 12.5 mg every 2 hours subcutaneously

The maximum where the book gives none — THE AMH GIVES NO 24-HOUR MAXIMUM FOR OXYCODONE AND NO FORMAL AUSTRALIAN RULE EXISTS. THE EXAMINER ACCEPTS MULTIPLICATION — 10 mg × 12 DOSES = 120 mg, OR 7.5 mg × 12 = 90 mg — OR A SEDATION-SCORE LIMIT, OR A RESPIRATORY-RATE LIMIT. A CHOSEN NUMBER BEATS AN EMPTY BOX. If you use 'sedation score < 2' it barely fits, so write it small and legibly or multiply instead

The serotonin syndrome answer, in forty seconds — 'This patient takes citalopram, an SSRI. Tramadol also increases serotonin, and the combination carries a significant risk of serotonin syndrome — agitation, tremor, clonus, sweating, hyperthermia, which can be life-threatening. So I have ceased tramadol, both the regular and the as-required orders, documented the reason, dated and signed it, and charted oxycodone 10 mg subcutaneously 2 hourly as required with a maximum of 120 mg in 24 hours'

'Why oxycodone rather than morphine?' — 'Both are appropriate and the stem allowed either. I chose oxycodone for its more predictable subcutaneous absorption and fewer active metabolites in a patient whose renal function I have not been given. I would ask nursing staff to check a sedation score before each dose and to hold the dose and call me if the score is 2 or more, or the respiratory rate is below 12'

Date prescribed · medicine gentamicin, generic name printed · route IV · dose 300 mg · date and time of dose — for example today at 1400, roughly the time you think it is — or the word 'Stat' · prescriber signature, small, because the box is small · and your printed name

back.dx: A ONCE-ONLY PRESCRIBING STATION — the first stat order the AMC has set — testing three things at once: that you know which box a stat dose lives in, that you can dose per kilogram within a renal band, and that the housekeeping boxes are still completed when the stem is silent. The numbers: gentamicin at CrCl above 60 is 5 to 7 mg/kg, and at CrCl 30 to 60 it is 4 to 5 mg/kg · eGFR 60 is treated as CrCl 60 for the exam · 5 mg/kg × 60 kg = 300 mg IV · the once-only box is on the front page · and the weight of 60 kg goes in the ID box VERIFY all against the AMH and local protocol. The marking brief's outright fails: charting gentamicin in the regular box for one day, which is the 2025 failing move · writing '5 mg/kg' or '300' with no unit · writing your own name as the patient · missing the ID box on the back · and leaving the VTE box blank. Omitting the weight is amber to some examiners and a fail to others, and filling in 'Given by' or 'Time given' is amber. Both 'Stat' and a date with an approximate time pass. Choosing 4 mg/kg for 240 mg, or 7 mg/kg for 420 mg, passes if the band is defensible and you can justify it — so know why you picked your number. And if you ask the examiner whether eGFR equals CrCl, they are briefed to shrug and say nothing. The variants. eGFR 45 at 80 kg puts you in the 30 to 60 band — 5 × 80 = 400 mg, or 4 × 80 = 320 mg, and you write the milligrams. 'Chart gentamicin daily for three days' makes it a regular order on page 3 with a daily frequency, a time such as 0800, three dated columns and the rest blocked — a course needing levels could sit in the variable-dose box, but for the exam a fixed daily dose for three days is regular. If you chart it as regular by mistake, the correction is one line, two lines, 'Ceased — written in error', date and signature, then re-chart in the once-only box — do not panic, because the examiner sees a correct correction. And for a one-word slip such as IM written for IV, a single line through the wrong word, initialled, with the correct word beside it is enough — full re-ordering is for anything larger. The principle underneath this station, which generalises to every chart: the box you choose is itself a clinical decision. A stat dose in the regular section reads as a course; a course in the once-only box reads as one dose; and the person who has to interpret it is not in the room with you.

back.dx: A PRESCRIBING STATION BUILT AROUND THE MEDICINES-TAKEN-PRIOR-TO-PRESENTATION BOX — the first time the AMC used it — plus transcribing home medicines as regular orders from pharmacy stickers, generic names, and withholding one drug around surgery. The numbers: perindopril 8 mg orally daily · atorvastatin 20 mg orally daily, with Lipitor on the box and the generic on the chart · aspirin 100 mg orally daily, blocked today and on the surgery day · 0800 mane and 2000 nocte · and the surgeon's rule, aspirin withheld seven days pre-operatively. The AMH maximums — perindopril 8 mg a day and atorvastatin 80 mg a day — are ceilings, not this patient's dose VERIFY all. The marking brief's outright fails: skipping the medicines-prior box · writing 'Lipitor' anywhere · charting the three only in the prior box so no inpatient orders exist · leaving aspirin open today and tomorrow, which is the point of the case · and missing the ID box on the back. Amber items, two of which together also fail: blocking aspirin for the next seven days, which is a misread worth discussing afterwards · never looking at the boxes and charting AMH maximums · writing 'Htn' or 'Ihd' instead of the indication in full · and entering no administration times. Writing 'Withhold' rather than crossing out passes, and so does also blocking perindopril and atorvastatin on the surgery day. The variants. If the stem gives the doses in words and there are no boxes, chart exactly the doses stated, and put a duration in the prior box only if one is given — 'Four years' becomes '4 years'. If a fourth drug is 'Ventolin as needed', the prior box gets salbutamol with dose and frequency blank if not given, the regular page gets nothing, and the PRN page gets salbutamol 100 micrograms by metered aerosol 4 hourly as required for asthma — or nothing at all if no dose is given and you are unsure, because you do not invent one. And if the patient is post-operative today, aspirin restarts on the surgeon's instruction only — withhold today and note 'Withhold — surgeon to review' — while VTE prophylaxis becomes a live question, with enoxaparin 40 mg subcut daily in the VTE box if the stem asks VERIFY. The principle underneath this one: a medication chart has to survive the handover. The prior box tells the pharmacist what he takes at home; the regular orders tell the nurse what to give; and the blocked columns tell both of them what not to give tomorrow morning when nobody who wrote the chart is on the ward.

Date · prednisolone · PO · 50 mg · daily · indication asthma, or COPD exacerbation · signature, print, contact · times 0800 in days one to five, because morning dosing is conventional · and days six onward crossed out. Leaving the course open-ended — a steroid with no stop date — is the fail
The salbutamol order, field by field

Date · salbutamol · MA · 100 micrograms — 200 micrograms for two puffs is also defensible · hourly frequency 4 hourly, or 1 to 4 hourly, which is accepted for salbutamol · indication asthma · signature, print, contact · and the year on the PRN page · with the administration record left completely empty

back.dx: A two-order prescribing station where the easy half is a fixed-dose steroid course and the hard half is an inhaler — generic name, metered-aerosol route, micrograms written in full, a chosen hourly frequency, the PRN box, and an honestly empty maximum. The numbers: prednisolone for asthma is 37.5 to 50 mg daily for 5 to 10 days and for COPD 40 to 50 mg daily for 5 to 14 days, with therapeutic guidelines giving 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg — so 50 mg orally daily for 5 days · salbutamol is 100 micrograms per puff, with 4 to 12 puffs, or 400 to 1200 micrograms, via spacer every 20 minutes acutely and then every 1 to 4 hours — so 100 micrograms by metered aerosol 4 hourly as required · and no 24-hour maximum for salbutamol exists VERIFY all. The marking brief's outright fails: writing 'Ventolin' · writing 'Mcg' or 'Ug' · charting salbutamol as a regular order · leaving prednisolone open-ended when the stem gave a duration · missing the ID box on the back · and leaving the VTE box blank. Amber items: putting prednisolone in the variable-dose box, which the examiner will ask about · writing 'Inh' or 'Mdi' as the route · and writing 'Every 20 min' as '20 minly'. Things that pass and are worth knowing pass: '1 puff' as the dose, which is common practice though less formal than 100 micrograms · '1 to 4 hourly' as the frequency · and an empty maximum PRN dose. The variants. A COPD exacerbation takes the same two orders with the indication changed, a course that may run to 14 days though five remains the taught default, and any antibiotic as a separate regular order with its own duration blocked. If asked to chart the acute regimen in emergency: salbutamol, MA, 1200 micrograms for 12 puffs via spacer, 'Every 20 minutes for 3 doses' written in words, for asthma — in the PRN box, or the once-only box if a single loading dose is asked — and then hand over to the 4-hourly PRN order. If a nebuliser is ordered, the route is neb and the adult dose is 5 mg, still salbutamol and still PRN unless told regular VERIFY. And if he has a maintenance inhaler at home such as budesonide with formoterol, it goes in the prior box under its generic names and on the regular page twice daily at 0800 and 2000 if the stem gives the dose — with the route as MA, or written in words for a dry-powder device, since dpi has no single approved abbreviation VERIFY. The two sentences worth having ready for the examiner: 'Salbutamol is a reliever, so it is as-required' and 'The AMH gives no maximum for salbutamol, so I have left the box empty'. And the generalisable point: the unit and the box are both clinical decisions. 'Mcg' misread as mg is a thousand-fold overdose, and a reliever in the regular section is a drug given on a schedule to someone who may not need it.

The AMH is actually useful in this one, unlike the home-medicines case: prednisolone has an indication-specific range and a duration, and salbutamol has a dose per actuation and an acute-versus-maintenance frequency. Open it at both drugs rather than working from memory.

The four things the marker is watching for are all visible at a glance: the word in the medicine column · the unit on the dose · which page the reliever is on · and whether the steroid course has an end.

A fixed dose is a regular order — Prednisolone at the same dose every day goes in the regular box, not the variable-dose box — that one is for tapers, where the dose changes. 'Steroids go in the variable-dose box' is the trap, and the examiner will ask why

The dose and the duration — The AMH gives asthma 37.5 to 50 mg once daily for 5 to 10 days and COPD 40 to 50 mg for 5 to 14 days; therapeutic guidelines' 1 mg/kg to a maximum of 50 mg lands in the same place. Choose 50 mg for 5 days — 40 or 37.5 mg also pass
Ventolin is a brand — WRITE SALBUTAMOL. The stem uses the brand name deliberately, AND WRITING 'VENTOLIN' IN THE MEDICINE COLUMN IS AN OUTRIGHT FAIL
A reliever is always PRN — A short-acting beta-agonist goes in the PRN box on the back page. Charting salbutamol as a regular order is a fail

The unit is the other outright fail — Dose per actuation is 100 micrograms, and you write '100 micrograms' in full — or 'Microg'. Never 'Mcg' and never 'Ug': 'Mcg' reads as mg on paper, which is a thousand-fold error
The route — The taught abbreviation is MA for metered aerosol. 'Inh' or 'Mdi' is an amber mark — use MA, or write the route in words

The empty max-dose box, and why — Leave the maximum PRN dose empty and be ready to say why: 'The AMH gives no maximum for salbutamol, so I have left the box empty' — because in a severe attack 12 puffs every 20 minutes may be needed. This is the one PRN box where empty is the correct answer rather than a gap

The acute regimen has no abbreviation — The AMH adult line is 4 to 12 puffs — 400 to 1200 micrograms — via spacer every 20 to 30 minutes initially, then every 1 to 4 hours. If you chart the acute regimen you must write 'Every 20 minutes' in words, because there is no abbreviation for it — '20 minly' is an amber mark

The medicines-prior box, if he uses it at home — If the stem says he uses Ventolin at home: salbutamol in the prior box with dose and frequency blank unless given, then sign, print and date. Do not invent 'Two puffs four hourly' if the stem did not say it

The four-point re-check — 'NOT VENTOLIN — YES. NOT mcg — YES. PRN, NOT REGULAR — YES. PREDNISOLONE BLOCKED AFTER FIVE DAYS — YES.' Plus the back ID box and the VTE box, both of which fail on their own if left
