ask: THE HONEST REASSURANCE: 'I want to answer that properly rather than quickly. Of all the cancers a person can be told they have, this is one of the most treatable there is. The great majority of people with this are cured and go on to live a completely normal length of life. I am not saying that to soften it — I am saying it because it is true.' SHE REPLIES 'but it is still cancer' → 'It is. BOTH OF THOSE THINGS ARE TRUE AT ONCE.'

THE PERMISSION LINE: 'Would you rather we talked about what happens next another day, and just stop here for now?' THE SIGNPOST INTO TASK THREE: 'There is one more thing I want to make sure we cover, because it is important and people often are not told it properly. What the treatment itself means for you.'

THE SHARED-DECISION PHRASE ON SURGERY: 'the surgeon will go through that with you RATHER THAN DECIDING AT YOU.' THE THYROXINE SENTENCE: 'It is one tablet, it is cheap, and people live completely normally on it — BUT YOU SHOULD HEAR IT FROM ME NOW RATHER THAN FIND OUT LATER.'
pefe: THE ONLY EXAMINATION IN THE STATION IS THE ONE YOU DESCRIBE RATHER THAN PERFORM: NECK EXAMINATION PLUS ULTRASOUND, AND IT COMES FIRST. Say why — it looks at the gland and at the glands around it, and it changes the operation, because a node found after surgery means a second operation.

THE FOLLOW-UP INVESTIGATION WORTH EXPLAINING RATHER THAN NAMING: THYROGLOBULIN is made by thyroid cells, so once the gland is gone the level should be very low. A RISING LEVEL MEANS RESIDUAL OR RECURRENT DISEASE and prompts a radioiodine scan. Naming the test without explaining why it works is recitation; explaining it is understanding.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: never said 'cancer' · delivered management over the top of the crying · never reached the consequences · told her thyroxine was a short course · promised categorically that she would be cured.

Two sentences on what it is, then stop — 'Your results have confirmed a condition called PAPILLARY THYROID CARCINOMA — WHICH IS A TYPE OF THYROID CANCER. The thyroid is the butterfly-shaped gland at the front of your neck.' Then one more: 'Papillary is the most common type, and it is the type we know the most about treating.' NOBODY NEEDS TO KNOW WHY IT IS CALLED PAPILLARY or how it differs from follicular — a histology lecture here is a marked failure

You are allowed to reassure — after the emotion, never instead of it — 'I want to say something, and I want you to know I am NOT SAYING IT TO MAKE YOU FEEL BETTER. Of all the cancers a person can be told they have, THIS IS ONE OF THE MOST TREATABLE THERE IS. Most people with this are cured, live a completely normal length of life, and the main thing they are left with is a tablet every morning.' In most bad-news stations optimism is a trap; HERE THE HONEST ANSWER IS A REASSURING ONE — but never 'you'll be fine', which she is briefed to reject with 'you can't know that'

The permission line, needed more here than anywhere — She is briefed to CRY LONGER THAN YOU EXPECT and not to settle at the first empathic line. At about four minutes: 'WOULD YOU RATHER WE TALKED ABOUT WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ANOTHER DAY, AND WE JUST STOP HERE FOR NOW?' She almost always says no, tell me now — THAT IS THE POINT OF ASKING. If you never offer, she keeps crying and lets the station run out: that is the failure being tested

Management in four steps, in this order — ONE — EXAMINE THE NECK AND ULTRASOUND IT FIRST, to map the gland and the nodes, BECAUSE A NODE FOUND AFTER THE OPERATION MEANS A SECOND OPERATION. TWO — SURGERY, NAMING BOTH lobectomy and total thyroidectomy, with the decision shared with the surgeon. THREE — RADIOACTIVE IODINE, possible not certain, and say WHY it works: thyroid cells take up iodine. FOUR — FOLLOW-UP WITH THYROGLOBULIN, made by thyroid cells, so once the gland is gone the level should be very low; if it stays up, cells remain and you scan to find them

The three consequences — all come from what sits behind the gland — ONE, THE NERVE: 'a nerve runs very close behind the thyroid and controls the VOICE BOX — small risk it is bruised or damaged, and your voice can become hoarse or weak. Sometimes that settles; occasionally it is permanent.' Say VOICE BOX to her and RECURRENT LARYNGEAL NERVE to the examiner. TWO, THE TABLET: 'if the whole gland comes out your body can no longer make thyroid hormone, so we replace it with thyroxine, one a day, first thing. THAT IS NOT A COURSE OF TREATMENT. THAT IS FOR THE REST OF YOUR LIFE' — patients routinely leave thinking it is a course. THREE, THE CALCIUM: four tiny glands behind the thyroid control blood calcium, can be bruised or removed, and TINGLING AROUND THE MOUTH AND IN THE FINGERS is the symptom to report

'I teach. I teach year threes' — the hidden agenda, offered once — Her voice is her livelihood, and she says it ONCE, in the middle of the consequences. A candidate reciting the three consequences as a list talks straight past it — and she then goes quiet and answers in one word for the rest of the station. PICK IT UP: 'then that matters a great deal, and I want you to raise it with the surgeon directly — they look for the nerve deliberately during the operation'

stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 30-year-old man who has come to you asking about haemochromatosis.
His brother has recently been diagnosed, and his brother's GP advised that family members should be screened. He has no symptoms. 8 minutes.

A single wide task — which is an invitation, not a constraint. The examiner wants the condition, the complications, the clinical features, the diagnosis, the treatment, the inheritance and the lifestyle advice. Cover all of it, unhurried.
tasks: Counsel the patient regarding the condition and the management plan
time: No bad news · no emotional set piece · no time pressure, and if anything you will have time spare · work the content checklist out loud and go slowly — the only way to fail is to be brief
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: The complications — and at 30 it is not only the liver

LIVER: raised enzymes, hepatomegaly, eventually CIRRHOSIS, which carries a risk of LIVER CANCER — the most important. JOINTS: arthritis characteristically IN THE HANDS, often the first symptom people notice. PANCREAS: diabetes, the old name 'bronze diabetes'. HEART: cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. HORMONAL: ERECTILE DYSFUNCTION and reduced libido, common in men and rarely volunteered. SKIN: bronze or slate-grey discolouration. GENERAL: fatigue. NAMING ONLY CIRRHOSIS IS A COMMON THIN ANSWER — at 30 the joints and the sexual function are what he will actually notice

back.dx: AT-RISK ASYMPTOMATIC FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVE OF A MAN WITH HEREDITARY HAEMOCHROMATOSIS. Uncommon in many parts of the world but RELATIVELY COMMON IN POPULATIONS OF NORTHERN EUROPEAN ANCESTRY and therefore in Australia, which is why candidates trained elsewhere often meet it for the first time here. CORRECTION — DO NOT PRESCRIBE A LOW-IRON DIET: candidates instinctively tell these patients to stop eating red meat. Reducing dietary iron does modestly reduce how often venesection is needed, BUT THE EFFECT IS SMALL, THE DIET IS HARD TO SUSTAIN, AND IT DOES NOT REPLACE VENESECTION — imposing it on a well man is an unnecessary burden with little benefit, and the role-player is briefed to look dismayed and say 'for the rest of my life?', which is a scored error. Examiner challenge 'should he avoid red meat?' → 'I would not put him on a restrictive low-iron diet — the benefit is marginal and venesection does the work. WHAT I WOULD ADVISE is avoiding iron and high-dose vitamin C supplements, and minimising alcohol, because THE LIVER IS WHAT WE ARE PROTECTING.' ADDED — RAW SHELLFISH is best avoided, because of VIBRIO VULNIFICUS infection, which is more severe in iron overload VERIFY. ASSESSING WHETHER DAMAGE HAS ALREADY OCCURRED, which the source omits: LIVER FUNCTION TESTS and examination for HEPATOMEGALY · FASTING GLUCOSE OR HbA1c for diabetes · ECHOCARDIOGRAM if there are cardiac symptoms or signs · A MARKEDLY RAISED FERRITIN, with a commonly quoted concern threshold above 1000 µg/L VERIFY, raised liver enzymes or hepatomegaly raise the possibility of CIRRHOSIS and may prompt elastography or biopsy · where cirrhosis is established, HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA SURVEILLANCE is indicated. INHERITANCE, EXPLAINED WITHOUT A PUNNETT SQUARE: 'It is AUTOSOMAL RECESSIVE. Everyone has two copies of each gene, one from each parent. To be at real risk you generally need a faulty copy FROM BOTH. If you have only one you are a CARRIER — very unlikely to have problems yourself, but you can pass it on.' THEN WHAT IT MEANS FOR HIM: 'Because your brother has it, BOTH YOUR PARENTS MUST CARRY AT LEAST ONE FAULTY COPY, which means each of their children has a meaningful chance of having inherited two — which is exactly why you have been asked to come in.' IF HE ASKS FOR A NUMBER, the classical figure for two carrier parents is ONE IN FOUR per child VERIFY — give it if asked, do not lead with arithmetic. WHO ELSE SHOULD BE TESTED: ALL FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVES of the diagnosed brother — the other siblings, and the parents if living · HIS OWN CHILDREN, BUT NOT YET, because this is an ADULT-ONSET condition with an entirely effective adult treatment, so testing is deferred to adulthood rather than done in childhood VERIFY · HIS PARTNER, if the question is the risk to their children, since a child is only at high risk if both parents carry it · SECOND-DEGREE RELATIVES are a case-by-case decision and are not routinely covered. THE LINE FOR THE FOUR-YEAR-OLD, WHICH IS HIS REAL REASON FOR COMING: 'The honest answer is that THERE IS NO URGENCY. This does not cause problems in childhood, and the treatment works just as well whenever we find it. So the usual approach is to test them AS ADULTS rather than now — and if you would find it useful, we can talk it through again when they are older.' HIS SECONDARY WORRY, RAISED ONLY IF YOU ASK ABOUT CONCERNS A SECOND TIME: whether a genetic result affects LIFE INSURANCE. CONFIRM EVERY THRESHOLD AND INTERVAL HERE AGAINST CURRENT AUSTRALIAN GUIDANCE BEFORE QUOTING IT; the RACGP has an accessible summary VERIFY.
plan: OPEN ON HIS BROTHER, NOT ON A LECTURE: 'I can see your brother has recently been diagnosed — can you tell me a bit more about what has brought you in?'
TWO QUESTIONS BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN ANYTHING: 'is there anything in particular you are worried about today?' and 'how much do you already know about it?' THE HIDDEN AGENDA LIVES IN THE FIRST.
REASSURE EARLY — found before it does damage, the treatment is simple and prevents essentially all of this. THEN the content lands differently.
THE CONDITION: too much absorbed, no route out, builds up over decades, men earlier than women, and why he is well now.
THE COMPLICATIONS, ALL SEVEN: liver and cirrhosis with liver cancer risk · joints · diabetes · heart · sexual function · skin · fatigue.
DIAGNOSIS IN ORDER: iron studies — ferritin and transferrin saturation — THEN the HFE gene test, C282Y and H63D. And the Medicare point.
GENE IS NOT DISEASE. Say it explicitly, and say that treatment follows iron loading rather than genotype.
TREATMENT: venesection, how, HOW OFTEN and FOR HOW LONG, then chelation named as second line.
LIFESTYLE, PRECISELY: alcohol · no vitamin C supplements · no iron supplements · AND EXPLICITLY NO LOW-IRON DIET.
FAMILY: autosomal recessive in plain words · the other siblings and his mother · his daughter as an adult, with the reason.
ARRANGE IT: blood test booked TODAY, a results appointment booked, written information.
TEACH-BACK: 'what will you tell your wife tonight?'

ask: THE REFRAME: 'This is one of the very few serious conditions where, if we find it before it has done damage, the treatment is simple, cheap, and prevents essentially all of the complications. You are thirty and you are well. That is the best possible position to be in.'

THE GENE-VERSUS-DISEASE LINE: 'If the gene test is positive, that does NOT mean you have the condition today. It means you are at risk of developing it. Plenty of people carrying those genes never develop a problem at all.' ON THRESHOLDS, IF PRESSED: 'I would interpret them against the reporting laboratory's reference range and current guidance rather than quote a figure from memory.'

THE DIET ANSWER: 'No, and I am glad you asked, because people often assume that. A strict low-iron diet makes surprisingly little difference and it is miserable to stick to. Taking blood off does the work. Eat normally.' THE CHILD: 'Not yet, and there is no urgency at all — the usual approach is to test as an adult.'
pefe: THERE IS NO EXAMINATION TASK, AND THE 'FINDINGS' ARE WHAT HE TELLS YOU: NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL, brother diagnosed at 36 on blood tests, mother alive and well, father died three years ago, one sister aged 33, around six to eight beers on a Saturday, a multivitamin he has never checked the label of.

ASK THE SYMPTOM SCREEN ANYWAY AND ASK IT PROPERLY — joints, fatigue, and sexual function, which he will answer 'no, nothing like that' to, but which shows you know what iron overload does to a 30-year-old man rather than only what it does to a liver.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: told him a positive gene test means he has the disease · sent the genetic test before iron studies · prescribed a restrictive low-iron diet · never asked what he already knew or what worried him · finished substantially early with the content list incomplete.

The sentence that reframes the whole consultation — say it early — 'I want to say something up front, because it changes how you should hear everything else. THIS IS ONE OF THE VERY FEW SERIOUS CONDITIONS WHERE, IF WE FIND IT BEFORE IT HAS DONE DAMAGE, THE TREATMENT IS SIMPLE, CHEAP, AND PREVENTS ESSENTIALLY ALL OF THE COMPLICATIONS. That is why your brother's doctor asked you to come in. You are thirty and you are well — that is the best possible position to be in.' Without this counterweight, the complication list is just a catalogue of organ failure

What it is, and why he feels perfectly well — 'The body absorbs too much iron from food and then CANNOT GET RID OF THE EXCESS — there is no real way for the body to excrete what it does not need, so over many years it builds up and deposits in organs.' WHY MEN EARLIER: women lose iron every month through their periods; men have no route out at all. WHY HE IS WELL: 'the iron has to build up for a long time, so people are usually completely well until somewhere between THIRTY AND SIXTY. BEING WELL NOW TELLS US NOTHING EITHER WAY — which is exactly why we test rather than wait for symptoms'

Two steps in order — and the Medicare point — STEP ONE, IRON STUDIES: FERRITIN, how much iron is in storage, and TRANSFERRIN SATURATION, how loaded the carrying protein is. BOTH RAISED is the pattern that takes you to step two. STEP TWO, THE HFE GENE TEST: two faults, C282Y AND H63D, AND C282Y IS THE IMPORTANT ONE — homozygous C282Y carries the highest risk of iron overload; H63D alone or one of each carries much lower risk and usually means monitoring. SENDING THE GENETIC TEST FIRST SKIPS THE CHEAPER, FASTER AND MORE INFORMATIVE TEST. 'Because your brother has been diagnosed, THIS TEST IS COVERED BY MEDICARE FOR YOU' — practical, reassuring and specific VERIFY

Correction — the genotype is not the disease — The source moves briskly from two copies of C282Y to lifelong venesection, and that OVERSTATES IT for a well 30-year-old. A SUBSTANTIAL PROPORTION OF C282Y HOMOZYGOTES NEVER DEVELOP CLINICALLY SIGNIFICANT IRON OVERLOAD. Genotype identifies RISK; IRON STUDIES OVER TIME determine whether and when treatment starts. SAY IT OUT LOUD: 'If the gene test comes back positive, THAT DOES NOT MEAN YOU HAVE THE CONDITION TODAY. It means you are at risk of developing it. What we would do is keep an eye on your iron levels, and only start treatment if and when they start climbing.' Examiner challenge 'would you start venesection on a positive genotype?' → 'No. I would TREAT ON IRON LOADING, NOT GENOTYPE — penetrance is incomplete'

Venesection, and the three lifestyle points said precisely — 'WE TAKE BLOOD OFF, THE SAME WAY AS DONATING. The body then uses up its stored iron to make new red cells.' INITIALLY FREQUENT, OFTEN WEEKLY, until ferritin reaches target · THEN MAINTENANCE EVERY ONE TO THREE MONTHS, guided by ferritin · LIFELONG, with ongoing monitoring · often done through LIFEBLOOD in Australia so the blood is used VERIFY. CHELATION IS SECOND LINE, for those who cannot tolerate venesection. LIFESTYLE: MINIMISE ALCOHOL, the most important point, because this is fundamentally a liver disease · NO HIGH-DOSE VITAMIN C SUPPLEMENTS, which increase iron absorption · NO IRON SUPPLEMENTS OR IRON-CONTAINING MULTIVITAMINS, check the label. DO NOT PRESCRIBE A LOW-IRON DIET

setting: The first ninety seconds are spent not talking, and that is the intervention, not wasted time. Then hold the line between blame and exoneration without becoming defensive. The station puts you between two cliffs and the role-player is briefed to push you towards both in turn — the appeaser who admits a mistake he is not in a position to admit, and the defender who protects the institution so hard he never hears the man in front of him.
stem: A 45-year-old woman underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy four hours ago. Post-operatively she has had a drop in her blood pressure and a drop in her haemoglobin, and has already been transfused.

The surgical team suspect a slipped clip from the cystic artery and she is being taken back to theatre for an open exploration to find and stop the bleeding. Her partner is outside and is angry. He wants to speak to a doctor. 8 minutes.

There is no examination, no investigation and no management plan to deliver. A pure communication assessment, in circulation since around 2017–2018 VERIFY. Almost no knowledge in it — a slipped clip, a return to theatre, and four questions.

back.dx: POST-OPERATIVE HAEMORRHAGE FROM A SLIPPED CYSTIC ARTERY CLIP, RETURNING TO THEATRE FOR OPEN EXPLORATION. There is almost no medicine in this station, and people fail it because they PANIC WHEN THE ROLE-PLAYER STARTS SHOUTING and then either apologise for something that was not negligent or defend the surgeon so hard they stop listening. THE TWO CLIFFS. THE APPEASER: 'you're right, I'm so sorry, it shouldn't have happened, I'll make sure someone is held accountable' — it FEELS KIND, and it is an admission of fault the candidate is not in a position to make about an event they did not witness. It is also UNTRUE, since a slipped clip is a recognised complication rather than negligence, AND IT SETS THE FAMILY UP FOR A GRIEVANCE THAT HAS NO FOUNDATION. THE DEFENDER: 'no, no, the surgeon is very experienced, these things happen, there's no problem here at all' — technically accurate and COMPLETELY DEAF; he has not been heard, his wife is bleeding, and the doctor is protecting the institution, so the role-player escalates. OPEN DISCLOSURE, WHICH THE SOURCE NEVER NAMES: the process of communicating openly with a patient or family when something goes wrong in their care. Its elements are AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT that something has happened · AN EXPRESSION OF REGRET, INCLUDING THE WORDS 'I AM SORRY' · A FACTUAL EXPLANATION of what is known and what is not yet known · AN EXPLANATION OF THE CONSEQUENCES and what is being done · A DESCRIPTION OF WHAT WILL BE DONE TO REVIEW IT. CRUCIALLY, AN EXPRESSION OF REGRET IS NOT AN ADMISSION OF LIABILITY, AND OPEN DISCLOSURE EXPLICITLY DOES NOT REQUIRE YOU TO ATTRIBUTE BLAME. If an examiner asks what framework you are working within → 'I'd be following OPEN DISCLOSURE principles — acknowledge what's happened, say I'm sorry it's happened, explain what we know and what we don't yet, and tell him what will be reviewed. That doesn't require me to attribute blame, and it doesn't stop me being honest.' Examiner challenge 'wasn't she consented?' → 'She will have been, and there'll be a signed form — but I DIDN'T TAKE THE CONSENT MYSELF, so I'd describe the process rather than claim to know what was said.' SAY 'WE THINK': nobody knows for certain until the surgeon looks, and OVERSTATING CERTAINTY TO A RELATIVE WHO LATER HEARS SOMETHING DIFFERENT IS HOW TRUST IS DESTROYED. ON PROGNOSIS: 'I CAN'T PROMISE YOU AN OUTCOME AND I WON'T. What I can tell you is that this was found early, she's stable enough for surgery, and this is an operation the team does to control exactly this kind of bleeding. Those things are all in her favour.' HIS HIDDEN AGENDA: he is not actually litigious. He is TERRIFIED AND HAS BEEN MADE TO FEEL INVISIBLE FOR FOUR HOURS, and underneath he feels GUILTY — he pushed her to have the operation because he was sick of watching her in pain. He gives it only if you ask an open question about how HE is, or near the end if you have handled him well: 'I talked her into having this done, you know.' THE BRIEFED SIGNAL THAT YOU HAVE PASSED is 'sorry for shouting at you' — do not answer 'that's alright' and walk off; close properly, confirm where you will find him, and make your commitments clear. THREE PRACTICE CARDS, SAME SKILL AT DIFFERENT HEAT: THE ACCUSER, who names the surgeon, says he has looked her up online and demands a different one — tests refusing to discuss a colleague's competence without sounding evasive, redirecting to what is happening now and offering the formal route · THE THREAT, who says he will sue and demands your name and the surgeon's — tests giving your name calmly and NOT LETTING A LEGAL THREAT CHANGE HOW MUCH YOU EXPLAIN · THE COLLAPSE, where anger turns to sobbing halfway through, 'I can't lose her too, I lost my brother last year' — tests switching from de-escalation to breaking-bad-news empathy mid-station: tissues, silence, and STOP DELIVERING FACTS.
plan: INTRODUCE, MOVE SOMEWHERE PRIVATE, OFFER A SEAT: 'tell me what's happened from your side.' Then stop talking.
HE RUNS HOT FOR A MINUTE OR MORE. Nod. Wait. Do not correct him. Do not explain. He will end with 'well? Say something.'
NAME THE FEELING BEFORE ANY FACT — the four hours, the routine operation, nobody telling him why.
THE SAFE APOLOGY: 'I'm very sorry this has happened.' Then ASK PERMISSION to explain.
THE EXPLANATION IN FOUR SENTENCES: the clip · it has worked loose · how the falling BP and haemoglobin told us · the transfusion already given.
QUESTION ONE — why did this happen: uncommon, but a RECOGNISED COMPLICATION that can happen when everything is done properly.
QUESTION TWO — was this a mistake: serious, not minimised, NOT A MISTAKE, picked up quickly. Do not appease and do not lecture.
QUESTION THREE — should we have been told: describe the CONSENT PROCESS, and say plainly you were not in that room.
QUESTION FOUR — what happens next: open incision rather than keyhole and WHY, blood already given, close monitoring afterwards.
'IS SHE GOING TO BE ALRIGHT?' — honest uncertainty plus what is in her favour. Never a promised outcome.
THE COMMITMENTS: your update · the surgeon · the patient liaison officer · where to wait · and offer to call someone for him.
ACKNOWLEDGE THE FOUR HOURS WITH NO INFORMATION, pick up the guilt if he offers it, check for remaining questions, and close properly.

pefe: THERE IS NOTHING TO EXAMINE AND NOTHING TO INVESTIGATE. THE 'FINDINGS' ARE THE FOUR HOURS HE HAS SPENT IN A CORRIDOR AND THE BAG OF BLOOD HE SAW RUNNING INTO HER AS SHE WAS WHEELED PAST. Read the situation rather than the patient: he is frightened, it is coming out as rage, and he has decided somebody made a mistake and wants a name.

THE CLINICAL FACTS YOU DO HAVE, AND THE ONLY ONES YOU NEED: laparoscopic cholecystectomy four hours ago · falling blood pressure · falling haemoglobin · already transfused · suspected slipped cystic artery clip · going back for OPEN exploration, because the surgeon needs to see the area properly.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: interrupted the opening and never recovered · admitted a mistake or promised someone would be held accountable · blamed a named colleague · defended the team without ever acknowledging his distress · promised his wife would be fine · left him with no commitment, no timeframe and nowhere to wait.

Move one — let him vent, and do not interrupt — He will be loud, he may swear, he may accuse you personally. DO NOT INTERRUPT · DO NOT CORRECT A FACTUAL ERROR · DO NOT START EXPLAINING. Anger burns out faster when it meets no resistance, and EVERY INTERRUPTION RESETS IT — the role-player is briefed to ESCALATE FOR THE REST OF THE STATION if you cut across his opening run. The commonest failure is starting to explain within the first fifteen seconds. Open with almost nothing: 'I'm Dr —, one of the doctors here. Please, SIT DOWN — tell me what's happened from your side.' Move somewhere private, offer water: THESE ARE SCORED BEHAVIOURS, NOT STAGE DIRECTIONS

Move two — acknowledge before you explain, then the safe apology — 'I can see how frightened you are, AND I'D BE EXACTLY THE SAME. You brought her in for a routine operation this morning and now she's going back to theatre and nobody's told you why. That's an awful position to be in.' THEN: 'I'M VERY SORRY THIS HAS HAPPENED' — an apology for the SITUATION, not an admission of fault. It is always safe, and WITHHOLDING IT MAKES YOU LOOK COLD. Then ask permission: 'can I explain what we think has happened?' — a small move that hands him control in a situation where he has none

The explanation, in four sentences and no jargon — WHAT WAS DONE: 'the small artery that supplies the gallbladder has to be sealed off, and we do that with a SMALL METAL CLIP.' WHAT HAPPENED: 'WE THINK the clip has worked loose, and that artery has started bleeding inside her abdomen.' HOW WE KNEW: 'after any operation WE WATCH THE BLOOD PRESSURE AND OBSERVATIONS VERY CLOSELY FOR EXACTLY THIS REASON' — which reframes the drop from a disaster into a system doing its job. WHAT IS DONE: transfusion already given, stable enough for surgery. CYSTIC ARTERY, HAEMOSTASIS AND HAEMODYNAMIC INSTABILITY HAVE NO PLACE IN THIS CONVERSATION

Question two is the station — 'Was this a mistake?' — THREE THINGS HELD TOGETHER IN ONE ANSWER: 'This is a serious thing to have happened and I'M NOT GOING TO PRETEND OTHERWISE. But it isn't a mistake — IT'S ONE OF THE RECOGNISED COMPLICATIONS of this operation, and it can happen when everything has been done properly. What I can promise you is that IT WAS PICKED UP QUICKLY, she's being treated now, and I'll keep you informed at every stage.' Agreeing that someone erred is an AUTOMATIC FAIL; so is defending the team so vigorously that you stop listening to him

Question three — describe the process, do not vouch for the conversation — CORRECTION: the source suggests saying you believe his partner was already told. THAT STEPS A FRACTION TOO FAR — you know what the consent process involves, YOU DO NOT KNOW WHAT WAS SAID IN THAT ROOM, and being contradicted later is exactly how a complaint becomes a formal one. THE SAFER CONSTRUCTION: 'Before any operation the surgeon goes through the possible complications, gives written information, and takes a signed consent form that lists them. SO IT SHOULD HAVE BEEN COVERED. But I wasn't in that conversation, and I'M NOT GOING TO TELL YOU WHAT WAS SAID IN A ROOM I WASN'T IN. If you'd like, I can find the consent form and go through it with you'

What to commit to before he leaves — words alone will not do it — AN UPDATE AFTER THEATRE, and then keep it · A CONVERSATION WITH THE SURGEON · A PATIENT LIAISON OFFICER if he wants his concerns formally recorded · SOMEWHERE TO WAIT, and a phone number if he has to leave · HIS RIGHT TO MAKE A COMPLAINT, because offering it is not a concession, it is respect, AND IT DEFUSES FAR MORE THAN IT INVITES · ANYONE HE WANTS CALLED — he has been alone in a corridor for four hours. 'I want you to have SOMETHING CONCRETE RATHER THAN JUST REASSURANCE'
fails: ★ Starts explaining within the first fifteen seconds, interrupts the opening run, or corrects a factual error — the role-player then escalates for the whole station
★ Admits a mistake or promises someone will be held accountable — an admission of fault about an event you did not witness, for something that is a recognised complication
Defends the surgeon without ever acknowledging his distress, or answers all four questions in one reassuring paragraph and loses three of them
Vouches for a consent conversation you were not in, uses jargon like cystic artery or haemodynamic instability, or overstates certainty instead of saying 'we think'
Promises an outcome, or leaves him with no update, no named person, nowhere to wait and nobody called

Framework and services to name: open disclosure · the patient liaison officer or equivalent for formal concerns · the surgeon to speak to him after theatre · a quiet room and a phone number · an offer to call family · VERIFY the local title for the liaison role and the current open disclosure standard before quoting them

setting: Hearing 'I can't look after him' as information rather than as a failing — and answering it with a concrete plan. Two opposite responses fail. The moralist says 'He's your father, family support is important', the role-player shuts down, and the rest of the station happens without any honesty in it. The deaf takes a textbook dementia history, delivers a textbook plan, and never returns to what the son said — everything correct, task two never attempted.
stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 65-year-old man recently diagnosed with alzheimer disease. A CT brain showed mild cerebral atrophy and his MMSE was 25.
His son has come with him to discuss what happens next. 8 minutes.

The son does not want to look after his father, and he will not open with that — it surfaces in the open question or when you ask what is worrying him. Underneath: the relationship was never good, the patient's wife died nine months ago, and the patient is now depressed.

Address the son's concerns
Explain your management plan

back.dx: ALZHEIMER DISEASE, RECENTLY DIAGNOSED, WITH CARER STRAIN AND UNTREATED DEPRESSION. THE PASS RESPONSE TO THE REFUSAL: 'Thank you for being honest with me — that's genuinely MORE USEFUL than if you'd said yes and then couldn't manage it. A lot of people in your position feel they're supposed to say yes. MY JOB ISN'T TO PERSUADE YOU. It's to work out what your dad needs and GET IT FROM SOMEWHERE OTHER THAN YOU.' Then prove it with the assessment, the services, the respite and the helplines, because WORDS ALONE WILL NOT DO IT. AND THE SON IS A PATIENT TOO: he has also been bereaved and nobody has asked him — 'can I ask how YOU are doing? You lost your mum nine months ago as well.' CARER GATEWAY EXISTS FOR HIM, NOT FOR HIS FATHER, and offering it is the thing that most visibly changes the role-player's demeanour. INVESTIGATIONS TO EXCLUDE REVERSIBLE CAUSES, because dementia is a diagnosis that requires the treatable mimics to be excluded: TSH · LIVER FUNCTION TESTS · VITAMIN B12 AND FOLATE · UEC, CALCIUM, GLUCOSE · FULL BLOOD COUNT · GDS-15 · neuroimaging, already done · consider syphilis and HIV serology if indicated. THE SUPPORT SYSTEM AS IT NOW STANDS: MY AGED CARE 1800 200 422 is still the entry point, an assessment determines the level of need, and support is then provided under SUPPORT AT HOME, which can include personal care, cleaning and shopping, meals, nursing, allied health, home modifications and equipment, and respite. IF NEEDS EXCEED WHAT CAN BE SAFELY PROVIDED AT HOME, RESIDENTIAL AGED CARE IS ASSESSED SEPARATELY — frame that as a legitimate outcome, not a failure VERIFY. THE TEAM: GP coordinating with a GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement · geriatrician or memory clinic · practice nurse · pharmacist for a HOME MEDICINES REVIEW, deprescribing anticholinergics and benzodiazepines · OT for home safety · physiotherapist for falls · dietitian · SOCIAL WORKER for the family situation · AUDIOLOGY AND OPTOMETRY, because vision and hearing are MODIFIABLE DEMENTIA RISK FACTORS. CORRECTION — DONEPEZIL IS NOT 'THE BEST': the cholinesterase inhibitors DONEPEZIL, RIVASTIGMINE AND GALANTAMINE have broadly COMPARABLE MODEST EFFICACY, and choice is driven by tolerability, comorbidity and formulation. MEMANTINE is used in moderate to severe disease. PBS listing carries authority requirements including baseline cognitive assessment and demonstrated response. Benefits are MODEST AND SYMPTOMATIC — say so honestly. Gastrointestinal side effects and bradycardia are the common problems, initiation is usually specialist, and ANTIPSYCHOTICS ARE NOT FIRST-LINE for behavioural symptoms and carry INCREASED MORTALITY IN DEMENTIA VERIFY. DRIVING: assessment is against AUSTROADS ASSESSING FITNESS TO DRIVE (2022), and SOUTH AUSTRALIA IS THE ONE STATE WITH MANDATORY REPORTING — under s 148 of the MOTOR VEHICLES ACT 1959 a health professional must report a patient to the REGISTRAR OF MOTOR VEHICLES where there is reasonable cause to believe a physical or mental condition is likely to endanger the public if they drive; elsewhere in Australia reporting is discretionary. BUT A DEMENTIA DIAGNOSIS DOES NOT AUTOMATICALLY END A LICENCE — Austroads is explicit that it requires ASSESSMENT AND ONGOING PERIODIC REVIEW, and an OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY DRIVING ASSESSMENT is often the practical next step VERIFY. CAPACITY AND PLANNING: capacity is DECISION-SPECIFIC AND ASSESSED AT THE TIME, so do not assume incapacity. ADVANCE CARE PLANNING SHOULD START EARLY, while he can still express his wishes — in SA an ADVANCE CARE DIRECTIVE under the Advance Care Directives Act 2013, appointing a SUBSTITUTE DECISION-MAKER, plus an Enduring Power of Attorney for financial matters. THE LINE THAT SELLS IT: 'One of the reasons to do this now rather than later is that YOUR DAD CAN STILL TELL US WHAT HE WANTS. That takes an enormous weight off you down the track, BECAUSE YOU WON'T BE GUESSING.' ELDER ABUSE RISK: a dependent older adult, a reluctant carer, a difficult relationship and a recent bereavement is a RECOGNISED RISK CONSTELLATION, and abuse includes financial, emotional and neglect, not only physical — screen sensitively through the function and support questions. THE SON TELLING YOU HONESTLY THAT HE CANNOT COPE IS PROTECTIVE; IT IS THE FAMILIES WHO SAY NOTHING YOU WORRY ABOUT. SA Adult Safeguarding Unit 1800 372 310; 1800ELDERHelp 1800 353 374.
plan: CONSENT AND INCLUSION — two sentences, two easy marks. Then the open question, and then silence.
THE REFUSAL ARRIVES. DO NOT MOVE PAST IT. Thank him, do not negotiate, and say your job is to get support from somewhere other than him.
THE BRIDGING LINE, then history: onset and progression · behavioural and psychological symptoms.
RISKY BEHAVIOUR AND SAFETY AT HOME — the stove, getting lost, wandering. AND ASK ABOUT DRIVING.
FUNCTION: washing and dressing, then shopping, cooking, cleaning, bills, tablets. Then nutrition and weight.
Vision and hearing · alcohol · medications · falls.
MOOD SINCE THE BEREAVEMENT, then safety. Then: 'how are YOU coping?' — and let the answer sit.
PART ONE OF THE PLAN, THE SUPPORT: My Aged Care referral today, assessment, SUPPORT AT HOME, and residential care named as legitimate if needed. Then Carer Gateway and Dementia Australia for HIM.
PART TWO, THE MOOD: assess properly today, bereavement counselling, consider an SSRI — and say plainly it will not reverse the Alzheimer's.
PART THREE, SAFETY: the driving assessment and the SA notification duty, said as something you will handle with his father yourself. Plus OT home safety, pharmacist review, and the hearing aids.
PART FOUR, PLANNING: both of them back within a fortnight for advance care planning, while his father can still say what he wants.
WRITTEN INFORMATION AND TEACH-BACK: 'can you tell me what the first two steps are?'

ask: THE TWO OPENERS: 'Is your father happy for me to discuss his health with you?' and 'Is he with you today? I'd like to include him if he'd like to be.' THEN: 'Tell me what's been happening, and what's worrying you most.'

THE ANSWER TO THE REFUSAL: 'Thank you for being honest with me — that's more useful than if you'd said yes and then couldn't manage it. My job isn't to persuade you. It's to work out what your dad needs and get it from somewhere other than you.' AND THE BRIDGE: 'The reason I'm asking all this in detail is that it decides what level of support he's eligible for.'

THE DRIVING OPENER: 'There's something I have to raise, and I'd rather do it now than later. Is your father still driving?' … 'A diagnosis on its own doesn't automatically end someone's licence — but it does have to be assessed, and reviewed again as things change. I'll be the one who has that conversation with him.' AND FOR THE SON: 'Can I ask how you're doing? You lost your mum nine months ago as well. That's a lot in one year.'
pefe: THIS IS A COLLATERAL HISTORY, NOT AN EXAMINATION — THE 'FINDINGS' ARE WHAT THE SON GIVES YOU WHEN ASKED: eighteen months of memory problems, much worse since his mother died · repeats himself, forgets the day, LOST HIS WALLET THREE TIMES LAST MONTH · snappy, awake at all hours, stopped going to bowls · A PAN LEFT ON THE GAS A MONTH AGO, smelt by the neighbour · STILL DRIVING EVERY DAY · washes and dresses himself fine · CANNOT manage shopping, cooking, cleaning, bills or tablets, because his wife did all of it · eats mostly toast and has lost weight · very deaf and refuses his hearing aids · a couple of beers a night, more since the bereavement · FLAT AND WITHDRAWN, and said once that THERE WASN'T MUCH POINT ANY MORE.

THE ONE THING HE WILL NOT VOLUNTEER: he and his father were never close, and he left home at seventeen — he gives it only if you ask gently. And 'nobody's asked me that' is the briefed response to being asked how he is.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: the refusal was never surfaced · the candidate moralised about family duty · DRIVING WAS NEVER MENTIONED · the depression was missed entirely · the candidate claimed treating the depression would reverse the dementia · obsolete aged care programmes were named as the current system.

Two sentences before you start, both easy marks — CONSENT: 'Before we start — is your father happy for me to discuss his health with you?' He is 65 with an MMSE of 25 and VERY LIKELY HAS CAPACITY FOR THIS DECISION — DO NOT ASSUME A DEMENTIA DIAGNOSIS REMOVES IT. INCLUDE THE PATIENT: 'Is your father with you today? I'd like to include him in this if he'd like to be.' Talking about a competent adult in the third person while he sits in the waiting room is poor practice and EXAMINERS NOTICE IT. Then the open question: 'tell me what's been happening, and WHAT'S WORRYING YOU MOST' — and then be quiet

The functional assessment is the answer to the son, not a box-tick — ADLs and IADLs are WHAT DETERMINES WHAT SUPPORT THE SYSTEM WILL FUND, so when he says he cannot care for his father the honest response is not reassurance — it is 'LET ME WORK OUT EXACTLY WHAT HE NEEDS, BECAUSE THAT DETERMINES WHAT WE CAN GET FOR HIM.' THE BRIDGING LINE: 'The reason I'm asking all this in detail is that IT DECIDES WHAT LEVEL OF SUPPORT HE'S ELIGIBLE FOR. The more clearly I can describe what he can and can't manage, the more we can put in place.' That single sentence converts an interrogation into a plan and VISIBLY CHANGES THE ROLE-PLAYER'S ATTITUDE

The nine blocks — and the three people run out of time for — ONSET AND PROGRESSION · BEHAVIOURAL AND PSYCHOLOGICAL SYMPTOMS · RISKY BEHAVIOUR: 'has he ever got lost, even somewhere familiar? Anything at home — THE STOVE LEFT ON, a fall, a wander at night? IS HE STILL DRIVING?' · FUNCTION: washing and dressing, then shopping, cooking, cleaning, BILLS and TABLETS · NUTRITION: who cooks, is he eating, has he lost weight · SUPPORT: who lives with him, who is looking after him, what is already in place · MOOD SINCE THE BEREAVEMENT · SAFETY: 'has he ever said anything that made you worry he'd had enough?' · AND THE SON: 'AND HOW ARE YOU COPING WITH ALL THIS?' — the last three are where the marks are

Correction — the MMSE is not what Australian practice uses first — Take the 25, but know what it is and is not. THE MMSE IS COPYRIGHT-RESTRICTED and largely superseded in Australian primary care, and it is HEAVILY INFLUENCED BY EDUCATION AND LANGUAGE BACKGROUND, which makes it unreliable across much of the Australian population. 25 OUT OF 30 IS ONLY MILD IMPAIRMENT — consistent with early disease AND consistent with depression. USE INSTEAD: GPCOG, designed for Australian general practice with an informant section · MoCA, more sensitive to mild impairment · RUDAS, culturally and linguistically fair · KICA-Cog for older Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people · PLUS A GDS-15, essential here given the bereavement VERIFY

The two things that fail people — the system, and driving — CORRECTION: HOME CARE PACKAGES AND SHORT-TERM RESTORATIVE CARE CEASED ON 1 NOVEMBER 2025 and were replaced by SUPPORT AT HOME under the Aged Care Act 2024 — naming the old programmes dates you instantly VERIFY. AND THEY ARE CARE WORKERS OR SUPPORT WORKERS, NOT SOCIAL WORKERS; a social worker does psychosocial assessment, counselling, advocacy and complex care coordination, which is a genuinely valuable and DIFFERENT referral here. DRIVING IS THE LARGEST OMISSION IN THE SOURCE: 'There's something I have to raise, and I'd rather do it now than later. IS YOUR FATHER STILL DRIVING?' If you never ask, the role-player is briefed NOT to mention it — the omission must stand

Pseudodementia — treat it, but do not overclaim — Depression in an older person can produce a picture INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM DEMENTIA — poor concentration, apparent memory loss, withdrawal — and here it is a live possibility, because his wife died nine months ago. BUT THE SOURCE OVERSTATES THE CONSEQUENCE: treating depression can substantially improve function and cognition where depression is driving the picture, and IT DOES NOT REVERSE ALZHEIMER DISEASE. Examiner challenge 'will treating his depression fix his memory?' → 'It may improve it, sometimes markedly, because depression itself impairs concentration and memory — and given his bereavement I'd want it treated FOR ITS OWN SAKE regardless. But it won't reverse Alzheimer disease. I'd REASSESS HIS COGNITION ONCE HIS MOOD IS TREATED, because that tells us how much of this was the depression'

setting: One question and one distinction. The question: how old was your father when he was diagnosed — without it you cannot categorise her and everything afterwards is a guess dressed as advice, and it is the question candidates most reliably forget because it feels like small talk. The distinction: screening is for people without symptoms. The moment she has one she leaves the screening pathway and goes to colonoscopy as a diagnostic test.
stem: General practice, rural South Australia. You are the GP. A 47-year-old woman has presented because she is concerned about bowel cancer.
Her father has recently been diagnosed with bowel cancer. 8 minutes, no examination — roughly four to five minutes of history, then counselling.

A guidelines station dressed as a reassurance consultation. The history is short and the counselling is algorithmic, so there is nowhere to hide — you either know the three risk categories and what each one buys her, or you do not.
The version that catches people out: recalls report one in which she has symptoms — a change in bowel habit or blood in the stool — revealed only if you ask.

back.dx: ASYMPTOMATIC 47-YEAR-OLD IN CATEGORY 2 (MODERATELY INCREASED RISK) BECAUSE HER FATHER IS A FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVE DIAGNOSED UNDER 60. THE ARITHMETIC, SHOWN OUT LOUD: 'we start either at fifty, or TEN YEARS BEFORE THE AGE YOUR FATHER WAS DIAGNOSED, whichever comes first. He was fifty-seven, so ten years earlier is FORTY-SEVEN — which is your age now. So I'd refer you for a colonoscopy NOW, and then five-yearly up to seventy-four.' THE DEFINITIONS, WHICH DECIDE THE CATEGORY: FIRST-DEGREE is biological parent, full sibling or child · SECOND-DEGREE is grandparent, aunt, uncle, niece, nephew, grandchild, half-sibling or double cousin · A COUSIN IS THIRD-DEGREE AND DOES NOT COUNT towards the categories — but ask anyway, because three affected relatives changes the picture and because you are also listening for LYNCH SYNDROME. Her uncle is second-degree, and ONE FIRST-DEGREE PLUS ONE OR MORE SECOND-DEGREE RELATIVES AT ANY AGE IS ITSELF CATEGORY 2. THE QUESTION CANDIDATES SKIP: 'has anyone had cancer of the WOMB, OVARY, STOMACH, KIDNEY OR BLADDER?' — endometrial, ovarian, gastric, urothelial and small bowel cancers clustering in a family raise LYNCH SYNDROME, an entirely different pathway and a FAMILY CANCER CLINIC referral. It takes one sentence and it is a marked item. IF SHE HAS SYMPTOMS — THE PIVOT, VERBATIM: 'What you've just told me CHANGES MY PLAN. SCREENING TESTS ARE FOR PEOPLE WHO HAVE NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL. You've described [the symptom], and that means the right test isn't a screening kit — IT'S A COLONOSCOPY, and I'm arranging it now rather than putting you on a screening programme. That is NOT because I think you have cancer. It's because the only way to be sure is to look, and the sooner we look the better the options.' EXAMINER ANSWERS: 'why not just put her on the national programme?' → 'a first-degree relative diagnosed under sixty places her in category 2, and the guideline recommends five-yearly colonoscopy for that group; the faecal test only detects lesions that are ALREADY BLEEDING, while colonoscopy also REMOVES POLYPS before they become cancer.' 'What if her father had been seventy-one?' → 'one first-degree relative at sixty or older is CATEGORY 1 — two-yearly faecal testing from forty-five to seventy-four, like the general population.' 'Would you order a genetic test?' → 'NOT FOR CATEGORY 2. If the family pattern suggested Lynch syndrome I would consider TUMOUR TESTING IN THE AFFECTED RELATIVE FIRST, and refer the family to a family cancer clinic' VERIFY. 'What would change your plan today?' → 'ANY SYMPTOM — rectal bleeding, a persistent change in bowel habit, unintentional weight loss, iron-deficiency anaemia or an abdominal mass.' WHAT TO SAY ABOUT THE COLONOSCOPY ITSELF: a camera on a flexible tube under sedation · A BOWEL PREPARATION THE DAY BEFORE, which most people find the worst part · under an hour, home the same day, SOMEONE MUST DRIVE HER · polyps removed at the time and sent for testing · risks small but real, BLEEDING AND RARELY PERFORATION. If colonoscopy is contraindicated or incomplete, CT COLONOGRAPHY may be offered VERIFY. SOUTH AUSTRALIAN PRACTICALITIES: referral to the nearest colorectal or general surgical unit — TQEH, RAH or FMC by catchment — with endoscopy locally through COUNTRY HEALTH CONNECT where a list runs · PATS for travel and accommodation for a metropolitan colonoscopy · CANCER COUNCIL SA 13 11 20, useful for her father too · Aboriginal Liaison Officer, local ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment · TIS National 131 450 · healthdirect 1800 022 222. THE FIVE PRACTICE CARDS: the SYMPTOMATIC version, with looser stools three times a day for two months and one episode of fresh bleeding — abandon screening, colonoscopy, blood count and iron studies · FATHER AT 71 AND NOBODY ELSE — category 1, and the test is not to over-investigate but to explain population screening rather than dismiss it · FATHER AT 57, SISTER AT 49, AUNT WITH ENDOMETRIAL CANCER AT 45 — a Lynch-spectrum pattern, category 3, family cancer clinic, and tumour testing of the affected relative before genetic testing of the patient VERIFY · SHE IS 32 AND HER FATHER WAS DIAGNOSED AT 44 — the arithmetic gives 34, not 50, and the skill is handling a young woman's fear without dismissing it or colonoscoping her tomorrow · ABORIGINAL, TWO HOURS FROM THE NEAREST LIST AND NO CAR — PATS, the ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officer, Closing the Gap co-payment for aspirin, and ASKING DIRECTLY WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY STOP HER ATTENDING.
plan: INTRODUCE AND USE HER NAME, open question, then ACKNOWLEDGE HER FATHER SPECIFICALLY — she becomes tearful once, early, and whether you stop for it is marked.
ASK FOR CONCERNS AND WRITE THEM DOWN, then SIGNPOST: the father, then symptoms, then risk factors, then exactly what testing you would recommend and why.
THE FATHER: how is he, THEN HOW OLD WAS HE AT DIAGNOSIS, then where in the bowel and whether it had spread.
SYMPTOM SCREEN: weight, appetite, tiredness, lumps, fevers and night sweats.
Abdominal pain and bloating · diarrhoea or constipation · change of habit asked separately · vomiting · fresh blood and black tarry stools both by name.

THE WIDER FAMILY, BOTH SIDES, WITH AGES — and the Lynch-spectrum cancers: womb, ovary, stomach, kidney, bladder.

ask: THE OPENING SET: 'I'm very sorry to hear about your dad — that's a frightening thing to be going through, and it's completely understandable it's made you think about yourself. Thank you for coming in, that's exactly the right thing to do.' THEN THE ONE THAT MATTERS: 'CAN I ASK HOW OLD HE WAS WHEN HE WAS DIAGNOSED?'

THE TWO THAT GET MISSED: 'Has there been any CHANGE IN YOUR USUAL BOWEL HABIT — are you going more often, or less, or differently from how you used to?' and 'Any blood in the stool, OR ANY BLACK TARRY STOOLS?' AND THE LYNCH ONE: 'Has anyone had cancer of the womb, ovary, stomach, kidney or bladder?'

THE ANSWERS SHE WILL PUSH FOR: to 'am I going to get it too?' → 'I can't promise you won't. What I can do is FIND ANYTHING EARLY, when it's very treatable — and REMOVE GROWTHS BEFORE THEY EVER BECOME CANCER.' To 'can't I just do the poo test?' → the kit only finds what is already bleeding. To 'do I need a genetic test?' → not for category 2. AND THE CLOSE: 'if any of that happens, WE LOOK STRAIGHT AWAY — we don't wait.'
pefe: NO EXAMINATION IN THIS STATION — THE 'FINDINGS' ARE WHAT SHE GIVES YOU ONLY WHEN ASKED: FATHER 57, diagnosed six weeks ago and just started chemotherapy · NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL, and she checked for blood herself after his diagnosis · non-smoker · a glass of wine most nights, around seven a week · RED MEAT MOST NIGHTS AND BACON AT WEEKENDS · not especially active, desk job · no polyps, no Crohn's or colitis · NEVER SCREENED, because she thought it started at fifty · FATHER'S BROTHER had something bowel-related in his fifties · no Lynch-spectrum cancers · one brother and one sister, both well.

HER HIDDEN PRESSURE IS NOT A SYMPTOM, IT IS A REQUEST: she pushes for reassurance at least twice — 'but I'll be all right, won't I?' — AND A DOCTOR WHO PROMISES SHE WILL BE FINE HAS FAILED, while a doctor who says the risk is raised and explains what they are going to do about it has passed.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: the father's age is never asked · she is offered a screening kit as a category 2 patient · a symptomatic version is put on a screening pathway · she is told she will be fine.

The one question — ask it inside ninety seconds — 'How is your dad doing?' is WARMTH. 'CAN I ASK HOW OLD HE WAS WHEN HE WAS DIAGNOSED?' is THE CASE. Ask both, in that order, and DO NOT SETTLE FOR 'A FEW YEARS AGO' — you need the age at diagnosis. She is briefed to give it ONLY IF ASKED DIRECTLY, and if nobody asks she prompts once at about seven minutes: 'does it matter how old he was?' HE IS 57. A first-degree relative at 60 or older raises her risk LESS THAN TWOFOLD (category 1); the same relative at 57 AT LEAST DOUBLES IT (category 2) — a completely different screening plan

The symptom screen — two traps inside it — Weight loss, appetite, tiredness, lumps, fevers or night sweats, abdominal pain, bloating — then THE TWO THAT GET MISSED. ASKING 'DIARRHOEA OR CONSTIPATION?' DOES NOT COVER CHANGE OF HABIT: a change of habit is someone who went every second day and now goes three times a day, SO ASK IT SEPARATELY. AND ASK FOR BOTH FRESH BLOOD AND BLACK TARRY STOOLS BY NAME — dark stool means higher bleeding, fresh blood means lower

The three categories, and what each buys her — CATEGORY 1, near-average to slightly increased: iFOBT TWO-YEARLY FROM 45 TO 74. CATEGORY 2, moderately increased, RISK 2–4×: COLONOSCOPY FIVE-YEARLY, starting at 50 OR TEN YEARS BEFORE THE EARLIEST FIRST-DEGREE DIAGNOSIS, WHICHEVER COMES FIRST, to 74. CATEGORY 3, high risk, 4–20×: COLONOSCOPY FIVE-YEARLY FROM TEN YEARS BEFORE OR 40, whichever is earlier, PLUS FAMILY CANCER CLINIC. Her father at 57 puts her in CATEGORY 2 ON HIS OWN VERIFY

Correction — two figures worth updating in older notes — THE FIRST-DEGREE AGE THRESHOLD IS 60, NOT 55 — the 2023 update moved it in both category 1 and category 2, and older textbooks still say 55. AND POPULATION SCREENING NOW STARTS AT 45, NOT 50: iFOBT two-yearly from 45 to 74, with the National Bowel Cancer Screening Program aligning, though in practice people aged 45–49 have needed to REQUEST their first kit rather than being invited VERIFY THE CURRENT INVITATION AGE — the programme has changed twice in recent years. ALSO 2023: criteria for categories 2 and 3 can be met by relatives from EITHER SIDE OF THE FAMILY; the old same-side requirement has gone

Why colonoscopy and not the kit — said without disparaging the programme — 'The home test looks for INVISIBLE BLOOD. It's a good test for the general population, but IT ONLY FINDS THINGS THAT ARE ALREADY BLEEDING. A colonoscopy LOOKS DIRECTLY AT THE WHOLE BOWEL, and if there's a small growth — a polyp — IT CAN BE REMOVED DURING THE SAME TEST, BEFORE IT EVER BECOMES A CANCER.' Offering the kit to a category 2 patient is the commonest wrong answer, and it comes from anchoring on the national programme

Honesty about risk — she wants to be told she is fine — You cannot tell her that and YOU MUST NOT; she is briefed to accept it warmly AND MARK YOU DOWN. THE HONEST VERSION: 'Your risk is higher than average — probably two to four times — AND THAT'S EXACTLY WHY WE SCREEN YOU DIFFERENTLY. What screening does is find things early, when they're very treatable, and remove growths before they ever become cancer.' NEVER GIVE THE NUMBER AND LEAVE IT THERE — 'two to four times' sounds catastrophic to a frightened person, so PAIR IT WITH WHAT YOU ARE GOING TO DO ABOUT IT and with the fact that MOST PEOPLE IN CATEGORY 2 NEVER DEVELOP BOWEL CANCER

setting: Put cancer at the TOP of the list — in the history, in the differentials, and out loud. The functioning tumours are interesting and candidates enjoy them: phaeochromocytoma is memorable, Cushing has a picture attached, conn has a test. Cancer has none of that, so it gets forgotten — and it is the thing that kills. The failure has a recognisable shape: a history entirely about headaches, palpitations and weight gain, and a differential list that opens with phaeochromocytoma.
stem: A 57-year-old woman has been brought to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. The primary and secondary surveys have been completed and are unremarkable.
As part of your trauma assessment you arranged a CT scan, which reports an incidental 1.5 cm homogeneous opacity in the left adrenal gland. 8 minutes.

The stem says the surveys are complete and unremarkable, and that is deliberate — it closes off the trauma history so you cannot fill four minutes with mechanism of injury and head strike. Eight or nine specific questions, asked deliberately, is a complete history here.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Explain your diagnosis and, more importantly, your differentials
Explain the further investigations you would arrange

back.dx: 1.5 cm HOMOGENEOUS LEFT ADRENAL MASS FOUND INCIDENTALLY ON TRAUMA CT — IS IT MALIGNANT, AND IS IT FUNCTIONING? FRAME IT FIRST: 'when we do a scan for one reason and find something we weren't looking for, we call it an INCIDENTALOMA. In your case it's a small lump on one of the adrenal glands — two small glands that SIT ON TOP OF THE KIDNEYS and make several important hormones.' THE ANATOMY BEHIND THE TESTS: three cortical layers and a medulla, each giving rise to a functioning tumour with its own screening test — ZONA GLOMERULOSA → aldosterone → CONN · ZONA FASCICULATA → cortisol → CUSHING · MEDULLA → catecholamines → PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA. THE THREE FUNCTIONAL SCREENS, EXPLAINED RATHER THAN LISTED, BECAUSE THE TASK SAYS EXPLAIN THE INVESTIGATIONS: PLASMA OR 24-HOUR URINARY METANEPHRINES — 'a blood test, or a urine collection over 24 hours, measuring breakdown products of adrenaline'; there is no consensus on which is superior and either is acceptable, so say so if challenged VERIFY · 1 mg OVERNIGHT DEXAMETHASONE SUPPRESSION TEST — 'you take a single steroid tablet at night and we check your cortisol in the morning; NORMALLY THE TABLET SWITCHES YOUR OWN PRODUCTION OFF, and if it doesn't, that tells us the gland is making hormone on its own'; preferred over 24-hour urinary free cortisol or late-night salivary cortisol in this setting VERIFY · ALDOSTERONE–RENIN RATIO — 'a blood test measuring two hormones that control blood pressure and salt balance, and the ratio between them'; SEVERAL ANTIHYPERTENSIVES INTERFERE WITH IT, so the result is interpreted with the medication list in hand VERIFY. PLUS DEDICATED ADRENAL CT with contrast washout, or MRI — non-contrast attenuation and washout characteristics distinguish a LIPID-RICH ADENOMA from a suspicious lesion VERIFY. AND ELECTROLYTES INCLUDING POTASSIUM: cheap, and a LOW POTASSIUM supports the Conn pathway. WHAT SIZE AND TEXTURE TELL YOU: larger lesions carry higher malignant risk and A COMMONLY QUOTED THRESHOLD FOR CONCERN IS AROUND 4 cm — HERS IS 1.5 cm, WHICH IS REASSURING, AND SAY THAT TO HER · HOMOGENEOUS ON CT IS ALSO REASSURING, while heterogeneity, irregular margins and necrosis are not · if the lesion is NON-FUNCTIONING AND RADIOLOGICALLY BENIGN, management is SURVEILLANCE — repeat imaging and repeat hormonal screening over a defined interval · ADRENALECTOMY is considered for FUNCTIONING TUMOURS, for lesions with concerning imaging features, and for SIGNIFICANT GROWTH on follow-up VERIFY. THE CLOSING SENTENCE OF THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST, WHICH STOPS YOU LEAVING A FRIGHTENED PATIENT HOLDING A LIST OF CANCERS: 'I want to be clear about the balance here. I've listed all of those BECAUSE WE HAVE TO CHECK THEM PROPERLY. But THE GREAT MAJORITY OF THESE LUMPS TURN OUT TO BE THE LAST ONE ON MY LIST — harmless, not a cancer, and not making any hormone.' THE INCIDENTALOMA FAMILY, since the same stem runs three ways: the ADRENAL version tilts towards history, differentials and functional screening · the BREAST version, a mass on CT chest after the same accident, tilts towards explaining results and the TRIPLE TEST · the THYROID version, a nodule on CT angiogram after a stroke, tilts towards history and the TSH-FIRST pathway. THE OPENING SENTENCE TRANSFERS TO ALL THREE: 'the scan has found something we were not looking for. IT IS COMMON, IT IS USUALLY HARMLESS, BUT IT DOES NEED TO BE SORTED OUT PROPERLY, and this is how we do that.' HER HIDDEN AGENDA: HER SISTER DIED OF OVARIAN CANCER AT 54, three years ago, and she has been frightened of cancer ever since. She gives it if you ask an open question about her concerns or about family history of cancer — and if nobody asks, she says at about six minutes 'MY SISTER DIED OF CANCER. IS THAT WHAT THIS IS?' If you over-reassure her — 'no, it'll be nothing' — she goes quiet and then says flatly 'YOU CAN'T KNOW THAT YET.' THE THREE PRACTICE CARDS: A MELANOMA EXCISED FROM HER BACK FOUR YEARS AGO — metastasis moves to the top, full skin check and staging, and this is the scenario where BIOPSY MAY GENUINELY BE INDICATED, after excluding phaeo VERIFY · A 5 cm HETEROGENEOUS MASS WITH IRREGULAR MARGINS — size and phenotype both concerning, urgent endocrine and surgical referral, dedicated imaging, and a conversation now closer to breaking bad news · EPISODES OF POUNDING HEADACHE, SWEATING AND A RACING HEART LASTING TWENTY MINUTES — phaeochromocytoma to the top, urgent metanephrines, NO NEEDLE, alpha before beta blockade, and caution with contrast and anaesthesia.
plan: INTRODUCE, THEN ASK HOW SHE IS IN HERSELF AFTER THE ACCIDENT — before any of the rest of it.
GIVE THE GOOD NEWS FIRST: no injuries, nothing broken, no internal bleeding, nothing needing an operation.
SIGNPOST THE INCIDENTAL FINDING, explain WHERE THE ADRENAL GLAND IS, and FRAME THE TWO QUESTIONS. She will ask 'is it cancer?' immediately — answer honestly, do not over-reassure.
MALIGNANCY BLOCK: weight, appetite, fatigue, night sweats, lumps.
PRIMARY HUNT: mammograms and breast lump · cough and haemoptysis · bowels and bowel screening · moles · AND ANY PREVIOUS CANCER OF ANY KIND.
PHAEO: sudden severe headaches · racing heart · flushing and sweating episodes · tremor.
CUSHING: weight gain and where · easy bruising · proximal weakness on stairs and out of a chair.
CONN: has a doctor called your blood pressure high, how many tablets · CRAMPS AND POLYURIA. STOP ON THE 'STUBBORN ON TWO' ANSWER.
BACKGROUND: past history, MEDICATIONS INCLUDING STEROIDS, smoking, family history of endocrine or adrenal disease — and ASK ABOUT HER CONCERNS, which is where the sister surfaces.
Name it: incidentaloma, translated. Then the seven differentials, cancer and metastasis first, benign adenoma last.
BALANCE IT: small, homogeneous, and the great majority are the harmless one.
INVESTIGATIONS, EACH EXPLAINED: metanephrines · dexamethasone suppression · aldosterone–renin ratio · dedicated adrenal imaging · electrolytes today.
NO NEEDLE BEFORE PHAEO IS EXCLUDED · endocrinology referral with GP coordination · written information · TEACH-BACK: 'what will you tell your husband about the scan?'

ask: THE FRAME: 'There are two things we need to find out about this lump. Whether it's harmful — whether it could be a cancer. And whether it's making hormones. Everything I'm about to ask is aimed at one of those two questions.'

THE SENTENCE THAT EARNS THE DISCRIMINATOR: 'At the top of my list I have to put a cancer — either one arising in the gland itself, or, more commonly, A CANCER FROM SOMEWHERE ELSE THAT HAS SPREAD THERE. That is why I asked you about weight loss, about your mammograms, about your bowels and about your chest.'

THE BALANCE, AND THE NEEDLE: 'The great majority of these turn out to be a harmless lump that's not a cancer and isn't making any hormone. Yours is small — a centimetre and a half — and the scan describes it as even in texture, both of which are reassuring.' … 'If it were the adrenaline-producing kind, PUTTING A NEEDLE IN CAN CAUSE A DANGEROUS SURGE IN BLOOD PRESSURE. So we do the hormone tests first, always.'
pefe: No examination task — the findings are the CT report and the history. The scan: 1.5 cm, homogeneous, left adrenal — both features reassuring, and worth saying to her. The planted positives, given only if asked: a few kilos gained over two years around the middle · cramps in the calves at night · blood pressure on two agents for eight years and once called 'Stubborn'.

EVERYTHING ELSE IS NEGATIVE: no weight loss, no lumps, no night sweats, no severe headaches, no palpitations, no sweating episodes, no tremor, no easy bruising, no proximal weakness. Mammogram two years ago clear, bowel screening last year negative, NEVER HAD CANCER HERSELF, no relevant family history of endocrine disease, non-smoker, on two antihypertensives and a statin.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: cancer and metastasis never named · no malignancy questions asked · proposed biopsy as a first step · told her categorically it was nothing to worry about · spent the history re-taking the trauma story.

Say the two questions out loud — it frames the whole consultation — 'There are TWO THINGS we need to find out about this lump. THE FIRST IS WHETHER IT IS HARMFUL — whether it could be a cancer. THE SECOND IS WHETHER IT IS PRODUCING HORMONES, because the adrenal gland makes several, and a lump there can make too much of one. EVERYTHING I'M GOING TO ASK YOU, AND EVERY TEST I'M GOING TO ARRANGE, IS AIMED AT ONE OF THOSE TWO QUESTIONS.' And GIVE THE GOOD NEWS FIRST — no injuries, nothing broken, no internal bleeding — before you mention the lump at all

Block one and two — malignancy, and the primary hunt — ASK THIS FIRST, AND IT IS THE BLOCK MOST OFTEN OMITTED: 'Have you lost any weight without trying? Has your appetite changed? Unusually tired? Any night sweats? ANY LUMPS ANYWHERE?' THEN THE PRIMARIES THAT METASTASISE TO THE ADRENAL — LUNG, BREAST, BOWEL, KIDNEY, STOMACH, MELANOMA, LYMPHOMA: 'are you up to date with your mammograms? Ever had a breast lump? Any long-standing cough, or coughed up blood? Any change in bowel habit or blood in the stool, and are you up to date with bowel screening? Any moles that have changed?' AND THE ONE THAT TRANSFORMS THE PRE-TEST PROBABILITY: HAVE YOU EVER HAD A CANCER OF ANY KIND YOURSELF?

The hormone blocks — ask symptoms, not signs — PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA, the episodic triad: 'do you get headaches, particularly bad ones that come on suddenly? Episodes where your HEART RACES? Episodes of FLUSHING AND SWEATING? Any shakiness in your hands?' CUSHING: 'have you PUT ON WEIGHT and where? BRUISING more easily? WEAKNESS getting out of a chair or climbing stairs?' — DO NOT ASK ABOUT PURPLE STRIAE OR A BUFFALO HUMP; THOSE ARE QUESTIONS A DOCTOR ASKS THEMSELVES, NOT THE PATIENT. CONN, one question that gets left out because it is only one question: 'HAS ANY DOCTOR EVER TOLD YOU YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE IS HIGH, AND HOW MANY TABLETS ARE YOU ON?' plus cramps and passing a lot of urine

The planted clue — 'I'm on two, and they said it was stubborn' — RESISTANT HYPERTENSION ON TWO OR MORE AGENTS, WITH NOCTURNAL CALF CRAMPS, IS THE BRIEFED FINDING POINTING AT CONN SYNDROME. Candidates racing through the hormone blocks tick the box and move on — and if you ignore it SHE DOES NOT REPEAT IT, and the omission stands. STOP, ACKNOWLEDGE IT, AND CONNECT IT TO THE ALDOSTERONE–RENIN RATIO LATER: 'two tablets and still described as stubborn — I'll come back to that'

The seven differentials, in the order the order is doing work — ONE, ADRENAL CARCINOMA — rare, but it goes first because it is what we must exclude. TWO, METASTASIS TO THE ADRENAL — commoner than primary adrenal cancer, and the reason the primary-hunt block exists. THREE, PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA. FOUR, CORTISOL-PRODUCING ADENOMA, which may be SUBCLINICAL — biochemically abnormal with no obvious appearance. FIVE, ALDOSTERONE-PRODUCING ADENOMA. SIX, ADRENAL HAEMORRHAGE, WHICH IS WORTH NAMING PRECISELY BECAUSE SHE HAS JUST BEEN IN A CAR ACCIDENT. SEVEN, BENIGN NON-FUNCTIONING ADENOMA — the most likely answer, SAID LAST SO IT LANDS AS REASSURANCE AND SHE LEAVES HOLDING IT

The needle — the highest-yield safety point in the station — NEVER PUT A NEEDLE INTO AN ADRENAL MASS UNTIL PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA HAS BEEN EXCLUDED BIOCHEMICALLY. Biopsying one can precipitate a CATASTROPHIC CATECHOLAMINE SURGE — hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia, cardiovascular collapse. Examiner challenge 'would you biopsy it?' → 'NOT AS A FIRST STEP. I'd screen for phaeochromocytoma first. And BIOPSY DOESN'T RELIABLY SEPARATE A BENIGN ADENOMA FROM AN ADRENAL CARCINOMA anyway — I'd reserve it for CONFIRMING A METASTASIS where there's a known primary and it would change what we do.' And the classic follow-up: A PHAEOCHROMOCYTOMA REQUIRES ALPHA BLOCKADE BEFORE BETA BLOCKADE, and before any surgery VERIFY

stem: A 45-year-old man was admitted following a total knee replacement three days ago. He has developed confusion and agitation today. He is a heavy drinker — 25 standard drinks every day.
Pulse 120 · temperature 37.8 °C · no organomegaly · no ascites · cannula sites not infected. Bloods: ALT, AST and GGT raised · haemoglobin low · MCV high, a macrocytic anaemia. 8 minutes.

You are speaking to the patient's son, not the patient — check consent and pitch everything accordingly. His last drink was the day he came in, and day three is seventy-two hours: precisely the delirium tremens window.

back.dx: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL DELIRIUM ON DAY 3 AFTER TOTAL KNEE REPLACEMENT — MULTIFACTORIAL UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. TWENTY-FIVE STANDARD DRINKS A DAY IS ROUGHLY A BOTTLE OF SPIRITS DAILY, and it matters for three reasons: this is ALCOHOL DEPENDENCE and withdrawal at this level carries a GENUINE MORTALITY RISK IF UNTREATED · SEIZURES AND DELIRIUM TREMENS ARE BOTH LIKELY, NOT THEORETICAL · THIAMINE DEFICIENCY IS NEAR-CERTAIN, making Wernicke both a differential and a preventable harm. THE WITHDRAWAL TIMELINE: 6–12 HOURS tremor, anxiety, sweating · 12–48 HOURS SEIZURES and alcoholic hallucinosis · 48–96 HOURS DELIRIUM TREMENS, which is this patient VERIFY. CORRECTION — ALCOHOL IS NOT A TREATMENT FOR WITHDRAWAL: the source suggests that in very severe withdrawal you can give the patient alcohol. THAT IS NOT STANDARD AUSTRALIAN HOSPITAL PRACTICE AND YOU SHOULD NOT SAY IT IN AN OSCE. Management here is BENZODIAZEPINES TITRATED AGAINST A VALIDATED WITHDRAWAL SCORE, WITH THIAMINE REPLACEMENT. Administering ethanol is not recommended: the dosing is unpredictable, it is hepatotoxic, it interacts, and it does not treat the underlying neurochemistry any better than a benzodiazepine does. Examiner challenge 'I've heard some units give alcohol' → 'I'm aware it has been done historically and occasionally still is, but it isn't the recommended approach. Australian practice is SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED BENZODIAZEPINE AGAINST A CIWA-Ar SCORE, WITH THIAMINE REPLACEMENT, and I'd ESCALATE TO ADDICTION MEDICINE OR INTENSIVE CARE rather than reach for alcohol' VERIFY. THE TWO LAST RESORTS, FRAMED PROPERLY: AN ANTIPSYCHOTIC is considered ONLY for distressing hallucinations or agitation persisting despite adequate benzodiazepine — it is NOT FIRST-LINE, because BENZODIAZEPINES TREAT THE CAUSE AND ANTIPSYCHOTICS LOWER THE SEIZURE THRESHOLD VERIFY. PHYSICAL RESTRAINT is an ABSOLUTE LAST RESORT, only where there is genuine risk to the patient or others, using the LEAST RESTRICTIVE OPTION, under hospital policy, DOCUMENTED, TIME-LIMITED AND REGULARLY REVIEWED — say it in those terms, because 'we can restrain him if he's a problem' is a poor answer to give a frightened relative. THE QUESTION NOBODY ASKS, AND THE BRIEFED COMPLAINT: was he ever asked about his drinking before the operation? A patient on 25 standard drinks a day going into an ELECTIVE joint replacement should have had a WITHDRAWAL PLAN WRITTEN BEFORE THE ADMISSION — prophylactic thiamine, a scoring chart, and a benzodiazepine order. The son raises it at about four minutes: 'NOBODY ASKED HIM ABOUT THE DRINKING BEFORE THE OPERATION.' DO NOT DEFEND THE HOSPITAL AND DO NOT CONCEDE FAULT YOU CANNOT VERIFY — acknowledge it, commit to finding out, and pivot to what you can control: 'I can't tell you what was asked, but I WILL find out, and I'll come back to you about it. What I can do right now is make sure he's treated properly from here.' Raising it gently is honest and good practice; raising it as blame is not. ON PROGNOSIS, WHEN HE PRESSES: 'THIS IS A SERIOUS CONDITION AND I'M NOT GOING TO PRETEND OTHERWISE — severe withdrawal can be dangerous, which is why we treat it properly and watch him closely. MOST PEOPLE TREATED THE WAY WE'RE TREATING HIM COME THROUGH IT.' If you promise his father will definitely be fine he says 'YOU DON'T KNOW THAT' and goes cold. AND THE OPPORTUNITY: when he is better, talk to him about the drinking — DASSA ADIS 1300 13 1340, free, 8.30 am to 10 pm daily, WHICH SUPPORTS FAMILIES AS WELL AS PATIENTS, so that number is for the son too. DASSA also runs a CLINICAL ADVISORY SERVICE FOR PRESCRIBERS — say you would use it if the regimen is difficult. THE SON'S HIDDEN AGENDA: he believes the hospital did this by not asking, and underneath he FEELS GUILTY THAT HE NEVER GOT HIS FATHER HELP — 'I should've done something about it years ago', which he says only near the end and only if you handled the complaint well.
plan: INTRODUCE, OPEN QUESTION, AND ACKNOWLEDGE HOW FRIGHTENING IT WAS TO WALK INTO — he came in this morning and his father did not know who he was.
CONFIRM CONSENT TO DISCUSS. You are speaking to a relative, and not asking is a marked omission.
THE BLOODS: liver enzymes, one sentence · anaemia and the large cells, one sentence · then the bridge. NINETY SECONDS, NOT THREE MINUTES.
ASK HOW MUCH HE DRINKS ON A USUAL DAY, and thank him for being straight about it.
FRAME IT: confusion in hospital usually has more than one cause at once, so we look for all of them and treat all of them.
MOST LIKELY: ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL, AND EXPLAIN WHY DAY 3 FITS — delirium tremens typically comes on two to four days after the last drink.

THE THREE EMERGENCIES TO EXCLUDE TODAY: PULMONARY EMBOLISM, because day 3 post-arthroplasty with a pulse of 120 · INFECTION, because the temperature is up · MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION, because it can be silent.
EXPECT THE COMPLAINT HERE: nobody asked about the drinking. Acknowledge, commit to finding out, do not defend and do not concede.
THE REST OF THE LIST: pain · drugs · electrolytes and glucose · intracranial · retention and constipation · sensory input · hepatic encephalopathy · fat embolism.
STEP ONE, INVESTIGATE — say the word first: bloods, ECG, chest X-ray, cultures, urine, CTPA, CT brain, bladder scan, medication review, pain assessment.
STEP TWO, TREAT THE WITHDRAWAL: THIAMINE BEFORE GLUCOSE · CIWA-Ar · SYMPTOM-TRIGGERED DIAZEPAM, aiming for calm and rousable, not unconscious. Plus magnesium.
STEP THREE AND FOUR: treat what else is found, then supportive delirium care — AND GIVE THE SON HIS JOB.
