setting: Triage aloud, tailor to the itinerary, and never drop the bite protocol. The stem invites a vaccine list, but the things most likely to harm him are road trauma, an animal bite and inadequate insurance — and you will not reach them unless you triage aloud. The two AUTOMATIC FAILS: recommending vaccines without establishing the itinerary, and failing to give the 15-minute wash and same-day care instruction.
stem: General practice, South Australia — a standard consultation, not a dedicated travel clinic. Josh Delaney, 28, fit and well, no medications, no known allergies.
He leaves in six weeks for three months backpacking through Thailand, Vietnam, cambodia and Nepal, including rural trekking. He wants 'Whatever jabs I need'. 8 minutes.

Three things are withheld unless you ask directly: he intends to hire a scooter in every country and holds no motorcycle licence · his only cover is through his credit card and he has never read the policy · and he is getting a tattoo in Thailand.
His real concern is cost. He has budgeted tightly and is quietly hoping you will tell him he doesn't need much.
tasks: Focused pre-travel history
Advise on vaccination and other travel health measures
Address questions and agree a plan
time: Saying aloud that you are prioritising is the demonstration of judgement — and it protects the last two minutes, which is where the insurance and road-safety marks live · if you are short of time, drop a vaccine, not the road and insurance advice

back.dx: Pre-travel consultation for three months of largely rural backpacking in South-East Asia and Nepal. Malaria and bites: risk varies a lot by region — most cities and main tourist areas in Thailand and Vietnam are low risk, but border areas and rural cambodia are higher, so check the current recommendation for the exact route rather than guessing. But the part people skip: avoiding bites matters more than the tablets, and it also covers dengue, for which he has no tablet and no vaccine. DEET or picaridin at 20% or more, reapplied · covered arms and legs at dusk and dawn · permethrin-treated clothing · and a treated net where there are no screens. And the line that makes it stick: dengue mosquitoes bite in the daytime, malaria ones at night — so it is an all-day job, not just evenings. Food, water and a diarrhoea plan: traveller's diarrhoea is the commonest thing that will actually happen to him. 'Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it' — bottled or treated water, no ice, no unpasteurised dairy, wash hands. Most cases settle on their own and the mainstay is fluid, so carry oral rehydration sachets, which weigh nothing. A standby antibiotic to take only if it is severe — fever, blood in the stool, or simply cannot function — but with a high fever, blood in the stool or inability to keep fluids down, get seen rather than self-treating. And: fever while he is there, or after he gets back, is malaria until proven otherwise. The two things most likely to hurt him, and the most important things you will say: road trauma is the leading preventable cause of death in young travellers, well ahead of any infection — helmet even where nobody else wears one, never after drinking, and most insurance policies exclude motorbike accidents unless you hold a motorcycle licence, so read that clause before you ride · and insurance: check it specifically covers medical evacuation, because a serious problem in rural Nepal means an air ambulance costing tens of thousands, and credit card cover usually doesn't include it, or trekking above a certain altitude. A traveller who declines Japanese encephalitis but wears a helmet and holds evacuation cover is far safer than the reverse. On prices: do not invent them — offering to look up the current cost scores better than a confident guess. The variants, scripted: version B, five days in Bangkok in a four-star hotel — 'This needs a lot less than you might expect, and I'd rather not sell you things you don't need': routine vaccines, hepatitis a because food and water applies even in good hotels, typhoid offered though lower risk over five days, and Japanese encephalitis and rabies explicitly not recommended because they are for rural, prolonged stays. Restraint is the marked behaviour here, and saying explicitly that you are not recommending something scores better than silence. Version C, pregnant at twelve weeks — live vaccines are off the table, meaning yellow fever and oral typhoid capsules, while injectable typhoid and hepatitis a are not live and can be given, and influenza and DTPa are actively recommended in pregnancy anyway · malaria is more dangerous in pregnancy and some drugs are unsuitable, so real malaria risk becomes a serious argument against going, not just a prescribing problem · Zika in pregnancy can cause serious birth defects with no vaccine and no treatment, so bite avoidance becomes non-negotiable · and check the insurance covers pregnancy-related care abroad, because many exclude it. Version D, immunosuppressed and yellow fever required for kenya — 'This is genuinely complicated and I don't want to guess at it. Yellow fever vaccine is live, and on methotrexate and prednisolone that carries real risk — it isn't a formality. But yellow fever itself is serious, and some countries require a certificate for entry. Three possible routes, all needing specialist input: vaccinate anyway after a formal risk assessment · issue a medical waiver letter, which some countries accept and others don't · or change the itinerary. I'd refer to a specialist travel medicine or infectious diseases service and involve the rheumatologist, and I'd do that today rather than next month, because it takes time. In the meantime, don't book anything non-refundable on the assumption it'll be fine.' Version E, declining rabies on cost — 'You can, and plenty of travellers do — it's your money and I'm not going to pressure you. But let me make sure you're deciding with the right information… now — whether or not you have the vaccine, this next part is free and it's the bit that matters most… can you say that back to me?' Letting the declined vaccine end the conversation is the failure. He will also test you with 'My mate got bitten by a monkey in Bali and he was fine' — the answer is 'He was lucky. Genuinely.'
plan: GREET AND TRIAGE ALOUD — name the plan for the eight minutes and flag that some of it may need a second appointment.
THE TRIP: countries and route · RURAL VERSUS URBAN · duration and departure date · ACTIVITIES AND ALTITUDE · accommodation · purpose of travel.
THE TRAVELLER: conditions, medications, allergies · IMMUNE STATUS, because it decides whether live vaccines are on the table · vaccine history and LAST TETANUS · previous travel in the region.
The two practical questions: travel insurance and evacuation cover, and the scooter. Flag that you will come back to both.
ROUTINE CATCH-UP FIRST, MEASLES NAMED SPECIFICALLY — then hepatitis A with its schedule, and typhoid.
THE ITINERARY-SPECIFIC ONES, EACH JUSTIFIED: hepatitis B · JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS, with the Bangkok-versus-rural-Cambodia contrast said out loud.
RABIES: what it is, why pre-exposure vaccine matters for immunoglobulin access — AND THE 15-MINUTE WASH AND SAME-DAY CARE, GIVEN WHETHER OR NOT HE BUYS THE VACCINE.
MALARIA BY REGION, THEN BITE AVOIDANCE AHEAD OF TABLETS — DEET or picaridin ≥20%, covered limbs, permethrin, treated net, and dengue by day.
Food and water, oral rehydration, and a standby antibiotic with the limits on self-treating.
The two that matter most: road trauma, helmets, alcohol and the motorcycle licence exclusion · and medical evacuation cover.
SEXUAL HEALTH, THEN THE PLAN: what you give today, what needs a second visit, what you will check and ring him about, and written information.
FEVER ON RETURN IS MALARIA UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE — then teach-back: 'what are the two things you'd tell your mate?'

ask: THE TRIAGE AND HISTORY SET: 'There's a lot to cover and limited time, so let me tell you how I'll use it.' · 'HOW MUCH OF IT IS RURAL VERSUS CITIES?' · 'What will you actually be doing — trekking, water, caves, animals?' · 'DO YOU HAVE TRAVEL INSURANCE, AND DO YOU KNOW WHETHER IT COVERS MEDICAL EVACUATION?' · 'ARE YOU PLANNING TO HIRE A SCOOTER OR MOTORBIKE AT ANY POINT?'

THE VACCINE SET: 'Before anything exotic, I want your routine vaccines up to date — ESPECIALLY MEASLES.' · 'You get good protection from the first hepatitis A dose, so six weeks is plenty.' · 'FOR FIVE DAYS IN BANGKOK I WOULDN'T MENTION JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS. FOR THREE MONTHS INCLUDING RURAL CAMBODIA, I WOULD.' · 'Once rabies symptoms start it is essentially always fatal, and there's no treatment.'

THE SET THAT SAVES HIM: 'WASH THE WOUND WITH SOAP AND RUNNING WATER FOR FIFTEEN MINUTES. NOT THIRTY SECONDS.' · 'Get medical care that same day, wherever you are. DON'T WAIT UNTIL YOU'RE HOME.' · 'Avoiding bites matters more than the tablets — and it covers dengue, which has no tablet.' · 'Boil it, cook it, peel it, or forget it.' · 'MOST POLICIES EXCLUDE MOTORBIKE ACCIDENTS UNLESS YOU HOLD A MOTORCYCLE LICENCE.' · 'If you get a fever after you're back, see a doctor promptly AND TELL THEM WHERE YOU'VE BEEN.'
pefe: No examination — the history is the risk assessment, and the three hidden items are given only if asked directly: the scooter in every country with no motorcycle licence · credit-card-only insurance he has never read · and the tattoo planned in Thailand, which comes out only if you ask about tattoos, piercings or hepatitis B risk.

WHAT HE GIVES WHEN ASKED: Thailand, overland into Cambodia, Vietnam, then Nepal · A FAIR BIT RURAL, 'THAT'S KIND OF THE POINT' · three months, leaving in six weeks · TREKKING WITH A COUPLE OF DAYS ABOVE 3,000 m · hostels and homestays · street food, definitely · no conditions, no medications, no allergies, NO IMMUNE PROBLEMS · all childhood vaccines and hepatitis B at school 'I think' · LAST TETANUS 'AGES AGO' · and BALI FIVE YEARS AGO WITH NOTHING BEFOREHAND AND HE WAS FINE, which is part of why he thinks this is over the top.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: recommending vaccines without ever establishing the itinerary · and failing to give the post-bite instruction — the 15-minute wash and same-day care — PARTICULARLY AFTER HE DECLINES THE VACCINE.

Triage out loud in the first thirty seconds — 'There's a lot to cover and limited time, SO LET ME TELL YOU HOW I'LL USE IT: I'll ask about the trip and about you for a few minutes, then go through the priorities — THE VACCINES YOU NEED SOONEST, MALARIA, AND THE PRACTICAL THINGS THAT ACTUALLY KEEP TRAVELLERS SAFE. Some of it may need a second appointment, and I'll tell you if so.' LAUNCHING INTO VACCINES TO SEEM EFFICIENT IS THE TRAP — he opens with 'just give me whatever jabs I need', and if you start listing without asking about the itinerary he lets you, AND MARKS YOU DOWN FOR IT

Two history answers do all the work: rural versus urban, and duration — 'Which countries, and roughly what route? HOW MUCH OF IT IS RURAL VERSUS CITIES? How long altogether, and exactly when do you leave? WHAT WILL YOU ACTUALLY BE DOING — trekking, water sports, caves, ANY CONTACT WITH ANIMALS? Any altitude in Nepal? Where are you staying?' ACCEPTING THE COUNTRY NAMES AND STOPPING IS THE ERROR: RURAL VERSUS URBAN AND DURATION ARE WHAT MOVE JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS AND RABIES FROM OPTIONAL TO GENUINELY INDICATED, and without them you cannot justify a single recommendation

The two highest-yield questions in the whole consultation — 'DO YOU HAVE TRAVEL INSURANCE, AND DO YOU KNOW WHETHER IT COVERS MEDICAL EVACUATION?' and 'ARE YOU PLANNING TO HIRE A SCOOTER OR MOTORBIKE AT ANY POINT?' They are not clinical questions and they produce the highest-yield advice in the station — A CANDIDATE WHO NEVER ASKS THEM CANNOT GIVE IT. If you never raise road safety or insurance, he says at the end 'IS THAT EVERYTHING THEN?' and fails those items

Routine first, because they matter more than the exotic ones — 'Before anything exotic, I want your routine vaccines up to date': tetanus and whooping cough · measles, two documented doses, because it is common over there and catches travellers out · chickenpox if never had it · polio · flu and COVID. Then the two for essentially anyone doing what he is doing: hepatitis a, food and water, two doses 6–12 months apart with good protection from the first, so six weeks is plenty · and typhoid, a single injection covering about three years

The itinerary-specific ones — justify each, do not list them — HEPATITIS B: blood and sexual contact, and over three months WITH TATTOOS, PIERCINGS, A POSSIBLE ACCIDENT OR A NEW RELATIONSHIP it is worth having, though he may already be covered from school. JAPANESE ENCEPHALITIS: a mosquito-borne brain infection in RURAL RICE-GROWING AREAS — 'FOR FIVE DAYS IN BANGKOK I WOULDN'T MENTION IT. FOR THREE MONTHS INCLUDING RURAL CAMBODIA AND VIETNAM, I WOULD.' SAYING WHY EACH ONE APPLIES TO HIS ITINERARY IS WHAT SEPARATES A RISK ASSESSMENT FROM A MENU — and it lets him make a real decision about cost

Rabies, and the instruction that must survive his declining the vaccine — 'Endemic across South-East Asia and Nepal — dogs mostly, but also monkeys and bats. Once symptoms start it is essentially always fatal, and there's no treatment.' The pre-exposure vaccine doesn't mean you ignore a bite — you would still need two more doses — but it means you don't need rabies immunoglobulin, which is often unavailable, unaffordable or of uncertain quality in exactly the remote places he is going. Then the free part, which is the scoring hinge: 'If any animal bites you, scratches you, or licks broken skin — wash the wound with soap and running water for fifteen minutes. Not thirty seconds. Fifteen minutes. Then get medical care that same day, wherever you are.' He will ask to skip the vaccine on cost — the bite protocol is more important for an unvaccinated traveller, not less

numbers: Ideally seen 6–8 weeks before departure · hepatitis a 2 doses 6–12 months apart, protective after the first · typhoid single injection for about 3 years, and the oral form is live · hepatitis B 3 doses · Japanese encephalitis 2 doses · rabies pre-exposure 2–3 doses, with 2 further doses and no immunoglobulin after a bite if pre-vaccinated VERIFY · yellow fever is live, approved centre only, certificate valid from 10 days

Post-bite wash 15 minutes and care the same day · repellent DEET or picaridin ≥20% · dengue bites by day, malaria by night · altitude illness above about 2,500 m · road trauma is the leading preventable cause of death in young travellers · fever in a traveller is malaria until proven otherwise · do not quote vaccine prices from memory — offer to check

stem: General practice, Wallaroo (MM5). Jack Petersen, 62, retired shearer now doing casual farm maintenance. The practice nurse has already performed pre- and post-bronchodilator spirometry; the printed report is on your desk.
Eight months of breathlessness walking up the main street and a morning cough with clear sputum. RR 18, SpO2 94% on room air, afebrile, BP 138/84, BMI 27. 8 minutes.
The chart: FVC 4.15 → 4.20 L (Predicted 4.75, LLN 3.80; 87% predicted) · FEV1 2.78 → 2.90 L (Predicted 3.85, LLN 3.05; 72% → 75% predicted) · FEV1/FVC 0.67 → 0.69 (Predicted 0.81, LLN 0.71).
Three acceptable manoeuvres, best two FEV1 within 90 mL. Salbutamol 400 microgram via spacer, repeated at 15 minutes.
tasks: Interpret the spirometry — to the examiner face-to-face, to the patient online
Explain the diagnosis to Jack in plain language
Answer his questions and outline your initial management
time: Fifteen seconds to orientate yourself to the report, said out loud with a reason — silence without a stated reason reads as panic, silence with one reads as method · then the interpretation, then the same thing in plain English, then four management priorities

back.dx: COPD WITH MILD AIRFLOW LIMITATION — FIXED OBSTRUCTION, POST-BRONCHODILATOR RATIO 0.69, FEV1 72% PREDICTED, 45 PACK-YEARS. THE SMOKING QUESTION, WHICH IS THE SECOND AUTOMATIC FAIL: he volunteers only 'I GAVE THE SMOKES UP' and gives the amount and the years ONLY IF YOU ASK A SECOND QUESTION — 'CAN I ASK, WHEN DID YOU STOP, AND HOW MUCH WERE YOU SMOKING BEFORE THAT?' Rollies, about a pack a day from seventeen, stopped four years ago: AROUND FORTY-FIVE PACK-YEARS, WHICH FITS WHAT YOU ARE SEEING. THEN THE SCREENING QUESTIONS THAT BELONG HERE: any blood when you cough · any weight coming off without trying · any fevers · AND AN OCCUPATIONAL HISTORY — dust, welding, asbestos, grain. EXPLAINING IT TO JACK: 'the test measures TWO THINGS: THE TOTAL AMOUNT OF AIR YOU CAN BLOW OUT, AND HOW MUCH OF IT COMES OUT IN THE FIRST SECOND. Yours shows THE AIR IS COMING OUT MORE SLOWLY THAN IT SHOULD for a man of your age and height — WHICH TELLS ME THE AIRWAYS ARE NARROWED. We gave you Ventolin and repeated it, AND THE NUMBERS BARELY MOVED. That's important, BECAUSE IN ASTHMA THEY OPEN UP. When the narrowing stays fixed like this, in someone who has smoked, the name for it is CHRONIC OBSTRUCTIVE PULMONARY DISEASE — COPD, WHICH COVERS WHAT PEOPLE USED TO CALL EMPHYSEMA AND CHRONIC BRONCHITIS.' MANAGEMENT, FOUR THINGS IN THIS ORDER: STOPPING SMOKING COMPLETELY IS THE ONLY THING THAT CHANGES HOW FAST THIS WORSENS, and it still counts at 62 — offer patches or tablets and QUITLINE 13 7848 · PULMONARY REHABILITATION, an exercise and education programme that DOES MORE FOR BREATHLESSNESS THAN ANY INHALER · VACCINATIONS: flu yearly, plus pneumococcal and COVID · AND AN INHALER, WHICH YOU DEMONSTRATE AND THEN WATCH HIM USE. Plus a CHEST X-RAY AND BLOODS and a WRITTEN ACTION PLAN FOR CHEST INFECTIONS. HIS QUESTIONS: 'WILL I END UP ON OXYGEN?' → most people with mild COPD never need it, that is a much later stage and not where he is · 'CAN I STILL WORK THE HEADER?' → yes, and STAYING ACTIVE IS PART OF THE TREATMENT — just watch the dust, KEEP THE CAB SHUT AND THE FILTER SERVICED · and the rehab objection 'IS THAT IN ADELAIDE? I'M NOT DRIVING DOWN THERE EVERY WEEK' deserves a local answer. SAFETY-NET: come back sooner if MORE SHORT OF BREATH THAN USUAL, if the SPUTUM CHANGES COLOUR or there is a FEVER — AND THE SAME DAY IF HE EVER COUGHS UP BLOOD. Review in four weeks with the X-ray back. THE VARIANTS: VARIANT B, THE RESTRICTIVE CHART in a 58-year-old boilermaker with thirty years of welding — 'THE RATIO IS 0.89 AGAINST A PREDICTED 0.80 — NORMAL, IN FACT SLIGHTLY RAISED, SO THIS IS NOT OBSTRUCTIVE AND THE POST-BRONCHODILATOR COLUMN ISN'T RELEVANT. Looking instead at the volumes: FVC 2.35 L, 59% predicted, FEV1 2.10 L, 64% — BOTH REDUCED WITH A PRESERVED RATIO, A RESTRICTIVE PATTERN. SPIROMETRY CANNOT CONFIRM RESTRICTION, so I'd request LUNG VOLUMES AND TRANSFER FACTOR', with an HRCT and a respiratory opinion for likely OCCUPATIONAL INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE. AND WHEN HE SAYS 'DON'T PUT THAT IN WRITING — I'LL LOSE THE JOB': 'I hear you, and I'm not going behind your back. But I can't treat this properly without recording what caused it, and A WORK-RELATED LUNG CONDITION GIVES YOU ACCESS TO COMPENSATION THROUGH ReturnToWorkSA RATHER THAN TAKING ANYTHING AWAY.' VARIANT C, EXPLAINING THE PROCEDURE TO A PARENT — no needles and nothing goes inside her · a SOFT CLIP ON THE NOSE so all the air goes through the mouthpiece · biggest breath in, lips sealed, BLAST THE AIR OUT AS HARD AND AS LONG AS SHE CAN · THE NURSE WILL BE SHOUTING ENCOURAGEMENT, WHICH IS NORMAL AND IS HOW WE GET A GOOD EFFORT · AT LEAST THREE GOOD GOES THAT AGREE, so about fifteen minutes, then Ventolin and a repeat after a quarter of an hour · CHILDREN USUALLY MANAGE FROM ABOUT FIVE OR SIX. VARIANT D, THE BORDERLINE CHART AND THE EXAMINER WHO PUSHES — ratio 0.78 against a predicted 0.83: 'IT IS BELOW THE MEAN PREDICTED, BUT HIS LOWER LIMIT OF NORMAL IS 0.73, AND 0.78 IS ABOVE IT — so statistically this sits INSIDE THE NORMAL RANGE and I wouldn't call obstruction on these numbers alone. I'd interpret it AGAINST HIS SYMPTOMS: repeat spirometry when he's symptomatic, look for PEAK-FLOW VARIABILITY, and consider BRONCHIAL PROVOCATION TESTING rather than either labelling him or discharging him.'
plan: WASH HANDS, INTRODUCE, GAIN PERMISSION — and ask what he was hoping to get out of today.
ORIENTATE TO THE REPORT OUT LOUD, WITH THE REASON: predicted column, lower limit of normal, pre- and post-bronchodilator values.

The interpretation: technically acceptable and repeatable · ratio 0.67 against LLN 0.71, obstructive · FVC preserved at 87%, pure obstruction · 2.78 → 2.90 L = 120 mL = 4.3%, not reversible · post-bronchodilator 0.69, below 0.70 — COPD, mild.
THE SAME THING IN PLAIN ENGLISH FOR JACK — two things measured, air coming out slowly, Ventolin barely moved it, and in asthma it would have.
HE SAYS 'I GAVE THE SMOKES UP' — ASK THE SECOND QUESTION: when, and how much before that. Then pack-years said back to him.
RED FLAGS AND OCCUPATION: haemoptysis, weight loss, fevers · dust, welding, asbestos, grain.
He goes quiet about his brother. Notice it and ask what he is worried about, before he has to say it.
BE STRAIGHT: the test cannot tell you about cancer either way, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY YOU ARE ORDERING THE X-RAY — and you will ring him yourself with the result.
Management in four: smoking cessation first · pulmonary rehab · vaccinations · one inhaler, demonstrated and watched. Plus x-ray, bloods and an action plan.
ANSWER THE OXYGEN QUESTION AND THE WORK QUESTION HONESTLY — most people with mild COPD never need oxygen, and staying active is part of the treatment.
SUMMARISE, SAFETY-NET INCLUDING SAME-DAY REVIEW FOR HAEMOPTYSIS, review in four weeks — and check what he would do if he got a chest infection over the weekend.

ask: THE INTERPRETATION SET: 'I'd like fifteen seconds to orientate myself to this report, BECAUSE THE HEADINGS DIFFER BETWEEN MACHINES.' · 'This is a technically acceptable and repeatable spirogram.' · 'STARTING WITH THE RATIO, BECAUSE THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING AFTER IT.' · 'FVC is preserved, so this is pure obstruction rather than a mixed picture.' · 'A RISE OF 0.12 LITRES — 120 MILLILITRES — WHICH IS 4.3 PER CENT OF HIS OWN BASELINE.' · 'The post-bronchodilator ratio is below 0.70, which is what formally confirms COPD.'

The patient set: 'The air is coming out more slowly than it should, which means the airways are narrowed.' · 'Did you ever smoke — and how much, and when did you stop?' · 'You've gone quiet on me. Is there something you're worried this might be?' · 'This test can't tell me about cancer either way, which is exactly why I want a chest x-ray.'
And for the restrictive variant: 'That is a restrictive pattern. Spirometry can't confirm restriction — I'd want lung volumes and transfer factor.'
pefe: The observations are given and the chart is the examination: RR 18, SpO2 94% on room air, afebrile, BP 138/84, BMI 27 · three acceptable manoeuvres with best two FEV1 within 90 mL, so quality criteria are met · salbutamol 400 microgram via spacer, repeated at 15 minutes.

WHAT HE GIVES WHEN ASKED: eight months of breathlessness, STOPPING ONCE ON THE HILL AND PRETENDING TO LOOK IN A SHOP WINDOW · a morning cough with clear phlegm · NO HAEMOPTYSIS, NO WEIGHT LOSS, NO FEVERS · shearing sheds and some grain handling, NO KNOWN ASBESTOS · no birds, dog lives outside · perindopril, occasionally forgotten · NEVER BEEN IN HOSPITAL EXCEPT FOR A BUSTED COLLARBONE · AND A BROTHER WHO DIED AT 64 OF LUNG CANCER FOUR YEARS AGO, WHICH IS WHY HE FINALLY STOPPED SMOKING.
The scoring checklist's last two items are the global ones: did you keep to time without rushing him, and did you treat him as a person rather than a spirogram.

Orientate aloud before a single number — 'Before I interpret this, I'd like FIFTEEN SECONDS TO ORIENTATE MYSELF TO THIS PARTICULAR REPORT, BECAUSE THE HEADINGS DIFFER BETWEEN MACHINES. This one gives me a PREDICTED COLUMN AND A LOWER LIMIT OF NORMAL, then PRE- AND POST-BRONCHODILATOR VALUES with percent predicted for each. I'll use FVC, FEV1 and the ratio, AND I WON'T BE USING PEAK FLOW OR THE MID-FLOWS.' Candidates who skip this step then MISREAD 'BASELINE' AS THE PREDICTED VALUE

The ratio first, with its comparison point named — 'STARTING WITH THE RATIO, BECAUSE THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING AFTER IT. His FEV1/FVC is 0.67. His predicted ratio is 0.81 and HIS LOWER LIMIT OF NORMAL IS 0.71. 0.67 IS BELOW BOTH, so the ratio is reduced — THIS IS AN OBSTRUCTIVE PATTERN.' Examiner probe 'why not just use 0.70?' → 'A FIXED 0.70 OVER-CALLS OBSTRUCTION IN OLDER PEOPLE AND MISSES IT IN YOUNGER ONES, because the normal ratio falls with age. THE LOWER LIMIT OF NORMAL IS THE FIFTH PERCENTILE for someone of his age, height, sex and ethnicity. I'll still quote the POST-BRONCHODILATOR ratio against 0.70, because that is what Australian COPD guidance requires for the diagnosis'

The probe that catches people: 'The chart says 72 to 75 — isn't that 3 per cent?' — 'Those two columns are percentages of predicted; subtracting them measures the change against the population value, not against his own lungs. Reversibility is post minus pre, divided by pre, times a hundred — from his litres. That gives 4.3 per cent. I'm aware the 2022 ATS/ERS standard does express the change as a percentage of predicted, but Australian practice uses 12 per cent and 200 millilitres from baseline, and by either criterion this response is negative'

Convert the pattern into a named disease — the pattern is never the end — 'Fixed airflow obstruction, with a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.69, below 0.70, which is what formally confirms COPD in Australian practice. His FEV1 is 72 per cent of predicted, so the airflow limitation itself is mild, although his symptoms are what will drive treatment. Against asthma: no reversibility, no variability, no atopy. Against a restrictive process: the ratio is low with a preserved FVC.' Stopping at 'Obstructive pattern' is the trap

The moment that decides the station — he goes quiet — At four to five minutes he says 'MY BROTHER WENT THAT WAY. LUNGS. HE WAS SIXTY-FOUR' and then stops talking. 'YOU'VE GONE QUIET ON ME. IS THERE SOMETHING YOU'RE WORRIED THIS MIGHT BE?' — and when he says cancer: 'I'M GLAD YOU TOLD ME. THIS TEST CAN'T SHOW CANCER AND CAN'T RULE IT OUT EITHER, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY I WANT A CHEST X-RAY AS WELL.' REASSURING HIM THAT THE SPIROMETRY EXCLUDES CANCER IS THE FAILURE — NAME THE X-RAY INSTEAD OF OFFERING COMFORT YOU CANNOT BACK. If you never ask, he says it outright at about seven minutes and marks you down for making him ask

The arithmetic, spoken — the most heavily weighted line in the station — 'FVC is 4.15 litres, 87 per cent of predicted — essentially preserved, so this is pure obstruction rather than a mixed picture. Now the bronchodilator response. FEV1 goes from 2.78 to 2.90 litres. That is a rise of 0.12 litres — 120 millilitres. As a proportion of his own baseline, 0.12 divided by 2.78 is 4.3 per cent. The thresholds are 200 millilitres and 12 per cent, and neither is met, so this obstruction is not reversible.' Say the litres, then the millilitres, then the percentage, in that order

Salbutamol 400 microgram via spacer, repeat spirometry at 10–15 minutes · withhold before a diagnostic test: salbutamol 4 h, ipratropium 12 h, salmeterol and formoterol 24 h, ultra-laba and lama 36 h — never the inhaled steroid · services: Quitline 13 7848 · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · TIS National 131 450 · VERIFY every threshold against therapeutic guidelines, the Australian asthma handbook or COPD-X before quoting it

At about forty seconds — neither deflect nor blurt: 'There is something we need to talk about properly, and I will be straight with you — let me ask a couple more questions first'

back.dx: SEVERE RESTRICTIVE VENTILATORY DEFECT WITH SEVERELY IMPAIRED GAS TRANSFER, CONSISTENT WITH PARENCHYMAL INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE — AND GIVEN THE EXPOSURE HISTORY, MOST LIKELY SILICOSIS. ORIENTATE FIRST: 'this is a full lung function report with THREE BLOCKS — spirometry with pre- and post-bronchodilator columns, STATIC LUNG VOLUMES, and CORRECTED GAS TRANSFER. I'll take them in order — ratio, then FVC, then TLC, then DLCO.' NAMING THE THREE BLOCKS TAKES SIX SECONDS AND STOPS YOU SKIPPING THE BOTTOM HALF OF THE SHEET, WHICH IS WHERE THIS DIAGNOSIS LIVES. Two details worth adding: THERE IS NO BRONCHODILATOR RESPONSE, FEV1 1.57 TO 1.58 L, AS EXPECTED IN FIBROSIS · and THE RV/TLC OF 38% AGAINST A PREDICTED 30 REFLECTS THE SHRUNKEN TOTAL CAPACITY RATHER THAN AIR TRAPPING. THE PLAN, IN ORDER: FIRST AND MOST IMPORTANTLY, STOP THE EXPOSURE STARTING NOW, AND PUT IT IN WRITING FOR THE EMPLOYER · SECOND, AN HRCT — A PLAIN X-RAY ISN'T DETAILED ENOUGH FOR THIS · THIRD, A BLOOD TEST FOR TUBERCULOSIS AND AN AUTOIMMUNE SCREEN, BECAUSE SILICOSIS MAKES TB MORE LIKELY AND IT IS VERY TREATABLE · FOURTH, REFERRAL TO A RESPIRATORY PHYSICIAN AND AN OCCUPATIONAL PHYSICIAN · FIFTH, A WALKING TEST TO SEE WHAT HIS OXYGEN DOES ON EXERTION. SAFETY-NET: come back straight away, or go to hospital, if MUCH MORE BREATHLESS OVER DAYS RATHER THAN MONTHS, if he COUGHS UP BLOOD, or if he gets FEVERS OR DRENCHING NIGHT SWEATS. Then: ring him with the CT result either way rather than leaving him waiting, ASK HIM TO BRING HIS WIFE NEXT TIME BECAUSE THERE WILL BE A LOT TO TAKE IN, and teach-back. HIS HIDDEN AGENDA: he already half-suspects this is work-related — HE HAS SEEN THE NEWS STORIES ABOUT BENCHTOP WORKERS — BUT WHAT HE IS ACTUALLY FRIGHTENED OF IS LOSING HIS INCOME, AND THE MORTGAGE IS WHAT KEEPS HIM AWAKE. He will not say so until work is raised. He also does not volunteer that HE HAS LOST ABOUT 4 kg, that he has STARTED SLEEPING IN THE RECLINER BECAUSE LYING FLAT MAKES THE COUGH WORSE, or the two coughing workmates. THE VARIANTS: VERSION B, SPIROMETRY ONLY WITH NO LUNG VOLUMES — FVC 0.90 L = 28%, FEV1 0.78 L = 30%, ratio 87: 'both severely reduced with a preserved ratio, WHICH IS SUGGESTIVE OF A RESTRICTIVE PROCESS. I want to be careful here: SPIROMETRY ALONE CANNOT CONFIRM RESTRICTION — a low FVC can also arise from AIR TRAPPING IN SEVERE OBSTRUCTION, OR FROM A SUBMAXIMAL EFFORT. I would confirm with formal lung volumes, specifically the TLC, together with gas transfer.' IF THE EXAMINER PRESSES 'SO IS IT RESTRICTIVE?', DO NOT CAVE — SUGGESTIVE IS THE ANSWER, AND NAMING THE CONFIRMATORY TEST IS THE MARK. VERSION C, THE PSEUDORESTRICTION CHART — FVC 1.89 L at 41% LOOKS restrictive, BUT THE RATIO IS 47% AGAINST A PREDICTED 79, MARKEDLY REDUCED, SO THIS IS OBSTRUCTIVE. The volumes confirm it: RV 248% OF PREDICTED AND TLC 117%, so there is GROSS AIR TRAPPING AND HYPERINFLATION, and THE LOW FVC IS A CONSEQUENCE OF TRAPPED GAS, NOT OF A SMALL LUNG. DLCO 62%, and a striking bronchodilator response of FEV1 0.89 to 1.89 L — severe obstruction with marked reversibility and hyperinflation, where the reduced gas transfer raises emphysema and the size of the response favours severe asthma. A LOW FVC NEVER ESTABLISHES RESTRICTION ON ITS OWN: RATIO FIRST, THEN TLC. VERSION D, RESTRICTION WITH A NORMAL DLCO — that points AWAY from parenchymal disease and TOWARDS AN EXTRAPULMONARY CAUSE: obesity, chest wall deformity such as kyphoscoliosis, pleural disease, or RESPIRATORY MUSCLE WEAKNESS. MEASURE THE FVC ERECT AND SUPINE — A FALL OF MORE THAN ABOUT 20% LYING FLAT SUGGESTS DIAPHRAGMATIC WEAKNESS — examine for proximal and bulbar weakness, check the BMI, and consider neurology referral. VERSION E, 'JUST TELL ME STRAIGHT, HOW LONG HAVE I GOT?' — 'I'm not going to give you a number, AND I WANT TO EXPLAIN WHY RATHER THAN JUST DODGING IT. I honestly don't know, and ANY FIGURE I GAVE YOU TODAY WOULD BE INVENTED. What I do know is that THE RANGE IS WIDE, that it depends heavily on how much further scarring occurs, and that STOPPING THE DUST EXPOSURE IS THE SINGLE BIGGEST THING IN YOUR FAVOUR. WHAT I CAN PROMISE IS THAT I'LL TELL YOU WHAT I KNOW WHEN I KNOW IT, AND I WON'T DRESS IT UP.'

HE ASKS 'IS IT BAD?'. Neither deflect nor blurt — promise honesty and finish the history.

EXCLUDE THE OTHERS: birds, damp, mould · DRUG CAUSES NAMED · connective tissue symptoms · reflux · smoking.

WARNING SHOT, THEN PAUSE. Let the five seconds sit. Then the diagnosis in plain English, and an apology for the news.

THE PLAN IN ORDER: stop the exposure today and put it in writing · HRCT · TB AND AUTOIMMUNE SCREEN · respiratory and occupational referrals · walking test.

THE BAD-NEWS SET: 'I'm afraid the results do show a problem, and it's a significant one.' — THEN STOP · 'Your lungs have become stiffer and smaller, and oxygen isn't crossing into your blood the way it should.' · 'THE SCARRING THAT'S ALREADY THERE DOESN'T REVERSE — BUT WHAT WE CAN CHANGE IS WHETHER IT GETS WORSE.' · 'I honestly can't tell you that today, and I'd be making it up if I tried.' · 'THIS IS A CONDITION I'M REQUIRED TO REPORT — AND THE REPORTING IS WHAT PROTECTS YOU.' · 'STOPPING THE EXPOSURE DOESN'T HAVE TO MEAN STOPPING WORK.'
pefe: The findings are the report and the signs already given: RR 18, SpO2 95% at rest, afebrile, and finger clubbing. The full sheet has three blocks and the diagnosis lives in the bottom two — lung volumes and gas transfer — so read past the spirometry.

WHAT HE GIVES WHEN ASKED, IN FOUR OR FIVE WORDS AT A TIME: nine months of breathlessness, STOPPING TWICE ON THE HILL · dry tickly cough, worse at night · NO HAEMOPTYSIS, NO FEVERS · a few kilos lost, 'not been eating much' · eighteen years cutting benchtops · ENGINEERED STONE, CUT DRY · A PAPER MASK, NEVER FIT-TESTED · 'THERE'S A FAN' · TWO WORKMATES COUGHING FOR MONTHS, 'WE JOKE ABOUT IT' · no birds, house dry, no regular medications, quit smoking at 30 after five pack-years.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: never taking a proper occupational history — material, wet or dry, protection, years · and agreeing not to notify. AND THE GLOBAL QUESTION ON THE SHEET: DID THEY SIT WITH YOUR SILENCE, AND DID YOU FEEL LIKE A PERSON WITH A MORTGAGE OR A REPORT TO BE READ?

The six occupational questions that make the diagnosis — 'Tell me exactly what you do at work' gets you 'I cut and Polish kitchen benchtops', and accepting that and moving on is the AUTOMATIC FAIL. The string of six: what material — natural stone or the engineered kind? · do you cut it wet or dry? · what mask do you wear, and has it ever been fit-tested? · is there dust extraction? · how many years? · are any of your workmates coughing or short of breath? Answers: engineered stone, cut dry because wet makes a mess, a paper mask from the hardware shop never fit-tested, just a fan, eighteen years — and two workmates with a cough for months. Then previous exposures: asbestos, mining, foundry, boilermaking, sandblasting, home renovation

Screen TB and malignancy — here they are not box-ticking — Haemoptysis · fevers, night sweats, weight loss · chest pain · ankle swelling. In silicosis TB risk is genuinely increased and silica is a recognised lung carcinogen, so these questions are doing real work. And exclude the other causes of a stiff lung: birds, damp, mould or a spa · drugs — amiodarone, methotrexate, nitrofurantoin, bleomycin · connective tissue symptoms — joint pains, rashes, dry eyes, fingers that go white in the cold · reflux · and smoking. Naming the drug causes shows the examiner you have a differential rather than a hunch

The four steps, spoken — and step three is the one that proves it — Step one, the ratio: 91% against a predicted 84 — normal, in fact raised, so not obstructive. Step two, the FVC: 1.73 L against 4.37 predicted, 40% — severely reduced, which is suggestive of restriction. Step three, the lung volumes, and this is what confirms it: TLC 2.68 L against 6.12 predicted, 44% — a genuinely reduced total lung capacity, so this is true restriction and not a low FVC from air trapping. Step four, gas transfer: corrected DLCO 5.13 against 32.19, 16% — severely reduced, which localises the disease to the lung parenchyma rather than the chest wall or the respiratory muscles. Announcing 'Restrictive' from the FVC alone is the trap

Warning shot, then pause — and let the silence sit — 'Dan, before I go through this — I'M AFRAID THE RESULTS DO SHOW A PROBLEM, AND IT'S A SIGNIFICANT ONE.' THEN STOP. He is briefed to GO SILENT FOR A FULL FIVE SECONDS, and IF YOU KEEP TALKING THROUGH HIS SILENCE HE MARKS YOU DOWN. Then: 'your lungs have become STIFFER AND SMALLER than they should be, and THE TRANSFER OF OXYGEN FROM YOUR LUNGS INTO YOUR BLOODSTREAM IS SEVERELY REDUCED. Putting that together with EIGHTEEN YEARS OF DRY-CUTTING ENGINEERED STONE, the most likely explanation is SILICOSIS — scarring of the lung caused by breathing in very fine stone dust over many years. I'M SORRY TO BE GIVING YOU THIS NEWS'

The honest prognosis — neither extreme — 'THE SCARRING THAT'S ALREADY THERE DOESN'T REVERSE — there's no treatment that undoes it, AND I'M NOT GOING TO PRETEND OTHERWISE. But WHAT WE CAN INFLUENCE IS WHETHER IT GETS WORSE, and the single most important thing there is STOPPING THE DUST EXPOSURE.' 'WE'LL GET YOU SORTED' IS DISHONEST; 'THERE'S NOTHING WE CAN DO' IS UNTRUE AND CRUEL. AND IF HE ASKS HOW LONG: DO NOT GUESS A NUMBER — 'I honestly can't tell you that today, AND I'D BE MAKING IT UP IF I TRIED. What I can tell you is what the specialist will look at, and I'll go through the results with you every step'

Hold the notification — and frame it as protection — 'STOPPING THE EXPOSURE IS NOT THE SAME AS STOPPING WORK — the aim is DUTIES WHERE YOU'RE NOT BREATHING THAT DUST. Second, this is a condition I'M REQUIRED TO REPORT to the work health and safety regulator — SafeWork SA. I DON'T HAVE A CHOICE ABOUT THAT, AND IT ISN'T A JUDGEMENT ON YOU. And I'd say this: THE REPORTING IS WHAT PROTECTS YOU. It's what opens the compensation and income-support pathway through ReturnToWorkSA, AND IT'S WHAT GETS YOUR WORKMATES CHECKED — which, from what you've told me about the two blokes with the cough, matters.' AGREEING NOT TO NOTIFY FAILS; NOTIFYING COLDLY IS A BARE PASS; AND TELLING HIM TO RESIGN IS MARKED DOWN

back.dx: MILD OBSTRUCTIVE VENTILATORY DEFECT WITH SIGNIFICANT BRONCHODILATOR REVERSIBILITY — CONSISTENT WITH ASTHMA, AND POSSIBLY OCCUPATIONAL. THE THREE PRACTICAL THINGS THAT FINISH THE STATION: THE SPACER — 'used with a spacer, FAR MORE OF THE DOSE REACHES YOUR LUNGS. I'll show you now AND THEN WATCH YOU DO IT, because TECHNIQUE IS THE SINGLE COMMONEST REASON A PUFFER DOESN'T WORK' · A WRITTEN ACTION PLAN — a one-page sheet with WHAT TO TAKE WHEN YOU'RE WELL, WHAT TO CHANGE WHEN YOU'RE GETTING WORSE, AND EXACTLY WHEN TO SEEK URGENT HELP, kept on the fridge · AND TRIGGERS — 'your hay fever matters more than you'd think; TREATING THE NOSE IMPROVES THE CHEST', plus a TWO-WEEK PEAK FLOW DIARY COVERING WORK DAYS AND DAYS OFF, because if work is contributing THAT CHANGES WHAT WE DO. REVIEW IN FOUR TO SIX WEEKS. SAFETY-NET: come back sooner, or go to the emergency department, IF SHE NEEDS THE RELIEVER MUCH MORE OFTEN, IF SHE'S WAKING AT NIGHT MORE, OR IF SHE'S EVER BREATHLESS AT REST OR STRUGGLING TO FINISH A SENTENCE. ON THE JOB: she says 'COULD IT REALLY BE THE JOB? I LOVE THAT JOB' — DO NOT THREATEN IT. 'It might be, and IF IT IS, THE ANSWER USUALLY ISN'T LEAVING — IT'S IDENTIFYING WHAT THE TRIGGER IS AND REDUCING EXPOSURE. Let's find out first.' The centre has GUINEA PIGS AND A RABBIT IN THE TODDLER ROOM and THE CLEANERS USE A STRONG BLEACH SPRAY at the end of shift — both given only if you ask what she is exposed to at work. HER HIDDEN AGENDA: HER GRANDMOTHER DIED OF EMPHYSEMA AND SHE IS QUIETLY FRIGHTENED THIS IS 'THE START OF LUNG DAMAGE'. She will not say so unless asked about worries — and if you never ask, she raises it at about six minutes and marks you down. HER SECOND CONCERN IS STEROIDS, BECAUSE A FRIEND GAINED WEIGHT ON PREDNISOLONE. THE VARIANTS: VERSION B, THE BORDERLINE CHART — ratio 59%, clearly obstructive; FEV1 2.40 TO 2.77 L, WHICH IS 370 MILLILITRES AND 15 PER CENT OF BASELINE. 'The thresholds are 200 millilitres and 12 per cent, SO BOTH ARE MET, THOUGH NOT BY A WIDE MARGIN. Given a supportive history I would call this significant reversibility consistent with asthma, AND I WOULD BE REASSURED BY THE FACT THAT BOTH CRITERIA — NOT JUST ONE — ARE SATISFIED.' IF THE EXAMINER SAYS 'ARE YOU SURE?', RECALCULATE OUT LOUD RATHER THAN CHANGING YOUR ANSWER — THE QUESTION IS TESTING WHETHER YOUR FIGURE CAME FROM ARITHMETIC OR FROM A GUESS. VERSION C, THE NORMAL CHART WITH A CLASSIC HISTORY — FEV1 4.35 L at 98%, FVC 5.60 L at 104%, ratio 78 against a lower limit of 73: 'THIS IS A NORMAL SPIROGRAM. BUT NORMAL SPIROMETRY DOES NOT EXCLUDE ASTHMA — the airflow limitation is VARIABLE, and she may simply be well today. I WOULD NOT REASSURE HER ON THIS RESULT. I'd arrange a TWO-WEEK PEAK FLOW DIARY looking for excess variability, consider FeNO, and refer for BRONCHIAL PROVOCATION TESTING if it remained uncertain.' AND TO THE PATIENT: 'your breathing test today came back normal — AND I WANT TO EXPLAIN WHY THAT DOESN'T MEAN NOTHING IS WRONG. In asthma THE NARROWING COMES AND GOES. If we happen to test you on a good day, the numbers look fine. So rather than telling you it's all clear, I'd like you to blow into a small meter at home twice a day for a fortnight. IF THE READINGS SWING AROUND, THAT SWING ITSELF IS THE EVIDENCE.' VERSION D, THE SMOKER WITH FIXED OBSTRUCTION — ratio 0.54 against a predicted 0.83; FEV1 1.35 TO 1.37 L, WHICH IS 20 MILLILITRES AND 1.5 PER CENT, SO NEITHER CRITERION IS MET. 'With a POST-BRONCHODILATOR RATIO BELOW 0.70 in a long-term smoker, this is FIXED AIRFLOW OBSTRUCTION CONSISTENT WITH COPD, NOT ASTHMA. At 50 per cent of predicted FEV1 this is MODERATE airflow limitation. I would confirm the smoking history in pack-years, AND I WOULD NOT WITHHOLD A PREVENTER TRIAL IF THERE WERE ALSO FEATURES OF ASTHMA — ASTHMA-COPD OVERLAP IS COMMON AND WORTH NAMING RATHER THAN FORCING A BINARY CHOICE.'

SO THE NARROWING ISN'T FIXED DAMAGE — IT OPENS UP.' · 'THE RELIEVER IS THE FIRE EXTINGUISHER; THE PREVENTER STOPS THE FIRES STARTING.' · 'An inhaled dose is a tiny fraction of a tablet dose and goes straight to the airway — AND WE'LL STEP DOWN TO THE LOWEST DOSE THAT KEEPS YOU WELL.' · 'TECHNIQUE IS THE COMMONEST REASON A PUFFER DOESN'T WORK — let me show you, then I'll watch you do it.'
pefe: The three things she withholds: she was completely well over the Christmas break and for a week in April when the centre was closed · the Guinea pigs and rabbit in the toddler room and the cleaners' bleach spray · and her fear about her grandmother's emphysema. And if you hand her a device without demonstrating, she holds it upside down and waits.

THE ROLE-PLAYER'S AUTOMATIC FAILS: reversibility calculated by subtracting percentage-predicted values, or announced with no arithmetic at all · and using a normal chart to tell her she does not have asthma.

Establish the pattern, because the pattern is the diagnosis — Accepting 'a cough for five months' and moving on is the error — VARIABILITY IS THE DIAGNOSIS. 'Is it there all the time, OR DOES IT COME AND GO? HOW MANY NIGHTS A WEEK DOES IT WAKE YOU? What about exercise — DOES IT COME ON WHEN YOU RUN, AND HOW LONG DOES IT TAKE TO SETTLE? Is there anything that reliably sets it off — cats, dust, COLD AIR, a chest infection? Any wheeze or whistling?' AND THEN THE ONE MOST CANDIDATES NEVER ASK: 'IS IT ANY BETTER WHEN YOU'RE ON HOLIDAY OR AWAY FROM WORK?' — WHICH IS WHAT FINDS OCCUPATIONAL ASTHMA. She was completely fine over the Christmas break and hadn't put it together

The risk questions that get skipped — Atopy — eczema, hay fever, a wheezy chest as a child — and family history. Smoking or vaping. Medications including blood pressure tablets and eye drops, because beta-blocker eye drops are easy to miss, and any problem with aspirin or anti-inflammatories. And the one that is scored: 'Have you ever been admitted to hospital or intensive care with your breathing, or needed steroid tablets for it?' — these are the markers of future life-threatening attacks

The four steps, with the arithmetic spoken — Step one, the ratio: 67% against a stated lower limit of 71 — reduced, so obstructive. Step two doesn't apply: FVC is 114% of predicted, so nothing suggests restriction. Step three, reversibility: 'FEV1 rises from 3.00 to 3.70 litres. That's an increase of 0.70 litres — 700 millilitres — and 0.70 divided by 3.00 is 23 per cent of her baseline. Significant reversibility requires at least 200 millilitres and at least 12 per cent. Both criteria are met.' Step four, severity: baseline FEV1 92% of predicted, so the obstruction itself is mild. The commonest error in the station is subtracting the percentage-predicted figures — 114 minus 92 — instead of working from her own litres

Translate the graph, and do not disparage the antibiotics — 'The machine measures two things: HOW MUCH AIR YOU CAN BLOW OUT IN TOTAL, AND HOW MUCH YOU CAN BLOW OUT IN THE FIRST SECOND. Your total is completely normal — but THE AMOUNT YOU CAN SHIFT IN THAT FIRST SECOND IS LOWER THAN IT SHOULD BE, which tells me THE AIR TUBES IN YOUR LUNGS ARE NARROWER THAN THEY SHOULD BE. The nurse gave you the blue reliever, waited, and repeated the test — AND YOUR FIRST-SECOND READING JUMPED BY 700 MILLILITRES, NEARLY A QUARTER BETTER. That means THE NARROWING ISN'T FIXED DAMAGE; IT OPENS UP. And that opening-up is what points to asthma.' On the two failed antibiotic courses: ACKNOWLEDGE THAT THE PATTERN WAS EASY TO MISTAKE FOR INFECTION rather than disparaging the previous doctor

Preventer versus reliever — and pre-empt the steroid question — 'The lining gets swollen and irritated, and the muscle around the tube tightens up. That's why it comes and goes, why it's worse at night, and why running sets it off. The reliever works in minutes — it relaxes the muscle. It doesn't treat the inflammation. The preventer contains a small dose of steroid that settles the inflammation over weeks. The reliever is the fire extinguisher; the preventer stops the fires starting. Most of the benefit comes from the preventer, and it only works if you take it when you feel well.' Address the steroid concern before she raises it: an inhaled dose is a tiny fraction of a tablet dose, delivered straight to the airway, rinse after use to prevent thrush and hoarseness, and you will step down to the lowest dose that keeps her well

Orientate to the chart before you calculate — 'The reference column here is headed NORMAL RANGE, the pre-bronchodilator column is headed BASELINE, and there is a POSTBRONCHODILATOR column with a percentage change. I'd also want to confirm the trace was technically acceptable — AT LEAST THREE ACCEPTABLE MANOEUVRES WITH THE BEST TWO FEV1 AND FVC VALUES WITHIN 150 MILLILITRES.' THE LAYOUT, NOT THE ALGORITHM, IS WHAT CAUSES THE FREEZE — NAMING THE THREE COLUMNS TAKES EIGHT SECONDS AND STEADIES YOU

COPD ratio threshold is below 0.70 post-bronchodilator · review at 4–8 weeks · the ATS/ERS 2022 alternative expresses change as more than 10% of predicted VERIFY · normal spirometry does not exclude asthma — use a two-week peak flow diary, consider FeNO, and refer for bronchial provocation if uncertain

setting: There is no lipid profile and no blood glucose in this case, and that is deliberate. You cannot calculate an absolute risk and you must not ask the examiner for one. The station tests whether you know how the assessment is done — the inputs, the two missing bloods, the five-year window and the three categories — and whether you screen for symptoms before you ever start counting risk factors. If the words 'Blood test', 'Sugar' and 'Fats' never leave your mouth, you have counselled a man about risk assessment without knowing what it requires.
stem: Your general practice. John Miller, 45, has booked a consultation. He wants to discuss his concerns, as his brother has recently undergone coronary artery bypass surgery.
No current complaints recorded. No previous blood results and no recent observations are available. 2 minutes reading, 8 minutes in the room.

His hidden agenda: he wants a treadmill test or a scan to prove his heart is fine, because he is frightened of leaving two young children without a father. If you never ask what he was hoping for, he raises it at about seven minutes when you are trying to wrap up.

Ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings

time: Four minutes of history with a time prompt, then the PEFE, then the counselling and the plan · the symptom screen takes 25 seconds and most candidates skip it entirely, though everything downstream depends on it

BMI and waist circumference · vital signs, particularly blood pressure and pulse rate and rhythm · JVP and visible apex · apex displacement, heaves, thrills · S1 and S2, loud P2, murmurs, added sounds · lower-limb peripheral pulses · and bedside, a random blood sugar and a urine dipstick. Expect BMI 31, waist 106 cm, BP 148/92, pulse 78 regular, everything else normal, random glucose 6.4, dipstick negative. Do not ask for an ECG — he is asymptomatic — and do not ask for an ankle–brachial index, which AMC does not treat as a bedside test

back.dx: PRIMARY-PREVENTION CARDIOVASCULAR RISK ASSESSMENT IN AN ASYMPTOMATIC 45-YEAR-OLD WITH A STRONG FAMILY HISTORY — and no bloods available. The opening that buys the station: 'I'm sorry to hear about your brother — I completely understand why that has worried you. Let me ask you some questions, I'll work out your risk of heart disease, and then we'll make the best plan together. Before I start — is there anything in particular you were hoping we'd cover today?' On the family history: 'Having a family history does increase your risk. Your brother's surgery, and now your mum's heart trouble, both count. But a family history is not a sentence — most of what decides your risk is things we can change, and you already have several of them.' False reassurance is a marked fail — 'I'm sure you'll be fine' when you have measured nothing. The management plan, snap plus weight, with numbers every time because adjectives score nothing: smoking — the single biggest one, a separate appointment just for it, Quitline 13 7848, and nicotine replacement · nutrition — more vegetables, fruit and wholegrains, less takeaway and fried food, less salt, swap butter for olive oil, less red meat and more fish, and a dietitian referral for a mediterranean-style diet · alcohol — four full-strength cans a night is roughly 30 to 40 standard drinks a week, since a full-strength can is about one and a half standard drinks, so four is closer to six; there is no completely safe level, but under 10 standard drinks a week, no more than 4 on any one day, and at least two alcohol-free days · physical activity — at least 150 minutes a week, which is five sessions of thirty minutes, and a gentle weekend stroll does not count, with an exercise physiologist referral · weight — BMI under 25 and waist under 94 cm. On medication, conditional and not promised: 'I can't commit today, because it depends on that number. High risk and I'd start a cholesterol tablet and a blood pressure tablet. Intermediate and we'd work on lifestyle first and decide together. Low and it's lifestyle alone, rechecked in about five years.' then heart foundation reading, review in one to two weeks once the results are back, and the safety-net: chest pain or tightness lasting more than ten minutes, chest pain at rest, breathlessness, palpitations, fainting, or sudden weakness or trouble speaking — call an ambulance on triple zero and do not drive yourself. He is defensive about the smoking and goes quiet if lectured without acknowledgement — 'I'm not here to give you a hard time about it, I just need the picture' preserves the rapport while still delivering the hardest message. And he pushes once on alcohol: 'Four cans isn't that much, is it?' — convert it to standard drinks out loud rather than judging it. Variant B, he admits exertional chest pain: everything up to the symptom screen is identical, and the station diverges at one line. 'Thank you for telling me that — I'm glad you did. That changes my plan for today. Tightness in the chest that comes on with exertion and settles with rest can mean the heart muscle isn't getting enough blood, and I need to sort that out before we talk about long-term risk.' Characterise it — how long, how far before it comes on and is that shortening, radiation to jaw, arm or back, sweating, nausea, breathlessness, ever at rest or waking him — then ECG, troponin, treatment, cardiology referral, a sublingual spray, aspirin and a statin, and the 000 advice. Hearing the chest pain and continuing with snap counselling is the whole point of the variant — and note that stress testing is now appropriate, because there is finally a symptom to test. Variant C, the results are back: TC 6.8, HDL 0.9, ratio 7.6, fasting glucose 5.6, eGFR 84, BP 148/92, calculated five-year risk 14% — give the number, then the meaning: 'Out of a hundred men in your situation, around 14 would have a heart attack or stroke in the next five years, and 86 would not. It is not a prediction about you personally — it's a reason to act.' then both drugs, bloods again at six to eight weeks, and annual review. If the examiner asks for a dose: name the drug class and say you would confirm against current therapeutic guidelines before prescribing — safer and more accurate than guessing VERIFY.

MEDICATION AS CONDITIONAL ON THE NUMBER — then Heart Foundation reading and review in one to two weeks.

ask: THE OPENING SET: 'I'm sorry to hear about your brother — I completely understand why that's worried you.' · 'Let me ask you a few questions, I'll work out your risk of heart disease, AND THEN WE'LL MAKE THE BEST PLAN TOGETHER.' · 'Before I start — IS THERE ANYTHING IN PARTICULAR YOU WERE HOPING WE'D COVER TODAY?' · 'First, let me make sure you don't have any symptoms already.'

THE HISTORY SET: 'Have you ever been told that your blood pressure is high?' · 'HOW WOULD YOU DESCRIBE YOUR WEIGHT?' — never 'what is your BMI?' · 'APART FROM YOUR BROTHER — has anyone else in the family had a heart attack, heart disease or a stroke? AT WHAT AGE WERE THEY DIAGNOSED?' · 'For the risk calculation, may I ask your ethnic background, and the postcode where you live?'

THE COUNSELLING SET: 'We use an Australian cardiovascular risk calculator — it gives us your risk of a heart attack or a stroke IN THE NEXT FIVE YEARS.' · 'To run that I need two things I don't have yet, SO I'M GOING TO ARRANGE A BLOOD TEST — ONE TO CHECK YOUR SUGAR LEVELS, AND ONE TO CHECK THE FATS IN YOUR BLOOD.' · 'Specifically, I need the TOTAL CHOLESTEROL TO HDL RATIO.' · 'Above 10% is high risk, between 5 and 10% is intermediate, under 5% is low — and those categories decide whether you need medication.' · 'There is no completely safe level of drinking, but to keep the risk down: UNDER 10 STANDARD DRINKS A WEEK, NO MORE THAN FOUR IN ONE DAY, AND AT LEAST TWO ALCOHOL-FREE DAYS.'
pefe: Ask for each finding by name or you will be asked 'Looking for what?' and lose forty seconds you cannot spare. Expect: BMI 31 · waist 106 cm · BP 148/92, pulse 78 regular · JVP not raised, apex not visible and not displaced · dual heart sounds with no murmurs or added sounds · all peripheral pulses present and equal · random blood sugar 6.4 mmol/L · urine dipstick negative. The figures vary between recalls; the shape of the reply does not.

WHAT HE GIVES ON HISTORY: FOUR FULL-STRENGTH CANS MOST NIGHTS · blood pressure NEVER CHECKED · TWENTY KILOS GAINED SINCE THE DESK JOB · cholesterol and sugar NEVER TESTED · NO VEGETABLES, FISH AND CHIPS THREE OR FOUR NIGHTS A WEEK, SALT ON EVERYTHING · a ten to fifteen minute weekend walk and NINE HOURS AT A DESK · Australian-born, postcode given · MOTHER'S STENTS IN HER EARLY SIXTIES AND FATHER'S HYPERTENSION, BUT ONLY IF ASKED BEYOND THE BROTHER · A PACK A DAY SINCE EIGHTEEN, defensively · work stress since the restructure · occasional ibuprofen, no allergies, ANXIOUS SINCE THE SURGERY.

The star items on the scoring sheet: screened symptoms before risk factors · asked about relatives other than the brother and their ages · said a blood test was needed for sugar and fats · and declined the treadmill test with a reason.

Screen symptoms before you count a single risk factor — 'FIRST, LET ME MAKE SURE YOU DON'T HAVE ANY SYMPTOMS ALREADY. Any CHEST PAIN, TIGHTNESS OR HEAVINESS, particularly when you exert yourself, that settles with rest? SHORT OF BREATH more easily than you used to be, especially on stairs? Any PAIN OR CRAMPING IN YOUR CALVES WHEN YOU WALK, especially uphill, that eases when you stop? Any PALPITATIONS, BLACKOUTS, OR EPISODES OF WEAKNESS OR SLURRED SPEECH?' In the standard version he is genuinely asymptomatic — but the order is a MARKED JUDGEMENT, NOT A COURTESY, because absolute risk assessment only applies to someone without established disease

The risk-factor run — a B C d E F s, in layman's words — A alcohol, how much and how often · B blood pressure ever checked, and how would you describe your weight — never 'What is your BMI?', because no patient knows · C cholesterol ever tested, and kidneys · d diet, pushed past the non-answer, and sugar ever tested · E exercise per week, work and sitting, and — for the calculator — ethnic background and postcode · F family history beyond the brother, with ages · s smoking, how many and how long, and stress. Then the short tail: medications, allergies, past history, mood

The mother is the reward for asking properly — If you ask only 'any family history?', he says 'WELL — MY BROTHER, LIKE I TOLD YOU' AND VOLUNTEERS NOTHING ELSE. Ask 'APART FROM YOUR BROTHER, HAS ANYONE ELSE — FATHER, MOTHER, BROTHERS, SISTERS — HAD A HEART ATTACK, HEART DISEASE OR A STROKE? AT WHAT AGE WERE THEY DIAGNOSED?' and you get his mother's stents in her early sixties and his father's hypertension. AND HE WILL SAY 'MY DIET'S ALRIGHT I SUPPOSE' — PUSH TO VEGETABLES, FRIED FOOD AND SALT, and he admits no vegetables, fish and chips three or four nights a week, salt on everything

Decline the treadmill test — and the explanation is the mark — 'A treadmill test is designed for someone who IS GETTING SYMPTOMS — chest pain on exertion — so we can see what the heart does under load. IN SOMEONE WITH NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL IT ISN'T ACCURATE ENOUGH: IT MISSES REAL DISEASE AND IT FLAGS PROBLEMS THAT AREN'T THERE, and then we end up doing more invasive tests for nothing. The blood tests and the calculator will tell us far more about your risk than a treadmill would. AND IF YOU EVER DO START GETTING CHEST PAIN ON EXERTION, THAT CHANGES COMPLETELY — COME STRAIGHT BACK.' AGREEING TO IT TO KEEP HIM HAPPY LOSES THE MARK, AND SO DOES REFUSING WITHOUT A REASON. He pushes once: 'BUT WHY NOT?'

The mark the station was built around — the two missing bloods — 'To run that calculation I NEED TWO THINGS I DON'T HAVE YET, so I'm going to arrange a blood test — ONE TO CHECK YOUR SUGAR LEVELS, AND ONE TO CHECK THE FATS IN YOUR BLOOD. Specifically, from the lipids I need the TOTAL CHOLESTEROL TO HDL RATIO — THAT IS THE NUMBER THE CALCULATOR USES. I'd also check your KIDNEY FUNCTION at the same time.' THEN THE CALCULATOR AND THE WINDOW: an Australian calculator giving RISK OF A HEART ATTACK OR STROKE IN THE NEXT FIVE YEARS, using age, sex, smoking, blood pressure, diabetes, a cholesterol measurement AND POSTCODE. THEN THE THREE CATEGORIES: ABOVE 10% HIGH · 5 TO 10% INTERMEDIATE · UNDER 5% LOW — and those categories are what decide medication

stem: General practice. Mr James Whitcombe, 50, has come in because his brother, 54, had coronary artery bypass surgery two weeks ago. He is anxious about his own heart. He smokes 15 a day and is otherwise well. 8 minutes.

Results: BP 148/94 (Average of two seated in-clinic readings) · BMI 29 · waist 102 cm · total cholesterol 6.8, LDL 4.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 2.6 · fasting glucose 5.2 and HbA1c 5.5%, normal · eGFR 82 · ECG sinus rhythm.
Cardiovascular risk assessment already calculated: 12% over five years.
tasks: Take a focused history
Explain the investigation results to the patient
Explain your management plan
Answer the examiner's questions
time: The plan has three limbs and all three are marked: medicines with monitoring · lifestyle · services and dated review · and every drug is a package — choice, side effect, monitoring, target, and when I see you
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Limb one — both drugs, each as a complete package

High risk with both the blood pressure and the fats up means two tablets, not one. An ACE inhibitor: the thing to know is a dry, tickly cough, and if it happens you switch to a closely related tablet that doesn't — with a blood test at two weeks for potassium and kidney function. A statin such as atorvastatin: the side effect is muscle aches, and most aches people get aren't the tablet, but if the pain or weakness is genuinely bad, come back for a creatine kinase. Then give him the targets, because people work towards numbers: total cholesterol under 4 · the bad type under 2 · stored fat under 2 · the good type above 1 · blood pressure consistently under 140/90 · and repeat lipids at three months

back.dx: High cardiovascular risk at 12% over five years, with the numbers already in the stem. Limb two, lifestyle, with the smoking first and without lecturing: 'The biggest single thing on this list is the smoking. Stopping would do more for that 12% than either tablet. Is that something you'd consider?' — ask permission, ask what he has tried, and offer something concrete: Quitline, and patches or a tablet, which roughly doubles the chances of it sticking. Food: more vegetables, fish, wholegrains, olive oil instead of butter, less red meat, and the salt is worth tackling — under a teaspoon a day and none at the table. Alcohol: no more than 10 standard drinks a week, no more than 4 in a day, and a couple of alcohol-free days. Activity: 150 minutes a week of something that gets him a bit puffed, which is thirty minutes on five days, plus resistance work twice a week. And on weight: 'Any weight you lose is a win — I'm not going to give you a target you'll hate.' Do not repeat the smoking message three times — if you lecture him he shuts down with 'Yeah, I know'. Limb three, services and review: a dietitian who will build an actual eating plan rather than a leaflet · an exercise physiologist who will write a programme for someone who has not exercised in a while · set up under a GP management plan so the visits are subsidised · heart foundation reading and today's plan written down · two weeks for the blood test and to check how he is going on the tablets, and three months to recheck the fats. And the principle worth saying: 'We don't need to keep recalculating that percentage — you're in the high group, so we just treat it.' Red flags: chest pain or tightness, pain into the jaw or arm, sudden breathlessness, or sudden weakness, numbness or slurred speech — ring 000, don't drive yourself. Then close the loop on the question he came in with: 'You came in asking whether you're next. You're not where your brother was — he already had blockages when they operated, and nothing today suggests you do. What you've got is a set of risks we've caught while there's still time to change them.' What a failing run looks like, with every fact correct: explains how a risk assessment is performed when the stem already gives 12% · never asks about chest pain · reads the lipid numbers aloud without translating them · gives the percentage bare · starts a statin only · names two drugs with no side effects, no bloods, no targets and no review dates · no referrals · recommends aspirin because the brother is on it · and never returns to 'Am I next?'. The harder moments, scripted: 'Can I just try the diet first and see how I go?' → 'I'm all for the diet, and it will do more than people expect. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I let you leave thinking diet alone will take a cholesterol of 6.8 down under 4. How about this: we start the lifestyle changes and the smoking work today, start one tablet, and I'll see you in two weeks — then you decide about the second with the numbers in front of you.' 'My cholesterol's only 5.6 — the lab says that's in range' → 'The lab range describes the general population. It doesn't describe what's safe for someone in the high risk group. It's not that your result is abnormal for everyone — it's that it's not low enough for you.' and the examiner's hardest question, 'He declines both tablets, have you failed?' → 'No — provided the refusal is informed. I would document that I explained his high-risk category, the recommended treatment and the reasoning, and that he declined. I would secure what he has agreed to — here, smoking cessation, which is the single highest-yield intervention available — arrange review in two weeks, and leave the offer open. A patient who leaves feeling heard is far more likely to come back and reconsider than one who has been argued at.' This station can be passed with the patient declining medication and failed with the patient accepting it — what is marked is whether the results were explained, the risk translated, the plan given in three limbs with dates attached, and the decision shared.

IT ISN'T A PREDICTION — IT'S A MEASURE OF WHAT'S STILL CHANGEABLE.' · 'FEELING WELL DOESN'T MEAN WE'RE SAFE. IT MEANS WE'VE GOT TIME.'

In someone who doesn't, the bleeding risk cancels out the benefit.' · AND THE CLOSING LOOP: 'You're not where your brother was — he already had blockages when they operated, and nothing today suggests you do.'
pefe: Everything is in the stem and the task is to translate it: BP 148/94 as the average of two seated readings · BMI 29, waist 102 cm · total cholesterol 6.8, LDL 4.6, HDL 0.9, triglycerides 2.6 · fasting glucose 5.2 and HbA1c 5.5%, both normal · eGFR 82 · ECG sinus rhythm · and a calculated five-year risk of 12%.

WHAT HE GIVES ON HISTORY: 15 CIGARETTES A DAY FOR 30 YEARS, stopped for a fortnight once · nobody has ever mentioned blood pressure or cholesterol · no diabetes · BROTHER PAUL IS 54, and his father died at 78 of cancer · MEAT AND POTATOES, REGULAR TAKEAWAY, AND HE SALTS EVERYTHING · six or seven beers across a weekend · NO EXERCISE BEYOND BEING ON HIS FEET AT WORK · kidneys and mood fine · AND WHAT HE ACTUALLY WANTS IS TO BE TOLD HE IS ALRIGHT. He does not volunteer the salt, the alcohol, his brother's exact age, or his expectations unless asked directly.

He is briefed to say 'But I feel fine' at least twice and to stay unconvinced if it is never addressed · to latch onto the normal sugar and try to treat the whole visit as reassuring · to test the number with 'So 88 out of 100 don't, that's not terrible, is it?' and disengage if you simply agree · and to ask for aspirin because his brother is on it.

Symptoms first, and the brother's age is the mark — Chest pain or tightness on exertion · pain into the jaw, neck or arm · breathlessness on exertion, lying flat, or waking him · calf cramping that eases when he stops · palpitations, dizziness, blackouts · weakness, numbness or trouble speaking, even briefly. Then: 'Your brother — how old is he exactly?' A first-degree relative with coronary disease before 55 is premature cardiovascular disease, and his brother at 54 qualifies — say it out loud. It does not change this man's management because he is already high risk, but in an intermediate patient it is exactly the reclassification factor that pushes them into treatment

Explain the lipids as four fats, not as a list of numbers — 'THE TOTAL AMOUNT is the overall figure, and yours is high — 6.8. Inside that there's A BAD TYPE — THAT'S THE ONE THAT BUILDS UP ON THE WALLS AND BLOCKS THE TUBES SUPPLYING THE HEART, THE SAME PROCESS YOUR BROTHER HAD. Yours is high. There's also A GOOD TYPE, WHICH HELPS CLEAR THAT BUILD-UP AWAY — we want it as high as possible and AT LEAST ABOVE 1; yours is 0.9. And a fourth, TRIGLYCERIDES, WHICH IS FAT YOUR BODY STORES — that's a bit high too.' RECITING 'LDL 4.6, HDL 0.9, TRIGLYCERIDES 2.6' IS NOT EXPLAINING

Give the good news honestly, then bring him back — 'YOUR SUGAR IS NORMAL, AND THAT'S GENUINELY GOOD NEWS — it means you don't have diabetes, WHICH WOULD HAVE MADE ALL OF THIS CONSIDERABLY HARDER.' Do not bury it: one piece of real good news MAKES THE REST LAND BETTER. But he will latch onto it and try to treat the whole visit as reassuring — SO BRING HIM BACK TO THE THREE THINGS THAT ARE NOT FINE: THE SMOKING, THE BLOOD PRESSURE AT 148/94, AND THE FATS

Translate the 12% — the sentence the guideline asks for — 'If we imagine 100 people the same age as you, the same sex, and in the same circumstances, 12 of those 100 will have a heart attack or a stroke in the next five years. That puts you in the high risk group.' He will minimise it — 'So 88 are fine? That doesn't sound too bad' — and do not simply agree. Benchmark it: 'For a man of 50 that figure should be around 2 or 3. Twelve is high — and it isn't a prediction, it's a measure of how much of this is still changeable.' and when he says 'But I feel fine': 'The furring-up builds silently over years — your brother felt fine too, until he didn't. Feeling well doesn't mean we're safe. It means we've got time'

The aspirin question, and the 'Normal for the lab' question — 'Should I be on aspirin? He's on aspirin.' → 'Aspirin is for people who already have the disease, like your brother. In someone who doesn't, the extra bleeding risk cancels out the benefit, so we don't use it routinely.' and from the examiner — 'His total cholesterol is 5.6 and his BP 140/95, still treat?' → 'Yes. Those figures sit inside the laboratory reference range but they are not target for a high-risk patient. The question is never whether a number is normal — it is whether it is normal for this patient's risk category'

numbers: Risk 12% over 5 years, high — bands <5 low, 5–10 intermediate, ≥10 high · lipid targets for high risk: total cholesterol <4, LDL <2, triglycerides <2, HDL >1 · BP target <140/90, lower if tolerated · ACE inhibitor: dry cough means switch to an ARB, review at 2 weeks with potassium and creatinine, and a fall in kidney function of more than about 25% prompts review · statin: muscle aches, creatine kinase if severe, repeat lipids at 3 months · aspirin is not for primary prevention VERIFY

Snap: Quitline 13 7848 · salt under 5 g a day · alcohol ≤10 standard drinks a week, ≤4 in a day, 2 alcohol-free days · activity ≥150 minutes a week plus resistance training twice weekly · BMI <25, waist <94 cm in men and <80 cm in women · premature family CVD is a first-degree relative before 55 · do not repeat the risk score in a high-risk patient, repeat the monitoring instead · if challenged on a number, say you would confirm against current lipid and hypertension guidance VERIFY

setting: There is no complaint in the stem — there is an agenda. Within the first minute he will tell you, in some form, that he has stopped his cholesterol tablet because it was giving him muscle aches. That sentence is the case, and it surfaces out of your open question or your concerns question — if you ask neither, it may never surface at all.
stem: Your general practice. John Reid, 55, attending for a vaccination. Known hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, on perindopril and atorvastatin. Family history of ischaemic heart disease.
Presenting complaint: none stated. 2 minutes reading, 8 minutes in the room.
In version A he volunteers it with the flu jab request. In version B he does not volunteer it at all, and only the concerns question — or a drug-by-drug compliance question — will catch it.
tasks: Take a relevant history from the patient
Counsel him regarding his cardiovascular risk and management
time: Five things are being paid for: finding the agenda · validating it rather than arguing · exploring the pain with the four discriminating questions · restarting the statin with the ladder ready · and an explicit benefit-versus-risk conversation that ends by handing the decision back

back.dx: STATIN-ASSOCIATED MUSCLE SYMPTOMS AND NON-ADHERENCE IN A MAN WITH HYPERTENSION, HYPERCHOLESTEROLAEMIA AND A FATHER WHO HAD A HEART ATTACK AT 58. THE EDUCATION THAT TARGETS THE ACTUAL HEALTH BELIEF: 'it's from a group called STATINS, and its job is to lower the fats in your blood. That matters because high fat levels increase your risk of a heart attack, a stroke and other heart disease — AND THEY CAUSE NO SYMPTOMS AT ALL, WHICH IS EXACTLY WHY THEY'RE SO EASY TO IGNORE. You said you feel completely fine, AND YOU DO — BUT THE RISK IS BUILDING QUIETLY IN THE BACKGROUND. And in your case there's MORE THAN ONE THING STACKING UP: having high blood pressure as well increases that risk further, and YOUR FATHER HAD A HEART ATTACK AT 58. By controlling both, we bring that risk down together.' THEN OPEN THE DOOR TO OTHER CAUSES BEFORE BLAMING THE DRUG: JOINT PROBLEMS LIKE ARTHRITIS, AN UNDERACTIVE THYROID, LOW VITAMIN D, FIBROMYALGIA, OR SIMPLY DOING MORE PHYSICALLY THAN USUAL — 'so before we decide the tablet is the culprit, WE NEED TO BE SURE THE PAIN REALLY IS COMING FROM IT.' THE BENEFIT-VERSUS-RISK ANALYSIS, SAID IN THESE TERMS: 'THE BENEFIT is that it lowers your chance of a heart attack, a stroke, or developing heart disease — SERIOUS, LIFE-CHANGING EVENTS, AND ONES WE WOULD FAR RATHER PREVENT. THE RISK is muscle aching. It's uncomfortable, and I'M NOT DISMISSING IT — but IT IS NOT LIFE-THREATENING, AND IT GOES AWAY WHEN WE STOP. ON BALANCE, THE BENEFITS CLEARLY OUTWEIGH THE RISK. That's why I'd like you back on it — AND IT'S WHY I'VE GOT A STEP-BY-STEP PLAN IF IT DOES HAPPEN AGAIN, RATHER THAN JUST TELLING YOU TO PUT UP WITH IT.' THE LADDER, IN ORDER: RESTART → IF ACHES RETURN, CHECK THE CK → IF RAISED, STOP FOR A FEW WEEKS TO LET THE MUSCLES SETTLE → THEN RESTART AT A LOWER DOSE, OR SWITCH WITHIN THE FAMILY, ATORVASTATIN TO ROSUVASTATIN → IF IT RECURS, CHECK CK AGAIN AND TRY INTERMITTENT DOSING, EVERY SECOND DAY OR TWICE A WEEK, BECAUSE TAKING SOME IS MUCH BETTER THAN TAKING NONE → AND ONLY THEN A DIFFERENT CLASS ALTOGETHER, EZETIMIBE. 'SO THERE'S A LOT OF ROAD BEFORE WE GIVE UP ON PROTECTING YOU' VERIFY. THEN LIFESTYLE WITH NUMBERS AND REFERRALS — diet with a DIETITIAN for a Mediterranean pattern · 150 MINUTES A WEEK with an EXERCISE PHYSIOLOGIST built around the driving · alcohol UNDER 10 STANDARD DRINKS A WEEK, ≤4 IN A DAY, TWO FREE DAYS · BMI UNDER 25 AND WAIST UNDER 94 cm. THE CLOSING BLOCK HAS TWO TRAPS IN IT: ENDING WITH 'SO YOU'LL RESTART IT THEN' INSTEAD OF HANDING THE DECISION BACK — 'BUT I WANT TO BE CLEAR, THIS IS YOUR DECISION, NOT MINE. Take the Heart Foundation reading home, have a think, and come back and we'll make the plan together. THERE'S NO PRESSURE FROM ME — I'D JUST RATHER WE DECIDED IT DELIBERATELY THAN BY ACCIDENT' — AND RUNNING THE WHOLE CONSULTATION WITHOUT EVER GIVING HIM THE VACCINATION HE ACTUALLY CAME IN FOR. Bloods in two weeks: cholesterol, kidneys and liver, PLUS A THYROID TEST AND VITAMIN D GIVEN THE ACHING, because both cause muscle pain in their own right. SAFETY-NET: GO STRAIGHT TO HOSPITAL IF THE PAIN BECOMES SEVERE, IF REAL WEAKNESS DEVELOPS, OR IF THE URINE TURNS DARK. THE VARIANTS: B, HE NEVER VOLUNTEERS IT — the compliance question drug by drug is what catches it, and if you never ask he mentions it at about six minutes as you wrap up. C, COST IS THE REAL BARRIER — 'I lost the depot job in March, I've been stretching the blood pressure ones too, taking them every other day.' DO NOT MOVE ON: STRETCHING THE ANTIHYPERTENSIVES IS RISKIER THAN THE MUSCLE ACHES, SO FIX THAT FIRST — both are on the PBS, a GENERIC BRAND is often considerably cheaper, a CONCESSION CARD lowers the copayment, the PBS SAFETY NET drops it further once reached, and a PHARMACIST MEDICATION REVIEW goes through the whole list. NON-ADHERENCE RARELY STOPS AT ONE DRUG. D, THE RED FLAG — weakness on the stairs and urine 'like Coke' for two days, still taking the tablet: STOP EVERYTHING, THIS IS NO LONGER A COUNSELLING STATION. 'Muscle pain with weakness and dark urine can mean THE MUSCLE IS BEING DAMAGED AND RELEASING A SUBSTANCE THAT CAN HARM THE KIDNEYS — that's RHABDOMYOLYSIS, and it needs sorting out TODAY. STOP THE STATIN NOW — THIS IS ONE SITUATION WHERE STOPPING IS EXACTLY RIGHT.' Urgent CK, kidney function and urine test, possible fluids in hospital, DON'T DRIVE YOURSELF — AND WE WOULD NOT SIMPLY RESTART THIS TABLET AFTERWARDS. And if weakness is PROGRESSIVE AND PERSISTS WEEKS AFTER STOPPING WITH A VERY HIGH CK, think IMMUNE-MEDIATED NECROTISING MYOPATHY — specialist referral, ANTI-HMGCR ANTIBODIES, AND DO NOT RECHALLENGE VERIFY. E, HE REFUSES OUTRIGHT — 'THAT'S YOUR RIGHT, AND I'M NOT GOING TO PUSH YOU. Everything we said about lifestyle matters MORE, NOT LESS. PLEASE KEEP TAKING YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE TABLET; THAT'S DOING HALF THE JOB ON ITS OWN. I'll arrange the blood tests anyway and see you in a fortnight. AND THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.' A COMPETENT REFUSAL IS NOT A FAILED STATION — WHAT FAILS IS PRESSURING HIM, OR LETTING THE REFUSAL COLLAPSE THE REST OF THE PLAN.
plan: OPEN QUESTION — he says he is here for the flu jab. THEN ASK THE CONCERNS QUESTION ANYWAY.
ACKNOWLEDGE AND VALIDATE: thank him for raising it rather than stopping quietly, and confirm the side effect is recognised.
THE TWO CONDITIONS: when diagnosed · what he takes for each · COMPLIANCE WITH THE PERINDOPRIL TOO · cough and postural dizziness · follow-up and bloods.
COMPLICATIONS SCREEN IN TWENTY SECONDS: chest pain or breathlessness on exertion · leg pain on walking · blurred vision.
THE FOUR DISCRIMINATING PAIN QUESTIONS: side · muscle or joint · dull or sharp · TIMING AFTER STARTING.
THEN: did it settle on stopping · WEAKNESS · morning stiffness · DARK URINE · any new medicine including from the chemist.
THE ADHERENCE SCREEN: what he understands the tablet is for · memory · AND COST.
Risk factors briskly — a B C d E F s, including the father's heart attack at 58.
EDUCATE: what a statin is, what it prevents, THAT THE RISK IS SILENT, and that the two conditions compound.
Other causes of muscle pain, then the rechallenge and why a ck today would be meaningless.
The explicit benefit-versus-risk comparison, then the ladder in order.
Lifestyle with numbers, dietitian and exercise physiologist.
HAND THE DECISION BACK · reading material · bloods including THYROID AND VITAMIN D · review in two weeks · SAFETY-NET FOR SEVERE PAIN, WEAKNESS AND DARK URINE · AND GIVE THE VACCINATION.
