The most likely cause in your case is the steroid nasal spray you use for your hay fever. These sprays are very effective, but over time they dry out the lining of the nose, and the dry lining cracks and bleeds. The nose picking will have contributed too, and the hay fever itself makes the lining inflamed and fragile.' then the other causes checked and excluded: injury or surgery, bleeding or clotting problems including liver disease, infections and allergies, and rarely a growth inside the nose. The management ladder: option one, co-phenylcaine spray to numb and vasoconstrict, then look — 'If I can see the bleeding vessel, I can burn it off using silver nitrate, which sits on the tip of a stick.' Name the risk: a small chance of a hole in the septum, which is why it is done gently and on one side only. Option two, packing — a Merocel sponge that expands when wet, or a rapid rhino, an inflatable balloon with a clot-promoting coating, in for about 24 hours, with an antibiotic while the pack is in. If nothing works, ENT and admission. The Merocel demonstration itself: blow the nose gently, co-phenylcaine, antibiotic ointment on the sponge so it slides in, and slide it straight back along the floor of the nose, horizontally — not upwards — then wet the end with saline so it swells. Warn of discomfort and ask permission; miming it in silence loses the mark. Act on the positive finding: 'I'd like you to stop the steroid nasal spray for now. It's protecting you from a stroke because of your irregular heartbeat, and it isn't what caused this bleed. If — and only if — we can't control the bleeding despite cautery and packing, we'd hold it temporarily, after discussing it with the specialist team, and restart it as soon as it's safe. Please don't stop it on your own at home.' Announcing cessation as step one is the error, and so is refusing to discuss it at all — use the word temporarily. Investigation is a full blood count; INR only if he were on warfarin, and there is no routine apixaban assay. Then four separate marks that are lost by omission: follow-up — back in 24 to 48 hours to have a pack removed, then the GP, and ENT if these keep happening · re-bleed first aid, repeated in full · general advice — no picking, don't blow hard, avoid very hot food and drinks, and no heavy exercise or lifting for a few days · and red flags: bleeding that won't stop after 15 minutes of pressure, fever or thick green discharge while the pack is in, faintness, or haematemesis or melaena. Say them fast if you must, but say them. The variants: one, a DVT three weeks ago instead of AF — 'That changes my thinking, and it makes me more reluctant to interrupt it, not less. The first few weeks after a clot are the highest-risk period for it coming back', so work harder locally and do not withhold even a single dose without discussing it first. Two, warfarin with a mechanical valve — check the INR now and be guided by it, hold temporarily and discuss reversal if it is high, but with a mechanical valve do not interrupt lightly and involve the cardiologist. Three, still bleeding through an anterior pack at twenty minutes — this suggests a posterior bleed: reassess haemodynamics, IV access, FBE, coagulation profile and group and hold, call the ENT registrar, and definitive control is a posterior balloon or a Foley catheter passed along the nasal floor and inflated, with admission. In a regional or MM5 site with no on-site ENT: stabilise, pack, and contact MedSTAR retrieval and the receiving ENT service early — a posterior pack that keeps bleeding is a transfer decision, not a wait-and-see. And if challenged on the anticoagulation controversy: 'The evidence is limited and practice varies. My principle is that local haemostasis comes first, and that any interruption is temporary, individualised to the thrombotic indication, and made in discussion with the treating team' VERIFY.
plan: Ask the examiner for saturation and conscious state — ten seconds, then move.
WIPE, NAME THE FEAR, AND SEQUENCE THE STATION ALOUD: stop the bleeding first, questions after.
The first-aid demonstration, one instruction at a time — and correct his technique specifically.
ASK PERMISSION TO SWITCH TO HISTORY WHILE HE HOLDS PRESSURE, THEN THE SIX BLEED QUESTIONS — and redirect him to spit rather than swallow.
The three red-flag blocks as one continuous run: anaemia, GI bleed, tumour.
Causes: trauma · inflammation and dryness, where you ask about the steroid spray by name · bleeding tendency.
The anticoagulant explored — why, when, missed doses, and anything else — then SADMA.
The diagnosis and causes in plain English, and defuse both distractors.
THE MANAGEMENT LADDER: numbing spray, cautery with its perforation risk, packing, antibiotic cover — and ENT if it fails.
Stop the spray and substitute, with the hay fever plan — then the full blood count.
The anticoagulant decision, reasoned out loud, with the word temporarily.
Follow-up · re-bleed first aid · general advice · red flags · summary and check understanding.
back.planNote: four tasks in eight minutes; the closing four blocks are four separate marks
ask: The opening and first-aid set: 'I'm here to help you, and my first priority is to stop this bleeding.' · 'Stay sitting up, lean forward, head tilted slightly down — not back.' · 'Pinch the soft part of your nose, not the bone, firmly for ten to fifteen minutes.' · 'Don't let go to check whether it has stopped.' · 'If blood runs down your throat, spit it out rather than swallowing it.'

THE HISTORY SET: 'Do you get hay fever? … AND ARE YOU USING A STEROID NASAL SPRAY FOR IT?' · 'WHY WERE YOU STARTED ON THE APIXABAN, AND WHEN WAS YOUR LAST DOSE?' · 'Any long-standing blockage of one side of your nose? Any lumps in your neck? HAVE YOU LOST WEIGHT WITHOUT TRYING?'

The counselling set: 'The most likely cause is the steroid spray you use for hay fever — it dries the lining of the nose, and dry lining cracks and bleeds.' · 'Your blood thinner is not the cause — but it can make the bleeding more severe and harder to stop.' · 'I won't stop it unless we can't control the bleeding — and then only temporarily, after discussing it with the specialist. Please don't stop it on your own.' · 'Your reading of 140 over 90 is where we want it for someone on treatment — it's not what caused this, and I won't be changing it today.' · 'Stop the spray for now, use a moisturiser inside the nostril, and we'll find another way to control your hay fever.'
pefe: No physical examination is required, but ask the examiner for the two missing observations: saturation 98% on room air and alert. The stem gives BP 140/90, HR 84 regular, RR 16, T 36.8 °C, GCS 15.

WHAT HE GIVES ON HISTORY: two hours, CONTINUOUS BUT SLOWING AND RESTARTING, LEFT NOSTRIL ONLY · one small self-limiting bleed last month · BLOOD AT THE BACK OF HIS THROAT WHICH HE HAS BEEN SWALLOWING — CORRECT THIS ON THE SPOT · NOSE PICKING, ADMITTED SLIGHTLY EMBARRASSED · no dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness, haematemesis or melaena · SPRING BLOCKAGE OF BOTH SIDES BUT NO UNILATERAL BLOCKAGE, FACIAL OR EAR PAIN, NECK LUMPS OR WEIGHT LOSS · no injury or nasal surgery, no easy bruising, no family bleeding history, no liver disease · APIXABAN FOR AF FOR TWO YEARS AND PERINDOPRIL FOR FIVE · non-smoker, a few weekend beers, no drugs.

The two things he withholds: the steroid nasal spray, which he does not think of as a medicine, and his plan to stop the anticoagulant himself. He also performs the first aid wrong until corrected, asks what jargon means if you use it, and if you blame his blood pressure he looks relieved and asks whether he needs stronger tablets.

Stability in ten seconds, then reassure before you treat — 'Before I start, could you tell me the oxygen saturation, and whether the patient is alert or drowsy? I'd like to confirm he is haemodynamically stable in the setting of active bleeding.' Two vital signs are missing from the stem. Then the greeting that buys the station: 'I can see this is frightening. I'm here to help you, and my first priority is to stop this bleeding. Once we've got it under control, I'll ask you some questions to work out why it happened'

The first aid, one instruction at a time — and he does it wrong on purpose — Sit up · lean forward with the head tilted slightly down, not back · pinch the soft part of the nose, just below the bony bridge · firm steady pressure for ten to fifteen minutes · 'And the important part: don't let go to check whether it has stopped. Most people release after a minute or two to have a look, and that undoes it' · spit blood out rather than swallowing it · ice on the forehead or back of the neck. He is briefed to tip his head back and pinch the bone, and to keep doing it wrong if you don't correct him: 'A little lower — the soft part, not the bone — and bring your head forward for me' is a marked item

The six bleed questions and the three red-flag blocks — When it started · continuous or stop-start and worsening · first time or recurrent · one nostril or both · blood dripping down the throat · and what set it off. Then, as one continuous run: blood loss — dizziness, chest pain, breathlessness · GI bleeding — haematemesis, black or tarry stools · and nasal tumour — long-standing unilateral blockage, facial or ear pain, headaches, neck lumps, unintentional weight loss. Do not omit the tumour block because he is only 40, and if he asks why: 'These are questions I ask everyone with a nosebleed, to make sure I'm not missing something growing inside the nose. Nothing you've told me suggests that'

The highest-value question in the station — Run the causes as trauma → inflammation and dryness → bleeding tendency. Inside the middle block: 'Any recent cold? A runny or blocked nose? Do you get hay fever? … and are you using a steroid nasal spray for it?' He confirms hay fever and is briefed not to volunteer the spray, because patients do not think of nasal sprays as medicines. He uses nasonex every morning. He also picks his nose and is slightly embarrassed about it

Explore the anticoagulant properly — why and when — 'Why were you started on the apixaban? … when did you take your last dose? … do you ever miss doses? … and are you taking anything else — aspirin, anti-inflammatories, anything over the counter?' Atrial fibrillation for two years, last dose about 8 am, next due tonight, never misses. Recording 'On apixaban' and moving on loses the mark — why and when are what make your later decision defensible, and they are what the examiner is listening for

Defuse the two distractors he plants — 'Should I stop the blood thinner?' — he has already decided to stop it himself, and volunteers it in the last minute if you never invite concerns. And 'My wife reckons it's my blood pressure': 'Your reading today is 140 over 90, which is where we want it to be for someone on treatment. High blood pressure is rarely the direct cause of a nosebleed, and being anxious and bleeding pushes the reading up anyway. I'm not going to change anything about it today.' Never say 'Yes, your blood pressure did this', and never start an antihypertensive — if you do, he looks relieved and says 'So I need stronger tablets then?' and lets you dig the hole
fails: ★ Never asks about the steroid nasal spray, so the actual diagnosis is never found
★ Stops the anticoagulant as step one — or refuses to discuss it at all — instead of reasoning it out loud and saying temporarily
Blames the blood pressure, or starts an antihypertensive at a reading of 140/90 in an anxious, actively bleeding patient
Never corrects his technique when he tips his head back and pinches the bone, or mimes the Merocel insertion without warning of discomfort and asking permission
Offers cautery without naming septal perforation, stops the spray without substituting anything, or runs out of time before follow-up, re-bleed first aid, general advice and red flags
numbers: 10–15 minutes of uninterrupted pressure · two hours' duration in this stem · 140/90 is target, not a problem · about 90% of bleeds are anterior · pack in situ 24 hours, up to 48 · about 10 mL of saline to expand a Merocel, swelling in about 30 seconds · co-phenylcaine is lignocaine plus phenylephrine · silver nitrate on one side only, with septal perforation as the risk

FBE is the investigation; INR only for warfarin, and there is no routine apixaban assay · the three red-flag blocks are tumour, anaemia and GI bleed · antibiotic cover while a pack is in · the word is temporarily · posterior bleeding needs ENT, a posterior balloon or Foley, and admission — and from a rural site, early MedSTAR and receiving-ent contact VERIFY

mnem.title: Causes and history — A GUSHING NOSE IS TERRIBLY BLOODY, STOP PICKING
rows: A · Anaemia
**How much blood, over how long** — and what it has cost him: **dizziness, light-headedness, chest pain, breathlessness, fatigue.**
G · GI bleeding
Blood that went **down** rather than out: **swallowing it, vomiting blood, black tarry stools.**
N · Nasal tumour
**Unilateral blockage · facial or ear pain · numbness · neck lumps · weight loss.** Candidates skip this because he is only 40 — ask it anyway.
I · Inflammation
**Hay fever, recent cold, allergic rhinitis** — and the question the station turns on: **"do you use anything up your nose — any spray?"** He will not volunteer the steroid spray.
T · Trauma
**Picking · forceful blowing · knocks or injury · recent nasal surgery · foreign body** (in a child).
B · Bleeding tendency

**Blood thinners and aspirin** — why he takes it, and **when was the last dose** · **easy bruising · bleeding gums · heavy periods · prolonged bleeding after cuts, dental work or surgery** · known clotting disorder.
S · SADMA

**S**moking · **A**lcohol · **D**rugs (**cocaine** is a real cause) · **M**edications — you already have the blood thinner from B, so sweep for the rest, including **over-the-counter aspirin, NSAIDs and fish oil** · **A**llergies.
P · Past & family

**Previous nosebleeds and what was done** (cautery, packing, ENT) · **why he is anticoagulated** · **liver or kidney disease** · **hypertension — ask it, do not blame it** · **previous nasal surgery** · **family history of bleeding disorders or telangiectasia** (HHT: recurrent epistaxis running in families).
mnem.note: Six minutes will not hold all eight. A–G–N–I–T–B is the discriminating half and earns the marks; S and P are a fast sweep at the end if time allows. Blood pressure is deliberately not a branch of its own — 140/90 in an anxious, actively bleeding man is at target and reads high for the wrong reasons, so ask it under P, but blaming it or starting an antihypertensive fails the station. S and P deliberately do not re-ask the apixaban: it is captured in B, where it matters.

setting: This is a decision, not a diagnosis: weigh procedural and patient bleeding risk against thrombotic risk, then commit — interrupt or continue, when to stop, bridge or not, when to restart. Three rules. If the operation cuts into the body, the anticoagulant is interrupted. Never bridge a DOAC or an antiplatelet — timing is the only lever. And before stopping an antiplatelet, ask why it was started and when the stent went in.
stem: Pre-admission clinic, regional South Australian hospital. Mr Peter Hallam, 72, a retired shearer who lives 90 minutes from town, is booked for an elective open right inguinal hernia repair in three weeks. 8 minutes.

Warfarin 5 mg daily for permanent atrial fibrillation, target INR 2–3, last INR 2.4, stable for two years. TIA 20 months ago. Also hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Weight 82 kg, eGFR 68. Observations normal.
Be ready for version B — the same station on apixaban 5 mg BD with CrCl 34 and a high-bleeding-risk bowel resection — and version C, aspirin plus clopidogrel six months after a drug-eluting stent.
tasks: Take a focused history directed at his bleeding risk and clotting risk
Explain your peri-operative anticoagulation plan in plain language
Address his concerns and questions
Answer the examiner's questions
time: Suggested clock: WIPE and signpost at 0:00 · the drug at 0:30 · clotting risk at 1:15 · bleeding risk at 2:15 · procedure and concerns at 3:15 · the plan at 4:00 · questions at 6:30 · summary and safety-net at 7:30

back.dx: HIGH THROMBOTIC RISK, MODERATE BLEEDING RISK, ELECTIVE SURGERY ON WARFARIN — interrupt with bridging. The plan in plain language: 'We stop the warfarin five days before the operation — so your last tablet is on the Thursday. The day before surgery we do a blood test, the INR, and we want it below 1.5; if it's still a bit high, there's a small dose of vitamin K we can give by mouth to bring it down safely. Because of your mini-stroke, I don't want you completely unprotected in those last few days, so we'll cover you with a small injection under the skin. It works within hours and wears off within hours, which is exactly what we want. You'd start those about three days before, and the last one is 24 hours before the operation.' The restart, which is half the plan: 'After the operation, once the surgeon is happy there's no bleeding, you go straight back onto your usual warfarin dose — the same 5 mg, no extra loading — usually that evening or the next day. It takes about five days to build back up, so we keep the injections going until your INR is back in range, then stop them.' then a written dated calendar — which day the warfarin stops, which day the injections start, when the blood test is — copied to the GP and the surgeon, and the INR arranged at his local clinic so he isn't driving three hours. Two sets of red flags, separately marked: bleeding that won't stop, black or bloody bowel motions, vomiting blood, a bad headache after a knock to the head — and any weakness, numbness or slurred speech. His questions, answered: 'Will I have a stroke like my brother?' → 'I can't promise nothing will happen — but what we're doing is designed exactly to prevent it. The gap is short, we're covering you through it, and we restart the moment it's safe. Your brother's situation and yours are not the same.' 'Can't I just stay on the warfarin?' → 'For some small procedures, yes — a tooth out, a cataract. But this operation cuts through the muscle wall.' 'I'm no good with needles' → tiny needle into the fat of the tummy, the nurse will teach him and his wife, or the community nurse can do it. 'Could we do the operation sooner and skip all this?' → 'The timing is what makes it safe rather than what delays it.' The examiner's summary answer: 'Cease warfarin day minus five. Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily from day minus three once the INR falls below range — 80 mg BD at his weight — with the last dose at least 24 hours pre-operatively. INR the day before, target below 1.5, with oral vitamin K 1–2 mg available if higher. Restart usual-dose warfarin the evening of surgery once haemostasis is secure, resume enoxaparin at 24 hours and overlap until the INR is therapeutic. Stop NSAIDs and fish oil now. Written dated plan copied to the GP, surgeon and anaesthetist.' and if he were on apixaban instead: 'Then I would not bridge at all. I'd calculate his creatinine clearance by cockcroft-gault, look at the procedural bleeding risk, and interrupt for 24 hours for a low-bleeding-risk procedure with normal renal function, 48 hours for a high-bleeding-risk one, extending to 72 hours or more if the clearance is reduced. No INR is needed. Restart at 24 hours after low-risk surgery and 48 to 72 hours after high-risk.' Version B, apixaban with CrCl 34 and a hemicolectomy: check the clearance yourself and say it — 'At 54 kg and 79, her cockcroft-gault clearance is about 34, lower than the eGFR suggests' · no INR, no vitamin K, no bridging, with three separate marks for saying so · a professional interpreter rather than her daughter, addressing the patient · and the restart timing is the mark most often dropped — 48 to 72 hours after a high-bleeding-risk bowel resection, with VTE prophylaxis in between. When she asks for the injections her friend had: 'With this type of tablet we don't use those injections. They're used to cover the long gap that warfarin leaves. Yours doesn't. Adding them would increase your bleeding risk without adding protection — I know that feels like less is being done, but in your case less is safer.' Version C is the hardest and carries an AUTOMATIC FAIL: aspirin plus clopidogrel six months after a drug-eluting stent, where 'We'll stop both a week before' is a single-item fail. The safe answer has three parts every time: delay if you can → keep the aspirin → involve cardiology. 'Those two tablets are keeping the stent open while it settles in, and stopping both in the first year carries a real risk of the stent blocking off — which would be a heart attack. If it truly can't wait, we stop only the clopidogrel, seven days before, and you keep taking the aspirin right through.' Elective non-cardiac surgery is ideally deferred until at least six months after a drug-eluting stent and a minimum of one month after a bare-metal stent VERIFY.
plan: WIPE and consent, open question — and SIGNPOST THE TWO HALVES: bleeding risk, then clotting risk.
The drug by name, dose, duration, who monitors it, last INR and stability — and any second antiplatelet.
CLOTTING RISK: PREVIOUS CLOT, STROKE OR TIA AND WHEN · VALVES, METAL OR TISSUE · AF, heart failure, diabetes, hypertension. Score it aloud to the examiner.
BLEEDING RISK: previous bleeding or transfusion · kidneys · LIVER AND ALCOHOL · NSAIDs AND COMPLEMENTARY MEDICINES · blood pressure control.
The procedure, the anaesthetic, the social situation and access to pathology — then the concerns question.
Acknowledge the brother properly before moving on.
WEIGH THE TWO RISKS OUT LOUD, THEN THE PLAN WITH NUMBERS: stop day minus five · INR day minus one under 1.5 · vitamin K if needed · BRIDGING FROM DAY MINUS THREE WITH THE LAST DOSE 24 HOURS BEFORE.
THE RESTART PLAN — usual dose, no loading, injections overlapped until the INR is therapeutic.
Modify what is modifiable: stop the Nurofen and fish oil today, paracetamol instead.
HIS QUESTIONS — the stroke fear, the needles, whether he can stay on it, and the three-hour round trip for a blood test.
Written dated calendar copied to the GP and surgeon, both sets of red flags, and confirmation with the surgeon and anaesthetist.
Summarise and share the decision: 'Is there any part of it you'd want done differently?'
back.planNote: the station's own suggested clock
ask: THE HISTORY SET: 'I NEED TO ASK ABOUT TWO THINGS — YOUR RISK OF BLEEDING, AND YOUR RISK OF CLOTTING.' · 'WHICH BLOOD THINNER IS IT, AND ARE YOU ON ANY OTHER ONE AS WELL?' · 'HAVE YOU EVER HAD A CLOT, A STROKE OR A MINI-STROKE — AND WHEN?' · 'Do you have any heart valve problem, or a valve replacement — METAL OR TISSUE?' · 'Any kidney trouble? Any liver trouble, and how much alcohol?'

The reasoning set: 'Thank you for telling me — that changes what I'm going to recommend.' · 'My job is not to choose one risk over the other — it's to make the gap as short and as safe as I possibly can.' · 'If the operation cuts into the body, the blood thinner has to be stopped.' · 'A small injection under the skin that works within hours and wears off within hours.' · 'With the newer tablets we don't use those injections — they'd add bleeding risk without adding protection.'

The closing set: 'I'll write it out as a dated calendar and send a copy to your GP and your surgeon.' · 'Come straight in for bleeding that won't stop, black motions, vomiting blood, a bad headache after a knock, or any weakness, numbness or slurred speech.' · 'How does that sit with you — is there any part you'd want done differently?' · 'Before I do anything, I'd confirm this with your surgeon and the anaesthetist.'
pefe: NO EXAMINATION — THE TWO HISTORIES ARE THE ASSESSMENT. WHAT HE GIVES: warfarin 5 mg for seven years, NEVER MISSED, monthly INRs with the GP, LAST 2.4 AND STEADY FOR YEARS · NO SECOND ANTIPLATELET · NO VALVE PROBLEM, no heart failure · NEVER A BLEEDER, no transfusion, kidneys and liver fine, two beers on a Friday · hernia repair three weeks on Tuesday under GENERAL ANAESTHETIC, day surgery, his wife driving · AND PATHOLOGY AN HOUR AND A HALF EACH WAY.

The three things he withholds: the TIA eighteen to twenty months ago, given only when asked about clots, strokes or why the warfarin was started · the Nurofen and fish oil, given only if you ask about pain relief, anti-inflammatories or over-the-counter medicines · and his brother's stroke after an operation, given only if you ask about worries. If you never ask, he volunteers the brother at about seven minutes and goes quiet and flat so you have to respond to it.

HE OPENS WITH THE PRESSURE — 'DO I STOP THE WARFARIN OR NOT? MY MATE HAD NEEDLES IN HIS BELLY — DO I NEED THOSE?' — AND PUSHES ONCE MORE IF YOU STALL: 'CAN YOU JUST GIVE ME A YES OR NO?' He resists the injection once with 'I'M NO GOOD WITH NEEDLES', and asks what every piece of jargon means without pretending to understand.

Identify the drug by name before anything else — 'Which blood thinner are you taking, and what dose? How long, and who looks after it? When was your last INR and what was it? Has it been steady, or does it bounce around? And are you on any other blood thinner as well — aspirin, clopidogrel, plavix, brilinta — even one you buy yourself?' 'Blood thinner' in the stem is not a diagnosis: candidates who assume warfarin and are handed apixaban give a five-day answer and an enoxaparin bridge, and both are wrong

Clotting risk — the three must-asks, then score it aloud — 'Have you ever had a clot — in the leg or the lung — or a stroke or mini-stroke? When was that?' · 'Do you have any heart valve problem, or a valve replacement — and is it a metal one or a tissue one?' · and the AF, heart failure, diabetes and blood pressure. The TIA is the whole point of the case and it is volunteered only if you ask about previous clots or strokes, or why the warfarin was started. Miss it and you will confidently decide not to bridge a patient who needs bridging. Then to the examiner: 'That gives him a CHA2DS2-VASc of six — hypertension, age over 65, diabetes, and a prior TIA scoring two'

Bleeding risk — and the two modifiable things he hands you — Previous bleeding hard to stop, transfusion, anaemia · kidneys · liver and alcohol · blood pressure control · and 'Do you take anti-inflammatories — Nurofen, Voltaren — or fish oil, turmeric, ginkgo?' He takes Nurofen most days for his knee and fish oil his wife buys. Say it out loud and act on it in the room: 'I'd like you to stop the Nurofen and the fish oil now and use paracetamol for the knee instead.' Silence here costs a mark, and he does not volunteer either

The procedure, the anaesthetic, the access — and the concerns question — What exactly is planned and when · has the anaesthetist mentioned a spinal or an epidural · going home the same day and who is at home · how far from a place that can do a blood test, which is an hour and a half each way · and then: 'Before I give you a plan — what were you hoping I'd say today, and is there anything about this that particularly worries you?' The hidden agenda arrives only in response to that question: his brother had a stroke after an operation and never came right. Everything you say afterwards must answer that fear

Name the balance before you name the plan — 'There are two risks I have to balance. On one side, warfarin is doing an important job: it's protecting you from a stroke, and we know that matters for you because of the irregular heartbeat and the mini-stroke. On the other side, if we operate while your blood is fully thinned, the bleeding during and after the operation can be very hard to control. So my job is not to choose one risk over the other — it's to make the gap as short and as safe as I possibly can.' Jumping straight to 'Stop it five days before' scores the fact and loses the reasoning, and the reasoning sentence is the discriminating item

Switch register between the patient and the examiner — To the patient: 'A small injection under the skin that works within hours and wears off within hours.' To the examiner: 'Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily.' Examiners notice candidates who can do both, and mark down candidates who talk to the patient in drug names. And when he says his mate had the same needles before a knee: 'Similar injection, but the reason matters. We use it here to cover the gap in your warfarin. If you were on one of the newer tablets like apixaban, we wouldn't use it at all — those wear off so quickly that the injections would only add bleeding risk'
fails: ★ Answers 'stop it five days before' in the first thirty seconds without weighing the two risks out loud
★ Never asks about the TIA, so decides against bridging a patient who needs it — or never asks about a second antiplatelet
Ignores the Nurofen and fish oil instead of stopping them in the room
Never asks about concerns, so the brother's stroke never surfaces and the whole explanation answers the wrong question
Gives no restart plan, no written dated calendar and no red flags — or recites 'therapeutic LMWH one milligram per kilogram BD' to the patient
numbers: Warfarin stop 5 days · INR on day minus one target under 1.5 · oral vitamin K 1–2 mg if still high · restart usual dose the evening of surgery · therapeutic again in 5–7 days · enoxaparin bridge for high thrombotic risk only at 1 mg/kg subcut BD from day minus three, last dose at least 24 hours pre-op, restart 24 hours after low-bleed-risk and 48–72 after high, and 1 mg/kg daily if CrCl under 30 VERIFY

DOACs are never bridged: CrCl ≥50 means 24 hours low risk and 48 high · CrCl 30–49 means 48 and 72 · dabigatran out to 96 hours · restart 24 hours or 48–72 · antiplatelets: aspirin 5 days, clopidogrel 7, ticagrelor 5, prasugrel 7 · DAPT within 12 months of ACS or PCI means delay surgery, and if impossible stop the p2y12 and keep the aspirin · HAS-BLED ≥3 is high bleeding risk; CHA2DS2-VASc ≥7, a mechanical valve, or stroke or VTE within 3 months is high thrombotic risk · neuraxial: therapeutic enoxaparin 24 hours, prophylactic 12, DOAC 72

must: FAIL — Answering 'stop it five days before' in the first thirty seconds without weighing the two risks out loud — the reasoning sentence is the discriminating item: 'my job is not to choose one risk over the other, it's to make the gap as short and as safe as I possibly can'

FAIL — Never asking the drug by NAME or about a second antiplatelet, and never asking about the TIA — 'blood thinner' in the stem is not a diagnosis, and the TIA comes only if you ask about previous clots or strokes; miss it and you confidently decide not to bridge a patient who needs it

FAIL — ★ AUTO-FAIL in the stent variant: 'we'll stop both a week before' — ceasing dual antiplatelet therapy within 12 months of a drug-eluting stent without cardiology risks stent thrombosis. Three parts every time: delay if you can, keep the aspirin, involve cardiology
FAIL — Bridging a DOAC or an antiplatelet — never done; timing is the only lever, and on apixaban there is no INR, no vitamin K and no bridging, which are three separate marks for saying so

FAIL — Ignoring the Nurofen and the fish oil instead of stopping them in the room, or never asking about concerns, so the brother's stroke never surfaces and the whole explanation answers the wrong question

FAIL — Giving no restart plan, no written dated calendar and no red flags — or reciting 'therapeutic LMWH one milligram per kilogram BD' to the patient instead of 'a small injection under the skin', then giving the dose to the examiner

setting: Two lines carry this station. 'Your INR is 2.4 — that is in the target range of 2 to 3, exactly where we want it' — never the word 'Normal', because a normal INR is about 1.0 and would mean the drug wasn't working. And 'Keep eating your green vegetables — what matters is consistency, not avoidance', which is the single most-tested error in the station.
stem: General practice. James Whelan, 50, known atrial fibrillation and chronic kidney disease, started on warfarin three weeks ago. He has had his INR checked and has come for the result. 8 minutes.
Result: INR 2.4.

Version B is the same drug with a different shape — Jane Petrakis, 55, on warfarin six months for AF, attending for a routine INR of 1.4, where the tasks are to take a history to find the reason, explain the finding, and counsel about it.
tasks: Explain the result to the patient
Explain the follow-up schedule
Counsel him regarding the specific points of warfarin use and its side effects
time: In this station the test is whether you can still be saying something useful at seven minutes — there are eight content blocks so you never run dry · and finish with a teach-back, which is quick, is explicitly good practice for a narrow-therapeutic-index drug, and rescues you if you left the hidden agenda unanswered

back.dx: Warfarin counselling in AF with chronic kidney disease, INR 2.4 and in target. Interactions: 'Tell every health professional you're on it — your GP, your pharmacist and your dentist, especially before any procedure. And check with me or the pharmacist before you start or stop anything, including things you buy off the shelf and herbal products — people often don't think of those as medicines. Two in particular: anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen, and ST John's wort. For everyday aches, paracetamol is the safer choice.' He takes ibuprofen for his back after heavy days on site, plus fish oil and a multivitamin, and volunteers none of it. Alcohol: avoid excess, particularly binge drinking, and he drinks two beers most nights. The supports block, which is where the spare minutes go: a medical alert bracelet, 'So that if you were ever found unwell, whoever helps you knows you're on a blood thinner' · a printed medication list for his wallet · tell his wife and family · a pharmacist medication review · and written information. Sick-day advice: 'If you become unwell — especially vomiting, diarrhoea, or not eating and drinking properly — or if you're started on antibiotics, come and see me, because those can change how the warfarin works and we may need to check your INR sooner.' then the summary and the teach-back: 'Could you tell me the two things you'll do differently, just so I know I've explained it well?' Version B, the INR of 1.4, is a history-first station in three groups. Group one, the condition and adherence: when diagnosed, whether anyone explained why she needs it, whether she is taking it exactly as prescribed and what is getting in the way, bleeding episodes, whether she has been getting her blood tests, palpitations or chest pain. Group two, the interactions: brand change · diet and specifically more green leafy vegetables · new medicines · and separately, herbal remedies, vitamins and supplements. Group three if time: memory, mood, home support, who cooks, and falls. Her answer: her mother was admitted six weeks ago, she has been visiting daily, sleeping badly, eating on the run, missing the tablet about three days a week and skipping her last two blood tests. The counselling has to do two things in order — 'Thank you for being honest with me — that sounds like an extremely difficult few months, and I'm not here to tell you off' — and then state the risk plainly: 'Yours today is 1.4, which is below that — and it means the warfarin isn't currently protecting you from a stroke. That's what I want us to fix together.' then problem-solve: a webster or blister pack, a calendar or phone alarm, a pharmacist medication review, the warfarin clinic, the generic brand if cost is part of it — and support for her: 'If your mother needs more support at home, I can involve a social worker or arrange an aged care assessment, which might take some of the load off you', with review in a week or two. Two failures live there: blaming by leading with 'You must take your medication', and being so sympathetic that you never say plainly that at 1.4 she is not protected. The other variants: an INR of 6.2 without bleeding — 'The good news is you're not bleeding, and at this level the bleeding risk is only moderate, so this is a matter of adjusting, not an emergency': withhold and recheck, consider a small dose of vitamin K, and find the cause, which is often recent antibiotics. 'Can I switch to one of the new tablets?' — the appeal is real, but they are cleared by the kidneys and are less safe and less predictable with his renal function, and warfarin has an antidote that can be given quickly; it isn't a life sentence and can be revisited if his kidney function changes. And 'I'm having a tooth out next month' — please don't stop the warfarin yourself; tell the dentist you're anticoagulated, because many dental procedures can be done safely without stopping it, often with a recent INR and local measures; for anything bigger, plan it with the proceduralist and cardiologist VERIFY.
plan: GREET, OPEN QUESTION, AND ASK THE AGENDA — the brain-bleed fear surfaces here. Promise to return to it.
Check prior understanding before explaining anything.
The indication in plain words, then the result: 2.4, in the target range of 2 to 3 — and why 'Normal' is the wrong word.
Why warfarin rather than a DOAC, because of his kidneys.
The schedule, both HALVEs — every one to two days at initiation, every four to six weeks once stable — then the warfarin clinic and self-testing.
The five dosing rules, then the four-hour missed-dose rule — and correct his 'Take two to catch up'.
Side effects and red flags, including the neurological one and the abdominal or back-pain one — and answer the sister's claim here.
INTERACTIONS: tell the GP, pharmacist and dentist · check before starting or stopping anything · NSAIDs AND ST JOHN'S WORT NAMED · paracetamol instead.
The diet correction, then cranberry and grapefruit juice, then alcohol.
Supports: bracelet, wallet card, tell the family, medication review, written information.
SICK-DAY ADVICE — vomiting, diarrhoea, not eating, or new antibiotics.
Summarise, then teach-back: 'Tell me the two things you'll do differently.'

ask: The opening set: 'Before I take you through the result — is there anything worrying you, or anything you'd especially like me to cover?' · 'Can I ask what you already understand about why you were started on warfarin?' · 'Warfarin is a blood thinner — it increases the time it takes your blood to clot.'

The result and schedule set: 'Your INR is 2.4 — that's in the target range of 2 to 3, exactly where we want it.' · 'A completely normal result would be about 1 — and that would mean the tablet wasn't working.' · 'Because of your kidneys, warfarin is the right choice for you.' · 'At the start we check every one to two days; once it's stable, every four to six weeks.'

The safety set: 'Same dose, same time every day, same brand — and tick it off on a calendar.' · 'If you remember within four hours, take it. Longer than that, skip it — never double up — and let me know.' · 'Bleeding can be hidden — it isn't always blood you can see.' · 'A severe headache or weakness, or back pain shooting down your leg — come in straight away. And after any head knock, even if you feel fine.' · 'Keep eating your green vegetables — what matters is consistency, not avoidance.'
pefe: No examination — the result is the finding, and the stem's chronic kidney disease is a marked item rather than scenery. INR 2.4 against a target of 2 to 3, three weeks into treatment.

What he volunteers: almost nothing. He answers only what is asked, and withholds the missed doses, the brand change, the ibuprofen and the cranberry juice. When asked: he takes it in the morning with his other medicines and has missed it twice since starting, and took two the next day to catch up · the pharmacy gave him a different-looking box last month · ibuprofen for his back after heavy days on site, plus fish oil and a multivitamin · cranberry juice most days for his waterworks · two beers most nights · a couple of forearm bruises from work · no falls, though he works on scaffolding · and a dental clean due next month.

He says 'So it's normal, then?' To see whether you correct the word, offers the 'Take two to catch up' line and waits, and looks satisfied if you tell him to avoid green vegetables — which he marks as an error. His hidden agenda is his sister's claim that these tablets cause bleeding into the brain, and if concerns are never invited he raises it in the last minute.

Ask the agenda even though it is a counselling station — 'Before I take you through the result — is there anything in particular that's worrying you, or anything you'd especially like me to cover today?' and 'Can I ask what you already understand about why you were started on warfarin?' Recalls differ and role-players are sometimes given a concern — his sister told him these tablets cause bleeding into the brain. If you never ask, you deliver eight perfect minutes to the wrong agenda, and he raises it in the last minute

The result — and why the CKD in the stem is a marked item — 'Your heart beats irregularly — atrial fibrillation — and that lets blood pool and form a clot, which can travel to the brain and cause a stroke. The warfarin is there to prevent that. Your result today is 2.4 — that is exactly where we want it. Below 2 we're not protecting you from clots; above 3 the bleeding risk starts to climb.' then volunteer the kidney explanation: 'Because of your kidneys, warfarin is the right choice for you. The newer blood thinners are cleared by the kidneys, so they aren't as safe or as predictable when kidney function is reduced.' He asks why his mate has one with no blood tests

Both HALVEs of the schedule, and something practical — 'When we first start warfarin we check the INR every one to two days, because we're adjusting the dose to find the right one for you. Once it's stable in range — as yours now is — we check it every four to six weeks.' Both intervals are marked even though he is past the first phase. Then the warfarin clinic: 'You have the blood test there; they text you your result and the dose to take, and the result comes through to me as well' — plus self-testing with a finger-prick device if travel is an issue. Offering nothing practical is the difference between reciting a schedule and running a follow-up plan

The five dosing rules and the four-hour rule — Exactly the prescribed dose — too little and you clot, too much and you bleed · the same time every day · a warfarin calendar on the fridge, ticked off · and don't change brands, because different brands aren't identical and switching makes the INR swing. Then: 'If you remember within about four hours of your usual time, take it. If it's longer than four hours, skip that dose — do not take two tablets to catch up — take your next dose at the usual time, and let me know, because a missed dose will show up on your next INR.' He offers 'I took two the next day to catch up' and waits to be corrected — 'Take two tomorrow' is an automatic-fail answer. He also mentions a different-looking box from the pharmacy, which needs acting on with an earlier INR

Red flags — including the two people don't think of — 'The main side effect is bleeding, and the important thing is that bleeding can be hidden — it isn't always blood you can see.' Unexplained bruising · a nosebleed that won't stop · blood in bowel motions or black tarry stools · vomiting or coughing up blood · blood in the urine · a cut that won't stop with pressure. Then the two that earn the marks: 'A severe or unusual headache, dizziness, confusion, weakness or slurred speech — that can mean bleeding into the brain' · and 'Pain in your abdomen, or back pain shooting down your leg with numbness or weakness — that can be bleeding deep inside the abdomen, and it can feel just like a slipped disc.' plus: any head injury or significant fall, come in even if you feel completely fine

The diet correction, which is itself a marked item — He has stopped eating salad and broccoli because his neighbour told him to. 'That's the most common wrong advice, so I'm glad you asked. Keep eating them. Green leafy vegetables do affect warfarin, but what matters is consistency, not avoidance — no dramatic changes. Don't suddenly go vegetarian, and don't suddenly start eating big bowls of spinach every day.' Two things to avoid: cranberry juice and grapefruit juice, which increase the effect. And he drinks cranberry juice most days for his 'Waterworks' — swap it, and flag the urinary symptoms for separate review
fails: ★ Calls the INR 'normal' rather than in the target range, or never says the target range at all
★ Tells him to avoid green leafy vegetables instead of correcting the advice to consistency, not avoidance
Accepts 'I took two the next day to catch up' without correcting it to the four-hour rule and never doubling
Never explains why warfarin rather than a DOAC, when the chronic kidney disease in the stem is a marked item
Gives only the stable-phase testing interval, says only 'watch for bleeding' without the specific red flags, or finishes without a teach-back
numbers: Target INR 2.0–3.0 · this patient 2.4 · version B 1.4 · a 'Normal' INR is about 1.0 · testing every 1–2 days at initiation and every 4–6 weeks once stable · missed-dose cut-off 4 hours, and never double · the antidote is vitamin K1

High INR without bleeding: under 4.5 adjust the dose · 4.5–10 withhold with or without vitamin K · above 10 withhold and give vitamin K · any significant bleeding gets vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate · bleeding risk is low under 5, moderate 5–9, and climbs steeply above 9–10 · no bridging for AF, but bridge for acute VTE · avoid cranberry and grapefruit juice · name NSAIDs and ST John's wort VERIFY

setting: The single point the examiner is listening for: 'We can't use these medications if you have chronic kidney disease, because the kidneys have to filter the medication out of your blood — so I need to check your eGFR before we change anything.' and the stem hands you his agenda, which is exactly why you must still ask whether there is another one.
stem: General practice. Jack Mannering, 67, attends concerned about his medication. Known atrial fibrillation, hypertension and type 2 diabetes. CHA2DS2-VASc score 2. 8 minutes.
Currently on warfarin; he wants to stop it because he is unhappy with the repeated blood tests, which are time consuming.

Task: counsel the patient about anticoagulant use and suggest other options. In the 2023 face-to-face recall a medicines book on the desk was tagged open at apixaban — which is a prompt, not an instruction to name only one drug.
His second worry, given only if you ask: a mate ended up in hospital bleeding on a blood thinner, and it shook him. If you never ask, he raises it in the last thirty seconds and marks you down.
tasks: Counsel the patient about anticoagulant use
Suggest other options
time: Done well this runs four to five minutes, so plan what fills the rest — announced components rather than drift: 'Can I tell you a bit more about…' warfarin diet and interaction counselling · the triple whammy · stopping before surgery, warfarin five days and a NOAC one to two · or what to do about a missed dose

back.dx: ATRIAL FIBRILLATION ON WARFARIN, REQUESTING TO STOP BECAUSE OF THE MONITORING BURDEN — a counselling station about offering options safely, not about talking him out of anything. Why the blood tests exist, explained rather than assumed: 'Warfarin needs its dose adjusted based on those blood tests — the right dose is different for every person, and it drifts. Warfarin also interacts with food and with other medicines, which is why we ask you not to change your diet suddenly and to tell every doctor and pharmacist you're on it. And we're concerned about serious bleeding if the level goes too high — the blood test is how we keep it in the safe range.' that also loops back to his mate in hospital. When he asks to stop altogether: 'Stopping altogether isn't something I'd recommend, because the stroke risk is real. But wanting to get off the monthly tests is a completely reasonable goal, and there may well be a way to do that' — safe without being confrontational, and it validates the underlying goal rather than the request. The close: reading material to take home and think about · cardiologist liaison and valve confirmation · bloods · red flags that are the same whichever drug he ends up on — any bleeding, coughing up blood, vomiting blood, blood or black stools, any severe headache or dizziness, or any abdominal or back pain — teach-back, and a review to decide together. The variants: one, he has chronic kidney disease — 'Because your kidneys aren't working at full capacity, these newer medications aren't safe for you: your body wouldn't clear them properly and they'd build up, which raises the bleeding risk. I'm sorry, because I know the tests are the very thing you wanted to avoid — but warfarin is the safer option for you, and we can reverse it if anything goes wrong. What I can do is look at making the monitoring easier — longer intervals once you're stable, testing closer to home or at work, or home INR testing.' Two, mechanical valve or mitral stenosis — 'When someone has a mechanical heart valve, or significant narrowing of the mitral valve, warfarin is the only anticoagulant we can use — the newer medications haven't been shown to be safe or effective in that situation, and there's a real risk of a clot forming on the valve. So switching isn't an option for you, and I'd rather be clear about that than raise your hopes.' Three, he wants to stop anticoagulation altogether — 'I hear you, and I'm not going to force you to take anything — that's your decision. But I'd be failing you if I didn't tell you what stopping means: your risk of a stroke would go up substantially, and a stroke can be life-changing. Can I ask what it is about the medication that's the biggest problem? Because if it's the testing, there may be a way around it that doesn't mean giving up the protection.' Four, 'How would I bleed if I take it exactly as prescribed?' — 'The usual answer is the kidneys. If you become dehydrated or unwell, or if someone adds an anti-inflammatory tablet like ibuprofen on TOP of your blood pressure tablet and a fluid tablet, your kidney function can drop suddenly and the medication builds up. That's why I'd ask you not to take anti-inflammatories without checking with us, and to let us know if you become unwell' — the triple whammy, and he does take ibuprofen for his back if you ask.
plan: WIPE, open question — he states the agenda firmly in his first answer.
Acknowledge the frustration explicitly, ask permission to explain, then ask for the second agenda.
WHY HE IS ANTICOAGULATED AT ALL: AF, clot, STROKE — and the CHA2DS2-VASc score named and explained.
HANDLE 'CAN I JUST STOP IT?' — decline to endorse stopping while validating the underlying goal.
WHY WARFARIN NEEDS THE TESTS: dose adjustment, food and drug interactions, AND THE BLEEDING RISK HE ALREADY RAISED.
INTRODUCE THE NOACs AND NAME ALL THREE — and say plainly that they need no regular monitoring.
The kidney point, said clearly and early, with an eGFR ordered before anything changes.
THE TWO HONEST DOWNSIDES: SHORT HALF-LIFE AND ADHERENCE, THEN REVERSAL AGENTS — which answers his bleeding worry.
The switch schedule with the daily-INR caveat said honestly.
Exclude valvular AF via the cardiologist, and order renal function, liver function and a blood count.
Red flags and teach-back, then reading material and a review to decide together.
FILL THE REMAINING TIME WITH AN ANNOUNCED COMPONENT — warfarin diet and interactions, the triple whammy, stopping before surgery, or missed doses.

ask: The opening set: 'Thank you for coming in to talk about it. I understand — regular blood tests are time consuming, and I'd be frustrated too.' · 'Before I start — is there anything else about this medication that's worrying you?'

THE JUSTIFYING SET: 'Blood thinners are used when someone has a high risk of forming clots. YOUR IRREGULAR HEARTBEAT INCREASES THAT RISK.' · 'We calculate a score that predicts the risk of clotting. YOURS IS 2, WHICH IS HIGH ENOUGH THAT WE SHOULD BE TREATING IT.' · 'NOT TAKING A BLOOD THINNER INCREASES THE RISK OF A CLOT, WHICH CAN LEAD TO A STROKE.' · 'Warfarin's dose has to be adjusted based on the blood test, and IT INTERACTS WITH FOOD AND OTHER MEDICINES.'

The options set: 'Three are approved in Australia: apixaban, rivaroxaban and dabigatran.' · 'These don't need regular monitoring — their effect is predictable and the dose is fixed.' · 'We can't use these if you have chronic kidney disease, because the kidneys clear the medication — so I need to check your eGFR before we change anything.' · 'They have a shorter half-life, so taking them at the same time each day and not missing doses matters more than with warfarin.' · 'Dabigatran has a reversal agent available here. For apixaban and rivaroxaban one exists overseas but isn't in routine Australian use yet.' · 'We stop the warfarin, check the INR daily, and start the new medication once it's below 2.5 — I have to be straight with you, that means a few days of daily tests first. Then none.'
pefe: No examination — the relevant facts come from questions, and most of them are negative: no stroke, heart attack, heart failure, valve surgery or known valve problem · no known kidney or liver disease, though the diabetes nurse checks something yearly and nobody has raised it · never a bleeding episode · INR reasonably stable. He takes warfarin, an antihypertensive and metformin reliably.

The two things worth asking for because they change the advice: alcohol — two or three beers most evenings — and anti-inflammatories, because he sometimes takes ibuprofen for his back and asks 'Should I not?'. Neither is volunteered.

He is pragmatic and a bit blunt, wants a straight answer and dislikes being managed. He pushes once on stopping altogether to see whether you stay safe without lecturing him · reacts with real irritation to the daily INR and accepts it only if it is framed as short-lived · and if you name only apixaban he asks 'Is that the only one there is?'

Acknowledge before informing, then ask for the second agenda — 'Thank you for coming in to talk about this rather than just stopping — that's the right thing to have done. And I completely understand: regular blood tests are time consuming, and I'd find that frustrating too. Is it alright if I explain a bit more about the medication and the other options we have?' then, before you start: 'Is there anything else about this medication that's worrying you?' Accepting the stem's agenda without asking whether there is another one is the trap — the bleeding worry changes what you emphasise later

Name all three, not just the one the book was open at — 'There is a newer group — the non-vitamin-k, or direct-acting, oral anticoagulants. There are three currently approved in Australia: apixaban, rivaroxaban and dabigatran. And here's the part that matters to you: these don't need regular monitoring. Their effect is predictable and the dose is fixed, so you wouldn't need the monthly blood tests.' Naming only apixaban is marked down — he asks 'Is that the only one there is?' — because a patient who cares about having an antidote may specifically want dabigatran, and offering options is the whole point of a counselling station

The two honest downsides — one of which answers his second agenda — First, the shorter half-life: 'They stay active in your blood for a shorter time, which means taking them at the same time each day and not missing doses matters more than it does with warfarin. With warfarin a late dose is fairly forgiving; with these it isn't.' Second, reversal: 'If someone bleeds badly on warfarin we can reverse it. Of the newer ones, dabigatran has a reversal agent available. For apixaban and rivaroxaban, a reversal agent exists overseas and has provisional approval here, but it isn't in routine use in Australian hospitals yet. I'd rather you knew that.' He then asks whether he should want the one with the antidote — dabigatran has that advantage but is the most dependent on kidney function and more often causes indigestion, while apixaban is the one most commonly started VERIFY

The switch schedule, with the caveat said honestly — 'We stop the warfarin, then measure your INR daily — and I have to be straight with you, since you came in about blood tests: that means daily tests for a few days. Once the INR drops below 2.5, we start the new medication. After that, no routine monitoring at all.' He reacts with genuine irritation — 'Daily? You're joking, that's worse than what I've got' — and accepts it only if you frame it as a short inconvenience for a long-term one. If you never mention it, he marks you down: this is consenting, not selling

Exclude valvular AF before promising anything — 'I'd like to speak with your cardiologist, both to make sure he's happy with the change and to confirm there's no problem with the valves in your heart — if there were, warfarin would be the safer choice for you.' and the bloods before any switch: kidney function, liver function and a blood count. Then hand it back: reading material to take home, nps medicinewise, and a decision made together once the results are in

Justify the treatment before you discuss changing it — and say the score out loud — 'Blood thinners are used when someone has a high risk of forming clots. You have atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat, and that lets blood pool and clots form. We also calculate the CHA2DS2-VASc score, which predicts the risk of clotting. Yours is 2, which means your risk is high enough that we should be treating it. And this matters because not taking a blood thinner increases the risk of a clot, which can lead to a stroke.' Some will say a patient doesn't need to hear about a risk score — say it anyway, because you are speaking to the examiner as much as the patient, and it demonstrates you know why he is anticoagulated rather than just that he is
fails: ★ Never states the renal contraindication or orders an eGFR before offering a switch
★ Never excludes valvular atrial fibrillation, where warfarin is the only option and switching is not on the table
Accepts the stem's agenda without asking whether anything else is worrying him, so the bleeding fear arrives in the last thirty seconds
Names only apixaban, or never mentions the difference in reversal agents that bears directly on his worry
Sells the switch without the daily-INR caveat, or never justifies the anticoagulation through stroke risk and the score in the first place
numbers: Three DOACs approved in Australia — apixaban, rivaroxaban and dabigatran — with no routine monitoring and fixed dosing · CHA2DS2-VASc 2 in this patient, high enough to treat · switching from warfarin means stop, daily INR, and start the DOAC once the INR is below 2.5 · bloods before switching: eGFR, LFTs and FBC VERIFY

Dabigatran has a reversal agent available in Australia, while the apixaban and rivaroxaban agent has provisional approval but is not in routine hospital use · dabigatran is the most renally dependent and more often causes dyspepsia; apixaban is the least restricted by kidney function · mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis require warfarin · pre-operative cessation is warfarin 5 days and a DOAC 1–2 days · the triple whammy is ACE inhibitor plus diuretic plus NSAID, causing kidney injury, drug accumulation and bleeding

FAIL — Naming only apixaban because the medicines book was tagged open at it — all three are approved here: apixaban, rivaroxaban and dabigatran; only dabigatran has a reversal agent in routine Australian use, which bears directly on his worry

FAIL — Selling the switch without the daily-INR caveat — stop the warfarin, INR every day, start once it is below 2.5, so there is a short run of daily tests first — or skipping the shorter half-life, which makes a missed dose matter more than it does on warfarin

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town (MM5). You are the GP. James Halloran, 50, with pain in the leg. Some recalls word it as shin pain — same station.
Also in the stem: known hypertension, on treatment. An x-ray of the leg is available in the room.
8-minute station, 2 minutes reading.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient
Explain the X-ray to the patient
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: THE X-RAY, available in the room

AP AND LATERAL of tibia and fibula. A SUBTLE BREAK IN THE CORTEX OF THE TIBIAL SHAFT, with THICKENING OF THE BONE'S OUTER SURFACE around it — PERIOSTEAL REACTION, the bone repairing itself. Easy to miss unless you deliberately TRACE THE CORTEX — the dense white outline — down BOTH bones on BOTH views, looking for a step, a lucent line or a thickened patch
How to orient yourself on the film
Knee at the top, ankle at the bottom. TIBIA is the thick weight-bearing bone MEDIALLY; FIBULA the slender one LATERALLY. TWO VIEWS, ALWAYS
What an EARLIER injury looks like

The crack is ABSENT and ONLY the periosteal swelling is visible. And PLAIN X-RAY IS NORMAL FOR THE FIRST TWO TO THREE WEEKS in most stress fractures, and stays normal throughout in a bone stress REACTION. A NORMAL FILM NEVER EXCLUDES THE DIAGNOSIS
The site he points to

ONE FINGERTIP on the MID-SHIN, FRONT of the right leg — and that is EXACTLY where the crack is on the film. TIE THE TWO TOGETHER OUT LOUD: ‘exactly where you put your finger.’ It makes the diagnosis feel earned rather than announced
The lump he volunteers
‘There's a bit of a firm lump on the bone if I press.’ THAT IS THE PERIOSTEAL REACTION — new bone being laid down to repair itself. Register it; you will use it as a reason
What the history gives you instead of an examination

NO colour or temperature change · NO hair loss over the shin · NO slow-healing sores · no swelling, redness or rash · no injury · NO back pain, paraesthesiae or weakness · NO night or rest pain, NO weight loss, NO fevers, no previous cancer. THESE NEGATIVES ARE YOUR DIFFERENTIAL REASONING — collect them, then quote them back
MRI — the investigation of choice
It detects bone stress injury BEFORE the cortex breaks, and it GRADES the severity. A BONE SCAN is sensitive but NOT specific and is now second line VERIFY
Bloods — only if the picture is atypical or recurrent
Vitamin D, calcium, phosphate, ALP; consider thyroid and coeliac screening. Consider a DXA after RECURRENT or UNEXPLAINED stress fractures VERIFY
If the vascular screen HAD been positive
ANKLE–BRACHIAL INDEX, then duplex ultrasound — instead of, not as well as, the bone workup
THE HIGH-RISK SITES — these do NOT get relative rest in general practice

ANTERIOR CORTEX OF THE TIBIA — the ‘DREADED BLACK LINE’, on the tension side · FEMORAL NECK, especially the superior (tension) side · NAVICULAR and the BASE OF THE FIFTH METATARSAL · medial malleolus, talus, patella. Poor blood supply or tension-side loading means non-union or complete fracture: ORTHOPAEDIC REFERRAL, often non-weight-bearing, sometimes surgery

dx: **Stress fracture of the tibia — a bone stress injury.** A fracture produced by **repetitive submaximal load on NORMAL bone**, rather than by a single injury: **resorption outstrips formation, microcracks accumulate, and eventually the cortex breaks.** The tibia is the commonest site in runners.

**THE TRAP IS IN THE STEM. ‘Known case of hypertension, on treatment’ is there to make you walk in thinking peripheral arterial disease** — it appears in the genuine PAD recalls in the same words. **A candidate who spends the history on claudication, colour change and cardiovascular risk factors will find nothing, and will still be at four minutes with no exercise history and no red-flag screen.** **Screen the vascular group in THREE questions, find it negative, and say so later as a reason.**

**THE FINDING THAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS BEFORE YOU SEE THE FILM**: **‘It makes no difference whether I go uphill or downhill.’** **Claudication is a DEMAND problem — uphill loads the calf harder, so it comes on sooner. Pain that ignores the gradient but tracks total distance and impact is MECHANICAL.** That single answer moves arterial disease down the list before any imaging.

**The second sorting question is how FAST rest helps.** **Vascular claudication settles within a few minutes of standing still; a bone or soft-tissue injury aches on for much longer** — his is *‘an hour or two afterwards’*.

**The third is the natural history**: **‘it used to come on at the end of a run, now it starts after ten minutes.’** **Bone stress injury arrives PROGRESSIVELY EARLIER. Shin splints do the OPPOSITE — sore at the start and WARMS UP as the run continues.**

**Explain the film in FOUR SENTENCES and sixty seconds, then stop**: **‘This is the X-ray of your right leg, and the white shadows are the bones. You have two bones in the lower leg — this thick one at the front is the shin bone, the tibia, and this thinner one beside it is the fibula. Now here on your shin bone, just at this point — which is exactly where you put your finger — I can see a small crack in the surface of the bone, and a little swelling of the bone's outer surface around it, which is the bone repairing itself. That is what we call a stress fracture. It is not a broken bone in the way you're imagining — nothing has snapped or moved out of place. It's a small crack that builds up over time from repeated pounding, and it's common in runners.’** **No cortices, no periosteum, no trabeculae.**

**Three reasons, then WHY IT HAPPENED — which is what the treatment follows from**: **‘You went from about 40 kilometres a week to nearly 70 in six weeks, and added hill sessions, on shoes that are a couple of years old. Bone adapts to load, but it needs TIME to do it. When the load goes up faster than the bone can strengthen, tiny cracks build up faster than they heal — and eventually you get one you can see on an X-ray.’**

**CORRECTION — the family history is a second decoy.** *‘My mother died at 85 with heart disease’* is **NOT a significant family history of premature cardiovascular disease.** Australian absolute risk assessment counts **a first-degree relative affected before 55 in men and 65 in women.** VERIFY **Say so out loud**: **‘Your mother developed heart disease in her eighties, which is common and doesn't particularly raise your own risk.’** **Counting it is a small error; recognising that it is not one separates candidates.**

**Answer the race question honestly, then constructively** — he has entered a half marathon in March: **‘I'm going to be straight with you: not this one. You need about six to eight weeks without running for that crack to heal, and then a gradual build back up. If you run on it, the crack can get bigger, and that turns six weeks into six months. But you don't have to stop TRAINING — from today you can swim, cycle or do deep-water running and keep almost all your fitness. Let's pick a race in the second half of the year and build towards it properly.’**

**Management: STOP RUNNING — that is the treatment, and it is the hardest part of the conversation.** **Weight-bearing as tolerated for a low-risk tibial shaft stress fracture; a CAM walker or moon boot for a few weeks if walking is painful** VERIFY · **paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, max 4 g in 24 hours**, ice after activity · **non-impact cross-training offered STRAIGHT AWAY** · **physiotherapy for calf and hip strengthening and running technique; podiatry for footwear and orthoses** · **optimise vitamin D, calcium and energy intake** · **graded return at six to eight weeks once pain-free walking with no local bony tenderness, building by the 10% RULE — no more than a 10% increase in weekly volume** VERIFY · **replace shoes roughly every 600–800 km** · **review 4–6 weeks, and again before he resumes.** SA — **telehealth sports medicine or orthopaedics through the regional LHN; MRI may mean travel, with PATS**; allied health under a **GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement, up to five subsidised visits a year** VERIFY ; **check the MRI item number before promising it will be bulk-billed.**
plan: **WIPE, then name what he has lost — four seconds, and it makes the ‘stop running for two months’ conversation land far better later**: **‘That must be frustrating if running is a big part of your life.’** Then signpost: **‘I'll ask about the pain first, then some questions that may seem unrelated — they help me rule other causes out — and then we'll look at the X-ray together.’**

**Site — OPEN, then CLOSED, then ONE FINGER.** **‘Where exactly is the pain?’** → *‘My leg.’* **‘Can you be more specific — buttock, thigh, knee, calf or shin? One leg or both? Front or back?’** → the shin. **‘Can you put ONE FINGER on the worst spot?’** **A single point on the bone is a stress fracture until proven otherwise; a spread of 5 cm or more along the medial border is shin splints.**

**The rest of SOCRATES**, then **THE TWO SORTING QUESTIONS**: **‘Is it worse when you walk, or when you stand?’ · ‘Is it worse going UPHILL, DOWNHILL, or does it make NO DIFFERENCE?’ · ‘Does it get better with rest — and HOW SOON after you stop does it settle?’** **Two questions and you have separated the vascular group from everything else.**
**The stress-fracture question almost nobody asks**: **‘Does the pain come on EARLIER in each run than it used to — or does it WARM UP once you get going?’**

**Pattern, then weight-bearing.** **‘Do you get pain at night, or does it wake you?’** — **this is the branch point: mechanical bone pain is LOAD-related, and pain worse at night and unrelated to activity belongs to the RED-FLAG group and changes the station completely** · morning or end of the day · after rest or after activity · **limping, and can you put your full weight on it.**

**General MSK screen, five questions in one breath**: swelling · redness or rash · stiffness and how long in the morning · change in the shape of the leg · **any injury or trauma, even minor.** *He volunteers the firm lump on the bone here.*

**Vascular — THREE questions and move on.** **Colour change, pale or bluish; does it feel cold; hair loss over the shin; sores slow to heal** · **smoking, diabetes, cholesterol, heart disease in himself or the family — AND AT WHAT AGE** · **prominent veins, previous clots, recent travel, surgery or immobility.**
**Neurogenic — four questions, no more.** **Back pain · pins and needles or numbness · weakness, does the foot ever slap or catch · any change in bladder or bowel control.**

**Red flags, ANNOUNCED as a block whatever the stem suggests.** **‘A few I ask everybody with this problem, to make sure nothing serious is being missed.’** Weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness, **previous cancer** · **fevers, sweats or chills, recent infection or break in the skin.**

**THE TRAINING HISTORY — THIS BLOCK IS THE DIAGNOSIS.** **‘How many kilometres a week, and has that CHANGED recently? Have you added hills, speed sessions or a new surface? HOW OLD ARE YOUR SHOES? Were you off running for a while before this started?’** Then **occupation, previous fractures, steroids, and the concerns question — where the March half marathon arrives.** **Then at 3:40 the film in four sentences, and from 4:40 the diagnosis, the mechanism, the differentials by group, the race answer and the plan.**
pefe: **There is no examination task — the X-ray is the investigation handed to you, and the history is where everything else comes from.** **Plan the LAST TWO MINUTES before you go in: one minute on the film, then diagnosis, differentials and management, which together are worth more marks than the film.**

**Four rules for the film**: **ORIENT first** — patients cannot follow a finding until they know what they are looking at · **NAME ONLY WHAT YOU NEED** — two bones, tibia and fibula · **POINT**, or if it is on a screen say ‘about a third of the way down’, and **do not stand up and walk to the screen mid-consultation** · **STOP at one minute.**

**‘What if the X-ray had been normal?’** → **‘A normal plain film does not exclude a stress fracture — it is often normal for the first two to three weeks, and in a bone stress REACTION it stays normal. With this history and focal bony tenderness I would treat him as having a bone stress injury regardless, and arrange an MRI if the diagnosis needed confirming or if he was not improving.’**

**‘Does it matter WHERE on the tibia the fracture is?’** → **‘Yes. A stress fracture of the POSTEROMEDIAL tibial shaft is low risk and heals with relative rest. One in the ANTERIOR CORTEX is on the tension side, has poor healing potential — the dreaded black line — and needs orthopaedic referral because it can progress to complete fracture or non-union. The same applies to the femoral neck, navicular and base of the fifth metatarsal.’**

**‘His mother had heart disease — is that a risk factor?’** → **‘Only if it was premature. A first-degree relative with cardiovascular disease before 55 in a man or 65 in a woman counts; his mother developed it in her eighties, so it does not meaningfully change his risk. I would still manage his blood pressure and calculate his absolute cardiovascular risk, but not because of that history.’**

**The bone-health questions almost nobody asks** — recurrent or unexplained bone stress injury should prompt a look at **bone health and ENERGY AVAILABILITY**: dietary intake and any deliberate restriction, sun exposure and vitamin D, calcium intake, previous fractures, corticosteroid use, **and in women the menstrual history, since amenorrhoea in an athlete is part of RELATIVE ENERGY DEFICIENCY IN SPORT.** **In a 50-year-old man, ask about weight loss and steroid use rather than assuming it is purely a training error.**

**Avoid**: **accepting a normal X-ray as excluding a stress fracture** · **injecting corticosteroid, or ultrasound-guided injection, for bone stress injury** · **diagnosing shin splints when there is a single tender point and localised bony swelling** · **attributing exertional leg pain in a hypertensive patient to arterial disease without checking the gradient question and the pulses.**

**The safety-net, and the last clause is the one that matters**: **‘Come back sooner if the pain becomes constant or starts waking you at night, if you develop a fever, if the leg swells or changes colour, or if the pain suddenly becomes much worse — particularly if you feel something give way. AND COME BACK BEFORE YOU START RUNNING AGAIN, NOT AFTER.’**
ddx: **Tibial stress fracture — the answer**
Runner or new load; **pain begins EARLIER in each successive run**, then with walking; relieved by rest but SLOWLY; **NO uphill–downhill difference**
**Focal tenderness at ONE POINT on the bone**, localised swelling, pain on hopping on that leg
**X-ray — often normal for 2–3 weeks; MRI is the test of choice.** Relative rest and graded return. Soon
**Medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints) — the closest mimic**
**Diffuse ache along the INNER BORDER of the shin**; sore at the start of a run and **WARMS UP**; sore again afterwards
**Tenderness spread over 5 cm or more** along the medial border, **NOT one point**; no bony swelling
Clinical. **X-ray normal.** Load reduction, calf and foot strengthening, footwear and gait review. Routine
**Chronic exertional compartment syndrome**
**Tightness and pain at a REPRODUCIBLE time or distance every run**, with numbness or foot slap, **resolving within minutes of stopping**
**Normal examination at rest**; tense compartments or a fascial defect AFTER exercise
Referral for intracompartmental pressure testing after exercise; fasciotomy if refractory. Soon
**Bone tumour or metastasis**
**NIGHT AND REST PAIN UNRELATED TO ACTIVITY**, progressive, weight loss, known primary; or a young patient with an **osteoid osteoma** whose pain is **dramatically relieved by anti-inflammatories**
Weight, appetite, lumps, fatigue, previous cancer; a palpable mass or localised bony swelling
X-ray; FBE, ESR/CRP, calcium, ALP, LFT; MRI and urgent referral. **Do NOT label activity-unrelated night pain as overuse.** Urgent
**Osteomyelitis · septic arthritis**
**Fever**, rapidly worsening pain, unable to weight-bear, systemic upset; diabetes, immunosuppression, a break in the skin
Fever, chills, redness, warmth; **a hot swollen joint with pain on passive movement**
FBE, CRP, ESR, blood cultures; **urgent orthopaedic referral — aspiration for a joint, MRI for bone.** Emergency
**Peripheral arterial disease — what the stem points at**
Calf pain at a **predictable distance, WORSE UPHILL, relieved by standing still within minutes**; smoker, diabetic, hypertensive, hyperlipidaemic
**Absent or weak pedal pulses**, prolonged capillary refill, hair loss, cool shiny skin, positive Buerger's
**Ankle–brachial index, then duplex ultrasound**; risk factor management and vascular referral. Soon
Deep vein thrombosis · venous insufficiency
DVT: **unilateral calf swelling and tenderness** after travel, surgery or immobility. Venous: aching, varicose veins, ankle swelling worse by evening
Calf circumference difference, pitting oedema, dilated superficial veins, haemosiderin staining
Wells score and compression ultrasound for DVT; compression and elevation for venous insufficiency. Soon
Lumbar radiculopathy · spinal canal stenosis
Back pain radiating down the leg, pins and needles, weakness; **stenosis eased by SITTING or LEANING FORWARD rather than by standing still**
Dermatomal radiation, reduced reflexes, weakness; **bladder or bowel change suggests cauda equina**
Neurological examination; MRI lumbar spine if a deficit or red flags. **Cauda equina is an emergency.** Soon
Tendinopathy · muscle strain · arthritis
Pain localised to a tendon or muscle belly, or to a joint; **sudden onset during activity** for a strain
Tenderness over the tendon, pain on resisted movement; joint line tenderness, crepitus, morning stiffness
Clinical; ultrasound if unclear. Load management and physiotherapy. Routine
**Relative energy deficiency in sport**
**Recurrent stress fractures**, restricted diet, hard training; **in women, amenorrhoea**
Energy availability, dietary restriction, menstrual history, previous fractures
**Vitamin D, calcium, DXA and a dietitian.** Think of it after a THIRD stress fracture, not the first. Soon
