stem: General practice in regional South Australia. You are the GP. David Whitmore, 60.
History given to you: pain in both knees for six months, constant, worse at the end of the day, worse on the left. No injury, trauma or fracture. Past history hypertension, on perindopril.
8-minute station. No further history-taking and no physical examination are required.
tasks: State your most likely diagnosis
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management plan to the patient, including non-pharmacological and pharmacological options
Explain the side effects of the treatments you offer
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: The examination is ALREADY DONE and handed to you

CREPITUS in both knees · PAINFUL ACTIVE AND PASSIVE MOVEMENT in both knees · BMI 32 · NO hot, red or swollen joint · AFEBRILE. These are not scenery — they are the evidence you hand back to the patient
The FIVE REASONS, counted out on your fingers

ONE — six months, so it is LONG-STANDING · TWO — WORSE AT THE END OF THE DAY and after being on his feet, the classic wear-and-tear pattern · THREE — NO INJURY or accident to explain it · FOUR — BILATERAL, which fits a wear pattern rather than one damaged structure · FIVE — CREPITUS with painful restricted movement. THIS IS THE HIGHEST-YIELD THIRTY SECONDS IN THE STATION
Investigations — NONE, routinely

The diagnosis of osteoarthritis is CLINICAL: history, examination and functional assessment. THIS IS THE ANSWER THE STATION WANTS. Say out loud: ‘I would not order an X-ray, because the diagnosis is clinical and the result would not change my management’
The diagnostic rule worth quoting
AGE 45 OR OVER + ACTIVITY-RELATED JOINT PAIN + EITHER NO MORNING STIFFNESS OR STIFFNESS LASTING 30 MINUTES OR LESS → diagnose knee OA WITHOUT imaging. Mr Whitmore meets all three VERIFY
UEC and eGFR

Before or during ANY NSAID use, and as BASELINE in a patient on an ACE inhibitor. In version B the disclosure ‘I've been buying them for months’ CONVERTS STRAIGHT INTO THIS TEST — that is the scoring moment
FBE, CRP/ESR, RF, anti-CCP, urate
ONLY if inflammatory or crystal disease is suspected. In osteoarthritis inflammatory markers are NORMAL or minimally raised
JOINT ASPIRATION
Suspected SEPTIC ARTHRITIS or crystal arthropathy. Cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystal microscopy — BEFORE antibiotics. NEVER inject steroid into a joint you suspect is infected
Weight-bearing AP + lateral ± skyline X-RAY
Diagnostic doubt, RED FLAGS, or SURGICAL PLANNING — NOT to confirm a diagnosis you have already made clinically
If you DID X-ray, the four cardinal features

JOINT SPACE NARROWING · OSTEOPHYTES · SUBCHONDRAL SCLEROSIS · SUBCHONDRAL CYSTS — classically worst in the MEDIAL compartment, which is why long-standing knee OA drifts into VARUS alignment. Know them; do not order the film
Lipids, HbA1c, absolute CVD risk

Opportunistic and appropriate in a hypertensive man with a BMI of 32 — mention it BRIEFLY. MRI is rarely indicated: suspected osteonecrosis, or a mechanical lesion where the result would genuinely change management

dx: **Bilateral primary knee osteoarthritis, left worse than right, in a 60-year-old man with obesity (BMI 32) and hypertension.** Chronic, non-inflammatory, mechanical pattern; no red flags. **A WHOLE-JOINT disease** — cartilage loss plus **subchondral remodelling and sclerosis, osteophytes, low-grade synovitis, capsular thickening and periarticular muscle weakness.** ‘Wear and tear’ is the lay phrase: **use it with the patient, but know it is a simplification you can defend.**

**NOTHING IN THE STEM IS DECORATIVE.** **Perindopril is there to make you refuse oral NSAIDs. BMI 32 is there to make you raise weight loss. Six months and worse at the end of the day are there so you can quote them back as your reasoning. No trauma closes off the post-traumatic story. Bilateral steers you away from a single mechanical lesion.** **Finish the station without using one of those five out loud and you have left marks on the table.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: name oral NSAIDs, rule them out, say why, and offer the topical alternative.** **Candidates who sail through and then say ‘I'll start you on some anti-inflammatories’ have failed the point the station was built around. Candidates who quietly never mention NSAIDs score poorly too — the examiner cannot tell whether you avoided them deliberately or simply forgot.**

**The words**: **‘They push blood pressure up, and yours is already something we're treating. They work against the perindopril. And the two together put a strain on the kidneys, which matters even more if you ever get a tummy bug or become dehydrated. You'd be taking these long-term, not for a few days. What I'll do instead is give you the same kind of medicine as a GEL you rub into the knee — very little gets into the bloodstream.’**

**THE TRIPLE WHAMMY — say the MECHANISM, not just the rule.** **ACE inhibitor or ARB + diuretic + NSAID.** **The ACE inhibitor dilates the EFFERENT arteriole, the NSAID constricts the AFFERENT arteriole, and the diuretic drops volume — glomerular perfusion collapses, and you get acute kidney injury, hyperkalaemia, rising blood pressure and fluid retention.** **Version B's patient is on indapamide as well — name it.** **Sick-day rule: withhold the ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever.**

**The honest sentence, and it must NEVER be left hanging**: **‘I need to be straight with you. This is a long-term condition. We are not able to reverse or repair the damage already done to the joint.’** → immediately → **‘But that is a long way from saying nothing can be done, because we can do a great deal about the symptoms.’** → then a concrete action. **The role-player is briefed to go flat and quiet if you pause after the bad news, and the examiner marks that down.**

**Non-pharmacological FIRST, and NUMBER the seven out loud**: **1 weight — 5–10% loss, with a DIETITIAN not an instruction · 2 EXERCISE, the single most effective treatment — physiotherapist for quadriceps strengthening, exercise physiologist, building to ~150 min/week · 3 aids — a stick in the OPPOSITE hand to the worse knee, cushioned footwear · 4 falls — OT home review · 5 the mental side — psychologist and pain strategies · 6 heat and pacing · 7 blood pressure control.** **Add: ‘I'll put a chronic disease management plan in place so Medicare helps with those visits, and I'll write the referrals today.’** VERIFY **GLA:D Australia is worth naming and is available in SA.**

**The ladder**: **1 TOPICAL diclofenac 1% gel, 2–4 g, 3–4 times daily** · **2 REGULAR paracetamol — 1 g qid, max 4 g/24 h; or modified release 665 mg × 2 tds, max 6 tablets/24 h** VERIFY · **✗ oral NSAIDs — named and ruled out** · **3 intra-articular corticosteroid — methylprednisolone acetate 40 mg or triamcinolone 40 mg, ultrasound-guided, FLARE ONLY, relief 4–12 WEEKS, not repeated as maintenance, ABSOLUTELY contraindicated if infection is suspected** · **4 duloxetine 30 mg daily for a week then 60 mg** VERIFY (not PBS-subsidised for OA) · **✗ opioids — decline and explain** · **5 pain clinic, and orthopaedics for TKR.**

**DIVERGENCE on paracetamol, and the answer that wins either way**: older Australian teaching puts it first; **the RACGP guideline is more sceptical because the effect size in knee OA is small.** If challenged: **‘I accept the effect size is modest and that exercise and weight loss are the higher-value interventions, which is why I led with them. I'm offering paracetamol as an adjunct, and I've chosen it because oral anti-inflammatories are relatively contraindicated by his hypertension and perindopril. I'd review its benefit at four to six weeks and stop it if it isn't helping.’**

**Surgery framed honestly**: **‘It gives most people a real improvement in pain and function — but it's a BETTER knee, not a YOUNG knee.’** **DO NOT QUOTE A WAITING-LIST NUMBER** — figures circulate from months to a decade. **‘Waits in the public system can be long and vary a lot depending on where you are and how urgent it's judged to be — which is exactly why we don't just wait, we keep working on the knee.’** SA — **PATS** for orthopaedic travel from an MM5 town; **telehealth** through the country LHN; **ALO or ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS co-payment, which matters when the plan is lifelong**; **ReturnToWorkSA and SafeWork SA** if work-aggravated; **Austroads driving — SA is one of only two jurisdictions with MANDATORY practitioner reporting**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for a septic joint needing retrieval.
plan: **WIPE — then OPEN WITH A QUESTION, even though the task says ‘explain the diagnosis’.** **‘Before I start — how can I help you today, and what were you most hoping to get out of coming in?’** **Fifteen seconds buys the hidden agenda — the X-ray, the Nurofen, the wheelchair fear, the trip he has booked — and gives you a place to return at the end.**

**Check understanding — ten seconds, never skip it**: **‘Has anyone talked to you about what might be causing the knee pain, or is there anything you've read or been told about it?’** *His mother had arthritis and ended up in a wheelchair.* **Acknowledge it immediately and PROMISE TO RETURN TO IT.**

**Name it, then justify it with the FIVE REASONS.** **‘What you have is a condition called osteoarthritis, and it's in both of your knees, a bit worse on the left. In everyday language it's what people call wear and tear — the smooth, slippery cushion that covers the ends of the bones gradually thins, so the bones don't glide over each other as easily.’** Then the five, counted. **Anyone can say ‘you have osteoarthritis’; very few then hand the patient five pieces of his own history as evidence — and it pre-empts the X-ray request before it is made.**

**Decline the X-ray without a power struggle**: **‘It wouldn't change what we do today. Osteoarthritis is diagnosed from the story and the examination, and the pictures often don't match how much pain people have — plenty of people with normal-looking knees are in agony, and plenty with very worn X-rays feel fine. I'd order one if I were worried about something else, or if we were planning surgery. If you'd still like one after we've talked, we can revisit it.’**

**Causes and risk factors, honestly flagged as changeable or not**: age · **weight — ‘your body mass index is 32, and that's one we can work on’** · previous knee injuries, which he has not had · repetitive loading · **the shape of the leg — varus or valgus concentrates load on one compartment and is an independent risk factor** · family tendency.

**Clinical features and course**, then **THE HONEST SENTENCE followed immediately by the positive one and the three goals**: **reduce the pain as much as we can; keep you doing your daily activities; keep you independent.** Then: **‘when I talk about painkillers later, hear this now — the aim is to bring the pain down enough that you can do what you need to do. It does NOT mean you'll be pain-free.’**

**The pivot line, memorised**: **‘So that's what it is and why I'm confident about it. Now — the part that matters more — what we can actually do about it.’** Then **the seven non-pharmacological items, NUMBERED, each with ONE CLAUSE SAYING WHAT THEY DO** — ‘a physiotherapist, to strengthen the thigh muscles so the joint is better supported’. **A referral list with no explanation reads as a dump.**

**The weight moment, and the repair line loaded in advance.** If he bristles — *‘so it's my fault then’* — **do not retreat and do not lecture**: **‘I'm not blaming you at all, and I'm sorry if it landed that way. I raise it because it's the thing that gives us the biggest return, and I'd rather help you with it than just tell you to do it. Would it be alright if I keep going?’** **Candidates who repair rapport after a misstep score better than candidates who never touch the difficult topic.**

**Frame the ladder before you climb it**, then the steps — **and when he asks for Nurofen at about five minutes, that is the station.** If he says *‘I've been buying them for months, nobody said anything’*, **DO NOT simply repeat the warning — convert it into action**: **‘That's really useful to know, and it's exactly why I'd like to check your kidney function and blood pressure today, because this combination can cause harm quietly, without any symptoms.’**

**Side effects in one sentence each — task four, and skipping it because the clock is against you scores nothing.** Then **surgery with the realistic picture**, then the **safety-net: hot, red, swollen knee or fever → SAME DAY; sudden locking or giving way; night or rest pain; unintended weight loss.** Then **review 4–6 weeks, referrals written today, and a summary that CLOSES THE LOOP on the wheelchair fear.**
pefe: **TASK 4 — SIDE EFFECTS, in the patient's language, and several recalls ask it explicitly.** **Gel** — *‘mostly just skin things: IRRITATION, redness or a rash where you rub it in, and the skin can be more SUN-SENSITIVE. Wash your hands afterwards, and not on broken skin.’* **Paracetamol** — *‘very well tolerated at the right dose. The one rule that matters: never more than four grams in twenty-four hours — and watch cold-and-flu PRODUCTS, because most already contain it.’* **Oral NSAIDs, which we are AVOIDING** — *‘they raise blood pressure, can cause STOMACH BLEEDING, and can strain the kidneys.’* **Injection** — *‘a small risk of infection getting into the joint — that's the one that matters. A day or two of worse pain first. Sometimes a pale dent in the skin. And if you're DIABETIC your SUGARS may run high for a few days.’* **Opioids** — *‘CONSTIPATION, DROWSINESS, nausea — and they stop working as well over time, so people end up on higher doses for the same relief.’* **Surgery** — *‘infection, clots, the ANAESTHETIC ITSELF, and the joint doesn't last FOREVER.’* **If the clock is against you, compress to one sentence each — a rapid accurate sweep scores; silence scores nothing.**

**The verbatim safety-net, and the review**: **‘If the knee BECOMES hot, red and swollen, or you get a fever or feel unwell with it, I need to see you that day, because we'd need to rule out an infection in the joint. Same if the knee SUDDENLY locks or gives way, or if the pain STARTS waking you at night, or you're losing weight without TRYING.’** Then **‘I'd like to see you in four to six weeks to check how you're going, recheck your blood pressure and weight, and see whether the pain relief is doing enough. I'll write the physio, exercise physiology and dietitian referrals today.’**
**This station gives you findings, not a patient to examine — no further history-taking or physical examination is required.** The marks sit almost entirely in how you talk.

**HEDGING COSTS THE MARK TWICE — once for the diagnosis and once for over-investigation.** ‘Possible osteoarthritis, I'd need an X-ray to be CERTAIN’ fails the thing the station was built to test: **will you COMMIT clinically?** When he pushes — *‘but wouldn't an X-ray make it certain?’* — **‘It wouldn't change what we do today. The pictures often don't match the pain — plenty of people with worn-looking X-rays feel fine, and plenty with normal ones are in real TROUBLE. I'd order one if I were worried about something else, or if we were planning an OPERATION.’** **And no ‘crepitus’, ‘DEGENERATIVE change’ or ‘REDUCED range of movement’ to the patient — say GRATING SOUNDS from the ROUGHENED SURFACES instead.**

**The diagnostic rule worth quoting**: **AGE 45 OR OVER + ACTIVITY-RELATED PAIN + MORNING STIFFNESS OF 30 MINUTES OR LESS → diagnose without imaging.** **DO NOT QUOTE public joint-REPLACEMENT waiting times, and do not quote a PRECISE post-injection septic arthritis rate** — *‘long and VARIES, I'd check the CURRENT local time rather than quote a number I couldn't stand behind’*, and *‘rare, but the one that matters’*.
**Examine the hip in every knee-pain patient** — hip pathology presents as knee pain alone, and **painful, restricted internal rotation is the giveaway.**

**Red flags that must make you abandon the script**: **hot, red, swollen, exquisitely tender knee ± fever → septic arthritis until proven otherwise** · rapid onset over hours to days in a single joint · **morning stiffness >30–60 minutes with symmetrical small-joint involvement and systemic features → inflammatory arthritis** · **pain at rest and at night, waking from sleep** · weight loss, fever, night sweats, bone pain, known cancer → malignancy · **true locking, giving way, effusion after a twist → mechanical or meniscal** · groin pain or pain on hip rotation → referred hip disease.

**Avoid**: **a reflex X-ray ‘to confirm it’** · **oral NSAIDs in this patient** · **opioids** · **repeated intra-articular steroid as maintenance** · **glucosamine, chondroitin, fish oil and turmeric as promised treatments — acknowledge respectfully rather than mocking** · **arthroscopic lavage or debridement for OA — not indicated** · **PRP and stem-cell injections** · **promising a pain-free knee, or the opposite — ‘it's bone on bone, nothing can be done’.**

**Do not miss**: **depression, social isolation and deconditioning in chronic pain** · **falls, and the consequences of a fall on a patient with weak quadriceps** · **driving — severe pain or restricted movement can impair emergency braking.**

**Version B — 68 F on perindopril AND indapamide, opening with ‘I just want some Nurofen’.** Two refusals to deliver kindly in one station. **Name the triple whammy explicitly, order UEC and eGFR, and decline the X-ray without being dismissive.** **If she says the gel didn't work, don't collapse into prescribing tablets** — check how she used it (amount, frequency, duration, whether she rubbed it in) and pair it with REGULAR paracetamol and physiotherapy before declaring it failed.

**Version C — 62 M, severe flare after a walking holiday, wanting an injection and a new knee.** **Before arranging ANY injection, check the joint is not infected: ‘Has the knee been hot or red? Have you had any fevers or felt unwell with it?’** A hot febrile joint is not a flare — it is possible septic arthritis, and injecting it is an automatic fail. **Frame the injection as temporary (4–12 weeks) and as a window to get the exercise and weight work going, not as the treatment.**

**Version D — the case that is NOT osteoarthritis.** 58 F, four months, **both knees AND both hands, stiff for well over an hour every morning, eases with use, puffy fingers, exhausted.** **Abandon the OA script.** **FBE, CRP/ESR, RF, anti-CCP, and an URGENT rheumatology referral — say the word urgent and say why: there is a window early on where treatment works much better.** **Recognising it and then referring ‘routinely’ is the trap.**
ddx: **Knee osteoarthritis — the answer**

**Stiffness ≤30 min**; better with rest; crepitus; **painful restricted active AND passive range**; bony enlargement; varus alignment; quadriceps wasting
**No test needed. Diagnose clinically and treat.** Imaging only for doubt, red flags or surgical planning. Routine
**Septic arthritis — must not miss**
**Hot, red, exquisitely tender, swollen joint over hours to days**; fever; systemically unwell; unable to weight-bear
Fever, rigors; immunosuppression, diabetes, IV drug use, **recent injection or skin breach**; prosthetic joint
**Urgent joint aspiration BEFORE antibiotics** (cell count, Gram stain, culture, crystals) + blood cultures, FBE, CRP. Urgent orthopaedic discussion. **NEVER inject steroid.** EMERGENCY
**Rheumatoid / inflammatory arthritis**
**Morning stiffness >30–60 min**; symmetrical small joints (MCPs, wrists, MTPs); fatigue; boggy synovial swelling; **BETTER with use**
Hand and foot joints; nodules; family history; psoriasis, nail changes, iritis, IBD, back pain

Gout
**Abrupt severe monoarthritis peaking in 12–24 h**; red shiny skin; prior first MTP attacks

Aspiration: **positively birefringent rhomboid crystals**; chondrocalcinosis on X-ray. Urgent

Clinical; physiotherapy-led rehabilitation. Routine

Aspirate if infection suspected; antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines. Urgent

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town. James Kellner, 57, a retired truck driver, with leg pain. Known type 2 diabetes, hypertension and hyperlipidaemia.
On the door: HR 82 · BP 152/90 · RR 16 · BMI 32 · temperature not given — you have to ask for it.

8-minute station. History 4 minutes, then the examination findings from the examiner, then diagnosis and differentials. Four recall versions run off this one stem: pad · pad plus cellulitis · spinal canal stenosis · statin myositis.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (4 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: How to OPEN the request — and call it a LOWER LIMB examination

‘Thank you. I'd now like to perform a LOWER LIMB examination. I'd start with the general appearance and gait, then the vital signs, then inspect, palpate and move the limb, and finish with some specific tests.’ NOT a knee, calf or thigh examination. And ask ITEM BY ITEM — THE EXAMINER ANSWERS WHAT YOU ASK, AND ONLY WHAT YOU ASK
1–2 · General appearance and gait, then VITALS WITH TEMPERATURE FIRST

Body habitus and BMI · level of consciousness, alert or drowsy · any distress · gait and any walking aid. Then ‘TEMPERATURE FIRST, PLEASE’ — then BP, heart rate, respiratory rate, saturations. TEMPERATURE IS THE SINGLE HIGHEST-YIELD VITAL SIGN IN THIS STATION — IT IS HOW THE MIXED CASE DECLARES ITSELF
3 · Inspection

Any REDNESS OR RASH · any PALLOR or HYPERPIGMENTATION · any ULCERS, and where · any HAIR LOSS on the legs · any swelling of the joints · any varicose veins or oedema. Rash screens infection. PALLOR AND HAIR LOSS ARE ARTERIAL; HYPERPIGMENTATION AND VARICOSITIES ARE VENOUS
4 · Palpation — NAME ALL FOUR PULSE SITES

Temperature of the legs, are they cool · CAPILLARY REFILL TIME · PULSES: FEMORAL, POPLITEAL, POSTERIOR TIBIAL AND DORSALIS PEDIS, BOTH SIDES · tenderness over muscles and joints · calf tenderness or asymmetry. OMITTING PULSES IN A CLAUDICATION CASE IS INDEFENSIBLE
5 · Movement
Any pain or restriction on ACTIVE AND PASSIVE movement of the HIP, KNEE AND ANKLE. Normal here excludes the joint group — ten seconds, and it closes a whole differential box
6 · SPECIAL TESTS — the two you cannot omit

‘I would like to perform BUERGER'S TEST.’ · ‘I would like to perform a SENSORY NEUROLOGICAL EXAMINATION of the lower limbs.’ Then femoral bruit · is an ANKLE–BRACHIAL INDEX available · version B: inguinal lymphadenopathy · a brief cardiovascular examination. STRAIGHT-LEG RAISE AND LIMB-LENGTH ARE OPTIONAL. THESE TWO ARE NOT
7 · Office tests
BLOOD SUGAR LEVEL and a URINE DIPSTICK. Glucose as a risk factor; dipstick for PROTEINURIA — chronic kidney disease travels with vascular disease — and glycosuria
THE CARD — VERSION B, the mixed case

BMI 32, alert. TEMPERATURE 38.7°C, BP 148/86, HR 96. Legs PALE with HAIR LOSS. A RASH on the left shin. Legs COLD. CAPILLARY REFILL OVER 3 SECONDS. POSTERIOR TIBIAL AND DORSALIS PEDIS ABSENT BILATERALLY; femoral present. No muscle or joint tenderness. Movements normal. BUERGER'S POSITIVE. FEMORAL BRUIT PRESENT. ABI UNAVAILABLE. SENSORY EXAMINATION NORMAL. INGUINAL NODE PALPABLE ON THE LEFT. Dipstick: glucose, no protein
When the examiner says ‘there is a rash’ — SIX QUESTIONS, FIFTEEN SECONDS

Primary morphology — macular, papular, a PATCH or a PLAQUE? · secondary change — blistering, discharge, WEEPING or pus? · is it WARM to touch? · is it TENDER on palpation? · where is it, is the EDGE WELL DEMARCATED, is it SPREADING? · any INGUINAL LYMPHADENOPATHY on that side? Noting ‘rash present’ and moving on loses the second diagnosis
How to READ THE CARD ALOUD, finding by finding

Pale legs with hair loss → ‘chronic arterial changes.’ Refill >3 s → ‘delayed; normal is under two seconds.’ Cold legs → ‘cool peripheries fit reduced perfusion.’ Absent pulses → ‘THE KEY FINDING.’ Buerger's positive → ‘pallor on elevation with dependent rubor confirms significant arterial insufficiency.’ Femoral bruit → ‘turbulent flow through a stenosed vessel.’ Normal neurology → ‘makes neurogenic claudication unlikely.’ ABI unavailable → ‘I would arrange it — it is the objective measure.’ Temp 38.7 with a warm tender weeping rash and a node → ‘THAT CHANGES THINGS: A SECOND, CONCURRENT DIAGNOSIS’

dx: **Peripheral arterial disease — and in version B, PAD WITH CRITICAL LIMB ISCHAEMIA PLUS CELLULITIS OF THE SAME LIMB.** **Everybody reaches PAD; the stem hands it to you.** **The examiner is not scoring the answer — they are scoring whether you knew there were TWO KINDS OF CLAUDICATION and did the work to tell them apart.**

**THE TWO QUESTIONS TO TAKE INTO THE ROOM, and both are about RELIEF, not pain**: **‘When you stop walking, does the pain go straight away or does it linger?’** proves arterial claudication. **‘Is it any better when you lean forward?’** excludes the nerve type — **and skipping it fails the station on its own.**

**‘Better with rest’ ON ITS OWN EXCLUDES NOTHING.** Osteoarthritis is better with rest. Tendinopathy is better with rest. Cellulitis is better with rest. **What is specific is the SPEED of relief**: arterial claudication is supply-and-demand, so the moment the muscle stops working the pain goes — **within a minute or two. Nothing else behaves like that.** **The second discriminator is a SHRINKING claudication distance.**

**VASCULAR vs NEUROGENIC**: **uphill** — arterial WORSE, neurogenic also worse, no real difference · **downhill** — arterial BETTER, neurogenic also worse · **relief** — arterial settles on STOPPING within a minute, neurogenic needs **SITTING OR LEANING FORWARD** · **character** — cramping tight ache vs **heaviness, weakness, burning, pins and needles** · **neurology** — normal vs numbness, weakness, sometimes continence change · **pulses** — reduced or absent with hair loss and cool shiny skin vs **normal pulses, normal skin** · **test** — ABI then arterial duplex vs MRI lumbar spine.

**DIVERGENCE, handled carefully**: some texts teach neurogenic claudication is BETTER uphill because the trunk flexes forward; this source teaches emphatically that **direction makes no difference in neurogenic claudication.** VERIFY **The safe OSCE wording avoids the shortcut**: **‘the vascular type is worse uphill and settles as soon as he stops; the nerve type happens in both directions and only settles when he sits or leans forward.’** If challenged: **‘I wouldn't rely on gradient alone — I'd use the relief posture, the neurology, the pulses and the ABI.’**

**NIGHT PAIN HERE IS NOT THE MALIGNANCY RED FLAG.** **Rest pain at night, relieved by hanging the leg out of bed, is the clinical marker of CRITICAL LIMB ISCHAEMIA — Fontaine stage III.** **Gravity is being used to perfuse the foot.** **Saying ‘stage III, critical limb-threatening ischaemia’ out loud is what converts a routine referral into an urgent one on your mark sheet.**

**FONTAINE**: **I asymptomatic · IIa claudication over 200 m · IIb under 200 m or lifestyle-limiting · III REST PAIN · IV ULCERATION OR GANGRENE.** **III or IV = urgent.** **ABI** VERIFY : **>1.4 non-compressible calcified vessels — common in diabetes and CKD and FALSELY REASSURING, use a toe–brachial index · 1.0–1.4 normal · 0.9–1.0 borderline · ≤0.9 diagnostic of PAD · <0.5 severe · <0.4 critical ischaemia.**

**Version B — COMMIT TO BOTH, and explain the LINK**: **‘Mr Kellner, there are two things going on at the same time.’** Then each with its reasons, then: **‘And the two are linked. When the blood supply is poor the skin becomes dry and cracks — you told me your toes crack — and it heals slowly, so infection takes hold easily.’** **Poorly perfused skin is dry, cracks, heals slowly and is often colonised with tinea between the toes. That is not a coincidence — it is what the mixed case is testing.**

**The amputation question, answered honestly and then made actionable**: **‘I'll be straight with you. Amputation is what can happen when this goes untreated for a long time, and I'm not going to pretend the situation isn't serious — it is, which is why I'm sending you in today. But you have come in at the point where we can act. Treating this infection now, seeing the vascular team, and stopping smoking — which will do more for your legs than any tablet I can prescribe — are the three things that most change how this goes.’**

**Management in four blocks** VERIFY : **1 RISK FACTORS — smoking cessation is the single most effective intervention (Quitline 13 7848, NRT, varenicline); BP, glucose, weight, diet.** **2 MEDICATION — antiplatelet AND a statin for EVERY PAD patient, for cardiovascular protection as much as for the leg; an ACE inhibitor where indicated.** **3 EXERCISE — a supervised programme, walking to near-maximal claudication pain, resting, repeating, ~30 minutes three times weekly. It genuinely works and is under-prescribed.** **4 FEET AND REFERRAL — podiatry, daily foot inspection, treat tinea and skin cracks; vascular referral for lifestyle-limiting claudication, URGENTLY for rest pain or tissue loss.** **Cellulitis: flucloxacillin, IV rather than oral if systemically unwell or the limb is ischaemic — oral therapy penetrates poorly perfused tissue badly. Mark the edge, elevate, review 24–48 h.** SA — **vascular services at the RAH and Flinders with telehealth triage before travel; PATS; SA Health HIGH RISK FOOT SERVICES — refer early rather than after tissue loss; ALO and ACCHS with Closing the Gap, since antiplatelet and statin here are lifelong.**
plan: **WIPE, concern in ONE sentence, then THE AGENDA SENTENCE — eight seconds of a four-minute history, and worth it**: **‘Leg pain can come from the circulation, from the nerves in the back, from the joints, or from the muscles and soft tissues. I'm going to work through each of those so we don't miss anything. Some questions won't seem connected — please bear with me.’** **It pre-announces the neurogenic group, and this station is marked on groups.**

**The pain, sub-localised**: **‘Which part of the leg — buttock, thigh, calf, or the whole leg? One side or both? If it's the thigh, front or back?’** Then out of ten, **‘a dull cramping ache, or a BURNING pain?’**, how long, getting worse.

**THE CLAUDICATION TRIAD — ask all three**: **‘Is the pain worse when you walk?’ · ‘Is it worse going UPHILL, DOWNHILL, or both the same?’ · ‘When you stop walking, does it settle STRAIGHT AWAY, or does it hang around for a while?’** Then **‘How far can you walk before it starts — and has that distance been getting SHORTER?’** **Two extra questions worth ten seconds each in a longer version: ‘can you CYCLE further than you can walk?’ (yes suggests neurogenic) and ‘any problems with erections?’ in a man with buttock claudication (aorto-iliac — Leriche).**

**Pattern and general screen.** **‘Do you get any pain at NIGHT, at rest?’** — and if yes, **‘does hanging the leg out of bed help?’** · morning or evening · limping, weight-bearing · swelling, redness or rash, joint stiffness, injury.

**GROUP 1 — VASCULAR.** ‘Now the circulation.’ Colour change, pale or bluish · ulcers slow to heal · dilated or bulging veins · previous clot · recent long travel, surgery or time in bed. **Then the cardiovascular risk factors as a BLOCK**: BP, sugar, cholesterol · **smoking — how much and for how long** · alcohol · **medications** · heart disease, angina, MI in him or the family · stroke or TIA.

**GROUP 2 — NEUROGENIC. THE FIFTEEN SECONDS THAT DECIDE THE STATION.** **‘Any back pain, now or in the past? … Any pins and needles or numbness in the legs? … Any weakness, or catching your toe when you walk? … Any problems with bladder or bowel control, or numbness around the back passage? … And is the pain any better when you lean forward or sit down?’** **Ask them even when the diagnosis is obvious — ESPECIALLY when it is obvious. The negative answers are what you quote later to exclude canal stenosis.**

**GROUP 3 — RED FLAGS, and this is the block that decides version B.** **INFECTION FIRST**: **‘Have you had any fever or chills? … Any redness, warmth or rash on the leg? … Any break in the skin, a cut, an ulcer, or cracking between the toes?’** Then malignancy: weight loss, appetite, lumps, tiredness, night sweats. **Candidates argue that a two-month history in obvious PAD does not need infection screening. IT IS EXACTLY THE CASE THAT DOES.**

**GROUPS 4 & 5 — joints and muscles.** Other joint pains · occupation · excessive exercise · family arthritis · **shoulder pain or stiffness and new headaches (PMR and giant cell arteritis)** · **‘any muscle aches or weakness climbing stairs or getting out of a chair — and has any medication been STARTED OR INCREASED recently?’** **MEDICATIONS ARE ASKED THREE TIMES IN THIS STATION, DELIBERATELY — in risk factors, for myositis, and in closure for compliance. Propranolol and the statin are the two answers hiding there.**

**Closure — diagnostic here, not administrative.** For EACH condition in the stem, four questions: **‘When were you diagnosed? What treatment are you on? Are you taking it regularly? Are you having your regular check-ups?’** Then **‘Is there anything you were particularly worried about today?’** — the amputation fear lives here, and if you never ask, he raises it himself at the end.

**The PEFE, requested in structure, temperature first, ending with Buerger's and the sensory examination.** **6:30 → 8:00: two diagnoses each with reasons, stage it as critical ischaemia, explain the link, answer the amputation question, then the differentials BY GROUP WITH NEUROGENIC NAMED FIRST, then the plan and safety-net.**
pefe: **THE COMPRESSION TEST FOR THIS STATION — if you can say these two sentences at the end, you have passed**: **‘It settles within a minute of stopping and leaning forward makes no difference, so this is arterial rather than neurogenic’** and **‘there are two things going on at once.’**

**BUERGER'S TEST, described**: supine, **leg raised to about 45° and held.** In significant arterial disease the foot goes **PALE and the superficial veins collapse into gutters — VENOUS GUTTERING.** The angle at which pallor appears is **Buerger's angle; below about 20° indicates severe ischaemia.** The leg is then **hung over the side of the couch: reactive hyperaemia produces a DUSKY RUBOR**, often after many seconds. **Pallor on elevation PLUS rubor on dependency is a positive test.**

**Investigations**: **bedside — ABI, blood sugar, urine dipstick, ECG.** **Bloods — FBE, U&E and creatinine, HbA1c, fasting lipids, LFT, and CREATINE KINASE where myositis is possible; CRP and cultures if febrile.** **Imaging — ARTERIAL duplex ultrasound first line: SPECIFY ARTERIAL, not simply ‘a Doppler’, because a venous duplex answers a different question.** CT or MR angiography if revascularisation is being considered; **MRI lumbar spine for the neurogenic version.**

**AVOID**: **compression bandaging before arterial disease is excluded** — on an ischaemic limb it causes tissue damage · **stopping a beta blocker or statin unilaterally** · **reassuring a diabetic foot because it does not hurt** — a PAINLESS ulcer in a diabetic is worse news than a painful one · **treating cellulitis orally in an ischaemic limb with systemic upset** · **attributing everything to one diagnosis when the findings need two.**

**THE PROPRANOLOL QUESTION**: a non-selective beta blocker **can worsen claudication and is suboptimal here — but it is NOT an absolute contraindication, and you never stop a cardiac drug unilaterally in an OSCE.** **‘I'd review this with your usual doctor; there are better options for your blood pressure.’**

**‘His ABI is 1.3 — doesn't that exclude PAD?’** → **‘Not in a diabetic. Medial calcification makes the vessels non-compressible and falsely elevates the index. I'd ask for a toe–brachial index or an arterial duplex, and I'd weight the clinical findings — absent pulses and a positive Buerger's — heavily.’** **‘Two diagnoses seems like hedging.’** → **‘It is not hedging — the findings require both, and they are causally linked. Treating only one would leave the patient at risk.’**

**VERSION C — spinal canal stenosis.** Both legs heavy and weak after a couple of hundred metres, **no difference up or down, standing still is not enough — he must SIT or LEAN ON THE TROLLEY**, longstanding back pain, numb feet, **can cycle for miles, pulses NORMAL.** **‘Standing and walking EXTEND the spine and narrow the canal; leaning forward OPENS it — which is exactly why the trolley helps and why you can cycle further than you can walk.’** MRI lumbar spine. **THE TRAP: calling it PAD because the stem is stuffed with cardiovascular risk factors. The risk factors do not make the diagnosis — the relief posture and the pulses do.**

**VERSION D — statin myositis.** Both thighs ache, **NO relation to walking distance**, difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs, **the statin was doubled two months ago**, pulses normal. **Check creatine kinase, U&E and TFT; withhold the statin and reassess; rechallenge at a lower dose or a different statin once settled.** **Severe pain with DARK URINE and a very high CK is rhabdomyolysis — urgent, with a risk of acute kidney injury.** **THE TRAP: never asking about medications.**

Cramping buttock, thigh or calf pain on walking, **worse uphill, settling within a minute or two of stopping**; **shrinking claudication distance**; cardiovascular risk factors
**Pallor, hair loss, cool limb, delayed capillary refill, absent pulses, Buerger's positive, femoral bruit**
**ABI, then arterial duplex.** Antiplatelet, statin, BP and glucose control, smoking cessation, supervised exercise. Soon
**Critical limb-threatening ischaemia**
**REST PAIN, worse at night, relieved by hanging the leg down**; ulceration; gangrene
**Very low ABI, tissue loss, Buerger's angle under 20°**
**URGENT vascular referral for revascularisation assessment.** Analgesia, foot protection. **Fontaine III–IV.** Urgent
**Acute limb ischaemia**
**Sudden onset: the six Ps — pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia, paralysis**
Atrial fibrillation, recent MI, aneurysm, bypass graft
**EMERGENCY — immediate vascular referral, anticoagulation, revascularisation within hours.** Emergency
**Lumbar spinal canal stenosis — name this group FIRST**
Bilateral leg pain, heaviness or weakness on walking, **up and downhill alike, relieved by LEANING FORWARD or SITTING**; variable walking distance
Back pain, numbness, weakness; **better pushing a trolley or cycling; PULSES NORMAL**
**MRI lumbar spine.** Physiotherapy, analgesia; decompression if disabling or progressive. Soon
Lumbar radiculopathy
Pain radiating below the knee in a **dermatomal band**, worse on coughing or straining
Straight-leg raise, dermatomal sensory loss, myotomal weakness, reflex change
Clinical ± MRI. **Saddle numbness or retention → CAUDA EQUINA, emergency.** Soon
Peripheral neuropathy / nerve entrapment
**Burning, glove-and-stocking numbness, worse at night, symmetrical**
Diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, thyroid disease
HbA1c, B12, TFT; foot protection and podiatry. **Often COEXISTS with PAD — both can be present.** Soon
**Cellulitis**
**Fever, spreading erythema with a defined edge, warm, tender, sometimes weeping; regional lymphadenopathy**
**Break in the skin, tinea between the toes, ulcer, oedema, diabetes. PAD PREDISPOSES — dry cracked poorly perfused skin**
Clinical; **mark the edge.** Antibiotics per Therapeutic Guidelines; **admit if systemically unwell.** VERIFY Same day
Osteomyelitis · septic arthritis
Deep bone or joint pain, fever, **chronic ulcer probing to bone**, unable to weight-bear
Diabetes, previous ulcer or surgery, immunosuppression
Bloods and cultures, MRI, joint aspiration; urgent referral. Emergency
Bone malignancy — primary or metastatic
**Night pain UNRELATED to activity**, progressive, weight loss, known primary
Weight, appetite, lumps, tiredness, night sweats, previous cancer
X-ray then MRI; bloods including calcium and ALP; staging. Urgent
Chronic venous insufficiency · DVT
Venous: aching heavy tight legs **worse on STANDING and by evening, better on elevation**. DVT: **unilateral** calf swelling over days
Oedema, varicosities, **haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis, medial gaiter ulcers**; or recent travel, surgery, immobility
Venous duplex. **Compression ONLY once arterial disease is excluded.** Wells score and compression duplex for DVT. Routine / Urgent
Osteoarthritis — hip, knee or ankle
Activity-related, worse through the day, stiffness under 30 minutes, restricted joint movement
Occupation and load, previous injury, joint swelling and crepitus
Weight-bearing X-ray. **Pain LINGERS after stopping, unlike arterial claudication.** Routine
**Statin-induced myositis**
**Symmetrical PROXIMAL muscle ache and weakness — thighs and shoulders — NOT related to walking distance**; onset after starting or increasing a statin
**‘Has any medication been started or increased recently?’** Difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs; **dark urine in severe cases**
**Creatine kinase, U&E, TFT.** Withhold or change the statin and recheck. **Very high CK with dark urine → rhabdomyolysis, urgent.** Soon
Polymyalgia rheumatica · herpes zoster · Osgood–Schlatter
Age over 50 with girdle pain and profound morning stiffness; band-like burning pain preceding a rash; anterior knee pain in an active teenager
**Always ask: new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual change**; dermatomal distribution; tender tibial tubercle
ESR and CRP; **visual symptoms = same-day ophthalmology.** Antiviral within 72 hours of rash. Soon

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town. James Doherty, 52, with right ankle pain. He mentions he had been gardening before it started.
On the door: temp 36.8°C · HR 78 · BP 148/88 · RR 14 · BMI 31.

8-minute station. History 6 minutes, the examination findings on a card, then diagnosis, differentials and investigations. Two recall versions off one stem: a, acute gouty arthritis · B, Achilles tendinopathy.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings, provided on a card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses
Outline your investigations
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: ASK FOR THE CARD AT 6:00 — never asking is task 2 scoring ZERO

‘I'd now like to examine your ankle — I'd look at BOTH ankles for swelling, redness and any deformity, feel for warmth and tenderness and CHECK THE PULSES AND SENSATION, then assess the range of movement and the tendons. Examiner, may I have the physical examination findings?’ And do NOT read the card silently — INTERPRET IT OUT LOUD
VERSION A card — gout
AFEBRILE. RIGHT ANKLE SWOLLEN, RED, WARM TO TOUCH, TENDER ON PALPATION. MOVEMENTS PAINFUL
VERSION B card — Achilles
PAINFUL DORSIFLEXION AND PAINFUL PLANTAR FLEXION. THE ACHILLES TENDON APPEARS WIDER THAN THE NORMAL SIDE
VERSION C card — vascular and neuropathic
ABSENT DORSALIS PEDIS AND POSTERIOR TIBIAL PULSES. REDUCED SENSATION TO MONOFILAMENT
VERSION D card — trauma
TENDER TIP OF THE LATERAL MALLEOLUS. UNABLE TO TAKE FOUR STEPS. That is TWO positive Ottawa criteria
Reading ‘AFEBRILE’

Argues against, but DOES NOT EXCLUDE, septic arthritis or cellulitis. Say: ‘he's afebrile, which makes infection less likely — BUT A SIGNIFICANT PROPORTION OF SEPTIC JOINTS ARE AFEBRILE AT PRESENTATION, so I still want the aspirate’
Reading ‘swollen, red, warm, tender, movements painful’
An INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS is confirmed. THE CARD HAS TOLD YOU THE PATHOLOGY, NOT THE CAUSE. Say: ‘that confirms an inflamed joint — the question is now which kind: crystal, infective or autoimmune’
Reading the Achilles card

BOTH movements hurt, so the structure that ACTIVELY MOVES and PASSIVELY STRETCHES in those planes is the Achilles. And ‘wider than the other side’ is FUSIFORM THICKENING — CHRONIC tendinopathy, not an acute strain, which fits three weeks of load
OTTAWA ANKLE AND FOOT RULES — X-ray if malleolar or midfoot pain PLUS any one

Bony tenderness over the posterior edge or tip of the LATERAL malleolus, distal 6 cm · the same for the MEDIAL malleolus · bony tenderness at the BASE OF THE FIFTH METATARSAL · bony tenderness over the NAVICULAR · OR INABILITY TO BEAR WEIGHT BOTH IMMEDIATELY AFTER THE INJURY AND IN THE DEPARTMENT — four steps, limping permitted VERIFY
THE TWO INVESTIGATIONS FOR GOUT — naming only one does not pass

JOINT ASPIRATION for POLARISED LIGHT MICROSCOPY (negatively birefringent NEEDLE-SHAPED urate crystals) WITH cell count, Gram stain and culture in the same procedure · AND SERUM URATE, accepting it is OFTEN NORMAL OR LOW DURING AN ATTACK — repeat at 4–6 weeks. Plus FBE, CRP, RENAL FUNCTION (it decides which drugs are safe), glucose and lipids. AN X-RAY IS NOT NEEDED

dx: **One stem, four recall versions, and the findings change between candidates in the same morning**: **A — acute gouty arthritis · B — Achilles tendinopathy · C — peripheral arterial disease with diabetic neuropathy · D — lateral ligament injury.** **Treat the foot, heel and ankle as ONE system with FIVE differential groups, then let the site, the character of the pain and one card of findings decide.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE, in one sentence: DIFFERENTIALS ARE SCORED AS GROUPS, NOT AS A LIST.** **‘Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, gouty, psoriatic, reactive, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, cellulitis’ is EIGHT conditions and TWO boxes — joint and infection.** **Red flags · bone and joint · soft tissue · vascular · neurological, with one or two examples inside each, scores FIVE. Same knowledge, different architecture, different result.**
**TWO QUESTIONS IN THE FIRST NINETY SECONDS DECIDE WHERE YOU SPEND THE STATION**: **‘Is it the front, the side, the back, or the whole ankle?’** and **‘Is it a dull ache, or a burning pain?’**

**‘BONE AND JOINT PROBLEMS DO NOT BURN.’** **DULL, ACHING, THROBBING → arthritis of any cause, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, tendinopathy, bursitis, fat pad, stress fracture, ligament injury, bone tumour.** **BURNING, TINGLING, ELECTRIC → peripheral arterial disease, peripheral neuropathy, tarsal tunnel, Morton's neuroma, lumbar radiculopathy, restless legs.** **If he says burning, your next four questions are pulses and colour, claudication and rest pain, pins and needles and numbness, and diabetes — IN THAT ORDER. SAY THE SWITCH OUT LOUD so the examiner hears you re-plan.**

**SITE DECIDES THE SHORTLIST**: **back of ankle → Achilles tendinopathy or rupture, retrocalcaneal bursitis** · **under the heel → plantar fasciitis, tender heel fat pad, calcaneal stress fracture** · **lateral → ligament injury (ATFL), peroneal tendinopathy** · **medial → tibialis posterior tendinopathy, tarsal tunnel** · **front → ankle osteoarthritis, anterior impingement** · **forefoot → Morton's neuroma, metatarsal stress fracture, hallux valgus, first MTP gout** · **the whole ankle → arthritis of any cause including gout, infection, ischaemia.**

**THE GARDENING IS A DECOY.** In older recalls it meant a scratch and cellulitis; here **the patient is afebrile with intact skin.** **Ask the two infection questions — skin break and fever — then MOVE ON, and bank the negative to quote later: ‘no fever and no break in the skin makes cellulitis unlikely.’** **Five minutes of cellulitis questions and the rest of the history never happens.**

**PROBING THE POSITIVE IS WHERE THE MARK SITS.** Many candidates ask the red meat and alcohol question, get a yes, and move on. **The examiner is watching the next thirty seconds.** **The eight-question gout cluster: what and how soon after · how much alcohol and WHAT SORT · sugary soft drinks · WATER TABLETS OR LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN · previous attack in this joint or the big toe · kidney problems or stones · LUMPS at joints, elbows or ears (tophi) · family history of gout.** **Beer is the highest-risk alcohol because it carries PURINES as well as ethanol.**

**Then quote the cluster back — that sentence is worth more than the diagnosis. Verbatim**: **‘Mr Doherty, I think you have gout — gouty arthritis. Arthritis means INFLAMMATION in a joint, and that's what makes your ankle swollen, red and painful to touch and move. The cause is a MINERAL called uric acid: when the level is high it forms tiny sharp crystals in the joint and the body REACTS to them. The REASONS I think that are the way it came on over hours in one hot swollen joint, plus the steak and PRAWNS two days before, four beers most NIGHTS, the sugary drinks, the water tablet for your blood pressure, your weight, and your FATHER's gout — that's a STRONG cluster.’** **Say MOST LIKELY until the aspirate is back, and never say ‘negatively birefringent MONOSODIUM urate’ to the patient.** **In version B the equivalent moment is the OCCUPATION: ‘painter’ is not background, it is the AETIOLOGY.**

**THE THREE THE COLLEGE LOVES — whatever the version, actively exclude INFECTION, PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE and GOUT.** Infection and PAD because missing them is dangerous; **gout because it is the one arthritis that only reveals itself if you ask a specific question nobody asks.** **A hot red swollen joint is SEPTIC ARTHRITIS UNTIL THE ASPIRATE SAYS OTHERWISE — and gout and sepsis CAN COEXIST IN THE SAME JOINT.**

**Treatment** VERIFY — **GOUT, acute, any one chosen by comorbidity**: **NSAID at full anti-inflammatory dose, short course** (avoid in CKD, heart failure, peptic ulcer, or with an ACE inhibitor plus diuretic) · **prednisolone 15–30 mg daily for 3–5 days** · **COLCHICINE LOW-DOSE ONLY — 1 mg then 500 micrograms at one hour, then 500 micrograms once or twice daily; high-dose regimens cause diarrhoea without added benefit** · intra-articular corticosteroid once sepsis is excluded. **Urate-lowering: allopurinol 50–100 mg daily, lower in renal impairment, titrated to urate BELOW 0.36 mmol/L (below 0.30 with tophi), with colchicine 500 mcg daily cover.** **Do NOT stop allopurinol during an attack in someone already established on it.** **Screen HLA-B*5801 before allopurinol in Han Chinese, Thai or Korean patients.**
plan: **WIPE, concern, and OFFER ANALGESIA — four seconds, scored in every painful presentation.** Then **THE AGENDA SENTENCE, the cheapest mark in the station**: **‘Pain in the foot and ankle can come from several different places — the bones and joints, the soft tissues like tendons and ligaments, the blood supply, or the nerves. I'm going to work through each of those in turn so we don't miss anything. Some questions won't seem connected — please bear with me.’**

**The pain.** Open question, **20 seconds uninterrupted.** Then **site, THEN SUB-SITE** · out of ten now and at worst · **DULL ACHE OR BURNING** · onset sudden or gradual · constant or intermittent, getting worse · radiation up the calf, into the toes, down from the back · better or worse with walking, standing, **taking the shoes off** · effect on work and home.

**The pattern — four questions that sort the list.** **‘Does it wake you at night?’** — red flag for malignancy and infection, **BUT night pain relieved by HANGING THE LEG OUT OF BED is critical limb ischaemia, and burning discomfort at night relieved by WALKING is restless legs.** **‘Morning or end of the day, and how long is the stiffness?’** **‘Worse with activity, or after rest?’** — **first steps after rest easing as you walk = plantar fasciitis.** **‘Limping — can you bear weight?’**

**General MSK screen, four questions**: swelling · redness or rash · stiffness · **‘any trauma or injury — even a minor twist, and EVEN YEARS AGO?’** — one recall turns on ‘I broke that ankle ten years ago’, setting up post-traumatic osteoarthritis.

**RED FLAGS, ANNOUNCED AND UNCONDITIONAL — age, duration and an obvious answer never excuse skipping them.** **Malignancy**: weight loss, appetite, lumps, unusually tired, night sweats. **Infection**: fever or chills, **any cut, scratch or break in the skin**, recent infections or procedures. **In the gardening stem these are also what let you SAY OUT LOUD that you considered and excluded cellulitis and septic arthritis — which is where the mark actually is.**

**GROUP 2 — BONE AND JOINT. ‘First the joints themselves.’** Occupation and load · other joints · family history of arthritis · **rash on elbows, knees or scalp, nail changes** · **THE GOUT TRIGGER QUESTION — the single highest-yield question in the station** · recent diarrhoea or urethral discharge. **Then PROBE the positive with the eight-question cluster.**

**GROUP 3 — SOFT TISSUE. ‘Now the tendons and ligaments.’** **Giving way or instability** · been over on it before · **tight shoes, better with them off** · **a PEBBLE under the ball of the foot** · change in footwear, training or walking distance. **Short by design — occupation and exercise were already asked.**

**GROUP 4 — VASCULAR. ‘Now the circulation.’** Colour change · slow-healing ulcers · **claudication, and IS IT WORSE GOING UPHILL** · **rest or night pain relieved by hanging the leg down** · unilateral calf swelling, travel, surgery, immobility.

**GROUP 5 — NEUROLOGICAL. ‘Last group — the nerves.’** Back pain now or in the past · pins and needles or numbness · **weakness, or catching the toe** · diabetes and when last checked · **restless legs at night relieved by getting up and walking.** **Naming the group is what turns a systems review into a scored differential block — two words, ‘now the circulation’, do it.**

**CLOSURE — SADMA is DIAGNOSTIC here, not administrative.** Smoking · **alcohol quantity AND type** · **sugary soft drinks** · drugs · **medications including over the counter, WATER TABLETS OR ASPIRIN, and RECENT ANTIBIOTICS (fluoroquinolones)** · allergies · conditions, operations, fractures · family history · **‘and is there anything you were particularly worried about today?’** — the hidden concern about work lives there. **Then at 6:00 ASK FOR THE CARD.**
pefe: **Answer the walking-stick fear DIRECTLY**: **‘Gout DOESN'T leave you NEEDING a walking stick if it's treated. Attacks settle in days with the right medicine, and we can prevent FUTURE ones. UNTREATED and repeated, it can DAMAGE a joint — which is EXACTLY why we're DEALING with it now.’** And **‘is it the beer? Or the blood pressure tablet?’** → **both CONTRIBUTE, along with the seafood, the soft drinks and your weight. ‘I WOULDN'T stop the blood pressure tablet today, but I will review it — there are ALTERNATIVES that don't raise uric acid.’** **Being dismissive or evasive when asked directly about the effect on work is an automatic fail.**
**Interpret the card out loud before you name anything.** Reading it silently and announcing a diagnosis loses the reasoning mark.

**ALWAYS EXCLUDE ACHILLES RUPTURE where there is any sudden snap**: **SIMMONDS' (Thompson) CALF-SQUEEZE TEST — patient prone, feet over the end of the couch; squeeze the calf; ABSENT PLANTAR FLEXION MEANS A RUPTURED TENDON.** Plus **a palpable gap** and **inability to do a single-leg heel raise.** **The pain SETTLES after the initial snap, so a patient can walk in flat-footed and be sent away.** Same-day orthopaedics, immobilise in equinus.

**VERSION B management**: **relative rest and LOAD MODIFICATION, not immobilisation.** **A structured ECCENTRIC LOADING programme with physiotherapy is the mainstay and takes TWELVE WEEKS OR MORE — tell the patient this at the outset or they will stop at three weeks and think it failed.** Heel raise, footwear review, calf stretching, simple analgesia. **Address the load — this man stands and climbs ladders all day.**

**TWO THINGS YOU MUST NOT DO in version B**: **never inject corticosteroid into the Achilles — it is associated with rupture** · **review any FLUOROQUINOLONE (ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin) — associated with tendinopathy and rupture, and stopped if implicated.** *He finished ciprofloxacin a fortnight ago and will only say so if asked about recent antibiotics.*

**VERSION C**: *‘a BURNING, both feet, worse at night — I hang the foot out from under the COVERS and that helps’* → **say the switch aloud: ‘burning POINTS me to the circulation and the nerves.’** Then: **calf CRAMPS at a HUNDRED METRES, worse uphill · dusky feet · FIFTEEN years of type 2 diabetes · FORTY a day since he was TWENTY.** **The decisive line: ‘pain at rest that eases when you hang the leg down suggests the blood supply is CRITICALLY reduced, not just narrowed — that needs an ankle–brachial index and a vascular surgical opinion URGENTLY, not a routine referral, and stopping smoking will do more for this than anything I can prescribe.’** **ABI, duplex, HbA1c, lipids, U&E, B12, TFT, ferritin; meticulous foot care and podiatry.** **Never compress before excluding arterial disease, and in diabetes A PAINLESS ULCER IS WORSE NEWS THAN A PAINFUL ONE.**

**VERSION D**: apply the **Ottawa rules**; otherwise **EARLY PROTECTED MOBILISATION BEATS PROLONGED REST** — relative rest, ice, compression, elevation, analgesia, then a **proprioceptive and strengthening programme to prevent recurrent instability.** **Review at 5–7 days — persisting inability to weight-bear suggests an occult fracture, osteochondral lesion or syndesmotic ‘high ankle’ injury.**

**VERSION B, said to him verbatim**: **‘The Achilles is the thick rope-like tendon at the back of your ankle JOINING your calf MUSCLE to your heel bone. It has become IRRITATED and thickened.’** Then the part that decides whether he follows the plan: **‘This IMPROVES with the right kind of loading, NOT rest alone — a specific exercise programme with a PHYSIOTHERAPIST. At least three MONTHS, and it feels slow at first. I'm TELLING you now so you don't stop at three weeks THINKING it hasn't WORKED. I won't inject steroid into the tendon — that carries a real risk of rupture.’** Plus **‘did it ever come on SUDDENLY — a snap, or a feeling like someone KICKED you in the back of the leg? Can you rise up onto the toes of that foot?’** — and **RECORD the ciprofloxacin and avoid that class in future.** **Ordering an MRI or a BATTERY of BLOODS for a clinical diagnosis reads as INSECURITY, not thoroughness.**

**VARIANT E — all the gout risk factors PLUS a temperature of 38.4°C with rigors, and he cannot weight-bear at all.** **New information OUTRANKS a diagnosis you had already settled on.** **‘You have several things that point to gout, and I do think that's possible. But you also have a fever and shivers with a hot swollen joint you can't stand on, and that combination has to be treated as an infection in the joint until proved otherwise. Gout and infection can also occur TOGETHER. So rather than treating you here, I'm SENDING you to HOSPITAL today for the joint to be ASPIRATED and for BLOODS — and I WON'T START ANTIBIOTICS BEFORE THOSE SAMPLES ARE TAKEN.’** **Sending him home on oral treatment is an automatic fail.**

**Examiner challenges, scripted**: *‘His urate came back at 0.33 — doesn't that exclude gout?’* → **‘No. Serum urate is frequently normal or even low during an acute attack, because urate is being deposited in the joint. I'd diagnose on the aspirate and repeat the urate in four to six weeks.’** *‘He's afebrile — why aspirate?’* → **‘Because a significant proportion of septic joints are afebrile at presentation, and gout and sepsis can occur in the same joint. The aspirate gives crystals, cell count, Gram stain and culture in one procedure, and the consequences of missing sepsis are far worse than the cost of the tap.’**

**Equity and access**: **gout is substantially more prevalent, presents younger and is more often undertreated in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and in Māori and Pacific Islander communities — consider urate-lowering therapy EARLIER rather than waiting for repeated attacks.** **Closing the Gap PBS co-payment makes lifelong allopurinol and statin sustainable, and adherence is the whole game.** **In a regional setting, joint aspiration for polarised microscopy may not be locally available — say you would refer to the nearest facility with the service, or to ED, RATHER THAN TREATING BLIND.** **PATS; telehealth rheumatology and vascular; podiatry and physiotherapy via a GP Management Plan.**

back.dx: PERIPROCEDURAL MANAGEMENT OF A DIRECT ORAL ANTICOAGULANT AND AN SGLT2 INHIBITOR, WRAPPED IN A CONCERNS BARRAGE — two named key points and everything else communication. The numbers: stop before a low bleeding risk procedure, apixaban and rivaroxaban 24-48 h, dabigatran 24-72 h and up to 96 h with poor renal function · high bleeding risk such as major bowel surgery 48-72 h, longer for dabigatran · minimal risk procedures such as dental, cataract or a diagnostic scope often need no interruption at all · restart is surgeon-decided, about 24 h after low or moderate risk and 2-3 days after high risk · SGLT2 inhibitor stops at least 3 days before and restarts when eating and drinking normally · bridging is never used for a NOAC · eGFR roughly 30-50 lengthens the interruption for apixaban and rivaroxaban, and dabigatran extends earlier and further VERIFY all. The examiner questions and their answers. 'Would you bridge her?' → 'No. Bridging is not recommended when interrupting a direct oral anticoagulant, because these agents have a rapid onset on restarting, so there is no therapeutic gap to cover. Bridging is a warfarin concept, where the delay to therapeutic effect creates that gap. Her clotting risk is low in any case.' 'If her eGFR came back at 35?' → 'The interruption lengthens — for apixaban at a low bleeding risk procedure, from around 24 hours to about 48. On dabigatran, which is substantially more renally cleared, it could extend to 72 or even 96 hours and I'd seek specialist advice. I'd also review her anticoagulant dose longer term, be cautious about perioperative nephrotoxins, and be cautious about restarting metformin until renal function returned to baseline.' 'Why stop the dapagliflozin three days before rather than on the morning like the metformin?' → 'Because SGLT2 inhibitors carry a risk of euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis, precipitated by fasting, dehydration and surgical stress. The glucose can be normal or only mildly elevated, so the usual warning sign is absent and the diagnosis is easily missed. The effect on ketogenesis persists beyond a single dose, so omitting it only on the morning is not sufficient.' 'She is having a colonoscopy with bowel preparation instead?' → 'For the SGLT2 inhibitor, no change — bowel preparation causes significant dehydration and the same risk applies. For the anticoagulant it depends: a purely diagnostic colonoscopy is low bleeding risk, but if polypectomy is anticipated I'd plan as for a low-to-moderate risk procedure and discuss it with the proceduralist.' The variants. B, sigmoid resection — a higher bleeding risk procedure, so 48-72 hours rather than 24-48, and the surgeon most likely waits 2-3 days to restart; the colostomy question is answered with the emergency-versus-planned distinction and deferred to the surgeon, never with a flat promise. C, dabigatran — widen to 24-72 hours and the kidney point gets stronger still. E, a mechanical valve or a mini-stroke six weeks ago disclosed in the history — change gear and escalate: 'That changes how we approach this. NOACs are not used for mechanical valves and bridging does apply here. This isn't a decision I'd make on my own today — I'll discuss it with your cardiologist and the surgical team before anything is changed, and please don't stop any medication on your own.' Recognising that you are outside the routine algorithm is the mark.
plan: WIPE, confirm identity and preferred name, then an open question — and let the barrage run without interrupting and without answering.
Acknowledge, reserve, collect anything else, count them back, and ask permission to take the history (see findings).

BLOCK ONE, MEDICATIONS — how long she has had the AF and diabetes · talk me through your medicines and are you taking them regularly · WHEN DID YOU LAST TAKE THE BLOOD THINNER · side effects, unusual bruising or bleeding · GP reviews and recent bloods · AND ANYTHING OVER THE COUNTER, FISH OIL, ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES OR HERBAL.

BLOCK TWO, BLEEDING RISK — high blood pressure · THE KIDNEY QUESTION ASKED AS TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS · liver problems · stroke or TIA · ANY SERIOUS BLEED, ULCER, BLOOD IN URINE OR BOWELS · alcohol per week. Answer the 'why my kidneys' question there and then.
BLOCK THREE, CLOTTING RISK — is the AF constant or paroxysmal · previous clot, stroke or TIA · HAVE YOU EVER HAD A HEART VALVE REPLACED · heart failure, heart attacks or leg circulation problems.

BLOCK FOUR, DIABETES AND SURGICAL BASICS — usual sugars and home monitoring, hypos, any admission or ketones · WHEN IS THE OPERATION and has she been told when to stop eating and drinking · allergies and previous anaesthetic trouble · and who is at home.
Team framing first, because it pre-answers two of her concerns — then her own cardiologist, with the promise, the fallback and the check.
The framework — bleeding if we keep it going against clotting if we stop it — then her actual scores on each side.

The NOAC plan — quick offset in one sentence · the eGFR decides · 24 to 48 hours with the exact day confirmed by phone and in writing · no bridging, and hold that line if she pushes · and the surgeon restarts, usually about 24 hours after, with 'Please don't restart it yourself'.

The SGLT2 plan as its own numbered item — three days, the reason in plain words, hydration, glucose monitoring and insulin cover, and when to restart — then the remaining tablets, which continue to the day with the morning oral glucose-lowering dose omitted.
BACK THROUGH EVERY CONCERN BY NAME — bleeding, stroke, the surgeon, the cardiologist, the neighbour, the brother-in-law (see findings). She raised them; the examiner wrote them down.

Safety-net — bleeding that won't stop, black or bloody motions, blood in urine or unusual bruising → contact us or ED · sudden weakness, face droop, trouble speaking or chest pain → triple zero · and feeling unwell, nauseated, vomiting or breathless in the days around surgery even with a normal sugar → ring us. Then summarise, ask her to tell it back, and offer a family meeting.

ask: The control line, learned whole: 'I appreciate you sharing your concerns with me and I can hear how worried you are... Before I start — is there anything else you're worried about? Tell me now, so I know to cover everything. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions first, so that when I answer them my answers are actually about you?'

The two key points, said plainly: 'I'll need to check your kidney function, with a test called the eGFR, to decide exactly when we stop it — your kidneys are how this medicine leaves your body.' and 'The dapagliflozin we stop three days before, because around an operation it can cause a build-up of acid in the blood even when your sugar looks normal.'
The bridging refusal, kindly: 'You won't need any injections in the gap. Yours starts working within hours, so there's nothing to cover.' Explain the warfarin difference; never concede.

The honest-reassurance line, which is the hardest thing here to get right: 'On a planned operation we have time to prepare — bloods, medication decisions, getting you in the best shape. That's why it carries less risk than emergency surgery. It doesn't mean no risk, and I won't tell you it does.'

Challenges: 'Am I going to bleed to death?' · 'But you're still stopping it — that's when the stroke happens, isn't it?' · 'Why do you keep asking about my kidneys?' · 'Can't you just tell me a day? I need to write it on the calendar.' · 'My friend had injections in her stomach — why don't I need those?' · 'Insulin? I don't want to end up on needles for good.' · and 'That's what they told my neighbour' if you reassure without a reason.
pefe: There is no examination, and the one number that decides the plan is deliberately withheld from the stem: the eGFR. The correct response is to name the test, give the range, order it today and commit to ringing with the exact date — not to invent a day to sound decisive.

Role-player: Jane Whitcombe, 60, a retired bookkeeper living with her husband Ken. Paroxysmal AF for about six years, type 2 diabetes for about twelve. Apixaban twice daily, dapagliflozin, metformin, atorvastatin, atenolol — taken reliably, last apixaban last night, paracetamol occasionally and nothing else. Blood pressure always normal, no kidney or liver problems, no stroke or TIA, no clots, no valve replacement, no heart failure, never a serious bleed, a little arm bruising she has always had, two glasses of wine at weekends, sugars seven or eight, no hypos, no allergies, a gallbladder out years ago. Surgery is a week on Thursday and nobody has told her anything about her tablets.

How she plays it: frightened underneath, coming out as sharp and demanding — not rude for its own sake; she feels ignored and unprepared. She delivers four or five concerns in one breath and does not let the doctor in until she runs out. She holds the cardiologist back for 'Anything else?' and drops it mid-explanation if never asked. She interrupts the history once with 'But you still haven't told me if I'm going to bleed to death' — and if the doctor abandons the history to answer, she keeps interrupting so they never get through it. She asks why the kidneys keep coming up, pushes for one fixed date, pushes for the injections, and panics about insulin. She softens only in response to specific answers — 'Don't worry' or 'You'll be fine' gets 'That's what they told my neighbour.' She accepts a family meeting warmly.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE, WITH FIVE FLAGGED CRITICAL: let her finish the barrage without interrupting · acknowledged before answering any of them · ASKED WHETHER THERE WAS ANYTHING ELSE · asked permission before the history · completed a structured history despite the interruption · ASKED ABOUT KIDNEY FUNCTION TWICE, AS TWO SEPARATE QUESTIONS (CRITICAL) · liver, previous bleeding, alcohol and other drugs · ASKED ABOUT A PROSTHETIC VALVE (CRITICAL) · previous clots or strokes · diabetes control and the operation date · explained the team decision · PROMISED TO TRY HER OWN CARDIOLOGIST WITH A FALLBACK AND CHECKED SHE AGREED · low bleeding risk procedure and no HAS-BLED factors · clotting risk low and why · the quick offset explained · SAID THE eGFR DECIDES EXACTLY WHEN TO STOP IT (CRITICAL) · GAVE A 24-48 HOUR RANGE RATHER THAN AN INVENTED DATE · SAID NO BRIDGING AND DID NOT AGREE TO ARRANGE INJECTIONS (CRITICAL) · surgeon restarts at about 24 hours · IDENTIFIED THE DAPAGLIFLOZIN AND SAID STOP 3 DAYS BEFORE (CRITICAL) · explained why, plus hydration, monitoring, insulin cover and restart · other medications and the omitted morning dose · reframed insulin as short-term · answered the surgeon concern without simply defending him · ANSWERED THE NEIGHBOUR CONCERN HONESTLY AND DID NOT PROMISE ZERO RISK · safety-netting and a written plan · summary and teach-back · CAME BACK TO EVERY CONCERN RAISED AT THE START · offered a family meeting.

The opening barrage — do not start answering — 'I'm on a blood thinner — am I going to bleed to death? And if you stop it, am I going to have a stroke? My brother-in-law had a stroke after an operation. My neighbour went in for a routine operation and she never came home. I don't know your surgeon from a bar of soap' — five in one breath, with 'I want to speak to my cardiologist, not one of yours' held back for 'Anything else?'

The line that takes control without dismissing her — 'I appreciate you sharing your concerns with me, and I can hear how worried you are — those are all reasonable things to be thinking about. I'll be doing my best to address every one of them and we'll make the best plan together. Before I do — is there anything else you're worried about? Tell me now, so I know to cover everything. Then, is it okay if I ask you a few questions first?' Counting them back — 'That's five, I've got all five' — is itself scored

If she interrupts the history — ONE LINE, THEN CONTINUE: 'THAT'S IMPORTANT AND I PROMISE I'LL ANSWER IT PROPERLY IN A MOMENT — CAN I JUST FINISH THESE FEW QUESTIONS SO MY ANSWER IS A GOOD ONE?' If you abandon the history to answer her, she is briefed to keep interrupting and you never get through it

Key point one — ask the kidney question twice, as two questions — 'HAVE YOU EVER HAD AN ABNORMAL KIDNEY FUNCTION TEST?' AND, SEPARATELY, 'HAS ANYONE EVER TOLD YOU THAT YOU HAVE CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE?' Buried once in a list, or not at all, is a single-item automatic fail

'Why do you keep asking about my kidneys?' — a gift, take it — 'That's a really good question and I'm glad you noticed. Your kidneys are how this particular blood thinner leaves your body. So how well they're working decides exactly how long before surgery we need to stop it. It's the single most important piece of information I need' — the examiner hears the reasoning twice

The valve question rules out a different station — 'Have you ever had a heart valve replaced?' → no. A mechanical valve would mean a NOAC is not the right drug at all, bridging would apply, and the whole plan changes. One question rules it out

Lead with the team, which pre-answers two concerns — 'This decision isn't made by one person — we make it as a team: your surgeon, your regular GP, the anaesthetist and a cardiologist, and I'll make sure they're all talking to each other'

Bleeding versus clotting, with her actual scores — Bleeding: a keyhole hernia repair is a low bleeding risk procedure, and on HAS-BLED her blood pressure is fine, no previous bleed, no kidney or liver problem, not over 65, no anti-inflammatories — no risk factors at all · clotting: diabetes counts for a point, but no heart failure, no hypertension, not 75, no previous clot or stroke and no artificial valve — low, which is what makes a short planned gap safe

The pharmacology in one sentence — 'Your blood thinner has a quick offset of action — the effect wears off within a few hours of stopping it, and it starts working again just as fast when you restart. That's quite different from warfarin, which hangs around for days'

The timing — give the range, name the test, commit to confirming — 'Most likely 24 to 48 hours before your surgery, and I'll confirm the exact day once I have the eGFR.' when she presses for one day: 'I'd rather give you an accurate answer than a quick one. I'll organise the blood test today and ring you with the exact date and put it in writing.' Naming a single invented day to sound decisive is the trap

No bridging — and do not be talked into it — 'My friend had injections in her stomach before her hip replacement. Why don't I need those?' → 'Your friend was almost certainly on warfarin, which takes days to start working again, so there's a real gap to cover. Yours starts working within hours, so there isn't one. Adding injections wouldn't make you safer — it would only add bleeding risk.' Agreeing to arrange bridging is an AUTOMATIC FAIL

Key point two — the planted tablet — 'There's one other tablet and this one's important — the dapagliflozin. We stop that one three days before. Around an operation, when you're not eating or drinking, it can cause a serious build-up of acid in the blood — and it can happen even when your sugar reading looks perfectly normal, so it's easy to miss.' Lumping it in with 'Your diabetes tablets stop on the morning' is a single-item AUTOMATIC FAIL

The three things that go with it — One, keep drinking plenty of fluids while she is still taking it, because dehydration is what sets it off · two, closer glucose monitoring once it stops, with insulin if sugars run high · three, restart it once she is eating and drinking normally. And if she panics about insulin: 'This would only be short-term cover around the operation, if your sugars needed it — not a permanent change'

Going back through the concerns by name — The surgeon — ask what specifically worries her, then offer a sit-down with him before the operation rather than defending him · the neighbour who died — 'With a planned operation we have time to prepare... That's why planned surgery generally carries lower risk than emergency surgery. It doesn't mean there's no risk, and I won't tell you it does' · the brother-in-law's stroke — his situation may be quite different; speak to her numbers · and in the bowel-surgery version, the colostomy question

Her cardiologist — promise, fallback, then check she agrees — 'I will do my best to get hold of him and speak to him directly. If I can't reach him before your surgery, I'll ask one of our experienced cardiologists to come and see you, so the decision is still made properly and you still get to ask your questions. How does that sound — are you happy for me to do that?' 'We have our own cardiologists here' reads as brushing her off; the check is what converts it into shared decision-making
fails: ★ Never asking about kidney function, or burying it once in a list — the eGFR is what decides the interruption, and it is the named key point of the case
★ Lumping the dapagliflozin in with 'your diabetes tablets stop on the morning of surgery' instead of stopping it three days before and explaining euglycaemic ketoacidosis
★ Agreeing to arrange bridging injections to keep her happy — bridging is never used when interrupting a direct oral anticoagulant
Starting to answer the first concern of the barrage, so the other six arrive one at a time and the three-minute history never happens

Inventing a single fixed stop date to sound decisive; never asking about a prosthetic valve; brushing off her request for her own cardiologist with 'we have our own here'; or running out of time so the concerns she raised at the start are never revisited by name
numbers: Stop before a low bleeding risk procedure: apixaban and rivaroxaban 24-48 h · dabigatran 24-72 h, up to 96 h with poor renal function · high bleeding risk: 48-72 h, longer for dabigatran · minimal risk (Dental, cataract, diagnostic scope): often no interruption · restart surgeon-decided, about 24 h low or moderate risk and 2-3 days high risk · bridging never for a NOAC; warfarin stops about 5 days before and may need it VERIFY

SGLT2 inhibitor: stop at least 3 days before, restart when eating and drinking normally · eGFR roughly 30-50 lengthens the interruption for apixaban and rivaroxaban, and dabigatran extends earlier and further · HAS-BLED: hypertension, abnormal renal or liver function, stroke, bleeding, labile INR (Warfarin only), elderly over 65, drugs or alcohol — hers is nil · cha2ds2-va/vasc: CHF, hypertension, age 75 or over (2), diabetes, stroke or TIA or thromboembolism (2), vascular disease, age 65-74, sex category — hers is 1 to 2 and low · VERIFY all
