stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town. Peter Baros, 60, has taken an urgent appointment with right groin pain. He arrived on a borrowed walking frame and would not put weight on the right leg.
Nurse's observations: temp 38.6°C · HR 104 regular · BP 126/78 · RR 18 · SpO2 97% on air · BGL 6.8. No physical examination is required and no examination findings will be provided.
8-minute station with a bell at 6 minutes. Everything after that bell is tasks 2, 3 and 4, which carry about 40% of the mark sheet.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (approximately 6 minutes)
Explain what you think is most likely causing his pain, and why
Explain the other conditions you considered and have been ruling out
Tell him what you are going to do next

dx: **Septic arthritis of the right hip — and because a prosthesis is in place, a PROSTHETIC JOINT INFECTION.** Specifically a **LATE ACUTE HAEMATOGENOUS infection, six years after a well-functioning replacement, seeded from a recent dental procedure.** **The organism forms a BIOFILM on the metal that antibiotics alone cannot penetrate — so cure normally needs SURGERY PLUS antibiotics, not antibiotics alone.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE, in one sentence: THE DIAGNOSIS IS NOT THE MARK. The audible, grouped exclusion of the other four differential groups AFTER you already have the answer is the mark.** **Nearly every candidate finds the fever and says septic arthritis. A large proportion still fail.** What separates them is the three minutes after the fever: **the passing candidate announced a switch and worked through kidney, bowel, genital and skin systematically; the failing candidate either closed early into past medical history, or kept asking more detailed questions about the same hip. Both read as PREMATURE CLOSURE — the single commonest reason this station is failed.**

**THE SWITCH LINE, verbatim, at about three minutes**: **‘Thank you — the temperature is important and I'll come back to it in a moment. Before I do, I want to make sure I'm not missing anything else that causes pain in this area. I'll ask about the hip itself, then your waterworks, then your tummy, then some private questions, then the skin. A lot of these will be a no — that's exactly what I'm checking.’**

**THE FIVE GROUPS, named out loud before the questions inside them**: **1 HIP AND MUSCULOSKELETAL — septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, the arthritides, AVN, PMR, greater trochanteric pain syndrome, implant loosening, fracture · 2 KIDNEY, URETER, BLADDER · 3 ABDOMEN AND PELVIS · 4 GENITAL · 5 SKIN AND LYMPH NODE.** Plus **neurological (L1/L2 radiculopathy) and vascular (femoral aneurysm, iliofemoral DVT)** if time allows. **Two groups is a fail even with the right diagnosis.**

**WHY THERE IS NO SWELLING OR REDNESS — and candidates hesitate because of it.** **The hip is a DEEP joint, encased in muscle on every side — iliopsoas and pectineus in front, the glutei behind, the adductors medially.** A septic knee is red, hot and visibly swollen because it sits under skin. **A septic hip shows you almost nothing: what you get instead is FEVER, SEVERE PAIN ON ANY MOVEMENT, and COMPLETE REFUSAL TO WEIGHT-BEAR.** **ABSENCE OF REDNESS ARGUES FOR A DEEP JOINT, NOT AGAINST INFECTION.**

**THE WEIGHT-BEARING LOGIC IS THE CENTRAL PLANK OF THE EXPLANATION**: **‘If this were a boil in the skin, a swollen gland, or a strain, you could still stand. NOT BEING ABLE TO LOAD THE LEG TELLS ME THE PROBLEM IS INSIDE THE JOINT.’** **Do not accept ‘it hurts to walk’ — ask ‘can you put ANY weight on it at all?’**

**THE SECOND DISCRIMINATING LAYER — THE PROSTHESIS.** Two candidates both say ‘septic arthritis’. One adds: **‘and because there is an artificial joint in there, this is a PROSTHETIC JOINT INFECTION — which usually needs an OPERATION as well as antibiotics, so I'm not going to start antibiotics here.’** **Ask WHY the hip was replaced, WHEN, and HOW IT HAS BEEN SINCE — and say the words prosthetic joint infection out loud.**

**Explaining it to him, in plain words and with the reasoning**: **‘The most likely cause of your pain is an infection inside the hip joint itself — septic arthritis. And because you have an artificial hip, we give it a specific name, a prosthetic joint infection. First, you have a temperature that isn't settling with paracetamol, so there is an infection somewhere. Second — and this is the important part — you can't put any weight on that leg at all. Third, germs travelling in the bloodstream can settle on artificial joints. That tooth extraction three weeks ago is ONE POSSIBLE WAY germs could have got in — I can't say for certain, and NOTHING WAS DONE WRONGLY.’** **Never say ‘haematogenous seeding’ or ‘biofilm’ to him.**

**The dental prophylaxis question he will ask** VERIFY : **current Australian guidance — Therapeutic Guidelines and the Australian Dental Association — is that routine antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures is NOT recommended solely because a patient has a prosthetic joint.** **Answer honestly and WITHOUT BLAME: ‘nothing was done wrongly, and we also can't be certain the tooth is the source — it's one possibility among several.’** **Blaming the dentist is an error of both fact and manner.**

**The hidden agenda, raised at six minutes if you never ask**: **‘Doctor, be straight with me — is this cancer? My BROTHER had SOMETHING in his bones and it STARTED like this.’** **Answer it DIRECTLY, with the specific negatives**: **‘I did think about it, which is why I asked about weight, appetite, lumps, night sweats and blood in your urine and bowels. Everything you told me was reassuring, and a three-day illness with a fever is much more likely to be infection. I'm not dismissing it, and the tests in hospital will look at that too.’** **IGNORING OR EVADING a directly asked question about cancer is an automatic fail.** And on the implant: **‘sometimes the surgeon can wash the joint out and keep the replacement, changing only some parts; sometimes it does need replacing. The surgeon will tell you once they've looked — I don't want to promise you either way.’**
plan: **WIPE, then comfort first — he is in pain and febrile.** **‘I can see you're in a lot of discomfort, so I'll be as quick as I can. Are you in pain right now?’** Then **THE AGENDA SENTENCE, which is what makes the next five minutes read as a plan rather than a fishing trip**: **‘Groin pain can come from a few different places — the hip joint, the kidneys and bladder, the tummy, the private parts, or the skin and glands. I'm going to go through each area in turn so we don't miss anything. Some questions won't seem related — please bear with me.’**

**The pain — nine questions, NINETY SECONDS, then move on.** Point with ONE finger · out of ten now and at worst · **dull ache or sharp and stabbing, does it come in WAVES** · when and sudden or gradual · constant or intermittent, better, worse or the same · **does it travel — down the leg, into the back, into the private parts** · better or worse with anything, and **has what you've taken helped** · effect on sleeping, washing, getting to the toilet.

**Pattern and general screen.** Night pain · activity versus rest · morning stiffness and **how long** · **‘CAN YOU PUT ANY WEIGHT ON IT AT ALL?’** · swelling or a lump · redness or rash · stiffness moving the hip · **any injury, fall or knock, even minor.**

**RED FLAGS, ANNOUNCED AND UNCONDITIONAL.** **Malignancy**: weight loss, appetite, lumps anywhere, unusually tired, **night sweats soaking the sheets**, long-standing cough, **blood in urine or bowel motions.** **A 60-year-old with new hip and groin pain has BONE, BOWEL, PROSTATE AND BLADDER malignancy on the list — there is no version of this station where you may skip this block.** **Infection**: fevers, **‘any SHIVERING AND SHAKING — rigors?’**, **‘have you taken anything for it, and is it bringing the temperature down?’** — *38.6 since FRIDAY and paracetamol is not SHIFTING it, which means an ESTABLISHED infection rather than a transient viral temperature* — recent infections — skin, chest, urine, teeth — **and RECENT PROCEDURES, OPERATIONS OR DENTAL WORK.**

**THE FEVER LANDS HERE AND MOST CANDIDATES STOP. DO NOT STOP. Say the switch line.** Then **GROUP 1 — HIP**: occupation and lifting · other joints · family arthritis · rash on elbows, knees or scalp, nail changes · **diarrhoea or urethral discharge** (which doubles as a bowel and genital screen) · **medications, and EVER had steroid tablets or injections** · alcohol · **previous hip surgery, fracture or dislocation → WHY, WHEN, AND HOW HAS IT BEEN SINCE** · painful to lie on that side · **shoulder stiffness, new headache, tender scalp, jaw ache on chewing.**

**GROUP 2 — KIDNEY, URETER, BLADDER. ‘Now your waterworks.’** Burning passing urine · frequency or urgency · **blood in the urine** · **getting up at night, and has the stream changed — slow, dribbling, hard to start** (worth adding in a man over 50; it also picks up prostate pathology, which refers to the groin and perineum).

**GROUP 3 — ABDOMEN AND PELVIS. ‘Now your tummy and bowels.’** **A lump or bulge in the groin, especially on coughing or straining** · tummy pain · vomiting · **passing wind and opening bowels normally** · constipation, diarrhoea, blood · overall change in bowel habit. **Pain plus vomiting plus no flatus is obstruction or strangulation — a surgical emergency.** **In a woman add: last period, heavy or painful periods, bleeding between periods or after menopause, and any chance of pregnancy.**

**GROUP 4 — GENITAL. Ask permission first: ‘I need to ask a few personal questions — is that alright?’** Testicular pain, swelling or lump · discharge, ulcers, blisters or sores · sexual activity and STI risk. Then **GROUP 5 — SKIN AND NODES. ‘Last area.’** **Boils, cuts, ulcers or infected hair follicles — ESPECIALLY IF HE SHAVES THERE** · **a band of rash, blisters or burning skin round to the back** · rash, redness, swelling or a break in the skin anywhere on that leg or foot · **tender lumps in the groin creases.** **Nodes have now been asked three times — deliberately.**

**CLOSURE, LAST AND FAST.** Conditions · medications and allergies · other operations · family history · smoking, alcohol, **injecting drugs** · who is at home · **‘and is there anything you were particularly worried about today?’** **Reaching past medical history at three minutes is the tell-tale sign the sweep was skipped — examiners watch for it. But NEVER drop the final open question: the hidden concern lives there and task 2 is marked partly on whether you answer it.**

**Diagnosis with the reasoning → differentials BY GROUP, each with a reason it is less likely → the plan.** **‘This needs to be sorted out today, in hospital — not next week. I'm going to ring the orthopaedic doctor on call now and arrange an ambulance. Please don't eat or drink anything from now, in case they need to take you to theatre.’** Then **safety-net: ‘if you feel confused or drowsy, if the temperature climbs, or if you feel much worse in any way, tell the staff straight away.’** **If the bell goes before you finish, get the three words out — HOSPITAL TODAY, BY AMBULANCE.**
pefe: **No physical examination is required and no findings will be provided.** In a history-predominant station **the examiner is scoring the ARCHITECTURE of your questioning, not the answer you land on.**

**DO NOW, in the consulting room**: **do not let him walk out — lie him down and keep him NIL BY MOUTH, he is likely going to theatre** · reassess for sepsis using the SA Health sepsis pathway · **IV access and BLOOD CULTURES ×2 SETS FROM SEPARATE SITES BEFORE ANY ANTIBIOTIC** · analgesia — paracetamol 1 g plus a short-acting opioid if severe, **avoiding NSAIDs where sepsis, dehydration or renal impairment is possible** VERIFY · **SPEAK DIRECTLY TO THE ON-CALL ORTHOPAEDIC REGISTRAR — do not send a letter with the patient** · ambulance transfer, or **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 or RFDS from a remote site.**
**IF HE IS SEPTIC, ANTIBIOTICS MUST NOT BE DELAYED FOR ASPIRATION — give within one hour, after cultures, and resuscitate with IV fluids.** That is the only exception to samples-before-antibiotics.

**In hospital**: **FBE, CRP and ESR, UEC, LFTs, coagulation, group and hold, blood cultures ×2** · **AP pelvis and lateral hip X-ray** for prosthesis position, **periprosthetic lucency ≥2 mm**, osteolysis, migration, fracture · **ultrasound for effusion and to guide aspiration** · **CT abdomen and pelvis if a psoas abscess or intra-abdominal source is possible** · **MRI where osteomyelitis or occult fracture is suspected and films are normal.** **THE DEFINITIVE TEST is IMAGE-GUIDED ASPIRATION of the hip — cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture and sensitivity, and crystals.**

**Synovial white cell thresholds, and the trap inside them** VERIFY : **native joint, above roughly 50 × 10⁹/L with >90% neutrophils strongly supports sepsis. FOR A PROSTHETIC JOINT THE THRESHOLDS ARE FAR LOWER — of the order of >10 × 10⁹/L in acute infection and >3 × 10⁹/L in chronic.** **Applying the native-joint number to a prosthesis will FALSELY REASSURE you.** **Quote the principle, not the figure, unless pressed.**

**Treatment** VERIFY : empirical cover aims at **Staphylococcus aureus** — native joint, **flucloxacillin 2 g IV six-hourly**, with **vancomycin where there is MRSA risk or severe penicillin hypersensitivity.** **Where a prosthesis is involved, therapy is BROADER and specialist-directed — typically prolonged, often a rifampicin-containing combination once the joint has been debrided.** **In the OSCE say ‘antibiotics after cultures, guided by orthopaedics and infectious diseases’ and only quote a dose if pressed.** **SURGERY IS THE TREATMENT — acute infection with a well-fixed implant is usually managed by DAIR (debridement, antibiotics and implant retention with exchange of modular components); a loose implant or long-standing infection needs one- or two-stage revision.**

**AVOID**: **starting oral antibiotics and reviewing in 48 hours — it sterilises cultures and delays surgery** · **intra-articular corticosteroid into a possibly infected joint** · **‘it's just your old arthritis’ — inappropriate reassurance is an automatic fail** · **waiting for CRP or ESR before referring; NORMAL INFLAMMATORY MARKERS DO NOT EXCLUDE A SEPTIC JOINT** · **attempting aspiration in general practice — a prosthetic hip is aspirated under imaging, in hospital** · **blaming the tooth and treating the dental problem instead of the hip.**

**VARIANT B — 71 F, both groins and shoulder girdles, 8 weeks, afebrile, morning stiffness 90 minutes.** The discriminating moment moves to **asking about the head and eyes UNPROMPTED**: new temporal headache, tender scalp, **jaw ache when chewing**, visual change. **POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA with suspected GIANT CELL ARTERITIS — start steroid TODAY, before the tests come back** (PMR prednisolone 15 mg; **GCA 40–60 mg**) VERIFY **, and any visual symptom is a 000 emergency. Waiting for the ESR costs sight.**

**VARIANT C — 55 M, colicky loin-to-groin-to-testis pain, restless, vomiting, haematuria — PLUS a fever.** **The discriminating moment is NOT stopping at the stone.** **‘Stones are usually painful rather than dangerous — but you also have a temperature, and a stone blocking the tube with an infection behind it is an EMERGENCY. That combination means hospital today, not waiting for a scan next week.’** **An infected obstructed kidney needs DRAINAGE, not analgesia and antibiotics.**

**VARIANT D — the same case, harder.** He is **ANGRY** (‘the last doctor told me it was nothing’) and the fever is **subtle at 37.5°C because he is on prednisolone 7.5 mg for polymyalgia.** **‘I'm sorry you were sent away feeling unheard.’ Acknowledge, do NOT defend, and never criticise a colleague.** Then: **‘your temperature is only mildly raised, but you're taking steroids, and STEROIDS CAN MASK A FEVER COMPLETELY. So I'm treating a normal temperature as much less reassuring than usual, and I'm going on the fact that you can't weight-bear at all.’**

stem: Your next patient presents with right-sided groin swelling for two months.
Tasks: take a history for six minutes — then explain your diagnosis and your differentials. No examination. No investigations.
The budget that makes six minutes enough: 40 seconds opening · 80 characterising · 40 skin · 80 hernia · 30 hip · 70 lymph nodes · 20 to close.
tasks: Take a history for six minutes
Explain your diagnosis and your differentials

dx: **THE ONE IDEA TO CARRY IN: the structure is the mark, not the answer.** **This station has run at least twice in 2025 and the AMC gave DIFFERENT FINDINGS TO DIFFERENT CANDIDATES SITTING THE SAME EXAMINATION.** One met a 50-year-old with cough, constipation, prostatism, heavy lifting, obesity and a previous appendicectomy — a textbook hernia. Another met a 22-year-old who noticed it playing basketball, not using condoms, with a male partner and a previous STI. **Same stem. Completely different answer. Anyone who walks in knowing ‘the groin swelling case is a hernia’ asks hernia questions, collects a page of negatives, and cannot name a diagnosis.**

**THE FOUR BUCKETS, run in EVERY version whatever the stem says**: **1 HERNIA — inguinal, femoral, incisional, ± strangulation · 2 SKIN AND SOFT TISSUE — boil, abscess, folliculitis, cellulitis, lipoma · 3 HIP AND MUSCULOSKELETAL — effusion, arthritis, septic arthritis, fracture, psoas abscess · 4 LYMPH NODES — infection or cancer, EACH LOCAL OR GENERALISED.** Plus a fifth worth one sentence: **VASCULAR AND DEVELOPMENTAL — saphena varix, femoral aneurysm, undescended testis, hydrocele of the cord.**

**THE SECOND-ORDER TRAP: asked for differentials, candidates say ‘inguinal, femoral, direct, indirect, incisional’. THAT IS ONE BUCKET AND THE EXAMINER MARKS IT AS ONE.** **Say instead: ‘my differentials fall into four groups — a hernia; a skin or soft tissue problem such as a boil or abscess; a hip problem; and enlarged lymph nodes, which I'd divide into infective and malignant, each of which can be local or generalised.’ That sentence alone covers the whole marking grid.**

**THE ANATOMICAL FACT THAT DECIDES HALF THIS STATION: THE TESTIS DOES NOT DRAIN TO THE INGUINAL NODES.** It descends from the posterior abdominal wall and takes its lymphatics with it, so **it drains to the PARA-AORTIC nodes.** **The inguinal nodes take the LOWER LIMB, the PERINEUM, the ANAL CANAL BELOW THE DENTATE LINE, and the SKIN OF THE SCROTUM AND PENIS.** **So a testicular tumour does not explain a groin node — but epididymo-orchitis with scrotal skin inflammation, a penile ulcer, a foot infection, leg cellulitis, a melanoma on the calf or an anal squamous cell carcinoma all can. Say it out loud and it reads as reasoning rather than recall.**

**THE CHARACTER BLOCK IS YOUR EXAMINATION — give it the time it deserves.** **Site (‘closer to your hip, or closer to your private parts?’) · size (‘the size of a coin, or bigger?’) · CONSISTENCY, offered as three options: ‘soft, or firm and rubbery, or hard?’ · tenderness, warmth, redness · duration · ‘constantly there, or does it come and go?’ · getting bigger · and THE HERNIA QUESTION: worse on standing, coughing or straining, and gone on lying flat.**

**What each consistency means**: **SOFT AND SQUASHY — hernia sac or lipoma · FIRM, RUBBERY, MOBILE — reactive lymph node · HARD, FIXED, CRAGGY — malignancy until proven otherwise · FLUCTUANT, HOT, EXQUISITELY TENDER — abscess.** **An open ‘what does it feel like?’ gets you ‘like a lump’ — the three options force a discriminating answer.** **And ‘comes and goes’ is close to diagnostic of a reducible hernia: a node does not disappear and reappear.**

**TAKE A SEXUAL HISTORY IN EVERY VERSION, NOT JUST THE ONE WHERE YOU SUSPECT IT.** **The candidate who reached the diagnosis in version B did so because they asked about condoms as a ROUTINE, got an unexpected answer, and followed it.** Normalise it: **‘I'd like to ask a few questions about sexual health. I ask everyone, because infections in that area are a common cause of swelling in the groin — is that all right?’** **In the married 50-year-old it finds nothing, and THAT IS THE POINT — a candidate who asks only when they already suspect will miss the case where the suspicion has to come FROM the question.**

**The six questions, learned verbatim — partners, practices, protection, past infections, testing**: **‘Are you sexually active at the moment? Are your partners MEN, WOMEN, OR BOTH? Do you use condoms — ALWAYS, SOMETIMES, OR NOT USUALLY? How many partners in the last six months or so? Have you ever been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted infection before? And have you ever been tested for HIV, or used PrEP?’** **If risk emerges, two follow-ups: SITES OF EXPOSURE (oral, anal), because that decides whether you swab throat and rectum, and vaccination status.** **Ask flatly, without commentary and without flinching — the role-player is briefed on whether you become awkward, and will close down if you do.**

**VERSION A explanation**: **‘The wall of your abdomen is a sheet of muscle holding everything in, and in the groin there's a naturally weaker point. Over time that point can stretch, and when it does a small sac of the lining of your abdomen — sometimes with a bit of fat or bowel in it — pushes out through the gap. That bulge is what you're feeling.’** Then **TWO reasons: how it behaves (soft, pushes back, out on standing and coughing, gone by morning) and the risk factors he disclosed — cough, straining with constipation, straining to pass urine, thirty years of bricklaying, extra weight. EVERY ONE IS A MECHANISM. Feed them back — that is what converts a diagnosis into a JUSTIFIED diagnosis.**

**VERSION B explanation — mechanism first, and DO NOT NAME AN ORGANISM YOU CANNOT SUPPORT**: **‘That lump is most likely a swollen gland — a lymph node. Glands like that are part of your immune system, and the ones in your groin drain the skin of your legs and your genital area. When there's an infection anywhere in that territory, the gland that drains it swells and becomes tender — that's the gland doing its job. Putting that together with the stinging when you pass urine and what you've told me about your sexual health, the most likely cause is an infection passed on through sex. I'm not going to guess which one, because the treatment depends on it — but they're all treatable, and I'd test for the others at the same time, because they often travel together.’**
plan: **Open, and ACKNOWLEDGE THE WORRY BEFORE YOU INTERROGATE.** He volunteers it — *‘it's not going away, so it's been playing on my mind’* — precisely so you have something to respond to. **‘That sounds like it's been on your mind, and I can understand that — a lump that doesn't go away is worrying. Let me ask you some questions and we'll work out what's going on together.’** **Eight seconds, and it is scored.**

**CHARACTERISE THE SWELLING — this replaces the examination.** Site oriented, size, **consistency in three options**, tenderness and skin change, constant or intermittent, enlarging, **and the standing/coughing/lying-flat question.** **Listen to the patient's own words — ‘when it's out’ reveals intermittency before you have asked.**

**BUCKET 2 — SKIN. Forty seconds, and it goes EARLY on purpose**: it is the shortest bucket, and the fever-and-chills question it opens with does **double duty** for the infective half of the lymph node bucket. **Fevers, chills or shivers · redness or rash · discharge · previous boils or infected hair follicles — DO YOU SHAVE OR WAX THE AREA?** **The groin is among the commonest sites for folliculitis and furuncles precisely because of shaving, sweat and friction.**

**BUCKET 1 — HERNIA. Symptoms first, then THE OBSTRUCTION SCREEN — fifteen seconds, and it is the safety item of the station.** **‘Any pain in the groin itself, separate from the lump? Any pain in your abdomen? Any nausea or vomiting? Are you opening your bowels normally — and passing wind? And HAS IT EVER GOT STUCK — been impossible to push back in?’** **Ask it even though the lump has been painless for two months, BECAUSE THAT IS EXACTLY THE PATIENT WHO PRESENTS STRANGULATED NEXT WEEK.**

**Then the risk factors, every one a mechanism**: **constipation and straining · long-standing cough and smoking · straining to pass urine, poor stream, nocturia** (two questions and you have both a hernia risk factor AND a second diagnosis to mention) **· occupation and heavy lifting — AND WHAT HE DID BEFORE HE RETIRED** · **previous abdominal operations** (version A plants an appendicectomy on the same side) · **‘how would you describe your weight?’** — asked explicitly, because with no examination there is no BMI available · family history of hernias.

**BUCKET 3 — HIP. Four questions, thirty seconds, and version C turns entirely on them.** **‘Any pain in the hip itself? Any stiffness moving the leg or hip? Are you limping — can you put your full weight through that leg? Any injury, fall or trauma, including during sport?’** **Inability to weight-bear moves hip pathology to the top of the list; WITH FEVER it becomes a septic hip and an emergency.** **The source is explicit that a candidate who never asked these would deserve to fail.**

**BUCKET 4 — LYMPH NODES. First the DRAINAGE TERRITORY**: **lower limb — cuts, ulcers, rashes, athlete's foot, ingrown toenail · genital skin — rash, blisters or ulcers · scrotum — swelling, pain, redness · urethral — discharge, burning passing urine · ANORECTAL — pain, bleeding, discharge or ulcers around the back passage,** because the anal canal below the dentate line drains here.

**Then the SEXUAL HISTORY, normalised and asked in full.** Then **THE CONSTITUTIONAL BLOCK — the only route to a malignant node**: **weight loss and how much over what period · appetite · unusually tired · NIGHT SWEATS SOAKING THE SHEETS · lumps or bumps anywhere else, neck or armpits · ANY UNUSUAL OR CHANGING MOLES ON YOUR LEGS OR FEET · ulcers or sores on the genitals that haven't healed · and recent travel.** **The mole question is not filler — a nodular melanoma on the calf can present as a groin node.**
**Close the history. Past medical, medications and family history ONLY if time survives — the source is explicit that these are the FIRST things to sacrifice here.**

**Leading diagnosis, named and explained with a mechanism the patient could repeat → justified from what he ACTUALLY SAID → the four groups, with ONE CLAUSE each saying why it is less likely, referencing the history → a next step → and a safety-net, even though the task did not ask for management.** **Two sentences at the end cost nothing and read as competence.**
pefe: **There is no physical examination and no investigation results — you diagnose on history alone.** That is why the character block carries so much weight.

**THE DECISION PATH, in order.** **FIRST: irreducible, painful and tender with abdominal pain, vomiting, distension or no flatus → STRANGULATED HERNIA, surgical emergency. Or fever plus inability to weight-bear → SEPTIC HIP. Stop and escalate.** **SECOND: does it come and go, worse standing or coughing, gone lying flat → hernia until proven otherwise.** **THIRD: a source in the drainage territory → reactive lymphadenitis — and take the full sexual history BEFORE concluding there is not.** **FOURTH: hip pain, limp, weight-bearing, sporting mechanism → hip pathology.** **FIFTH: hard, fixed, painless, growing, with weight loss, night sweats, nodes elsewhere or a changing mole → MALIGNANT lymphadenopathy, investigate rather than reassure.**

**INGUINAL versus FEMORAL is the distinction that matters clinically**: **inguinal emerges ABOVE AND MEDIAL to the pubic tubercle; femoral sits BELOW AND LATERAL, alongside the femoral vessels.** **A femoral hernia has a NARROW, RIGID NECK and a much higher strangulation risk — it is repaired EVEN WHEN ASYMPTOMATIC, and it is commoner in women and easily missed because it is small.** VERIFY **Direct versus indirect, by contrast, is largely a surgical distinction made at operation — do not over-claim it from a history alone.**

**Investigations if asked** VERIFY : **HERNIA — largely clinical; ultrasound if uncertain or the patient is obese; CT for complex or recurrent. Surgical referral; watchful waiting is accepted for a minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia in a man, but a FEMORAL hernia is repaired regardless. Treat the drivers — constipation, cough, smoking, prostatic symptoms, weight.** **SUSPECTED STI — nucleic acid amplification on first-void urine, plus THROAT AND ANORECTAL SWABS where the sexual history indicates; HIV and syphilis serology; hepatitis B and C; swab any ulcer for herpes and syphilis PCR; consider LGV testing on a positive chlamydia result in a man who has sex with men.** **Contact tracing, vaccination for hepatitis A and B and HPV, PrEP discussion, and several are NOTIFIABLE in South Australia.**

**LYMPHADENOPATHY of unclear cause**: FBC and film, ESR or CRP, LDH; EBV and CMV serology; HIV and syphilis serology; chest X-ray; ultrasound of the node. **Examine the ENTIRE drainage territory including the soles and between the toes, and the whole skin for melanoma.** **If the node is hard, fixed, over about 2 cm, or persists beyond four to six weeks without explanation, refer for CORE OR EXCISIONAL BIOPSY — fine-needle aspiration is generally inadequate when lymphoma is suspected, because architecture is needed for classification.** VERIFY

**Scripted examiner challenges**: *‘Why isn't this a hernia?’* (version B) → **‘Three reasons. He has none of the risk factors — no cough, no constipation, no straining, no heavy lifting, and he's twenty-two. The swelling doesn't behave like a hernia: it isn't worse on standing or coughing and doesn't reduce on lying flat. And the mechanism doesn't fit — hernias don't appear suddenly during a game of basketball. What he does have is a set of clear risk factors for sexually transmitted infection, and the inguinal nodes drain exactly that territory.’** *‘Could a testicular tumour cause this node?’* → **‘Not typically — the testis drains to the para-aortic nodes because of its embryological origin.’**

**The difficult moments, scripted**: *‘It doesn't hurt — can't we just leave it?’* → **‘For a hernia that isn't bothering you, watching and waiting is sometimes reasonable. But occasionally the contents get trapped and the blood supply is squeezed — that's an emergency needing surgery within hours. So even if we watch it, you need to know the warning signs.’** *‘Does this go on my record? My family use this clinic.’* → **‘What we discuss is confidential and isn't shared with your family. If you'd feel more comfortable, SHINE SA provides sexual health testing separately from your usual practice.’** *‘Do I have to tell my partners?’* → **‘You don't have to do that alone — there are services that will notify people ANONYMOUSLY on your behalf.’**

**VARIANT C — THE HIP.** Same 22-year-old and the same basketball, but **hip ache, stiffness, limping, cannot weight-bear.** **‘The hip sits deep inside, wrapped in muscle, so a problem there often shows up as swelling or fullness in the groin rather than anything you can see from outside.’** X-ray, inflammatory markers, ultrasound for effusion. **Add FEVER and it is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — and because the hip is deep, the ABSENCE of visible redness argues for a deep joint, NOT against infection.**

**VARIANT D — THE MALIGNANT NODE.** Hard, fixed, progressively enlarging, with six kilos of weight loss and drenching night sweats. **Investigate urgently rather than watch: bloods, a scan, and most likely a biopsy.** **Two things candidates miss: examine the whole drainage territory INCLUDING THE SOLES AND BETWEEN THE TOES for a melanoma or a penile, scrotal or anal lesion; and insist on CORE OR EXCISIONAL biopsy rather than FNA if lymphoma is possible.**

**VARIANT E — STRANGULATION.** *‘It's been out since yesterday and I can't get it back in. It's really tender, my stomach's aching, and I threw up this morning.’* **Recognition and escalation, NOT a differential discussion — everything else in your plan is suspended.** **Nil by mouth, IV access, analgesia, call the surgical team now; in regional SA, MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval coordination.** **VARIANT F — the femoral hernia in an older, thinner woman: small, below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, easily missed, and the safety-net becomes MORE emphatic, not less.**

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town. James Whitfield, 60, a storeman, with burning pain in both feet.
On the door: BP 148/86 · HR 78 regular · T 36.8°C · RR 14 · BMI 31 · random capillary glucose 12.4 mmol/L. Not in acute distress.

8-minute station with a bell at 6 minutes. History 6 minutes · ask the examiner for the findings, which come on a card, and do not examine the patient · explain the diagnosis in language he understands · explain the other diagnoses and why they are less likely.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings — you will be handed a card
Explain the most likely diagnosis to the patient in language he can understand
Explain the other diagnoses you considered and why they are less likely
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: ASK FOR IT BY NAMING THE SYSTEMS — a vague ‘can I have the findings?’ throws away the marks

‘Vital signs and BMI · a VASCULAR assessment — dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, capillary refill, temperature, hair distribution and BUERGER'S TEST · inspection of both feet INCLUDING BETWEEN THE TOES AND THE SOLES for ulceration, callus, deformity or infection · a NEUROLOGICAL assessment — light touch, pinprick, 10 g MONOFILAMENT AT TEN SITES, 128 Hz VIBRATION, proprioception, power, ankle and knee reflexes, ROMBERG and gait · lumbar spine with STRAIGHT LEG RAISE · and the special tests, MULDER'S CLICK and TINEL'S over the tarsal tunnel’
General and vascular

Overweight, comfortable at rest, AFEBRILE. Both feet WARM AND WELL PERFUSED. DORSALIS PEDIS AND POSTERIOR TIBIAL PULSES PALPABLE BILATERALLY. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. NO elevation pallor or dependent rubor
Skin

DRY SKIN, CALLUS OVER BOTH FIRST AND FIFTH METATARSAL HEADS. NO ULCER, no erythema, no swelling, no interdigital maceration. Nails thickened. The callus is where the ulcer will form — it is the reason blanket reassurance fails this station
Sensation

Reduced light touch and pinprick in a STOCKING DISTRIBUTION TO MID-SHIN bilaterally. 10 g MONOFILAMENT NOT PERCEIVED AT 6 OF 10 SITES ON EACH FOOT. Vibration (128 Hz) ABSENT at both great toes, PRESENT at both tibial tuberosities. Proprioception IMPAIRED at both great toes
Motor, reflexes and gait
Power 5/5 in all groups, NO WASTING. Knee jerks present, ANKLE JERKS ABSENT BILATERALLY, plantars downgoing. ROMBERG POSITIVE. Gait mildly broad-based, NO FOOT DROP
Spine and special tests — the ones that EXCLUDE

Lumbar spine non-tender, normal movements, STRAIGHT LEG RAISE NEGATIVE bilaterally (excludes radiculopathy). MULDER'S CLICK NEGATIVE (excludes Morton's neuroma). TINEL'S AT THE TARSAL TUNNEL NEGATIVE (excludes tarsal tunnel)
READ THE CARD ALOUD IN ONE INTERPRETIVE SENTENCE before you turn to the patient

‘So the findings show reduced sensation in a stocking pattern with absent vibration and absent ankle jerks, but with NORMAL PULSES and NO ULCERATION — that fits a SENSORY NERVE problem rather than a CIRCULATION problem, which is reassuring in one important respect.’ This tells the examiner you INTERPRETED the card rather than merely received it
VERSION B card — forefoot

TENDERNESS IN THE THIRD WEBSPACE, POSITIVE MULDER'S CLICK, sensation and reflexes NORMAL → Morton's neuroma. Ultrasound of the forefoot first in Australian practice; MRI only for equivocal or pre-surgical cases
VERSION C card — vascular
PULSES ABSENT, foot COOL, HAIR LOSS, ELEVATION PALLOR, ABI 0.35 → CRITICAL LIMB ISCHAEMIA, same-day vascular referral
The numbers on this card

10 g monofilament, 10 sites — FAILURE AT ANY SITE IS LOSS OF PROTECTIVE SENSATION · ABI <0.40 critical ischaemia · 0.40–0.90 PAD · 0.91–1.30 normal · >1.30 FALSELY HIGH from medial calcification · TOE–BRACHIAL INDEX <0.70 IS ABNORMAL, and it is the number to use in diabetes · a temperature difference over 2°C between feet supports ACTIVE CHARCOT VERIFY

dx: **Distal symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy — length-dependent, from chronic hyperglycaemia PLUS chronic alcohol excess.** **THE LINE THE WHOLE STATION TURNS ON: ‘You have a sensory neuropathy — and there are TWO things driving it.’** **Not ‘diabetic neuropathy’. Naming the alcohol alongside the glycaemia is what separates a pass from the crowd of candidates who all reached the same diagnosis.**

**THE STATION IS BUILT TO PUNISH PREMATURE CLOSURE.** The moment you read ‘burning pain in the feet’ in a 60-year-old you know it is diabetic neuropathy — **so does everyone else, and the case was designed by someone who knew you would know. The marks were therefore placed everywhere EXCEPT the diagnosis.** **A candidate who ‘knows’ the answer takes a DIABETES history and finishes with four minutes of confirmed diabetes and zero minutes of excluded alternatives — and that history would be identical whether the man had claudication, an ulcer, restless legs or a neuroma. AN IDENTICAL HISTORY CANNOT DEMONSTRATE CLINICAL REASONING.**

**SAY THE FIVE HEADINGS OUT LOUD, IN THIS ORDER — the examiner is marking whether your history has a VISIBLE SKELETON**: **1 RED FLAGS — infection, osteomyelitis, Charcot, malignancy, cauda equina · 2 VASCULAR — claudication, rest pain, colour change, ulcers, risk factors · 3 NEUROLOGICAL — diabetes, ALCOHOL, B12, thyroid, uraemia, back pain, drugs · 4 SOFT TISSUE — Morton's, footwear, standing, fasciitis, injury · 5 OTHER — restless legs and ferritin, diet, occupation.**

**THE QUALITY QUESTION IS A SCORING QUESTION. Burning has THREE quite different meanings**: **NEUROPATHIC — with pins and needles or numbness · ISCHAEMIC — with claudication, worse elevated, better dependent · INFLAMMATORY or INFECTIVE — with redness, heat, swelling.** **One extra question — ‘do you get pins and needles or numbness with it?’ — splits all three. Ask it, and say why you are asking.**

**‘WHEREABOUTS IN THE FOOT?’ is the single highest-yield question, and the map does the diagnostic work before you ask a single risk factor**: **WHOLE FOOT AND BILATERAL → polyneuropathy · FOREFOOT → Morton's · HEEL, first steps → plantar fasciitis · ONE SIDE, medial ankle → tarsal tunnel or radiculopathy.** **‘Where is it?’ ‘My feet.’ ‘Okay, and how long?’ leaves Morton's, tarsal tunnel and fasciitis all still open.**

**DO NOT SKIP THE VASCULAR BLOCK BECAUSE YOU KNOW IT IS NEUROPATHY.** **Peripheral arterial disease and neuropathy share EVERY risk factor and coexist in a large minority of people with diabetes.** **Skipping it is the commonest content failure in this station.** The highest-yield vascular question: **‘Do you get pain in the foot at rest, or at night in bed — and DOES HANGING YOUR LEG OUT OF THE BED HELP?’** — a yes is **critical limb ischaemia, and it is a same-day vascular referral, not a gabapentinoid and a routine review.**

**CAP DIABETES AT FOUR QUESTIONS AND STOP**: when were you diagnosed · what are you taking · how often do you manage to take it · when were you last reviewed and do you know your HbA1c. Then a **30-second complications sweep** — vision, kidneys, dizziness on standing, erections or bladder.

**THE ALCOHOL QUESTION IS THE PASS POINT, AND IT MUST BE QUANTIFIED.** **‘Do you drink?’ → ‘socially’ → move on is the commonest way the second aetiology is lost.** The role-player is briefed to give ‘a few, socially’ to the vague question and the real figure — **six to eight stubbies most nights plus scotches on Saturday** — only to **‘On a day when you do drink, roughly how many would you have, and what sort?’**, and **only if the tone is neutral. If you sound disapproving he becomes guarded and says ‘not that much really’.**

**Explaining it — name it, translate it in the same breath, then CHECK**: **‘You have a condition called a SENSORY NEUROPATHY. The nerves that carry sensation from your feet up to your brain have been damaged, and when nerves are damaged they MISFIRE, which you feel as burning and pins and needles. Where they've stopped working altogether you feel numbness — that's why parts of your feet feel like they're wrapped in a THICK SOCK. Does that make sense so far?’** Then **the two causes: ‘the first is your blood sugar — running high over years damages the small nerves and the tiny vessels that feed them. The second is the ALCOHOL — six to eight drinks most nights is directly TOXIC to nerves, and it also affects the vitamins nerves need.’**

**THE HIDDEN AGENDA, and the second discriminator: his father lost a leg.** **Ask for his concern in the FIRST 45 SECONDS — if you leave ‘any concerns?’ to the end, the role-player drops it at 7:30 and you have no time to respond, and ‘addresses patient concerns’ is marked down.** Then answer it directly: **‘That must sit in the back of your mind every time your feet hurt. Let me be straight with you — you are NOT in that position today. Your circulation is good, your pulses are strong, and there's no ulcer or infection. What happened to your father is NOT INEVITABLE for you — it is largely PREVENTABLE, and I'll show you exactly how. Three things make the difference: the sugar, the alcohol, and looking after the skin on your feet.’**
plan: **WIPE and agenda, then the three opening questions**: **‘Are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it? And is there anything in particular you're worried this might be?’** **The third one converts a lost mark into a strong one.**

**Characterise the pain — SITE FIRST, quality second.** **‘Whereabouts in the foot exactly — the ball of the foot, the heel, the whole foot, or between the toes? And one foot or both?’** Then onset and gradient · **‘burning, aching, shooting — and DO YOU GET PINS AND NEEDLES OR NUMBNESS WITH IT?’** · does it travel or shoot down from the back · **timing: night, morning, end of day; worse after activity or after resting** · out of ten, and effect on sleep and work. **‘Same day and night, no difference with walking’ ACTIVELY excludes claudication, inflammatory arthritis and restless legs on pattern alone — use negative history, don't just collect positives.**

**‘First I want to make sure nothing serious is going on.’** Fever, chills or sweats · **redness, warmth or swelling spreading up the foot** · **any break in the skin, ulcer or BLACK AREA** · weight loss, night sweats, lumps · **leg weakness, difficulty lifting the foot, bladder or bowel change, numbness around the back passage** — the cauda equina screen.

**‘Now I'd like to check the blood supply to your legs.’** **Cramping in the calves on walking, ESPECIALLY UPHILL — how far before it starts, does it settle standing still** · **REST OR NIGHT PAIN, AND DOES HANGING THE LEG OUT OF BED HELP** · colour change, cold feet · hair loss, non-healing sores · **swelling, varicose veins, brown staining** · then risk factors: smoking, BP, cholesterol, sugar, heart attack, stroke, angina, family history before 60. **Six questions, 45 seconds — there is time.**

**‘Now I want to check the nerves.’** Weakness lifting the foot or on stairs · unsteadiness or falls · back pain shooting down the leg · **the four diabetes questions and STOP** · the complications sweep · **thyroid: cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, dry skin** · **THE ALCOHOL QUESTION, quantified** · **diet and B12: vegetarian? stomach surgery? long-term reflux tablets? — and note METFORMIN ITSELF LOWERS B12** · kidney and liver · **other drugs, including past metronidazole, isoniazid, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, phenytoin or chemotherapy.**

**‘Now the structures in the foot itself.’** **Tight or narrow shoes; worse with shoes ON and better when they come OFF; a PEBBLE under the ball of the foot** · occupation, standing, new exercise · injury. **Then ‘one more pattern I want to exclude’: RESTLESS LEGS — ‘do you get an URGE TO MOVE your legs when you're sitting or lying still, and does getting up and WALKING make it better? Is it worse in the evening?’** Then close: **‘anything else you've noticed that I haven't asked about, and what were you hoping we might do today?’**
6:00 — HARD STOP

**Stop the history when the bell goes, WHATEVER is unasked.** **An incomplete history with a complete explanation scores far better than the reverse, because tasks 3 and 4 carry their own marks.** Ask for the findings **by naming the systems**, then **read the card aloud in one interpretive sentence.**
**‘What do you already understand about why your feet might be burning?’** Then **name the syndrome, translate it, check understanding, then BOTH causes.**

**Answer the amputation fear directly**, then **the differentials in FIVE NAMED GROUPS, each with the discriminating negative** — infection and Charcot excluded by no fever, redness, swelling or skin break; vascular by strong pulses, no claudication, no rest pain; radiculopathy by bilateral non-dermatomal symptoms and a negative SLR; Morton's and tarsal tunnel by diffuse pain with negative Mulder's and Tinel's; restless legs by no urge to move.

**The plan and the safety-net, delivered even if you are 20 seconds over — it is worth more than a tidy finish.** **‘Look at your feet EVERY DAY including the soles — use a mirror or ask your wife. NEVER walk barefoot, and NEVER use a hot water bottle or heater on your feet, because you won't feel a burn. If you see a break in the skin, blister, redness, swelling or any black area, or if you get a fever, come in THAT SAME DAY, not next week. If the foot becomes suddenly painful, pale or cold, that's an emergency — go straight to the emergency department.’**
pefe: **Investigations — one blood test covers most of it**: **HbA1c and fasting glucose · FBC (macrocytosis suggests alcohol or B12) and FERRITIN/iron studies · U&E, eGFR and urine albumin:creatinine · LFT and GGT · TSH · SERUM B12 ± folate** — **and a NORMAL serum B12 does not exclude functional deficiency; add methylmalonic acid or homocysteine if low-normal** · fasting lipids · ESR/CRP if infection is possible.

**Calculate the ABI — and if it is above 1.30, or he has long-standing diabetes, OBTAIN A TOE–BRACHIAL INDEX, because medial arterial calcification makes the vessels incompressible and falsifies the ABI.** **Naming the toe–brachial index rather than the ABI is one of the few sentences in this station that marks you out as above the line.**

**NERVE CONDUCTION STUDIES ARE NOT ROUTINE** — reserve them for **asymmetric, motor-predominant, rapidly progressive or diagnostically uncertain** cases. Ordering them as a reflex reads as insecurity.

**Management — treat the CAUSES, treat the PAIN, protect the FOOT.** **Glycaemia**: restart and re-titrate metformin, and **explore WHY adherence lapsed rather than assuming non-compliance**; HbA1c target generally around 53 mmol/mol (7.0%), individualised VERIFY ; diabetes annual cycle of care, educator, dietitian. **Alcohol**: non-judgemental brief intervention; **NHMRC — no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 on any one day; a 375 mL full-strength stubby is about 1.4 standard drinks, so six to eight most nights is roughly 50–70 per week, five to seven times the limit.** **Assess dependence and withdrawal risk BEFORE advising abrupt cessation. Thiamine 100 mg orally daily, higher and parenteral if Wernicke's is a risk.** VERIFY

**Neuropathic pain — choose one and titrate** VERIFY : **amitriptyline 10 mg nocte, up by 10 mg every 1–2 weeks to 25–75 mg** (caution in the elderly — anticholinergic effects, falls, cardiac conduction) · **duloxetine 30 mg daily for a week then 60 mg** · **pregabalin 25–75 mg nocte titrating to 150–300 mg daily in two divided doses, REDUCED IN RENAL IMPAIRMENT.** Topical capsaicin 0.075% as an adjunct. **Set the expectation honestly: a good response is roughly a 30–50% REDUCTION in pain, not abolition.**

**Foot protection is the management, not an afterthought**: podiatry referral and a **formal high-risk foot assessment**; daily self-inspection including the soles with a mirror; never barefoot; check inside shoes before putting them on; **test bath water with the hand or elbow, never a hot water bottle or heater**; professional callus and nail care; well-fitting footwear. **And DRIVING — assess against Austroads; in South Australia there is a MANDATORY REPORTING DUTY for a driver believed unfit.**

**AVOID**: labelling it ‘diabetic neuropathy’ and stopping the search · reassuring him it is nothing to worry about · **relying on a normal ABI in long-standing diabetes** · long-term NSAIDs with reduced eGFR · **opioids for chronic neuropathic pain** · starting a gabapentinoid without discussing sedation, falls, weight gain and misuse potential · **moralising about the drinking — it closes the conversation and loses the second diagnosis.**

**Examiner challenges, scripted**: *‘Isn't this just diabetic neuropathy?’* → **‘It is very likely predominantly diabetic, but he drinks 8–10 standard drinks daily, which is independently neurotoxic, and metformin lowers B12. I would not attribute it solely to diabetes without excluding the reversible causes, because two of them are treatable.’** *‘His ABI is 1.20 — that's normal, isn't it?’* → **‘In long-standing diabetes medial arterial calcification makes the vessels incompressible, so the ABI can be falsely normal or high. I'd obtain a toe–brachial index; below 0.70 is abnormal.’**

**VERSION B — 45 F, forefoot, Morton's neuroma.** *‘Right at the front, on the ball of my right foot. Like a stone in my shoe, with an electric shock into the third and fourth toes. Within a minute of getting my shoes off it's gone.’* **‘That points to a MORTON'S NEUROMA — a thickened, irritated nerve running between the bones of your toes. It isn't a cancer, and it isn't a nerve disease affecting the whole body.’** **Wider flatter shoes with a roomy toe box and a metatarsal pad first; ultrasound to confirm; corticosteroid injection; surgery only if those fail.** **THE TRAP: candidates who rehearsed version A take a diabetes history from a 45-year-old with no diabetes.**

**VERSION C — 68 M smoker, critical limb ischaemia.** *‘Worst when I lie down. I sit on the edge of the bed at three in the morning with my leg hanging down, and that eases it. Cramping at eighty metres.’* Card: **cool hairless foot, absent pulses, elevation pallor, ABI 0.32.** **‘The blood supply to your foot is severely reduced — that's why the pain comes on when you lie flat and eases when you hang the leg down, because GRAVITY is doing the work your arteries can't.’** **Vascular team TODAY, urgent arterial duplex, aspirin and a statin; keep the foot DOWN rather than elevated, protected and warm but NEVER with direct heat.** **THE TRAP: prescribing a gabapentinoid and booking a routine review.**

stem: General practice in a regional South Australian town (MM5). James Whitcombe, 58, runs a hardware store and is on his feet most of the day. Right heel pain for four months.
Also in the stem: he injured that same ankle about ten years ago. Given to you: temp 36.6°C · HR 72 · BP 132/80 · RR 14 · BMI 30. He walked in unaided.
8-minute station. History in 6 minutes, then the examination findings on a card when you ask, then the diagnosis and differentials explained to the patient in plain language with your reasons.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings, provided on a card
Explain your most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient, in plain language, with the reasons you have reached them
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: ASK AS A STRUCTURE, NOT A WISH

‘General appearance — CAN HE WEIGHT-BEAR, what is his gait? · vital signs, PARTICULARLY THE TEMPERATURE · inspection: swelling, redness, rash, any SKIN BREAK OR ULCER, and any DEFORMITY · palpation: local temperature, PEDAL PULSES AND CAPILLARY REFILL, and tenderness over the PLANTAR HEEL, the ACHILLES AND ITS INSERTION, the malleoli and the JOINT LINE · movement: dorsiflexion, plantarflexion, inversion and eversion — IS THERE PAIN, AND IS THE RANGE RESTRICTED? · a brief NEUROLOGICAL examination of the foot · special tests: WINDLASS, THOMPSON, ANTERIOR DRAWER AND TALAR TILT, TINEL'S.’ Pulses and weight-bearing are the two candidates leave out
General
AFEBRILE. ABLE TO WEIGHT-BEAR; mild ANTALGIC GAIT favouring the right
Inspection — THE FIRST DECISIVE FINDING

THE RIGHT HEEL APPEARS WIDENED compared with the left. No redness, no rash, no skin break or ulcer. DO NOT OVERTHINK THE WORD ‘WIDENED’ — IT IS A DEFORMITY, and deformity means STRUCTURAL JOINT OR BONE DISEASE, not tendinopathy
Palpation

NO local rise in temperature. DORSALIS PEDIS AND POSTERIOR TIBIAL PULSES PRESENT, capillary refill under 2 seconds. TENDERNESS OVER THE ANKLE JOINT LINE. NO discrete tenderness at the MEDIAL CALCANEAL TUBERCLE or at the ACHILLES INSERTION
Movement — THE SECOND AND THIRD DECISIVE FINDINGS
PAINFUL IN ALL FOUR DIRECTIONS. Dorsiflexion 20° · plantarflexion 20° · inversion 20° · eversion 10°
The four normal ranges — without them you cannot say ‘reduced’

DORSIFLEXION about 20° · PLANTARFLEXION 30–50° · INVERSION 20–30° · EVERSION 15–25°. So: plantarflexion 20° and eversion 10° are CLEARLY REDUCED; inversion 20° is at the LOWER LIMIT; dorsiflexion 20° is WITHIN NORMAL BUT PAINFUL. Say it that way — A GLOBAL RESTRICTION WITH PAIN, not ‘all the numbers are abnormal’ VERIFY
Neurovascular and special tests — what each one EXCLUDES

Power, sensation and reflexes intact. WINDLASS NEGATIVE and no tubercle tenderness → argues against PLANTAR FASCIITIS. THOMPSON NEGATIVE and no insertional tenderness → argues against ACHILLES tendinopathy or rupture. NO LAXITY on anterior drawer or talar tilt → argues against chronic LIGAMENT instability, because chronic ligament injury produces EXCESS movement, not restriction
READ THREE FINDINGS ALOUD, IN THESE WORDS

‘A WIDENED right heel — that is a DEFORMITY; pain on ALL FOUR movements; and a REDUCED RANGE, with plantarflexion 20° against a normal 30 to 50 and eversion 10° against a normal 15 to 25.’ Taking the card and going silent loses the reasoning mark — this IS the reasoning
THE TRAP SITTING IN THIS CARD

Candidates see ‘heel’, remember plantar fasciitis is the commonest heel diagnosis, and announce it — IGNORING a negative windlass, absent tubercle tenderness, a deformity and a globally restricted painful joint. THE CARD OVERRIDES YOUR PRIOR. Read it TO TEST your hypothesis, not to confirm it
THE OTHER VERSION CARDS

B — tender MEDIAL CALCANEAL TUBERCLE, POSITIVE WINDLASS → plantar fasciitis. C — tender 2–6 cm ABOVE the insertion, thickened tendon, recent CIPROFLOXACIN → fluoroquinolone-associated Achilles tendinopathy, and NEVER INJECT STEROID. D — FEBRILE, ULCER UNDER THE HEEL, cannot weight-bear, diabetic → osteomyelitis ± septic arthritis, same-day referral, and MRI IS THE IMAGING OF CHOICE

dx: **Post-traumatic osteoarthritis of the ankle** — osteoarthritis in a joint whose surfaces or alignment were disrupted by a previous injury. **Any intra-articular fracture, dislocation or major ligament rupture raises the long-term risk — the same reason an ACL tear is repaired promptly.** Calling it osteoarthritis alone is also accepted.

**THE LINE IN THE STEM THAT IS THE WHOLE CASE: ‘He injured that ankle ten years ago.’ That is not background colour — it is the MECHANISM.** **If you never ask what the injury was, what he was diagnosed with and how it was treated, you cannot say the word POST-TRAUMATIC.** **And the recalls disagree about whether it was ‘an injury’ or ‘a fracture’ PRECISELY BECAUSE CANDIDATES DID NOT ASK.**

**THREE INJURY QUESTIONS, IN THIS ORDER**: **‘Can you describe what happened?’ · ‘WHAT WERE YOU TOLD IT WAS — WHAT WAS THE DIAGNOSIS?’ · ‘And what treatment did you have?’** **He will not volunteer the word FRACTURE unless you ask the middle one.** Answers: came off a ladder and twisted it badly ten years ago · they said he'd fractured it · cast for six to eight weeks then physiotherapy, settled fine at the time.

**THE CLINICAL RULE THAT DECIDES THE CARD: A TENDON hurts when you LOAD OR STRETCH it. A LIGAMENT hurts when you stretch it IN ONE DIRECTION, and when chronically injured it gives you LAXITY, NOT RESTRICTION — more movement than normal, not less. A JOINT hurts in EVERY direction and LOSES RANGE.** **So pain on inversion AND eversion AND plantarflexion AND dorsiflexion, with reduced range, cannot be a lateral ligament and cannot be the Achilles.**

**SITE SORTS THE SOFT TISSUE — ask it first and two thirds of the list disappears.** **UNDER the heel → plantar fascia, fat pad, calcaneal stress fracture, Baxter's nerve · BEHIND the heel → Achilles tendinopathy, retrocalcaneal bursitis, Haglund's · ALL OVER, deep, with restriction → THE JOINT.** **Heel, foot and ankle pain share ONE differential list — what changes between them is only the ORDER.**

**ASK THE PLANTAR FASCIITIS PAIR EVEN WHEN YOU THINK IT IS ARTHRITIS**: **‘Are the first few steps when you get out of bed painful? And does it ease off after you have walked for a few minutes?’** **Pain worst on the first steps after rest that eases with a few minutes of walking is close to diagnostic of plantar fasciitis. It costs eight seconds, it is the single most likely heel diagnosis in general practice, and in version B it is the entire station.** **The NEGATIVE answer is worth as much as a positive one — it lets you say WHY plantar fasciitis is not the diagnosis rather than never mentioning it.**

**Three gifts the role-player hands you, each of which you must catch and REUSE**: **‘It looks a bit thicker than the other one — WIDER’** — he offers the deformity before you ever see the card · **‘stiff for about FIFTEEN MINUTES first thing’** — quantified, mechanical, and it argues against an inflammatory arthropathy (‘a bit stiff’ is not an answer) · **‘it doesn't give way — it's STIFF RATHER THAN WOBBLY’** — chronic ligament instability gives LAXITY, and he reports the opposite.

**Name it, then TRANSLATE it — and no ‘intra-articular’, ‘congruity’ or ‘degenerative change’ to a shopkeeper**: **‘The most likely diagnosis is osteoarthritis of your ankle joint. Because it has followed your old fracture, we call it POST-TRAUMATIC osteoarthritis. A joint has a smooth CUSHION of cartilage on the ends of the bones that lets them GLIDE over each other. When a fracture involves a joint, it disturbs those smooth surfaces and the way the joint LINES UP — and over the years that means more WEAR AND TEAR. The cushion thins, the bone underneath thickens, and the joint gets stiff and sore. That process has been going on quietly since your injury, and it has now CAUGHT UP with you.’**

**THE THREE REASONS — THIS IS THE SCORED HALF OF THE TASK**: **‘First, the pain is MECHANICAL — worse when you walk and better when you rest. That is how a worn joint behaves. Second, your right heel is WIDER than the left, which you had noticed yourself — the shape of the bone and joint has changed. Third, and most importantly, the movements of your ankle are PAINFUL IN EVERY DIRECTION AND REDUCED — that points at the joint itself rather than at a tendon or a ligament, because those would hurt in only one direction. And it fits with the fracture you had ten years ago.’**

**The hidden agenda arrives at the end — ‘am I going to end up needing a new ankle? My father had both knees replaced.’** **Park it, then answer it specifically**: **‘Almost certainly not yet. Most people are managed with footwear, exercises, weight management and simple pain relief, and that is where we'll start. Surgery — either FUSING the joint or REPLACING it — is reserved for people whose pain stays severe despite all of that. We're a long way from that conversation.’** **Talking over it to finish your list costs the easiest communication marks in the station.**
plan: **WIPE with consent and confidentiality, acknowledge, check comfort, and SIGNPOST — because you are about to ask this man about diarrhoea, psoriasis and antibiotics in a consultation about his heel.** **‘I'll ask about the pain first, then some general health questions, then a few to make sure nothing serious is being missed — and then I'll examine the foot and ankle.’** Tell him now and none of it seems strange when you get there.

**SITE — OPEN, THEN CLOSED.** **‘Where exactly do you feel the pain?’** → *‘My right heel.’* and he stops. **‘Can you be more specific — is it UNDER the heel, BEHIND the heel, or ALL OVER the heel and ankle?’** → *‘All around it — deep inside more than on the bottom.’* Then the rest of SOCRATES: out of ten · dull or sharp · when it started and is it changing · does it travel · better or worse with anything · **worse standing and walking** · effect on work and home.

**PATTERN — four questions plus the pair.** Wakes him at night · morning or end of the day · **after rest or after activity** · **‘are the first few steps out of bed painful — and does it ease off after a few minutes of walking?’** Then **weight-bearing and gait, asked as BOTH**: **‘have you been limping, or is walking painful?’** and **‘are you able to put your FULL WEIGHT on that foot?’**

**GENERAL MSK SCREEN, five questions in one breath**: swelling · redness · rash · **any change in the SHAPE of the heel or ankle** · **stiffness, and HOW LONG it lasts in the morning** · **‘and have you had any trauma or injury to that ankle?’** **Trauma sits INSIDE the standard screen, which is your safety net — even if you meant to explore the old injury separately and forgot, this catches it. When he says yes, STOP and open it up.**
**EXPLORE THE OLD INJURY IN FULL — the three questions. This is the block the station is built around.**

**RED FLAGS, ANNOUNCED.** **‘These next few I ask everybody with this problem, to make sure nothing serious is being missed.’** **Fevers, sweats or chills · any break in the skin, any sore or ULCER on the foot · DO YOU HAVE DIABETES · change in weight or appetite, lumps, more tired than usual · and IS THERE PAIN THAT IS THERE ALL THE TIME, at rest and at night, THAT DOESN'T CHANGE WITH MOVEMENT.**

**BONE AND JOINT.** Job and how much standing · exercise · **pain in other joints** · family history of arthritis · **rashes or psoriasis** · triggered by red meat, seafood or alcohol · **recent diarrhoea or urethral discharge** · back or buttock pain with prolonged morning stiffness.

**SOFT TISSUE, NERVE AND VESSEL.** **‘Does your ankle ever GIVE WAY, or feel unsteady or wobbly on uneven ground?’** · back pain, pins and needles, numbness or burning in the foot, weakness · **calf or foot pain after a set walking distance that eases when you stand still; colour or temperature change.**

**DRUGS, THEN CLOSURE.** **‘What medications do you take, including anything from the chemist? HAVE YOU HAD ANY ANTIBIOTICS RECENTLY — ANYTHING LIKE CIPROFLOXACIN? Any steroid tablets? Any cholesterol tablets?’** Then other conditions, operations, allergies, smoking, mood, **and ‘was there anything you were hoping I'd cover today?’**

**Ask for the card as a named structure → READ THE THREE DECISIVE FINDINGS ALOUD → name the diagnosis and translate it → THE THREE REASONS → the differentials in plain words with why each is excluded → answer the new-ankle question → the plan → the safety-net → summary.** **Explain to the PATIENT, not the examiner — the stem says so. Turn your chair.**

**Bloods only if red flags or an inflammatory picture**: FBE, CRP and ESR, urate, RF and anti-CCP, HbA1c.

**Management**: paracetamol **1 g up to four times daily, maximum 4 g in 24 hours** · **topical NSAID — diclofenac 1% gel three to four times daily** VERIFY · **footwear and orthoses: cushioned supportive shoes with a STIFF OR ROCKER SOLE to reduce ankle motion; a lace-up brace or a custom ankle-foot orthosis if severe; a walking stick in the OPPOSITE hand during flares** · **physiotherapy for range, calf and peroneal strengthening, balance and gait; podiatry for footwear and orthoses** · **weight reduction — BMI 30, and every kilogram is multiplied through the ankle at every step** · a short oral NSAID course if not contraindicated · **intra-articular corticosteroid for a flare** VERIFY · **orthopaedic referral if refractory: arthroscopic debridement, realignment osteotomy, ARTHRODESIS or total ankle replacement.** **Review 4–6 weeks with the imaging.**

**AVOID**: **corticosteroid injection into or around the Achilles — it precipitates rupture** · **diagnosing plantar fasciitis when the range is painful and restricted in every plane** · oral NSAIDs in the elderly, in renal impairment, or with an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus a diuretic (the TRIPLE WHAMMY) · MRI first line for uncomplicated mechanical heel pain · **continuing a fluoroquinolone in a patient with new Achilles pain** · **reassuring before the red-flag screen is complete.**

**FLUOROQUINOLONES — the drug question that changes the answer.** **Ciprofloxacin, norfloxacin, moxifloxacin cause tendinopathy and tendon RUPTURE, most often the Achilles, and THE RISK PERSISTS FOR WEEKS TO MONTHS AFTER THE COURSE** — higher over 60, with corticosteroids, and in renal impairment. If posterior heel pain follows a quinolone: **stop the drug in consultation with the prescriber, unload the tendon, and NEVER inject corticosteroid into or around the Achilles.**

**Examiner challenges, scripted**: *‘Dorsiflexion of 20° is normal — so is the range really reduced?’* → **‘Dorsiflexion of 20° is within the normal range, but it is PAINFUL. Plantarflexion of 20° against a normal 30–50, and eversion of 10° against a normal 15–25, are clearly reduced, and inversion of 20° is at the lower limit. So my reading is a globally painful ankle with a genuine restriction in at least two planes — which still localises the problem to the JOINT rather than to a single tendon or ligament.’** *‘Could this be a ligament injury from the old sprain?’* → **‘Chronic ligament injury produces LAXITY, not restriction, and pain in the direction that stretches the ligament rather than in all four. His drawer and talar tilt showed no laxity, and he has a DEFORMITY, which a ligament injury does not cause.’**

**DO NOT MISS**: **osteomyelitis or septic arthritis** — fever, a skin break or ulcer, especially in diabetes; SAME-DAY · **Achilles rupture** — a sudden snap, a palpable gap, a positive Thompson; same-day orthopaedics · **calcaneal stress or insufficiency fracture** — a NORMAL X-RAY DOES NOT EXCLUDE IT, the next test is MRI · **malignancy** — rest and night pain unchanged by movement, weight loss · **critical limb ischaemia** · **the diabetic foot — neuropathy plus an ulcer plus deformity is a HIGH-RISK FOOT, not a heel strain.** **A heel spur is a common INCIDENTAL finding and is NOT the cause of the pain — do not offer it as the explanation.**

**VERSION B — 45 F, BMI 32, standing job.** *‘Right under the heel. The first few steps out of bed are agony, then it loosens off after a couple of minutes. By the end of a shift it's back.’* **Plantar fasciitis: stretching the calf and sole, a cushioned heel cup, supportive shoes, less standing, weight loss, simple analgesia.** **‘Slow — months, not weeks — but most settle without any procedure.’** Ultrasound only if unclear; **a fascia over about 4 mm thick supports it.**

**VERSION C — 52 M, new runner, ciprofloxacin a month ago for prostatitis.** **‘Two things loaded that tendon: the new running, and the antibiotic — ciprofloxacin weakens tendons, and the risk lasts weeks after the course. Rest from running, a small heel raise, a physio-guided loading programme. NEVER inject steroid around this tendon — it can rupture. Return at once for a sudden snap or inability to push off.’** **VERSION D — 68 F, diabetic, febrile, ulcer under the heel, struggling to weight-bear.** **‘Fever, a break in the skin over the heel and diabetes together can mean infection that has reached the BONE. Bloods and an X-ray now, and referral to hospital today. The scan that shows this best is an MRI. Please don't weight-bear meanwhile.’**
