stem: General practice. You are the GP. Your next patient is Jenny, a 40-year-old woman, complaining of foot pain. No site is given in the stem.
Tasks: take a focused, relevant history — 6 minutes · physical examination findings will be given to you on a card · explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient.
The same stem has been recalled with three different cards: a, hallux valgus — B, hallux rigidus — C, acute gout.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history (6 minutes)
Receive the physical examination findings on a card
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: THE THREE-QUESTION RULE — ask these of the card, in this order, and the station is over

1 IS THERE A DEFORMITY? Yes → HALLUX VALGUS. 2 IS THERE REDNESS, WARMTH AND MARKED SWELLING? Yes → GOUT (or SEPTIC ARTHRITIS if febrile). 3 IS MOVEMENT REDUCED WITHOUT EITHER OF THOSE? Yes → HALLUX RIGIDUS
CARD A — hallux valgus

DEFORMITY AND SWELLING seen at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. NORMAL MOVEMENTS. NO REDNESS. No other features of arthritis. No fever. Peripheral pulses present, sensation intact. Remaining joints of the foot and ankle normal. Skin intact, no ulcer, no lesion between the toes
CARD B — hallux rigidus
PAIN at the first MTP joint. DECREASED RANGE OF MOVEMENT. NO REDNESS. NO DEFORMITY. Pain NOT triggered by alcohol or red meat. No fever
CARD C — acute gout
REDNESS, WARMTH AND SWELLING of the first MTP joint. PAINFUL ON PALPATION AND ON MOVEMENT, restricted range. NO DEFORMITY. NO FEVER
THE SENTENCE THE EXAMINER IS WAITING FOR — card A

‘There is DEFORMITY, WITH a NORMAL range of movement, and WITHOUT redness — that makes a bunion far more likely than osteoarthritis or gout.’ THREE FINDINGS IN ONE BREATH, each tied to the diagnosis it excludes. A candidate who simply says ‘bunion’ and a candidate who says that sentence SCORE VERY DIFFERENTLY
The one-liners for the other two cards

CARD B: ‘REDUCED RANGE OF MOVEMENT, NO REDNESS AND NO DEFORMITY — hallux rigidus, that is, OSTEOARTHRITIS of the first MTP joint.’ CARD C: ‘RED, WARM, SWOLLEN, EXQUISITELY TENDER with restricted movement, NO DEFORMITY and NO FEVER — acute gout’
Do NOT recite the card item by item, and do NOT say ‘examination is normal’
IT IS NOT NORMAL — there is a deformity. SYNTHESISE: ‘ABNORMAL SHAPE, NORMAL FUNCTION, NO INFLAMMATION’
What you must ask for beyond the joint

TEMPERATURE · inspect the WHOLE foot INCLUDING BETWEEN THE TOES AND THE SOLE · warmth and point tenderness · range of movement, ESPECIALLY DORSIFLEXION of the first MTP · PEDAL PULSES, CAPILLARY REFILL AND MONOFILAMENT SENSATION · gait and FOOTWEAR inspection · AND THE OTHER FOOT
Investigations — and when NOT to order them

IF THE JOINT IS RED, HOT AND SWOLLEN: JOINT ASPIRATION for Gram stain, culture and POLARISED-LIGHT MICROSCOPY — THE ONLY TEST THAT SEPARATES GOUT FROM SEPSIS. Plus FBE, CRP, urate, UEC. IF THE PICTURE IS MECHANICAL: USUALLY NO INVESTIGATION IS NEEDED. Weight-bearing AP, lateral and oblique films only if the diagnosis is uncertain or surgery is contemplated — saying that distinction out loud is a MATURITY MARK
What each film would show

HALLUX VALGUS — lateral deviation of the hallux, WIDENED INTERMETATARSAL ANGLE, lateral subluxation of the sesamoids, medial eminence; joint space often PRESERVED. HALLUX RIGIDUS — joint-space narrowing with a DORSAL OSTEOPHYTE BEST SEEN ON THE LATERAL, subchondral sclerosis and cysts — which is WHY you request a lateral as well as an AP. GOUT — NORMAL IN A FIRST ACUTE ATTACK; chronic disease shows PUNCHED-OUT erosions with OVERHANGING EDGES, PRESERVED JOINT SPACE and normal bone density VERIFY

dx: **ONE HISTORY, ONE EXAMINATION CARD, THREE DIFFERENT ANSWERS — and the card decides.** **DEFORMITY without inflammation is a BUNION. STIFFNESS without inflammation is OSTEOARTHRITIS of the first MTP joint. INFLAMMATION without deformity, with a trigger in the history, is GOUT.** **The station is not testing whether you know what gout is — it is testing whether you READ THE FINDINGS YOU WERE GIVEN instead of the recall you memorised.**

**‘FIRST MTP JOINT’ IS A LOCATION, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.** **The recall circulating after the exam said ‘first MTP joint — gout’, and people repeated it. Three completely different conditions live there.** **Candidates who fail this station almost always fail the same way: they recognised ‘first MTP joint’, retrieved ‘gout’ from the recall, and never looked at what they had been handed.**

**Definitions, for the patient and the examiner**: **HALLUX VALGUS — a progressive DEFORMITY in which the first metatarsal deviates medially and the great toe deviates laterally, producing a prominent MEDIAL EMINENCE that becomes painful in footwear. It is a DEFORMITY, NOT AN ARTHRITIS.** **HALLUX RIGIDUS — simply OSTEOARTHRITIS: cartilage loss with DORSAL OSTEOPHYTE formation, progressive loss of movement, most obviously of DORSIFLEXION, and pain on PUSH-OFF. There is NO angular deformity.** **GOUT — acute inflammatory arthritis from monosodium urate crystal deposition, classically the first MTP joint (PODAGRA), abrupt onset PEAKING WITHIN 12–24 HOURS.**

**SAY BOTH NAMES AND TRANSLATE THE LATIN — it scores the terminology mark AND the communication mark in one sentence**: **‘a bunion — the medical name is HALLUX VALGUS’** · **‘osteoarthritis of the big toe joint, sometimes called HALLUX RIGIDUS’.** **Mnemonic: VALgus = VALgus deformity; RIGIDus = RIGID, stiff joint.** **Calling a bunion ‘hallux rigidus’ in front of the examiner is a named fail.**

**THE SITE QUESTION IS THE HIGHEST-YIELD QUESTION IN ANY FOOT, ANKLE OR HEEL STATION — and it is the one candidates skip because the patient said ‘my foot’ and they accepted it.** **The stem DELIBERATELY WITHHOLDS the site.** **‘Where exactly in the foot — the FRONT, the MIDDLE, the HEEL, or the ANKLE? Can you point with one finger? Is it one spot or spread out? IS IT ONE FOOT OR BOTH?’** **One question and your differential list has halved.** **Bilateral points to a systemic or biomechanical cause; a single hot joint points to crystal or septic arthritis.**

**KNOWING THE SITE NARROWS EMPHASIS — IT DOES NOT LICENCE A ONE-DIAGNOSIS HISTORY.** The full foot structure still runs: bone and joint, soft tissue, neurovascular, skin and nails. **Three questions about the big toe and nothing else is a named fail.**

**‘Worse in shoes’ belongs to TWO diagnoses — the bunion (pressure on the medial bump) and MORTON'S NEUROMA (compression of the interdigital nerve). Separate them with one question**: **‘Do you wear tight or narrow shoes? Is it a BURNING pain BETWEEN THE TOES, or an ACHE AT THE BUMP?’**

**ASK THE GOUT QUESTION THE RIGHT WAY.** **‘Do you eat red meat?’ is the WRONG question — almost everyone does, and a ‘yes’ will lure you towards gout.** **The question is whether it BRINGS THE PAIN ON.** Here it does not — and **that NEGATIVE is worth saying out loud when you present.**

**CORRECTION — why contraception is in this case.** **The oral contraceptive pill is NOT a gout risk factor.** What it tells you is that **she is PREMENOPAUSAL — and primary gout is UNCOMMON BEFORE THE MENOPAUSE, because oestrogen is uricosuric.** **That is a genuine reason to be cautious about diagnosing gout in a 40-year-old woman on the basis of joint site alone.** **The medications that DO matter are DIURETICS and LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN — ask for those by name.**

**SERUM URATE IS A TRAP IN AN ACUTE ATTACK.** **It is frequently NORMAL OR LOW during a flare, because urate shifts into the joint — and a raised level in an asymptomatic person does not diagnose gout.** **Check it 2–4 WEEKS AFTER the attack settles, and use it to GUIDE URATE-LOWERING THERAPY rather than to make the diagnosis.** VERIFY **Target below 0.36 mmol/L, or below 0.30 with tophi.**
plan: **WIPE with confidentiality, then ‘are you in pain right now? Would you like something for it?’** — four seconds, and it is on the mark sheet in almost every pain station. Then the open question.

**THE SITE QUESTION, asked properly — front, middle, heel or ankle; point with one finger; one spot or spread out; ONE FOOT OR BOTH.** *‘It's here — at the base of my big toe. Mostly the right, but the left is starting too.’*

**Explore the pain.** How long · **suddenly or gradually** · any injury before it started · dull ache, sharp, or **burning** · does it travel · out of ten · what makes it worse and what helps · **‘IS IT WORSE WHEN YOU WEAR YOUR SHOES?’** · impact on daily life and work. **Gradual over years + worse in shoes + better barefoot is a MECHANICAL, pressure-related forefoot problem — and that already makes gout unlikely BEFORE you have seen the card.**

**Pattern, weight-bearing and footwear.** Night pain or waking · **morning or end of the day** · **rest or activity** · **able to put full weight on it** · **limping** · **what shoes — narrow across the front? heels?** · **‘is it worse when you PUSH OFF, or walk UPHILL?’** **Weight-bearing and limp are compulsory in every lower-limb station; footwear is compulsory in every foot station — and asking it earns marks TWICE, as a clue and as the first line of treatment.**
**General MSK screen**: swelling · redness or warmth · rashes anywhere · stiffness in the joint · **any DEFORMITY or change in the shape of the toe** · any injury, trauma or accident.

**RED FLAGS, ANNOUNCED**: **‘I'm now going to run through a checklist of possible causes; some questions will sound unrelated but I ask them of everyone.’** Fever, chills or sweats · unwell in herself · **lumps or bumps** · weight loss without trying · **night pain that wakes her** · **any break in the skin, ulcer or infection on the foot.**

**BONE AND JOINT.** **OA** — occupation, long periods standing or walking, excessive exercise. **RA** — other joint pains, family history of arthritis, **morning stiffness and HOW LONG.** **Psoriatic** — rash, scaly patches, **nail changes.** **GOUT** — **does red meat or beer BRING THE PAIN ON**, previous attacks, **lumps around joints or ears (tophi).** **Reactive** — recent diarrhoea, vaginal discharge, **red or painful eyes.**

**SOFT TISSUE, NEUROVASCULAR, SKIN AND NAILS.** **Plantar fasciitis** — heel pain worst with the first few steps in the morning. **Morton's neuroma** — burning or electric pain between the toes, a pebble in the shoe, relieved by removing the shoe. **Vascular** — calf pain on walking relieved by rest, cold feet, smoking. **Neurological** — numbness, pins and needles or burning especially at night, back pain down the leg, weakness or tripping. **Skin and nails** — ingrown toenail, corn, callus, wart, ulcer, **itching or peeling between the toes.**

**SADMA, with the deliberate items.** Smoking · **how much alcohol and what kind** · recreational drugs · **medications INCLUDING FLUID TABLETS, ASPIRIN and anything from the chemist** · **contraception** · allergies · **diabetes, high blood pressure or kidney problems** · operations · family history · **‘and is there anything I haven't asked that you were hoping to discuss?’**

**Functional and psychosocial impact, closure and summary. Her hidden agenda is SURGERY — her mother had the same deformity and had both feet operated on. If she does not raise it, you should.** Then **read the card as a PATTERN, name it, translate it, give the THREE FINDINGS that drove it, the differentials each with one clause, the plan, and the safety-net.**
pefe: **The numbers** VERIFY : **INTERMETATARSAL ANGLE NORMALLY UNDER ABOUT 9°, HALLUX VALGUS ANGLE UNDER ABOUT 15°** — these guide the CHOICE of surgical procedure, they do not decide whether to operate · **inflammatory morning stiffness is OVER 30–60 minutes, mechanical is UNDER 30 — hers is five** · **trauma plus inability to weight-bear FOUR STEPS means image for fracture** · **the OCP MATTERS only as a MARKER of premenopausal STATUS, since oestrogen is uricosuric** · gout peaks within 12–24 hours · urate target below 0.36 mmol/L, below 0.30 with tophi. **VERIFY every dose, angle and THRESHOLD against CURRENT THERAPEUTIC GUIDELINES before quoting it.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS NOT THE DIAGNOSIS. It is whether your formulation is visibly built from HISTORY PLUS EXAMINATION, and whether you say WHICH FINDINGS DROVE IT.** **Two candidates can both say ‘bunion’; the one who says ‘deformity with normal movement and no redness’, from the card, passes.**

**SAYING IT TO HER, verbatim**: **‘Jenny, I think the pain is COMING from a bunion. The medical name is hallux valgus. It's a change in the shape of the joint at the base of the big toe: over years the big toe gradually leans across towards the other toes, and the bone BEHIND it DRIFTS the other way, so a bump forms on the INSIDE of your foot. Because that bump STICKS out, it PRESSES INSIDE your shoe — which is exactly why you told me it's worse in shoes and fine barefoot. The hard patch of skin over it is from that RUBBING. It does tend to run in FAMILIES, which fits with your mother.’** **Then the plan: ‘the most IMPORTANT thing is footwear — wide, deep, soft-FRONTED shoes with a low heel. I'll add a bunion pad, SIMPLE pain relief, and refer you to a PODIATRIST for the hard skin and for an INSOLE. I'll be HONESTLY clear with you: splints and exercises will NOT straighten an established bunion. Surgery works well, but we reserve it for when pain is LIMITING what you can do — not for appearance.’** **Safety-net: come back if it becomes red, hot and much more painful, if you get a fever, or if the skin BREAKS down. Review in six to eight weeks.**

**Her differentials, in plain words with the REASONS**: **hallux rigidus — but your joint isn't stiff · gout — no redness or heat, gradual not overnight, and food and alcohol don't TRIGGER it · infection in the joint — no fever and you're well · rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis — no other joints, no prolonged morning stiffness, no rash or nail change · a TRAPPED nerve between the toes — your pain is at the joint, not burning between the toes · a stress fracture — nothing has changed in your activity and the tenderness isn't over the other bones.**

**HALLUX VALGUS management — FOOTWEAR IS THE TREATMENT.** **Wide, deep, soft toe-box; low heel; lace or strap so the foot does not slide forward** · **bunion pad or silicone shield over the medial eminence, toe spacer, orthosis if there is associated pronation** · paracetamol and topical NSAID · **podiatry for callus and pressure management, physiotherapy for foot intrinsic strengthening** · **surgery (osteotomy ± soft-tissue realignment) ONLY if pain persistently limits function despite conservative measures.** **Be honest: SPLINTS AND EXERCISES WILL NOT STRAIGHTEN AN ESTABLISHED DEFORMITY, and surgery for APPEARANCE ALONE is not recommended.**

**HALLUX RIGIDUS management** — **a STIFF-SOLED OR ROCKER-SOLE shoe, or a carbon-fibre plate / MORTON'S EXTENSION orthosis, to stop the toe dorsiflexing at push-off. THIS IS THE HIGHEST-YIELD INTERVENTION.** Activity modification — reduce hill walking, sprinting and deep squatting; low-impact exercise instead. Paracetamol and topical NSAID first. Physiotherapy and weight management. **Intra-articular corticosteroid for temporary relief. Surgery if refractory — CHEILECTOMY (removal of the dorsal osteophyte) for earlier disease, ARTHRODESIS for advanced.**

**GOUT — acute attack, CHOOSE ONE, started as early as possible** VERIFY : **NSAID at full anti-inflammatory dose** if renal, cardiovascular and GI risk allow · **COLCHICINE, low-dose regimen** — reduce in renal impairment, alert to interactions · **PREDNISOLONE, a short oral course**, particularly where the other two are contraindicated. dx: **Cellulitis of the right lower leg, on a background of PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE — a deliberately MIXED case.** **You are marked on a comprehensive LEG PAIN history that ARRIVES at cellulitis — not on a cellulitis history that never asked the vascular, neurogenic and red-flag groups.**

**WHY CANDIDATES FAIL: the stem says leg pain and 39°C, and the whole room reaches for cellulitis.** The candidate asks about rashes, gardening, bushwalking, scratches and insect bites, **finds every positive, is delighted, and runs out of four minutes having never asked a single vascular, neurogenic or red-flag question. They then fail — WITH THE CORRECT DIAGNOSIS.**

**THE ROLE-PLAYER IS THE BAIT.** She hands you cellulitis in the first fifteen seconds and **keeps handing it to you, and is briefed to steer back to it if you move on.** **Every positive she gives you is bait. Acknowledge it, PARK it — ‘thank you, I'll come back to the rash, I promise’ — and keep working through your groups. You can return to the rash with ninety seconds left and still get every mark for it.**

**FOUR BLOCKS, ROUGHLY ONE MINUTE EACH, and the infection detail is LAST**: **PAIN AND SWELLING · VASCULAR · NEUROGENIC · MSK, SKIN AND RED FLAGS.** **Four minutes is about TWENTY-FIVE QUESTIONS — budget them before you go in: six on pain and swelling, six vascular, four neurogenic, the rest on MSK, red flags and infection. Anything you have not planned, you will not ask.**

**THE SWELLING IS IN THE PRESENTING COMPLAINT, SO IT IS ON THE MARK SHEET — three questions, three differentials moved**: **HOW FAR UP** tells you the extent to mark and follow · **ONE LEG OR BOTH** separates cellulitis and DVT from venous eczema and heart failure · **DOES IT SETTLE OVERNIGHT** separates dependent oedema from an acute inflammatory process.

**THE QUESTION THAT FINDS THE SECOND DIAGNOSIS — and the whole reason the station exists.** **Do NOT ask ‘any circulation problems?’ and accept ‘no’. Patients do not know they have arterial disease; they know they get a cramp when they walk to the shops.** **ASK THE SYMPTOM, NOT THE LABEL: ‘did you get cramping in the calf after walking a certain distance? HOW FAR — and does it settle if you STAND STILL?’** **That pair also distinguishes VASCULAR claudication (a predictable distance, relieved by standing still within minutes) from NEUROGENIC (variable distance, relieved only by SITTING OR LEANING FORWARD, often with back pain and paraesthesiae).**

**THE FEVER DOES NOT NARROW THE LIST AS MUCH AS YOU THINK.** Fever with a painful leg fits cellulitis — **but also septic arthritis, necrotising fasciitis, osteomyelitis, an abscess, an infected ulcer, GOUT (which can produce a low-grade fever and a hot red joint), and DVT, which classically produces a low-grade temperature.** **Treat the fever as a reason to WIDEN the red-flag screen, not as permission to stop thinking.**

**Two answers doing quiet work in the history**: **‘spread since yesterday’ — DAYS, NOT HOURS, which argues AGAINST necrotising fasciitis** · **‘I can still get about’ — she is WEIGHT-BEARING, which argues against a septic joint.** **Notice both and quote them back later.**

**EXPLAIN BOTH PROBLEMS — two diagnoses were put in this leg deliberately**: **‘Marion, there are two things going on in that leg. The first is why you're unwell today: an infection of the skin and the tissue just under it, called CELLULITIS. Bacteria that normally live harmlessly on the skin have got in through a break — most likely that scratch, and the cracked skin between your toes — and are spreading through the tissue. The second I found while examining you, and it has been building far longer. I can't feel the pulses in your right foot, the skin is cool and the hair has worn away over your shin. That fits with NARROWED ARTERIES — the pipes carrying blood down to the foot have furred up — and it explains the cramp you get after two hundred metres. It matters today because A LEG WITH A POOR BLOOD SUPPLY HEALS MORE SLOWLY.’**

**THE DISPOSITION SENTENCE — DO NOT SOFTEN IT**: **‘Your temperature is 39, your blood pressure is lower than I'd like at 90 over 60, and your heart is running at 110. That combination tells me the infection is affecting your WHOLE BODY, not just the leg. So I'm NOT going to send you home with tablets today. I'm going to put a drip in, take blood cultures, give you fluids and start intravenous antibiotics, and arrange for you to be seen in hospital. I know that's more than you came in expecting.’**

Have you felt FAINT, CONFUSED or very unwell in yourself? Any chest pain or shortness of breath? Any weight loss or night sweats?’**

**ONLY NOW, THE INFECTION DETAIL.** The rash — when it appeared, spreading, blisters or discharge · fevers or shakes · **any break in the skin: a scratch, bite, cut, gardening, bushwalking** · **ANY CRACKING OR ITCHING BETWEEN THE TOES** — tinea pedis is one of the commonest portals of entry, treating it prevents recurrence, and almost no candidate asks · leg ulcers · previous cellulitis in this leg · swelling that never fully settles.

**BACKGROUND, FAST — and the allergy question is NOT optional because you are about to prescribe a penicillin.** Other conditions, **especially diabetes** · medications · **‘any allergies, particularly to penicillin — AND WHAT HAPPENED?’** — a rash decades ago is not the same as anaphylaxis · **tetanus status** · smoking · **‘who is at home with you?’** — if the observations are borderline, social circumstances are part of the disposition decision, and saying so shows you are thinking about disposition, not just diagnosis.

But a systolic of 90 with a pulse of 110 and a temperature of 39 in a patient with a clear source meets RED-FLAG CRITERIA on our sepsis pathway, and qSOFA counts a systolic of 100 or below. I would manage her as sepsis: access, cultures, lactate, fluids, intravenous antibiotics, and reassess.’**

**‘Would you put compression on that leg?’** → **‘NOT before I know the arterial supply. Her pedal pulses are absent and Buerger's is positive, so compression could cause ISCHAEMIC DAMAGE. I would elevate the leg, treat the infection, and measure an ankle–brachial index once the acute episode settles before considering any compression.’**

**‘When would you stop calling this cellulitis?’** → **THREE findings would change it: ‘if the JOINT were swollen with pain on PASSIVE movement, it becomes SEPTIC ARTHRITIS. If the pain were OUT OF PROPORTION, with bullae, crepitus or tenderness spreading BEYOND the red margin, it becomes NECROTISING FASCIITIS. And if there were NO RASH AT ALL with a swollen tender calf, I would be investigating for a DEEP VEIN THROMBOSIS instead.’**

**AVOID**: **treating bilateral chronic red legs as cellulitis — that is VENOUS ECZEMA until proven otherwise** · **compression before excluding arterial disease** · **prescribing a penicillin without asking about allergy and what happened** · **sending home a hypotensive tachycardic febrile patient on oral antibiotics** · **swabbing intact erythematous skin and calling it a microbiological diagnosis** · **spending your four minutes on the rash.**

**The safety-net, verbatim**: **‘Come back immediately — or go to the emergency department — if the redness SPREADS PAST THE LINE I'VE DRAWN, if the pain becomes MUCH WORSE THAN THE LEG LOOKS, if BLISTERS appear, if you get shakes or feel FAINT OR CONFUSED, if you start vomiting, or if you cannot walk on it. Otherwise I'll see you in 24 to 48 hours to check the mark.’**

**VERSION B — septic arthritis.** *‘My knee's swollen too and I can't bend it — any movement is agony.’* **‘What concerns me MORE than the skin is the knee joint itself. A swollen joint where every movement hurts means we assume infection INSIDE the joint until proven otherwise. A specialist needs to take fluid from it with a needle, IDEALLY BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS START, because that identifies the bug.’** **Cellulitis overlying a joint leaves that joint moving FREELY AND PAINLESSLY.**

**VERSION C — necrotising fasciitis.** Twelve hours, **pain far out of proportion, spreading while you watch, early blisters, dusky skin, vomiting, hypotension.** **‘I'm calling an ambulance and the surgical team NOW. You'll need an operation as well as antibiotics into the vein, and WE CAN'T WAIT FOR SCANS.’** **VERSION D — DVT.** Unilateral calf swelling and tenderness, **no rash**, low-grade temperature, five days after knee replacement. **Wells score and compression ultrasound — antibiotics would not treat this.**

**VERSION E — the mimic.** Both legs red, scaly and itchy for months, varicose veins, ankles swell by evening, **afebrile**, third antibiotic course this year. **‘Cellulitis is nearly always in ONE leg, comes on over DAYS and causes FEVER; yours is in BOTH legs, has been MONTHS, and you have no temperature. Moisturiser, a short course of steroid ointment and compression — BUT I'll check the circulation FIRST, because compression is only safe if the arteries are healthy.’** SA — **SA Health sepsis pathway · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Hospital in the Home or OPAT through the regional LHN · PATS for vascular review in Adelaide · ACCHS and Closing the Gap, relevant when adherence over seven days matters.**

**Gout: sudden, exquisite, often first MTP — CAN MIMIC CELLULITIS AND CAUSE FEVER.** Baker's: sudden calf pain and swelling with knee arthritis. Trauma: a clear precipitant
Joint involvement, previous attacks, diuretics and alcohol; **a popliteal swelling that has disappeared**; history of injury
Urate (unhelpful acutely), aspiration if uncertain; ultrasound for a Baker's cyst; X-ray if trauma. Soon

stem: General practice. James Whitlock, 45, with left knee pain present for six months. He is concerned there is something wrong with his knee. Afebrile with normal observations.

Tasks: take a focused, relevant history — 6 minutes · ask the examiner for the physical examination findings, given on a card at six minutes · explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient.
The concern is written into the stem, which means it is scored — acknowledge it in your opening statement, because saying it at the end does not recover the mark.
tasks: Take a focused, relevant history from the patient (6 minutes)
Ask the examiner for the physical examination findings, given on a card at six minutes
Explain your diagnosis and your differential diagnoses to the patient
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: ASK AS A STRUCTURE — and do NOT forget the hip and the lumbar spine

‘INSPECTION for swelling, redness, DEFORMITY, ALIGNMENT and QUADRICEPS WASTING, compared with the other side · PALPATION for warmth, an EFFUSION, JOINT LINE tenderness, tenderness OVER THE PATELLA and AT ITS INFERIOR POLE, and the POPLITEAL FOSSA · ACTIVE AND PASSIVE range and CREPITUS · then CLARKE'S PATELLAR GRIND TEST, McMURRAY'S, and the LIGAMENT STRESS TESTS · and I would also examine THE HIP AND THE LUMBAR SPINE, check GAIT, and assess NEUROVASCULAR STATUS.’ In a knee station the referred causes are EXAMINED, not just asked about — and it costs one sentence
VERSION A card — chondromalacia
INSPECTION NORMAL — no swelling, no redness, no deformity. PAIN ON PRESSURE OVER THE PATELLA. NO Clarke's test result given
Reading version A aloud

‘So a NORMAL-LOOKING knee with NO swelling or redness, and TENDERNESS ON DIRECT PRESSURE over the patella itself.’ The NORMAL inspection is POSITIVE EVIDENCE — a bursitis you can SEE, so a normal-looking knee ranks it second
VERSION B card — chronic meniscal tear
Inspection NORMAL. Palpation NORMAL. McMURRAY'S TEST POSITIVE
VERSION C card — osteoarthritis
GENU VARUM. QUADRICEPS WASTING. CREPITUS. REDUCED FLEXION. MEDIAL JOINT LINE TENDERNESS. NO WARMTH, no erythema
CLARKE'S TEST (patellar grind, Zohlen's sign)

Supine, leg extended. PRESS THE PATELLA DOWN into the trochlear groove and ask the patient to TIGHTEN THE QUADRICEPS. RETROPATELLAR PAIN is a positive test. VERIFY — a useful bedside pointer but NOT SPECIFIC; it can be uncomfortable in normal knees, so NEVER rest the diagnosis on it alone
Investigations — OFTEN NONE, and saying so is a MARK, not a gap
Chondromalacia, prepatellar bursitis and patellar tendinopathy are CLINICAL diagnoses. SAY THAT OUT LOUD
When to image, and only if it changes something

WEIGHT-BEARING X-RAY (AP, lateral, SKYLINE) if osteoarthritis is uncertain, if there is deformity, or if surgery is being considered · BLOODS if inflammatory features: FBE, ESR, CRP, URATE, RF and anti-CCP (HLA-B27 only on specialist advice) VERIFY · JOINT ASPIRATION for crystals and culture if the joint is hot and swollen — diagnostic for gout and MANDATORY if sepsis is possible · ULTRASOUND for a suspected Baker's cyst, bursitis or possible DVT · MRI ONLY where the result would change management, typically a suspected mechanical meniscal tear with TRUE LOCKING
What the X-ray shows in knee OA

JOINT SPACE NARROWING, usually the MEDIAL compartment, with SUBCHONDRAL SCLEROSIS and OSTEOPHYTES. But THE DIAGNOSIS IS CLINICAL — radiographic change correlates POORLY with symptoms, and imaging everyone is a named error
The pictures worth recognising

PREPATELLAR BURSITIS — a WELL-DEFINED swelling sitting IN FRONT OF the patella, NOT inside the joint; direct pressure hurts, walking and stairs relatively spared; HOT WITH FEVER means SEPTIC bursitis. BAKER'S CYST — fluid-filled swelling in the POPLITEAL FOSSA, usually secondary to OA, RA or internal derangement; RUPTURE causes sudden calf pain, swelling and bruising and MIMICS A DVT — ultrasound answers BOTH questions

dx: **Chondromalacia patellae / patellofemoral pain syndrome (version A), with PREPATELLAR BURSITIS as the close second** · **chronic meniscal tear (version B)** · **knee osteoarthritis (version C).** **THE PREDOMINANT ASSESSMENT AREA IS DIAGNOSTIC FORMULATION — everything else is scaffolding.**

**THE TWO WORDS THAT CHANGE EVERYTHING ARE ‘SIX MONTHS’.** **This is NOT the acute traumatic knee station.** **ACUTE: the trigger is a single named injury, the key block is the MECHANISM, the top answers are meniscal and ACL tears, and you ask how FAST it swelled.** **CHRONIC: no injury or an old one, the key block is RED FLAGS AND DIFFERENTIALS, the top answers are chondromalacia, bursitis, OA and an old meniscal tear, and you ask whether there is swelling WITHOUT ANY TRAUMA.** **Candidates fail both stations because they cannot tell which one they are in.**

**TWO THINGS DECIDE THIS STATION.** **(1) DID YOU ASK THE RED FLAGS?** Candidates reason that six months of pain cannot be infection or cancer, so they skip the questions. **The examiner is not scoring your PROBABILITY ESTIMATE — they are scoring whether a doctor faced with six months of unexplained joint pain EXCLUDED MALIGNANCY AND INFECTION OUT LOUD.** **(2) WAS YOUR DIFFERENTIAL LIST UNGROUPED AND BROAD?**

**DO NOT GROUP. ‘Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid, gout, psoriatic and reactive arthritis’ is ONE differential box, not five.** **Give one or two from the joint bucket, then MOVE TO A DIFFERENT BUCKET — soft tissue, neurovascular, referred, red flag.** **BREADTH ACROSS BUCKETS IS WHAT SCORES.** The debrief question that matters: **how many BUCKETS did your list cover, not how many diagnoses did you name.**

**THE SITE NARROWS IT BEFORE YOU ASK ANYTHING ELSE.** **FRONT, on or behind the kneecap** → chondromalacia, prepatellar bursitis, patellar tendinopathy, fat pad impingement, Osgood–Schlatter in an adolescent. **MEDIAL** → medial compartment OA, medial meniscal tear, MCL strain, pes anserine bursitis. **LATERAL** → lateral meniscal tear, LCL strain, iliotibial band syndrome in runners. **POSTERIOR** → Baker's cyst, hamstring or gastrocnemius strain, DVT, popliteal artery. **DIFFUSE or cannot localise** → inflammatory arthritis, referred from hip or lumbar spine, generalised OA.

**THE SIX KEY KNEE QUESTIONS — if you forget reactive arthritis nobody minds; if you forget LOCKING and GIVING WAY you have a problem.** **1 LOCKING — ‘does it get stuck so you have to wiggle it free?’ → meniscal tear, loose body, osteochondritis dissecans. 2 GIVING WAY → cruciate insufficiency, patellar instability, quadriceps inhibition. 3 RANGE — ‘can you fully bend and fully straighten it?’ → mechanical block or effusion. 4 PROLONGED SITTING → THE THEATRE SIGN of patellofemoral pain. 5 STAIRS AND SQUATTING → patellofemoral loading, BUT OSTEOARTHRITIS DOES THIS TOO, so it is supportive not diagnostic. 6 CLICKING → the history version of crepitus.**

**THE PATTERN SEPARATES MECHANICAL FROM INFLAMMATORY, and you say the conclusion out loud**: **MORNING-PREDOMINANT with stiffness over 30–60 minutes, several joints, BETTER WITH USE → INFLAMMATORY.** **END-OF-DAY, activity-related, worse with use and better with rest, stiffness lasting a few minutes → MECHANICAL.** **NIGHT PAIN that wakes him is the single most efficient question in the station — it halves the differential list and it is your malignancy and infection screen for the joint.**

**THE THREE-PART FORMULA FOR THE EXPLANATION**: **1 NAME IT simply, in plain English. 2 EXPLAIN what has gone wrong in ONE sentence. 3 GIVE THREE REASONS, NUMBERED — site, aggravating pattern, examination finding.** Then the second differential, the wider list by bucket, the plan and the safety-net. **‘The cartilage on the back of your kneecap has become damaged. Cartilage is the smooth coating that lets the kneecap GLIDE over the bone underneath. When it's worn or softened, the kneecap RUBS rather than glides, and that causes pain.’**

**IN VERSION A, TWO DIAGNOSES SIT CLOSE TOGETHER — and the discriminators are specific.** **A BURSITIS DOES NOT CHANGE WITH STAIRS, and the card says inspection is NORMAL — no swelling, no redness. A BURSITIS YOU CAN SEE.** So chondromalacia goes first and **bursitis goes second, NAMED EXPLICITLY**: *‘a small cushion in front of the kneecap that can become inflamed, usually in people who kneel a lot. Less likely here because there's no swelling or redness to see, you don't kneel at work, and a bursitis doesn't usually get worse on stairs.’*

**ANSWER THE ARTHRITIS FEAR WITH EVIDENCE, NOT BLANKET REASSURANCE — that is the whole skill being tested.** His father had a knee replacement at 60 and he is 45. **‘I thought hard about that, because of your dad. Against arthritis: your morning stiffness lasts a MINUTE OR TWO rather than an hour, only ONE joint is involved, there's no swelling, redness or heat, and no family history of the inflammatory types. I also deliberately checked for the serious causes — a growth in the bone and an infection in the joint — and nothing points that way. I can't be certain from one visit, and if you don't improve I'd reconsider. But I don't think you're heading for your father's knee at 45.’**
plan: **WIPE — and ADDRESS THE STATED CONCERN IN THE OPENING STATEMENT.** The concern is written into the stem; **if you don't acknowledge it now you have lost the communication marks before asking a single question, and saying it at the end does not recover them.** **‘Six months is a long time to be putting up with something, and I can hear you're worried about it. I'm here to help.’** Then agenda, permission, **and ‘are you in any pain right now?’** — still ask, even in a chronic case.

**BOX 1 — the pain (SIQORA).** **SITE offered as FOUR OPTIONS** · out of ten · dull or sharp · how long, constant or intermittent, getting worse · **does it radiate — radiation reopens the back and hip as the source** · better or worse with anything, **and specifically worse on standing and walking** — **weight-bearing pain suggests a joint or cartilage problem; A BURSITIS HURTS ON PRESSURE, NOT ON LOAD** · **‘how is this affecting your life, at home and at work?’**

**BOX 2 — the pattern, five questions.** **‘Any pain at night that wakes you?’** · **morning or end of the day, and HOW LONG is the morning stiffness** · **after rest or after activity** · **limping** · **able to bear weight** — asked twice, deliberately, because it is the most commonly forgotten lower-limb question.

**GENERAL MSK SCREEN, four questions, thirty seconds.** **Swelling — and SWELLING WITHOUT TRAUMA IS A RED FLAG** · redness or rash anywhere · stiffness · **‘have you EVER injured this knee — even years ago?’** **If yes, SWITCH MODES: what happened, was there a twist, any POP, could you weight-bear afterwards, what treatment, DID IT EVER FULLY SETTLE. Version B turns on that answer.**

**RED FLAGS, SIGNPOSTED.** **‘There are a few questions I ask everyone with long-standing joint pain.’** **MALIGNANCY: unintended weight loss · change in appetite · lumps or bumps anywhere · unusual tiredness · night sweats · EVER BEEN TREATED FOR CANCER.** **INFECTION: fevers or chills · has the knee been HOT OR RED · any recent skin infection, cut or injection near the knee.** **SIX MONTHS DOES NOT EXEMPT YOU.**

**THE SIX KEY KNEE QUESTIONS, rehearsed as a block — locking, giving way, full bend and straighten, prolonged sitting, stairs and squatting, clicking.** **Do NOT stop at the stairs answer and announce chondromalacia — osteoarthritis is also worse on stairs. These questions BUILD a case, they do not close it.**

**BOX 3 — JOINT BUCKET.** Other joints — hands, wrists, feet, hips · **family history of arthritis** · rashes, scaly patches, nail changes · **gout: does it come on quickly and go red and hot, triggered by red meat or alcohol, any big toe attacks, any fluid tablets** · **reactive/IBD: recent diarrhoea or blood in the stool, urethral or vaginal discharge, burning on passing urine** · **‘any recent or recurrent sore throats?’** — acute rheumatic fever remains an important cause of joint pain in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, **a genuine equity point, not a throwaway.**

**SOFT TISSUE BUCKET** — occupation, **‘do you do much kneeling, or put direct pressure on your knees at work?’**, jumping sports or a recent increase in training, **‘any lump behind the knee?’** **NEUROVASCULAR AND REFERRED** — back pain now or in the past, pins and needles, weakness, **colour change or coldness in the leg, calf pain on walking relieved by rest**, **‘any hip or groin pain?’** — **in an adolescent that is SUFE until proven otherwise.**

**BOX 4 — CLOSURE.** Occupation and hobbies · impact on work and life · past history, **medications INCLUDING DIURETICS** · allergies, smoking, alcohol · **and the ideas and concerns question, which in this station is scored because the concern is in the stem.**

**Ask for the card as a structure INCLUDING the hip and lumbar spine → read it aloud → NAME IT, explain it in one sentence, give THREE NUMBERED REASONS → the ranked second differential with why it is less likely → the wider list ACROSS BUCKETS in lay language → answer the arthritis fear with evidence → the plan → the safety-net and review at 4–6 weeks.**
pefe: **Management — in a chronic condition THE EXPLANATION IS THE INTERVENTION.** Then: **paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, max 4 g in 24 hours** · **TOPICAL NSAID (diclofenac gel) PREFERRED OVER ORAL for knee pain in older patients**; oral ibuprofen 200–400 mg three times daily with food if no contraindication VERIFY · **activity modification — REDUCE the aggravating load (stairs, squatting, kneeling), DO NOT REST COMPLETELY** · **knee pads and a change of work technique if kneeling is the cause** · **PHYSIOTHERAPY REFERRAL — the mainstay for patellofemoral pain (quadriceps, VMO and hip abductor strengthening), for OA, and for degenerate meniscal tears** · weight management raised gently and without judgement.

**DO NOT MISS**: **septic arthritis or septic bursitis — hot, red, febrile: ASPIRATE AND REFER THE SAME DAY** · **malignancy — night pain, weight loss, a mass, or a history of cancer** · **a TRULY LOCKED knee — a mechanical block needs orthopaedic assessment, not a physiotherapy trial** · **inflammatory arthritis — delayed diagnosis of rheumatoid costs joints, refer early** · **ruptured Baker's cyst versus DVT — they look identical, SCAN** · **referred hip pathology — hip OA in adults, SUFE in adolescents: EXAMINE THE HIP** · **gout presenting in the knee rather than the toe — and urate can be NORMAL during the attack.**

**AVOID**: grouping every arthritis as a single differential and calling it five · **labelling it ‘wear and tear’ and stopping — that is not a plan** · **ARTHROSCOPY for a degenerate meniscal tear or for osteoarthritis — current Australian guidance does NOT support it in the absence of TRUE MECHANICAL LOCKING** VERIFY · **imaging everyone — radiographic osteoarthritis is common and correlates poorly with pain** · long-term oral NSAIDs without reviewing renal function, blood pressure and ulcer risk · **opioids for chronic non-cancer knee pain** · **reassuring without a review plan, or promising a knee replacement.**

**THE JARGON TRANSLATOR — use it, and check understanding twice.** ‘Chondromalacia patellae’ → **‘the cartilage on the back of your kneecap is damaged, so it rubs instead of gliding’** · ‘bursa’ → **‘a small cushion in front of the kneecap that has become inflamed’** · ‘meniscus’ → **‘a cushion-like pad of cartilage inside the knee’** · ‘Baker's cyst’ → **‘a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee’** · ‘inflammatory arthritis’ → **‘a type of arthritis where the body's immune system attacks the joints’** · ‘radiculopathy’ → **‘a pinched nerve in the back sending pain down the leg’** · ‘crepitus’ → **‘the grinding or clicking you can feel in the joint’** · ‘metastasis’ → **‘a cancer that has spread to the bone’**.

**The safety-net — say all four**: **‘Come back sooner if the knee becomes HOT, RED AND SWOLLEN or you develop a FEVER; if it LOCKS and won't straighten; if the pain starts WAKING YOU AT NIGHT; or if you start LOSING WEIGHT without trying.’** Then **review in four to six weeks**; **‘if it isn't improving by then, we'll reconsider the diagnosis and think about scans or a specialist opinion’**; and written information.

**‘What would you do if he doesn't improve?’** → **‘I would REASSESS THE DIAGNOSIS rather than repeat the same plan. I'd check adherence to the physiotherapy programme, re-examine including Clarke's test, the hip and the lumbar spine, and then consider a weight-bearing X-ray. If inflammatory features had emerged I'd send FBE, ESR, CRP, urate, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, and refer to rheumatology. MRI I would reserve for genuine mechanical symptoms.’**

**VERSION B — the chronic meniscal tear.** *‘It's worse when I walk on it. And now you ask — it does lock sometimes; I have to wiggle it to free it. I twisted it playing football about fifteen years ago.’* **‘The most likely problem is a tear of the MENISCUS — a cushion-like pad of cartilage inside the knee — most likely dating from that old twisting injury. My reasons: the knee LOCKS, which happens when a torn flap catches in the joint; there was an UNTREATED twisting injury; and McMURRAY'S TEST IS POSITIVE.’** **THE TRAP: referring straight for arthroscopy. In a middle-aged knee with a degenerate tear and NO TRUE MECHANICAL BLOCK, PHYSIOTHERAPY COMES FIRST — surgery is for the genuinely locked knee.**

**VERSION C — osteoarthritis.** *‘It aches after I've been on my feet. Worse going downstairs. Stiff for about ten minutes in the morning. The knee grinds and clicks.’* **‘My reasons: age over 45 with activity-related pain relieved by rest; morning stiffness lasting only about TEN MINUTES, which fits a MECHANICAL rather than an inflammatory arthritis; and on examination bow-leg alignment, wasting of the thigh muscle, crepitus and medial joint line tenderness with NO WARMTH. THIS IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS — I would not routinely X-ray, since radiological change correlates poorly with symptoms.’** **Plan: EXERCISE AND WEIGHT MANAGEMENT ARE FIRST LINE — NOT REST.** Physiotherapy, **GLA:D** where available, topical NSAID, a walking aid if needed. **Surgery is for people whose function and quality of life are significantly limited despite all of that.**

**Curveballs a partner can add**: **GOUT** — flares after barbecues and beer, red and hot, on a thiazide → **aspiration for crystals is definitive, urate may be normal during the attack, review the diuretic.** **RHEUMATOID** — stiff over an hour, both hands, exhausted → **switch buckets, FBE/ESR/CRP/RF/anti-CCP, EARLY rheumatology referral.** **SEPTIC JOINT** — swollen and feverish → **stop the differential list, urgent aspiration and same-day referral.** **RED FLAG** — wakes at night, five kilos lost → complete the malignancy screen, examine for masses and nodes, X-ray, urgent review. **ADOLESCENT** — 14, normal knee, limping → **examine the hip: SUFE until proven otherwise; night pain plus weight loss means OSTEOSARCOMA at the distal femur or proximal tibia.**

SA — **physiotherapy is the mainstay, so use a GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement for subsidised visits, regional LHN telehealth physiotherapy and rheumatology, and GLA:D programmes for osteoarthritis** VERIFY · **PATS for travel to Adelaide for rheumatology, orthopaedics or MRI** · **kneeling trades — carpet layers, tilers, concreters: ReturnToWorkSA and a work capacity certificate, SafeWork SA for the hazard, knee pads and task rotation** · **ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officer, Closing the Gap PBS, and remember ACUTE RHEUMATIC FEVER — ask about sore throats and skin sores** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** for a septic joint in a remote setting · **name the out-of-pocket cost of private physiotherapy, imaging and orthopaedic review against public waiting times, and offer the bulk-billed pathway.**
ddx: **Bone tumour or metastasis**
**NIGHT PAIN, weight loss, known cancer**; an ADOLESCENT with persistent pain
Night sweats, lumps, appetite, tiredness, **focal bony tenderness**
**X-ray, then urgent referral; bloods including CALCIUM and ALP.** Urgent
**Septic arthritis / septic bursitis**
**FEVER, hot red swollen joint, unwell**, immunosuppression, skin breach over the knee
**Exquisite pain on ANY movement, warmth**
**Urgent ASPIRATION and hospital referral — never delay for imaging.** Emergency
**Chondromalacia patellae / patellofemoral pain**
**RETROPATELLAR or peripatellar pain, worse on STAIRS, SQUATTING and after PROLONGED SITTING (the THEATRE SIGN)**
**Pain on pressure over the patella, positive CLARKE'S test, NO swelling, NO redness**
**Clinical diagnosis; imaging rarely needed. PHYSIOTHERAPY IS THE MAINSTAY.** Routine
**Prepatellar bursitis**
**Repetitive KNEELING — carpet layers, tilers, carpenters, hockey goalkeepers, cleaners**
**Localised swelling and redness OVER the patella, warm, tender to DIRECT PRESSURE, JOINT MOVEMENT ITSELF PRESERVED**
Clinical; **aspirate only if SEPTIC bursitis is suspected**; avoid kneeling, use knee pads. Routine unless septic
**Osteoarthritis**
**Age over 45, activity-related pain, morning stiffness UNDER 30 min, worse DOWNSTAIRS**, obesity, prior injury or malalignment
**Crepitus, GENU VARUM, quadriceps wasting, reduced flexion, medial joint line tenderness, NO warmth**

Rheumatoid arthritis
**Morning stiffness OVER 30–60 min, SEVERAL joints, SYMMETRICAL, hands and wrists**, systemic symptoms
Other joints, family history, fatigue, **swelling WITHOUT trauma**
RF, anti-CCP, ESR/CRP; **EARLY rheumatology referral — delay costs joints.** Semi-urgent
Gout / pseudogout
**Rapid-onset attacks, red hot swollen joint**, triggered by red meat, alcohol, dehydration or **DIURETICS**
**Previous first MTP attacks, tophi, diuretic use**, renal impairment
**Joint aspiration for crystals is definitive; SERUM URATE MAY BE NORMAL DURING AN ACUTE ATTACK.** Semi-urgent
Psoriatic · reactive · IBD-associated arthritis
Rash, **NAIL PITTING**, recent gastro or genitourinary infection, bowel symptoms, eye inflammation
**Examine the SKIN AND NAILS**; diarrhoea, urethral or vaginal discharge, back pain and enthesitis
Inflammatory markers; rheumatology referral. Routine
**Chronic or degenerate meniscal tear**
**OLD injury, often untreated; MECHANICAL symptoms — LOCKING, catching, giving way**; worse on walking and twisting
**Joint line tenderness, POSITIVE McMURRAY'S, effusion, inability to fully extend**
**MRI if it would change management. ARTHROSCOPY FOR A DEGENERATE TEAR IN A MIDDLE-AGED KNEE IS NOT RECOMMENDED.** Routine unless locked
Patellar tendinopathy · old cruciate injury
**JUMPING sports; pain BELOW the patella**, worse with activity · injury years ago with **ongoing GIVING WAY**
**Tenderness at the INFERIOR POLE — tilt the patella by pressing on the superior pole** · Lachman, drawer and stress tests, quadriceps wasting
Clinical; **ECCENTRIC LOADING programme** · physiotherapy, specialist opinion if instability limits function. Routine
**Baker's (popliteal) cyst ± rupture**
**Lump BEHIND the knee**, usually secondary to OA, RA or internal derangement; **RUPTURE gives sudden calf pain and BRUISING**
Posterior fullness; sudden calf pain and bruising around the ankle
**ULTRASOUND — and it EXCLUDES THE DVT IT MIMICS.** Treat the underlying joint disease. Routine; urgent if DVT possible
Osteochondritis dissecans · Osgood–Schlatter
**Adolescent or young adult**; OCD gives locking and effusion; **Osgood–Schlatter gives TIBIAL TUBEROSITY pain with jumping**
Age, sport, localised tenderness at the tibial tuberosity, mechanical symptoms
X-ray; **OCD needs orthopaedic referral, Osgood–Schlatter is self-limiting.** Routine
Lumbar radiculopathy · PAD · DVT
Back pain radiating to the knee, dermatomal · **calf or thigh pain on walking relieved by rest** · **unilateral calf swelling with recent immobility or travel**
Pins and needles, weakness, straight-leg raise, reflexes · pulses, colour, temperature, hair loss · calf tenderness, swelling, warmth
Normal back and neurological examination excludes it clinically · **ABI and duplex** · **Wells score and duplex — consider especially with a ruptured Baker's cyst.** Routine to urgent
**Referred hip pathology — OA in adults, SUFE in adolescents**
**KNEE pain with a NORMAL KNEE**; limp; groin pain; **obligate EXTERNAL ROTATION on hip flexion**
**EXAMINE THE HIP IN EVERY KNEE CASE**
**Hip X-ray INCLUDING FROG-LATERAL.** URGENT in adolescents

stem: General practice. James Corrigan, 40, with left knee pain for two weeks and similar episodes before that settled without treatment. No fever. No injury.
A known hypertensive taking hydrochlorothiazide. Non-smoker, four standard drinks of beer daily, an accountant, otherwise well, no other past or family history.

Examination already performed: the knee is swollen and red, warm and tender on palpation. Temperature normal. Tasks: explain your most likely diagnosis and differentials — request further investigations and explain them — explain your immediate management.
tasks: Explain your most likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses to the patient
Request further investigations and explain them
Explain your immediate management to the patient
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: VERSION 1 — the findings are GIVEN in the stem

The knee is SWOLLEN AND RED on inspection, WARM AND TENDER on palpation. TEMPERATURE IS NORMAL. That last line is the examiner HANDING YOU the exclusion of septic arthritis — SAY IT OUT LOUD, it is a scored point
VERSION 2 — you must REQUEST it, and the examiner answers ONLY what you ask specifically

‘I'd inspect, palpate and move the joint’ RETURNS NOTHING and scores three out of ten while you think you did fine. Everyone does look-feel-move; the marks that separate a 3 from a 6 are THE NAMED FINDINGS, THE EFFUSION TEST, THE JOINT ABOVE AND BELOW, AND THE OFFICE TESTS
General appearance and vitals

‘Is the patient ALERT OR DROWSY, and does he look SYSTEMICALLY UNWELL?’ — that is the sepsis screen. Then ‘TEMPERATURE FIRST, please’, then blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate. Plus BMI AND WAIST CIRCUMFERENCE — obesity is a gout risk factor. And GAIT AND THE FOOTWEAR HE IS WEARING
The knee — named at every step

INSPECTION: swelling? redness? any deformity — SPECIFICALLY GENU VARUM OR VALGUM? ANY TOPHI visible around the joint? ANY SKIN BREACH OR CELLULITIS? PALPATION: local rise in temperature? tenderness? MOVEMENT: pain on ACTIVE AND PASSIVE movement, and is range restricted?
The ONE special test that matters here
PATELLAR TAP OR SWEEP TEST — IS THERE AN EFFUSION? SKIP the ligament and meniscal tests; they are not what this station is about
Beyond the knee

EXAMINE THE JOINT ABOVE AND BELOW — the hip and the ankle · THE FIRST METATARSOPHALANGEAL JOINTS and other joints for signs of PREVIOUS attacks · LOOK FOR TOPHI AT THE EAR HELIX, OLECRANON AND ACHILLES TENDON · a brief cardiovascular examination — heart sounds, murmurs, peripheral pulses
OFFICE TESTS — a separate task from investigations, and the thing that makes the examiner happy

BLOOD GLUCOSE LEVEL, and say whether FASTING OR RANDOM · URINE DIPSTICK — and NAME WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR: GLUCOSE, KETONES, PROTEIN, BLOOD, NITRITES AND LEUCOCYTES · blood pressure · height, weight, BMI and waist · temperature. ANSWERING THE OFFICE-TEST TASK WITH PATHOLOGY REQUESTS IS THE VERSION 6 TRAP
VERSION 3 — the crystal report, and TWO traps inside one result

‘URIC ACID CRYSTALS SEEN, NEGATIVELY BIREFRINGENT. LEUCOCYTES PRESENT. CULTURE NEGATIVE.’ ‘NEGATIVELY BIREFRINGENT’ IS NOT A NEGATIVE TEST — it is the OPTICAL FINGERPRINT of urate and it CONFIRMS gout. And LEUCOCYTES ARE EXPECTED IN ANY INFLAMED JOINT — IT IS THE NEGATIVE CULTURE THAT EXCLUDES INFECTION
The crystals, either way round

GOUT — NEEDLE-SHAPED, STRONGLY NEGATIVELY birefringent, YELLOW when aligned PARALLEL to the polariser. PSEUDOGOUT — RHOMBOID, WEAKLY POSITIVELY birefringent, BLUE when parallel. Calling a negatively birefringent needle ‘pseudogout’ is a named fail
VERSION 6 — reading the dipstick

GLUCOSE 3+ = blood glucose has exceeded the RENAL THRESHOLD OF ROUGHLY 10 mmol/L, so it spills into the urine. KETONES 3+ = fat being broken down for fuel — from FASTING, DEHYDRATION or INSULIN DEFICIENCY, and with high glucose THIS MUST BE TAKEN SERIOUSLY: exclude DKA with symptoms, blood ketones and a venous gas. PROTEIN = consider CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE, follow with a urine ACR

dx: **Acute gouty arthritis — urate crystallises in and around the joint and triggers an intense inflammatory response.** **The AMC has run this topic in SIX recall versions, each examining a DIFFERENT SEGMENT of one management plan — which is why the only safe preparation is to know the ENTIRE management: flare, long-term, non-pharmacological, reversible causes, cardiovascular risk and follow-up.**

**THE SIX COMPONENTS, and the version that punishes you for missing each**: **1 TREAT THE FLARE — version 5, where candidates restarted allopurinol and forgot he is in an attack. 2 CONFIRM BY ASPIRATION — version 1. 3 LIFELONG URATE-LOWERING, TREAT-TO-TARGET — version 4, where the stem already gave the acute treatment. 4 FLARE PROPHYLAXIS FOR SIX MONTHS — any version, and it is why patients abandon allopurinol. 5 TRIGGERS AND REVERSIBLE CAUSES — versions 2 and 5, where ‘contributing factors’ IS the task. 6 CARDIOVASCULAR RISK AND FOLLOW-UP — version 4, where BMI 34 and waist 105 are in the stem for that reason.**

**SAY THE STRUCTURE OUT LOUD BEFORE YOU DELIVER IT so the examiner can tick as you go**: **‘I'd like to cover three things — treating this attack, preventing future attacks, and the things you can change yourself. And the one condition I must exclude first is an infection in the joint.’**

**SEPTIC ARTHRITIS IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT SENTENCE IN THE STATION.** **‘The one I'm most concerned to rule out is an infection inside the joint. It looks ALMOST IDENTICAL — red, hot, swollen, painful. It's serious, because an infected joint can be damaged QUICKLY. In your favour you have no fever and you're not unwell in yourself — and the fluid sample will settle it definitively.’** **Gout and sepsis CAN COEXIST.**

**EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS IN TWO LAYERS, then link them.** **LAYER 1: ‘Arthritis simply means INFLAMMATION IN A JOINT — and when a joint is inflamed it goes RED, it SWELLS, and it becomes PAINFUL. That's exactly what I found in your knee.’** **LAYER 2: ‘Gout is what's causing it. There's a natural substance in your blood called URIC ACID. When there's too much of it, it forms TINY CRYSTALS that settle inside the joint, and your body reacts to them with this intense inflammation. So — too much uric acid, crystals in the knee, a hot swollen painful joint. Does that make sense so far?’**

**THEN THREE NUMBERED REASONS**: **‘First, the PATTERN — sudden attacks in a single joint that have come and gone by themselves before; that's exactly how gout behaves. Second, the APPEARANCE — red, warm, swollen and tender. Third, you have things that push the uric acid UP: the beer, and one of your blood pressure tablets.’**

**UNDER-EXCRETION ACCOUNTS FOR THE LARGE MAJORITY OF CASES — which is why THE MEDICATION REVIEW AND THE KIDNEYS MATTER MORE THAN THE DIET DOES.** **PRODUCTION ↑**: purine-rich food (red meat, offal, seafood), alcohol especially BEER, fructose-sweetened drinks, high cell turnover. **EXCRETION ↓**: **THIAZIDE AND LOOP DIURETICS, ciclosporin and tacrolimus, LOW-DOSE ASPIRIN, chronic kidney disease, dehydration.**

**THE THIAZIDE IS THE REVERSIBLE CAUSE YOU MUST NAME — and the commonest omission.** **‘Your blood pressure tablet makes the kidneys HOLD ON TO uric acid. There are three main groups of blood pressure medicines — ACE inhibitors or ARBs, calcium channel blockers, and thiazides. I'd like to SWAP you to one of the other groups: it would control your blood pressure just as well and give you fewer flares.’** **DO NOT simply STOP it and leave the hypertension untreated — SUBSTITUTE, then RECHECK.** **Many patients are on a COMBINATION tablet — check the actual product or you will miss the thiazide entirely.** **Losartan has a mild uricosuric effect and is a sensible substitute** VERIFY. **Also review low-dose aspirin — but do NOT stop it if it is for secondary cardiovascular prevention.**

**GOUT TRAVELS WITH CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASE — every classical cardiovascular risk factor is also a gout risk factor: hypertension, chronic kidney disease, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes and obesity.** **So in EVERY gout case: perform a cardiovascular risk assessment, check renal function, glucose and lipids, and review the antihypertensive. Saying this out loud is a reliable mark.** VERIFY

**THE COMPLIANCE MOMENT — version 5, and DO NOT SCOLD.** *‘I stopped the allopurinol six months ago. You'd checked my uric acid and told me it was normal, so I thought I was fixed.’* **‘Thank you for telling me — that makes complete sense, and it's a really common misunderstanding. THE URIC ACID WAS NORMAL BECAUSE THE TABLET WAS WORKING. IT'S A TREATMENT, NOT A CURE — when you stop it, the uric acid climbs back up and the attacks return, which is exactly what's happened.’** **Explore the reason first, then correct the belief.**
plan: **The opening you must not skip.** This is an ARTIFICIAL case — you walk in already knowing the diagnosis, and candidates either **sit down and lecture** or **try to take a history and get stopped by the examiner. Neither passes.** WIPE, then **ONE open question — ‘just so I've heard it from you, what's been happening with the knee?’** — then the agenda, **then the ICE question, which is the whole rapport mark in a counselling station.**
**The diagnosis in TWO LAYERS, then the THREE NUMBERED REASONS.** **Chunk and check — ‘does that make sense so far?’ — at least twice. Six uninterrupted minutes of information is a named fail.**

**Differentials, KILLER FIRST.** Septic arthritis with why it matters and how you will exclude it. Then **by bucket, in plain words**: pseudogout · rheumatoid, reactive or psoriatic arthritis — *‘those usually affect several joints, often symmetrically, and cause long morning stiffness’* · wear-and-tear arthritis — *‘doesn't usually cause this much heat and redness’* · bursitis · cellulitis over the joint · and nothing to suggest a problem from the back or hip, or a clot in the leg.

**INVESTIGATIONS, RANKED — two, then two, each with a reason.** **Reciting ‘FBE, ESR, CRP, UEC, LFT, TFT, X-ray, aspiration, urate, calcium’ FAILS: it shows you cannot prioritise.** **1 SERUM URATE — a baseline before long-term treatment, AND SAY THE CAVEAT: it is often normal or low during an attack, and a high urate alone does not diagnose gout. 2 JOINT ASPIRATION, ultrasound-guided — POLARISED LIGHT MICROSCOPY to confirm, AND microscopy, Gram stain and CULTURE to exclude infection. 3 RENAL FUNCTION — UEC, eGFR and urine ACR, because urate is cleared by the kidneys and it changes the doses. 4 FASTING GLUCOSE or HbA1c and LIPIDS — because they travel with gout and matter for the heart.** Then only if indicated: FBE/ESR/CRP, X-ray, blood cultures.

**Handle the needle reluctance with REASONS, not instruction.** *‘A needle in my knee? Is that necessary?’* → **‘We use local anaesthetic and it's usually quick. I'm recommending it for two reasons: it's the ONLY way to be certain there isn't an infection, and it CONFIRMS the gout — which matters, because I'm going to suggest a tablet you'd take LONG TERM, and I'd rather be sure before asking that of you. We can also put a little steroid into the joint at the same time, which settles the pain quickly.’**

**TREAT THE FLARE — OFFER OPTIONS, NOT ORDERS.** **‘For the pain right now we have three options, and we can choose what suits you best’ is itself a mark; ‘I'll start you on indomethacin’ is doctor-centred.** **NSAID at full anti-inflammatory dose with food** — avoid in CKD, peptic ulcer, heart failure, anticoagulation, the elderly. **CORTICOSTEROID — oral prednisolone or an INTRA-ARTICULAR injection, conveniently at the same sitting as the diagnostic aspiration — but NEVER inject until infection is excluded.** **COLCHICINE 1 mg orally immediately then 500 MICROGRAMS one hour later** VERIFY — reduce in renal or hepatic impairment and with interacting drugs. **Plus rest, keep weight off it, ice and elevation.**

**TRIGGERS, framed as ‘avoiding triggers’.** **DIET: ‘cut back red meat and offal, and seafood — NOT NONE, but as little as possible: the less you take, the fewer attacks.’** **ALCOHOL: ‘alcohol raises uric acid, and BEER IS THE WORST, with spirits next. NONE IS BEST; the less, the fewer flares.’** **NEVER offer ‘two standard drinks is safe’ as reassurance — that is a SCRIPTED TRAP in version 5.** **SUGARY DRINKS, HYDRATION — dehydration brings attacks on.** **WEIGHT — gradual loss lowers urate, but AVOID CRASH DIETING AND FASTING, which can trigger a flare.** **FOOTWEAR.** Then **THE THIAZIDE.**

**LONG TERM — allopurinol, treat-to-target.** **Start 50 mg daily, increase by 50 mg every 2–4 WEEKS, rechecking urate at each step, to a target BELOW 0.36 mmol/L — or BELOW 0.30 if tophaceous.** **Lower and slower in chronic kidney disease. Then LIFELONG.** **THREE things he must be told: a dose that never reaches target IS DOING NOTHING · it is a TREATMENT, NOT A CURE · and STARTING IT CAN TRIGGER AN ATTACK, so colchicine 500 micrograms once or twice daily runs alongside it for AT LEAST SIX MONTHS.** **And the side effect to name: ‘IF YOU DEVELOP A RASH, STOP THE TABLET AND CONTACT ME STRAIGHT AWAY.’**

**CLOSURE — the FOUR Rs.** **RISK ASSESSMENT** — cardiovascular risk assessment because gout travels with heart and kidney disease. **READING** — a gout fact sheet and **specifically a FOOD AND DRINK fact sheet, which patients find far more useful than general advice.** **REVIEW** — 1–2 weeks for the flare, every 2–4 weeks while titrating, then 6–12 monthly once at target. **RED FLAGS** — fever or feeling unwell, the joint rapidly worsening, or a rash on the new tablet.
Then summarise

**‘This is gouty arthritis; we'll confirm it with a fluid sample and rule out infection; we'll settle this attack; then we'll lower the uric acid long term, change the blood pressure tablet, and work on the alcohol and diet.’**
pefe: **THE HIDDEN AGENDA IS THE RICHEST MARK IN THE STATION and he withholds it until asked about concerns**: *‘My uncle had gout. His hands ended up covered in chalky lumps and he could barely hold a cup. I don't want to end up like that.’* **Answer it SPECIFICALLY: ‘Those lumps are called TOPHI — deposits of uric acid that build up after YEARS of attacks that weren't controlled. They're NOT INEVITABLE, and they're exactly what we're going to prevent. Controlled gout does not damage joints. The two things that get you there are keeping the uric acid at target and staying on the treatment.’**

**Answering ‘can't I just watch my diet instead?’ HONESTLY**: **‘Diet genuinely helps, and I'd like you to make those changes. But I want to be honest with you: DIET ON ITS OWN USUALLY LOWERS THE URIC ACID ONLY MODESTLY. THE TABLET DOES THE HEAVY LIFTING. And it's a small tablet with a low side-effect rate, against attacks like this one and long-term joint damage. It's your decision, and we can review it together.’**

**CORRECTION — the lecture quotes colchicine as ‘1 GRAM stat’. That is a SLIP OF THE TONGUE. The dose is 1 MILLIGRAM stat then 500 MICROGRAMS one hour later. A GRAM WOULD BE A LETHAL OVERDOSE.** **Colchicine has a narrow therapeutic index — NEVER QUOTE GRAMS.**

**DIVERGENCE 1 — must every patient have an aspiration?** VERIFY **The lecture's position, and the one to say: YES — confirm at least once, because you are about to commit the patient to a LIFELONG medication.** Australian guidance sits slightly differently: **aspiration is the gold standard and is MANDATORY whenever septic arthritis is possible or the diagnosis is uncertain, but a confident clinical diagnosis of classical podagra with typical risk factors is widely accepted in practice.** **If challenged, say both.**

**DIVERGENCE 2 — does every confirmed patient need allopurinol?** VERIFY **The lecture: yes, offer it to everyone with confirmed gout.** Australian guidance defines indications: **recurrent flares (commonly two or more a year), tophi, erosive damage, urate stones and CKD — with a move toward offering it after a FIRST attack where urate is high or risk factors persist.** **In every recall version the patient has recurrent attacks, so both positions give the same answer — you just need to defend it.** **And DO NOT treat asymptomatic hyperuricaemia.**

**VERSION 4 — THREE separate investigation boxes, and NAMING WHY you are grouping them is what passes**: **1 THE GOUT — serum urate, aspiration for polarised microscopy and MCS. 2 CARDIOVASCULAR RISK — BMI 34, waist 105, so fasting glucose or HbA1c, lipids, eGFR, urine ACR, blood pressure, then a formal CVD risk assessment. 3 THE NOCTURIA — he was started on PREDNISOLONE, which raises blood glucose; glucose spills into the urine and drives an OSMOTIC DIURESIS. Blood glucose, urine MCS for infection, and in an older man consider PSA after discussing its limitations.** VERIFY

**THE STEROID–GLUCOSE CHAIN, in one line**: **prednisolone → insulin resistance and increased hepatic glucose output → HYPERGLYCAEMIA → glucose exceeds the renal threshold → GLYCOSURIA → OSMOTIC DIURESIS → polyuria, nocturia, thirst.** **Steroid hyperglycaemia with once-daily MORNING prednisolone is typically AFTERNOON and POST-PRANDIAL predominant, so A FASTING GLUCOSE ALONE CAN MISS IT — check a level after lunch as well.** **And the HbA1c caveat: it reflects 2–3 MONTHS, so one month of prednisolone can give a NORMAL HbA1c, which DOES NOT EXCLUDE steroid-induced hyperglycaemia.**

**Naming it to the patient, carefully**: **‘Your blood sugar is high, and that's why you're passing more urine, especially at night. The most likely cause is the prednisolone — steroids push the blood sugar up. That IS a form of diabetes, but it's caused by the MEDICATION rather than the usual type, and it often improves once the steroid is stopped. I'd like to confirm it with blood tests and keep an eye on it.’** **Describe the finding, name the likely cause, and CONFIRM BEFORE YOU LABEL.** **And the task asks for the causes, PLURAL — urinary tract infection, previously undiagnosed type 2 diabetes unmasked by the steroid, chronic kidney disease, prostate in a man over 50, diuretics, hypercalcaemia, evening fluid, alcohol, caffeine, sleep apnoea and heart failure.**

**Examiner follow-ups, scripted**: *‘What if the culture grows an organism?’* → **‘Then this is septic arthritis until proven otherwise. Urgent referral, blood cultures, IV antibiotics AFTER cultures are taken, and joint washout — and note the two can coexist.’** *‘His eGFR is 34 — does anything change?’* → **‘Yes. AVOID NSAIDs, REDUCE the colchicine dose, and PREFER a corticosteroid for the flare. Allopurinol still applies but I'd start LOWER and titrate MORE SLOWLY, and be alert to hypersensitivity.’** *‘Would you treat a urate of 0.49 with no attacks?’* → **‘No. Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is not treated — I'd address the cardiovascular risk factors instead.’**

**The allopurinol rash matters more than it sounds**: rarely it causes a SEVERE cutaneous reaction, and **the risk is higher with the HLA-B*58:01 allele, more common in people of Han Chinese, Thai and Korean ancestry, and in chronic kidney disease.** VERIFY **If allopurinol is not tolerated: febuxostat, or probenecid (avoid with urate stones or significant renal impairment), on specialist advice.** SA — **gout is MORE COMMON, OFTEN MORE SEVERE AND UNDER-TREATED in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people: register for Closing the Gap PBS co-payment relief for allopurinol and colchicine, involve the ACCHS and an Aboriginal Liaison Officer, and use a GP Management Plan for structured review** · **if ultrasound-guided aspiration is not locally available, arrange it through the regional LHN or discuss with rheumatology by telehealth, use PATS for travel — and if sepsis is suspected DO NOT WAIT: MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**
