stem: Emergency department. Mark, 30, has attended after trauma to his leg with pain on movement of the ankle. He has been examined: no neurovascular injury, closed fracture.
An ankle x-ray is displayed. Tasks: explain the x-ray to the examiner, with a prompt at three minutes — explain the diagnosis to the patient — explain your management plan.
8 minutes. The structure invites you to walk past the patient to get to the film. Do not.
tasks: Explain the X-ray to the examiner
Explain the diagnosis to the patient
Explain your management plan
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: THE TWO EXCLUSIONS IN THE STEM ARE DOING WORK — say out loud that you noted them

NEUROVASCULAR STATUS INTACT and THE FRACTURE IS CLOSED. That is not scene-setting: it is the examiner REMOVING TWO MANAGEMENT PATHWAYS so the one they want to test is the one you deliver. An OPEN fracture would mean washout, antibiotics, tetanus and theatre within hours; NEUROVASCULAR COMPROMISE would mean urgent reduction. Both excluded → the station is CLASSIFICATION, STABILITY, IMMOBILISATION AND REFERRAL
THE FIVE-STEP REPORTING SPINE — step 1, orient

‘This is a plain radiograph of the ankle. IDEALLY I'D REVIEW THREE VIEWS — AP, LATERAL AND MORTISE — and I'd confirm the patient's identity and the date of the film first.’ Free marks, and it pre-empts the examiner asking what else you would want
Steps 2 and 3 — the highest-value sentence in the station

‘There is a FRACTURE OF THE DISTAL FIBULA. It lies ABOVE THE LEVEL OF THE ANKLE JOINT LINE AND THE SYNDESMOSIS, which makes this a WEBER TYPE C. That's important, because a fracture at this level carries a HIGH RISK OF SYNDESMOTIC INJURY, and therefore a HIGH RISK THAT THE ANKLE JOINT IS UNSTABLE.’ LEVEL → LETTER → CONSEQUENCE, in one breath. The letter alone is worth NOTHING
Steps 4 and 5 — pattern, then displacement and the mortise

PATTERN: transverse, OBLIQUE, spiral or comminuted — four seconds, and candidates skip it. Then DISPLACEMENT and ANGULATION described HONESTLY, and ‘I would specifically assess THE MORTISE — the MEDIAL CLEAR SPACE for talar shift, and the TIBIOFIBULAR CLEAR SPACE AND OVERLAP for syndesmotic widening’
The three measurements that prove instability VERIFY

MEDIAL CLEAR SPACE UNDER 4 mm — widening means THE TALUS HAS SHIFTED LATERALLY. TIBIOFIBULAR CLEAR SPACE UNDER 6 mm. TIBIOFIBULAR OVERLAP OVER 1 mm. Quote these and you move from ‘it looks unstable’ to ‘HERE IS WHY’
Step 6 — rule out the rest, which is how you show you LOOKED

‘I can see NO OTHER FRACTURE — the TIBIA, the MEDIAL MALLEOLUS, the POSTERIOR MALLEOLUS and the TALUS all appear intact, the joint space appears preserved, and I see NO DISLOCATION.’ Two malleoli fractured is a BIMALLEOLAR and by definition UNSTABLE; add a posterior malleolus and it is TRIMALLEOLAR. Both are surgical
THE SENTENCE THAT MAKES YOU STAND OUT — twelve seconds

‘I'd also want to examine THE WHOLE LENGTH OF THE FIBULA UP TO THE KNEE. If there were proximal fibular tenderness, I'd X-ray the FULL TIBIA AND FIBULA to exclude a MAISONNEUVE FRACTURE, because a syndesmotic injury can be associated with a fracture MUCH FURTHER UP THE LEG THAN THE ANKLE FILM SHOWS.’ It is the single most commonly missed injury in this presentation and IT IS NOT ON THE FILM AT ALL
What else hides on an ankle film

DELTOID LIGAMENT INJURY WITHOUT FRACTURE — widened medial clear space with an INTACT medial malleolus, functionally equivalent to a medial malleolar fracture · TALAR SHIFT OR DISLOCATION — urgent, skin and neurovascular structures at risk · TALAR DOME OSTEOCHONDRAL LESION — a subtle flake, a common cause of persistent pain later · TIBIAL PLAFOND (PILON) FRACTURE — comminution into the weight-bearing articular surface, a different and much more serious injury · BASE OF THE FIFTH METATARSAL — often at the EDGE of the film, same inversion mechanism, commonly missed because everyone is looking at the malleoli
The specialist's reading of THIS film — know it, because it differs from the presenter's

The fibula is DEFINITELY ANGULATED, roughly 10–15° · the displacement is DEFINITE, not minimal · the MEDIAL CLEAR SPACE IS WIDENED beyond normal, confirming syndesmotic injury · and the smooth continuous curve beneath the distal fibula and talus is INTERRUPTED. His conclusion: THIS ANKLE CERTAINLY REQUIRES ORIF; at least three views are needed; a CT would be required before contemplating non-operative management; and OFFERING NON-OPERATIVE MANAGEMENT ON THIS FILM WOULD BE A SIGNIFICANT ERROR VERIFY
Extra imaging to name if pressed

THREE VIEWS — AP, LATERAL AND MORTISE. A CT TO ASSESS THE SYNDESMOSIS if non-operative management is being contemplated. A POST-IMMOBILISATION FILM after splinting to confirm position has not been lost. And WEIGHT-BEARING OR GRAVITY STRESS VIEWS are sometimes used to settle a Weber B VERIFY

dx: **Displaced oblique WEBER C fracture of the distal fibula — an UNSTABLE ankle injury with probable syndesmotic disruption.**

**THE ONE IDEA TO CARRY IN: YOU ARE BEING EXAMINED AT INTERN LEVEL. YOU ARE NOT THE PERSON WHO DECIDES WHETHER THIS ANKLE IS PLATED.** **Your job is to CLASSIFY it, call it UNSTABLE, IMMOBILISE it, and REFER it — and to say that the orthopaedic team makes the definitive call.** **Candidates fail this station by committing to a definitive management decision they are not qualified to make — and it does not matter which decision they pick.**

**THE WEBER SYSTEM IS ONE QUESTION: where is the fibular fracture RELATIVE TO THE SYNDESMOSIS?** **A — BELOW it: the ligaments above the break are intact, the mortise holds, usually STABLE.** **B — AT the level of it: typically spiral, and stability depends on whether the syndesmosis and the MEDIAL SIDE have gone with it.** **C — ABOVE it: the syndesmosis has ALMOST BY DEFINITION been torn to allow the fibula to break where it did, so the ankle is PRESUMED UNSTABLE.**

**THE ANATOMY IN ONE SENTENCE**: **the ankle is a MORTISE — a socket formed by the tibia above, the medial malleolus inside and the lateral malleolus outside — holding the talus. IT ONLY WORKS IF THE SOCKET KEEPS ITS EXACT WIDTH. The syndesmosis is what holds that width.** **That is why a break in a bone that carries almost no body weight can nonetheless need plating.**

**THE CHOREOGRAPHY — DO NOT WALK PAST THE PATIENT.** The station has TWO AUDIENCES and its structure invites you to ignore one. **‘Hello, you must be Mark — I'm going to look at your X-ray with my colleague for a moment, and then I'll come straight back and go through everything with you. Is that all right?’** **Thirty seconds, and it converts an awkward structural quirk into two communication marks — and it PRE-COMMITS you to analgesia so it cannot be forgotten later.**

**THE PATIENT EXPLANATION IN FOUR BEATS, AND BEAT ZERO IS COMFORT.** **BEAT 1 — name the bone: ‘you've broken a bone called the FIBULA; let me show you on the picture.’** **BEAT 2 — two bones, one joint, one band: ‘this thick one is the TIBIA, your shin bone, which carries your weight. This thinner one on the outside is the FIBULA. At the bottom they form THE SOCKET of your ankle joint — the ankle bone sits in between them, A BIT LIKE A HINGE SITTING IN A BRACKET. For that to work they have to stay EXACTLY THE RIGHT DISTANCE APART, and what holds them there is A STRONG BAND just above the ankle — the SYNDESMOSIS.’**

**BEAT 3 — why the level matters**: **‘If the fibula breaks LOW DOWN, below that band, the band is usually intact and the ankle stays stable. But your break is ABOVE the band — and for the bone to break up there, THE FORCE HAS USUALLY TRAVELLED THROUGH THE BAND ON ITS WAY. So the band may well be TORN. We call a break at this level a WEBER TYPE C. And because of that, this type of fracture can leave the ankle joint UNSTABLE — the two bones can DRIFT APART and the ankle bone stops sitting properly in its socket.’** **BEAT 4 — the bridge: ‘so this is a break we definitely need the bone surgeons to look at BEFORE we decide anything. Is that making sense so far?’**

**THE SOCKET-AND-BRACKET IMAGE DOES ALL THE WORK. Once the patient understands the two bones must stay a fixed distance apart, EVERYTHING ABOUT INSTABILITY AND SURGERY FOLLOWS WITHOUT FURTHER EXPLANATION.**

**PRESENT BOTH PATHWAYS, WEIGHT THEM, AND ATTRIBUTE THE DECISION.** **‘Because of the level of this break and the risk to that band, we treat this as an UNSTABLE fracture — so the MOST LIKELY outcome is an OPERATION to stabilise it, with a PLATE AND SCREWS holding the bone, and sometimes AN EXTRA SCREW ACROSS to hold the two bones the correct distance apart while the band heals. Afterwards you'd be in a backslab or cast, and OFF THAT LEG, for around SIX WEEKS. There is a SMALLER possibility that if the specialists are satisfied there's minimal displacement and the ankle is genuinely stable on all the views, they'd manage it in a cast without operating. They may want extra X-rays or a CT to work that out.’** **NEVER present them as equally likely, and NEVER commit to non-operative management yourself.**

**THE RETURN-TO-WORK QUESTION HAS NO NUMBER — ‘six weeks’ is a WRONG ANSWER, and so is ‘four’.** **The right answer begins with a question: WHAT DOES HE DO FOR WORK? A desk worker and a baggage handler have entirely different answers to the same fracture.** **The examiner is testing whether you know the answer is OCCUPATIONAL, not orthopaedic.** **Frame the question if you are worried it will be objected to: ‘to answer that properly I need to ask what your job involves.’**
plan: **Enter, greet the patient, PARK HIM POLITELY, get permission** — and acknowledge the pain now, promising to act on it.

**Report the film — the six steps, out loud, in order. Roughly seventy to eighty seconds of real content.** **Then a SUMMARY SENTENCE that does the examiner's job for them: ‘a displaced oblique Weber C fracture of the distal fibula, WHICH I WOULD TREAT AS AN UNSTABLE ANKLE INJURY REQUIRING ORTHOPAEDIC ASSESSMENT.’** **If the examiner says move on, MOVE ON IMMEDIATELY — do not finish the sentence for your own satisfaction.**

**Return to the patient and RESET DELIBERATELY. Comfort before content.** **‘Thanks for waiting, Mark. Before anything else — how are you feeling? Are you in much pain? Let me get you something for that straight away, and we'll talk while it takes effect.’** **This is the single easiest mark in the station to drop, and it is dropped constantly by candidates who arrive still thinking in radiology.**

**The four beats, then check understanding.** **And when he says ‘sounds worse than I thought’ — ACKNOWLEDGE, THEN REFRAME. DO NOT MINIMISE: ‘it's a significant injury, but it's a very treatable one, and we see a lot of them.’**

**IMMEDIATE CARE, described concretely.** **ANALGESIA — regular paracetamol plus an oral or IV opioid titrated to effect** VERIFY · **CONFIRM AND DOCUMENT the exclusions: distal pulses, capillary refill, sensation, motor function, and inspect the skin for wounds, TENTING and fracture blisters** · **BELOW-KNEE POSTERIOR BACKSLAB at NINETY DEGREES, well padded — NOT a circumferential cast, because a slab ACCOMMODATES SWELLING and a cast in an acutely swelling limb risks compartment problems** · **NON-WEIGHT-BEARING with crutches, elevation and ice** · **POST-IMMOBILISATION FILM** · **NIL BY MOUTH, IV access, pre-operative bloods — if they operate today this saves hours** · **consider VTE risk given lower-limb immobilisation, raised as a consideration rather than prescribed yourself.** VERIFY

**REFER — orthopaedic REVIEW BEFORE DISPOSITION. Not ‘I'll book you into fracture clinic’, which is discharging an unstable ankle without a specialist opinion.** **EVERY Australian guideline, including the most permissive, requires distal fibular fractures to be DISCUSSED with orthopaedics.** Then **both pathways, weighted, with the decision attributed.**

**Follow-up, rehabilitation and red flags.** Fracture clinic within days; immobilisation and weight-bearing status set by orthopaedics; **physiotherapy once permitted — range of motion, calf and peroneal strengthening, proprioception and gait retraining, and WARN HIM that stiffness and swelling persist LONG AFTER THE BONE UNITES** · **NO DRIVING while in a backslab or non-weight-bearing; ask which leg and whether the vehicle is manual, and he should notify his insurer** VERIFY.

**THE RETURN-TO-WORK PLAN — five beats, and the STRUCTURE is what scores.** **1 NAME THE OBSTACLES — non-weight-bearing for several weeks, AND ongoing swelling even once the cast is off. 2 CERTIFICATE NOW. 3 ARRANGE REVIEW — the fracture clinic follows the bone, you follow how he is FUNCTIONING. 4 MODIFIED DUTIES as the intermediate step — ‘something seated for a few weeks while we review again’. 5 FULL DUTIES when function is restored.** **Learn those five and the answer works for any occupation the role-player gives you.**

**Close — recap, check understanding, invite questions, confirm the safety-net.** **THE RED FLAGS, said without the words ‘compartment syndrome’: ‘pins and needles or numbness in your toes, any change in COLOUR of your toes, PAIN THAT KEEPS GETTING WORSE DESPITE THE PAINKILLERS, or if the slab starts to feel TOO TIGHT — come straight back, don't wait.’ After an operation add fever or wound discharge.**
A note on the clock

**This station usually finishes EARLY — the three-minute prompt is far more than the film needs, and candidates report being told to move on after about a minute.** **Use the surplus for a proper analgesia enquiry, a thorough explanation and a complete return-to-work discussion — DO NOT respond to it by INVENTING RADIOLOGICAL DETAIL YOU CANNOT DEFEND.**
pefe: **WHERE THE SOURCES GENUINELY DISAGREE — and the position that is safe under all of them.** VERIFY **A Victorian emergency guideline takes a PERMISSIVE line: distal fibular fractures across Weber types may be managed initially in a CAM boot or backslab — BUT still requires that ALL distal fibular fractures be DISCUSSED with orthopaedics.** **NSW ACI: a fibular fracture above the syndesmosis WITH THE ANKLE IN NORMAL ANATOMICAL POSITION may be backslabbed, non-weight-bearing, with orthopaedic follow-up within one to two days — note the CONDITION, which is NOT MET if the film shows displacement, angulation or a widened medial clear space.** **Orthopaedic sources: Weber C fractures are USUALLY UNSTABLE and MOST REQUIRE SURGICAL EVALUATION.** **Lead with the orthopaedic position, because it generalises.**

**THE DIVERGENCE INSIDE THE SOURCE LECTURE: the presenter reads this film as minimally displaced with no angulation; the orthopaedic specialist, live in the same session, reads it as definitely angulated, definitely displaced, with a widened medial clear space.** **HOW TO RESOLVE IT IN THE EXAM: THE SPECIALIST IS RIGHT ABOUT THE FILM, AND THE PRESENTER IS RIGHT ABOUT HOW A JUNIOR DOCTOR SHOULD HEDGE. DO BOTH — describe what you actually see, and let your conclusion follow it.**

**Challenge 1 — ‘IS IT DISPLACED?’** → **‘To my eye there IS displacement of the distal fragment and I think some angulation — I'd estimate in the order of ten to fifteen degrees. I'd want the lateral and mortise views to quantify that properly. EITHER WAY IT DOESN'T CHANGE MY IMMEDIATE MANAGEMENT: I'm treating this as an unstable injury and asking orthopaedics to review before disposition.’**

**Challenge 2 — ‘SO WOULD YOU SEND HIM HOME IN A BACKSLAB?’** → **‘NOT ON THIS FILM, no. Some Australian emergency guidelines do allow a backslab and early orthopaedic follow-up for a Weber C, but ONLY WHERE THE ANKLE IS IN NORMAL ANATOMICAL POSITION — and here I think there's displacement and a widened medial clear space, so THAT CONDITION ISN'T MET. I'd backslab him, keep him non-weight-bearing and nil by mouth, and ask orthopaedics to see him IN THE DEPARTMENT.’**

**Challenge 3 — ‘WHAT WOULD YOU DO IF YOU WERE THE ORTHOPAEDIC SURGEON?’** → **‘I'd EXPECT open reduction and internal fixation — a plate and screws to the fibula, and possibly a syndesmotic screw. But I'd want three views and, if there were any question of managing it without surgery, a CT to assess the syndesmosis. THAT DECISION SITS ABOVE MY LEVEL and I'd want it made by the orthopaedic team.’**

**The patient's pressure tests, scripted.** *‘Can't you just plaster it and let me go home? I've got a shift tomorrow.’* → **‘I understand, and I'm sorry — but I can't do that with THIS break. Because it's above that band, the ankle may not be stable, and if we plaster an unstable ankle and send you home IT CAN SHIFT OUT OF POSITION. I need the bone surgeons to look at it before you go anywhere. What I CAN do is get your pain properly sorted and sort the paperwork for work.’** *‘Just tell me straight — do I need surgery or not?’* → **‘The honest answer is that it's MOST LIKELY, and I'd plan on it. But I'd be MISLEADING you if I said it was certain, because that call belongs to the orthopaedic team and they may want extra imaging first. I'd rather be straight with you than guess.’**

**The jargon translator**: fibula → **‘the thinner bone on the outside of your lower leg — the bump on the outside of your ankle’** · mortise → **‘the socket your ankle bone sits in’** · syndesmosis → **‘a strong band holding the two leg bones exactly the right distance apart’** · unstable → **‘the two bones can drift apart, so the ankle bone stops sitting properly in its socket’** · ORIF → **‘an operation to line the bone back up and hold it there with a metal plate and screws’** · syndesmotic screw → **‘an extra screw going across from one bone to the other, holding them at the right width while the band heals’** · backslab → **‘a plaster splint along the back of your leg rather than a full cast — it leaves room for the swelling’** · nil by mouth → **‘nothing to eat or drink for now, just in case you need an operation today’**.

**VARIANT — WEBER A.** *‘A TRANSVERSE fracture of the distal fibula lying BELOW the level of the ankle joint and the syndesmosis — a Weber type A. Because the fracture is below the syndesmosis, the syndesmotic ligaments are USUALLY INTACT and the ankle is generally a STABLE injury. No displacement, mortise congruent, normal medial clear space.’* **Symptomatic treatment, a boot or backslab, weight-bearing as tolerated in many cases, routine fracture clinic — though local practice still favours discussing distal fibular fractures with orthopaedics.** VERIFY **THE REASONING YOU SAY ALOUD IS THE SCORED ITEM, NOT THE DISPOSITION.**

**VARIANT — WEBER B, the genuinely uncertain one, and examiners like it for that reason.** **Stability turns on TWO questions you must NAME OUT LOUD: (1) is there displacement, and IS THE MORTISE CONGRUENT — check the medial clear space; (2) IS THERE A MEDIAL-SIDE INJURY — a medial malleolar fracture, or medial tenderness suggesting a DELTOID LIGAMENT TEAR?** **A lateral malleolar fracture PLUS a medial-side injury is a FUNCTIONALLY BIMALLEOLAR, UNSTABLE ankle even if only one bone is broken.** **Undisplaced with a congruent mortise and no medial-side injury is often non-operative; displaced, or with medial-side injury, is usually surgical.** VERIFY

**VARIANT — TALAR SHIFT OR DISLOCATION: the ONLY version of this station that is TIME-CRITICAL.** **A talus displaced out of the mortise puts skin and neurovascular structures at risk and needs URGENT REDUCTION, usually under procedural sedation, BEFORE definitive imaging or referral discussions. Reassess neurovascular status before AND after, splint, and get a post-reduction film. DO NOT deliver a leisurely six-step report while the foot is dislocated.** SA — **most country hospitals have no on-site orthopaedic service: the pathway is TELEPHONE DISCUSSION with the on-call orthopaedic registrar at the receiving metropolitan unit, and transfer for operative management** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 coordinates transfer, but a CLOSED, NEUROVASCULARLY INTACT ankle fracture is usually a ROAD TRANSFER rather than an emergency retrieval — saying that shows you know when NOT to escalate** · **PATS for fracture clinic travel; country LHN fracture clinics, telehealth orthopaedics and Country Health Connect physiotherapy for a patient facing repeated 200 km round trips** · **if it happened at work: ReturnToWorkSA and a WORK CAPACITY CERTIFICATE rather than an ordinary medical certificate; if a motor vehicle accident, a CTP claim** · **Aboriginal Liaison Officer early where transfer to Adelaide takes the patient far from community.**

Fibular fracture **ABOVE the joint line and the syndesmosis**
**Level relative to the syndesmosis**; displacement, angulation; medial clear space
**PRESUME UNSTABLE. Backslab, non-weight-bearing, nil by mouth, orthopaedic review BEFORE disposition. ORIF is the more probable outcome.** Urgent
Weber B
Fracture **AT the level of the syndesmosis**, typically SPIRAL
**Displacement and mortise congruence; AND a medial-side injury — medial malleolar fracture or medial tenderness**
**Undisplaced with congruent mortise and no medial-side injury → often non-operative. Displaced or medial-side injury → usually surgical. Stress views sometimes settle it.** VERIFY Urgent

Fracture **BELOW the syndesmosis**, often transverse
Mortise congruent, normal medial clear space, no displacement
**Syndesmotic ligaments usually intact — generally STABLE. Boot or backslab, weight-bearing as tolerated, routine clinic.** VERIFY Routine
**Maisonneuve fracture**
**PROXIMAL fibular fracture near the knee with syndesmotic injury, often with a medial malleolar fracture or deltoid tear — IT IS NOT ON THE ANKLE FILM AT ALL**
**Syndesmotic widening with NO fibular fracture on the ankle film, or a very high one. PALPATE THE WHOLE FIBULA TO THE KNEE**

Deltoid ligament injury without fracture

**Report the medial clear space EXPLICITLY — this is why the measurement matters**
**Functionally equivalent to a medial malleolar fracture — the mortise is unstable even though only one bone is broken.** Urgent

Skin tenting; neurovascular status before and after
**URGENT REDUCTION under procedural sedation, splint, post-reduction film. An urgent problem, not a clinic problem.** Emergency

Wound over the fracture; or pale, pulseless, paraesthetic foot
**The stem EXCLUDED both — but re-check and DOCUMENT them**
**Open: washout, antibiotics, tetanus, theatre within hours. Compromise: urgent reduction.** Emergency
Tibial plafond (pilon) fracture

High-energy mechanism; articular involvement
**A completely different and much more serious injury with a WORSE prognosis — this is not a fibular fracture case, escalate.** Urgent
Talar dome osteochondral lesion · base of 5th metatarsal

**CHECK THE EDGES OF EVERY ANKLE FILM**

stem: General practice. A 50-year-old presented with pain and itchiness in both legs and was investigated. He has returned for results.
Ankle-brachial index 0.9 left, 1.0 right. Venous duplex ultrasound: incompetence of the sapheno-femoral junction and the perforating veins.
Tasks: explain the investigations and the diagnosis — take a history, five minutes — explain your management plan. 8 minutes total.
tasks: Explain the investigations and the diagnosis
Take a history (five minutes)
Explain your management plan
findingsLabel: Results and findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: THE RESULTS YOU ARE HANDED
ANKLE–BRACHIAL INDEX: 0.9 LEFT, 1.0 RIGHT. VENOUS DUPLEX ULTRASOUND: INCOMPETENCE OF THE SAPHENO-FEMORAL JUNCTION AND OF THE PERFORATING VEINS, BILATERALLY
THE ABI READ AS A TREATMENT DECISION, NOT A NUMBER VERIFY

BELOW 0.50 severe arterial disease — NO COMPRESSION · 0.50–0.79 moderate — REDUCED ONLY, SPECIALIST-GUIDED · 0.80–0.90 mild/borderline — CAUTION · 0.91–1.40 NORMAL, FULL COMPRESSION SAFE · ABOVE 1.40 NON-COMPRESSIBLE CALCIFIED VESSELS, UNRELIABLE — DO TOE PRESSURES
A CORRECTION TO CARRY IN — the source teaching gives ‘normal’ as 0.9–1.0, which is NOT the standard reading

The conventional interpretation is 1.00–1.40 NORMAL · 0.91–0.99 BORDERLINE · 0.90 OR BELOW DIAGNOSTIC OF PERIPHERAL ARTERIAL DISEASE · above 1.40 uninterpretable VERIFY. THIS CHANGES THE CASE: on the standard reading the LEFT LEG AT 0.9 SITS EXACTLY AT THE DIAGNOSTIC BOUNDARY, not comfortably inside normal. The right at 1.0 is normal
Scripted reply if an examiner quotes 0.9–1.0 back at you

‘I'd interpret 1.0 to 1.4 as the normal range, with 0.91 to 0.99 borderline and 0.9 or below suggesting arterial disease — so I'd call the right leg normal and THE LEFT BORDERLINE rather than normal. I appreciate some sources quote 0.9 as the lower limit of normal. PRACTICALLY IT DOESN'T CHANGE MY PLAN, because either way 0.9 is the point at which I STOP AND CONFIRM THE ARTERIAL SUPPLY before applying firm compression, and I'd repeat the measurement and examine the pulses myself before committing to a compression class.’ SAY IT ONCE, CALMLY, AND STOP. DO NOT ARGUE — it defends THE ACTION, not the number
What the duplex actually tells you

PRIMARY SUPERFICIAL VENOUS REFLUX WITH PERFORATOR INCOMPETENCE — the commonest pattern — and IMPORTANTLY THE DEEP SYSTEM IS NOT REPORTED AS OBSTRUCTED. Two consequences: this is a CANDIDATE FOR DEFINITIVE TREATMENT of the superficial system if conservative measures fail; and a normal-looking deep system makes a CURRENT DVT unlikely but says NOTHING ABOUT A PAST ONE — so you still ask about previous clots. Reflux lasting MORE THAN ABOUT HALF A SECOND on augmentation is taken as pathological VERIFY
THE CEAP CLINICAL STAGES — stage it aloud in one sentence, it reads as expertise and takes three seconds

C0–C1 no signs or spider veins · C2 VARICOSE VEINS · C3 OEDEMA · C4a PIGMENTATION OR ECZEMA · C4b LIPODERMATOSCLEROSIS · C5 HEALED ULCER · C6 ACTIVE ULCER. This stem patient, with pain, itch and presumed skin change but no stated ulcer, is around C4a VERIFY
THE THREE ULCERS — the single highest-yield discrimination in the whole lower-limb cluster

VENOUS: MEDIAL GAITER, SHALLOW, WET, irregular border, surrounding PIGMENTATION, PULSES PRESENT, EASED BY ELEVATION. ARTERIAL: TOES AND PRESSURE POINTS, PUNCHED OUT, DRY NECROTIC base, cold hairless pale skin, ABSENT PULSES, WORSE ON ELEVATION. NEUROPATHIC: PLANTAR pressure points, CALLUSED RIM, PAINLESS, pulses often normal
Venous versus lymphatic oedema

VENOUS oedema PITS, SETTLES OVERNIGHT, and typically SPARES THE TOES AND DORSUM of the foot. LYMPHOEDEMA is NON-PITTING, does NOT settle overnight, INVOLVES the toes and dorsum, skin thickened and warty, POSITIVE STEMMER SIGN
What you would ADD to the investigations

HbA1c OR FASTING GLUCOSE — mandatory in any patient with chronic leg symptoms and skin change; undiagnosed diabetes drives neuropathy, impairs healing, and CALCIFIES VESSELS SO THE ABI MISLEADS · FULL BLOOD COUNT AND FILM — answers the itch question and lets you reply to ‘how do you know it isn't something in the blood?’ WITH A TEST RATHER THAN AN ASSERTION · U&E, LFT, ALBUMIN for renal, hepatic and hypoalbuminaemic causes of bilateral oedema · LIPIDS, BP AND A FULL CARDIOVASCULAR RISK ASSESSMENT, because the left ABI of 0.9 flags arterial disease VERIFY
Wound swabs — when NOT to

ONLY if there is an ulcer with CLINICAL SIGNS of infection — increasing pain, spreading erythema, purulence, fever. DO NOT swab a colonised ulcer routinely: EVERY CHRONIC ULCER GROWS ORGANISMS, and treating the swab rather than the patient drives resistance

dx: **Chronic venous insufficiency from primary superficial venous reflux with perforator incompetence, clinically around CEAP C4a.**

**THE ONE IDEA: COMPRESSION IS THE TREATMENT FOR VENOUS DISEASE — AND COMPRESSION IS DANGEROUS ON AN ARTERIAL LEG.** **That is why the ankle–brachial index was done BEFORE anyone reached for a stocking.** **THE EXAMINABLE BEHAVIOUR IS SAYING THAT CONNECTION OUT LOUD: the ABI is not a result to report, IT IS THE SAFETY GATE THAT PERMITS THE TREATMENT.** **‘That's why we checked your arteries before prescribing compression — and yours are fine, so it's safe for you.’**

**THE TIMING ARITHMETIC, DONE BEFORE YOU KNOCK.** Eight minutes, three tasks, **and the stem itself assigns FIVE to history — which leaves three for tasks 1 and 3 combined.** **TAKE FOUR. The history is genuinely thin because the diagnosis has already been made for you; what you are really being asked for is a SYMPTOM-AND-RISK INVENTORY, and that is a four-minute job done well.** **The minute you save is the minute that buys you a complete management plan.** **An examiner has never failed a candidate for a slightly short history; they fail candidates who run out of time with no plan.**

**EXPLAIN IN FOUR BEATS, and BEAT ONE IS THE TWO-PIPE MODEL — do not skip it, it takes twelve seconds and everything after it is unintelligible without it**: **‘There are two kinds of blood tube in your legs. The ARTERIES bring blood DOWN from the heart into the legs. The VEINS take it back UP to the heart — which is the HARDER job, because it's UPHILL, AGAINST GRAVITY. Two different systems, and we tested both.’** **The uphill-against-gravity image pre-explains why standing makes it worse, why elevation helps, and why the calf muscles matter.**

**BEAT TWO — the arterial test**: **‘The first test compared the blood pressure at your ANKLE with the blood pressure in your ARM. That one looks at the arteries. Yours came back essentially in the normal range — so blood IS getting down into your feet properly, and this isn't a blockage of that kind. THAT MATTERS FOR TREATMENT, AND I'LL COME BACK TO IT.’** **Flagging it lets you close the compression loop later without re-explaining, and that closure is the discriminating item of the station.**

**BEAT THREE — the venous test, and the word is FLAPS, not valves**: **‘Veins have little ONE-WAY FLAPS inside them, like valves. Every time your CALF MUSCLE SQUEEZES it pushes blood up through the flaps toward your heart, and the flaps stop it falling back. The scan shows that in several places — A MAJOR JUNCTION UP AT YOUR GROIN, and some of the SMALL CONNECTING VEINS in your calves — those flaps aren't SEALING any more. So some of the blood FALLS BACK DOWN and POOLS in your lower legs. That pooling, and the pressure it builds up, is exactly what's causing the aching and the itch.’**

**BEAT FOUR — NAME IT, which is a scored item; do not leave the patient to infer it**: **‘The condition has a name — CHRONIC VENOUS INSUFFICIENCY. VENOUS means the veins; INSUFFICIENCY means they're not doing quite enough of their job. It's very common, IT'S NOT A CLOT, AND IT'S NOT CANCER. It's LONG-TERM, so we MANAGE it rather than CURE it — but it responds well and there's a great deal we can do. Is that making sense so far?’** **Then ONE check-back and MOVE — a second and third eat your management plan.**

**ANSWER THE FEAR BEFORE THE PHYSIOLOGY.** The open question at 0:20 almost always surfaces either *‘is it a clot?’* or *‘will I lose my leg?’* — **and an anxious patient does not process a mechanism explanation until the fear is addressed.** Put **‘it is not a clot, and it is not cancer’** FIRST, then build the model.

**TWO QUESTIONS SEPARATE VENOUS FROM ARTERIAL PAIN IN TEN SECONDS**: **‘Is it worse when you're STANDING?’ and ‘is it BETTER when you put your feet UP?’** **Yes to both is VENOUS. ARTERIAL IS THE EXACT REVERSE — worse elevated, eased by HANGING THE LEG DOWN — and if he said that, you would be re-examining that left ABI of 0.9 rather than reaching for a stocking.**

**THREE THINGS NOT TO SAY.** **NO DIURETIC for venous oedema — a common wrong answer. The problem is LOCAL VENOUS HYPERTENSION, not fluid overload; a diuretic depletes intravascular volume without fixing the leg and invites acute kidney injury, hyponatraemia and falls.** **NO ANTIBIOTICS for red, scaly, itchy gaiter skin — that is VENOUS ECZEMA. Bilateral simultaneous cellulitis is RARE; bilateral venous eczema MISDIAGNOSED as cellulitis is COMMON.** **AND DO NOT PROMISE A CURE — it loses honesty marks and sets the patient up to abandon the stockings at six weeks when the legs are better but not perfect.**
plan: **Open, confirm identity, and ONE open question even though this is not a history station.** **‘Before I go through them — what have you been told so far, and what's been worrying you most?’** Twenty seconds that confirms identity, relieves the main anxiety immediately, and **surfaces the fear AND often hands you the family history for free.**

**TASK 1 — the four beats. NINETY SECONDS. Set that intention before you walk in.** This is a results station wearing a history station's clothing, and the explanation is genuinely harder than usual — two tests, two vascular systems, one anatomical junction. **That difficulty IS the trap: it invites you to spend three minutes here.**

**HISTORY BLOCK A — SYMPTOMS AND COMPLICATIONS, signposted.** Pain — where, how long, what it feels like · **worse standing, better elevated** · **swelling, and does it settle overnight** — venous oedema improves overnight, cardiac, renal and hepatic oedema tend not to · **ULCERS, sores, or anything slow to heal — NEVER OMIT** · rash, dryness, cracking, colour change · numbness or pins and needles — **heaviness is part of the syndrome, FRANK NUMBNESS IS NOT, and stocking numbness means screen for diabetes** · **‘does either calf ever get SUDDENLY hot, red, tender or much more swollen than the other?’ — screens cellulitis AND DVT in nine seconds.**

**BLOCK B — RISK FACTORS IN TWO TIERS.** **TIER ONE, venous-specific, ASKED BY NAME: previous CLOT or DVT or blood thinners — a past DVT destroys valves directly, making this POST-THROMBOTIC rather than primary, with a worse prognosis · VARICOSE VEINS, the visible face of the same reflux · PROLONGED STANDING AT WORK · FAMILY HISTORY of varicose veins or leg ulcers**, plus pregnancies, previous leg fracture, orthopaedic surgery or immobility. **TIER TWO, cardiovascular — BUNDLE IT INTO ONE QUESTION. These are cardiovascular, not arterial, risk factors and the link is WEAKER for venous than arterial disease. Smoking impairs healing and obesity defeats the calf pump, so they still matter — but DO NOT spend ninety seconds here.**

**BLOCK C — FUNCTION, FALLS AND HOME. The block most candidates never reach, and where the general-practice marks live.** Impact on day, work, sleep, walking · **falls, near-misses, unsteadiness** · activities of daily living — **and SPECIFICALLY ‘can you reach your own feet?’, because it determines whether he can apply a stocking or inspect for ulcers unaided** · home hazards — stairs, loose rugs, lighting · **‘who's at home with you? Anyone who could help with the stockings or check your feet?’**
5:30 — MOVE, MID-SENTENCE IF NECESSARY

**TASK 3 — and STATE THE TWO GOALS BEFORE THE PLAN.** **‘There are two reasons we treat this. The first is to STOP IT GETTING WORSE — left alone it tends to progress. The second, and the bigger one, is to PREVENT AN ULCER. Once the skin properly breaks down on a leg like this, it can take MONTHS to heal, it can get INFECTED, and it's genuinely hard to get back. Everything I'm about to suggest is aimed at making sure that doesn't happen.’** **Fifteen seconds, and it converts a list of chores into a rationale — the difference between a patient who wears the stockings and one who does not.**
BLOCK 1 — COMPRESSION, the cornerstone

**‘Firm elastic stockings, TIGHTEST AT THE ANKLE and easing off up the leg. That squeeze NARROWS the stretched veins so the FLAPS CAN MEET AGAIN, stops fluid leaking into the tissues, and helps push blood back up.’** **Then CLOSE THE LOOP: ‘we can only use firm compression safely if the arteries are supplying the leg properly, and yours are — that's why we checked before prescribing.’** **ON FIRST THING IN THE MORNING, BEFORE YOU GET OUT OF BED and before the swelling builds; OFF AT NIGHT.** **Around 20–30 mmHg at the ankle for skin changes; 30–40 for healed or active ulceration, and MULTILAYER BANDAGING rather than stockings while an ulcer is open** VERIFY. **MEASURED, NOT GUESSED — and offer a donning aid or a lighter class they will actually wear: AN UNWORN CLASS-3 STOCKING ACHIEVES NOTHING.**
BLOCKS 2 AND 3 — skin, and elevation

**PODIATRY, and say what they will DO: a DAILY EMOLLIENT, plain and unperfumed; teach DAILY inspection of the feet and lower legs including between the toes and behind the malleoli; and go through exactly what INFECTION looks like.** **WARN EXPLICITLY ABOUT CONTACT ALLERGY — this population sensitises to lanolin, fragrances and topical antibiotics at high rates, and the ‘worsening eczema’ is often THE CREAM.** A short topical corticosteroid course for an active flare, then stop VERIFY. **ELEVATION: ‘above the level of your HEART — pillows under the ankles, NOT JUST A FOOTSTOOL’ — a footstool does not remove the hydrostatic column, and that phrase is the scored one.** Half an hour, three or four times a day; avoid long stretches of standing still.
BLOCKS 4 AND 5, then escalate and close

**EXERCISE, SUPERVISED — physiotherapist or exercise physiologist, with TWO reasons: his legs hurt, so you cannot simply tell him to walk for an hour; and they will teach CALF PUMPING exercises, because the calf muscles ARE the pump doing the job the valves aren't.** **Preserve ankle range of motion — a stiff ankle disables the calf pump entirely.** **RISK FACTORS: weight with a dietitian — MECHANISTIC here, because abdominal adiposity raises intra-abdominal pressure and directly worsens venous return; smoking, because HEALING IS THE WHOLE GAME — Quitline 13 7848; alcohol; occupational modification.** **ESCALATE to vascular surgery if symptoms progress despite adequate conservative treatment or an ulcer develops.** **Then SAFETY-NET: any break in the skin, spreading redness, fever, increasing pain. Written information. Review in four to six weeks.**
pefe: **HIS ANSWERS, so you know what you are fishing for** (each given ONLY if asked): pain **eight or nine months, both legs, heavy and aching — ‘by the end of a shift they weigh a tonne’** · **worse STANDING, much better with feet up** · swelling **builds through the day — ‘by four o'clock my socks leave a ring’** · **no ulcer, but a graze CAUGHT on the tow bar took three weeks to close over** · skin **brown around both ankles, dry and flaky, ITCHES worst at NIGHT — his wife says he scratches in his sleep** · no numbness · no sudden hot red PAINFUL leg · **never a DVT** · **varicose veins behind the left calf for years** · **LOADING dock SUPERVISOR, ten hours a shift on concrete** · **MOTHER had varicose veins AND a leg ulcer; older SISTER has the veins** · **fifteen CIGARETTES a day since twenty, tried quitting twice** · four or five beers most NIGHTS · **blood pressure ‘a bit up’ two years ago and UNTREATED** · **OVERWEIGHT, ‘diet's whatever's quick’** · sleep poor from the itch, **STOPPED walking the dog** · no falls · **reaching his feet is a struggle — his wife cuts his TOENAILS** · **SUPPORT at home: wife Karen, would help with anything.**

**And what that last answer CHANGES — this is why the functional block exists.** He cannot reliably inspect his own lower legs or don a firm stocking unaided, **so the daily skin check and the donning aid become HIS WIFE'S job or the community nurse's, AND YOU MUST SAY SO.** **Examiners notice when a plan is TAILORED to something the patient actually said** — it is the difference between a plan and a recitation. **Bundle the cardiovascular sweep into ONE question to buy the forty seconds this block needs, but ask the tier-one venous risks INDIVIDUALLY AND BY NAME, because those are the scored ones.**

**Endovenous thermal ablation — radiofrequency or laser — is now the usual FIRST-LINE intervention for saphenous reflux; ultrasound-guided foam sclerotherapy and open ligation and stripping are alternatives.** **Refer when symptoms persist despite adequate conservative treatment; for an ACTIVE OR NON-HEALING ULCER, because treating superficial reflux EARLY alongside compression improves ulcer healing** VERIFY; **for recurrent ulceration; for a BLEEDING VARICOSITY or SUPERFICIAL THROMBOPHLEBITIS NEAR THE SAPHENO-FEMORAL JUNCTION — within a few centimetres may warrant anticoagulation; and for diagnostic uncertainty or an ABI below 0.8.**

**Answering ‘could this be leukaemia?’ — a fair question with a clean answer.** **Generalised pruritus IS a recognised presentation of myeloproliferative and lymphoproliferative disease — polycythaemia vera classically (itch after a hot shower, plethora, splenomegaly), Hodgkin lymphoma and CLL less so.** **What excludes it here is THE DISTRIBUTION AND THE COMPANY THE ITCH KEEPS: this itch is CONFINED to the lower legs in the gaiter area, accompanied by pigmentation and skin thickening, on a background of demonstrated venous reflux. HAEMATOLOGICAL PRURITUS IS GENERALISED, has no dermatological substrate at the site, and is not confined to a vascular territory.** **If it were generalised, or with night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy or a palpable spleen, a FBC and film would be entirely reasonable — and it's a cheap test if you're unsure.**

**Scripted difficult moments.** *‘Can't I just have a water tablet like my neighbour?’* → **‘I can see why that seems logical, but it wouldn't help. Water tablets take fluid out of your WHOLE BODY, and your problem isn't too much fluid overall — it's PRESSURE BUILDING UP IN THE LEGS SPECIFICALLY. So it wouldn't fix the leg, and it could do your kidneys harm.’** *‘Aren't stockings for old ladies?’* → **‘They're the single most effective treatment we have, and there are much better-looking options than there used to be — including ones that just look like sports socks. Let's find a pair you'd ACTUALLY BE WILLING TO WEAR, because A STOCKING IN THE DRAWER DOES NOTHING.’**

*‘How much will they cost?’* → **‘I won't pretend they're cheap — there's NO GENERAL SUBSIDY, and a good pair is a real expense. But they last, and I'd rather find you something AFFORDABLE THAT YOU'LL WEAR than prescribe the perfect stocking you'll give up on.’** *‘Do I have to wear them forever?’* → **‘Realistically, long-term, yes. They're MANAGING the problem rather than CURING it, and I'd rather be straight with you about that than have you stop in six weeks when the legs feel better. We'll find a pair you can actually live with.’** **Honest rather than comfortable — and that last sentence is what keeps the stocking in use.**

*‘My mate just had his veins done — why can't I?’* → **‘That may well be where we end up. But the evidence is that we get the best results by STARTING with compression and the other measures and ADDING a procedure if that isn't enough — not the other way round.’** *‘I can't stop smoking, I've tried.’* → **‘Most people who succeed have tried several times first, so having tried twice puts you AHEAD, not behind. This is the one that matters MOST for your legs, because it slows healing and healing is the whole game here. Can I start you on something to make it easier this time?’**

**The single most persuasive move available in a chronic disease consultation: REUSE HIS OWN EVIDENCE.** He mentions a graze on the ankle that took three weeks to heal. **Not an ulcer — but DELAYED HEALING AT THE GAITER AREA IS THE WARNING SHOT.** **Name it back to him inside the management rationale: ‘you told me a graze took three weeks to heal — that's the early warning.’** It makes the prevention argument concrete instead of theoretical.

**VARIANT B — a clinical photograph in the stem.** **DESCRIBE IT OUT LOUD — it earns marks AND saves history time.** *‘There's a brownish staining around both ankles — that's IRON from blood cells that have leaked into the skin, and it tells me this has been going on a while. The skin's dry and scaly, which is what's itching, and it's thickened and tight low down. The good news is THE SKIN IS STILL INTACT — there's no ulcer — and that's exactly what I want to keep.’* **Stage it silently: pigmentation and eczema C4a, thickened narrowed lower leg C4b. Then SKIP the ‘have you noticed any discolouration’ question and spend the time on the functional block.**

**VARIANT C — an ACTIVE VENOUS ULCER, and the plan CHANGES SHAPE in four ways.** **1 COMPRESSION BANDAGING, NOT STOCKINGS, while the ulcer is open — multilayer compression is what HEALS venous ulcers; stockings come later for maintenance** VERIFY. **2 COMMUNITY NURSING for dressings and bandaging — not optional for a patient who cannot reach his own feet. 3 EARLY vascular referral, NOT deferred — an ulcer moves referral from ‘if things worsen’ to ‘NOW’.** **4 Check HbA1c, and SWAB SELECTIVELY.** *‘The most important treatment is FIRM BANDAGING, which a community nurse will do and change regularly. That's what heals these. Once it's closed over you'll move on to stockings TO STOP IT COMING BACK — and it does come back if you stop.’*

**VARIANT D — history first, results at the end.** Now you must GENERATE the diagnosis. **Say your differential GROUPS aloud before narrowing — venous, arterial, lymphatic, systemic oedema, dermatological, neurological, and systemic causes of itch.** **Request examination findings EXPLICITLY: peripheral pulses and capillary refill; distribution of oedema and whether it PITS; whether the TOES AND DORSUM are involved; gaiter skin changes; ulceration site and character; STEMMER SIGN; temperature and asymmetry; sensation, MONOFILAMENT and vibration; abdominal and cardiac examination if bilateral oedema; BMI.** **Then request investigations WITH REASONS ATTACHED.**

**VARIANT E — the AMC's lower-limb cluster is RECOMBINED EVERY SITTING: peripheral arterial disease, cellulitis and diabetic sensory neuropathy, in every pairing.** **THREE RULES THAT SURVIVE EVERY RECOMBINATION: (1) ALWAYS establish arterial status before committing to compression, whatever the venous findings say. (2) BILATERAL, GRADUAL, ITCHY, GAITER-DISTRIBUTED IS VENOUS; UNILATERAL, ACUTE, HOT, TENDER IS INFECTIVE OR THROMBOTIC — and if both pictures are present, TREAT THE ACUTE ONE FIRST AND SAY SO. (3) ANYONE WITH CHRONIC LEG DISEASE GETS AN HbA1c AND A SENSATION CHECK — the neuropathy is the layer that turns a manageable leg into an ulcerated one, and it is the layer candidates forget.** SA — **GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangements to fund podiatry, physiotherapy and dietetics** VERIFY · **COUNTRY HEALTH CONNECT community nursing for compression bandaging and wound care — the practical route for an MM5 patient who cannot manage a dressing alone** · **public vascular at RAH, Flinders and TQEH, with telehealth review through the country LHNs** · **PATS for travel over 100 km each way** VERIFY · **NO universal SA subsidy for compression stockings — cost is a genuine adherence barrier and should be NAMED in the consultation; DVA covers eligible veterans and some LHN wound clinics supply garments** · **Quitline 13 7848, ADIS 1300 13 1340** · **chronic leg ulceration carries a substantially higher burden in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people — lower threshold for community nursing.**

Tasks: explain the results and the most likely diagnosis — explain the cause and the likely course — discuss the initial management plan.

Tasks: explain the management of rheumatoid arthritis — explain what he needs checked while on methotrexate.

findings: THE RESULTS YOU ARE HANDED — case A
RHEUMATOID FACTOR POSITIVE. ANTI-CCP ANTIBODY POSITIVE. Mother has rheumatoid arthritis. Diclofenac has not helped
WHICH RESULT ACTUALLY MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS

RHEUMATOID FACTOR IS A SCREENING TEST — neither sensitive nor specific enough alone, and positive in other autoimmune disease, chronic infection AND IN HEALTHY OLDER PEOPLE. ANTI-CCP IS THE SPECIFIC TEST, around 95–98% specificity VERIFY, and it often turns positive YEARS BEFORE SYMPTOMS. Say it out loud: ‘it is the ANTI-CCP that carries the weight here, in a patient with the right symptom pattern and a first-degree family history’
CORRECTION — ‘a positive anti-CCP means RA 100% of the time’. IT DOES NOT

It appears in PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS, some chronic infections, INTERSTITIAL LUNG DISEASE and occasionally in healthy people. It is also NEGATIVE IN SERONEGATIVE RA, so a negative does NOT exclude the diagnosis. RA IS A CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS supported by serology, inflammatory markers and imaging
If the examiner challenges you on that

‘Anti-CCP is the most specific serological test available and in this clinical context it STRONGLY SUPPORTS the diagnosis, but I would NOT make the diagnosis on a single antibody. I am relying on the SYMMETRICAL SMALL-JOINT PATTERN, the PROLONGED MORNING STIFFNESS, the FAMILY HISTORY and the SEROLOGY TOGETHER’
The pattern that makes it
SYMMETRICAL · POLYARTICULAR · SMALL JOINTS OF THE HANDS (MCP, PIP) AND WRISTS · DIP SPARED · MORNING STIFFNESS LASTING MORE THAN 30–60 MINUTES · BETTER WITH USE, WORSE WITH REST VERIFY
INVESTIGATIONS YOU WOULD ORDER TODAY

BLOODS: FBE · ESR and CRP · UEC · LFT · TSH · ANA (and ENA if positive) · uric acid if the story allows · HEPATITIS B AND C SEROLOGY AND A CHEST X-RAY AS BASELINE BEFORE IMMUNOSUPPRESSION. IMAGING: plain films of HANDS AND FEET — THE FEET OFTEN ERODE FIRST AND ARE OFTEN FORGOTTEN; ultrasound of the hands detects synovitis earlier than plain films where available. ALSO: urinalysis, BLOOD PRESSURE, LIPIDS AND GLUCOSE — baseline cardiovascular risk, WHICH THIS DIAGNOSIS RAISES
THE FOUR-SENTENCE MONITORING ANSWER — the task in case B is asking for exactly this

‘BEFORE STARTING: bloods, a CHEST X-RAY, HEPATITIS AND VARICELLA serology, VACCINATIONS and a PREGNANCY TEST. Then FULL BLOOD COUNT, LIVER FUNCTION AND KIDNEY FUNCTION EVERY TWO TO FOUR WEEKS for the first few months, and AFTER ANY DOSE CHANGE. Once stable, EVERY ONE TO THREE MONTHS — THREE MONTHS IS THE LONGEST I WOULD LEAVE IT. And I'd check in on side effects, alcohol and ANY NEW COUGH at each of those visits’
CORRECTION — monitoring is NOT just FBE and LFT

ADD RENAL FUNCTION. METHOTREXATE IS CLEARED BY THE KIDNEYS, so falling renal function causes the drug to ACCUMULATE and is a well-recognised route to SEVERE TOXICITY. FBE + LFT + UEC TOGETHER, EVERY TIME VERIFY
CORRECTION — folic acid TIMING

Give folic acid ON A DIFFERENT DAY from the methotrexate (commonly the day after), or daily EXCEPT on the methotrexate day. TAKING BOTH TOGETHER ON THE SAME DAY REDUCES THE DRUG'S EFFECT. Commonly 5 mg weekly in Australian practice VERIFY
VACCINATION — BEFORE, NOT AFTER

Check and update BEFORE starting: INFLUENZA (annual), COVID-19, PNEUMOCOCCAL, dTpa, and HEPATITIS B serology. CHECK VARICELLA IMMUNITY AND VACCINATE IF NON-IMMUNE, because VARICELLA VACCINE IS LIVE AND CANNOT BE GIVEN once he is immunosuppressed. SHINGRIX IS NON-LIVE and can be given during therapy. RESPONSE TO VACCINES IS BLUNTED after immunosuppression starts — which is the reason for doing it first VERIFY

dx: **TWO COUNSELLING CASES ON ONE SPINE.** **CASE A — a new diagnosis of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis in a 25-year-old PIANIST.** **CASE B — a 45-year-old man who has read that METHOTREXATE CAUSES CANCER and has come in ANGRY.** **Case B's first task is the WHOLE of case A's task 3, delivered to someone who is furious — learn case A properly and case B becomes a communication problem with a familiar core.**

**ONE POINT DECIDES CASE A: NAME THE DMARD AND REFER URGENTLY, EARLY.** **Candidates explain rheumatoid arthritis beautifully, cover painkillers and physiotherapy, and NEVER SAY THE WORD METHOTREXATE OR THE WORD RHEUMATOLOGIST.** **Say DMARD · METHOTREXATE · RHEUMATOLOGIST · EARLY in one sentence, and say it BEFORE MINUTE SIX.** **Miss it and nothing else rescues the station.**

**ONE POINT DECIDES CASE B: AGREE THAT HIS CONCERN IS VALID BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN ANYTHING.** **‘I completely understand why you're angry, and I want to be honest with you: YOU ARE POINTING AT SOMETHING REAL. I'd be worried too if I'd read that. Can I take you through the condition and the medication properly, and then WE'LL MAKE A PLAN TOGETHER?’** **The examiner is watching for one thing: do you DENY, MINIMISE or ARGUE — or do you say ‘you are not wrong’? Everything else is recoverable. That is not.**

**THE TRAP IN CASE B: some recalls render task 1 as ‘convince him to keep taking the medication’. YOU ARE NOT BEING ASKED TO CONVINCE HIM. You are being asked to INFORM him properly so HE can decide.** **A candidate who bullies, minimises, or says ‘methotrexate does not cause cancer’ FAILS.** **A COMPETENT ADULT WITH CAPACITY MAY DECLINE ANY TREATMENT.**

**THE CANCER ANSWER, VERBATIM — three parts**: **‘ONE: rheumatoid arthritis ITSELF increases the risk of certain cancers, particularly LYMPHOMA. That is the DISEASE, not the drug. TWO: methotrexate MAY ADD A SMALL AMOUNT to that risk. I'm not going to tell you it doesn't. THREE: in a person who HAS RA AND TAKES METHOTREXATE, we genuinely CANNOT SEPARATE THE TWO — and because methotrexate CONTROLS THE INFLAMMATION THAT DRIVES THE RISK in the first place, IT MAY ACTUALLY LOWER IT. So: possibly a small added risk, and we can't say for certain where it comes from. WHAT WE ARE CERTAIN ABOUT ARE THE RISKS OF LEAVING THE ARTHRITIS UNCONTROLLED.’** VERIFY **Speak in DIRECTION OF EFFECT AND UNCERTAINTY, never invented percentages.**

**EXPLAINING WHAT RA IS, in plain words**: **‘It's an AUTOIMMUNE condition — your immune system, which normally fights infection, MISTAKENLY STARTS ATTACKING YOUR OWN BODY. It mainly attacks the LINING OF THE JOINTS, causing pain, swelling, stiffness and redness. But this is the important part: IT IS NOT ONLY A JOINT DISEASE. The same process can affect your EYES, your LUNGS, your HEART AND BLOOD VESSELS, and the NERVES. That is exactly why we take it seriously and treat it properly.’** **NAME THREE ORGANS, not a list.**

**THE CAUSE — BE HONEST, AND REMOVE BLAME**: **‘The truthful answer is that we DON'T KNOW EXACTLY. It's a combination of GENES — which is why it runs in families — and things in the ENVIRONMENT, of which SMOKING is the one we know most about. IT IS NOT SOMETHING YOU DID, not something you ATE, and not something you could have PREVENTED.’** **THE COURSE: ‘it settles and then FLARES. Each flare is a burst of inflammation, and IT IS THE REPEATED FLARES that gradually damage the joints and cause deformity — AND THAT DAMAGE DOESN'T REVERSE. So everything we do is aimed at PREVENTING flares rather than just treating them once they arrive.’**

**CORRECTION — DO NOT SAY ‘THERE IS NO TREATMENT FOR THIS’.** There is no CURE, but **rheumatoid arthritis is now one of the MOST TREATABLE chronic diseases in medicine, and SUSTAINED REMISSION IS A REALISTIC GOAL.** **Saying ‘there's no treatment’ to a 25-year-old is both INACCURATE AND CRUEL, and examiners mark it down.** **Say: ‘we can't CURE it, but we can CONTROL it very well — and THE EARLIER WE START, THE BETTER WE DO.’**

**AND CORRECTION — NSAIDs ARE NOT ‘LONG-TERM TREATMENT’ for RA.** They relieve pain and swelling but **DO NOT MODIFY THE DISEASE and DO NOT PREVENT EROSION.** In Australian practice they are **ADJUNCTIVE, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest sensible period, with a PPI if GI risk is present.** If challenged: **‘I'd use an NSAID for symptom control WHILE THE DMARD TAKES EFFECT, but THE DMARD IS THE TREATMENT.’** Steroids are **a BRIDGE, not long term — prednisolone works fast, but raises BP and blood sugar, causes weight gain, thins the bones and upsets the stomach.**

**HER HEALTH BELIEF IS THE THING DRIVING THE FEAR — find it and correct it.** She goes quiet and says **‘Like Mum.’** **Walk through that door: ‘tell me what happened to your mum's hands.’** Then: **‘Treatment for this has changed ENORMOUSLY since your mum was diagnosed. What we can do now is NOT what was available then, and THE WHOLE REASON I WANT TO MOVE QUICKLY is to make sure your hands do not follow that path.’**
plan: CASE A · open

**WIPE, then ONE open question BEFORE the results**: **‘I do have your blood results back today. BEFORE we get to them, can you tell me what has happened so far? … And is there anything in particular you're WORRIED about, or hoping I can help with today?’** **Opening with ‘I've got your results, they're positive’ loses rapport and you never find out that her mother's deformed hands are the picture in her head.**
CASE A · task 1

**REASON IT OUT BEFORE YOU NAME IT** — symptoms, then family history, then why the tests were done, then RF as the screen and anti-CCP as the specific one. **Then: ‘Putting all of that together, I'M AFRAID this does look like rheumatoid arthritis.’** **Then STOP: ‘that's a lot to take in. HOW ARE YOU FEELING ABOUT THAT?’ — and WAIT. DO NOT FILL THE SILENCE. Examiners mark the pause.**
CASE A · task 2
**What RA is → whole-body, three organs → the cause, honestly, with blame removed → the course, flares and irreversible damage → no cure but very treatable, remission as the goal.**
CASE A · task 3, part one

**SYMPTOM CONTROL — two halves, and name the side effects.** NSAIDs with the stomach and kidney caveats; **prednisolone as a FAST-ACTING BRIDGE with its four downsides.** **Read ‘initial management’ GENEROUSLY — give the WHOLE package anyway. Nobody has ever lost a mark for completeness here, and the single item that decides the station sits inside it.**
CASE A · task 3, part two ★

**THE DMARD REFERRAL, scripted**: **‘The second half is the important one. I'm going to refer you to a RHEUMATOLOGIST, and I want that to happen SOON. They will start you on DISEASE-MODIFYING ANTI-RHEUMATIC DRUGS — DMARDs — and the usual first choice is METHOTREXATE. These are DIFFERENT from painkillers: they don't just MASK the symptoms, they CALM DOWN THE IMMUNE SYSTEM and STOP THE DISEASE DAMAGING YOUR JOINTS. The reason I want you seen quickly is that THE EARLIER THESE ARE STARTED, THE MORE JOINT DAMAGE WE PREVENT, and that damage DOESN'T COME BACK once it's done.’**
CASE A · task 3, part three ★

**PREGNANCY — ASK IT, IN THIS PATIENT.** **‘Before we go further, there's something I need to ask because IT CHANGES WHAT WE CHOOSE. Are you planning a pregnancy in the foreseeable future, and what are you using for contraception? METHOTREXATE IS ONE MEDICINE WE CANNOT USE IN PREGNANCY OR WHILE TRYING — IT HARMS THE BABY. That doesn't mean you CAN'T have children; it means WE PLAN IT, and there are OTHER DMARDs that are safe in pregnancy.’** **The source lecture does not mention any of this. In an OSCE with a young woman, OMITTING IT IS A SERIOUS SAFETY MISS.**
CASE A · task 3, the rest

**THE TEAM — physiotherapist** (stronger muscles mean less load through the joints) · **occupational therapist / HAND THERAPIST for splints and aids** · **psychologist, because this is a lot to absorb at 25.** **LIFESTYLE — exercise, diet, weight, and specifically SMOKING (‘makes RA worse AND makes the medicines work less well’) and alcohol; plus BP, lipids and sugars because RA ITSELF RAISES HEART RISK.** **SUPPORT — written material, and Arthritis Australia** VERIFY. Then **summary, safety-net, follow-up.**

**LISTEN, AND BE SEEN LISTENING.** He opens fast and loud. **NOD. MAKE EYE CONTACT. DO NOT INTERRUPT, do not put your hand up, DO NOT START A SENTENCE WITH ‘BUT’. **Re-explain RA, then give TWO IRREVERSIBLE CONSEQUENCES: repeated inflammation DESTROYS THE JOINTS and that damage is irreversible; the same inflammation DAMAGES OTHER ORGANS — lungs, heart and vessels, eyes, nerves — and that is irreversible too.** **Then FRAME RISK BEFORE DISCUSSING IT: ‘every medicine has side effects — EVEN PARACETAMOL. And if, after all that, you STILL WANT TO STOP IT, THAT IS YOUR DECISION — we'd then talk through the other options. MY JOB IS TO MAKE SURE WHATEVER YOU CHOOSE IS AN INFORMED CHOICE. pefe: **THE PIANO — case A's hidden agenda, released at about six minutes if you never ask.** *‘I'm a professional pianist with the symphony orchestra. It's my job, not a hobby. Should I stop playing?’* **DO NOT ANSWER YES. DO NOT ANSWER NO.** You do not know the severity, her hand function, how many hours she plays or how it affects her. **This question needs EDUCATION, NOT A VERDICT — and it is the single most memorable moment in the case.**

**THE DIPLOMATIC ANSWER, IN FIVE MOVES**: **‘1 That's the most important question you've asked me, and I want to answer it PROPERLY rather than QUICKLY. 2 Your symptoms — the pain and the swelling — CAN certainly interfere with playing, so what you can do will VARY. 3 But if we start the right treatment, get you onto a DMARD like methotrexate and get a PHYSIOTHERAPIST AND HAND THERAPIST working with you, THERE IS A REAL CHANCE YOU WILL BE ABLE TO KEEP PLAYING. I'm not PROMISING, but I'm not WRITING IT OFF either. 4 What I would say is: AVOID PLAYING THROUGH A FLARE — when the joints are hot, swollen and painful, playing through it MAKES THE INFLAMMATION WORSE. 5 And I'll follow you closely. If it turns out you can't sustain performing, I CAN WRITE TO YOUR EMPLOYER to help you find a suitable role — teaching, or another position in the orchestra — RATHER THAN YOU SIMPLY LOSING YOUR CAREER.’**

**THE PREMATURE-CLOSURE TRAP: do NOT jump to ‘I'll give you a certificate and send you to Centrelink.’** She has a **TREATABLE condition that HAS NOT BEEN TREATED YET**, and an income-support pathway would assess her as able to do other work anyway. **TREAT FIRST, ADAPT SECOND, and only discuss income support if genuine long-term incapacity develops** — then Services Australia, with a supporting report from you and the rheumatologist.

**TWO THINGS THAT KILL PEOPLE.** **1 DAILY DOSING. Methotrexate for RA is taken ONCE A WEEK. ACCIDENTAL DAILY DOSING CAUSES FATAL BONE-MARROW FAILURE and is a recognised Australian medication-safety alert. SAY THE DAY OF THE WEEK OUT LOUD, WRITE IT ON THE BOX, and check it at every review.** **2 TRIMETHOPRIM. Trimethoprim and trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole with methotrexate can cause SEVERE PANCYTOPENIA. AVOID THE COMBINATION and make sure any other prescriber knows he is on methotrexate.** **Plus: keep alcohol low or none, because BOTH ALCOHOL AND THE DRUG WORK ON THE LIVER.**

**Explaining methotrexate, and answering ‘isn't that chemotherapy?’**: **‘It IS used at much higher doses in cancer treatment, yes — but for arthritis it's used at a LOW dose, ONCE A WEEK, and it works by CALMING THE IMMUNE SYSTEM rather than as chemotherapy. It takes SEVERAL WEEKS to work — which is why steroids are often used at the start to cover the gap. You'd have FOLIC ACID with it to reduce side effects, and regular blood tests.’** **Side effects SANDWICHED: nausea, mouth ulcers, tiredness, dry skin, hair thinning; the two watched with bloods are LIVER and BLOOD COUNT; rarely LUNG INFLAMMATION — ‘and the good news is the FOLIC ACID reduces a lot of those.’**

**THE SAFETY-NET on immunosuppression — say it, or the station is marked down**: **‘See a doctor THE SAME DAY if you get a FEVER, SORE THROAT OR MOUTH ULCERS, any unusual BRUISING OR BLEEDING, YELLOW EYES OR DARK URINE, or a NEW DRY COUGH OR BREATHLESSNESS. Those are the ones we don't wait on.’**

**Scripted variants.** *‘We've been trying for a baby for six months.’* → **‘I'm really glad you've told me, because it CHANGES THINGS. Methotrexate cannot be used in pregnancy or while trying. That does NOT mean you can't have children and it does NOT mean we leave the arthritis untreated — HYDROXYCHLOROQUINE AND SULFASALAZINE are considered safe in pregnancy, and I'll make sure the rheumatologist knows this is a priority from the FIRST appointment. Can I also ask — IS THERE ANY CHANCE YOU COULD BE PREGNANT RIGHT NOW? I'd like to do a test TODAY before anything is started.’** **The trap is reassuring her that ‘we'll sort that out later’ — the DRUG CHOICE CHANGES NOW.** **Methotrexate must be stopped and washed out before conception, FOR BOTH WOMEN AND MEN** VERIFY.

*‘I want to stop it and try herbal medicine.’* → **‘That is YOUR decision to make and I'll respect it — it's your body. What I'd ask is THREE things. First, let me tell you what STOPPING means, so the decision is fully informed: without a disease-modifying medicine the inflammation continues, and the joint and organ damage doesn't reverse. Second, TELL ME WHAT YOU PLAN TO TAKE, because some herbal preparations affect the LIVER or interact with other medicines. Third — PLEASE KEEP SEEING ME AND KEEP THE BLOOD TESTS GOING, whatever you decide, so that if things change we can act early. And I'll still arrange that joint appointment, because there are other DMARDs, including injections and biologicals, that might suit you better.’** **EITHER CAPITULATING WITHOUT EXPLAINING CONSEQUENCES, OR REFUSING TO ACCEPT HIS DECISION — BOTH FAIL.**

**Examiner interruptions, scripted.** *‘Why not just start methotrexate yourself?’* → **‘In Australian practice DMARDs are usually INITIATED BY A RHEUMATOLOGIST, with defined pre-treatment screening, monitoring and PBS authority requirements. My role is to refer PROMPTLY, arrange BASELINE investigations, and then SHARE the monitoring.’** VERIFY *‘What is treat to target?’* → **‘Setting a DEFINED TARGET — remission or low disease activity — and ESCALATING therapy at regular reviews UNTIL IT IS REACHED, judged on symptoms, swollen joints and inflammatory markers.’** *‘Can you force him to take it?’* → **‘NO. He has capacity. My obligation is to inform him fully, offer alternatives, and CONTINUE TO CARE FOR HIM WHATEVER HE DECIDES.’**

**If she asks about diet, turmeric or going gluten free**: **‘There's NO DIET THAT CURES rheumatoid arthritis, and I'd be cautious of anyone who says otherwise. A Mediterranean-style diet and a healthy weight are sensible and may help how you feel. If you want to try a supplement, TELL ME WHAT IT IS FIRST — some affect the liver or interact with the medicines. What I would NOT want is for a supplement to be used INSTEAD OF the treatment that prevents joint damage.’** **And ‘will my children get it?’ → ‘having a parent with it raises the risk, but MOST CHILDREN OF PEOPLE WITH RA NEVER DEVELOP IT. There's no genetic test we'd do and nothing to screen for now. THE MOST USEFUL THING ANYONE IN YOUR FAMILY CAN DO IS NOT SMOKE.’** SA — **mark the rheumatology referral URGENT (suspected early inflammatory arthritis) to RAH, Flinders or Lyell McEwin; telehealth rheumatology for country patients** · **PATS for travel** · **GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangement for physiotherapy, OT and psychology; GP Mental Health Treatment Plan** · **ACCHS and Closing the Gap PBS — relevant BECAUSE DMARD THERAPY IS LIFELONG** · **Quitline 13 7848** · **NOT a ReturnToWorkSA matter — this is not a work-caused injury.**

stem: General practice in regional South Australia, routine booked appointment. Nancy Pearce, 74, a retired schoolteacher who lives alone, attending for her annual review of hand osteoarthritis diagnosed about eight years ago. No new complaint in the stem.
T 36.5°C · HR 74 · BP 142/84 · BMI 27 · walks in unaided.

Tasks: take a focused history in four minutes — describe the relevant findings on a photograph of her hands to the examiner — explain the diagnosis and your differential diagnoses. In the hybrid version, task 2 becomes 'Describe how you would examine her hands'.
tasks: Take a focused history (four minutes)
Describe the relevant findings on the photograph to the examiner
Explain the diagnosis and your differential diagnoses
findingsLabel: The photograph and the findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: DESCRIBE FIRST, CONCLUDE SECOND — the examiner is scoring OBSERVATION, not recognition
Saying ‘this is osteoarthritis’ and THEN describing loses the mark. Use a FIXED ORDER: DISTRIBUTION → NAMED SIGNS → DEFORMITY → WASTING → SKIN AND NAILS
DISTRIBUTION

‘The changes are at the DISTAL AND PROXIMAL INTERPHALANGEAL JOINTS and at the BASE OF THE THUMB. THE METACARPOPHALANGEAL JOINTS LOOK SPARED.’ OA loves DIP, PIP and thumb base; RA loves MCP, PIP and WRIST and SPARES the DIP
NAMED SIGNS

‘HEBERDEN'S NODES at the DISTAL interphalangeal joints, BOUCHARD'S NODES at the PROXIMAL interphalangeal joints, and SQUARING at the BASE OF THE THUMB.’ Mnemonic: HEBERDEN = HIGHEST joint, furthest out (DIP). Bouchard is the one before it
DEFORMITY
‘There is LATERAL ANGULATION of the fingers at the affected interphalangeal joints. I see NO ULNAR DEVIATION at the knuckles and NO SWAN-NECK OR BOUTONNIÈRE deformity’
WASTING, SKIN AND NAILS

‘There is WASTING OF THE SMALL MUSCLES of the hand, with HOLLOWING BETWEEN THE METACARPALS. No redness, no rash, NO NAIL PITTING OR ONYCHOLYSIS, no nail-fold changes, NO TOPHI. These appearances are TYPICAL OF OSTEOARTHRITIS’
CORRECTION — ‘radial deviation’ is NOT an osteoarthritis sign

Source material states OA causes radial deviation and RA causes ulnar deviation. The pairing that ACTUALLY matters is THE RHEUMATOID ZIG-ZAG: RADIAL DEVIATION AT THE WRIST WITH ULNAR DEVIATION AT THE MCPs, in the SAME hand, in OPPOSITE directions. In hand OA you see LATERAL ANGULATION AT THE INTERPHALANGEAL JOINTS from the nodes themselves, and in advanced thumb-base disease an ADDUCTED THUMB WITH COMPENSATORY HYPEREXTENSION at the MCP joint. If challenged: ‘I describe the DIRECTION and the JOINT SEPARATELY rather than attributing a direction to a disease’
CORRECTION — the thumb joint

The joint OA prefers at the thumb is the FIRST CARPOMETACARPAL (TRAPEZIOMETACARPAL) joint AT THE BASE OF THE THUMB — NOT the first metacarpophalangeal joint. ‘SQUARING’ refers to the BASE of the thumb
For contrast — the RHEUMATOID hand

THE KNUCKLES are the swollen joints (boggy swelling at the MCPs), the FINGERS DRIFT TOWARDS THE LITTLE-FINGER SIDE, the WRIST DRIFTS THE OTHER WAY, and the back of the hand is HOLLOWED BY WASTING. Plus nodules and nail-fold infarcts
VERSION B — the HYBRID, where task 2 becomes ‘describe how you would EXAMINE her hands’

HEADLINES ONLY, ABOUT NINETY SECONDS — no technique, no explanation of what each step tests. A LIST, DELIVERED BRISKLY. THE TRAP is starting a real examination and narrating each step; candidates fail this by attempting a complete hand examination and running out of time
The hybrid script, verbatim

‘After consent, exposure to the elbows and asking about pain, with the hands resting on a pillow: INSPECTION — both hands, DORSAL THEN PALMAR: swelling, Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes, squaring, deformity and deviation, wasting, skin and nail changes, scars. PALPATION — TEMPERATURE over the joints, then each small joint BIMANUALLY IN TWO PLANES for tenderness, bony swelling and synovitis; the wrists; the ANATOMICAL SNUFFBOX; a THUMB GRIND TEST. MOVEMENT — active then passive: finger flexion, extension, abduction, adduction; thumb flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and OPPOSITION; wrist flexion, extension and deviation. FUNCTION — GRIP STRENGTH, PINCH GRIP ON A COIN, THE OK SIGN, KEY GRIP, AND UNDOING A BUTTON. I would complete by examining THE ELBOWS for nodules and psoriasis, and the joint above’

dx: **Nodal osteoarthritis of the hands, established, with PROGRESSIVE FUNCTIONAL IMPAIRMENT and an INADEQUATELY REVIEWED ANALGESIC REGIMEN.**

**THE DIAGNOSIS IS GIVEN TO YOU IN THE STEM. That is deliberate, and it is what unsettles candidates: if you already know it is osteoarthritis, what is the history FOR?** **This is a CHRONIC-DISEASE ANNUAL REVIEW, not a diagnostic case. THE MARKS LIVE IN FUNCTION, TREATMENT REVIEW AND SUPPORT — not in grinding through arthritis differentials for four minutes.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: do you convert a chronic-disease review into a FUNCTIONAL AND SOCIAL ASSESSMENT, and ACT on what you find?** **Candidates fail by taking a competent four-minute pain history and stopping.** **THE EXAMINER IS WAITING FOR ‘WHO COOKS FOR YOU?’** **If you finish the station without having asked it, you have failed however fluent the rest was.**

**TWO OPEN QUESTIONS, NOT ONE — and the SECOND is what releases the case.** She opens with **‘I'm just here for my yearly check.’** **If you accept that, you have four minutes of nothing.** The role-player is briefed to **STAY CLOSED and give short answers if you move to a rote pain history — that IS the test.** **‘Of course. TELL ME HOW THINGS HAVE BEEN GOING WITH YOUR HANDS SINCE I LAST SAW YOU.’** → *‘Well, since you ask — they've got worse. The tablets aren't doing much any more, and I can't open jars at all now.’*

**THE COMPARISON TECHNIQUE — USE IT TWICE.** **‘Out of ten, how bad is the pain today? … AND WHAT WOULD YOU HAVE SAID A YEAR AGO?’** and **‘A year ago, could you open a jar? Can you now?’** **An annual review IS a comparison. Anyone can take a pain history; SHOWING CHANGE OVER A YEAR is what marks this out as a review.**

**ACCEPTING ‘I MANAGE’ IS THE NAMED FAILURE. ‘Manage’ IS NOT AN ANSWER.** Every limitation she has — jars, tins, buttons, chopping, the car key — **comes out ONLY because the tasks are NAMED.** **A person who cannot cook, wash or dress is a person who needs SUPPORT, not just a stronger tablet.**

**THE NSAID QUESTION IS A SCORED ITEM, and ‘heartburn’ is a clue you must ACT on.** An anti-inflammatory in a 74-year-old carries risk of **GASTROINTESTINAL BLEEDING, RENAL IMPAIRMENT, FLUID RETENTION AND RISING BLOOD PRESSURE — and her BP is already 142/84.** **Ask by SYMPTOM, not by naming the drug class** — indigestion, heartburn, stomach pain, **BLACK OR TARRY BOWEL MOTIONS**, ankle swelling. **And ask about OVER-THE-COUNTER ibuprofen and combination cold remedies; patients often do not count them as medication.**

**WHAT THE PATTERN TELLS YOU.** **Osteoarthritis is MECHANICAL: worse WITH USE, worse AT THE END OF THE DAY, morning stiffness UNDER 30 MINUTES.** **ADVANCED osteoarthritis DOES ache at rest and at night — that is NOT automatically an alarm in someone with eight years of disease.** **Stiffness lasting OVER AN HOUR with HOT SWOLLEN KNUCKLES is a DIFFERENT DISEASE.** VERIFY thresholds

**Explaining it to her, and the sentence that prevents harm**: **‘The smooth lining that lets the small joints GLIDE has worn thin, and the bone around it has THICKENED — those are the firm lumps you can feel at your fingertips. It is common with age and it IS slowly progressive, BUT THERE IS A LOT WE CAN DO about the pain and about KEEPING YOUR HANDS WORKING.’** Then, when she asks whether to rest them: **‘RESTING THEM COMPLETELY ACTUALLY MAKES IT WORSE — the muscles waste and the joints stiffen. KEEPING THEM MOVING, with the right aids and a splint, IS A LARGE PART OF THE TREATMENT.’** **Say ‘WEAR AND REPAIR’ rather than ‘wear and tear’ — more accurate and less defeating.**

**THE CYCLE YOU ARE TRYING TO INTERRUPT, and naming it out loud explains WHY hand therapy matters as much as analgesia**: **PAIN stops the hand being used → DISUSE wastes the small muscles → WEAKNESS makes every task hurt more.**
plan: **WIPE, then OPEN TWICE.** ‘How can I help you today?’ → *‘just here for my yearly check’* → **THE SECOND OPEN QUESTION.** If she is STILL giving you nothing: **‘Is there anything about your hands that has been bothering you, or anything you were hoping we could sort out today?’** **Then ACKNOWLEDGE the loss she discloses: ‘having to ask for help with something you have always done yourself is HARD. That is worth our whole appointment.’** Then **SIGNPOST: ‘I'd like to ask about the pain, then about the treatment and how it's working, then about how you're managing at home.’**

**BLOCK 1 — PAIN AND PATTERN, BRIEFLY. SIXTY SECONDS, THEN MOVE.** Which joints — **fingertips, middle knuckles, base of the thumb, or wrists** · **out of ten today AND a year ago** · constant or intermittent, getting worse · does it spread up the forearm · better or worse with what · **effect on life.** Then the three pattern questions: **night pain · worse with activity or aching at rest too · morning or later in the day, AND HOW MANY MINUTES to loosen up.**

**BLOCK 2 — GENERAL JOINT SCREEN, twenty seconds.** Swelling · redness or warmth · stiffness or difficulty moving the fingers · **crepitus — cracking or grating** · **have the joints CHANGED SHAPE** · **any other joints — knees, hips, neck.**

**BLOCK 3 — THE CHRONIC-DISEASE REVIEW: FIVE QUESTIONS, IN THIS ORDER.** **1 When were you diagnosed, and has anything been done since? 2 What are you taking NOW, and how often? 3 Are you able to take it AS PRESCRIBED? 4 Is it helping — AND IS IT HELPING LESS THAN IT USED TO? 5 Any SIDE EFFECTS — indigestion, heartburn, stomach pain, BLACK OR TARRY BOWEL MOTIONS, ankle swelling?** **Then act: screen for melaena, dizziness and anaemia, ask about over-the-counter medicines, and CHANGE THE DRUG.**

**BLOCK 4 — FUNCTION, THE HEART OF THE STATION. Start general, then GET SPECIFIC.** ‘Are you managing your usual daily activities?’ → *‘I manage’* → **then, whatever she answers: ‘WHO COOKS FOR YOU? Are you able to PREPARE A MEAL yourself? Can you WASH AND SHOWER yourself? Can you DRESS yourself — BUTTONS, ZIPS, bra fastenings? Can you OPEN A JAR, TURN A TAP, TURN A KEY, USE A PEN? Are you still DRIVING — can you GRIP THE WHEEL and turn it safely?’**

**BLOCK 5 — SUPPORT AND THE GERIATRIC SCREEN.** **Who do you LIVE with** · family or friends nearby who can help · **who does your SHOPPING, who helps with the HOUSEWORK** · **how has your MOOD been, are you still ENJOYING things** · sleep · **‘TELL ME WHAT YOU ATE YESTERDAY’** · **any FALLS in the last year.**
The diet question is not filler

**If she cannot grip a knife or open a tin, she is eating packet food or skipping meals.** **Ask what she ACTUALLY ATE YESTERDAY, not whether she eats well.** **And add a WEIGHT question — unintentional weight loss in an older person is NEVER explained by osteoarthritis.**
If time remains
**Other conditions — blood pressure, kidney trouble, stomach ulcers · other medications INCLUDING OVER THE COUNTER · allergies · smoking and alcohol.**
Task 2, then task 3

**Describe the photograph in the fixed order → explain the diagnosis in PLAIN WORDS → then the differentials to the examiner, EACH WITH A REASON IT IS LESS LIKELY.** **Reciting a list scores nothing — knuckles spared, stiffness brief, no nail or skin changes, no acute attacks.**
Then ACT on what you found — do not just record it

**‘From what you have told me, the hands are now LIMITING COOKING AND DRESSING, and you are managing ALONE. I'd like to arrange an OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY ASSESSMENT AT HOME for aids and a thumb splint, and refer you to MY AGED CARE for help with shopping and housework. And I'd like to CHANGE YOUR ANTI-INFLAMMATORY because of the heartburn.’** **Then the safety-net: come back sooner if the joints become HOT AND RED, if you get BLACK BOWEL MOTIONS or stomach pain, or if you have a FALL. Review in THREE MONTHS after the medication change.**

**THE MEDICATION LADDER.** **TOPICAL NSAID to the affected joints — a reasonable FIRST pharmacological step in hand OA and SAFER THAN ORAL in an older patient** VERIFY · **PARACETAMOL — safe, but MODEST benefit; do not present it as a solution on its own** VERIFY · **ORAL NSAID — lowest effective dose, shortest course, WITH A PPI; check RENAL FUNCTION and BLOOD PRESSURE; avoid with anticoagulants** · **INTRA-ARTICULAR CORTICOSTEROID to the first carpometacarpal joint for a persistent flare** · **DULOXETINE for persistent pain in some patients** VERIFY PBS criteria · **SURGERY — TRAPEZIECTOMY or joint fusion for refractory thumb-base disease.** **NOT RECOMMENDED: glucosamine, chondroitin, and LONG-TERM OPIOIDS.** VERIFY
