findings: ASK FOR IT AS A STRUCTURE

‘I would INSPECT for swelling, redness and SKIN BREAKS, PALPATE for site, TEMPERATURE and FLUCTUANCE, test ACTIVE THEN PASSIVE movement, examine THE JOINT ABOVE AND BELOW, and check NEUROVASCULAR STATUS. May I have the findings?’
THE CARD, handed to you at 6 minutes with a photograph

AFEBRILE, systemically well. LEFT ELBOW: a DISCRETE, TENDER, FLUCTUANT SWELLING OVER THE OLECRANON, ABOUT 5 cm ACROSS. Overlying skin WARM AND PINK; NO SPREADING ERYTHEMA, NO LYMPHANGITIS, NO SKIN BREAK. MOVEMENT: flexion and extension RESTRICTED AT THE END OF RANGE BY PAIN ONLY; THE JOINT LINE ITSELF IS NOT TENDER. Neurovascular intact. Right elbow normal. NO OTHER SWOLLEN JOINTS
READING THE CARD IN SILENCE LOSES THE MARK — say the two findings that decide the case
‘The two findings that matter to me are that the swelling is FLUCTUANT AND SITS ON THE OLECRANON, and that THE JOINT STILL MOVES — which places the problem OUTSIDE THE JOINT, IN THE BURSA’
THE ANATOMICAL REASON THE ELBOW STILL BENDS

The bursa is a FLAT SAC BETWEEN SKIN AND THE POINT OF THE ELBOW, OUTSIDE THE JOINT CAPSULE. That is why a bursitis leaves flexion and extension ALMOST INTACT, while a SEPTIC ARTHRITIS INSIDE the joint does not
The photograph

A DISCRETE, WELL-DEMARCATED swelling sitting ON THE POINT of the elbow, skin PINK AND SHINY over it, THE REST OF THE ELBOW CONTOUR NORMAL. DESCRIBE THE SITE BEFORE YOU NAME THE DIAGNOSIS. Bursitis can get LARGE — candidates doubt the diagnosis because the swelling looks too big. It is still DISCRETE, still ON THE POINT, and the joint below it STILL MOVES
Contrast — UPPER-LIMB DVT, the differential for the 2025 ‘swelling’ stem
THE WHOLE LIMB is swollen, the contour SMOOTH AND FEATURELESS and the skin SHINY — rather than a discrete lump. Dilated surface veins, dusky colour. Think of it after REPETITIVE OVERHEAD WORK
THE BEDSIDE DECISION — two questions do almost all the work
IS HE SEPTIC? and DOES THE JOINT STILL MOVE? Everything downstream follows from those
INVESTIGATIONS

IF INFECTION IS POSSIBLE: ASPIRATE THE BURSA — LATERAL, OBLIQUE APPROACH — and send for FOUR TESTS: CELL COUNT, GRAM STAIN, CULTURE AND CRYSTALS · FBE, CRP, ESR; URATE (interpret with care); BLOOD CULTURES if febrile · ULTRASOUND confirms bursal fluid, SEPARATES BURSA FROM JOINT EFFUSION and guides aspiration · X-RAY if there was a blow, if there is bony tenderness, or if you suspect a loose body or chronic gout
THE APPROACH MATTERS
DO NOT PUNCTURE STRAIGHT THROUGH THE POINT OF THE ELBOW — thin skin, poor healing, RISK OF A CHRONIC SINUS. And DO NOT START ANTIBIOTICS BEFORE ASPIRATING IF YOU CAN ASPIRATE — YOU LOSE THE DIAGNOSIS
Two numbers to carry

SERUM URATE IS OFTEN NORMAL DURING AN ACUTE ATTACK — recheck at 2–4 WEEKS, not during it. LOSS OF ACTIVE EXTENSION AGAINST GRAVITY AFTER A BLOW = FRACTURE OR TRICEPS AVULSION UNTIL X-RAY SAYS OTHERWISE

dx: **Non-septic OLECRANON BURSITIS, precipitated by a direct blow, in a man with a background of GOUT.** **Inflammation of the subcutaneous bursa lying between the skin and the olecranon. It sits OUTSIDE the joint capsule, which is why the elbow still bends.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE IS NOT THE DIAGNOSIS — almost everyone names the bursitis once they see the photograph.** **TWO OTHER THINGS SEPARATE CANDIDATES.** **1 SUSTAINING SIX MINUTES OF STRUCTURED HISTORY. Candidates run dry at three minutes, repeat SADMA, and the examiner watches a doctor with no system.** **2 ACTIVELY EXCLUDING INFECTION AND NAMING A CAUSE. ‘Bursitis’ alone is HALF an answer. ‘NON-SEPTIC olecranon bursitis, PRECIPITATED BY A DIRECT BLOW, IN A MAN WITH GOUT’ is the whole answer.**

**READ THE STEM LIKE AN EXAMINER: HE IS A CARPENTER, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE MISDIRECTION TOWARDS EPICONDYLITIS.** **A carpenter also KNEELS AND RESTS HIS ELBOWS ON HARD SURFACES — which is the REAL mechanism.** **DO NOT ask ‘do you play tennis or golf?’; ask ‘WHAT DOES YOUR WORK INVOLVE, and do you do any sport or exercise?’** **He will mention golf. NOTE IT, DO NOT CHASE IT — the swelling is POSTERIOR, not at an epicondyle, and A LUMP ON THE POINT OF THE ELBOW IS NEVER AN EPICONDYLITIS.**

**THE SITE QUESTION IS THE WHOLE CASE, AND MOST CANDIDATES NEVER ASK IT.** He says ‘it's my left elbow’ and the role-player is briefed to **give a vague answer to a vague question and WAIT TO BE ASKED WHICH PART.** **‘IS IT THE FRONT OF YOUR ELBOW, THE BACK, OR THE WHOLE ELBOW?’** → *‘Right on the point, at the back.’* **FOUR ZONES, FOUR DIFFERENTIAL SETS — which is why the site question comes before everything else.**

**THE QUALITY QUESTION SPLITS TWO WHOLE DIFFERENTIAL GROUPS IN ONE SENTENCE.** **A DULL ACHE points to BONE, JOINT AND SOFT TISSUE. SHARP, ELECTRIC OR SHOOTING pain points to NERVE — a cervical radiculopathy or an entrapment.**

**THE FIVE DIFFERENTIAL GROUPS ARE THE SPINE OF THE HISTORY AND THEY TAKE TWO FULL MINUTES ON THEIR OWN — which is the answer to the silence-at-four-minutes problem.** **1 RED FLAGS — malignancy, infection, DVT. 2 JOINT AND BONE. 3 SOFT TISSUE. 4 NEUROLOGICAL. 5 REFERRED.** **LEARN THE GROUP NAMES, NOT THE LIST — the same five buckets work for the knee, the hip, the foot and the hand; only the contents change.**

**CORRECTION — NIGHT PAIN.** Source material suggests lateral epicondylitis characteristically gives night and rest pain. **IT DOES NOT.** **Epicondylitis pain is ACTIVITY-RELATED — gripping, lifting, turning a handle.** **PAIN THAT RELIABLY WAKES A PATIENT IS A RED FLAG and should push you towards INFECTION, INFLAMMATORY ARTHRITIS OR MALIGNANCY.** **Carpal tunnel is the classic benign exception.** If challenged: **‘I treat night pain as a RED FLAG rather than a feature of tendinopathy, so I screened for infection and malignancy on that basis.’**

**MECHANICAL OR INFLAMMATORY — say the conclusion out loud.** **Worse WITH ACTIVITY, better with rest, worse at the END OF THE DAY, stiffness UNDER 30 MINUTES = MECHANICAL — osteoarthritis, tendinopathy, bursitis.** **Worse AFTER REST, better with movement, worse IN THE MORNING, stiffness OVER 30–60 MINUTES = INFLAMMATORY — rheumatoid, psoriatic, reactive.** VERIFY

**Explaining it to him, in plain words**: **‘James, you have a condition called OLECRANON BURSITIS. A BURSA IS A SMALL CUSHION that sits between the SKIN and the BONY POINT of your elbow and STOPS THEM RUBBING. Yours has become inflamed and FILLED WITH FLUID. TWO THINGS EXPLAIN IT: the knock on the door, AND YOUR GOUT — crystal problems inflame these cushions as well as joints. And KNEELING AND LEANING ON THE ELBOW ALL DAY KEEPS IT GOING.’**

**HIS HIDDEN AGENDA IS MONEY AND SURGERY, NOT CANCER — and he mentions the lost work in his opening line.** *‘I'm self-employed, so no work, no money.’* **If you never ask what he is worried about, he volunteers it at around four minutes: ‘am I going to need surgery? I can't afford to be off.’** **NAME IT EARLY — ‘three weeks is a while, and I can hear it is COSTING YOU WORK, which is stressful’ — then ASK THE CONCERN QUESTION, and CLOSE THE LOOP in the plan with A WORK CAPACITY CERTIFICATE FOR MODIFIED DUTIES.**
plan: **WIPE, then ‘before we start — ARE YOU IN ANY PAIN RIGHT NOW that we need to deal with first?’, then confidentiality, then ‘tell me about your elbow.’** **ACKNOWLEDGE the impact on work, then ASK THE AGENDA EARLY, NOT AT THE END: ‘was there anything in particular you were WORRIED this might be? And what were you HOPING we would sort out today?’** Then **SIGNPOST: ‘I'll ask about the pain first, then some questions to rule out the serious causes, then your general health. SOME MAY SOUND UNRELATED — bear with me.’**
**THE SITE QUESTION — front, back, or the whole elbow.**

**BLOCK 1 — EXPLORE THE PAIN, ninety seconds.** Out of ten · **dull ache or sharp, electric, shooting** · when it started, constant or intermittent, getting worse · **does it spread — up to the shoulder, down to the hand** · worse and better with what · **effect on work and daily life.**

**BLOCK 2 — THE PATTERN, ALL THREE, EVERY TIME.** **‘Does the pain WAKE YOU AT NIGHT?’ · ‘Is it worse AFTER REST, or AFTER ACTIVITY?’ · ‘Worse FIRST THING IN THE MORNING or at the END OF THE DAY?’** **Skipping these to save time loses the mechanical-versus-inflammatory split, which is scored.**

**BLOCK 3 — GENERAL MUSCULOSKELETAL SCREEN, four questions, twenty seconds.** **Swelling · redness or rash · stiffness or difficulty moving it · AND HAVE YOU HAD ANY INJURY OR KNOCK TO THAT ELBOW.** **When he says yes: TWO QUESTIONS ONLY — how hard was it, and CAN YOU STRAIGHTEN THE ELBOW FULLY YOURSELF? That is your fracture screen. Then MOVE ON — ninety seconds on the angle at which he hit the door is a named waste.**

**BLOCK 4 — THE FIVE GROUPS, OUT LOUD. TWO MINUTES.** **RED FLAGS: weight loss, appetite, lumps, unusual tiredness, night sweats · fevers, chills or shivers · IS THE WHOLE ARM SWOLLEN OR JUST THE ELBOW · any repeated overhead movements — painting a ceiling, overhead work, basketball · clots in you or the family · ANY RECENT HOSPITAL STAY, DRIP OR LINE IN YOUR ARM.**
Groups 2 and 3

**JOINT AND BONE: what does your work involve day to day; any sport; heavy or repeated lifting · other joints painful or swollen; family history of arthritis; rashes or patches on elbows, knees or scalp · DOES IT FLARE AFTER RED MEAT, SEAFOOD OR ALCOHOL; HAVE YOU EVER BEEN TOLD YOU HAVE GOUT · recent diarrhoea or blood in the stool; burning on passing urine or discharge.** **SOFT TISSUE: occupation, exercise and trauma already asked — add the one that is easy to forget: ‘DOES THE ELBOW EVER LOCK OR CATCH, so you cannot straighten it?’ — the question for a LOOSE BODY or OSTEOCHONDRITIS DISSECANS.**
Groups 4 and 5

**NEUROLOGICAL: any NECK PAIN; any numbness, tingling or pins and needles in the arm or hand; any WEAKNESS gripping or lifting.** **REFERRED: any CHEST PAIN; any COUGH, or coughing up blood; any SHOULDER PAIN.** **Two questions, ten seconds — and DROPPING THEM BECAUSE ‘IT'S ONLY AN ELBOW’ IS A NAMED ERROR. The examiner notes that you thought beyond the joint.**

**BLOCK 5 — CLOSURE.** Smoking · alcohol in a usual week · recreational drugs · **medications INCLUDING OVER THE COUNTER** · allergies · **other conditions — DIABETES, KIDNEY PROBLEMS, ANYTHING THAT AFFECTS YOUR IMMUNE SYSTEM.** **TWO QUESTIONS THE SOURCE OMITS, both five seconds, both changing how hard you push on septic bursitis: ‘ARE YOU ON STEROIDS, or any medication that lowers your immunity?’ and ‘IS THERE ANY BREAK, GRAZE OR CUT IN THE SKIN OVER THE ELBOW?’**

**Ask for the card as a structure → READ THE TWO DECIDING FINDINGS ALOUD and interpret them → explain in plain words WITH A CAUSE → the differentials GROUPED, each with why it is less likely → the plan → the safety-net → summary.** **If he is silent or gives short answers, MOVE TO THE NEXT DIFFERENTIAL GROUP. NEVER REPEAT SADMA TO FILL TIME.**

**CORRECTION — DO NOT INJECT CORTICOSTEROID AS FIRST-LINE TREATMENT.** Source material offers intrabursal steroid as an option. **Current practice DISCOURAGES it in the olecranon bursa — SKIN ATROPHY, CHRONIC PAIN and a HIGHER RATE OF SECONDARY INFECTION.** **Reserve it for REFRACTORY, CONFIRMED NON-SEPTIC disease, after specialist discussion.** VERIFY If challenged: **‘I'm aware steroid injection is described. **SEPTIC BURSITIS — commonly Staphylococcus aureus, and FEVER IS ABSENT IN MANY CASES** VERIFY. **ASPIRATE FIRST, THEN empirical antibiotics: di/flucloxacillin orally for a well patient; INTRAVENOUS if systemically unwell.** VERIFY against Therapeutic Guidelines — Antibiotic. **If the examiner says ‘he's afebrile, so it isn't septic?’ → ‘Fever is absent in a SUBSTANTIAL PROPORTION of septic bursitis, so I don't rely on it. I use the whole picture: SPEED OF ONSET, WARMTH, SPREADING ERYTHEMA, A SKIN BREAK, TENDERNESS OUT OF PROPORTION, and HOST FACTORS such as diabetes or immunosuppression. If any were present I would aspirate.’**

**THE SAFETY-NET, SAID OUT LOUD**: **‘Come back IMMEDIATELY if the elbow becomes HOT AND RED, if the redness starts SPREADING UP THE ARM, if you get FEVERS OR SHAKES, or if you feel GENERALLY UNWELL. Those would mean the fluid has become INFECTED and you would need antibiotics, possibly drainage.’**

**Would you aspirate THIS one?** → **‘Not mandatory here, since he is AFEBRILE with NO CELLULITIS. I WOULD aspirate if he were FEBRILE, if the skin were SPREADING RED, if he were IMMUNOSUPPRESSED OR DIABETIC, if there were a SKIN BREAK, or if the swelling were TENSE AND VERY PAINFUL. I'd send it for CELL COUNT, GRAM STAIN, CULTURE AND CRYSTALS.’** **Is trauma a differential?** → **‘Trauma is a MECHANISM rather than a diagnosis, but it OBLIGES me to exclude an OLECRANON FRACTURE and a TRICEPS AVULSION, which I did by testing ACTIVE EXTENSION AGAINST GRAVITY.’**

**THE ONE LINE THAT SHOWS A CAUSE WAS FOUND**: **‘TWO THINGS in his history explain why this bursa became inflamed: he KNOCKED THE ELBOW on a door, and he has a HISTORY OF GOUT — CRYSTAL DISEASE IS A RECOGNISED CAUSE OF BURSITIS, NOT JUST OF JOINT PAIN.’** **And he only reveals the gout if asked about OTHER JOINTS, ARTHRITIS, FAMILY HISTORY, or ALCOHOL AND RED MEAT TRIGGERS.**

**VERSION B — the 2025 ‘SWELLING’ stem. Identical case, identical findings, identical differentials. ONLY THE OPENING BLOCK CHANGES.** **‘Tell me about the swelling. WHERE EXACTLY — the whole elbow, the back of it, or one side? Is it ONE SIDE OR BOTH? ANY SWELLING ANYWHERE ELSE IN YOUR BODY? Is it painful?’** Then add ONE line to the presentation: **‘because SWELLING was the complaint, I gave EXTRA WEIGHT to UPPER-LIMB DVT and asked whether the WHOLE ARM was involved. Here the swelling is LOCALISED TO THE POINT and the joint MOVES — so it is a bursa, not the joint and not a vein.’**

**VERSION — THE SEPTIC ONE.** *‘It came up over two days. It's hot. I've been shivery. I grazed it at work last week.’* → **‘This looks INFECTED rather than simply inflamed. I'd like to DRAW A SAMPLE OF THE FLUID OFF WITH A NEEDLE and send it to the laboratory, take blood tests and BLOOD CULTURES, and start antibiotics STRAIGHT AFTER THE SAMPLE IS TAKEN. If you were more unwell you'd need those antibiotics THROUGH A DRIP IN HOSPITAL.’** **VERSION — THE LOCKING ELBOW.** → **‘TRUE LOCKING points to something MECHANICAL INSIDE the joint — a LOOSE BODY or OSTEOCHONDRITIS DISSECANS of the capitellum. X-ray the elbow, refer for orthopaedic assessment, MRI if the X-ray is normal.’**

**NEVER SAY**: ‘it's just a bursitis, nothing to worry about’ · **‘you're a carpenter, so this is tennis elbow’** · **‘I'll give you some antibiotics to be safe’ (without aspirating)** · **‘we'll inject some steroid into it today’.**

stem: General practice in regional South Australia, 8 minutes. Jack Brennan, 62, an office manager, has come to discuss the ultrasound of his right shoulder. His physiotherapist referred him after two months of physiotherapy failed to settle the pain. The report is available to you.
Tasks: explain the ultrasound findings to the patient — take a further focused history. You are not required to examine the patient.
The shape of the eight minutes: 0:00 open · 0:30 to 3:15 explain · 3:15 to 6:00 history · 6:00 to 7:15 the sweep · 7:15 to 8:00 impact, plan and close.
tasks: Explain the ultrasound findings to the patient
Take a further focused history from the patient
findingsLabel: The ultrasound report and the imaging — open only when you would read it
findings: THE REPORT YOU ARE HANDED

RIGHT SHOULDER ULTRASOUND. SUBSCAPULARIS: FULL-THICKNESS TEAR. SUPRASPINATUS: PARTIAL-THICKNESS TEAR. INFRASPINATUS: PARTIAL-THICKNESS TEAR. TERES MINOR: NORMAL. NO subacromial–subdeltoid bursitis. NO calcific tendinopathy. NO significant joint effusion. LONG HEAD OF BICEPS INTACT AND NORMALLY LOCATED. NO acromioclavicular joint abnormality
THE FOUR CUFF MUSCLES, and what each does

SUPRASPINATUS — ABDUCTION · INFRASPINATUS AND TERES MINOR — EXTERNAL ROTATION · SUBSCAPULARIS — INTERNAL ROTATION, AND REACHING BEHIND THE BACK. INSERTIONS: THE THREE POSTERIOR ONES ON THE GREATER TUBEROSITY, SUBSCAPULARIS ON THE LESSER TUBEROSITY. TERES MAJOR IS NOT A CUFF MUSCLE — DO NOT NAME IT AS ONE. DELTOID IS NOT EITHER, AND IT IS THE MUSCLE THAT WILL COMPENSATE
PARTIAL versus FULL-THICKNESS — define these BEFORE you give the findings

PARTIAL = part of the tendon THICKNESS is torn, the rest still pulls. FULL-THICKNESS = the defect runs FROM THE JOINT SURFACE TO THE BURSAL SURFACE, so that tendon NO LONGER TRANSMITS FORCE. The word the radiologist uses is a statement about HOW FAR THROUGH THE TENDON THE DEFECT GOES — NOTHING MORE. IT DOES NOT TELL YOU HOW MUCH PAIN HE HAS, AND IT DOES NOT DECIDE WHETHER HE NEEDS SURGERY
What the ultrasound images show

NORMAL SUPRASPINATUS in long axis — a SMOOTH CONVEX BAND OF EVEN ECHOTEXTURE arching over the humeral head. A PARTIAL-THICKNESS defect — a DARK (HYPOECHOIC) FOCUS within an otherwise BRIGHT tendon. A FULL-THICKNESS subscapularis tear — the tendon fibres REPLACED BY A DEFECT THAT RUNS THE WHOLE WAY THROUGH. Layers from the surface: SKIN, DELTOID, the THIN SUBACROMIAL–SUBDELTOID BURSA, then TENDON, then BRIGHT CORTEX of the greater tuberosity
WHY YOU STILL ORDER A PLAIN FILM — the cuff itself is INVISIBLE on X-ray

What you look for is THE GAP BETWEEN THE ACROMION AND THE HUMERAL HEAD. When a LARGE TEAR has been there FOR YEARS THE HEAD RIDES UP AND THAT INTERVAL NARROWS. It also EXCLUDES FRACTURE AND CALCIFIC DEPOSITS — and it shows GLENOHUMERAL OSTEOARTHRITIS (narrowed joint space, inferior humeral osteophyte), WHICH IS THE DIFFERENTIAL THE ULTRASOUND CANNOT ANSWER, and the reason the ‘grinding, cracking, locking’ questions earn marks
Views to request
SHOULDER X-RAY — AP PLUS AXILLARY OR SCAPULAR Y VIEW
MRI — and why NOT now

RESERVED for DIAGNOSTIC DOUBT or SURGICAL PLANNING. It shows TEAR SIZE, TENDON RETRACTION AND MUSCLE QUALITY, which decide WHETHER A REPAIR IS WORTH ATTEMPTING. IT IS NOT THE FIRST TEST AND IT IS NOT NEEDED TO START TREATMENT. If asked: ‘the ultrasound has already answered the diagnostic question’
Bloods — only if the sweep turns something up

IF GIRDLE FEATURES: ESR, CRP, FBE, UEC, LFT, TSH, CK; add RF and ANTI-CCP if inflammatory · HbA1c if not recent — DIABETES CHANGES PROGNOSIS AND REHABILITATION · ECG IN THE ROOM if any chest or exertional symptoms
THE CLINICAL PEARL THAT JUSTIFIES THE WHOLE HISTORY

AN ULTRASOUND REPORTING SEVERAL TORN TENDONS IN A 62-YEAR-OLD IS DESCRIBING WEAR, NOT AN ACCIDENT. DEGENERATIVE CUFF TEARING IS COMMON AND OFTEN ASYMPTOMATIC — imaging findings rise steeply with age. SAY THAT OUT LOUD: it reassures him, AND IT IS THE HONEST REASON YOU KEEP ASKING QUESTIONS AFTER THE SCAN. VERIFY exact prevalence before quoting a percentage
THE SHAPE OF THE EIGHT MINUTES

0:00 OPEN · 0:30–3:15 EXPLAIN · 3:15–6:00 HISTORY · 6:00–7:15 THE SWEEP · 7:15–8:00 IMPACT, PLAN, CLOSE. YOU WILL HAVE SPARE TIME. SPEND IT ON THE SWEEP, NOT ON SILENCE — this station's failure mode is FINISHING EARLY, not running out

dx: **Chronic DEGENERATIVE rotator cuff tear — full-thickness SUBSCAPULARIS with partial-thickness SUPRASPINATUS and INFRASPINATUS tearing, in a 62-year-old with NO TRAUMA.**

**THE TASKS FEEL BACKWARDS, AND THAT IS THE DESIGN.** **Almost every station gives you history first and the result last. THIS ONE REVERSES IT: the scan is handed to you, so THE DIAGNOSIS IS ALREADY MADE BEFORE YOU OPEN YOUR MOUTH.** **The history is therefore NOT DIAGNOSTIC — it is there to CHARACTERISE the problem, MEASURE ITS IMPACT, and PROVE THE TEARS EXPLAIN EVERYTHING.** **Candidates who treat task 2 as an afterthought FAIL.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: candidates fail this station by treating the ultrasound as the FINISH LINE.** They explain the tears beautifully, take a textbook cuff history, run out of things to ask — and stop. **RECALLS ARE CONSISTENT: THE CASE WAS REPEATEDLY FAILED UNTIL CANDIDATES ADDED AN EXPLICIT SWEEP OF THE OTHER CAUSES OF SHOULDER PAIN, SAID OUT LOUD.** **It is an odd design — the history comes after the diagnosis, and NOBODY ASKS YOU FOR A DIFFERENTIAL — but the marks are there. DO IT ANYWAY, AND SIGNPOST IT SO THE EXAMINER CANNOT MISS IT.**

**THE FIVE GROUPS TO SWEEP: NECK · GIRDLE · JOINT · CHEST · LUNG. Ninety seconds.** **Running the sweep SILENTLY IN YOUR HEAD SCORES NOTHING — if you do not signpost it and say the questions out loud, you get nothing for it.** **A run of negatives IS the point: you are being marked for ASKING, not for what he answers.**

**EXPLAIN IN FOUR LAYERS, AND DEFINE THE WORDS BEFORE THE RESULT.** **LAYER 0 — what were you told the scan was looking for? LAYER 1 — the JOINT: ‘a ball and socket, and unlike your hip that socket is VERY SHALLOW, a bit like a GOLF BALL SITTING ON A TEE. That gives you a huge amount of movement, but it makes the joint NATURALLY UNSTABLE, so it depends on the muscles around it to hold it in place.’ LAYER 2 — the FOUR MUSCLES: ‘they move the shoulder, and just as importantly THEY HOLD THE BALL CENTRED ON THE SOCKET. Together they're called the ROTATOR CUFF. THE NAMES DON'T MATTER — what matters is that the scan looked at all four.’ LAYER 3 — partial versus full. LAYER 4 — THE RESULT, ONE TENDON AT A TIME.**

**NEVER SAY ‘THREE OUT OF FOUR OF YOUR MUSCLES ARE TORN’ — that is CATASTROPHISING BY ARITHMETIC, and the role-player is briefed to become distressed and say ‘so my shoulder's wrecked then’, which derails the consultation.** **NAME EACH TENDON SEPARATELY AND FINISH ON THE NORMAL ONE: ‘the muscle at the FRONT has a full-thickness tear — torn right through. TWO of the muscles at the BACK have partial tears — damaged, but STILL PARTLY ATTACHED AND STILL WORKING. And the FOURTH ONE IS COMPLETELY NORMAL. The scan also shows NO inflammation of the cushion, NO calcium build-up, and your BICEPS TENDON IS EXACTLY WHERE IT SHOULD BE.’**

**THEN FRAME IT AND CHECK IT**: **‘I want to be straight with you: this is WEAR AND TEAR THAT HAS BUILT UP OVER YEARS, NOT SOMETHING YOU DID LAST WEEK, and it is VERY COMMON AT YOUR AGE. Plenty of people have changes like these and manage very well. IT DOES NOT MEAN YOUR SHOULDER IS FINISHED. Does that make sense so far?’**

**TWO FUNCTIONAL QUESTIONS YOU MUST NOT SKIP.** **OVERHEAD ACTIVITY — the single most discriminating functional question in cuff disease, AND THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR THE WORD.** **REACHING BEHIND THE BACK — THAT IS SUBSCAPULARIS, THE TENDON TORN RIGHT THROUGH IN THIS MAN. Asking it SHOWS YOU UNDERSTOOD THE REPORT RATHER THAN RECITED IT.**

**THE SECOND DISCRIMINATOR IS EXPECTATION, and he WILL ask whether he needs an operation — at about three minutes and again at seven.** **A CANDIDATE WHO ANSWERS YES OR NO LOSES THE MARK EITHER WAY. THE MARK IS FOR THE PROCESS**: **‘That's exactly the right question. MOST TEARS LIKE THESE ARE MANAGED WITHOUT SURGERY TO BEGIN WITH, and a lot of people do well. Whether an operation would help YOU depends on how much it's LIMITING you and how you go with a proper REHABILITATION programme — so what I'd suggest is that we give that a REAL GO, and if you're still stuck, I'll refer you to a shoulder surgeon and YOU DECIDE WITH THEM. IT WON'T BE SOMETHING THAT HAPPENS TO YOU. Would that be reasonable?’**

**HIS HIDDEN AGENDA: HIS BROTHER HAD A SHOULDER RECONSTRUCTION, WAS OFF WORK FOR MONTHS, AND STILL CANNOT THROW A BALL — and he is frightened of ending up the same way and LOSING HIS JOB.** **He does NOT volunteer it early. If you ask about concerns at the start he says only ‘I just want to know what's going on.’ HE RELEASES IT IF YOU ASK ABOUT CONCERNS A SECOND TIME, OR ASK ABOUT MOOD OR COPING — and if you never ask, at about seven minutes.** **SO ASK FOR CONCERNS TWICE: once at the start, once near the end.**
plan: **WIPE — and OPEN BEFORE YOU EXPLAIN.** **‘I DO have the results of your shoulder scan with me. BUT BEFORE WE GET TO THOSE, can you tell me what has happened so far?’** **Walking in talking — ‘hello Jack, I've got your results, let me explain’ — costs you rapport, his agenda, and any idea of what he already understands.** Then **ACKNOWLEDGE the two months of physiotherapy — ‘that must be frustrating’ — then THE AGENDA QUESTION, then SIGNPOST THE WHOLE CONSULTATION.**

**TASK 1 — the four layers, permission first (‘can I take you through it step by step, so it makes sense?’), definitions BEFORE findings, findings ONE TENDON AT A TIME ending on the normal one, frame, and CHECK UNDERSTANDING AT LEAST TWICE.** **If he goes quiet and looks away, NAME IT: ‘I can see that's a lot to take in.’** **If he asks about surgery here, DEFER IT EXPLICITLY AND PROMISE TO ANSWER: ‘that's exactly the right question, and I'll answer it properly — but let me ask you a few things first so my answer is WORTH something.’**

**THE PAIN, fully characterised — you have the time.** Where exactly, **point with ONE FINGER** · does it travel · aching, sharp or burning · **out of ten at its worst AND right now** · constant or intermittent · better, worse or the same · what makes it worse, what helps · what he has taken and whether it helped · **‘DO YOU GET PAIN AT NIGHT — CAN YOU LIE ON THAT SHOULDER?’** — the classic cuff question · **‘HOW IS THIS AFFECTING YOUR LIFE?’ asked as ITS OWN QUESTION, not tacked on.**

**THE SHOULDER ITSELF.** Stiff? · anything you can't do · **OVERHEAD — a high shelf, hanging washing, an overhead cupboard** · **BEHIND THE BACK — a back pocket, a seatbelt, a bra strap** · does it feel WEAK · does it ever feel UNSTABLE, like it might give way or pop out · **any CLICKING, CATCHING OR LOCKING.**

**WORK, SPORT, DOMINANCE, TRAUMA AND WHAT HAS BEEN TRIED.** **Right or left handed** · what do you do for work, **and does any of it involve reaching ABOVE SHOULDER HEIGHT — DO NOT ASSUME ‘OFFICE JOB’ MEANS NO OVERHEAD LOAD** · sport or hobbies using the arm overhead · **‘what CAN'T you do now that you could six months ago?’** · managing dressing, showering, driving · **‘have you EVER injured this shoulder?’** · **‘WHAT DID THE PHYSIO ACTUALLY HAVE YOU DOING, and did any of it help EVEN A LITTLE?’** — he tailed off at six weeks and admits it ONLY IF ASKED DIRECTLY. **Hearing ‘physio didn't work’ and re-referring to physio without asking what it was is a named fail — ADHERENCE IS THE ANSWER HERE.**

**THE SWEEP. SIGNPOST IT, THEN RUN IT.** **‘The scan explains a lot of what you've told me. EVEN SO, shoulder pain can occasionally come from SOMEWHERE OTHER THAN THE SHOULDER, and I don't want to miss anything — can I ask a few quick questions that may sound unrelated?’**
The five groups, verbatim

**NECK: neck pain or stiffness · numbness or pins and needles in the arm or hand · weakness, dropping things, trouble with buttons.** **GIRDLE: is the OTHER shoulder painful · pain or stiffness around the HIPS OR THIGHS · HOW LONG are you stiff in the mornings · unusually tired, or lost weight — THEN, WITHOUT PAUSING: any NEW HEADACHES, TENDERNESS ON THE SCALP, PAIN IN THE JAW WHEN YOU CHEW, OR ANY CHANGE IN YOUR VISION.** **PMR QUESTIONS AND GCA QUESTIONS ARE ONE BLOCK, NEVER SEPARATED.** **JOINT: grinding, cracking or popping · catching or locking · other joints · family history of arthritis.** **CHEST: ‘a routine question I ask about ANY shoulder or arm pain — any chest pain or tightness, any shortness of breath, ESPECIALLY ON EXERTION?’** **LUNG AND SYSTEMIC: smoking · cough, haemoptysis, hoarse voice, weight loss, fevers or night sweats · any history of cancer.**

**IMPACT, MOOD AND SUPPORT — soft marks, easily won.** How are you COPING · how has your MOOD been · how is your SLEEP · who's at home with you · are things alright at home, relationships, money, work · **and ‘what were you HOPING we'd be able to do about this today?’ — THE SECOND CONCERNS QUESTION, which is what releases the brother.** Then **SADMA, past and family history, rapid fire — including DIABETES AND THYROID, both strongly associated with ADHESIVE CAPSULITIS, which shows the examiner your differential list is LIVE, NOT DECORATIVE.**

**SUMMARISE — and the summary is where a scrappy consultation is RESCUED, because it demonstrates the NEGATIVES you elicited.** Then the plan, **the answer to the agenda**, and the safety-net. **Note the NUROFEN + BLOOD PRESSURE TABLET + BORDERLINE DIABETES combination — it changes your analgesia advice and it is a FREE MARK if you comment on it.**
pefe: **Management — conservative first for a chronic degenerative tear.** **MOST PATIENTS IMPROVE THEIR FUNCTION AND PAIN WITH A STRUCTURED PROGRAMME EVEN THOUGH THE TENDON DOES NOT HEAL BACK TOGETHER.** **Give it a REAL trial — typically around THREE MONTHS** VERIFY — **with a WRITTEN GOAL.** **Paracetamol 1 g up to four times daily, max 4 g in 24 h** VERIFY · **short course oral NSAID if no contraindication — CHECK BLOOD PRESSURE, KIDNEYS, STOMACH AND CARDIAC RISK FIRST** VERIFY dose · **topical NSAID as a lower-risk alternative** · **RELATIVE REST FROM OVERHEAD LOADING — NOT A SLING, NOT IMMOBILISATION** · **structured physiotherapy: PROGRESSIVE LOADING of the INTACT cuff and the SCAPULAR STABILISERS, DELTOID RETRAINING** · ice or heat, whichever helps · **consider a subacromial corticosteroid injection for pain that BLOCKS REHABILITATION — discussing that benefit is SHORT-TERM** VERIFY · **REVIEW IN 4–6 WEEKS WITH A FUNCTIONAL GOAL WRITTEN DOWN.**

**REFER to an orthopaedic upper-limb surgeon if**: **an ACUTE TRAUMATIC FULL-THICKNESS TEAR in a functionally demanding patient** · **PSEUDOPARALYSIS — he cannot ACTIVELY lift the arm at all although you can move it PASSIVELY** · **a LARGE SUBSCAPULARIS TEAR with functional loss** · **persistent disabling pain or weakness after an ADEQUATE conservative trial** · **diagnostic uncertainty.** **WHAT SURGERY IS AND IS NOT: repair MAY improve pain and strength but is NOT GUARANTEED, needs MONTHS of rehabilitation, and RE-TEAR IS COMMON IN LARGE DEGENERATE TEARS. SAY THAT, RATHER THAN PROMISING.**

**AVOID**: **promising surgery, or promising it will fix him** · **saying ‘it's all torn’ or ‘there's nothing to be done’** · **a sling or prolonged rest — risks a STIFF SHOULDER** · **repeated corticosteroid injections** · **long-term oral NSAIDs in an older patient without checking kidneys and blood pressure** · **ordering MRI reflexively when ultrasound has already answered the question** · **closing on the tear without the differential sweep.**

**SAFETY-NETTING — say it, then write it**: **‘Come back sooner if the pain SUDDENLY GETS MUCH WORSE, if you CAN'T LIFT THE ARM AT ALL, if you develop a FEVER WITH A HOT SWOLLEN SHOULDER, if you get NUMBNESS OR WEAKNESS IN THE HAND, or if you get any CHEST PAIN OR BREATHLESSNESS. If you get a NEW HEADACHE, TENDERNESS ON THE SCALP, JAW PAIN WHEN YOU CHEW, or ANY CHANGE IN YOUR VISION, that's a SAME-DAY problem — ring us or go to the emergency department.’**

**Examiner challenges, scripted.** *‘Why did you ask about HEADACHES in a shoulder case?’* → **‘Because he is OVER 50 with a SHOULDER GIRDLE complaint, and POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA is on my list. If polymyalgia is possible I MUST screen for GIANT CELL ARTERITIS, because untreated it can cause IRREVERSIBLE VISUAL LOSS and it is a SAME-DAY problem.’** *‘The scan gave you the diagnosis — why keep asking?’* → **‘Because DEGENERATIVE CUFF TEARS ARE COMMON AND OFTEN ASYMPTOMATIC, so finding one DOES NOT PROVE IT IS THE CAUSE OF HIS PAIN. I wanted to be satisfied that the findings ACCOUNT FOR HIS WHOLE STORY before I commit him to a management plan.’** *‘Why not MRI?’* → **‘The ultrasound has already answered the diagnostic question. I'd reserve MRI for SURGICAL PLANNING or genuine diagnostic doubt.’**

**His answers, so you know what you are fishing for — AND HE DOES NOT OFFER NEGATIVES; he says ‘no’ ONLY WHEN ASKED, because THE WHOLE POINT OF THE STATION IS WHETHER YOU ASK.** Pain **over the OUTER shoulder (lateral deltoid), DOWN TO ABOUT THE ELBOW, NEVER INTO THE HAND; a deep ACHE, SIX at worst, three now; SLOWLY WORSE OVER SIX MONTHS; WORSE REACHING OVERHEAD; PANADOL takes the edge off** · **NIGHTS ARE THE WORST — CANNOT LIE ON THAT SIDE, WAKES 2–3 TIMES** · **stiff TEN MINUTES first thing** · **cannot get anything off the TOP SHELF, stopped hanging the washing; TWISTS to do the SEATBELT; feels WEAK LIFTING; no giving way, no locking** · **RIGHT-handed and it is the RIGHT shoulder; OFFICE MANAGER, mostly desk BUT STACKS FILES AND BOXES ON HIGH SHELVES; LAWN BOWLS on Saturdays, had to stop** · **NO trauma, never dislocated, no accident at work.**

**And the background he gives ONLY IF ASKED**: **gave up smoking about 22 years ago, smoked from 18 to 40** · **four or five beers a week** · **A BLOOD PRESSURE TABLET; PANADOL most days; NUROFEN ‘when it's bad’** · **HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE; told last year he was ‘BORDERLINE DIABETIC’** · **father had bad arthritis in his hands** · **physio: TWO MONTHS, A SHEET OF BAND EXERCISES, AND HE TAILED OFF AFTER ABOUT SIX WEEKS BECAUSE IT WASN'T HELPING — admitted ONLY if asked directly whether he kept them up.** **If you say ‘I'll refer you to a physio’, he replies flatly: ‘I've just done two months of physio.’**

**VERSION B — THE TRAUMATIC TEAR AT WORK.** 45M painter or storeman, **sudden onset after lifting a pallet or a fall, ISOLATED FULL-THICKNESS SUPRASPINATUS TEAR WITH RETRACTION.** **Hidden ask: ‘will I get back on the tools?’** → **‘That CHANGES things, and in a GOOD way — a tear that happens SUDDENLY in someone who uses the arm all day is one we refer EARLY rather than waiting. Tell me exactly what happened. Could you use the arm at all afterwards? Any numbness or weakness in the hand? I'm going to refer you to a shoulder surgeon NOW rather than in three months, get an X-ray today, and complete a WORK CAPACITY CERTIFICATE. Because it happened at work, we'll lodge it with ReturnToWorkSA, and I'll write to your employer about MODIFIED DUTIES — NO OVERHEAD LIFTING.’**

**VERSION — THE GIRDLE PATIENT.** *‘It's the other shoulder too. My hips ache getting out of the car. I'm stiff till about eleven in the morning.’* → **‘That CHANGES MY THINKING. When BOTH shoulders and BOTH hips are involved with that much morning stiffness, I have to consider POLYMYALGIA RHEUMATICA, which is QUITE DIFFERENT from a tendon problem and is TREATED DIFFERENTLY. Unusually tired, or lost weight? AND THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE: any new headaches, tenderness when you brush your hair, pain in the jaw when you chew, or any change in your vision?’** **ESR and CRP THE SAME DAY.** **VERSION — THE ANGRY PATIENT.** *‘So that's it then — I'm stuffed. Two months of exercises for nothing. When do I get the operation?’* → **‘I can hear how frustrated you are, and I don't blame you. Can I ask what makes you feel it's finished? … I want to give you a STRAIGHT answer rather than a COMFORTABLE one. THE TENDONS DON'T KNIT BACK TOGETHER ON THEIR OWN, that's true. BUT THE PAIN AND WHAT YOU CAN DO ARE NOT THE SAME THING AS THE PICTURE ON THE SCAN. Can we agree on a proper trial first, WITH A DATE TO REVIEW IT?’** **VALIDATE, THEN HOLD THE PLAN — do not match his frustration with defensiveness, and do not capitulate.**

SA — **orthopaedic upper limb: outpatient referral to RAH or Flinders; Yorke and Northern LHN visiting specialist clinics where available** · **PATS subsidises travel and accommodation for a country patient attending a specialist MORE THAN 100 km away — OFFER THE FORM AT THIS VISIT** VERIFY · **physiotherapy through Country Health Connect and local private practice; a GP MANAGEMENT PLAN AND TEAM CARE ARRANGEMENT unlocks Medicare-subsidised allied health visits** · **Version B work injury: notify ReturnToWorkSA, complete a Work Capacity Certificate, discuss modified duties; SafeWork SA if there is an unsafe practice** · **Aboriginal Liaison Officer or local ACCHS, and Closing the Gap PBS registration** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · Quitline 13 7848.**
ddx: **Rotator cuff tear — the answer**
**INSIDIOUS, over 40, LATERAL DELTOID ache, NIGHT PAIN, WEAKNESS ON LIFTING, worse OVERHEAD**
**Overhead limitation, REACHING BEHIND THE BACK, WEAKNESS RATHER THAN STIFFNESS**
**Ultrasound already done. PLAIN FILM FOR BONE. Physiotherapy trial; MRI only if surgery contemplated.** Routine
Subacromial impingement / bursitis
**PAINFUL ARC, pain on overhead reach, NO TRUE WEAKNESS**
**PAIN rather than WEAKNESS; often COEXISTS**
**The report here EXPLICITLY SAYS NO BURSITIS** — treat as part of the cuff spectrum. Routine
**Adhesive capsulitis**
**STIFFNESS DOMINATING PAIN; GLOBAL loss of movement, ESPECIALLY EXTERNAL ROTATION; DIABETES or THYROID disease**
**‘Is it stiff?’ · ‘Can SOMEONE ELSE move it further than you can?’**
**Clinically PASSIVE movement is ALSO lost, and IMAGING IS NORMAL — and here it is not.** Routine
Glenohumeral or AC joint OA
**CREPITUS, CATCHING, LOCKING, stiffness, older patient, prior trauma**
**‘Grinding, cracking, popping? Does it LOCK?’**
**PLAIN X-RAY — joint space narrowing, osteophytes. ULTRASOUND DOES NOT SEE THIS.** Routine
**Polymyalgia rheumatica ± GIANT CELL ARTERITIS**
**OVER 50, BILATERAL SHOULDER AND HIP GIRDLE pain, PROLONGED morning stiffness (typically over 45 min), FATIGUE, WEIGHT LOSS**
**BOTH girdles, stiffness DURATION, systemic symptoms — THEN HEADACHE, SCALP TENDERNESS, JAW CLAUDICATION, VISION**
**ESR and CRP, FBE. GCA features → SAME-DAY assessment and urgent steroid decision — UNTREATED IT CAUSES IRREVERSIBLE VISUAL LOSS.** GCA: same day
Rheumatoid / inflammatory arthritis
**OTHER joints, SYMMETRY, SWELLING, morning stiffness OVER AN HOUR, family history**
‘Any other joints? Swollen? Stiff for how long?’
RF, anti-CCP, ESR/CRP; rheumatology referral if positive. Soon
**Cervical radiculopathy (C5)**
**NECK PAIN, pain radiating PAST THE ELBOW, DERMATOMAL numbness, weakness, WORSE WITH NECK MOVEMENT OR COUGHING**
**Neck pain, tingling, weakness, BAND-LIKE numbness over the deltoid**
Neurological examination of the limb; cervical imaging **only if a deficit persists or progresses.** Soon
**Referred cardiac pain**
**LEFT shoulder or arm, EXERTIONAL, tightness, breathlessness, sweating, nausea**
**ASK ABOUT CHEST PAIN AND EXERTIONAL BREATHLESSNESS IN EVERY SHOULDER CASE**
**ECG THE SAME VISIT; troponin and acute referral if the story is suggestive.** Immediate
Apical lung tumour
**SMOKER, weight loss, UNREMITTING pain, HOARSENESS, HAND WASTING, DROOPING EYELID**
Smoking, cough, haemoptysis, voice change, weight loss
Chest X-ray; CT chest if abnormal or suspicion high. Urgent
Septic arthritis / bursitis
**FEVER, HOT SWOLLEN shoulder, SEVERE pain on ANY movement, immunosuppression**
Fever, rigors, redness, **whether he can move it AT ALL**
**DO NOT ASPIRATE IN GENERAL PRACTICE — HOSPITAL TODAY.** Emergency
Bone metastasis / myeloma
**Known cancer, NIGHT PAIN UNRELIEVED BY POSITION, weight loss, bone pain elsewhere**
Cancer history, weight loss, **pain that NEVER EASES**
Plain film, then FBE, ESR, CALCIUM, ALP and specialist referral. Urgent
Neuralgic amyotrophy
**Severe shoulder pain followed by PROFOUND WEAKNESS as the pain settles**; often post-viral or post-immunisation
The SEQUENCE — pain THEN weakness; winging of the scapula
Clinical; nerve conduction studies; neurology referral. Soon

stem: General practice in regional South Australia. James Doyle, 26, a storeman who played country football until a few years ago. The stem says 'A problem with his shoulder' or 'Shoulder pain' — but his opening line is not about pain: 'My shoulder keeps falling out.'
Afebrile · HR 70 · BP 122/76 · walks in unaided, no sling.

Tasks: take a focused history — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings, given on a card — explain your diagnosis to the patient, with differentials not asked for — and describe the course of the disease to the patient, with management not asked for.

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: ASK FOR IT AS A STRUCTURE

‘I would INSPECT both shoulders for WASTING, DEFORMITY AND SCARS, PALPATE the ACROMIOCLAVICULAR JOINT, GREATER TUBEROSITY AND BICEPS GROOVE, assess ACTIVE AND PASSIVE RANGE AND POWER, perform special tests including APPREHENSION, RELOCATION AND SULCUS, and check NEUROVASCULAR STATUS INCLUDING THE AXILLARY NERVE. May I have the findings?’
THE CARD

INSPECTION: no wasting, no deformity, no scars, shoulders symmetrical. PALPATION: no tenderness over the acromioclavicular joint, greater tuberosity or biceps groove. MOVEMENT: FULL ACTIVE AND PASSIVE RANGE IN ALL DIRECTIONS; POWER NORMAL THROUGHOUT, including resisted abduction and external rotation. SPECIAL TESTS: APPREHENSION TEST POSITIVE; SULCUS SIGN POSITIVE. IMPINGEMENT TESTS NEGATIVE. NEUROVASCULAR: INTACT, including SENSATION OVER THE REGIMENTAL BADGE AREA AND DELTOID POWER
READ IT OUT LOUD — say the three things that decide the case

‘FULL RANGE AND NORMAL POWER — so the ROTATOR CUFF IS WORKING, which argues AGAINST A CUFF TEAR. NO TENDERNESS AND NEGATIVE IMPINGEMENT — so this is NOT A TENDINOPATHY. A POSITIVE APPREHENSION TEST — which REPRODUCES THE POSITION IN WHICH THE JOINT COMES OUT, and tells me the problem is INSTABILITY’
THE APPREHENSION TEST

The arm is ABDUCTED TO 90° AND EXTERNALLY ROTATED. A POSITIVE TEST IS THE PATIENT'S LOOK OF APPREHENSION AND RESISTANCE — THE SENSE THAT IT IS ABOUT TO COME OUT — NOT PAIN. It reproduces the position in which the humeral head displaces ANTERIORLY. ABDUCTION PLUS EXTERNAL ROTATION IS THE PROVOCATIVE POSITION
CORRECTION — what the SULCUS SIGN actually shows

Source material states that a positive sulcus sign demonstrates a LABRAL TEAR. IT DOES NOT. The sulcus sign indicates INFERIOR CAPSULAR LAXITY — downward traction on the arm produces a VISIBLE GROOVE BELOW THE ACROMION as the head drops inferiorly — and WHEN PRESENT BILATERALLY it points to MULTIDIRECTIONAL INSTABILITY, a different, usually ATRAUMATIC pattern managed with PHYSIOTHERAPY RATHER THAN SURGERY. IT IS THE APPREHENSION TEST that reflects anterior instability from a labral lesion
Scripted reply if challenged on the sulcus sign

‘I read the APPREHENSION TEST as evidence of ANTERIOR INSTABILITY. I take the SULCUS SIGN as evidence of INFERIOR CAPSULAR LAXITY rather than of the labral tear itself, and ITS PRESENCE MAKES ME CONSIDER A MULTIDIRECTIONAL COMPONENT — which matters because IT MAKES ME MORE CAUTIOUS ABOUT A PURELY ANTERIOR SURGICAL REPAIR’ VERIFY
WHAT IS NOT ON THE CARD, AND WHY THAT MATTERS

NO WASTING, NO SCARS, NEUROVASCULARLY INTACT INCLUDING THE REGIMENTAL BADGE AREA AND DELTOID POWER. THAT IS THE AXILLARY NERVE CLEARED — THE NERVE MOST OFTEN INJURED IN ANTERIOR DISLOCATION. SAY THAT YOU LOOKED FOR IT
The two named lesions

A BANKART LESION is AVULSION OF THE ANTEROINFERIOR LABRUM, sometimes with a fragment of glenoid rim. A HILL–SACHS LESION is the IMPACTION FRACTURE OF THE POSTEROLATERAL HUMERAL HEAD where it strikes the glenoid rim as it dislocates. THEIR PRESENCE CONFIRMS A TRAUMATIC ANTERIOR MECHANISM
Imaging

PLAIN FILMS FIRST, INCLUDING AN AXILLARY VIEW, which may show a HILL–SACHS DEFECT or a BONY BANKART. PLAIN FILMS ARE OFTEN NORMAL BETWEEN DISLOCATIONS, so for a suspected labral tear THE INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE IS MR ARTHROGRAPHY — contrast outlines the labrum and shows the DETACHED ANTEROINFERIOR FRAGMENT against the INTACT POSTERIOR LABRUM VERIFY
WHY THERE IS NO DIFFERENTIAL TASK

For a shoulder that REPEATEDLY POPS OUT there are realistically TWO answers: A LABRAL TEAR AND A ROTATOR CUFF TEAR. That is why the case writer asks for DIAGNOSIS rather than differentials — AND WHY THE MARKS MOVED INTO THE HISTORY AND THE EXPLANATION INSTEAD

dx: **ANTERIOR SHOULDER INSTABILITY following a traumatic first dislocation, due to a LABRAL TEAR — a BANKART LESION when the anteroinferior labrum is avulsed.** **The humeral head no longer stays reliably in the glenoid, because the structures that hold it there have been damaged.**

**AN UNUSUAL TASK LIST — READ IT TWICE.** **This is an older online-exam format designed to FILL THE TIME: DIAGNOSIS ONLY, THEN COURSE.** **DIFFERENTIALS ARE NOT ASKED FOR. MANAGEMENT IS EXPLICITLY EXCLUDED.** **Candidates lose it by delivering a management plan NOBODY ASKED FOR and running out of time before the course.** **IF YOU ARE ASKED FOR THE COURSE, GIVE THE COURSE.** **Answering the question you EXPECTED rather than the one that was SET is the commonest way this station is lost.**

**THE TERMINOLOGY POINT: ‘RECURRENT SHOULDER DISLOCATION SYNDROME’ APPEARS IN NO STANDARD REFERENCE.** **The formal term, and the one used in Murtagh, is SHOULDER INSTABILITY.** Lead with that, then explain the underlying labral tear in plain words. If challenged: **‘because that describes the SYMPTOM rather than the PATHOLOGY. SHOULDER INSTABILITY names the problem, and the LABRAL TEAR names the cause.’**

**THE QUESTION THE STATION TURNS ON, asked in the first thirty seconds**: **‘CAN YOU DESCRIBE EXACTLY WHAT YOU MEAN BY FALLING OUT? Do you feel the joint POP OUT OF PLACE? Or is it more that it feels WEAK when you move it? Or that it is STIFF and hard to move?’** **Patients use ‘falling out’ for instability, for weakness, for subluxation AND for pain. Everything downstream — labrum versus cuff versus capsulitis — is decided by this answer.** **Candidates who assume they know what he means LOSE THE STATION IN ITS FIRST THIRTY SECONDS.**

**TWO STABILISERS, AND WHICH ONE FAILED.** **STATIC — the LABRUM, the JOINT CAPSULE and the GLENOHUMERAL LIGAMENTS. Damaged here.** **DYNAMIC — the ROTATOR CUFF, pulling the head into the socket. INTACT here, which is why his POWER AND RANGE ARE NORMAL.** **CORRECTION: source material states the shoulder has no significant ligaments. IT HAS THREE GLENOHUMERAL LIGAMENTS AND A CORACOHUMERAL LIGAMENT, and the INFERIOR GLENOHUMERAL LIGAMENT COMPLEX IS THE PRINCIPAL RESTRAINT IN ABDUCTION AND EXTERNAL ROTATION — exactly the position of apprehension.**

**THE MOST EMBARRASSING OMISSION IN THIS STATION: THE STEM SAYS SHOULDER PAIN. THE PATIENT NEVER MENTIONS PAIN. CANDIDATES THEREFORE NEVER ASK ABOUT IT.** **ASK ABOUT THE SHOULDER PAIN IN THE SHOULDER PAIN STATION — put it FIRST in the symptom sweep, before locking and stiffness.** He will say it aches for a day or two after it goes back, **and only if the question is put.**

**THE QUESTION THAT GIVES YOU THE COURSE FOR FREE: ‘IS IT HAPPENING WITH LESS AND LESS FORCE?’** → *‘it used to take a proper knock. Now it goes reaching for a seatbelt, or turning over in bed.’* **When he says he dislocated it turning over in bed, YOU ALREADY HAVE THE NATURAL HISTORY TO DESCRIBE BACK TO HIM IN TASK 4.** **Hearing it and not registering it is the wasted opportunity of the station.**

**WHY THE IMAGING QUESTION MATTERS: if the first episode was X-RAYED AND REPORTED AS A DISLOCATION, you have DOCUMENTED TRAUMATIC INSTABILITY. That distinguishes it from ATRAUMATIC MULTIDIRECTIONAL INSTABILITY, which is managed VERY DIFFERENTLY — physiotherapy, rarely surgery.**

**THE FIVE-STEP EXPLANATION — name it → describe the joint → name the two stabilisers → say which one tore → connect it back to his symptom.** **‘James, most likely you have a condition called SHOULDER INSTABILITY. The shoulder is a BALL-AND-SOCKET joint, but unlike the hip, THE SOCKET IS VERY SHALLOW — MORE LIKE A SAUCER THAN A CUP. That is what lets you move your arm in every direction, but it also makes it THE LEAST STABLE JOINT IN THE BODY. TWO THINGS hold the ball in place. The first is A RIM OF FIRM GRISTLE around the edge of the socket, called the LABRUM, which DEEPENS it. The second is a group of muscles that wrap around the joint, the ROTATOR CUFF, which PULL THE BALL INTO THE SOCKET. When you were tackled and landed on that shoulder, the ball came out of the socket, AND AS IT DID, IT TORE THAT RIM. With the rim torn, the socket is SHALLOWER than it should be, and the ball SLIPS OUT AGAIN. THAT IS WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING.’** **IF YOU SAY ‘LABRUM’, DEFINE IT IN THE SAME SENTENCE.**

**WHY OVERHEAD ACTIVITY IS ALWAYS ASKED: OVERHEAD FUNCTION IS ROTATOR CUFF FUNCTION.** **Normal overhead activity with recurrent dislocation POINTS AT THE LABRUM AND AWAY FROM THE CUFF — and it is the sentence you will use in the explanation to say WHY YOU ARE NOT CALLING IT A CUFF TEAR.** **If asked for a second possibility: ‘the other thing that can cause a shoulder to feel unstable is A TEAR OF THE ROTATOR CUFF MUSCLES. I think that is LESS LIKELY, because you have NO WEAKNESS and NO TROUBLE WITH OVERHEAD ACTIVITIES, and your power and movement were normal on examination.’**
plan: **‘Are you in any pain at the moment? … Tell me about your shoulder.’** → **a LONG RAMBLING ACCOUNT — the bed, the door frame, the footy injury, all in one go. THIS IS A DELIBERATE TEST of whether you can take control POLITELY. LET HIM FINISH, THEN TAKE CONTROL: ‘that sounds really unsettling, and having to put your own shoulder back is not something anyone should be doing. That's helpful — LET ME GO THROUGH IT PROPERLY WITH YOU.’** **If you interrupt him rudely he becomes TERSE; if you let him finish and then structure it, he engages fully.** Then **THE DESCRIBE QUESTION.**

**BLOCK 1 — DESCRIBE IT, THEN TIME IT.** **Does it go back on its own, or do you have to put it back — HOW do you put it back** · **‘does anything go NUMB OR TINGLE when it is out?’** · how long has this been going on · constantly or once in a while, roughly how often now · **IS IT GETTING WORSE — happening MORE OFTEN, or WITH LESS AND LESS FORCE** · what sort of things bring it on now · anything that makes it better · **‘how is this affecting your life — your work, your sport, your SLEEP?’**

**BLOCK 2 — MINE THE ORIGINAL INJURY.** **‘Take me back to the FIRST time it happened. What exactly were you doing, and HOW DID YOU LAND?’** · any SWELLING, BRUISING OR REDNESS at the time · **‘did you HEAR OR FEEL A POP?’** · did you see a doctor, or go to hospital · **‘did you have any SCANS OR X-RAYS, and were you told what they showed?’** · **how was it put back — did someone REDUCE it, were you given a SLING** · **‘did you have any PHYSIOTHERAPY afterwards?’**

**BLOCK 3 — SWEEP THE REST OF THE SHOULDER, EVERY ONE OF THEM.** **‘DO YOU HAVE ANY PAIN IN THE SHOULDER?’ (if yes, a brief SOCRATES)** · does it ever LOCK OR CATCH · any STIFFNESS · any difficulty with the RANGE OF MOVEMENT, can you get it ALL THE WAY UP · any SWELLING in the joint · any REDNESS OR RASH over it · any CLICKING, POPPING OR GRATING · any WEAKNESS lifting or reaching · **any NUMBNESS OR PINS AND NEEDLES in the shoulder, arm or hand.**

**BLOCK 4 — FUNCTION AND RISK.** **‘What is your OCCUPATION, and what does it involve PHYSICALLY?’** · any SPORT or exercise, and how much · **‘any difficulty or pain with OVERHEAD ACTIVITIES — reaching above your head, putting things on a high shelf?’**
6:00 → 6:30, if time remains

**BLOCK 5 — CLOSURE.** Other joints · morning stiffness over half an hour · family history of arthritis · neck pain · smoking, alcohol, medications, allergies, conditions. **BE HONEST ABOUT THIS BLOCK: screening for OA and RA in a 26-year-old with a traumatic labral tear is LOW-YIELD, and the source says as much. It is there because THE STATION ALLOTS MORE TIME THAN THE HISTORY NEEDS. DO NOT START IT UNTIL THE SHOULDER SWEEP IS COMPLETE.**
**Ask for the card as a structure, then READ IT OUT LOUD and interpret ALL THREE findings.**
**TASK 3 — the five-step explanation.**

**TASK 4 — THE COURSE, IN FOUR SENTENCES.** **‘I'll be straight with you. FIRST, THE TEAR ITSELF DOES NOT HEAL. Unlike a bruise or a pulled muscle, THAT RIM HAS A POOR BLOOD SUPPLY, so once it is torn it STAYS torn, and the socket stays shallower than it should be. SECOND, that means this is A LONG-TERM CONDITION, AND A RECURRENT ONE — we expect the shoulder to keep coming out. THIRD, and this is what you have already noticed — IT TENDS TO HAPPEN WITH LESS AND LESS FORCE OVER TIME. The first time it took a football tackle. Now it happens turning over in bed. That pattern usually continues. FOURTH, EACH DISLOCATION CAN DO A LITTLE MORE DAMAGE to the rim and to the bone at the edge of the socket, which is ONE REASON NOT TO SIMPLY LIVE WITH IT.** VERIFY **So: it is PERSISTENT, RECURRENT, and it WILL NOT RESOLVE ON ITS OWN — but that does not mean nothing can be done.’**
STOP THERE UNLESS INVITED

**The task said COURSE and explicitly EXCLUDED management.** **If you find yourself saying ‘so we'd start with physiotherapy’, STOP — that was not the task.** **OFFER it instead: ‘There is a lot that can be done about it — WOULD YOU LIKE ME TO GO THROUGH THE TREATMENT OPTIONS?’ and let them invite you.** Then close: **‘I know that's not the easiest thing to hear. The important message is that this is MANAGEABLE, and there are GOOD OPTIONS. What questions do you have for me?’**
pefe: **ONLY IF INVITED — the management.** **‘CONSERVATIVE TREATMENT FIRST for most people — PHYSIOTHERAPY to strengthen the ROTATOR CUFF so the muscles COMPENSATE FOR THE TORN RIM, and AVOIDING THE POSITION THAT PROVOKES IT, WHICH IS ARM UP AND ROTATED OUTWARDS. SURGERY to repair the rim is offered when symptoms are SEVERE, when it KEEPS DISLOCATING DESPITE PHYSIOTHERAPY, or in a YOUNG PERSON WHO WANTS TO RETURN TO CONTACT SPORT.’** VERIFY thresholds. **Given his job and frequency, an ORTHOPAEDIC OPINION AND A SCAN OF THE JOINT.**

**HIS HIDDEN AGENDA: whether it will EVER HEAL, and whether he will END UP UNABLE TO WORK.** He asks **‘so is it going to heal up eventually?’** near the end, and if you answer honestly, **‘will I be able to keep working?’** **He is matter-of-fact and a bit fed up, SLIGHTLY EMBARRASSED ABOUT RELOCATING IT ON A DOOR FRAME — not distressed.**

**DO NOT MISS**: **ASSOCIATED ROTATOR CUFF TEAR — the rule in a FIRST DISLOCATION OVER 40, where WEAKNESS rather than INSTABILITY dominates** VERIFY age threshold · **AXILLARY NERVE INJURY — numbness over the REGIMENTAL BADGE AREA, DELTOID WEAKNESS. Ask about it in the history** · **FRACTURE — GREATER TUBEROSITY or GLENOID RIM** · **a shoulder that WILL NOT RELOCATE, or NEUROVASCULAR COMPROMISE — EMERGENCY** · **POSTERIOR DISLOCATION — after a SEIZURE or an ELECTRIC SHOCK; arm held INTERNALLY ROTATED and WILL NOT EXTERNALLY ROTATE.**

**Prognosis points worth knowing** VERIFY figures before quoting any: **RECURRENCE RISK IS STRONGLY AGE-DEPENDENT — VERY HIGH after a first traumatic dislocation in a YOUNG ATHLETE, and MUCH LOWER in older patients** · **a first dislocation OVER 40 should raise suspicion of an ASSOCIATED ROTATOR CUFF TEAR rather than a labral tear** · **REPEATED DISLOCATION CAUSES PROGRESSIVE GLENOID BONE LOSS, WHICH CAN CHANGE THE OPERATION FROM A LABRAL REPAIR TO A BONE-BLOCK PROCEDURE.**

**NEVER SAY**: **‘you've got recurrent shoulder dislocation syndrome’** · **‘you have a labral tear’ (WITHOUT DEFINING THE LABRUM)** · **‘it'll heal up with rest’** · **‘there's nothing much to be done’** · **a MANAGEMENT PLAN when the task asked for the COURSE.**

**If he asks ‘CAN I KEEP PLAYING FOOTY?’** → **‘Contact sport with an unstable shoulder means IT WILL KEEP COMING OUT, and EACH TIME RISKS A BIT MORE DAMAGE. I wouldn't tell you NEVER — I'd tell you it's THE SINGLE STRONGEST REASON TO SEE A SURGEON about repairing it.’** **If he asks for a certificate** → **‘Yes, and I'd rather write you onto MODIFIED DUTIES than off altogether — STAYING AT WORK IN A RESTRICTED ROLE GIVES BETTER OUTCOMES than being off. I'll specify NO OVERHEAD WORK and a LIFTING LIMIT. If this started at work, we should also lodge a ReturnToWorkSA claim.’**

**VARIANT — THE OVER-40 FIRST DISLOCATION.** *‘I'm 58. I fell three weeks ago and they put it back in hospital. Now I can't lift my arm and it feels weak.’* → **‘In someone OVER FORTY, a first dislocation carries a HIGH CHANCE OF AN ASSOCIATED ROTATOR CUFF TEAR, and WEAKNESS RATHER THAN INSTABILITY IS THE CLUE. I would examine the cuff specifically and arrange an ULTRASOUND OR MRI.’** VERIFY

**VARIANT — ATRAUMATIC MULTIDIRECTIONAL INSTABILITY.** *‘Both of them feel loose. I've never injured either. I've always been double-jointed.’* → **‘BILATERAL, ATRAUMATIC, HYPERMOBILE — that is MULTIDIRECTIONAL INSTABILITY from GENERALISED CAPSULAR LAXITY rather than a traumatic labral tear. The SULCUS SIGN IS TYPICALLY POSITIVE ON BOTH SIDES. It is managed with a STRUCTURED PHYSIOTHERAPY PROGRAMME; SURGERY IS A LAST RESORT AND DOES LESS WELL.’** VERIFY

**VARIANT — POSTERIOR DISLOCATION.** *‘It came out during a fit. It's stuck by my side and I can't turn it outwards.’* → **‘A shoulder that dislocates during a SEIZURE OR AN ELECTRIC SHOCK, held INTERNALLY ROTATED and UNABLE TO EXTERNALLY ROTATE, is a POSTERIOR DISLOCATION — CLASSICALLY MISSED ON A SINGLE ANTEROPOSTERIOR FILM. I would request an AXILLARY OR SCAPULAR Y VIEW and involve orthopaedics URGENTLY.’** **VARIANT — ADHESIVE CAPSULITIS:** 62M, gradual pain and stiffness over five months, cannot reach behind his back, **PASSIVE MOVEMENT AS RESTRICTED AS ACTIVE — PASSIVE LOSS IS THE DISCRIMINATOR.**

SA — **MR ARTHROGRAM and orthopaedic review generally require Adelaide: PATS travel subsidy applies; RAH, Flinders or Lyell McEwin** · **Country Health Connect physiotherapy through the Yorke and Northern LHN, with TELEHEALTH review where travel is a barrier** · **if the injury is WORK-RELATED, a ReturnToWorkSA claim and a WORK CAPACITY CERTIFICATE — a storeman doing overhead lifting will need MODIFIED DUTIES** · **an IRREDUCIBLE dislocation or one with NEUROVASCULAR COMPROMISE in a small rural site: ANALGESIA, DO NOT PERSIST WITH REPEATED ATTEMPTS, and call MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** · **ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officer; Closing the Gap PBS co-payment.**

setting: Two of the most commonly dropped marks here are not clinical at all. One — the son does the talking, the candidate answers him, and nobody ever asks the patient whether that is alright; that is a confidentiality breach and is explicitly examinable. Two — task 2 says request the report, and candidates sit waiting for it to be handed over. Both take seconds.
stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 60-year-old man, a known case of ischaemic heart disease, who has come for a medication review. A medication review has already been carried out by the pharmacist and a report is available. His son is here with him.

Current medications: simvastatin for cholesterol · aspirin for ischaemic heart disease · allopurinol for gout prevention · paracetamol · temazepam for sleep · and diltiazem, recently added by his cardiologist.
Tasks: take a history from the son for three minutes — request the pharmacist's report from the examiner — explain the report to the son and the required actions.
tasks: Take a history from the son for three minutes
Request the pharmacist's report from the examiner
Explain the report to the son and the required actions
time: Fifteen seconds for consent, first thing · then why they came and why the son came · three minutes of history using the medicines themselves as the structure, because there is no presenting complaint · ask for the report the moment the three minutes are up · then the three actions in order — the interaction, the temazepam taper, and the dose administration aid — each translated out of pharmacological language
findingsLabel: The report has three findings — read them back in your own words, not theirs
findings: The three findings
1. Diltiazem and simvastatin should not be used together at this dose — risk of muscle damage · 2. Temazepam should be considered for cessation · 3. A medication aid could be provided

back.dx: POLYPHARMACY — six regular medicines plus over-the-counter ibuprofen — with a clinically significant drug interaction that is already symptomatic, a benzodiazepine to deprescribe, and an adherence problem that may be cognitive. The interaction, translated: 'His cholesterol tablet and the new heart tablet don't sit well together. The heart tablet slows down how the body clears the cholesterol tablet, so the level builds up higher than it should — and at high levels those tablets can damage muscle, which causes aching and weakness and very occasionally something more serious that can affect the kidneys.' then connect it to the aching legs the son has just given you. What you do: ask about muscle symptoms today and, if present, stop the statin and check creatine kinase and renal function · either lower the simvastatin to the dose considered safe with diltiazem or switch to a statin not affected by that pathway · keep the diltiazem, because the cardiologist added it deliberately · write to the cardiologist · and check liver and kidney function and repeat the lipids. The safety-net is specific: 'If he gets aching, tenderness or weakness in his muscles — especially the thighs or shoulders — or if his urine goes dark like tea, I want him to stop the cholesterol tablet and contact us that day.' The temazepam: 'It works well for a few weeks, but after that the body gets used to it and it stops helping the sleep — while it keeps causing drowsiness, unsteadiness, falls and problems with memory.' and then the safety point that is non-negotiable: 'We don't stop it suddenly. Stopping a tablet like this abruptly can cause serious withdrawal, including fits. We bring it down slowly, in small steps, over weeks to months, at a pace he's comfortable with — and only if he agrees.' Treat the sleep rather than just the tablet: ask what the problem actually is — getting off, staying asleep, early waking — and screen for depression, pain, sleep apnoea, nocturia, alcohol, caffeine and restless legs, with sleep hygiene and cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, which is more effective than a hypnotic and without the harms VERIFY. The dose administration aid is the one that solves what the son described: 'Each day of the week has its own row, and morning, lunch and night each have their own sealed compartment. You just pop out the compartment — and if a compartment is still full, you know a dose has been missed.' What else a good review covers: is anything missing for his ischaemic heart disease · is anything doubled up across prescribers · allopurinol dose against renal function and whether the gout is actually controlled · the total daily paracetamol and whether anything else contains it · aspirin continued for secondary prevention with reflux and bleeding asked about · and stopping the over-the-counter NSAID, which does not sit well with aspirin, gout or cardiac disease. And the person rather than the list: cognition if he is muddling tablets — assess it rather than assuming age · falls on a benzodiazepine and a rate-limiting calcium channel blocker · driving · who supports him and whether they need support · cost and a home medicines review · and a written medication list for both to carry. The pressure points, scripted. 'Can't you just stop the sleeping tablet?' → 'No — and this is important. Stopping a tablet like that suddenly can cause serious withdrawal, including fits.' 'Should he stop the new heart tablet?' → 'No. The cardiologist added it deliberately and it's doing an important job. It's the cholesterol tablet I'll change, and I'll write to them.' 'He won't agree to any of this' → 'Then we go at his pace. These are suggestions, not orders, and the one I'd least like to leave is the tablet combination, because that one can actually hurt him.' and if the son asks you to stop telling his father things because it only worries him — explore the concern, but the patient's right to information stands; negotiate how, not whether.
plan: WIPE, THEN CONSENT IN FIFTEEN SECONDS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE: 'MR AZIZ — AND YOU MUST BE HIS SON? BEFORE WE START: MR AZIZ, ARE YOU HAPPY FOR ME TO DISCUSS YOUR MEDICINES WITH YOUR SON HERE?' If the patient is not present or not able to answer, ask the son whether he has his father's consent or is the substitute decision-maker — and if only the examiner is available, ask the examiner. THE MARK IS FOR RECOGNISING THAT CONFIDENTIALITY APPLIES.

FIND OUT WHY THEY CAME, AND — SEPARATELY — WHY THE SON CAME: 'WHAT MADE YOU COME IN FOR A MEDICATION REVIEW?' AND 'CAN I ASK WHAT PROMPTED YOU TO COME ALONG TODAY?' The second answer is the clinical information the stem has deliberately left out. Then signpost the shape of the consultation.

THE THREE-MINUTE HISTORY, USING THE MEDICINES AS THE STRUCTURE BECAUSE THERE IS NO PRESENTING COMPLAINT. WHO AND HOW: who looks after the tablets · HOW DOES HE KEEP TRACK OF WHAT TO TAKE WHEN · does he ever miss doses or take them twice · DOES HE GET THEM ALL FROM THE SAME PHARMACY. You already have the list — what you need is how he takes it.

Side effects, with the one that matters most: 'Any muscle aches, pains or weakness — particularly since the new heart tablet was started?' · 'Any dark or tea-coloured urine?' · falls, dizziness or daytime drowsiness · and any recent slowing of the pulse or feeling faint, given newly added diltiazem.

COMPLETENESS AND CONTEXT — 'ANYTHING OVER THE COUNTER: ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES, VITAMINS, HERBAL THINGS?', which is never on the list and always in the cupboard · allergies · anything changed recently, new specialists or new tablets · HOW IS HIS MEMORY · how is he sleeping and how long has he been on the temazepam · who picks the tablets up and is cost a problem · does he live alone, does he drive, does he drink.
Ask the examiner for the report out loud, then read it back in your own words (see findings).
Action one, the interaction — explain it in lay terms, connect it to the aching legs, say what you will change and what stays, and give the safety-net sentence (see dx).
Action two, the temazepam — why it should come down, then the safety point that it is never stopped abruptly, then negotiate rather than announce. Deprescribing without agreement does not happen.

ACTION THREE, THE DOSE ADMINISTRATION AID, EXPLAINED PRACTICALLY — AND THEN THE REST OF THE REVIEW: stopping the Nurofen, assessing his memory properly rather than assuming age, and checking the allopurinol against renal function.

Close: 'So: three changes. I'll change the cholesterol tablet because of the interaction, start bringing the sleeping tablet down slowly if he agrees, and organise a pack from the pharmacy that sorts everything by day and time. I'll do blood tests today and write to the cardiologist. Come back straight away for muscle aches, weakness or dark urine, and I'll see you both in two weeks.' and speak to the patient directly at least once rather than letting the son answer everything.

Role-player: Nadeem Aziz, 34, a schoolteacher, who has brought his father Farouk, 60, for a medication review. Farouk is in the room and will answer if spoken to directly, but the son does most of the talking — worried, and slightly embarrassed about raising it in front of him. His opening is polite and a little anxious: 'The specialist added a new one, and I wanted someone to look at the whole lot.'

setting: A station that looks easy and empties fast. 'Healthy diet, exercise, less alcohol, stop smoking' takes twenty seconds and you have six minutes. Every recommendation must carry a number or a specific — not 'Exercise more' but '150 minutes a week over at least three days, never two days off in a row, plus two resistance sessions'. And protect two minutes for the glucometer, because it is a whole task.
stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 40-year-old woman recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Her HbA1c is 7.5%.

A glucometer is provided — on screen in the online format, on the desk in a face-to-face station. If it is on the desk, pick it up and demonstrate while narrating, then hand it to her and ask her to show you.
Tasks: discuss the lifestyle modifications with the patient — you have six minutes for this — and explain how to use a glucometer.

Explain how to use a glucometer

back.dx: NEWLY DIAGNOSED TYPE 2 DIABETES AT 7.5% — diagnostic, but only modestly above target, which is exactly why a lifestyle-first approach is reasonable and why this consultation matters. She is at risk of large-vessel disease — heart attack, stroke, peripheral arterial disease — and small-vessel disease of the eyes, kidneys and nerves, and lifestyle addresses both. The advice, with a number on every item. Food, asked about first: more vegetables at two meals a day, wholegrain cereals and breads, one and a half to two serves of dairy daily, fish twice a week, legumes and nuts, and olive oil as the main fat · less sugary drinks, which are the single biggest easy win, less saturated fat, smaller and less frequent red and processed meat, less takeaway and smaller portions · and alcohol within national guidelines. Frame it as swaps and additions and keep 'Nothing is completely banned' in the script, because a prohibition list is the failure mode. Exercise, after the cardiac question: 150 minutes a week of moderate to vigorous activity — enough to make her puff, so a gentle stroll does not count — spread over at least three days with never more than two consecutive days off, plus two or three resistance sessions totalling about an hour. Weight and waist: 5 to 10 per cent weight loss meaningfully improves glucose and cardiovascular risk — about five kilos for her — and waist under 80 cm for women and 94 cm for men. BMI under 25 is the ideal, not the starting target, and setting it as one is demotivating. Then the domains candidates forget: smoking cessation as the highest-value single change with Quitline 13 7848 · sleep, asking about snoring and daytime sleepiness because obstructive sleep apnoea is common and worsens control · daily foot checks including the soles and between the toes, never barefoot, well-fitting shoes · optometry at diagnosis · influenza and pneumococcal vaccination · driving, and never driving below 5 mmol/L · a sick day plan — keep taking medication, test more often, keep fluids up, seek help if vomiting · and mood, because diabetes distress and depression are common at diagnosis. The negotiation is the marked behaviour, not comprehensiveness: 'Of everything we've discussed — the drink, the bread, the vegetables, the walking — which two would you be willing to start this week?' and 'Two changes you keep beat twelve you abandon.' Hypoglycaemia — teach the rule of 15 but put it in context, because a patient on lifestyle or metformin alone is at very low risk: symptoms, then check, and if below 4.0 take 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate — half a glass of juice or regular soft drink, three teaspoons of sugar or honey, six or seven jelly beans, or glucose tablets — wait 15 minutes, recheck, repeat if still below 4, then a longer-acting snack or meal. Before exercise aim above 5, and watch for delayed lows after prolonged exercise. The team, named: credentialled diabetes educator, who gives her an hour you cannot · dietitian · exercise physiologist or physiotherapist · optometrist and podiatrist · pharmacist · under a GP management plan with team care arrangements. Baseline screening at diagnosis: eyes, feet with pulses and monofilament, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR, lipids, blood pressure, cardiovascular risk, liver function, mood and dental. Review in two to four weeks to see how the changes are going, repeat HbA1c at three months, NDSS registration for subsidised strips, and red flags: very thirsty, passing lots of urine, losing weight, blurred vision, or a foot wound that is not healing. What else to consider: do not assume type 2 at 40 — a lean, rapidly symptomatic, ketotic patient is type 1 or lada and needs antibodies and c-peptide VERIFY · steroid-induced hyperglycaemia · and a misleading HbA1c in anaemia, recent transfusion, iron therapy or chronic kidney disease, where fasting glucose or an OGTT is used instead VERIFY.
plan: Open by asking rather than telling: 'Before I go through them — what do you already know about diabetes? And is there anything in particular worrying you?' Her mother's diabetes is the frame she hears everything through, and it must be addressed early: 'Your mother's diabetes is not your diabetes. Hers was probably found late; yours has been found early and is only a little above target.' and to 'I feel completely fine': 'That's the difficulty with diabetes — it does its damage quietly for years before anyone feels anything. That's exactly why acting now works.'
Explain the number and the condition in one paragraph, then signpost the three things you will cover (see findings).

THIRTY SECONDS OF DIETARY AND ACTIVITY HISTORY BEFORE ADVISING: 'TALK ME THROUGH A NORMAL DAY'S EATING. BREAKFAST, LUNCH, DINNER, SNACKS, DRINKS.' AND 'WHAT ACTIVITY DO YOU DO NOW?' It makes everything afterwards specific and credible instead of generic — and it is how you find the two or three cans of Coke a day.
Dietary advice built out of her answers, leading with her biggest single win — the soft drink — then the specifics, and 'Nothing is completely banned' (see dx).

The cardiac question before prescribing exercise: 'Before I ask you to push yourself — do you get any chest tightness, pressure or breathlessness when you exert yourself? I ask everyone, because diabetes raises the risk of heart disease and can make it silent.' if yes: examination, ECG, and consider stress testing before recommending vigorous activity VERIFY. Then the prescription with its numbers.

NEGOTIATE RATHER THAN REPEAT. When she says she has two kids and a full-time job and it is not happening, DO NOT SAY THE TARGET AGAIN LOUDER — she becomes resigned and stops engaging. 'THEN LET'S NOT START WITH THE GYM. WHAT ABOUT A TEN-MINUTE WALK AFTER DINNER, AND THE STAIRS AT WORK?' Then ask which two she will start this week.

WEIGHT, WAIST AND THE REMAINING DOMAINS — a realistic 5 to 10 per cent rather than an unreachable BMI target, waist, alcohol, smoking, sleep and snoring, daily foot checks, eyes, vaccination and driving (see dx).
PROTECT THE LAST TWO MINUTES AND TEACH THE METER, NARRATING ALL NINE STEPS — then TEACH-BACK, and correct the deliberate error when she says she would use the pad of her finger (see findings).
How often to test, answered honestly — then the rule of 15 with the risk put in context, so she is not frightened of something she is not yet at risk of.

The team, the baseline screening, NDSS registration, a review in two to four weeks, repeat HbA1c at three months and the red flags. And if she asks about tablets or remission: 'If you do need metformin, that isn't you failing — diabetes is progressive and the medication is a tool, not a punishment' and 'Some people with early type 2 get their sugar back into the normal range with weight loss and activity — we call that remission. I can't promise it, and it isn't a cure, but it is a real possibility' VERIFY.

Role-player: Sarah Kennelly, 40, an office administrator with children aged 8 and 11, who had blood tests two weeks ago because she was tired and feels completely well. About 88 kg at 165 cm, having put on 10 kg since her second child. Toast and coffee, a white-bread sandwich at work, whatever the children are eating for dinner, and two or three cans of coke a day — mentioned only if asked what she drinks. No exercise beyond walking around the office, and a gym membership unused for two years. No smoking, two glasses of wine most evenings. No exertional chest pain. She snores and her husband says she stops breathing — mentioned only if asked about sleep.

How she plays it: anxious, leading with her mother, who ended up on insulin and lost a toe before she died. If told only that she has diabetes with no reassurance she goes quiet and frightened; if the doctor addresses her mother's story directly she relaxes and engages. She says once 'But I feel completely fine'. She pushes back on exercise, and if the target is simply repeated louder she becomes resigned and stops engaging — but agrees enthusiastically to something small and negotiated. On teach-back she gets one step wrong on purpose, saying she would use the pad of the finger, to see whether she is corrected. Her hidden concern, volunteered late or only if asked what worries her most, is that she and her husband have been talking about a third child and she is frightened this rules it out — which matters, because preconception care changes in diabetes: glucose well controlled before conception, high-dose folate, medication review, and HbA1c unreliable in pregnancy VERIFY.

HbA1c 7.5% — explain it in one breath — 'The test is called HbA1c. It tells us your average blood sugar over about three months. Below 6 is normal. 6.5 and above means diabetes. Yours is 7.5. So it is diabetes — but it is only a little above where we'd like it, and that is a good place to be starting from.' then the condition in one sentence: 'Your body still makes insulin, but it doesn't work as well as it should, so sugar builds up in the blood'

The glucometer, narrated — 1. Wash hands in warm water and dry completely — residue gives a false reading and warm hands bleed more easily · 2. Check the strips are in date, take one out and close the pot · 3. Put the strip in the meter, which turns itself on · 4. New lancet, set the depth, and prick the side of a fingertip not the pad — less painful and more blood — rotating fingers · 5. Let a drop form without squeezing hard, which dilutes the sample · 6. Touch the drop to the edge of the strip and let it draw in · 7. Wait for the reading · 8. Write it down with the time · 9. Lancet into a sharps container, not the bin

setting: You have been sent to tell a daughter that her father is dying. The clinical content is small and the communication content is the whole station. The single commonest failure is letting 'Palliative care' sound like 'We are stopping treatment'. And do not open with 'How can I help you?' — you asked to see her, about her dying father.
stem: Hospital ward. You are the treating junior doctor. A 90-year-old man admitted with lower lobe pneumonia and started on antibiotics has been having episodes of hypoxia and hypotension.

He has an advance care directive for no CPR and no enteral feeding. The consultant has suggested palliative care and asked you to discuss this with the family. His daughter is here and wishes to discuss his condition.
Tasks: explain the measures being taken — what is happening with her father — and explain what further can be done for the patient.
