time: The opening shape is memorised, not improvised — introduce as her father's doctor, express sorrow, offer a seat · then two questions in the first minute, both separately marked: what do you already know, and are you his substitute decision-maker · then the story in order so the conclusion arrives as something she can see coming · then the directive as his voice · then palliative care, defined properly · then the person, the family, the supports and the meeting

back.dx: A 90-year-old dying of severe pneumonia that is not responding to full treatment, with a valid advance care directive. The story is built in order so the conclusion arrives as something she can see coming: what he has → how serious → what we are doing → how he is responding → what we are worried about → what he himself asked for → what we propose. By the time you say the words palliative care, she should already be most of the way there. The warning shot and the reassurance belong together, in that order: 'He is not responding as well as we had hoped. He has had further episodes of low blood pressure and low oxygen' — pause — 'We are concerned his condition may get worse, and we will keep doing everything we can for him. He is not going to be left without care.' when she asks whether he is dying, answer it: 'I think he may be. He isn't responding to the treatment and I'm worried he will get worse rather than better. I can't tell you how long and I won't guess — but I'd rather you knew exactly where we stand.' then stop talking; silence after bad news is part of the answer, not dead air. The directive is handed back to her rather than used against her: 'That was his decision, made when he could make it, and we will respect it. Did the two of you ever talk about what he wanted?' then the three sentences the whole station is built around, and all three must be said: 'Palliative care is not giving up.' · 'It runs alongside what we are already doing, not instead of it — the antibiotics, the oxygen and the fluids carry on as long as they help him.' · 'What changes is what we are aiming for — comfort, rather than cure at any cost. Nothing is being taken away from him.' then be concrete, because detail is what makes palliative care sound like care rather than withdrawal: symptom medicines charted ready in advance for pain, breathlessness, nausea, secretions and restlessness, so nobody waits while he is uncomfortable · stopping medicines that cannot help him now, like the cholesterol tablets · mouth care, positioning and gentle nursing · fewer needles, observations and blood tests that will not change anything · and a quiet room with unrestricted visiting. The second half of the discriminating issue is not making her decide — she is the substitute decision-maker, not the person who must authorise her father's death: 'The medical recommendation is ours to make, and I don't want you carrying that. Your role is to help us understand who your dad is and what he would have wanted' — often the most relieving sentence in the station. Then the person and the family: what mattered most to him · was he religious and is there anyone to call · any cultural things to get right · did he ever say where he would want to be · who else needs to be here · and how is she, sleeping, eating, working, and is anyone else depending on her. The supports: specialist palliative care and the hospital social worker today · pastoral care · carer gateway 1800 422 737 with centrelink carer allowance and carer payment VERIFY · country health connect and community palliative care if home becomes the plan · bereavement support offered in advance rather than afterwards · an Aboriginal liaison officer where relevant, because practices and language around dying differ and must be led by the family · and TIS National 131 450, never using a family member to interpret an end-of-life discussion. And the plan: a family meeting with the consultant and the palliative care team, documented goals of care consistent with the directive, and overnight contact arrangements with her best number. Before concluding he is dying, still review the reversible: culture results and antibiotic cover, fluid status and heart failure, empyema, pulmonary embolism, and delirium — which is distressing, treatable and frequently missed at the end of life.
plan: THE OPENING, WHOSE SHAPE IS MARKED: 'HELLO, I'M DR [NAME], ONE OF THE DOCTORS LOOKING AFTER YOUR FATHER. ARE YOU SAMANTHA? I'M SO SORRY TO HEAR YOUR FATHER HAS BEEN UNWELL. PLEASE, TAKE A SEAT.' Introduction, your relationship to the patient, an expression of sorrow, a seat — and then her understanding before yours.

THE TWO QUESTIONS, BOTH SEPARATELY MARKED: 'BEFORE I SAY ANYTHING — CAN YOU TELL ME HOW MUCH YOU ALREADY KNOW ABOUT YOUR FATHER'S CONDITION?' AND 'CAN I CHECK — ARE YOU NAMED AS HIS SUBSTITUTE DECISION-MAKER?' Then ask whether there is anything in particular she wants covered, and signpost the three things you will do.

The situation in four short blocks, pausing after each — what he has · how serious, and why low oxygen and low blood pressure make it severe · what you are doing, which she needs to hear before she can hear that it is not working · and how he is responding, with the reassurance sentence attached (see dx).

Answer 'Are you telling me he's dying?' Honestly and directly — then stop, offer tissues, and let her react. 'Take whatever time you need. This is an enormous thing to be told.' Continuing the explanation while she is crying is the error.

The advance care directive, brought in respectfully as his voice in the room and then handed back to her — and if she says he signed it years ago and didn't mean this: 'That's a fair thing to raise. The directive isn't a rule that overrides you — it's his voice in the room. Tell me what you think he'd say if he could.'
If she asks about the ventilator, answer it in terms of benefit and burden rather than of what the document does or does not list (see findings).

NAME WHO ASKED, DEFINE PALLIATIVE CARE, AND THEN SAY ALL THREE CORRECTING SENTENCES — NOT GIVING UP, ALONGSIDE NOT INSTEAD OF, NOTHING BEING TAKEN AWAY. When she says 'so you're giving up on him', that is the moment the station turns.

What it looks like in practice, concretely — the anticipatory medicines, the medicines stopped, the mouth care, the reduced needles and the open visiting (see dx). And make clear the decision is not hers to carry alone.

THE PERSON AND THE FAMILY — what mattered most to her dad, whether he was religious and who to call, cultural needs, who else needs to be here, and how SHE is. Four separately marked items live in this last stretch, and candidates end on the definition of palliative care and never reach them.
Supports, the family meeting with the consultant and the palliative care team, overnight contact with her best number, and a summary that ends on 'Nothing is being taken away from him.'

ask: The opening shape, which is marked: 'I'm one of the doctors looking after your father.' · 'I'm so sorry to hear your father has been unwell.' · 'Can you tell me how much you already know?' · 'Are you named as his substitute decision-maker?'

The three sentences that prevent the misunderstanding the station is built on: 'Palliative care is not giving up.' · 'It runs alongside what we're doing, not instead of it.' · 'Nothing is being taken away from him.'
The honest answer and the relieving one: 'I think he may be dying. I can't tell you how long, and I won't guess.' · 'The medical recommendation is ours to make — I don't want you carrying that.'

The ones that reach the person: 'His directive is his voice in the room — did the two of you ever talk about it?' · 'What mattered most to your dad?' · 'We don't wait for him to be uncomfortable before we treat it.' · 'If anything changes overnight, the ward will call you.'

Challenges: 'Are you telling me he's dying?' · 'So you're giving up on him' · 'Can't you just put him on a ventilator?' · 'He signed that form years ago — he didn't mean this' · 'Are you going to stop his antibiotics?' · 'Will he be in pain?' · 'Can we take him home?' · 'It's my decision then?' · and 'My brother will want everything done.'
pefe: There is no examination and no history task — but two questions must still be asked in the first minute and both are separately marked: what she already knows, and whether she is the substitute decision-maker. Discussing treatment decisions with a relative of unconfirmed standing is the procedural failure here.

Role-player: Samantha Hobbs, 58, a school administrator whose father Ronald, 90, was admitted three days ago. She has visited daily, nobody has updated her since Tuesday, and she has been waiting outside the ward all morning — not aggressive, but frightened, tired and slightly aggrieved at the lack of communication. Ronald lived independently until this admission, was widowed six years ago, and is devoutly catholic — he would want the priest. He completed the directive about four years ago after a friend died badly in intensive care, and told her plainly that he had had a good innings and did not want to be kept alive by machines — said only if asked whether they ever discussed it.

How she plays it: she listens quietly to the explanation, then goes silent when told he is not responding and asks directly whether he is dying. If answered honestly she cries, accepts tissues and recovers in about thirty seconds; if evaded she asks again more sharply — 'I need you to tell me straight.' She asks once about the ventilator. When palliative care is mentioned she says flatly 'So you're giving up on him' and waits — and if it is not corrected clearly she becomes upset and hostile for the rest of the station, while a good 'Alongside, not instead of' settles her visibly and she starts asking practical questions. She has a brother Greg interstate who will want everything done and whom she dreads telling — raised only if asked who else needs to be involved. She has not eaten or slept properly in three days, said only if asked. Her hidden fear, volunteered late or if asked what worries her most, is that he will be in pain and will die alone while she is at home. If the doctor never asks about her father as a person or about her, she does not volunteer the priest or the brother.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: INTRODUCED AS ONE OF HER FATHER'S DOCTORS AND OFFERED HER A SEAT · EXPRESSED SORROW RATHER THAN SAYING 'HOW CAN I HELP YOU' · ASKED WHAT SHE ALREADY KNEW BEFORE EXPLAINING · CONFIRMED SHE WAS THE SUBSTITUTE DECISION-MAKER · explained the pneumonia and why it was severe · explained the antibiotics, oxygen and fluids · GAVE A CLEAR WARNING SHOT · SAID EXPLICITLY THEY WOULD KEEP DOING EVERYTHING THEY COULD · ANSWERED 'IS HE DYING?' HONESTLY · PAUSED AND LET HER REACT, OFFERING TISSUES · raised the directive as HIS WISHES and asked whether they had discussed it · ADDRESSED THE VENTILATOR IN TERMS OF BENEFIT AND BURDEN · SAID PALLIATIVE CARE IS NOT GIVING UP · SAID IT RUNS ALONGSIDE AND NOTHING IS BEING TAKEN AWAY · DESCRIBED SYMPTOM CONTROL CONCRETELY · MADE CLEAR THE DECISION WAS NOT HERS TO CARRY ALONE · asked about her father as a person and about his spiritual needs · ASKED HOW SHE WAS AND ABOUT OTHER FAMILY · offered a family meeting, palliative care team and social worker · and gave a clear overnight contact plan and closing summary.

The clinical picture — Lower lobe pneumonia on intravenous antibiotics, with episodes of hypoxia and hypotension — which is what makes it a severe pneumonia, and it is failing to respond to appropriate therapy in a 90-year-old

The directive — No CPR and no enteral feeding. It does two things: records refusals of specific treatments, which are legally binding when valid, and appoints a substitute decision-maker. It does not replace a conversation with the family, it never means withdrawal of comfort care, and it is not a document to hide behind — never say 'He signed a form'

The intubation question — where the obvious reasoning is wrong — The directive says nothing about intubation, and it is tempting to conclude that intubation is therefore the next step. That is unsafe: a directive lists what a person refuses, and does not oblige you to provide everything they did not think to refuse. Clinicians are not obliged to offer treatment that is not clinically indicated VERIFY

So say this instead — 'If he continues to worsen, the only remaining option would be a breathing tube and intensive care. His directive doesn't mention that specifically — so the question is whether it would help him, and whether it fits what he would have wanted. In someone of 90 whose pneumonia isn't responding, it is very unlikely to give him more good time, and it would almost certainly mean he died in intensive care rather than with you'

South Australian terminology — Under the advance care directives act 2013 the appointed person is a substitute decision-maker — not a 'Medical decision maker', which is Victorian, and not 'Next of kin', which has no decision-making status in law. Ask: 'Are you named as your father's substitute decision-maker in his advance care directive?' VERIFY

setting: It looks like a dermatology station and it is not. Acne cases are designed around the psychosocial impact, and the role-player will show you — poor eye contact, a quiet voice, a story about school. A candidate who counts spots and lists side effects and never asks how he is coping has missed the station. And note the task wording: the impact of the condition is a marked task, not a throwaway phrase.
stem: General practice. Your next patient is a 17-year-old boy who has had acne for about a year. He has already tried topical treatments and a course of oral antibiotics without success, and oral isotretinoin is now being considered.
Tasks: take a history from the patient — explain the impact of the condition and the treatment, including the side effects of retinoid therapy.
If he is accompanied, offer him part of the appointment alone and explain confidentiality in one sentence.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain the impact of the condition and the treatment, including the side effects of retinoid therapy
time: Open by letting him describe the skin in his own words, which is neutral ground and his area of expertise · classify it, including the scarring question · take a treatment history that asks how, not just what · then normalise and ask the question the station is built on · explore what he discloses and respond to it with named supports · then explain acne and de-blame it · then isotretinoin, benefit first and side effects in full
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: Severity is not a lesion count

Any scarring means severe, whatever the count — and scars are permanent, which is why severe acne is treated aggressively and early VERIFY. And significant psychosocial impact is itself a recognised reason to escalate treatment, even when the skin looks moderate — so asking about it is taking a severity history, not being pastoral VERIFY
His skin

Mixed comedonal and inflammatory — blackheads and whiteheads plus deeper sore lumps · face mainly with some on the back and shoulders · and some spots on his cheeks have left small dents, which he mentions only if asked about marks or scars · he picks and squeezes them

back.dx: ACNE VULGARIS — mixed comedonal and inflammatory, with established atrophic scarring, which classifies it as severe irrespective of lesion count — on a background of inadequate rather than ineffective previous treatment, and with significant undisclosed psychosocial impact. Explain the condition and de-blame it in the same breath: 'Under the skin you have tiny oil glands. In your teens, hormones make them produce more oil. The opening gets blocked by dead skin, the oil builds up behind it, and bacteria that normally live on the skin multiply in there — which is what makes it red and sore. It is not caused by being dirty, and it is not caused by chocolate. It is hormones and genetics, and it is not your fault.' Scrubbing makes it worse; gentle wash twice daily, oil-free non-comedogenic moisturiser and sunscreen, and no picking, which causes scarring. Isotretinoin is indicated here on three separate grounds — scarring, failure of prior therapy, and psychological impact — and the other indications are severe or nodulocystic disease and frequent relapse VERIFY. Lead with the benefit because it is real: 'It is the most effective treatment we have — it shrinks the oil glands, and for many people a single course clears the acne for good. But it has real side effects, and you need to know them before you decide.' The common ones: dryness, especially the lips, in almost everyone — constant lip balm, moisturiser and artificial tears, and contact lenses may become uncomfortable · nosebleeds from a dry nose · sun sensitivity, with spf 50+, hat and shade · and it often gets worse before it gets better, with a flare in the first few weeks expected · muscle and joint aches, especially with heavy exercise · and night vision can be affected, which matters for driving. The ones requiring action rather than mention: blood tests before and during for liver enzymes and blood fats · pregnancy, where the drug is severely harmful to a developing baby and any patient who could become pregnant needs pregnancy testing and strict reliable contraception before, during and for a defined period after treatment, with explicit documented counselling VERIFY — mention it even for a male patient as part of explaining what the drug is · no blood donation during treatment or for a period afterwards · never with a tetracycline, because of raised pressure around the brain · and no waxing, laser or skin resurfacing during and for a period after. Sexual dysfunction is now noted in the Australian product information after a TGA review — mention it if asked and take a report seriously. The mood question is answered honestly and safely, and the honest position is neither 'There's no link' nor 'This drug causes depression': the Australasian college of dermatologists states that current evidence does not point to a causal relationship and that severe acne itself carries psychological risk, while the TGA concluded an association with psychiatric and sexual adverse effects could not be ruled out and had the product information updated as a precaution, with psychological monitoring recommended for anyone with a history of mental illness VERIFY. So: reported, not proven causal, taken seriously, actively monitored, report immediately. In Australia isotretinoin sits under appendix d of the poisons standard and is restricted to specialist dermatologists, with an RACGP application before the TGA to allow accredited GPs to prescribe — check whether that has changed before telling a patient what will happen VERIFY. PBS listing is for severe cystic acne unresponsive to other therapy, authority required streamlined VERIFY. And consider the other causes: drug-induced acne from anabolic steroids, corticosteroids, some anticonvulsants and lithium — abrupt, monomorphic, often truncal, and easily missed in a 17-year-old who trains · rosacea, which flushes and has no comedones · folliculitis, which is itchy and hair-follicle centred · and in a female patient, polycystic ovary syndrome with irregular periods, hirsutism or rapid weight change.
plan: Open and give him some control: 'Tell me about your skin, in your own words.' then, if a parent is present, offer privacy as routine: 'It's something I offer everyone your age — would you like some of this appointment on your own?' and confidentiality in one sentence — what he tells you stays between you, unless you were worried about his safety, and you would talk to him first.

CLASSIFY THE ACNE — how long · WHAT SORT OF SPOTS, BLACKHEADS AND WHITEHEADS OR THE DEEPER SORE LUMPS · where, face or chest and back too · is it getting worse · anything that makes it better or worse including stress, sweating, products, helmets or sports gear · DO YOU PICK OR SQUEEZE THEM · AND THE ONE THAT CHANGES THE PLAN: 'HAVE ANY OF THEM LEFT MARKS OR SCARS?'

THE TREATMENT HISTORY THAT ASKS HOW, NOT JUST WHAT: what have you tried · FOR HOW LONG EACH TIME · DID YOU PUT THE CREAM ON THE WHOLE AREA, OR JUST ON THE SPOTS · did you use it every day · did anything irritate your skin · how long were you on the antibiotic and did you take it every day. Then other causes — medications, ANYTHING FROM THE GYM INCLUDING SUPPLEMENTS AND PROTEIN, and family history.

Normalise, then ask — the single most useful sentence in the station and the difference between passing and failing: 'Can I ask you something a bit different? A lot of people your age find this really gets to them — how they feel about themselves, how school is. How much does it affect you?' Normalising is what converts a closed adolescent into an open one.

EXPLORE IT PROPERLY RATHER THAN ABSORBING IT AND MOVING ON — 'THANK YOU FOR TELLING ME, THAT TOOK SOMETHING' · what sort of things do they say · HOW OFTEN ARE THERE DAYS YOU DON'T GO IN · does anyone at school know · have you stopped doing things you used to do · HOW'S YOUR MOOD BEEN IN YOURSELF · still enjoying things · sleep and appetite · AND, IF THE PICTURE WARRANTS IT, WHETHER HE HAS FELT REALLY DOWN OR HOPELESS · plus who he talks to when things are tough.

RESPOND WITH ACTION, NOT SYMPATHY — 'NONE OF THIS IS YOUR FAULT, AND BEING TEASED ABOUT IT IS NOT SOMETHING YOU SHOULD HAVE TO JUST PUT UP WITH' · THEN NAMED SUPPORTS: THE SCHOOL COUNSELLOR, headspace, AND KIDS HELPLINE 1800 55 1800 ANY TIME · ENCOURAGE HIM TO TELL A TRUSTED ADULT AND OFFER TO SUPPORT THAT · AND A LONGER FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT. If he discloses persistent low mood or hopelessness, ASSESS IT PROPERLY AND SUPPORT IT RATHER THAN PRESCRIBING AND MOVING ON — and say 'the two go together', because clearing the acne often lifts the mood and neither is a reason to ignore the other.
Explain acne and say explicitly that it is not his fault, then the everyday measures (see dx).

ISOTRETINOIN — WHY IT IS INDICATED FOR HIM SPECIFICALLY, THEN THE BENEFIT, THEN THE SIDE EFFECTS IN FULL (see dx). Listing them so alarmingly that he refuses an effective treatment is its own failure.

The mood question, answered honestly: 'Mood changes have been reported and we take that seriously. What that means in practice is that I'll ask about your mood before we start and at every single visit, and I want you — and your mum — to tell me straight away if anything changes, even a bit. We don't wait and see with that.' A flat 'No, that's a myth' leaves him unconvinced and is inaccurate.

CLOSE BY CONNECTING THE PLAN BACK TO WHAT HE DISCLOSED: dermatology referral for the tablet, baseline bloods, current treatment used properly in the meantime — whole area, every day, six weeks before judging it — AND A LONGER APPOINTMENT ABOUT SCHOOL. 'I WANT TO TREAT YOUR SKIN — AND I DON'T WANT TO TREAT ONLY YOUR SKIN.'

The one question that changes the severity classification: 'Have any of them left marks or scars?' and the one that changes the treatment history: 'Did you put the cream on the whole area, or just on the spots?'

The follow-ups that turn a disclosure into a plan: 'Are there days you don't want to go in?' · 'Does anyone at school know?' · 'Have you stopped doing things you used to do?' · 'How's your mood been in yourself?'

The de-blaming line and the honest one: 'It's not because you're dirty, and it's not chocolate. It's not your fault.' · 'Mood changes have been reported and we take that seriously — tell me straight away if anything changes, even a bit.'

Challenges: 'It's just spots. Mum made me come' · 'Isn't that how you do it?' About applying cream to the spots · 'So washing more won't fix it?' · 'That's a lot' at the side effects · 'Isn't that the one that makes you depressed?' · and, only if asked what worries him most, 'That I'll be left with scars and nothing will ever work.'
pefe: There is no examination task — the history is the assessment, and the scarring question is what stands in for grading the skin. The role-player's non-verbal behaviour is the other half of the data: poor eye contact, a flat quiet voice and short answers are cues, not scenery.

Role-player: Nathan Cullity, 17, in year 12, whose mother made the appointment and who is embarrassed to be there. He plays it quietly — little eye contact, short answers, looking at the floor or his hands — and volunteers nothing. If the doctor only asks about the skin he answers factually and reveals nothing about school. If the doctor normalises and asks how it affects him, he pauses and then opens up gradually — names first, then the days off school, then the football.

The two behaviours that tell you how you are doing: if the doctor responds warmly he makes eye contact for the first time. If the doctor moves straight from his disclosure to the medication, he closes down again and gives short answers for the rest of the station. He is not in crisis — he is worn down and lonely — and if the mood question is dismissed with 'No, that's a myth' he looks unconvinced and says 'Right.' At the end, if school has been asked about and support offered, he says: 'No one's asked me about any of that before.'

Mark them against these: spoke to him, not over him, and offered time on his own · explained confidentiality in a sentence · asked what sort of spots and where · asked whether any had left marks or scars · asked whether he picks or squeezes · asked what he had tried, and how he used it and for how long · explained that the cream goes on the whole area and takes six to eight weeks · asked about supplements or anything from the gym · family history · normalised and asked how much it affects him · asked about school and being teased · asked whether there were days he did not go in · asked whether he had stopped doing things · asked about his mood · thanked him and said it was not something to put up with · offered named support and encouraged telling a trusted adult · explained acne clearly and said explicitly that it is not his fault · explained the benefit as well as the side effects · covered dryness, sun sensitivity, early flare, aches, blood tests and pregnancy · and answered the mood question honestly with monitoring at every visit and follow-up for more than just his skin.

The treatment that did not fail — He applied the cream only to the visible spots rather than the whole area, and stopped at two weeks because his face went red. That is not treatment failure — topicals go on the whole affected area because they prevent the next spots rather than treat the visible ones, they need six to eight weeks, and early irritation is expected and settles VERIFY. Saying so is marked clinical reasoning

What he will not volunteer — Kids at school call him names · he misses about one day a week · he stopped playing football this year · nobody knows, not his mother and not a teacher · his mood is 'Alright — bit flat, I suppose' · and his hidden concern is that he will be left with scars and nothing will ever work. He takes protein powder, and his father had bad acne

setting: A high-failure-rate station with a simple trap: the stem hands you one abnormal number and candidates blame it. Delirium is almost always multifactorial and the task says reasons, plural — a candidate who names the sodium and stops has answered one third of one task. The other half is behavioural as well as medical management, and the daughter is part of the treatment.
stem: Hospital ward. An 80-year-old woman admitted and diagnosed with lower lobe pneumonia and heart failure, started on antibiotics. She is a chronic smoker.
She has become restless and agitated and is shouting in Greek. Her oxygen saturation is 93% on 4 litres of oxygen. Bloods are all normal except the sodium, which is abnormal.

Her daughter is here to speak with you. Tasks: explain the condition to the next of kin — explain the possible reasons — explain your management plan, with later recalls specifying both behavioural and medical management.
tasks: Explain the condition to the next of kin
Explain the possible reasons
Explain your management plan — behavioural and medical
time: Open by asking what she has been told and what she has noticed · then lead with the reassurance about the nature of the condition — sudden, fluctuating, reversible, not dementia — before going anywhere near causes · then the Greek explained and an interpreter arranged · then six causes applied to her mother · then medical management, then the behavioural half where most marks are lost · then sedation and restraint · then safety, prognosis and close

back.dx: Multifactorial hyperactive delirium. Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness caused by an underlying physical problem, and the three features you give the family are: it comes on suddenly, it comes and goes through the day, and it is usually reversible once the cause is treated. The contrast that reassures must be said explicitly, because it is the question she actually asked: 'This is not dementia. Dementia comes on slowly over years and doesn't go away. This came on over hours, and we expect it to improve.' Be honest about the caveat too — it can take days to weeks, and cognition is rechecked afterwards because delirium can uncover or be followed by longer-term change VERIFY. Hypoactive delirium — quiet, withdrawn, drowsy — is commoner, carries a worse prognosis and is routinely missed, so quiet is not the same as better. The reasons, plural and applied to her: the chest infection itself · low oxygen at 93% even on oxygen, and the brain is very sensitive to that · the low salt level · the heart failure · her medications, reviewing the whole chart for anything sedating or anticholinergic and anything started or stopped on admission · withdrawal, including nicotine in a chronic smoker who has been in a smoke-free hospital for days, and alcohol or sedatives if relevant · pain, often untreated because she cannot tell you · a full bladder or constipation, both common and both easily fixed · and the environment — an unfamiliar place, no clock, no window, lights and noise at night, broken sleep, glasses and hearing aids not in, and not being able to understand or be understood. Say the mnemonic silently and the list out loud: drugs · electrolytes and endocrine · lack of drugs meaning withdrawal · infection · reduced sensory input · intracranial · urinary and faecal retention · myocardial and pulmonary · sleep, stress and environment — or pinch me: pain, infection, nutrition, constipation, hydration, medication, environment. Investigations, with reasons: bedside glucose first, always · observations and saturations · FBC, UEC, LFT, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, CRP · urine microscopy and culture, blood cultures if febrile · bladder scan for retention · chest x-ray · ECG, cheap and quick, for a silent infarct or arrhythmia · CT brain if there is a head injury, focal neurology, anticoagulation or no other explanation · thyroid function and B12 where relevant · medication review as an investigation in its own right · and a pain assessment using an observational tool if she cannot report it. Medical management: continue and review the antibiotics · optimise oxygen and treat the heart failure · correct the sodium carefully and slowly, guided by volume status · rationalise the drug chart · treat pain, constipation and retention · and nicotine replacement for a chronic smoker. The behavioural half, which is the evidence-based core of delirium care and is explicitly requested by the task: family at the bedside · glasses on and hearing aids in · orientation with a clock, a calendar, a window, and staff saying who they are and where she is at every interaction · day-night rhythm, with light and activity by day and dark and quiet at night, and not waking her for non-essential observations · early mobilisation, sitting out of bed, eating and drinking normally · removing tethers — unnecessary cannulas, catheters and monitoring leads · and an interpreter. Medication only if safety demands it: when she is a danger to herself or others, or so distressed that essential treatment is impossible — low dose, single agent, shortest course, reviewed daily, with an ECG for QT where practical, and benzodiazepines avoided except in alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal where they are the treatment VERIFY. Avoid physical and chemical restraint, because both worsen delirium and cause injuries. Safety: falls precautions with a low bed, close observation, a clear floor and the call bell in reach — an agitated 80-year-old who climbs out of bed can turn pneumonia into a fractured hip and a subdural. And the sentence that recruits the daughter: 'You are part of the treatment. Someone familiar sitting with her, holding her hand, telling her where she is — that does more for delirium than most of what we can prescribe.' In a small rural hospital where one-to-one nursing may not be available, family presence is not just kind, it is the practical alternative to restraint. Prognosis: most people recover, it can take days to weeks, it is often worse before it is better and worse at night, she may not remember much of it, and cognition is reassessed once she is physically well VERIFY.
plan: Open and check perception before explaining anything: 'Before I start — what have you been told so far, and what have you noticed yourself? And is there anything in particular worrying you?' Her fear — dementia — is what your whole first block should be aimed at.
Name it and give the three features, then the contrast that reassures — and say 'This is not dementia' explicitly, because it is the question she asked (see dx).

Explain the Greek as language reversion, arrange a professional interpreter, and decline her offer to translate kindly: 'Thank you — for something like this we use a professional interpreter, so nothing gets lost and you can just be her daughter.'

Frame the causes before listing them — 'Delirium almost never has a single cause. In someone of your mother's age it's usually several things at once, each of which on its own she might have coped with' — then give six applied to her. When the daughter says the nurse told her it was the sodium: 'It's one of the reasons, and we're treating it. But it isn't the whole answer.'
MEDICAL MANAGEMENT, WITH THE SODIUM HANDLED BY VOLUME STATUS RATHER THAN REFLEX FLUIDS — saying 'we'll give her a drip to fix the sodium' may be exactly wrong in heart failure (see findings and dx).

THE BEHAVIOURAL HALF, IN DETAIL — THIS IS WHERE MOST MARKS ARE LOST AND LATER RECALLS ASK FOR IT BY NAME (see dx). Then the sentence that recruits her, and answer 'is there really anything I can do?' with 'you are part of the treatment', meant literally.

Sedation and restraint, explained rather than refused: 'We can, and we will if she's at risk of hurting herself — but sedatives tend to make delirium last longer and cause falls, so they're a last resort: lowest dose, one medicine, shortest time, reviewed every day. And we avoid tying people down — restraints make agitation worse and cause injuries.' when she asks about the drip being pulled out, offer the alternatives: someone familiar with her, removing the drip if it is not essential, close observation.

Safety and prognosis — falls as the biggest risk with a low bed and close observation · days to weeks, often worse at night, and she may not remember much of it · and cognition rechecked once she is physically well. Do not promise full recovery.

Role-player: Maria Stavros, 54, a bookkeeper, whose mother Eleni, 80, was admitted four days ago with a chest infection and heart failure. Eleni migrated from greece at 22, is normally fluent in English, lives alone, does her own shopping and plays cards weekly, with no memory problems at all before this. She has smoked since she was eighteen and still smokes about ten a day. She takes tablets for blood pressure and her heart and has recently been given something for pain in hospital. She has not opened her bowels since admission, and her glasses and hearing aids are at home in a drawer — both mentioned only if asked.

How she plays it: frightened and slightly accusatory, opening with the fact that nobody has explained anything and asking immediately whether her mother has gone senile. If the doctor says clearly that this is not dementia and is usually reversible she visibly relaxes and becomes cooperative; if they do not address dementia she asks again more insistently and stays anxious for the rest of the station. She says once 'The nurse said it was her sodium' — and if the doctor agrees that the sodium is the cause she accepts it readily, so the examiner sees they settled for one answer. She offers to interpret, and if they accept, she does it. Her hidden fear, volunteered late or if asked what worries her most, is that her father had dementia and she nursed him for six years, cannot face doing it again, and feels guilty for thinking that.

How to handle it in the room — 'Her salt level is low, and that can certainly make confusion worse. What we do about it depends on whether she is carrying too much fluid or too little — with heart failure and a chest infection it could be either, so we examine her, and if she is fluid-overloaded we restrict fluids and may use a diuretic rather than give more fluid. We also correct it slowly, because correcting sodium too quickly is itself dangerous' VERIFY

The Greek is a clue, not a symptom — People with delirium or dementia often revert to their first language. back.dx: POORLY CONTROLLED CHRONIC ASTHMA WITH OVER-RELIANCE ON RELIEVER THERAPY — not an exacerbation. Control is not the same as severity: control describes how she is now and is assessed with four questions, while severity describes how much treatment she needs to achieve it. And frequent reliever use is a risk marker, not just a control marker — heavy short-acting beta-agonist use is associated with worse outcomes VERIFY. The contributing factors must be named individually and tied to her answers, not offered as 'Various triggers': her nose — perennial allergic rhinitis, blocked all year and never treated, because the nose and the chest are one airway and treating the nose often improves the chest VERIFY · the cat acquired in March, which matches her deterioration timeline exactly once you anchor it with 'And when did the symptoms start getting worse?' · her glaucoma eye drops, some of which are beta-blockers and can tighten the airways VERIFY · and simply that her preventer dose is not enough for how much asthma she has. The key explanation she needs: 'Your blue puffer is a reliever — it opens the airways for a few hours and then it wears off. It does nothing to the inflammation underneath. Your preventer treats that inflammation, but only if the dose is enough. So needing the reliever most days isn't you overusing it — it's the signal that the preventer needs to go up.' Telling her to cut down the reliever without increasing the preventer is both wrong and dangerous. The plan, in six parts: confirm the diagnosis with spirometry including reversibility if it has never been done VERIFY · watch her use the inhaler and spacer once anyway, saying so explicitly because it earns credit rather than losing it — 'I can see technique and adherence have been checked, I'd still watch you use it once, because it's the commonest reason for this and it takes twenty seconds' · treat the comorbidities with an intranasal corticosteroid for rhinitis, plus reflux, weight and sleep apnoea VERIFY · remove the triggers — cat out of the bedroom at minimum with weekly hot bedding washes, damp addressed, household smoke eliminated, and the eye drops reviewed with her ophthalmologist · step up the preventer — a higher-dose inhaled corticosteroid, or adding a long-acting bronchodilator, or a combination inhaler used as both preventer and reliever, selected against the current Australian asthma handbook rather than quoted from memory VERIFY · and a written action plan, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination, and review in four to six weeks, stepping down only after about three months of good control VERIFY. The action plan is written, on paper, in her hand — not 'I'll explain it' — and contains what to take when she is well, exactly what to increase when things slip, what to do when it is severe and to call the same day, and the emergency steps: four puffs of reliever through a spacer, one at a time, wait four minutes, repeat, call 000 VERIFY. Red flags for coming back sooner: the reliever not lasting the usual few hours or needed more often than every three to four hours · too breathless to speak in full sentences · waking repeatedly at night · not improving after reliever · and 000 for severe breathlessness, blue lips or drowsiness. And ask the question that reframes the whole station: 'Has anyone ever formally confirmed the asthma with breathing tests?' — because not everything that wheezes is asthma. Vocal cord dysfunction gives difficulty getting air in, throat tightness and no response to reliever, and needs a flow-volume loop and speech pathology rather than more asthma medication VERIFY · COPD or asthma-copd overlap in a smoker with incomplete reversibility · heart failure with orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea · bronchiectasis with chronic daily sputum · pulmonary embolism · and obesity, reflux or anxiety as contributors. Refer to a respiratory physician if control is not achieved despite a stepped-up regimen and treated comorbidities, if the diagnosis is uncertain, if she has had a life-threatening attack, or if she needs frequent oral corticosteroids.

RISK AND SEVERITY, WHICH CHANGE THE URGENCY OF EVERYTHING THAT FOLLOWS: how many flare-ups in the last year · HOW MANY COURSES OF PREDNISOLONE · any hospital admissions · HAVE YOU EVER BEEN IN INTENSIVE CARE OR NEEDED A BREATHING TUBE · how many canisters this year · and do you have an asthma action plan. Previous intensive care or intubation is the single strongest predictor of a future near-fatal attack, and naming that risk out loud is separately marked.

TRIGGERS, COMORBIDITIES AND MEDICINES. ENVIRONMENT: what sets it off · HAS ANYTHING CHANGED AT HOME — NEW PET, NEW CARPET, DAMP, MOULD, WOOD HEATER · who smokes · occupation, and IS IT BETTER ON WEEKENDS OR HOLIDAYS · worse in spring, with colds, with exercise, in cold air. COMORBIDITIES: ANY HAY FEVER, BLOCKED OR RUNNING NOSE · reflux · snoring or daytime sleepiness · weight change · anxiety or panic with the breathlessness. MEDICINES: beta-blocker tablets · ANY EYE DROPS · aspirin or anti-inflammatories · anything new in the last few months · and whether she is getting her preventer refilled on time.

back.dx: TYPE 1 DIABETES — autoimmune destruction of beta cells producing absolute insulin deficiency, requiring insulin for life, which is why 'I stopped my insulin because I wasn't eating' is dangerous rather than sensible. A 22-year-old is a different problem from a 60-year-old with type 2: he faces decades of injections and finger-pricks at the age when he is starting work, studying, drinking, driving and forming relationships, and psychological burden, diabetes distress and disordered eating are all commoner, with adherence the central clinical problem. The immediate management starts with his agenda, and for version A that means options rather than instructions: basal-bolus, which is the most flexible but has the most needles · a premixed pen twice daily, which is far fewer injections but requires regular meals and gives less fine control · and an insulin pump, a small device delivering insulin continuously through a tiny cannula changed every two or three days, usually paired with a sensor that reads glucose without finger-pricks — fewest needles and the best control, but worn all the time, and if it fails the sugar rises fast. Refer for pump assessment rather than promising a pump VERIFY. If he admits skipping doses, do not lecture — 'Thank you for telling me. What makes that one the hard one?' — and then change the regimen, because burden responds to redesign rather than repetition. The safety block is given in every version: hypoglycaemia and the rule of 15 — below 4, take 15 g of fast sugar, wait 15 minutes, recheck, then a proper snack — with glucagon for someone at home to use VERIFY · sick day rules, and this is the one that matters most: never stop insulin because he is not eating, because he usually needs more not less — test more often, check ketones, keep fluids up, and present if vomiting, drowsy or if ketones are climbing · driving — above 5 to drive, glucose in the car, and not within two hours of a severe hypo VERIFY · alcohol, which can drop the sugar several hours later and often overnight, so eat carbohydrate with it, check before bed and tell whoever he is with · and medical identification. The long-term plan: the team — an endocrinologist, because type 1 is specialist-led and his lapsed when he left paediatrics; a credentialled diabetes educator for technique, dose adjustment and carbohydrate counting; a dietitian; an optometrist and podiatrist — all under a GP management plan with team care arrangements. Annual screening: HbA1c three to six monthly with an individualised target · retinal examination · urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR · foot inspection with pulses and monofilament · lipids and blood pressure · and coeliac and thyroid screening, because other autoimmune conditions cluster with type 1 VERIFY. And the things easy to forget at 22: mood and diabetes distress, asked about directly · insulin omission for weight control, asked sensitively if there are clues · sexual health, contraception and preconception planning · work, study and disclosure · vaccination · travel letters and insulin storage · NDSS registration · and doing the script, because he came for it and it is both courteous and marked. On continuous glucose monitoring: a sensor worn on the skin giving real-time glucose and trend arrows without finger-pricks, with alarms, particularly valuable in type 1 and in hypoglycaemia unawareness. All people with type 1 can apply through the NDSS, with full subsidy for under-21s, concessional cardholders aged 21 and over, and in pregnancy, and a co-payment otherwise — and a GP cannot certify the access form, which must be signed by an endocrinologist or credentialled diabetes educator, which is another reason to refer VERIFY. Watch for the things that change the station: hypoglycaemia unawareness, which is safety-critical and usually improves if lows are avoided for a few weeks VERIFY · lipohypertrophy · diabetes distress or depression, which changes control more than any dose adjustment · disordered eating with insulin omission, suggested by weight preoccupation and an unexplained high HbA1c with normal-looking records · and DKA risk behaviours.
plan: Open, agree to the scripts, and then ask the question the station is built on — before the history, so the history is aimed at something: 'Of course, I can sort the scripts out. Before I do — is there anything in particular you'd like me to address while you're here? Anything about the diabetes that's been bothering you?' It costs eight seconds and it is the station.

Acknowledge warmly and contract for the history: 'That's a very fair thing to be fed up with, and I'm glad you told me rather than quietly skipping them. We'll come back to it properly. Can I ask you some questions first so I've got the whole picture?'

BLOCK ONE, DIAGNOSIS AND TREATMENT — when diagnosed · what insulin and how many injections a day · SAME DOSE AND TIME, OR DOES HE EVER MISS ONE. If he admits missing doses, thank him and explore why rather than reacting with disapproval.
The two questions nobody asks — technique and site rotation, and hypoglycaemia warning (see findings).

BLOCK TWO, SIDE EFFECTS AND FOLLOW-UP — hypos and how often · weight gain · WHO FOLLOWS HIM UP AND DOES HE SEE A SPECIALIST · WHEN WAS HIS LAST HbA1c · does he check at home and what numbers does he see.

Blocks three to five, complications and life — tired, polyuric, thirsty · blurred vision and when his eyes were last checked · pins and needles or numbness in his feet · does he drive, drink, smoke · and 'How are you going in yourself — mood, work, study?', because diabetes distress at 22 is common and he will not raise it.
Answer the agenda first, with options rather than instructions — and tailor to whichever version you are in (see findings and dx).

The safety block, in every version — hypos and the rule of 15 with glucagon · sick day rules and never stopping insulin · driving · alcohol and delayed overnight lows · and medical identification (see dx).
Long-term — the team under a care plan, the annual screening, vaccination and NDSS registration, with the bloods overdue today.

Do the scripts — he came for them — and close the loop explicitly, which is a distinct scored behaviour taking one sentence: 'You came in fed up with the injections. Have I answered that? And is there anything else on your mind?'

ask: The question the whole station is built on, asked in the first thirty seconds: 'Is there anything in particular you'd like me to address today?' and the closing half of it: 'You came in worried about the injections — have I answered that?'
The response to an admission of skipped doses: 'I'm glad you told me rather than quietly skipping them.' and 'What makes that one the hard one?'
The two five-second questions: 'Has anyone ever actually taught you how to inject — and do you rotate the sites?' and 'When you go low, do you get warning — or does it come out of nowhere?'

The safety lines: 'Never stop your insulin because you're not eating — you usually need more, not less.' · 'Above 5 to drive, and glucose in the car.' · 'Alcohol can drop your sugar hours later, often overnight.' · and 'Those lumps make the insulin absorb unpredictably.'

Challenges: 'Just after repeats for my insulin, thanks' · 'I don't want to be the bloke going off to the toilet with a needle' · 'A pump — could I actually get one?' · 'I stopped it once when I had gastro. Nobody ever told me that' · 'What are ketones?' · 'Seriously? Hours later?' About the alcohol · 'Will that cost me?' · and, if you forget, 'So … the scripts?'
pefe: There is no formal examination, but two things are done in the room: watch him demonstrate an injection, and palpate the sites for lipohypertrophy — look, do not just ask. Technique means a new needle each time, pinch-up if needed, insertion at 90 degrees, delivery, then counting to ten before withdrawing, and systematic rotation — and absorption from lumpy areas is unpredictable, so dose requirements will change once he moves away from them VERIFY.

Role-player: Jack Merrilees, 22, a delivery driver with type 1 diabetes since 14, on long-acting insulin at night and quick-acting with meals — four injections a day. He has come only for repeat scripts and expects to be out in three minutes, and his opening is brisk and transactional. No specialist since he left the children's hospital at 16, last blood test about two years ago, testing morning and night with readings usually 8 to 14. He still gets warning before a hypo. He drives for work and drinks on weekends.

What he withholds: the agenda itself — he is sick of four injections a day and sometimes skips the night one when he is out, because he does not want to be seen using a needle — given only if asked whether he has any concerns · that he was shown how to inject once in hospital at 14 and nobody has checked since, and that he uses the same spot with a firm lump there · that he stopped his insulin for two days last year with gastroenteritis because he was not eating and nobody told him not to · and a second hidden concern, given only if asked how he is in himself: he is worn down by it, 'Some days I'm just over it', and has not told anyone. If the doctor never asks about concerns he says nothing about the injections, answers briefly and takes the script. If the doctor responds with disapproval about skipped doses he closes down for the rest of the station. And if the script is never mentioned he prompts: 'So … the scripts?'

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: ASKED WHETHER HE HAD ANY CONCERNS, EARLY AND UNPROMPTED · ACKNOWLEDGED IT WARMLY AND PROMISED TO RETURN TO IT · asked when diagnosed, what insulin and how many injections · ASKED ABOUT MISSED DOSES AND EXPLORED WHY WITHOUT JUDGEMENT · ASKED WHETHER ANYONE HAD TAUGHT HIM TO INJECT, AND ABOUT SITE ROTATION · IDENTIFIED OR ASKED ABOUT THE LUMP · ASKED ABOUT HYPOS AND WHETHER HE GETS WARNING · asked who follows him up and when his last HbA1c was · asked about home readings · asked about eyes and feet · ASKED ABOUT DRIVING AND ALCOHOL · ASKED HOW HE WAS GOING IN HIMSELF · OFFERED THREE INSULIN DELIVERY OPTIONS WITH HONEST PROS AND CONS · REFERRED FOR PUMP ASSESSMENT RATHER THAN PROMISING ONE · taught the Rule of 15 and mentioned glucagon · GAVE SICK DAY RULES AND SAID NEVER TO STOP INSULIN · gave driving advice and delayed-hypoglycaemia advice about alcohol · RE-REFERRED TO AN ENDOCRINOLOGIST AND A DIABETES EDUCATOR · arranged bloods and complication screening and mentioned the NDSS · DID THE SCRIPTS · AND CLOSED THE LOOP ON HIS ORIGINAL CONCERN.

Version A — the injection burden — 'I'M DOING EVERYTHING RIGHT, BUT I'M SICK OF STICKING NEEDLES IN MYSELF FOUR TIMES A DAY.' The station becomes a discussion of insulin delivery options including the pump

Version B — no specialist, doesn't understand the numbers — 'I HAVEN'T SEEN A SPECIALIST SINCE I WAS A KID, AND HONESTLY I DON'T REALLY KNOW WHAT THE NUMBERS ON THE MACHINE MEAN.' The station becomes education and referral — endocrinologist, diabetes educator, what the numbers mean, how to adjust

Version C — 'Am I doing it properly?' — 'I worry I'm not doing it properly — the injections, the monitoring, all of it.' The station becomes technique, reassurance and structured review: 'Let's not guess — show me how you'd do an injection now, and let me have a look at the spots you use. Checking is quicker than worrying'

The two history questions nobody asks — 'Has anyone ever actually taught you how to inject — and do you rotate the sites?' and 'When you go low, do you get warning — or does it come out of nowhere?' The first uncovers years of poor technique and lipohypertrophy, which makes absorption erratic and explains poor control better than anything on the drug chart; the second uncovers a driving hazard. Both take five seconds, and with the lumps you look rather than just ask
fails: ★ Never asking for concerns — a flawless diabetes consultation with no agenda elicited fails this station
★ Handing over the script and ending the consultation, or finding the agenda and never returning to it
★ Omitting sick day rules, when 'I stopped my insulin because I wasn't eating' is the sentence that precedes a DKA admission
Lecturing a non-adherent 22-year-old instead of exploring why and redesigning the regimen, or promising an insulin pump rather than referring for assessment

Skipping the technique and site questions so years of lipohypertrophy are missed; missing hypoglycaemia unawareness and its driving implications; giving no driving or alcohol advice to a man who drives for work; never assessing mood; or forgetting the script he actually came for
numbers: Hypoglycaemia under 4.0 mmol/L with the rule of 15, and above 5 to drive VERIFY · basal-bolus is about 4 or more injections daily, premixed is 2, and a pump cannula is changed every 2-3 days · HbA1c 3 to 6 monthly with an individualised target VERIFY

Annual screening: eyes, feet, urine ACR, eGFR, lipids, TSH and coeliac serology VERIFY · sick days: glucose every 2-4 hours and ketones whenever high or unwell, and never stop insulin · CGM is available to all type 1 through the NDSS with full subsidy for under-21s, concessional cardholders 21+ and in pregnancy, and the access form cannot be certified by a GP VERIFY · NDSS · diabetes Australia · PATS · Quitline 13 7848 · VERIFY all

setting: A discharge-planning station with a conflict built into it. The trap is treating it as a binary — home or a nursing home. It is not: the report says 'Not safe unless proper support is available', which is a condition to be satisfied rather than a door closed. And the patient is missing from the conversation entirely — two people are deciding where a competent 70-year-old will live, and she has not been asked.
stem: Orthopaedic ward. A 70-year-old woman admitted with a hip fracture has already undergone surgery and is planned for discharge soon. The occupational therapist has completed an assessment.

The report: she can perform basic activities of daily living such as going to the toilet and showering, but has problems with cooking and needs assistance. She has balance issues, has to hold on to something while walking, and has poor mobility. She is not safe to be discharged home unless proper support is available.

Her son is here. He lives in a rural area an hour away, says he cannot take care of her, and is insisting that she be discharged home. Tasks: explain the report to the son — discuss the discharge planning for this patient.
tasks: Explain the occupational therapist's report to the son
Discuss the discharge planning for this patient
time: Open by asking what he understands and how he is going · then defuse in ten seconds, before explaining anything, because almost all the conflict comes from two fears · then the report in plain language, positives first, with the conditional intact · then explore what is driving him · then break the binary with the pathway · then put the patient back in the room · then the medicine everyone forgets in a social station

back.dx: A 70-year-old recovering from operative fixation of a hip fracture who is independent in personal care but cannot run a household and has impaired balance — not unsafe to go home, but unsafe to go home without support. Defuse before you explain, because his insistence is a defence against two fears: 'Nobody is asking you to become her carer. And nobody is talking about a nursing home.' Ten seconds, and most of the conflict in the station dissolves. Then explore rather than argue: 'You've said a couple of times that you can't look after her. What's making this hard for you?' — because it is nearly always distance and work, guilt, cost, or fear of a nursing home, and each has a different answer. Distance and work → services come to her, he does not have to be the carer. Guilt → name it and relieve it: 'You're not failing her. Most families can't do this on their own — that's exactly what these services exist for.' Cost → much is government subsidised and the social worker will confirm eligibility, so do not rule anything out on cost before finding out, and do not promise funding you have not confirmed VERIFY. Then break the binary with a pathway. First, rehabilitation — a few weeks of daily physiotherapy and occupational therapy to rebuild strength, balance and confidence, and if she was independent before the fall the odds are good. Then transition care — short-term support after hospital, at home or in a facility, designed to get people back on their feet before anyone makes long-term decisions VERIFY. Then home with services — an acat assessment through my aged care for meals, showering, cleaning, shopping and nursing visits, plus rails, a shower chair, a raised toilet seat, a four-wheeled walker, lighting, removal of rugs and a personal alarm VERIFY. And name the option you are not proposing, because he is dreading it: 'Permanent residential care is not what I'm proposing. It would only come into the conversation if, after all of that, she still couldn't be kept safe at home — and even then it would be a decision made with her, not for her.' then the sentence that distinguishes a good candidate: 'We've spent ten minutes talking about your mother without her. She's 70, she's alert, and this is her home and her life we're discussing. Nothing gets decided without her.' that is not only ethical but clinical — she is the decision-maker unless she lacks capacity and nothing in the stem suggests she does; a competent adult can discharge herself and the son cannot discharge her or prevent her going; and her goals change the plan, because someone determined to get home engages with rehabilitation very differently. Arrange a multidisciplinary family meeting with her in it. And do not assume cognition either way — delirium complicates a large proportion of hip fracture admissions and is frequently missed at discharge, so ask the son whether she was getting more forgetful before the fall and whether she has seemed herself since the operation, and test formally if there is any doubt VERIFY. Then the medicine. Her bones: a minimal trauma hip fracture means bone-protective treatment regardless of the T-score, with vitamin d and calcium, calcium and renal function checked, and a dental review before an antiresorptive VERIFY. Her falls: medication review for sedatives, antihypertensives and anticholinergics · lying and standing blood pressure · vision and footwear · home hazards · and a strength and balance programme, which is the single most effective intervention VERIFY. Her operation: wound review and suture removal · thromboprophylaxis duration · analgesia adequate to allow mobilising · constipation from opioids · anaemia · nutrition, because protein and energy intake drive rehabilitation outcomes · and confirm the weight-bearing status with the surgeon before planning anything. Also consider depression and fear of falling, both of which are barriers to rehabilitation; carer strain in the son; and, if something does not add up — reluctance to have her home, questions about the house, unexplained pressure — the possibility of neglect or financial pressure, which means speaking with the patient alone and involving social work VERIFY. If he says he is taking her home today, do not escalate: 'I'm not going to stop you, and I don't want this to be a fight — we're both trying to do right by your mum. Can you give me five minutes to show you what's actually on the table?' and note that discharge against advice is a competent patient's right, not the son's — another reason to bring her into the room.
plan: OPEN AND CHECK WHERE HE IS BEFORE GIVING THE REPORT: 'BEFORE I GO THROUGH THE ASSESSMENT — WHAT'S YOUR UNDERSTANDING OF HOW SHE'S BEEN GOING? AND HOW ARE YOU GOING WITH ALL THIS?' He is braced for bad news and will hear everything as a prelude to being asked to give up his life.

Defuse before you explain — the two sentences that remove the two fears (see dx). Then signpost: 'Three things: what the occupational therapist found, what that means for going home, and what the options actually are — because I don't think the choice is what you think it is.'

TRANSLATE THE REPORT, POSITIVES FIRST, THEN WHAT SHE CANNOT DO, THEN THE MOBILITY AND WHY IT MATTERS — AND DELIVER THE CONCLUSION WITH THE CONDITIONAL INTACT AND THE LAST FOUR WORDS EMPHASISED (see findings). No untranslated allied health language: not 'independent in basic ADLs but requires assistance with IADLs'.
Explore what is driving him rather than treating him as an obstacle — one question uncovers guilt, distance, work or cost and changes the whole tone (see dx).
The pathway, in order — rehabilitation, then transition care, then home with services — and then name the option you are not proposing, because saying it out loud is what lets him stop fighting.
Put the patient back in the room, kindly, and ask what she wants — then offer a family meeting with her, the occupational therapist, the physiotherapist and the social worker in it.
THE MEDICINE — HER BONES, HER FALLS AND HER OPERATION (see dx). Bone protection after a minimal trauma hip fracture is a scored item and a major real-world omission.

Close with concrete next steps and named people: social worker today · acat referral · rehabilitation referral · a family meeting with a date · bone treatment and falls prevention. 'Nobody is asking you to give up your job, and nobody is putting her in a home.'
back.planNote: two tasks, but the second one contains the whole conflict — and the defusing has to come before the explaining or he will hear the report as a verdict
ask: The two sentences that dissolve the conflict: 'Nobody is asking you to become her carer.' and 'Nobody is talking about a nursing home.'
The one that distinguishes a good candidate: 'We've been talking about your mother without her. Nothing gets decided without her.' and its follow-up: 'What does she want?'
The question that changes the tone: 'What's making this hard for you?' and the reply to the guilt: 'You're not failing her. This is exactly what these services exist for.'

The conditional, quoted with its last words intact: 'Not safe to go home — unless proper support is in place. Those last words matter.' and the reframe: 'When she goes home, she doesn't go home to nothing.'

Challenges: 'I can't look after her' · 'She'll hate a nursing home' · 'Just let her go and she'll manage' · 'Who's going to pay for all this?' · 'I'm taking her home today' · 'She'll refuse rehab' · 'My father died in one. It was awful' · and, only if asked what is making it hard, 'I feel bloody awful about it. She looked after me my whole life.'
pefe: There is no examination — the occupational therapy report is the data, and the skill is translating it without losing the conditional. But two clinical things still have to be checked before the plan is final: her cognition, because post-operative delirium is common and missed, and her weight-bearing status from the surgeon, because every rehabilitation plan depends on it.

Role-player: David Pethick, 45, a farm machinery mechanic, whose mother Joan, 70, fell at home three weeks ago and broke her hip. He lives an hour away, works full time and has two teenagers. He is defensive rather than aggressive, and arrives braced to be told that either he must move in with her or she is going into a home — and he cannot face either. Joan lived completely independently until the fall and drove until last year, which he says if asked about her baseline. His father died in a nursing home and it was, in his words, awful — mentioned only if a nursing home is raised.

How he plays it: if the doctor does not address the two fears he stays defensive and keeps repeating that she has to go home; if they do, he visibly relaxes and becomes cooperative. If told flatly 'She can't go home' he becomes firm — 'Then what are you saying, a nursing home? Because that's not happening.' He has never heard of rehabilitation, transition care or my aged care as options and is genuinely surprised by them. He asks once who pays. His hidden feeling, given only if asked what is making this hard, is guilt. And he has not actually asked his mother what she wants — admitted if asked, and never raised by him if the doctor does not mention her at all.

MARK THEM AGAINST THESE: asked what he understood and how he was going · EXPLICITLY SAID NOBODY IS ASKING HIM TO BE HER CARER · EXPLICITLY SAID NOBODY IS PROPOSING A NURSING HOME · EXPLAINED THE REPORT IN PLAIN ENGLISH, POSITIVES FIRST · DISTINGUISHED PERSONAL CARE FROM RUNNING A HOUSEHOLD · explained why the balance matters — the risk of another fall · QUOTED THE CONCLUSION WITH THE 'UNLESS SUPPORT IS AVAILABLE' PART INTACT · ASKED WHAT WAS MAKING THIS HARD FOR HIM · responded to the guilt without dismissing it · OFFERED REHABILITATION AS THE FIRST STEP · offered transition care or an equivalent bridge · OFFERED HOME SERVICES THROUGH AN AGED CARE ASSESSMENT · named equipment and home modifications INCLUDING A PERSONAL ALARM · handled the cost question honestly and referred to the social worker · ASKED WHAT HIS MOTHER WANTS AND SAID NOTHING WOULD BE DECIDED WITHOUT HER · OFFERED A FAMILY MEETING INCLUDING HER · EXPLAINED THAT HER BONES NEED TREATMENT AFTER A FRACTURE LIKE THIS · covered falls prevention · used no untranslated jargon and NEVER TREATED HIM AS THE PROBLEM · and gave a clear list of next steps with people and timing attached.

What she can do — lead with this — Basic activities of daily living: toileting, showering, dressing, grooming, feeding, transferring. 'She can get to the toilet on her own. She can shower herself. Those are the things people most fear losing, and she hasn't lost them.' It buys you the credibility to deliver the rest

What she cannot do — Instrumental activities of daily living: cooking, shopping, cleaning, laundry, transport, managing medications and finances. It is IADLs, not ADLs, that determine whether someone can live alone — and she cannot manage cooking without help

The mobility, which is what actually worries you — Balance impairment and furniture-walking after a hip fracture mean a very high risk of a second fall. About a third of people are left with significant functional loss after a hip fracture and first-year mortality is substantial VERIFY — this is not over-caution

And the fracture is itself a diagnosis — A hip fracture from a fall at standing height is a minimal trauma fracture, which means she needs bone-protective treatment regardless of her bone density result VERIFY — the item most often forgotten because this feels like a social station

The conditional — read it literally — 'Not safe to discharge home unless proper support is available' is a conditional statement, not a prohibition. Candidates who read it as 'She can't go home' end up in a fight with the son; candidates who read it as 'She can go home once we put the support in' end up with a plan
fails: ★ Presenting it as home versus a nursing home, which is the frame he is already fighting and which turns the consultation into an argument
★ Making decisions about a competent 70-year-old without her, or never mentioning her at all
★ Agreeing to a discharge you believe is unsafe — a second fall at home alone with a fresh prosthesis is a catastrophic and foreseeable outcome
★ Forgetting bone-protective treatment after a minimal trauma hip fracture because this feels like a social station

Reading the conclusion as a refusal rather than a condition; never asking why he is insisting and treating him as an obstacle; promising funding you have not confirmed; using untranslated allied health jargon; or finishing with no concrete next step and no named person

setting: Widely regarded as the hardest counselling case in the set, because three conditions have to be covered in eight minutes: COPD, recurrent falls and osteopenia. A candidate who touches all three passes; a candidate who does one of them beautifully fails. Breadth beats depth — write the three words at the TOP of your paper before you go in, and number everything out loud.
stem: General practice. A 55-year-old man, a known case of COPD, has come concerned about his recurrent falls. He uses budesonide as an inhaler, and his GP prescribes prednisolone for eight days whenever he has an exacerbation.

Results: DEXA — T-score between −1 and −2.5 at all three sites · full blood examination normal · blood glucose normal · urea, electrolytes and creatinine normal · liver function normal · serum calcium normal · vitamin d 30 nmol/L, reference above 50.

Tasks: explain the results to the patient — take a history from the patient — explain the contributing factors and your management plan. A workable split is two minutes on results, three on history, three on factors and management.
tasks: Explain the results to the patient
Take a history from the patient
Explain the contributing factors and your management plan
time: Acknowledge why he actually came — he is frightened of falling alone at home — then contract for the order of the tasks and say it out loud · two minutes on the results and no more · three minutes of history that must cover bones, falls and chest, with the fracture question asked first · then three minutes on contributing factors and a three-part plan · you cannot afford a single question that is not on your list
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: The bloods — fast, but say them

Blood count, sugar, kidneys, liver and calcium all normal — naming them reassures him and takes fifteen seconds · but vitamin d is 30 when it should be above 50: 'Vitamin d is what lets your body absorb calcium, so low vitamin d means weaker bones. That one is easy to fix'

back.dx: THREE PROBLEMS FEEDING EACH OTHER — osteopenia, recurrent falls and COPD with repeated glucocorticoid exposure — and the conceptual core of the station is one sentence: 'Soft bones on their own don't break. Why he is falling: breathlessness and deconditioning from COPD · steroid myopathy, meaning proximal muscle weakness from repeated courses · medications, particularly sedatives and antihypertensives · postural hypotension · and vision, footwear, home hazards and night-time toilet trips. The plan has three parts and is delivered as headings, not a pharmacology lecture. If drug treatment is indicated, headlines only: alendronate weekly on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, upright for 30 minutes and separated from calcium and antacids · zoledronic acid yearly with renal function, corrected calcium and vitamin d checked first · denosumab six-monthly, where adherence is critical because delay beyond about four weeks risks rebound vertebral fractures and stopping it requires replacement with a bisphosphonate VERIFY · dental review before starting, for osteonecrosis of the jaw · and bisphosphonates reconsidered at five to ten years with a repeat DEXA at two years VERIFY. Falls: name the people, not just the idea — a physiotherapist for a supervised strength and balance programme, which is the single most effective falls intervention VERIFY · an occupational therapist for home hazards, rails, lighting and bathroom modifications · a podiatrist for feet and footwear · medication review and deprescribing, with the sleeping tablet weaned slowly rather than stopped abruptly · optometry, with caution about multifocals on stairs · postural blood pressure today · and a personal alarm, because he lives alone and that was his opening line. Second, it is hypocalcaemia, not hypercalcaemia: the risk before and during zoledronic acid and denosumab is a low calcium, which is exactly why calcium, vitamin d and renal function are corrected before the first dose VERIFY. And do not stop the inhaled steroid to protect his bones — that would worsen COPD control and lead to more oral prednisolone, which is far worse for bone. The DEXA, explained in two minutes — 'It measures how dense and strong your bones are, at three places — spine, hip and the TOP of your thigh bone. It gives two numbers: a T-score comparing you to a healthy young man, and a Z-score comparing you to someone your own age and sex.' T above −1 is normal, −1 to −2.5 is osteopenia, and −2.5 or below is osteoporosis

The verdict, in plain words — 'Your T-score is between minus one and minus two and a half at all three sites. That means osteopenia — your bones are softer than they should be. It is not osteoporosis, which is when they become fragile and break easily. You are in between, and the point of today is to stop you going any further'

The question the whole station turns on — 'Have you ever broken a bone?' — then which one, and how much force. Hip or vertebral minimal trauma fracture → treat whatever the T-score is · any other minimal trauma fracture at 50 or over → presumptive osteoporosis, with frax run on the BMD where T sits between −1.5 and −2.5, treating if major fracture risk is 20% or more or hip 3% or more · no fracture → assess risk factors and use frax VERIFY. Without the answer you literally cannot produce a management plan

Which sites count — Minimal trauma means a fall from standing height or less, and the sites that count are vertebra, hip or proximal femur, distal radius, proximal humerus and pelvis. Fingers, toes, skull and face do not
