back.dx: EPISODIC MIGRAINE WITHOUT AURA — a clinical diagnosis that the imaging was not required to make, and which you explain by showing your working rather than announcing a label: 'I don't want you to just take my word for it — let me show you how I know.' then what migraine actually is: 'It isn't just a bad headache. It's a condition of the brain and its blood vessels, where the nerve pathways that carry pain become over-sensitive and over-react to certain triggers. That's why the light hurts, why you feel sick, and why it knocks you out for hours. It is real, it is common, and it is treatable.' The management is delivered in three named parts and counted out loud, because a candidate who says the right drug names in the wrong shape has lost the structure mark. Part one, things she can do herself: a migraine diary started today, recording when, how bad, how long, what she ate and drank, how she slept and what she took · and the common triggers — missed or late sleep including sleeping in at weekends, skipped meals, dehydration, alcohol, caffeine both excess and withdrawal, stress and the let-down after stress, and hormonal timing around periods · plus a cold pack on the forehead, a warm pack on the neck, and a dark quiet room. Be honest about trigger avoidance rather than handing over a list of banned foods: triggers are usually cumulative, and the glass of wine that is fine on a well-slept Saturday causes an attack on a tired, dehydrated Thursday VERIFY. Part two, treating the attack: take it early, at the first hint, rather than waiting to see whether it turns into a bad one — the single most important thing about migraine treatment · a simple anti-inflammatory at a proper dose, because half a tablet will not touch it · then an antiemetic, explained properly or the mark is lost: 'It isn't only for the nausea. During a migraine your stomach almost stops emptying, so painkillers sit there and don't get absorbed. The anti-sickness tablet helps the painkiller actually get into you' · then triptans, which are migraine-specific and act on the process rather than dulling the pain, offered as a choice of tablet, wafer that dissolves on the tongue, or nasal spray that bypasses the stomach — and offering the three forms is the patient-centred mark, with the wafer being the answer to a woman who vomits her tablets. Triptans are serotonin agonists, so check for SSRIs and mao inhibitors, and they come in small packs on purpose so that overuse is noticed VERIFY. Avoid opioids — poorly effective in migraine and a major cause of overuse headache VERIFY. Part three, prevention: for roughly two to four or more attacks a month, or attacks disabling enough to cost days even if fewer — so at eight a year the honest answer today is not yet, and saying why is the useful part, because it tells her when to come back. If one is started it is taken daily whether or not she has a headache, given two to three months before judging it — impatience is the commonest reason preventers 'Fail' — and aimed at fewer and milder attacks rather than zero, with general-practice options including a beta-blocker, amitriptyline, pizotifen and candesartan, and pregnancy suitability checked first in a 25-year-old VERIFY. Then the two forgotten items. Medication overuse headache: 'If you take painkillers too often, they start causing headaches. Keep painkillers to fewer than 15 days a month, and triptans to fewer than 10. If you're needing them more often than that, come and see me — that means you need a preventer, not more painkillers' VERIFY. And the contraceptive pill: migraine with aura is an absolute contraindication to combined hormonal contraception because of ischaemic stroke risk, while migraine without aura is more nuanced — generally acceptable to initiate, with a lower threshold to stop if aura develops or vascular risk factors accumulate. Progestogen-only methods, the implant, the injection and both intrauterine devices are not restricted, so there is always an alternative and she is never left without contraception VERIFY. Red flags to give her explicitly, because the normal MRI does not cover future presentations: the worst headache of her life coming on in seconds · fever, neck stiffness or a rash · weakness, numbness, slurred speech or confusion · a headache that wakes her or is worse lying flat or on coughing · a change in pattern · headache after a head injury · and visual loss or double vision VERIFY. Review in six to eight weeks with the diary. And keep in mind the other things a young woman on the combined pill can have: cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension with visual obscurations and pulsatile tinnitus VERIFY.

Read task 3 again: 'The diagnosis and the causes'. The word causes is the whole station, and the 'Strange' examination from the examiner only makes sense once you understand that.
stem: General practice. A 60-year-old man presents complaining of a rash. A photograph is provided, showing a vesicular rash in a unilateral, dermatomal distribution. On history it is extremely painful.
Tasks: take a history for four minutes — ask the examiner for your physical examination findings — explain your diagnosis and the causes to the patient — request your investigations.
The examination is not of the rash. You already know what the rash is.
tasks: Take a history for four minutes
Ask the examiner for your physical examination findings
Explain your diagnosis and the causes to the patient

time: Ninety seconds on the rash and the pain, including the eye and ear questions · then signpost the shift, because you are about to ask about weight loss, night sweats and sexual history · then two and a half minutes on the immune screen, which is the station · then request a general examination with the reason attached · then the diagnosis and the causes · then investigations in two groups
findingsLabel: Ask for a general examination, not a dermatological one — and name the reason as you ask
findings: What the examiner may hand back

Afebrile · BMI down from 25 to 22 · firm, non-tender lymph nodes in the left supraclavicular fossa and both axillae · spleen tip palpable · mouth clear · chest clear · rash confined to one dermatome — which changes the station, and you must be honest with him about it

back.dx: HERPES ZOSTER — reactivation of varicella zoster virus that has lain dormant in a sensory nerve root since chickenpox — and the real diagnosis is whatever let it reactivate. To him, in plain words: 'When you had chickenpox as a child, the virus didn't leave your body — it went to sleep in a nerve root next to your spine. Years later it can wake up, travel down that one nerve, and cause pain and a rash in exactly the strip of skin that nerve supplies. That's why it's a band on one side and stops in the middle.' then the part the task actually asks for: 'Why now? The virus is kept asleep by your immune system, so shingles appears when the immune system DIPs. Most often that is simply age — immunity to this virus fades as we get older, which is why it is common at 60. But sometimes there is another reason: diabetes, medicines that suppress immunity like steroids, a blood or other cancer, or an infection such as HIV. Physical or emotional stress and poor nutrition also play a part. That's why I asked all those questions, and it's why I want some blood tests.' Age is a diagnosis of exclusion, not a first answer. And the immune screen is not academic — it changes what you prescribe: in an immunocompetent patient antivirals are given within 72 hours of rash onset, while in an immunocompromised patient they are given regardless of how long the rash has been present, with a much lower threshold for admission and intravenous therapy VERIFY. The history is weighted accordingly. Malignancy: unintentional weight loss · drenching night sweats · lumps in the neck, axillae or groins · change in bowels or blood in urine or stool · cough or haemoptysis · and screening status. Diabetes and chronic disease: thirst and nocturia · recurrent infections or thrush · slow-healing wounds · renal or hepatic disease · family history. Drugs, HIV and lifestyle: steroids in tablet or strong inhaled form · methotrexate, azathioprine or biologics for arthritis, bowel disease or transplant · any chemotherapy ever · splenectomy · alcohol, smoking and injecting drug use · and sexual history, raised with framing rather than bluntly: 'One of the things that can allow shingles to happen is an infection that quietly weakens the immune system — including HIV. I ask everyone about this, and I'd like to include an HIV test in the bloods. Is that alright with you?' The treatment of the shingles itself: antiviral tablets started as soon as possible VERIFY · pain relief given regularly rather than as needed, with early consideration of a neuropathic agent, because under-treated pain is the commonest real-world failure in zoster VERIFY · skin care, keeping it clean, dry and covered with loose clothing and a non-stick dressing · contagion advice, because the fluid can give chickenpox rather than shingles to someone never infected, so keep it covered until every blister has crusted and avoid newborns, non-immune pregnant women and immunosuppressed people · review in two to three days · and vaccination once recovered, since shingles can recur VERIFY. Investigations in two groups. Group one, confirmation: the diagnosis is clinical — say so — with VZV PCR on a de-roofed vesicle only if atypical and never delaying treatment for the result, and fluorescein examination if there is any ocular involvement VERIFY. Group two, the cause: full blood count and film for lymphoma, leukaemia and cytopenias · blood glucose and HbA1c · HIV serology with consent · urea, electrolytes and creatinine, which are also needed for antiviral dosing · liver function · ESR or CRP, and LDH if lymphoma is a concern · chest x-ray for mediastinal nodes and lung malignancy · and hepatitis serology, protein electrophoresis and age-appropriate cancer screening depending on the history VERIFY. The complications that change the station: herpes zoster ophthalmicus, where involvement of the forehead, upper eyelid or tip of the nose means same-day ophthalmology and immediate antivirals, with tip-of-nose lesions predicting ocular involvement VERIFY · Ramsay hunt syndrome, with ear pain, canal vesicles, facial palsy, vertigo or hearing loss, needing urgent ENT VERIFY · disseminated zoster, with lesions well outside the dermatome or a systemically unwell patient, needing admission and intravenous therapy and implying significant immunosuppression · bacterial superinfection · and post-herpetic neuralgia, whose risk rises with age, severe acute pain and severe rash, and whose prevention includes treating the acute pain properly now VERIFY.
plan: Open and get the rash story fast — when it started, which fixes the 72-hour window · whether anything came before it · where exactly and whether it crosses the midline · whether it is spreading beyond the band · and the two same-day referral questions: any blisters near the eye or on the nose, and any in or around the ear with facial weakness or dizziness.
The pain — severity out of ten, character, whether light touch hurts, whether it is keeping him awake — and the systemic screen for fever, headache, neck stiffness or confusion.

Signpost the shift, or the next two minutes land as an interrogation: 'I'm fairly confident I know what this is, and I'll tell you in a moment. But I want to spend most of our time on why it has happened now, because that matters more than the rash itself. Some of my questions will seem unrelated — bear with me.'
THE IMMUNE SCREEN — MALIGNANCY, THEN DIABETES AND CHRONIC DISEASE, THEN DRUGS, HIV AND LIFESTYLE (see dx). This is the two and a half minutes that decide the station.
Request the general examination by name, with the reason attached — not a description of the rash (see findings).

Explain the diagnosis in plain words, then the causes — which is the half the task asks for and the half most candidates omit (see dx). If the examination has given you weight loss and lymphadenopathy, be honest: 'I'm not telling you what it is, because I don't know — but I'm not going to pretend I'm not concerned.'
Treatment today — antivirals started now rather than after the bloods, proper regular analgesia because nine out of ten is not something to put up with, skin care and contagion advice.
Investigations in two groups, saying that the diagnosis itself needs no test and that the second group is for the cause (see dx).

Safety-net and review — back sooner if it spreads well beyond the band, if the eye becomes red or painful, if he develops fever, headache or confusion, or if the pain is uncontrolled — with review in two to three days and urgent haematology referral if the film or count is abnormal.

ask: The sentence that carries the station: 'Shingles happens when the immune system drops its guard. At 60 that is usually just age — but I'd rather look for another reason than miss one.'

The signpost that makes the next two minutes acceptable: 'Some of my questions will seem unrelated — bear with me.' and the framing that makes the HIV question land: 'I ask everyone — there are infections that quietly weaken the immune system and are very treatable if we find them.'
The two same-day referral questions: 'Any blisters near your eye or on your nose?' and 'Any in or around the ear, or any weakness of your face?'

The examination request with its reason, and the contagion line: 'Because I'm looking for an underlying cause rather than examining the rash…' · 'The fluid can give chickenpox — not shingles — to someone who's never had it. Keep it covered until every blister has crusted.'

Challenges: 'Why are you asking me about weight loss? It's a rash' · 'What's that got to do with a rash?' when sexual health is raised · 'Is it catching? Can I give it to the grandkids?' · 'Will the pain go away?' · 'Cancer? … my brother had lymphoma' · and 'Thanks for not fobbing me off with a cream.'
pefe: The examination feels strange only if you have misread the station. Candidates ask the examiner to describe the rash and get told something they already know — the examination here is a general one looking for an underlying immunosuppressive illness, and naming the reason as you ask is what shows the examiner you understand that.

Role-player: Kevin Beattie, 60, a warehouse supervisor. Four days ago he developed a band of blisters around his left ribs, preceded by two days of burning. The pain is nine out of ten and he cannot bear his shirt touching it. He has come expecting a cream and is irritated that it is taking so long. He had chickenpox as a child. No blisters near the eye, nose or ear, no facial weakness, no fever or confusion. Medications: one blood pressure tablet, no steroids, no methotrexate, no chemotherapy ever. He smokes ten a day and drinks four or five beers most nights.

What he gives only if asked: about five kilos of unintentional weight loss over a few months, which he blames on stress at work · waking at night sweating, which he blames on the weather · and getting up at night to pass urine more than he used to. He is initially uncomfortable being asked about sexual health — 'What's that got to do with a rash?' — but answers if it is explained well. If the doctor spends the whole history on the rash he answers briefly and volunteers nothing; if they signpost that they want to know why it happened, he becomes cooperative. If cancer is mentioned he goes quiet and then says 'My brother had lymphoma' — which is his hidden concern, and he has been quietly frightened by the weight loss for weeks. If the doctor is honest about being concerned but has a clear plan, he is grateful rather than panicked.

Mark them against these: took a brief, focused rash history rather than an exhaustive one · asked about the eye, the nose and the ear · asked about severity and character of the pain including light touch · signposted that they wanted to explore why it had happened · asked about weight loss and night sweats · asked about lumps, bowels, blood and cough · asked about thirst and nocturia · asked about steroids and immunosuppressive medications · raised sexual health and HIV testing with a proper explanation · asked the examiner for a general examination, naming lymph nodes, spleen, weight and mouth · explained shingles as reactivation in a nerve, in plain words · explained why the rash is one-sided and stops at the midline · explained the causes — age, diabetes, medications, cancer, HIV · was honest about their concern given the weight loss and the glands · started antiviral treatment and did not wait for results · took the pain seriously and offered adequate analgesia · gave contagion advice · ordered investigations aimed at the cause · gave clear red flags and a review date · and responded to his brother's lymphoma with empathy rather than deflection.

How to ask — 'I'd like the examination findings, please. Because I'm looking for an underlying cause rather than examining the rash, I would specifically like: vital signs and temperature · weight · lymph nodes in the neck, axillae and groins · abdominal examination for hepatomegaly or splenomegaly · the mouth for oral candida · the chest · the skin generally for lesions outside the dermatome · and the eye, if there is any facial involvement'

What each finding would mean — Lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly → lymphoma or leukaemia · oral candida → significant immunosuppression · weight loss or cachexia → malignancy or chronic disease · lesions beyond the dermatome → disseminated zoster · red eye or corneal involvement → ophthalmic zoster · facial weakness → Ramsay hunt

The rash description — one line, then move on — 'I'd also confirm the rash is a grouped vesicular eruption in a single dermatome that does not cross the midline, and note whether the lesions are vesicular, pustular or crusted, which tells me how far through the illness he is.' that is all you need
fails: ★ Spending the history characterising a rash you have already been shown in a photograph
★ Never screening for immunosuppression — no questions about weight, sweats, lumps, diabetes, steroids or HIV — when that is the purpose of the case and it changes the treatment
★ Asking the examiner to describe the rash instead of requesting a general examination for a cause
★ Explaining what shingles is and never explaining why, when the task says 'the diagnosis and the causes'

Missing ophthalmic or otic involvement, both of which are same-day referrals; delaying antivirals until the bloods return; ordering a VZV PCR as though the diagnosis were in doubt; under-treating pain scored at nine out of ten; giving no contagion advice; or asking about HIV bluntly and without framing
numbers: Antivirals are most effective within 72 hours of rash onset, and are given regardless of duration if immunocompromised VERIFY · the rash is confined to one dermatome and does not cross the midline · contagious until every lesion has crusted · tip-of-nose lesions, the hutchinson sign, predict ocular involvement VERIFY

Investigations for the cause: FBC and film · blood glucose and HbA1c · HIV serology with consent · UEC, which also guides antiviral dosing · LFT · CRP and LDH · and chest x-ray · review in 2-3 days and vaccination once recovered VERIFY · post-herpetic neuralgia risk rises with age, severe acute pain and severe rash, and treating the acute pain properly is part of prevention VERIFY · SHINE SA for HIV testing advice · cancer council SA 13 11 20 · Quitline 13 7848 · VERIFY all

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: never screening for immunosuppression — weight loss, night sweats, lumps, thirst and nocturia, steroids and immunosuppressants, and HIV raised WITH framing ('I ask everyone, because there are infections that quietly weaken the immune system and are very treatable'). It is the purpose of the case, and it changes the treatment

setting: This is a framework card, not only a single case. The examiners can place an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient into any station — antenatal, chest pain, paediatric, palliative or emergency — and when they do, the same small set of behaviours earns marks and the same small set loses them. Whatever the tasks say, there is an additional unwritten task: demonstrate culturally safe practice, assessed through how you open, who you offer, what you assume and how you plan.
stem: Worked case — general practice, rural South Australia. A 45-year-old Aboriginal man has come because his sister told him he should get a check-up. He has not seen a doctor in several years and says he feels 'All right'.
His file records blood pressure 152/94 at a community screening event eighteen months ago, never followed up. No current medications. A family history of diabetes and kidney disease.
Tasks: take a history — explain what a health assessment involves and what you would check — discuss your management plan, including follow-up.
tasks: Take a history from the patient
Explain what a health assessment involves and what you would check
Discuss your management plan, including follow-up
time: Spend the first minute earning the rest of the consultation — the identification question asked routinely so it is clearly not about him, then the offers · then the person before the organ · then the medical and family history · then risk factors asked neutrally and social and emotional wellbeing · then the access question · then the assessment explained and the blood pressure acted on · then the practical levers and the return negotiated

back.dx: Untreated hypertension with substantial undifferentiated cardiometabolic and renal risk, in a man with significant access barriers — and the most important clinical outcome of this consultation is the second consultation. Why the framework exists: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians experience a substantially lower life expectancy and a higher burden of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, respiratory disease, rheumatic heart disease and ear disease, with onset at younger ages VERIFY. The causes are structural rather than personal — dispossession, intergenerational trauma, racism, and inequitable access to housing, education, employment and health services — and if it comes up, say it correctly and never in a way that locates the problem in the patient. Say it to the examiner if asked; do not lecture the patient about his own community. What follows clinically: screening starts earlier and is repeated more often, access barriers must be actively removed rather than noted, and care works best when it is community-controlled, family-inclusive and continuous. The history takes the whole person: medical, including previous rheumatic fever or a heart murmur and the routinely under-asked ears, eyes, teeth and skin · social and emotional wellbeing — who is at home, what he does, where he is from because country and community matter, how he is travelling in himself, any sorry business or loss, housing, and who he goes to when things are hard · and risk factors asked neutrally and never assumed, in exactly the tone you would use with anyone. The wording that separates a pass from an offence: never 'I assume you'd be drinking a fair bit?', 'People in your community often…', 'Do you have a job at all?' or 'You people are at high risk of…'; instead 'Do you drink? If so, how much and how often?', 'Tell me about your situation at home', 'What do you do day to day?' and 'There are some things I'd check earlier for you than for others — can I explain why?' The health assessment, explained plainly as broader than a normal appointment and free: measure and examine — blood pressure, height, weight, waist · heart and chest, listening deliberately for a murmur · ears with otoscopy and hearing, because chronic ear disease is common and under-treated · eyes including vision and retinal screening · teeth and gums · skin, feet and pulses. Investigate — blood glucose and HbA1c · lipids and cardiovascular risk assessment commenced at a younger age than in the general population VERIFY · eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, which is the test that gets left off · full blood count and iron studies · sexually transmitted infection screening where appropriate · and age-appropriate bowel, cervical and breast screening. Prevent and support — immunisation per the indigenous schedule VERIFY · smoking cessation with Quitline 13 7848 and the Aboriginal Quitline where available · alcohol and other drug support if wanted · social and emotional wellbeing supports · hearing and dental referral · and the follow-up items attached to the assessment for nurse, health worker and allied health VERIFY. The blood pressure is acted on rather than repeating the last CLINICIAN'S omission, and acknowledging that failure honestly — 'That's not good enough and I'm sorry' — builds more trust than any reassurance. The enabling is where marks are won or lost, because noting a barrier scores nothing and removing it scores: cost → closing the gap PBS registration done today in the practice, bulk billing, generic options VERIFY · transport → one visit for everything, health worker transport, telehealth, PATS for specialist travel · time off work → batch the bloods and appointments · fear or past experience → an Aboriginal health worker, a support person, and continuity with one clinician · literacy → plain-language written information and checking understanding rather than asking 'Do you understand?' · distance → shared care with the local clinic and a named contact. And the follow-up is the treatment: 'What would make it easier for you to come back?' · 'Would you rather see me, or one of the Aboriginal health workers first?' · 'Is it alright if we ring you if we don't see you?' — with a recall set and named, one named contact at the practice, the next appointment booked before he leaves, everything batched into as few visits as possible, shared care with the ACCHS if he prefers, and family involved if he wants them. In hospital stations, ask about cultural obligations, family presence and practices around serious illness and dying — and let the family lead.
plan: Open, ask what brings him in, and then ask the identification question of everyone — framed as such, so it is clearly not about him: 'Before we go on, I ask everybody this: are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?'

Explain why you asked, then make the offers — an Aboriginal health worker to sit in · a support person or family · an interpreter if a traditional language is preferred, through TIS National 131 450 and never a family member for clinical content · and a choice of clinician gender where the consultation involves men's or women's business. Offer once, accept the answer gracefully, move on.

Signpost and hand over some control: 'I'd like to hear about you first, then talk about a check-up that's available to you, then work out a plan together. Stop me any time, and tell me if there's something you'd rather not talk about today.'

THE PERSON BEFORE THE ORGAN — WHO IS AT HOME, WHAT HE DOES, WHERE FAMILY IS FROM, AND HOW HE IS TRAVELLING IN HIMSELF. Sixty seconds of genuine interest buys the rest of the consultation, and going straight to risk factors forfeits it.

Medical and family history — known problems, medications, allergies, immunisation · any rheumatic fever or heart murmur, which is a specific and important question in this population and changes your examination · and what runs in the family, which here is dialysis and diabetes and drives the testing.
RISK FACTORS ASKED NEUTRALLY AND SOCIAL AND EMOTIONAL WELLBEING ASKED USING THAT FRAMING — INCLUDING SORRY BUSINESS OR RECENT LOSS. Then WAIT after the question rather than rephrasing it three times.

THE ACCESS QUESTION, WHICH IS THE ONE THAT EXPLAINS THE LAST FIVE YEARS: 'HAS SOMETHING MADE IT HARD TO COME IN TO A DOCTOR BEFORE?' — then LISTEN, and do not defend the system or explain the experience away.

Explain the health assessment plainly and say what you would check and why — linking the kidney and sugar tests to his own family history (see dx). And answer 'I feel fine' honestly: 'A lot of these things don't make you feel anything until quite late. That's exactly why the check is worth doing.'
The blood pressure — repeated today, acted on, and the previous omission acknowledged honestly.

The practical levers, named and done rather than mentioned — closing the gap PBS registered today · a care plan for free allied health · health worker support with appointments · and shared care with the ACCHS if he prefers it.

Negotiate the return, book the next appointment before he leaves, set a recall and name a contact — because for a man who has not seen a doctor in years, the follow-up plan is the treatment and 'Come back if you're worried' is not one.
back.planNote: the framework applies whenever an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander patient appears in any station — you do not abandon the station to talk about culture, you do four small things inside it
ask: The sentence to open with in any station: 'I ask everybody this: are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin? … thanks — the reason I ask is that it opens up some things that are there for you. Would you like one of our Aboriginal health workers to sit in?'

The questions that reach the person: 'Tell me a bit about you — who's at home, what you do, where family's from.' · 'How are you travelling in yourself?' · 'Has there been any sorry business or loss in the family?' · and 'Has something made it hard to come in to a doctor before?'

The two clinical questions specific to this population: 'Were you ever told you had rheumatic fever, or a murmur?' and the kidney screen that must include a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, not just a creatinine.

The enabling lines, said as actions rather than observations: 'There's a scheme that makes your medicines much cheaper or free — I can register you today.' · 'If you'd rather go through the Aboriginal health service, that's completely fine and I'll work with them.' · 'What would make it easier for you to come back?'

Challenges: 'My sister made me come' · 'I feel fine, but' · 'I don't really come to doctors' · 'My uncle went into hospital and never came home' · 'Nobody ever rang me' about the blood pressure · 'Can't afford the tablets anyway' · 'I'd have to get a lift into town' · and, only if asked what worries him most, 'Ending up on the machine like mum. And the grandkids.'
pefe: The examination is the health assessment itself and is deliberately broad — blood pressure and anthropometry, heart and chest with deliberate listening for a murmur, ears, eyes, teeth, skin, feet and pulses. The characteristic gaps are the ears and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and both are marked.

Role-player: Trevor Karpany, 45, who does fencing and seasonal farm work and lives with his partner and two grandchildren, with family from up the river. He has not seen a doctor in about five years and is here because his sister kept nagging him. Polite but reserved, he does not volunteer things. He does not know his blood pressure was high, because nobody rang him after the community screening day. His mother is on dialysis and his father had 'The sugar'. He may have had rheumatic fever as a child and is not sure. He smokes about ten a day and drinks on weekends, and food is expensive and limited at the local store.

How he plays it, and what it tells you: he takes pauses before answering and makes limited eye contact, which is normal for him rather than evasion. If the doctor fills his pauses or talks over him, he gives shorter answers for the rest of the station; if they wait, he gives a fuller answer. If the identification question is never asked he does not volunteer it; if it is asked routinely and explained he answers readily and warms slightly. If the doctor makes an assumption — 'I assume you'd be drinking a fair bit' — he goes flat and closed for the rest of the consultation. His brother died last year, mentioned only if asked how he is going or about loss, and only after a pause. He does not like hospitals because his uncle went in and never came home, mentioned only if asked whether something has made it hard to come in. He could not afford tablets in the past, which is the real reason he stopped going. His hidden concern, given only if asked what worries him most, is ending up on dialysis like his mother and the grandchildren being left without him.

Mark them against these: asked whether he is of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin and framed it as asked of everyone · explained why they were asking · offered an Aboriginal health worker and accepted the answer gracefully · offered to include a family member or support person · asked about him as a person before asking about his body · asked where family is from · allowed silence and did not talk over him · did not require eye contact or treat its absence as a problem · asked about loss or sorry business · asked about smoking, alcohol and food neutrally without assuming · asked whether something had made it hard to come in, and listened without defending · asked about rheumatic fever or a murmur · took the family history seriously and linked it to the tests · explained the free annual health check and what it covers · included ears, eyes, teeth, skin and feet rather than just blood pressure · arranged kidney tests including a urine test · acknowledged honestly that the blood pressure had been missed · registered him for cheaper medicines rather than just mentioning cost · offered a care plan and the Aboriginal health service as an option · and asked what would make it easier to come back, batched the visits, and set up a recall and a named contact.

In any station, whatever it is about — 1. Offer an Aboriginal health worker or liaison officer, and a support person · 2. Adjust your screening thresholds and say so — earlier cardiovascular and diabetes assessment, rheumatic heart disease in the differential for a sore throat or murmur, ear disease in a child · 3. Name the practical supports — closing the gap PBS, care plan, ACCHS, transport · 4. Ask about family and community and include them if he wants VERIFY

The identification question, and why it is clinical — 'I ask everybody this: are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?' then explain why: it opens up the yearly health assessment, the closing the gap PBS co-payment, and specific immunisation and screening schedules. Not asking is not neutral — it withholds access. And you cannot guess: identification is a matter of identity, not appearance VERIFY

What cultural safety actually means — It is defined by the recipient, not the provider — not a checklist you complete but whether the patient experiences the encounter as safe, respectful and free of judgement. Cultural awareness is knowing difference exists; cultural competence is having skills to work across it; cultural safety goes further and requires you to examine your own assumptions and the power imbalance in the room VERIFY

And the term to use — Social and emotional wellbeing is commonly preferred over 'Mental health' and is broader — connection to body, mind and emotions, family and kinship, community, culture, country and spirituality. Using the phrase signals that you understand health is not only individual VERIFY

Communication habits that are themselves marked — Allow silence — a pause is thinking time, not a gap for you to fill, and filling it is the commonest cultural-safety error candidates make · do not require eye contact, because avoiding it may be respect rather than evasion · yarn, because an unhurried conversation gets more than a question list · plain English and checking back gently · and earn the right to sensitive questions rather than opening with them
fails: ★ Never asking the identification question, or guessing from appearance — the single commonest dropped mark, and not asking withholds access to funded care
★ Deficit assumptions about alcohol, smoking, employment or education — asking 'I assume you'd be drinking?' does more damage to your score than omitting an investigation
★ Never offering an Aboriginal Health Worker, Liaison Officer, support person or interpreter
★ Noting barriers without removing them — 'cost can be a problem for a lot of people' scores nothing where 'I'll register you today' scores

Filling the silences or demanding eye contact; using a family member as interpreter for clinical content; treating all Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people as one culture; reciting life expectancy statistics at the patient about his own community; omitting the urine ACR, the ears, or the rheumatic fever question; or ending with 'come back if you're worried' instead of a booked appointment, a recall and a named contact
numbers: Ask every patient: 'Are you of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin?' · annual health assessment available at any age, with linked follow-up items VERIFY · closing the gap PBS co-payment relief, registered in the practice · cardiovascular risk assessment and diabetes screening commenced earlier than in the general population VERIFY · kidney screening is eGFR plus urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio

13yarn 13 92 76 — a national crisis support line staffed by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander crisis supporters VERIFY · Quitline 13 7848, including Aboriginal Quitline services · TIS National 131 450 where a traditional language is preferred · Aboriginal community controlled health services across SA — refer to them, work with them, and accept the patient's preference · Aboriginal health workers, practitioners and liaison officers, involved early rather than at discharge · country health connect and PATS · VERIFY all

must: FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: never asking the identification question, or guessing from appearance — the single commonest dropped mark; ask it of everyone, frame it as such, and explain why: it opens the yearly health check, cheaper medicines and Aboriginal Health Worker support

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: deficit assumptions about alcohol, smoking, employment or education — 'I assume you'd be drinking?' does more damage to your score than omitting an investigation; ask exactly what you would ask anyone, in the same tone. And never recite gap statistics at the patient

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: never offering an Aboriginal Health Worker or Liaison Officer, a support person or an interpreter — offer all three, accept the answer gracefully, and never use a family member as interpreter for clinical content

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: noting barriers without removing them — 'cost can be a problem for a lot of people' scores nothing where 'I'll register you for Closing the Gap today' scores; plus a care plan, transport help, batched visits, and shared care with the ACCHS if he prefers

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: ending with 'come back if you're worried' — for a man who has not seen a doctor in years the follow-up plan IS the treatment: ask what would make it easier to come back, book the next appointment before he leaves, set a recall and name a contact. And act on the blood pressure that was never followed up rather than repeating the last clinician's omission

DO — Ask about rheumatic fever or a murmur, and screen the kidneys with eGFR AND a urine albumin–creatinine ratio, not just a creatinine — plus ears, eyes, teeth and skin, which are routinely left off. And let the silences sit: filling a pause is the commonest cultural-safety error, and absent eye contact is not evasion

stem: Version A, the current recall — Jenny, 28, 35 weeks pregnant, presents to your rural general practice or emergency department concerned about her pregnancy. In her opening statement she says she is leaking fluid from the vagina. Tasks: take a history (6 minutes) — physical examination findings are on a card, read them — explain the diagnosis to the patient.

Version B, the older recall — Jenny, 28, 33 weeks pregnant, complaining of passing fluid from the vagina since one hour ago. Tasks: take a history (4 minutes) — ask the examiner for physical examination findings — explain the diagnosis with reasons — explain your management plan.
In both: she had a LLETZ or cone for abnormal cells before this pregnancy, and at the 20-week scan the cervix was short so a cerclage was placed. On speculum the suture may be visible.
tasks: Take a history (6 minutes in Version A, 4 in Version B)
Physical examination findings — from the card, or requested from the examiner
Explain the diagnosis with reasons
Explain your management plan

dx: **Preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes at 35 weeks with a cervical cerclage in situ; no infection, no labour, GBS unknown.** **Definition: spontaneous rupture of the membranes BEFORE the onset of labour — 'preterm' if before 37 completed weeks. About 3% of pregnancies, and it precedes a third of preterm births.** At term it is simply PROM.
**★ EVERY DECISION COMES BACK TO TWO ENEMIES: INFECTION AND IMMATURITY OF THE LUNGS. Say it to the patient and to the examiner — it makes the whole plan explain itself.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE HAS TWO MOMENTS. FIRST, the examination: you must say the word 'STERILE speculum', look for POOLING in the posterior fornix, the OS, a CORD, take SWABS and a FLUID TEST — and must NOT do a digital examination. SECOND, the plan: the examiner is not looking for 'admit and induce' or 'send home and wait', but for a candidate who screens out infection, labour and fetal distress, gives antibiotics (and steroids under 35 weeks) to everyone, then presents EXPECTANT VERSUS ACTIVE and HOSPITAL VERSUS HOME as HER choices with pros and cons, and closes with red flags.**

**Why no digital examination — have the sentence ready**: **'it increases ascending infection and adds nothing, because the speculum shows the os. I'd only do one if delivery were imminent and I needed a Bishop score.'** **A bimanual is equally unnecessary — the uterus is abdominal.**

**THE DIAGNOSIS WITH ITS TWO REASONS, in lay words**: **'your waters have broken early — before 37 weeks and before labour started. I think that for two reasons: first, the fluid you describe — a gush, clear, no smell, no blood — is typical of the water around the baby; and second, when I examined you I could see fluid collected at the top of the vagina, and I've taken a sample to confirm it. Importantly, labour hasn't started and there's no sign of infection in the fluid — both of those would change what we do.'**

**THE RISKS IN TWO SENTENCES: 'it raises the risk of INFECTION in the fluid around the baby, because the seal is broken. And because labour can start at any time, the baby may be born early — and a baby born early can have BREATHING PROBLEMS, because the lungs are the last thing to mature.'** Add that it can occasionally cause the cord to slip down, which is why you examined carefully.

**THE NUMBERS. ERYTHROMYCIN 250 mg orally 6-hourly for 10 DAYS or until labour** — **NOT amoxicillin-clavulanate, because of necrotising enterocolitis.** **BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg IM × 2, 24 hours apart, if UNDER 35 WEEKS** (routine before 34+6, considered 35+0 to 36+6; **the teaching cut-off of 35 weeks is a safe exam answer**). **MAGNESIUM SULFATE for neuroprotection if birth is expected before 30 WEEKS.** **Intrapartum GBS: benzylpenicillin 3 g IV then 1.8 g 4-hourly.** VERIFY

**TIMING OF BIRTH — and the trial behind it: the PPROMT trial (2016) found that for 34 to 36+6 weeks with no infection, expectant management to 37 weeks reduced neonatal respiratory morbidity WITHOUT increasing sepsis. So the plan is EXPECTANT TO 36 COMPLETED WEEKS (37+0), THEN INDUCE** — but deliver at ANY gestation for **chorioamnionitis, abruption, abnormal CTG, meconium, cord prolapse or established labour.** VERIFY If challenged on why not induce at 35 weeks: **'both are acceptable; PPROMT favoured expectant management for respiratory morbidity when there is no infection — so I offer both.'**

**THE CERCLAGE — the bonus, and there is no dogma: 'I'll discuss it with the obstetrician today.' REMOVE if infection, bleeding, labour, or OVER 32 WEEKS. UNDER 32 weeks with none of those, LEAVE IT IN while the steroids work and reassess at 48 hours.** VERIFY (evidence limited) **Elective removal happens at 36–37 weeks anyway.** At 35 weeks: **most likely out, because it is a foreign body and the lungs are mature enough.**

**TOCOLYSIS: only WITH contractions, NEVER with any sign of infection, and only to buy 48 hours for steroids or transfer.** SA: **an MM5 unit cannot care for a 33–35 week neonate.** After speculum, swabs, the first antibiotic dose, steroids and a CTG, **arrange transfer by MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 or RFDS** to Lyell McEwin, Flinders or the WCH by gestation and cot availability VERIFY — **and give the first betamethasone dose BEFORE transport.** **PATS** for travel and accommodation; **Country Health Connect**; **TIS National 131 450**; **Aboriginal Family Birthing Program**. **Sending a rural 33–35 weeker home 'to wait' is a named error.**
plan: **WIPE, confirm name and date of birth, open question**: **'can you tell me why you're concerned about your pregnancy?'** *'I'm leaking fluid from down below — it started about an hour ago with a big gush.'*

**Empathy and signpost**: **'I understand, and I know how frightening this is. I'll ask some questions, then examine you, and we'll take good care of you. Let me ask about the fluid itself, because that tells me a lot.'**

**CHARACTERISE THE FLUID — five things**: **'when did it start? Is it continuous or on and off? Getting worse? Has this ever happened before? WHAT COLOUR IS IT — clear, yellow, green, brown? Any blood or tissue? How many pads, and were they fully soaked? AND DOES IT HAVE A BAD SMELL?'** **Colour and smell are the two everyone forgets, and they detect meconium and chorioamnionitis.**

**★ THE THREE SYMPTOM QUESTIONS, announced**: **'three things I must check.'** **'Any tummy pain or tightenings?'** — if yes, where, how long, how often, getting closer? **'Any vaginal bleeding?'** **'Any fever or chills — do you feel unwell?'**

**★ RISK FACTORS — and the twist lives here**: **'any trauma or knock to the tummy? Did it start after sex? ANY PREVIOUS EARLY RUPTURE OF THE WATERS, OR ANY PROBLEMS WITH YOUR CERVIX — SURGERY, OR A STITCH?'** *The LLETZ and the cerclage.* Then **'any burning, frequency, or leaking of urine before this?'** — one question that shows you thought of incontinence.
**OBSTETRIC HISTORY**: booking bloods and blood group · dating scan · screening · **the 18–20 week scan — normal apart from the cervix** · the sweet drink test · vaccinations.
**★ THE SWAB AND THE KICKING**: **'have you had the swab test from your private parts?'** *'Not yet.'* **So GBS is unknown — say that out loud.** Then **'is the baby kicking as usual?'**

**Pre-eclampsia screen and the closing block**: headache, blurred vision, swelling, right upper quadrant pain, nausea · first pregnancy · past medical history, medications, **allergies — especially penicillin** · smoking and alcohol · partner support, mood, safety at home · **and HOW FAR SHE LIVES FROM THE HOSPITAL, because it decides the disposition.**

**ASK FOR THE FINDINGS IN ORDER**: general appearance · **all vital signs, and name the TEMPERATURE first** · abdomen — fundal height, **lie and presentation**, fetal heart rate, tenderness, **'am I feeling any contractions?'**

**★ THE SPECULUM — say 'STERILE'**: **'with consent and a chaperone — inspection of the vulva for fluid, blood, discharge, a cord. Then a STERILE SPECULUM: is the os open or closed? Do I see POOLING of fluid in the posterior fornix? Any CORD? The colour and smell of the fluid? A CERVICAL SUTURE?'**

**The samples, then the refusal**: **'I'd like to take a sample of the fluid for an AMNISURE or NITRAZINE test, and low and high vaginal swabs plus an ANORECTAL SWAB FOR GBS.'** Then: **'I will NOT do a digital vaginal examination — it increases infection and adds nothing, because the speculum shows me the os.'**

**THE DIAGNOSIS WITH ITS TWO REASONS**, in lay words — the character of the fluid, and the pooling seen on speculum — **and name the two relevant negatives: no contractions, and no fever or offensive fluid.**
**THE TWO RISKS**: infection now the seal is broken, and early birth with breathing problems because the lungs mature last.

**INVESTIGATIONS IN THREE GROUPS**: **to rule out infection** — FBC, CRP, the swabs, a urine test · **to check the baby** — ultrasound for liquor volume, position and size · **and a CTG**, 'and if the trace is abnormal the plan changes to delivery.'

**MANAGEMENT TODAY, EVERY CASE**: **erythromycin for ten days** · **(Version B) betamethasone, two doses 24 hours apart, which speeds the maturing of the lungs** · **and penicillin through a drip when labour starts, because the swab wasn't done.**

**★ THE CHOICE, OFFERED NOT DICTATED**: **'as long as there's no infection, no labour and the baby is well, we have two options. We can wait, with close monitoring, until the end of 36 weeks and then induce — a more mature baby, but we watch for infection. Or we can induce now, which at 35 weeks is also reasonable. It's your decision, and I'll tell you what's safer.'**

**HOSPITAL VERSUS HOME, with the rural reasoning**: **'hospital is safer — temperature, bloods and the baby's trace, and we're right there if labour starts. Home is possible for some women after a couple of stable days — but you're an hour and a half away, and this hospital can't care for a 35-week baby, so my advice is to stay and be transferred to a unit with a nursery.'**

**THE AVOID LIST, THE RED FLAGS, AND THE STITCH**: **no sex, no tampons, no swimming or baths.** **Come straight back for fever or feeling unwell; smelly, yellow, green or brown fluid; tightenings or pain; bleeding; the baby moving less; or feeling anything in the vagina.** Then: **'about the stitch — there's no single right answer, and I'll discuss it with the obstetrician today. At 35 weeks they'll most likely take it out.'**
pefe: **Name the TEMPERATURE first in the vital signs** — it is the infection question.

**Abdomen: fundal height, Leopold's for LIE AND PRESENTATION (a non-cephalic presentation with ruptured membranes is a CORD-PROLAPSE risk), fetal heart rate, tenderness, and whether contractions are palpable.**
**★ STERILE SPECULUM — say the word. Look for: POOLING in the posterior fornix · the OS open or closed · ANY CORD · the colour and smell of the liquor · a CERVICAL SUTURE.**

**AMNISURE (PAMG-1) or NITRAZINE.** Two lines is positive and faint lines are read as positive; **nitrazine turns blue at the alkaline pH of liquor but gives false positives with blood, semen and bacterial vaginosis.**
**Swabs: low and high vaginal, PLUS an anorectal swab for GBS** — the 36-week swab has not been done. **Then FBC, CRP, MSU, group and antibodies.**
**NO DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION unless delivery is imminent. NO BIMANUAL — the uterus is abdominal.**

**ERYTHROMYCIN 250 mg QID × 10 days (not amoxicillin-clavulanate). BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg IM × 2 if under 35 weeks. MAGNESIUM SULFATE if under 30 weeks. BENZYLPENICILLIN 3 g IV then 1.8 g 4-hourly in labour.** VERIFY
**CHORIOAMNIONITIS: temperature over 38, maternal HR over 100, fetal HR over 160, tender uterus, offensive liquor, raised WCC and CRP → IV antibiotics and DELIVER regardless of gestation.**

**Expectant monitoring: 4-hourly temperature and pulse; twice-weekly CRP, FBC and CTG; weekly to fortnightly ultrasound for liquor and growth.** **Home only after 48–72 hours stable, singleton, cephalic, no infection, living close to a maternity unit — rarely met in MM5.**

**CERCLAGE: remove if infection, bleeding, labour, or over 32 weeks; under 32 weeks leave it while steroids work and reassess at 48 hours.** VERIFY **Give the first betamethasone dose BEFORE transport, and transfer to a unit with a nursery — MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33.**

setting: An examination-first station with an anxious parent left waiting — so greet her before you turn to the examiner, and validate her early. Two traps define it: asking only about the ears when a child who is not talking needs the brain examined, and naming the audiogram pattern without narrating how you got there. The marks are in the narration.
stem: You are a general practitioner in Wallaroo, South Australia. Cooper Nguyen, aged 2 years and 9 months, has been brought in by his mother, who is worried about his speech. He uses only about six words.
He has had recurrent ear infections — around eight episodes in the past year, the most recent about six months ago. Audiometry has been performed and the results are available to you.
Tasks: ask the examiner for the relevant physical examination findings — interpret the audiometry to the examiner — explain the diagnosis and management to the mother. The role player is the mother.

time: Twenty-five seconds greeting the mother before you turn to the examiner — it buys her cooperation for the three minutes at the end · three minutes of examination delivered as one continuous run · ninety seconds narrating the audiogram axis by axis and ear by ear · then three minutes of explanation and management in plain English
findingsLabel: The examination — and the audiogram narration the marks are in
findings: Ask for more than the ears

General appearance — alert and interactive, any dysmorphic features · behaviour — eye contact, response to name, consistent response to sound, repetitive behaviour · growth centiles including head circumference, and temperature · and neurology: tone, reflexes and gait. These feel irrelevant in an ENT station, which is exactly why they are in the marking scheme
The ears, characterised not just named

Otoscopy of both ears — canal clear of wax · drum dull or retracted · bubbles or an air-fluid level · red or bulging · perforation or discharge · cone of light. Accepting 'Abnormal drums' is not enough: the explicit absence of redness, bulging, perforation and discharge is how you justify not prescribing an antibiotic
The audiogram, narrated in full

'Frequency is on the horizontal axis in hertz, and hearing level on the vertical axis in decibels, increasing downwards — so the lower the mark, the louder the sound needed to be. The normal range is 0 to 20 decibels.' then right ear: air conduction 45-50 dB, outside the normal band; bone conduction 5-10 dB, within it; an air-bone gap of roughly 40 dB. Then the left ear, same pattern. Only then name it

back.dx: BILATERAL OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION — glue ear — causing a bilateral moderate conductive hearing loss and consequent expressive language delay. To the mother, in plain English and without the terminology you already used with the examiner: 'Cooper has fluid sitting behind both of his eardrums. It is not an infection at the moment — there is no redness and he is not in pain — but the fluid is there. It is very common after repeated ear infections.' then the mechanism and the analogy: 'The eardrum has to be able to move to pass sound through to the hearing nerve. With fluid behind it, it cannot move properly, so everything he hears arrives muffled — as if he were listening from underwater.' then the reassuring half of the test: the part that goes through the eardrum is reduced, the part that goes straight to the hearing nerve is completely normal, so the problem is mechanical and mechanical problems can be fixed. And the link that explains why she came: 'Children learn to talk by hearing words clearly. If everything is muffled during the years they are learning language, speech falls behind. It is not that he is not bright, and it is not anything you have done.' The management has four parts and two referrals that go together rather than in sequence. First, ENT referral — because the fluid is bilateral, long-standing and affecting speech, he is likely to be offered grommets, tiny ventilation tubes that let the fluid drain and air back in, with hearing usually improving straight away and the tubes extruding themselves over six to twelve months. Second, and just as important, speech pathology — started today, not after the ears are fixed, because he has ground to make up. Third, repeat the hearing test after treatment. Fourth, review the rest of his development rather than just his talking. Then the antibiotic sentence, said explicitly and held under pressure: 'Antibiotics will not fix this, and neither will antihistamines, decongestants or steroid sprays. Those treat infection, and what cooper has now is fluid rather than infection. I know he has had a great deal of antibiotics over the last year, and I do not want you to think we are simply not trying.' if she pushes: they genuinely do not clear the fluid and each course carries side effects and resistance, but another acute infection with pain and fever is different and would be treated. Home advice: keep him away from cigarette smoke in the house and the car · get down to his level and have his attention before speaking · turn the television off when talking to him · read to him close up, face to face · and no bottle lying flat. The examiner's three follow-ups have set answers. Type B versus type C: type C is a peak shifted into negative pressure, meaning the Eustachian tube is not ventilating but there is air in there; type B is flat, the drum is not moving at all, and with a normal canal volume that means fluid — a large canal volume would suggest a perforation or a patent grommet instead. Why bone conduction is unaffected: the transducer sits on the mastoid and vibrates the skull directly, bypassing the canal, drum and ossicles, so it tests the cochlea and nerve alone. Could it be mixed: no — in a mixed loss the bone conduction line would also fall below the normal band. And if the audiogram is sensorineural instead, with air and bone together at 60-70 dB and no gap, the effusion does not explain it: ask about newborn hearing screening, family history of childhood deafness, meningitis, congenital CMV and ototoxic medication, and refer urgently — grommets are not the answer.
plan: GREET THE MOTHER FIRST AND BY NAME, BEFORE TURNING TO THE EXAMINER — AND VALIDATE HER IMMEDIATELY: 'YOU WERE ABSOLUTELY RIGHT TO BRING HIM IN.' It is true, and it pre-empts the guilt she will otherwise express at minute six.
The examination request, delivered as one continuous run — general, behaviour, growth, ears characterised, nose, palate and tongue tie, nodes, neurology and chest (see findings).

THE AUDIOGRAM — AXES FIRST, THEN RIGHT EAR AIR THEN BONE THEN THE GAP, THEN THE LEFT EAR, THEN THE CONCLUSION, THEN THE TYMPANOGRAMS. Saying 'bilateral conductive hearing loss' and stopping shows pattern recognition rather than interpretation.

TURN BACK TO HER — 'THANK YOU FOR WAITING' — AND EXPLAIN THE DIAGNOSIS IN PLAIN ENGLISH WITH THE UNDERWATER ANALOGY AND THE LINK TO HIS SPEECH (see dx). Expect her four questions: is he deaf, is it my fault, will he catch up, how bad is it.
The four-part plan — ENT for grommets, speech pathology in parallel, a repeat hearing test, and developmental review.
THE ANTIBIOTIC SENTENCE, SAID EXPLICITLY — AND HELD WHEN SHE ASKS FOR ANOTHER COURSE. Caving to satisfy her is the easiest way to lose the management domain.
Home advice, safety-net and summary: 'Come back sooner if he gets a painful ear, a fever, any discharge from the ear, if he seems to be hearing less than he was, or if he loses words he already had.'
back.planNote: an examination-first station with a waiting parent — twenty-five seconds of greeting at the start buys the three minutes of explanation at the end
ask: The three sentences that carry the station: 'What is his tone, and are his reflexes normal?' · 'Bone conduction is normal in both ears, so the cochlea and the nerve are working — the problem is in the conducting apparatus.' · 'Everything he hears is muffled, as if he were listening from underwater.'

The opening that pre-empts the tears: 'You were absolutely right to bring him in.' and the reassurance she is waiting for: 'His hearing is reduced, not absent, and the nerve itself is working perfectly.'

The line that must be said and held: 'Antibiotics will not fix this, and neither will antihistamines or decongestants.' and the pairing that is separately marked: 'ENT for grommets, and speech pathology — both today, not one after the other.'

The examination questions most often omitted: 'Are there any dysmorphic features? What are his growth centiles?' · 'Does he make eye contact and respond when his name is called?' · 'Is the palate intact? Is there a tongue tie?'

Challenges: 'So he is not deaf?' · 'Is it my fault? I did not realise' · 'Will he catch up?' · 'An operation? He is only two' · 'Can we not just try another course of antibiotics first?' · 'How long will we wait to see the specialist?' · 'Is there anything I can do at home?' · and, tearful at about minute six, 'I keep thinking I should have brought him in sooner.'
pefe: Role-player: cooper's mother. He is 2 years 9 months and uses about six words — mum, dad, more, no, ball, dog — never putting two together, pointing and pulling her by the hand instead. Normal pregnancy and birth, passed the newborn hearing check, walked at 13 months, happy and sociable with plenty of eye contact. About eight ear infections in the past year with antibiotics every time, the last six months ago. Childcare two days a week. His father smokes, mostly outside but sometimes in the car. English at home plus Vietnamese from his grandmother, and he says little in either.

What she has noticed and what she hides: he often does not turn when called from another room, which she assumed was toddler behaviour; he turns the television up; he is increasingly frustrated. Her hidden agenda is a fear that he is autistic, after her neighbour's son was diagnosed last year — raised only if the doctor asks whether anything in particular is worrying her, or mentions development. She also carries guilt about not coming sooner, and becomes tearful once at about minute six.

How she plays it: anxious, articulate and paying close attention. When surgery is mentioned she pushes back once — 'An operation? He is only two' — and then asks for another course of antibiotics. She accepts the plan only if the doctor explains why antibiotics will not work. If they simply prescribe antibiotics to please her, she accepts cheerfully and marks them down for it.

Mark them against these: greeted her before turning to the examiner · validated her concern early · asked about dysmorphic features and growth centiles · asked about eye contact and response to name · asked otoscopy of both ears and characterised the drums · explicitly excluded redness, bulging, perforation and discharge · asked about the palate and tongue tie · asked about tone and reflexes · explained the audiogram axes before interpreting · narrated air, then bone, then the gap, for the right ear, and the same for the left · named bilateral conductive loss after the narration · mentioned the tympanograms · explained glue ear in plain English with no jargon · used the underwater analogy · explained that the nerve is normal · linked the hearing loss to the speech delay · told her it was not her fault · handled the autism worry seriously if raised · referred to ENT for grommets · referred to speech pathology as well and in parallel · said antibiotics will not fix this and explained why · held that position when pushed · mentioned a repeat hearing test · mentioned smoke avoidance and home strategies · and safety-netted and summarised.

back.dx: A SELF-LIMITING DIVERTICULAR BLEED THAT HAS STOPPED — but the clinical point the station is really testing is that fresh rectal bleeding in a 73-year-old is colorectal cancer until a lumen view says otherwise. A five-year-old colonoscopy showing diverticulosis does not exclude an interval cancer, and diverticular disease is so common that its presence proves nothing about the source of today's bleed VERIFY. Handing over 'Known diverticular bleed, settled, for discharge' without raising re-scoping closes a diagnosis on the telephone. The call: identify yourself by name and role, confirm who you are speaking to, and name the patient, the age and the bed. Situation in one sentence with your level of concern — 'He was admitted two days ago with fresh rectal bleeding, he has settled completely and he's stable. I'm calling because I think he's ready for discharge planning and I'd like your view on whether that happens today and what follow-up he needs.' Background: relevant only — the bleeding pattern, the five-year-old scope and the absence of a repeat, and the aspirin 100 mg named explicitly alongside the absence of any other agent that affects bleeding. Assessment: observations in a fixed order — temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, saturations, GCS — including the admission postural drop; the examination positives and relevant negatives; the haemoglobin with its trend and what you make of it; then your impression, which is the half candidates omit and where the marks are. Recommendation, which here has two parts: first a decision on discharge today after 48 stable hours with a stable haemoglobin, and second — the part that matters more — that he needs a colonoscopy, with an explicit ask about whether that is inpatient or booked as an outpatient before he leaves. Also flag the aspirin: the indication is not documented anywhere in the notes, and primary versus secondary prevention give different answers, so say you will check it rather than deciding blind added. His family history and screening status are also absent from the notes — saying so is better than assuming either way. Close with a read-back of the plan and the timeframe, and say who you will tell.
plan: READ THE NOTES BACKWARDS — the most recent progress note and observations tell you what you are handing over NOW; the admission note tells you how it started. Reading forwards through five pages means arriving at the current state with ninety seconds left.
PLAN THE CALL ON PAPER — one line per letter, and WRITE THE IMPRESSION AND THE ASK FIRST, because they are the two things you will otherwise leave out.
IDENTIFY — you, them, the patient, and the bed and ward. Ten to fifteen seconds, and do not apologise for calling.
SITUATION — one sentence, with your level of concern stated in words: stable, settling, ready for planning (see dx).
BACKGROUND — relevant only, with the aspirin and the absence of other bleeding agents said explicitly, and the five-year-old scope flagged.
ASSESSMENT — observations in order including THE ADMISSION POSTURAL DROP, examination, the haemoglobin trend with your reading of it, then YOUR IMPRESSION.
RECOMMENDATION — the two-part ask, with the colonoscopy as the substantive one, plus what has been done and what you will do meanwhile.
THE REGISTRAR'S QUESTIONS — expect three to five, answered in one sentence each.
READ BACK the plan and the timeframe, and state who you will tell.

ask: THE SENTENCE THAT SEPARATES REPORTING FROM HANDING OVER: 'MY CONCERN IS THAT THIS IS A SELF-LIMITING DIVERTICULAR BLEED THAT HAS STOPPED, AND WHAT I WOULD LIKE IS…' — an impression followed by an ask. Everything before that sentence is data, and data alone is what a fax does.

The substantive ask: 'He's 73 with rectal bleeding and his last scope was five years ago, so I don't think we can put this down to diverticular disease without looking. I'd like to know whether you want that as an inpatient or booked as an outpatient before he leaves.'

The honest line about the numbers: 'Repeat haemoglobin today is 129 — that's three down from admission, which I read as stable rather than an ongoing bleed.' and the one about the aspirin: 'I don't have the indication documented, so I'll check that.'
The close: 'Can I read that back to make sure I've got it?'

pefe: There is no examination task — the clinical notes are the data, and the skill is translating a document written in the order things happened into a call delivered in the order the listener needs them.

Role-player: the on-call surgical registrar — busy, not hostile, somewhere else in the hospital and unable to see the patient. Answers the phone with 'Surgical registrar.' and nothing else. Interrupts once early with 'Sorry — how sick is he? Do I need to come now?' and, if the candidate starts with the admission history rather than the current state, cuts in with 'Just tell me the obs first.'

How the registrar scores it in real time: if the candidate never gives an impression, ask 'So what do you think is going on?' and mark them down for having needed to be asked. If they never make a specific request, ask 'Ok — so what do you want me to do?' and mark them down. End with 'Anything else?' and wait to see whether they read back the plan.

back.dx: Contained ruptured infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm with haemorrhagic shock. Say the triad out loud, because it is what converts this from abdominal pain to a vascular emergency: pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass VERIFY. The call opens with identification and the request together: 'It's Dr [name], intern in the emergency department at [hospital]. I need you to come to resus now — I have a 65-year-old man with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm on ultrasound and he's hypotensive. Can I give you the details while you're on your way?' Situation: name, age, resus Bay, two hours of sudden severe central abdominal pain radiating to the back at 9 out of 10, now shocked, with an 8 cm infrarenal aneurysm and retroperitoneal blood on bedside ultrasound. Background: ex-smoker with twenty pack-years, hypertension on perindopril and atorvastatin, no anticoagulant and no antiplatelet said explicitly, no allergies, independent and well until two hours ago. Assessment: observations in order, the pallor and diaphoresis, the weak pulses and delayed capillary refill, the pulsatile mass, the lumbar tenderness, and the anuria since onset — then the impression stated as such. Recommendation, which is two questions rather than one: come and see him now, and tell me whether you are taking him straight to theatre or whether he needs retrieval to a vascular centre — followed by the list of what is already done so it is not repeated, and an explicit offer: 'Do you want me to activate the massive transfusion protocol and call MedSTAR while you're coming?' Two points the registrar may probe. First, resuscitation target: in ruptured AAA the aim before definitive repair is permissive hypotension — enough perfusion to maintain consciousness and urine output, not a normal blood pressure — because aggressive fluid loading raises pressure against a contained rupture, dislodges clot and worsens bleeding; say you would titrate to conscious state rather than to a number and confirm the current threshold against local protocol VERIFY. Second, rural reality: a rural site cannot repair this, so the call is actually two calls — the surgical or vascular registrar, and retrieval on MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 — and saying that you have started the retrieval conversation in parallel rather than sequentially is the point, because time to theatre is the outcome determinant and a candidate who waits for permission before ringing retrieval has lost time they cannot get back added. Close with a read-back and say that you will update his family.

back.dx: Upper gastrointestinal bleed, most likely an nsaid-induced peptic ulcer, currently haemodynamically stable. The aetiology is the whole story and fits in one line: longstanding reflux plus three weeks of NSAIDs two to three times daily with no gastroprotection. Naming that link is the assessment. Stopping the NSAID is part of the handover rather than an afterthought — the cause of the bleed is still being administered unless someone stops it, and saying 'I've stopped his nsaid' out loud demonstrates that you have identified the cause and acted on it, which is a scored behaviour. The call: identify yourself and the patient with the bed; situation in one sentence — 24 hours of melaena and postural dizziness, stable, awaiting endoscopy, and you are ringing to ask when that should happen and whether it needs to be tonight. Background: the reflux, the hypertension, and the NSAIDs given the weight they deserve, with the explicit absence of anticoagulant and antiplatelet; the family history of bowel cancer in his mother and the absence of any screening are worth flagging as an incidental issue for later rather than as the acute problem. Assessment: observations in fixed order, the mild pallor, the epigastric tenderness, the rectal finding of black tarry stool with no fresh blood, the two episodes of postural dizziness with none since admission and no haematemesis at any point — then the missing haemoglobin named plainly: 'I don't have his haemoglobin back yet — the bloods went at [time] and I'll ring you the moment I have it' — then the impression. Inventing a number, or quietly skipping it and hoping the registrar does not ask, both fail. Recommendation: a decision on the timing of endoscopy — tonight's list or tomorrow morning's — followed by what is already in place (Pantoprazole 40 mg IV, nil by mouth, IV access with fluids, two-hourly observations, stool chart), the fact that the NSAID has been stopped, and explicit call-back criteria: if he drops his pressure, has haematemesis, or when the haemoglobin arrives. The registrar may ask about risk scores for upper GI bleeding — Glasgow-Blatchford and Rockall exist and stratify the need for intervention, and the honest answer is to name them and say you would confirm the cut-offs before quoting them VERIFY. A transcription note in the source: the document header names the patient mr tony stark while the body of the history refers throughout to mr Z — use one name consistently, because the discrepancy is an artefact of the source rather than a detail of the case correction.

back.dx: BENIGN FAMILIAL MACROCEPHALY — a large head crossing up to a familial centile, with normal development, a soft flat fontanelle, a normal neurological examination and a macrocephalic parent. Macrocephaly means an ofc above the 97th centile or more than 2 SD; concern is proportional to the rate of crossing and to symptoms, and crossing two major centile lines warrants assessment. To Kate, in plain English: 'Noah does have a big head and the nurse was right to check, because the serious cause is fluid building up inside the skull. I have looked for the signs of that — a tight bulging soft spot, vomiting, drowsiness, eyes turning down, losing skills — and none are there. His body is growing normally, his development is on track, and Dave's head is also above the TOP line. Big heads run in families, and babies with a family big head grow into it in the first year, crossing the lines exactly as Noah has.' Differentials, each with its discriminator: hydrocephalus, obstructive or communicating — bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, sunset eyes, vomiting, irritability, rapid crossing, and a history of prematurity with IVH or past meningitis · benign enlargement of the subarachnoid spaces — often familial and self-limiting, with enlarged extra-axial spaces on ultrasound · subdural haematoma or effusion from non-accidental injury — irritability, retinal haemorrhages, bruises, an inconsistent history, and a mandatory report · intracranial mass or cyst — focal signs, regression, seizures · neurofibromatosis 1 — six or more cafe-au-lait spots, axillary freckling, family history · achondroplasia or skeletal dysplasia — short limbs, frontal bossing, short length · metabolic and storage disease such as glutaric aciduria or canavan — regression, hypotonia, dystonia · and overgrowth syndromes such as sotos — tall and large with developmental delay and facial features. Safety-netting is the other half of the diagnosis: return immediately for vomiting, drowsiness, irritability, a bulging soft spot, eyes turning down, a seizure, loss of skills, or a head growing faster than expected — and if the curve keeps diverging rather than running parallel, urgent paediatric review and MRI, with neurosurgery at WCH via MedSTAR if there is acute raised pressure.
plan: Open with the nurse's concern and the mother's own observations — 'The nurse asked me to see Noah about his head size; tell me what you have noticed.' She has noticed nothing, and saying so is itself a finding.

Birth and neonatal: gestation, birth weight and head circumference, instrumental or traumatic delivery, NICU, intraventricular haemorrhage if preterm, neonatal infection or meningitis, jaundice.
THE DECISIVE QUESTION: 'DO YOU OR HIS DAD HAVE BIG HEADS? WHAT HAT SIZE?' Then family history of hydrocephalus, neurofibromatosis, developmental delay or short stature.

back.dx: Ileocolic intussusception, peak incidence 6-18 months, with post-viral lymphoid hyperplasia as the lead point after last week's upper respiratory infection. The classic triad is intermittent colicky pain with pallor and drawing up the legs, vomiting that becomes bilious, and red-currant-jelly stool — but only about a third of children have all three, which is why the interval lethargy is the clue that actually discriminates. To Priya: 'Part of Oliver's bowel has slid into the next section, like a telescope. That explains the waves of pain when the bowel squeezes, the green vomit because the bowel is blocked, and the jelly-like blood because the trapped bowel oozes. His age and last week's cold fit — the glands in the bowel swell and act as the lead point.' Differentials with their discriminators: malrotation with midgut volvulus — bilious vomiting at any age, usually continuous pain without the episodic pattern, and a surgical emergency with the same first steps · incarcerated inguinal hernia — a groin lump, so always examine · acute gastroenteritis — no mass, no bile, watery stool rather than jelly · testicular torsion — scrotal swelling and tenderness in an inconsolable infant · meckel diverticulum — painless bleeding · henoch-schonlein purpura — purpuric rash and joint swelling, and itself a lead point · and sepsis, UTI or meningitis — lethargy and fever without the colic pattern. Management is a sequence, not a list: nil by mouth · IV access with FBE, UEC, glucose, venous gas and lactate, group and hold · a fluid bolus if compromised then maintenance with dextrose · nasogastric tube on free drainage if vomiting or distended · analgesia · urgent ultrasound for the target sign, which must not delay the referral · paediatric surgical referral now to WCH via MedSTAR · air (Pneumatic) enema reduction by radiology with the surgeon present as the definitive treatment · and operative reduction only if the enema fails or there is perforation, peritonitis or shock, in which case resuscitate, give broad-spectrum antibiotics and go straight to a theatre pathway. Safety-netting: observe 24 hours after reduction because about one in ten recur, and tell the mother explicitly that the same screaming episodes mean coming straight back.
