Vomit and stool, asked for specifically: how many vomits and what colour — milk turning bile-stained · last normal stool, diarrhoea, and any blood or mucus.
Hydration and intake: last feed tolerated, wet nappies in 12 hours, tears · then recent URTI or gastro in the last two weeks, and fever now.
Red flags for the other causes — groin or scrotal swelling, rash, trauma, ingestion — and background: birth, growth, development, previous abdominal surgery, rotavirus vaccine timing, family history.

The examination request as one run: appearance and hydration between episodes, vitals, abdomen for the mass and the empty right iliac fossa, peritonism, hernial orifices, testes, rectal examination, skin (see findings).
Name the diagnosis with three reasons and give the differentials in one breath each — volvulus and incarcerated hernia as the must-excludes (see dx).
Management in order: NBM · IV fluids and bloods · analgesia · NGT · ultrasound without delaying referral · the surgeon at WCH via MedSTAR · air enema with the surgeon present · theatre if it fails.

Explain the transfer to the mother — retrieval flies them both and she stays with him — then the 24-hour observation, the one-in-ten recurrence and the instruction to return immediately if the episodes restart.

dx: **Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction — ABO incompatibility from a MIS-IDENTIFIED UNIT.** **Fever, rigors, hypotension, loin or back pain and haemoglobinuria WITHIN THE FIRST 15–30 MINUTES.** **DIC and acute kidney injury follow.**

**THE FIRST SENTENCE MUST BE ‘STOP THE TRANSFUSION’ — before questions, before examination.** Then, in order, to the nurse: **‘Disconnect the giving set and KEEP THE PACK AND SET — don't discard them.’ · ‘Keep the cannula, flush with saline and start 0.9% saline VIA A NEW GIVING SET.’ · ‘ABC: oxygen if saturations under 94, full obs every 15 minutes, call the registrar and notify the blood bank.’ · ‘Check the patient's wristband against the blood pack label and the compatibility form WITH ME NOW.’**

**The three discriminators, in order**: **(1) STOP, first sentence. (2) CHECK THE IDENTITY of unit and patient and recognise the mismatch as the cause. (3) OPEN DISCLOSURE — tell Helen plainly that THE WRONG UNIT WAS GIVEN, rather than hiding behind ‘a reaction’.**

**THE FIVE REACTIONS** VERIFY — **ACUTE HAEMOLYTIC (ABO)**: fever, rigors, hypotension, loin or back pain, haemoglobinuria, oozing, identity mismatch. **FEBRILE NON-HAEMOLYTIC**: fever rise ≥1°C, chills, **no hypotension, otherwise well.** **ALLERGIC (mild)**: urticaria and itch, no systemic features. **ANAPHYLAXIS**: wheeze, stridor, angioedema, hypotension within minutes. **BACTERIAL CONTAMINATION (especially platelets)**: high fever, rigors, shock. **TACO**: dyspnoea, **HYPERTENSION**, raised JVP, crackles, elderly or cardiac. **TRALI**: hypoxia, bilateral infiltrates, fever, hypotension within 6 hours.
**TIME COURSE sorts them**: **haemolytic and anaphylaxis — MINUTES** · FNHTR — during or within 4 hours · **TACO and TRALI — within 6 hours** · **delayed haemolytic — 3 to 14 days.**

**RENAL PROTECTION, QUANTIFIED — this is a scored item, not a gesture.** **IV 0.9% saline bolus 500 mL to 1 L, then an infusion to maintain URINE OUTPUT ABOVE 1 mL/kg/h** — free haemoglobin is what damages the kidney. **Catheter and HOURLY urine measures.** **Consider furosemide 40 mg IV ONLY if oliguric DESPITE adequate filling.** VERIFY

**Escalate and report**: registrar and physician, **ICU or HDU review**; **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if deteriorating at a rural site; haematology advice via the blood service. **DIC — FFP, cryoprecipitate and platelets UNDER HAEMATOLOGY GUIDANCE ONLY.** **Notify the blood bank and Australian Red Cross Lifeblood, RETURN the unit and set, file an incident report, and expect a root-cause analysis of the identification error.**

**DO NOT RESTART ANY BLOOD until a full investigation is complete.** Re-crossmatch new units when needed. **Treat the anaemia later with correctly crossmatched blood or IV iron, and manage the menorrhagia that caused it.**

**OPEN DISCLOSURE, in these words**: **‘Helen, I need to explain what's happened. The blood you were being given was NOT the unit matched for you — the label has a different hospital number. Your immune system is breaking down those blood cells, which is causing the fever, the back pain and the dark urine. We've stopped it, we're giving you fluid to protect your kidneys, and we'll watch your blood counts, clotting and kidney function closely with the senior team. I'M SORRY THIS HAS HAPPENED; IT'S AN ERROR, AND IT WILL BE FULLY INVESTIGATED AND YOU'LL BE TOLD THE FINDINGS.’**

**Answering ‘Am I going to be all right?’**: **‘Most people recover with the treatment we've started, and we've caught it early. The next hours matter, so you'll be closely monitored, possibly in the high-dependency unit. No more blood will be given until everything has been re-checked. Would you like us to call your husband?’** **Then document, and inform next of kin with consent.**
plan: 0:00 — to the NURSE, before anything else

**‘STOP THE TRANSFUSION NOW. Disconnect the giving set and keep the pack and set — don't throw them away. Keep the cannula, flush it and start normal saline through a new giving set. Oxygen if her sats drop below 94, obs every 15 minutes, and call the registrar and the blood bank. I'm coming.’**
**‘Helen, I'm Dr ___. We've stopped the blood. Tell me what you're feeling.’** Let her give the sequence: **hot and shivery, then the back ache, then the pounding head, and she is frightened.**

**The anaphylaxis screen in one question**: **‘Any chest tightness, trouble breathing, itching or hives, swelling of the lips?’** → no. **That is TACO, TRALI and anaphylaxis screened in a single breath.**

**Timing and the first unit**: **‘How far into this unit did it start? How was the first unit?’** → about half an hour; the first was fine. **The first unit being uneventful is what makes a unit-specific problem likely.**

**Previous transfusions, pregnancies and allergies** — **pregnancies matter because of alloantibodies.** Then known antibodies, previous reactions, **IgA deficiency**, cardiac or renal disease for fluid tolerance, medications.

**‘Nurse, let's check her wristband against the pack together.’** Then to the examiner: **‘May I have the examination, THE URINE IN THE CATHETER BAG, and THE PACK LABEL CHECK?’** **Not asking for the urine and the label is a named trap.**

**Name it the moment the mismatch appears**: **‘This is an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction — the unit is not hers.’** Then the bloods **from the other arm**, the urine for haemoglobin, and **the pack and giving set to the blood bank.**

**The fluid order, with a number**: **‘Give a 500 mL saline bolus now and then run fluids to keep her urine output above about 70 mL an hour; measure it hourly. ECG for potassium.’** Then **call the physician and ICU, and notify the blood bank and the incident system.**
**Open disclosure — the apology, the mechanism in plain words, the plan, and the promise that she will be told the findings.**
**Answer ‘will I be all right’ honestly, offer to call Tom, and say you will come back as results arrive.** Then the examiner presentation if asked.

dx: **Rh(D) ALLOIMMUNISATION — a SENSITISED Rh-negative mother with an anti-D titre of 1:16 at 12 weeks. ★ THE PASS/FAIL HINGE IS RECOGNISING SENSITISED VERSUS UNSENSITISED. If you say 'we'll give you the anti-D injection at 28 weeks', the examiner marks the diagnosis as MISSED.**

**The sentence that carries the station**: **'this is NOT the routine anti-D injection situation — your body has ALREADY made antibodies, so this pregnancy needs specialist monitoring of the baby's blood count.'**

**THE MECHANISM, in her words**: **'fetal Rh-positive red cells crossed into your circulation in the last pregnancy — most likely at the fall or at the birth — and your immune system learned to make antibodies against them. In a normal Rh-negative pregnancy we give an anti-D injection to prevent exactly this. ONCE THE ANTIBODIES EXIST, THE INJECTION CANNOT UNDO THEM.'**

**THEN THE RISK, GRADED AND BALANCED**: **'in this pregnancy, if this baby is also Rh positive, those antibodies can cross the placenta and break down some of the baby's red blood cells. In mild cases the baby is a bit anaemic or jaundiced after birth; in more serious cases the baby can become anaemic before birth. Your level — 1 in 16 — is the point where we watch closely. The important thing is that we now have very good ways of monitoring and, if needed, TREATING THIS BEFORE BIRTH, and most babies do well.'** **Never give the risk without the second half — she is briefed to become tearful and ask 'should I not have this baby?'**
**DECLINE THE NEEDLE WITH THE REASON, NOT JUST A REFUSAL**: **'no — it wouldn't help now, and that's an important thing to understand. What helps is monitoring.'**

**THE HISTORY THAT MATTERS IS NOT A GENERIC ANTENATAL ONE. Hunt five things: SENSITISING EVENTS in the last pregnancy (antepartum haemorrhage, a fall, amniocentesis, ECV, miscarriage, termination, ectopic) · WHETHER ANTI-D WAS GIVEN, and within 72 hours · the PREVIOUS BABY'S blood group, jaundice, phototherapy or transfusion · the PARTNER'S blood group and whether it is the same father · and PREVIOUS BLOOD TRANSFUSIONS, the other route to sensitisation.** **Spending four minutes on a generic antenatal history is the named trap.**

**THE PATHWAY, IN ORDER. 1. REFER NOW to maternal-fetal medicine — do not wait for the next titre. 2. FETAL Rh STATUS by CELL-FREE FETAL DNA on maternal blood from about 12 weeks** VERIFY, **with the paternal group as a supplementary check only. IF THE FETUS IS Rh NEGATIVE THERE IS NO RISK AND SHE RETURNS TO ROUTINE CARE — say that early, because it is the most reassuring thing you can offer. 3. TITRES every 4 weeks to 28 weeks, then every 2 weeks** VERIFY. **4. MCA PEAK SYSTOLIC VELOCITY DOPPLER from 18–20 weeks, 1–2 weekly, with MoM >1.5 indicating moderate to severe anaemia.** VERIFY

**5. TREATMENT IF ANAEMIC: intrauterine (cordocentesis) transfusion at the tertiary centre. 6. BIRTH at a tertiary hospital with neonatology, generally 37–38 WEEKS** VERIFY, **with cord blood group, DAT, haemoglobin and bilirubin; phototherapy or exchange transfusion if needed, and IVIG in some protocols.** VERIFY

**7. ANTI-D PROPHYLAXIS IS NOT INDICATED. CORRECTION — this is the common error and the auto-fail.** **8. THE FUTURE: each subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy is usually MORE SEVERE, so preconception MFM counselling, partner testing, and documenting it on My Health Record or an alert card.**

**Do not neglect the rural logistics — it is a named fail risk.** She is from Kadina with a three-year-old and is worried about getting to Adelaide. SA: refer to **maternal-fetal medicine at the Women's and Children's Hospital**, or via the local obstetric unit; **PATS** for travel and accommodation; **Country Health Connect**; social work; partner involvement; a mental-health check; **TIS National 131 450**; ACCHS support if she identifies as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander. **Finish with a teach-back — ask her to say the plan in her own words.**
plan: **WIPE, congratulate, and signpost BEFORE the result**: **'your booking bloods are back and I'd like to go through one result carefully. Before that — how are you feeling?'** *'Fine, a bit of nausea. Is something wrong?'* → **'one result needs explaining and some planning, and I'll walk you through it.'**
**Confirm the basics quickly**: dates, LMP and dating scan, pregnancy symptoms, **any bleeding or pain now.** **Do not spend four minutes here.**

**★ THE PREVIOUS PREGNANCY — the block the station is built on**: **'do you know Liam's blood group?'** *No.* **'Did you have anti-D injections DURING that pregnancy — around 28 and 34 weeks?'** *'I don't think so — I moved practices.'*

**★ THE SENSITISING EVENT**: **'was there any bleeding, any fall, or any procedure during that pregnancy?'** *'I fell down the steps at about 30 weeks and went to hospital; they checked the heartbeat and sent me home.'* Then the question that completes it: **'WAS ANY INJECTION GIVEN AFTER THAT FALL?'** *No.*
**The previous baby's outcome**: **'was Liam jaundiced? Did he need lights, or a transfusion?'** *A bit yellow, no lights.* **And the delivery type.**

**The partner and the other routes**: **'is Liam's father also this baby's father, and do you know his blood group?'** *Same dad, group unknown.* **'Any miscarriages, terminations or ectopic pregnancies? Any amniocentesis or a procedure to turn the baby? And have you ever had a blood transfusion?'** *No to all.*

**Close the history**: past medical history, medications, allergies, smoking and alcohol, supports, **distance from the tertiary centre**, and Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander status for ACCHS support. Then **ideas and concerns: 'what have you heard about anti-D?'**

**★ THE EXPLANATION — name the sensitised status in the FIRST sentence**: **'your blood group is O negative, which we knew. What is NEW is that your blood contains antibodies against the D factor. That means some of Liam's blood mixed with yours — probably around that fall or at the birth — and your immune system learned to make antibodies against it.'**

**Then the key distinction, said plainly**: **'in a normal Rh-negative pregnancy we give an anti-D injection to prevent exactly this. Once the antibodies exist, the injection can't undo them. So this is a DIFFERENT situation from the routine anti-D pregnancy.'**

**She asks 'what does it do to this baby?' — give the graded risk**: if this baby is also Rh positive, the antibodies cross the placenta and break down some of the baby's red cells; **mildly, jaundice after birth; more seriously, anaemia before birth.** Then **the titre: 'your level is 1 in 16, which is the point where we watch closely.'**

**★ THE BALANCING SENTENCE — never omit it**: **'the important thing is that we now have very good ways of monitoring this, and of treating the baby before birth if we ever need to. Most babies in this situation do well.'**

**★ THE NEEDLE REQUEST — decline WITH the reason**: *'can you just give me the needle anyway?'* → **'no — it wouldn't help now, and that's an important thing to understand. What helps is monitoring.'**
**THE PLAN, STEP 1 — refer today**: **'I'll refer you today to the maternal-fetal medicine team at the Women's and Children's.'** **Not 'refer to the obstetrician' with no pathway.**

**STEP 2 — and lead with the reassuring possibility**: **'a blood test on YOU can tell us the baby's blood group from the baby's DNA in your blood. If the baby is Rh NEGATIVE, none of this applies and we go back to routine care.'** Add that **Josh's blood group is worth checking as a supplementary piece.**

**STEP 3 — the surveillance**: **'if the baby is Rh positive, we repeat your antibody level every four weeks, then every two weeks from 28 weeks. And from about 18 to 20 weeks the specialists do a Doppler ultrasound of a blood vessel in the baby's head that shows whether the baby is becoming anaemic.'**
**STEP 4 — she asks 'and if it is?'**: **'then the specialists can give the baby a blood transfusion through the cord, in the womb.'**

**STEP 5 — the birth**: **'birth would be planned at the Women's and Children's around 37 to 38 weeks, with the newborn team ready, and they check the baby's blood at birth — the group, the blood count and the jaundice level — and treat with lights or an exchange transfusion if needed.'**

**THE RURAL LOGISTICS — a named fail risk if skipped**: **PATS for travel and accommodation, Country Health Connect for follow-up, social work** — and answer her actual worry: **who cares for Liam while she travels.**

**THE FUTURE, then the TEACH-BACK**: **'any later pregnancy needs this same planning from the start, ideally before you conceive, and each Rh-positive pregnancy tends to be more affected than the last — so it's worth having this on your record.'** Then: **'can you tell me in your own words what the plan is?'** Written information, review in two weeks, and the WCH will call.

stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Frank Doyle, 67, a retired truck driver, returns for results. Four months of dull epigastric pain radiating to the back, worse after meals and lying flat, 8 kg weight loss, and two weeks of painless jaundice with pale stools and dark urine. New type 2 diabetes was diagnosed 3 months ago. He smokes 30 a day.

CT abdomen: a 3 cm hypodense mass in the head of the pancreas with dilatation of the common bile and pancreatic ducts — the double-duct sign · two indeterminate 8 mm liver lesions · encasement of the superior mesenteric vein over 180 degrees. LFTs: bilirubin 180, ALP 640, GGT 900, ALT 110. Ca 19-9 2,400.
Tasks: take a brief focused history (2 minutes) — explain the results and the most likely diagnosis to the patient — outline the next steps and management plan, addressing his questions.

back.dx: Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma, locally advanced with SMV encasement and possible liver metastases, causing obstructive jaundice, with new-onset diabetes as the herald in a heavy smoker. The sequence is the station: warning shot — 'Frank, I have the scan and blood results, and I am afraid it is serious news, not what either of us hoped for' · invitation — 'Would you like Maureen in the room?' · then the word itself: 'The scan shows a growth in the head of the pancreas, and with the jaundice, the weight loss and the blood marker I am almost certain this is cancer of the pancreas' · then stop. Silence, tissues, 'I am so sorry. Take your time.' Only then chunk and check: what the pancreas does and why his sugar Rose and he lost weight · why he is yellow and itchy, because the growth is blocking the bile duct · what the scan shows about spread, in plain words — wrapped around a large vein, with two small liver spots not yet certain · and what happens next. The pathway in patient order: confirm the diagnosis with EUS-guided fine needle aspiration and stage with a CT chest · take it to the multidisciplinary team at RAH or FMC, who are the decision-makers on surgery, not you · relieve the jaundice with an ERCP and a metal stent, which fixes the itch and makes him well enough for treatment · keep him strong with pancreatic enzyme replacement at every meal, a dietitian, diabetes optimisation and analgesia that actually works, with a coeliac plexus block later if needed · and involve palliative care now, framed explicitly as symptom expertise rather than surrender, because people seen early live better and often longer. Chemotherapy — folfirinox or gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel if he is fit — is the MDT's discussion VERIFY. The practical layer: INR and vitamin K before any procedure · a glucose plan · paracetamol then a low-dose opioid with a laxative and no NSAIDs VERIFY · driving advice while opioids are adjusted · smoking cessation, which genuinely improves treatment tolerance · Trousseau DVT awareness · a mood and risk check · carer support, centrelink and financial counselling · advance care planning over time · a cancer nurse, cancer council SA 13 11 20, PATS for Adelaide travel · and GP review within days, sooner for fever or rigors.

Warning shot, then the invitation to have Maureen in the room — he declines, which is his choice and should be respected, not overridden.
SAY IT: CANCER OF THE PANCREAS. THEN STOP TALKING. Silence, tissues within reach, 'I am so sorry.' The commonest error here is filling the silence with the plan.
When he asks about his brother, acknowledge it and separate it gently: 'I can hear how frightening that is' — and later, 'Your brother's story is not automatically yours.'
Chunk and check the explanation: what the pancreas does, why he is yellow, what the scan shows about the vein and the liver spots (see findings).

THE PATHWAY IN FIVE NUMBERED STEPS — BIOPSY AND CT CHEST, MDT, STENT, NUTRITION AND ENZYMES AND DIABETES AND PAIN, PALLIATIVE CARE NOW (see dx). Do not promise surgery; name the MDT as the decision-maker.

The prognosis answer when he asks, bounded and honest: months to a year or two rather than many years when it cannot be removed — depending on the biopsy, the liver spots and his response — with three promises: straight answers, symptom control, and him in charge of decisions.

What happens this week: clotting and vitamin K today · enzymes, sugar and analgesia started · calls to the surgical unit and cancer nurse · PATS and cancer council 13 11 20 · review in three days · and the same-day return rule for fever or shivers.

back.dx: MILD VIRAL UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION, ALREADY IMPROVING — and a hidden agenda: a backdated certificate for an exam missed before the illness began, which he missed because of exam panic. The rule, which must be said plainly: a medical certificate is a legal document, so you certify the date you saw him, the findings you made, and your opinion on fitness from today — and you never backdate the date of examination or state as fact anything you did not observe (Ahpra good medical practice and medical board guidance on certificates) VERIFY. What you can write: a certificate dated today stating you examined him today and found a mild viral illness, unfit for study for a day or two from today · a clearly labelled line of reported history — 'Mr Reid reports that he has been unwell since Thursday with sore throat and fatigue' · and a factual letter for the special-consideration panel setting out his account and today's findings. What you cannot: certify unfitness on a day you did not see him as fact, backdate the consultation, invent findings, or retrospectively certify 'Unfit for exam'. How to say it: 'I can only certify what I have seen — I saw you today. What I cannot do is write, as if I had examined you, that you were unfit on Tuesday. That is not me doubting you — it is the rule every doctor works under, and a backdated certificate can void your application and get us both in trouble.' then the thing that turns a refusal into help: an honest letter about exam panic is a legitimate ground for special consideration and is often stronger than a cold. Differentials for the illness itself: infectious mononucleosis — exudative tonsillitis, posterior nodes, splenomegaly, weeks of fatigue · streptococcal pharyngitis — fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough · influenza or COVID — fever, myalgia, cough, test if in window · and the real differential for the missed exam, which is exam-related anxiety, panic or depression, or a substance-related night. Management: symptomatic care with fluids, rest, paracetamol or ibuprofen, saline spray and lozenges, and no antibiotics VERIFY · safety-net for fever, tonsillar exudate, neck swelling, prolonged fatigue or breathing difficulty, with EBV serology then · treat the anxiety as the main problem, with a mental-health assessment and GP mental-health treatment plan, free and fast university counselling, study skills and headspace for 12-25 · assess risk first if there is hopelessness or self-harm ideation, before any paperwork · keep the diagnosis off the certificate unless he consents, and ask him · keep a copy in the notes · and review in a week or sooner.

The mental-health screen, which is expected and separately marked: mood, anhedonia, panic before exams, sleep, concentration, hopelessness, self-harm thoughts, supports — plus previous missed exams, workload, hours and financial stress.

back.dx: SPASTIC DIPLEGIC CEREBRAL PALSY SECONDARY TO PERIVENTRICULAR LEUKOMALACIA OF PREMATURITY — legs more than arms, velocity-dependent hypertonia, hyperreflexia, clonus, scissoring and persistent primitive reflexes, with motor delay but preserved social, visual and communication milestones. The explanation, in plain words: 'Cerebral palsy is the name for a group of conditions that affect movement and posture, caused by an injury to the developing brain — in Liam's case the areas that control the legs, damaged around the time of his very early birth by the bleeding and the fragile blood supply premature brains have. The MRI shows exactly that pattern.' then the three sentences the examiner is listening for: 'It happened once and it does not get worse — it is not a disease that spreads. What changes is how it shows up as he grows, which is why the stiffness is more obvious now than at three months.' · 'Spastic means the muscles are tight; diplegic means mainly the legs, with the arms much less affected — and children with this pattern usually have normal or near-normal thinking, which his smiling, babbling and reaching support.' · 'This is nobody's fault — nothing you did or did not do in pregnancy or since caused this.' On walking, honest and bounded: most children with diplegia do walk — some independently, some with a frame or sticks and a wheelchair for distance — the picture is clearer by two to three years, and sitting unaided by two is a good predictor and exactly what therapy targets now VERIFY. What to exclude: hereditary spastic paraplegia or leukodystrophy — progressive with regression and a family history · a spinal cord lesion such as a tethered cord — legs only with sphincter or back signs · dopa-responsive dystonia — diurnal variation, worth a levodopa trial · global developmental delay or a genetic syndrome — all domains delayed, dysmorphism · and muscular dystrophy — weakness and hypotonia rather than spasticity, check ck. Any loss of skills means this is not cerebral palsy and needs urgent neurology. The team and the plan: paediatrician as coordinator with paediatric neurology and rehabilitation at WCH, and SA cp register notification · physiotherapy for goal-directed task-specific practice, positioning, standing frames and ankle-foot orthoses when standing · occupational therapy for hand function, equipment and home adaptations · speech pathology for feeding and later communication · NDIS early childhood approach for under-sixes as the funding route, applied for today, with novita or kids plus, country health connect, telehealth therapy and PATS for Adelaide trips · spasticity management later with botulinum toxin to calves and adductors from about two years, casting, and oral baclofen if generalised · orthopaedic hip surveillance, because spastic hips sublux silently · and comorbidity surveillance across ophthalmology for the esotropia, audiology, epilepsy vigilance, growth and nutrition, reflux, constipation, dental, sleep and pain. And the family is part of the plan: written information, carer gateway, carer allowance, a separate appointment for Sarah's own sleep and mood, and an offer to go through it all again with her husband present.

dx: **Acute periapical (dentoalveolar) abscess of the lower left first molar, with LOCALISED BUCCAL-SPACE CELLULITIS, systemic features and MILD TRISMUS.**

**THE THREE DISCRIMINATORS**: **(1) check the airway-threatening spread — floor of mouth, tongue elevation, drooling, dysphagia, voice change, stridor, severe trismus = LUDWIG'S ANGINA or a deep neck space infection, and that is an emergency.** **(2) Recognise that THE GP CANNOT CURE A DENTAL ABSCESS — antibiotics are an adjunct; definitive treatment is DRAINAGE or EXTRACTION by a dentist.** **(3) SOLVE THE ACCESS PROBLEM — public dental emergency pathway, cost, transport, PATS.**

**‘Candidates who write amoxicillin and “see a dentist” fail on BOTH counts.’** Say the negatives of the airway screen out loud, then say plainly that the dentist is the treatment, **and show him how he gets there.**

**Explaining it**: **‘You have an abscess — a pocket of pus — at the root of that broken tooth, and the infection has spread into the cheek. The tooth is DEAD and infected, and ANTIBIOTICS ALONE WON'T FIX IT: the pus has to be drained and the tooth root-treated or, more likely, taken out by a dentist. What I can do today is get the infection under control, get you pain relief that's safe, and get you to a dentist quickly and affordably. The one thing I've checked carefully is that the infection hasn't spread under your tongue or into your neck, because that can block the airway — yours hasn't.’**

**ANALGESIA — the combination, and it beats either alone for dental pain**: **paracetamol 1 g QID PLUS ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food.** VERIFY **Warn of the paracetamol maximum of 4 g a day — he is taking ten tablets daily.** **AVOID escalating opioids.**

**ANTIBIOTICS AS ADJUNCT, because of the spreading swelling and fever**: **amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days PLUS metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5 days.** VERIFY **NO ALCOHOL with metronidazole.** **Clindamycin 300 mg 8-hourly if penicillin allergic.** **IV benzylpenicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate or clindamycin AND admission if systemic toxicity, more than moderate trismus, or deep space involvement.**

**THE ACCESS PLAN, which is half the station**: **Health Care Card → eligible for SA DENTAL SERVICE EMERGENCY CARE. PHONE THE REGIONAL COMMUNITY DENTAL CLINIC NOW for an urgent appointment within 24–48 hours.** Explain the private alternative and its cost. **PATS if referred to the Adelaide Dental Hospital.** Aboriginal dental programs where applicable. **ASK ABOUT TRANSPORT — community transport, or family.** *His brother can drive him.*

**Also**: warm salt-water mouth rinses, soft diet, fluids, keep hygiene up · **if fluctuant and accessible intra-orally, incision and drainage can be done under local anaesthetic; otherwise extraction IS the drainage** · **review in 48 hours, or by phone** · **medical certificate.**

**THE RED FLAGS, given verbatim**: **‘Go straight to emergency, day or night, if the swelling moves UNDER YOUR TONGUE or INTO YOUR NECK, you CAN'T SWALLOW YOUR SPIT, you DROOL, your VOICE CHANGES, you CAN'T OPEN YOUR MOUTH TWO FINGERS, the swelling reaches your EYE, or you get SHAKING CHILLS.’**

**Prevention, raised without moralising**: **smoking cessation (Quitline 13 7848) — ‘the smoking is the biggest thing for your gums, when you're ready’** · sugar reduction · brushing and fluoride · regular dental checks.
plan: **The pain** — site, character (throbbing, **worse lying down and at night**, hot or cold sensitivity), duration, previous episodes, **the broken tooth history**, and **the over-the-counter analgesia with doses.**
**The swelling** — onset, **spread: cheek, under the jaw, neck, eye** · **trismus in finger widths** · bad taste or discharge, which means spontaneous drainage.

**THE AIRWAY AND DEEP-SPACE SCREEN, asked as the SECOND question of the consultation**: **‘Any trouble swallowing your spit? Any drooling? Any muffled or “hot potato” voice? Does your tongue feel pushed up? Any neck stiffness? Any difficulty breathing, or lying flat?’**
**Systemic**: fever, rigors, malaise, appetite. *He was hot and sweaty last night.*
**Dental history and the barriers**: last visit, hygiene, other bad teeth, dentures — **and then the barriers explicitly: cost, distance, fear.** *Ten years, cost, and 90 km.*

**Medical**: **diabetes, immunosuppression** · **heart valve disease or a prosthetic valve** for endocarditis considerations · **bleeding disorders or anticoagulants**, because extraction is coming · allergies, particularly penicillin · medications.

**Social and habits**: smoking, alcohol, sugar-sweetened drinks, **methamphetamine — ‘meth mouth’** · **Health Care Card status for public dental eligibility** · transport · work impact · living alone.

**Ask for the examination, naming the airway items**: **‘I'd like the facial and intra-oral findings, SPECIFICALLY the floor of the mouth, tongue position, trismus, swallowing, voice, and any neck or periorbital swelling, plus vitals and a fingerprick glucose.’**
**Name it, state the airway negatives out loud, and say plainly that antibiotics won't cure it.** Then the differentials.
**The access plan — phone the clinic in the room** — then the analgesia correction, the antibiotics, the rinses, the bloods, the 48-hour review, and the red flags.

back.dx: LARYNGOMALACIA — the commonest cause of chronic infant stridor, where soft supraglottic tissues collapse inward on inspiration: onset at 2-4 weeks, inspiratory, positional, in a thriving infant, self-resolving by 12-24 months. To Bec: 'The tissue at the TOP of the voice box is soft and floppy in the first months, so when he breathes in — especially on his back, feeding or upset — it gets sucked inward and makes that squeak. It is not an infection, it is not croup, and it is not his windpipe collapsing. He is feeding beautifully, gaining weight, pink, and the noise vanishes when he is upright or asleep. The tissue stiffens as he grows — it usually peaks around six to eight months and is gone by his first or second birthday.' The differentials, dismissed with reasons rather than listed: tracheomalacia — present from birth, expiratory or biphasic, rattly with a washing-machine cough · croup — acute, febrile, barking cough in a 6-month to 3-year-old, not a chronic noise from two weeks of age · vascular ring — biphasic with feeding difficulty, dysphagia and recurrent chest infections · subglottic haemangioma — biphasic and worsening between one and three months, with a cutaneous haemangioma in the beard distribution in about half · vocal cord palsy — from birth, weak or hoarse cry, aspiration, after forceps or cardiac surgery · subglottic stenosis — biphasic after neonatal intubation · foreign body — sudden onset in an older infant · and epiglottitis or bacterial tracheitis — acute, toxic, drooling, an emergency. The diagnosis is clinical; flexible nasolaryngoscopy by ENT confirms it with an omega-shaped epiglottis and prolapsing arytenoids, and imaging or bronchoscopy is for atypical features only. Management: no treatment today, but warn that the noise usually gets louder before it improves and is worse with colds, which is expected rather than deterioration · feeding upright and paced, smaller and more frequent if he tires, frequent burping and 20-30 minutes upright afterwards · conservative reflux measures, with acid suppression only for clear GORD VERIFY · safe sleep, which is the second scoring point: on his back in his own cot despite the noise, because prone sleeping on a parent's chest is a SIDS risk — said with empathy, acknowledging why she does it · fortnightly weights with CaFHS · ENT referral for poor weight gain or feeding difficulty, apnoea or cyanosis, stridor with retractions at rest, worsening beyond expectations, cough or aspiration, hoarse cry, any haemangioma, or parental anxiety, with supraglottoplasty for the roughly 10% who are severe VERIFY · and red flags straight to emergency: blue or grey colour, pauses in breathing, sucking in at the ribs or neck when calm, fast breathing at rest, refusing feeds, fever with a barking cough, drooling or lethargy. Review in 4 weeks with a written factsheet, a smoke-free home and immunisations on time.

Vitals: HR 92 · BP 124/78 · RR 16 · SpO2 99% · T 36.9. He is walking and talking.

findings: Primary survey and general

Airway, breathing and circulation intact · GCS 15 · no cervical spine tenderness · comfortable at rest, not pale or sweaty, vitals as per the stem. Say 'Primary survey intact, proceeding to a focused secondary examination' out loud — it is a scored sentence
Inspection, including the back you have to roll him for

An 8 cm bruise over the left flank and lower ribs in a developing grey turner pattern, abrasions to the left forearm · no seat-belt or handlebar mark · abdomen not distended. He will not volunteer his back — 'Can you roll onto your right side for me'
Palpation and percussion

Tender left flank and left upper quadrant with no guarding and no rebound · no palpable mass and no ballottable kidney · left renal angle markedly tender to fist percussion, right side normal — percuss both and compare · resonant with no shifting dullness, bowel sounds present
The chest, pelvis and perineum

Tenderness over left ribs 10-11 with no crepitus, equal air entry, no surgical emphysema · pelvis stable on a single gentle compression · no perineal or scrotal bruising, no blood at the meatus, testes normal — check the meatus before anyone mentions a catheter
The urine and the bedside tests
Frank haematuria with no clots on inspection · dipstick large blood · fingerprick Hb 138 · fast shows no free fluid — which does not exclude renal injury and is not the definitive test

back.dx: BLUNT LEFT RENAL TRAUMA — contusion or laceration — with gross haematuria in a haemodynamically stable patient, plus probable left lower rib fractures and a splenic injury still to exclude. To Tom: 'You landed hard on your left side and there is bruising over the left kidney, tenderness over the kidney, and blood in your urine. That tells me the kidney has been bruised or torn. You are stable, which is reassuring, but blood in the urine after this kind of injury always needs a CT with contrast dye — it shows how deep any tear goes, whether the drainage system is leaking urine, and whether the spleen next door is injured.' The investigation must be named precisely: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast, arterial and portal venous plus a 10-minute delayed excretory phase to detect collecting-system or ureteric leak, with a chest x-ray and CT chest if rib fractures are suspected. Ultrasound or non-contrast CT as the definitive test is a marked error. Differentials with discriminators: splenic injury — left upper quadrant tenderness, referred left shoulder tip pain, tachycardia or hypotension, positive fast · rib fractures with pneumothorax or haemothorax — rib tenderness, crepitus, reduced air entry · bladder or urethral injury — pelvic fracture, blood at the meatus, inability to void, perineal bruising · hollow viscus injury — peritonism, evolving pain, free air · and musculoskeletal contusion alone, which does not produce gross haematuria and so does not excuse skipping imaging. Immediate management: two IV cannulas with FBE, UEC, group and hold, coags and a venous gas and lactate · urinalysis · nil by mouth until the CT is reviewed · analgesia with IV paracetamol and titrated opioid, avoiding NSAIDs while bleeding and renal injury are in play · tetanus status for the abrasions. Disposition by grade: stable grades i-iii are managed non-operatively with admission, bed rest until the gross haematuria clears, serial haemoglobin, hourly to two-hourly observations, repeat examination and urology notification · grades iv-v, haemodynamic instability or an expanding haematoma mean resuscitation, massive transfusion if needed, and urology with interventional radiology for angioembolisation or laparotomy, transferred to the RAH trauma service via MedSTAR. Discharge advice when the time comes: no contact sport or heavy lifting for 4-6 weeks, return for increasing flank pain, fever, recurrent haematuria or dizziness, follow-up imaging for grade III and above, and a blood pressure check at follow-up for post-traumatic hypertension VERIFY.
plan: Introduce, consent, warn it may be tender, wash hands, expose chest to groin, lie him flat with one pillow.

The scored sentence: 'From the triage sheet — airway patent, breathing and circulation stable, GCS 15, no neck tenderness. Primary survey is intact, so I will proceed to a focused secondary examination.' then general appearance, pallor, sweating and repeated vitals.
Inspection front, then roll him: bruising including grey turner in the flank and Cullen periumbilically, abrasions, seat-belt or handlebar marks, distension, asymmetry, penetrating wounds.

Palpation starting away from the pain — light then deep in four quadrants, guarding, rebound, rigidity, masses including an expanding flank haematoma, liver, spleen, bimanual ballottement of the kidneys, bladder.
Renal angle percussion on both sides with a comparison stated · then percussion for shifting dullness and auscultation for bowel sounds and bruits.

The chest and pelvis: palpate ribs 9-12 for tenderness and crepitus, compare air entry, feel for surgical emphysema · a single gentle pelvic compression · perineal and scrotal bruising, blood at the meatus, testes — PR only if pelvic or urethral injury is suspected.
Look at the urine yourself, then request dipstick, fingerprick haemoglobin or venous gas, and a bedside fast — and summarise the findings to the examiner as a trauma summary.

To the patient: the provisional diagnosis, the CT with contrast and delayed phase and why, then IV access, bloods, analgesia, nil by mouth, admission with serial haemoglobin, urology, and the transfer criteria — finishing with the four-to-six-week activity restriction and return advice.

stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Emily Ross, 24, a hairdresser, presents with a 3-month itchy rash in the elbow creases, behind the knees and on the neck and eyelids, worse at night. She scratches until it bleeds and sleeps poorly.

She has hay fever and had 'Baby eczema'. She has been using a supermarket moisturiser and a 1% hydrocortisone cream 'When it's bad'. A photograph of the antecubital fossae is provided: ill-defined erythematous, excoriated, lichenified plaques with some crusting.
Tasks: take a focused history (4 minutes) — describe the rash to the examiner and state your diagnosis with differentials — explain the diagnosis and management to the patient.

findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: THE PHOTOGRAPH — describe it with the formula, do not say ‘red itchy rash’
SITE → DISTRIBUTION → MORPHOLOGY (macule/papule/plaque) → COLOUR → SURFACE (scale, crust, excoriation, lichenification) → BORDER → SECONDARY CHANGE → ASSOCIATED FEATURES
The description, word for word

‘SYMMETRICAL, BILATERAL ANTECUBITAL FOSSAE. ILL-DEFINED ERYTHEMATOUS PLAQUES with LICHENIFICATION — thickened skin with accentuated markings — multiple LINEAR EXCORIATIONS, and on the left several HONEY-COLOURED CRUSTS suggesting SECONDARY BACTERIAL INFECTION. No vesicles, pustules or scale, no punched-out erosions. In keeping with chronic flexural atopic dermatitis with impetiginisation’
Skin examination on request
Flexural lichenified plaques with excoriations. A FEW HONEY-COLOURED CRUSTS on the LEFT antecubital fossa. NO VESICLES. No pustules
The negatives that exclude the differentials
NAIL PITTING ABSENT · NO SCALY SCALP · PALMS CLEAR · NO BURROWS IN THE WEB SPACES. Those four exclude psoriasis, seborrhoeic dermatitis and scabies in one sweep
Vitals and nodes
TEMPERATURE 36.8, NO LYMPHADENOPATHY — she is not systemically unwell
What you are LOOKING FOR and did NOT find
NO MONOMORPHIC PUNCHED-OUT VESICLES OR EROSIONS. That is ECZEMA HERPETICUM, and excluding it explicitly is part of the description
The treatment history — ask exactly what, how much, how often, how long
A SUPERMARKET MOISTURISER ‘when I remember’ and 1% HYDROCORTISONE ‘when it's bad’. THAT IS UNDER-TREATMENT, and it is why it ‘never works’. You cannot diagnose under-treatment without asking HOW MUCH
Steroid phobia — ask it DIRECTLY
‘How do you feel about steroid creams?’ → ‘I've read they thin your skin.’ If you do not ask, she will not tell you, and she will not use what you prescribe
The occupation
HAIRDRESSER — WET HANDS ALL DAY, rarely gloves. Long hot showers. Irritant and allergic contact overlap, and a patch-test question
Swab and bloods
SWAB THE CRUSTED AREA FIRST, then treat. No routine bloods

dx: **Adult atopic dermatitis — flexural, lichenified — with likely SECONDARY STAPHYLOCOCCAL INFECTION (impetiginisation) of the left elbow.**

**THE FIVE DISCRIMINATORS**: **(1) describe the rash SYSTEMATICALLY; (2) recognise the atopic triad and the FLEXURAL pattern; (3) treat with the RIGHT-POTENCY topical steroid, NOT 1% hydrocortisone, plus a proper emollient regimen; (4) spot the IMPETIGINISED patch and treat it; (5) the OCCUPATIONAL trigger — wet work as a hairdresser.**

**THE EXAMINER IS LISTENING FOR POTENCY.** **Naming a MODERATE–POTENT steroid for the body and a MILD one for the face, used DAILY UNTIL CLEAR, alongside a QUANTIFIED emollient regimen.** **Candidates who prescribe ‘hydrocortisone cream and moisturiser’ repeat the failed plan.**

**Explaining it**: **‘Eczema is a condition where the SKIN BARRIER IS LEAKY and the immune system in the skin OVER-REACTS — it isn't an infection or an allergy to one thing. It runs with hay fever and asthma. It's CONTROLLED RATHER THAN CURED, and the two pillars are restoring the barrier with moisturiser and calming the flare with the right-strength steroid cream used properly.’**

**PILLAR ONE — EMOLLIENT, QUANTIFIED**: thick, fragrance-free (sorbolene with glycerine, or an ointment), **twice daily to the WHOLE BODY and after every wash — 250 to 500 g PER WEEK for an adult.** VERIFY **Soap substitute, short lukewarm showers, pat dry, cotton clothing.** To her: **‘a 500-gram tub should last about a week or two.’**

**PILLAR TWO — POTENCY MATCHED TO SITE**: **TRUNK AND LIMBS — moderate/potent: methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% or mometasone 0.1% ONCE DAILY.** **FACE, EYELIDS AND NECK — mild to moderate: hydrocortisone 1% or desonide.** VERIFY **Use ENOUGH — a fingertip unit — daily for one to two weeks until clear, then TWICE-WEEKLY ‘weekend’ maintenance on trouble spots.** **1% hydrocortisone on lichenified elbows is too weak, and that is why it never works.**

**Answering steroid phobia with a SPECIFIC safety explanation, not reassurance**: **‘Skin thinning happens with STRONG steroids used CONTINUOUSLY on THIN skin for MONTHS. Used this way — to clear a flare and then stopped — it's safe, and the untreated scratching does more damage.’**

**THE INFECTION**: the crusted left elbow — **swab first, then flucloxacillin 500 mg QID for 7 days** VERIFY **(cephalexin if penicillin allergic).** **Dilute bleach baths twice weekly for recurrent infection.** VERIFY

**The rest**: **sedating antihistamine at night SHORT TERM — for sleep, NOT for the itch itself** · keep nails short · **wet wraps for a severe flare** · **face and eyelids: if a steroid is needed beyond two weeks, a calcineurin inhibitor — pimecrolimus 1% or tacrolimus** VERIFY · **OCCUPATION: nitrile gloves with COTTON LINERS for wet work, hand emollient at every break, consider occupational advice, and PATCH TESTING via dermatology for PPD, fragrance and preservatives.**

**Step-up via dermatology**: phototherapy, methotrexate or ciclosporin, **dupilumab under PBS criteria.** VERIFY **Give a WRITTEN ECZEMA ACTION PLAN and review in 2 weeks.** **RED FLAGS — same day: fever, a rapidly spreading painful rash, CLUSTERS OF SMALL BLISTERS OR PUNCHED-OUT SORES (eczema herpeticum), and eye involvement.**
plan: **The rash** — onset, **sites over time**, **itch severity and timing**, **sleep loss**, bleeding or weeping, **any blisters**, **fever or feeling unwell** (herpeticum).
**The atopic background** — childhood eczema, asthma, hay fever, food allergy, **family atopy.** *Baby eczema, spring hay fever, mother has asthma.*
**Triggers** — heat, sweat, wool, soaps, **hot showers**, stress, seasonal — **and the occupation: hairdresser, wet work, shampoos, dyes, gloves?**

**TREATMENTS — EXACTLY what, HOW MUCH, HOW OFTEN, HOW LONG.** *Supermarket moisturiser ‘when I remember’, 1% hydrocortisone ‘when it's bad’.* **That answer IS the diagnosis of under-treatment.** Also emollient type and frequency, over-the-counter or ‘natural’ remedies, previous steroid courses.
**Infection** — crusting, oozing, pain, spreading redness, **cold sores in the household.**
**Impact and background** — work, relationships, mood, cost · PMHx, medications, allergies, **pregnancy plans, because they affect therapy choice** · smoking and alcohol.

**Steroid phobia, asked directly**: **‘How do you feel about steroid creams?’** → *‘I've read they thin your skin.’* **Surface it now, answer it in the management block — do not discover it after you have prescribed.**

dx: **Erythema nodosum — a SEPTAL PANNICULITIS — as an EXTRA-INTESTINAL MANIFESTATION of NEW INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE.** Bloody diarrhoea, urgency, left lower quadrant pain, weight loss, an oral ulcer and peripheral arthritis **favour ulcerative colitis (or Crohn's colitis).**

**THE EXAMINER IS SCORING WHETHER YOU TREAT THE SHIN LUMPS AS A SIGN, NOT A DIAGNOSIS.** The bowel history must be taken **PROACTIVELY**, and the EN cause list run through. **The second scoring point is INFECTION BEFORE IMMUNOSUPPRESSION — stool cultures and C. difficile before steroids — and a SEVERITY ASSESSMENT to decide outpatient versus admission.**

**THE THREE-LAYER DIFFERENTIAL — think in this order.** **WHAT ARE THE LUMPS?** erythema nodosum · cellulitis (unilateral, spreading) · superficial thrombophlebitis or DVT · **nodular vasculitis / erythema induratum (POSTERIOR calves, they ULCERATE, TB)** · insect bites · other panniculitis. **WHY HAS SHE GOT EN?** **IBD · streptococcal pharyngitis · sarcoidosis · drugs (OCP, sulfonamides) · TB · PREGNANCY · mycoplasma, Yersinia, Campylobacter · Behçet · lymphoma · IDIOPATHIC in up to half.** **WHAT IS THE BOWEL DISEASE?** ulcerative colitis · Crohn's colitis · infective colitis · coeliac · microscopic colitis · colorectal cancer · **and IBS does NOT bleed or cause weight loss.**

**The description, word for word**: **‘Bilateral, symmetrical, tender, warm, erythematous subcutaneous nodules 2 to 4 cm in diameter on the anterior shins, poorly demarcated, non-ulcerated, some evolving to a bruise-like yellow-purple colour — the appearance of erythema nodosum. Combined with three months of bloody diarrhoea, weight loss, an aphthous ulcer and peripheral arthritis, the likely underlying cause is inflammatory bowel disease, probably ulcerative colitis.’**

**Explaining it to Zoe**: **‘The lumps on your shins are called erythema nodosum — inflammation of the fat under the skin. They're NOT DANGEROUS THEMSELVES and they fade like bruises over a few weeks, but they're A SIGNAL THAT SOMETHING IS INFLAMED ELSEWHERE, and the bowel symptoms you've described are the likely reason. Three months of bloody diarrhoea with urgency, weight loss, mouth ulcers and joint pains fits inflammatory bowel disease — most likely ulcerative colitis, where the lining of the large bowel becomes inflamed. IT'S A LONG-TERM CONDITION BUT VERY TREATABLE, and people live full lives with it.’**

**SEVERITY TODAY, out loud**: six stools a day with blood, **but HR 88 and T 37.6 → MODERATE.** **Check Hb, CRP and albumin.** **ADMIT if severe criteria are met: ≥6 bloody stools PLUS HR >90, T >37.8, Hb <105, or raised CRP/ESR.** VERIFY **Ask the severity questions directly: nocturnal stools, fever, dizziness on standing, inability to keep fluids down.**

**DO NOT START STEROIDS before infection is excluded and gastroenterology is contacted, unless she is severe.** **Initial UC treatment after diagnosis is usually ORAL PLUS RECTAL 5-ASA (mesalazine), with ORAL PREDNISOLONE 40 mg for moderate–severe flares** VERIFY **— and that can begin on gastro advice once the stool tests are back.**

**THE NSAID TRAP, and it is specific to this case**: **NSAIDs are usually first line for erythema nodosum — but AVOID THEM HERE, because they worsen IBD.** **Stop her ibuprofen, use paracetamol, and manage the EN with REST, LEG ELEVATION and COMPRESSION STOCKINGS. The EN settles as the colitis is treated.**

**Before immunosuppression — a whole block candidates forget**: **vaccination review (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID, hepatitis B, HPV, varicella status), TB and hepatitis screening, contraception counselling, and document the smoking status.** **Smoking is PROTECTIVE in UC and HARMFUL in Crohn's — ask.** **Iron replacement (IV if intolerant or severe) once the bleeding is controlled. Dietitian — and AVOID RESTRICTIVE DIETS.**

**Support and safety-net**: **Crohn's & Colitis Australia**, a work certificate, a mental-health check, and an explanation of the **chronic flare–remission course and later cancer surveillance.** **Review in 1 week with results, sooner if worse.** **RED FLAGS TO ED: fever, more than 8 stools a day, severe pain or distension, dizziness, heavy bleeding.** SA — gastroenterology via **RAH or FMC outpatients or telehealth, with PATS.**

**THE DISCRIMINATOR, in one line: name PPD, explain delayed allergy and PERMANENT sensitisation, treat with a moderate-potent topical steroid to the neck and ears and a mild one to the eyelids (or a short oral prednisolone course if the facial oedema is severe), and give a LIFELONG AVOIDANCE PLAN with patch testing and cross-reactors.**
**‘The candidate who treats it as “a rash — hydrocortisone and antihistamine” and lets her use a different brand next time FAILS THE PREVENTION TASK.’**

**Explaining it**: **‘This is an allergic reaction to a chemical in permanent hair dye called PPD. It's a DELAYED allergy — your immune system reacts ONE TO THREE DAYS after contact — which is why it came on after the dye, and why you could use it for years and then suddenly react. ONCE SENSITISED, IT STAYS FOR LIFE. The pattern along the hairline, ears and neck, WHERE THE DYE RUNS OFF, is typical. Your eyelids react because the skin there is thin and you've transferred it with your hands.’**

**TREATMENT, BY SITE** VERIFY : **wash residual dye out with a mild shampoo; COOL COMPRESSES to weeping areas; saline wet soaks for crusts.** **Moderate–potent steroid — methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% or mometasone 0.1% — to HAIRLINE, EARS AND NECK, once to twice daily for 7–14 days.** **MILD — hydrocortisone 1% — to the EYELIDS for 5–7 days only.** **A lotion formulation for the scalp.**

**SYSTEMIC STEROID, justified by the eyelid oedema**: **if severe facial or periorbital oedema, or more than about 20% body surface — oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg (25–50 mg) daily for 5–7 days THEN TAPER OVER 2 WEEKS.** VERIFY **A short course that stops abruptly REBOUNDS.**

**Plus**: non-sedating antihistamine by day, sedating at night for sleep — **it helps the itch only modestly, and it is NOT the main treatment** · emollient to settled areas · avoid fragranced products until healed · **review in 3–5 days, earlier if worsening** · **medical certificate — she works at a bank and can't go in like this.**

**PREVENTION — the half of the station candidates skip.** **PERMANENT AVOIDANCE of PPD and related dyes: check ingredients for p-phenylenediamine, TOLUENE-2,5-DIAMINE (PTD) and p-aminophenol.** **‘PPD-FREE’ DYES MAY CONTAIN CROSS-REACTORS.** **Refer for PATCH TESTING via dermatology to confirm PPD and identify what else she reacts to.**

**THE CROSS-REACTORS, and one of them matters to an anaesthetist**: **azo textile dyes · BLACK RUBBER · sulfonamides · BENZOCAINE and PABA sunscreens · some LOCAL ANAESTHETICS.** **Document the allergy in the record, give a WRITTEN ALLERGY CARD, and note the benzocaine cross-reaction for future anaesthesia.**

**Answering ‘can I just use a different brand?’ — this is the scored moment**: **‘No — that's the key message. Both drums dull, grey-yellow and retracted with a visible fluid level on the right · no perforation, no discharge, no erythema · afebrile · mouth-breathing with mild nasal speech and 2+ tonsils, which is the adenoid story · no craniofacial abnormality

back.dx: BILATERAL CHRONIC OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION — glue ear — causing a moderate conductive hearing loss with speech and language delay, with adenoidal obstruction feeding it. To Jess: 'After her ear infections, thick fluid has stayed behind the eardrums instead of draining. The eardrum cannot vibrate properly, so sound reaches her muffled — about the level of hearing through earplugs. That is why she says what, turns the TV up, and why her words are unclear: she is learning speech from muffled sound. The hearing nerve itself is normal, which is the good news — when the fluid goes, hearing returns.' Differentials: sensorineural loss, where bone conduction is also reduced — congenital CMV, genetic causes, post-meningitis, ototoxicity, and a failed newborn screen · mixed loss with both components · cholesteatoma or chronic suppurative otitis media — discharge, perforation, an attic retraction pocket · wax or foreign body on otoscopy · autism spectrum or global delay, where the response is inconsistent and social communication is abnormal while hearing may be fine · and adenoid hypertrophy with obstructive sleep apnoea, which coexists here and shapes the surgery. The pathway VERIFY: she meets criteria for ENT referral for ventilation tubes now — bilateral effusion, present more than three months, hearing loss at or above 25-30 dB and speech delayed — with adenoidectomy considered given the snoring and mouth breathing. Watchful waiting for three months is right only for shorter, milder, unilateral effusions without language impact. Speech pathology is referred now, not after surgery. Hearing strategies at home and kindy are separately marked: face her and get her attention first, reduce background noise, sit her at the front, speak clearly rather than loudly, repeat and check understanding — and write to the kindy. Repeat audiology after grommets, or three-monthly if waiting. Reduce risk with a smoke-free home, treating nasal congestion, no bottle in bed and up-to-date pneumococcal and influenza vaccination. There is no evidence for antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants or steroids in OME VERIFY, though autoinflation may help older children. And if speech does not track once hearing is restored, reassess for language disorder or autism. Rurally: ENT via PATS and WCH or a visiting service, Aboriginal ear health programs where relevant, and grommet aftercare advice.

dx: **Preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at 31 weeks COMPLICATED BY UMBILICAL CORD PROLAPSE with fetal bradycardia — an obstetric emergency.**

**★ THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: the examiner gives the cord finding AND WAITS. The first words out of your mouth after hearing 'cord at the os' must be: 'THIS IS A CORD PROLAPSE — CALL FOR HELP, KNEE–CHEST, ELEVATE THE PRESENTING PART.'** **Candidates who continue with the PPROM checklist — swabs, erythromycin, expectant management — without first relieving the compression fail the station.**

**THE SET-UP IS IN THE STEM: the head is 4/5 PALPABLE — high and unengaged — which is exactly the situation in which a cord prolapses when the membranes rupture. And the only abnormal number in the stem is the FETAL HEART AT 88.**

**SPEAK IN THE ORDER YOU ACT: help → position → relieve pressure → oxygen and IV → tocolysis bridge → steroids → MedSTAR → theatre.** **1. DECLARE AND CALL: 'this is an obstetric emergency — umbilical cord prolapse. I'm calling for help now' — a second doctor, senior nurse or midwife, theatre notified if there is local caesarean capability, and MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 SIMULTANEOUSLY for retrieval and obstetric advice.** **Never leave the patient to make the phone calls yourself.**

**2. RELIEVE THE COMPRESSION, PHYSICALLY. KNEE–CHEST position, or steep left-lateral Trendelenburg. MANUAL ELEVATION of the presenting part with two fingers via the vagina — gloved, AND THE HAND STAYS IN until delivery or theatre. This is THE ONE SITUATION IN PPROM WHERE YOU ENTER THE VAGINA.** **Alternatively, or in addition, FILL THE BLADDER with 500 mL of saline via an indwelling catheter and clamp it for transfer.** VERIFY

**3. DO NOT HANDLE OR REPLACE THE CORD.** If it is outside the introitus, keep it warm and moist within the vagina. **Attempting to push it back is an auto-fail, and she is briefed to ask 'is that safe?' if you say you will.**

**4–5. HIGH-FLOW OXYGEN, two large-bore cannulas, FBE, group and hold, coagulation profile, IV fluids. Then TOCOLYSIS AS A BRIDGE — TERBUTALINE 250 microg subcutaneously** VERIFY **— which reduces contractions and therefore compression, if delivery is not immediate.**

**6–8. CONTINUOUS fetal monitoring — if the heart recovers with positioning, maintain it and move. BETAMETHASONE 11.4 mg IM now** VERIFY **— there is benefit even if birth is within hours, so give it. MAGNESIUM SULFATE for neuroprotection under 30 weeks** VERIFY **— at 31 weeks, discuss with MedSTAR or the obstetrician rather than deciding alone. ERYTHROMYCIN 250 mg QID for the PPROM** VERIFY, **and BENZYLPENICILLIN for GBS if she is in labour, because the swab has not been done.**

**9. DEFINITIVE CARE IS AN EMERGENCY CAESAREAN — not 'transfer and see'. If this hospital has a surgeon and anaesthetist able to operate, PROCEED LOCALLY with MedSTAR's neonatal team en route. If not, retrieve WITH THE PRESENTING PART ELEVATED AND THE BLADDER FILLED, left lateral, oxygen, continuous monitoring.** **10. ANTI-D if Rh negative** VERIFY **— she is A positive here. NIL BY MOUTH, document the times, and make sure someone calls her partner.**

**EXPLAIN WHILE YOU ACT, in plain words**: **'Lena, your waters have broken early and the baby's cord has come down in front of her head. That squashes the cord and drops her heart rate, so we need to take the pressure off it right now and deliver her by caesarean. I'm going to ask you to get on your hands and knees with your chest down, I'll keep my hand inside to hold the baby's head up off the cord, and the team is calling the retrieval service and theatre.'** SA: **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33**, RFDS; tertiary neonatal care at **WCH or Flinders**; **PATS**; **Country Health Connect**; **TIS National 131 450**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**.
plan: **Open while the nurse takes the vitals — do not stop the clinical work to take a history**: **'Lena, I'm Dr ___. I can see you're worried — tell me exactly what happened.'** *A gush at the sink, clear, still trickling.*

**The fluid and the three symptoms, fast**: **'what colour was it — clear, green, blood-stained? How much, and is it still coming? Any tightenings or pain? Any bleeding? IS THE BABY MOVING?'** *'She moved in the car, less since we got here.'* **Note that — it is the second soft sign after the Doppler.**

**Infection and dates**: **'any fever, offensive discharge, or burning passing urine? How many weeks are you, and when was your last scan — was the placenta at the top?'** *31+2; 20-week scan normal, placenta high.*

**The pre-theatre and pre-transfer block — and these are the ones people skip in a rush**: **'have you had the GBS swab? Any diabetes or blood pressure problems? Any previous operations on the cervix? What's your blood group? Any allergies? AND WHEN DID YOU LAST EAT?'** *No swab, A positive, no allergies, lunch at one.*
**Social, in one line**: **'who's with you, how far do you live, and is your partner contactable?'** *Farm 40 minutes out; Marek at work.* **Do not run a long social history — it is a named trap.**

**ASK FOR THE FINDINGS — and ask for the cord BY NAME**: **'Examiner, may I have maternal vitals; the abdominal examination — fundal height, lie, presentation, ENGAGEMENT, contractions, tenderness; a STERILE SPECULUM looking for pooling of liquor, CORD, blood or cervical dilatation; and a CTG?'**
**THE FINDING LANDS: a loop of pulsating cord at the os, CTG baseline 90 with variable decelerations. THE STATION HAS CHANGED.**

**★ DECLARE IT IN THE FIRST BREATH**: **'this is a CORD PROLAPSE with fetal bradycardia — an obstetric emergency. I'm calling for help NOW: a second doctor, the senior midwife, theatre notified, and I want MedSTAR on the line on 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval and obstetric advice.'**

**POSITION AND RELIEVE — physically, and say it as an instruction**: **'Lena, I need you on your hands and knees with your chest down on the bed. I'm going to put two fingers inside and hold the baby's head up off the cord, AND KEEP THEM THERE.'** **Do not touch or attempt to replace the cord.**

**Explain while you act, in plain words**: waters broken early; the cord has slipped down in front of her head; it is being squashed and her heart rate has dropped; **'we need to take the pressure off right now and deliver her by caesarean.'** *'Oh God — is she going to be okay?'* → **'we're acting immediately, and the retrieval team is on their way.'**

**The nursing orders, in one run**: **'catheter in, fill the bladder with 500 mL of saline and clamp it; oxygen 15 litres via mask; two large cannulas; FBE, group and hold, coags; start fluids; continuous CTG.'**

**The drugs, in order of priority**: **'terbutaline 250 micrograms subcut to relax the uterus'** · **'betamethasone 11.4 mg IM now for the baby's lungs'** — give it even if birth is within hours — · **'and erythromycin.'** **Nil by mouth.** **At 31 weeks, discuss magnesium with the MedSTAR obstetrician rather than deciding alone.**
**The heart recovers to 120 — say what that means and do not relax the relief**: **'the heart rate has recovered with the pressure off. My hand stays where it is and the bladder stays filled.'**

**THE DISPOSITION DECISION — surgeon 20 minutes here, MedSTAR 60 minutes away**: **'with a surgeon and anaesthetist available and the baby at 31 weeks, we proceed to caesarean HERE, NOW, with MedSTAR's neonatal team coming to us. I'll confirm that plan with the MedSTAR obstetrician on the phone.'** **'Transfer and see' is the failure.**

**If there were NO local capability**: retrieve **with the presenting part elevated and the bladder filled, left lateral, on oxygen, with continuous monitoring** — the pressure relief travels with her.
**Tell her what happens next, plainly**: **'the operation is here, now, under anaesthetic. The newborn team will be here to look after her.'** Then **consent for caesarean.**

**The things that are marked and easily dropped at the end**: **anti-D if she were Rh negative** (she is A positive) · **nil by mouth confirmed** · **document the times** · and **'who can we call for you?'** — *Marek* — **'we'll call him.'**

**The forty-second summary if asked**: 31-week primigravida with PPROM complicated by cord prolapse and fetal bradycardia; help and MedSTAR, knee–chest, manual elevation and bladder filling, oxygen, IV access, terbutaline, betamethasone, erythromycin, **emergency caesarean locally given local capability**, anti-D if Rh negative.

**NEVER a digital vaginal examination in PPROM WITHOUT cord prolapse.** **The prolapse is the one exception — and then the fingers are there to ELEVATE THE PRESENTING PART, not to assess the cervix.**
**NEVER handle or attempt to replace the cord.** If it is outside the introitus, keep it warm and moist within the vagina.

**Relief options: KNEE–CHEST or steep left-lateral Trendelenburg · MANUAL ELEVATION with the hand left in situ · BLADDER FILLING with 500 mL saline via IDC, clamped** — the last is what makes transfer possible. VERIFY

Amy Lawson, 32, PRIMIGRAVIDA at 36 weeks. TEN DAYS of an intensely itchy bumpy rash that STARTED IN THE STRETCH MARKS on her abdomen and spread to thighs and buttocks. It keeps her awake. NO BLISTERS. Baby moving normally
★ THE BLOODS ARE ALREADY DONE AND NORMAL
LFTs NORMAL · BILE ACIDS 6 micromol/L (normal) · BP 118/72 · urine protein NEGATIVE. The cholestasis question is answered — but you must SAY you checked
★ THE SKIN FINDINGS ON REQUEST

Erythematous URTICARIAL PAPULES coalescing into PLAQUES WITHIN AND AROUND THE ABDOMINAL STRIAE, spreading to proximal thighs and buttocks · a few excoriations · PERIUMBILICAL SKIN SPARED · NO vesicles or bullae · FACE, PALMS, SOLES AND MUCOSAE SPARED
Obstetric findings
Fundal height 36 cm, cephalic, FHR 140. NO jaundice. Observations normal
What she gives on history

First bumps RIGHT IN THE STRETCH MARKS BELOW the belly button; THE BELLY BUTTON ITSELF IS FINE. No blisters. PALMS AND SOLES FINE. No dark urine, pale stools or yellow eyes. No fever. NOTHING NEW used. NOBODY ELSE ITCHY. No eczema or hay fever. Baby kicking plenty. MILD ANKLE SWELLING ONLY
★ SHE DOES NOT VOLUNTEER THE TWO DISCRIMINATORS
If you do not ask about BLISTERS or about PALMS AND SOLES, she says nothing about either
★ THE TRAP SHE IS BRIEFED TO SPRING

'CAN I USE ANYTHING? I THOUGHT NOTHING WAS SAFE IN PREGNANCY.' If you refuse all treatment she says 'I HAVEN'T SLEPT IN A WEEK.' Withholding steroids and antihistamines 'because pregnant' is a named fail
★ THE SECOND TRAP
'AND THE BABY?' — if you mention risk to the baby WITHOUT IMMEDIATELY CLARIFYING, she becomes anxious
VARIANT — bile acids 45, itch on palms and soles, NO rash
INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS: obstetric referral, ursodeoxycholic acid VERIFY, weekly bile acids and LFTs, fetal surveillance, planned birth 36–39 weeks by level VERIFY, vitamin K if the PT is prolonged
VARIANT — periumbilical urticaria then TENSE BLISTERS at 30 weeks
PEMPHIGOID GESTATIONIS: urgent dermatology and obstetrics, biopsy with DIRECT IMMUNOFLUORESCENCE, potent topical or oral steroids, growth surveillance — and a NEONATAL RASH IS POSSIBLE
VARIANT — twin pregnancy with rapid weight gain
PEP is MORE LIKELY. Same management
VARIANT — flexural eczema at 20 weeks with an atopic history
ATOPIC ERUPTION OF PREGNANCY — earlier in pregnancy, flexural, atopic history. Emollient, topical steroid, antihistamine

dx: **Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP; also PUPPP — pruritic urticarial papules and plaques of pregnancy): a primigravida in the third trimester with striae-based urticarial papules and plaques, UMBILICUS SPARED, NO BLISTERS, and NORMAL LFTs AND BILE ACIDS. Benign for mother and baby, and it resolves within days to weeks of birth.**

**★ THREE WORDS WIN THE DIFFERENTIAL, AND YOU MUST SAY THEM EXPLICITLY: UMBILICUS SPARED (against pemphigoid gestationis) · NO BLISTERS · BILE ACIDS NORMAL (against cholestasis). Then the reassurance has to be SPECIFIC: no risk to the baby, and no change to the birth plan.**

**DESCRIBE THE RASH SYSTEMATICALLY BEFORE NAMING IT**: **'erythematous, urticarial papules coalescing into plaques distributed WITHIN AND ALONGSIDE THE ABDOMINAL STRIAE, extending to the proximal thighs and buttocks, with excoriations. THE PERIUMBILICAL REGION IS SPARED. There are NO vesicles or bullae, and the face, palms, soles and mucosae are clear. Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is the pattern.'** **'Pregnancy rash' is the named trap.**

**THE TWO CONDITIONS THAT ACTUALLY MATTER. INTRAHEPATIC CHOLESTASIS — itch WITHOUT a primary rash, on the PALMS AND SOLES, worse at night, with only excoriations to see; raised bile acids and ALT; carries FETAL RISK and needs obstetric management. PEMPHIGOID GESTATIONIS — PERIUMBILICAL urticarial plaques that then blister into TENSE BULLAE; second to third trimester; autoimmune; preterm and SGA risk; needs dermatology and obstetrics, biopsy with immunofluorescence, and systemic steroids.**

**THE REST OF THE LIST, each with its discriminator: ATOPIC ERUPTION OF PREGNANCY — earlier than the third trimester, flexural eczema or prurigo papules, atopic history · SCABIES — burrows, web spaces, ITCHY CONTACTS · DRUG ERUPTION or VIRAL EXANTHEM — a temporal drug link, fever, morbilliform, mucosal involvement · URTICARIA — wheals that last under 24 hours and migrate.**

**THE EXPLANATION, in her words**: **'this is polymorphic eruption of pregnancy — also called PUPPP. It happens in about ONE IN 160 pregnancies, usually FIRST pregnancies in the last few weeks, and it typically starts in the stretch marks as the skin is pulled. It's uncomfortable, but it's HARMLESS: it doesn't affect the baby, it doesn't affect the birth, and it clears within days to a few weeks after the baby arrives.'**

**THEN THE TWO EXCLUSIONS, SAID ALOUD TO HER**: **'your liver tests and bile acids are normal, so it's not the itch of pregnancy that affects the liver — that's the one that does need special care. And there are no blisters and your belly button is spared, which rules out the rarer blistering condition.'**

**TREATMENT, AND SAY 'SAFE IN PREGNANCY' EXPLICITLY EACH TIME. 1. EMOLLIENT thickly and often; cool showers; light cotton clothing; cold compresses; oatmeal or bicarbonate baths. 2. MODERATE-POTENCY TOPICAL CORTICOSTEROID — betamethasone valerate 0.02–0.05% or methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% — once to twice daily for 1–2 weeks** VERIFY. **3. ORAL ANTIHISTAMINE: loratadine or cetirizine by day; CHLORPHENAMINE (sedating) at night for sleep** VERIFY. **4. If severe and sleep-destroying: short oral PREDNISOLONE 20–30 mg daily tapering over 1–2 weeks** VERIFY, **after obstetric discussion.**

**5. NO CHANGE to the antenatal plan; birth at term as planned; BREASTFEEDING IS FINE; the rash resolves postpartum; RECURRENCE IN LATER PREGNANCIES IS UNCOMMON.** **6. SAFETY-NET: return if BLISTERS appear, if the itch spreads to PALMS OR SOLES, if there is JAUNDICE or DARK URINE — repeat the LFTs and bile acids — if fetal movements reduce, or for headache, visual change, swelling or fever. 7. Review in 1–2 weeks and at routine visits, with written information.**

**The observations are on the card for a reason — comment on them. PRE-ECLAMPSIA IS UNRELATED to the rash, but BP 118/72 with negative protein is a relevant negative, and asking about fetal movements and pre-eclampsia symptoms is separately marked.** **PEP is more common with TWINS and RAPID WEIGHT GAIN, so ask.** SA: shared antenatal care in regional SA; dermatology referral only for the blistering or refractory cases — **PATS** if metropolitan review is needed; **Country Health Connect**; **TIS National 131 450**; **healthdirect 1800 022 222**; **CaFHS 1300 733 606** postnatally.
plan: **WIPE, then an open question**: **'Amy, tell me about this rash.'** *Ten days, started in the stretch marks, now on thighs and bottom, itches so badly she can't sleep.*

**★ THE FIRST DISCRIMINATING QUESTION**: **'where exactly did the first bumps appear — and IS YOUR BELLY BUTTON INVOLVED?'** *'Right in the stretch marks below the belly button. The belly button itself is fine.'* **Say what that means later; note it now.**

**★ THE SECOND AND THIRD**: **'any BLISTERS, fluid-filled bumps or oozing? And any itch on your PALMS OR SOLES, or itching ANYWHERE WITHOUT a visible rash?'** *No to all.* **She volunteers neither unless asked.**
**Characterise the itch and the rash**: severity, timing, sleep loss · any wheals that come and go within hours (urticaria) · any target lesions · how it spread.

**THE CHOLESTASIS SCREEN, symptomatically**: **'any dark urine, pale stools, yellowing of your eyes, or pain under the right ribs?'** Then **'you had bloods last week — I want to check your bile acids and liver tests were done.'** *They were, and they are normal.*

**Systemic and exposure**: **'any fever, feeling unwell, sore throat or joint pains?'** · **'any new medications, supplements, creams or washing products?'** · **'is anyone else at home itchy? Any pets?'** — the scabies and drug-eruption screen in three questions.

**Atopy and obstetric background**: **'any eczema, asthma or hay fever, in you or the family? Any rashes in previous pregnancies?'** · **'is this a single pregnancy, and has your weight gain been rapid?'** — **PEP is commoner with twins and rapid weight gain.**

**★ PREGNANCY WELLBEING — separately marked, and skipped by candidates who treat this as a pure dermatology case**: **'is the baby moving normally? Any tightenings, bleeding or leaking of fluid? Any headaches, vision changes or swelling?'** *Baby kicking plenty; mild ankle swelling only.*
**Impact and expectations**: **'how is it affecting your sleep and your mood? What have you already tried? And is there anything you're particularly worried about?'**
**ASK FOR THE FINDINGS**: **'Examiner, may I have the skin findings and the obstetric observations?'**

**★ DESCRIBE BEFORE YOU DIAGNOSE** — erythematous urticarial papules and plaques within and around the striae, spreading to thighs and buttocks; **umbilicus spared; no vesicles or bullae; palms, soles, face and mucosae clear**; excoriations. **Then the obstetric observations: normal, fetal heart 140, no jaundice.**

**NAME IT WITH THE NUMBERS**: polymorphic eruption of pregnancy, also called PUPPP — **about one in 160 pregnancies, mostly first pregnancies in the last few weeks, starting in the stretch marks as the skin stretches.**

**★ THE THREE EXCLUSIONS, SAID TO HER**: **'your liver tests and bile acids are normal, so this isn't the liver itch of pregnancy — the one that does need special care. And there are no blisters and your belly button is clear, which rules out the rare blistering rash of pregnancy.'**

**THE REASSURANCE, SPECIFIC NOT GENERAL**: **'it's miserable, but it's harmless. It doesn't affect the baby, it doesn't affect the birth or breastfeeding, and it clears within days to a couple of weeks after delivery.'**
**★ SHE ASKS 'CAN I USE ANYTHING? I THOUGHT NOTHING WAS SAFE' — and the answer is 'PLENTY IS SAFE'**: a thick moisturiser several times a day, cool showers, cotton clothes, cold compresses.

**The steroid, with the safety statement attached**: **'a moderate-strength steroid cream — methylprednisolone aceponate — once or twice a day to the rash for a week or two. That amount IS SAFE IN PREGNANCY.'**
**The antihistamines, aimed at her actual problem — sleep**: **'loratadine by day, and chlorphenamine at night to help you sleep. Both are fine in pregnancy.'**
**The escalation**: **'if it's still unbearable in a week we can use a short course of prednisolone tablets, after a word with the obstetric team.'**
**'AND THE BABY?' — answer it cleanly, with no hedging**: **'nothing changes. Same birth plan, same checks, and you can breastfeed normally.'**

**THE SAFETY-NET, and it is specific**: **'come back straight away if BLISTERS appear, if your PALMS OR SOLES start itching, if your urine goes dark or your eyes yellow — we'd repeat the liver tests — or if the baby's movements drop, or you get headaches, vision changes or a lot of swelling.'** Then **review in one to two weeks, a factsheet, and a teach-back.**

**BILE ACIDS AND LFTs — check them, don't assume.** They are already done and normal here, **but not mentioning them is a named fail.**

**Comment on the obstetric observations on the card: BP, urine protein, fundal height, presentation, fetal heart** — and **ask about fetal movements and pre-eclampsia symptoms**, which is separately marked.

setting: The crying is scripted to eat two to three minutes and it will not stop while you talk — it stops for a tissue, a glass of water, silence, or the offer of another appointment. The marks lost most often are in task two: candidates go straight from the tears to the management list and never explain what melanoma is or why depth matters.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia — Yorke Peninsula. Your next patient is Josh carter, a 55-year-old farmer, who has come to discuss the results of an excisional biopsy of a mole on his forehead performed by your colleague last week.

Histopathology conclusion: malignant melanoma, superficial spreading type, clark level II, breslow thickness 0.45 mm, no ulceration, mitotic rate under 1/mm², completely excised, all margins clear with the nearest at 2 mm.

time: Thirty seconds to sit down and ask what has happened so far · thirty more on perception · one minute for warning shot, invitation and the diagnosis in one sentence · two minutes of emotion handled with objects and silence, with a hard stop at about three minutes · one minute explaining the condition and why depth matters · three minutes on the five management points, red flags and support · thirty seconds of teach-back
