ask: The consent line: 'Because Ryan's an adult, I just need to confirm he's happy for me to discuss his condition with you.'

The two sentences that replace the grade: 'His blood pressure is drifting down and there's blood collecting in his abdomen — that tells us the bleeding hasn't stopped' and 'The grade doesn't decide the operation. His blood pressure does.'

The specifics that are the pass mark: 'Pneumococcal, meningococcal — both ACWY and B — and Hib. Plus the flu vaccine every year.' · 'Hib is a bacterium. The flu vaccine is a virus. He needs both.' · 'Amoxicillin 250 milligrams once a day, for at least three years.'

The fever rule, given as an instruction and not softened: 'If he gets a fever, or shivers or shakes — he takes the emergency antibiotic and goes straight to an emergency department.' and its companion: 'The daily tablet is a small preventive dose. It won't treat a serious infection.'

Challenges: 'Is he going to be alright?' Early and again at the end · 'Take it out? Can he live without it?' — answered plainly, not hedged · 'Against what?' and 'Which one, for how long?' when you speak in categories · 'Three years? Every single day?' · 'Even though he's already taking the other one?' · 'So I could just ring the GP in the morning?' if you soften the rule, which is marked as a fail · 'We've got a dog — does he have to get rid of her?' · and 'What about his ribs?' At about seven minutes if you never mention them.
pefe: Role-player: Jane Mercer, 51, Ryan's mother, rung ninety minutes ago and drove straight in. She has seen him briefly — awake, in pain, told her to talk to the doctors — and nobody has told her anything about the scans. Ryan is 24, an apprentice electrician who plays local football and lives at home, healthy, no allergies, no medications. She is frightened and holding it together, asking rapid-fire questions, and becomes tearful at the words operation or remove.

What she holds back: the dog at home and Ryan's Bali trip in October, raised only if the candidate mentions travel or animals or asks about concerns. Her agenda is 'Is he going to be alright?' and, once surgery is mentioned, 'Can he live without it?' — and what she wants to leave with is something concrete she can do, so she visibly relaxes when the fever rule is given clearly.

How she tests them: she makes them be specific — categories get 'Against what?' and 'Which one, for how long?' · if they use 'Grade ii' she asks whether two out of five is good · if they hedge on living without a spleen she asks again · if they talk over her tears she goes quiet and withdrawn, and recovers only if they pause · if they never ask about consent she says nothing and marks it.

Mark them against these: confirmed the patient's consent to discuss with his mother · open question then about twenty seconds of empathy and reassurance · explained the three scan findings in plain English · explained what the spleen is before discussing removing it · justified theatre by the falling BP and free fluid rather than the grade · mentioned preservation or embolisation · said clearly that people live normal lives without a spleen · named pneumococcal · named both meningococcal ACWY and B · named Hib and distinguished it from influenza · named annual influenza · gave the timing rule · named the daily antibiotic with dose and duration · gave the standby supply as a separate thing · stated the fever rule as an instruction and held it when pushed · explained why prophylaxis does not replace the standby dose · covered travel and malaria · covered animal bites · gave MedicAlert with a reason · arranged a vaccination card and recall · educated the family · addressed the rib fractures · and finished with teach-back of the fever rule.

The ten seconds that must not be skipped — Ryan is 24 and an adult, so his information is confidential to him: 'Before we start — because Ryan is an adult, I just need to confirm he's happy for me to discuss his condition with you. Have you been able to speak with him?' She says yes. Tick it and move on. If the candidate never asks, the role-player says nothing and marks it as a fail

Why he is going to theatre — Grades I and II are usually managed non-operatively, so the grade is not the decision — the physiology is. A falling blood pressure with free intraperitoneal fluid means the bleeding has not settled: failed non-operative management. Say 'The grade doesn't decide the operation — his blood pressure does'

The rib fractures, which almost every candidate ignores — They do not need an operation — ribs heal over six to eight weeks and you cannot cast a chest. The point is analgesia, because pain means shallow breathing, atelectasis and then pneumonia — so proper pain relief, deep-breathing exercises, physiotherapy, and watching for air or blood around the lung. Thirty seconds, and she asks about them at seven minutes if you do not

The three scan findings, said in plain words — Broken ribs on the left · a tear in the spleen · blood collecting inside the abdomen. Do not lead with 'Grade ii' — it means nothing to her, and if you say it she asks whether two out of five is good

What the spleen is, before you talk about removing it — 'An organ about the size of a fist, sitting in the upper left part of the tummy, tucked up under the ribs — which is why a blow to that side can injure it. It is part of the immune system: its main job is helping the body fight off certain serious infections in the blood.' Saying 'Under the ribs' ties the two injuries together for free

Confusing Hib with influenza, or giving 'the meningococcal vaccine' without splitting ACWY and B; leading with the grade instead of the physiology; failing to say plainly that life without a spleen is normal, or over-reassuring that there is nothing to worry about; no MedicAlert and no family education; unexplained jargon like OPSI, encapsulated organisms and laparotomy

Daily prophylaxis amoxicillin 250 mg once daily or phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg twice daily for at least 3 years — not 500 mg and not six months to two years correction VERIFY · standby amoxicillin 2 g stat as four 500 mg capsules, then 1 g eight-hourly if review is delayed, or cefuroxime 500 mg for non-severe penicillin hypersensitivity VERIFY · trigger: fever 38 or above, or rigors · OPSI risk is lifelong with about 30% in year one and 50% by year two VERIFY · ribs unite in 6-8 weeks · tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury VERIFY · spleen Australia covers VIC, WA, QLD and TAS but not SA correction VERIFY · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 · VERIFY all

setting: The diagnosis is easy, which is exactly why the failure rate is high. Candidates say 'It's viral, it's self-limiting, take paracetamol and fluids' and stop. She will say 'My throat really hurts' up to three times — she is not asking for a diagnosis, she is asking for relief, and the mark is the lignocaine spray used before she eats and drinks.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Jane Whitmore, 19, a university student, saw your colleague two days ago with a severe sore throat, a cough and marked tiredness. She has returned today for the results and still feels unwell.

Examination two days ago: redness and exudate on both tonsils · multiple tender cervical lymph nodes, soft on palpation · no rash · mild splenomegaly and mild hepatomegaly. Results: FBE shows a raised white cell count with lymphocytosis and atypical lymphocytes, Hb and platelets normal · EBV IgM positive · CMV IgG positive · LFTs show a mild rise in AST and ALT under three times the upper limit, bilirubin normal.
Tasks: explain the investigation results to the patient — explain the diagnosis and its implications — discuss your management plan — address the patient's concerns.

time: Forty-five seconds to introduce, ask how she is feeling and acknowledge the throat before any result · two minutes on the results in a building sequence, chunked and checked · seventy-five seconds naming the syndrome and mapping its features onto her · forty-five seconds on implications, where most marks are lost · then nearly two minutes of management led by the throat · and the last minute for red flags, review and teach-back
findingsLabel: Examination findings — open only when you would ask the examiner
findings: The liver function tests, which are there deliberately

A mild rise in the enzymes under three times the upper limit with a normal bilirubin — mild EBV hepatitis, expected, settling, and not liver damage. It sets up two practical things: no alcohol until it settles, and repeat bloods at review. Skipping it because it is the least dramatic result loses a marked item
If the examiner probes the serology

Monospot is quick but insensitive in the first week, so a negative does not exclude EBV · ebv-specific serology is more reliable, with VCA IgM positive and EBNA IgG absent indicating acute infection, because EBNA IgG only appears at 6-12 weeks · and naming HIV seroconversion, CMV, toxoplasmosis and acute viral hepatitis shows you have not anchored VERIFY

back.dx: ACUTE EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS INFECTION PRESENTING AS INFECTIOUS MONONUCLEOSIS — glandular fever — with mild hepatitis and mild splenomegaly. Use the syndrome name with the patient and mention EBV as the virus behind it, then map the features onto her rather than reciting them into the air: severe exudative sore throat, fever, tender swollen neck glands, marked and prolonged tiredness, enlarged spleen and inflamed liver — 'You have almost the full picture, which is why I am confident rather than going on one blood test.' 'Implications' means three blocks — complications, prognosis, and what it means for her life over the next few weeks — and candidates who do only the first lose marks. Frame before naming: most people recover completely, and these are mentioned so she knows when to seek help — the spleen, which can tear if it takes a knock · tonsillar swelling enough to obstruct the airway · rarely neurological, cardiac or haematological involvement · and the fatigue that genuinely drags for weeks and sometimes a couple of months. On the cancer link: do not lead with it and do not hide it — 'There is a very small, long-term association between this virus and some rare blood and throat cancers. To put that in perspective, the large majority of adults carry this virus for life and never have any problem from it.' Management is where the station is won, and 'Supportive' is a list with numbers on it. The throat first, because it is her agenda: paracetamol 1 g four times daily to a maximum of 4 g in 24 hours, taken regularly rather than when unbearable · ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily with food if not contraindicated · codeine added if that is not enough · and the item that actually helps, a lignocaine or benzydamine throat spray or gargle used a few minutes before eating and drinking so she can swallow — which is the point, because it keeps fluids going · plus cool fluids, ice blocks, soft food and saline gargles VERIFY. Then hydration with oral rehydration solution and small sips, rest while febrile and then graded activity rather than a month in bed. Then the spleen, specific and with a duration: no contact or collision sport and no heavy lifting for at least four weeks from symptom onset, walking and light activity fine, and clinical review before return — individualised, with longer for persistent splenomegaly or high-impact sport, and no routine serial ultrasound because it does not predict rupture VERIFY. Then what you are not doing, each with a reason: no antibiotics, because it is viral — and critically because amoxicillin or ampicillin causes a florid morbilliform rash in the large majority of acute EBV, which is not a true penicillin allergy and must be documented as such, with phenoxymethylpenicillin preferred if a bacterial tonsillitis genuinely needs treating · no antivirals, because aciclovir reduces shedding without improving outcomes · and no routine corticosteroids — not because they 'Trigger the malignant associations of ebv', which is a theoretical concern rather than the reason correction, but because there is no demonstrated benefit in uncomplicated disease and there are risks, reserving them for impending airway obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy or severe haemolysis or thrombocytopenia VERIFY. Then transmission and life admin: saliva spread, so no kissing or sharing drink bottles, cutlery, toothbrushes or lip products while symptomatic · no work, school or university exclusion, because shedding continues for months and exclusion is pointless — she returns when she feels well enough · no alcohol while the enzymes are raised · blood donation deferred · a medical certificate · and missed-pill rules if she has been vomiting on the combined pill VERIFY. Red flags with actions: inability to swallow saliva, drooling, voice change or noisy breathing — airway · inability to keep fluids down or minimal urine — dehydration · severe abdominal pain, especially left-sided, or pain at the left shoulder tip, or faintness — the spleen, and that is a triple-zero call · severe headache, neck stiffness, confusion or seizure · chest pain or palpitations · jaundice or dark urine · and new petechiae or bleeding gums. Review in one week with repeat LFTs, a spleen check and written information.
plan: Open with 'How are you feeling today?' and let her describe the throat — then validate it honestly: 'This is one of the sorest throats there is, and I'm going to make that the first thing we deal with.' then permission, signpost, and the first concern check.
The results in a building sequence — infection, then viral, then this virus, then the liver — chunking and checking after each (see findings).
Name the syndrome and the virus, say it spreads by saliva and is extremely common, then map its features onto her own findings so the diagnosis is evidenced rather than asserted.

Implications as a framed block: most people recover fully, then the spleen, the airway, the rare neurological, cardiac and haematological ones, and the fatigue — each attached to when to seek help, not left as frightening nouns.

Management led by the throat: regular paracetamol, an NSAID, a step up if needed, and the lignocaine spray before eating and drinking — then fluids with oral rehydration and small sips, and rest with graded return.
The spleen with its duration and the pre-return review — and hold it when she pushes about finals, with empathy and a reason rather than a lecture.
What you are not giving and why — no antibiotics with the amoxicillin rash named, no antivirals, no routine steroids — plus transmission, no exclusion from university, no alcohol and a certificate.

Red flags each with an action including the left shoulder-tip pain and the triple-zero call · review in one week with repeat liver tests · written information · second concern check and a teach-back of the sport advice and the red flags.

ask: The opening that earns the rest: 'This is genuinely one of the sorest throats there is — I'm going to make that the first thing we sort out.'
The principle, given before the result: 'IgM means recent or current. IgG means past.' then 'EBV now; CMV some time in the past, and it isn't causing this.'
The marked item every other candidate misses: 'Use the numbing spray a few minutes before you eat or drink, so you can actually swallow.' and its companion, 'Small sips count.'

The spleen advice with its duration and its reason: 'No contact sport and no heavy lifting for at least four weeks from when you got sick — and see me before you go back' · 'An enlarged spleen can tear from a knock that wouldn't normally hurt you.'

Challenges: 'My throat really hurts', repeated up to three times if you move on · 'Atypical? That sounds bad. Is it leukaemia?' · 'So I've got two viruses?' · 'Is my liver damaged? Can I still take Panadol?' · 'I read online it's linked to cancer' · 'Four weeks? We've got netball finals in three' — and if you soften to 'See how you feel', she says 'Great, I'll play then' and marks it as a fail · 'My flatmate said I should ask for antibiotics' · 'Can my boyfriend catch it?'
pefe: Role-player: Jane Whitmore, 19, a second-year university student in a share house who plays Saturday netball, unwell about five days. The worst sore throat she has ever had — swallowing feels like swallowing glass — with fevers and sweats, sore neck glands, exhaustion after fourteen hours' sleep, and a dry cough. She has barely eaten in three days and is drinking much less because it hurts, though she is not vomiting and is still passing urine. On the combined pill, taking one paracetamol 'When I remember', no allergies, six standard drinks on a Saturday, has a boyfriend. Flat and miserable rather than anxious.

Her two agendas: the throat, said early and repeated if nothing better than paracetamol is offered — this is the engine of the station · and netball finals in three weeks, which she fully intends to play and pushes back on once. The worry she voices only if asked about concerns is that she googled 'Atypical lymphocytes' last night and read about leukaemia, and she asks the cancer question at about five minutes if complications were mentioned and it was skipped.

How she scores it: she warms noticeably when the lignocaine spray is offered · she accepts the sport advice if given a clear reason, and accepts it enthusiastically if softened to please her, which is marked as a fail · and she asks what any unfamiliar word means rather than helping the candidate out.

Mark them against these: acknowledged the throat before the results · checked concerns twice · explained the FBE including 'Atypical' and defused it · gave IgM versus IgG as a principle · explained CMV as past infection only · explained the liver result with the alcohol advice and repeat testing · named glandular fever and the virus · mapped the features onto her · delivered complications framed with actions attached · answered the cancer question honestly and proportionately · gave paracetamol dose and frequency with an NSAID and a step-up · offered the lignocaine spray before eating and drinking · gave hydration advice with oral rehydration and small sips · gave the spleen advice with a duration and a pre-return review · held it when pushed · stated no antibiotics and why including the amoxicillin rash · stated no antivirals and when steroids are used · gave transmission advice and said there is no exclusion period · named red flags with actions including left shoulder-tip pain · arranged a one-week review with repeat bloods and a certificate · and closed with teach-back.

The full blood count — 'Your white cells — the cells that fight infection — are higher than normal. The type that is raised is called lymphocytes, and that pattern usually points to a virus rather than a bacteria. Some of them look bigger and different from usual — we call them atypical, and that is a very typical finding in this infection, not something sinister.' The antibodies, and the CMV distractor — Give the principle first: IgM is the early one and means recent or current; IgG is the later one, stays for years and means past. So EBV IgM positive is the infection she has now, and CMV IgG positive means she met that virus at some point and it healed — it is not causing today's illness. 'EBV now, CMV in the past'

The paracetamol question candidates freeze on — Yes — therapeutic doses for a short course are safe. Mildly raised transaminases from EBV are not a contraindication; the concern is overdose and chronic high-dose use. Do not exceed 4 g in 24 hours, avoid combination products that double-dose, and avoid alcohol VERIFY

findingsLabel: What to ask for, and what the examiner gives back
findings: What comes back

Well, comfortable, afebrile, no pallor or jaundice · hands on photograph: flat erythema involving both hands and fingers roughly symmetrically — a patch rather than raised plaques — with mild scaling and some crusting and no purulent discharge · scalp: small papules and vesicles, no discharge · no burrows in the web spaces · no lymphadenopathy and no supraclavicular nodes · thyroid normal · no hepatosplenomegaly · dipstick normal

back.dx: ALLERGIC CONTACT DERMATITIS TO HAIR DYE — a type IV delayed hypersensitivity, most often to para-phenylenediamine, in the exact distribution of contact. The reasoning given out loud, in three parts: she has an itchy rash, so the problem is inflammation in the skin rather than elsewhere · it is confined to two areas rather than being all over, and when itch is that localised something has usually touched those places · and those two places are exactly where the dye went — the scalp, and the ungloved fingers that applied it — with an onset 24 to 72 hours later, which is the timing of delayed hypersensitivity rather than an immediate reaction. The point candidates fold on: previous uneventful use does not exclude it — sensitisation develops over time, and it is the second and subsequent exposures that react. She pushes once with 'But I've used it for years', and a candidate who changes diagnosis has failed the point. The differentials, each with why it fits less well: irritant contact dermatitis — same distribution but burns rather than itches, needs no prior sensitisation, often coexists, and patch testing separates them · atopic dermatitis — no personal or family atopy, no flexural involvement, first episode with an obvious trigger · pompholyx — deep-seated vesicles on palms and finger sides, recurrent, and would not explain the scalp · scabies — no burrows, no itchy contacts, and in adults it characteristically spares the head and neck, which hers does not · psoriasis — a flat patch rather than a thickened silvery plaque, normal nails, no family history · tinea — symmetrical and not annular, with scrapings if it fails to respond · urticaria — wheals are raised, individually resolve within 24 hours and migrate, whereas hers is flat, fixed and contact-shaped · lichen planus — violaceous flat-topped polygonal papules · herpetic whitlow — usually one digit, painful more than itchy · secondary bacterial infection — afebrile with crusting but no purulence, though worth rechecking · and drug eruption — no new medications and the wrong distribution. Then the systemic group, said briefly but said: lymphoma and leukaemia, cholestatic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, thyroid disease, coeliac disease and iron deficiency — none supported by the history or examination, and with the clinching general point that a systemic cause almost always causes itch all over rather than in two specific spots. Management is brief but should not be omitted: stop and wash off the product · a moderate to potent topical corticosteroid such as methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% or mometasone 0.1% to hands and scalp, as a lotion or foam in hair, with a mild steroid only if face or eyelids are involved VERIFY · emollient and a soap substitute · a sedating antihistamine at night, which helps sleep more than itch · oral prednisolone only for severe or extensive disease or significant facial swelling VERIFY · swab and flucloxacillin if pustules or honey-coloured crust appear VERIFY · dermatology patch testing once the acute episode settles, to confirm PPD and map cross-reactors · and review in three to five days. Prevention is parked and then answered properly when she asks whether she can ever dye her hair again: lifelong avoidance of PPD and its relatives p-phenylenediamine, toluene-2,5-diamine and p-aminophenol, with 'Ppd-free' not guaranteed because cross-reactors exist — azo textile dyes, black rubber, sulfonamides, and benzocaine and paba sunscreens and local anaesthetics, which is worth documenting for future dental and surgical work · never a black henna tattoo · the box's 48-hour patch test is unreliable once sensitised and can itself provoke a reaction · and an allergy card with the record documented VERIFY.
plan: Open, empathise with the itch and ask about concerns — then the framing sentence that shows you have a system before you have an answer: 'I divide the causes into problems in the skin itself and problems elsewhere in the body that show up as itch, and then I ask whether there is a rash, because that splits it further.'

The itch: onset, first episode or recurrent, all over or localised, severity out of ten, does it wake her at night, and is it worse after a hot shower — the last two are the scabies pair and both are expected.
'Is there a rash?' — then explore it rather than ticking it: where exactly, what colour, any blisters, any discharge, painful as well as itchy, symmetrical.

The contact history, which solves it: new soaps, shampoos and conditioners · creams, makeup, nail and hair products — 'Have you dyed or treated your hair recently?' · then 'Did you wear gloves?' and 'Have you used that product before?' · plus perfumes, clothes, washing powder, jewellery, occupation and hobbies.

Differential-specific questions — atopy and family history, family psoriasis, travel or new accommodation and whether contacts are itching, new medications, recent viral illness — then the systemic red-flag screen even though you already know the answer: weight loss, night sweats, lumps, jaundice or dark urine, kidney problems, heat intolerance and tremor, chronic diarrhoea.
Ask the examiner in the fixed sequence, naming what you are looking for (see findings).
Describe the photograph to formula, then name contact dermatitis and give the three reasons — and address the prior-tolerance objection head-on when she raises it.
The differentials with a reason each, skin then systemic — then park-and-return to her 'Can I ever dye my hair again?' Question, a brief plan, the safety-net and a teach-back.

ask: The question that splits the differential and must be asked by two minutes: 'Is there a rash where it itches?'
The two scabies questions, asked as a pair: 'Does it wake you at night? And is it worse after a hot shower?'
The two that turn a product into a mechanism: 'Did you wear gloves?' and 'Have you used that product before without any trouble?'

The reasoning, said in her language: 'When itch is that localised, something has usually touched those particular places' · 'You can become allergic to something you've used safely for years' · and the line that closes the systemic group, 'A cause inside the body almost always causes itch all over, rather than in two specific spots.'

Challenges: 'But I've used it for years' — pushed once, and folding on it fails the point · 'So can I never dye my hair again?' Asked the moment you name it, which tempts you to skip the differentials — park it and come back · 'But why do you think it's not one of those?' if you list differentials without reasons · and, only if you ask about concerns, 'My aunt had lymphoma and I read that itching can be a sign of cancer.'
pefe: Role-player: Lily Barnett, 24, a university student who works part-time in a bookshop and lives in a share house, normally very healthy. Four days of itch at 8/10 in her fingertips and across her scalp and nowhere else, waking her at night, with red flaky hands and tiny blisters on the scalp, no pus and no pain. She scratches her hands and head throughout, and is fed up and practical rather than frightened.

The key fact and when she gives it: she dyed her own hair at home on the weekend with a permanent box dye and did not wear the gloves, having used that brand for years without a problem, which is why she does not believe it could be the cause. The itch started the next day or the day after. She volunteers it only if asked about new products, cosmetics, hair products or contacts — and if nobody asks, she offers it at about six minutes.

Everything else is negative: no atopy in her or her family, no family psoriasis, no travel or new accommodation, nobody else itchy, no new medications or herbal products, no recent illness, no weight loss, night sweats, lumps, jaundice, dark urine, bowel symptoms, heat intolerance or joint pains, not pregnant, no known allergies. Her hidden worry, given only if asked about concerns, is that her aunt had lymphoma.

Mark them against these: opened with empathy and asked about concerns · established timing and that it was a first episode · established that the itch is localised · asked about severity and night waking · asked about hot showers · asked 'Is there a rash?' · took a mini rash history · took a contact history including hair products · asked about gloves and previous use · asked about occupation and hobbies · asked atopy and family history · asked the scabies questions about travel, accommodation and itchy contacts · asked about new medications and recent viral illness · ran the systemic red-flag screen · asked for general appearance and temperature · asked for a full skin examination · specifically asked for the web spaces, wrists and axillae · asked for lymph nodes including supraclavicular · asked for thyroid and abdomen · described the rash with primary and secondary morphology and negatives · named contact dermatitis with reasons · explained that prior tolerance does not exclude allergy · gave differentials with reasons, skin and systemic · and finished with a brief plan, patch testing, safety-net and teach-back.

Ask in sequence and say what you are looking for — General appearance — cachexia, pallor, jaundice · vital signs, particularly temperature for secondary infection · a full skin examination · the hands and scalp, and specifically the web spaces, wrists, axillae and waistline for scabies burrows, plus the nails · a full lymph node examination including supraclavicular · thyroid · abdomen for hepatosplenomegaly · and a urine dipstick. Asking for 'A general examination' and waiting costs thirty seconds

Describing it to formula — Site and distribution · primary morphology — flat patch, so not urticaria which is raised and oedematous, and not psoriasis which is a thickened plaque · secondary morphology — scale and crust · then the negatives that matter: no purulent discharge, no burrows, no nail pitting · then interpret

Do not be thrown by the vesicles — Candidates learn that dermatitis is flat, then hear 'Papules and vesicles on the scalp' and abandon the diagnosis. Acute contact dermatitis is vesicular, weeping and crusted; the flat scaly lichenified picture is the chronic phase, and both can coexist

The history detail the case turns on — She dyed her own hair at home a few days ago and did not wear gloves. She has used that brand for years without trouble. The itch began 24 to 48 hours later, confined to scalp and fingertips — exactly where the dye touched her. She volunteers it only if asked about new products or hair products

findings: Blood pressure
NORMAL
Temperature
Fundal height, fetal heart rate and lie
NORMAL
Renal angle tenderness
POSITIVE — ask for it BY NAME, even after a general tenderness question. Some examiners answer 'no tenderness' generally and then give you a positive renal angle only when you name it
Urine dipstick
BLOOD, PROTEIN and NITRITES
Trap on the card — the blood
Blood on the dipstick does NOT mean a stone. Infection causes haematuria. Do not switch to renal colic
Trap on the card — the protein
1+ protein does NOT mean pre-eclampsia when the blood pressure is normal and there are no neurological features. Infection causes proteinuria too. NITRITES are what confirm the urinary tract

dx: **Acute pyelonephritis at 20 weeks.** Say it with the reasons attached: **the pain is on the right and drags downward, which is the pattern kidney pain follows · burning on passing urine and going more often · a fever · nitrites on the dipstick, which come from bacteria · and tenderness when I tapped over your kidney at the back**.

CORRECTION — **cystitis does not usually cause fever.** Systemic upset — **fever, rigors, vomiting, loin pain** — is what moves you from the lower tract to the upper. **Fever with urinary symptoms in pregnancy is pyelonephritis until proven otherwise.**

**The two dipstick traps.** **Blood does not mean a stone** — infection causes haematuria, and switching to renal colic is a named fail. **1+ protein does not mean pre-eclampsia** when the blood pressure is normal and there are no neurological features — infection causes proteinuria too. **Nitrites are what tie this to the urinary tract.**
**This is not managed in general practice.** Transfer to the emergency department for **admission**. It is a different disease in pregnancy.

**Urine for microscopy, culture and sensitivity BEFORE the first dose.** Then **intravenous antibiotics, continued until she is clinically improving** — **not a single stat dose, and not oral**. VERIFY the current first-line agent against Therapeutic Guidelines; **do not memorise a combination**.
**Analgesia and antipyretics safe in pregnancy, and intravenous fluids.** **Bloods including FBE and inflammatory markers. CTG to monitor the baby.**
**Post-treatment culture**, and **consider prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy**. **Significant bacteriuria is 10⁵ CFU/mL on culture.**

Keep screening after you know the answer — say the bridging sentence out loud: **'That does sound like a urine infection, and I'll come back to it. Before I do, I need to check a few things about the pregnancy itself — any bleeding? Any leaking of fluid? Is the baby moving normally?'**

Deliver the differentials **in named groups, three Ps leading**: **the pregnancy-related causes — pre-eclampsia, the labour starting early, the afterbirth separating** · other kidney and bladder causes — cystitis, a stone · gastrointestinal causes · liver and gallbladder causes. **Seven names in four groups beats twelve recited flat.**

The numbers and the SA plan: **20 weeks is the line above which pre-eclampsia exists at all · 140/90 hypertension, 160/110 severe · fetal heart rate 110–160 · CTG from about 26–28 weeks** VERIFY. From an MM5 site this is **stabilise and transfer** — Wallaroo and Kadina do not manage it; receiving units are the **WCH, Lyell McEwin or FMC**. **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33** if she is unstable. **PATS** for the partner's travel, said aloud. **TIS National 131 450** — never a family member.
plan: **'Examiner, could I have her vital signs — blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature and saturations?'** In this version the **temperature is the station** — 39 °C.
Open question, then acknowledge the concern in one sentence and signpost.

The pain: **where exactly · out of ten · what sort of pain · when did it start · constant or coming and going · does it radiate · anything better or worse**. Here: right-sided, **dragging down to the right lower abdomen**, two days, on and off then constant, getting worse.

The bridging sentence, out loud, the moment the answer appears: **'that does sound like a urine infection, and I'll come back to it. Before I do, I need to check a few things about the pregnancy itself.'** **The marks are for exclusion, not arrival.**
General gastrointestinal screen: **any nausea or vomiting · bowels normal · passing wind · any bloating · any fevers or chills · any change in appetite**.

The obstetric block, the three Ps, asked even though the pain is urinary: **any bleeding from down below · any discharge or leaking of fluid · is the baby moving as much as usual, when did you last feel it**.

**Preterm labour specifically: does the pain come in waves that last longer and arrive closer together?** **Abruption specifically: is the pain constant, and is the uterus tender?** One question each.

The pre-eclampsia set in full: **headaches · change in vision, blurring, flashing lights, spots · swelling in your legs, hands or face, and is it there when you wake · pain up under the ribs on the right · yellowing of the skin · chest pain or breathlessness · passing less urine**.
Routine antenatal history, briskly: **routine bloods, dating scan, the 18–20 week scan, the sweet drink test · previous pregnancies and any problems**.

Gastrointestinal rule-outs: **appetite · any lump in the groin · worse after fatty meals · aspirin or anti-inflammatories**. Then kidney and bladder: **burning on passing urine · going more often · blood in the urine**.
Travel, social history, and **'what were you most worried this might be?'** — deliberately last, and deliberately brief.

Ask for the card, in order: **general appearance · vital signs including temperature · neurological, fundoscopy, reflexes and specifically ankle clonus · chest · abdomen, distension and tenderness over the liver and the uterus · then the uterus: fundal height, fetal heart rate, tenderness, palpable contractions · bowel sounds · RENAL ANGLE TENDERNESS BY NAME · inguinal orifices and a rectal examination · speculum with consent and a chaperone — os open or closed, blood or fluid · lower limbs · urine dipstick**.

Give the diagnosis **with the reasons attached**: the site and pattern of the pain, the dysuria and frequency, the fever, **the nitrites**, and **the positive renal angle**. Explain nitrites as **'a chemical that comes from bacteria'**.

Handle the two dipstick traps **before the examiner raises them** — the blood is from the infection, not a stone; the protein is from the infection, not pre-eclampsia, because the blood pressure is normal.

Differentials **in named groups**, three Ps first, then kidney and bladder, then gastrointestinal, then liver and gallbladder. Close with the six-bullet plan in thirty seconds: **transfer and admit · culture before antibiotics · IV antibiotics until improving · analgesia, antipyretics and fluids · bloods and CTG · post-treatment culture and consider prophylaxis.**
pefe: The examination is **handed to you already written**. **Read it top-down: blood pressure and dipstick first, the uterus second, the os third, everything else last.**
**Ask for renal angle tenderness BY NAME.** This is the version where it decides the answer, and a general tenderness question may be answered 'no'.
**Four things about the uterus by name**: **fundal height · fetal heart rate · is it tender · are there palpable contractions.**

The dipstick here reads **blood, protein and nitrites**. **Nitrites confirm the urinary tract.** Blood is from the infection. Protein is from the infection, given a normal blood pressure and no neurological features.
**Urine for microscopy, culture and sensitivity BEFORE the first antibiotic dose.** This is the single most commonly lost step.

**Intravenous antibiotics, continued until clinically improving.** Not oral, not a single stat dose. VERIFY the current first-line agent against Therapeutic Guidelines rather than memorising a combination.
**Bloods: FBE and inflammatory markers**; **UEC with creatinine**. **Intravenous fluids** if she is febrile or vomiting.
**CTG** to monitor the baby — from about 26–28 weeks, so at 20 weeks it may not apply; VERIFY the local gestational threshold and say so rather than requesting it reflexively.
**Post-treatment culture** to confirm clearance, and **consider antibiotic prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy**.
**Significant bacteriuria is 10⁵ CFU/mL.** Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated, unlike outside pregnancy.

**This is the diagnosis.** Admission and IV antibiotics; culture first. **Emergency in pregnancy**

**Do not switch to this on dipstick blood alone.** Ultrasound. Urgent

**Against — normal blood pressure, no neurological features. Proteinuria alone does not make it.** Ask the set anyway. Emergency

Ultrasound. Urgent

dx: **TWO VERSIONS, IDENTICAL STEM, DIFFERENT ANSWERS.** **VERSION A — the bloating SETTLES AFTER SHE OPENS HER BOWELS, stools ALTERNATE hard then loose, stress at work → IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME (Rome IV, a diagnosis of EXCLUSION).** **VERSION B — WORSE AFTER PIZZA AND BREAD, stools GREASY, BULKY, HARD TO FLUSH, FLOAT, STICK TO THE PAN, background IRON DEFICIENCY ANAEMIA ‘they told me it is my heavy periods’, now on iron tablets → COELIAC DISEASE, with ORAL IRON AS A SECONDARY CONTRIBUTOR.** **Red flags are all negative in BOTH.**

**THE ONE BEHAVIOUR THAT SEPARATES A PASS FROM A FAIL: WHETHER YOU INTERROGATE THE ANSWER THE PATIENT HANDS YOU, OR ACCEPT IT.** **This station is BUILT on a supplied explanation.** **In Version B she tells you her anaemia is ‘just heavy periods’. THE CANDIDATE WHO ACCEPTS THAT LOSES COELIAC DISEASE.** **In Version A she says the bloating settles when she opens her bowels, and THE CANDIDATE WHO TAKES THAT AS PERMISSION TO STOP ASKING LOSES THE EXCLUSION MARKS THAT MAKE IBS DEFENSIBLE.**

**REFUSING THE HANDED EXPLANATION, verbatim**: **‘You mentioned you're LOW IN IRON and that it was put down to HEAVY PERIODS. That MAY WELL BE PART OF IT, but LOW IRON CAN ALSO MEAN THE BOWEL ISN'T ABSORBING PROPERLY, so I'd like to ask a few questions about your stools. Have you noticed them being GREASY OR BULKY, FLOATING, or HARD TO FLUSH AWAY?’** → *‘Now that you mention it, yes — they're pale and they stick to the bowl. I have to flush twice. I thought that was normal.’*

**DEFINE THE WORD BEFORE YOU ASK ANYTHING ELSE. FOUR DIFFERENT COMPLAINTS HIDE BEHIND ‘BLOATING’, and they point to FOUR DIFFERENT DIFFERENTIAL GROUPS.** **‘When you say bloated, can you describe it — is it that you're BURPING a lot, or passing MORE WIND than usual, or is it that your TUMMY ACTUALLY LOOKS AND FEELS SWOLLEN?’** **Candidates open with ‘how long has this been going on?’ and NEVER DEFINE THE SYMPTOM — and the examiner is watching for this question specifically.** **BLOATING is the SENSATION of trapped gas or fullness; DISTENSION is the MEASURABLE increase in girth. THEY ARE NOT THE SAME, and the second one is the one that GETS A MASS OR ASCITES FOUND.**

**THE NOCTURNAL QUESTION EARNS MARKS AND TAKES ONE LINE.** **‘Does it ever WAKE YOU AT NIGHT, or is it only when you're awake?’** **SYMPTOMS THAT WAKE A PATIENT FROM SLEEP POINT AWAY FROM FUNCTIONAL DISEASE AND TOWARDS ORGANIC PATHOLOGY. It is one question and IT REFRAMES THE WHOLE DIFFERENTIAL.**

**THE STOOL DESCRIPTORS ARE THE HIGHEST-YIELD QUESTION IN VERSION B, AND YOU MUST NAME ALL FOUR.** **GREASY · BULKY · FLOATS · HARD TO FLUSH, STICKS TO THE PAN.** **Asking ‘are your bowels normal?’ instead of naming the four descriptors GETS A YES — the role-player is briefed to give the description ONLY WHEN ASKED DIRECTLY.**

**IN ANY WOMAN WITH PERSISTENT BLOATING, THE PHRASE ‘I WOULD WANT TO EXCLUDE OVARIAN CANCER’ MUST BE SPOKEN.** **Ovarian cancer produces EXACTLY these non-specific symptoms and is THE CLASSIC MISSED DIAGNOSIS in this presentation.** **THE CLUSTER: BLOATING, EARLY SATIETY, PELVIC PAIN, URINARY FREQUENCY — PERSISTENT AND MORE THAN 12 TIMES A MONTH.** **The fixed rule: bloating in a female patient means ovarian cancer is NAMED, WHATEVER HER AGE.**

**RED FLAGS ARE ASKED UNCONDITIONALLY, REGARDLESS OF AGE OR DURATION** — ‘she's 25, it's functional’ is a named fail. **THE TEN: WEIGHT LOSS · BLOOD IN STOOL OR MELAENA · ANAEMIA · NOCTURNAL SYMPTOMS · PERSISTENT CHANGE IN BOWEL HABIT · ABDOMINAL OR PELVIC MASS · FAMILY HISTORY OF BOWEL OR OVARIAN CANCER · ONSET OVER 50 · FEVER.**

**CORRECTION TO A COMMONLY TAUGHT VERSION OF ROME IV.** **It requires ABDOMINAL PAIN AT LEAST ONE DAY PER WEEK OVER THE LAST THREE MONTHS, WITH ONSET AT LEAST SIX MONTHS BEFORE DIAGNOSIS — plus TWO OF THREE: related to defecation, change in stool frequency, change in stool form.** **It is often taught as ‘six months of pain’, WHICH CONFLATES THE TWO WINDOWS.** If challenged: **‘the SYMPTOM WINDOW is THREE months; the SIX months refers to the TIME SINCE ONSET.’** **AND STRESS IS NOT A CRITERION.**

**EARNING IBS OUT LOUD, rather than defaulting to it**: **‘My provisional diagnosis is IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME. I say that POSITIVELY rather than BY DEFAULT: she has recurrent abdominal discomfort RELIEVED BY DEFECATION, an ALTERNATING STOOL FORM, and a clear STRESSOR. IMPORTANTLY, I HAVE EXCLUDED THE ALTERNATIVES — no weight loss, no rectal bleeding, no anaemia, no nocturnal symptoms, no family history of bowel or ovarian cancer, no travel, no gluten or dairy relationship, and SHE IS NOT PREGNANT.’** **PLACE IBS LAST.**
plan: **WIPE — the sanitiser is on the desk and THE EXAMINER WILL POINT AT IT.** Then **acknowledge, signpost the bowels-and-periods questions, AND ELICIT THE AGENDA IN THE FIRST MINUTE, NOT THE LAST**: **‘Before I start, was there anything in particular that worried you, or something you were hoping we'd do today?’** **If you leave this to the closing seconds you will RUN OUT OF TIME AND LOSE THE MARK.** **Her concern, if you ask: her aunt had bowel cancer.** **She is a little self-conscious and SLIGHTLY BRACED FOR BEING TOLD IT IS NOTHING — if you sound bored SHE STOPS VOLUNTEERING, and Version B never surfaces the stool description.**

**BLOCK 1 — DEFINE AND CHARACTERISE.** The definition question · how long, constant or intermittent, getting worse · **worse at any particular time of day, AND DOES IT WAKE YOU AT NIGHT** · anything better or worse, **and SPECIFICALLY: is it worse after eating, AND IS THERE ANY FOOD THAT SETS IT OFF?** **She answers a general aggravating-factor question with ‘not really’ — SHE ONLY REVEALS BREAD AND PIZZA WHEN FOOD IS NAMED SPECIFICALLY.**

**BLOCK 2 — GENERAL GI SCREEN, the safety net everyone skips.** Nausea · vomiting · abdominal pain · **CONSTIPATION · DIARRHOEA** · fever. **Constipation and diarrhoea are the two you MUST have an answer to before you move on.**

**BLOCK 3 — RED FLAGS AND THE MALIGNANCY GROUPS, ANNOUNCED: ‘I ask everybody these next questions, just to be safe.’** **GENERAL: weight loss without trying · change in appetite · lumps or bumps · more tired than usual.** **BOWEL CANCER: blood in your stool or very dark stools · any LASTING change in bowel habit · anyone in the family with bowel cancer.** **OVARIAN: DO YOU GET FULL VERY QUICKLY, after only a small amount of food · any change in how often you pass urine · family history of OVARIAN OR BREAST cancer.** **OBSTRUCTION: any SURGERY on your tummy · any LUMP OR SWELLING IN YOUR GROIN · ARE YOU PASSING WIND NORMALLY — the cardinal obstruction question in EVERY GI station.**

**BLOCK 3 continued — the dietary, infective and motility groups.** **LACTOSE: worse after dairy — milk, cheese, yoghurt, ice-cream.** **COELIAC: THE FOUR STOOL DESCRIPTORS · does bread or pasta make it worse · ANYONE IN THE FAMILY WITH COELIAC DISEASE** (her sister ‘was told she has something to do with gluten’ — only if asked). **INFECTION: travel, camping, tank water, fever, anyone else at home unwell.** **MOTILITY: medications INCLUDING OVER THE COUNTER AND SUPPLEMENTS — the iron tablets are THEMSELVES A DIFFERENTIAL · diabetes · do you feel the cold or the heat more than others.** **IBD: joint pains · mouth ulcers · red or sore eyes · RASHES — and the itchy blistery rash on both elbows comes out ONLY IF ASKED.**

**BLOCK 3 ends with IBS AND GYNAE — MOVE THESE TO 5:00 AT THE LATEST.** **IBS: do your stools ALTERNATE hard and loose · DOES OPENING YOUR BOWELS MAKE THE BLOATING BETTER · how are things at home, at work.** **GYNAE: when was your LAST PERIOD, are they REGULAR · IS THERE ANY CHANCE YOU COULD BE PREGNANT · are you sexually active, and what are you using for contraception.** **In a 25-year-old woman with bloating, ‘I DIDN'T GET TO IT’ READS THE SAME AS ‘I DIDN'T THINK OF IT’.**

**BLOCK 4 — ROUND OFF.** SADMA · past medical history · family history · occupation and living situation · **a mini-HEADSS for stressors: ‘who do you live with? How are things at work? Anything stressful going on at the moment?’** **STOP AT 6:00.**
Task 2 — the diagnosis
**SPEAK IT OUT LOUD AND IN FULL SENTENCES. NODDING, OR WRITING IT DOWN AND SLIDING IT ACROSS, DOES NOT SCORE — FAILING TO SPEAK THE ANSWER IS A SINGLE-ITEM FAIL.**
Task 3 — the differentials, BY GROUP

**SIX NAMED GROUPS BEAT A FLAT LIST OF TWELVE DIAGNOSES: MALIGNANCY · OBSTRUCTION · DIET · INFECTION · MOTILITY · FUNCTIONAL.** **‘MALIGNANCY — bowel cancer and, IMPORTANTLY, OVARIAN cancer, which presents with exactly these non-specific symptoms; less likely here with no red flags. OBSTRUCTION — adhesions, hernia, volvulus or constipation; less likely with NORMAL FLATUS and no previous surgery. DIETARY — coeliac disease and lactose intolerance. INFECTION — giardiasis or post-infectious change; less likely with no travel. MOTILITY — medication effect, diabetic enteropathy or hypothyroidism. INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE. And FUNCTIONAL — irritable bowel syndrome, WHICH I PLACE LAST BECAUSE IT IS A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION. I would also exclude PREGNANCY in any woman of this age.’**
Explaining coeliac to her, and the sentence that protects the test

**‘Your BOWEL IS SENSITIVE TO GLUTEN — a protein in WHEAT, RYE, BARLEY AND OATS. When you eat it, the LINING OF THE BOWEL BECOMES INFLAMED and STOPS ABSORBING FOOD PROPERLY. That explains the bloating after bread and pizza, the greasy stools that are hard to flush, the LOW IRON, and the ITCHY RASH ON YOUR ELBOWS.’** Then, when she asks whether to stop gluten: **‘That's the important part — PLEASE KEEP EATING GLUTEN UNTIL WE'VE TESTED YOU, because STOPPING IT MAKES THE TESTS COME BACK FALSELY NORMAL.’** **The role-player is briefed to look relieved and say ‘I'll start tonight’ if you get this wrong — AND TO MARK IT AS AN ERROR.**
pefe: **Management — VERSION B, COELIAC DISEASE.** **LIFELONG STRICT GLUTEN-FREE DIET: wheat, rye, barley, oats and their derivatives** · **referral to an ACCREDITED PRACTISING DIETITIAN** · **SCREEN AND REPLACE DEFICIENCIES: iron, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium, zinc** · **BONE DENSITOMETRY — COELIAC DISEASE CAUSES OSTEOPOROSIS** · **OFFER SEROLOGICAL SCREENING TO FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVES** · **PNEUMOCOCCAL VACCINATION — FUNCTIONAL HYPOSPLENISM IS RECOGNISED IN COELIAC DISEASE** · **review symptoms and REPEAT SEROLOGY to confirm dietary adherence.** **Associated with TYPE 1 DIABETES and AUTOIMMUNE THYROID DISEASE.**

**Management — VERSION A, IBS.** **EXPLAIN POSITIVELY, NOT AS ‘NOTHING IS WRONG’** · regular meals, adequate fluid, SOLUBLE fibre, reduce caffeine and alcohol · **LOW-FODMAP TRIAL WITH STRUCTURED DIETITIAN-SUPERVISED REINTRODUCTION** · **symptom-targeted: ANTISPASMODIC for pain, LAXATIVE OR LOPERAMIDE by predominant stool pattern** · address the stressor; consider psychological therapy where stress is prominent · **REVIEW, AND RE-OPEN THE DIAGNOSIS IF ANY RED FLAG APPEARS.**

**The safety-net, verbatim**: **‘Come back sooner if you LOSE WEIGHT without trying, SEE BLOOD in your stool, develop a FEVER, or CAN'T KEEP FLUIDS DOWN.’** Then **‘CAN I JUST CHECK WHAT YOU'LL DO BETWEEN NOW AND THEN?’** — and her answer should be *‘keep eating normally, have the blood test, and come back for the results.’**

**VARIANT — SHE HAS ALREADY STARTED A GLUTEN-FREE DIET.** → **‘Thank you for telling me — THAT CHANGES WHAT I DO NEXT. The blood test ONLY WORKS WHILE YOU'RE EATING GLUTEN, so if we test you now it may come back NORMAL EVEN IF YOU DO HAVE COELIAC DISEASE. I'd ask you to go back onto a normal diet for ABOUT SIX WEEKS before we test. I know that's not what you want to hear, but A WRONG ANSWER HERE WOULD FOLLOW YOU FOR LIFE.’**

**VARIANT — ‘ISN'T THIS JUST IBS? MY FRIEND HAS THAT.’** → **‘It MIGHT be, and irritable bowel syndrome is very common. But it's a diagnosis we ONLY MAKE ONCE WE'VE EXCLUDED OTHER CAUSES — and you have TWO THINGS THAT DON'T FIT IT: your stools suggest YOU'RE NOT ABSORBING FAT PROPERLY, and YOU'RE SHORT OF IRON. I'd rather CHECK THAN ASSUME.’**

**VARIANT — THE OVARIAN VERSION, SHE IS 52.** Bloating four months, waistband tight, full after half a meal, passing urine more often, mother had breast cancer at 46. → **‘Some of what you've described — the bloating, FEELING FULL QUICKLY, and needing to PASS URINE MORE OFTEN — can occasionally come from THE OVARIES, so I'd like to arrange an ULTRASOUND OF YOUR PELVIS and a blood test called CA-125. I'M NOT TELLING YOU THAT YOU HAVE ANYTHING SINISTER; I'M TELLING YOU IT'S SOMETHING I ALWAYS CHECK FOR.’**

**Clue–response table for the moments that decide it.** *‘It settles after I go to the toilet’* → Rome IV criterion 1 — **ask stool form and frequency change, then stress, BUT STILL FINISH THE RED FLAGS. Version A hands you the criterion at NINETY SECONDS. THAT IS BAIT TO CLOSE EARLY.** *‘Milk seems to set it off’* → **quantify: how much, how soon after, DOES HARD CHEESE DO IT TOO.** *‘It's worse in the morning with my coffee’* → **pattern, not pathology — NOTE IT, DO NOT CHASE IT; ask whether it wakes her at night.** *‘Do you think it's cancer?’* → **‘That's a VERY REASONABLE thing to worry about, and IT'S EXACTLY WHAT THESE QUESTIONS ARE FOR.’**

**Other practice stems worth running.** **25F, bloating and foul wind for six weeks AFTER CAMPING AND DRINKING TANK WATER, partner also unwell → GIARDIASIS; did you ask about travel, camping and contacts?** **25F, bloating two days, VOMITING, NO FLATUS, appendicectomy at 15, visibly distended and LOOKS UNWELL → BOWEL OBSTRUCTION; this needs ESCALATION, NOT A CLINIC PLAN.** **25F, bloating and constipation four weeks AFTER STARTING ORAL IRON for a low ferritin → DRUG-INDUCED; did your medication history include SUPPLEMENTS?**

**AVOID**: **false reassurance — ‘it's nothing serious, don't worry’ before the investigations are back. REASSURE ABOUT PROCESS, NOT OUTCOME.** · a flat, ungrouped differential list · **skipping red flags because she is 25** · **missing the stool-character question, which diagnoses Version B as IBS.**

findings: WHEN THIS PANEL APPLIES
ONE SITTING ran this as FIVE MINUTES of history, then a PHYSICAL EXAMINATION REQUEST, then diagnosis and differentials. TREAT FIVE MINUTES AS THE SAFE ASSUMPTION AND FINISH EARLY RATHER THAN LATE
Steps 1–3 — before you touch the abdomen

GENERAL APPEARANCE: pallor, cachexia, jaundice, hydration, comfort — AND RASHES: DERMATITIS HERPETIFORMIS ON ELBOWS AND KNEES, ERYTHEMA NODOSUM ON SHINS. VITAL SIGNS, TEMPERATURE ESPECIALLY. HANDS AND FACE: KOILONYCHIA, pallor of palmar creases and conjunctivae, ANGULAR CHEILITIS, GLOSSITIS, MOUTH ULCERS, clubbing
Steps 4–7 — the abdomen

INSPECTION: distension, flanks, scars, HERNIAL ORIFICES WITH A COUGH, visible peristalsis, everted umbilicus, SISTER MARY JOSEPH NODULE. PALPATION: light then deep, tenderness, guarding, masses, organomegaly, A PELVIC MASS RISING OUT OF THE PELVIS. PERCUSSION: liver span, splenic dullness, SHIFTING DULLNESS FOR ASCITES. AUSCULTATION: bowel sounds — absent, normal, or OBSTRUCTIVE TINKLING
Steps 8–9 — completing it
INGUINAL AND FEMORAL ORIFICES · DIGITAL RECTAL EXAMINATION · AND OFFER A PELVIC EXAMINATION IF OVARIAN PATHOLOGY IS ON YOUR LIST. OFFICE TESTS: URINE DIPSTICK, URINARY β-hCG, BLOOD SUGAR LEVEL
HOW TO RAISE THE PELVIC EXAMINATION SAFELY

A bimanual examination for isolated bloating CAN LOOK EXCESSIVE, so FRAME IT AS CONDITIONAL AND CONSENTED: ‘Given the possibility of an OVARIAN cause, I would like to OFFER a pelvic examination WITH A CHAPERONE PRESENT, if that's acceptable to you.’ OFFERING IT CORRECTLY SCORES; PERFORMING IT UNANNOUNCED DOES NOT
THE RASH THAT HANDS YOU THE DIAGNOSIS

An ITCHY VESICULAR rash on ELBOWS, KNEES, BUTTOCKS OR SCALP in a patient with chronic bloating, loose stools and iron deficiency is DERMATITIS HERPETIFORMIS UNTIL PROVEN OTHERWISE. It is COELIAC DISEASE OF THE SKIN, it responds to a GLUTEN-FREE DIET, and ITS PRESENCE ALONE IS ENOUGH TO COMMIT TO THE DIAGNOSIS IN THE ROOM. Herpetiform means HERPES-LIKE, i.e. VESICULAR — but unlike herpes it is INTENSELY ITCHY RATHER THAN PAINFUL
WHICH RASH BELONGS TO WHICH DIAGNOSIS — a favourite examiner probe

DERMATITIS HERPETIFORMIS (grouped vesicles and excoriated papules over EXTENSOR surfaces — elbows and knees) = COELIAC. ERYTHEMA NODOSUM (TENDER RED NODULES ON THE SHINS) = INFLAMMATORY BOWEL DISEASE, NOT coeliac. KOILONYCHIA = spooning of the nail in LONGSTANDING IRON DEFICIENCY. ANGULAR CHEILITIS = fissuring at the mouth corners — look for GLOSSITIS at the same time
BEDSIDE AND FIRST-LINE INVESTIGATIONS

BEDSIDE: URINARY β-hCG · abdominal examination INCLUDING HERNIAL ORIFICES · blood sugar level · weight and waist · blood pressure. BLOODS: FBE · IRON STUDIES AND FERRITIN · CRP and ESR · UEC, LFT · TSH · COELIAC SEROLOGY: tTG-IgA WITH TOTAL SERUM IgA, TAKEN WHILE SHE IS STILL EATING GLUTEN · HbA1c if indicated
DO NOT MISS, and AVOID

DO NOT MISS: PELVIC ULTRASOUND AND CA-125 in any woman with persistent bloating · faecal occult blood or CALPROTECTIN where the picture is inflammatory · ERECT AND SUPINE ABDOMINAL X-RAY if obstruction is suspected · A RECTAL EXAMINATION. AVOID: STARTING A GLUTEN-FREE DIET BEFORE SEROLOGY — IT INVALIDATES BOTH THE ANTIBODY TEST AND THE BIOPSY · CA-125 as a SCREENING test in an asymptomatic woman · LABELLING IBS AT THE FIRST VISIT WITH AN UNEXPLAINED ANAEMIA SITTING IN THE NOTES · empirical antispasmodics instead of a diagnosis
The confirmatory test

DUODENAL HISTOLOGY graded by the MODIFIED MARSH CLASSIFICATION, from normal villi through to TOTAL VILLOUS ATROPHY. BIOPSY REMAINS THE CONFIRMATORY TEST IN AUSTRALIAN ADULTS. Numbers VERIFY : coeliac affects about 1 IN 70 Australians and the MAJORITY REMAIN UNDIAGNOSED; FIRST-DEGREE RELATIVES carry roughly a 1 IN 10 risk; gluten challenge is commonly quoted as THE EQUIVALENT OF 4 SLICES OF BREAD DAILY FOR 6 WEEKS before testing

MORBILLIFORM RASH, GENERALISED LYMPHADENOPATHY, INFLAMED TONSILS WITH EXUDATE. Temperature 38.2°C. NO jaundice, NO organomegaly, NO MURMUR, injection sites unremarkable, DIPSTICK NEGATIVE
VERSION 3 CARD — endocarditis
MURMUR, PLUS RAISED JVP, BIBASAL CREPITATIONS AND ANKLE OEDEMA. THIS IS THE CONFUSION THE EXAMINERS BUILT DELIBERATELY: HEART FAILURE IS THE COMPLICATION, ENDOCARDITIS IS THE DIAGNOSIS
THE URINE DIPSTICK, read properly
UROBILINOGEN IS NORMALLY PRESENT; BILIRUBIN IS NOT. Its presence means CONJUGATED bilirubin is spilling into the urine — hepatitis, cholestasis or obstruction
EXPOSE THE ARMS
The card may say ‘injection sites’ and EXPECT YOU TO HAVE ASKED ABOUT THEM. Look at BOTH ANTECUBITAL FOSSAE, BOTH FOREARMS AND THE GROINS for TRACKS, CELLULITIS, ABSCESS AND THROMBOPHLEBITIS
Peripheral stigmata in Version 3

SPLINTER HAEMORRHAGES, JANEWAY LESIONS AND OSLER NODES are individually non-specific but count as MINOR CRITERIA when there is FEVER AND A MURMUR. OSLER EQUALS OUCH — PAINFUL, ON THE PULPS; JANEWAY LESIONS ARE PAINLESS AND ON THE PALMS AND SOLES
INVESTIGATIONS — in the room

Vital signs; LOOK AT BOTH ARMS AND THE GROINS · skin, sclerae, mouth, NAILS, PALMS AND SOLES · abdomen: liver size and tenderness, spleen · cardiovascular: MURMUR, JVP, chest, ankles · ALL NODE GROUPS · URINE DIPSTICK · bedside blood glucose
INVESTIGATIONS — the bloods

FBE with film, EUC, CRP, LFT, INR (SYNTHETIC FUNCTION) · HEPATITIS A IgM; HBsAg, ANTI-HBc IgM, ANTI-HBs; HCV ANTIBODY AND HCV RNA · HIV ANTIGEN/ANTIBODY TEST — NAMED, WITH CONSENT · SYPHILIS EIA AND RPR; NAAT SWABS FROM EXPOSED SITES · THICK AND THIN MALARIA FILMS × 3 PLUS RAPID ANTIGEN if febrile after South-East Asian travel · arbovirus serology by exposure · BLOOD CULTURES × 3 BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS, PLUS ECHOCARDIOGRAM, if a murmur or embolic signs
NOTIFIABLE, and the confidentiality line that follows from it

HEPATITIS A, B, C, HIV AND MALARIA ARE ALL NOTIFIABLE IN SOUTH AUSTRALIA. So NEVER promise unqualified confidentiality: ‘what you tell me is confidential, THOUGH SOME INFECTIONS HAVE TO BE REPORTED TO PUBLIC HEALTH SO CONTACTS CAN BE TRACED — that's done sensitively and YOUR NAME ISN'T GIVEN TO YOUR CONTACTS.’ The role-player is briefed to ask ‘so nobody else will ever know?’ AND SEE WHETHER YOU CORRECT YOURSELF

dx: **THREE VERSIONS, ONE STRUCTURE, AND EVERY ANSWER IS A CONSEQUENCE OF SHARED NEEDLES.** **VERSION 1 — abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea, jaundice → ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS, most likely B or C.** **VERSION 2 — NO abdominal pain, NO jaundice; rash, sore throat, night sweats → HIV SEROCONVERSION (and EBV is what most candidates say instead).** **VERSION 3 — chest pain and palpitations with fever → INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS, COMPLICATED BY heart failure. NOT a diagnosis of heart failure.** **BUILD ONE STRUCTURE AND LET THE ANSWERS TELL YOU WHICH.**

**THE STEM GIVES YOU THREE PIECES OF INFORMATION AND EVERY ONE CARRIES MARKS: the UNWELLNESS, the TRAVEL, the HEROIN.** **SIGNPOST THEM OUT LOUD: ‘there are THREE things I want to cover — what the unwellness actually feels like, your trip, and the heroin. I'll take them in that order.’** **Twelve seconds, and it tells the examiner your ENTIRE PLAN BEFORE YOU EXECUTE IT.**

**DEFINE ‘UNWELL’ FIRST, EVERY TIME — the question decides which cluster you are in.** **‘When you say you feel unwell — do you mean LOW IN ENERGY, do you mean SLEEPY, or do you mean FEVERISH?’** **‘Low in energy’ puts you in the TIREDNESS cluster. ‘Sleepy’ puts you in SLEEP DISORDERS. ‘FEVERISH’ puts you in INFECTION — and in this station, with travel and needles, THAT IS WHERE YOU WANT TO BE.**

**THE TRAVEL HISTORY IS EIGHT QUESTIONS, NOT TWO — A B C D E F G S — and it is the LARGEST SINGLE SCORING BLOCK AFTER THE DIAGNOSIS.** **ACTIVITIES · BITES · CONTACT (sick people, animals, farms) · DRUGS · EXPOSURE TO BLOOD (tattoos, piercings, dental work, surgery, TRANSFUSION) · FOOD AND WATER · GP BEFORE TRAVEL · SEX.** **He answers ‘just having fun with mates, nothing special’ — RUN THE WHOLE MNEMONIC ANYWAY. THE SCRIPTED FINDINGS SIT IN THE SPECIFIC QUESTIONS, NEVER IN THE SUMMARY.**

**WHY BLOOD TRANSFUSION OVERSEAS IS A REAL QUESTION.** It sounds odd in an Australian consultation. **IT IS NOT. Cosmetic surgery, dental work and elective procedures cost a FRACTION overseas, and HEALTH TOURISM IS COMMON. People DO have transfusions abroad, in systems with DIFFERENT SCREENING STANDARDS.**

**THE VACCINATION QUESTION, AND THE TRAP INSIDE IT.** He says he saw his GP and had ‘a hepatitis shot’. **THAT IS A SCRIPTED FINDING PLACED TO TEST WHETHER YOU KNOW WHAT IT COVERS.** **HEPATITIS A AND HEPATITIS B ARE VACCINE-PREVENTABLE. HEPATITIS C IS NOT — THERE IS NO VACCINE. A hepatitis shot before the trip DOES NOT TAKE ACUTE HEPATITIS OFF YOUR LIST.** Say so out loud.

**THE HEROIN HISTORY IS THREE QUESTIONS AND THE ORDER IS ITSELF A COMMUNICATION SKILL.** **‘CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THAT?’ → (let him talk, DO NOT INTERRUPT) → ‘CAN YOU TELL ME HOW YOU USED IT — HOW IT WENT IN?’ → ‘AND DID YOU SHARE NEEDLES?’** **ASKING ‘DID YOU SHARE NEEDLES?’ FIRST ANNOUNCES THAT YOU HAVE MEMORISED THE RECALL. It is also poor practice: an open question first gets you THE GUILT, THE FREQUENCY, WHETHER IT WAS A ONE-OFF, AND WHETHER THERE IS ONGOING USE — none of which a closed question yields.** **The role-player is briefed: if you lead with needles, he answers ‘yes’ FLATLY AND VOLUNTEERS NOTHING ELSE.**

**SHARED NEEDLES OPENS ONE BOX, WHICH CONTAINS THREE. ASK ALL THREE IN EVERY VERSION.** **BOX 1 HEPATITIS: yellowing of skin or eyes · right upper quadrant pain · nausea or vomiting · DARK URINE OR PALE STOOLS · appetite · itch.** **BOX 2 HIV: sore throat · rash · fever, chills, NIGHT SWEATS · weight loss · LUMPS in neck, armpits or groin · diarrhoea.** **BOX 3 INJECTION-RELATED: redness, swelling or pain AT THE INJECTION SITE · chest pain · racing or pounding heart · breathlessness · MARKS OR SPOTS ON HANDS, FINGERS OR PALMS.** **THE ANSWERS, NOT YOUR MEMORY OF THE RECALL, TELL YOU WHICH CASE YOU ARE IN — and the NEGATIVES are what let you say ‘I excluded that’ out loud.**

**THE SINGLE MOST DESIGNED TRAP IN THE STATION: GO BACK FOR THE SEXUAL HISTORY.** **‘No sex overseas’ is written into the role-player brief PRECISELY SO THAT CANDIDATES TICK THE BOX AND MOVE ON.** **THE VIRUS WAS NOT CONTRACTED OVERSEAS BY SEX — IT WAS CONTRACTED BY A NEEDLE. BUT THE MAN IN FRONT OF YOU CAN NOW TRANSMIT IT, AND TO WHOM IS A QUESTION YOU MUST ASK.** **THE REFRAME: ‘I asked earlier whether you had sex while you were away and you said no, and I accept that — but THESE SAME INFECTIONS ARE ALSO PASSED ON SEXUALLY, so if you have picked one up I NEED TO KNOW WHO ELSE MIGHT NEED TESTING. HAVE YOU EVER BEEN SEXUALLY ACTIVE?’** → **he then answers fully: never uses condoms, multiple partners at times, partners are women. THE BRIEF SAYS NO THE FIRST TIME AND FULLY THE SECOND — WHICH MEANS THE MARK EXISTS AND IS SIMPLY WAITING FOR YOU.**

**‘I FEEL SO GUILTY’ IS SAID AT LEAST THREE TIMES, AND A FOURTH MORE HEAVILY IF YOU DO NOT PICK IT UP. IT IS A DELIBERATE CUE.** **FOUR QUESTIONS, TWENTY SECONDS, AND ONE OF THEM MUST BE ABOUT SELF-HARM**: **‘How are you COPING with what happened? … How's your MOOD been? … Are you still ENJOYING the things you used to? … Have you had any THOUGHTS OF HARMING YOURSELF?’**
plan: **WIPE, then ACKNOWLEDGE THE FEAR HE HAS JUST VOICED — he has told you he thinks something is seriously wrong.** **‘I'm sorry — a week of feeling that unwell, to the point you can't get out of bed, is FRIGHTENING, and I understand why you're worried something serious is going on.’** Then **SIGNPOST THE THREE LEADS.**
**BLOCK 1 — DEFINE THE UNWELLNESS.** Low in energy, sleepy, or feverish · how long · constant or coming and going · getting worse · anything better or worse · **how is it affecting your life.**

**BLOCK 2 — THE TRAVEL HISTORY IN FULL, A B C D E F G S, OUT LOUD.** Where and how long · **‘WHAT DID YOU ACTUALLY DO while you were over there?’** · insect or tick bites, bushwalking · contact with anyone unwell, animals or farms · **tattoos, piercings, DENTAL WORK, SURGERY OR A BLOOD TRANSFUSION** · street food or unbottled water · **did you see a doctor before you went, for VACCINATIONS OR MALARIA TABLETS** · **and did you have any sexual contact while you were away** — **WRITE THE ‘NO’ DOWN; YOU ARE COMING BACK TO IT.**
**BLOCK 3 — THE HEROIN HISTORY, THREE STEPS, IN ORDER.**
**BLOCK 4 — THE THREE BLOOD-BORNE VIRUS BOXES, prefaced: ‘thank you for being honest, that helps me a lot. SHARING A NEEDLE CAN PASS ON INFECTIONS CARRIED IN BLOOD, so I need to check for those.’**

**BLOCK 5 — GO BACK FOR THE SEXUAL HISTORY, with the reframe.** Have you ever been sexually active · do you use condoms · have you ever had multiple partners · **are your partners male, female, or both.**

**BLOCK 6 — THE PSYCHOLOGICAL CUE, then close out.** Coping, mood, anhedonia, **self-harm** · **‘has there been any use since you got back?’** · medications, allergies, conditions · alcohol, smoking · family history of cancer · **‘and was there anything you were PARTICULARLY WORRIED this might be?’** — his hidden agenda: **‘I'm scared I've given myself something I can't get rid of.’**
HARD STOP ON HISTORY AT SIX MINUTES

**The grouped differential list is worth MORE than the last question.** If time remains, sweep the tiredness mnemonic — haemochromatosis, diabetes, thyroid, anaemia, autoimmune disease, coeliac, heart failure, sleep apnoea. **YOU WILL RARELY GET THERE. DO NOT SACRIFICE THE DIFFERENTIAL LIST TO REACH IT.**
**Ask for the card AND INTERROGATE IT — the four things it does not mention.**

**Name the diagnosis with REASONS, give the differentials BY GROUP, name the HIV test and seek consent, handle confidentiality accurately, offer harm reduction WITHOUT JUDGEMENT, safety-net, summarise.** **When you name it he pauses long and says ‘I've ruined my life over one stupid night’ — PAUSE WITH HIM: ‘that's a hard thing to hear. WHAT'S GOING THROUGH YOUR MIND?’ IF YOU RUSH TO REASSURE WITHOUT PAUSING HE SAYS ‘YOU'RE JUST SAYING THAT.’** Then the two things to hold on to: **‘FIRST, WE DON'T KNOW YET — THIS IS A CONCERN, NOT A RESULT. Second, if it IS HIV, treatment today is EXTREMELY EFFECTIVE: people live a NORMAL LIFE SPAN and, ON TREATMENT, CANNOT PASS IT ON TO ANYONE ELSE. THIS IS NOT THE ILLNESS IT WAS THIRTY YEARS AGO.’**
pefe: **VERSION 1 — naming acute hepatitis.** **‘Your LIVER IS INFLAMED, and it is most likely caused by a VIRUS you picked up when you injected and shared a needle.’** **CORRECTION: the teaching says THE TYPE DOES NOT MATTER. For the patient that is true; FOR YOUR MANAGEMENT IT IS NOT.** **Given the needle sharing, the likely types are HEPATITIS B OR C, and that matters because IT CHANGES WHO WE VACCINATE, WHO WE TEST, AND WHETHER WE CAN CURE IT.** If he asks which type: **‘If it's hepatitis B WE CAN VACCINATE THE PEOPLE AROUND YOU. If it's hepatitis C THERE'S NO VACCINE — BUT IT IS NOW CURABLE WITH TABLETS, usually over two to three months.’** VERIFY

**VERSION 3 — naming endocarditis, NOT heart failure.** **‘An INFECTION OF THE INNER LINING OF YOUR HEART, usually one of the valves. You most likely caught it when you injected and shared a needle — BACTERIA FROM THE SKIN GET INTO THE BLOODSTREAM AND SETTLE ON A VALVE. Those heart-failure signs are A COMPLICATION OF THE INFECTION, NOT A SEPARATE ILLNESS. This needs HOSPITAL TODAY.’** **If challenged: ‘I've made endocarditis PRIMARY because the heart failure here is explained by ACUTE VALVULAR REGURGITATION from the infection. Heart failure is ONE OF THE TWO CLASSICAL COMPLICATIONS of endocarditis, THE OTHER BEING SYSTEMIC EMBOLISM. Diagnosing heart failure alone in a FEBRILE INJECTING DRUG USER WITH A NEW MURMUR would MISS THE TREATABLE CAUSE and DELAY BLOOD CULTURES AND ANTIBIOTICS.’**

**Definitions to have ready.** **BLOOD-BORNE VIRUSES — hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV. ALL THREE ARE TRANSMITTED BY BLOOD AND BY SEX, WHICH IS WHY THE SEXUAL HISTORY MUST BE REVISITED.** **HIV SEROCONVERSION ILLNESS — the acute symptomatic phase 2–4 WEEKS AFTER INFECTION: fever, sore throat, rash, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, headache, sometimes diarrhoea and weight loss. INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM INFLUENZA OR GLANDULAR FEVER.** **INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS — infection of the endocardial surface, usually a valve. IN INJECTING DRUG USE THE TRICUSPID VALVE IS CLASSICALLY INVOLVED, AND STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS IS THE COMMONEST ORGANISM.**

**DO NOT MISS**: **INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS — FEVER PLUS A MURMUR IN AN INJECTING DRUG USER IS ENDOCARDITIS UNTIL BLOOD CULTURES SAY OTHERWISE** · **FALCIPARUM MALARIA — South-East Asian travel with undifferentiated fever. IT KILLS IN DAYS. THICK AND THIN FILMS, THREE SETS** · **SEPSIS FROM INJECTION-SITE CELLULITIS OR ABSCESS — LOOK AT THE ARMS** · **ACUTE LIVER FAILURE — encephalopathy, coagulopathy, worsening jaundice** · **SUICIDAL IDEATION — he says ‘guilty’ repeatedly. ASK.**

**AVOID**: **antibiotics before cultures if endocarditis is possible** · **diagnosing heart failure in Version 3** · **NSAIDs or aspirin if dengue is possible** · **telling him a hepatitis vaccine protects him from hepatitis C** · **moralising about the heroin** · **promising confidentiality you cannot keep for a notifiable disease.**

**Treatment by version** VERIFY: **ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS — mostly SUPPORTIVE. Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs; MONITOR INR AND ENCEPHALOPATHY. Vaccinate and test household and sexual contacts. HEPATITIS C IS NOW CURABLE — direct-acting antivirals, typically 8–12 WEEKS, PBS-listed and prescribable in general practice with support.** **HIV — SAME-DAY sexual health or infectious diseases referral. ANTIRETROVIRAL THERAPY IS STARTED AS SOON AS POSSIBLE AFTER DIAGNOSIS, REGARDLESS OF CD4 COUNT. If an exposure were WITHIN 72 HOURS, POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS would apply — it does not here, BUT KNOW THE WINDOW.** **ENDOCARDITIS — ADMIT. Empirical therapy in an injecting drug user MUST COVER STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS INCLUDING MRSA — typically vancomycin based; confirm before quoting a dose. Cardiology and cardiothoracic input; SURGERY for heart failure, abscess, large vegetations or embolic events.**

**The numbers**: **station 8 min, history 6 min** · **HIV seroconversion at 2–4 WEEKS; 4th-generation antigen/antibody test; REPEAT AT 6 WEEKS; PEP WINDOW 72 HOURS** · **hepatitis serology: hepatitis A IgM; HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HBs; HCV antibody PLUS HCV RNA** · **endocarditis: THREE SETS OF BLOOD CULTURES FROM SEPARATE SITES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS; TTE THEN TOE; MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA** · **malaria: THICK AND THIN FILMS × 3 plus rapid antigen** · **dengue: NO NSAIDs, NO ASPIRIN.**

**Other practice stems.** **Same stem, incomplete recall: fever, raised JVP, INGUINAL LYMPHADENOPATHY, SPLENOMEGALY → STILL ENDOCARDITIS. Tests whether your structure survives an AMBIGUOUS card.** **24F back from PAPUA NEW GUINEA eight days ago, rigors and headache, NO PROPHYLAXIS, platelets 88 → FALCIPARUM MALARIA; tests whether FILMS are requested URGENTLY.** **29M one week after a shared injection: fever, a RED TENDER SWELLING IN THE ANTECUBITAL FOSSA, HR 118, BP 96/58 → INJECTION-SITE ABSCESS WITH SEPSIS; tests whether YOU LOOKED AT THE ARMS.**

**The safety-net, verbatim**: **‘If you become CONFUSED OR DROWSY, if you TURN YELLOW, if you get CHEST PAIN OR BREATHLESSNESS, or if you get MUCH WORSE — go straight to the emergency department or call 000.’** **And offer harm reduction WITHOUT ASSUMING: ‘I'd also like to give you information about free needle and syringe services and TAKE-HOME NALOXONE — NOT BECAUSE I ASSUME YOU'LL USE AGAIN, BUT BECAUSE IT COSTS NOTHING TO HAVE.’**

SA — **harm reduction: NEEDLE AND SYRINGE PROGRAM sites through SA Health and participating pharmacies; TAKE-HOME NALOXONE FREE WITHOUT PRESCRIPTION; opioid dependence treatment through DASSA; ADIS 1300 13 1340** VERIFY · **ADELAIDE SEXUAL HEALTH CENTRE (CLINIC 275) and SHINE SA — HIV and STI testing, treatment and CONFIDENTIAL PARTNER NOTIFICATION** VERIFY · **SA Health COMMUNICABLE DISEASE CONTROL BRANCH — notification and contact tracing** · **MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 and RFDS for retrieval of a septic or unstable patient; PATS for travel to metropolitan cardiology or hepatology** · **Country Health Connect for follow-up** · **ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officers; Closing the Gap PBS** · **TIS National 131 450 · healthdirect 1800 022 222 · GP MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT PLAN; LIFELINE 13 11 14.**

The two that get mixed up

‘So he is FEBRILE, with a MURMUR, and he has RAISED JVP, BIBASAL CREPITATIONS AND ANKLE OEDEMA. I read the murmur and the fever in an INJECTING DRUG USER as INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS, and I read the raised JVP, crepitations and oedema as HEART FAILURE ARISING FROM IT — a COMPLICATION, not a second diagnosis’

THREE SETS OF BLOOD CULTURES FROM SEPARATE SITES, BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS. Saying ‘I'd start antibiotics’ without mentioning cultures is a NAMED AUTOMATIC FAIL — you lose the organism and therefore the targeted therapy

IN INJECTING DRUG USE THE TRICUSPID VALVE IS CLASSICALLY INVOLVED, AND STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS IS THE COMMONEST ORGANISM. A RIGHT-SIDED vegetation embolises TO THE LUNGS — so look for PLEURITIC PAIN, HAEMOPTYSIS AND MULTIPLE PERIPHERAL LUNG OPACITIES rather than for stroke
