Heart failure is ONE OF THE TWO CLASSICAL COMPLICATIONS of endocarditis, THE OTHER BEING SYSTEMIC EMBOLISM. Diagnosing heart failure alone in a febrile injecting drug user with a new murmur WOULD MISS THE TREATABLE CAUSE AND DELAY CULTURES AND ANTIBIOTICS.’**

**THE STEM STILL GIVES YOU THREE LEADS, AND THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT CHANGE BETWEEN VERSIONS: the UNWELLNESS, the TRAVEL, the HEROIN.** **SIGNPOST THEM OUT LOUD — twelve seconds, and it shows the examiner your whole plan before you execute it.** **DEFINE ‘UNWELL’ FIRST: low in energy, sleepy, or FEVERISH — and feverish puts you in infection, which is where you want to be.**

**THE TRAVEL HISTORY IS EIGHT QUESTIONS, NOT TWO — A B C D E F G S** — ACTIVITIES · BITES · CONTACT · DRUGS · EXPOSURE TO BLOOD (tattoos, piercings, dental work, surgery, TRANSFUSION) · FOOD AND WATER · GP BEFORE TRAVEL · SEX. **He answers ‘just having fun with mates, nothing special’ — RUN THE WHOLE MNEMONIC ANYWAY. THE SCRIPTED FINDINGS SIT IN THE SPECIFIC QUESTIONS, NEVER IN THE SUMMARY.** **And MALARIA STILL HAS TO BE MENTIONED — South-East Asian travel with fever means THICK AND THIN FILMS, whatever else you have found.**

**THE HEROIN HISTORY IS THREE QUESTIONS AND THE ORDER IS ITSELF A COMMUNICATION SKILL**: **‘CAN YOU TELL ME MORE ABOUT THAT?’ → (let him talk) → ‘HOW DID YOU USE IT — HOW DID IT GO IN?’ → ‘AND DID YOU SHARE NEEDLES?’** **Leading with needles announces a memorised recall, and the role-player is briefed to answer ‘yes’ FLATLY AND VOLUNTEER NOTHING ELSE — you lose the guilt, the frequency and whether use has continued.**

**ASK ALL THREE BLOOD-BORNE VIRUS BOXES EVEN THOUGH THIS IS THE CARDIAC VERSION.** **HEPATITIS: jaundice, RUQ pain, nausea, dark urine or pale stools.** **HIV: sore throat, rash, night sweats, weight loss, lumps, diarrhoea.** **INJECTION-RELATED — the one that pays off here: REDNESS OR SWELLING AT THE INJECTION SITE · CHEST PAIN · RACING OR POUNDING HEART · BREATHLESSNESS · MARKS OR SPOTS ON HANDS, FINGERS OR PALMS.** **The NEGATIVES in the other two boxes are what let you say ‘I excluded that’ out loud.**

**THE TWO TRAPS THAT RUN IN EVERY VERSION, INCLUDING THIS ONE.** **(1) GO BACK FOR THE SEXUAL HISTORY: ‘no sex overseas’ is in the brief PRECISELY SO CANDIDATES TICK IT AND MOVE ON — he answers fully the SECOND time, so the mark is waiting for you.** **(2) THE GUILT: ‘I feel so guilty’ is said at least THREE times, and a FOURTH more heavily if unacknowledged. FOUR QUESTIONS, TWENTY SECONDS, AND ONE MUST BE ABOUT SELF-HARM.**
plan: **WIPE, then ACKNOWLEDGE THE FEAR HE HAS VOICED** — ‘a week of feeling that unwell, to the point you can't get out of bed, is FRIGHTENING.’ Then **SIGNPOST THE THREE LEADS: the unwellness, your trip, and the heroin — in that order.**
**DEFINE THE UNWELLNESS.** Low in energy, sleepy, or feverish · how long · constant or intermittent · getting worse · anything better or worse · **effect on life.**

**THE TRAVEL HISTORY IN FULL, OUT LOUD.** Where and how long · **what did you ACTUALLY DO** · bites, bushwalking · sick contacts, animals, farms · **tattoos, piercings, dental work, surgery, BLOOD TRANSFUSION** · street food and unbottled water · **pre-travel GP visit, VACCINATIONS AND MALARIA TABLETS** · **sex while away — WRITE THE ‘NO’ DOWN, YOU ARE COMING BACK TO IT.**
**THE HEROIN HISTORY, THREE STEPS, IN ORDER.**

**THE THREE BBV BOXES — and in this version the INJECTION-RELATED box is where the case turns.** When he reports chest pain, palpitations and breathlessness, **FOLLOW IT: how long has the chest pain been there, is it worse lying flat or on exertion, any breathlessness at night or on climbing stairs, ANY SUDDEN WEAKNESS, VISUAL LOSS OR LIMB PAIN (embolism), and ANY PLEURITIC PAIN OR COUGHING BLOOD (septic pulmonary emboli from a right-sided vegetation).**
**GO BACK FOR THE SEXUAL HISTORY, with the reframe: ‘these same infections are ALSO passed on sexually, so if you have picked one up I need to know WHO ELSE MIGHT NEED TESTING.’**

**THE GUILT, then close out.** Coping · mood · anhedonia · **self-harm** · any use since you got back · medications, allergies, conditions · alcohol, smoking · **‘was there anything you were particularly worried this might be?’**
**Ask for the card AND INTERROGATE IT — and REQUEST THE PERIPHERAL STIGMATA BY NAME. Then read the decisive findings aloud and separate the infection from its complication.**

**Name endocarditis with reasons → say the heart failure is a COMPLICATION → the differentials BY GROUP → THREE SETS OF BLOOD CULTURES BEFORE ANTIBIOTICS → hospital TODAY → safety-net → summary.** **Do not forget the consented HIV test and the malaria films just because the cardiac answer is in front of you — he shared a needle, and ALL THREE BBVs still need testing.**
The confidentiality line

**NEVER promise unqualified confidentiality.** **‘What you tell me is confidential, THOUGH SOME INFECTIONS HAVE TO BE REPORTED TO PUBLIC HEALTH SO CONTACTS CAN BE TRACED — that's done sensitively and YOUR NAME ISN'T GIVEN TO YOUR CONTACTS.’** **The role-player is briefed to ask ‘so nobody else will ever know?’ AND SEE WHETHER YOU CORRECT YOURSELF.**
pefe: **MANAGEMENT — ADMIT.** VERIFY **Empirical therapy in an injecting drug user MUST COVER STAPHYLOCOCCUS AUREUS INCLUDING MRSA — typically VANCOMYCIN BASED, with the regimen guided by Therapeutic Guidelines and local policy. CONFIRM BEFORE QUOTING A DOSE.** **CARDIOLOGY AND CARDIOTHORACIC INPUT. SURGERY for HEART FAILURE, ABSCESS, LARGE VEGETATIONS OR EMBOLIC EVENTS — and heart failure is itself one of the commonest surgical indications, which is another reason naming it as ‘the diagnosis’ misses the point.**

**THE MODIFIED DUKE CRITERIA, to frame the answer**: **MAJOR — positive blood cultures with a typical organism from two separate sets, and EVIDENCE OF ENDOCARDIAL INVOLVEMENT on echocardiography (vegetation, abscess, new valvular regurgitation).** **MINOR — PREDISPOSITION (including INJECTING DRUG USE), FEVER ≥38°C, VASCULAR PHENOMENA (septic emboli, Janeway lesions, conjunctival haemorrhage), IMMUNOLOGICAL PHENOMENA (Osler nodes, Roth spots, glomerulonephritis), and MICROBIOLOGICAL EVIDENCE not meeting a major criterion.** VERIFY

**DO NOT MISS, alongside the endocarditis**: **SEPSIS — he may be septic before he is diagnosed; vital signs and lactate** · **SEPTIC PULMONARY EMBOLI from a tricuspid vegetation — pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, multiple peripheral opacities** · **SYSTEMIC EMBOLISM if there is left-sided disease — stroke, splenic or renal infarct, acute limb ischaemia** · **AORTIC ROOT ABSCESS — new conduction delay on the ECG** · **FALCIPARUM MALARIA, which still has to be excluded in a febrile returned traveller from South-East Asia** · **INJECTION-SITE ABSCESS OR SEPTIC THROMBOPHLEBITIS — LOOK AT THE ARMS** · **SUICIDAL IDEATION — he says ‘guilty’ repeatedly.**

**AVOID**: **antibiotics before cultures** · **diagnosing heart failure as the primary problem** · **stopping the BBV screen because the cardiac answer arrived first** · **moralising about the heroin** · **promising confidentiality you cannot keep for a notifiable disease** · **an HIV test without named consent.**

**The safety-net, verbatim**: **‘If you become CONFUSED OR DROWSY, if you get WORSE BREATHLESSNESS or CANNOT LIE FLAT, if you get SUDDEN WEAKNESS, VISUAL LOSS OR A COLD PAINFUL LIMB, or if you COUGH UP BLOOD — go straight to the emergency department or call 000.’** **But in this version the realistic disposition is ADMISSION TODAY, not a safety-net and review.**

**Harm reduction, offered WITHOUT ASSUMING**: **‘I'd also like to give you information about free needle and syringe services and TAKE-HOME NALOXONE — NOT BECAUSE I ASSUME YOU'LL USE AGAIN, BUT BECAUSE IT COSTS NOTHING TO HAVE.’**

**The variant that tests whether your structure survives an AMBIGUOUS card**: same stem, incomplete recall — **FEVER, RAISED JVP, INGUINAL LYMPHADENOPATHY, SPLENOMEGALY.** → **STILL ENDOCARDITIS.** Splenomegaly is a recognised finding in subacute disease, lymphadenopathy is non-specific, and the fever with a raised JVP in an injecting drug user keeps the diagnosis where it was. **Say what you would ask for to resolve it: a murmur, peripheral stigmata, blood cultures and an echocardiogram.**

AUREUS in injecting drug use** · **complications: HEART FAILURE and SYSTEMIC EMBOLISM** · **OSLER = OUCH (painful, pulps); JANEWAY = painless, palms and soles** · **malaria: thick and thin films × 3** · **HIV seroconversion 2–4 weeks, repeat at 6 weeks, PEP window 72 hours** · **no hepatitis C vaccine.**

findingsLabel: The results, the ECG and the doses — open only when you would ask for them
findings: VERSION A — the sick one

68M, CKD stage 4, two days of lethargy and GENERALISED MUSCLE WEAKNESS after gastroenteritis. On RAMIPRIL, SPIRONOLACTONE, metformin, atorvastatin. BP 104/62 · PR 52 · RR 16 · SpO2 97% · 36.4°C. POTASSIUM 7.2 (3.5–5.2) · SODIUM 134 · UREA 24.1 (3–8) · CREATININE 312 (60–110) · eGFR 16 · BICARBONATE 16 (22–32) · CORRECTED CALCIUM 2.18
VERSION B — the well one

44F, ENTIRELY WELL, routine pre-procedure bloods. Lab PHONES a potassium of 6.1. No symptoms, no relevant medications, NORMAL RENAL FUNCTION, and THE LAB COMMENTS ‘SPECIMEN HAEMOLYSED’. ECG NORMAL. Answer: PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA — but the ORDER OF OPERATIONS is the mark: ECG FIRST, REPEAT SECOND, CONCLUDE THIRD
THE ECG PROGRESSION, in order

TALL PEAKED, NARROW-BASED, SYMMETRICAL T WAVES appear first → then the P WAVE FLATTENS and the PR INTERVAL LENGTHENS → then the QRS WIDENS → P WAVES ARE LOST ENTIRELY → the widened QRS MERGES WITH THE T WAVE to give a SINE WAVE, which is PRE-TERMINAL. The end point is VF OR ASYSTOLE
READ IT OUT LOUD IN SIX STEPS — a short ordered read-out beats a list of adjectives

1 RATE AND RHYTHM — ‘bradycardic at 52, and I cannot clearly identify P waves.’ 2 P WAVES — ‘flattened and of low amplitude.’ 3 PR — ‘prolonged.’ 4 QRS — ‘broad at approximately 130 MILLISECONDS, WITH NO TYPICAL BUNDLE BRANCH MORPHOLOGY.’ 5 T WAVES — ‘tall, NARROW-BASED, SYMMETRICAL and peaked, MOST MARKED IN THE MID-PRECORDIAL LEADS.’ 6 CONCLUSION — ‘these are the changes of SEVERE HYPERKALAEMIA and this patient needs treatment NOW’
TWO ECG TRAPS

PEAKED T WAVES ARE NOT SPECIFIC. HYPERACUTE T WAVES OF EARLY STEMI ARE BROAD-BASED AND ASYMMETRICAL; benign early repolarisation gives tall T waves in a well patient. IT IS THE COMPANY THEY KEEP — FLAT P, LONG PR, WIDE QRS — THAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS. And A BROAD COMPLEX REGULAR TACHYCARDIA IN A DIALYSIS PATIENT MAY BE HYPERKALAEMIA, NOT VT
SEVERITY — and the row that overrides all the others

MILD 5.5–5.9: find the cause, stop the culprit drug, review intake, recheck. MODERATE 6.0–6.4: ECG and monitoring; treat if ANY ECG change or if RISING RAPIDLY. SEVERE ≥6.5: treat IMMEDIATELY, regardless of symptoms. ANY LEVEL WITH ECG CHANGE = TREAT AS SEVERE — THIS ROW OVERRIDES EVERY ROW ABOVE IT
THE RULE THAT GENERATES THE FOLLOW-UP QUESTION

ECG CHANGES CORRELATE POORLY WITH THE SERUM LEVEL. A CKD patient may sit at 7.0 with a NEAR-NORMAL ECG because the rise was SLOW; a previously normal patient may develop a SINE WAVE AT 6.2 because the rise was FAST. TREAT THE ECG AND THE RATE OF RISE, NOT THE NUMBER. Equally — A NORMAL ECG AT K 7.2 IS NOT REASSURANCE. IT DOES NOT MEAN YOU CAN WAIT
STEP 1 · PROTECT — CALCIUM GLUCONATE 10%, 10 mL IV OVER 2–3 MINUTES, with cardiac monitoring

REPEAT IF THE ECG HAS NOT IMPROVED AFTER ABOUT 5 MINUTES. Indicated whenever there are ECG CHANGES or the patient is HAEMODYNAMICALLY UNSTABLE. ONSET WITHIN MINUTES; EFFECT LASTS ONLY 30–60 MINUTES — IT IS A BRIDGE, NOT A TREATMENT. CALCIUM CHLORIDE gives more elemental calcium but is MORE SCLEROSANT — reserve for CENTRAL ACCESS OR PERI-ARREST
STEP 2 · SHIFT

INSULIN 10 UNITS SHORT-ACTING IN 50 mL OF 50% GLUCOSE IV OVER 15–30 MINUTES. ONSET 15–30 min, PEAK AROUND 1 HOUR, LASTS 4–6 HOURS. HYPOGLYCAEMIA IS THE COMMONEST COMPLICATION AND OFTEN OCCURS AFTER THE POTASSIUM HAS BEEN RECHECKED — MONITOR BLOOD GLUCOSE HOURLY FOR AT LEAST 6 HOURS. If the glucose is already high, insulin may be given with LESS OR NO ADDED GLUCOSE — but still monitor. SALBUTAMOL 10–20 mg NEBULISED — onset about 30 minutes, ADDITIVE to insulin; expect tachycardia and tremor; NOT RELIABLE AS SOLE THERAPY, a proportion do not respond. SODIUM BICARBONATE ONLY where there is significant metabolic acidosis — WEAK AND INCONSISTENT EVIDENCE alone
STEP 3 · REMOVE — and this is the ONLY step that takes potassium out of the body

HAEMODIALYSIS — DEFINITIVE. Indicated for REFRACTORY OR SEVERE hyperkalaemia, particularly with ANURIA, ESTABLISHED RENAL FAILURE, or ONGOING POTASSIUM RELEASE. LOOP DIURETIC with volume replacement — ONLY useful if the patient IS MAKING URINE and is NOT VOLUME DEPLETED. POTASSIUM BINDERS — SODIUM ZIRCONIUM CYCLOSILICATE and PATIROMER act within hours and are NOW PREFERRED OVER OLDER RESINS. RESONIUM IS SLOW, POORLY EVIDENCED FOR ACUTE USE, AND SHOULD NOT BE RELIED ON AS YOUR ACUTE ANSWER

dx: **TWO THINGS DECIDE THIS STATION.** **FIRST, YOU ASK FOR AN ECG BEFORE YOU FINISH READING THE BLOOD RESULTS — AND YOU SAY SO OUT LOUD.** **SECOND, YOU KNOW THAT CALCIUM DOES NOT LOWER POTASSIUM; IT BUYS YOU THE FIFTEEN MINUTES IN WHICH INSULIN DOES.** **Candidates who recite a drug list without that distinction GET TAKEN APART ON THE FOLLOW-UP QUESTION.**

**THE SINGLE HIGHEST-SCORING SENTENCE IN THE STATION, said BEFORE you read down the rest of the panel**: **‘Before I interpret these results in full, this potassium is in the SEVERE range and I would ATTACH CARDIAC MONITORING AND OBTAIN A 12-LEAD ECG IMMEDIATELY, and I would ask WHETHER THE SAMPLE WAS HAEMOLYSED.’** **The role-player brief says: if they never ask for an ECG, NEVER GIVE ONE — AND MARK THAT AS A FAIL.**

**THE THREE JOBS, AND SAY WHICH DRUG DOES WHICH.** **CALCIUM PROTECTS THE HEART. IT DOES NOT LOWER THE POTASSIUM.** **INSULIN AND SALBUTAMOL SHIFT potassium INTO CELLS — they lower the MEASURED level TEMPORARILY but DO NOT REMOVE A SINGLE MILLIMOLE FROM THE BODY.** **ONLY DIALYSIS, DIURESIS AND BINDERS ACTUALLY REMOVE IT.** **PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE.**

**THE QUESTION THAT SEPARATES A PASS FROM A DISTINCTION, AND IT IS ASKED ALMOST EVERY TIME**: *‘Does the calcium lower his potassium?’* → **‘NO. It STABILISES THE MYOCARDIUM against the EFFECT of the potassium — THE SERUM LEVEL IS UNCHANGED. That is why it must ALWAYS be given ALONGSIDE something that actually shifts or removes potassium, NEVER INSTEAD OF IT.’**

**VERSION A IS MULTIFACTORIAL AND NAMING ONE CAUSE IS THE COMMONEST WEAK ANSWER. THERE ARE FOUR IN FRONT OF YOU**: **‘His STAGE 4 CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE sets the BASELINE inability to excrete. His GASTROENTERITIS AND POOR INTAKE have precipitated an ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY ON TOP — the urea of 24 with a creatinine of 312 fits a PRERENAL component. He is on RAMIPRIL AND SPIRONOLACTONE TOGETHER, which is ADDITIVE potassium retention and a well-recognised combination in advanced renal disease. And his BICARBONATE OF 16 tells me he is ACIDOTIC, which SHIFTS POTASSIUM EXTRACELLULARLY.’**

**THEN ASK BY NAME FOR THE THREE HE WILL NOT VOLUNTEER: OVER-THE-COUNTER ANTI-INFLAMMATORIES, RECENT TRIMETHOPRIM, AND POTASSIUM-BASED SALT SUBSTITUTES.** **The brief says: if asked specifically about anti-inflammatories, HE ADMITS TO IBUPROFEN FOR HIS KNEE. IF NOT ASKED, HE DOES NOT MENTION IT.** **Patients do not think of salt substitutes, ibuprofen or ‘the tablet for my water’ as medications.**

**THE DRUG SWEEP, as a class list**: **ACE INHIBITORS / ARBs** — ramipril, perindopril, candesartan · **POTASSIUM-SPARING DIURETICS** — spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride · **NSAIDs** — including over the counter · **TRIMETHOPRIM**, alone or as co-trimoxazole · **HEPARIN** — suppresses aldosterone, INCLUDING PROPHYLACTIC DOSING · **BETA-BLOCKERS** — impair cellular uptake, mainly non-selective · **CALCINEURIN INHIBITORS** — ciclosporin, tacrolimus · **DIGOXIN** in toxicity — blocks the Na/K-ATPase pump · **POTASSIUM SUPPLEMENTS AND SALT SUBSTITUTES.**

**CAUSES BY MECHANISM — FOUR BUCKETS, AND SPURIOUS ALWAYS COMES FIRST.** **SPURIOUS: haemolysed sample · TIGHT TOURNIQUET OR FIST CLENCHING · delayed processing or a cold sample · MARKED THROMBOCYTOSIS OR LEUCOCYTOSIS (potassium released during clotting — a PLASMA sample rather than SERUM resolves it) · DRIP-ARM CONTAMINATION.** **REDUCED EXCRETION: AKI · CKD · drugs · ADDISON DISEASE and other hypoaldosteronism · TYPE 4 RENAL TUBULAR ACIDOSIS.** **SHIFT OUT OF CELLS: metabolic acidosis · DKA and insulin deficiency · RHABDOMYOLYSIS · TUMOUR LYSIS · burns or crush injury · in vivo haemolysis · digoxin toxicity · SUXAMETHONIUM.** **INCREASED INTAKE: rarely sufficient alone — salt substitutes, supplements, large transfusions of STORED BLOOD, in a patient who already cannot excrete.**

**ALWAYS ASK THESE THREE.** **1 WAS THE SAMPLE HAEMOLYSED? Check the lab comment BEFORE you commit.** **2 IS THE PATIENT PASSING URINE? ANURIA REMOVES YOUR SLOWEST AND SAFEST ROUTE OF EXCRETION AND MOVES DIALYSIS UP THE LIST.** **3 IS THERE ANYTHING THAT WILL KEEP MAKING IT WORSE? Ongoing rhabdomyolysis, tumour lysis, or a drug still in the system means ONE ROUND OF TREATMENT WILL NOT HOLD.**

**HYPERKALAEMIA IS OFTEN SILENT UNTIL IT IS LETHAL.** When symptoms occur they are NON-SPECIFIC: generalised muscle weakness, fatigue, paraesthesiae, palpitations, and in severe cases **ASCENDING FLACCID PARALYSIS WITH SPARING OF THE DIAPHRAGM AND CRANIAL NERVES. BRADYCARDIA IS A LATE AND OMINOUS SIGN.** **THE EXAMINATION POINT: YOU CANNOT EXCLUDE HYPERKALAEMIA CLINICALLY — WHICH IS PRECISELY WHY THE ECG COMES FIRST.**
plan: Reading time — write FIVE things

**1 ECG + MONITOR NOW, and ask about haemolysis. 2 PROTECT · SHIFT · REMOVE, and which drug does which. 3 Ca gluconate 10% 10 mL · insulin 10 u + 50 mL 50% glucose · salbutamol 10–20 mg neb. 4 STOP ramipril, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim. 5 FOUR CAUSES: CKD · AKI on top · ACEi + spironolactone · acidosis.** **SAY UNPROMPTED: hourly BGL for 6 hours · recheck K at 1–2 hours · involve renal and retrieval early.**
TASK 1a — the opening sentence ★

**Say it BEFORE reading the rest of the panel. If you read the whole panel first and ask for the ECG at the end, YOU HAVE ALREADY SHOWN YOU DO NOT TREAT THIS AS AN EMERGENCY. The station is effectively decided here — everything after this is CONTENT; this was JUDGEMENT.**
TASK 1b — interpret the ECG

**The six-step read-out. If challenged ‘could the T waves be ischaemic?’ → ‘HYPERACUTE T WAVES OF INFARCTION ARE BROAD-BASED AND ASYMMETRICAL. It is the COMBINATION with FLAT P WAVES, a LONG PR and a WIDE QRS that makes hyperkalaemia the explanation.’**
TASK 1c — interpret the biochemistry

**‘SEVERE hyperkalaemia at 7.2. The creatinine of 312 and eGFR of 16 indicate ADVANCED RENAL IMPAIRMENT, and with a urea of 24 and a UREA-TO-CREATININE PATTERN SUGGESTING A PRERENAL COMPONENT, this looks like ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY ON CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE. The bicarbonate of 16 shows a METABOLIC ACIDOSIS, which itself SHIFTS POTASSIUM OUT OF CELLS. The mild hyponatraemia fits VOLUME DEPLETION.’**
TASK 2 — the causes, all four at once
**Then the three you must ask for by name.**
TASK 3 — immediate management, said as THREE JOBS

**PROTECT: calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV over 2–3 min with continuous monitoring, REPEATED AT 5 MIN IF THE ECG HAS NOT IMPROVED; lasts 30–60 min; DOES NOT LOWER THE POTASSIUM.** **SHIFT: 10 units short-acting insulin in 50 mL of 50% glucose over 15–30 min, WITH HOURLY BLOOD GLUCOSE FOR AT LEAST SIX HOURS — HYPOGLYCAEMIA IS THE COMMONEST COMPLICATION AND IS OFTEN DELAYED; plus salbutamol 10–20 mg nebulised, ADDITIVE. Given the bicarbonate of 16, CONSIDER sodium bicarbonate, RECOGNISING THE EVIDENCE IS WEAK.** **REMOVE: he is oliguric with an eGFR of 16, so HAEMODIALYSIS IS DEFINITIVE — involve the renal team AND ARRANGE RETRIEVAL NOW RATHER THAN AFTER FAILED MEDICAL THERAPY.** **Alongside: WITHHOLD ramipril and spironolactone, CAUTIOUSLY restore volume, RECHECK THE POTASSIUM AT 1–2 HOURS on continuous monitoring.**
TASK 4 — explain to the patient, and NEVER QUOTE THE NUMBER

**‘Your blood tests show that a SALT called POTASSIUM is MUCH HIGHER than it should be. Potassium is essential — it helps your NERVES AND MUSCLES work — but when it climbs too high IT UPSETS THE ELECTRICAL RHYTHM OF YOUR HEART. Your heart tracing is ALREADY showing some of those changes, WHICH IS WHY I AM TREATING THIS STRAIGHT AWAY RATHER THAN WAITING.’** **Then the three things: ‘CALCIUM FIRST — THAT DOES NOT LOWER THE POTASSIUM, BUT IT PROTECTS YOUR HEART WHILE THE OTHER TREATMENTS WORK. Then INSULIN WITH SUGAR, which drives the potassium OUT OF YOUR BLOODSTREAM AND BACK INTO YOUR CELLS. And a NEBULISER that helps do the same. Then we work on CLEARING IT FROM YOUR BODY.’** **The role-player is briefed: IF YOU USE THE NUMBER 7.2 AT HIM, HE LOOKS BLANK AND SAYS ‘IS THAT BAD?’**
Then the drugs, and the instruction that matters
**‘Two of your tablets — THE BLOOD PRESSURE ONE AND THE FLUID ONE — HOLD POTASSIUM IN. I AM STOPPING BOTH TODAY. PLEASE DO NOT RESTART THEM UNTIL WE REVIEW YOU.’**
His three questions, in order

*‘Am I going to have a heart attack?’* → **‘NOT A HEART ATTACK IN THE USUAL SENSE — this affects the RHYTHM rather than BLOCKING AN ARTERY. But I DO NOT WANT TO UNDERSTATE IT: at this level the rhythm can become dangerous, and that is exactly why you are on a monitor and why I am treating you BEFORE we have finished all the tests. The good news is that this is VERY TREATABLE, and I am starting now.’** *‘Is it something I did?’* → **‘YOU HAVE NOT DONE ANYTHING WRONG. Being unwell and dehydrated has put extra strain on kidneys that were ALREADY STRUGGLING, and two of your regular tablets hold potassium in.’** *‘Do I have to go to Adelaide?’* → **‘POSSIBLY, YES. If the potassium does not come down, the most effective way to remove it is DIALYSIS, and that means transferring you. I am arranging that conversation NOW rather than waiting, so we are not delayed if you need it. IS THERE SOMEONE YOU WOULD LIKE ME TO CALL?’**
VERSION B — the order of operations IS the mark

**‘A potassium of 6.1 is in the MODERATE range and I CANNOT IGNORE IT. Even though she is well, I would obtain an ECG AND REVIEW HER OBSERVATIONS BEFORE I DECIDE ANYTHING. I would also ask the laboratory WHETHER THE SAMPLE WAS HAEMOLYSED, WHETHER THERE WAS A DELAY IN PROCESSING, AND WHAT HER PLATELET AND WHITE CELL COUNTS WERE.’** Then, once the ECG is normal and the haemolysis is confirmed: **‘the most likely explanation is PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA. RED CELLS CONTAIN POTASSIUM AT ROUGHLY 25 TIMES THE PLASMA CONCENTRATION, so even modest haemolysis raises the measured value substantially. I would REPEAT THE SAMPLE with a WIDER-BORE NEEDLE, avoiding a PROLONGED TOURNIQUET AND FIST CLENCHING, and get it to the laboratory PROMPTLY. I would NOT TREAT, AND I WOULD NOT CANCEL HER PROCEDURE, until I have a clean result.’** **CANDIDATES SPLIT TWO WAYS AND BOTH FAIL: some treat a haemolysed sample with insulin–dextrose in a well patient; others dismiss it as artefact WITHOUT an ECG or a repeat, AND WOULD MISS A GENUINE RESULT IF THE HAEMOLYSIS WERE COINCIDENTAL.**
pefe: **Examiner probes to have ready.** *‘How long does calcium last?’* → **‘30 to 60 minutes. REPEAT IF THE ECG HAS NOT IMPROVED.’** *‘What is the commonest complication of your treatment?’* → **‘HYPOGLYCAEMIA from the insulin — OFTEN DELAYED, hence HOURLY GLUCOSE MONITORING FOR AT LEAST SIX HOURS.’** *‘His ECG is normal at 7.2 — can you wait?’* → **‘NO. A normal ECG DOES NOT EXCLUDE RISK; changes can appear ABRUPTLY. Monitor and treat.’** *‘When is dialysis indicated?’* → **‘REFRACTORY hyperkalaemia, ANURIA or established renal failure, ONGOING POTASSIUM RELEASE, or the other indications for dialysis in acute kidney injury.’**

**CORRECTION — the digoxin ‘stone heart’ teaching.** **The old teaching that CALCIUM IS CONTRAINDICATED IN DIGOXIN TOXICITY IS NOT SUPPORTED BY CURRENT EVIDENCE AND IS NO LONGER AN ABSOLUTE BAR.** **In digoxin toxicity the DEFINITIVE treatment is DIGOXIN IMMUNE FAB.** **Safe wording: ‘I would give DIGOXIN-SPECIFIC ANTIBODY FRAGMENTS and DISCUSS CALCIUM WITH THE TOXICOLOGIST.’** **And hyperkalaemia in digoxin toxicity is A MARKER OF SEVERITY and an INDICATION for Fab.**

**VARIANT — THE SINE WAVE.** K 8.4, QRS merging with T, patient DROWSY AND HYPOTENSIVE. → **‘This is PERI-ARREST. Calcium IMMEDIATELY and REPEATED, insulin–dextrose and salbutamol SIMULTANEOUSLY RATHER THAN SEQUENTIALLY, call for help and the ARREST TROLLEY, and DIALYSIS AS AN EMERGENCY.’**

**VARIANT — DKA, and the one hyperkalaemia you end up TREATING WITH POTASSIUM.** K 5.9, glucose 28, ketones 5.2, pH 7.12. → **‘The TOTAL BODY POTASSIUM IS DEPLETED DESPITE THE HIGH SERUM LEVEL. Once insulin and fluids start, the potassium WILL FALL RAPIDLY. I would follow the DKA protocol and BEGIN POTASSIUM REPLACEMENT ONCE THE LEVEL IS BELOW 5.5 AND THE PATIENT IS PASSING URINE.’**

**VARIANT — THE WELL DIALYSIS PATIENT.** K 6.9, no symptoms, NORMAL ECG, dialysis due tomorrow. → **‘CHRONIC TOLERANCE means the ECG may be UNREMARKABLE at levels that would be dangerous acutely — BUT THAT IS NOT PERMISSION TO WAIT. I would monitor, treat medically, and BRING THE DIALYSIS SESSION FORWARD.’** **And the related trap: a BROAD COMPLEX REGULAR TACHYCARDIA at 140 in a dialysis patient who missed two sessions is HYPERKALAEMIA MIMICKING VT — CALCIUM FIRST, AND GET HIM DIALYSED.**

**VARIANT — THE ANGRY PATIENT.** *‘You lot gave me those tablets. Now you're telling me they nearly killed me?’* → **‘That is a FAIR thing to be upset about, and I want to be STRAIGHT with you. BOTH TABLETS WERE PRESCRIBED FOR GOOD REASONS — they protect your heart and your kidneys. WHAT HAS CHANGED is that your kidneys have TAKEN A HIT from being unwell, and at that point THE SAME TABLETS BECOME A PROBLEM. It is NOT that they were the wrong choice; it is that THEY NEED REVIEWING WHEN THINGS CHANGE. I am stopping them today and we will work out a safer plan TOGETHER.’**

**Other practice stems.** **24M, CRUSH INJURY under a fallen gate for three hours. K 6.8, CK 48,000, dark urine → RHABDOMYOLYSIS. Treat the potassium, then AGGRESSIVE FLUIDS — AND EXPECT IT TO RISE AGAIN as muscle continues to break down.** **62M, lymphoma, 48 h after chemotherapy. K 6.6, phosphate high, calcium LOW, urate high → TUMOUR LYSIS SYNDROME. Hydration, RASBURICASE, involve renal early.** **31F, weight loss, PIGMENTATION, postural dizziness. Na 126, K 6.0, glucose 3.1 → ADDISON DISEASE — THE HYPERKALAEMIA IS A CLUE, NOT THE DIAGNOSIS. Hydrocortisone and fluids.** **78F on ramipril, started TRIMETHOPRIM three days ago for a UTI. K 6.3, creatinine up 40% → DRUG INTERACTION. Stop both, rehydrate, recheck.**

**The one-line summary to the examiner**: **‘SEVERE hyperkalaemia at 7.2 WITH ECG CHANGES, in the context of ACUTE-ON-CHRONIC KIDNEY INJURY, an ACE INHIBITOR AND SPIRONOLACTONE, and a METABOLIC ACIDOSIS. I would MONITOR, give CALCIUM GLUCONATE, then INSULIN–DEXTROSE AND NEBULISED SALBUTAMOL, WITHHOLD ALL CONTRIBUTING DRUGS, RECHECK AT ONE TO TWO HOURS, and INVOLVE RENAL AND RETRIEVAL EARLY given his eGFR of 16.’**

**AVOID**: **no glucose monitoring after insulin — say it UNPROMPTED** · **Resonium as the acute answer** · **being reassured by a normal ECG** · **missing the multifactorial picture** · **quoting the number to the patient** · **concluding ‘it is just haemolysis’ BEFORE the ECG — the error that would kill THE ONE PATIENT IN FIFTY WHERE THE HAEMOLYSIS WAS COINCIDENTAL.**

SA — **in an MM5 setting the practical constraints matter AND ARE WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD.** **POINT-OF-CARE BLOOD GAS ANALYSERS give a potassium IN MINUTES and are often the FASTEST confirmation available — TREAT ON THE ECG WHILE AWAITING THE FORMAL LABORATORY RESULT.** **NEBULISED SALBUTAMOL AND CALCIUM GLUCONATE ARE USUALLY AVAILABLE WHERE INSULIN INFUSION PROTOCOLS AND DIALYSIS ARE NOT.** **DIALYSIS REQUIRES TRANSFER — INVOLVE MedSTAR RETRIEVAL ON 1300 13 12 33 EARLY RATHER THAN AFTER TWO FAILED ROUNDS OF MEDICAL THERAPY, BECAUSE THE TRANSFER TIME, NOT THE DRUG, IS THE RATE-LIMITING STEP.**
ddx: **Spurious — pseudohyperkalaemia. ALWAYS CONSIDER IT FIRST**
**A WELL patient with an unexpected high potassium; lab comment ‘specimen haemolysed’**
**Haemolysis · TIGHT TOURNIQUET OR FIST CLENCHING · delayed or cold processing · THROMBOCYTOSIS OR LEUCOCYTOSIS · DRIP-ARM CONTAMINATION**
**ECG FIRST, THEN REPEAT THE SAMPLE properly, THEN conclude. A PLASMA sample resolves the cell-count cause.** Do not treat until confirmed
**Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease**
**Diarrhoea, vomiting, poor intake on a background of CKD; lethargy and MUSCLE WEAKNESS**
**Urea disproportionately raised (PRERENAL); eGFR; URINE OUTPUT**
**Treat the potassium, restore volume CAUTIOUSLY, withhold nephrotoxins, renal referral. ANURIA MOVES DIALYSIS UP THE LIST.** Emergency
**Drugs — the commonest reversible cause**
**ACEi/ARB · SPIRONOLACTONE · NSAIDs · TRIMETHOPRIM · heparin · beta-blockers · calcineurin inhibitors · digoxin · SALT SUBSTITUTES**
**ASK EACH BY NAME — patients do not count ibuprofen, salt substitutes or ‘the water tablet’ as medications**
**WITHHOLD EVERY CONTRIBUTOR and tell the patient NOT TO RESTART until reviewed.** Immediate
**Metabolic acidosis**
**Bicarbonate low; shifts potassium OUT of cells**
Bicarbonate on the panel; the clinical context
Treat the cause; **sodium bicarbonate ONLY if significantly acidotic — WEAK evidence as a potassium-lowering agent alone.** Same admission
**Rhabdomyolysis**
**Crush injury, prolonged immobility, DARK URINE, very high CK**
The mechanism and the urine colour
**Treat the potassium, then AGGRESSIVE FLUIDS — AND EXPECT IT TO RISE AGAIN as muscle continues to break down.** Emergency
**Tumour lysis syndrome**
**48 h after chemotherapy; HIGH phosphate, LOW calcium, HIGH urate**
Recent chemotherapy, tumour bulk
Hydration, **RASBURICASE**, involve renal early. Emergency
**Diabetic ketoacidosis / insulin deficiency**
**High glucose, ketones, acidosis — with a HIGH serum potassium but DEPLETED total body potassium**
Glucose, ketones, pH
**DKA protocol; START POTASSIUM REPLACEMENT once below 5.5 and passing urine. THE ONE HYPERKALAEMIA YOU TREAT WITH POTASSIUM.** Emergency
**Addison disease / hypoaldosteronism**
**LOW sodium, HIGH potassium, LOW glucose, PIGMENTATION, postural dizziness, weight loss**
Pigmentation, postural BP, the electrolyte pattern
**Short synacthen test; HYDROCORTISONE AND FLUIDS. The hyperkalaemia is a CLUE, NOT THE DIAGNOSIS.** Urgent
**Digoxin toxicity**
**Nausea, YELLOW-GREEN VISUAL DISTURBANCE, bradyarrhythmia; hyperkalaemia is a MARKER OF SEVERITY**
Digoxin level, renal function, interacting drugs
**DIGOXIN IMMUNE FAB is definitive. Discuss calcium with toxicology — the historical absolute contraindication is now questioned.** Emergency
Increased intake alone
**Salt substitutes, supplements, large transfusions of STORED BLOOD**
Diet and supplement history by name
**Rarely sufficient alone — only in a patient who ALREADY CANNOT EXCRETE.** Routine
**Early STEMI — the ECG mimic**
**Tall T waves that are BROAD-BASED AND ASYMMETRICAL**, chest pain
**The COMPANY the T waves keep — flat P, long PR, wide QRS point to hyperkalaemia instead**
Serial ECGs, troponin. **Do not let a tall T wave alone decide either diagnosis.** Emergency

versions.doorStem: A results-interpretation station: a potassium result is handed to you. Tasks are the same in both versions — interpret the results and any further investigation to the examiner → state the likely causes → outline immediate management → explain the situation to the patient. The two versions land on DIFFERENT answers.
rows: A · the sick one

68-year-old man, CKD stage 4, rural ED, two days of lethargy and generalised muscle weakness after gastroenteritis last week, drinking little. On ramipril, spironolactone, metformin, atorvastatin. BP 104/62, PR 52. K⁺ 7.2, urea 24.1, creatinine 312, eGFR 16, bicarbonate 16. ECG: bradycardic, flat P, long PR, broad QRS, peaked T.

SEVERE HYPERKALAEMIA with ECG changes — MULTIFACTORIAL: CKD sets the floor, acute illness and dehydration precipitate, ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone are additive, acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells. Treat now.
B · the well one

44-year-old woman, entirely well, routine bloods before a minor procedure. Lab phones K⁺ 6.1. No symptoms, no relevant medications, normal renal function, lab comments 'specimen haemolysed'. ECG normal.
PSEUDOHYPERKALAEMIA — repeat the sample properly. But get the ECG FIRST and confirm it is normal before concluding the result is spurious, not after.
versions.note: The trap in version B splits candidates two ways and both fail: treating a haemolysed sample with insulin–dextrose in a well patient, or dismissing it as artefact with no ECG and no repeat. ECG first, repeat second, treat only if confirmed. Severity: mild 5.5–5.9 · moderate 6.0–6.4 · severe ≥6.5 · ANY level with ECG change = severe, and that row overrides the rest. A normal ECG at 7.2 is not reassurance. Practice cards in the source (crush injury/rhabdomyolysis, Addison, trimethoprim interaction, tumour lysis, dialysis patient with broad-complex tachycardia) are partner drills, not recalls.

findings: VERSION B — the stem you are in

35M, RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT ABDOMINAL PAIN. AST AND ALT RAISED, LESS THAN TWICE THE UPPER LIMIT · TRIGLYCERIDES ELEVATED (ref <1.7 mmol/L) · TOTAL CHOLESTEROL ELEVATED (ref <5.5 mmol/L). Tasks: take a history; EXPLAIN THE INVESTIGATION RESULTS TO THE PATIENT; explain your diagnosis and differentials. EVERYTHING IS NEGATIVE — no red flags, no hepatitis risk factors, no surgery, no fever, AND NO ALCOHOL AT ALL. LIFESTYLE QUESTIONS ARE THE ONLY POSITIVE GROUND
VERSION A — for contrast

40M attending TO DISCUSS RESULTS, NO PRESENTING COMPLAINT. AST about 95 (ref <40) · ALT about 40–50 (ref <45) · GGT ELEVATED (ref <50) · ALP and bilirubin NEAR NORMAL. ONE BOTTLE OF WINE EVERY NIGHT FOR TWENTY YEARS. Restaurant owner. Examination entirely normal → ALCOHOLIC HEPATITIS, ratio about 2.4
MAGNITUDE FIRST, THEN RATIO — and quoting the ratio is EXPLICITLY REWARDED

MILD rise = UNDER ABOUT 5× the upper limit. MARKED = OVER 10×. AST:ALT ABOVE 2 FAVOURS ALCOHOL; BELOW 1 FAVOURS FATTY LIVER OR VIRAL. A VIRAL HEPATITIS WOULD HAVE GIVEN A FAR LARGER RISE — say that out loud as a reason
THE STANDARD-DRINK ARITHMETIC — getting it wrong undermines an otherwise good station

A STANDARD DRINK IS 10 g OF ALCOHOL. A 750 mL BOTTLE OF WINE AT 13% IS ABOUT 7.7 STANDARD DRINKS — NOT 12 TO 14. A nightly bottle is ROUGHLY 54 A WEEK. NHMRC: NO MORE THAN 10 STANDARD DRINKS A WEEK AND NO MORE THAN 4 IN A DAY
THE SEVEN-STEP EXAMINATION REQUEST

GENERAL APPEARANCE: jaundice, cachexia, SCRATCH MARKS, oedema, and STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE such as SPIDER NAEVI AND PALMAR ERYTHEMA · VITAL SIGNS, PARTICULARLY TEMPERATURE · ABDOMEN: inspection for distension and scars; superficial and deep palpation for tenderness and masses, SPECIFICALLY HEPATOMEGALY AND SPLENOMEGALY; PERCUSSION FOR SHIFTING DULLNESS; auscultation for bowel sounds · OFFICE TEST: URINE DIPSTICK FOR BILIRUBIN · ‘I would skip a rectal examination unless there were bowel symptoms’
A NORMAL EXAMINATION IS A FINDING — say so

‘The examination is NORMAL, WHICH IS WHAT I WOULD EXPECT AT THIS STAGE — there are NO STIGMATA OF CHRONIC LIVER DISEASE and NO EVIDENCE OF DECOMPENSATION. THAT IS REASSURING BUT IT DOES NOT EXCLUDE ONGOING DAMAGE’
INVESTIGATIONS — do now and do next

REPEAT AND EXTEND THE LFT with GGT, ALBUMIN, INR AND A FULL BLOOD COUNT — A LOW PLATELET COUNT IS AN EARLY CLUE TO FIBROSIS · EXCLUDE THE TREATABLE CAUSES: HEPATITIS B SURFACE ANTIGEN AND HEPATITIS C ANTIBODY; IRON STUDIES (FERRITIN AND TRANSFERRIN SATURATION) for haemochromatosis; AUTOIMMUNE SCREEN; COELIAC SEROLOGY; THYROID FUNCTION; CAERULOPLASMIN IF UNDER 40 · METABOLIC WORK-UP: fasting lipids, HbA1c or fasting glucose, blood pressure, WAIST CIRCUMFERENCE and BMI · UPPER ABDOMINAL ULTRASOUND
What the ultrasound shows in steatosis
A BRIGHT, ECHOGENIC LIVER returning brighter echoes than the ADJACENT RIGHT KIDNEY, with the deeper structures POORLY SEEN. LOSS OF THE NORMAL HEPATORENAL CONTRAST IS THE FINDING TO NAME
STAGING THE FIBROSIS — and enzymes do NOT do it

CALCULATE A FIB-4 SCORE, which combines AGE, TRANSAMINASES AND PLATELET COUNT; TRANSIENT ELASTOGRAPHY (FibroScan) where available. RE-STAGE FIBROSIS PERIODICALLY RATHER THAN REPEATING ENZYMES ALONE. PERSISTENT LOW PLATELETS, LOW ALBUMIN, A RISING INR OR SPLENOMEGALY SUGGEST ESTABLISHED CIRRHOSIS and change follow-up to SURVEILLANCE FOR VARICES AND HEPATOCELLULAR CARCINOMA
DO NOT MISS, and AVOID

DO NOT MISS: a MARKED rather than mild rise — THAT IS A DIFFERENT DISEASE · ESTABLISHED CIRRHOSIS — low platelets, low albumin, raised INR, splenomegaly · ALCOHOL WITHDRAWAL RISK if abrupt cessation is advised in a heavy drinker. AVOID: DIAGNOSING FATTY LIVER BEFORE EXCLUDING THE OTHER CAUSES — it is a DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION and EXAMINERS TEST THAT EXPLICITLY · and AVOID LECTURING: use BRIEF INTERVENTION, NOT MORALISING

dx: **VERSION B — FATTY LIVER DISEASE (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis).** A MILD transaminase rise with DYSLIPIDAEMIA and NO ALCOHOL, **after EVERY OTHER CAUSE HAS BEEN EXCLUDED.** **IT IS A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION AND BELONGS AT THE BOTTOM OF THE LIST, NOT THE TOP.**
**THE WHOLE APPROACH: A RESULT WITH NO COMPLAINT BECOMES A LIVER CASE — YOU MAKE THE ABNORMAL LFT THE COMPLAINT and run the standard blocks against it.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: QUOTE YOUR OWN NUMBERS BACK AS REASONS.** **Both diagnoses are GUESSABLE FROM THE STEM. What separates candidates is WHETHER THE REASONING IS SPOKEN.** **A PASS SAYS THREE THINGS: THE MAGNITUDE OF THE RISE AS A MULTIPLE OF THE UPPER LIMIT, THE AST:ALT RATIO, AND THE FACT THAT THE OTHER CAUSES HAVE BEEN ACTIVELY EXCLUDED. A FAIL NAMES THE DISEASE AND STOPS.**

**NAMING A DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION, verbatim**: **‘Fatty liver disease is what we call a DIAGNOSIS OF EXCLUSION, so I want to be CLEAR ABOUT HOW I GOT THERE. I have ruled out CANCERS of the liver, gallbladder and pancreas; VIRAL infections of the liver; GALLSTONE disease; a SERIOUS DUCT INFECTION, BECAUSE YOU HAVE NO FEVER; and MEDICATIONS. YOU DO NOT DRINK AT ALL. What is LEFT is the MILD ENZYME RISE together with the RAISED CHOLESTEROL AND TRIGLYCERIDES, and that combination points to FAT STORED IN THE LIVER.’**

**CORRECTION — FATTY LIVER DOES NOT CAUSE ABDOMINAL PAIN.** **Version B pairs a PAIN complaint with a FATTY LIVER diagnosis, WHICH IS A WEAKNESS IN THE CASE DESIGN RATHER THAN A CLINICAL FACT.** If challenged: **‘That is correct, and I agree. Fatty liver disease is USUALLY ASYMPTOMATIC and is NOT A RECOGNISED CAUSE OF ABDOMINAL PAIN. So I would TREAT THE STEATOSIS ON ITS OWN MERITS, but I would CONTINUE TO LOOK FOR A SEPARATE EXPLANATION FOR THE PAIN — BILIARY DISEASE, PEPTIC ULCER DISEASE OR REFLUX — rather than assume the two findings are connected.’**

**ASK THE SPECIFIC QUESTION, NOT THE POLITE ONE. ‘HOW IS YOUR DIET?’ INVITES ‘HEALTHY AND BALANCED’ AND THE BLOCK SCORES NOTHING.** **The specific question SHOWS THE EXAMINER WHAT YOU ARE SCREENING FOR: in fatty liver ask about A TYPICAL DAY'S FOOD, SUGARY DRINKS AND TAKEAWAY; in iron deficiency ask about RED MEAT; in osteoporosis ask about DAIRY.** **Pressed for a typical day he gives: COFFEE AND A PASTRY, TAKEAWAY AT LUNCH, BIG DINNER LATE, TWO OR THREE SOFT DRINKS A DAY, NO EXERCISE — NO TIME.**

**QUANTIFY THE ALCOHOL EVEN WHEN THE ANSWER IS NONE — and in Version A the role-player DEFLECTS THE FIRST QUESTION LIGHTLY.** ‘I have a drink most nights — I own a restaurant, it goes with the job.’ **IF THE DOCTOR ACCEPTS THAT AND MOVES ON, THE BRIEF SAYS: DO NOT HELP THEM — MARK IT AS A FAIL.** **The specific follow-up — WHAT do you drink, HOW MUCH, HOW MANY NIGHTS, HOW LONG — is what yields ‘a bottle of wine, most nights, probably every night, for twenty years’.**

**CONVERT IT OUT LOUD, WITHOUT JUDGEMENT**: **‘Thank you for being straight with me, that helps a great deal. Just so we are working with the same picture: A BOTTLE OF WINE IS ABOUT SEVEN TO EIGHT STANDARD DRINKS, so that is ROUGHLY FIFTY IN A WEEK. The recommended maximum for a healthy adult is TEN A WEEK. I AM NOT SAYING THAT TO MAKE YOU FEEL BAD — IT IS DIRECTLY RELEVANT TO THE RESULT I AM ABOUT TO SHOW YOU.’**

**CAGE AND AUDIT-C — naming one of these and saying you would use it is a strong answer even without time to run it.** **CAGE: have you ever felt you should CUT DOWN · been ANNOYED by criticism · felt GUILTY about it · needed a drink in the morning (EYE-OPENER). TWO OR MORE POSITIVES SUGGEST PROBLEM DRINKING.** **AUDIT-C is the three-question screen used in Australian general practice: HOW OFTEN you drink, HOW MANY on a typical day, and HOW OFTEN you have SIX OR MORE on one occasion.**

**NOMENCLATURE, worth a sentence.** **Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease has been REDEFINED INTERNATIONALLY as METABOLIC DYSFUNCTION-ASSOCIATED STEATOTIC LIVER DISEASE (MASLD), with the inflammatory form termed MASH.** **Australian examiners will accept NAFLD, NASH or fatty liver disease; saying ‘FATTY LIVER DISEASE, ALSO CALLED NON-ALCOHOLIC STEATOHEPATITIS OR THE NEWER TERM MASLD’ is SAFE AND SHOWS CURRENCY.**
plan: 0:00 → 0:40 — opening a station with no complaint

**THE BRIDGE THAT STOPS IT FEELING AWKWARD: ‘Thank you for coming in to discuss them. I DO have your results here, and I WILL go through them with you. BEFORE I DO, may I ask you a few questions SO THAT THE RESULTS MAKE MORE SENSE WHEN WE GET TO THEM? Then we will look at them together and talk about what they mean. Is that all right?’** **Candidates who sit down and START RECITING ENZYME VALUES LOOK MECHANICAL, and the approach-to-patient domain suffers BEFORE THE CLINICAL CONTENT EVER STARTS. Two sentences of bridging protects that domain AND BUYS YOU PERMISSION to take a history in a station that never asked for a complaint.**
**BLOCK 2 — SYMPTOMS OF LIVER DISEASE.** Any YELLOWING of skin or the whites of your eyes · any ITCHING · has your URINE GONE DARK, or your STOOLS PALE.
**BLOCK 3 — RED FLAGS AND FAMILY HISTORY.** Weight loss without trying · change in appetite · lumps or bumps · unusually tired · **family history of cancer of the BOWEL, LIVER, PANCREAS OR STOMACH.**
1:40 → 2:10 ★ HARD RULE

**BLOCK 4 — ALCOHOL QUANTIFIED IN STANDARD DRINKS BY 2:10.** Do you drink · how much and how long at that level · what do you drink and what SIZE GLASS · roughly how many NIGHTS a week. **Then CAGE if time.**

**BLOCK 4 continued — the rest of ABP FIT NO SEX.** Recent ANTIBIOTICS · BLOOD — transfusions, tattoos, piercings, injected drugs · FOOD — unusual food · TRAVEL · OCCUPATION and any chance of a NEEDLE-STICK · SEXUAL history and condom use · **regular medications INCLUDING OVER-THE-COUNTER, HERBAL OR GYM SUPPLEMENTS.**

**BLOCKS 5 TO 7 — GALLBLADDER, SURGERY, FEVER.** ‘Have you ever had PAIN AFTER A LARGE FATTY MEAL?’ · any operations · **‘and any FEVER or shaking chills?’** — **FEVER CLOSES EVERY LIVER BLOCK, NO EXCEPTIONS.**
3:20 → 4:00 ★ Version B only
**BLOCK 8 — LIFESTYLE, and this is the only positive ground in Version B.** A typical day's food, from morning to night · sugary drinks · takeaway · **and do you exercise regularly.**
4:00 — HARD RULE: HISTORY STOPS
**Request the examination as the seven-step structure.**
5:00 → 6:20 — explain the results, NINETY SECONDS MAXIMUM

**VERSION B: ‘We checked your LIVER ENZYMES, which are CHEMICALS THAT LEAK OUT OF LIVER CELLS WHEN THE LIVER IS IRRITATED. Yours are up, BUT ONLY MILDLY — LESS THAN TWICE WHAT WE EXPECT — and that tells me there is SOME INFLAMMATION in the liver, BUT NOT A SEVERE ONE. The SECOND thing we checked was THE FAT IN YOUR BLOOD. There are two main types, CHOLESTEROL AND TRIGLYCERIDES, and BOTH are higher than we would like. WHEN THERE IS A LOT OF FAT CIRCULATING, SOME OF IT GETS STORED IN THE LIVER, AND THAT STORED FAT CAUSES THE IRRITATION WE ARE SEEING. That condition is called FATTY LIVER.’**
6:20 → 7:00 — the diagnosis WITH THE NUMBERS AS REASONS

**VERSION A, for comparison: ‘I am making this diagnosis for THREE reasons. FIRST, you are drinking about a BOTTLE OF WINE A NIGHT, which is roughly SEVEN TO EIGHT STANDARD DRINKS, so around FIFTY IN A WEEK — ABOUT FIVE TIMES THE RECOMMENDED MAXIMUM — and you have done so for TWENTY YEARS. findingsLabel: The ECG, the glucose and the numbers — open only when you would ask
findings: VERSION A — the older recall, and the one this card is built on

THE ECG IS SINUS RHYTHM WITH NO ACUTE ST OR T WAVE CHANGE. Capillary glucose taken at the shopping centre by a first aider was 2.7 mmol/L. ANSWER: HYPOGLYCAEMIA — missed meal plus UNACCUSTOMED EXERTION on insulin. CANDIDATES FAIL NOT BECAUSE THEY MISS THE DIAGNOSIS, BUT BECAUSE THEY ANNOUNCE ‘IT'S A HYPO' AND OFFER NOTHING ELSE. THE DIFFERENTIAL IS MARKED EVEN WHEN THE ANSWER IS OBVIOUS
VERSION B — the 2019 recall, identical history

ST ELEVATION IN II, III AND aVF WITH RECIPROCAL ST DEPRESSION IN aVL — ACUTE INFERIOR STEMI, PAINLESS because of DIABETIC AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHY. Hypoglycaemia MAY STILL COEXIST. Candidates fail here by having ALREADY DECIDED IT IS A HYPO, glancing at the ECG, and MISSING AN EVOLVING STEMI IN FRONT OF THEM
ASK FOR A BEDSIDE GLUCOSE ANYWAY — three seconds, and it changes the station

The stem says vitals are stable, so DO NOT waste 20 seconds asking for them again. BUT in a patient on insulin who felt faint after skipping breakfast, say ONCE: ‘COULD I PLEASE HAVE A BEDSIDE BLOOD GLUCOSE WHILE WE TALK?' If the examiner gives a NORMAL figure it QUIETLY REMOVES HYPOGLYCAEMIA AS THE WHOLE ANSWER BEFORE YOU EVER SEE THE ECG
THE ECG DRILL — say it in THIS ORDER, EVERY TIME, whatever the history led you to expect

RATE · RHYTHM (P wave before every QRS) · PR INTERVAL, and IS THERE HEART BLOCK · QRS WIDTH · AXIS · ST SEGMENTS · T WAVES · Q WAVES. THE MARKS ARE IN THE ORDER, and in NAMING THE RECIPROCAL CHANGE, which is what distinguishes infarction from PERICARDITIS OR EARLY REPOLARISATION
The Version B hand-over, in one breath

‘Rate approximately 70. Rhythm regular and sinus. PR normal, NO HEART BLOCK. QRS narrow. Axis normal. THERE IS ST ELEVATION IN LEADS II, III AND aVF, THE INFERIOR LEADS, WITH RECIPROCAL ST DEPRESSION IN aVL AND LEAD I. No established Q waves yet, T waves upright. I would ALSO look for ST DEPRESSION IN V1–V3 that might indicate POSTERIOR EXTENSION, and I would IMMEDIATELY do RIGHT-SIDED LEADS, PARTICULARLY V4R, to look for RIGHT VENTRICULAR INVOLVEMENT. My interpretation is an ACUTE INFERIOR ST-ELEVATION MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION'
Territories and what to watch for

INFERIOR — II, III, aVF (reciprocal I, aVL); RIGHT CORONARY IN ABOUT 80%, left circumflex in the rest; WATCH FOR BRADYCARDIA, AV BLOCK, RV INFARCT, HYPOTENSION. RIGHT VENTRICULAR — V4R; proximal RCA; PRELOAD-DEPENDENT, SO NITRATES CAN CAUSE PROFOUND HYPOTENSION. POSTERIOR — V7–V9; TALL R AND ST DEPRESSION IN V1–V3; EASILY MISSED, LOOKS LIKE ANTERIOR ISCHAEMIA. ANTERIOR/LATERAL — V1–V4 / I, aVL, V5–V6; larger infarcts, pump failure
STEMI VOLTAGE CRITERIA

NEW ST ELEVATION AT THE J POINT IN TWO CONTIGUOUS LEADS: ≥1 mm in all leads OTHER THAN V2–V3; in V2–V3, ≥2.5 mm in MEN UNDER 40, ≥2 mm in MEN 40 AND OVER, and ≥1.5 mm in WOMEN. RECIPROCAL DEPRESSION STRONGLY SUPPORTS TRUE INFARCTION
HYPOGLYCAEMIA — the numbers for Version A

BGL BELOW 4.0 mmol/L: 15 g FAST CARBOHYDRATE, REPEAT AT 15 MINUTES. IF UNCONSCIOUS: GLUCAGON 1 mg IM or 50 mL OF 50% GLUCOSE IV. Then a LONGER-ACTING carbohydrate once conscious, and REVIEW the insulin, meal timing and snacks
REPERFUSION NUMBERS — for the Version B answer

PRIMARY PCI PREFERRED: first medical contact to device ≤90 MINUTES, up to 120 minutes acceptable if TRANSFER is required. If that cannot be met, FIBRINOLYSIS WITHIN 30 MINUTES of first medical contact — WEIGHT-ADJUSTED TENECTEPLASE — and TRANSFER FOR ANGIOGRAPHY AT 3–24 HOURS, or immediately if reperfusion fails. TOTAL ISCHAEMIC TIME IS WHAT DETERMINES MYOCARDIUM SAVED
The acute drugs, and the one you must withhold

ASPIRIN 300 mg CHEWED · TICAGRELOR 180 mg or CLOPIDOGREL 300–600 mg loading, as directed by the receiving centre · GTN 300–600 µg SL — NOT IF HYPOTENSIVE, BRADYCARDIC, RV INFARCT SUSPECTED, OR A PDE5 INHIBITOR IN THE LAST 24–48 HOURS · MORPHINE 2.5–5 mg IV titrated · OXYGEN ONLY IF SpO2 BELOW 93% · NEVER DELAY REPERFUSION FOR A TROPONIN

dx: **VERSION A — HYPOGLYCAEMIA: a missed meal plus UNACCUSTOMED EXERTION on insulin, with a NORMAL ECG.** **VERSION B — ACUTE INFERIOR STEMI, painless because of diabetic autonomic neuropathy.** **IDENTICAL HISTORY IN BOTH. The ECG is the only thing that separates them.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: YOU MUST LET THE ECG OVERRULE YOUR HISTORY.** **Everything in the first five minutes points to a hypo — insulin, a skipped breakfast, an apple, hours of walking. THE EXAMINER HAS BUILT THAT PATH DELIBERATELY.** **The pass is reserved for the candidate who READS THE ECG SYSTEMATICALLY AS THOUGH THE HISTORY HAD NEVER HAPPENED.** **In Version A the failure is the MIRROR IMAGE: the diagnosis really IS a hypo, and candidates lose marks because they ANNOUNCE IT WITHOUT EVER GIVING A DIFFERENTIAL.**

**PRESYNCOPE = SYNCOPE. Same questions, same differentials, SAME SERIOUSNESS.** **‘I was about to faint but I didn't' DOES NOT SEND YOU DOWN A FALLS PATHWAY** — trip hazards, footwear, home safety. **Presyncope is the PRODROME of syncope — light-headedness, greying vision, feeling about to fall — WITHOUT actual loss of consciousness. IT IS NOT A BENIGN VERSION.**

**THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT CHANGE: syncope, presyncope, seizure and unexplained collapse ALL RUN ON THE SAME SPINE.** **The ONLY thing this case adds is a FULL DIABETES BLOCK — and the reason to add it is THE CONTEXT, NOT A MEMORISED RECALL.**

**‘NO WARNING AT ALL' IS A DISCORDANT FINDING AND YOU MUST FLAG IT.** **ABSENT PRODROME ARGUES AGAINST VASOVAGAL AND RAISES CARDIAC CAUSES.** Carry that thought into the ECG and ask for it WITH REAL INTENT.

**‘NO CHEST PAIN' IS A CLUE, NOT A CLOSED DOOR.** **In diabetes, PAINLESS ISCHAEMIA IS COMMON. ABSENCE OF CHEST PAIN DOES NOT REMOVE ACS — SAY THIS TO THE EXAMINER.** **Roughly a QUARTER TO A THIRD of infarcts are CLINICALLY UNRECOGNISED at the time, and painless presentation is DISPROPORTIONATELY COMMON IN DIABETES, WOMEN AND OLDER PATIENTS.**

**WHAT THE COMPLICATIONS SCREEN IS REALLY FOR — it is NOT box-ticking.** **Established microvascular disease tells you TWO THINGS AT ONCE: AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHY CAN CAUSE ORTHOSTATIC PRESYNCOPE, AND CAN ABOLISH THE PAIN OF MYOCARDIAL ISCHAEMIA.** **A patient with RETINOPATHY AND PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY IS EXACTLY THE PATIENT WHO HAS A PAINLESS INFARCT. SAY THIS OUT LOUD WHEN YOU PRESENT.** **She mentions the tingling feet and the early retinal changes ONLY IF ASKED DIRECTLY.**

**THE TRAP IN THE RISK FACTORS: ASK THEM IN THEIR PROPER PLACE, EVERY TIME.** **You ask about smoking, cholesterol and family history BECAUSE EVERY LOSS-OF-CONSCIOUSNESS HISTORY INCLUDES A CARDIOVASCULAR SCREEN — not because you happen to know how this recall ends.** **IF YOU ONLY START ASKING THEM AFTER THE ECG APPEARS, THE EXAMINER CAN SEE YOU WERE RECITING AN ANSWER.**

**VERSION A, said properly — the diagnosis AND the list**: **‘The most likely explanation is a LOW BLOOD SUGAR. You take insulin, you SKIPPED BREAKFAST and had only an APPLE, and you then WALKED FOR SEVERAL HOURS — MORE ACTIVITY THAN USUAL BURNS THROUGH SUGAR and makes a low far more likely. BUT I DON'T WANT TO STOP AT THE OBVIOUS ANSWER, so let me tell you what else I've considered: a HEART RHYTHM OR HEART ARTERY problem, a DROP IN BLOOD PRESSURE ON STANDING, DEHYDRATION, a MINI-STROKE, a SEIZURE, an INFECTION, ANAEMIA, a SALT DISTURBANCE, and any MEDICATION EFFECT. Your tracing is NORMAL, which is reassuring. I'd like some blood tests today, I'd like you to HAVE SOMETHING TO EAT NOW, and we'll review your insulin, your MEAL TIMING and your SNACKS together — particularly on days when you'll be on your feet for hours.'**

**THE COMMUNICATION CHALLENGE in Version B: telling a woman who LOOKS ENTIRELY WELL, FEELS BETTER, AND HAS A PARTY TONIGHT that she is having a heart attack, MUST NOT DRIVE, and is LEAVING BY AMBULANCE NOW — without panicking her and WITHOUT SOFTENING IT INTO SOMETHING SHE CAN DECLINE.** **The brief: she is determined not to miss tonight and INTENDS TO DRIVE HOME. IF THE CANDIDATE AGREES, HESITATES, OR FAILS TO ARRANGE AN AMBULANCE, MARK IT AS A FAIL. IF THE CANDIDATE NEVER GIVES AN ASPIRIN, MARK IT AS A FAIL.**
plan: Timing — be ruthless
**2 min reading · 8 min station. HISTORY 5:00 · ECG 1:15 · EXPLANATION AND CLOSING 1:45.** **THE LAST 1:45 CARRIES A THIRD OF THE MARKS.**

**WIPE, acknowledge, signpost — and ASK FOR THE GLUCOSE.** **‘Thank you for coming in to get checked — YOUR FRIENDS GAVE YOU VERY GOOD ADVICE. Let me ask you some questions, look at your heart tracing, and find the cause, SO WE KNOW EXACTLY WHERE WE STAND BEFORE THIS EVENING. And could I please have a bedside blood glucose while we talk?'**

**BLOCK 1 — EXPLORE THE EPISODE.** **‘Did you LOSE CONSCIOUSNESS COMPLETELY, or were you AWARE of your surroundings?'** · **any JERKING of the arms or legs, or TWITCHING ON ONE SIDE; did you WET OR SOIL yourself** — **FOCAL SEIZURES CAN OCCUR WITH PRESERVED AWARENESS, so the seizure screen is still worth ten seconds** · how long did it last · **is this the FIRST time.**

**BLOCK 2 — CONTEXT, ENVIRONMENT AND THE ‘BEFORE' QUESTIONS.** What were you doing just before · **was it HOT, had you been STANDING a long time, did it come on when you CHANGED POSITION** · any stressful or upsetting news · **ANY WARNING AT ALL — light-headed, sweaty, shaky, hungry, palpitations, vision greying, ringing in the ears** · **have you MISSED ANY MEALS today, were you drinking enough FLUIDS** · any knock to the HEAD · any FEVER OR RASH.
**BLOCK 3 — THE ‘AFTER' QUESTIONS.** Were you CONFUSED or DROWSY, and how long before you felt normal · did you INJURE yourself or hit your head · **did anyone say you looked PALE, GREY OR SWEATY.**

**BLOCK 4 — THE DIABETES BLOCK.** When diagnosed · **taking your insulin EXACTLY as prescribed, AND DID YOU TAKE IT TODAY** · **has the DOSE been CHANGED recently, by you or your doctor** · **any NEW medicines, OVER-THE-COUNTER products, SUPPLEMENTS, or TRADITIONAL OR HERBAL remedies** · **talk me through what you eat in a day — DO YOU TAKE YOUR MID-MORNING AND MID-AFTERNOON SNACKS** · do you TEST at home, what do they usually run, **DO YOU GET WARNING SYMPTOMS WHEN YOU GO LOW** · regular reviews and HbA1c.
Then the complications, and say WHY

**Numbness, tingling or burning in the feet; any ULCERS** · **change or blurring of VISION — when was your last EYE CHECK** · any KIDNEY problems on your blood tests · **do you get DIZZY ON STANDING, feel FULL VERY QUICKLY after meals, or have BLADDER trouble.**

**BLOCK 5 — SYSTEM SCREEN, QUICK AND COMPLETE.** **CNS**: headache, weakness, numbness, slurred speech, double vision, unsteadiness. **CVS**: **chest pain, tightness or heaviness — EVEN A LITTLE** · breathlessness on exertion or lying flat · racing or thumping of the heart · ankle swelling. **GI**: nausea, vomiting, tummy pain, diarrhoea, **black or bloody stools**. **SADMA**. **PSYCHOGENIC**: breathing very fast, stress, panic episodes. **EXERTION**: more physical activity than usual today. **RISK AND BACKGROUND**: blood pressure, cholesterol, weight, **family history of heart disease or a heart attack at a young age**. **IMPACT: DO YOU DRIVE, and who is at home with you** — you will need that fact in your closing.
**THE ECG HAND-OVER, in the fixed order.**

**Name hypoglycaemia with its THREE supporting facts, then THE FULL DIFFERENTIAL, then the plan: FOOD NOW, bloods today, and a REVIEW of insulin, meal timing and snacks — particularly on days of unaccustomed activity.** **Then SICK-DAY and hypo-awareness education, a diabetes educator, and follow-up.**

**WARNING SHOT → the diagnosis in plain English → the TWO-PART DIABETES EXPLANATION (vessels blocked → heart attack; nerves damaged → no pain) → the DIFFERENTIAL SHE MUST STILL HEAR → ASPIRIN, AMBULANCE, MONITORING → NO DRIVING, CALL FAMILY → summary.** **THE MOMENT YOU SAY STEMI, THE NEXT SENTENCE IS ASPIRIN AND 000.**

**THE CLOSING SHE FORCES, VERBATIM — she ALWAYS finishes with ‘can I still go to the party? MY CAR'S OUTSIDE — I'LL DRIVE MYSELF'**: → **‘I'M SORRY — TONIGHT ISN'T POSSIBLE, AND YOU MUST NOT DRIVE: NOT TODAY, AND NOT UNTIL THE SPECIALIST CLEARS YOU, WHICH IS USUALLY ABOUT TWO WEEKS AFTER SUCCESSFUL PCI. YOUR CAR CAN STAY HERE SAFELY. IS THERE SOMEONE I CAN CALL — YOUR HUSBAND?'** **AGREE, HESITATE, OR FAIL TO ARRANGE THE AMBULANCE AND IT IS MARKED AS A FAIL.**

**VERSION B — the diagnosis, verbatim**: **‘Mrs Rowe, I need to tell you something important, and I want you to hear THE WHOLE OF IT. Your heart tracing shows that you are HAVING A HEART ATTACK RIGHT NOW. It's called a MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION. Here is what has happened: DIABETES, OVER TIME, DAMAGES THE SMALL BLOOD VESSELS THAT SUPPLY THE HEART. When one of them SUDDENLY BLOCKS, part of the heart muscle STOPS GETTING BLOOD — that's a heart attack. Now you'll be asking me WHY YOU HAVE NO CHEST PAIN, and that's the second part: DIABETES ALSO DAMAGES THE NERVES, INCLUDING THE NERVES THAT CARRY PAIN FROM THE HEART. So instead of pain, the only thing you felt was BEING UNWELL AND ABOUT TO FALL. That's why we call it a SILENT heart attack, and IT'S THE REASON THE TRACING MATTERS MORE THAN HOW YOU FEEL.'**

**Then the action, in the same breath**: **‘What happens now is that I GIVE YOU AN ASPIRIN TO CHEW, WE CALL AN AMBULANCE, and you go STRAIGHT TO HOSPITAL where they can OPEN THAT BLOCKED VESSEL — THE SOONER THAT HAPPENS, THE MORE HEART MUSCLE WE SAVE. I'M SORRY, BUT TONIGHT'S PARTY ISN'T POSSIBLE, AND YOU MUST NOT DRIVE. IS THERE SOMEONE I CAN CALL FOR YOU?'** **And ‘am I going to die?' → ‘THIS IS SERIOUS, AND IT'S ALSO VERY TREATABLE — THE SAFEST THING IS EXACTLY WHAT WE'RE DOING NOW.'**

**DO NOW**: bedside glucose · **12-LEAD ECG WITHIN 10 MINUTES**, repeat if it evolves · **ASPIRIN 300 mg CHEWED** unless true allergy · **CALL 000 for an ambulance to a PCI-CAPABLE CENTRE — DO NOT LET HER DRIVE OR TAKE A TAXI** · IV access, continuous monitoring, **DEFIBRILLATOR TO HAND** · oxygen only if SpO2 <93% · **repeat blood pressure and DO V4R.** **DO NEXT**: notify the receiving team DIRECTLY and TRANSMIT THE ECG · antiplatelet loading and anticoagulation as directed · troponin, FBE, UEC, CMP, lipids, HbA1c, coagulation — **BUT NEVER DELAY REPERFUSION FOR A TROPONIN** · contact her family; document everything.

**DO NOT MISS**: **RIGHT VENTRICULAR INFARCTION — CHECK V4R BEFORE NITRATES** · **BRADYCARDIA AND COMPLETE HEART BLOCK** · **POSTERIOR EXTENSION (V1–V3 ST depression)** · **COEXISTING HYPOGLYCAEMIA — BOTH CAN BE TRUE** · driving advice and a clear handover · **that she may MINIMISE symptoms because she HAS none.**

**Examiner challenges, scripted.** *‘Why did you not simply treat the hypoglycaemia?'* → **‘Because the two are NOT MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE, and the ST elevation is the finding that determines THE NEXT HOUR. I would check and correct the glucose, but THE REPERFUSION PATHWAY IS WHAT I ACT ON FIRST.'** *‘How can she have an infarct with no pain?'* → **‘DIABETIC AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHY IMPAIRS THE AFFERENT PAIN PATHWAY FROM THE MYOCARDIUM; painless infarction is well described in DIABETES, IN WOMEN AND IN OLDER PATIENTS, and the presenting complaint is often something NON-SPECIFIC such as BREATHLESSNESS, NAUSEA, FATIGUE OR PRESYNCOPE, AS HERE.'** *‘Which artery?'* → **‘Most often the RIGHT CORONARY, in about 80% of inferior infarcts; the LEFT CIRCUMFLEX in the remainder. ST ELEVATION TALLER IN III THAN II FAVOURS THE RIGHT CORONARY.'**

**VARIANT — SHE REFUSES THE AMBULANCE.** → **‘I can hear how much tonight matters, and I'm not going to pretend this is a small thing. PART OF YOUR HEART MUSCLE IS LOSING ITS BLOOD SUPPLY RIGHT NOW, and every minute counts. The reason it must be an AMBULANCE rather than your car is that THE MOST DANGEROUS MOMENTS ARE THE FIRST HOURS, WHEN THE HEART'S RHYTHM CAN GO WRONG VERY SUDDENLY; THE PARAMEDICS CARRY THE EQUIPMENT TO FIX THAT, AND I DON'T WANT YOU AT THE WHEEL IF IT HAPPENS. You can ABSOLUTELY DECLINE — it's your decision and I'll respect it — BUT I'D BE FAILING YOU IF I DIDN'T TELL YOU PLAINLY THAT I THINK IT WOULD BE A VERY DANGEROUS CHOICE. Can I call your husband, and would it help to speak to him before you decide?'**

**VARIANT — HYPOTENSION AFTER THE ECG (right ventricular infarction).** BP 82/54, pulse 46. → **‘That raises RIGHT VENTRICULAR INVOLVEMENT, which often accompanies an inferior infarct. I would LIE HER FLAT, WITHHOLD NITRATES and AVOID MORPHINE, obtain RIGHT-SIDED LEADS to confirm, give a CAUTIOUS IV FLUID BOLUS of normal saline SINCE THE RIGHT VENTRICLE IS PRELOAD-DEPENDENT, prepare ATROPINE 600 MICROGRAMS for symptomatic bradycardia and have TRANSCUTANEOUS PACING available, and ESCALATE IMMEDIATELY.'**

**Other practice stems.** **68M with diabetes, two days of nausea, vomiting and breathlessness, NO chest pain; ST elevation II, III, aVF AND HYPOTENSION → INFERIOR MI WITH RV INFARCTION. FLUIDS, NOT GTN.** **52F, recurrent presyncope ON STANDING, on insulin, an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic, POSTURAL DROP OF 30 mmHg → ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION from autonomic neuropathy PLUS medications. REVIEW THE DRUGS, DON'T IMAGE THE BRAIN.** **44F, presyncope WITH PALPITATIONS WHILE SITTING STILL; SHORT PR AND A DELTA WAVE → WOLFF–PARKINSON–WHITE. Cardiology referral, AVOID AV NODAL BLOCKERS if she develops AF.** **44F on insulin with presyncope; ST DEPRESSION IN V1–V3 WITH TALL R WAVES and no elevation anywhere → POSTERIOR MI. DO V7–V9; THIS IS A STEMI EQUIVALENT, NOT ‘ISCHAEMIA'.**

**LONGER TERM, once through the acute phase**: dual antiplatelet therapy, a STATIN, an ACE INHIBITOR and a BETA BLOCKER unless contraindicated · **CARDIAC REHABILITATION referral** · tightened diabetes review with the GP and diabetes educator, **including SICK-DAY AND HYPOGLYCAEMIA MANAGEMENT** · smoking cessation, blood pressure and lipid targets · GP Management Plan and Team Care Arrangements · **DRIVING: under Assessing Fitness to Drive, a PRIVATE driver is generally NOT FIT TO DRIVE FOR ABOUT 2 WEEKS after a STEMI treated with successful PCI, and COMMERCIAL drivers considerably longer — CONFIRM THE PERIOD WITH THE TREATING CARDIOLOGIST BEFORE ADVISING.**

SA and equity — **from an MM5 or MM6 practice, primary PCI is RARELY REACHABLE INSIDE 120 MINUTES. The pathway is: ACTIVATE MedSTAR (or the RFDS) EARLY AND IN PARALLEL WITH TREATMENT — NOT AFTER — give PRE-HOSPITAL FIBRINOLYSIS under the SA Health STEMI pathway, and TRANSMIT THE ECG for remote cardiology confirmation. Check contraindications — particularly recent STROKE, BLEEDING, SURGERY OR UNCONTROLLED HYPERTENSION.** · **WOMEN, OLDER PEOPLE AND PEOPLE WITH DIABETES ARE THE GROUPS MOST LIKELY TO HAVE AN INFARCT WITHOUT CHEST PAIN, AND THEREFORE THE GROUPS MOST LIKELY TO BE SENT HOME.** · **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians develop ischaemic heart disease YOUNGER and die of it at MARKEDLY HIGHER RATES — A LOW THRESHOLD FOR AN ECG IN AN ABORIGINAL PATIENT WITH VAGUE SYMPTOMS IS GOOD PRACTICE, NOT OVER-INVESTIGATION. Closing the Gap PBS co-payment; involve an Aboriginal Liaison Officer early.**

setting: An easy station with a low recalled pass rate, and the reason is narrow. Every candidate lists painkillers, breathing exercises and red flags. The pass is decided by whether you say out loud that pain causes shallow breathing, shallow breathing causes collapse, and collapse causes pneumonia — and then hang every part of the plan off that chain. The role-player asks 'But how do painkillers help my ribs heal?' even if you have already explained it, to see whether you can say it a second way.
stem: Emergency department, regional South Australia, 21:40. Jenny Kowalski, 42, came off her bicycle at speed onto her left side about three hours ago. She wore a helmet, did not hit her head and did not lose consciousness. She is fully alert and haemodynamically stable throughout.

Chest x-ray and CT chest: fractures of the left 4th, 5th and 6th ribs, all minimally displaced · mild pulmonary contusion of the left lower lobe · no pneumothorax and no haemothorax. Observations: BP 128/76, HR 84, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8, GCS 15. Abdomen soft and non-tender. The ED consultant has reviewed her, cleared her for discharge, and has asked you to speak to her.

Tasks: explain the x-ray and CT findings and the diagnosis — explain the discharge plan including analgesia and breathing care — explain the red flags and when she must return — address her questions and concerns. No examination required.
tasks: Explain the X-ray and CT findings and the diagnosis to the patient
Explain the discharge plan, including analgesia and breathing care
Explain the red flags and when she must return
Address the patient's questions and concerns
time: Forty-five seconds on WIPE, name, 'How are you feeling' and an offer of analgesia · fifteen seconds on the first agenda check · two minutes translating the three imaging findings · a minute on the chain, which is where the station is decided · two minutes on analgesia, breathing numbers, cough splinting and mobilising · a minute on red flags with actions and follow-up · and the last minute on the two agendas and teach-back

back.dx: UNCOMPLICATED MULTIPLE RIB FRACTURES — left 4th to 6th, minimally displaced — with a mild left lower lobe pulmonary contusion, no pneumothorax and no haemothorax, haemodynamically stable and dischargeable. Rib level is the whole point of the stem: 4–6 sits below the great vessels (Ribs 1–3) and above the solid organs (Ribs 9–12), so aortic, cardiac, splenic and hepatic injury are argued away by position rather than ignored. The defensive differential, grouped: rs — pneumothorax, haemothorax, atelectasis, pneumonia, flail chest (≥ 3 contiguous ribs in ≥ 2 places, not present here) · CVS — blunt cardiac and aortic injury · GI — splenic, hepatic and diaphragmatic injury · MSK — sternal, scapular, clavicular and thoracic spine injury · CNS — head and C-spine · other — was the fall itself syncope, arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia or alcohol. The three that can still declare themselves after discharge are delayed pneumothorax, delayed haemothorax and a progressing contusion — that is what the safety-net is built around. Management is multimodal analgesia, then breathing, then mobilising, in that order because each depends on the one before: paracetamol 1 g QID by the clock (Max 4 g/24 h) · ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food where not contraindicated · a short small supply of oxycodone IR 5 mg 4–6 hourly PRN with a laxative started the same day · regional blocks (Serratus anterior, erector spinae, intercostal) named as the next step if pain stops her breathing deeply · incentive spirometry · cough with pillow splinting · early mobilisation with no bed rest and no chest binders · chest physiotherapy referral named · written handout, work certificate, smoking cessation, and review at about one week in fracture clinic or with the GP, often by telephone. Repeat imaging is symptom-driven, not routine. VERIFY all doses. The discharge decision should be said out loud as reasoned rather than inherited: stable, normoxic, mobile, pain controlled orally, someone at home — if any one of those fails, she stays.
plan: WIPE, name and role, then 'How are you feeling right now?' and — before any content — offer another dose of pain relief. Ten seconds, and it is a free empathy mark. Then permission and signpost.
First agenda check: 'Before I go through the plan — is there anything in particular worrying you?' Ask again before you close; the bike question usually only comes the second time.
The three imaging findings in plain English, chunked, with a check after each (see findings).
The chain, unprompted — pain → shallow breathing → collapse → pneumonia — so the agenda question is already answered when it arrives.
Screen before you prescribe: allergies, ulcer, renal, asthma, pregnancy, other medicines, driving or caring for small children. Then the drugs with names, doses and side effects (see dx).

Breathing with numbers: ten slow deep breaths, hold 3–5 seconds, every 1–2 hours while awake, incentive spirometer if available · cough hugging a pillow · short walks from day one, no bed rest, no binders · chest physio referral.
Red flags, each paired with its action · then follow-up, written information, work certificate, smoking, and who is at home — a rural address changes the threshold.
The two agendas: painkillers do not heal bone, they buy back the deep breath · the bike answered by principle then range then safety, never a bluffed number · then teach-back.
back.planNote: generous time for the content — the risk is running dry at five minutes, so bank the teach-back, written information, smoking, work certificate and second agenda check for the tail
ask: The chain, verbatim: 'Pain makes you breathe shallowly; shallow breathing lets parts of the lung collapse; collapse plus phlegm is how a chest infection starts.' and its companion: 'The painkillers are not to heal the bone — they are so you can take a deep breath and cough. That is the treatment.'

The breathing prescription, which is the sentence the examiner is listening for: 'Ten slow deep breaths, hold each for three to five seconds, every one to two hours while you are awake.' plus 'Hug a pillow against your ribs when you cough — it hurts less and the cough is stronger. Please do cough.'

Red flags with actions: sudden or worsening breathlessness · chest pain suddenly much worse or different · coughing blood, or green phlegm with fever or shivers · dizziness, faintness or racing heart · pain the tablets are not touching so she cannot breathe deeply · any tummy pain or left shoulder-tip pain → straight back to ED or 000; healthdirect 1800 022 222 if unsure.

The bike answer, without a bluffed number: 'There is no fixed number of weeks — it depends on your healing, not the calendar. Once you have no pain at rest and can take a deep breath and cough, build back up gradually — for most people with three broken ribs that is around six to eight weeks for proper riding.' then helmet, not while on the stronger tablets, and not if unwell — and the same for driving a car, which is the free mark candidates drop.

Challenges: 'It really hurts when I breathe in' · 'How do painkillers help my ribs heal?' Asked even after you have explained it · 'A bruised lung? Is that serious?' · 'Will I get addicted?' · 'Every one to two hours? Even at work?' · 'Coughing is going to be agony' · 'I live forty minutes out — can I drive myself in?' · 'My friend was back on after two weeks — is that definite?' · and, if you moralise about cycling, 'It is how I get to work. I am not giving it up.'
pefe: Role-player: Jenny Kowalski, 42, a primary school teacher in a country town who commutes by bike. Pain 7/10 at rest and 9/10 on deep breathing, visibly guarding and breathing shallowly throughout — that is the visual cue the candidate is meant to notice. Stoic, slightly impatient, wants a plan; she only goes quiet if the candidate is dismissive.

What she volunteers only if asked: smokes five a day, two wines most weekends, on the oral contraceptive pill only, no allergies, not pregnant, no past history, helmet worn, no dizziness or blackout before the fall, partner at home forty minutes out of town.

Her hidden agenda is that she fears being told to give up cycling. She will not raise it until asked about concerns; if the candidate never asks, she raises it herself at about six and a half minutes. She pushes the painkiller question once even if it has been answered, and asks what any jargon means every time.

Mark them against these: asked how she feels and offered analgesia first · permission and signposting · asked about concerns twice · explained the fractures, the negatives and the contusion in plain English including the 1–3 day worsening · explained the chain · screened before prescribing · named drug, dose and frequency · added a laxative and the no-driving advice · gave the breathing numbers · pillow splinting · mobilise, no bed rest, no binder · chest physio · red flags each with an action · named the follow-up · answered both agendas · smoking, written information and work certificate · teach-back at the close.

Variants to rehearse: a 74-year-old ex-smoker with COPD and SpO2 91% — the hidden discriminator is that he may not be safely dischargeable and you must say so · ribs 9–11 — add the delayed splenic rupture warning with left shoulder-tip pain · an anticoagulated patient — drop the NSAID and lower the return threshold · refusal of opioids — structured shared decision-making, not persuasion · a rural patient ninety minutes out with no reception and alone — the discharge is not safe as written.

The fractures — 'Three of your ribs are broken — the fourth, fifth and sixth on the left. The broken ends are still lined up.' that matters because lined-up ribs heal themselves over six to eight weeks — nothing to pin or plate, and you cannot cast a chest. Minimise the treatment, never the injury: 'Only three ribs' is a trap

The contusion — the one candidates skip — 'A small part of your left lung is bruised — exactly like the bruise on your skin where you landed, a little bleeding and swelling in the tissue. It is not a hole and it is not an infection.' It evolves over 24–72 hours and then settles over about a week — which is the honest justification for the safety-net, and the answer if the examiner asks why a mild contusion needs red flags at all

The chain — the single most important thirty seconds — 'When a rib is broken, a deep breath hurts, so people breathe shallowly and avoid coughing. But the bottom of the lung needs a deep breath to stay open. Without it small areas collapse and the phlegm sits there — and that is how a chest infection starts. So the painkillers are not there to heal the bone. They are there so you can take a deep breath and cough. That is the treatment'

The mechanism question almost nobody asks — 'Did you feel unwell, dizzy or black out before you came off?' A syncopal fall is a different presentation entirely. Also worth asking: helmet and head injury, alcohol, whether this is a workcover or third-party matter, and who is at home tonight

The reassuring negatives — 'There is no air leaking around the lung and no blood collecting around it — the two things we look hardest for, and neither is there.' Plain phrase first, the words pneumothorax and haemothorax second, never the other way round

setting: Almost every candidate knows the number six. This station separates those who know the number from those who know what the six months is counted from. Both clocks — time on treatment and time seizure-free — started four months ago, so the answer is two months, not six. The role-player is briefed to ask 'So six months from today?' Precisely to give you the chance to get it right or wrong.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Julie Nguyen, 28, a university student, comes to see you to discuss her driver's licence. She had a seizure four months ago and was diagnosed with epilepsy. Her neurologist started her on anti-seizure medication. She wants to know when she can drive again.
Tasks: take a focused, relevant history from the patient (4 minutes, prompted) — counsel the patient appropriately regarding her driving licence.

Some recent sittings hand you a printed extract of the fit to drive standards table in the stem. If so, read it with her and point to the row that applies — that is better counselling than reciting from memory. The marks are still in the history and in applying the criteria.
