Counsel the patient appropriately regarding her driving licence
time: Forty seconds on introduction, open question, the agenda and empathy · three and a quarter minutes of focused history, where four AUTO-FAIL items live · thirty seconds on empathy again and the public-safety reason · seventy-five seconds explaining the three criteria as criteria · forty-five seconds applying them to her · fifty seconds on compliance, triggers, contraception and non-driving safety · and the last forty seconds on the reporting duty, reading, the neurologist letter, review and teach-back

back.dx: EPILEPSY TREATED FOR THE FIRST TIME — fitness-to-drive assessment, private vehicle, in a non-adherent patient with three modifiable seizure triggers. The standard that applies is the first-time-treatment variation (Treatment started within the preceding 18 months), not the default: a conditional licence with at least annual review may be considered if she has been treated for at least 6 months, has had no seizures in the preceding 6 months, any seizures after starting treatment were only in the first 6 months and not the last 6, and she follows medical advice including adherence. She is four months in and seizure-free, so she is two months away. The other private standards worth holding: default 12 months seizure-free · first seizure 6 months, with an unconditional licence possible after 2 years seizure-free and 12 months off medication · breakthrough seizure in previously well-controlled epilepsy 4 weeks if there is an identified, reliably avoidable provoking factor that has not caused seizures before, otherwise 3 months · acute symptomatic seizures 6 months · sleep-only seizures 12 months, or 2 years if there were previous awake seizures · no driving during a medication taper or switch and for 3 months after the last dose · unconditional licence again after 5 years seizure-free and 12 months off medication · commercial default 10 years seizure-free plus EEG, specialist-led, with no reductions. Three rules override the table: adherence is a licence condition and a patient who refuses medical advice should be assessed as not fit to drive, with periodic drug levels available as a condition where there is doubt · a crash caused by a seizure removes every reduction · and if more than one standard could apply, the longest non-driving period wins. Two corrections: sleep deprivation is clinically a major trigger but is explicitly not accepted as a licensing provoking factor because it cannot be reliably avoided, so it cannot shorten a period to four weeks; and weight gain is not a carbamazepine effect — that is valproate, gabapentin and pregabalin. Carbamazepine causes drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, diplopia, nausea, rash and hyponatraemia, with rare blood dyscrasias and severe cutaneous reactions, and hla-b*1502 screening is recommended before starting it in people of han Chinese, Thai and other South-East Asian ancestry added. Take her actual side effects at face value and discuss them with the neurologist rather than assuming a class effect. VERIFY all figures against Austroads assessing fitness to drive.
plan: Open question, acknowledge the agenda, empathy for the lost independence — then permission: 'Is it alright if I ask a few questions first, so what I tell you is actually right for your situation?' Do not answer the licence question yet.
The four key questions, asked explicitly and separately (see findings), then the rest of the history.
Empathy again, then the reason before the rule: not a punishment — a seizure at the wheel could hurt her and others.

The three criteria explained as criteria: six months on treatment so we know it is working · no seizures in those six months · taking it as prescribed, which is written into the standard as a licence condition.
Apply them: four months in, seizure-free — two months away, not six. Then conditional licence, annual review, and that the licensing authority decides, not you.

Fix the adherence problem rather than naming it: letter to the neurologist about the side effects, possible dose or drug change, phone alarm, pill box or blister pack — and the honest blocker that missed doses mean she does not meet the standard even at six months.
Triggers with numbers not disapproval · contraception and pre-conception folate on an enzyme-inducing teratogen · non-driving safety and seizure first aid for flatmates · seizure diary.
Her duty to notify and the SA mandatory reporting duty, stated calmly as information and never as leverage · reading material · review in two months · teach-back of the three criteria.
back.planNote: keep the criteria explanation tight — the safety, women's health and legal blocks are all marked items and they are what candidates run out of time for
ask: The four questions, verbatim: 'And when was your last seizure?' · 'Are you able to take it every day exactly as prescribed — and what gets in the way?' · alcohol, drugs, sleep, other medicines and herbal products · 'Do you drive a private car only, or do you drive for work — truck, bus, taxi or rideshare?'

The answer that decides the station: 'Your six months started when your treatment started. You are two months away, not six.' then 'It is called a conditional licence and it needs a medical review every year' and 'I do not issue the licence — the licensing authority decides, based on what I send them. What I can promise is that if those three things are true, I will support it.'

The compliance move: 'That is a real problem, not an excuse — I will write to your neurologist about the drowsiness, because sometimes the dose can be adjusted and sometimes a different medication suits better.' plus the honest line: 'If you are missing doses you do not meet the standard even at six months, and if there is doubt the authority can require periodic blood-level checks.'

The two things almost nobody says: 'Carbamazepine can make the contraceptive pill less reliable' — the combined pill, mini-pill and implant are affected, an IUD or depot generally is not; and 'If you were ever thinking about pregnancy, come and see me first — there is a high-dose folate we start beforehand and any change is planned by your neurologist, never stopped abruptly.' Note that a drug switch itself triggers the three-month non-driving period.

Challenges: 'I just want my licence back' · 'So six months from today?' — the scripted opening for the key answer · 'What does conditional mean?' · 'Every year? Forever?' · 'Are you definitely going to give it to me?' — saying yes is a fail · 'They would actually test me?' · 'Nobody told me that about the pill — could I have got pregnant?' · 'Are you going to report me?' · and if you lecture her, 'I know. It is just not that simple' and one-word answers thereafter.
pefe: Role-player: Julie Nguyen, 28, a third-year university student in a share house with casual cafe shifts. First seizure four months ago — a witnessed convulsion at home — diagnosed with epilepsy, saw the neurologist once, started on carbamazepine, has not driven since. Frustrated and deflated rather than hostile; she brightens if the candidate is warm about how hard the two-hour bus trip has been, and goes quiet and monosyllabic if lectured.

She misses two or three doses a week. She wants a yes today and expects to be told six months. The worry she voices only if asked about concerns is that she will never be allowed to drive again and will have to defer her degree.

How she tests them: she volunteers nothing about the last seizure unless asked directly, and marks it as a fail if the question never comes · she admits non-adherence but gives the reasons only if asked why · she does not mention rideshare unless asked whether she drives for work · she asks 'So six months from today?' after the criteria, and marks six months as a fail and two months as a pass · she marks any promise of the licence as a fail · and if threatened with reporting she goes cold.

Mark them against these: empathy and agenda acknowledged · permission before the history · asked the last-seizure date separately from the diagnosis date · asked about adherence and then why · alcohol with quantity, drugs, sleep, other medicines and supplements · private versus commercial vehicle · neurologist follow-up · mood and psychosocial impact · the public-safety reason before the rules · the three criteria explained before being applied · the correct answer of two months · conditional licence explained · annual review · the authority decides, not the doctor · a concrete plan for the side effects · trigger counselling with a figure for alcohol · contraception and pre-conception folate · non-driving safety and seizure first aid · both legal duties stated factually · review, reading and a neurologist letter · teach-back.

Variants: last seizure two weeks ago — six months runs from that seizure, so about five and a half months, and the treatment needs review now · long-standing epilepsy seizure-free 20 years with one seizure after six beers — four weeks, because alcohol is identified, avoidable and novel; if the trigger was an all-nighter it is three months because sleep deprivation does not count · rideshare driver — commercial, specialist-led, handle the livelihood conversation · she says she will drive anyway — not fit to drive, explore, document, involve the neurologist, disclose the duty without threatening · neurologist weaning the drug — no driving during the taper and for three months after · crash caused by the seizure — full twelve months, no reductions.

Are you taking it as prescribed — and what gets in the way — 'Not really, I miss it a fair bit.' The mark is in the second half: 'It makes me feel dopey in the mornings, I have put on weight, and I forget when I am busy.' if you just say 'You must take it' she goes quieter and marks it

What increases your risk of a seizure — Alcohol five or six wines on a Saturday · sleep up until 2 or 3 am most nights with assignments · ST John's wort daily for stress, which induces enzymes and lowers her drug level · no recreational drugs · plus missed doses, illness and fever

What do you drive — private or commercial — 'Just my own car.' In the variant she has started driving for a rideshare app and only says so if you ask whether she drives for work — which is commercial, specialist-led, ten years seizure-free with an EEG, and no first-time-treatment reduction

The rest of the history, not optional — Seizure description and any subtle episodes since · sleep-only or time-of-day pattern · neurologist follow-up (Seen once, not since), EEG and MRI · contraception and pregnancy plans — she is on the combined pill · home safety — she has baths most nights · mood, study and stigma · SADMA, past history and family history

When was your last seizure — not when were you diagnosed — 'Four months ago — that was the one. Nothing since.' The whole clock hangs off this date and she volunteers nothing unless asked directly. In the harder recall variant she answers 'Actually… two weeks ago', and the seizure-free clock restarts from then
fails: ★ Never asking when the last seizure was, and taking the four-month diagnosis date as the seizure date
★ Asking about compliance but never asking why — 'are you taking it? no? well, you need to'
★ Never establishing the vehicle type, and assuming private because she is a young student
★ 'Wait six months from today' — the commonest wrong answer in this station

Telling her the plan before explaining the criteria; never saying conditional licence or annual review; promising the licence; skipping triggers; using the reporting duty as a threat; missing contraception and pregnancy on an enzyme-inducing teratogen; no non-driving safety advice; no empathy before the regulation; and blaming her for the non-adherence
numbers: Private standards: default 12 months seizure-free · first seizure 6 months · epilepsy treated for the first time (Treatment started within 18 months) 6 months treated and 6 months seizure-free — this case · breakthrough in previously well-controlled epilepsy 4 weeks with an identified avoidable provoking factor, 3 months without · acute symptomatic 6 months · sleep-only 12 months, or 2 years after previous awake seizures · taper or switch: no driving during and for 3 months after · unconditional again after 5 years seizure-free and 12 months off medication · commercial default 10 years plus EEG, first seizure 5 years, no reductions · two or more seizures in 24 hours count as one · Austroads assessing fitness to drive 2022, paraphrased — VERIFY

SA is the jurisdiction detail that decides the station: reporting is mandatory under the motor vehicles act 1959 section 148 — a health professional who believes a licence holder's condition makes driving likely to endanger the public must inform the registrar in writing and then tell the person that the report was made and what was in it · most other states are discretionary · the patient also has her own duty to notify service SA · for a private licence the GP may liaise with the authority, for commercial only a specialist may · folic acid 5 mg daily pre-conception · people with epilepsy are around twice as likely to be in a crash added · telehealth neurology supported rurally, PATS over 100 km, TIS National 131 450 · VERIFY all

source: Epilepsy_Driving_Licence_Counselling_Notability.pdf (Julie Nguyen, 28, epilepsy treated for the first time four months ago, non-adherent on carbamazepine, private vehicle — four history questions decide the station and the correct answer is review in two months, not six, with a conditional licence and annual review)
drive: AMC Clinical Notability › Counselling › Epilepsy_Driving_Licence_Counselling_Notability.pdf
must: FAIL — Never asking when the LAST SEIZURE was, and taking the four-month DIAGNOSIS date as the seizure date — the whole clock hangs off that one date, and without it every number you quote afterwards is invented: 'I know you were diagnosed four months ago; when was the most recent seizure you had?'; she volunteers nothing, and in the harder variant the answer is TWO WEEKS AGO, which restarts the seizure-free clock and changes the entire answer (★)

FAIL — Asking about compliance but never asking WHY — 'are you taking it? no? well, you need to' scores the first half and loses the second, because you cannot fix what you have not named: 'what gets in the way of taking it?' → side effects, forgetting, cost, denial of the diagnosis, not wanting to be 'on tablets', fear of dependence; she is briefed to go quieter and say 'I know, it's just not that simple' if you simply tell her to try harder (★)

FAIL — Never establishing the VEHICLE TYPE, and assuming private because she is a young student — 'do you drive a private car only, or do you drive for work: a truck, bus, taxi or rideshare?'; she mentions the rideshare app ONLY if asked, and rideshare and taxi driving are COMMERCIAL, where the first-time-treatment reduction does not apply at all, the default is TEN YEARS seizure-free with an EEG, and the assessment must come from a SPECIALIST rather than from you (★)

FAIL — 'Wait six months from today' — the commonest wrong answer in this station, and what separates candidates who know the number from those who know WHAT THE SIX MONTHS IS COUNTED FROM: both clocks started when TREATMENT started, so she is TWO MONTHS AWAY, NOT SIX; explain the criteria AS CRITERIA before applying them, because the examiner is marking the explanation — and she is briefed to ask 'so six months from today?' precisely to give you the chance to get it right or wrong (★)

DO — The three criteria, in this order, for EPILEPSY TREATED FOR THE FIRST TIME on a PRIVATE licence: treated for AT LEAST SIX MONTHS, so the medication has had time to show it works; NO SEIZURES in those six months; and TAKING THE MEDICATION AS PRESCRIBED, because adherence is WRITTEN INTO THE STANDARD as a condition of the licence — then 'your six months started when your treatment started, and you've had no seizures since, so you're TWO MONTHS away, not six'; name CONDITIONAL LICENCE and explain it (you can drive, but the licence carries a medical condition and needs review EVERY YEAR rather than the ten-year licence most people have), and say explicitly that THE LICENSING AUTHORITY DECIDES, NOT YOU ('I can't promise the outcome; I can promise I'll support the application if those three things are true'); give the public-safety reason BEFORE the rules and the empathy before both, because she has lost her independence on top of a diagnosis she did not ask for; other private standards — 12 months seizure-free by default; 6 months after a first seizure; 4 WEEKS for a breakthrough seizure in previously well-controlled epilepsy IF there is an identified, reliably avoidable provoking factor that has not caused seizures before, and 3 MONTHS if no cause is found; 6 months for acute symptomatic seizures; and NO DRIVING during a medication taper or switch AND FOR THREE MONTHS AFTER THE LAST DOSE (VERIFY against Austroads); three rules override the table — compliance is a licence condition, a crash caused by a seizure removes every reduction, and where more than one standard could apply THE LONGEST NON-DRIVING PERIOD WINS

DO — The compliance move: 'that is a real problem, not an excuse — I will write to your neurologist about the drowsiness, because sometimes the dose can be adjusted and sometimes a different medication suits better', with practical aids (a phone alarm, a weekly pill box, a pharmacy blister pack) and the honest blocker named ('if you're missing doses you don't meet the standard even at six months, and if there's doubt the authority can attach a condition that we check the drug LEVEL in your blood'); then the blocks candidates run out of time for — TRIGGERS with numbers rather than disapproval (no alcohol is safest and certainly not five or six in a night; a regular sleep pattern matters almost as much as the tablets, though SLEEP DEPRIVATION IS NOT ACCEPTED AS A LICENSING 'PROVOKING FACTOR' because it cannot be reliably avoided; and tell every doctor and pharmacist about the epilepsy medication, because ST JOHN'S WORT induces enzymes and lowers her drug level); CONTRACEPTION AND PREGNANCY, which almost nobody raises — carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer that reduces the effectiveness of the combined pill, the mini-pill and the implant while an IUD or depot is generally unaffected, and it is teratogenic, so pre-conception FOLIC ACID 5 MG DAILY with any change planned by the neurologist and never stopped abruptly (VERIFY); NON-DRIVING SAFETY in thirty seconds (showers not baths, never swim alone, care on ladders and around the stove, seizure first aid for flatmates — protect the head, do not restrain, nothing in the mouth, recovery position, call 000 if over five minutes or she does not wake), plus a seizure diary and medical identification; and the LEGAL part stated calmly as information and NEVER as a threat — her own duty to notify the licensing authority, and in SOUTH AUSTRALIA a MANDATORY doctor's duty to report under the Motor Vehicles Act 1959 s148, with 'that's not something I'm doing today, and I'd always tell you if I did'; do not say WEIGHT GAIN is a carbamazepine side effect if challenged, because that belongs to valproate, gabapentin and pregabalin, while carbamazepine causes drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, diplopia, nausea, rash and hyponatraemia, with HLA-B*1502 screening recommended before starting it in people of Han Chinese, Thai and other South-East Asian ancestry; close with teach-back

setting: The varicose vein is scenery. This is ANZCOR first aid for bleeding delivered down a phone line to a frightened husband, and the clinical content is first-aid level. The failing candidate hands the crisis back — tells a panicking 71-year-old to hang up and ring triple zero himself, then delivers a correct list into a phone nobody is listening to. The passing candidate takes the emergency off him in the first minute, gives one instruction at a time in kitchen words, and does not hang up.
stem: General practice, regional South Australia. Your next case is a telephone appointment. It concerns a 68-year-old woman who is a known case of varicose veins. She has just cut her leg on broken glass and is bleeding. Her partner is on the telephone and both of them are at home.
Tasks: take a history / assessment from the partner — explain your immediate management to the partner.

Some recalls give task 1 as 'Take a history' and others as 'Do an assessment' — they are the same instruction. You are on a telephone, so the assessment is the history, asked of a frightened third party. The station may be converted to face-to-face mid-station; say nothing down the phone you would not say in the room. Stem reconstructed from 2024 recalls.
tasks: Take a history / assessment from the partner
Explain your immediate management to the partner
time: Ten seconds for his name · twenty seconds addressing the panic properly, once · twenty seconds stating that you are arranging the ambulance · two and a half minutes of closed binary questions in order · three and a half minutes of instructions, one action each, each closed with 'Tell me when that is done' · and the last minute on monitoring, the three do-nots, what the crew will do, and reassurance — not on vein education

back.dx: Bleeding varicosity of the lower leg after a glass laceration, managed by telephone through a panicking third party. The varicosity exists in the stem only to make prolonged, non-self-limiting bleeding plausible — incompetent valves leave the superficial venous system under sustained high pressure and the overlying skin is thin and poorly nourished, so a minor knock opens a vein that is already hypertensive and it flows faster the longer the leg stays dependent. It changes nothing you do. The sequence is DRSABCD adapted to a phone: danger from the glass · response, with 'She is talking' said aloud as a positive airway and breathing finding · then haemorrhage control. Firm direct pressure on or around the wound is the fastest, easiest and most effective measure and everything else is an adjunct to it or a consequence of it failing: lie her flat · any clean cloth, folded, both hands, press harder than feels polite and do not let go · if it soaks through, a second pad on TOP and never lift the first, because lifting strips the clot · stacking pads is not pressure — absorbent layers feel productive while the pressure at the bleeding point falls, so the answer is a firmer more focused push and a bandage over the TOP added · embedded glass stays in and he presses either side of it, because the fragment may be plugging the vessel it cut and blind removal can extend the injury to vessels, tendons and nerves · blanket on for warmth, because cold blood clots badly · nothing by mouth · and she does not stand, because standing puts the venous pressure straight back up. Elevation is the one place the common teaching needs resolving correction: ANZCOR does not recommend routine elevation for bleeding in general — no evidence of benefit and potential for pain or injury — while the vascular literature for a bleeding varicosity specifically does recommend lying flat and raising the leg above heart level with a compression bandage not removed until review, because this bleeding is pressure-driven. The exam position: pressure first always, elevation as an adjunct added after pressure is on, never interrupting it, and not if fracture is suspected. The tourniquet is last resort only — life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure has failed to control — and must be described properly: a belt or folded strip, 5–10 cm above the wound, not over a joint, not over the wound, not covered by clothing, tightened until the bleeding stops and then left alone, time written down and handed over, and keep pressing anyway — because an improvised band that is too loose occludes venous return only and makes the bleeding worse added. Commercial windlass tourniquets outperform improvised ones; say so. Afterwards: paramedic pressure dressing, haemostatic dressing or tourniquet if uncontrolled, IV access and fluids, analgesia, oxygen, transport · ED assessment for blood loss and shock, FBC and group and hold, wound exploration and glass removal with imaging if retained fragments are suspected, closure · tetanus booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago for a tetanus-prone wound, 10 years for a clean minor one, with immunoglobulin if the primary course is incomplete or uncertain · and venous duplex then endovenous ablation, sclerotherapy or surgery, with graduated compression and skin care meanwhile — a bled varicosity recurs if the reflux is not treated, so this is a referral, not a reassurance. VERIFY all.
plan: 'Who am I speaking with?' — get his name and use it. Then address the fear once, properly: 'Ben, I can hear how frightening this is and you have done exactly the right thing ringing. Stay with me — I will tell you exactly what to do and I am not going to hang up.' Do it well and he cooperates for the rest of the call.

Help first, history second: 'Before anything else — I am getting an ambulance to you now. My nurse is dialling triple zero on the other line while we talk. She has your address. You do not have to make that call.' Pre-empts the scripted objection.

Closed binary questions in order — response, danger, timing and trajectory, lay quantity, oozing or spurting, glass in the wound, shock signs, anticoagulants, comorbidities, address and access (see findings). No SADMA, no pulse count, no blood pressure.
Danger first: clear patch of floor, do not kneel in the glass. Then lie her down flat and keep her still.

Cleanest cloth, folded, straight on the cut, both hands, press hard, do not let go — speakerphone or phone on the floor. Then: soaked means a second on TOP, never lift the first. Glass stays in, press either side.
Pillow or folded coat under the calf without interrupting the pressure · blanket on · nothing to eat or drink · she does not stand.

The tourniquet, labelled as last resort as you say it, with placement and the time noted (see dx). Then the three do-nots said out loud, including the explicit refusal of the car when he offers it at about six minutes.

Monitoring instructions — tell me if she stops answering, if her breathing changes, or if she goes grey and sweaty · what the crew will do · reassurance that most bleeds like this stop with the pressure he is already applying · tetanus and vascular referral flagged for later · and you stay on the line.
back.planNote: eight minutes is generous for first-aid content — candidates fail on sequence and on losing the caller, not on time; spend any spare minute on monitoring and reassurance rather than vein education
ask: The four rules of a panic call: one instruction per sentence, then stop and let him do it · kitchen words not clinical words — tea towel not compress, press hard not apply firm digital pressure · close the loop with 'Tell me when you have the towel on it' · and address the fear once, properly, at the start.

The five scripted obstacles and their answers. 'I called you — why should I ring triple zero?' → 'You do not have to. My nurse is dialling right now. Your job is your wife's leg, nothing else.' · 'How can I press on it while I am talking to you?' → 'Put me on speakerphone, or put the phone down on the floor next to you. Both hands on the leg.' · 'I am on my own, I cannot do all that' → 'Then do one thing: press on it and do not let go. Everything else can wait for the ambulance.' · 'I have got the car — should I just drive her in?' → 'No. If you drive, nobody is pressing on that leg, and she can faint on the way. Stay where you are and keep pressing.' · he goes quiet or repeats himself → 'Ben, you are doing this right. Take one breath with me. Now — both hands, press hard. Tell me what you can see.'

The three do-nots, said out loud: do not drive her to hospital · do not remove embedded glass · do not lift the pad to check. Plus no creams or ointments, nothing to eat or drink, and she does not stand up.

The examiner challenge on elevation — 'Why did you elevate? ANZCOR does not recommend it.' → 'You are right that ANZCOR does not recommend routine elevation for bleeding in general. I raised this leg because the bleeding is venous and pressure-driven, so lowering the venous pressure reduces flow at the bleeding point, and there was no suspected fracture. I did it only after direct pressure was on, and it did not interrupt the pressure.'

Traps to name before they happen: launching into questions before saying the ambulance is coming · treating 'Take a history' as an invitation to a full SADMA · letting him dodge a question instead of asking it again shorter — 'Ben, just yes or no. Is she talking to you?' · forgetting that 'She is talking' is a positive airway and breathing finding · offering the tourniquet early because it sounds decisive · giving the whole list in one breath · and ending the call.
pefe: Role-player: Ben Halloway, 71, a retired shearer, at home with his wife Marge, 68, who has bad varicose veins on her right shin and has just dropped a glass jar and cut her leg. He is frightened and not thinking clearly. He opens fast and loud, talking over the doctor: 'My wife's bleeding, there's blood everywhere, you have to help me.'

How he plays it: he avoids the first question he is asked, answering a different one or just repeating that she is bleeding · if the doctor uses clinical words like compress, elevate or apply pressure to the wound site he says 'I don't understand what you're telling me to do' · if the doctor does not arrange the ambulance and tells him to call 000 he gets cross: 'I've called you for help and you want me to make another call?' · he objects once about holding the phone, says once that he is on his own, and at about six minutes offers to drive her in · he settles as soon as he is named, told to breathe, and given one clear instruction at a time.

What he reports if asked: she is awake and talking, scared · it started about five minutes ago and has not stopped · a soaked tea towel and a puddle on the floor · steady dark red, not spurting · glass on the floor and he thinks a bit is in the cut · no blood thinners, just a fluid tablet · blood pressure, nothing else · she is a bit pale and says she feels funny · tetanus unknown.

Mark them against these: got his name and used it · addressed the panic before instructing · arranged the ambulance themselves · asked about danger from the glass · confirmed she was awake and talking · asked about blood thinners · had her lie down · cloth and firm pressure with both hands · second pad on TOP and never lifted the first · left the glass in and pressed around it · explicitly refused the car · gave monitoring instructions · described the tourniquet as a last resort · used words he could understand · one instruction at a time, confirmed · and stayed on the line at the end.

Variants: she slumps and stops answering — leave the bleeding, look listen and feel, compressions if not breathing normally · bright red and spurting — arterial, harder more focused pressure and a much lower tourniquet threshold, tell the crew · she takes apixaban for AF — it will not self-arrest, continuous pressure to handover and she goes to hospital whether or not it stops · 'It has stopped, can we stay home?' — no, the dressing stays on until review and a bled varicosity rebleeds added · a neighbour rings with a forearm cut on a circular saw — identical sequence, plus any amputated part goes dry in a sealed bag and that bag on ice, never directly on ice or in water added · 'What would you do if you were there?' — same order, upgraded tools.

Danger — the written-in hazard — 'Is there broken glass on the floor where you are?' — 'There is glass everywhere, she dropped a jar.' Danger to him as much as to her: find a clear patch of floor, do not kneel in it

Characterising the bleed — Started about five minutes ago, has not stopped, looks worse · quantity in lay terms — 'A soaked tea towel and a puddle on the floor', never ask a frightened man for millilitres · 'Oozing steadily or spurting?' — steady dark red, so venous as expected; bright red spurts would be arterial and a much lower tourniquet threshold

The answers that change what you say — Glass: he thinks there is a bit in the cut — so it stays in and he presses around it · shock: she is a bit pale and says she feels funny · anticoagulants: no, just a fluid tablet — if she were on apixaban or warfarin this would not stop on its own and pressure is continuous until handover · other conditions: blood pressure only · address and front-door access, worth ten seconds rurally · tetanus: he has no idea, and that is a question for the end, not the third slot

The branch you must be able to take — If she slumps or stops answering, leave the bleeding: 'Look at her chest — is it rising and falling? Put your ear close to her mouth and tell me if you can hear or feel any air.' Occasional gasping is not normal breathing — chest compressions now, hard and fast in the centre of the chest, and upgrade the ambulance. Circulation to the brain comes before haemorrhage control

Response, airway and breathing — 'Is she awake? Is she talking to you?' — 'Yes, she is talking, she is scared.' Say out loud that this tells you her airway is clear and she is breathing; that is how the examiner sees you doing a and B without ever saying DRSABCD down the phone
fails: ★ Telling him to hang up and ring 000 himself, and leaving it there
★ Agreeing to private-car transport, or failing to rule it out when he offers
★ Instructing removal of embedded glass, or offering a tourniquet as the first or second step

★ Missing danger entirely — no mention of the broken glass on the floor — or, in the unresponsive variant, controlling the bleeding on a patient who is not breathing normally instead of starting compressions

★ Ending the call before help arrives. Borderline: clinical jargon he cannot follow; stacking the whole list into one speech; arguing with him; running a full past history; leaving tetanus, monitoring or the vascular referral unmentioned
numbers: Direct pressure is the single most effective measure · pad soaked → add another on TOP, never lift the first · glass stays in, press around it · tourniquet 5–10 cm above the wound, not over a joint, not covered, time noted, for life-threatening limb bleeding pressure has failed to control — harm reported with prolonged application in the order of hours VERIFY · tetanus booster if over 5 years for a tetanus-prone wound, 10 years for a clean minor wound VERIFY · definitive care: venous duplex then ablation, sclerotherapy or surgery

In an MM5 rural town the responding SA ambulance crew may be volunteer and the response long — plan instructions for a caller who has to keep pressing for 20–30 minutes, not 5 · 000 SA ambulance · MedSTAR 1300 13 12 33 for retrieval and coordination from a small country hospital · healthdirect 1800 022 222 for the after-hours version of this call · TIS National 131 450, a credible extra mark in a station built around a caller who cannot follow instructions · country health connect for ongoing wound and compression dressings · PATS for the later vascular outpatient appointment · VERIFY all

must: FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: telling him to hang up and ring 000 himself — YOU arrange it: 'I'm getting an ambulance to you now, my nurse is dialling triple zero on the other line, you do not have to make that call.' Say it in the first thirty seconds, before any questions

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: agreeing to private-car transport, or failing to rule it out when he offers at about six minutes — nobody maintains pressure in a car and she can faint on the way; the ambulance comes to them

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: instructing removal of embedded glass — it may be plugging the vessel it cut, and blind removal extends the injury, so press firmly either side of it — or offering a tourniquet as the first or second step rather than a last resort for life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure has failed to control

Circulation to the brain comes before haemorrhage control

FAIL — AUTO-FAIL: ending the call before help arrives — 'put me on speakerphone or put the phone on the floor; I'm staying on the line until they walk through the door'. Soaking through means a second cloth ON TOP — never lift the first, because lifting strips the clot. Pillow under the calf only after pressure is on, blanket over her, nothing by mouth, and tell me if she stops answering you

stem: General practice, Wallaroo, South Australia (MM5). Endoscopy and ENT services are in Adelaide. Susan Hartley, 57, presents with new difficulty swallowing.

Version C: solids stick in the chest, but there are no red flags at all — no weight loss, no appetite change, not tired, and it is not progressive. What she does have is heartburn, a metallic taste, water brash and a lot of spicy food.
Tasks: take a focused history (6 minutes) — explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons — give your differential diagnoses.

Explain your most likely diagnosis, with your reasons, to Susan
Give your differential diagnoses

dx: **VERSION C — OESOPHAGEAL STRICTURE SECONDARY TO CHRONIC GASTRO-OESOPHAGEAL REFLUX DISEASE.** **NOTE THE WORDING CAREFULLY — NOT ‘GORD’.**

**WHY THE ANSWER IS NOT SIMPLY ‘GORD’: GORD DOES NOT ITSELF CAUSE DYSPHAGIA. It causes HEARTBURN, REGURGITATION AND OESOPHAGITIS.** **What causes the swallowing difficulty is THE STRICTURE — SCARRING FROM YEARS OF INFLAMMATION THAT NARROWS THE PIPE. SAY THE MECHANISM, NOT JUST THE PARENT CONDITION.** If challenged: **‘GORD is the UNDERLYING CONDITION, but the swallowing difficulty is caused by a PEPTIC STRICTURE — FIBROUS NARROWING that has developed as a COMPLICATION of years of reflux. I WOULD STILL BIOPSY IT, BECAUSE A MALIGNANT STRICTURE CAN LOOK BENIGN.’**

**THE DISCRIMINATING BEHAVIOUR RUNS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** **In Versions A and B the failure is LETTING A NORMAL EXAMINATION OR A PLAUSIBLE BENIGN STORY DISPLACE CANCER FROM THE TOP WHILE RED FLAGS ARE STILL ON THE TABLE — half the cohort on the day answered ‘stricture’ and were WRONG.** **THE MIRROR ERROR IS VERSION C: RED FLAGS ARE GENUINELY ABSENT, AND THE CANDIDATE WHO STILL SHOUTS CANCER AS THE ANSWER HAS STOPPED LISTENING.**

**BUT CANCER IS STILL DIFFERENTIAL 2, AND IT MUST BE SAID OUT LOUD**: **‘I do want to say that A CANCER OF THE FOOD PIPE IS STILL ON MY LIST AND I HAVE NOT RULED IT OUT. You don't have the warning signs I look for — NO WEIGHT LOSS, NO BLEEDING, YOUR APPETITE IS FINE — which is REASSURING, BUT THE CAMERA TEST IS WHAT TELLS US FOR CERTAIN.’**

**NAME BOTH AXES ALOUD BEFORE LISTING ANYTHING.** **AXIS 1 — OROPHARYNGEAL vs OESOPHAGEAL: trouble INITIATING with coughing or choking, pointing to the THROAT, versus food that goes down and STICKS SECONDS LATER, pointing to the CHEST.** **AXIS 2 — OBSTRUCTIVE vs MOTILITY: SOLIDS ONLY = OBSTRUCTIVE; SOLIDS AND LIQUIDS = MOTILITY.** **If you can say ‘this is a LOW, OBSTRUCTIVE dysphagia’ before you name a disease, THE LIST WRITES ITSELF.**

**SEPARATE DYSPHAGIA FROM ODYNOPHAGIA FIRST — PATIENTS USE THE SAME WORDS FOR BOTH.** **Dysphagia = DIFFICULTY swallowing. Odynophagia = PAIN on swallowing.** **PAINFUL swallowing points to INFECTION, ULCERATION, PILL OESOPHAGITIS OR AN ULCERATED TUMOUR — A DIFFERENT LIST.**

**THE SOLIDS-VERSUS-LIQUIDS QUESTION DOES MORE DIAGNOSTIC WORK THAN ANYTHING ELSE YOU WILL ASK. ASK IT BY 1:30.** **Caveat worth adding if challenged: A VERY ADVANCED OBSTRUCTION EVENTUALLY AFFECTS LIQUIDS TOO, SO PROGRESSION AND RED FLAGS OUTRANK THE PATTERN.**

**THE RED FLAGS ARE GENERIC FIRST, THEN SITE-SPECIFIC — AND THE SITE-SPECIFIC SETS ARE THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN A PASS AND A BORDERLINE.** **GENERIC: weight loss QUANTIFIED, appetite, lumps and bumps, tiredness, night sweats.** **OROPHARYNGEAL: LONG-STANDING SORE THROAT · EAR PAIN · VOICE CHANGE — the two the recalls say candidates ALMOST NEVER ASK.** **OESOPHAGEAL/GASTRIC: HAEMATEMESIS · MELAENA.** **THYROID: NECK LUMP · WEATHER PREFERENCE.** **LUNG/MEDIASTINAL: COUGH · HAEMOPTYSIS.**
**THE SMOKING TRAP IS DELIBERATE. ‘DO YOU SMOKE?’ GETS A FLAT NO.** **The brief says: only ‘HAVE YOU EVER SMOKED?’ gets ‘yes, twenty a day, I gave up ten years ago’.**

**RESPOND TO WHAT SHE ACTUALLY SAID, NOT TO A SCRIPT.** **The recalled openings differ — some role-players volunteer worry, some simply state the problem.** **DO NOT DELIVER A CANNED ‘I UNDERSTAND YOUR CONCERN’ TO A PATIENT WHO HAS NOT EXPRESSED ONE — THE EXAMINERS HAVE SPECIFICALLY PENALISED THAT.** **If she is worried: ‘That does sound worrying, and you were right to come in.’ If matter-of-fact: ‘Thank you for coming in to get this checked.’**
plan: **WIPE, open question, and RESPOND TO HER STATEMENT.** Then signpost: **‘I'd like to ask a number of questions so I can work out what's causing it. Is that alright?’**

**DESCRIBE IT — and these two questions carry more diagnostic weight than the rest of the history combined.** **‘Can you tell me what you mean by difficulty swallowing — IS IT HARD TO SWALLOW, OR PAINFUL TO SWALLOW?’** · **‘Is it hard to START the swallow — DO YOU COUGH OR CHOKE as you begin? Or does it GO DOWN AND THEN GET STUCK? And if it sticks, IS THAT IN YOUR THROAT OR IN YOUR CHEST?’**

**THE PATTERN AND THE COURSE.** **‘Does it happen with SOLID FOOD ONLY, or with LIQUIDS as well?’** · how long, first time or before, every day or on and off, **is it GRADUALLY GETTING WORSE** · anything better or worse, any particular food · **‘how is this affecting your day-to-day life — ARE YOU MANAGING TO EAT ENOUGH?’** **She has moved to SOFT AND SEMI-SOLID food — that is BOTH a SEVERITY MARKER AND AN IMPACT ANSWER. Use it in your summary.**
**GENERAL GI, FAST.** Nausea, vomiting, bloating, bowels, fevers.
**GROUP 1 — CANCERS: the generic four, then the FOUR SITE-SPECIFIC SETS.** Signpost it: **‘now some questions we ask everybody with swallowing problems — yes or no is fine.’**

**GROUPS 2 AND 3 — STRICTURES AND REFLUX, THEN INFECTIONS.** **‘Do you get HEARTBURN? Any ACIDIC, METALLIC OR BITTER TASTE in your mouth? A SUDDEN RUSH OF SALIVA? Have you TAKEN anything for it — AND IS IT STILL WORKING?’** · fevers, sore throat now, painful swallowing.

**GROUP 4 — MOTILITY, NEUROLOGICAL THEN AUTOIMMUNE.** **‘Any WEAKNESS anywhere? Any NUMBNESS or PINS AND NEEDLES? Any BLURRING OR DOUBLE VISION? Any DROOPY EYELIDS, or worse at the END OF THE DAY? Any TREMOR or slowing up? Any PREVIOUS STROKE? ARE YOU DIABETIC?’** — **STROKE IS THE COMMONEST CAUSE OF OROPHARYNGEAL DYSPHAGIA; omitting this group because ‘she has reflux’ is a named fail.** Then **‘any RASHES? JOINT PAINS? TIGHTENING OF THE SKIN ON YOUR HANDS? DRY EYES OR A DRY MOUTH?’**

**GROUP 5 — MEDICATIONS, then close.** **‘Are you on any medications at all?’** — **and ASK THE TIMING: DID THE SWALLOWING TROUBLE START WHEN THE DRUG DID?** Then **‘do you smoke, OR HAVE YOU EVER? Alcohol? Spicy food, coffee?’** · other conditions, **family history of stomach or bowel problems.**

**Diagnosis with reasons → the grouped differential list → the plan → nutrition → safety-net.** **Version C, verbatim: ‘The most likely cause of your swallowing difficulty is NARROWING OF THE FOOD PIPE — what we call a STRICTURE. These are SCARS, caused by LONG-TERM INFLAMMATION FROM ACID COMING UP FROM THE STOMACH. The scarring narrows the pipe, and THAT IS WHY SOLID FOOD CATCHES.’** Then **differential 2.**
THE GROUPED DIFFERENTIAL LIST — 45 seconds, NINE SECONDS PER GROUP

**‘The other things I considered were: OTHER CANCERS THAT CAN PRESS ON THE FOOD PIPE — in the THROAT, the THYROID GLAND or the LUNG; NARROWING FROM LONG-STANDING REFLUX; INFECTIONS in the throat; PROBLEMS WITH THE MOVEMENT of the food pipe — that group includes conditions of the NERVES such as STROKE, MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS, MYASTHENIA GRAVIS AND DIABETES, conditions of the IMMUNE SYSTEM such as SCLERODERMA, and a condition called ACHALASIA; and finally SOME MEDICATIONS can cause it. THE CAMERA TEST IS WHAT SORTS BETWEEN THEM.’** **GROUPS, NOT A FLAT LIST — the examiner is marking COVERAGE OF GROUPS, not the number of questions.**
Her hidden agenda, and when it lands

**HER SISTER-IN-LAW DIED OF OESOPHAGEAL CANCER FOUR YEARS AGO and she has been PUTTING OFF COMING IN BECAUSE OF IT.** **She does NOT volunteer it unless you ask what she is WORRIED about, what she THINKS it might be, or whether anything is ON HER MIND.** **If you never ask, she says it AT THE VERY END: ‘My sister-in-law died of cancer of the gullet. That's what's been in my head.’** **She also pushes once at the end: ‘AM I GOING TO BE ALRIGHT?’ — MARK WHETHER YOU FALSELY REASSURE.**
pefe: **THE KEY LINE SHE DELIVERS WITH EMPHASIS, and if you move straight past it SHE DOES NOT REPEAT IT — IT IS MARKED AS MISSED**: **‘MYLANTA USED TO HELP. IT DOESN'T DO ANYTHING NOW.’** **ACKNOWLEDGE IT EXPLICITLY: A TREATMENT THAT STOPS WORKING IN A CHRONIC UPPER GI COMPLAINT IS A CHANGE THAT NEEDS EXPLAINING.**

**VERSIONS A AND B — the naming, verbatim**: **‘Susan, I've been thinking about a number of conditions that can cause difficulty swallowing. In your case I AM CONCERNED ABOUT THE POSSIBILITY OF A CANCER IN THE FOOD PIPE. I want to be clear IT IS NOT CONFIRMED — THAT IS WHY I WANT TO ARRANGE A TEST.’** Then the reasons: **‘you've had REFLUX FOR A LONG TIME and the MYLANTA THAT USED TO HELP HAS STOPPED WORKING, and IT IS GETTING WORSE. You have LOST WEIGHT WITHOUT MEANING TO. And importantly, your swallowing problem happens ONLY WITH SOLID FOOD — that pattern suggests SOMETHING IS PHYSICALLY BLOCKING THE WAY, rather than a problem with the muscle movement.’**

**VERSION B — the normal card, and the sentence that fails half the cohort.** **TO THE EXAMINER: ‘I note the examination is ENTIRELY NORMAL. A NORMAL EXAMINATION DOES NOT EXCLUDE AN OESOPHAGEAL MALIGNANCY AND MY CONCERN IS UNCHANGED.’** **TO THE PATIENT: ‘I've examined you and I could not find anything abnormal today. I WANT TO BE HONEST WITH YOU: A NORMAL EXAMINATION DOES NOT RULE OUT A CANCER. EARLY TUMOURS VERY OFTEN CAUSE NO SIGNS AT ALL. My concern is based on your SYMPTOMS, and IT HAS NOT CHANGED.’** **The brief makes her pushback COMPULSORY — ‘but you said the examination was normal?’ — then she WAITS. IF YOU SOFTEN OR BACKTRACK, THAT IS A FAIL.**

**ADDED — GLOBUS PHARYNGEUS, one line.** **A sensation of a LUMP IN THE THROAT BETWEEN MEALS, with ENTIRELY NORMAL SWALLOWING. IT IS NOT DYSPHAGIA.** **If a patient tells you the lump is there WHEN THEY ARE NOT EATING and food goes down NORMALLY, YOU ARE IN A DIFFERENT CASE.** It is a diagnosis of exclusion after a normal endoscopy — **NEVER THE FIRST ANSWER.**

**WHY MEDICATIONS GET THEIR OWN GROUP — several classes cause dysphagia by DIFFERENT MECHANISMS and they are EASY MARKS.** **ACE INHIBITORS** (cough and throat symptoms) · **SEDATIVES AND ANTIPSYCHOTICS** (impaired swallow coordination) · **ANTICHOLINERGICS, SSRIs AND DECONGESTANTS** (dry mouth) · **BISPHOSPHONATES AND DOXYCYCLINE** (PILL-INDUCED OESOPHAGITIS, usually with ODYNOPHAGIA).

**Examiner challenges, scripted.** *‘Which cancers other than oesophageal?’* → **‘OROPHARYNGEAL, THYROID causing EXTRINSIC COMPRESSION, and LUNG OR MEDIASTINAL masses. EACH HAS ITS OWN SCREENING QUESTIONS, WHICH I ASKED.’** *‘The examination was normal. Are you sure?’* → **‘Yes. Early oesophageal tumours very often produce NO PHYSICAL SIGNS. THE ONLY INVESTIGATION THAT REMOVES CANCER FROM THE TOP OF MY LIST IS A NORMAL ENDOSCOPY.’** *‘Why does the pattern of onset matter in achalasia?’* → **‘Achalasia affects SOLIDS AND LIQUIDS FROM THE OUTSET and progresses SLOWLY OVER YEARS, often with REGURGITATION OF UNDIGESTED FOOD and CHEST PAIN. PROGRESSIVE SOLIDS-ONLY DYSPHAGIA OVER WEEKS IS A DIFFERENT PROBLEM.’**

**Other practice stems.** **62M heavy smoker and drinker, COUGHS AND SPLUTTERS AS HE STARTS to swallow, persistent sore throat, RIGHT EAR PAIN, hoarse for two months, NECK LUMP → OROPHARYNGEAL CARCINOMA. URGENT ENT, NOT GASTROENTEROLOGY.** **38-year-old, three years of trouble with BOTH SOLIDS AND LIQUIDS FROM THE OUTSET, regurgitates undigested food at night, chest pain → ACHALASIA. Barium shows a BIRD'S BEAK; MANOMETRY confirms; SCOPE STILL NEEDED TO EXCLUDE PSEUDOACHALASIA.** **44-year-old, six months of a LUMP IN THE THROAT THAT IS WORST WHEN SHE IS NOT EATING and disappears when she swallows food, no weight loss, very stressed → GLOBUS PHARYNGEUS.**

**The 40-second model answer structure**: age and duration and pattern → **POSITIVES** → **NEGATIVES, and the negatives are long in this station** (no odynophagia, no difficulty initiating, no choking, no ear pain, no voice change, no neck lump, no cough or haemoptysis, no haematemesis or melaena, no neurological or connective tissue symptoms) → most likely diagnosis **with the reason it outranks the alternative** → differential 2 with why it is less likely → the other groups considered → **the plan, including the referral pathway and the nutrition.**

**The cross-references worth knowing, so you do not rebuild them here**: dyspepsia and the ALARM framework, GORD endoscopy-results counselling and the PPI ladder, the hiatus hernia explanation, haematemesis, peptic ulcer disease and H. pylori eradication, and GORD as a chest-pain differential are each owned by other pairs in this cluster.

**The three lines that decide the station**: **‘IS IT HARD TO SWALLOW, OR PAINFUL TO SWALLOW?’** · **‘DOES IT HAPPEN WITH SOLID FOOD ONLY, OR WITH LIQUIDS AS WELL?’** · **‘A NORMAL EXAMINATION DOES NOT RULE OUT A CANCER.’**

dx: **VERSION B — INFECTIVE GASTROENTERITIS, viral, bacterial or protozoal, acquired from the sewage. NOT hepatitis.** **VERSION A — ACUTE VIRAL HEPATITIS, most probably A, with E named alongside it.** **BOTH VERSIONS SHARE ONE STEM AND ONE HISTORY; ONLY THE SYMPTOM SET AND THE EXAMINATION CARD DIFFER.**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: WHETHER YOU LET THE EXAMINATION CARD OVERRULE THE RECALL.** **Almost every candidate knows this as ‘THE SEWER HEPATITIS CASE’. THE EXAMINERS KNOW THAT TOO, which is why they wrote a second version in which the card shows NO JAUNDICE, NO HEPATOMEGALY AND A NORMAL URINE DIPSTICK — AND STILL HEAR CANDIDATES ANNOUNCE HEPATITIS.** **READING THE CARD AND CHANGING YOUR ANSWER IS THE SINGLE BEHAVIOUR BEING TESTED.**

**ITS TWIN: WHETHER YOU OPENED THE INCIDENT AT ALL.** **A candidate who diagnoses correctly WITHOUT ASKING ONE QUESTION ABOUT THE SEWER has failed the APPROACH AND DIFFERENTIAL DOMAINS EVEN WITH THE RIGHT DIAGNOSIS.** **It is the LEAD POINT OF THE STEM and THE SINGLE COMMONEST REASON candidates fail this station.**

**VERSION B, SAID PROPERLY — and do NOT hedge**: **‘Jane, I want to be careful here, BECAUSE THE EXAMINATION CHANGES WHAT I THINK. You are NOT YELLOW, your liver is NOT ENLARGED OR TENDER, and your URINE TEST IS NORMAL — SO THIS IS NOT HEPATITIS. What you have is GASTROENTERITIS: an INFECTION OF THE BOWEL, most likely from a BUG YOU SWALLOWED when you fell into the sewage. That fits your FEVER, the LOWER TUMMY PAIN, the NAUSEA and the DIARRHOEA.’** **SAYING ‘IT IS PROBABLY EARLY HEPATITIS’ READS AS AN UNWILLINGNESS TO ABANDON THE RECALL, AND IT COSTS YOU THE DIAGNOSIS DOMAIN.**

**OPEN THE INCIDENT, THEN THE FOUR SPECIFICS.** **Open first: ‘You mentioned an incident at work. Can you tell me more about it?’** → *‘I collect samples from the sewer. I slipped climbing in and fell into the sewage.’* **THEN SAY THE PIVOT OF THE CASE ALOUD: ‘SO YOU WERE EXPOSED TO URINE AND FAECES.’** **Then: 1 WERE YOU WEARING PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT? 2 DID ANY OF THE FLUID GET INTO YOUR EYES OR YOUR MOUTH? 3 DID YOU FILE AN INCIDENT REPORT? 4 DID YOU HIT YOUR HEAD, OR INJURE YOURSELF ANYWHERE ELSE?**

**THE TRAP INSIDE THE EXPOSURE BLOCK: ASKING ONLY ‘WERE YOU WEARING PPE?’ AND STOPPING.** **PPE DOES NOT PROTECT THE MOUTH RELIABLY, and THE WHOLE FAECAL–ORAL ROUTE RUNS THROUGH THE MOUTH.** **THE EYES-AND-MOUTH QUESTION IS THE ONE THAT JUSTIFIES YOUR DIFFERENTIAL LIST — and she will say she CANNOT REMEMBER.**

**THE INCIDENT REPORT IS NOT TRIVIA.** **Ask it, CONFIRM it, and REINFORCE it — ‘good, that matters, because it is WHAT PROTECTS YOU if you need time off’. THE REPORT IS WHAT OPENS HER ReturnToWorkSA CLAIM.** **And the HEAD INJURY question matters because this was a FALL INTO A CONFINED SPACE — four words, and missing it is an automatic fail.**

**CHARACTERISE THE DIARRHOEA BY CONSISTENCY AND BLOOD — AND NOTHING ELSE.** **CONSISTENCY GRADES SEVERITY — watery is worse than loose. BLOOD SEPARATES INVASIVE BACTERIAL COLITIS from viral and toxin-mediated illness.** **VOLUME AND ODOUR ADD NOTHING YOU WILL ACT ON, and asking whether the stool smells bad WASTES A QUESTION YOU CANNOT AFFORD.** **In Version B: loose, four or five times a day, NO BLOOD, fever and chills, nausea WITHOUT vomiting, LOWER abdominal pain.**

**A BARE ‘GASTROENTERITIS’ SCORES FAR LESS THAN A SPECIFIC LIST. NAME ONE OR TWO FROM EACH SUBGROUP OUT LOUD**: **VIRAL — ROTAVIRUS, NOROVIRUS, ADENOVIRUS · BACTERIAL — SALMONELLA, SHIGELLA, E. COLI, CAMPYLOBACTER · PROTOZOAL — GIARDIA, CRYPTOSPORIDIUM, ENTAMOEBA.** **And NAME LEPTOSPIROSIS, THE SEWER-SPECIFIC ORGANISM: RODENT URINE is the classic vector; SEVERE CALF MYALGIA, CONJUNCTIVAL SUFFUSION, headache; JAUNDICE WITH ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY in Weil disease. IT IS TREATABLE, SO YOU TEST FOR IT EVEN WITH A NEGATIVE SCREEN.**

**THE PSYCHOLOGICAL SCREEN IS BUILT INTO THIS CASE DELIBERATELY — AND THE NIGHTMARE AND AVOIDANCE QUESTIONS ARE WHAT TELL THE EXAMINER YOU ARE SCREENING FOR PTSD RATHER THAN DEPRESSION.** **‘Falling into a sewer would SHAKE ANYONE. How have you been COPING since it happened? How has your MOOD been? How has your SLEEP been — any NIGHTMARES OR FLASHBACKS? Have you found yourself AVOIDING going back to work? Any other stress at work or at home?’** **Her hidden agenda: she has NOT BEEN BACK INTO A SEWER SINCE, has DREAMT ABOUT IT TWICE, and is quietly worried SHE WILL NOT BE ABLE TO DO HER JOB ANY MORE. IF YOU ARE WARM SHE VOLUNTEERS THE DREAMS; IF YOU ARE BRISK AND CLINICAL SHE KEEPS THEM TO HERSELF.**
plan: **WIPE — in the online format you cannot wash your hands, so SAY IT: ‘I would normally wash my hands here.’** Then **‘I understand you have been feeling unwell and that SOMETHING HAPPENED AT WORK’** and **THE AGENDA QUESTION: ‘Before I start — is there anything in particular you are WORRIED this might be?’ — EIGHT SECONDS, AND A MARKED ITEM.**

**BLOCK 1 — EXPLORE ‘UNWELL’, FOUR QUESTIONS, NO MORE.** **‘Can you describe what you mean by feeling unwell — is it TIREDNESS, FEELING FEVERISH, PAIN, or something else?’** · how long, constant or coming and going, getting worse · anything better or worse · **how is it affecting your day-to-day life.** **Spending two minutes here is a named trap.**

**BLOCK 2 — THE INCIDENT: open first, then the FOUR SPECIFICS.** **Acknowledge before you ask: ‘THAT SOUNDS HORRIBLE. Thank you for telling me — THAT CHANGES WHAT I NEED TO CHECK FOR.’** **She is embarrassed and a bit disgusted, trying to be matter-of-fact — ACKNOWLEDGE THE UNPLEASANTNESS WITHOUT MAKING A JOKE OF IT.**

**BLOCK 3 — THREE INFECTION GROUPS, signposted: ‘I am going to run through some symptoms quickly — mostly yes or no.’** **HEPATITIS A AND E: yellowing of skin or eyes · TUMMY PAIN, AND WHERE · nausea or vomiting · DARK URINE OR PALE STOOLS.** **GASTROENTERITIS: any diarrhoea · LOOSE OR COMPLETELY WATERY · ANY BLOOD · any mucus · fever or chills.** **WATER CONTACT AND RARER: any RASH · LUMPS OR BUMPS in the neck, armpits or groin · SEVERE MUSCLE ACHES, ESPECIALLY IN YOUR CALVES · RED OR SORE EYES** — **the calf and eye questions are your LEPTOSPIROSIS SCREEN, AND EVEN A NEGATIVE ANSWER EARNS THE MARK BECAUSE YOU ASKED IT.**

‘Could I have the examination findings, please: GENERAL APPEARANCE AND HYDRATION, JAUNDICE IN THE SCLERAE AND UNDER THE TONGUE, TEMPERATURE AND VITAL SIGNS, LYMPH NODES, ABDOMINAL TENDERNESS AND ITS SITE, LIVER SIZE AND TENDERNESS, SPLEEN, CALF TENDERNESS AND CONJUNCTIVAL SUFFUSION, ANY RASH, AND A URINE DIPSTICK.’ The dipstick and the calves are the two candidates leave out
VERSION B CARD — the one this card is built on
NO JAUNDICE. NO HEPATOMEGALY. MILD LOWER ABDOMINAL TENDERNESS. URINE DIPSTICK NORMAL. Temperature 38.1°C, pulse 92, BP 118/72, RR 16, SpO2 98%
VERSION A CARD — for contrast

NO JAUNDICE. Temperature 38.1°C. TENDER HEPATOMEGALY WITH RIGHT UPPER QUADRANT TENDERNESS. No splenomegaly, no rash, no calf tenderness. URINE DIPSTICK POSITIVE FOR BILIRUBIN → acute viral hepatitis A or E
WHY THE DIPSTICK DECIDES IT

BILIRUBIN APPEARS IN THE URINE BEFORE THE SKIN TURNS YELLOW — which is why Version A can have a positive dipstick and NO VISIBLE JAUNDICE. So in Version B, a NORMAL dipstick with no hepatomegaly takes hepatitis off the top. JAUNDICE BECOMES VISIBLE AT A BILIRUBIN OF ROUGHLY 40–50 µmol/L; BILIRUBINURIA COMES FIRST VERIFY
THE SENTENCE THAT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

‘Why not hepatitis?’ → ‘Because there is NO JAUNDICE, NO HEPATOMEGALY AND NO BILIRUBIN IN THE URINE. In acute hepatitis I would expect AT LEAST BILIRUBINURIA, since CONJUGATED BILIRUBIN APPEARS IN URINE BEFORE THE SKIN DISCOLOURS.’ And ‘could it be both?’ → ‘It COULD — a single sewage exposure can transmit MORE THAN ONE ORGANISM. I would still call GASTROENTERITIS the leading diagnosis and check liver function and hepatitis serology to be sure’
DO NOW
VITAL SIGNS AND HYDRATION · POSTURAL BLOOD PRESSURE if she has been vomiting or has diarrhoea · URINE DIPSTICK — bilirubin, blood, protein · NEUROLOGICAL SCREEN if she struck her head
DO NEXT

FBE, UEC, LFT, INR, CRP, lipase, blood glucose · FAECAL PCR / MCS — in Version B, and in either version if there is diarrhoea, and ESPECIALLY given the OCCUPATIONAL source · HEPATITIS SEROLOGY: anti-HAV IgM, hepatitis E IgM, HBsAg and core IgM, HCV antibody · LEPTOSPIRA SEROLOGY AND PCR — BECAUSE OF THE SEWER
RESULTS THAT CHANGE MANAGEMENT

ALT and AST in the HUNDREDS OR THOUSANDS with a modest ALP → HEPATOCELLULAR injury · RISING INR OR FALLING ALBUMIN → failing synthetic function; THE FINDING THAT TURNS AN OUTPATIENT INTO AN INPATIENT · anti-HAV IgM positive → confirms acute hepatitis A; notify · BLOODY STOOL WITH ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY AND ANAEMIA → HAEMOLYTIC URAEMIC SYNDROME; WITHHOLD ANTIBIOTICS AND REFER · ultrasound showing a collection → LIVER ABSCESS, not hepatitis
AVOID

ANTIBIOTICS FOR UNDIFFERENTIATED DIARRHOEA, and SPECIFICALLY IF SHIGA-TOXIN E. COLI IS POSSIBLE · ANTIMOTILITY AGENTS SUCH AS LOPERAMIDE IN BLOODY OR FEBRILE DIARRHOEA · paracetamol above the reduced ceiling in acute hepatitis, and alcohol entirely VERIFY · naming a hepatitis subtype you cannot prove on history · REASSURING HER THE SEWAGE WAS HARMLESS

dx: **MAJOR DEPRESSIVE DISORDER — Version B of the MDD stem: JANE, 25, whose opening line is 'I've been feeling out of sorts.' Flat, slowed, and giving you nothing until you ask a second time.**

**THE SECOND OPEN QUESTION IS WHAT MAKES THIS STATION WORK. 'Out of sorts' is a deliberate non-answer; 'CAN YOU TELL ME A LITTLE MORE ABOUT WHAT YOU MEAN BY THAT?' converts it into a mood presentation. Going straight to a symptom checklist loses the history and the rapport at once.**
**Then the three Ts: how long · every day or coming and going · getting worse · did anything happen before it started · how is this affecting your life?**

**Run the criteria in order and FOLLOW UP EVERY POSITIVE: mood · SLEEP with the type — initiation versus maintenance · appetite, then weight · ANHEDONIA asked explicitly · concentration · energy · guilt and worthlessness. Stop counting once you have the number.**
**'I haven't checked my weight' is NOT a negative — appetite change alone ticks the criterion, and chasing the number costs you the thyroid question.**

**THE MANIA GATE CLOSES BEFORE THE WORD DEPRESSION IS USED: 'has there ever been a time, even a few days, when you felt unusually high or energetic, extremely good about yourself, didn't need much sleep, or did things out of character?'**

**THE AMC GREY ZONE: a vague answer about life not being worth it is NOT a no. Count to three, then climb — have you ever acted on it · do you have a plan · have you done anything to prepare · WHAT HAS STOPPED YOU · any thoughts of harming anyone else.** **Protective factors are scored.**

**Close the psychosis box in FOUR questions — hallucinations, strange ideas, special powers, control or persecution. Running the whole delusion catalogue costs you the social history, the drug history and the thyroid screen.**

**NAME IT, EXPLAIN IT IN ONE LINE, THEN COUNT THE REASONS ALOUD. The reasoning is the only evidence the examiner has that you know how a psychiatric diagnosis is made — and add the negative mania screen as positive evidence: 'you've never had a period of feeling unusually high, which tells me this is depression on its own, not a bipolar condition.'**

**THE SAFETY NET WITH A NAMED SERVICE AND HER AGREEMENT: 'come back to me, go to the emergency department, or ring Lifeline on 13 11 14. Can you agree to that?'** **Plus CBT with a mental health treatment plan, an SSRI with the activation warning, sleep hygiene, exercise, less alcohol, and review at four weeks — ONE WEEK IF UNDER 25.**

stem: General practice, South Australia. A 60-year-old man has come in complaining of dizziness. The reception note reads 'Dizzy spells, 5 days'. Information on the door: HR 78 regular · BP 132/80 sitting · RR 14 · SpO2 98% RA · T 36.7 · BGL 5.8 · GCS 15.
At the defining question he says: 'It's not spinning. I go light-headed and grey when I stand up out of the chair, and twice my legs have gone from under me.'

Tasks: take a focused, relevant history — ask the examiner for the physical examination findings you require — explain the most likely diagnosis and your differential diagnoses — outline your management plan. You do not perform the examination; findings are supplied only for what you name.

findingsLabel: The examination request and the findings — open only when you would ask
findings: THE VERSION B STEM, as recalled

Margaret Doyle, 74, dizziness and TWO FALLS IN THE LAST MONTH. Medications: PERINDOPRIL, INDAPAMIDE, TAMSULOSIN, SERTRALINE. LIVES ALONE. Door: BP 138/82 LYING, 106/64 STANDING · HR 72 · BGL 5.2. SAME WORD ON THE STEM AS THE VERTIGO STATION — COMPLETELY DIFFERENT STATION
THE DEFINING ANSWER THAT TELLS YOU WHICH STATION YOU ARE IN

‘It's NOT SPINNING. I go LIGHT-HEADED AND GREY WHEN I STAND UP out of the chair, and TWICE MY LEGS HAVE GONE FROM UNDER ME.’ The moment you hear this you are in a POSTURAL HYPOTENSION / RECURRENT FALLS station, NOT a vestibular one
THE POSTURAL DROP DEFINITION
A FALL OF ≥20 mmHg SYSTOLIC OR ≥10 mmHg DIASTOLIC WITHIN 3 MINUTES OF STANDING. Hers is 138 → 106 — A 32 mmHg SYSTOLIC DROP. Say the arithmetic out loud
ASK FOR IT BY NAME — the examination request changes in this version

‘I'd particularly like a LYING AND STANDING BLOOD PRESSURE AT ONE AND THREE MINUTES, PULSE RATE AND RHYTHM, GAIT AND BALANCE, a FULL FALLS-RISK ASSESSMENT including VISION AND FOOTWEAR, and a MEDICATION REVIEW.’ The ONE-AND-THREE-MINUTE timing is what makes it a proper postural BP, and a pulse that does NOT rise with the drop points towards an AUTONOMIC or DRUG cause
The rest of the request — you still clear the same groups

General appearance, hydration, pallor · CARDIOVASCULAR examination — murmurs, especially AORTIC STENOSIS · NEUROLOGICAL examination including SENSATION IN THE FEET and PROPRIOCEPTION · VISUAL ACUITY · office tests: BLOOD GLUCOSE and an ECG. The ECG is not optional — ARRHYTHMIA CAN PRESENT AS A FALL
WHY EACH DRUG ON HER LIST MATTERS — name the mechanism, not just the drug

PERINDOPRIL — ACE inhibitor, VASODILATES · INDAPAMIDE — thiazide-like DIURETIC, DEPLETES VOLUME and can cause HYPONATRAEMIA · TAMSULOSIN — ALPHA-1 BLOCKER, a classic cause of FIRST-DOSE AND POSTURAL HYPOTENSION · SERTRALINE — SSRI, HYPONATRAEMIA (especially COMBINED WITH A THIAZIDE in an older woman) and an independent FALLS RISK. FOUR DRUGS, FOUR CONTRIBUTIONS
Bloods to order

UEC — SODIUM AND RENAL FUNCTION, because a thiazide PLUS an SSRI in a 74-year-old woman is the textbook set-up for HYPONATRAEMIA · FBE (anaemia) · BGL/HbA1c · TSH · VITAMIN D if falls and bone health are in play
THE FALLS PACKAGE — this is where the general-practice marks live

Falls RISK FACTORS: vision, FOOTWEAR, feet, cognition, continence and night-time toileting, alcohol · HOME SAFETY: loose rugs, lighting, stairs, bathroom rails, a clear path to the toilet at night · GAIT AND BALANCE assessment · a PERSONAL ALARM for someone who lives alone · BONE HEALTH — a fall with a fracture is the outcome you are preventing
THE CLINICAL POINT UNDER THE WHOLE STATION

The stem word NEVER decides your structure — THE PATIENT'S DEFINITION DOES. The AMC re-labelled the falls stem ‘dizziness’ PRECISELY BECAUSE candidates memorised recalls by title. Running the vertigo structure here — ear questions, Dix–Hallpike, Epley — means SIX MINUTES ANSWERING A QUESTION NOBODY ASKED
AVOID

FORCING THE EAR QUESTIONS ONTO THIS PATIENT · offering a Dix–Hallpike or an Epley · ADDING A DRUG (a vestibular sedative, or a new antihypertensive) instead of REVIEWING THE ONES SHE IS ON · stopping all antihypertensives abruptly without a plan · missing HYPONATRAEMIA · forgetting that she LIVES ALONE

dx: **VERSION B — POSTURAL (ORTHOSTATIC) HYPOTENSION causing RECURRENT FALLS, most likely DRUG-INDUCED — perindopril, indapamide and TAMSULOSIN together, with sertraline adding a hyponatraemia and falls risk.** **Version A of this stem — posterior-canal BPPV — is a separate card (MED-101).**

**THE DISCRIMINATING ISSUE: SWITCHING STRUCTURE OUT LOUD.** **The AMC RE-LABELLED THE FALLS STEM ‘DIZZINESS’ because candidates MEMORISED RECALLS BY TITLE. It PUNISHES RECALL MEMORISATION AND REWARDS A STRUCTURE.** **Candidates who skip the definition question and launch into ear questions on a Version B patient FAIL BEFORE MINUTE TWO.**

**THE SECOND DISCRIMINATOR: REVIEWING THE DRUGS RATHER THAN ADDING ONE.** **Four medications, each contributing a mechanism. The instinct to PRESCRIBE something for ‘dizziness’ is the trap — THE FIX HERE IS SUBTRACTION.**

**THE TRIAGE TRIAD — ASK ALL THREE, IN THIS ORDER, IN THE FIRST 90 SECONDS.** **1 ‘DIZZINESS MEANS DIFFERENT THINGS TO DIFFERENT PEOPLE — do you mean a SPINNING sensation, the room going round? Or LIGHT-HEADED, as if you're about to FAINT? Or OFF-BALANCE and unsteady on your feet?’ 2 ‘Any FAINTING or BLACKING OUT, even briefly?’ 3 ‘And any FALLS?’** **SPINNING → vertigo structure. LIGHT-HEADED → syncope/pre-syncope structure. UNSTEADY, KEEPS GOING OVER → recurrent falls structure. VERSION B IS THE SECOND AND THIRD TOGETHER.**

**SWITCH OPENLY — say it, so the examiner hears the reasoning**: **‘Thank you — THAT TELLS ME SOMETHING DIFFERENT IS GOING ON, SO LET ME CHANGE THE QUESTIONS I'M ASKING.’** Then: **does it happen SPECIFICALLY WHEN YOU STAND UP from sitting or lying · HOW QUICKLY after standing · ANY WARNING before the falls · did you BLACK OUT, or were you AWARE throughout · any INJURIES · tell me about ALL YOUR MEDICATIONS AND WHEN YOU TAKE THEM.**

**THE THREE PRESENTATIONS SHARE ONE WORD AND OVERLAP HEAVILY.** **Syncope (transient loss of consciousness), recurrent falls (no LOC, repeated falls) and dizziness/vertigo.** **HYPOGLYCAEMIA, ARRHYTHMIA AND NEUROLOGICAL DISEASE APPEAR IN ALL THREE** — so the cardiac, metabolic and neurological screens STILL RUN in Version B. **Only the EAR group drops out.**

**THE TIMING OF THE DRUGS IS A QUESTION WORTH ASKING.** **‘When do you take each of them?’** A diuretic and an alpha-blocker taken together in the morning, with falls in the mid-morning, is a pattern you can FIX BY STAGGERING OR DEPRESCRIBING. **TAMSULOSIN is the one to name first — an ALPHA-1 BLOCKER, a classic cause of POSTURAL HYPOTENSION, and often continued without review.**

**THE GERIATRIC SCREEN IS NOT OPTIONAL HERE — SHE LIVES ALONE.** **Memory · mood (and the SERTRALINE tells you there is a mood history) · who is at home · managing cooking, shopping and washing · falls or near-misses at home.** **A 74-year-old who lives alone and has fallen twice is ONE FALL AWAY FROM A HIP FRACTURE AND A LONG LIE ON THE FLOOR.**

**EXPLAINING IT TO HER, verbatim**: **‘Margaret, your dizziness is coming from your BLOOD PRESSURE DROPPING WHEN YOU STAND UP — it fell from 138 TO 106 TODAY. That's very likely being CAUSED OR WORSENED BY YOUR BLOOD PRESSURE TABLETS AND THE TABLET FOR YOUR WATERWORKS. I'd like to REVIEW THOSE DOSES, and I want to talk about PREVENTING FALLS, because THAT'S WHAT WORRIES ME MOST.’**

**WHY THE ECG AND THE NEURO SCREEN STILL MATTER.** **A fall is not automatically postural.** **ARRHYTHMIA (including heart block and SICK SINUS) presents as falls in older people; AORTIC STENOSIS gives EXERTIONAL presyncope; PARKINSONISM and AUTONOMIC NEUROPATHY give postural drops independent of drugs.** **The postural drop is the most likely answer — but you have to have looked for the others to say so.**
plan: **Confirm haemodynamic stability, WIPE, open question, and ELICIT THE AGENDA EARLY — ‘was there anything in particular you were worried this might be?’** — not at 7:30.
**THE TRIAGE TRIAD. Define → LOC → falls.** **When she says light-headed on standing and her legs giving way, SWITCH STRUCTURE OUT LOUD.**

**CHARACTERISE THE EPISODES.** When they happen · how quickly after standing · how long they last · any warning (light-headed, grey vision, sweating, palpitations) · **any loss of consciousness** · any injury from the falls · **after meals, in the heat, or after passing urine at night?** (post-prandial, heat and micturition are postural triggers too).

**THE MEDICATION REVIEW — every drug, the dose, WHEN it is taken, and WHEN it was started or changed.** **Specifically: ‘has any tablet been STARTED OR INCREASED recently?’** Then **over-the-counter, alcohol, and fluid intake.**

**CARDIAC, METABOLIC, NEURO — still run.** Chest pain, palpitations, exertional symptoms · diabetes, thyroid, tiredness (anaemia) · **tremor, slowness, stiffness (Parkinsonism)** · numbness in the feet · eyesight.

**FALLS AND THE GERIATRIC SCREEN.** Footwear, vision, **night-time toileting**, continence · home hazards · **who is at home, managing daily tasks, memory, mood** · **CAN SHE GET UP IF SHE FALLS, and does she have a PERSONAL ALARM?**

**Ask for the examination BY NAME — lying and standing BP at 1 AND 3 minutes, pulse rate and rhythm, gait and balance, falls-risk assessment including vision and footwear, cardiovascular, neurological including feet, and office tests.**
**Name it with the numbers — ‘138 TO 106, a 32 mmHg drop’ — then the likely cause (the drugs), then the differentials by group, each with why it is less likely.**

**MANAGEMENT — REVIEW, DON'T ADD.** **Review and DEPRESCRIBE or reduce the most likely culprit, starting with the ALPHA-BLOCKER and the DIURETIC — discuss the tamsulosin with her urinary symptoms in mind, and consider whether she needs BOTH antihypertensives at her current BP** · **stagger doses rather than taking them together** · **check SODIUM AND RENAL FUNCTION** · **rise slowly and in stages — sit on the edge of the bed first** · adequate fluids · **FALLS PREVENTION: physiotherapy for strength and balance, OT home assessment, personal alarm, footwear, vision check** · **review in 1–2 weeks with a repeat postural BP.**

**Safety-net, then teach-back.** **‘Come back immediately, or call an ambulance, if you BLACK OUT, if you have CHEST PAIN OR PALPITATIONS, if you HIT YOUR HEAD in a fall, or if you get WEAKNESS, NUMBNESS OR SLURRED SPEECH.’** Then **‘just so I know I've explained it properly — what will you do if you fall again?’**
pefe: **DEPRESCRIBING — do it with a plan, not by stopping everything.** **Start with the drug MOST LIKELY to be responsible and LEAST NEEDED at her current BP.** **TAMSULOSIN: discuss her urinary symptoms first — it may be reducible, switchable, or unnecessary.** **INDAPAMIDE: a common first candidate to stop in a falling older woman, ESPECIALLY IF SODIUM IS LOW.** **Recheck BP LYING AND STANDING at review; the target in a frail older faller is AVOIDING SYMPTOMATIC POSTURAL DROPS, not a textbook sitting BP.** VERIFY

**SERTRALINE — do not stop it abruptly, but DO check the sodium.** **An SSRI with a thiazide in a 74-year-old woman is the textbook set-up for HYPONATRAEMIA, which itself causes unsteadiness, confusion and falls.** **If the sodium is low, the thiazide goes first; the SSRI is reviewed rather than stopped cold.**

**NON-DRUG MEASURES FOR POSTURAL HYPOTENSION** VERIFY: **rise slowly and in stages** · **adequate fluid intake** unless restricted · **avoid large carbohydrate-heavy meals and alcohol** (post-prandial drops) · **head-of-bed elevation** · **compression stockings** in selected patients · **counter-pressure manoeuvres** (crossing the legs, clenching the buttocks) when light-headed. **Drug treatment for postural hypotension (such as fludrocortisone or midodrine) is SPECIALIST territory and comes AFTER removing the culprits — never instead of it.**

**THE FALLS PREVENTION PACKAGE**: **PHYSIOTHERAPY for strength and balance training — the single best-evidenced falls intervention** · **OCCUPATIONAL THERAPY HOME ASSESSMENT** — rails, lighting, rugs, bathroom, a clear night path to the toilet · **PERSONAL ALARM** for someone who lives alone · **VISION** review · **FOOTWEAR** · **BONE HEALTH** — vitamin D, and consider osteoporosis assessment, because a fracture is the outcome you are preventing · **My Aged Care** referral if she needs support at home.

**DRIVING — still part of your management.** **Recurrent pre-syncope and falls can impair safe driving; assess against AUSTROADS.** **In SOUTH AUSTRALIA the doctor has a STATUTORY DUTY to report a patient believed unfit to drive (Motor Vehicles Act 1959).** **‘I'd rather we sort this out together and get you back to driving safely.’**

**If she says ‘so you want to take my tablets away — won't my blood pressure go up?’** → **‘That's a very fair worry. Your blood pressure LYING DOWN is actually quite reasonable, and what's causing the falls is the DROP WHEN YOU STAND. At your age, a FALL is a much bigger danger than a blood pressure reading a little above the textbook number. I'll ADJUST ONE TABLET AT A TIME and RECHECK IT, so we find the balance safely.’**

**Contrast with Version A — the SAME STEM, the OPPOSITE STRUCTURE.** **Version A: ‘SPINNING, the whole room takes off’ → vertigo → the five ear questions, the neuro screen, nystagmus by name, Dix–Hallpike, Epley.** **Version B: ‘LIGHT-HEADED AND GREY WHEN I STAND’ → postural hypotension → medication review, postural BP, falls risk, home safety, gait.** **THE PATIENT'S DEFINITION DECIDES — never the stem word.**

**The variants from the same stem worth knowing**: **unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus → NOT BPPV; audiometry and MRI internal acoustic meati** · **continuous vertigo with ataxia and thick speech → posterior circulation stroke; ambulance, not an Epley** · **‘I tripped twelve days ago and hit my head — I'm on apixaban’ → urgent non-contrast CT for SUBDURAL HAEMATOMA; the patient volunteers it ONLY IF ASKED DIRECTLY.** **Each one punishes running a memorised recall.**

**The 40-second answer shape**: one-line summary → key positives (light-headed on standing, two falls, the four drugs, lives alone) → **key negatives (no spinning, no loss of consciousness, no ear symptoms, no focal neurology, no chest pain or palpitations)** → the postural drop WITH THE NUMBERS → most likely diagnosis and the drug cause → differentials with why each is less likely → **the plan: review the drugs, check sodium, falls prevention, review with repeat postural BP.**

SA — **physiotherapy and OT through a GP MANAGEMENT PLAN AND TEAM CARE ARRANGEMENTS** · **COUNTRY HEALTH CONNECT** for community allied health and home visits in a rural setting · **MY AGED CARE** for a home-support assessment · **a personal alarm service** for someone living alone · **DRIVING: SA doctors have a statutory reporting duty** · **ACCHS and Aboriginal Liaison Officer where relevant; Closing the Gap PBS.**
